units.la: FFERO vobis posthumam PIERII WINSEMII vestri Historiam, cui quidem vivus supremam manum imposuerat, ac in Comitijs vestris obtulerat, eoq; ut typis mandaretur decreto cautum erat: sed cum præsaga mens, quodammodo mortem præsentiens, testaretur, hoc ipso vivo in effectum perduci non posse, illam mihi curam pro veteri familiaritate, commendavit, quod acriter instanti denegare religio mihi fuit: voluit, ut & debuit, illam Illustriss. Dominationibus offerri & inscribi, utpotè quorum autoritate & jussu eam conscripserat: Laudabili sanè ab omni ævo, instituto, ut posteritati constaret ante actorum memoria, & à quam parvis initijs, Majores vestri (benedictione divinâ adjuvante,) supra captum humanum Provinciam ad florissentem præsentem statum deduxerint, ut à cunabulis propemodum jam adolevisse dici posit.
units.tr: I bring you the posthumous history of your Pierius Winsemius. He had put the final touches to it while alive and had presented it at your assembly, and it was decreed that it be committed to print. But his foreboding mind, sensing his death in some way, declared that this could not be brought to completion while he lived. On account of our old friendship, he entrusted that task to me, and it would have been scrupulous of me to refuse him as he pressed hard. He wished, as was fitting, that it be offered and dedicated to your Illustrious Lordships, by whose authority and command he had written it. This is a praiseworthy practice from every age, so that posterity may know the memory of past deeds and how, from such small beginnings, your ancestors (with divine blessing assisting) brought the Province beyond human comprehension to its present flourishing state, so that it may be said to have grown up almost from the cradle.

units.la: Edidit quidem Historicus vester ante annos aliquot, Historiæ partem primam, & postmodum etiam secundam, sed defectu multorum autographorum, non ut in præsenti absolutam: etenim multa ex illo tempore in archivis vestris & alibi reperta sunt, quæ ut fidem majorem Historiæ faciunt, sic lucem clariorem Lectori præbent; quæ posteriori huic editioni inserta sunt.
units.tr: Your historian indeed published some years ago the first part of the History, and afterwards the second as well. But for lack of many autographs, it was not in the complete form it has now. For much from that time has since been found in your archives and elsewhere, which gives the History greater credibility and gives the reader a clearer light. These things have been inserted into this later edition.

units.la: Placuit Illustriss. Dominationib. vestris initium Historiæ sumeret, ex illo tempore quo maximus Cæsar Carolus V. abdicavit Provincias Belgicas, & in Philippum filium heredem unicum uno quasi ore transtulit, cum placuisset maximo Cæsari, morti donum præripere, & mortalitatis donum in vita antevertere, raro sane exemplo ut desinas imperare, cum posis.
units.tr: It has pleased your Illustrious Lordships that the history should begin from the time when the greatest Emperor Charles V abdicated the Belgic Provinces and transferred them, as with one voice, to Philip his son and only heir. For it pleased the greatest Caesar to snatch from death its gift and to anticipate in life the gift of mortality, a truly rare example of ceasing to rule while one is still able.

units.la: Et quamquam plurimi Scriptores, de causis impulsivis abdicationis curiosius indagent, satius est cuique judicium suum relinquere, cum revera, magis in conjectura positum sit, quàm quod quid certi jam statui posit. Hoc saltem verum, quod domus Austriaca in Carolo V. Cæsare, summum majestatis & gloriæ fastigium viderit, ex quo sensim & quasi sine sensu paulatim retrocedere cæpit, sive quod dies decretorius ac fatalis periodus immineat, sive quod ob tyrannidem, religionis causa effusi sanguinis guttulæ, & ex eo renascentes surculi (Deo eorum injuriam vindicante) eveniat: judicio divino relinquimus, nos latet, ut & quæ præsentis status catastrophe futura sit: sane periodus lenta nunc violentior esse videtur.
units.tr: Although very many writers inquire rather curiously into the impelling causes of the abdication, it is better to leave each person his own judgment, since the matter rests more on conjecture than on anything that can now be stated as certain. This at least is true: the House of Austria saw under Charles V the highest summit of majesty and glory, and from that point it began gradually, and almost without feeling, to fall back. Whether this is because the decisive and fatal period is at hand, or because of tyranny, and drops of blood shed for religion, and shoots springing up from them (God avenging their wrong), we leave to the divine judgment, since it is hidden from us what the outcome of the present state's catastrophe will be. Surely the slow period now seems to be becoming more violent.

units.la: Incidit abdicatio Cæsaris, noviq; Principis Philippi ininauguratio, in annum millesimum quingentesimum quinquagesimum quintum. Quamquam & verum sit, ut ex actis publicis in archivis vestris repartis, ac Historiae insertis pateat, Caesarem jam praevie Dominium Frisiae, (quod a Duce Saxoniae obtinuerat. Qui anno millesimo quadringentesimo nonagesimo octavo, Snecae Archi-Gubernator Dominij Frisiae salutatus erat, & ad annum decimum quintum supra sesqui millesimum obtinuerat) anno millesimo quingentesimo quinquagesimo, xviii. Ianuarij, transtulisse in principem Philippum filium, eumq; & tum Dominum Frisiae salutatum fuisse, imo & indicto Ordinum conventu proclamatum esse, interveniente solemni juramento, quod Ioannes Lignaeus Arembergiae Comes, Leoverdiae die qua supra, solemni ritu praestitit. Quod & ipse princeps Philippus (novus dominus) inviolabiliter se servaturum, in majorem populi securitatem, solenni corporali juramento interveniente, expromisit. Continebat illud juramentum, confirmationem privilegiorum ac tractatuum a Ducibus Saxoniae & Caesarea majestate obtentorum, & juxta, omnia alia Philippum principem facturum ad qua justus & bonus princeps ac dominus fidelibus subditis suis tenetur.
units.tr: The abdication of the Emperor and the not yet inaugurated new prince Philip fell in the year one thousand five hundred and fifty-five. Yet it is also true, as is evident from the public acts preserved in your archives and inserted into the History, that the Emperor had earlier transferred the Lordship of Friesland to his son Philip. He had obtained it from the Duke of Saxony, who in the year 1498 had been hailed as Archgovernor of the Lordship of Friesland at Sneek and had held it for fifteen years beyond a thousand and a half. This transfer took place on 18 January 1550, and Philip was then acclaimed Lord of Friesland. Indeed, it was proclaimed at a summoned assembly of the Orders, with a solemn oath intervening, which John Lignaeus, Count of Aremberg, performed in ritual form at Leeuwarden on the day stated above. The prince Philip himself, the new lord, promised with a solemn bodily oath that he would keep this inviolably, for the greater security of the people. That oath contained confirmation of the privileges and treaties obtained from the Dukes of Saxony and from the Caesarean majesty, and likewise a pledge that Prince Philip would do all that a just and good prince and lord is bound to do for his faithful subjects.

units.la: Magno sane applausu procerum & populi proclamatio & inauguratio novi domini celebrata est, ut de novo Cajo sibi congratulantes, dum spes erat patribus & populo, mitius (ut plerumque fieri solet) sub novo Domino imperium fore, & severiora Caesaris Edicta, de Religione, introductione novorum Episcoporum, & exosae inquisitionis insolito judicio, mite temperamentum acceptura, patriasque leges & privilegia salva ac intacta fore. Et quamquam merito majores tenere debuisset, Hispanica indoles, educatio & aversi à Belgis mores & solitæ tyrannidis suspicio, vicit tamen in avidis libertatis ingenijs salso sperata clementia & Edictorum mitigatio. Sed tanta est mentis humanæ caligo, ut etiam in multum nocitura, cum applausu ruamus, dum futuri temporis exitum caliginosa noƈte premit D E U S.
units.tr: The proclamation and inauguration of the new lord were celebrated with great applause from the nobles and the people, who congratulated themselves on the new lord. The fathers and the people hoped that, as usually happens, the rule under the new lord would be milder, that the harsher edicts of the Emperor concerning religion, the introduction of new bishops, and the unusual procedure of the hated Inquisition would receive a gentle moderation, and that the country's laws and privileges would remain safe and intact. And although they ought rightly to have feared more, given the Spanish character, his upbringing, his manners turned away from the Belgians, and the suspicion of his customary tyranny, nevertheless in minds eager for liberty the hoped-for clemency and mitigation of the edicts prevailed. But such is the darkness of the human mind that we rush with applause into what will greatly harm us, while God holds the outcome of the future time under a dark night.

units.la: Evenit etenim Majoribus vestris, quod in proverbio est, Fortuna vitria est cum spendet frangitur; &
units.tr: For it happened to your ancestors as the proverb says: "Fortune is glass: when it shines, it is broken;"

units.la: Aspera, sub dulci melle, venena latent.
units.tr: "Bitter poisons lie hidden under sweet honey."

units.la: Omnis enim illa concepta spes de miti imperio ac patriarum legum conservatione subitò evanuit & stultæ lætitiæ populus graves pœnas dedit. Quamquam enim & Cæsar, præsentibus provinciarum Deputatis, Bruxellis in ipso solemni renuntiationis omnium provinciarum actu, Philippum filium (provinciarum jam dominum (serio monuerat de confervanda populi (utpote meritis in donum Austriacam illustris) libertate & privilegiorum jure, utque princeps paternum amorem, ex anticipati temporis usura sibi debitum, in amore & cura populi Belgici compensaret, jure postulasset, sub hac comminatione, fore alias ut populus patriarum legum tenax & servitutis impatiens jugum excuteret, ac Philippus princeps id se facturum spopondisset Cæsari, frustra fuit & repromissio in ventum abijt: atq; alia se rerum facies mox obtulit, dum imperium quod mite sub novo domino speraverant patres, crudele & intolerabile factum est. Idque non solum severiorum edictorum Cæsaris confirmatione tam de religione, Episcoporumq; introductione quam &, qua arbiter conscientijs dabatur, inquisitione. Sed & insuper novorum eorundemque severiorum edictorum promulgatione, atque eorum rigida ac severa executione, dum immemor Rex omne imperium violentum non esse diuturnum. Tum mox exauditur detestabilis & execrabilis vox: Ure, Seca: Non curamus privilegios vestros, laniatibus carnificum, exilio, tortura, gladio, patibulo, aqua, confiscatione bonorum, jus edictorum vindicatur. Luctu; armis, caede, cadaveribus, cruore incendio omnia complentur; sic
units.tr: For all that hope of a mild rule and of the preservation of the country's laws vanished suddenly, and the people, foolish in their joy, paid heavy penalties. The Emperor, in the presence of the deputies of the provinces at Brussels, in the very solemn act of renouncing all the provinces, had earnestly admonished Philip his son, already lord of the provinces, concerning the preservation of the people's liberty (a people deserving well of the Austrian house) and the right of their privileges. He had asked that the prince make up, by the usury of anticipated time, the paternal affection owed to him through love and care for the Belgic people. He had warned under this threat that otherwise the people, tenacious of the country's laws and impatient of servitude, would throw off the yoke, and Philip had promised Caesar that he would do so. Yet the promise was in vain and went off into the wind. Soon another face of affairs presented itself, and the rule which the fathers had hoped would be mild under the new lord became cruel and intolerable. This happened not only through the confirmation of the harsher edicts of the Emperor, both concerning religion and the introduction of bishops, and through the inquisition by which judgment over consciences was given to an arbiter, but also through the promulgation of new and yet harsher edicts and their rigid and severe execution, the King forgetting that every violent rule is not lasting. Then soon was heard the detestable and execrable cry: "Burn, cut! We do not care about your privileges!" By the butchering of executioners, exile, torture, sword, gallows, water, and confiscation of goods, the right of the edicts is vindicated. Everything is filled with mourning, arms, slaughter, corpses, blood, and fire; thus

units.la: Nulla dies mœrore caret, ——— — —— — sed nova fletum causa ministrat.
units.tr: No day is free of grief ... but each new cause supplies fresh tears.

units.la: Urbes, castella præsidijs firmata, legiones scriptæ, novæ arces extructæ, in consilium patriarum legum exteri vocantur. Hispanus per omnia dominatur, quasi à rege sibi omnis juris dicundi potestas data, & pro lege sit;
units.tr: Cities and castles are fortified with garrisons, legions are enrolled, new citadels are built, and foreigners are called into the council concerning the laws of the country. The Spaniard rules in everything, as if all power of pronouncing law had been given him by the King and his will were the law:

units.la: Sic volo, sic jubeo, stat pro ratione voluntas.
units.tr: "Thus I wish, thus I command; my will stands in place of reason."

units.la: Ad hæc, merito obstupescunt & presis labijs exhorrescunt Patres, cum omnia undique nil nisi tyrannidem redolerent; consternatio omnes occupavit, dum libertas & vita in dubio sunt, nec amisso patrimonio corpus liberum habere liceret; & vim atque injuriam strictus tueretur ensis.
units.tr: At these things the Fathers were rightly struck dumb, and they shuddered with pressed lips, since everything on every side smelled only of tyranny. Consternation seized all, while liberty and life were in doubt, nor was it permitted to keep a free body once property was lost, and the drawn sword defended force and injury.

units.la: Sed quid consilijs? cum huic nodo non esset æqualis cuneus? & vix moles sine exitio convellentium convelli posse videbatur. In jus namq; Princeps, (jam Rex & dominator in Asia & Africa) trahi non poterat: Patres tranquillitatis amantes, supplices, precibus clementiam Regis edictorumque mitigationem implorandam ducunt eamq; ut tutissimam viam cum omomni animi fubmissione ingrediuntur, supplicesque libellos, Austriacæ, Regis locum tenenti, regisque consilio, multa cum humilitate offerunt, oblationemq; repetunt, non honores, divitias ac imperium petentes, sed patriarum legum conservationem, edictorum mitigationem & conscientiarum libertatem. Sed quid his precibus, lamentationibus, se fatigantes promeriti sunt Patres? hoc unum quod Geusij, hoc est, mendicantis nomen datum sit, in contumeliam, contemptum & risum, quasi catervæ ex decoctoribus mendiculisque collectæ. Cujus nominis, Geusij, dico, ignominiosa nota partibus inusta, tantæ efficaciæ habita ut nondum cicatricem obduxerit, sed etiamnum aculeum dedignationis obtineat, ut & hodie apud hostes quisquis quenquam Geusium dixerit, omnia opprobria dixisse videatur. Et quod magis mirere, nec Cæsareæ, nec Regiæ, nec Principum intercessiones, postmodum quidquam valuere ad demulcendum Regis animum. Adde in testimonium alienati à Belgis animi, intercessores supplices in Hispania morte mulctatos: Adde & in testimonium alienati Regis à Belgis animi, quod efserissimus Tyrannus Ferdinandus de Toledo Albæ Dux in Belgium, cum Hispano milite mittatur, ut omnes vi atque armis subigat ac internecioni devoveat, utpote criminis Læsæ majestatis reos, Bona fisco Regio addicat, & de Belgio in illum modum disponat, quasi de Regno vi ac armis subacto ac devicto, in quod Regi jus vitæ ac necis erat: dicam uno verbo ut falsis nominibus jus & leges inverteret.
units.tr: But what counsels could help? What wedge was equal to this knot? The mass seemed hardly able to be pulled apart without destroying those who pulled it apart. For the Prince, already king and ruler in Asia and Africa, could not be summoned to law. The Fathers, lovers of tranquillity, resolved that the king's clemency and the mitigation of the edicts should be implored with prayers, and they entered upon this as the safest way with all submission of spirit. With great humility they offered supplicating petitions to the Austrian regent's deputy and to the King's council, seeking not honors, riches or rule, but the preservation of the country's laws, the mitigation of the edicts and freedom of conscience, and they repeated the offer. But what did the Fathers earn by wearying themselves with these prayers and lamentations? Only this: they were given the name "Geuzen," that is, beggars, as an insult, a contempt and a laughingstock, as if a troop gathered from bankrupts and beggars. The disgraceful brand of this name, "Geuzen," I say, was stamped upon the party, and it was held in such efficacy that it has not yet closed its scar, but still keeps the sting of disdain. Even today among the enemies, whoever calls anyone a Geuzen seems to have spoken every reproach. What is more to be wondered at, neither the intercessions of the Emperor, nor of the King, nor of the princes availed anything afterwards to soothe the King's mind. Add, as evidence of the King's estranged mind from the Belgians, the supplicating intercessors put to death in Spain. Add also that the most savage tyrant Ferdinand of Toledo, Duke of Alba, is sent into Belgium with Spanish soldiers, so that he may subdue all by force and arms and devote them to slaughter as guilty of treason, hand over their goods to the royal fisc, and dispose of Belgium as if it were a kingdom subdued and conquered by force and arms, over which the King had the right of life and death. In one word, he was to pervert right and laws under false names.

units.la: Hunc effectum in Regis animo sortitæ sunt supplicationes: jura, leges & privilegia provinciarum, paterna monita, & juramentum provincijs datum, de confervandis legibus & privilegijs. Hinc pau-latim, patrum & populi magis magisq; à Rege Regioque consilio alienata mens est, seclusa omni clementiæ & commiserationis spe, Rege ad preces surdo, & animum in patres indies exasperante & in pejus obstirmante, consiliaq; ventilare cœperunt Patres, cum flecti Rex non posset, ut quoquo modo frangi executio, & invisum Tyrannicum Regis imperium posset, & si non executi, saltem enervari aliquantulum posset, crescente ex desperatione audacia (quæ inermes in arma & periculi societate animos conjungente trudit) cum libertatem conscientiarum nemo bonus nisi cum vita simul amittat. Non contumacia aut malevolo in Regem animo, (quis enim gentem ullam magis supplicem regi vidit? ) sed quod viderent Patres, aut perpetuo læsa conscientia abjectissime vivendum, serviendum, & moriendum esse, aut Regis injustum imperium dum supplicationibus non poterat armis enervandum, aut relictis aris & focis, in exilio mendicandum esse. Quod equidem tandem, tandem, obtinuerunt Majores vestri, ut hodierna tempora & præsens vester status testantur. Idque maxime eo tempore cœptum, ex piscatorijs quodammodo navibus cum nulla vel minima eluctandi spes apparebat, atque omne humanum auxilium sublatum videbatur, dum nulla provincia, nulla urbs, castellum aut oppidum erat, quod non absolute sub Tyrannide (quæ est violentum unius imperium præter mores & leges) Hispanica suppressa libertate ac religione ingemiscebat, dum Albani tyrannis omnes subegerat, & prædæ expositerat, in tantum ut ne hiscere quidem quisquam auderet. Atq; ij quibus vires aut divitiæ erant, patria profugi aut proscripti exulabant. Imo & qui in Angliam profugi, qui æquatiles Geusij indigetabantur (procurante hoc Albano, crudeli & Belgicæ libertatis osori efferisimo) portubus exire, & prohibito commeatu, mare petere jusi erant: Unde tamen, sublato omni auxilio humano, Deo omnia dirigente, divinum auxilium remedium tulit, dum Brila ab exulibus capta, respiratio quædam, quasi novum sydus subortum, ut Belgis testatum faceret Deus divina auxilium non desiderare, nec juvari posse: Et quamquam Albanus nihili faceret hunc exulum conatum & Brilæ occupationem: docuit tamen posterior ætas, quod Brilam nunquam in potestatem reduxerit Dux Albanus. Et quod ex illo fonte exopinato, cepta in servitute respiratio, & multorum animorum erectio, quibus hoc divinum auxilium, majora sperandi ansam præbuit. Unde & multis civitatibus occasio nata ab Albani Tyrannide se subtrahendi.
units.tr: This was the effect that the petitions produced in the King's mind: the rights, laws and privileges of the provinces, his father's admonitions, and the oath given to the provinces to preserve their laws and privileges. From this point the minds of the nobles and the people were gradually and increasingly estranged from the King and his council. With every hope of mercy and compassion cut off, the King was deaf to their prayers and hardened himself ever more against the nobles, who grew more exasperated each day. When the King could not be moved, the nobles began to consider ways in which the execution of his orders might be broken in some fashion, and the hated tyrannical rule of the King might be weakened, if not overthrown, at least somewhat enfeebled. Desperation made them bold, for it drives unarmed men to take up arms and to share the danger together, since no good man can lose freedom of conscience without losing his life as well. They were not moved by obstinacy or ill will towards the King (for who ever saw a people more suppliant before a king?), but because the nobles saw that they must either live, serve and die with their consciences forever wronged and abased, or else, while their petitions could not prevail, must break the King's unjust rule by force, or abandon their altars and hearths and go begging in exile. This, at last, your forefathers did secure, as the present times and your present state bear witness. This began chiefly at the time when, in what were almost fishing boats, there appeared not even the smallest hope of resisting, and every human aid seemed removed, while there was no province, city, castle or town which did not groan under the Spanish tyranny (which is the violent rule of one man against custom and law), its liberty and religion suppressed. Alva had subdued everyone with tyranny and exposed them to plunder, so that no one dared even to open his mouth. Those who had strength or wealth fled their country as exiles or were proscribed. Indeed, those who had fled to England, who were called the Geuzen (the Beggars), were ordered, at Alva's instigation (he was cruel and most hostile to Belgian liberty), to leave the harbours and to make for the sea, with supplies forbidden to them. Yet from there, with all human help removed, God directing all things, divine aid brought the remedy: Brill was taken by the exiles, and a kind of breathing space arose, as though a new star had risen, to show the Belgians that God does not need human aid, nor can be helped by it. And although Alva made nothing of this attempt of the exiles and their seizure of Brill, later ages have taught that Duke Alva never recovered Brill. And from that unexpected source came a respite amid servitude and the raising up of many spirits, to whom this divine aid gave greater cause for hope. Hence many cities also had the occasion to withdraw from Alva's tyranny.

units.la: Ac didicit Albanus, quod Brila à Lumæo ipsi imposita, in tantum lumina ejus obscuraverit, quod lucem Belgicam ulterius non ferens, Hispaniam repetere coactus sit, suo exemplo confirmans quod tyrannorum execrabilis & brevis potestas sit. Et sic paulatim succesu temporis, Deo & proram & puppim gubernante, provinciæ in illum statum adoleverunt, de cujus honore, gloria, ac divitijs nihil attinet dicere, dum arma Hispanica terra non metuat mari leges quodammodo det. Dum excusso tyrannidis jugo, jam majestas singulis inest. Sed quales quantique casus obvenerit & provinciam angiaverint, quam aspera ad libertatem & statum præsentem clivus fuerit, quantas miserias, clades & calamitates perpesi sint majores, quantæ vicissitudines quassarint & concusserint, quam-que que accipiti marte, sæpè dimicatum sit cum parvis copijs, & quantum in-noxij sanguinis effusum sit.
units.tr: Alva learned that Brill, placed in his way by Lumey, so obscured his light that, unable to bear the Belgian light any longer, he was compelled to return to Spain, confirming by his own example that the power of tyrants is hateful and brief. And so, little by little, as time went on, with God steering both prow and stern, the provinces grew to that state of which there is no need to speak in terms of honour, glory and riches, since Spanish arms no longer fear the land and, as it were, they give laws to the sea. Now that the yoke of tyranny has been shaken off, majesty dwells in each one of them. But of what kind and how great the disasters were that befell and afflicted the province, how harsh the slope to liberty and to the present state was, what great miseries, defeats and calamities your forefathers suffered, what changes shook and battered them, how often they fought with small forces against a doubled sword of war, and how much innocent blood was poured out.

units.la: Hæc animus meminisse horret luctuque refugit.
units.tr: My mind shrinks from remembering these things and turns away in grief.

units.la: Argumenti loco est quod Albanum excedentem provincijs gloriabundum dixisse ferunt: sexennio quo regio nomine provincijs præfuerat, 18. millia hominum carnificis manu (exhorresco) perempta esse, eorum qui in acie & exilio occubuere infinitus est numerus.
units.tr: As evidence of this, they report that Alva, as he left the provinces, boasted that in the six years in which he had governed them in the King's name, eighteen thousand men had been put to death by the executioner's hand (I shudder to say it), and that the number of those who fell in battle or died in exile is beyond counting.

units.la: Illa sunt quæ ordine deducit Historicus vester, non in globo ut dici solet, sed veris & ex archivis deductis documentis eo ordine quo gesta sunt, specialius in Frisia hac vestra: Idq; ex commisso in illud usq; tempus, quo Provinciæ in Libertatem sese vindicarunt, & Philippum tunc Hispaniarum Regem ob Tyrannidem omni jure cecidisse judicarunt, nomenq; regium, sygilla, atq; omnia Regis insignia, sustulerunt & dominium ejurarunt, ac Remp. Liberam constituerunt, quod publico edicto, rationibus insertis ad longum, promulgatum anno supra CIↄ. Iↄ. LXXXI. XII. Kalend. Septemb. quo Lectorem remittimus.
units.tr: These are the things that your historian sets out in order, not in a lump, as is commonly said, but with documents drawn from the true records and archives, in the order in which the events occurred, especially in this your Frisia. He does so from the crime committed up to that time, when the provinces claimed their liberty for themselves and judged that Philip, then King of the Spains, had by his tyranny forfeited every right, and so they removed the royal title, the seals and all the King's insignia, renounced his lordship and established a free commonwealth. This was proclaimed by a public edict, with its reasons set out at length, in the year 1581, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, and to that edict we refer the reader.

units.la: In Historiæ commendationem me non dabo, ne huic tam vendibili vino hederam suspendere videar, cum & multorum celeberrimorum doctissimorumq; virorum testimonia de excellentia Historiæ extent, quæ brevi forte in lucem prodibunt; ausim dicere neminem ante hac majori studio & curiosa indagatione scripsisse, magisq; facta verbis exæquasse. Finio in voto, & apprecor ut in florenti rerum statu Ill. D.D. vestras, diu conservet magnus ille arbiter rerum Deus, à quo, in quo & ad quem sunt omnia. Cui sit laus, honos & gloria in æternum.
units.tr: I shall not give myself over to praising the History, lest I seem to hang an ivy bush over such saleable wine. There exist testimonies of many most famous and learned men to the excellence of the History, which will perhaps soon come to light. I venture to say that no one before has written with greater zeal and more curious investigation, and has matched deeds with words more faithfully. I bring my remarks to a close with this wish and pray that the great Judge of all things, God, from whom, in whom and to whom are all things, may long preserve your Illustrious Lordships in the flourishing state of affairs. To him be praise, honour and glory for ever.

units.la: ALLOR? an in nostri redierunt tempora saecli Historiae Princeps sapienti nobilis ore, Nobilis & gemmis Latij SALUSTIUS aevi? Nec minor hoc TACITUS, victuris Nomina chartis Gestaque Romulidum tradens annalibus orbi?
units.tr: Or has our age produced again a prince of history, noble in his wise speech, and as noble in his gems of the Latin age, Sallust? Is Tacitus not equal to him, who hands down to the world in his annals the names and deeds of the Romulids, names destined to live on the page?

units.la: Credite! non alius stylus est: Nec dignius unquam Majestas meminit sese Romana locutam.
units.tr: Believe me, there is no other style. Never did Roman majesty speak of itself in a more worthy way.

units.la: Res alia & seges est. Tua, FRISIA, Bella, DUCESQUE Jura, POTESTATES aeterna luce beantur.
units.tr: Your theme is different and a richer field, O Frisia: your wars and leaders, your laws and powers, are blessed with eternal light.

units.la: Hei mihi! quam latum quondam mea Patria Regnum, STAURIA cum Ducibus Septem, clara inde Novenis Regibus & Danis fuit & contermina Gallis.
units.tr: Alas, how wide my fatherland's kingdom once was, with its seven chiefs of Stavoren, and thereafter famous for its nine kings and the Danes, and bordering on the Gauls.

units.la: Nunc alius patriae limes, quam Lavica claudit, Et mare Flevanis infusum terminat undis.
units.tr: Now another boundary marks our country, that which the Lek closes off, and the sea, poured in by the Flevo waters, sets its limit.

units.la: Scilicet instabilem variata potentia mundum Voluit, & aeternum nihil est. Regnisque negatum Stare diu, veniente die, quo gloria rerum Sistitur, & caeco succisa potentia fato.
units.tr: Surely changeable power has willed the world to be unstable, and nothing is eternal. Kingdoms are denied lasting existence; the day comes when the glory of things is brought to a halt, and power is cut down by blind fate.

units.la: Cui fecere viam bellis & sanguine gaudens RHADBODI genius, sed post civilis Erynnis Frisiacas totis concussit viribus oras Inque novas secuit parteis. Hinc turbida dudum.
units.tr: For the genius of Radbod, delighting in war and blood, cleared the way for this; but afterwards the civil Fury shook the Frisian shores with all her might and cut them into new factions. From here the turbulent Vetcopers raised their banners, and the Schyrings their opposing signs.

units.la: VETCOPERI tollunt, contraria signa SCHYRINGI, In sua crudeles vertentes viscera dextras Vastarunt patrios ferro flammaque penates.
units.tr: Turning their cruel right hands against their own vitals, they laid waste the ancestral household gods with sword and fire.

units.la: Sic caput & mundi terror, quae fortibus armis Imperium terris, animos aequarat olympo, Martia ROMA suis struxit sibi funera telis.
units.tr: So Rome, the head and terror of the world, which by her brave arms had made her empire equal to the earth and her spirit equal to Olympus, built her own funeral pyre with her own weapons, Mars's city.

units.la: Ast animus meminisse horret, luctuque refugit, Quanta per Hollandos Frisiosque effusa PHILIPPO Tempestas ierit campos, quibus actus uterque Europae atque Asiae satis concurrerit orbis, Ut Libertatem, patria ut funditus aras Diruerat. Fuit ergo truci crudelior ALBA
units.tr: But my spirit shudders to remember, and shrinks back in grief, what storm Philip let loose across the fields of Holland and Friesland, where each side clashed, as much of the world of Europe and Asia as there was room for, so that he had utterly overturned liberty and the altars of the fatherland. Alba was therefore crueller than the savage Tigris,

units.la: Tygride, vel tristi Busyride saevior ipso
units.tr: and more fierce than Busiris himself, the sad Busiris.

units.la: Missus in has oras, juratas frangere leges
units.tr: Sent into these shores, he was ordered to break the laws sworn to,

units.la: Jussus, & hostiles veluti devincere terras,
units.tr: and to conquer the hostile lands as if they were his own,

units.la: Mancipioque suo bellis asscribere Regi.
units.tr: and to bind them by war as slaves to his King.

units.la: Ille per innocuos grassatus caede penates
units.tr: He raged through the harmless households with slaughter,

units.la: Obvia quaeque metit ferro, non flectitur annis,
units.tr: and cut down with the sword whatever stood in his way; he was not softened by years,

units.la: Non ullis precibus, crudeli sanguine mactat
units.tr: nor by any prayers; with cruel bloodshed he slew

units.la: Uxoresque Virum, Puerosque ante ore Parentum.
units.tr: wives and husbands, and boys before the eyes of their parents.

units.la: Nec generi parcit, Nec stirpi saevus equestri.
units.tr: Nor did he spare rank, nor the cruel family of the knights.

units.la: Illustres Patriae Proceres, clarissimus HORNAE
units.tr: The illustrious nobles of the fatherland, most famous Horne

units.la: EGMONDAEQUE comes, tum millia multo virorum
units.tr: and Egmond the count, then thousands of men

units.la: Carnifici trucidata manu. Fit Belgica tota
units.tr: were butchered by the executioner's hand. All Belgium became

units.la: Exul, inops, terras alio sub sole jacentes
units.tr: an exile, a beggar, and begged for a small home for her gods

units.la: Dis sedem exiguam patriis, littusque rogavit
units.tr: among the lands lying under another sun, and a shore

units.la: Innocuum, & cunctis undamque auramque patentem.
units.tr: that was harmless, and a sea and air open to all.

units.la: Haud aliter stimulante fame tygrisve lupusve
units.tr: Not otherwise, when hunger drives them on, does a tiger or wolf

units.la: Mansuetas praedatur oves, vigilique remoto
units.tr: prey upon the gentle sheep, and with the watchman removed,

units.la: Terribilis miti Balautum sanguine longam
units.tr: the terrible beast sates its long rage with the gentle blood of Balaut,

units.la: Exsaturat rabiem, & totis dat funera campis:
units.tr: and brings death across all the fields.

units.la: Illae, qua data porta, ruunt, in montibus, antris
units.tr: Those who find a gate open rush into the mountains and caves,

units.la: Se tegere, & letum tutis evadere sylvis.
units.tr: to hide themselves, and to escape death in the safe woods.

units.la: Sed redijt tandem vetus in praecordia virtus
units.tr: But at last the old virtue returned to their hearts

units.la: Sub duce ARAUSIADA, & pro libertatis amore
units.tr: under the leadership of Orange, and for love of liberty

units.la: Creverunt animi, civilis maxima quercus
units.tr: their spirits grew, and the greatest oak of civil glory

units.la: Gloria fit, miserosque rogo servare penates.
units.tr: became a refuge for the wretched households, which they begged to save.

units.la: Suasit amor Patriae, libertas pristina gentis,
units.tr: The love of the fatherland urged them on, the ancient liberty of the nation,

units.la: Religioque viris animoso occumbere leto.
units.tr: and religion, to die in a manly way.

units.la: Ergo per adversas sortes erecta resurgens
units.tr: Therefore, raised up by adverse fortunes and rising again,

units.la: Juncta Philippeos excussit Belgica fasces,
units.tr: Belgium, joined together, shook off the Philippine fasces,

units.la: Terribilemque Ducem, qui tum felicibus armis
units.tr: and the terrible leader, who then with fortunate arms

units.la: Imperium Oceano, famamque aequarat Olympo.
units.tr: had made his empire equal to Ocean and his fame equal to Olympus.

units.la: Salve laeta Dies, Niveo signanda Lapillo,
units.tr: Hail, joyful day, to be marked with a snow-white stone,

units.la: Salve laeta Dies; qua non felicior orta,
units.tr: hail, joyful day, than which none more fortunate has arisen,

units.la: Natalis Patriae, tum Libertatis avitae.
units.tr: birthday of the fatherland, and of our ancestral liberty.

units.la: Candida Relligio FRATERNIS saucia flammis,
units.tr: Bright religion, wounded by brotherly flames,

units.la: Et SPE pollenti clypeos armata FIDEQUE
units.tr: and armed with a shield of mighty hope and faith,

units.la: Libera tum coluit sacra, Libera vota Tonanti
units.tr: then worshipped in freedom, and offered its free vows to the Thunderer,

units.la: Obtulit; & licitum templis indixit honorem.
units.tr: and proclaimed honour lawful for the temples.

units.la: Nataque Libertas Suffragia libera liquit
units.tr: And born Liberty left her free votes,

units.la: Libera Frisiadis Patriae moderamina terrae.
units.tr: the free government of the Frisian fatherland's land.

units.la: Haec meus aeternis consignat tempora chartis
units.tr: These times my pen sets down in eternal pages,

units.la: VINSEMIUS Patriae celeberrima gloria terrae
units.tr: I, Winsemius, the most celebrated glory of my fatherland,

units.la: Gloria, lingua, manus. Latiae facundia Stuadae
units.tr: glory of tongue and hand. Eloquence of the Latin Stua,

units.la: Sive undare foro; numerosque referre solutos,
units.tr: whether to pour forth in the forum, or to bring back loose numbers,

units.la: Seu libet Aonias sub leges cogere voces.
units.tr: or as I please, to bring the Aonian voices under the rule of law.

units.la: Ast nunc illa jacet Patriae celeberrima terrae
units.tr: But now that glory of my fatherland, most celebrated, lies

units.la: Gloria, & elinguis, qui nuper lingua manusque
units.tr: silent, who lately was the sole glory

units.la: Sola fuit Patriae. Fatis concessit ab atro
units.tr: of his fatherland in tongue and hand. He has yielded to the fates, from the dark

units.la: Ordine fatorum Patrias qui vindicat oras.Mens verò è claustris fugiens mortalibus interAgmina caelitum victrix migravit ad astra,Et sanctos coeli cives & amoena piorumConcilia, Elysios celebrans jam carmine campos. Patria quas grates solves? quae praemia fastis? Praelia, queis, Regesque tui, praeclaraque facta,Libertatis amor, jurataque Regibus olimPacta triumphali ducuntur ad ultima curruSaecula, & extremos aeterna laude nepotes. Hoc opus (exstat enim de te non dignius ullum) Sede loca illustri, magnis & honoribus auge.Haereat in memori VINSEMIUS ore manuque, Nec pretium, nec tanti abolescat gratia facti.Sit, pete, terra levis, multaque in pace quiescat,Et violis sacrum consperge, rosisque sepulcrum,Ac cineri tanto magna cum laude parenta, Nos quoque, nos curam veteris servamus amici,Et memores nostri, quamvis rude, pignus amorisDistichon hoc meritae grati sacravimus URNAE.
units.tr: order of fates, which claims back the ancestral shores. But his mind, fleeing from the cloisters among mortals, has migrated, victorious, among the ranks of the heavenly host to the stars, and, now celebrating the blessed citizens of heaven and the pleasant assemblies of the pious, the Elysian fields in song. What thanks will you pay, fatherland? What rewards will you give in the annals? The battles, your kings, and your famous deeds, the love of liberty, and the pacts once sworn to kings are led in triumphal chariot to the furthest ages, and to the furthest descendants by eternal praise. This work (for no worthier one exists about you) place in an illustrious seat and increase with great honours. Let Winsemius remain in your memory, in mouth and hand, nor let the reward and the grace of so great a deed grow old. Be light, earth, and may he rest in much peace; sprinkle his sacred tomb with violets and roses, and with great praise, to such ashes, we, too, who keep the care of an old friend, and mindful of ourselves, though rough, have consecrated this couplet as a pledge of love to the deserving grateful urn.

units.la: OS magnum, quod magna Dei miracula narrat, Quae nostros tantum cernere fecit avos, Dum vox imbellis populi & suspiria mixta Sanguine ruperunt vincula dura Erebi, Regnaque quaßarunt, & celso culmine structum Mundique æquatum finibus imperium, Pondere sub cuius, nutantis vulnere vasto, Iam pridem rerum machina tota gemit: Dum tener astuti rejecit frena PHILIPPI Belga vovens soli libera corda Deo. Qualia non Tacitus non aurea vena Maronis Explicuit sive bis doctius ingenium. Os felix, cui tanta datum est nudare nepoti Risuro fumos labilis imperij, WINSEMII; quod nec voluit mors dura silère. Verba etenim seclis pagina tradet anus:
units.tr: O great mouth, which tells of the great miracles of God, which made our forefathers alone to see, when the unwarlike voice of the people and sighs mixed with blood broke the hard bonds of Erebus, and shook the kingdoms, and the empire built on a lofty summit and made equal to the boundaries of the world, beneath whose weight, tottering from a vast wound, the whole machinery of affairs has long groaned; when the tender Belgians threw off the reins of crafty Philip, vowing their hearts free for God alone. Such things neither Tacitus nor the golden vein of Maro unfolded, nor a genius twice as learned. Happy mouth, to which it was given to lay bare for a later generation the smoke of the fleeting empire, WINSEMIUS; which cruel death did not wish to keep silent. For the page will hand down the words to the ages, as an old woman would:

units.la: Honori Collegae dum vivebat amandi & observandi, post obitum desiderati, raptim ponebat.
units.tr: Hastily written while he was alive, to be loved and respected by his colleague, and lamented after his death.

units.tr: JOHANNES COCCEIUS, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Professor of Hebrew Language, and at the time Rector in the Academy of Franeker.
