units.tr: On the Frisian History

units.la: CLARISSIMI VIRI DOMINI PIERII WINSEMII, IC. Ordinum Frisiae Historiographi & Historiarum atque Eloquentiae Professoris, inter operas Typographicas, ante editum opus, defuncti.
units.tr: Of the most distinguished man, Master Pierius Winsemius, Doctor of Law, Historiographer of the Frisian Orders, and Professor of History and Eloquence, who died while the work was in the printers' hands, before it was published.

units.la: DNVIDA mors nulli mortali parcere docta, Saepius egregios, suspiciosa, premens, Viderat hunc prodire librum, qui reddaret ævum Exstinctis longo tempore funeribus. Qui Soli exhibeat res gestas luce Carentum Lethe devicta, Tartareoque specu. Scilicet hic veterum patrata leguntur avorum, Quos tenet inferni regia muta poli. Ferratæ patuêre fores, calamoque potente Pieridum magnos vivere fecit avos. WINSHEMI calamus duxit de nocte profundâ PIERIUS Frisios restituitque Patres, Quotquot in Hispanos animosi ivêre secures, Et soboli dederunt libera regna suæ. Vidit & ingemuit torsitque volatile ferrum, Invisumque malo vulnere stravit humi. Sic quicunque, inquit, mortem violare deinde Speret & è Stygia victor abire domo. Sic invisè jaces, solâ tamen utere vitâ, Quam potuit functis addere docta manus. Ergo parte sui subijt WINSEMIUS umbras, Et non emissum morte reliquit opus: Parte sui meliore viget, vivetque per illos, Quibus tribuit nunquam posse deinde mori.
units.tr: Death, which has learned to spare no mortal, and often hovered over the eminent, watching with hostility and pressing hard, had seen this book come forth, one that would give life again to those long buried in their funerals. It shows the deeds of the dead to the light of the sun, Lethe conquered and the Tartarean cave overcome. Indeed, here are read the deeds of our ancient forefathers, whom the silent kingdom of the infernal pole holds. The iron gates have been thrown open, and with the powerful pen of the Muses he has made the great ancestors live again. The pen of Winsemius drew the Frisian fathers, Pierius, out of the deep night and restored them, all those who, bold, had gone against the Spaniards with their axes and given free realms to their offspring. He saw this, groaned, and hurled the flying iron, and laid low on the ground the hated one with a grievous wound. So, he said, let whoever hopes afterwards to violate death and depart victorious from the Stygian house. So you lie, hated, yet you enjoy only the life which the learned hand could add to the dead. Therefore Winsemius went down into the shadows with part of himself, and left behind a work that death had not sent forth. With his better part he flourishes, and he will live on through those to whom he has granted that they can never die again.

units.la: C. SCHOTANUS, Graec. Litt. & Histor. Lulef. Profess.
units.tr: C. Schotanus, Professor of Greek Letters and History at Leeuwarden

units.la: I N HISTORIAM PHILIPPICO-FRISICAM CLARISSIMI, AMPLISSIMIQUE VIRI D. PIERI WINSEMI, I. C. & Historio-graphi Frisiorum integerrimi, ac Eloquentiæ & Historiarum Professoris Celeberrimi; Amici & Collegæ quondam intimi ac desideratissimi.
units.tr: IN THE PHILIPPICO-FRISIAN HISTORY OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED AND MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN DR PIERUS WINSEMIUS, Doctor of Law, the most upright historiographer of the Frisians, and most celebrated Professor of Eloquence and History; once my closest and most lamented friend and colleague.

units.la: ERGONE PIERIDES meritis nec præmia constant? Nec sua Musarum cultori, & honesta Professo Nomina sunt clari concessa brabeia laboris? Ergonè post rigido consumtas frigore noctes Egelidas, lucemque datam melioribus actis, Non licuit superesse sibi, superesse suorum Effectis operum, dignosque hinc carpere fructus? Sed fuit in fatis, ut quem diversa decerêt Sæcula nosse suum, vel qui, si commoda nostra Spectassèt, si PIERIDUM juga sacra sororum Difficilis Natura gradus servare secundos Curasset, multos tempus traxisse per annos Debuerat, Pylio longè dignissimus ævo; Hunc (veniam fasso da numen) magna gerentem, Complexumque suâ præclaros mente labores, Ultrà quos dederat, cunctisque sacraverat ævis, In medio rerum cursu, Mors sæva Lycæis Eriperet nostris, ac funere mergeret atro? Exueretque citum moribundæ carcere molis Invida vis fati? Quem nunc, heu! squallida gestans, Oraque, & incomptos jaciens Academia crines, Luget; & expresso lachrymarum fonte, Patrono Orba suo, fugiens oculis solatia, questus Concoquit intempesta suos, gemitusque per auras Nequidquam evanidas fundit, concussa recenti Vulnere; cujus agit nunc, præstans ante, profundum Justitium densis Facundia mersa pruinis. Quid quod sistra silent præcocis conscia fati? Et tripodes, & muta chelys, & marcida laurus Squallent? nec Cyrrhæ cortina remugit ab antro? Claraque ob abruptam cessant oracula vocem?
units.tr: Are the Pierides, then, without reward for their merits? Are the names of a devotee of the Muses and an honourable professor not granted as prizes of renown for labour? Was it not allowed him, after nights worn away in rigid cold and days given to better deeds, to survive for himself, to survive in the fruits of his works and to gather from them the worthy harvest? But it was fated that he, whom diverse ages should have known as their own, who, had he considered our advantages and cared to keep the second rank on the difficult slopes of the sacred Sisters of the Pierides, ought to have spent many years, far most worthy of a Pylian age; this man, bearing great tasks and embracing with his mind glorious labours beyond those he had already given and had consecrated to all ages, in the middle course of affairs, cruel Death was to tear from our Lyceum and plunge into dark funeral? Did envious force of fate strip him from the prison of the dying body? Whom now, alas, Academia mourns, squalid in face and casting down her unkempt hair; and, with a fountain of tears pressed out, bereft of her patron and shunning every comfort, she digests her complaints through the untimely hours and pours out groans into the air, vainly dissipating them, shaken by the recent wound; by whose loss Eloquence, formerly outstanding, now lives in profound mourning, sunk in dense frost. What of the fact that the sistra fall silent, aware of his premature fate? And the tripods, the mute lyre and the withered laurel grow squalid? Nor does the curtain of Cirrha resound from its cave? And the famous oracles cease their clear voice?

units.la: Sic miseri morimur nascendo, horæque rapacisPræda sumus, vitæ florem sic singula carpitÆtas, sic vixdum meditantes lubrica vita, Alternasque vices rerum, sortemque malignamNequidquam, humanis nos tandem excedere rebusMandat summa dies, & ineluctabile fatum.
units.tr: Thus we wretched mortals die by being born, and we are the prey of greedy hour; thus each age plucks the flower of life, thus life, slippery, has scarcely begun to think; and the highest day, and inescapable fate, commands us at last to depart from human affairs, in vain, with their alternating changes and their malignant lot.

units.la: Non tamen interijt totus, depasta nec omnemEst inopina Virum supremi funeris hora. Terra tenet corpus, tumuloque recondita tristiViscera, mortali quæ sanguine creta, quietumIn vitam exspectant reditum. Nam parte superstesIpse sui meliore manet, mortique relinquitQuod mortale fuit: sed vivax particula auraeDivinæ ætthereas conscendit Spiritus arces, Regna beata colens: ac Nobis magna relinquensIngenij documenta sui, mirandaque mentisLumina, doctrinæque suæ pollentis acervosImmodicos, sacro quos fudit pectora motuPulsus, & æthereo perfusus numine mentem.
units.tr: Yet he did not perish wholly, nor has the unexpected hour of the last funeral devoured the whole of the man. The earth holds his body, and his sorrowful entrails, hidden in the tomb and formed from mortal blood, await a quiet return to life. For the living spirit, the better part of himself, remains and leaves to death what was mortal; but the spirit, a lively particle of divine air, has climbed to the ethereal citadels, dwelling in the blessed kingdoms; and it leaves to us great proofs of its genius, the wonderful lights of its mind, and the immoderate heaps of its mighty learning, which, struck by a sacred impulse and filled with the heavenly divinity, it poured forth from its breast.

units.la: Quem quoque Thymbræus puerum formavit ApolloObsequio clarere bono, primaque JuventâMagna rudimenta & tenerae cunabula linguaeEdere clara satis, cum prima elementa laborumPercurrit, titubansque ratos industria gressusDiscendique sibi callem legit. Aucta LycæoGloria cum crevit, curisque Academia primisSuccessit, roburque dedit juvenilibus annis:Tum vero pariter mens ingeniosa, laborqueVires commisere suas, quo se quoque possetPIERIIS gaudens studijs, attollere victorClaraque Magnatum præcox volitare per ora; Cecropiaeque simul versans consulta Minervae,Scandere Doctrinæ Sapientum templa serenæ.
units.tr: Him also Thymbraean Apollo formed as a boy to shine with good obedience, and in his early youth to put forth clear enough great beginnings and the tender cradle of the tongue, when he ran through the first elements of study and, with diligent effort, his faltering steps found their way and he chose for himself the path of learning. When the glory of the Lyceum grew and Academia succeeded to his first cares and gave strength to his youthful years, then truly his ingenious mind and his labour together committed their strengths, so that he too, rejoicing in the Pierian studies, might raise himself up as a victor, and fly early through the famous mouths of the great; and at the same time, turning over the counsels of Cecropian Minerva, he might climb to the temples of the serene Wisdom of the learned.

units.la: Inde Machaoniam natura ductus ad Artem, Pergameos, Coösque senes, & Græcia quotquotDocta dedit Medicos, vel quotquot Roma superbit,Barbarus aut Arabs, sibi vult fecisse frequentes, Ingenio studioque suo complexus, in imumCorporis humani perspexit, & intima lustransQuæ sapiens Natura tegit, penetralia parvæInspexit Mundi machinæ, si forte labaretFabrica, vel languor popularet corpore vires, Posset ut obscuras morborum pandere causas. Quin quod & ulterius, quo sævis pharmaca morbisAptaret, dextraque manu medicamina ferret,Non minor hæc tum cura fuit, cognoscere Plantas,Quas Oriens Eous habet, quas sidere seroSpectat pulcra dies, septem gelidique TrionesAspiciunt, pluvijs perfususque imbribus Auster.
units.tr: Thence, led by nature to the Machaonian art, he wished to make himself one of the frequent physicians whom Pergamum and the old men of Cos, and whatever learned Greece gave, or whoever proud Rome boasts, whether barbarian or Arab, embraced with his genius and zeal; he surveyed to the depths the human body and, searching its inmost parts, looked into the hidden recesses of the machinery of the world which wise Nature conceals, if perchance the frame should totter or languor should lay waste the strength of the body, so that he might be able to lay open the obscure causes of diseases. Moreover, and further, so that he might fit remedies to savage diseases and bring medicines with a skilled hand, no less care was given to learning the plants which the Eastern Dawn has, which the fair day, late in the year, watches under the star, which the seven cold Triones behold, and which the South Wind, drenched with showers and rains, sees.

units.la: Sed quoniam quò fata trahunt; retrahuntq; sequendum; Præcipuè Juveni bona jussa capescere fas sit; Ergò sanctarum fisus moderamine Legum, En vestras Astræa fores, edictaque pandit Vestra, triumphantes quos vidit Roma Quirites, Et Bizantinis suffragia condita regnis.
units.tr: But since fate draws whither, and draws back, one must follow; and chiefly it is right for a young man to take up the good commands: therefore, trusting in the guidance of the holy laws, behold, Astraea opens your doors and proclaims your edicts, which Rome saw when her Quirites were triumphant, and the suffrages established for the Byzantine kingdoms.

units.la: Quin & ut optatam studijs contingere metam, Ac dignam meritis mercem sufferre laborum Posset, terrarum longos invisere tractus Maluit, atque sitas alio sub cardine gentes Quærere longinquas peragratus sedulus oras, Ne quid inexpertum studijs relinqueret usquam; Sed posset varios hominum cognoscere mores, Atque alios casus Legum, diversaque Jura. Igitur Hercinios saltus, Fuldaeque rigentes Legit aquas, Vesaraeque vias, transfivit & Albim; Et sæpè Hesperio mutatum sanguine Mosam, Cornigerumque patrem Rhenum, Viadrique ruentis Fluminaque, & celebres Meliboco vertice Cattos; Et Nemetos, & quæ nostris contraria terris, Albiona, immensis quâ circumfunditur undis: Et Te, quæ Batavas inter caput exeris urbes, Ingens Leida sacris semper domus hospita Musis, Perque alios plures tractus, populosque remotos; Quos fluvijs diversa suis intervolat unda, Et varias ivit terras: dum præmia laudum Et voluit, simul & meruit retulisse decora.
units.tr: Moreover, so that he might attain the goal desired by his studies and receive the reward for his labours worthy of his merits, he preferred to visit the long tracts of lands, and, travelling diligently over distant shores, to seek nations situated under another pole, so that he might leave nothing untried anywhere in his studies, but might be able to know the varied customs of men and the different cases of the laws and the diverse laws. Therefore he passed through the Hercynian woods and the cold waters of the Fulda, and the roads of the Weser, and crossed the Elbe; and often the Meuse, changed by Hesperian blood, and the horned father Rhine, and the rushing rivers of the Oder, and the famous Catti on the Meliboean peak; and the Nemetes, and the lands opposite to ours, Albion, where the wide waves surround it; and you, Leiden, who lift your head among the Batavian cities, a vast house always hospitable to the sacred Muses; and through many other tracts and remote peoples, whom a wave flying through with its own rivers divides; and he went through various lands, while he wished to bring back the prizes of praise, and at the same time earned the honours.

units.la: Rettulit & mercem studiorum, ac digna probatus Præmia ferre, Gradum titulis comitantibus auget, Quam dedit ambiguis natalibus acta Cadomum.
units.tr: He also brought back the reward of his studies, and, proved worthy, he bears the prizes; he increases his rank with accompanying titles, which the event at Caen gave, a city of uncertain birth.

units.la: Hunc tum mirata est ingens, quæ lumina vitæ Dulcia præclaro tribuit Leovardia Alumno; Dum plausu exceptus populi, non voce clienti Emtâ, non pretio, sed juri obnoxius uni, Ancipites casus, litesque absolvit amaras, Adversasque suo pressit sub Judice partes.
units.tr: Then the great Leeuwarden admired him, which offers the sweet lights of life to its distinguished alumnus; while, received with applause of the people, not bought by a client's voice, not by price, but bound to justice alone, he resolved doubtful cases and bitter lawsuits, and held down the adverse parties under his one judge.

units.la: Ast quem Pierides sibi primis semper ab annis Sacravère, suo quem perfudère liquore, & Innocuæ pietatis amor ducebat, & almæ Pacis honos, Litisque ferae contraria Virtus; Huic quoque tum querulas vulgi, plebisque profanæ Pertæso facilè curas, semperque calentis Officium servile fori, strepitusque clientum, Blanda quies placuit, nec desidiosa; sed inter Munia curarum tranquillam carpere vitam.
units.tr: But him whom the Pierides had consecrated to themselves from his earliest years, whom they had bathed in their own liquor, whom the love of innocent piety led, and the honour of nourishing peace, and the virtue opposed to fierce strife; to him too, weary of the querulous cares of the common crowd and the profane populace, the servile duty of the ever-heated forum and the noise of clients, a soft and not idle quiet pleased; and among the duties of cares he chose to pass a tranquil life.

units.la: Igitur urbano; quia sic tum fata volebant, Jam procul à strepitu, & primâ statione recedens; Excludensque simul populique forique calores;
units.tr: Therefore, since the fates then so willed it, withdrawing now far from the din of the city and from his first post, and at the same time shutting out the heat of the people and the forum;

units.la: Prætulit exculti vernantia gaudia ruris: Arboreosque inter medius, gelidosve recessus, Et virides læto ridentes gramine campos, Et liquidas inter fluviorum ac æquoris undas, Otia PIERIDUM carpit, devotaque Musis Tempora diverso rerum oblectamine fallit: Posthabitisque bonis, quæ pellax gloria mundi Æstimat, & studio vulgus sectatur hiante, Altius insurgit, studiumque effusus in omne, Exerit ingenium, & divinæ semina mentis Inserit haut ullo perituris tempore chartis.
units.tr: he preferred the joys of the cultivated countryside in spring: and in the middle of the tree-shaded or cool retreats, and the green fields smiling with joyful grass, and between the clear waters of rivers and the sea, he gathered the leisure of the Pierides and, devoting his times to the Muses, beguiled them with varied delight in affairs. Having set aside the goods which the deceitful glory of the world esteems, and which the gaping crowd pursues with eager zeal, he rose higher, and, poured out into every zeal, put forth his genius and sowed the seeds of his divine mind in pages that will never perish in time.

units.la: Sive suos ardens Tibi MINCIA cantat AMORES, Sive dolet, nullos cum mœstus in ignibus ignes Invenit, & tristi modulatur carmen avena. Sive tuos ignes, Cererem qui sævus in æstu SYRIUS eludis medio, cum torridus iras Evomis in campos, avidisque in lucra colonis Spes messis tardare vales Latrator anhelus, Cum premit indomiti trux Phœbus terga Leonis. Sive etiam ulterius tendit, mirandaque tractat Divinæ monumenta manus, nec clara parentum Gesta silet, nec voce suâ profitetur inertes Frisiacos rexisse Duces, dum stare quietas Res nostras Fortuna vetat, servatque tenorem Ipsa suum, ac luctu gaudet turbare triumphos. Nec laudes ô Magne tuas GUSTAVE, nec ista Invictæ documenta manus, nec fortia facta, Nec cum Phœbæo diffusum lumine Nomen, Præterit, at scriptis donat vivacibus orbi. Ah quoties curis defixum talibus, atque Magnæ molis opus rimantem, & pectore toto Absentem penitus, vidit cum surgeret undis Purpureis ventura dies, cum lumine pleno Umbras contraheret tenues altissimus orbe Sol medio, vel cum claro nox sidera cælo Spargeret, & rebus cæcas induceret umbras.
units.tr: Whether the Mincius sings to you of his burning loves, or grieves, mournful, when he finds no fires among the fires, and modulates his song on the sad oaten pipe; whether you, Sirius, the cruel dog-star, mock your fires in the middle of the heat, when you, parched, vomit your rage over the fields, and, a panting barker, you are able to delay the hopes of harvest for the greedy farmers, when savage Phoebus presses the back of the untamed Lion; whether he extends further still and treats the wonderful monuments of the divine hand, nor is silent about the famous deeds of his ancestors, nor by his voice does he profess that the Frisian leaders, idle, governed, while Fortune forbids our affairs to stand quiet, and herself keeps her own course, and rejoices to disturb triumphs with grief; nor, O great Gustavus, does he pass over your praises, nor the proofs of that invincible hand, nor your brave deeds, nor your name spread with Phoebean light, but he gives them to the world in lasting writings. Ah, how often, when he saw the coming day rising from the purple waves, or when the highest sun with full light contracted the faint shadows in the middle of the sphere, or when the night scattered stars across the clear sky and brought dark shadows over things, how often did he see him fixed in such cares, probing the work of a great undertaking, and wholly absent in his whole heart.

units.la: Donec & ad curas nova cura accederet istas, Expeteretque sibi luxata Academia tantum Depositum, quò læsa suos sanare labores Posset, & auspicio Procerum præclara per orbem, Præsidio tali, diffundere nomina totum. Hïc curæ indomitæ; nullisque interrita Virtus Adversis satis emicuit, dum victa fatiscit Undique barbaries, & labem inferre vetatur Moribus ingenuis, sed passim Legibus æquis Vivitur, officioque bono: quin docta Juventus, Felix voce illâ, semperque assueta doceri Annuit, & totam se ipsi debere fatetur, Nec dignum meritis unquam statuisse brablum,
units.tr: Meanwhile the Academy, its strength broken, sought for itself this trust, so that, under the patronage of the nobles, it might heal its wounded labours and spread its famous name throughout the world. Here an undaunted courage, unshaken by any adversity, has shone forth, while barbarism, beaten on every side, wastes away, and it is forbidden to bring disgrace upon honourable customs. Instead, everywhere men live under fair laws and in good duty. Indeed the learned youth, glad at that voice and always accustomed to being taught, assents and confesses that it owes everything to them, and never judged any prize worthy of its deserts.

units.la: Dum tali auxilio res quondam Academica tuta, Contra Barbaricos ausus, Cyclopiaque arma, Perstat ovans; dumque hic altis Palinurus in undis Puppe sedet celsa, clavoque intentus adhæret Intrepidus, fragilem queat ut dissolvere navim Syrtibus, & decimis subducere sedulus undis. Nec tentant peccare mali, nec præmia desunt Ingenuis, cunctos regit at Prudentia casus, Consilijs matura suis; quidquid vel Erinnijs, Seque vorans Livor, toto molimine tentent, Vel quæ vibratæ decernant vulnera linguæ, Vel quæ feralis recinat convitia Bubo.
units.tr: While, with such help, the Academy, once in danger, now safe against barbarous assaults and Cyclopean weapons, stands triumphant, and while here Palinurus sits at the high stern in the deep waters, intent on the helm and fearless, so that he may steer the fragile ship clear of the Syrtes and draw it diligently from the tenth wave, the wicked do not dare to offend, and rewards are not lacking for free minds. But Prudence, ripe in her counsels, governs all chances. Whatever the Erinyes and Envy, devouring itself, attempt with all their efforts, whatever wounds the hurled tongue may decree, and whatever ill omens the baleful owl sings, all these are held in check.

units.la: Interea totum sibi tandem vendicat omnis Historie, jussu Procerum: quis justa petenti Deneget officia, & monumenta sacrata futuris? Igitur exæquans præclari coepta laboris, Altæ mentis opus, documentaque maxima laudum Aggreditur mandatque suis memorabile chartis Quidquid nostra tulit Tellus sub Rege PHILIPPO Quidquid & à primâ nascentis origine juris Obtigit Hesperij Patriæ, Laribusque paternis: Donec ad excussum jure & victricibus armis Gens properat pertæsa jugum crudelis Iberi, Belgica, nec sceptris se vult submittere Regis Perjuri de more suo. Fidusque recenset, Quæ fuerint tanti nobis cunabula belli, Qui dubij fluctus, & quæ d scriu ina, cum post Invidiam factura a'ijs, nos pilea sanctæ Libertatis apex ursit, timidosque coëgit Omnia dura pati, jugulisque admittere ferrum, Sospite pro Patriâ, quam Regem ferre Tyrannum. Et medias Syrtes, inter mediasque Charybdes, Insontem dubijs patriam committere bellis: Cum quidquid præstare potest, vel publicus horror, Vel suadet commune malum, tentavimus omnes, Quos Patriæ conjunxit amor, conjunxit iniquis Religio vexata motis, expulsaque Terris, Quin & ab Hesperio pessundata Jura PHILIPPO: Indociles tam dura pati, sed vivere ferro, Et pariter didicisse mori, quam templa, focosque, Nostraque perjuris committere rostra PHILIPPIS, Scilicet atroci vapulavit Belgica Monstro, Tutoris vim passa sui, perpessaque sævi ALBANI furias Ducis; atque experta nefandis Corpora supplicijs devota, & millia ferro Carnificum demissa neci, fœdaraque slupris Barbaricis sacra, & stagnantes sanguine rivos, Et prædâ invalidos agros, & cœdibus urbes Exhaustas, raptasque nurus, socrusque peremtas;
units.tr: Meanwhile, by the command of the nobles, the whole of history at last claims for itself what is its due. Who would deny due service to one who asks for it justly, or sacred records to the future? Therefore, matching the beginnings of his distinguished labour, the work of a lofty mind and the greatest proofs of praise, he undertakes and commits to his pages worth remembering whatever our land has borne under King Philip, and whatever has befallen the Western fatherland and its household gods from the first origin of its nascent law. Until the people, weary of the cruel yoke of the Spaniard, hastens to cast it off by right and by victorious arms, the Belgian nation, which does not wish to submit to the sceptre of a king perjured after his own fashion. The faithful writer recounts what were the cradles of so great a war, what doubtful waves there were, and what things were to be described, when, after envy had made things, the cap of holy Liberty urged us on, and forced the timid to endure all harshness and to offer the sword to their throats, for the sake of the safety of the fatherland, which they could not bear as a tyrant king. And between the Syrtes and between Charybdis, he committed the innocent fatherland to doubtful wars. Whatever public horror can achieve, or common misfortune urge, we all attempted, all whom love of country joined together, and whom religion, harried by unjust disturbances, joined together, driven out from their lands, and even the laws of the West overthrown by Philip. Unused to enduring such hardships, but learning to live by the sword and to die together, as they had learned to entrust temples, hearths, and our rostra to the perjured Philips, the Belgian land was indeed scourged by a savage monster, having suffered the violence of its own guardian and endured the furies of the cruel Duke of Alba. Having experienced bodies devoted to unspeakable tortures, and thousands given over to death by the sword of executioners, sacred things defiled by barbarous outrages, streams flowing with stagnant blood, fields stripped of plunder, cities exhausted by slaughter, daughters-in-law seized and mothers-in-law slain.

units.la: Et dulces mixto maculatas sanguine Matres Heu ! prolis, fructûsque sui: glomeratáque tandem Funera funeribus densis, bonaque omnia tanquam, Ut fera diluvies solet, uno mersa profundo. Donec fata viam faciunt, & gnava Potentum Sedulitas exosa scelus, furiasque Philippi, Asseruit belloque Lares, Mavortiaque arma Strinxit, & incolumem spretâ defendere vitâ Ausa fuit Patriam, victricia signa per orbem Gestans, & veteri sub Libertate triumphans Marani contra rabiem, dum vulnere multo Pressus, dejurata sibi sua nomina sentit Et sceptra, oppositis jam fractus viribus Hostis.
units.tr: And mothers, stained with mingled blood, alas, of their offspring and their own fruit; and funerals piled upon funerals in dense heaps, and all goods, as a savage flood is wont to do, submerged in one deep abyss. Until the fates made a way, and the diligent zeal of the powerful, hateful to crime and to the furies of Philip, asserted the household gods by war, drew the weapons of Mars, and dared to defend the fatherland, its life unharmed and disregarding its own, bearing victorious standards throughout the world and triumphing in its ancient Liberty against the raging Maranus, while, pressed by many wounds, the enemy, now broken by opposing forces, feels that the names and sceptres sworn to him are his own.

units.la: Hæc pandit nunc cura Viri suprema, laborum Materiem complexa sinu, dum dura retexit Tempora, fortunasque Ducum; dum pace vel armis Inclyta perpetuis Annalibus acta revolvit.
units.tr: This is what the supreme care of the man now sets forth, having embraced the matter of his labours in his bosom, while he unfolds the hard times and the fortunes of the leaders, while he rehearses in the perpetual annals the famous deeds done in peace or in arms.

units.la: Quod superest, ô Vos Proceres, Patriaéq; Parentes, Magnanimi Heroës, quos inter maximus arte Consiliisque valens summo Scheltinga favore Assidet, & rerum fidus Secreta gubernat. Cernite, quàm vestris aspirent Numina factis: Cernite, quam Patriam nunc prospera cuncta sequantur, Excusso cervice jugo, pulsisque Philippis: Tutaque præsidio Libertas Patria vestro Extolli laetetur ovans: spectate labores Preclaros meritis, animisque, ut & auguror, æquis Accipite hæc vestris Monumenta sacrata trophæis: Hoc Opus Historiæ Frisicæ, quod marmora vincet, Mansurum sine fine bonum, cui nulla nocebunt, Aut nocitura suos evertent tempora leges.
units.tr: As for what remains, O you nobles and fathers of the fatherland, magnanimous heroes, among whom Scheltinga, most powerful in skill and counsel, sits in highest favour and faithfully governs the secrets of affairs, behold how the divine powers favour your deeds. Behold how all prosperous things follow our fatherland now that the yoke has been shaken from its neck and the Philips driven out. Liberty, safe under your protection, rejoices to be exalted in triumph. Regard the labours, distinguished by their merits, and, as I augur, accept with fair minds these sacred monuments, placed among your trophies: this work of Frisian history, which will outlast marble, a good that will endure without end, which no times will harm, or whose laws, though harmful in the future, will overturn its own.

units.la: IOH. PHOCYLIDES HOLWARDA.
units.tr: IOH. PHOCYLIDES HOLWARDA.

units.la: ALLOQUIUM AD Authorem Celeberrimum.
units.tr: ADDRESS TO THE MOST CELEBRATED AUTHOR.

units.la: SÆclo, Cognate, dignus hoc Scripto fugis, Ereptus Orbi, quinque bis ævi videns: Peracta Lustra, & annos novem, sic homo est Inane nomen, fumus, aura, vanitas: Solâ superstes mente, quæ cœlum tenet.
units.tr: Kinsman of the age, worthy of this writing, you have fled, snatched from the world, having seen five times two spans of life, the lustra completed and nine years more. Thus man is an empty name, smoke, breath, vanity, surviving only in the mind, which holds heaven.

units.la: L. M. P.
units.tr: Gladly and deservedly set up (L. M. P.).

units.la: V. REVIUS, Med. D.
units.tr: V. REVIUS, Doctor of Medicine.

units.la: Nempe tantillum est homo.
units.tr: Indeed, man is but a tiny thing.

units.la: IN OBITUM CLARISSIMI per terrarum orbem VIRI, D. PIERII WINSEMII, Frisiæ Historiographi, & in Patriâ Academiâ Historiarum & Eloquentiæ Professoris;
units.tr: IN MEMORY OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN KNOWN THROUGHOUT THE WORLD, MR PIER WINSEMIUS, HISTORIOGRAPHER OF FRIESLAND AND PROFESSOR OF HISTORY AND ELOQUENCE IN THE NATIVE ACADEMY

units.la: Ad Amplissimos D. D. Curatores.
units.tr: To the Most Illustrious Curators

units.la: EHEU! WINSEMII referunt mala nuncia mortem: Nuncia Pieridum collachrimanda Choro. Huius fata Viri Musarum pulpita plorant: Et Themis in pullo conspicienda gemit. Quis nunc Eloquijs Franicas mulcebit Athenas? Pulsabit doctam quis, velut ille, lyram? WINSEMII occubuit facilis cum funere Vates; Et Gravis Orator conditur in tumulo. Quàm mirum! semper quo vindice Frisia vivet; Vindictam mortis WINSEMIUS patitur. Vos, quèis Franagrij committa est cura Lycæi Insignes quatuor Palladis arte Viri; Hoc agite! ut viduas scandat dignissimus Arces Et par WINSEMIO plectra diserta sonet. Sit procul hinc Favor, & procul hinc eat improba Pestis Ambitio, laurum sola Minerva ferat. Eia agite! ut stent firma Dei fundamina magni, Et solitis habitet Patria Musa locis. Non melius ferro potuisti excindere regnum Obversum Christo cor Iuliane fovens; Otia quàm sacris indicere signia ludis, Legibus & Patrium dividuare forum. Libertas, sincera Fides, & gloria Christi, Heie fecit sacras ædificare Domus: Tolle Scholas, expelle Viros, & supprime Leges: Nos premet antiquo Vultur Iberque jugo.
units.tr: Alas! Messages of ill tidings report the death of Winsemius, a messenger to be mourned by the choir of the Muses. The fates of this man are lamented by the Muses' stage, and Themis groans, to be seen in mourning dress. Who now will soothe Franeker's Athens with eloquence? Who, like that man, will strike the learned lyre? Winsemius, a poet of easy grace, has fallen with his death, and the grave orator is laid in his tomb. How strange! Frisia will always live under his protection, yet Winsemius suffers the vengeance of death. You, to whom the care of the Franeker Lyceum has been entrusted, four men distinguished in the art of Pallas, take heed! Let the most worthy man climb the widowed citadels, and let an eloquent lyre sound equal to Winsemius. Let favour stay far away, and let shameless ambition, that plague, depart far from here, so that Minerva alone may bear the laurel. Come, then! Let the firm foundations of great God stand, and let the Fatherland's Muse dwell in her accustomed places. You could not have destroyed the kingdom by the sword better, Julian, who cherished a heart hostile to Christ; nor could you have proclaimed idleness by sacred games and divided the national forum by laws. Liberty, sincere faith, and the glory of Christ, the man made sacred houses to be built. Remove the schools, expel the men, and suppress the laws: the vulture and the Spaniard will press us under the old yoke.

units.la: HÆ C olim, scripsisque tuo Vir Clare sepulchro, Cum mea sub salsis Musa natabat aquis. Integer à luctu quia nunc elabitur annus, NEUHUSIUS leto succinet ore melos. Plaudite Pierij, Parnassi Numina collis! Plaudite Castalij turba novena fori! Plaudite! PIERIUS mundani luminis ofor Hospes in Aonidum maluit esse Choro; Atque ibi divino vobiscum nectare pasci, Et facilem tecum, Clio, sonare Lyram;
units.tr: Once, illustrious man, I wrote these lines for your tomb, when my Muse was swimming in salt waters. Because the year is now passing without mourning, Neuhusius will sing a song with a voice of grief. Applaud, Pierian divinities of Parnassus' hill! Applaud, ninefold company of the Castalian forum! Applaud! Pierius, a guest of the worldly light, preferred to be in the choir of the Aonian Muses, and there to feed with you on divine nectar, and, Clio, to sound with you the easy lyre;

units.la: Longius ac triste vita servare figuram, Et curis plenos continuare dies.
units.tr: to preserve a long and sad figure of life, and to continue days full of cares.

units.la: Felix WINSEMI! qui post tua terga relinquis, Et rides quae nos tristia fata premunt.
units.tr: Happy Winsemius, who leave behind your back, and laugh at the sad fates that press upon us.

units.la: Felix WINSEMI! cui nunc meliore theatro Quam FRISIAE rostris scribitur Historia.
units.tr: Happy Winsemius, whose History is now written in a better theatre than the rostra of Friesland.

units.la: Scilicet hoc nostro vix tutum est scribere saclo! Difficile est omni posse placere viro.
units.tr: Surely it is scarcely safe to write in our age! It is hard to please every man.

units.la: Ille novus, plebi sua qui natalia debet, Vult sibi prisca dari nomina Nobilium.
units.tr: That new man, who owes his birth to the common people, wishes the ancient names of nobles to be given to himself.

units.la: Si Proavum narras quae sors, quae vita manebat, Non moritura tuas obsidet ira fores.
units.tr: If you tell of his ancestor, what fate and what life awaited him, an anger that will not die will besiege your doors.

units.la: Iste, malis quaerit conscendere culmen honoris Artibus, Ambitio sola cui pretium.
units.tr: That man seeks to climb the summit of honour by evil arts, for whom ambition alone is the prize.

units.la: In laudes te accinge viri, sit dignior, ex quo Et Patrum & Patriae pendeat una Salus.
units.tr: Gird yourself to praise men, so that the one on whom the safety of both the Fathers and the Fatherland depends may be more worthy.

units.la: Illum si contra Calami distrinxeris arma, En! suprema leves sors jacet ante pedes.
units.tr: If you draw the sword of the pen against him, behold! Lightly regarded, the last lot lies before your feet.

units.la: Frisonis referes quae prima potentia Regis? Quasve sibi tenuit Stauria divitias?
units.tr: Of the Frisian: What first power of the king will you relate? Or what riches did Stavoren hold?

units.la: Vel faciles scribes Radbodi ad Tartara gressus? Inveniet nusquam pagina vestra fidem.
units.tr: Or will you write of Radbod's easy steps into Tartarus? Your page will nowhere find belief.

units.la: Si Satyris, tecto sub nomine, crimina culpes, Te vocat in crimen conscius ipse sibi.
units.tr: If you accuse crimes under a hidden name in satires, the conscience of him calls you to a charge.

units.la: Disce, quod obsequium dubios tibi reddat amicos. Scribere vera, nocet: scribere falsa, nefas.
units.tr: Learn that obsequiousness makes doubtful friends for you. To write the truth harms; to write falsehoods is wicked.

units.la: Felix WINSEMI terrarum exempte periclis! Felix praeteritis cui vacat urna malis!
units.tr: Happy Winsemius, freed from the dangers of the world! Happy the urn that is free of past evils!

units.la: Fallor? an in vestros recidit labor iste lacertos KOLDE, Leoninae cui data cura Scholae?
units.tr: Am I mistaken, or does this labour fall upon your shoulders, Kolde, to whom the care of the Leonine School has been given?

units.la: Ille sequere ingenio rutilantem lampada Phoebi: WINSEMIUS, fama non moriente, praeit.
units.tr: You, follow the shining lamp of Phoebus with your genius: Winsemius goes before, with a fame that does not die.

units.la: Invida WINSEMIO quae scribere Fata negarunt, Absolvat pensum KOLDIUS Historiae:
units.tr: What the envious fates denied to Winsemius in writing, let Koldius complete as the task of History:

units.la: Historijs comprende, potens qui Roma ruinam Sentiat & Meretrix de Babylone cadat.
units.tr: Comprehend in histories how powerful Rome feels its ruin and how the harlot falls from Babylon.

units.la: Qui Grex Christiadum, justis satiata Triumphis, Sub Pace in toto praedicet orbe Deum.
units.tr: Let the flock of Christians, sated with just triumphs, proclaim God under peace throughout the whole world.

units.la: Haec sunt vota tui quondam divina Parentis, Quae toties templis sunt memorata sacris;
units.tr: These are the prayers of your divine parent long ago, which have so often been recalled in sacred temples;

units.la: Illa eadem a nostro praedicta & scripta Parente, Cujus in aeternum non morietur Opus.
units.tr: the same that were foretold and written by our parent, whose work will never die.

units.la: Sic tibi KOLDE, novos una gratamur Honores: Et flemus magni funera WINSEMII.
units.tr: So, Kolde, we together welcome new honours for you, and we weep for the funeral of the great Winsemius.

units.la: HENR. NEUHUSIUS.
units.tr: HENR. NEUHUSIUS.

units.la: Curiae Frisiae Advocatus.
units.tr: Advocate of the Court of Friesland.

units.la: LECTORI.
units.tr: To the Reader.

units.la: BENEVOLUS Lector, ut vitia Typographica pro benevolentiâ suâ corrigat, rogat Typographus: Irrepsere ob mortem Authoris, absentiam Correctoris & hyemis injuriam, cum Corrector quandoque in loco non esset.
units.tr: The printer asks the kindly reader to correct the typographical errors out of his goodwill. They crept in because of the author's death, the corrector's absence, and the harm done by winter, since at times there was no corrector on the spot.

units.la: VALE
units.tr: Farewell.

units.la: PIERIVS WINSEMIVS, I.C. Illustr. Ordinum Frisiae Historiogr. ac Eloquent. & Historiar. Professor Celeberrimus.
units.tr: Pierius Winsemius, Doctor of Law, Historiographer of the Illustrious Orders of Friesland, Professor of Eloquence and History, most distinguished.

units.la: Ætat. Suae 58. Obiit cIↄ IↄCXLIV.
units.tr: In the 58th year of his age. He died in 1644.

units.la: I. Suydenhoef Sculp.
units.tr: I. Suydenhoef engraved.

units.la: C. Fontanus excud.
units.tr: C. Fontanus printed.

units.la: Posteritas venerare Virum qui hoc cingitur ære:
units.tr: Posterity, venerate the man whom this bronze encloses:

units.la: Ingenium & Virtus hoc meruere Viri.
units.tr: Genius and virtue earned this man.

units.la: Ille fuit Doctus, Facilis, Gravis, atqʼ Disertus,
units.tr: He was learned, easy, grave, and eloquent,

units.la: Orator, Vates, Doctor, et Historicus.
units.tr: An orator, poet, teacher, and historian.

units.la: Qualibet Ars toto vix uni addiscitur ævo:
units.tr: Scarcely can any art be learned by one man in a whole lifetime:

units.la: WINSEMIUS quatuor prævalet Ingeniis.
units.tr: Winsemius excels with four talents.

units.la: Os, Oculi, Facies, Sensus, Miracula ponunt:
units.tr: Mouth, eyes, face, and senses: the marvels proclaim him.

units.la: Fama per Historias non moritura viget.
units.tr: Through his histories his fame lives on, not doomed to die.

units.la: H. NEVHVSIVS. Fris. Advoc.
units.tr: H. Nevhusius, Advocate of Friesland.

units.la: P. WINSEMII Historiarum LIBER PRIMUS.
units.tr: The First Book of P. Winsemius' Histories

units.la: MORTE Maximiliani Burani Cæsarei per Frisiam Præfecti, qui ingenti Provinciæ luctu Brux-ellis anginâ extinctus erat, suffectus à Carolo Cæsare Joannes Lignæus Arembergiæ Comes. Cuius tristem ac turbulentam Præfecturam sævissima bellorum per Belgicam tempestas, mutatioq; civilium animorum subsecuta. Postquam enim Carolo Cæsari gravis senecta, & animus tranquillitatis avidus tædia regni, & fluitantium per Europam bellorum peperere, destinatumq; Philippo filio (quem Anno M. D. XXVII. XII. Kalend. Jun. ex Isabella Emanuelis Lusitaniæ Regis filiâ Carolus Cæsar susceperat) Belgarum Imperium fuit, tum, velut infausto sydere, commoti animi præsagio eventuræ calamitatis fluctuavere. Iudicantibus, ut in tali statu fieri solet, plerisque, Philippum Hispaniæ & circumjacentium Regnorum Principem, à suo cœlo aut educatione alium, vel potentiâ gravem fore. Alij verò novo in successore mitissimam rerum sortem & conditionem intuebantur, validis tum adhuc patrijs legibus, nec adultâ; ut solent; potentiâ infractis. Ita promiscuè Belgarum gentem spes; metusque agitabant, donec ille terrarum gentiumque victor, terror Europæ, in Asiâ, Africâq;, dominator Carolus Cæsar conventu omnium Belgicæ Ordinum ad IIX. Kalend. Novemb. Bruxellis indicto fidem faceret placituri in filio Imperij. Se Fato, ac divini numinis ope ad fastigia rerum evectum, sed nunc gravem annis, neque oblitum humanæ sortis melioribus desiderijs agitari. Continuam sibi invaletudinem, nec parem molestijs senectam, esse aliquid in principe animo, quod post decurrentis ævi legem æterna spectet, ad quæ perveniri non nisi per tranquillitatem solitariæ, & nihil molestum versantis vitæ posset. Itaq; validis annis plurima bellorum per Europam, Asiam, atq; Africam gessisse, ultra Herculis sui columnas, & mare Oceanum, velut destinatum magnitudini suæ gyrum circumacta, quorum potissima subsidia à Belgicâ gente accepisset. Inde propensum sui in Provincias animum, quibus si satisfactum non esset, ut molestum lubricumque tam multa regendi onus est, darent patres veniam imbecillitati suæ, spemq; in Philippo filio Angliæ regë (id enim quod post mortem Mariæ Portugallicæ, Mariam Anglorum Reginam matrimonio teneret addi placuit) ponerent.
units.tr: On the death of Maximilian of Buren, the emperor's prefect in Friesland, who had died of quinsy at Brussels to the great grief of the province, Charles Caesar appointed in his place John Lignaeus, Count of Aremberg. His sad and turbulent prefecture was followed by the most savage storm of wars across Belgium and a change in the minds of the citizens. For when heavy old age, a spirit longing for tranquillity, and weariness of rule and of the wars drifting through Europe had weighed on Charles Caesar, and the rule of the Belgians had been destined for his son Philip (whom Charles Caesar had begotten on 21 May 1527 by Isabella, daughter of Emanuel, King of Portugal), then the minds of men, as if under an unlucky star, wavered in foreboding of the calamity to come. Most people, as is usual in such a situation, judged that Philip, Prince of Spain and of the surrounding kingdoms, would be a man of a character different from his upbringing and his heaven, or that he would be heavy in power. Others looked to the new successor and expected the mildest fortune and condition of affairs, since the native laws were still strong and his power, as usual, was not yet full-grown and unbroken. Thus hope and fear stirred the Belgian people alike, until that conqueror of lands and peoples, terror of Europe, and master of Asia and Africa, Charles Caesar, summoned a meeting of all the orders of Belgium at Brussels on 24 October, to make it plain that he would hand over the empire to his son. He said that he had been raised by fate and by the aid of the divine power to the heights of affairs, but that now, heavy with years, he was not forgetful of human destiny and was moved by better desires. A continual ill health, and an old age not equal to its burdens, had set in his princely mind a concern which looked beyond the law of the passing age to eternity, a goal that could be reached only through the tranquillity of a solitary life free of all troubles. So, in his stronger years, he had waged many wars through Europe, Asia and Africa, beyond the pillars of his Hercules and the Ocean sea, turning himself around a circuit as if it had been set for his greatness, and in these undertakings he had received his chief support from the Belgian people. Hence his inclination towards the provinces; if they were not satisfied, the burden of ruling so many is as irksome and slippery as it is. Let the fathers, he said, grant pardon to his weakness and place their hope in Philip his son, king of England (for it had been decided that the title of King of England should be added, since he held Mary, Queen of the English, in marriage after the death of Mary of Portugal).

units.la: Arent, beneficia fidemque Belgici populi, & si quæ sint, paterni principatus deliquia novis virtutibus pensaturo. Quare Cæsar filium monere moderati & clementis Imperij, populumque magnis in Burgundicam Austriamque domum meritis illustrem, è præscripto patriarum legum, ac avitæ libertatis regat. Fore alias, ut sæviore dominatu fidâ, sed bellaci gente commotâ intestinæ in eum partes exsurgant, cum ipsis civilium bellorum initijs terminum occasumque suæ potentiæ habiturum. Quibus stabiliendis valida cani atque augusti vultus majestas erat. Tum Cæsari Gulielmi Nassovij Principis Aurantij humeris innixo lacrymæ fluxerunt, ut creditum fuit, miseratione, aut reverentiâ coëuntium Ordinum, vel paterni erga Belgicam gentem, & natales sibi cunas (Gandæ enim Flandrorum natus erat) affectus argumenta. Dein precatus Deum prospera sibi, & successori solio excessit, filiumque in eo collocavit tantarum rerum vivo patre hæredem. Præter Galliam enim Belgicam, quam Oceanus ingens Rhenique flumen, tum Sequanæ fontes, & Vogesi juga claudunt, regna mox Hispaniarum ac Siciliæ, noviterque repertus Indiarum orbis Philippo accessere, translato quoque postmodum, (ne quid animus Caroli mortale curaret) in Ferdinandum fratrem majoris Germaniæ Imperio. Ita omne Burgundicæ domus patrimonium, quod occasu, & sterilitate principum familiarum in Philippo Bono, post Carolo Audace coaluerat, à morte Mariæ Charlesiæ, quæ Maximiliano Frederici III. Imperatoris filio nupserat, in Philippum Austrium, ac post Carolum Cæsarem, & Philippum filium justâ successione devolutum est. Qui, etsi robustæ ætatis Princeps, veniam imbecillitati orare, ac testari de affectu. Contra Ordines prompta obsequia polliceri, Cæsarique Carolo imprimis grates agere, quod tot nationum in successore filio prospexisset incolumitati. Ut, quia Cæsar ampli & diu gesti Imperij pertædus quieto otio se dare, ac experiri privatæ vitæ felicitatem constituisset, Provinciæ Belgicæ conceptam ex abitu Cæsaris ægritudinem successione filij, tanquam justo solatio, levarent. Id sibi gravissimi mœroris non leve remedium, &, si pericula post ingruant, grande munimentum fore. Se interim daturos operam, ut regiæ Majestatis splendor justa sui Principatus subsidia habeat, sentiatque se populum regere Principis sui reverentem. Hæc à Legatis Provinciarum, quæ jam ante Burgundicæ domui paruerant, pulchrâ cum obtestatione fidei, ac integritatis Carolo coram Philippoque dicebantur. Quare Maria gubernatrix Philippo nepote principatum adepto Præfecturâ Provinciarum se abdicavit, Emanuelemque Philibertum Sebaudum Philippi consobrinum successorem accepit. Hoc verò solummodò restabat, ut Transrhenana Frisiorum ora, (quam Maximilianus Austrius Cæsar Frisicæ libertatis æmulus pro jure, ut ferebat, Imperij, etsi verius prolatandæ Burgundicæ domus potentiæ, in Albertum Saxonem, Saxo in Carolum cessione transtulerat) eodem Carolo Cæsare adhuc rerum potiunte, & vergentibus sensim ejusdem annis, Burgundicis ditionibus in Philippo filio jungeretur. Itaque Carolus rerum humanarum inconstantiam, & fortunæ (quæ consilia eius per Germaniam confuderat) mutabiles, & incertas vices, tum brevitatem mortalis ævi expendens Anno M. D. XLIX. de ma-
units.tr: Let them, he said, make up with new virtues for the benefits and the loyalty of the Belgian people and for whatever lapses his father's rule may have shown. Therefore let the Caesar advise his son to rule with a moderate and merciful government, and to govern the people, illustrious for their great services to the house of Burgundy and Austria, according to the prescription of the native laws and ancestral liberty. Otherwise, he said, if he ruled more harshly, the intestine factions would rise against him among a people faithful yet warlike, and with the very beginnings of civil wars his power would meet its end and fall. To secure these things, the majesty of the aged and august countenance was a strong support. Then, leaning on the shoulders of William of Nassau, Prince of Orange, Charles shed tears, as was believed, out of pity or reverence for the assembled orders, and as evidence of his paternal affection for the Belgian people and for the cradle of his birth (for he had been born at Ghent in Flanders). Then, having prayed God for prosperity for himself and his successor, he withdrew from the throne and placed his son in it, the heir of great affairs while his father was still alive. For besides Gaul-Belgium, which the great ocean, the Rhine river, the sources of the Seine and the ridges of the Vosges enclose, the kingdoms of Spain and Sicily and the newly discovered world of the Indies soon came to Philip; and afterwards, lest Charles's mind should be troubled by anything mortal, the imperial power over greater Germany was transferred to his brother Ferdinand. Thus the whole patrimony of the house of Burgundy, which had grown together through the failure and barrenness of princely families, in Philip the Good and afterwards in Charles the Bold, passed by lawful succession, after the death of Mary of Burgundy, who had married Maximilian, son of the Emperor Frederick III, to Philip of Austria, and then to Charles Caesar and his son Philip. Although Philip was a prince in the vigour of his age, he prayed for pardon for his weakness, and he bore witness to his good will. On the other side, the orders promised ready obedience and especially gave thanks to Charles Caesar, because he had provided for the safety of so many nations by a son as successor. And so, since the Caesar, weary of a great and long-held empire, had resolved to give himself to a quiet leisure and to try the happiness of a private life, the provinces of Belgium should lighten the sorrow they had conceived at the Caesar's departure by the succession of his son, as by a lawful consolation. This, they said, would be a not slight remedy for their most grievous sorrow and, should dangers arise afterwards, a great defence. Meanwhile they would take care that the splendour of the royal majesty should have just support for its princely rule, and that it should feel that it was ruling a people reverent towards its prince. These things were spoken before Charles and Philip by the envoys of the provinces, which had already before obeyed the house of Burgundy, with a fine solemn oath of faith and integrity. Therefore Mary, the governess, when Philip her nephew had gained the principate, resigned the prefecture of the provinces, and received as her successor Emanuel Philibert of Savoy, a cousin of Philip. Only this remained, that the Frisian coast beyond the Rhine (which Maximilian of Austria, Caesar and rival of Frisian liberty, had transferred to Albert of Saxony, on the pretext, as he put it, of the right of the empire, though more truly to extend the power of the house of Burgundy, and Albert of Saxony had transferred it to Charles), while Charles Caesar was still in control of affairs and his years were gradually waning, should be joined to Philip his son's Burgundian dominions. And so Charles, weighing the inconstancy of human affairs, the changeable and uncertain turns of fortune (which had thrown his plans into confusion in Germany), and the brevity of mortal life, in the year 1549 began to plan the speedy inauguration of his son Philip in Friesland, so that, having confirmed an heir and successor, he might leave the earth, as one subject himself to the law of man, with less restlessness of mind and less care for mortal affairs. This was not a difficult or hard thing to do in those times. For not only did the greatness of so great a Caesar not allow anyone to resist his counsels, nor did the height of so imperious and lofty a power permit it; but also this helped most to carry out Charles's will and to win over the hearts of the people, that he had secured peace for his provinces for so many years by foreign arms and illustrious victories, and the people, flourishing at that time in a golden happiness of the age, enjoyed it. Therefore, when Philip the son had been proclaimed heir throughout all Belgium, and an assembly of the orders of Friesland had been convened at Leeuwarden in January 1550, Charles Caesar had caused Philip his son to be also declared heir and successor by the same orders, and had obtained documents to this effect, procured by John Lignaeus of Aremberg, prefect of Friesland and the neighbouring territories:

units.la: Carolus imperium transfert in filium. maturandâ Philippi filij per Frisiam inauguratione cogitaverat, ac ut ipse humanæ legi obnoxius, confirmato hærede, & successore, minore mentis inquietudine & mortalium rerum curâ terris excederet. Quod factu ijs temporibus arduum, ac difficile non erat. Præterquam enim, quod tanti Cæsaris consilijs refragari, tam Imperiosæ, & sublimis potentiæ fastigium non sinebat, ita hoc maxime ad exequendam Caroli voluntatem, & concilianda populi ingenia faciebat, quod tot annorum pacem suis Provincijs per externa arma, & illustres victorias peperisset, aureaque velut temporum felicitate florentissimus etiam tum populus uteretur. Quare per omnem Belgicam Philippo filio hæredè proclamato, conventuque Ordinum Frisiæ Ianuario mense Anno MDL. Leovardiæ coacto, Carolus Cæsar Philippum quoque filium hæredem ac successorem ab ijsdem Ordinibus renunciari fecerat, tabulasq; huiusmodi, procurante Ioanne Lignæo Arembergio, Frisiæ vicinarumque ditionum Præfecto, hac de re impetraverat:
units.tr: Charles transfers the empire to his son. For this matter he had intended to hasten the inauguration of his son Philip throughout Friesland, so that, with the heir and successor confirmed, he might leave the earth with less mental disquiet and less care for mortal affairs, as one himself subject to the human law. This was not difficult or hard to accomplish in those times. For not only did it not allow anyone to oppose the plans of so great a Caesar, nor did the summit of so imperious and lofty a power permit it, but this too helped most to carry out Charles's will and to win over the minds of the people: that for so many years he had secured peace for his provinces through foreign arms and illustrious victories, and the people, most flourishing at that time, enjoyed a golden happiness of the age. Therefore, when Philip the son had been proclaimed heir throughout all Belgium, and an assembly of the orders of Friesland had been held at Leeuwarden in January 1550, Charles Caesar had caused Philip his son also to be declared heir and successor by those same orders, and had obtained documents on this matter, procured by John Lignaeus of Aremberg, prefect of Friesland and the neighbouring territories:

Valerius Herama Iureconsultus, & Pastor Novolandius, Abbæus Pastor Tyallehusius, Ulricus Oenema, Loingius, Elingus Hora-tius pro Goingiis, Regnerus Hotsemius, Iustus Emius, Auco Heronius, pro Wimbritseriis; Pibo Annius, & Gosuinus Haionius pro Bolsuerdiis, Ielmerus Ielmerius, pro Hemclumolpherdÿs; Saco Wibrandius, & Ultius Lollius, pro Worcumanis; Titus Suffridæus pro Eloftanis; Kempo Donia, Hector Hemmema, Haringus Glinzius pro Menaldumanis; Wibrandus Sellingwirtius pro Hindelopiis, omnes Westergoi; Hommius Haersma, pro Slotanis; Hubertus Schofius Commendator Nessanus, pro me & Cœnobio Aelsumano, Foc-co Iskius Bornensis, Franciscus Tiepkonius, Sicco Pierius, Epo Femmius, pro Haskeriis quinque pagicis; Feddo Pastor Oelanus, Gabinius Andringa, Ferco Intiæus, & Annas Tiarckenius pro Domewerstalliis; Idsardus Pastor Echtnanus, Christianus Pierius; Annas Emius, & Hanco Meiczius pro Lem-steranis quinque pagicis; Vibius Pastor Wikelius, Ioannes Ietsomius, Rinco Sipkonius, Gasparus Hermanni pro Gasterlandis; Ioannes Luydens Pastor Olbercopius; Ioannes Franck, Prætor, & Christianus Lutgenius pro Stellingu-erfiis Orientalibus; Wigerus Pastor Idsartius, Lubbertus Lyclesius Prætor; Folckerus Everardus, & Andreas Sinæus pro Stellinguerfiis Occidentalibus; Eylardus Tyssenius, & Annas Poppius pro Scoterlandis; Gerbrandus Mintianus Prætor, Hanco Nicolaus, & Tiebbo Sanmius pro Enguerdiis, Douwo Pastor Leppenbusanus, Focco Teius Prætor, & Vitus Brunius pro Opsteranis. Notum facimus: Quandoquidem Frisiæ Ordinibus de voluntate Caroli Cæsaris Do-mini nostri Clementissimi, placuit Illustrissimum Philippum Principem Hispa-niarum, utriusque Siciliæ, & Hierosolymæ, Archiducem Austriæ, Ducem Burgundiæ & Brabantiæ, Comitem Habspurgi, Flandriæ, Hollandiæ, Dominum Frisiæ, unicum Cæsareæ Majestatis filium, ut verum heredem declarare, ac pro eo, à morte Caroli Patris, in successorem recipiendo fidem juramentumque interponere, ita nos prædicto nomine & de mandato Ordinum No-bili viro Ioanni Lignæo Comiti Arembergio, Equiti Aurei Velleris, & Cæsareæ Majestatis per Frisiam, Trans-Isulaniam & Groningam Præfecto, jus-jurandum fecimus hoc modo:
units.tr: WE, Gerardus Wittemius, prelate of the Fosuerdienses, Gerardus of Zutphen, prelate of the Clare-campenses, Gerardus Duingelius, Gerco of the monastery, Henricus Smeinsius of Hortus Mariae, Henricus of Zutphen, prelate of the Doccomienses; Serapius Hania, Doctor of Laws, and Albertus Franciscus, consuls and delegates of the Leovardienses; Petrus Dekema, knight, for the Ielsumani; Botto Wibrandius for the Corniumani, Feico Tiallengius for the Britsumii, Gisbertus Gerritius for the Stenani, Haringus Heringa for the Fintzumani and Hiumani, Goffo Douma and Martinus Ioannis for the Husumani and the Hempenii, Hero Doconius for the Goutumani, Geroldus Feytzma, Douwo the priest, and Igo Petraeus for the Wirdumani, Benedictus Renicius for the Leccumani, Ioannes Buygerius for the Medumani, Haringus Sytzma, magistrate, Ernestus Goslinga, R. Feytzma, Feico Ritskenius for the Ferverdici, Olphardus Tennartius, minister, Feddo Haerda, Sibrandus Edsardius, Worperius Tyessenius, Geroldus Montzma, Worperius Peyma, Sipco Monickhusius, and Bernardus Ioannis for the Western Dongyri; Franciscus Aylva; Saco Ringia, Worperius Ropta, magistrate, Andreas, minister of Oestrum; Iouco Aebema and Ieldertus Popkonius for the Eastern Dongyri; Leo Ielgersma and Leo Harckema for the Otto-Pagici; Scipio de Meckmans, Tammo Eaus, Folkerus Buvinga, Gaius Folkertius, Tyspco Hesselius, deputy magistrate, for the Collumani; Ioannes Wopconius, magistrate, Leo, priest of Dantum, Feio Eysingha and Feio Iornsma for the Dantumani; Gosuinus Petraeus, deputy magistrate, Iouco, minister of Zuydwold, Feio Hemstra, Ado Eysingha, for the nobility; Prior of Bergum; Wopko Suffridaeus, Iuco Tennius, Briuchtus Atteius, Gailco Ielcomus, Bonno Bennenius for the Zietzerchii; Emcko Genckius, magistrate, and Arnoldus Oedzius for the Smallingi; Feddo Sixtinus Ielgersma, Hector Gerritius, Petrus Tetardus, Douwo Pibenius, and Feico Diricius, magistrates and delegates for the Idaerderani; Wibrandus Albada, minister of Rauwerd, Hector Albada, magistrate, Suffridus Regnerius for the Soelani, Sibrandoburani, Enguirdi, Ernsumani and Poppingaverii; Gerbrandus Gulielmus for Rauwerd, vicar and prebendary; Petrus Ioannis for the Deersumani; Broerius Hansonius for the new monastery; Leo Mellaeus, consul of Doccum; all of Oostergo. Ioannes Buscoducis, abbot in Hemelum; Godefridus Zuollis, prelate of Lidlum; ...nomine prose, with Cornelius, minister of Firdgum, and the monastery of Tiumarum; Gerbrandus Aysma, provost of Angium; Petrus Purmeranus, prior of Achlem; Stephanus Eaeus, cellarist of Floridum Campum, in the name of the prelate; Petrus Ruardus for Gerardus Siuckis, prior in Thabor; Iarichus Dekema and Nicolaus Hansonius, jurists, for Franeker; Iarichus Dekema, Andreas Waltinga, and Hanso Douwonius for the territory of Franeker; Horatius Fons, Wopko Albada, priests; Iulius Botnia, Petrus Walta, Sidsius Sidzii, and Iarichus Tadaeus for Baerderland; Gerardus, minister of Oosterend, Siricius Donia, magistrate, Ruardus Roorda, Gaius Petraeus for Hemmardia; Adrianus Michaelius, deputy magistrate, Ielgerus Tierkenius, Sipko Iasperius, Suffridus Tiallesius, and Hero Lollius for Barra; Adrianus Michaelius for Harlingen; Ioannes Herama, magistrate, Uldricus, minister of Ferwold, Dodo Sixtinus, Martinus Haiomius, Ruardus Feitesius, and Sibrandus Tiallengius for Wonseradeel; Epo Petraeus, Annas Feddonius, Vibius Tzommerius, and Kempo Gellius, consuls, for Sneek; Valerius Herama, jurist, and Novolandius, minister, Abbaeus, minister of Tyallehuis, Ulricus Oenema, Loingius, Elingus Horatius for Goingi; Regnerus Hotsemius, Iustus Emius, Auco Heronius for Wimbritseria; Pibo Annius and Gosuinus Haionius for Bolsuerdia; Ielmerus Ielmerius for Hemclumolpherdi; Saco Wibrandius and Ultius Lollius for Workum; Titus Suffridaeus for Eloftum; Kempo Donia, Hector Hemmema, Haringus Glinzius for Menaldum; Wibrandus Sellingwirtius for Hindeloopen, all of Westergo; Hommius Haersma for Slotum; Hubertus Schofius, commendator of Ness, for myself and the monastery of Aelsum; Focco Iskius of Born, Franciscus Tiepkonius, Sicco Pierius, Epo Femmius for the five rural districts of Haskerland; Feddo, minister of Oele, Gabinius Andringa, Ferco Intiaeus, and Annas Tiarckenius for Domwerstal; Idsardus, minister of Echtenen, Christianus Pierius; Annas Emius and Hanco Meiczius for the five rural districts of Lemsterland; Vibius, minister of Wikel, Ioannes Ietsomius, Rinco Sipkonius, Gasparus Hermanni for Gaasterland; Ioannes Luydens, minister of Olterterp; Ioannes Franck, magistrate, and Christianus Lutgenius for Eastern Stellingwerf; Wigerus, minister of Idsart, Lubbertus Lyclesius, magistrate; Folckerus Everardus and Andreas Sinaeus for Western Stellingwerf; Eylardus Tyssenius and Annas Poppius for Schoterland; Gerbrandus Mintianus, magistrate, Hanco Nicolaus, and Tiebbo Sanmius for Enkhuizen; Douwo, minister of Leppenbus, Focco Teius, magistrate, and Vitus Brunius for Opsterland. We make known: Since it has pleased the Estates of Friesland, by the will of Charles Caesar, our most gracious lord, to declare the most illustrious Philip, Prince of Spain, of both Sicilies and Jerusalem, Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy and Brabant, Count of Habsburg, Flanders and Holland, Lord of Friesland, the sole son of His Imperial Majesty, to be the true heir, and, on the death of his father Charles, to receive him as successor, pledging faith and oath, we have therefore, in the aforesaid name and by the mandate of the Estates, taken this oath to the noble Johannes Lignaeus, Count of Aremberg, Knight of the Golden Fleece, and prefect of His Imperial Majesty in Friesland, Trans-Isulania and Groningen, in this manner:

units.la: Nos Delegati Præsulum, Religiosorum, Nobilium, Oppidorum, Proprietariorumque Frisiæ, fidem facimus nos Carolo Cæsare (cui Deus longam felicemque vitam largiatur) humanis exempto Illustrissimo Duci, & Domino Phi-liplippo Principi Hispaniarum &c. Domino Frisiæ, Cæsareæ Majestatis unico filio, & hæredi, tum hæredibus, posterisque eius, ut veris hereditariisque Frisiæ Dominis fideles subditos fore, Præfectisque, Præsidibus, Senatoribus & Officialibus obsecuturos, neque facturos quidquam, quod Principi, hæredibus eius, Præfectis, Rectoribus, Præsidibus, & Officialibus, quoad jura Principis, contrarium, atque adversum sit. Pollicemur ea propter si quid tale contingat nos id vulgaturos Præfectis, Præsidi, & Senatoribus, omniaque facturos, ad quæ fideles subditi vero & hereditario Domino præstanda tenéri solent. Ita Nos Deus adjuvet, & omnes Sancti. Et quoniam jusjurandum, quod præstitimus ratum efficaxque esse volumus, ita nos prædicti rogavimus Joannem de Busco-Ducis Abbatem in Hemelum, Iarichum Dekema, Oldermannum civitatis Franequeranæ, Joannem Buygerium, Prætorem Territorij Leovardiensis, Iure-Consultos, ut sigillis, & subscriptione suâ muniant. Et nos Delegati oppidanorum potestatem fecimus Serapio Hania Iure Consulto, & Consuli civitatis Leovardiensis, suâ manu subscribendi, sigilloq; prædictæ civitatis roborandi. Quod nos Joannes de Busco-Ducis, Iarichus Dekema, Joannes Buygerius, & Serapius Hania fieri curavimus. Leovardiæ XVIII. die Januarij, Anno salutis M. D. L.
units.tr: We, the delegates of the prelates, religious, nobles, towns, and landowners of Friesland, pledge our faith that we will be faithful subjects to Charles Caesar (to whom God grant a long and happy life), released from human affairs, and to the most illustrious Duke and Lord Phi-liplippo, Prince of Spain, etc., Lord of Friesland, the sole son and heir of His Imperial Majesty, and to his heirs and descendants, as to true and hereditary lords of Friesland; and that we will obey the prefects, presidents, senators, and officials, and will do nothing that is contrary to or adverse to the prince, his heirs, the prefects, rulers, presidents, and officials, as far as the rights of the prince go. We therefore promise that if anything of this kind should happen, we will report it to the prefects, president, and senators, and will do all that faithful subjects are wont to owe to a true and hereditary lord. So help us God, and all the saints. And since we wish the oath we have taken to be valid and effective, we have asked Ioannes de Buscoducis, abbot of Hemelum, Iarichus Dekema, alderman of the city of Franeker, Ioannes Buygerius, praetor of the territory of Leeuwarden, and jurisconsults, to confirm it with their seals and signatures. And we, the delegates of the townsmen, have empowered Serapius Hania, jurisconsult and consul of the city of Leeuwarden, to subscribe with his own hand and strengthen it with the seal of the said city. This we, Ioannes de Buscoducis, Iarichus Dekema, Ioannes Buygerius, and Serapius Hania, have seen to be done. Leeuwarden, 18th day of January, in the year of salvation 1550.

units.la: Tum Philippi nomine reciprocum juramentum à Joanne Lignæo Arembergio dictum hoc modo.
units.tr: Then, in the name of Philip, the reciprocal oath was sworn by John Lignaeus Aremberg in this manner.

units.la: NOs Ioannes Lignæus Comes Arembergiæ, &c. Frisiæ, Trans-Isulaniæ, & Groningæ Præfectus, de speciali mandato Illustrissimi Philippi Principis Hispaniarum, Domini Frisiæ; Notum facimus hisce litteris; Quia Ordinibus Frisiæ visum est assentiri petitioni Caroli Cæsaris Domini nostri clementissimi & Philippum Caroli Cæsaris unicum hæredem, in futurum, hæreditarium Frisiæ Dominum & successorem, Caroli Cæsaris nuncupare, & declarare, eiusq; rei hoc die nobis ab ijsdem Ordinibus facta solemnia sunt, ita nos de mandato Principis Philippi reciprocè juramentum diximus hoc modo:
units.tr: WE, Ioannes Lignaeus, Count of Aremberg, etc., Prefect of Friesland, Trans-Isulana, and Groningen, by the special mandate of the most illustrious Philip, Prince of Spain, Lord of Friesland, make known by these letters: since the estates of Friesland have agreed to the petition of our most merciful lord Charles Caesar, and have resolved to name and declare Philip, the sole heir of Charles Caesar, the future hereditary lord and successor of Friesland, and the solemnities of this matter have today been performed for us by the same estates, we have therefore, by the mandate of Prince Philip, sworn reciprocally in this manner:

units.la: Nos Ioannes Ligmeus Comes Arembergiæ, & Eques Aurei Velleris, Præfectus generalis Cæsareæ Majestatis per Frisiam, Trans-Isulaniam, & Groningam, nomine & de speciali mandato Illustrissimi Principis Philippi Principis Hispaniarum, utriusque Siciliæ & Hierosolymæ, Archiducis Austriæ, Ducis Burgundiæ & Brabantiæ, Comitis Habspurgi, Flandriæ, & Hollandiæ, Domini Frisiæ, juramus ac fidem facimus, Illustrissimum Principem Philippum, Carolo Cæsare (cuius vitam Deus prorogare dignetur) vitâ defuncto, Frisiam ut Dominum Hæreditarium decet juste & decenter recturum, Matrem Ecclesiam, Religiosos, Viduas, Pupillos, tum Equestrem Ordinem, Dominos, Nobiles, Oppida & Agros defensurum, neque deserturum, daturumque operam ut eorum pacta, privilegia, immunitates, consuetudines & jura, primum ab Illustrissimo Saxoniæ Duce Georgio, dein Cæsarea Majestate. Anno millesimo quingentesimo decimo quinto concessa, confirmataque, integra manent, & servENTUR, omnesque subditi & incolæ Frisiæ clementer habeantur, prout ab hereditario Domino & Principe fieri æquum est. Ita nos Deus adjuvet, & omnes Sancti. Et quia hoc modo res confecta est, ita nos has litteras manu nostrâ signavimus, & nostro sigillo munimus. Datum Leovardiæ, XVIII. die Januar. Anno M. D. L.
units.tr: We, Ioannes Lignaeus, Count of Aremberg, Knight of the Golden Fleece, general prefect of His Imperial Majesty for Friesland, Trans-Isulana, and Groningen, in the name and by the special mandate of the most illustrious Prince Philip, Prince of Spain, of both Sicilies and Jerusalem, Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy and Brabant, Count of Habsburg, Flanders, and Holland, Lord of Friesland, swear and pledge that the most illustrious Prince Philip, when Charles Caesar (whose life God deign to prolong) has died, will rule Friesland justly and fittingly as a hereditary lord ought; that he will defend and not desert Mother Church, the religious, widows, orphans, the equestrian order, lords, nobles, towns, and fields; and that he will take care that their pacts, privileges, immunities, customs, and rights, first granted by the most illustrious George, Duke of Saxony, and then by His Imperial Majesty in the year 1515, and confirmed, remain whole and are kept; and that all subjects and inhabitants of Friesland are treated mercifully, as is right for a hereditary lord and prince. So help us God, and all the saints. And since the business has been concluded in this way, we have signed these letters with our hand and secured them with our seal. Given at Leeuwarden, 18th day of January, in the year 1550.

units.la: Quas tabulas ut accepto pridie Burgundicarum ditionum principatu confirmaret Philippus, evocatis ad se in atrium, quod regio ornatu instructum pellucebat, Frisiorum qui Flevum inter Lavicamque flumina colunt, Legatis, in eodem solio desedit, repetitoque paterni consilij secreto hunc in modum eos adlocutus est:
units.tr: When Philip had received the principality of the Burgundian lands, he wished to confirm these documents. He summoned to himself, into the hall, which shone with royal splendour, the envoys of the Frisians who dwell between the rivers Vlie and Lauwers. He sat down on the same throne and, resuming his father's secret counsel, addressed them in this manner:

units.la: Posteaquam Carolo Caesari patri meo certis de causis, (quarum rationes heri in Conventu omnium Belgicae Ordinum vobis etiam praesentibus exposuit) visum fuit, dimissa Principatus cura, Belgicae provincias, quas a majoribus longa traditione acceperat, in me filium transferre, ita paternae voluntati morem gessi, arduumque illud regendi onus in me recepi. Quapropter ut Principatum sumpsisse videar, qui obtestatione sanctissimi numinis firmetur, ac de libertate vestra, Patrioque jure non delibet, hac jurisjurandi formula me adstringo:
units.tr: Since it seemed good to my father, Charles Caesar, for certain reasons (the grounds of which he set out yesterday in the assembly of all the Belgian Estates, with you also present), to lay down the care of government and transfer to me, his son, the Belgian provinces which he had received from his ancestors by long tradition, I have complied with my father's wish and taken upon myself that heavy burden of ruling. Therefore, so that I may appear to have assumed the principality in a way that is confirmed by invoking the most holy Divine Majesty, and that does not detract from your liberty or paternal right, I bind myself by this form of oath:

units.la: EGO PHILIPPUS, Dei gratia Rex Angliae, Franciae, Neapolis, &c. Princeps Hispaniarum; Archidux Austriae; Dux Burgundiae, Lotharingiae, Brabantiae, Limburgi, Luxemburgi, Gelriae, & Mediolani; Comes Habspurgi, Flandriae, Artesiae, Burgundiae, Palatinus Hannoniae, Hollandiae, Zelandiae, Namurci, & Zutphaniae, Princeps Sueviae, Marchio Sacri Imperij, Dominus Frisiae, Salinarum, Mechliniae, Civitatis, Oppidorum & Territorij Trajectensis, Transisulaniae, Groningae, &c. Promitto & juro vobis Deputatis Terrarum & Oppidorum Frisiae, ab ijsdem Mandatum & Procurationem habentibus, & specialiter ad hoc authorisatis, quod facta nobis cessione per Sacratissimum Dominum & Patrem nostrum Carolum, eius nominis Quintum, Romanorum Imperatorem, de omnibus terris suis inferioris Germaniae, & nominatim Dominio Frisiae, inviolabiliter observanda, ita observari faciam omnia & singula quae mense Ianuario Anno millesimo quingentesimo quinquagesimo Comes de Aremberga Gubernator locum tenens Frisiae, ex nostro man{a}dato & nomine, cum in dicta Frisia in futurum Dominum & Principem, post dicti Domini Patris nostri decessum, reciperemur, tam generaliter quam particulariter communi terrae, Provinciae, Oppidis & Subditis eiusdem Frisiae promisit & juravit, & ad quae virtute juramenti tunc praestiti post obitum dicti Domini Patris nostri tenerer, & obligarer, cum confirmatione Privilegiorum & Tractatuum, à Ducibus Saxoniae, & Caesarea Majestate obtentorum, & quod omnia alia faciam, ad quae bonus justus Princeps ac Dominus fidelibus Subditis suis tenetur. Ita me Deus adjuvet, & omnes Sancti eius.
units.tr: I, Philip, by the grace of God King of England, France, Naples, etc.; Prince of Spain; Archduke of Austria; Duke of Burgundy, Lorraine, Brabant, Limburg, Luxemburg, Guelders and Milan; Count of Habsburg, Flanders, Artois, Burgundy; Palatine of Hainault, Holland, Zeeland, Namur and Zutphen; Prince of Swabia, Margrave of the Holy Empire, Lord of Friesland, the Salines, Mechelen, the City, Towns and Territory of Utrecht, Overijssel, Groningen, etc., promise and swear to you, the deputies of the lands and towns of Friesland, who hold a mandate and procuration from them and are specially authorised for this: that, since the cession has been made to us by our most holy lord and father Charles, the fifth of that name, Emperor of the Romans, of all his lands in Lower Germany, and particularly the lordship of Friesland, to be inviolably observed, I will cause all and each of the things to be observed which in January in the year 1550 the Count of Aremberg, governor and lieutenant of Friesland, promised and swore by our mandate and in our name, when we were received in the said Friesland as future lord and prince after the death of our said lord father. He promised and swore, both generally and particularly, to the common land, provinces, towns and subjects of the same Friesland, and to which, by virtue of the oath then taken, I would be bound and obligated after the death of our said father; with confirmation of the privileges and treaties obtained from the Dukes of Saxony and his Caesarean Majesty. And I will do all other things which a good, just prince and lord is bound to do for his faithful subjects. So help me God and all his saints.

units.la: Et quoniam Isbrandus Antistes Lidlumanus, Sixtus Dekema Equés, Ageus Albada Caesarei per Frisiam Senatores, Schelto Lyauckama, Gemma Burmania, pro Nobilitate, Tzomerus Vibenius, Oldermannus Snecensium, Iacobus Sibrandius Leovardiensium, & Regnerus Amius Bolsuerdiensium Consules, Delegati omnes Agrorum, Oppidorumque Frisiae, adstantibus Viglo Zuichemo Equite, Praeside Secreti Senatus, Reinoldo à Burmania Equite, Satrapa Coverdiensi & per Drentiam, Christophoro Sternzee, Satrapa Harlingensi, & Renico Camminga, praesente Ioanne Ligneo Equite nostri Ordinis, & Generali Frisiae, Trans-Isulanie, Groningae, & ditionis Lingae Praefecto, juse jurandum fecere hac forma:
units.tr: And since Isbrand, Bishop of Lidlum; Sixtus Dekema, knight; Ageus Albada, imperial senators throughout Friesland; Schelto Lyauckama and Gemma Burmania, for the nobility; Tzomerus Vibenius, Oldermann of Sneek; Jacob Sibrandi of Leeuwarden; and Regnerus Amius, consul of Bolsward; all the delegates of the fields and towns of Friesland, with Viglius Zuichemus, knight, president of the Secret Council, Reinold of Burmania, knight, governor of Coevorden and of Drenthe, Christopher Sternzee, governor of Harlingen, and Renicus Camminga present, and with John Ligne, knight of our order and general prefect of Friesland, Transisulania, Groningen and the district of Lingen, also present, took the oath in this form:

units.la: QVandoquidem nos Deputati & alij supra dicti, qui praesentes fuimus, Carolo Caesare clementissimo Domino nostro in Illustrissimum Philippum filium, Regem Angliae, & hereditarium Dominum ac Principem, & hic praesentem patrimonium ceterasq; Ditiones Belgicas, & Dominium Frisiae transferente, Illustrissimusq; Philippus, hereditarius Dominus noster, juramento se obstrinxit, se ea omnia quae tempore inaugurationis xviii. January M.D.L. per Arembergiae Comitem, Praefectum Frisiae, promissa & confirmata juramento sunt, tam generaliter, quam particulariter servaturum, prout Majestas regia post obitum Caroli patris tenebatur, & quidem eâ lege ac conditione ut e praescripto mandatorum nostrorum jusjurandum quoque Regiae majestati diceremus: Ita fidem facimus, & juramus nomine Agrorum ac Oppidorum Frisiae, Nos praedicto Regi fideles subditos fore, servaturosque ea omnia quae tempore Inaugurationis nos facturos promisimus, & in quae post decessum Caroli obligati eramus; Ita Deus nos adjuvet, & omnes Sancti. Propterea Nos Philippus ex Formula juramenti à Nobis praestiti confirmavimus, & confirmamus eorum privilegia, & conventiones cum Saxonia Principe & Caesarea Ma-jestate.
