units.tr: Since we deputies and the others named above, who were present, when Charles, our most merciful lord, transferred to the most illustrious Philip, his son, King of England and hereditary lord and prince, the present patrimony and the other Belgian dominions and the lordship of Friesland; and since the most illustrious Philip, our hereditary lord, has bound himself by oath to observe fully, both generally and particularly, all those things which were promised and confirmed by oath at the inauguration on 18 January 1550 by the Count of Aremberg, prefect of Friesland, just as the royal majesty was bound to do after the death of his father Charles; and indeed on this condition and law, that in accordance with the instructions of our mandates we should also give the oath to the royal majesty: so we pledge and swear, in the name of the fields and towns of Friesland, that we will be faithful subjects of the aforesaid king, and will keep all those things which we promised at the inauguration to do, and to which we were obligated after Charles's death. So God help us, and all the saints. Therefore we, Philip, on the basis of the form of oath sworn by us, have confirmed and do confirm their privileges and the agreements made by the country folk and townsmen with the Prince of Saxony and his Caesarean Majesty,

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. jestate per Agrarios Oppidanosq; initas, salvo tamen cuiusque jure. In quorum fidem, & testimonium, & ad petitionem Deputatorum has perscribi mandavimus, ac nostra manu ac Cæsareo sigillo, quo nos utimur, roboratifecimus. Datum Bruxellis xxvi. Octobris, Anno Domini millesimo, quingentesimo, quinquagesimo quinto. Subscript.
units.tr: Majesty, saving in each case the right of each party. In witness and testimony of which, and at the petition of the deputies, we have commanded these to be drawn up, and have confirmed them with our hand and with the Caesarean seal which we use. Given at Brussels, 26 October, in the year of our Lord 1555. Signed:

units.la: PHILIPPUS.
units.tr: PHILIPPUS.

units.la: Et ad mandatum Regis
units.tr: And by command of the King

units.la: D. OVERLOPE. HÆC TABULÆ.
units.tr: D. OVERLOPE. THESE DOCUMENTS.

units.la: Quæ etsi populo Frisico speciosæ viderentur, sive odio factionum; quæ ante Saxonum tempora exarserant, sive quod Caroli Cæsaris Saxonumq; memoriam innovarent, tamen sive gentis errore, aut in Philippum fiducia factum est, ut omissis aliorum Principum, qui à Francorum ætate hanc gentem nobilitaverant, tabulis, Romanorum Imperatorum diplomata vetustissimæ libertatis simulachra, & simul munimenta prætei irentur. Quæ res Philippo occasionem licentiosioris imperij, nobis fœdioris servitij, ac ultimæ rerum patientiæ dedit. Invenio in litteris secretioribus xvii. Octob. Bruxellis datis, Frisios ad Cæsarem Carolum, Bruxellis tum agentem, Renicum Cammingha; & Petrum Ruartium I C. stabiliendis patriæ suæ privilegijs tum ablegasse, impeditoq; ob instantia transferendi imperij solemnia Cæsare initos vt Bruxellis hæsisse. Magnam quoq;, præter Clivia Ducem, Episcopum Osnaburgensem, Aureique Velleris equites procerum frequentiam è Germania, Hispania & Gallia Belgica convenisse, eosq; in ipso apparatu magnam rerum mutationem ex futurâ imperij cessione formidasse. Frisios quoq;, etsi omnia præparante Viglio secreti Senatus Præsidc, tardiores in mittendis legatis fuisse, istamq; cunctationem, veluti taciti metus interpretem, siniistre ab aulicis acceptam. Traditum memoriæ est Frisiorum Legatos stantes & erectos, velut tacitâ utrinq; libertatis agnitione, Philippo Sacramentum dixisse, reliquarumque Provinciarum legatos, quas hæreditario jure Philippus tenebat, inclinato genu solemnia homagij recitavisse. Quæ ex magnâ domo & nobilissimi viri, qui actioni interfuit, ore profecta inserenda annalibus duxi, quo opera mea lecturis innotesceret, Frisiæ gentem præ cæteris magnâ libertatis prærogativâ valuisse.
units.tr: Although these documents seemed splendid to the Frisian people, whether from hatred of the factions that had blazed up before the time of the Saxons, or because they renewed the memory of Charles Caesar and of the Saxons, nevertheless, whether through an error of the nation or through trust placed in Philip, it came about that the charters of the other princes, who had ennobled this nation since the age of the Franks, were set aside, and the diplomas of the Roman emperors, images of the most ancient liberty and at the same time its safeguards, were put forward instead. This situation gave Philip the opportunity for a more licentious rule, and gave us a more foul servitude and the last degree of helplessness. I find in secret letters, dated Brussels 17 October, that the Frisians had then sent Renicus Cammingha and Petrus Ruartius, a jurist, to Charles Caesar, who was then staying at Brussels, to secure the privileges of their homeland; and that, because of the pressing preparations for the ceremony of transferring the empire, they had stayed on at Brussels to await the emperor. I also find that a large gathering of nobles had come from Germany, Spain and Belgian Gaul, besides the Duke of Cleves, the Bishop of Osnabrück and the knights of the Golden Fleece, and that they feared a great change in affairs from the future cession of the empire, even in the very preparations. The Frisians too, although Viglius, president of the secret Council, was arranging everything, were slower in sending envoys, and this hesitation, as an interpreter of silent fear, was taken unfavourably by the courtiers. It is recorded that the envoys of the Frisians, standing upright and with heads raised, as if by a silent acknowledgement of liberty on both sides, took the oath to Philip, while the envoys of the other provinces, which Philip held by hereditary right, bent the knee and recited the solemn formula of homage. I have thought fit to insert these facts in my annals, which came from the lips of a great house and of a most noble man who was present at the act, so that it may become known to my readers, through my work, that the Frisian nation was, beyond the others, strong in its great prerogative of liberty.

units.la: Itaq; peractis solemnibus, Frisiæq; Ditionibus è jure tabularum conventionumque, quas memoravi, in Philippum à Carolo Cæsare devolutis, Legati in Frisiam regressi. Tum Novembri mense Senatus per Frisiam regius (qui à Carolo Cæsare dicundi administrandiq; juris potestatem acceperat) à Philippo confirmatus, adactique ad sacramentum novi Principis Hippolytus Perfinius, Præses, Iacobus Roussellius, Petrus Dekama Eques, Upco Burmania, Ioannes Rommartius, Iulius Gelius Fisci Regii Procurator, Adrianus Vastartius, Antonius Lavailius, Alexius Gelius, Sixtus Dekama Eques, Aggæus Albada, & Valerius Ockingha Iure-Consulti, cum Godefrido Duvenæo Graphiario. Post, quod Caroli Principis ætate divisa in factiones, & non nisi Saxonum, Geldri, ac Burgundi, armis fatigata gens perfecerat, Magistratus quoque reliqui juf-jurandum homagij Philippo dixere, Philippusq; ut ante Anno M. D. L. filius ac hæres Caroli, ita hoc tempore successor nulla adhuc aut exili animorum dissensione per Frisiam renunciatus est. Hoc ut fieret, celebratum à Philippo aurei Velleris festum, & in istam societatem (quam ducentis abhinc annis ut munimentum imperij & concordiæ Philippus Burgundio instituerat) Principes adsciti, tum theatralium ludorum, & recentis magnificentiæ imago provincialium animos impellebant. Ad hæc Caroli patris in Philippum fidele monitum, & magni Cæsaris lachrymæ precesq; in ipso Patrum consessu fusæ, tum ceremonijs pactisq; conventis advocatum numen, velut adhuc intuentibus, percipientibusque, obversabantur. Vulgum verò novi, ut fieri solet, Imperij dulcedo (ac si illud libertati gentis parum derogaret) tum vernantes Principis anni, & gerendis bello paceque rebus habiles, universos, ut & Carolum Cæsarem, conciliatum per Mariæ nuptias Anglicum fœdus securitate atq; fiducia implebant. Eo namque inter cætera cautum erat, ut Philippi ex Maria primogenito cum patrij, avitique regni, tum universæ quoq; Belgicæ hæreditas obveniret, pactorumque dotalium ratione æterna ac inviolata Anglicæ Belgicæque gentium fœdera haberentur.
units.tr: Therefore, when the solemnities were completed, and the Frisian lands had passed to Philip from Charles Caesar by the law of the documents and agreements I have mentioned, the envoys returned to Friesland. Then in the month of November the royal Senate for Friesland, which had received from Charles Caesar the power of declaring and administering law, was confirmed by Philip; and Hippolytus Perfinius, president, Jacobus Roussellius, Petrus Dekama, knight, Upco Burmania, Ioannes Rommartius, Julius Gelius, royal procurator of the treasury, Adrianus Vastartius, Antonius Lavailius, Alexius Gelius, Sixtus Dekama, knight, Aggaeus Albada, and Valerius Ockingha, jurists, together with Godefridus Duvenaeus, registrar, were brought to take the oath to the new Prince. Afterwards the other magistrates also swore the oath of homage to Philip, since the nation, divided into factions in the age of Prince Charles and worn out by arms of the Saxons, Gelderlanders and Burgundians alone, had brought it about; and Philip, as before in the year 1550, so now at this time was proclaimed in Friesland as son and heir of Charles, and as successor, with no dissension of minds, or with only a slight one. To bring this about, the festival of the Golden Fleece was celebrated by Philip, and princes were admitted into that fellowship, which Philip the Burgundian had founded two hundred years earlier as a bulwark of empire and concord; and the image of theatrical games and of recent magnificence stirred the minds of the provincials. Besides this, the faithful admonition of Charles, the father, to Philip, and the tears and prayers of the great Caesar poured out in the very assembly of the Fathers, together with the ceremonies and the agreed pacts, kept before the eyes of all the god invoked as if still watching and hearing. But the sweetness of the new rule, as is usual, filled the common people, and indeed all, including Charles Caesar, with security and confidence (as if it detracted little from the liberty of the nation), as did the flourishing years of the Prince, and his ability to manage affairs both in war and in peace, and the English alliance secured through the marriage with Mary. For among other things it was provided there that Philip's first son by Mary should inherit both the paternal and ancestral kingdom and the whole of Belgium, and that by the terms of the marriage settlement the alliances of the English and Belgian peoples should be regarded as eternal and inviolate.

units.la: Cæterum ut res humanæ ultrò fluxæ ac instabiles sunt, ita novam rerum fœlicitatem velut cæcâ vertigine omnia rotantis fortunæ adversitas excepit. Philippus namque sive ut principatum suum (cuius solemnia proxumo mense celebraverat) Romanorum Pontificum Imperijs assimilaret, sive ut suspectam, quam plurimum regnantibus, populi libertatem, ipsâ teneritudine rerum, specioso adhuc Principatus sui exordio, perverteret, vulgato circâ medium Decembrem Inquisitionis Edicto, Ordinum populiq; spes non parum obturbavit. Itaque prioris fiduciæ, ut mobiles ad deteriora mortalium animi sunt, vis repente conversa, atqueante quinquennium admirandæ solemnitatis memoria perculsis animis se intorsit. Tum quippe certam spem futuri Principatus Philippo factam recordabantur, jactoq; simul cum Philippi imperio novæ servitutis fundamine primos Inquisitores per Carolum Cæsarem in Frisiam missos quinq; jam annorum insolentem dominatum exercuisse. Quare sagaciores nihil aliud sperari potuisse tum primum innuebant, quam ut post ordinatas cæptando Concilio (quod Paulus III. Pontifex consulto Carolo Cæsare Tridenti indixerat) per Frisiam mense Iulio, Anno MDL. Ioh. XLVI. supplicationes, ejusdem Concilij decreta, eodem Carolo adhuc rerum potiunte per Frisiam cæterasq; Provincias invalescerent, premendisq; conscientijs, & accidendæ Principum potestati repertum imperium Frisicæ quoque libertati contra datam à Cæsare fidem intorqueretur. Quod etsi edicto Anni MDL. Ioh. L. coercendis Anabaptistarum furoribus, Carolus Cæsar adumbrasset, ita arguebant Carolum Cæsarem, & Mariam Gubernatricem, promiscuè edicti legem in eos quoque strinxisse, qui caligine istorum temporum, & fædissimis cleri moribus offensi alio cultu adorandum numen, quærendumq; æternæ salutis mysterium arbitrabantur. Exindè namq; Anno MDL. Ioh. LIIII. Hyppolytum Persinium nium Regij per Frisiam Senatus praesidem, solenni Ordinum Frisiae conventu ad IV. Eid. Ianuar. Leovardiae indicto; multa acerbitate & vehementi oratione nomine Caroli Caesaris a Romana Ecclesia defectoribus atroces ex edictis poenas comminatum, Praetoribusq;, ut & Magistratibus, severioris per Frisiam Imperij praescriptum demandasse. Tum Hermannum quoque Letmatium, & Franciscum Sonnium, Inquisitores Friscae genti datos, rescriptoq; Mariae Gubernatricis, (quod XVI. Kal. Sept. Anno CIↄ. Iↄ. LIV. transmiserat) nova potestate auctos observandis Provincialium actionibus consilijsque praefuisse. Itaq; criminabantur Carolum Caesarem moderatum ante, & juris antiqui reverentem, procurato successore filio, & adulta potestate novis rebus se dedisse, Philippumque beneficio Frisiae gentis anticipatum imperium (quod ei Ordines non nisi expleta per Carolum mortalitate depacti erant) vivo patre, contra receptum regnantibus morem, quorum lenissimi primo dominatus esse solent, ijsdem auspicijs & fere peioribus ordiri. Qua de causa, quoque factum existimo, ut honorarium sexaginta millium aureorum, quod intra sexennium Carolo Caesari se datur Ordines Frisiae promiserant, non nisi recuperatis majorum immunitatibus, & patrio jure restituto, per abolitas intra annum conventiones ut libertati adversas, ita potentia regnantium, aut adulatione temporum introductas, se soluturos caverent, solemnesque ea de re tabulae approbante Carolo Caesare, ac Maria Gubernatrice, etsi, ut creditum fuit, invita, velut in gratiam laesi offensiqe populi Prid. Non. Iul. Anno CIↄ. Iↄ. LIV. conscriberentur.
units.tr: But, as human affairs are of their own accord fleeting and unstable, so the adversity of a Fortune that turns all things with blind whirling received this new happiness of affairs. For Philip, whether he wished to make his principate (whose solemnities he had celebrated the previous month) resemble the dominions of the Roman Pontiffs, or whether he wished to subvert the liberty of the people, which is very much suspected by rulers, while his principate was still in its specious beginning and in the tenderness of affairs, by the Edict of Inquisition published about the middle of December, greatly disturbed the hopes of the Orders and the people. So the force of their former confidence was suddenly turned around, as the minds of mortals are fickle toward worse things, and minds struck by the memory of the admirable solemnity, not yet a full five years old, turned about. For they recalled the certain hope of a future principate given to Philip, and, with the foundation of new servitude thrown in alongside Philip's rule, they said that the first Inquisitors sent into Friesland by Charles Caesar had exercised their insolent domination now for five years. Hence the more far-sighted began then first to hint that nothing else could have been hoped for, than that, after the supplications had been ordered and the council (which Pope Paul III had deliberately summoned to Trent with Charles Caesar's consent) had been held, the decrees of that same council, while Charles still held power, would gain strength in Friesland and the other provinces; and that the empire, found for the purpose of suppressing consciences and diminishing the power of princes, would be turned against Frisian liberty too, against the faith given by the emperor. Although Charles Caesar, by the edict of the year 1550, had outlined this as a means of curbing the rage of the Anabaptists, they argued that Charles Caesar and Mary the Regent had indiscriminately extended the law of the edict also to those who, offended by the darkness of those times and by the most foul morals of the clergy, judged that God must be worshipped in another way and the mystery of eternal salvation sought. For from that point, in the year 1554, Hippolytus Perfinius, president of the royal Senate through Friesland, was summoned to a solemn assembly of the Orders of Friesland at Leeuwarden on 10 January; and with great harshness and a vehement speech, in the name of Charles Caesar, he threatened the defectors from the Roman Church with severe penalties from the edicts, and gave the praetors, as well as the magistrates, the strict orders of the empire prescribed for Friesland. Then Hermannus Letmatius and Franciscus Sonnius, appointed as Inquisitors for the Frisian people, and strengthened with new authority by the rescript of Mary the Regent (which she had sent on 17 August in the year 1554), presided over the observation of the actions and counsels of the provincials. So they accused Charles Caesar, who had previously been moderate and respectful of ancient law, of having, after arranging a successor in his son and with his son's power now grown up, given himself to new measures; and they accused Philip of having anticipated the empire by the favour of the Frisian people (which the Orders had agreed only to grant after Charles's death was completed), while his father was still alive, and of beginning with the same auspices, and nearly worse ones, what in rulers is usually begun by their mildest acts at the first onset of their rule, contrary to accepted custom. For this reason, I think, it also happened that the honorary sum of sixty thousand gold pieces, which the Orders of Friesland had promised to Charles Caesar to be paid within six years, they agreed to pay only once the greater immunities had been recovered and their ancestral right restored, and once the agreements made within the last year had been abolished, as hostile to liberty and as introduced by the power of rulers or by the flattery of the times; and a formal document on this matter was drawn up, with the approval of Charles Caesar and of Mary the Regent, though, as was believed, unwillingly, as if in favour of a people who had been wronged and offended, on 6 July in the year 1554.

units.la: CIↄ. Iↄ. LVI.
Unde etiam factum est ut Anno LVI. praeside Senatuque regio secundam honorarij pensionem exigente Frisij eidem Senatui hunc in modum responderint:
units.tr: Hence it also came about that in the year 1556, while the president and the royal Senate were demanding the second instalment of the honorary payment, the Frisians answered the Senate in this manner:

units.la: Inter Carolum Caesarem & nos ante biennium procurante Arembergio Frisiae Praefecto conventum est, ut sexaginta aureorum millia titulo Honorarij (rogas vocabant) intra sexennium justis pensionibus Carolus Caesar acciperet. Hac tamen cautione interpositâ, ut si quid legibus nostris atq; Privilegijs adversum, durante Caroli imperio, actum foret, id omne intra breve tempus, & quidem ante unius anni effluxum per Delegatos Caesaris rescinderetur. Quâ pactione nos etiam cavimus, ut priusquam secunda pensio à Caesare exigi posset, postulatis nostris, quae ante biennium Caesari exhibuimus, benigne & ex patrio jure responderetur. Caeterum quoniam Philippo Caroli patris successori placuit legatos nostros ad Praesidem Senatumque regium remittere, quo quaedam postulata in judicio disceptarentur, quibusdam Philippus ipse rescriberet, ita censent Delegati nostri conventioni Carolo cum Caesare initae satisfactum non esse. Et quoniam Senatus regius secundae pensionis solutionem praestari sibi petit, ita protestamur exactionem illam frustraneam & irritam esse, nulloque jure subnixam; facimusq; copiam notarijs nostris Nicolao Clentinghio & Gualthero Coquillano qui hanc protestationem Regio procuratori exhibeant. Datum VI. Eid. Jan. CIↄ. Iↄ. LVI.
units.tr: Between Charles Caesar and ourselves, two years ago, through the agency of Aremberg, Prefect of Friesland, it was agreed that Charles Caesar should receive sixty thousand gold pieces under the title of honorary gift (which they called rogas), in lawful instalments within six years. Yet this condition was attached: that if anything were done against our laws and privileges during the reign of Charles, all of it would be rescinded through the delegates of Caesar within a short time, and indeed before the lapse of one year. By this agreement we also took care that, before the second instalment could be exacted from Caesar, our demands, which we presented to Caesar two years ago, should be answered kindly and in accordance with our ancestral right. Moreover, since it has pleased Philip, the successor of Charles's father, to send our envoys back to the president and the royal Senate, so that certain demands might be disputed in court, and Philip himself might reply to some of them, our delegates judge that the agreement made with Charles Caesar has not been fulfilled. And since the royal Senate asks that the payment of the second instalment be made to it, we declare that this demand is vain and void, and supported by no right; and we furnish our notaries, Nicolaus Clentinghius and Gualterus Coquillanus, with a copy, so that they may present this protest to the royal procurator. Given on the 6th day before the Ides of January, 1556.

units.la: Hoc modo dubijs Philippi subditorumq; animis, & lubricâ fide prima etiam principatus tempora fluebant, donec crescente Inquisitorum insolentiâ, contemptu ac detestatione tam enormis Imperij, magis magisque nexus infoelicis concordiae laxaretur. Quare Philippus, ne prima Principatus sui infantiâ Frisiorum animos à se alienaret, ex litteris Leovardiæ xii. Kalend. Martij autore, prout deprehendo, Regio Senatu, datis, de attemperanda mox Inquisitorum potestate cogitavit, demulcendisq; offensis mentibus, Edictum tale in Frisiam misit.
units.tr: In this way the minds of Philip and his subjects wavered, and the first days of his rule drifted with unreliable good faith, until, as the insolence of the Inquisitors grew and contempt and hatred for so monstrous a power increased, the bond of that unhappy concord was loosened more and more. Therefore Philip, lest in the very infancy of his reign he alienate the minds of the Frisians, thought, as far as I can detect, from letters written at Leeuwarden on the 12th day before the Kalends of March to the royal Senate, about moderating soon the power of the Inquisitors, and, to soothe the wounded minds, sent an edict of this kind into Friesland.

units.la: Quamvis ad præcavendas hæreses, & errores adversus Christianam fidem in his Belgicæ provincijs exortos plurima Edicta facta, ac vulgata fuere, pæneque isti rei decretæ deterrere animos hominum debuissent, quo minus in ijsdem erroribus perseverarent, ita deprehendo magnum pravis opinionibus incrementum per Frisiam accedere, cùm quod è vicinis locis illa contagio luesque proserpat, tum quod simplicissimi, innocentissimique ope seductorum corrumpantur inquinenturque. Et quia plurimæ difficultates super puniendis per Frisiam pro rigore Edictorum hæreticis ex hac causa emanant, quod Georgius Scencus Teutoburgius, nuper provinciæ istius Præfectus, in consessu regy Senatus fidem fecisset, Carolum Cæsarem patrem meum super hoc consultum singulari clementiâ indulsisse, veniamque eidem Senatui fecisse, quâ Edictorum asperitati temperamentum reperiret, judicaretque pro qualitate rerum personarumque conscientiæ magis norvnâ, quam pro scripti juris rigore. Ea propter perspectis visitatisque actis, quæ mitigandis corrigendisque Edictis perscripta erant, de consilio Senatus statui atque ordinavi: Vt ij, qui simplicitate suâ aut persuasione aliorum, ab Ecclesiâ desciverunt, contemnentes sacramenta, interrogatique de articulis fidei suæ, non respondent prout veros Christianos decebat, cæterum ut hæretici & contra doctrinam Ecclesiæ sentientes, nisi intra ternum decimum quartum diem toties moniti resipuerint, & ad communionem Ecclesiæ redierint, factâ errorum suorum confessione sine morâ punientur pro rigore Edictorum. Illi vero qui præmissis admonitionibus, intra illud tempus resipuerunt, redieruntque ad Ecclesiam damnantes errores suos, arbitrariâ à Senatu (qui hoc modo ex Edictis judicare non tenebitur) pœna corrigentur, cæterum hac lege & conditione missi res lapsi in hæreses, neque illarum Doctores fuerint, quibus id beneficij nequaquam dabitur. Quod ad eos verò attinet, qui errore seducti non baptizari liberos suos fecerunt, aut baptizari vetuerunt, vetabuntque; illi, & si hac de re convicti fuerint, & si prima, secunda, aut tertiâ admonitione emendaverint se, ac pœnitentiam egerint, oblata abjurationè errorum suorum, arbitraria pœna corrigentur, sin vero persistant etiam admoniti, à Senatu meo è formula Edictorum igne punientur, non requisita Inquisitorum sententia. Quapropter Senatui meo per Frisiam mando, ut sine ulla tergiversatione ea exequatur, quæ constituì, ac quæ publicè expedire judicavi. Datum Bruxellis ii. Non. Martij, Anno Domini millesimo quingentesimo, quinquagesimo sexto. Signatum
units.tr: Although many edicts have been made and published to guard against heresies and errors against the Christian faith that have arisen in these Belgic provinces, and although the very decrees on this matter ought almost to have deterred men's minds from persevering in the same errors, nevertheless I find that a great increase of perverse opinions is occurring throughout Friesland, both because that contagion and pestilence creeps in from neighbouring places, and because the most simple and most innocent are corrupted and defiled by the work of seducers. And since very many difficulties arise concerning the punishment of heretics in Friesland according to the rigour of the edicts, from this cause: that Georgius Scencus Teutoburgius, lately prefect of that province, had assured the assembly of the royal Senate that Charles Caesar, my father, had been consulted on this matter and had granted it with singular clemency, and had given that same Senate leave to find a means of tempering the harshness of the edicts, and to judge according to the nature of the affairs and persons, by conscience rather than by the rigour of the written law. Therefore, having examined and considered the records which had been drawn up for moderating and correcting the edicts, I have decided and ordained, on the advice of the Senate: that those who, through simplicity or the persuasion of others, have fallen away from the Church, despising the sacraments, and when questioned about the articles of their faith do not answer as true Christians ought, but are heretics and think contrary to the doctrine of the Church, unless within fourteen days, having been so often admonished, they repent and return to the communion of the Church, after confessing their errors, shall be punished without delay according to the rigour of the edicts. But those who, after the aforesaid admonitions, have repented within that time, and returned to the Church, condemning their errors, shall be corrected by an arbitrary penalty imposed by the Senate (which will not be bound to judge in this way by the edicts); yet only on this condition and law: that those who have lapsed into heresies and were not their teachers shall be sent away, and this benefit shall in no way be given to them. As for those who, led astray by error, have caused their children not to be baptized, or have forbidden, or will forbid, their baptism: if they are convicted of this matter, and after a first, second or third admonition they amend themselves and do penance, having offered an abjuration of their errors, they shall be corrected by an arbitrary penalty; but if they persist even when admonished, they shall be punished by fire, according to the form of the edicts, by my Senate, without the sentence of the Inquisitors being sought. Wherefore I command my Senate in Friesland to carry out without any delay what I have decreed, and what I have judged to be publicly expedient. Given at Brussels, on the 2nd day before the Nones of March, in the year of our Lord 1556. Signed

units.la: PHILIPPUS.
units.tr: PHILIP.

units.la: Et ad mandatum Regis
units.tr: And by command of the King

units.la: D. OVERLOPE.
units.tr: D. OVERLOPE.

units.la: Tum ut diversitati religionum, & simul asperitati publicorum judiciorum subveniret Philippus Georgium Egmondanum Præsulem Ultrajectinum, (cuius Ecclesiasticæ jurisdictioni clerus tum per Frisiam parebat) Bruxellas evocavit, deque mittendo in Frisiam Legato Sedis decretum fecit. Pensionem quoque ei ex aerario sacro, tum etiam suo assignavit, Ioannemq; Lignaeum Arembergium secretis hac de re mandatis instructum in Frisiam praemisit. Iis vero maxime caverat Philippus, ut foedis abominandisque monachorum sacerdotumque moribus asperius remedium ordinaretur, deficiscentiumq; ab Ecclesia dignitates, & sacerdotia, adstricti moris vitaeque cultoribus & incorruptam religionem professis, interpositâ Praesulum auctoritate, conferrentur. Itaque Arembergius evocatos ad se antistites sui officij serio commonefecit, evilescentisque divini cultus restaurationem imperavit. Litterae Philippi hac de re ad Senatum regium VIII. Eid. Mart. datae. Mox eodem Martio mense dirus Cometes exarsit, aucto adhuc animorum metu tristi illo prodigio imminentium rerum funesta initia signari.
units.tr: Then, that he might provide both for the diversity of religions and at the same time for the harshness of the public judgments, Philip summoned to Brussels Georgius Egmondanus, bishop of Utrecht (whose ecclesiastical jurisdiction the clergy in Friesland then obeyed), and decided to send him into Friesland as legate of the See. He also assigned him a pension from the sacred treasury, and also from his own purse, and sent ahead into Friesland Johannes Lignaeus Aremberg, instructed with secret orders in this matter. Philip had especially taken care that a sharper remedy be provided for the foul and abominable morals of monks and priests, and that the dignities and priesthoods vacated by those who had fallen away from the Church be conferred, with the authority of the bishops interposed, upon men who cultivated a settled discipline and way of life and professed an uncorrupted religion. Accordingly Aremberg seriously reminded the bishops summoned before him of their office, and ordered the restoration of the divine worship, which was growing weak. Philip's letters on this matter were dated to the royal Senate on the 8th day before the Ides of March. Soon afterwards, in the same month of March, a dire comet blazed forth, and with the fear of men increased still further, that sad portent was taken as a sign of the deadly beginnings of impending events.

units.la: Carolum quoque Caesarem conspecto crinito inusitateque sydere triste illud praesagium suis extremis, tanquam instantibus, applicasse Guiciardinus tradit, animumq; magni Caesaris jam ante inclinantis vitae sollicitudine occupatum, majoribus privatae fortunae desiderijs exarsisse.
units.tr: Guicciardini records that Charles Caesar, when he saw the long-haired and unusual star, applied that sad omen to his own last days, as though they were at hand, and that his mind, already inclining before by anxiety about life, was inflamed with greater longings for the fortunes of a private man.

units.la: Cornelius Gemma magni Gemmae Frisij filius celeberrimus illius temporis Mathematicus eadem fere, (cum de Carolo Caesare non pronuntiet) criniti syderis praesignificationes tradit, additque quarto post anno, dein septimo, nono, & undecimo, tempestatis futurae, quae tum adhuc latebant, semina, velut per Criticas indicationes toti Europae; & imprimis Belgicae populo aperuisse. Itaque Carolus instructa Liburnicarum classe mense Septembri Zelandico portu solvit, unaq; cum Eleonora, & Maria sororibus in desideratam diu Hispaniam navigavit, Cenobioque D. Justi se clausit. Scribit Strada Carolum Caesarem, velut desiderio veteris potentiae retractum, translati in filium imperij poenitentiam egisse, fastidioq; privatae vitae ductum imminutam antiquae majestatis venerationem, obvelatâ tamen animi aegritudine, dissimulasse. Certe credibile est tantum Principem, qui ex secundarum rerum continuo fluxu fortunam velut in potestate habuerat, tantâ ex vitae mutatione, quam brevem fore praenoverat, quadam generosae mentis concussione affectum fuisse, comparationeq; temporum instituta, amissum vetus imperium loco indecentis recentisque servitij habuisse. Tradit Demetrius Mariam Philippi amitam, ut non aequâ mente Praefecturâ Provinciarum defunctam, itaque renitentem Carolum fratrem in Hispaniam secutam, quod calidioris caeli inclementiam, quae causa mortis post fuisse creditur, dubiae per annos valetudini, & temperamento infirmi corporis obtenderet.
units.tr: Cornelius Gemma, son of the great Gemma Frisius, the most celebrated mathematician of that time, gives almost the same portents of the long-haired star (though he does not pronounce about Charles Caesar), and adds that in the fourth year after it, then the seventh, ninth and eleventh, he had revealed to all Europe, and especially to the people of Belgium, the seeds of a future storm, which at that time were still hidden, as if by critical indications. And so Charles, with a fleet of galleys made ready, sailed from the Zeeland harbour in September, and together with his sisters Eleanor and Mary sailed to Spain, which he had long desired, and shut himself up in the monastery of St. Just. Strada writes that Charles Caesar, drawn back as if by longing for his old power, repented of having transferred the empire to his son, and that, weary of private life, he concealed, though with a veiled sorrow of mind, the diminished reverence for his former majesty. Certainly it is credible that so great a prince, who had held fortune, as it were, in his power through a continuous flow of prosperous affairs, was shaken by a certain shock of a noble mind at so great a change of life, which he had foreseen would be brief, and that, comparing the times, he regarded the lost old empire as a shameful and recent servitude. Demetrius relates that Mary, aunt of Philip, having discharged the governorship of the provinces without an even mind, and therefore reluctant, followed her brother Charles into Spain, pretending that the inclemency of the warmer climate, which was believed to have been the cause of her death afterwards, was the reason, on account of her doubtful health for years and the weakness of her body.

units.la: Eam ipsam quoq; Mariam velut ab Hispanicae, (quae sensim in Belgicam immigrabat) gentis superbis consilijs abhorreret supremo conloquio, Belgicae nobilitatis fidem tanquam grande stabiliendi imperij secretum Philippo commendasse, vocemq;, si pondus habuisset, publicae rerum tranquillitati, & tot gentium sanguini profuturam veridico oraculo eloquutam. Caeterum Philippi animus suae magnitudinis, & potentiae immodicus, libertatis vero Belgicae & iniquus aestimator, alijs tum imperij arbitris utebatur. Quorum suasu hoc etiam factum est, ut vivo adhuc & agenti in Belgica Caesari, quod alias exempto humanis fieri consuevit, religio, & veluti consecratio decerneretur, Philippusq; Caroli patris de Religione rescripta, & praesertim
units.tr: Likewise Mary herself, shrinking in her last conference from the proud designs of the Spanish nation (which was gradually immigrating into Belgium), is said to have entrusted to Philip the loyalty of the Belgian nobility as the great secret of firmly establishing his empire, and to have spoken a word, which, if it had had weight, would have benefited the public tranquillity and the blood of so many peoples, in a truthful oracle. But Philip's mind, immoderate in its greatness and power, and an unjust judge of Belgian liberty, then used other counsellors of the empire. By their persuasion it also came about that, while Charles was still alive and active in Belgium, the reverence and, as it were, consecration which were usually bestowed on men after their death were decreed for him, and Philip confirmed by solemn edict, on the 12th of September, the rescripts of his father concerning religion, and especially the edict which he had drawn up in 1550 by decree of the Council of Trent.

units.la: Edictum (quod Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. L. ex decreto Concilij Tridentini conceperat) solenni Edicto xii. Septemb. confirmaret. LVI.
units.tr: The edict (which in the year 1550 he had drawn up by decree of the Council of Trent) he confirmed by a solemn edict on 12 September. LVI.

units.la: Edictum Caroli istiusmodi erat.
units.tr: The edict of Charles was of this kind.

units.la: QVanquam id operam semper dedi ut meos intra fines antiqua & vera religio servaretur, etsi totus in hoc semper fui, ut qui multis nunc annis disseminati sunt per orbem Christianum errores, haereses atque sectae funditus tollerentur, licet hoc nomine vana subinde proposui Edicta, gravissimasq; poenas, tamen magno cum animi dolore accepi, non meae solum Ditionis homines, verum exteros etiam qui nostris in Provinciis habitant atque negotiantur, huius mali contagionem longè latèq; in promiscuam multitudinem diffundere, sic ut planè sit opus acrem aliquam adhibere medicinam, & in fontes diligenter inquirere, ut ea pestis extirpetur radicitus, quemadmodum in postremis Provinciarum conventibus Praefectos & Ordines admonui, ut pro se quisque diligenter in hanc curam incumberent & in veteri atque Catholica Religione permanerent, praesertim cum sit omnium oculis expositum, quas turbas atq; seditiones in vicinis populis excitaret ea labes, ut interim de salutis & animarum dispendio nihil dicam. Itaque de consilio charissimae sororis germanae, & reliquorum procerum, novam hanc legem fero, & simul edico. Primum, ne quis omnium quicunque ille sit domi habeat, emat, aut distribuat, Lutheri, Oecolampadij, Zuinglij, Buceri, Calvini, & quoscunque tandem libros editos annis abhinc triginta incertis autoribus, ut amplius in Theologorum Lovaniensium Catalogo continentur.
units.tr: Although I have always taken care that the old and true religion be preserved within my borders, and although I have always been intent on having the errors, heresies and sects that have for many years been spreading through the Christian world utterly uprooted, and although I have repeatedly issued empty edicts to that end and proposed the gravest penalties, I have nonetheless received with great grief of mind the news that not only the people of my own dominions but also foreigners who live and trade in our provinces are spreading the contagion of this evil far and wide among the common multitude. So it is plainly necessary to apply some sharp remedy and to search diligently for the sources, so that this plague may be torn out by the roots. As I admonished the prefects and estates at the last assemblies of the provinces, each of them should apply himself diligently to this care and remain in the old Catholic religion. This is especially so since it is plain to everyone's eyes what disturbances and seditions this blight has stirred up among neighbouring peoples, not to mention the loss of salvation and of souls. Therefore, by the counsel of my dearest sister and German sister, and of the other nobles, I issue this new law and at the same time decree: first, that no one, whoever he may be, shall keep at home, buy, or distribute the books of Luther, Oecolampadius, Zwingli, Bucer, Calvin, and whatever other books have been published within the last thirty years by uncertain authors, as are listed more fully in the Catalogue of the Louvain theologians.

units.la: Item ne quis ullam habeat picturam atq; imaginem fictam in ludibrium Divae Virginis, atque Sanctorum, neve deiciat, aut infringat ullam imaginem in honorem alicuius Divi depictam; Ne quis domum suam occultis conventibus aperiat, in quibus & disseminari solent errores & homines rebaptizari, & conspirationes in Ecclesiam atque Rempublicam fieri. Ne quis de S. Scriptura maxime de rebus dubiis, atque difficilibus privatim aut publice disputet, aut eius interpretationem sibi sumat, nisi sit Theologus, qui probatae alicuius Academiae testimonium habeat, qui secus fecerint punientur ut seditiosi, & publicae tranquillitatis perturbatores, ac viri quidem gladio ferientur, feminae autem in terram defodientur, si quidem ab errore desistent; si vero pertinaces erunt, exurentur, publicatis illorum bonis utrumcunque luant supplicium. Ad haec testamenti faciendi potestatem nullam habebunt, & quicquid eius rei fecerint, à quo primum tempore hanc legem nostram violare caeperunt, irritum esse iubeo. Praeterea ne quis hospitium praebeat, aut ulla re subveniat iis, quos de haeresi novit suspectos, mando, verum denunciet statim Inquisitori, vel loci Praefecto subiturus poenam nisi faciat. Qui non malitia nec obstinatione, sed per infirmitatem lapsi fuerint in haeresin & errorem, neque tamen in hanc nostram legem commiserint, nec seditiose quid fecerint & sponte redierint ad sanitatem, & abjuratione facta recepti fuerint in gratiam, nullum posthac sermonem inter se conferant de rebus ad fidem ac religionem pertinentibus, alioqui plectentur ut in crimen relapsi. Qui non convictus quidem sed admodum suspectus de haeresi damnatus fuerit, ut vel publice satisfaciat, & idem post accusetur haereseos, multabitur ut in crimen relapsus. Iis, qui sunt haereseos, & id genus criminum macula polluti, licet in gratiam recepti fuerint, nullus honos, nullum munus publicum, nulla dignitas communicabitur. Nisi testimonium quis adferrat ab Ecclesiae ministro eius loci, ubi vixit postremo, non permittatur ei domicimiticilium, vel habitatio, nam ejusmodi pro suspectis haberi debent. Præfecti locorum, & reliqui nostri Beneficiarij, diligenter inquirant in eos, qui legem hanc violabunt, sed & Inquisitoribus, Iudicibusq; Ecclesiasticis opem serant, ut in quibus culpa resederit, comprehensi pœnam luant, juxta formulam quam Inquisitoribus præscripsi, misi faciant, arbitrio nostro luent. Procurator etiam publicus cognoscat, an suum illi munus faciant, & si negligentiam in iis deprehendet, in judicium venire jubeat, & si deliquisse apparebit, Magistratus illis abrogetur, aut alia, quæ videbitur, pœna constituatur. Episcopi prætera, & Archi-Diaconi, & Abbates, & in genus alij proceres investigent omni studio, si quis ordinis Ecclesiastici sit infectus eo morbo, & severè vindicent. Qui contaminatum aliquem hac peste norunt, vel quibus locis commorentur, & delitescant hæretici compertum habent, ilico deferant, nisi faciant, eandem, quam illi, pœnam luent. Delator, si modo non vana accusatio fuerit, dimidiam partem bonorum illius consequetur, si quidem bona sexcentos aureos non excedent, nam quicquid erit supra hanc summam, eius decima pars illi decidetur. Qui conventus occultos Inquisitori deteget, etiamsi cum illis conlia contulit, non plectetur, modo & de religione bene sentiat, & in posterum abstineat, sed qui remotus ab eorum societate deferet, præmium consequetur, ut supra dictum est. Pœnæ, quas constituimus, irrogentur tales omnino, neque sit in ullius potestate illas vel mutare, vel mitigare, quod sæpe factum esse intelligo. Nam qui Iudices in eo delinquent, non ferent impune. Qui de hæresi accusati, & in jus vocati profugerunt, ac postea proscripti sunt, ubi de sociis criminum jam mortuis acceperunt, supplicare solent, ut ad purgationem admittantur, quandoquidem probari crimen amplius non posse putant, eoque fit, ut reversi falsam doctrinam & errores iterum diffundant, id verò ne fiat, publicè interest. Itaq; mando, ne locus ullus detur ipsorum postulatis, verum, ut omnes, qui citati non comparuerunt, sed fugâ salutem quæverunt, habeantur pro convictis atq; damnatis. Qui pro suspectis & fugitivis, & proscriptis, & Anabaptistis intercedunt, habeantur pro fautoribus hæreticorum. Iudices autem & Præfecti neminem ex illis in gratiam recipiant, nisi vel meo, vel sororis germanæ permissu. Qui secus agent, ejus abrogabitur Præfectura. Librarij nihil excudant, nihil divendant, aut distrahant res sacræ, nisi de voluntate & consilio eorum, quibus hæc erit demandata cura, si quid etiam ipsorum operæ in eo deliquerint, ipsi præstabunt. Et quia Catalogus extat librorum, quos Academia Lovaniensis rejecit, Librarij in suis tabernis eum habeant suspensum, & ob oculos positum, ne post ignorantiam obducant vel ipsi, vel emptores, dein alterum habeant librorum suorum Catalogum. Qui non parebit, 100. aureis multabitur. Pueros etiam erudiendos nemo suscipiat, nisi permissu Magistratus, & præcipuè Ecclesiæ ministri. Nihil autem doceat aut proponat juventuti, nisi juxta formulam à Theologis Lovaniensibus conscriptam. Hæc Sleidanus.
units.tr: Likewise, no one shall keep any painted or fashioned picture or image that mocks the divine Virgin and the Saints, nor shall anyone cast down or break any image painted in honour of any saint. No one shall open his house for secret meetings, in which errors are usually spread, men are rebaptized, and conspiracies are formed against the Church and the commonwealth. No one shall dispute about Holy Scripture, especially about its doubtful and difficult matters, either privately or publicly, nor take its interpretation upon himself, unless he is a theologian who holds the testimony of some approved university. Those who act otherwise shall be punished as seditious persons and disturbers of public peace: men shall be struck down with the sword, but women shall be buried in the ground, provided they desist from their error; if indeed they remain obstinate, they shall be burned, and their goods confiscated, whichever way they pay the penalty. Moreover, they shall have no power to make a will, and whatever they have done in this matter, from the first time they began to violate this our law, I decree to be void. Furthermore, no one shall give lodging to, or offer any help to, those whom he knows to be suspected of heresy; I command rather that he report them at once to the Inquisitor or to the prefect of the place, or else he shall himself undergo the penalty. Those who have fallen into heresy and error not through malice or obstinacy but through weakness, and who have not transgressed this our law nor done anything seditiously, and who of their own accord have returned to soundness and, having made abjuration, have been received back into favour, shall not hereafter hold any conversation among themselves about matters pertaining to faith and religion; otherwise they shall be punished as relapsed offenders. Whoever has been condemned for heresy, not convicted indeed but strongly suspected, shall either make public satisfaction, and if afterwards he is accused of heresy again, he shall be fined as a relapsed offender. To those who are stained with heresy and crimes of that kind, no honour, no public office, and no dignity shall be granted, even if they have been received back into favour. Unless someone brings a testimonial from the minister of the church of the place where he last lived, he shall not be allowed a home or residence, for such persons must be regarded as suspect. The prefects of the localities and our other officials shall diligently inquire after those who violate this law, and they shall also lend aid to the Inquisitors and ecclesiastical judges, so that those in whom guilt is found, once seized, pay the penalty according to the formula that I have prescribed to the Inquisitors; let them pay it at our discretion, without fail. The public prosecutor shall also examine whether they perform their duty, and if he finds negligence in them, he shall summon them to court; and if it appears that they have offended, their magistracy shall be taken from them, or some other penalty that seems fitting shall be imposed. Moreover, bishops, archdeacons, abbots, and other nobles of every kind shall investigate with all zeal whether anyone of the ecclesiastical order is infected with this disease, and shall punish them severely. Those who know of anyone tainted with this plague, or who know the places where heretics live and hide, shall at once report them; otherwise they shall pay the same penalty as those men. An informer, provided his accusation is not false, shall receive half of the goods of the accused, if indeed the goods do not exceed six hundred gold coins; for whatever exceeds this sum, a tenth part of the excess shall be given to him. Whoever reveals secret meetings to the Inquisitor shall not be punished, even if he has contributed to them, provided he thinks soundly about religion and abstains from them in future; but whoever, having withdrawn from their company, informs against them shall receive the reward, as stated above. The penalties that we have laid down shall be imposed in exactly this way, and no one shall have the power to change or soften them, which I understand has often been done. For those judges who offend in this matter will not go unpunished. Those who have been accused of heresy and summoned to court, and who fled and were afterwards outlawed, when they learn that their accomplices in the crimes are now dead, are accustomed to petition to be admitted to clearing themselves, since they think the crime can no longer be proved; and so it comes about that, once returned, they spread false doctrine and errors again. That this must not happen is a matter of public concern. Therefore I command that no place be given to their requests, but that all who did not appear when summoned and sought safety in flight be regarded as convicted and condemned. Those who intercede for suspects, fugitives, outlaws, and Anabaptists shall be regarded as abettors of heretics. Judges and prefects shall receive none of these men back into favour, except by permission of myself or of my sister German. Whoever acts otherwise shall lose his prefecture. Booksellers shall print nothing, sell nothing, and shall not circulate sacred books, except by the will and counsel of those to whom this charge has been committed; and if they offend in this matter through any fault of their own work, they shall answer for it themselves. And since there is a catalogue of books that the University of Louvain has rejected, booksellers shall keep it hung up and in plain view in their shops, so that neither they nor their buyers may afterwards plead ignorance; and they shall keep a second catalogue of their own books. Whoever does not obey shall be fined one hundred gold coins. Moreover, no one shall take on the instruction of children unless by permission of the magistrate, and especially of the ministers of the Church. He shall teach or set before the young nothing except according to the formula drawn up by the Louvain theologians. So far Sleidanus.

units.la: Tum ne memoria superstitiosæ in Carolum patrem pietatis per injuriam temporum intercideret, solenne hac de re Edictum bis in anno publicari per Frisiam jussit, istique Actui viiii. Kalend. Iul. & ix. Kalend. Ianuar. dies redintegrandæ suæ, & juxta paternæ venerationi designavit. Legem quoque Carolo Cæsare Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xl. de legitimandis liberis latam Philippus tum confirmavit, antiquatoque Comitum, ut vocant, Palatinorum sordido, & venali jure legilegitimationes non nisi suo, aut Curiæ rescripto fieri præcepit, pecuniamque isti actui assignatam, ne quid detrimenti jus Principis pateretur, inferri in ærarium, legitimatorumq; nomina rationariorum tabulis perscribi jussit. Dein suæ & simul Belgicæ quietis pertæsus, Gallico bello, quod Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. ııı. Carolum inter Cæsarem Henricumque ıı. Gallorum Regem recruduerat, quinque annorum inducijs, ipso Paschæ festo per Frisiam publica supplicatione celebratis, silente ac suspenso, ex eodem Edicto constitutis Inquisitoribus ministeria delegavit, deq; Gulielmo Lindano, homine pro more illius ordinis, superbo in Frisiam mittendo cogitavit. Ei quoque, mutato Inquisitoris, quod eâ ætate invisum erat, nomine, quo invidiam apud Frisios declinaret Philippus, titulum Delegati generalis facere, summamq; ei rerum Ecclesiasticarum censuram committere constituit. Secus vero volebat Philippus, ut à communione Ecclesiæ licentiâ temporum secretos, profanatæque Romanæ religionis insimulatos arctius coerceret, eorumq; nomina actis perscripta ad Senatum Regium deferret. Qui æthereæ luis metu, ne socordiâ hominum inquinatus aër, pecori tum infestus, atrocem mortalibus pestilentiam daret, jacentia campis animalium cadavera humari jussit, Edictumq; eâ de re per Frisiam vulgavit. Sumptuum quoq; impensarumque, quæ ante annum habendæ, honorandæque Philippi Principis inaugurationi, factæ erant cum legatis rationes initæ, Opidanisq; seorsim, trecenti & quinquaginta septem Carolini notabili temporum frugalitate ac parsimonia à Delegatis Opidorum è suo Ærario assignati. Tum Reynoldus Brederodius eius nominis iii. vir illustris ex antiqua & nobili Ludigmannorum apud Frisios gente, quę Potestatis summum per Frisiam Imperium circa annum 988. in Gosuino Ludigmanno tenuerat, maternum genus ducens, litteras Leovardiam ad senatum dedit. Iis monebat: Ducendæ se per ditiones suas in Vahalim, Mosamque flumina, novæ ac navigabilis fossæ consilium cæpisse, expediendis Frisiorum vicinarumque gentium commercijs, quæ Frisij cum illius oræ populis multa per tempora magnâ onerum navigandiq; molestia egissent. Ita Frisios huc usque superato Austrini maris sinu, lecta potioris Hollandiæ ora Dordracum magno flexu petere coactos, dissitas navium stationes magnis sæpe portorijs telonijsque redemisse. Et quoniam consilij sui ratio non alia sit, quam ut Frisij compendijs locorum, & simul levamentis onerum fruantur, ita cælare rem non potuisse civitati Leovardiæ, cæterisq; per Frisiam Oppidis fructuosam. Monere ea propter ut Oppidani cæteriq; quorum interest, in commune consulant ocyus; decernantque quod maturando negotio, & suo simul commodo expedire judicaverint. Itaque Senatus Leovardiensium ne quid socias urbes clàm haberet, easdem Brederodij (quibus suas Prid. Non. Aug. subjunxerat) litteras ad vniversos oppidorum per Frisiam rectores misit, eorumque Delegatos, ut Leovardiæ quam primum adsint, quod res moram non ferret, hortatus est. Ibi oppidorum Delegati volutatis deducendi operis rationibus istaque re, Iacobo Ægidio Consuli, Hermanno Feltesio, & Alberto Iacobæo, Scabinis Leovardiæ urbis, Adriano Michaëlio Consuli Harlingano, & Ottoni Bauconio Ærarij apud Franequeranos Tribuno, commissâ, Tzcmerum Vibenium Oldermannum Snecensium, & nuperâ ad Carolum Philippumque legatione functum, delegavere, qui ad Brederodium eat, ac cum eo de telonio cæterisque rebus agat, deq; ijs ad suos referat. Tabulæ mandatorum Prid. Eid. Aug. per Leovardios nullo, ut post patuit, eventu signatæ, decreti operis consilio morte ejusdem Brederodij (quæ vii. Kal. Octob. cum terris exemit) interrupto. Eâ namque evenit ut Henricus filius Brederodiæ domus ditione potiretur, turbulentissimique, quod post subortum fuit, temporis fortunâ, declinante sensim Frisiorum cum Vahalis, Mosæque accolis commercio, consilia pacis, & florentium rerum non procederent. Mox enim gravis, & supra hominum memoriam memorabilis annona cum asperrimo gelu, mense Februario surgens, post in Martium ac Aprilem provecta, ac sensim asperior tantam frumenti caritatem attulit, ut ad famen fermè veniretur, absumptisq; aut suppressis hominum alimentis languentia corpora flaccescentis ferè animæ deliquio conciderent. Itaque plebes, ut solet ingruentibus adversis turbulenta, tum maximè inediæ impatiens, & structoribus annonæ infesta prærepta sibi infælicis vitæ subsidia querebatur. Esse domi inopem turbam, & infirmis præ inediâ corporibus alimenta poscentem, tum fæcundas matres desideria non implere enutriendis infantibus destinata. Fœtus quoq; ipsos acetabulis adhuc suis, & secreto matrum clausos injuriam miserrimi temporis sentire, cuius principium necdum ingressi sint. Id verò mali non ab inclementiâ syderum, aut annorum sterilitate, sed aliunde haberi. Quippe incuriâ, aut assensu dominantium annonam per homines flagellari inopum sanguine, & alienâ miseriâ fœlices, neq; absimiles lieni, quod viscus exarescente toto corpore solum intumescit. Ab ijs esse quod exportata in Hispaniam è Frisijs frumenta, gravius annonæ pretium parent, ac tot millium animæ facilioris alimoniæ egentes insatiabili paucorum cupidine, & avaritiâ crucientur. Ut id porrò non fiat statuendem lenitati, & incuriæ imperantium terminum esse reprimendis coëmptionibus, quas Carolus Cæsar Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xlvi. & post cIↄ. Iↄ. liv. asperis vulgatisque per Frisiam Edictis vetuisset. Quin satius esse res malis artibus, & damno humanæ societatis introductas, supinis civitatum rectoribus, & annonæ Prafectis, per vim subverti, omniumque vitam, & incolumitatem privatis dispendijs emi. Itaq; parum abfuit, quin florentissimarum urbium direptiones instituerentur, acriorque ferro famés mobilem & egenam plebem, quiete temporum etiam præter hoc infidâ, ad perpetranda enormia stimularet. Cæterum benignitate propitij numinis ea infœlicis mali vis diuturna non fuit. Notat Andreas Gryphius vir literatus, & apud Utingeranos, Præturam tum gerens, panem secalicium ii. libr. adultâ circa Kalend. Iun. frumenti caritate i 2. mox eâ inclinante quatuor sestertijs venisse, inopinâque rerum mutatione stupentes hominum animos vitæ velut remedium divinitus concessum reputasse. Ducentas quoque onerarias naves flante Euro Balthicum sinum, deïn Germanici maris, (quod à Sundâ Daniæ freto veterem Frisiorum oram, marginemque intuti littoris pulsat) partem tem emensas, frumentoque onustas confertim appulisse, eundemq; annum, cuius initium penuria ferme funestum fuerat, ut desperatio- nem mortalium eluderet, frugum, & annonae feracissimum fuisse. Gemma notat hoc anno, qui horrenda lampade in caelo visa, & se-cutis tempestatibus notabilis fuit, modij partem octavam tribus florenis cum semisse vaenijsse, intensioreq; annonae malo, ne frumenta quidem justum pretium excedentia aere aut argento haberi potuisse. Tum ut asperis fatis, & importuno syderi res Belgicae subjacerent, premente adhuc Provincias annona, resurgens e Gallia bellum ferbuit, Caroloq; Caesare, ac Francisco, Henricoque Regibus jam ante captum, Philippo Principi, cum ipso Belgicae imperio haereditario velut jure obvenit. Qui propterea ne Henrici II. Gallorum regis periniqua consilia, suam vero integritatem, & stabiliendae pacis studium caelaret, datis in Frisiam VI. Kal. April. litteris causam renascentis belli exposuit. Ijs significabat: Non alia mente se fuisse, quam ut diuturno, quod Carolus pater cum Gallorum regibus, gessisset, bello, finem imponeret, factaque ante annum Non. Febr. inducias tanquam auspices verae duraturaeque pacis integras, inviolatasque servaret, novoq; &, ut plurimum, lubrico principatui fundamentum servata quiete, & procurata florentis populi concordia substerneret. Id vero per Gallorum Regem non licere, occasionem rumpendi foederis, & quinquennalium Inducianum jam diu animo agitantem. Exinde violata per Hispaniam, Pede-montium atque Belgicam finium jura, foedatisque vastitie agris, & sacro limite, vim quoque commercijs libero mari intulam. Postremo ne vires nocendi deessent, sollicitata per Lavignium Legatum Turcarum foedera, quo Italiae, Hungariaeq; bellum, & juxta furorem Otthomannicae gentis sentirent, omnisque Tanaim intra atque Oceanum Europa illo foedere dissociaretur. Eius pessimi consilij Laubespinae (is Henrico regi a Secretis) ad Bassum Fontanum apud Belgas Legatum, indices litteras fuisse, quibus fidem faceret, Henricum regem mutare Inducias novo bello constituisse, & animum alere religioni foedenum, pactorum adversum. Quamobrem velle metu instantis periculi, ut Frisij per Galliam & istius regni confinia agentes in sua redeant, fruanturque domestica securitate commerciorum jure-foris, & praesertim per Galliam infido. Dein Philippus trajectu in Angliam e Pleumosijs facto Mariae Uxoris, Anglorumque auxilia popposcit, decretoq; procerum regni, tum assensu populi Anglici, qui pro more gentis interponi solet, voti compos factus, bellum per fœcialem Gallo denuntiavit. Mox classe in Belgicam revectus haberi delectum jussit, turmisque equestribus (quas nomine Caroli Caesaris Maria Gubernatrix Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xLvI. autoraverat) supplementa procuravit. Itaq; & Ioannem Lignaeum Arembergium Frisiae Praefectum, virum militiae egregium, & qui jam ante Carolo Caesare Gallicis bellis stipendia fecerat, adesse oeyus jussit, rogatisque voluntariorum (quod Frisium de jure patrio, & conventione Anni cIↄ. Iↄ. xxII. Provincia evocare fas non esset) auxilijs solemnia propitiando per Frisiam numini instituit. Post supremo belli imperio in Emanuelem Philibertum Belgicae Praesidem collato, circumferentibus arma
units.tr: Then, so that the memory of his father's pious conduct would not be lost through the injuries of the times, Philip ordered a formal edict on this matter to be published twice a year throughout Friesland, and he appointed for this act the 9th day before the Kalends of July and the 9th before the Kalends of January, as days to renew that memory and to honour his father. In 1540, when Charles was emperor, a law had been passed on legitimising children. Philip now confirmed it. He abolished the sordid and venal right of the so-called Count Palatines, and ordered that legitimations be made only by his own rescript or that of the Court. He also ordered that the fee assigned for this act be paid into the treasury, so that the prince's right would suffer no loss, and that the names of the legitimised be entered in the account books. Then, weary of his own quiet and of Belgium's, he entrusted the ministry to inquisitors appointed by the same edict, after the war with France, which Charles, between the emperor and Henry II, King of the French, had revived in 1543, had been suspended by a five-year truce. The truce was celebrated throughout Friesland with a public thanksgiving on Easter day. He also considered sending Willem Lindanus, a man proud in the manner of that order, into Friesland. To avoid the hatred that the name of inquisitor, then odious, would bring upon him among the Frisians, Philip resolved to give Lindanus the title of general delegate and to commit to him the supreme oversight of ecclesiastical affairs. Philip, however, wanted otherwise: he wished to restrain more strictly those who, in such a time of license, had cut themselves off from the communion of the Church and were accused of having profaned the Roman religion, and to have their names recorded in the acts and reported to the royal Senate. Fearing the heavenly fire, lest air polluted by human sloth, then hostile to cattle, should bring a dreadful pestilence on mortals, he ordered the carcasses of animals lying in the fields to be buried, and published an edict on this matter throughout Friesland. He also settled accounts with the envoys for the expenses and outlays incurred a year earlier for the inauguration of Prince Philip, which was to be solemnly honoured. The towns were assessed separately, and 357 Carolus guilders, a notable sum given the frugality and thrift of the times, were paid from their own treasuries by the town delegates. Then Reynold Brederode, the third of that name, an illustrious man of the ancient and noble Ludigman family among the Frisians, which around the year 988 had held supreme power in Friesland under Gosuin Ludigman, and which he traced through his mother's line, sent a letter to the Senate of Leeuwarden. In it he warned that he had resolved to dig a new, navigable canal through his lands to the rivers Waal and Maas, to ease the trade of the Frisians and of neighbouring peoples, which for a long time the Frisians had carried on with the inhabitants of that coast at great cost and difficulty of navigation. Thus, since the Frisians, having passed the bay of the Zuiderzee, were forced to make for Dordrecht by a great detour along the shore of the richer Holland, they often paid heavy tolls and dues to redeem their distant anchorages. And since the purpose of his plan was none other than that the Frisians should enjoy shorter routes and at the same time lighter burdens, he could not keep the matter hidden from the city of Leeuwarden and the other towns of Friesland, which would profit from it. He therefore advised the townsmen and others concerned to consult together quickly, and to decide what they judged expedient for the speedy conduct of the business and for their own advantage. Accordingly, so that the Senate of Leeuwarden would hide nothing from the allied cities, it sent the same letter of Brederode (to which it had added its own on the 4th day before the Nones of August) to the magistrates of all the towns in Friesland, and urged their delegates to come to Leeuwarden as soon as possible, since the matter would not brook delay. There the delegates of the towns entrusted the plans for the proposed work and the business to Jacob Egidius, consul, Hermann Feltesius and Albert Jacobaeus, aldermen of the city of Leeuwarden, to Adrian Michael, consul of Harlingen, and to Otto Bauconius, treasurer at Franeker. They sent Tzcmerus Vibenius, alderman of Sneek, who had lately been on an embassy to Charles and Philip, to go to Brederode, to deal with him about the toll and the other matters, and to report back to his people. The letters of commission were sealed by Leeuwarden on the 2nd day before the Ides of August, but as later appeared, with no result, since the project was interrupted by the death of Brederode himself, which took him from the world on the 7th day before the Kalends of October. For it happened that Henry, son of Brederode, came into possession of the family's lordship, and in the turbulent fortunes of the time that followed, as the trade of the Frisians with the inhabitants of the Waal and Maas gradually declined, the plans for peace and for prosperity did not go forward. Soon a grave scarcity, memorable beyond living memory, arose in February with bitter frost, and continued into March and April. Growing gradually more severe, it brought such a dearth of grain that people came near to famine, and with men's food used up or hoarded, their weakened bodies sank into near-fainting. So the common people, as is their wont in adversity, grew restive, most impatient of hunger and hostile to the profiteers in grain, and they complained that the means of their wretched life had been snatched from them. There were poor crowds at home, with bodies weakened by hunger, begging for food; fruitful mothers could not satisfy the cravings of the infants they were meant to nourish; even the unborn, still shut in their mothers' wombs, felt the injury of that most wretched time, whose beginning they had not yet entered. This evil, they said, came not from the harshness of the stars or from barrenness of the years, but from elsewhere. Indeed, through the negligence or connivance of the rulers, grain was being wrung from the poor at the price of their blood, and the rich were growing fat on another's misery, not unlike the spleen, which swells alone while the whole body withers. From them came the grain exported from Friesland to Spain, which made the price of bread heavier, and the lives of so many thousands, who needed easier nourishment, were tormented by the insatiable greed and avarice of a few. So that this should not continue, they said, the limit must be set to the lenity and negligence of the rulers, by restraining the purchases which Charles the Emperor had forbidden in 1546 and afterwards in 1554, by harsh and widely published edicts throughout Friesland. Rather, it was better that practices introduced by bad arts and to the harm of human society should be overthrown by force, against the lazy rulers of the cities and the prefects of the grain supply, and that the lives and safety of all should be bought at private loss. And so it was not far from happening that the sacking of the most flourishing cities should be begun, and that fiercer steel would urge on the restless and needy common people, already untrustworthy in the quiet of the times, to commit outrages. But by the kindness of a favourable divinity, the force of this unhappy evil did not last long. The learned Andreas Gryphius, who was then holding the office of praetor among the Utingeran people, notes that rye bread of two pounds, when the price of grain was at its height around the Kalends of June, came down to four sesterces after the price had fallen to twelve stuivers, and that men's minds, stunned by the unexpected change, reckoned it a remedy granted by God for their life. He also notes that two hundred merchant ships, driven by the east wind, sailed up the Baltic gulf and then part of the German sea, which beats against the old shore of the Frisians, through the Sound of Denmark and the margin of the safe coast, and came in a crowd laden with grain. And that same year, which had begun almost fatally with dearth, was most abundant in fruits and crops, so as to frustrate men's despair. Gemma notes that in this year, when a dreadful torch was seen in the sky and the storms that followed were notable, an eighth part of a measure sold for three and a half florins, and by the more intense evil of the grain supply, even grain exceeding its just price could scarcely be had for money or silver. Then, while the Netherlands were subject to harsh fates and an unfavourable star, and the grain supply still pressed on the provinces, war rose again from France and blazed up. Charles Caesar, and Francis and Henry, kings, having already been taken earlier, the war fell as it were by hereditary right to Prince Philip, together with the rule of the Netherlands itself. Therefore, so as to conceal the very unfair designs of Henry II, King of the French, and his own integrity and zeal for establishing peace, he set out the cause of the renewed war in a letter to Friesland dated the 6th day before the Kalends of April. In it he declared that he had no other intention than to put an end to the long war which his father Charles had waged with the kings of the French, and that he would keep the truce made before the Nones of February, as the auspices of a true and lasting peace, whole and inviolate, and that he would lay, by preserving quiet and securing the concord of a flourishing people, a foundation for a new and, for the most part, slippery rule. But this, he said, could not be done while the King of the French was willing to do so: he had long been turning in his mind an opportunity to break the treaty and the five-year truce. Thereafter the rights of the borders of Spain, Piedmont and Belgium had been violated, the fields had been defiled with devastation, and the sacred boundary, and violence had been done to trade on the open sea. Finally, lest the means of harming should be lacking, he had solicited through Lavignus, the envoy of the Turks, a treaty by which Italy and Hungary would feel war, and the Ottoman people, raging, would turn Europe, from the Don to the Ocean, against that treaty. Laubespina, secretary to King Henry, sent an accompanying letter to Bassus Fontanus, envoy among the Belgians, about this most wicked plan, by which he might give proof that King Henry had resolved to change the truce into a new war, and was nourishing a mind hostile to religion and foul toward treaties. Therefore, in fear of the imminent danger, he wished the Frisians, who were travelling through France and the borders of that kingdom, to return to their homes and to enjoy domestic security in their trade, which was unsafe abroad and especially through France. Then Philip, having crossed from Pleumosium to England, sought the help of Mary, his wife, and of the English; and when the decree of the nobles of the kingdom and the assent of the English people, which by custom of that nation is usually interposed, had been obtained, he declared war on the French through a herald. Soon he was carried back to Belgium with his fleet, and ordered levies to be raised, and he procured reinforcements for the cavalry troops which Mary, the governor, had enrolled in the name of Charles Caesar in 1546. Accordingly he also ordered John Ligne of Aremberg, prefect of Friesland, a man distinguished in war, who had already served under Charles Caesar in the French wars, to come at once; and, since it was not lawful to summon the Frisians from the provinces against their ancestral right and the agreement of 1522, to ask for volunteers' help, he instituted solemn rites through Friesland to propitiate the deity. Afterwards he conferred the supreme command of the war on Emanuel Philibert, president of Belgium, while the French, through Italy, were carrying arms about.

units.la: per Italiam Gallis, exercitum jam ante de more lustratum in Galliæ fines duci præcepit, vulgatoque, ac si in Rhemos expeditionem adornaret, eundem Philibertum cum copijs Marianum pergere, oppeririq; auxilia Germanorum jussit. Is, dum ea adventant, triduum moratus equitum turmas, cum expedita peditum manu Guisam, & mox Quintini fanum præmisit, subsecutusque cum reliquo exercitu, in quo Arembergius Frisiæ Præfectus voluntariorum ex illà gente auxilia ducebat, haud procul Sabi flumine, quod urbem eam modico alveo lambit, castra locavit. Mox suburbio, & propugnaculo, quod cis flumen erat, occupato, arctiore obsidio oppidum pressit, dispositisque tormentis & idoneo primum opere præparato oppugnare agressus est. Quà re excitì Galli Dandaloto nobili viro, mox ipso Connestablio duce castra propè posuere, præmissoque in locum solvendæ obsidioni opportunum prono flumine Dandaloto, de transmittendis quoque in adversam ripam reliquis copijs cogitavere. Cæterum per Lamoralium Egmondanum, qui in exercitu Philippi erat, detectum Gallorum consilium omninò infructuosum fuit. Itaq; Philibertus copiarum partem trajicere Sabim flumen, equitatumq; confestim subsequi jussit, assecutusque Gallorum exercitum, qui signum receptui jam dabat, fugæ, & per conturbatos ordines, confusioni proximum cæcidit, magnâq; clade affecit. Bis mille & quingenti ac inter eos nobilissimi Gallorum cæsi cruentatis sanguine campis jacuere. Præda ingens parta, omnisq; ferè Gallorum apparatus arma, & machinæ, cum signis militaribus victoribus obvenere. Tum Philippus primis principatus sui & juventæ annis præter spem hominum, qui Carolo Cæsare imperium ponente aliud augurati erant, id gloriæ adeptus in castra ad Quintini fanum contendit, confidenteq; Compendij Henrico Rege, nuniendis tantum locis, & petendis sociorum auxilijs post acceptam cladem occupato, urbem maxumam atque florentissimam Burgundicis itetum ditionibus adjecit. Ita Quintini fano potitus Philippus Ioannem Lignæum Arembergium Frisiæ Præfectum, cum delecta suorum manu, auxiliaribusque copijs Castellum amandavit. Qui ne tempus gerendis accelerandisque rebus destinatum muniendis castris insumeret, in circumjacentes campos, nullo vallo, aut fossâ præductis, repente effusus locum natura munitum tormentis aggressus est, murique parte per vim machinarum repentè subruta, cæptandæ oppugnationi se paravit. Cæterum præsidiarij ultro inbelles, tum sociorum ad Quintinum clade fracti, simulque rerum instantium metuentes Arembergio se permisere. Arembergius locato ibidem præsidio, ordinatisque rebus in Philippi ad Quintinum castra cum copijs revertit. Quâ in Galliam expeditione inofsenso cursu rerum peractâ de reducendo in Belgicam exercitu, Philippus mox consilium cæpit, motisque derepente per ingruentis brumæ incommoda, & dubij aëris inclementiam castris, in hyberna se recepit. Frisij quoque navatâ Philippo extra ordinem opera, ut periculorum ultrò socij, ita gloriæ consortes in sua redierę, illustreque ut Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. li. ad Metim, ita hoc tempore ad Quintini Fanum fidei in Principem virtutisque exemplum, ore gentis huc usque & memorabili fama celebratum edidere. Annotatum invenio Carolum Cæ-
units.tr: while the French were carrying arms through Italy, he ordered the army, which had already been reviewed in the customary way, to be led into the borders of France. He let it be published abroad that he was preparing an expedition against Reims, and he ordered the same Philibert to advance with his forces towards Marienburg and to wait there for the German auxiliaries. While these were on their way, Philibert delayed for three days. He then sent ahead squadrons of cavalry with a light body of infantry to Guise, and soon after to Saint-Quentin. Following with the rest of the army, in which Arembergius, the Frisian prefect, led the volunteers from that people, he pitched camp not far from the river Sambre, which washes that town with a shallow channel. Soon he seized the suburb and the outwork on this side of the river, and pressed the town with a closer siege. Having placed his artillery and first prepared a suitable position, he began to attack. Roused by this, the French soon pitched their camp nearby under the leadership of the noble Dandelot and then the Constable himself. They sent Dandelot ahead, by the river's downstream course, to a place suitable for relieving the siege, and also considered transferring the rest of their forces to the opposite bank. But the French plan, detected by Lamoral of Egmont, who was in Philip's army, came to nothing. Philibert therefore ordered part of his troops to cross the Sambre and the cavalry to follow at once. Overtaking the French army, which was already sounding the signal to retreat, he cut down the fleeing and disordered ranks, bringing them to near rout, and inflicted a great slaughter. Two thousand five hundred of them, and among them the most noble of the French, lay slain on fields soaked with blood. A huge booty was taken, and almost all the French equipment, arms and siege engines, together with their military standards, fell to the victors. Then Philip, in the first years of his rule and of his youth, achieved such glory, beyond the expectation of men who had predicted otherwise when Charles Caesar laid down the empire. He hastened to the camp at Saint-Quentin. King Henry, who had retreated to Compiègne and was occupied after the defeat only with fortifying positions and seeking help from his allies, was confident. Philip added to the Burgundian dominions the most large and flourishing city... Having thus taken possession of Saint-Quentin, Philip sent Lignaeus Arembergius, the Frisian prefect, with a chosen band of his own men and auxiliary forces, to Le Cateau. Lest he spend the time allotted for conducting and speeding up the operations on fortifying his camp, he suddenly poured out onto the surrounding plains, without any rampart or ditch drawn before them, and attacked the place, which was fortified by nature, with artillery. When part of the wall was suddenly broken down by the force of the machines, he prepared himself to begin the assault. But the garrison, unwarlike of its own accord and broken by the defeat of its allies at Saint-Quentin, and also fearing the impending danger, surrendered itself to Arembergius. Arembergius, having placed a garrison there and settled affairs, returned with his forces to Philip's camp at Saint-Quentin. When the expedition into France had been completed without any unfavourable turn of events, Philip soon formed a plan to lead the army back into Belgium. Suddenly, because of the discomforts of the approaching winter and the harshness of the uncertain air, he broke up the camp and withdrew into winter quarters.
