The Frisians also, since Philip had made use of their service beyond the ordinary, returned home as companions in dangers and sharers in glory, and they produced, as famous in this period at Saint-Quentin as they had been at Metz in the year 1551, an example of loyalty to their prince and of valour, which has been celebrated down to this day by the voice of their people and by a memorable reputation. I find it noted that Charles Caesar...

units.la: Frisiorum fides.
units.tr: The loyalty of the Frisians

units.la: Cæsarem eodem bello Gallico resurgente Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LII. mense Ianuario lustrandis per Frisiam armis Arembergium delegasse, eundemque Arembergium evocatis Leovardiam agrariorum civitatumque Syndicis diem armilustrio ad xiv. Kal. Mart. dixisse. Voluisse quoq; ut Urbanæ Rusticæq; tribus, tum ipsa quoque nobilitas more majorum arma in promptu haberet, ac tertius quisq;, prout fieri soleret, ferreo thorace, lorica, ac gladio, militari lege cingeretur. Tum Iacobus Osius Flandricæ gentis, in Frisia apud Harlinganos agens, ob suspectam, ut tum ferebant tempora, religionem, in carcerem Leovardiæ conjectus, ac non multo post à Senatu Provinciæ regio damnatus, excruciatum per tormenta spiritum acerba morte, & memorabili in extremis constantia effudit. Constat ipsum Philippum Regem datis ad Lalainium Brabantiæ Præfectum Eid. Novembris Antverpiam, quà in urbe Osius vixerat, litteris, de eodem captivo cognovisse, ac ut cum eo lege & ex Edictis Caroli patris ageretur, etiam detectà per Lalainium viri innocentiâ, Senatui per Frisiam regio demandasse. Vulgaris fama fuit eundem Osium Antonij Lavailij Senatoris regij nuper ministrum & Scribam ab hero suo proditum, domesticæ consuetudinis & in Lavailium officij triste præmium & sortem violentæ mortis retulisse. Legem namque asperam Anno cIↄ Iↄ. xxxv. contra Anabaptistas sanxerat Carolus, ut istius sectæ asseclæ, aut fautores, mares capite luerent, fœminæ verò in puteum, fluentemvè demergerentur. Quamobrem & Edicto Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xxxvii. publicato eosdem sectarios vinculis dari, Prætoresque per Provinciam constitutos navatæ operæ testimonium singulis mensibus exhibere suo per Frisiam Senatui sub pœnâ rogatæ legis jusserat. Qui propterea Mennonem quoque Symonium presbyterio apud Witmarsios jam ante functum, post hæresiarcham clam haberi, recipiq; vetuerat, deferentiq;, aut capienti ioo. Carolinorum mercedem ex ærario Cæsaris assignaverat. Neque ullâ magis de causâ Maria Gubernatrix Anno cIↄ Iↄ. liv. convocari Frisiæ Ordines, Hyppolitumque Persinium Præsidem Senatus verba facere in comitio jusserat, quàm ut eadem Secta extirparetur, Ordinesque Provinciæ statuendi in sectarios juris præsidium Cæsaris Præfecto, Senatuiq; commodarent. Criminatus namque Mariæ nomine Persinius erat, novarum religionum semina per Frisiam spargi, nihilq; aliud metuendum esse, quam ut invalescentibus indies sectis avita religio obscuretur. Inter omnes verò pessimam Anabaptistarum esse, cuius id propositum sit specie præstigij, aut simulatæ pietatis regna, & resp. turbare, subversisque legibus, & sublatâ Magistratuum autoritate damnatis moribus, & impiâ ad lubidinem superstitione uti. Hoc modo Floridi Campi cœnobium à fanaticâ gente occupatum, oppressos Monasterienses altosq; vicinos, ut sedem atq; officinam suæ impietati haberet, execrabilemq; dominatum, quem odio Principum & sua stoliditate somniaverat, muris moenibusq; præcinctum tueretur. Ita eosdem quoque sectarios plus quam belluinâ feritate suarum conjugum carnifices, & simul parricidas extitisse, dirâque regni sui imagine tamdiu usos, donec Principum armis repressi, ac in angustum redacti dignas facinoribus suis poenas referrent. Et quo-niam niam interesset humanae societatis, execrandum illud genus in naturâ rerum non extare, caeterum in ipso ortu extingui, ita Carolum Caesarem singularis prudentiae Principem Edictis rescriptisq; suis cavisse, ne in ditionibus suis haberentur, caeterum convicti reprobatae religionis & impietatis ex hominum coetu, tanquam usurâ lucis, & vitae munere indigni, exterminentur. Haec à PerfinioPraesidei v. Eid. Ian. Anno cIↄ Iↄ LVI. propósita. Idcirco Philippus confirmatis jam ante Caroli sanctionibus, exasperatâ Anno cIↄ Iↄ LVI. lege caverat, ut sectarij istiusmodi, pertinaces praecipuè & refractarij, igne punirentur, Senatusq; per Frisiam regius in eundem post Osium ex Edictis statueret. Tum, quod ante Philippus praeconceperat, ne Romanae religioni, quam solam teneri in ditionibus suis Carolus Caesar, & post Philippus sanciverat, aliquid contagij ex proserpentibus per Europam, ut vocabant, haeresibus accederet; Georgius Egmondanus Episcopus Ultraiectinus Gulielmum Lindanum sacrae paginae Doctorem titulo Vicarij per Frisiam potestate, ac Diplomate donavit, eundemq; pro jure, ut aiebat, sedis juris dictionem Ecclesiasticam exercere jussit. Diploma tale erat:
units.tr: I find it noted that in the same French war, which revived in the year 1552, in January, Charles Caesar had appointed Arembergius to review the arms throughout Friesland, and that Arembergius, having summoned the syndics of the agrarian and civic communities to Leeuwarden, had set the day of the muster for the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March. Charles also wished that the urban and rural tribes, and the nobility itself, in the manner of their ancestors, should keep arms at hand, and that every third man, as was customary, should be girded with an iron breastplate, a corselet and a sword, by military law. Then Jacob Ossius, of Flemish stock, working in Friesland among the people of Harlingen, was thrown into prison at Leeuwarden on account of his religion, which was then suspected, as the times were. Not long afterwards he was condemned by the royal Senate of the province, and he gave up his spirit to a bitter death by torture, with a memorable constancy at the end. It is established that Philip the King, by letters sent on the Ides of November to Lalaing, prefect of Brabant, at Antwerp, where Ossius had lived, learned of this captive, and ordered that the case be dealt with according to the law and the edicts of his father Charles. He also ordered the royal Senate in Friesland, once Lalaing had also uncovered the man's innocence, to act accordingly. It was a common report that this same Ossius had been betrayed by his master, Antonius Lavaillius, a recent royal councillor, and that his former minister and secretary, having been drawn into domestic intimacy, received the sorry reward of his service to Lavaillius, and the fate of a violent death. For Charles had enacted a harsh law in the year 1535 against the Anabaptists, that the followers or supporters of that sect, if men, should pay with their heads, while women should be drowned in a well or in a flowing stream. Therefore, by an edict published in the year 1537, he had also ordered these sectaries to be put in chains, and the magistrates appointed throughout the province to give monthly proof of their zealous work to the Senate of Friesland under penalty of the law. For this reason he had also forbidden Menno Simons, who had earlier held the office of elder at Witmarsum, to be kept in secret, after he became a heresiarch, or to be received, and he had assigned a reward of 100 Carolus guilders from the imperial treasury to whoever should inform against him or seize him. Nor for any other reason did Mary, the Regent, in the year 1554, order the Estates of Friesland to be summoned and Hippolytus Persinius, president of the Senate, to speak in the assembly, than that this same sect might be rooted out, and that the Estates of the province might lend to the imperial prefect and the Senate the protection of the law against the sectaries. For Persinius, speaking in Mary's name, had accused them of sowing the seeds of new religions throughout Friesland, and said that nothing was to be feared more than that, as the sects grew stronger day by day, the ancestral religion would be obscured. Among all, he said, the Anabaptists were the worst, whose purpose was, under the appearance of a trick or of feigned piety, to overturn kingdoms and commonwealths, to use the overturning of laws and the removal of the authority of magistrates, depraved morals and a superstition impious in its lust. In this way they had occupied the monastery of Floridus Campus, the Münsterites and the people of the neighbouring Altos, oppressed, to use as the seat and workshop of their impiety, and to protect with walls and ramparts the execrable domination which they had dreamed of out of hatred of princes and their own stupidity. So these same sectaries, executioners of their own wives with more than bestial savagery and at the same time parricides, had made use of this dire image of their kingdom for as long as they were checked by the arms of princes and reduced to a narrow compass, until they paid penalties worthy of their crimes. And since it was in the interest of human society that this detestable kind should not exist in the nature of things, but be extinguished at its very birth, Charles Caesar, a prince of singular prudence, had taken care by his edicts and rescripts that they should not be tolerated in his dominions, but that those convicted of a rejected religion and of impiety should be expelled from the company of men, as unworthy of the usufruct of light and of the gift of life. These things were set forth by Persinius, the president, on the thirteenth of January in the year 1556. Hence Philip, having already confirmed the sanctions of Charles, by a law sharpened in the year 1556 ordered that sectaries of this kind, especially the obstinate and the refractory, should be punished by fire, and that the royal Senate in Friesland should decree against the same, after Ossius, in accordance with the edicts. Then, because Philip had previously resolved that nothing of the contagion of the heresies which, as they called them, were creeping through Europe should attach itself to the Roman religion, which alone Charles Caesar, and afterwards Philip, had decreed should be held in their dominions, George Egmont, bishop of Utrecht, gave to William Lindanus, doctor of sacred Scripture, with the title of vicar and power throughout Friesland, and by a diploma, and ordered him to exercise ecclesiastical jurisdiction, as he said, by right of the see. The diploma was as follows:

units.la: Diploma Lindani.
units.tr: The Lindanus Diploma

units.la: GEorgius Egmondanus Dei & Apostolicae Sedis gratiâ Episcopus Trajectensis, Venerabili & eximio Viro D. Magistro Wilhelmo Lindano, sacrae Theologiae Professori, salutem in Domino, & in commissis debitam adhibere diligentiam de tuâ circumspectione & industriâ & expertâ providentiâ plenam in Domino fidem habentem. Te per Frisiam nostrae jurisdictioni subjectam, nostrum Decanum Commissarium, seu Officialem, & ad ordinariam nostram jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam, ibi nostro nomine exercendam constituimus, deputamus & ordinamus, dantes & concedentes tibi per praesentium tenorem liberam & plenam potestatem, & auctoritatem ac mandatum, generale ac speciale, de & super quibuscunque causis meris, & mixtis, matrimonialibus, civilibus, criminalibus cognoscendi, definiendi, sententiandi & exequendi super quibuscunque criminibus, culpis, delictis, & negligentiis quarumcunque personarum, communitatis vel universitatis ibidem ex officio, vel ad partium instantiam inquirendi, corrigendi & definiendi, in personas, universitates, Ecclesias, parochias & loca praedicta excommunicationis, suspensionis, & interdicti sententias aliasq; censuras & poenas canonicas fulminandi & infligendi, ac per te inflictas & fulminatas absolvendi, suspendendi, relevandi, & tollendi. Invocato etiam ad hoc, si opus fuerit, auxilio brachij secularis, nec non matrimonia clandestine contrahentes, & eosdem intereffentes corrigendi & ab huiusmodi excommunicationis sententiâ, quam propter hoc inciderant, absolvendi, quaecunque monasteria non exempta verò authoritate Apostolicâ nobis commissa, quam praesentibus tibi subdelegamus, visitandi authoritatem, abusus, negligentias & enormia ibidem inventa corrigendi, omniaque alia & singula faciendi & exercendi, quae in praemissis & circa ea fuerint necessaria, seu quotquot opportuna, etiamsi mandatum exigant aliud speciale & quae ad dictorum spectant officium de jure vel consuetudine (causa correctionum & absolutionum occisorum, vulneratorum & immutilatorum dericorum, Ecclesiasticarum personarum, ac violatarum immunitates ecclesiarum & caemiteriorum, aliorumque locorum sacrorum, exceptis, quas nobis specialiter reservamus, contradictores quoslibet & rebelles per censuras Ecclesiasticas comcompescendi, sententias quas praemissorum occasione rite tuleris, ratas habebimus, ac faciemus auctoritate nostrâ inviolabiliter observari praesentibus, usq; ad nostram notariam revocationem duraturis. Datum sub sigillo nostro ad causam praesentem appenso, die ultimâ mensis Julij, Anno Domini millesimo, quinquagesimo septimo.
units.tr: Georgius Egmondanus, by the grace of God and the Apostolic See Bishop of Utrecht, to the venerable and distinguished man, Master Wilhelm Lindanus, Professor of Sacred Theology, greetings in the Lord. Since we have full confidence in the Lord in your circumspection, your diligence in the matters entrusted to you, and your proven prudence, we appoint, depute and ordain you to exercise ecclesiastical jurisdiction in Friesland, which is subject to our authority, in our name, as our Dean, Commissary or Official, for our ordinary jurisdiction. By the tenor of these presents we grant you free and full power, authority and mandate, both general and special, to take cognizance of, decide, pass sentence on and execute all causes, whether purely spiritual, mixed, matrimonial, civil or criminal; to inquire into, correct and decide, whether by office or at the request of a party, all crimes, faults, offences and neglects of any persons, communities or corporations there; and to pronounce and inflict upon persons, corporations, churches, parishes and the aforesaid places sentences of excommunication, suspension and interdict, and other censures and canonical penalties, and to absolve, suspend, relieve and remove those so inflicted and pronounced by you. If need be, you may also call for the aid of the secular arm for this purpose. You may likewise correct those who contract clandestine marriages and those who attend them, and absolve them from the sentence of excommunication they have incurred for this reason. You have authority to visit all monasteries not exempt, committed to us by Apostolic authority, which we subdelegate to you by these presents, and to correct the abuses, negligences and outrages found there; and to do and exercise all other and single things that shall be necessary or as many as expedient in the aforesaid matters and concerning them, even if they require some other special mandate, and which belong by law or custom to the office of the said [visitors] (with the exception of the corrections and absolutions of the slain, the wounded and the maimed, of clerics and ecclesiastical persons, and of violations of the immunities of churches, cemeteries and other sacred places, which we reserve specially to ourselves). We will hold ratified, and will cause to be inviolably observed by our authority, the sentences which you shall duly pronounce on the occasion of the aforesaid matters, and to restrain all contradictors and rebels by ecclesiastical censures, these presents to last until our formal revocation. Given under our seal, appended to the present matter, on the last day of July, in the year of the Lord one thousand five hundred and fifty-seven.

units.la: Quod diploma an Philippo rege instigante Lindano concessum, an auctoritate Egmondani indultum sit, non reperio, hoc saltem constat, Philippum sequenti mense hoc ipsum Valencenis confirmasse die quarto Augusti. Antonium quoq; Perennottum Episcopum Attrebatensem ac Praepositum divae Mariae Trajectensis Ecclesiae mense Iulio signasse. Robertum quoq; de Bergis Episcopum Leodiensem, ac praepositum sancti Salvatoris Trajectensis una cum Iacobo Utenengio Decano sancti Petri, post approbavisse. Hoc vero Philippi diplomate cautum reperio, ne per hoc Lindani diploma moribus antiquis ac consuetudine receptis quid decederet & ne oppidanorum aliorumque privilegijs, tum Abbatum reliquorumq; Ecclesiasticorum jurisdictionibus quid derogaretur. Jus quoq; quod Philippus Senatusq; Regius in causis Ecclesiasticis haberet integrum inviolatumq; foret. Hoc modo Lindanus à Philippo in possessionem sui muneris missus, Ecclesiasticae concordiae destinata, severiore imperio pervertit.
units.tr: Whether this diploma was granted at the instigation of King Philip, with Lindanus, or was issued by the authority of Egmondanus, I do not find. This much is certain: Philip confirmed the same at Valenciennes on 4 August of the following month. I find also that Antonius Perrenotus, Bishop of Arras and provost of the church of St Mary at Utrecht, signed it in July; and afterwards Robertus de Bergis, Bishop of Liège and provost of the church of St Saviour at Utrecht, together with Jacobus Utenengius, dean of St Peter's, approved it. In Philip's own diploma, however, I find a proviso that the Lindanus diploma should not in any way detract from ancient customs and established practice, nor from the privileges of the townsmen and others, nor from the jurisdictions of the abbots and the other ecclesiastics; and that the right which Philip and the royal Senate had in ecclesiastical causes should remain whole and inviolate. In this way Lindanus, sent by Philip into possession of his office, which was destined to restore ecclesiastical harmony, by a harsher rule overturned it.

units.la: Itaq; curante per Belgicam religiones & trahente bellum segnius Philippo, qui cum Pontifice foedus inierat, factum est, ut Henricus Rex Gallorum Caletum ad Iccium portum in finibus Morinorum urbem validam occuparet, submotisq; omni Galliâ (ac si occasione Burgundicae societatis eorum per Galliam dominationi periodum tum fortuna pararet) Anglorum praesidijs, Divodurum Guisius cum valido exercitu positis ad Mosellam castris obsideret. Quapropter Philippus, velut excusso per discrimen torpore, qui etiam incubante Belgicae Gallorum exercitu de mittendo Romam Francisco Sonnio, nuper per Frisiam Inquisitore cogitabat, quo obsessis subveniret, repente copias contraxit, missis in Provincias, qui auxilia concirent, exercitumq; in bellum cogerent ocyus. Tum ne miles stipendij, & juxta animi egeret, ageretque laxius, demandato Praefectis Praesidibusque Provinciarum negotio populum tributum rogavit, eaque de re v. Eid. April. litteras in Frisiam ad Arembergium dedit. Qui propterea communicatis cum Senatu regio, qui tum comitiorum dies ordinabat, Philippi litteris, ad x'i. Kal. Maij Frisiae Ordines Leovardiam convenire fecit, Carolumq; Nitzenium virum Equestris dignitatis, & (ablegato ante annum Ultrajectum Hyppolito Persinio) Senatus tum Praesidem verba facere jussit. Ibi Nitzenius vir ut auctoritate ac facundiâ, ita (quod jam ante Carolo Caesare procuratorem Fisci Regij per provinciam egisset) peritiâ rerum excellens à Caroli Philippique regum in Frisios affectu orsus, periculosi temporis conditionem cum anteacti fortunâ composuit. Frisios quippe à recepto Carolo Principe faelices diu annos pace, & legibus florentes egisse, inturbataq; domi quiete usos Francisci Henricique Galliae regum vafris, & perniciosis consilijs subfuisse. Eos aliena namq; invadendi caeca cupidine impulsos bellum semper ab occasione caepisse, ruptisq; toties foederum sacris nullâ lege, aut conventione coercitos, ut veteris in Burgungundos odij, ita cupidinis professionem patefacere. Hoc modo Anno c Io. Io. xxxviii. decennales inducias per Frisiam solenni more promulgatas, easdemq; à Gallo violatas, mox Anno cIo. Io. xliv. repetitas, infidam pacem, & brevem, ut plurimum, circuitum habuisse. Tempus quoq; quinquennalibus inducijs pridem praefinitum eodem Gallo autore abrumpi, stratáq; armis via dubiam partium fortunam victorias damnis cladibusq; miscuisse. Nunc vero rem in summum discrimen adducam. Occupatum quippe à Gallis Caletum, & Anglos Philippi socios maritimis Galliæ, & littorali tractu submotos, nihilque aliud infstare, quàm ut Divoduro Gallicis insuper armis capto, reliqua Gallorum, & victrix manus in Pleumosios ac interiora Flandriæ caeterarumque Provinciarum pergat, depulsaq; avitis sedibus, aut excisa Belgica gente Philippum Principem possessione Burgundicæ domus exuat, veteri odio, & novo conatu non improspere caepto. Itaque usitato gentium more quibus necessitas mali semper remedium extorsisset, cbstandum consilijs hostium esse, & subveniendum ultimo exitio utili liberalitate, qua Principis imperium, patriæ sacra atque leges, privatorum pignora, atq; possessiones in tuto sint. Hæc Nitzenius. Caeterum Ordines agrarij sive quod Anno cIo. Io. liv. Carolo Caesari honorarium (ueq; enim de tributo loquutus erat Nitzenius) sexagenta millium aureorum justis pensionibus addixissent, sive quod fastidium declinantis à libertate majorum Imperij ureret, postulato Arembergij aegrius assensere. Recordabantur namque majores suos Carolo Caesari praeter agrum Biltanum, quem vectigalem ei reverentiâ Imperij fecerant, quatuordecim aureorum florenorum millia quotannis eâ lege ac conditione depactos, ut omnem Frisiam à Stavria in Gerricomium, qui Lavicæ amni imponitur, pontem, adversum externa arma, suis etiam viribus, & illo Provinciæ subsidio, defenderet. Caviisse quoque eosdem Anno cIo. Io. xxiv. ut ulterioribus actionibus Carolus abstineret, nulloq; titulo, aut specie, imponendis genti Friscæ novis oneribus se daret. Ab eo etiam fuisse, ut Caroli cum Imperio Romano, & Provincijs Belgicæ initam conventionem Anno cIo. Io. xlix. Frisij rejecerint, ipsque Maria Gubernatrix secessionem metuens, nihil acturos Frisios praeter quam proprio & arbitrario motu de speciali Caesaris Mandato rescripserit. Oppidanorum verò Delegatis, (in quibus pro Leovardiensibus Serapium Haniam, Iacobum Ægidium, Iacobum Sibrandium, & Dyonisium Wingiam, Consules, Tzomerum Vibenium, Oldermannum, & Andream Ocnonium pro Snecensibus, Adrianum Michaëlium pro Harlinganis, Nicolaum Hansonium pro Franequeranis, Regnerum Annium, pro Bolsuerdijs, Theodorum Theodoretum Oldermannum, & Hermannum Roswinckelium pro Doccomijs, Buwonem Diorræum, & Ulpium Nicolaum, pro Worcomijs, & Regnero Siboldio Delegato Hindelopæ, Scelconem Martinium pro Slotanis, Gajum Andreæ pro Staurijs, & Ausonium Popma pro Ilstanis fuisse comperio) alia, ab Agrarijs, mens erat. Quamobrem illi sive aemulatione in eosdem Agrarios, (quibuscum in constituenda tum Reipub. formâ dissidebant) sive affectu in Principem, negotio Dyonisio Wingiæ, Tzomero Vibenio, Adria-
units.tr: Thus, while religious strife was being stirred up throughout Belgium, and the war was being waged rather sluggishly by Philip, who had entered an alliance with the Pope, it came about that Henry, King of the French, seized Calais, a strong city, at the port of Ardres in the territory of the Morini, and, with the English garrisons removed from all of France, Guise besieged Thionville with a strong army, having pitched camp on the Moselle, as though fortune were then offering the French an opportunity to bring to an end the rule of the Burgundian house over France. Therefore Philip, as if roused from his torpor by the danger, who even while the French army lay in Belgium had been thinking of sending Francis Sonnius, lately Inquisitor in Friesland, to Rome, to bring aid to the besieged, suddenly gathered forces, sending men into the provinces to raise auxiliaries and to press the army into the field the more swiftly. Then, lest the soldiers lack pay and the enthusiasm of their spirit and act more loosely, he entrusted the matter to the prefects and governors of the provinces and asked the people for a tax; and on this matter he wrote a letter to Arenberg in Friesland on 9 April. Arenberg therefore, having communicated Philip's letter to the royal Senate, which was then fixing the days of the assembly, caused the Estates of Friesland to convene at Leeuwarden on 21 April, and ordered Carolus Nitzenius, a man of knightly rank, and (since Hippolytus Persinius had been sent to Utrecht a year before) the then President of the Senate, to address them. There Nitzenius, a man excellent both in authority and in eloquence, and also (because he had already served as procurator of the royal fisc throughout the province under Charles the Emperor) excellent in experience of affairs, began with the attitude of the kings Charles and Philip towards the Frisians, and set out the condition of the perilous time alongside the fortunes of the past. The Frisians, he said, had lived for many years happily in peace and under the laws since they received Prince Charles, and, enjoying undisturbed quiet at home, had been subject to the crafty and destructive counsels of the French kings Francis and Henry. For, driven by a blind desire to invade what belonged to others, they had always begun wars from opportunity, and, though so often bound by the sacred oaths of treaties, were restrained by no law or convention; and, just as they showed their old hatred of the Burgundians, so they revealed their avowed greed. In this way, in the year 1538, the ten-year truce proclaimed through Friesland with the customary solemnity, and violated by the Frenchman, was soon renewed in 1544, yet it had for the most part an unfaithful peace and a brief duration. The term of the five-year truce, too, which had long since been fixed, was broken by the same Frenchman's instigation, and the road having been cleared by arms, the uncertain fortune of the parties mingled victories with losses and disasters. Now, however, I shall bring the matter to the highest peril. Calais, occupied by the French, and the English, allies of Philip, removed from the maritime and coastal region of France, and nothing else threatens than that, with Thionville also taken by French arms, the remaining forces of the French and their victorious army should advance into the Pleumosii and into the interior of Flanders and the other provinces, and, driving out the people from their ancestral seats, or having exterminated the Belgian nation, should strip Philip, the Prince, of possession of the Burgundian house, an enterprise undertaken with an old hatred and a new attempt not unsuccessful. Therefore, according to the customary practice of nations, to whom necessity of evil has always forced a remedy, the counsels of the enemy must be resisted, and the last ruin must be averted by a useful generosity, by which the authority of the Prince, the sacred things and laws of the country, the pledges and possessions of private citizens may be kept safe. So spoke Nitzenius. However, the landed Estates, whether because in the year 1554 they had assigned sixty thousand gold pieces to Charles the Emperor as an honorarium, by regular payments (for Nitzenius spoke not of a tax), or because a distaste for abandoning the liberty of their ancestors burned within them, assented to Arenberg's demand with some reluctance. For they remembered that their ancestors, besides the Bilt territory, which they had made tributary to him out of reverence for the Empire, had bound themselves to Charles for fourteen thousand gold florins a year, on the condition and agreement that he would defend all Friesland, from Staveren to the bridge at Gerkesklooster, which is placed over the river Lauwers, against foreign arms, with their own strength as well as with that aid of the province. They had also provided, in the year 1524, that Charles should refrain from further proceedings and should not, under any title or pretext, impose new burdens on the Frisian people. It was also from this that the Frisians, in 1549, rejected the agreement made by Charles with the Roman Empire and the Belgian provinces, and Mary the Governess, fearing secession, wrote that the Frisians would do nothing beyond what they did of their own accord and at their own discretion, by special mandate of the Emperor. Of the delegates of the townsmen (among whom I find that for Leeuwarden Serapius Hania, Jacobus Aegidius, Jacobus Sibrandius and Dionysius Wingia were consuls; Tzomerus Vibenius, Oldermannus, and Andreas Ocnonius for Sneek; Adrianus Michaelius for Harlingen; Nicolaus Hansonius for Franeker; Regnerus Annius for Bolsward; Theodorus Theodoretus, Oldermannus, and Hermannus Roswinckelius for Dokkum; Buwo Diorraeus and Ulpius Nicolaus for Workum; Regnerus Siboldius, delegate for Hindeloopen; Scelco Martinius for Sloten; Gajus Andreae for Stavoren; and Ausonius Popma for Ilst), the intention was otherwise. Therefore they, whether from rivalry with those same landed Estates (with whom they disagreed on the form of the commonwealth at that time), or from affection for the Prince, committed the business to Dionysius Wingia, Tzomerus Vibenius, Adria-

units.la: Adriano Michaëlio, & Regnero Annio commisso, decretum de præstando subsidio perscripsere; honorariumque Philippo pro modo agrorum suorum, quos ipsi cæterique oppidani jure dominij per Provinciam tenerent, tum territoriorum Urbicorum quantitate, ac juris sui termino depacti sunt. Rogavere insuper Arembergium Senatumq; regium, ut de eo ad Philippum regem referant, deq; Oppidanorum promptitudine, si forte Agrarij dissentiant, testentur. Hæc v i i i. Kal. Maij perscripta, & à Tzomero Vibenio Rollema, D. Wingia, Adriano Michaëlio, & Regnero Annio Leovardiæ confirmata. Cæterum an Gallicæ expeditioni plenius subventum sit, in indigestis illorum temporum actis non reperio. Mihi verisimile est, Ordines Agrarios, ne discrepare illâ temporum teneritudine ab Oppidanorum sententiâ viderentur, consensum interposuisse, opeque tributi, honorarijve, quod è Frisiâ cæterisque Provincijs subministratum puto, vergente Augusto, stipendia veterano militi assignata.
units.tr: Adriano Michaëlio and Regnerus Annius being entrusted with the matter, they drew up a decree on providing aid. They agreed on an honorarium for Philip, in proportion to the size of the fields that they and the other townsmen held by right of ownership throughout the province, and to the extent of the urban territories and the limit of their jurisdiction. They further asked Arenberg and the royal Council to report this to King Philip, and to testify to the townsmen's readiness in case the Landowners should dissent. This was written down on the 8th day before the Kalends of May, and confirmed at Leeuwarden by Tzomerus Vibenius of Rollema, D. Wingia, Adrianus Michaëlis and Regnerus Annius. Whether the French expedition was more fully supported, however, I do not find in the unarranged records of those times. It seems likely to me that the Landowning orders, lest they appear to differ in opinion from the townsmen in such a delicate time, gave their consent, and that the money from the tax or honorarium, which I think was supplied from Friesland and the other provinces, was assigned to the veteran soldiers as the summer waned.

units.la: Tum Philippus acceptâ dediti Divoduri famâ, Thermumq; nobilem Gallum Pleumosijs imminere, Emanuelem Philibertum Belgicæ Præfectum cum parte copiarum in Condrusios præmisit, commeatumque ut & annonam, Edicto ea de re Leovardiæ xiv. Kal. Iul. publicato, è Frisia fertilissimâque Lavicam inter Flevumque orâ comportari in castra jussit. Post Emanuele Philiberto in Mediomatricum finibus relicto, Lamoralium Egmondanum virum illustrium natalium, & gestarum nuper ad Quintinum rerum gloriâ clarum, Grevelingam cum potissimâ exercitus parte ablegavit, gerendisq; cum imperio rebus præfecit. Ibi Thermus Gallus castra quoq; haud magno terrarum spatio discreta posuerat. Qui ubi circumventum se in hostico videt, Egmondanumq; animum pugnæ præferre, de receptu cogitavit. Quare relabente vicini maris æstu, & superato Ada amne sensim retrocessit, prémenteque tergum exercitùs Egmondano aciem instruere pro naturâ loci, temporisque coactus est.
units.tr: Then Philip, having received word of the surrender of Divodurum, and that the noble Frenchman Thermus was threatening the Pleumosii, sent ahead into the Condrusi Emanuel Philibert, prefect of Belgium, with part of the forces. By an edict published at Leeuwarden on the 14th day before the Kalends of July, he ordered that provisions and grain be brought into the camp from fertile Friesland and the shore between Lavicum and the Flevus. After leaving Emanuel Philibert in the territory of the Mediomatrici, he sent Lamoral of Egmont, a man of illustrious birth and famed for his recent exploits at St Quentin, to Gravelines with the greater part of the army, and placed him in charge of affairs with full command. There the Frenchman Thermus had also pitched his camp, not far away. When he saw himself surrounded in enemy territory, and saw that Egmont preferred battle, he considered retreating. So, as the tide of the nearby sea came in, and crossing the river Aa, he gradually withdrew; but with Egmont pressing on his rear, he was compelled by the nature of the place and the time to draw up his line.

units.la: Tum Egmondanus pro concione verba fecit, formatisque Ordinibus signum pugnæ dari jussit. Itaq; acies commissæ tamdiu dubiâ fortunâ & miro virtutis certamine pugnavere, donec Galli à præsidiarijs Anglorum navibus impetiti, equitatu insuper præter morem Gallicarum turmarum tardo, & mox in fugam acto peditum quoque ordines luxati in diversa spargerentur. Mille & quingentos Gallorum cecidisse fidus istorum temporum Scriptor annotavit. Thermus ipse gravi vulnere accepto, prædam omnem, quam Flandriæ municipijs extorserat, tum tormenta, signaque militaria Egmondano reliquit, cuius prudentiæ & virtuti illius ferè ævi Scriptores victoriam asignavere. Notat Cloutingius perlatâ Leovardiam Egmondani de Gallis victoriâ grates in templis publicè numini decretas, peractaque re divina populum sacris locis effusum, alterum illum Gallicæ cladis diem communi lætitiâ insignivisse.
units.tr: Then Egmont addressed the assembly, and having formed the ranks, ordered the signal for battle to be given. The lines engaged and fought for a long time with doubtful fortune and a remarkable contest of valour, until the French, attacked by the English ships stationed there, and with their cavalry, contrary to custom, slow, and soon put to flight, and their infantry lines broken, were scattered in different directions. A faithful writer of those times recorded that fifteen hundred Frenchmen fell. Thermus himself, having received a grave wound, left to Egmont all the booty he had extorted from the towns of Flanders, and also the artillery and military standards. Writers of almost that age ascribed the victory to Egmont's prudence and valour. Cloutingius notes that when news of Egmont's victory over the French reached Leeuwarden, thanks were publicly offered to God in the churches; and, the divine service being performed, the people poured out into the sacred places, and that second day of the French defeat was marked by common rejoicing.

units.la: Tum Philippus, ut eventum rerum specularetur, Attrebati diu commoratus, ultrò per ætatem, & regios spiritus (per quos ardua res, & fortunæ etiam imperio subjectæ factu faciles videntur) maximè verò recentis victoriæ fiduciâ luxurians de maturanda totis viribus, valida in Galliam expeditione cogitavit. Quare conquisito per omnem oram milite, atrematisnuatisque urbium præsidijs, ipse rectà in hosticum duxit, castraque prope Dorlentem Gallicæ ditionis oppidum metatus est. Pedestrem exercitum tricena millia, equestrem duodena conficiebant. In comitatu quoque regio clarissimi per Germaniam, Belgicam atque Hispaniam, Duces spectabantur, Ioannemque Ligneum Arembergium Frisiæ Præfectum, sua etiam provincià Philippi litteræ, tum clarissimæ expeditionis fortuna, velut optuma adipiscendæ gloriæ materies, exciverat. Militum quemque ut sacramenti religio, ita exoluta jam ante provinciarum subsidijs stipendia, universos virtutis & gloriæ contemplatio ad omne officium, & simul discrimen accendebant. Erant quoque, qui in opulenta hostium castra, & sumptuosam, etiam in bello, Gallorum luxuriem oculos converterent, quam Henricus rex, locato ad Petram pontem exercitu, haud vanà quoq; suarum virium fiduciâ ostentabat. Apparatus quoque Philippi castrorum multiplex, tormentorum machinarumq; variæ species, &, quod gerendo continuandoque bello primum esse solet, commeatuum ac annonæ copia è Frisiorum orâ, vicinoque tractu habebatur. Hoc modo comparatis necessarijs, & officio cuiq; militarium Ducum assignato, rem, prout erat, ultimi discriminis Philippus aggressus est, Dorlentemq; oppidum naturâ loci munitum, etiam Henrico rege stativa castrorum propiùs habente, oppugnare constituit. Cæterum persuasus à purpuratis, qui reprimendum lubricæ ætatis, & inconsulti impetûs ardorem sanioribus consilijs autumabant, cæpto destitit, contentusq; magnificâ castrorum, & potentiæ ostentatione ad Audiæ fluminis ripam haud procul Henrici castris desedit. Ita duorum potentissimorum Europæ regum capita, & fortunam angustis terrarum spatijs, appetitus gloriæ, & magnarum rerum insatiabilis cupido circumscripserat. Quare periculi metus, & sollicitudo obversantium extremorum (in quæ facilius, quam res prosperi ominis humanarum mentium imbecillitas se deflectit) omnium animos pervasit, ac si de alterutro regum subvertendo, & tot gentium internecione præceps proterendis rebus fortuna laboraret. Neq; aliud momenta temporum allatura videbantur, cum præter spem mortalium, quos vel arcano fatorum imperio duci tum observatum fuit, consilium cæptandæ pacis, velut cælo missum, animos regum, atq; ingenia occupavit. Itaq; Legatis Insulam Flandrorum misis, mox evoluto Octobri mense imperato armistitio castra mota, copiæque aut impetratâ missione exauctoratæ, aut in hyberna circa Vergiliarum occasum reductæ, non obscurum futuræ pacis auspicium fecere. Cuius belli Gallici mole, etsi haud dubiè Provinciæ gravarentur, ita maximè metuebant prudentiores, ne Philippus, stratis cum Gallorum rege odijs, & diuturnâ dissensione in fœdus, aut, ut Principumferè solet, in affinitatem versa, insitâ animi fluctuantiumque annorum mobilitate, exequendis per vim, quæ jam ante vulgaverat, Caroli Edictis se accingeret. Id nàmque curiosæ mentes, & velut anxiâ fatorum indagatione suspensæ secius interpretabantur, quod per Hispaniam equitum peditumq; delectus haberi dicerentur, copiæque Hispanorum, tanquam coloniam facturæ, Gallici belli prætextu, in Provincias Belgicæ magno numero se effunde-
units.tr: Then Philip, to watch how events turned out, stayed a long time at Arras. Partly this was because of his age and his royal spirit, through which difficult things, even those subject to fortune, seem easy to accomplish; but especially, exulting in confidence from the recent victory, he thought of pressing an expedition into France with all his strength and without delay. So, having gathered soldiers from every shore and strengthened the garrisons of the cities, he led the army straight into enemy territory and pitched camp near Dourlens, a town under French rule. The infantry numbered thirty thousand, the cavalry twelve thousand. In the royal retinue were seen the most famous commanders from Germany, Belgium and Spain, and Johann of Ligne, Arenberg, prefect of Friesland; Philip's letters had summoned him, and the glorious fortune of the expedition, as the best material for winning glory, had roused him from his own province too. Each soldier was spurred on to every duty, and at the same time to danger, by the religion of his oath, by the stipends already paid out from the provinces' subsidies, and by the contemplation of virtue and glory held out to all. There were also some who turned their eyes to the wealthy enemy camp and to the sumptuous luxury of the French, even in war, which King Henry, having stationed his army at Pont-à-Pierre, displayed with no empty confidence in his own forces. Philip's camp equipment was also varied, with many kinds of artillery and machines and, what is usually first in waging and sustaining war, a supply of provisions and grain was at hand from the Frisian shore and the nearby region. With the necessities thus prepared, and each military commander assigned his duty, Philip undertook the matter, which was, as it stood, of the utmost danger, and resolved to assault Dourlens, a town fortified by its location, while King Henry held his fixed camp rather close by. But he was persuaded by the nobles, who thought the ardour of his youthful and rash impulse should be restrained by wiser counsel, and so he abandoned the undertaking. Content with the magnificent display of camp and power, he settled on the bank of the river Oise, not far from Henry's camp. Thus the fortunes of the two most powerful kings of Europe were confined within narrow bounds of land by the desire for glory and the insatiable appetite for great enterprises. Fear of danger and anxiety about the extremes that threatened (into which the weakness of human minds turns more readily than toward a prosperous outcome) spread through all minds, as if fortune were labouring to overthrow one of the two kings and to ruin headlong so many nations by slaughter. Nor did the course of events seem about to bring anything else, when, beyond all human hope, and as if by a secret decree of fate, the plan of seeking peace, as though sent from heaven, took hold of the minds and dispositions of the kings. So envoys were sent to the island of Flanders, and soon, the month of October having run out, an armistice was ordered. The camps were moved, and the troops were either discharged with their release obtained, or led back into winter quarters about the setting of the Pleiades, which gave no small sign of a coming peace. Although the Provinces were undoubtedly burdened by the weight of this French war, the wiser sort feared most that Philip, once his hatreds with the French king were laid to rest and the long dissension turned into alliance or, as usually happens with princes, into kinship, would, through the restlessness of mind natural to fluctuating years, set himself to carry out by force the edicts of Charles that he had already made public. For curious minds, hanging in anxious inquiry as if into fate, interpreted it otherwise, because it was said that levies of horse and foot were being held in Spain, and Spanish forces, as though about to found a colony, were pouring into the Belgian Provinces in great numbers under the pretext of the French war.

units.la: Philippus præliium parat, & Gallia.
units.tr: Philip prepares for war, and France.

units.la: Conventus Insulæ Flandrorum. derent. Quamobrem dissitis oris, & longè post Pyrenæos non spiculatores tantum, custodesque regij corporis, sed copias armatorum, (etiam silente ad tempus Gallico Bello) evocari, ac per præsidia urbium disponi ægrius habitum, Philippumq; velut recentium pastorum, monitorumq; Caroli patris immemorem, novum imperium non favore fidissimi populi, sed peregrino stipatore, & præsidiario milite inchoare. Reperio in actis publicis, majores nostros Carolo Cæsare & Philippo rerum potiuntibus, quotannis è conventibus suis delegasse, qui læsæ libertati remedia peterent, omnibusq; quæ per dominantes abusu potentiæ, inrepserant, actis prolatis Cæsarem & Philippum, eorundemq; Præfectos decentis & simul exorbitantis imperij commonuisse. Comitium quoq; x I. Kal. Maii Leovardiæ habitum perpensisq;, quæ aut arcendo populi servitio, aut comprimendæ dominantium licentiæ profutura credebantur, tuendo juri publico, tam in Ecclesiasticis, quam politicis causis delectos. Decretum quoq; ut in Commissarios regios, Decanosq; inquirant delegati, faciantq;, dum de advocato provinciæ constituendo qui regio opponeretur deliberatum foret.
units.tr: Assembly of the Island of Flanders. Therefore, with distant shores, and far beyond the Pyrenees, it was harder to bear that not only spearmen and the guards of the royal person, but also troops of armed men, were being summoned, and disposed through the garrisons of the cities, even while the French war lay silent for the time being. Philip, as if forgetful of his recent shepherds of the people and of the warnings of his father Charles, was beginning a new rule not with the favour of a most loyal people, but with foreign attendants and garrison soldiers. I find in the public records that our ancestors, while Charles Caesar and Philip held power, sent delegates each year from their assemblies to seek remedies for injured liberty; and by bringing forward the acts, they reminded Caesar and Philip and their prefects of the proper yet exorbitant extent of their authority, and of everything that had crept in through the abuse of power by the rulers. An assembly was also held at Leeuwarden on the 11th day before the Kalends of May, and, having weighed what was thought useful either to ward off the servitude of the people or to check the licence of the rulers, it chose men to defend public law in both ecclesiastical and civil causes. It was also decided that the delegates should inquire into the royal commissioners and deans, and act, until it had been deliberated who should be appointed as the province's advocate to oppose the king's.

units.la: Magnam quoque & sub Carolo Cæsare institutam jam ante, dissensionem tum viguisse, repetitisq; in Senatu Philippi, quæ controversa erant, variös, prout affecti erant, animorum motus observatos. Volentibus Agrarijs, ut tota dominationis vis ad se pertineret, Oppidanisq; à corpore Provinciæ seclusi, tributa arbitrio Agrariorum conferrent. Ita domi forisq; dissensionibus occasiones quærebantur. Cæterum infidam Belgicæ concordiam importuna maximè Caroli Cæsaris, qui xı. Kal. Octob. naturæ legem impleverat; mors luxavit. Qui depósito imperio, etsi in Hispaniæ solitudinem amotus, Philippi tamen filij ponderosa consilia, & teneriores annos senili prudentiâ moderabatur. Quare vivo Carolo florens adhuc & sine motu Belgica, postquam lentâ febre sublatum in Hispaniâ Provinciæ flevere, maximi Cæsaris monumento libertas simul, & quies populi se conclusit. Unde publicus, domesticusque per Provincias mæror, dubium an Caroli Cæsaris immaturum funus, an instantia temporum præsagæ mentes lugerent. Idcircò & per primarias Belgicæ urbes tristes exequiarum pompæ, & mœrentium turbarum varij processus spectabantur, quos paternis manibus, ac (ut mihi videtur) fato quodam futurę civilium bellorum tempestati Philippus filius procurabat. Funus quoque Carolo Cæsari Leovardiæ factum, deductumq; ad D. Viti fanum, lamentantium præficarum, ut in Principum exequijs solet, luctumque universæ multitudinis secum traxit. Funestas quoque faces per Leovardiam urbem præluxisse funeri ferunt, adornatisq;, illorum temporum ritu, per delubra altaribus, magni Cæsaris umbræ, velut æternitatem ingressæ, Præsulum, Flaminumq; ministerijs consecrationes decretas. Gemma scribit, admirandum venti vorticem mense Iulio, toti Belgicæ vicinisq; locis incumbentem, ædificia passim arboresq; disjecisse, ortumq; rursus mense Augusto Cometen Carolo Cæsari imminentia extrema portendisse. Quamvis non ignorem, multos scriptores, priori Cometæ, qui anno quinquagesimo sexto magno cum horrore gentium illuxerat, Carolinæ mortis prædictionem assignasse, moreq; mortalium, quibus extraordinaria naturæ opera ad Principum exitus referre mos est, omnia illa, quæ cælo terrisq; apparuere, Carolino excessui applicata. Ut ut sit, novum & insolitum non fuit, tanti Principis obitum diversis naturæ prodigijs signatum, laboraturamq; eius morte tot gentium securitatem laboribus cælestium attributam. Strada notat, Carolum Cæsarem continuâ mortis & vergentis vitæ meditatione imaginarium funus suo in Secreto instituisse, solenniq; more, ac si rebus humanis excessisset, elatum, veri funeris secuturos apparatus, prævio, quasi spectaculo, oculis suis delibasse. Quæ res etsi religionis plena præludenti ad æterna crederetur, mihi tamen à superstitione aliena non fuisse videtur, quod præter commune mortalium officium, seria & severa futuræ mortis argumenta ludicris exemplis, velut mox ultra numine, dehonestaverit. Idem Gemma tradit, hyemem imbribus tempestatibusq; valde fædam fuisse, ipsceq; crinito, quod arserat, sidere discutiendis aëris squalloribus invalido, novis mortalium aut saltem insolitis morbis viam ortumq; præstructum. Eodem quoq; anno magnum frugum ubertatem fuisse, populumq; benignitate cæli abusum, luxu immodesto proventum felicioris anni prodegisse. Eandem quoq; anni, qui subsecutus est, temperiem fuisse, publicâq; terrarum fæcunditate, vitia quoq; hominum istius ætatis increvisse, præstruente quasi providentia, ut eventura tempestas nostro merito aut errore accidisse crederetur. Igitur Philippus peractis, mense Decembri, patri inferijs, Mariæ quoque amitæ, nuper Belgicarum Provinciarum Gubernatrici, post Mariæ conjugi (quæ durante legatorum ad sanciendam cum Gallorum rege pacem x v. Kal. Nov. repentinâ morte decesserat) justa persolvit, honorarioq; funeri per Frisiam faciendo tempus ordinavit. Iussit quoq;, ut toto quintiduo ternis in diem horis campani æris per omnem Provinciam pultatio fieret, diesq; postremus celebrandis Mariæ exequijs decerneretur. Qui casus, ut toti Belgicæ funestus, ita Phillippo regi maxume luctuosus fuit. Eius morte namque factum est, ut infælicis & non durabilis matrimonij pactione Anglicam inter Belgicamque gentem inita societas dissolveretur, Philippusque sociâ vitæ & consorte rerum orbus, Francici Anglicique regni titulis insignibusque è jure connubialium codicillorum cederet. Ijs quippe perscriptum erat, ut Mariâ sine liberis decedente, Angliæ, Franciæque regnorum titulos, (quorum speciem magis quam vim, vivâ etiam & superstite Mariâ tenuerat) Philippus amitteret, usurpandisque insignibus abstineret. Quapropter Philippus Elisabethâ Mariæ sorore ad regnum Angliç xvii. Kalend. Febr. evectâ, de omittendis Francicis Anglicisque titulis per Emanuelem Philibertum ad Senatum per Frisiam regium scripsit, eundemque vetere judicialium actorum formulâ uti jussit. Litteræ Philiberti Prid. Kal. April. Leovardiam missæ. Itaque Philippi regis consilia eo tum spectabant, ut concussum bello Gallico, & accisum Mariæ mortæ principatum, stabili, & incorruptâ pace muniret, Mariâque conjuge fato extinctâ, novâ matrimonij felicitate regiæ domus orbitatem repararet. Quare repetito fœcialium conventu, etsi dubio adhuc exitu consilia regum fortuna libraret, pax tandem Cambresij ix. Kal. April. facta. Traditum commentarijs est, Viglium Zuichemum
units.tr: A great dissension, already begun under Charles Caesar, was also flourishing at that time. When the disputed matters were raised again in Philip's Senate, the varying movements of minds were observed, according to how each man was disposed. The Agrarians wanted the whole force of government to rest with themselves, and the townsmen, shut out from the body of the Province, were to pay taxes at the Agrarians' discretion. Thus occasions for conflict were sought both at home and abroad. Moreover, the untimely death of Charles Caesar, who had fulfilled the law of nature on 21 September, broke up the uneasy harmony of the Netherlands. Though he had withdrawn into the solitude of Spain after laying down his power, he had still tempered the weighty plans of his son Philip, and his youthful years, with senile prudence. So while Charles lived, the Netherlands flourished and remained undisturbed. But after the Provinces had wept for him, who had been carried off by a slow fever in Spain, liberty and the people's peace seemed to be enclosed together in the monument of the great Caesar. Hence there was public and private mourning throughout the Provinces, and people doubted whether they were lamenting the untimely funeral of Charles Caesar or whether their minds, foreseeing the coming times, were grieving. So through the leading cities of the Netherlands sad funeral processions and the varied tumults of mourners were seen, which Philip, the son, directed with paternal shades, and, as seems to me, by a certain fate, for the coming storm of civil wars. Charles's funeral was also held at Leeuwarden and carried to the shrine of St Vitus, and it drew with it the wailing of hired mourners, as is customary at the funerals of princes, and the grief of the whole multitude. They also say that funeral torches shone through the city of Leeuwarden, and that, with altars decked out in the custom of those times in the shrines, consecrations were decreed by the ministries of prelates and priests for the shade of the great Caesar, as if it had entered eternity. Gemma writes that a remarkable whirlwind, falling in July on the whole of the Netherlands and neighbouring places, scattered buildings and trees everywhere; and that in August a comet, rising again, portended the last things impending for Charles Caesar. Although I am not unaware that many writers assigned the prediction of Charles's death to the earlier comet, which had shone with great horror on the nations in the fifty-sixth year, and that, following the custom of mortals who are wont to refer extraordinary works of nature to the ends of princes, all those things that appeared in heaven and on earth were attributed to the death of Charles. However that may be, it was not new or unusual that the death of so great a prince was marked by various prodigies of nature, and that the security of so many nations, which was about to suffer by his death, was ascribed to heavenly signs. Strada notes that Charles Caesar, through continual meditation on death and on the passing of life, held an imaginary funeral in his private retreat, and, in the customary manner as if he had departed from human affairs, was carried out, and by way of a foretaste, as it were a spectacle, he tasted with his own eyes the preparations for a real funeral to follow. Although this practice, full of religion as it was thought to be, in preparation for eternal things, does not seem to me alien to superstition, since, beyond the common duty of mortals, he dishonoured the serious and severe signs of future death with playful examples, as if by a power above. The same Gemma reports that the winter was very foul with rain and storms, and that, since the comet that had blazed was too weak to dispel the murkiness of the air, a way was prepared for new or at least unusual diseases among mortals. In the same year there was also great abundance of crops, and the people, abusing the kindness of the sky, squandered the yield of the more fortunate year in immoderate luxury. The following year likewise had the same mildness, and with the public fruitfulness of the lands the vices of men of that age also increased, as if providence were arranging things so that the coming storm might be believed to have come by our merit or error. Therefore, when the rites for his father had been completed in December, Philip also paid the due rites to his aunt Mary, lately Governess of the Belgian Provinces, and afterwards to Mary's husband, who had died suddenly on 17 October while the envoys were making peace with the king of the French; and he appointed a time for the honorary funeral to be held throughout Friesland. He also ordered that for five whole days, three times a day, the bell of the bronze be rung throughout the whole Province, and that a last day be fixed for celebrating Mary's funeral. This event, as it was mournful for the whole of the Netherlands, was especially sorrowful for King Philip. For by her death the alliance between the English and Belgian peoples, made by the agreement of an unhappy and short-lived marriage, was dissolved, and Philip, bereft of his partner in life and in affairs, lost the titles and insignia of the kingdoms of France and England, which came from the law of the marriage codicils. For it had been written in them that if Mary died without children, Philip would lose the titles of the kingdoms of England and France, which he had held in name rather than in power even while Mary was alive and surviving, and that he should abstain from using the insignia. Therefore, when Elizabeth, Mary's sister, was raised to the kingdom of England on 16 January, Philip wrote through Emmanuel Philibert to the Senate at Friesland, ordering that the English and French titles be dropped, and that the Senate use the old formula for judicial acts. The letters of Philibert were sent to Leeuwarden on 31 March. Thus the plans of King Philip were then directed to this end: to secure, with a stable and unbroken peace, the principate that had been shaken by the Gallic war and diminished by Mary's death, and, with Mary as his wife taken by fate, to repair the childlessness of the royal house by a new happy marriage. Therefore, after a repeated meeting of the envoys, though the fortune of the kings still weighed their plans with an uncertain outcome, peace was at last made at Cambrai on 24 March.

units.la: ANNO. MDXCVII. cIↄ. Iↄ. LVIII. LIX. mum, Frisicæ gentis, & equestris ordinis virum; Senatus secretiorum Præsidem, præter alios sanciendo fœderi à Philippo delegatum, valetudinēq; impeditum procerum conventui, & actioni pacis non interfuisse. Eâ præter cætera, cautum erat: Ut quicquid Gallico, Italicoq; bello vi, aut dolo partum, amissumvè foret, utrique Regum, eorum subditis, socijsque restitueretur, omnibus & singulis libera commercia, pax certa, atque constans esset. Emanuel quoque Philibertus Belgicæ Præfectus exceptis paucis, quæ, dum lege cognosceretur, pignori essent, omnia sua cis ac trans Alpes reciperet, Margaretamque sororem regiam nuptijs sibi adjungeret. Fœdus ipsum toti ferè Europæ fructuosum Carolo Hispaniæ Principi, & Delphinati Galliæ probaretur. Tum adimpleudæ conventioni Henrico regi trimestre, quadrimestre Philippo præstitutum, obsidesque arbitrio partium dati regum fœderi robur addidere. Quod ne Philippus Frisios clam haberet, litteras eâ de re confestim ad Arembergium Præfectum in Frisiam dedit, quibus certiores Frisios faciebat: Placuisse æterno numini post tot tædia & incommoda bellorum discordibus regum animis desiderium pacis instillare; asperitatemque durissimi temporis summo humani generis bono firmâ pace lenire. Ea propter velle, ut Frisij fato supplicationum die amburbia decernant, votaque duraturæ paci nuncupent tam fœcundæ mortalium fœlicitati solemnia. Hæc Bruxellis Non. April. Philippi manu signata, ac Leovardiam transmissa. Itaque publica lætitiæ signa per omnem Provinciam edita, structiqué in publico ignes, & accensa funalia, testandæ domesticæ rerum incolumitati colluxere. Post Margareta Marchica, (ea Arembergio uxor) litteris Philippi suas adjecit, procuratæq; interventu Christiernæ Lotharingicæ Gallicæ pacis nuntium Frisijs firmavit. Id verò seorsim addebat, eâdem Christierna, ut novi fœderis ita nuptiarum conciliatrice, Elisabetham Vallesiam Henrici regis filiam Philippo desponsatam, Philippumq; Gallici fœderis vinculum innovatâ matrimonij fide, & opportunis Elisabethæ amoribus geminasse. Hoc modo bellorum funerumq; facibus nuptialis fax subdita, Philippusq; securo per Belgicam principatu potitus de adijciendo Burgundicæ hæreditati Hispaniæ regno à morte Caroli patris agitavit. Cuius excessum ut surgens iterum mense Augusto Cometes portendisse, ut ante dixi, creditus est; ita magnæ rerum mutationis, & futuræ tempestatis signum infœlici Belgicæ attulisse. Ab eo namq; tempore evenit, ut Philippus Carolo patre finem mortalitatis adepto, velut amoto suarum actionum moderatore, definitum lege principatum immodestius gereret, secretisque à communione gerendarum rerum Belgicæ proceribus, suorum Hispanorum consilijs, & Antonij Perennotti Cardinalis post Granvellani vafro, & crudeli ingenio uteretur. Reputabat namq; Philippus, Carolum patrem in Germania res novas molitum, Nicolao Perennotto Antonij patre tanquam fidissimo, & principe Senatus usum, Antoniumque filium non alio à patre ingenio, magnæque per Belgicam autoritatis, stabiliendis ijsdem Caroli Edictis commodum instrumentum superesse. Mariæ verò, ut dixi, Austriacæ alia mens, atque consilium fuerat. Prævidebat namque prudens fœmina, & longo usu res Belgicas edocta,
units.tr: ANNO 1597. (1558, 1559). ...ium, of Frisian stock and a man of the equestrian order, President of the Privy Council, was delegated by Philip, among others, to ratify the covenant; but, hindered by ill health, he did not take part in the assembly of nobles or in the work of the peace. Among other things, it was provided by this peace that whatever had been won or lost by force or fraud in the Gallic and Italian war should be restored to both kings, their subjects and allies, and that free commerce, certain and constant peace, should exist for all and each. Emmanuel Philibert, Governor of the Netherlands, was to recover all his possessions on both sides of the Alps, except for a few which were to remain as pledges until the matter was examined by law; and he was to take as his wife Margaret, the king's sister. The treaty itself was approved as profitable for almost all of Europe, by Charles, Prince of Spain, and by the Dauphin of France. Then, to fulfil the agreement, a term of three months was set for King Henry and of four months for Philip, and hostages were given at the discretion of the parties, adding strength to the covenant between the kings. Lest Philip keep the Frisians in the dark about this, he at once sent letters on the matter to Aremberg, the Governor in Friesland, by which he informed the Frisians that it had pleased the eternal God, after so many weariness and calamities of war, to instil in the discordant minds of the kings a desire for peace, and to soften the harshness of this most hard time by a firm peace, for the highest good of mankind. Therefore he wished the Frisians to decree a day of thanksgiving in all their towns by the decree of fate, and to offer vows for a lasting peace, the solemnities of so fruitful a happiness for mortals. These things were signed by Philip's hand at Brussels on 5 April and sent to Leeuwarden. Thus public signs of joy were displayed throughout the Province, and fires were built in public places and torches lit, shining to attest the domestic safety of their affairs. Afterwards Margaret of Mantua (she was the wife of Aremberg) added her own letter to Philip's, and, through the agency of Christine of Lorraine, confirmed for the Frisians the news of the French peace. She added separately that the same Christine, as the mediator not only of the new alliance but also of the marriage, had betrothed Elizabeth of Valois, daughter of King Henry, to Philip, and that Philip, by renewed pledge of marriage and by Elizabeth's timely affections, had doubled the bond of the French alliance. In this way the nuptial torch was lit with the torches of wars and funerals, and Philip, having secured a safe principate throughout the Netherlands, began to consider adding to the Spanish kingdom the Burgundian inheritance, from the death of his father Charles. As I said before, a comet rising again in August was believed to have foretold his departure; so it brought to the unhappy Netherlands a sign of great change and of the coming storm. For from that time it came about that Philip, having obtained the end of mortality with his father Charles, and as if the moderator of his actions had been removed, governed the principate, which was fixed by law, more immoderately; and with the nobles of the Netherlands set apart from the common conduct of affairs, he used the counsels of his Spaniards and the crafty and cruel nature of Antony Perrenot, Cardinal, after Granvelle. For Philip reckoned that his father Charles, who had been planning new things in Germany, had used Nicholas Perrenot, Antony's father, as a most faithful man and the leading man of the Senate; and that Antony, the son, not unlike his father in nature and of great authority throughout the Netherlands, remained a convenient instrument for establishing the same edicts of Charles. But Mary of Austria, as I said, had another mind and plan. For the prudent woman, instructed by long experience in Netherlands affairs, foresaw

units.la: {li} Causa Belgii.
units.tr: The cause of the Low Countries.

units.la: Pierii Winsemii
units.tr: Pierius Winsemius

units.la: (xxiv. enim annis Provinciis præfuerat) communi hoc modo concor-diæ periculum fore, validâ utramq; inter gentem, Belgicam Hispani-camque, & pervetustâ æmulatione, quam à Philippi Austrij cum Io-annâ Ferdinandi Hispaniæ regis filiâ, matrimonio, post Hispaniam Belgicæ, Burgundiæque connexam, periti aulicarum rerum observas-sent. Itâ factum esse, ut Legati, (quos quotannis in Belgicæ Provincias Hispaniæ reges mittebant) regijs magis quam suis opibus nixi Belgicam nobilitatem magnificentiâ ac luxu provocarent, attritisq;, nullo ærarij regij subsidio, Illustrium familiarum facultatibus eosdem Belgicæ Principes reparandæ velut fortunæ avidos, ad captanda nova-rum rerum consilia, Carolum verò Philippumque ad frenandam mo-bilium, ut talia fere Principum sunt, ingeniorum cupiditatem propel-lere conarentur. Quam causam subsecutæ civilium bellorum tempestati, non ultimam fuisse Everardus Reidanus, qui in arcana istorum temporum penetravit, fidus autor est. Cui malo, etsi id occulto na-turæ odio inter eas gentes diu alitum esse, occasione belli Gallici grande incrementum accessisse haud dubium est. Criminabantur namq; intra se Hispani, ut Gallorum spolia, & manubias, ita omnis belli gloriam, & victoriæ decus Belgicæ genti cessisse, Lamoraliumque Egmondanum Belgici sanguinis Principem, qui Philippi partes cum imperio gesserat, cruentum illud diuturnumque bellum, Carolo etiam Cæsare varia fortuna motum, primo ad Quintini fanum, dein Grevelingam in littore Flandrico, Gallorum clade, & memorabili exitu finisse. Quare interveniente propria rebus prosperis invidia (quæ pravis aulæ artibus optime facta pessime interpretari solet) facilore Principis juventa, per æmulos, &, ut creditum fuit, Ferdinando Albano præcipuo autore actum est, ut omnis Gallici belli gloria obscuraretur, gestarumque rerum magnitudo, & simul fælicitas, quâ fatorum auspicio usus fuerat Lamoralius, invidentium studijs in fœdissimam post cœdem verteretur, populusque Belgicus tributi, & fidei suæ mercedem novi Principis odium, & mox omnis sævitiæ documentum acciperet. Ita libertati Belgicæ structæ clam insidiæ, quam Caroli, Philippiqué Principum inauguratione ratam semper inviolatamque Ordines Belgicæ caverant, & quæ Hispanos, cæterosque peregrinos dignitatibus, honoribusq; submovebat. Ad quos ut ipsis Hispanis aditus pateret, formâ regni, ut notat Demetrius, mutare Remp. in Secreto Hispaniæ diu constitutum erat, Philippumque lubricæ adhuc, & ambitiosæ ætatis Principem majoris imperij pollicitatione circumvenire. Quare Gallico bello sopito, & proclamatâ Philippum inter Henricumq; pace, hoc maxime quærebatur, ut exurgens per Philippi ditiones religio, & cum eâ libertas opprimeretur, invalefceretq; Philippi Imperium vi & armis stabiliendum. Scribit Borræus Henricum 11. Galliæ regem Gulielmo Nassovio Aurantio Principi Secretum ici fœderis clam communicasse, pronoq; in eum affectu, sive ut fato aut ordinatione numinis in plures arcanum fœdus dispalefceret, sanguinarium Philippi de subvertendo Belgicæ statu consilium aperuisse.
units.tr: (for he had governed the Provinces for twenty-four years), that concord would be endangered in this way: the Netherlanders and the Spaniards were strongly opposed to one another, and there was an ancient rivalry, which skilled observers of court affairs had noted, arising from the marriage of Philip of Austria with Joanna, daughter of Ferdinand, king of Spain, by which Spain was joined to the Netherlands and Burgundy. The result was that the envoys, whom the kings of Spain sent every year into the Provinces of the Netherlands, relied more on royal than on their own resources, and by their display and luxury challenged the Netherlandish nobility. Since no help came from the royal treasury, these envoys drained the wealth of the illustrious families, and the Netherlandish princes, eager to restore their fortunes, were led to seek new schemes; while Charles and Philip tried to restrain by force the restless ambition of minds, as is usually the case with princes. Everardus Reidanus, who penetrated the secrets of those times, is a reliable witness that this was no small cause of the storm of civil wars that followed. There is no doubt that, although this evil had long been nourished in secret by the natural hatred between those peoples, it received a great increase from the occasion of the French war. For the Spaniards charged among themselves that, just as the spoils and booty of the French had gone to the Spanish, so the entire glory of the war and the honour of victory had passed to the Netherlandish people. They also charged that Lamoral, Count of Egmont, a prince of Netherlandish blood, who had commanded with authority on Philip's side, had brought that bloody and long war, which had been waged with varying fortune even under Emperor Charles, to an end at St. Quentin first, and then at Gravelines on the Flemish coast, with the defeat and memorable death of the French. Therefore, envy intervening against his successes (which, through the wicked arts of the court, is wont to interpret good deeds in the worst light), it was done more easily, as was believed, through his rivals, and chiefly by the author Ferdinand of Alba, that the whole glory of the French war should be obscured. The greatness of his achievements, and at the same time the good fortune which Lamoral had enjoyed under the favourable auspices of fate, were turned by the zeal of his enemies into a most shameful end after his execution. The Netherlandish people received, in return for their taxes and their loyalty, the hatred of the new prince, and soon a proof of all cruelty. Thus secret plots were laid against the liberty of the Netherlands, which the Estates had always guarded against being violated, as the inauguration of Charles and Philip had ratified it; and which kept the Spaniards and other foreigners away from dignities and honours. In order that the Spaniards themselves might have access to these, it had long been decided in secret in Spain to change the form of the state, as Demetrius notes, and to win over Philip, a prince still of unstable and ambitious age, with the promise of greater power. Therefore, with the French war quieted and peace proclaimed between Philip and Henry, this above all was sought: that religion, rising up throughout Philip's dominions, together with it liberty, should be crushed, and that Philip's rule should be made firm by force and arms. Borrhaeus writes that Henry II, king of France, secretly communicated the secret of this treaty to William of Nassau, Prince of Orange, and, being inclined towards him, or perhaps by the fate or ordinance of heaven, revealed the bloody plan of Philip for overthrowing the state of the Netherlands, so that the secret treaty might be disclosed to many.

units.la: Tum missus in Frisiam à Margareta Arembergius cum mandatis; Ut Gulielmi Lindani delegati regij Ultrajectini Præsulis, tum extraordiordinarij per Frisiam Senatoris, autoritatem confirmaret, regisque Philippi in stabiliendâ Romanâ religione voluntatem aperiret. Quæ duo varijs conventibus agitata populum Frisicum ab ipsius Lindani actionibus, ipsoque Philippo, alienavere. Qui capto deserendæ Belgicæ consilio, quo Hispanias reviseret, Gandavo, ubi morabatur, litteras ad Præsidem Senatumque suum dedit, Frisiorumq; Legatos una cum cæteris Belgicæ Legatis adesse jussit: Litteræ hæ erant:
units.tr: Then Margaret sent Arembergius into Friesland with instructions: to confirm the authority of Gulielmus Lindanus, the royal delegate, Bishop of Utrecht, and also of the extraordinary senator for Friesland, and to make known King Philip's will regarding the establishment of the Roman religion. These two matters, debated at various meetings, alienated the Frisian people from the actions of Lindanus himself, and from Philip himself. Philip, having resolved to abandon the Netherlands so that he might revisit Spain, gave a letter from Ghent, where he was staying, to his president and senate, and ordered the Frisian envoys to attend together with the other envoys of the Netherlands. The letter was as follows:

units.la: GANDAVVM, civitatem meam, devectus sum, celebrando Aurei Velleris conventui, & ut rerum per Belgicam meam, antequam regna mea per Hispanias revisam, moderamini prospicerem. Quare Ordines mearum provinciarum convocare, & quidem quanto ocyus intra mensem hunc adesse volui, ne meum in Hispanias iter deliberatione, aut tarditate Legatorum retardetur. Igitur etiam mandabitis Frisijs, ut Legatos suos intra præscriptum tempus mittant, tardisq; & privilegium de Non Evocando obtendentibus, persuadebitis me in procinctu mei in Hispanias discessus stare. Per hoc etiam esse, quod ante animo agitaveram, ne in provinciam illorum excurrere queam. Igitur quoniam Belgicâ propediem excessurus sum, ne Frisijs quoque desim, persuadebitis ipsis ut Legatos suos salvo jure mittant, fidemq; facietis, hoc ipsum augendis illorum privilegijs commodisq; fore. Litteræ Non. Iul. Gandavo datæ.
units.tr: GHENT, my city, I have come to attend the assembly of the Golden Fleece, and to provide for the management of affairs throughout my Netherlands before I return to my kingdoms in Spain. Therefore I wish to summon the Estates of my provinces, and indeed as quickly as possible, within this month, so that my journey to Spain is not delayed by deliberation or by the tardiness of the envoys. Therefore you will also instruct the Frisians to send their envoys within the prescribed time; and if they are slow, and plead the privilege of Non Evocando, you will persuade them that I am on the point of departing for Spain. By this also, what I had previously intended will be achieved: that I may not be able to make an incursion into their province. Therefore, since I am about to leave the Netherlands shortly, so that I may not fail the Frisians either, you will persuade them to send their envoys with their right preserved, and you will assure them that this very thing will serve to increase their privileges and advantages. Letter dated at Ghent, the Nones of July.

units.la: Igitur repetito, & quidem acriore Philippi mandato, velut exulceratâ mente regiâ, quæ jus populi cum detrimento potentiæ suæ invalescere ægrius ferebat, comitium Delegatorum Frisiæ ad xii. Kal. Aug. Leovardiæ indictum, ibique recitatis per Alexium Gelium Senatorem regium Philippi litteris, Decretum factum.
units.tr: Therefore, with a repeated and indeed harsher command from Philip, as if his royal mind were inflamed, which could ill bear that the people's right should grow strong to the detriment of his power, a meeting of the Frisian deputies was summoned at Leeuwarden for the twelfth day before the Kalends of August. There, after Philip's letter had been read out by Alexius Gellius, the royal senator, a decree was made.

units.la: Non posse se (salvâ interim majestate Philippi) Legatos hoc tempore extra provinciæ suæ fines mittere, cæterum perstare in antiqui juris defensione, quod Frisios patriâ suâ evocari prohibuisset. Hoc à Regnero Meinardo Pastore Collumano, Gellio Bonnio Commendatore Hospitalis Snecani, & Guilielmo Hissio Advocato signatum.
units.tr: That they could not (saving meanwhile the majesty of Philip) send envoys beyond the borders of their province at this time; moreover, they persisted in defending their ancient right, which had forbidden them to be summoned out of their homeland. This was signed by Reinerus Meinardus, minister of Collum, Gellius Bonnius, commander of the Hospitallers of Sneek, and Gulielmus Hissius, advocate.

units.la: Quod rescriptum etsi jure subnixum foret, tamen asperius illis videbatur, qui in Philippo durius paterno ingenium, & valituram ex patientia Belgarum potentiam observabant. Itaq; x. Kal. Aug. conventus procerum Leovardiæ repetitus, suspensaque agrariorum oppidanorumque lite, quæ tum flagrabat, Isbrandus Hardervicenus Præsul Lidlumensis, Aggæus Albada IC. & Senator regius, Ruardus Roorda, & Serapius Hania Legum Doctor, & Consul Leovardiensis, ad Philippum Delegati. Illis mandatum erat, ut cum Belgicæ Provinciarum legatis, Gandavum irent, deq; Philippi regis, antequam Belgio excedat, voluntate & postulatis cognoscant. Præterea ut apud Regem populum Frisicum à pollutæ religionis suspicione purgarent, falsaque delationes apud Philippum professione Romanâ diluerent. His mandatis litteræ ad Philippum datæ, quæ juris antiqui non obscuram probationem, cum reverentiâ tamen dominantis conjunctam, præ se ferebant. Igitur ne Philippi evocatio Frisicæ genti in præjudicium cederet, Legati coram Præside Senatuque regio comparuere, eaq; de re acta perscribi
units.tr: Although this reply was supported by law, it nevertheless seemed harsher to those who observed in Philip a temper more severe than his father's, and a power that would grow from the patience of the Netherlanders. Therefore, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, the assembly of the nobles was reconvened at Leeuwarden; and, with the lawsuit between the landowners and townsmen, which was then raging, suspended, Isbrand of Harderwijk, Bishop of Lidlum, Aggaeus Albada, jurist and royal senator, Ruard Roorda, and Serapius Hania, Doctor of Laws and consul of Leeuwarden, were chosen as envoys to Philip. They were instructed to go to Ghent together with the envoys of the Netherlandish provinces, and to learn King Philip's will and demands before he left the Netherlands. Moreover, they were to clear the Frisian people before the king of any suspicion of a polluted religion, and to refute false accusations made to Philip by a profession of the Roman faith. Letters to Philip were given with these instructions, which displayed a clear proof of their ancient right, yet joined with reverence towards the ruling power. So that Philip's summons might not turn out to the prejudice of the Frisian nation, the envoys appeared before the president and the royal senate, and the matter was recorded in writing.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. LIX. — Non. Iul.: date line of the royal letter, as printed in the margin.
units.tr: 1559. — Nones of July.

units.la: Ita gens nostra dum juris sui ob potentiam dominantis vim non poterat, nudam speciem retinebat, aliquali solatio, ut cessante vetustæ, quam ab Imperatoribus Germaniæ, acceperat, & cuius libera atque socia provincia fuerat, immunitatis exemplo, in solis Philippi novam dominationem molientis actis, extaret. Unde Philippus confirmatā etiam per Belgicam eādem Gallicā pace retineri sub signis Hispanum militem jussit, comparatisque ad profectionem, quam in Hispaniam parabat, rebus, conventum omnium Belgicæ Ordinum Gandavi indixit, exhibitoque scripto hunc in modum disseruit:
units.tr: Thus our nation, while because of the power of the ruling force it could not maintain its right, kept only the bare appearance of it, and with some small consolation remained, as an example of the immunity it had received long ago from the Emperors of Germany, of whose free and allied province it had been, and which survived only in the acts of Philip, who was constructing a new domination. Hence Philip, having confirmed the same Gallic peace, ordered the Spanish soldiers to remain under their standards throughout the Netherlands. And, having made preparations for the journey he was planning to Spain, he summoned a meeting of all the Estates of the Netherlands at Ghent, and, having presented a written statement, spoke in this manner:
