units.la: IN Hispaniam, Ordines, curandis regni mei negotijs ire constitui, imitatus exemplum Caroli patris, quem è medià Hispaniâ vestri aliquando amor, & publicæ pacis cura protraxit. Itaque Carolus pater, ne quid adversum ordini ingrueret, ab Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xliii. tàm diu apud vos egit, donec in me filium Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. lv. senio aut invaletudine compulsus, Burgundicæ domus patrimonium transferret. Ipse reliquum vitæ, quam brevem, & angustis terminis circumscriptam post habuit, divinis meditationibus, tum curandæ valetudini destinaret. Ab eo tempore in Principem vestrum delectus hic quoque substiti, vestroque ac juxta regnorum meorum subsidio cruentum bellum, quo Gallia ruptis Induciis in me ardescebat, firmâ pace clausi. Neque excessurus adhuc Belgicâ meâ fuissem, nisi in motu Hispania, & nisi rationes mearum rerum, quas ipse expendo, postularent. Hac de causa, ut Gallicum & atrox bellum robustis nervis traherem, regnum meum non modico onere pressi, postquam tanti exercitus stipendijs vestra liberalitas par non fuit. Isto onere ut me levem, tributo, & ut illud exigam, impetremque, præsentiâ meâ opus est. Et quia hoc tempore omnem simul exercitum dimittere per inopiam aris non licet, ita legionem meam vestris in finibus relinquo, stipendia, prout confido, à vobis habiturus. Ut quoniam flagrante bello deesse vobis nolui, ita vos recuperatâ per me pace quieti, & felices simile mihi subsidium præstetis. Compositis per Hispaniam rebus idem addico, neque affectum in vos meum distantium locorum intercapedo imminuet. Quin daturus sum operam, ut ordinato per Hispaniam regni statu remigrem ad vos ocyus, modo res meæ, & simul vestræ exigant, quarum incolumitati catera mea posthabeo. Interim Emanuelì Philiberto nuper provinciarum Præfecto, & Gallico fœdere in res suas immissò (dum Carolum filium certis de causis, & antequam discors Hispaniæ regnum intravero, præficere vobis non licet) Margaretam sororem meam substitui, eiq; ut & singulis Provinciarum præfectis, in mandatis dedi, religionem Romanam certam tectam, curet, statuatq; in delinquentes è præscripto legum coërcendos. Vt idem faciatis, Ordines, moneo, hortorque, ita fiet, ut florentissimas Provincias, pronumq; in vos Regem me sitis habituri.
units.tr: I have resolved, Estates, to go to Spain to attend to the affairs of my kingdom, imitating the example of my father Charles, whom your affection at one time, and care for the public peace, drew away from the middle of Spain. Accordingly, my father Charles, so that nothing hostile should befall the Order, spent time with you from the year 1543 for so long, until, compelled by old age or ill health, in the year 1555 he transferred the patrimony of the house of Burgundy to me, his son. He himself set aside the rest of his life, which he regarded as short and confined within narrow limits, for divine meditations and for the care of his health. From that time I too have stayed here as your prince, and with your help and that of my kingdoms, which lie nearby, I have closed with a firm peace the bloody war with which France, having broken the truces, was blazing against me. I would not yet have left my Netherlands, were it not for the unrest in Spain and the reasons for my affairs, which I myself weigh, that demand it. For this reason, so that I might drag on the French and savage war with strong sinews, I have burdened my kingdom with no small weight, since your generosity was not equal to the pay of so great an army. To relieve myself of this burden, and to collect the tax and obtain it, my presence is needed. And because at this time it is not possible, for lack of money, to dismiss the whole army at once, I leave my legion within your borders, expecting, as I trust, that you will supply its pay. And since I did not want to fail you while the war was blazing, so may you, once peace has been restored through me, be quiet and happy and grant me a similar help. Once affairs in Spain are settled I will likewise promise the same, and the distance of places will not diminish my affection towards you. Indeed I will take care that, once the state of my kingdom in Spain is set in order, I return to you more quickly, provided my affairs and yours together require it; for the safety of these I set aside my other concerns. Meanwhile, since I may not set my son Charles over you for certain reasons, and before I enter Spain, where discord reigns, I have appointed in my place my sister Margaret, having lately placed Emanuel Philibert, the former governor of the provinces, who was engaged in the French alliance on his own account, in command; and I have ordered her, as I have ordered each of the governors of the provinces, to take care that the Roman religion is kept certain and protected, and to restrain offenders according to the prescription of the laws. If you do the same, Estates, I warn and urge you, it will come about that you will have flourishing provinces and a king well disposed towards you.

units.la: Ea Philippi Oratio, Legatis Ordinum mœrorem indignationemque simul incusserat. Dolebant quippe Provincias Gallicâ adhuc face calentes, ut ante à Carolo, ita nunc Philippo deseri, summæque rei regimen inquietis peregrinorum ingenijs, & muliebri Margaretæ imperio committi. Erant quoque qui eandem Margaretam, velut tantarum rerum incapacem, pronuntiarent, &, quod in matrimonio ut ante Alexandri Medicæi, ita tunc Octavij Farnesij viveret, haustos Italiæ mores criminarentur. Maxumè verò conquerebantur, militeni Hispanum, & regij exercitus reliquias in finibus Belgicæ confidere, omnis belli metu per Gallicam pacem sublato, & post mortem Mariæ Anglicæ Elisabethâ Vallesiâ in Philippi domum deruptâ. Idcircò è quiete publicâ fore, eum in Hispanias ablegari, alijs bellis usui futu-rum, allaturûmque interea Philippo securitatem per longinqua & infesta classibus maria ituro. Quæ Ordinum, Principumque Belgicæ supplicatio, ut tandem fructu suo, ita odio quoque apud Philippum non caruit. Præterquam enim, quod exautorandi exercitus, cuius operâ bello Gallico usus fuerat, & faciendæ intra trimestre militum missionis vanam spem faceret Philippus, ita creditus suit, eo tempore clam sententiam mortis in eos strinxisse, qui amoveri in Hispaniam eundem militem, & extrudi Belgicis terris sollicitaverant importunius. A quo etiam hoc suit, ut idem miles post Philippi discessum (qui vii. Kalend. Septem. Vlissingæ classem ingressus erat) annum & semestre in Belgicâ subsisteret, acturusque haud dubiè diuturnius præsidium, solius, quâ ad Zerbium Afri littoris insulam Philippus affectus erat, atrocissimæ cladis insperato vulnere revocaretur. Ita Philippus relictâ Belgicâ, quam pacatam à Carolo patre acceperat, turbatam verò reliquis vitæ, & regni sui annis habiturus erat, in Hispaniam profectus est. Tradit V. C L. Suffridus Petræus quondam Ordinum huius gentis Historiographus, Philippum non aliâ de causâ, quam ad capessendum Regni Hispaniæ diadema, Belgica excessisse, ac secundo vento usum ad vi. Eid. Septemb. in eandem Hispaniain appulisse. Alij addunt viso attactoque regni littore classem Philippi horrendâ tempestate disjectam, navesque plurimas ipso etiam Philippo spectante, turbatis supra modum aquis demersas. Gemmas quoq;, signa, toreumata, tum operis antiqui tabulas, mirâ Belgarum arte elaboratas ac per Germaniam Italiamq; à Carolo Cæsare regio paratui, ac domesticæ magnificentiæ congestas, mari haustas, ipsumque Philippum magno vitæ discrimine fluctibus expositum, suis terris restitutum. Tum è Philippi abitu & simul relicto in præsidijs milite, præscius velut eventuri mæror, & tacita simul indignatio omnem Belgicam pervasit. Ratiocinabantur quippe prudentiores Philippum Principem Belgicæ genti diffisum pignorandæ arctius fidei arma & militem delegisse, modumq; parando populi obsequio repertum, concordiæ quam maxume inimicum fore.
units.tr: This speech of Philip's had struck the envoys of the Estates with grief and indignation alike. The Provinces, still smarting from the French torch, grieved that they were to be abandoned now by Philip, as before by Charles, and that the direction of the highest affairs was to be entrusted to the restless minds of foreigners and to the rule of a woman, Margaret. Some even declared that Margaret was incapable of such great matters, and they blamed her for the habits of Italy she had absorbed: she had lived in marriage first with Alessandro de' Medici and then with Ottavio Farnese. Above all they complained that the Spanish soldiery and the remnants of the royal army were settling on the borders of Belgica. Now that all fear of war had been removed by the French peace, and after the death of Mary of England, Elizabeth of Valois had been married into Philip's house, they argued, the troops would be sent away to Spain, to be of use in other wars, and in the meantime they would bring Philip security as he sailed over distant seas dangerous to fleets. This petition of the Estates and Princes of Belgica did not lack its effect, but it also met with hostility from Philip. For Philip, while he offered vain hope of disbanding the army, by whose help he had carried on the French war, and of discharging the soldiers within three months, is believed to have secretly passed sentence of death at that time on those who had too importunately urged that the same soldiers be removed to Spain and expelled from Belgian lands. Because of this, the same soldiers remained in Belgica for a year and a half after Philip's departure (he had boarded the fleet at Flushing on the 26th of August), and they would undoubtedly have held the garrison longer, had they not been recalled by the unexpected blow of a most dreadful disaster, which befell Philip off the island of Djerba on the African coast. So Philip left Belgica, which he had received quiet from his father Charles, but which he was to have troubled for the rest of his life and the years of his reign, and set out for Spain. Lord Suffridus Petrus, once historiographer of this nation's Estates, records that Philip left Belgica for no other reason than to seize the crown of the kingdom of Spain, and that, using a favourable wind, he reached the same Spain on the 8th of September. Others add that when Philip's fleet sighted and touched the shore of the kingdom, it was scattered by a dreadful storm, and very many ships were sunk, with Philip himself watching, the waters being stirred beyond measure. Also sunk at sea were gems, statues, embossed vessels, and paintings of ancient workmanship, wrought with wonderful Belgian skill and gathered from Germany and Italy by Emperor Charles for royal display and domestic magnificence; and Philip himself, exposed to the waves at great peril to his life, was restored to his own lands. Then, with Philip's departure and the soldiers left in the garrisons, a grief as if of something about to happen, and a silent indignation together, spread through all Belgica. For the wiser sort reasoned that Philip, distrusting the Belgian people as a prince, had chosen to secure his faith more tightly by arms and soldiers, and that this method, devised to win the people's obedience, would be most hostile to harmony.

units.la: Strada notat, Ordinum supplicationem benignè à Philippo auditam, eandemque regia pollicitatione liberandi à milite Belgij firmatam. Cæterum properato Philippi abitu, & ut ille scribit, Belgicæ perincommodo, necdum rite constitutæ res evanuere, milesque Hispanus post anni effluxum per præsidia habitus. Quod ut argumentum suspectæ apud regem Belgarum fidei fuit, ita occasionem nascenti properantique ad sua initia fatali malo dedit, quod dein licentiâ Hispanorum auctum, ne moram daret, procerum quoque acrioribus ingenijs stimulabatur. Sunt qui tradant, Margaretam Gubernatricem moderamini rerum jam admotam, Philippi missionem dissuasisse, ne demisso quod petebatur milite periculum à finitimis civitatibus incumberet, quas rumpendam ad pacem, cem, ex se sæpe infidam opportunitas nocendi impelleret. Quibus Provinciarum querimonijs etiam hæc per Frisiam seorsim accessit, quod Gulielmus Lindanus Philippi, & Ultrajectinæ Sedis Legatus (de quo in Frisiam mittendo Philippus Anno CIↄ. Iↄ. LVI. cum Georgio Egmondano Præsule Ultrajectino consultaverat) insolentius ageret, mandatisque Philippi, & simul sanctionibus Romanæ Sedis subnixus, temerandis sacris, atque profanis sua ministeria adaptaret. Itaque Frisiæ Ordines ultrò superbiam hominis perosi, mox instigante clero, de cuius jure agebatur, inritati, ut pessimarum rerum principijs obstarent, prolixè apud Arembergium egere, deque ejusdem Lindani superbâ & insolenti dominatione hoc modo conquesti sunt:
units.tr: Strada notes that the petition of the Estates was kindly heard by Philip, and was confirmed by a royal promise to free Belgica from the soldiery. But with Philip's hasty departure, and, as he writes, to Belgica's great inconvenience, the matter, not yet properly settled, faded away, and the Spanish soldiers were kept in garrisons after the year had run out. This gave an occasion of suspicion about the Belgians' loyalty in the king's eyes, and it gave a fatal wound to a rising and hurrying beginning; afterwards, increased by the licence of the Spaniards, it also stirred the nobles, whose spirits were sharper, not to delay. There are those who relate that Margaret, the Regent, now brought to the management of affairs, had advised against Philip's dismissal of the soldiers, lest, with the requested troops sent away, danger should hang over them from neighbouring states, which the opportunity to harm would urge to break the peace, a peace they themselves were often unfaithful to. To these complaints of the Provinces there was also added, separately, this from Friesland: Gulielmus Lindanus, Philip's envoy and envoy of the See of Utrecht (about whose sending to Friesland Philip had consulted with Georgius Egmondanus, Bishop of Utrecht, in the year 1556), was acting more insolently, and, relying on Philip's commands and at the same time on the sanctions of the Roman See, was adapting his ministry to profane and sacred things alike, to their profanation. And so the Estates of Friesland, hating the man's arrogance of their own accord, and soon stirred up by the clergy, whose right was at issue, pleaded at length before Arenberg, so that they might oppose the beginnings of the worst things; and they complained of this proud and insolent domination of Lindanus in the following words:

units.la: ETSI libertatis nostræ diuturna possessio, quâ majores nostri anreâ illâ ætate rerum usi sunt, Præfecte, & nuperæ conventiones, quas cum Carolo Philippoq; non semel inijmus, movisse Philippum regem debuissent, ne vis ulla legibus nostris, ac religiosis ritibus, inferretur, ita præter spem nostram jam diu dispendium facimus nostræ libertatis, obtruso nobis Gulielmo Lindano commissario Fidei, etsi revera Inquisitori, homine peregrino, & supra quam ambitioso. Quod genus hominum, ut majoribus nostris infrequens fuit, qui à Sergio Pontifice post paganos ritus Friscis terris ejectos liberè ætatem egere, ita cum hoc ipso Philippi imperio, quod salvâ & incolumi libertate depacti eramus, novam servitutem accepimus. De patrijs legibus, quas suo huc usq; sanguine majores nostri tutati sunt, nunc non loquimur: Ne quis eas violaret Francorum impetus, & Normannicam vim, tum intentatum à Florentijs ac Albertis inclementius imperium sustinuimus, & ne corpora lege mancupij servirent, nosque ultimi nepotum cum traduce spiritu pessimam vivendi conditionem, & novorum juxta dominorum insolentiam acciperemus. Nunc verò animis, atq; conscientijs nostris tormenta parantur. Vt, quia ferrum & cauteria urendis secandisque mentibus non sunt, quas ut liberrimas, ita ab omni terrenâ illuvie secretas immortale numen hominj largitum est; cruciatibus corporum conscientiæ deterreantur, serviantq; superbis, importunisque dominatoribus, quorum speciosa pietas enormibus sæpè flagitijs obtenditur. Ab eo est, quod ambitioni suæ modum non ponant, Ecclesiasticas dignitates, contra leges patrias, à Carolo Cæsare Anno CIↄ. Iↄ. XXII. confirmatas conduplicent, auctoritatem, honores, opes, ut reliqui mortalium, & ferè sædius rapiant, nullo, aut minimo pietatis documento, quæ destinata divino cultui, & saluti hominum ministeria sædare curis sæculi, & ludicris quærendæ fortunæ cupiditatibus non solet. Hoc verò Lindani per Frisiam munus, hæ actiones sunt. Is namque imperia, æs, sacerdotia, aut suæ conditioni adjecit, aut pretio corruptus largientibus concessit, & quidem in fraudem Ecclesiastici per Frisiam Ordinis, qui Philippi inauguratione caverat: UT JUS EIUS INTEGRUM INTAMINATUMQUE ESSET, Philippusque intacto omnis statûs jure, ac beneficio, prout Carolinis temporibus factum erat, omnem imperij ac potentiæ gloriam confirmandis religiosæ vetustatis monumentis impenderet. Nunc verò ut patrij sacrorum ritus polluuntur, ita Præsulibus ac Decanis legitimum jus subtrahitur, quorum à tot sæculis fuissent, res sacras ordinare, ac clerum coërcere pudoris, & recti oblitum. Ea propter rogamus, PraPræfecte, ut te istiusmodi rebus interponas, procuresque in posterum, Ne quid novum & insolens, quod à majorum receptis ritibus declinet, per Frisiam in- valescat.
units.tr: Although the long possession of our liberty, by which our ancestors enjoyed the things of that golden age, Prefect, and the recent agreements we have made more than once with Charles and Philip, ought to have moved King Philip that no violence be done to our laws and religious rites, yet, beyond our hope, we have for a long time now been suffering the loss of our liberty, with Gulielmus Lindanus, a commissioner of the faith, though in truth an inquisitor, a foreigner, and more ambitious than is fitting, forced upon us. This kind of man was rare among our ancestors, who, after the pagan rites had been driven out of the Frisian lands by Pope Sergius, lived their lives freely; but with this very rule of Philip, under which we were bound by agreement with our liberty safe and intact, we have received a new servitude. We are not now speaking of the native laws, which our ancestors have defended up to now with their own blood, so that the attack of the Franks and the Norman violence should not violate them; and when, since the Florentines and Alberts, we endured a more merciless rule never before attempted, we did not let our bodies serve under the law of bondage. And we, the last of our descendants, with the disgrace of the age, receive the worst condition of living and the insolence of new masters alike. But now torments are being prepared for our minds and consciences. For since iron and cautery are not fit for burning and cutting the minds, which the immortal God has given to man as free and set apart from all earthly defilement, consciences are to be terrified by bodily torments and made to serve proud and importunate lords, whose showy piety is often held out to cover monstrous crimes. Hence they do not set any limit to their ambition: they double the ecclesiastical dignities which, against our native laws, were confirmed by Emperor Charles in the year 1522, and they seize authority, honours, and wealth like the rest of mortals, and even more shamefully, with no or very little sign of piety, which ministries destined for divine worship and the salvation of men are not accustomed to defile with worldly cares and the playful desires of seeking fortune. Such is this office of Lindanus in Friesland, and such are his actions. For he has added to his own position, or granted for a price to those who bribe him, commands, money, and priesthoods, and this in breach of the ecclesiastical order of Friesland, which at Philip's inauguration secured that its RIGHT SHOULD BE WHOLE AND UNSTAINED; and that Philip, with the whole right and benefice of every estate kept intact, as was done in the times of Charles, should devote all the glory of his rule and power to confirming the monuments of religious antiquity. But now, as our native sacred rites are polluted, so the lawful right is taken from the bishops and deans, who for so many centuries had the right to order sacred matters and to restrain the clergy, a clergy forgetful of shame and of what is right. Therefore we ask, Prefect, that you interpose yourself in such matters and take care for the future that nothing new and insolent, departing from the received rites of our ancestors, may gain strength in Friesland.

units.la: Cæterum, sive Legati reverentiâ, sive quod Caroli Philippique regum Edictis & sanctionibus Pontificum ultrò patrocinaretur Arembergius, parum profectum est. Hoc tantum subsecutum comperio, quod Arembergius spem Ordinibus redintegrandi Ecclesiastici juris faceret, ac de eâ re apud Margaretam Gubernatricem se acturum polliceretur. Verum in speciem, ut eo temporeferè omnia, sed maximè ut Philippi consilia morâ invalescerent, aulicâ lenitudine trahebantur. Quamobrem Lindanus ultrò præfractus & contumax, tum notatâ Arembergij conniventiâ insolentior in omnem immodestiam erupit, severumq; inquirendi officium fædiore post imperio exercuit. Cuius rei cum eum Ordines Frisiæ acrius monerent, Lindanus interminatam potestatem, & secretam licentiam comprimendis temporum vitijs obtendit, Ordinesque ac Senatum juxta regium puniendis flagitijs, pollutisque sacris tardos criminatus, fremens & indignabundus cætu excessit.
units.tr: However, whether out of reverence for the envoy, or because Arenberg of his own accord favoured the edicts of the kings Charles and Philip and the sanctions of the Popes, little was achieved. I learn only that this followed: Arenberg held out to the Estates hope of restoring the ecclesiastical right and promised that he would raise the matter with Margaret, the Regent. But in appearance, as at that time nearly everything was, and above all so that Philip's plans might grow strong through delay, matters were dragged along by courtly slowness. Therefore Lindanus, already stubborn and obstinate of his own accord, and now emboldened by noticing Arenberg's connivance, broke out into still greater insolence of every kind, and afterwards carried out his strict office of inquisition more foully. When the Estates of Friesland warned him more sharply about this, Lindanus pleaded the power to threaten and the secret licence to check the vices of the times, and accused the Estates and the Senate, as slow to punish crimes and polluted sacred things in the way the king would wish, and, raging and indignant, he left the assembly.

units.la: Quâ actione cum odia gentis & juxta superbia Lindani intenderetur, Ordines agrarij denuo libellum supplicem Præsidi Senatuique regio exhibuerunt, deque imminuto jure Ecclesiastico hoc modo conquesti sunt.
units.tr: Because of this action, the hatred between the peoples and Lindanus's arrogance both grew. The rural estates again presented a petition to the President and the royal Senate, complaining in these terms about the diminished ecclesiastical right.

units.la: Convenimus cum Saxone, Carolo Cæsare, & dein Philippo Caroli Patris Successore, privilegia & jura nostra salva fore. At vero Philippus Rex Gulielmo Lindano diploma concessit, quo rerum Ecclesiasticarum, judicandarum potestas ei demandatur. Quo ipso cum Ecclesiasticorum, qui tertium Provinciæ membrum constituunt, jus lædatur, duo tamen Philippus rex istâ dispositione cavisse videtur, ut privilegiis populi Lindani diploma non obstaret, & ne regij per Frisiam Senatus auctoritatem ac jus minueret. Et quoniam Senatui regio incumbit, jus suum per regium Procuratorem tueri, ac defendere, ita de nostro retinendo tantum laboramus, quod ab omni temporum memoriâ utque in hunc diem receptum Commissarios arbitrosque juris Ecclesiastici per Oofter-Goos, Wester-Goos, Silvestres, & quidem ex ipso sacro ordine accepit. Præterea longâ consuetudine presbyteri & pastores hoc obtinuere, ut Decanos in jurisdictione suâ nominent, eligantq;, quibus coram omnis quæstio, quæ judicio Senatus regij non subesset, in promptu decidebatur. Ad hoc compertum est Abbates, Lidlumensium, ut & alios suorum subditorum Archidiaconos esse, ipsosque per Frisiam Pastores jus instituendi Vicarios habuisse. Quæ omnia etsi retineri debuissent, utpote à Saxone, Carolo Cæsare, & ipso rege Philippo Frisicæ genti confirmata, ita Lindanus horum omnium & juris apud majores nostros quæsiti transgressor violatorque est. Præterquam enim quod Commissarios Ecclesiasticos neque ex Oofter-Goïs nec ex Wester-Goïs, nec ex Sylvestribus creatos admittat, ita Presbyteris Decani electionem negat, inque pastores presbyterosque alicuius facti criminisve insimulatos judicium exercet. Quod in Henrico Drolshagio perpetuo vicario Oldenhovia observatum est, quem à divinarum rerum administratione suo arbitratu semovit. Præterea pastorum jus, quo vicarios instituunt, ad se trahit, faciisque omnia, quæ immodicæ, & non legibus compressæ potestati conveniunt. Quod cum nobis intolerabile, ipsi indecens sit, petimus, Præses Senatusque, ut superbi hominis libidinem, insolentiamque castigetis,
units.tr: We agreed with Charles the Saxon, Emperor Charles, and afterwards with Philip, Charles's successor, that our privileges and rights would remain safe. But King Philip granted Gulielmus Lindanus a charter by which the power of judging ecclesiastical affairs was committed to him. By this very act the right of the clergy, who form the third member of the province, is violated. Yet King Philip seems to have provided in this arrangement two things: that the charter should not stand in the way of the privileges of the people of Lindanus, and that it should not diminish the authority and right of the royal Senate in Friesland. And since it is the business of the royal Senate to protect and defend its own right through the royal Procurator, we labour only to keep what we have, namely what has been received from all memory of time down to this day: that commissioners and arbiters of ecclesiastical right are taken from Oostergo, Westergo and the Sylvestres, and indeed from the sacred order itself. Moreover, by long custom the elders and ministers have obtained this, that they nominate and elect deans for their jurisdiction, before whom every question not subject to the judgement of the royal Senate was readily decided. In addition, it is established that the abbots of Lidlum, as well as those of other subject houses, are archdeacons, and that they have the right of appointing vicars throughout Friesland. Although all these things ought to have been kept, since they were confirmed for the Frisian people by Charles the Saxon, Emperor Charles, and King Philip himself, Lindanus has nevertheless been the transgressor and violator of all of them and of the right acquired by our ancestors. For, besides refusing to admit ecclesiastical commissioners chosen neither from Oostergo, nor from Westergo, nor from the Sylvestres, he also denies the deans' election to the elders, and he exercises judgement over ministers and elders accused of any act or crime. This was seen in the case of Henricus Drolshagius, perpetual vicar at Oldenhove, whom he removed from the administration of divine things at his own pleasure. Furthermore, he draws to himself the ministers' right by which they install vicars, and he does everything that belongs to an immoderate power not restrained by laws. Since this is intolerable to us and unseemly for him, we ask that you, the President and Senate, chastise the arrogant man's lust and insolence,

units.la: tis, illiusque Lindani immodestos mores rescripti severitate coërceatis.
units.tr: and check the immoderate conduct of that Lindanus with the severity of a rescript.

units.la: Quo facto Præses Senatusque regius Lindanum ad se vocavere, increpitumque turbati ordinis & violatorum rituum abstinere immodestis actionibus jussere. Hæc ix. Kal. Aug. acta, & ab Emskerchio Graphiario regio signata. Quod etsi se facturum polliceretur Lindanus, tamen sacræ et jam captæ dominationis cupido, hominem ex ingenio suo violentum magis efferavit, novisque Frisiorum querimonijs occasionem aperuit. Quippe ademptâ plurimis concionandi, sacraque celebrandi potestate, omne Ecclesiasticum judicium majore superbiâ, &, ut fieri in liberâ gente assolet, invidiâ exercuit, ipsosque Ordines, quasi ex Philippi ore pronuntiaret, acerbioribus dicterijs insectatus est. Itaque retracto ad judicium Senatus regij Lindano partes litis contestationem subiere, ipseque Lindanus, etsi favore, ut profitebatur, regis ac Viglij Præsidis subiutus, acrem juris processum, quo multa ei objectabantur, cum invidia provincialium sustinere coactus est. Invenio in actis Renicum Burmania Iuris Doctorem, Valerium Cammingha, Haringum Glinzium, Hesselum Aysma Iureconsultum, Frisiæ Delegatos causæ actores fuisse, ipsosque Leovardienses, alienis à Lindano animis agrariorum partibus se adjunxisse.
units.tr: After this was done, the royal President and Senate summoned Lindanus before them, rebuked him for disturbing good order and violating the rites, and ordered him to refrain from immoderate actions. This was done on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, and sealed by Emskerk, the royal registrar. Although Lindanus promised that he would do so, the desire for a sacred dominion he had already seized made the man, violent by nature, even fiercer, and opened the way to fresh complaints from the Frisians. For, having taken away from many the power of preaching and celebrating the sacred rites, he exercised all ecclesiastical judgement with greater arrogance and, as usually happens in a free nation, with resentment, and he assailed the estates themselves with harsher insults, as if he were pronouncing them from Philip's mouth. Therefore the case was brought back before the royal Senate, and the parties joined issue. Lindanus himself, although he professed to be supported by the favour of the king and of Viglius the President, was forced to endure a sharp legal process, in which many charges were brought against him, amid the hostility of the provincials. I find in the records that Renicus Burmania, Doctor of Law, Valerius Cammingha, Haringus Glinzius, and Hesselus Aysma, a jurist, were the delegates of Friesland and the advocates of the case, and that the people of Leeuwarden, their minds alienated from Lindanus, joined the side of the rural estates.

units.la: Post xvii. Kal. Decemb. ipso novilunio, quo maria ordinarijs vicibus majore æstu cientur, Oceanus intumuit, ruptoque multis in locis, qui Lemmarios spectat, aggere, depressa fere ac palustria regionis obtexit: Itaque Biltanus ager, per quem clementi, & insensili fere altitudine Frisia in Corum exsurgit, ut & maior Westergoæ pars, intactus ab aquarum salsedine mansit, toto Sylvestrium tractu, qui à Cunera, & Stellinguerfijs in Winbritzerios, ac Wonseranos protenditur, marinis undis operto. Oostergoos quoque plerosque Leppæo aggere, velut munimento agrorum suorum, clausos, ab hoc malo immunes fuisse Andreas Gryphius in suis notis autor est. Idem scribit aquam marinam eodem æstu circa nonam vespertinam repente Bornenfibus affusam, mox Coro vento auctam, areas domorum, villarumq; habiles ferendis navigijs fecisse. Post surgente Euro sensim relapsam eadem quâ perruperat, viâ, & laxantibus catarractis in suum alveum redijsse.
units.tr: After the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, at the very new moon, when the seas are stirred by their usual tides with greater force, the ocean swelled, and, breaking through the dyke in many places on the side facing Lemmer, it covered the low and marshy parts of the region. Thus the Biltish land, through which Friesland rises gently and at an almost uniform height towards the Coru, and also the greater part of Westergo, remained untouched by the saltness of the waters, while the whole tract of the Sylvestres, which stretches from Cunera and Stellingwerf to Winsum and Wonseradeel, was covered by the sea waves. Andreas Gryphius, in his notes, reports that most of Oostergo also was spared this calamity, being shut in by the Leppa dyke as by a bulwark of its fields. He writes that the same tide, about the ninth hour of the evening, suddenly poured sea water over Bornwird, and that soon, the wind from the northwest increasing it, it made the courts of houses and farms fit for ships to sail. Afterwards, when the east wind rose, the water gradually subsided by the same way by which it had broken in, and, with the sluices opened, returned to its channel.

units.la: Mox Arembergius ad viii. Eid. Iun. conventum Ordinum Frisiæ Leovardiæ indixit, postulataque quæ vigesimo mensis Anni lix. Gubernatrix Margareta ipsi commiserat, hoc modo Carolus Nitzenius, Præses Senatus, propositu.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Arembergius called a meeting of the Frisian estates at Leeuwarden for the eighth day before the Ides of June, and Carolus Nitzenius, President of the Senate, set out the demands which the Governess Margaret had entrusted to him on the twentieth day of the month of the year 1559, in these words.

units.la: ANNO LVIII. mense Aprili Arembergius Frisiæ Præfectus vos convocari fecerat, & quidem de mandato Philippi regis, ut indicaret quibus oneribus regiæ res premerentur. Quæ ipsa quoque non aliâ ex causâ regio ærario obvenere, quam quod Provincias hasce à Gallorum armis ac incursionibus liberaverit. Ita modo circa Rhenum, modo per Artesiam, Hannoniam atque Flandriam exercitum aluit, quo à vobis vestrisque finibus hostem averteret, qui regionem in vestram, & Transflavicanos, tum gentes circa Ijalam flumen sitas, excursurus dicebatur. Hoc modo Provinciæ aliâ pace & securitate beneficio regio floruere. Quod agnoscendo, dum Groningenses, Transfulani, Lingenses, Drentini, & ipsi Geldri Philippo subsidia determunt; vos soli perduci ad sublevandum regis aerarium non potuistis. Neque tamen eo minus a bello cessatum est, quod binis, & quidem felicibus ad Quintini fanum, & Grevelingam praelijs, utilem honestamque pacem, sed impensa regia dedit. Qui propterea res suas aut distrahere, aut pignori dare coactus, militem in armis, quantum potuit, ac fide retinuit, aliquos defectu aeris, non exsolutis stipendijs, exautoravit. Quae ut ad manum sint, ne fides, exercitus ac simul disciplina solvatur, & ut subveniatur rebus regijs diuturne ex bello impulsis, Margareta Gubernatrix conventum hunc habere voluit, quo subsidia regi praestaretis. Quod facere tanto vobis facilius erit, quanto minus provincia vestra onerum sustinuit, quae durante Arembergij Praefectura neque militem colligere, nec militarem manum recipere intra fines suos jussa sit. Cum e contra Brabantini, Flandri, Artesij, Hannonij, Namurcenses, Luxemburgij militaribus injuriis vexati sint, regisq; amore aut ipsi sub stipendijs fuerint, aut laudabili facilitate rogas concesserint. Quibus rationibus permotus Arembergius idem, quod anno LVIII. proponi per me fecit, ut in memoriam revocaret, quae isto conventu acta sunt. Quo tempore vos ipsi deprædicastis non minore affectu erga regem Philippum duci, quam quo Carolum patrem prosequuti estis. Ut istis vocibus fidem adstruatis, retinendis in obsequio ac disciplinâ egiomibus, sublevandaeque domui regiae, septuaginta aureorum millia hoc tempore exigit, utque intra quadriennium aequalibus pensionibus ea praestentur. Hac VIII. Iul. voce Nitzenij propositia.
units.tr: In the year 1558, in April, Arembergius, the Prefect of Friesland, had caused you to be summoned, by the command of King Philip, so that he might state with what burdens the royal affairs were pressed. These burdens too have come upon the royal treasury for no other reason than that he has freed these provinces from the arms and incursions of the French. Thus, now near the Rhine, now through Artois, Hainaut and Flanders, he maintained an army, by which he might turn the enemy away from you and your borders, which was said to be about to make a raid into your land, into the Transflavian region, and into the peoples living near the river Ijssel. In this way the provinces flourished in peace and security through the king's favour. Acknowledging this, while the Groningers, the Transfuli, the Lingenses, the Drentians, and Gelderland itself granted aid to Philip, you alone could not be brought to relieve the royal treasury. Yet the war was not for that reason ceased, since the two battles, indeed successful ones, at Saint-Quentin and at Gravelines gave a useful and honourable peace, but at the king's expense. Therefore he, being compelled either to sell or to pledge his own goods, kept the soldiers under arms and in loyalty as far as he could, and dismissed some for lack of money, their pay not being paid. So that these things may be at hand, lest the loyalty, the army and at the same time the discipline be dissolved, and so that the royal affairs, long battered by war, may be relieved, the Governess Margaret wished to hold this meeting, at which you would furnish aid to the king. This will be all the easier for you to do, the less your province has borne of burdens, which, while Arembergius was Prefect, was not ordered either to raise soldiers or to receive a military garrison within its borders. Whereas, on the other hand, the Brabanders, Flemings, Artesians, Hainaulters, the people of Namur and Luxembourg have been vexed by military injuries, and either themselves served for the king's love under pay, or with commendable readiness granted requests. Moved by these considerations, Arembergius has caused me to propose again the same matter that was proposed in the year 1558, so as to recall to memory what was done at that meeting. At that time you yourselves declared that you were led by no less affection towards King Philip than that with which you had followed Charles his father. So that you may confirm these words by deeds, by maintaining the army in obedience and discipline and by relieving the royal house, he demands seventy thousand gold pieces at this time, to be paid within four years in equal instalments. This was the proposal of Nitzenius, given on the eighth day before the Ides of July.

units.la: Quare x I. ad Arembergium ablegati Gerardus Duingelius Abbas Gericcensis, Ioannes Herama, & Hero Burmania, hoc modo responderunt.
units.tr: Accordingly, on 11 July, Gerardus Duingelius, Abbot of Gerkesklooster, Joannes Herama, and Hero Burmania, sent as envoys to Arembergius, answered in this way.

units.la: Non uno malo populus noster, Praefecte, gravatur, sed inter steriles annos inclementia coeli infelices, tum inter infrequens commercium, res provinciae trahantur. Unde annonae caritas, quae publicae infecunditatis individua comes est, per Frisiam suberta, intumescente ad hoc mari, quod ruptis, aut attritis littoribus salsedine agros corrupit. Inde pecorum passim interitus, & frugum penuria facultates nostras exhausit, quas, veluti confluentibus malis, praeter aggerum marinorum impendia, roga quoq; & precarium aes in Caesarem collatum attenuarunt. Et certè nisi perire terras nostras, quod in Zelandiâ evenit, aut arredi ab Oceano volumus, marinis æstubus fraugendis, reficiendisque aggeribus, omne, quod possidemus, impendendum est. Ut certè praestando beneficio, & liberalitati obvia quaeque calamitas nos invalidos fecerit, quorum insuper aerarium, sexaginta millibus aureorum, quos Caesari Carolo erogavimus, exhaustum scies. Tamen, ut in tantâ rerum angustiâ nos, quemadmodum ante Caesari, ita regi Philippo approbemus, offerimus quinquaginta aureorum millia sex pensionibus persolvenda, sub hac tamen cautione & curâ, ut salvo jure & immunitate nostrâ fiat, & ut ex conventione cum Carolo Caesare Anno xxxix. initâ, omne juri nostro adversum corrigatur.
units.tr: Our people, Prefect, are weighed down not by one evil, but between sterile years and unfavourable weather, and the affairs of the province are dragged down along with infrequent trade. Hence the dearness of grain, which is the inseparable companion of public barrenness, spreads through Friesland, while the sea swells for this purpose and, by breaking or wearing away the shores, spoils the fields with its saltness. Hence the death of cattle everywhere and the scarcity of crops have exhausted our resources, which, as the evils flow together, have been further diminished, besides the expense of the sea dykes, by the tax on the poll and the loan granted to the Emperor. And indeed, unless we wish our lands to perish, as happened in Zeeland, or to be torn away from the ocean, everything we possess must be spent in restraining the tides of the sea and in repairing the dykes. Thus, while we are weakened in our power to render benefits and in our liberality by every calamity that meets us, you should know that our treasury has been drained by the sixty thousand gold pieces that we paid to the Emperor Charles. Nevertheless, so that in so great a narrowness of affairs we may approve ourselves to King Philip as we did before to the Emperor, we offer fifty thousand gold pieces, to be paid in six instalments, yet under this caution and care, that it be done with our right and immunity preserved, and that everything contrary to our right be corrected in accordance with the agreement made with the Emperor Charles in the year 1539.

units.la: Quâ conditione lectâ offensus Arembergius, cum Senatus regij parte in arcem se contulit, sibique sexaginta millia aureorum assignari purè non adjectis conditionibus petijt, quas regis Philippi nomine, si imminutum gentis jus foret, suppleturum se dicebat.
units.tr: Having read these terms, Arembergius was offended. He went with some members of the Council of State to the citadel and asked that the sixty thousand gold pieces be assigned to him outright, without conditions. He said that if the nation's rights were diminished, he would make good the loss in King Philip's name.

units.la: Neque enim ante (inquit) civitate hac excedam, nisi quod regio Caroliquè nomine nomine vobis promissum est, praestetur, paratus, ut impendia conventuum publicorum evitemus, toto die ab ortu solis ad occasum reparandis rebus vestris vacare.
units.tr: "I will not leave this city," he said, "until what was promised to you in the name of the Regent and of Charles is delivered. I am ready to spend the whole day, from sunrise to sunset, settling your affairs, so that we avoid the expense of public assemblies."

units.la: Quare postero die, qui xii. erat, Arembergio per Ruardum Roorda & Heronem Burmania Delegatos, responsum:
units.tr: Therefore, on the next day, which was the twelfth, a reply was given to Arembergius through the delegates Ruardus Roorda and Heron Burmania.

units.la: Quamvis oblatio quinquaginta millium aureorum nostram liberalitatem, & in Regem affectum satis praedicaverit, tamen amore & reverentia regiae Philippi majestatis ducti, spondemus nos quinquaginta aureorum millia quinque justis pensionibus soluturos, sed hac cautione adjecta, ut laesi juris exempla aboleantur, & ut Lindani superbia actionibusque Ecclesiasticis occurratur.
units.tr: "Although the offer of fifty thousand gold pieces sufficiently proclaims our generosity and our devotion to the King, nevertheless, moved by love and reverence for the royal majesty of Philip, we promise to pay fifty thousand gold pieces, five instalments of equal size. But this condition is added: that examples of violated right be abolished, and that the arrogance and ecclesiastical proceedings of Lindanus be checked."

units.la: Haec ab Eysone Wiltinghio Praesule Clare-campio, Herone Burmania, Isbrando Harderviceno Antistite Lidlcmensi, Ruardo Roorda, Feddone Ockio, presbytero Oelano, & Ulrico Regnerio signata. Quae cum detrectaret Arembergius, qui puram & sine exceptione conventionem volebat, rursus conventum sibi dari petijt, novamque relationem ad Ordines instituit. Qui cum in priore decreto perfisterent, Arembergius pertinaciam, an libertatem gentis miratus, praestationem 5000. aureorum acceptavit, eâq; de re Margaretam Gubernatricem se moniturum fidem fecit. Ita res ad tempus interquievit, donec Margareta Gubernatrix, mobilitate animorum introspecta, libertati gentis aliquid daret, conventionemque cum Frisico populo initam, scriptis eâ de re solemnibus tabulis xiix. Augusti, ratam esse jussit.
units.tr: This reply was signed by Eyso Wiltingh, Prelate of Klarkamp, Heron Burmania, Isbrand Harderwijk, Bishop of Leeuwarden, Ruardus Roorda, Feddo Ockius, the elder Oela, and Ulricus Regnerus. Since Arembergius, who wanted an unconditional agreement without exceptions, rejected this, he again asked for a meeting to be granted to him and drew up a new report for the Estates. When the Estates held to their earlier decree, Arembergius, marvelling at their stubbornness or at the nation's liberty, accepted a payment of five thousand gold pieces, and he promised to inform Margaret the Regent of the matter. So the affair rested for a time, until Margaret the Regent, seeing into the fickleness of men's minds, granted something to the liberty of the nation, and on 12 August she ordered, by formal documents in writing, that the agreement made with the Frisian people be ratified.

units.la: Reperio in actis, eodem conventu de extruendâ Philippi Basilica, colloquium institutum, Ordinesque Frisiae, petente Arembergij nomine Nitzenio, tria millia aureorum erigendo operi, Leovardienses octingentos addixisse. Sub hac tamen formulâ, ut conclave aliquod conventui Ordinum habendo, reservaretur. Quae res etsi anno xlvi. Carolo adhuc Caesare & Maria Caroli sorore, rerum potiuntibus, tractata in curia oppidanâ fuisset, ita tunc in comitio confirmata vim ac robur accepit.
units.tr: I find in the records that at the same assembly a discussion was held about building a basilica for Philip. At the request of Nitzenius, on Arembergius' behalf, the Estates of Friesland agreed to give three thousand gold pieces toward the work, and the people of Leeuwarden eight hundred. This was on the condition that some room be reserved for the meetings of the Estates. Although this matter had been discussed in the town council in 1546, when Charles still held power with his sister Mary, it now received its force and validity from the assembly.

units.la: Mox vetus de Lindano querela recruduit, multaque odio illius & conciliandae invidiae Arembergio Senatuique regio oblata Lindani personam & simul dignitatem praegravavere. Quâ cum movere eum Ordines conarentur, non invalidis rationibus, quibus male administrati muneris urgebatur, tamen exteri hominis superbiae, quam aequiori causae plus datum, inrepente apud nonnullos metu, regiae majestatis voluntatem repetitis contra Lindanum obloquijs eludi. Quare multa in speciem acta, retinendique juris spe populo Frisico per Arembergium Senatumque regium facta Lindanus abjectum & humilem, quem simulabat, animum, majore mox superbiâ elevabat. Quod ab Arembergij, qui impense ei faciebat, consilio profectum illi non ignorabant, qui arcanos per litteras cum Margaretâ Gubernatrice Arembergij sermones, tanquam Lindano profuturos, evulgabant. Quippe illi Margareta rescripserat: Non videri sibi accusationum materiem amovendo Lindano satis validam, quin contra innocentiae ejus facere, quod ab objectis se purgare singulari constantiâ offerret. Interea moniturum se Episcopos & Archidiaconos jurisdictionem per Frisiam habentes, ut vetus mos in instituendis pastoribus servetur, & ut curarum, sicuti vocabant, beneficium nacti non nisi de consilio praesidis Senatusque regij, & ipsius quoque Lindani, repetito examini subijcerentur. Quod ad commissarios Episcopi Ultrajectini & Archidiaconorum, qui Oostergoïs, & Westergoïs pro more praesint, placuisse Philippo regi, & Episcopo Ultrajectino, non ita pridem defuncto, ut stabiliendam ad religionem, reformationemque status ordinisque Ecclesiastici per Frisiam, ut censor aliquis doctrinae & pietatis laude praecellens crearetur, qui in vitam ac mores coenobitarum pastorum; doctrinam inquirat. Cujus curationi, cum Rex, & Episcopus, tum ipsi Archidiaconi multum aeris impendant, non aliam Regis, Episcopi, aut Archidiaconorum intentionem esse, quam ut Romanae religioni consulatur, & ne Frisij onere sustentandi Episcopalis Vicarij, aut censoris, graventur. Praeterea addebat Margareta non esse suae potestatis, sine regis voluntate, aut mandato, hac in parte quid mutare, neque inconsulto novo Episcopo aut Archidiaconis aliud decernere quam quod Philippo regi visum fuisset. Se interim daturam operam, ut jus Frisijs sartum tectum servetur, moneaturque Lindanus, ut ex praescripto Philippi Regis agat. Haec Bruxellis v. Eid. Iul. acta, & Margaretae manu signata.
units.tr: Soon the old complaint about Lindanus broke out again. Many charges, offered to win the people's hatred of him and to gain favour for Arembergius and the royal Council of State, weighed heavily on Lindanus' person and his standing. When the Estates tried to move him from office, on grounds that were not weak, namely that he was badly managing his post, yet the arrogance of this foreigner, to which the more just cause gave more weight, and a fear creeping in among some people, led them to blunt the king's will by repeated objections against Lindanus. Therefore, Lindanus, whose humble and abject spirit was only pretended, soon raised himself with greater arrogance. Those who knew that this came from the advice of Arembergius, who was eagerly supporting him, circulated secret letters, in which Arembergius' conversations with Margaret the Regent were reported as though they would help Lindanus. Margaret had indeed written back to him that, in her view, removing Lindanus was not a strong enough ground for accusations, and that it was more in favour of his innocence that he offered himself to clear himself of the charges with remarkable steadiness. Meanwhile, she would warn the bishops and archdeacons who held jurisdiction throughout Friesland, so that the old custom in appointing ministers be kept, and so that those who had obtained the benefice of cures, as they were called, should be put to examination again, and only with the advice of the president and the royal Council of State, and of Lindanus himself. As for the commissioners of the Bishop of Utrecht and of the archdeacons, who preside over Oostergo and Westergo according to custom, it had pleased King Philip and the Bishop of Utrecht, who had died not long before, that for establishing religion and reforming the state and order of the clergy throughout Friesland, some censor distinguished by his praise for doctrine and piety should be appointed, who would examine the doctrine and the life and morals of the monks and ministers. Since the King, the bishop and the archdeacons themselves spent much money on this business, the intention of the King, the bishop and the archdeacons was none other than to safeguard the Roman religion, and that the Frisians should not be burdened with supporting an episcopal vicar or censor. Margaret added that it was not within her power to change anything in this matter without the King's will or command, nor to decree anything other than what seemed good to King Philip, without consulting the new bishop or the archdeacons. Meanwhile, she would take care that the rights of the Frisians were kept safe and whole, and Lindanus would be advised to act according to the instructions of King Philip. These things were done at Brussels on 5 July and were signed in Margaret's hand.

units.la: Tum ut res ultro per Edicta & Inquisitionem, deinde ob Hispanorum Legionem per praesidia distributam lubricae, validioribus machinis impulsae nutarent, vix reversus in Hispaniam Philippus post compressos primatum sanguine regni motus, & infaelices exitu cum Elisabetha Vallesia regij Francicique sanguinis faemina, celebratas nuptias, constituendorum per Provincias Episcopatuum negotio se dedit. Quapropter misso jam ante Romam, ubi Paulus IV. Pontificatum tum gerebat, & quo cum bellum in Italia Philippus gesserat, Francisco Sonnio Theologo Lovaniensi, & per Frisiam Inquisitore, de consilio Antonij Perrenoti, hoc maxime cavit, ut negotium Pontifex maturaret, ipseque occasionem obturbandae Belgicae nactus, Gallici foederis secretum, suo principatui, & juxta Provincijs fatale, & climactericum exequeretur. Itaque Paulus Pontifex, ne rei tam sanctae, & necessariae morae necterentur, XIV. Kal. Iun. Philippi mox consilium approbavit, confirmarique tabulis fecit. Quo Pontifice humanitus ab Ipto, & damnata cum eo ob foeditatem gesti Pontificatus omni memoria, Pius IV. successor eandem mox sanctionem confirmaverat, Philippiq; propositum, velut persanandis per Belgicam mentibus salubre, & Romanae Sedis Imperio conducens corroborari factis eâ de re VIII. Eid. Mart. tabulis fecerat. Ita Sonnius curatis, quas Romae voluerat, rebus, in Belgicam regressus ordinationes novorum Episcoporum, & simul fomitem civilis incendij clam adduxit. Reperio in litteris mandatorum Sonnij, causam constituendae per Frisiam Sedis luxui & corruptis caenobitarum moribus imputatam, reprimendisque adultis cleri vitijs unicum illud remedium sanandis malis repertum. Duorum quoque Caenobiorum Horti Mariae, & Lidlumani amplissimum censum Sedi destinatum, triaque millia ducatorum mensae Episcopali assignata. Reliquum dotis, quod ante monachorum luxus insumpserat, Canonicis attributum, eosq; e S. pagiuae Canonumq; Doctoribus, tum e Nobilitate creandos in ijsdem litteris Philippum constituisse. Ultrajectinae quocIↄ. Iↄ. quoque Sedi, ut ante Willebrordi ætate, Archiepiscopum ordinatum Suffraganeosq; Daventriensem, Leovardiensem, Groningensem, Harlemensem, & Middelburgicum eidem Archi-Episcopo subjunctos. Quibus in Hispaniam à Sonnio missis robur post additum, Philippusq; Iv. Eid Maij in ipso (ut habent tabulæ) consistorio eà de re Decretum fecit.
units.tr: Then, as matters were wavering unstably, first through the edicts and the Inquisition, and then, because of the Spanish legion distributed in garrisons, were being pushed by stronger machines, Philip, having barely returned to Spain after suppressing with blood the movements of the nobility of the realm, and having celebrated his marriage with Elizabeth of Valois, a woman of royal and French blood, turned to the business of establishing bishoprics throughout the provinces. Therefore, he had already sent Francis Sonnius, a theologian of Louvain and inquisitor for Friesland, to Rome, where Paul IV then held the papacy, against whom Philip had waged war in Italy. On the advice of Antoine Perrenot, Philip above all took care that the Pope should hasten the business, so that he himself, having found an occasion to disturb the Netherlands, might carry out the secret of the French alliance, which was fatal and climacteric for his principality and for the neighbouring provinces. So Pope Paul, lest the delay of so holy and necessary a matter be prolonged, soon approved Philip's plan on 19 May and had it confirmed by documents. When Paul died, and all memory of his disgraceful papacy was condemned, his successor Pius IV soon confirmed the same sanction. He had confirmed Philip's proposal by documents on 6 March, as something wholesome for healing minds throughout the Netherlands and conducive to the empire of the Roman See. Thus Sonnius, having arranged the business he had wished to arrange in Rome, returned to the Netherlands and secretly brought with him the ordinances for the new bishops, and at the same time the spark of civil fire. I find in the letters of Sonnius' instructions that the cause of establishing the See throughout Friesland was attributed to luxury and corrupt morals of the monks, and that to curb the grown vices of the clergy that single remedy was devised for healing the evils. In the same letters Philip also ordained that the very wealthy revenues of the two monasteries of Mariahoop and Lidlum were assigned to the See, and that three thousand ducats were assigned to the episcopal table. The rest of the endowment, which the monks' luxury had previously consumed, was given to the canons, and it was laid down in the same letters that Philip would appoint them from the canons of the Church and the doctors of the canons, and also from the nobility. Also to the See of Utrecht, as in the time of Willibrord, an archbishop was appointed, with the bishops of Deventer, Leeuwarden, Groningen, Haarlem and Middelburg placed under him as suffragans. When Sonnius had sent these arrangements to Spain, they gained strength, and Philip, on 4 May, in the consistory itself (as the documents state), made a decree on this matter.

units.la: Extat in Cornelij Gemmæ observationibus terribilem Solis defectum mense Augusto evenisse, multaque prodigia velut facem belli denuntiantia, curiosè notantibus apparuisse. Lucem quoque magnam cum levi terræ motu notatam, totumque annum tempestatibus & procellis, tum fulminibus fragoribusque cœli, turbidum fuisse. Præsagiente velut rerum naturâ, indicandis in hoc terrarum circulo motibus præludi.
units.tr: It is recorded in the observations of Cornelius Gemma that a terrible eclipse of the sun occurred in August, and that many portents appeared, which curious observers noted as announcing war like a torch. A great light was also observed together with a slight earthquake, and the whole year was turbulent with storms and tempests, with thunderbolts and crashes from the sky. Nature itself seemed to presage, and these were the preludes to movements to be shown throughout this circle of lands.

units.la: Dein Philippus regio luxu celebratis nuptijs Carolum filium unicum adhuc regiæ domus hæredem per omnem Hispaniam, juramento à proceribus regni subditisque accepto, designari successorem, confirmariqúe curavit. Ut scilicet dubio longioris vitæ spatio, & incertâ Elisabethæ fœcunditate, diffusum regni corpus, & haud pridem factionibus obnoxium, certo hærede, &, si quid humanitus accideret, majestate novi regnantis coërceret. Quarum rerum ut ignaræ adhuc per Frisiam mentes erant, ita domesticis econtra malis, & multo prædone adfligebantur. Interceptis namque Gallicâ pace stipendijs pessimos quosque, ut nuper militiæ, ita tum ignaviæ ac desidis vitæ cupido grassationibus per provinciam mancipabat, otiumque inutile, & turbidis rebus, aut perdendis Provincialium fortunis succrescens, fœdis & reprobatis bello sceleribus pascebatur. Quamobrem Senatus regius (quod jam ante sancitâ Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. XLIV. Gallicâ pace Carolo Cæsare evenerat) edicto in prædones statuit, deprehensisque cum telo conciliandæ securitati publicæ severam legem, poenam capitis, denuntiavit.
units.tr: Then Philip, having celebrated his marriage with royal splendour, arranged that his only son Charles, still the heir of the royal house, should be designated successor throughout all Spain, having received the oath from the nobles of the realm and the subjects, and he had this confirmed. Clearly, because of the uncertain length of his own life and the doubtful fertility of Elizabeth, he wished the far-flung body of the kingdom, which had lately been prone to factions, to be held together by a certain heir and, if anything should happen to him as a mortal, by the majesty of a new ruler. While the minds in Friesland were still ignorant of these matters, they were on the other hand troubled by domestic evils and a great band of robbers. For with the French peace having cut off the pay of the soldiers, the worst men, just as recently from the army, so now the desire for an idle and lazy life drove them through the province in raids, and idleness, useless and growing from troubled affairs or from the ruin of provincial fortunes, fed on foul and condemned crimes of war. Therefore the royal Council of State, as had already happened in 1544 by the French peace with Charles Caesar, issued an edict against the robbers, and it proclaimed a severe law, the penalty of death, against those caught carrying weapons, in order to secure public safety.

units.la: Invenio in actis circa Berlicomos, Vieranos, Beetgumanos & confines enormi licentiâ pecora promiscuè alienum in pascuum acta, ipsosque colonos agrorum & proprietarios eâ de vi apud Senatum regium conquestos, ad comitium provinciæ rescripto Curiæ remissos. Ad libellum quoque supplicem ab ijsdem Berlicomijs socijsque anno sequente III. Maii oblatum, velut distractis in graviora ingenijs, non rescriptum fuisse.
units.tr: I find in the records that around Berlikum, Vier, Beetgum and the neighbouring districts, cattle were driven onto other people's pasture with enormous licence. The farmers and landowners themselves complained of this violence to the royal Senate, which sent them back to the provincial assembly with a rescript. The petition that the Berlikumers and their allies presented the following year, on 3 May, was likewise not answered, since the minds of the men concerned had been turned to more serious matters.

units.la: Arembergius quoque Ægyptios paganis ritibus, & profanis superstitionibus imbutos, suaeque Præfecturæ graves & molestos Frisiâ ocyus excedere, similique gladij poenâ (quâ Carolus Cæsar ex Edicto Anni cIↄ. Iↄ. XXXIIIX.) coërceri jussit. Edictum VII. Kal. Octob. Vollenhovæ signatum. Cautum quoque, ut earum rerum merciumq; (quæ adulatione istorum temporum, ac discordi implicitoque factionibus populo Frisico, Carolo Cæsari Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. XXIV. vectigales factæ erant) apud Conductores Regios professio fieret, persolvereturq; vectigal importandis in Frisiam, rebus, mercibusque assignatum. Poena in Transgressores Edicti statuta, decretumque ut confiscationi rerum, mercium, naviumque pecuniaria quoque multa adijceretur à Carolo Cæsare Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. XLIV. fraudatoribus istiusmodi vectigalium irrogata. Ii fructus deperditæ per discordias libertatis fuere, quorum onera adolescente principatu, post etiam bello aucta, liberrimam tot sæculis gentem diuturnis armis, & succrescenti indies servituti implicuere.
units.tr: Arembergius also ordered that the Egyptians, steeped in pagan rites and profane superstitions and burdensome and troublesome to his prefecture, should leave Friesland more quickly, and that they be restrained by the same penalty of the sword that Charles Caesar had prescribed by his edict of the year 1533. The edict was signed at Vollenhove on 25 September. It was also provided that a declaration of those goods and wares, which in the flattery of those times and amid the discord and entanglement of factions had been made liable to duty for the Frisian people in the year 1524 under Charles Caesar, should be made to the royal collectors, and that the duty assigned to goods and merchandise brought into Friesland should be paid. A penalty was laid down for transgressors of the edict, and it was decreed that a fine of money should be added to the confiscation of goods, merchandise and ships, as had been imposed on defrauders of such duties by Charles Caesar in 1544. These were the fruits lost through the discords of liberty, whose burdens, increased in the youthful reign and afterwards by war, bound a most free nation for many centuries with lasting arms and with a servitude that grew daily.

units.la: Post partem Edicti à Carolo Cæsare Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. L. publicati Senatus per Frisiam regius renovavit, vetuitque; Ne quid in publicum, præterquam de consilio Censorum typis ederetur, vulgareturque poenâ ex eodem Edicto 100. aureorum constitutâ. Edictum IX. Kalend. Ian. Leovardiæ signatum. Hoc quippe Edicto obtendebatur, ne, serace istiusmodi librorum Germaniâ, quæ libertatem suam, invito etiam Cæsare, retinuerat, simile per Belgicam fieret, ætasque tenerior, propriâ animorum mollitie, cum ipso velut lacte præcepta purioris doctrinæ hauriret. Itaque Maria Gubernatrix nomine Caroli Cæsaris hoc etiam Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LIII. sanxerat, ut decretorum Germaniæ liber per Frisiam non valeret, nullaque aut inefficax ad Decreta Germaniæ Augustanis Comitijs Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. XLVIII. facta reorum, damnatorumq; in causa religionis provocatio haberetur. Ijs namq; caverat Carolus, ut partem onerum Imperij Belgæ ferrent, ad eos verò Rescriptorum, Statutorumque ejusdem Imperij (quibus libertatem Religionis coactus indulserat) communio, beneficiumve non perveniret. Quapropter ne jure ac immunitate Germaniæ (quâ ab omni memoriâ ex tot Cæsaris Diplomatis, tum ex ipsa quoque Carolinâ conventione anni cIↄ. Iↄ. XXII. debebant) Frisij fruerentur, promulgatis per Belgicam de Religione Edictis, Statutisque eos parere jusserat, omni exemptione fœdo exemplo antiquatâ. Ita namq; inter Frisios Carolumq; Cæsarem conventum erat: UT CAESAR JUS SAXONIS AC HAEREDITARII PRAEFECTI CESSIONE ACCIPERET, EIQUE JUS-JURANDUM, UT ET HAEREDIBUS, POSTERISQUE NOMINE ROMANI IMPERII DEFERRETUR. Neque aliam rationem ineundi inter Belgicæ Provincias, Frisiosque fœderis Mariam Gubernatricem, Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. XXXV. IV. Eid. Iun. proposuisse, quam ut ad mutua auxilia adversum vim externam Provinciæ se obligarent, suo verò jure, (ac si fœdus, Principisvè imperium nihil de eo delibaret) unaquæque Provincia frueretur. Cæterum robusto Cæsaris Principatu, & adultâ post partium, quæ à libertate majorum desciverant, adulatione, omnis aviti, patrijque juris memoria, atque vis sensim obliterata, Frisiorumque Ditiones Germaniæ Imperio subtractæ, duorum Cæsarum Maximiliani atque Caroli cupiditate, patrimonio Burgundicæ domus adscriptæ sunt. Ab eo namque fuit, ut solemnem illam cum Frisijs Anni cIↄ. Iↄ. XXIV. pactionem omisso Imperij, quod præferre debuerat, nomine, CAROLUS CAESAR, SE, ET HAEREDES, POSTEROSQUE, UT HOLLANDIAE COMITES servaturum caveret, nulloque tempore, ita pacisçente odio Geldricæ partis Burgundicæ factionis nobilitate, Frisiam ab Hollandiæ Comitatu se separaturum, fidem interponeret. Quod ne fieret subsecutis temporibus Maria quoque Gubernatrix, datis in Frisiam Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. XLIX. Prid. Eid. Iun. litteris, obnixè Frisios rogaverat, ut fœdus autore Cæsare, cum Romano Imperio, de præstandis auxilijs, Au-
units.tr: After the Senate, the royal authority through Friesland, renewed part of an edict published by Charles Caesar in the year 1550, and forbade that anything be printed or made public in the public domain except with the approval of the censors, under a penalty of 100 gold pieces set by the same edict. The edict was signed at Leeuwarden on 24 December. For the purpose of this edict it was argued that, lest such books from Germany, which had kept its liberty even against the will of Caesar, should be imported in the same way into the Low Countries, and lest a younger generation, through its own softness of mind, should drink in with its very milk the precepts of a purer doctrine. Accordingly, Mary the Regent, in the name of Charles Caesar, had decreed in this same year 1553 that the decrees of Germany should have no force through Friesland, and that no appeal of the accused and condemned in matters of religion, made according to the decrees of Germany at the Augsburg Diet of 1548, should be recognised or have any effect. For Charles had provided that the Netherlands should bear a part of the burdens of the empire, but that the communion and benefit of the rescripts and statutes of that same empire (by which he had been compelled to grant freedom of religion) should not reach them. Therefore, lest the Frisians should enjoy the right and immunity of Germany (which, from all memory, they owed to so many diplomas of the Caesars, and also to the Carolingian convention of the year 1522 itself), he had ordered them to obey the edicts and statutes on religion that had been published throughout the Netherlands, all exemption having been abolished by a shameful precedent. For this is what had been agreed between the Frisians and Charles Caesar: that Caesar should receive the right of the Saxon and hereditary prefect by cession, and that the oath should be rendered to him in the name of the Roman Empire, and likewise to his heirs and descendants. Nor did Mary the Regent, on 10 June 1535, propose any other basis for forming a covenant between the Netherlandish provinces and the Frisians than that they should bind themselves to mutual aid against external force, while each province enjoyed its own right, as though the covenant or the authority of the prince took nothing from it. But with the Caesar's principate strong, and with flattery grown up after the factions that had deserted the liberty of their ancestors, the memory and force of all ancestral and paternal right was gradually effaced. The territories of Friesland were withdrawn from the empire of Germany and assigned to the patrimony of the Burgundian house, through the greed of the two Caesars, Maximilian and Charles. For it was from Charles that the solemn compact with the Frisians of the year 1524 was obtained, and he gave his pledge that, leaving out the name of the empire, which he ought to have put first, he would keep, for himself, his heirs and his successors, the title of Counts of Holland, and that at no time would Friesland separate itself from the county of Holland. Lest this happen in the following times, Mary the Regent also, in letters sent to Friesland on 12 June 1549, had earnestly asked the Frisians to approve the covenant made at Augsburg under the authority of Caesar with the Roman Empire concerning the furnishing of aid, and to join with the Belgic peoples in a closer bond of fellowship on this very occasion.

units.la: Augustae Vindelicorum initum, Frisij approbarent, arctiorisque societatis vinculo hac ipsa occasione cum Belgicae populis coirent. Hoc namque illo consilij arcano tum agebatur, ut Frisij hortatu Mariae Gubernatricis, Principis faeminae, & civiles animos movere non imperiae, tum reverentiâ, cuius mandatum Maria praeferebat, Caroli Caesaris pelleċti, & firmiore cum caeteris provincijs nexu uniti, ab antiqua Romani Imperij societate divellerentur, communemque cum Belgico populo fortunam, & conditionem instantium temporum acciperent. Carolus quoque Caesar sociatâ Germaniae Belgicâ, discors religionibus, & laerum Principum armis Imperium commodius coerceret, compositoque, & pacato eodem Imperio Belgicam suam, novarum, ut aiebat, religionum faecundam, in speciem regni, & non disparatae cum Hispaniâ servitutis, subsidio eiusdem foederis formaret. Caeterum continuam in Carolo felicitatem fastidiente, & velut manum retrahente fortunâ factum est, ut sua Germaniae libertas constaret, Carolusque Caesar, prout incerti mortalium rerum eventus sunt, propositio excidens, praefractum illum & magnitudini suae fatalem in religione zelum, quietis Belgicae provincijs suo, & successoris filij damno inferret, Frisios etiam, ut naturae limite & ultimo Rheno, ita legibus, moribusque à Belgicae populis Burgundionum subditis discretos, ijsdem, quae de religione per Belgicam sanxerat, Edictis teneri obligarique pronuntiaret. Litterae Mariae Gubernatricis ad Senatum regium (qui judicium Caroli Caesaris super hac re per litteras xvi. Kal. Jun. Leovardiae datas requisiverat) Bruxellis iv. Non. Jun. Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LIII. signatae. Liber quoq; de Confessione Fidei incerto autore, & spretâ Censorum autoritate, editus, à Senatu per Frisiam regio damnatus est. Tum deducendâ reparandâque, quae à Sigeri Coenobio Garipam ducit, viâ, inter Tietzerchios, & Smallingaeos orta lis à Senatu regio definita, mandatumque agrarijs per Provinciam; ut vias publicas eluvie brumalium aquarum foedatas, ferendis equis, curribusque commodas curent. Cautum quoq; asperè, Ne quod maris ejectamentum, sive aestu è fundo actum, sive tempestate disjectum, sine Praetorum consensu à litore asportaretur, caeterum omne fluitans, naufragumve, ut ante ex pacto Caesari, ita Philippo pro more cederet, denunciatione eius rei intra xxi v. horas Praetori, triduum verò Senatui regio facienda.
units.tr: Augsburg [Augusta Vindelicorum]. For this was the secret purpose of that plan then in hand: that the Frisians, by the urging of Mary the Regent, a princess, should stir up civil spirits not yet subject to empire, and, out of reverence for the command that Mary put forward, be drawn to Charles Caesar and, bound by a firmer tie with the other provinces, be torn away from the ancient fellowship of the Roman Empire and receive a common fortune and condition with the Belgic people in the pressing times. Charles Caesar also, by joining the Netherlands to Germany, would more conveniently restrain an empire divided by religions and the arms of the discordant princes, and, once that same empire was composed and pacified, would shape his Netherlands, fertile in what he called new religions, into the appearance of a kingdom and a servitude not dissimilar to that of Spain, with the aid of the same alliance. But fortune, growing weary of Charles's continual success and drawing back its hand, brought it about that the liberty of Germany held firm, and Charles Caesar, as the outcome of mortal affairs is uncertain, fell from his purpose; and that stubborn zeal in religion, fatal to his own greatness, brought loss to the quiet Netherlandish provinces, to his own and to his son's detriment. He also declared that the Frisians, separated from the Netherlandish peoples, subjects of the Burgundians, not only by the natural boundary of the Rhine but also by their laws and customs, should be held and bound by the same edicts on religion that he had sanctioned throughout the Netherlands. The letters of Mary the Regent to the royal Senate (which had requested Caesar's judgement on this matter by letter given at Leeuwarden on 16 May) were signed at Brussels on 2 June 1553. A book on the Confession of Faith, published by an unknown author and in contempt of the authority of the censors, was condemned by the royal Senate throughout Friesland. Then a dispute between the Tietzerchiers and the Smallingers, arising over the making and repair of the road that leads from the monastery of Sieger to Garipa, was settled by the Senate, and the land stewards throughout the province were ordered to keep the public roads, fouled by the flooding of winter waters, fit for horses and carts. It was also strictly provided that no piece of wreckage cast up by the sea, whether driven ashore by the tide or scattered by a storm, be carried away from the shore without the consent of the praetors; and that all floating or shipwrecked goods should, as before by agreement with Caesar and now likewise with Philip, pass by custom, the matter being reported to the praetor within twenty-five hours, and to the royal Senate within three days.

units.la: Ideni statuit, Ut ij, qui tabulationibus littorum, portuumve (arcas veteres achitectonicae autores, ut & hodie, vocabant) manus admovissent, earum asseres, sublicas, tigna rupissent, abstuhissentve, capite luerent, ablatorum verò ejectamentorum convicti, pecuniariâ multâ, post arbitrariâ poenâ corrigerentur. Hoc quippe nolebat Senatus, ut Frisica gens navigiorum spolijs ceustum faceret, munimentumque infidi littoris immenso sumptu arcendo mari à majoribus fundatum privati licentia, & rapacitate nudaretur. Mox ingravescenti rursum annonae prospectum, publicatumque à Margaretâ Gubernatrice; Ne quod frumentum Frisiâ exportaretur. Quod decretum, quia Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LX. Carolo Caesare impediendis, minuenciisque commercijs videbatur, ita per Legatos coram Mariâ agrarij tum egerant, ne quid tale in posterum manifesto Provincialium damno perscribere-tur. tur. Ostendebant namque exportatis frumentis annonæ periculum non strui, quod ea foli Frisici natura esset, minimum secalis, hordei verò ac avenæ plurimum ferre. His quoque solis stare, & florere commercia, ijsq; fieri, ut per mercatores aliunde advectos pecuniæ haud parum agrarijs accedat, quâ marinorum aggerum, tum regiorum vectigalium onera ferri queant. Sine hoc verò subsidio, nec privatas agrariorum res consistere, nec statas vectigalium pensiones præstari posse. Neq; enim tantas oppidanis opes, atq; facultates esse, ut omni frumento paratum æs assignare queant, etiam extemplo persolutum, caritatem annonæ datum. Ita namq; fore, ut ipsi pretium quod volent, statuant, agrariorumq; sæpe angustiâ malè usi per damnatas legibus coemptiones, frumento caritatem, egestatem plebi, penuriam universis sint paraturi. Idcirco rogabant Carolum Cæsarem, ut habitâ libertatis ratione, decretum antiquaret, durantéq; bello Gallico, aut caritate rerum tantummodò valiturum, fidem daret.
units.tr: The same body decreed that those who had laid hands on the planking of the shores or harbours (which the old architectural writers, as today, called chests) and had broken or carried off its boards, piles or beams should pay with their heads; and those convicted of carrying off the wreckage should be punished with a fine of money and afterwards with an arbitrary penalty. For the Senate did not wish the Frisian people to make a habit of plundering the spoils of ships, and the defence of the treacherous shore, raised by their ancestors at immense cost to keep off the sea, to be stripped bare by private licence and rapacity. Soon, as the price of grain rose again, a prohibition was published by Margaret the Regent that no grain be exported from Friesland. This decree seemed to hinder and diminish commerce in the year 1560 under Charles Caesar, so the land stewards, through envoys, then pleaded before Mary that nothing of the kind be decreed in future to the manifest loss of the provincials. For they showed that a danger to the food supply was not created by exporting grain, since the nature of the Frisian soil was such that it bore very little rye but a great deal of barley and oats. Commerce too depended on these alone and flourished through them, and it came about that, through merchants brought in from elsewhere, no small amount of money came to the land stewards, by which they could bear both the burdens of the sea dykes and the royal taxes. Without this aid, neither the private affairs of the land stewards could stand, nor the fixed payments of the taxes be made. For the townspeople did not have such wealth and resources that they could assign ready money for all their grain, even if paid immediately, once the price of grain had risen. For it would follow that they would set whatever price they wished, and the land stewards, often ill served by their straitened circumstances, would through purchases condemned by the laws prepare a dearth of grain, want for the common people and scarcity for all. Therefore they asked Charles Caesar that, having regard to liberty, he should annul the decree and give his word that it would hold only while the Gallic war lasted, or while goods were dear.

units.la: Id Mariæ Gubernatricis rescripto (additâ obtestatione integrum agrarijs jus, inviolatumque fore) VI. Eid Ian. confirmatum, ut ijsdem agrarijs tum damnosum, ita hoc tempore sublevandæ communi annonæ remedium fuit. Eò namque Margaretæ consilium atque Edictum spectabat, ut coemptiones cessarent, omneq; frumentum in promiscuos populi usus erogatum istius anni præsentaneæ sterilitati mederetur. Æstas enim ut multo imbre madens, ita torpido aëre putredinem frugum, mox animalium luem, atque pestilentiam invexerat, stagnantesq; pœt planitiem aquæ campis suopte ingenio humentibus ægrius laxabantur. Inveno in Annalium libro Kemponis Martenæ, graffantibus adhuc per Provinciam Burgundicarum Geldricarumque partium reliquijs, Frisiæ Ordines Georgij Scenci & suorum dominatione offensos, Margaretam Cæsaris amitam Provinciarum tum Gubernatricem suppressæ, aut sterili annonæ simile remedium orasse, querimoniamque Ordinum eidem Edicto, per Carolum sæpius Cæsarem vulgato, causam dedisse. Idem quoque Edictum vehementibus oppidanorum studijs anno sequente confirmatum, pœnamque lege constitutam violatoribus Edicti à Magistratibus per Frisiam irrogatam esse, Hobbio Baerdio, Cornelio Fonckio, Tarquinio Vallesio, Iacobo Iacobæo, G. Wallema, Theodoro Theodoreto, Foccone Andreæ, Ioanne Iulio Beima, & Bonnone Petræo III. Eid. Mart. subscribentibus. Legem quoq; de ponderibus, & mensuris, Saxonum ætate latam, ab ijsdem innovatam, statutumque ut per oppida Saxonicæ legis ratio atque formula observaretur.
