Thus the English had moved their cloth market from Belgium into the territory of the empire at Emden, for no other purpose than that the fortunes of the Belgian people might decline, and that a long-unfaithful alliance might be loosened by a new quarrel. For this reason he wished the Frisians to leave the kingdom of England and to abstain likewise, until Elizabeth should rescind the edict, and disputes arising from this cause should be settled by arbiters. Meanwhile English cloths were to be forbidden in Friesland, and not received or sold there; on the contrary, it was to be decreed that any that were received and sold should go to the treasury. The letters of Margaret, the Regent, were sent from Brussels into Friesland on 29 July and published at Leeuwarden on 11 August. It is clear from these letters that, since a plague and pestilence was then raging through England, the edict had been put forward, and that the English goods and the breath of the merchants had made commerce slow. Then Philip, intending to avenge the insult of the rejected bishop as contempt for his rule, sent to Margaret the Regent letters full of threats, in which strict orders for the reception of the Inquisition and of the Council of Trent were contained. Therefore Margaret, having called together the Senate of the Belgian Estates, showed them Philip's letters, so that she would have nothing hidden; these were variously interpreted, according to each man's temper or disposition, in those doubtful and harsh times. Some thought that Philip's decrees should be published through the provinces at once; on the other hand, the wiser counsel, and among them Viglius of Zuichem, was that the publication of the decrees should be postponed until the Belgian Senate had reported to Philip on the state of the provinces. Others add that Viglius took upon himself whatever harm or danger to the king's anger might result from the delay, and offered a guarantee to Margaret in person. But Viglius's wholesome counsel, which loved public peace, then prevailed through the votes of the others. And so the bridle was loosened for the evils, and Margaret the Regent wrote at once to the Frisians on 19 December, signifying that Philip wished the people to obey his edicts concerning religion. She also warned the magistrates of the towns that, under the penalty laid down in those same edicts, they should each quarter send one from the number of the Senators or Scabins, and give him power to see that the decrees of the Council of Trent were kept safe and sound. The most distinguished man Abel Franckena writes in his historical fragments that the Council of Trent, begun at Trent on the river Adige by Pope Paul III, became the mother of the movements through all Germany and likewise in Belgium, and that Charles, and soon afterwards Philip, out of reverence for the leading men of that Council, as if driven by divine inspiration, and with the Perrenots, father and son, as instigators, neglected every law and principle of the civil government.

units.la: Tum rursum prætoribus regijs à Iulio Gelio procuratore Fisci, dies dictus, missusq; Ianuario mense Bruxellas (cuius nomen actis reticetur) vir nobilis, qui coram Viglio Præside & Ioachimo Hoppero Senatore regio quereretur. Publicanos, aut conductores regiorum vectigalium per Frisiæ portus fraudem Regi, ac commercijs facere. Prætoris morte aut alia ex causa vacuis successores dandos, eosq; à populo electos offerendos Senatui regio esse. Conventiones cum Saxone ac Carolo Cæsare initas renovandas esse. Satrapas arcium coram judicio regio conveniendos. Privilegiorum Frisiæ pactorumque publicorum instrumenta à Viglio Præside, ac Hoppero, repetenda esse. Ad quæ responsum in commentarijs istius viri nobilis reperio. Non interesse tantum provinciæ, sed & regis, ut publicanorum fraudibus subveniatur, eligunturque prætores more antiquo, constituunturque à Curiâ, sed ut conventionibus Saxonicis ac Caroli Cæsaris cum hac gente initis firmamentum accedat, archivorumque acta à Viglio, & Hoppero, qui se ad hoc offerrent, provinciæ restituantur. Quod ad satrapas attineret, eos, qua prætores forent, coram regio Senatu sistendos, donec aliter à Philippo statutum sit. C. Gemma notat, non uno huius anni prodigio insignitam civilis belli tempestatem, æmulationesq; ac discordias virorum Principum, velut ipso conciente cælo, plebem quoque ipsam instantium pavidam funestis partibus miscuisse.
units.tr: Then again a day was set by the royal praetors, at the instance of Julius Gellius, the procurator of the treasury; in January a noble man (whose name the records do not give) was sent to Brussels to complain before Viglius, the President, and Joachim Hopper, a royal Senator. He said that the tax-farmers, or collectors of royal revenues, through the Frisian ports were defrauding the King and commerce. When praetors died or were vacant for some other reason, successors ought to be appointed, and those chosen by the people should be offered to the royal Senate. The agreements made with the Saxons and with Charles Caesar ought to be renewed. The governors of the fortresses should be summoned before the royal court. The documents of the Frisian privileges and of the public pacts ought to be demanded back from Viglius the President and from Hopper. I find in the commentaries of this noble man the reply to these points. It was not only in the interest of the province but also of the king that the frauds of the tax-farmers be checked, and that praetors be chosen in the ancient manner and appointed by the Court; but the agreements with the Saxons and with the treaties of Charles Caesar made with this people should receive confirmation, and the archives' records should be restored to the province by Viglius and Hopper, who offered themselves for this purpose. As for the governors, they should, while they were praetors, be placed before the royal Senate until Philip decided otherwise. C. Gemma notes that the storm of civil war was marked by more than one portent in this year, and that the rivalries and discords of the leading men, as if heaven itself were stirring, had mixed the common people, too, fearful of the threatening dangers, into its deadly parties.

units.la: Tum vulgatis per Frisiam Margaretæ litteris altiore metu trepidatum, perculsarumq; mentium sollicitudinem inauspicati prodigiorum monitus auxere. Tradunt monstrorum ortu deformes partus tum notatos, horrendaque per vicinos Frisios vaticinia maturum exitium ceciniße. Cæteris laborantium tabescentiumve velut rerum mœstarum & incompositæ facies, & per omnem Provinciam manifesta civilis concordiæ deliquia, ut certioris mali præludia observabantur. Quare
units.tr: Then, when Margaret's letters had been published through Friesland, the people trembled with greater fear, and the anxiety of their terrified minds was increased by the warnings of ill-omened portents. They relate that deformed births were then noted in the birth of monsters, and that dreadful prophecies among the neighbouring Frisians foretold an approaching ruin. In the rest of the suffering and wasting people, the faces of things both sad and disordered were observed, and throughout the whole province the clear signs of a collapse of civil concord, as the preludes of a worse evil. Wherefore

units.la: Margareta Gubernatrix prodigiorum fide conterrita, & ut mollitiem sexus, animumque miseratione tristiorum omnium motum ostentaret, de mittendo in Hispaniam ad Philippum Legato cogitavit, convocatoq; ocyus Status Belgici Senatu Principes Aurei Velleris, & provinciarum Præfectos adesse Bruxellas jussit. Ibi ponderato temporum discrimine de Legato proposuit, perrogatisque sententijs Lamoralium Egmondanum virum illustrium natalium, & Carolo Philippoque regibus Gallicis alijsque bellis clarum, expediendæ in Hispaniam Legationi designavit. Strada scribit, Egmondanum ab illâ legatione alienum non fuisse, publicæq; Belgarum causæ prætextu usum, sua quoque desideria, in spem privatæ utilitatis exposuisse. Quod arcanum Margaretæ Gubernatrici fœminæ, nobilitati Belgicæ haud satis æquæ, aperire magnæ temeritatis fuisse videtur, hominemque laudis & simul opum potentem æmulæ (nam id Regi indicaverat) principi devium ab honesto consilium instillasse.
units.tr: Margaret the Regent, terrified by the credibility of the portents, and wishing to show both the gentleness of her sex and her heart moved with pity for all who were sadder, thought of sending an envoy to Philip in Spain. Having quickly called together the Senate of the Belgian Estates, she ordered the Knights of the Golden Fleece and the governors of the provinces to come to Brussels. There, having weighed the danger of the times, she proposed the matter of an envoy; and when opinions had been asked in turn, she chose Lamoral of Egmont, a man of illustrious birth and famous in the French wars of Charles and Philip, for the business of the embassy to Spain. Strada writes that Egmont was not averse to that embassy, and, using the pretext of the common cause of the Belgians, also laid before the king his own desires, in hope of private advantage. This secret matter seems to have been a great rashness to reveal to Margaret the Regent, a woman, and not sufficiently fair to the Belgian nobility; and to have insinuated to the prince, who was powerful in fame and likewise in wealth, a rival (for she had made this known to the King), a counsel turned aside from honesty.

units.la: Illius mandata habebant, ut omnium Ordinum nomine Philippum Regem de statu suarum ditionum doceret, Edictorumque asperitati salubre remedium oraret. Quapropter Egmondanus in Hispaniam non segni itinere contendit, salutatoque, pro more, Philippo rege, in hunc modum differere potuit:
units.tr: Egmont's instructions were that, on behalf of all the Estates, he should inform King Philip of the state of their domains, and beg a healthful remedy for the harshness of the edicts. Therefore Egmont hastened into Spain by no sluggish journey, and, having greeted King Philip in the customary way, was able to speak to this effect:

units.la: NON veni ad te latorum, prosperorumque nuntium ferens, PHILIPPE REX, nec reporto manubias Gallorum, quibuscum bella nuper illustria victoriis gessisti. Caeterum accedo tristium & infaelicium veri narrator. Belgicam florem regnorum, & hereditatis tuæ non leviter commotam, metuentemq; graviorum turbarum, quas decreta tua, & si in ea perseveres, nova severitatis imperium dabunt. Neq; enim edicta tua minore curâ (quam quâ olim Carolo patre per Germaniam Principes) Belgæ, cæteraque nationes expendent, supra omnium gentium fastigium, quas Sol videt, suâ, nec inverâ opinione libertatis ac armorum gloriâ evecti. Quos cogitabis suis fortunis, ac virtute usos maioribus tuis præclaras victorias, & secura imperia peperisse. Id patris Caroli voce, cum imperio se abdicaret in concessu Patrum, ac honorati Ordinis expositum. De tuis bellis, cum Gallorum vires nuper in te versæ, ipse testaberis, reputabisque (si pacatam florentemque Belgicam tuam vis) beneficia populi illis præmijs, & gravi dominatu non pensari. Quin elementiam potius ostende iis, qui fide ac obsequio erga te cum omni terrarum gente certabunt, modo consensum tui imperij cum illorum libertate non auferas. Certè majores tuos, etiam offensos, non deposuit, odia simul cum armis ponere, donaretq; clementiam Arteveldis ac Agricolis, qui frenandis majorum tuorum imperijs intestina ac victricia arma per Flandriam circumtulere. Ita reputa Carolum Burgundionem atavum tuum suetum bellis & ferocem, amore pacis Gandensium licentiam tolerasse, & ne arma in suos verteret, adprobasse, quæ fastidiret. Idem si facias, PHILIPPE REX, obsequia populi tui, opes, & tributa, ex te ipso gloriam ac decus habiturus es. Caeterum si arma, & vis apud te prevalebunt, contumaciam tuorum, deinde egestatem sustinabis, & transfire aliò terrarum commercia, quibus majores tui suam potentiam debuerunt. Fiet inde, ut in antiquas Sedes (quod olim sub Ludovico Maleano Flandriæ Comite, Anglica, glica gens faciebat) ac tutiora loca, & bellis inaccessa populi remigrent, relinquaturque Provincijs solitudo, & post inopiam omnium rerum etiam optu-marum confusio. Quare vota, quae omnium subditorum nomine Legatus offero, ac desideria tuorum implebis, temperabisque severius imperium clementia, cui soli, tuam, & florentis nuper Belgicae fortunam, conjugum ac liberorum nostrorum, tum carissimi cuiusque pignoris incolumitatem commissam scies. Eam si mihi addixeris Legato, PHILIPPE Rex, non indignos hac legatione fructus feram, quorum is primus sanctissimusque erit, tibi ditiones tuas, quas à praeclaris majoribus longâ traditione accepisti, caeterum mihi, & subditis tuis dulcissimam patriam ab imminenti periculo liberasse.
units.tr: I HAVE NOT come to you, KING PHILIP, bringing news of successes, nor do I bring back the spoils of the French, against whom you recently waged famous wars and won victories. Rather I come as a narrator of sad and unhappy truths: Belgium, the flower of your kingdoms and of your inheritance, is not lightly stirred, and fears more grievous troubles, which your decrees, and a new empire of severity, if you persist in it, will bring. For the Belgians and the other nations will weigh your edicts with no less care than that with which the princes of Germany once weighed those of your father Charles; raised above the summit of all the nations the sun sees, by their own opinion, and not an untrue one, of liberty and the glory of arms. You will reflect that they, using their own fortunes and virtue, won for your ancestors famous victories and secure dominions. That was declared in the voice of your father Charles, when he gave up his power in the assembly of the Fathers and of the honoured Order. As to your wars, when the forces of the French were recently turned against you, you yourself will bear witness, and you will consider (if you wish Belgium, your peaceful and flourishing land, to be) that the people's services are not repaid by those rewards and by harsh rule. Rather, show clemency to those who will vie with the whole world in faith and obedience towards you, provided you do not take away the agreement of your rule with their liberty. Certainly your ancestors, even when offended, did not lay down their hatred together with their arms; they pardoned the Arteveldes and the Agricolas, who carried intestine and victorious arms through Flanders to curb the rule of your ancestors. So consider that Charles the Burgundian, your great-grandfather, accustomed to wars and fierce, tolerated the licence of the Ghentese out of love for peace, and approved, rather than turn his arms against his own people, what he scorned. If you do the same, KING PHILIP, you will have the obedience, the wealth and the taxes of your people, and you will have glory and honour from yourself. But if arms and force prevail with you, you will endure the stubbornness of your subjects and then their poverty, and the commerce on which your ancestors built their power will move to other lands. The result will be that the people will migrate to their old homes (as once under Louis of Male, Count of Flanders, the English nation did), and to safer places inaccessible to wars; and the provinces will be left in solitude, and after the lack of all things, even the best, confusion. Therefore, you will fulfil the prayers, which I offer as envoy in the name of all your subjects, and the wishes of your people, and you will temper your harsh rule with clemency, to which alone you will know that your fortune and that of the recently flourishing Belgium, the safety of our wives and children, and of every most dear pledge, are entrusted. If you grant it to me as envoy, KING PHILIP, I will bear fruits not unworthy of this embassy, the first and holiest of which will be to have freed your domains, which you received by long tradition from your illustrious ancestors, and, for me and your subjects, our most sweet homeland, from imminent danger.

units.la: Ferunt eâ Egmondani legatione delinitum Philippum spem clementiae, & mitioris imperij fecisse, eundemq; Egmondanum festino itinere ex Hispania in Belgicam revectum, magno gaudio, etsi non diuturno, Provincialium animos perfudisse. Ab eius namq; reditu factum est, ut omne restituendae quietis consilium protraheretur, conceptaeq; meliores fortunae spes, & desideria longiore apud populum morâ evanescerent. Hoc tantum subsecutum Demetrius tradit, ut leniendis Philippi Edictis Legati à Margareta ederentur, eorumque officia, attemperandae Edictorum severitati destinata, Hispaniae Senatus, Inquisitorum interventio perverteret. Fuere, qui Barlamontium, hominem ex imo ad res magnas, &, ut plurimum, invidiae expositas, evectum, Margaretaeque Gubernatricis muliebri gratiâ subnixum, autorem fotoremq; pessimorum consiliorum criminarentur, eumque secreto commercio Hispaniae familijs, & magnatum negotijs innexum grande obstaculum impudentibus ausis quieti Belgicae substernere. Itaque Philippum jam ante monuisse, ut suae animae & legis conscius patris Caesaris Edictis robur adstrueret, duplicatâque hoc modo in paternos manes, & simul Ecclesiam Romanam pietate, etiam inter homines agens, quod patri evenerat, consecrationis velut gloriam & simul imaginem futurae aeternitatis acciperet. Quare Philippus, Barlamontij aliorumq; consilijs impulsus, etiam reversô in Belgicam Egmondano, edixit. Ut rescripta de Religione integra, & inviolata essent, cultaque imprimis Inquisitione, Tridentinum Concilium per Episcopos stabiliendum Belgicae genti, caeterisque trans Rhenum Frisiorum populis sacro-sanctum haberetur:
units.tr: They report that Philip was won over by Egmont's embassy, and that he gave hope of clemency and a milder rule. Egmont then hurried back from Spain to the Netherlands, and his return brought great joy to the provincials, though it did not last long. From the time he returned, the plan for restoring peace was put off, and the hopes of better times and the people's longing for them faded through long delay. Demetrius records that the only result was that Margaret's letters were published to soften Philip's edicts, and that the Spanish Council and the intervention of the Inquisitors undid the work of the officials appointed to temper the severity of the edicts. Some accused Barlaymont, a man raised from the lowest rank to great office, and usually exposed to envy, who relied on the feminine favour of the Governess Margaret, of being the author and supporter of the worst policies. They said that, being bound by secret dealings to Spanish families and the affairs of great lords, he was a great obstacle that laid low the peace of Belgium with shameless daring. So Philip had already been advised beforehand to strengthen his father the Emperor's edicts, as one aware of his own soul and of the law, so that, by doubling his devotion to his father's memory and at the same time to the Roman Church, he might receive the glory of consecration, as his father had, and at once an image of future eternity. Therefore Philip, moved by the counsels of Barlaymont and others, also issued an edict after Egmont's return to the Netherlands: that the decrees on religion should be kept whole and inviolate, and that, above all, the Inquisition being maintained, the Council of Trent should be established among the Belgian people, and held sacred by the other peoples of Frisia across the Rhine.

units.la: Cui malo ne fomes quoq; per Frisiam deesset, Fredericus Tautoburgius Archi-Episcopus Ultrajectinus, sive Philippi impulsu, sive ut novam dignitatem acrioribus studijs exornaret, datis ad Praesulem Staurium litteris, omnes Frisiae Abbates Ultrajectum evocavit, habendoque ibidem Concilio adesse jussit. Litterae hae erant:
units.tr: So that this evil might not lack a spark in Frisia either, Frederick Tautenburg, Archbishop of Utrecht, whether at Philip's urging, or so as to adorn his new dignity with more zealous efforts, sent letters to the prelate Staurius and summoned all the abbots of Frisia to Utrecht, ordering them to attend a council held there. The letters were these:

units.la: Reverende Domine Abbas sincere dilecte: Metropolitica nostra auctoritate Regiae Majestatis atq; Illustrissimae Dominae Ducissae Gubernatricis harum ditionum Generalis ordinatione submixa, vobis indicimus & denuntiamus, Concilium provinciale inchoandum auspicandumq; mensis Octobris proxime futuri, die decimâ mane, apud Ecclesiam nostram Metropolitanam, & Cathedralem in civitate Trajectensi, cum solemnitatibus debitis & consuetis fineq; Canonico (Dei opitulante gratiâ) terminandum. Ad quod quidem cIↄ.Iↄ. LXV. dem provinciale Concilium; qui de jure ad id vocari debent, vocati sunt; prout & vos praesentes serio vocamus, una cum aliis Abbatibus circumvicinis ordinis vestri nostrae Metropolitanae superioritati subjectis, quos tecum adducas, idq; sub poenis Ecclesiasticis in vos, si emanseritis, per dictum Concilium infligendis (quod fore non speramus) ad consultandum, & tractandum super iis, quae Dei gloriam, Ecclesiae decus, unitatem fidei, morum emendationem, atq; animarum salutem, respicere & concernere dinoscantur. Valete in Domino; ex Arce nostra Duerstede. 15. Septemb. Anno 1565.
units.tr: Reverend Lord Abbot, sincerely beloved: By the ordinance of the Royal Majesty and of the most illustrious Lady Duchess, the General Governess of these lands, subject to our metropolitan authority, we declare and announce to you that a provincial council is to be opened and begun on the tenth morning of the coming month of October, in our metropolitan and cathedral church in the city of Utrecht, with the due and customary solemnities, and, God helping by his grace, to be concluded in the canonical manner. To which 1565 indeed the provincial council, those who ought by law to be summoned to it have been summoned; as we now seriously summon you too, together with the other abbots of your order in the neighbourhood, subject to our metropolitan supremacy, whom you shall bring with you. This is under ecclesiastical penalties to be inflicted on you by the said council if you stay away (which we do not hope will happen), for consulting and treating on those matters which are recognised as concerning the glory of God, the honour of the Church, the unity of the faith, the amendment of morals, and the salvation of souls. Farewell in the Lord; from our castle at Duurstede, 15 September, in the year 1565.

units.la: FREDERICUS, Archi-Episcopus Trajectensis.
units.tr: FREDERICK, Archbishop of Utrecht.

units.la: Caeterum clerus spreto Archi-Episcopi mandato, veteris potentiae libertatis; reminiscentia, contumaciam induit, fiduciaq; sociae potestatis (qua Ordines & Leovardienses complectebatur) detrectantem immodesta absentiam professus est. Quod sive antiqui Iuris obtentu, quod evocari finibus Frisium non sinebat, sive instinctu politicae autoritatis factum, in commentarijs istorum temporum non observo. Hoc saltem verum est, totum provinciae, cuius membrum clerus constituebat, corpus, Episcopali potentiae tum oblectatum, civilem potius regnandi in Philippo modum, quam novam sacri ordinis dominationem expetivisse. Quare Ultrajectinus excussam a Frisiorum Praesulibus, Sedis suae reverentiam indignatus, contumacem clerum, dato duodecim dierum tempore, rursum ad Concilium evocavit, ac ut adesset, cum aliqua severitate edixit.
units.tr: But the clergy, scorning the Archbishop's command and recalling their old power and liberty, assumed obstinacy and, relying on the confidence of their allied power (which included the Orders and the Leeuwarden churches), openly declared an unrestrained absence. Whether this was done under the pretext of ancient law, which did not allow the Frisians to be summoned beyond their borders, or was prompted by political authority, I do not find in the records of those times. At least this is true: the whole body of the province, of which the clergy formed a part, was then pleased with episcopal power, and sought rather the civil manner of ruling under Philip than a new lordship of the sacred order. Therefore the Archbishop of Utrecht, indignant that the reverence due to his see had been shaken off by the prelates of Frisia, again summoned the obstinate clergy to the council, giving them a period of twelve days, and ordered them, with some severity, to attend.

units.la: FREDERICUS à Tautenburg, Dei & Apostolicae Sedis gratia, Archi-Episcopus Trajectensis; Notum facimus, universis & singulis; Quod cum nos insequendo sacri Oeconomici & generalis Concilij decretum, sanctaeq; Sedis Apostolicae confirmationem & mandatum (quo omnia & singula dicti Concilij decreta conservando, eadem ab omnibus Christi fidelibus suscipienda & servanda esse decrevit, ac in virtute sanctae obedientiae & sub poenis ijsdem sacris canonibus constitutis, aliisque gravioribus etiam privationis arbitrio eiusdem sanctae Sedis Apostolicae infligendis, universis & singulis Patriarchis, Archi-Episcopis, Episcopis, & aliis quibusdam Ecclesiarum Praelatis, ut eadem decreta in judicio & extra diligenter observent, & a subditis quisq; suis faciat inviolabiliter observari, district praecepit, & mandavit (ne nostro deessemus officio) Synodum provincialem ad decimam diem huius mensis Octobris indixerimus, & ad eandem omnes nostri comprovinciales Episcopi & seu Suffraganei aliq; Praelati & capitula per nos evocati, tanquam obedientiae filij comparuerunt, in tantum quod divina gratia idipsum provinciale Concilium faeliciter fit inchoatum. Cumq; nonnulli, & inter hos potissimum Praelati Frisiae, atq; Transisulaniae, per nos tamen serio evocati in praedicto Provinciali Concilio desiderarentur, Seq; contumaciter absentassent. Nos matura cum Venerabilibus fratribus nostris comprovincialibus & Suffraganeis, Episcopis nimirum Harlemensi, Middelburgensi, Groningensi, Leovardiensi & Daventriensi, nec non Episcopo Ruremundensi, deliberatione praehabita, eosdem sic evocatos, prout revera sunt, contumaces reputavimus, non indignum fore censentes; reliquis exemplo paena aliqua salutari feriri, nisi antiquius duxisse-mus, mus, de nimiâ argui misericordiâ, quàm rigore. Quapropter eosdem Prælatos omnes & singulos, tam prius vocatos, quam nunc primo vocandos; (etiamsi exemptionem ab ordinaria nostra jurisdictione, quavis etiam Apostolicâ autoritate prætendant, & habeant Commissarium etiam nostrum, & Archidiaconorum Trajectensium, Leovardiæ residentem) Iterato evocandos esse duximus, prout præsentium tenore evocamus, ýsdem & eorum cuilibet tam ordinariâ nostrâ, quam sanctæ Sedis Apostolicæ (cuius hac in parte tanquam eiusdem sub titulo nostræ Archiepiscopalis dignitatis delegatus) vice fungimur, totiusq; Concilij provincialis inchoati autoritate districtè mandantes, sub inobedientiæ ac arbitrariæ correctionis pœnis, nostro tam in qualitate prædictâ, quam aliàs, ac totius Concilij provincialis arbitrio infligendis, ac moderandis, quatenus infra duodecim dierum spatium à receptione & intimatione præsentium compareant, & quilibet eorum compareat personaliter Trajecti ad Concilium provinciale inchoatum; Ibidem ipsis injungenda incumbentiaq; officia & munia obituri, quo omnia communiter ad Dei gloriam omniumq; Christi fidelium salutem tractari & concludi possint. Nisi tamen ýdem Prælati, & seu eorum aliquis legitimam & in jure fundatam (præter tamen quamcunq; exemptionem quæ hac in parte militare non potest) causam & excusationem habeant, seu habeat, quominus personaliter comparere possint, seu possit, ad quam coram nobis dictoq; Concilio provinciali allegandum, & simul ipsorum seu ipsius constituendum præstandum, & subeundum, omniaq; alia & singula faciendum & gerendum, quæ ipsi constituere, facere & gerere possent, & deberent, seu posset, & deberet, si personaliter comparuissent, vel comparuisset, procuratorem cum sufficienti mandato mittant, seu mittat, ne ulterior eorum seu ipsius contumacia & inobedientia nos, alioqui invitos, ad pœnarum aliquarum declarationem, & seu, tanquam inobedientium, imò rebellium constrictionem contra eosdem procedere cogat. Ad evidentiam atq; robur præmissorum; Nos, atq; comprovinciales nostri Episcopi his litteris subscripsimus, easq; nostri sigilli appensione munivimus. Datum Trajecti sub anno à nativitate Domini millesimo, quingentesimo sexagesimo quinto, mensis Octobris die decimâ quintâ. Sic subscriptum, Fredericus, Archiepiscopus Trajectensis; Nicolaus, Episcopus Harlemensis; Nicolaus de Castro, Episcopus & Prælatus Middelburgensis; Ioannes Knyff, Episcopus Groningensis; Remigius Drutius, Electus Leovardiensis; Ioannes Mahusius, Electus Daventriensis. Et sic subscriptum de mandato supra fati amplissimi Domini Archi-Episcopi.
units.tr: FREDERICK of Tautenburg, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See Archbishop of Utrecht: We make known to all and each that, while we were following the decree of the sacred and general council, and the confirmation and mandate of the holy Apostolic See (by which it decreed that all and each of the decrees of the said council are to be preserved, and are to be received and observed by all the faithful of Christ, and which strictly commanded and enjoined all and each of the Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, and certain other prelates of the churches, under the virtue of holy obedience and under the penalties laid down by the sacred canons, and other heavier penalties to be inflicted at the discretion of the same holy Apostolic See, including deprivation, that they diligently observe the same decrees in judgment and outside it, and that each of them make their subjects observe them inviolably), we, lest we fail in our office, appointed a provincial synod for the tenth day of this present October month. To it all our fellow provincial bishops, or suffragans, and other prelates and chapters summoned by us appeared, as obedient sons, so that by divine grace that same provincial council was happily begun. But since some, and chiefly the prelates of Frisia and Overijssel, though seriously summoned by us to the aforesaid provincial council, were missed, and had stubbornly absented themselves, we, after mature deliberation with our venerable brothers, our fellow provincials and suffragans, namely the Bishops of Haarlem, Middelburg, Groningen, Leeuwarden and Deventer, and also the Bishop of Roermond, judged these men, summoned as they were, to be truly contumacious, and thought it not unfitting that others should be struck by some salutary penalty as an example, unless we had preferred to be accused of excessive mercy rather than of severity. Wherefore we have judged that all and each of the said prelates, both those summoned before and those now summoned for the first time (even though they claim exemption from our ordinary jurisdiction on any apostolic authority whatever, and have our own commissary residing at Leeuwarden, and the archdeacons of Utrecht), are to be summoned again. Accordingly, by the tenor of these present letters we summon them, and we act in place of our ordinary authority and of the holy Apostolic See (of which, in this matter, we are delegate under the title of our archiepiscopal dignity), and by the authority of the provincial council now begun we strictly command them, under the penalties of disobedience and of arbitrary correction, to be inflicted and moderated at our discretion, in this capacity as well as otherwise, and at the discretion of the whole provincial council, that within twelve days of the receipt and notice of these present letters they appear, and that each of them appear in person at Utrecht before the provincial council now begun, there to undertake the offices and duties enjoined on them, so that all matters may be commonly treated and concluded for the glory of God and the salvation of all the faithful of Christ. Unless, however, the said prelates, or any one of them, have a lawful cause and excuse founded in law (apart from any exemption, which cannot apply in this matter) why they, or he, cannot appear in person, they, or he, shall send a proctor with sufficient mandate, to be presented before us and the said provincial council, and in their or his name to take on and perform whatever they, or he, could and should do if they, or he, had appeared in person; lest their or his further contumacy and disobedience compel us, against our will, to declare penalties and to proceed against them as disobedient, indeed as rebellious. In evidence and confirmation of the foregoing, we and our fellow provincial bishops have subscribed these letters and fortified them with the appending of our seal. Given at Utrecht in the year of our Lord 1565, on the fifteenth day of October. Signed: Frederick, Archbishop of Utrecht; Nicholas, Bishop of Haarlem; Nicholas de Castro, Bishop and Prelate of Middelburg; John Knyff, Bishop of Groningen; Remigius Drutius, Elect of Leeuwarden; John Mahusius, Elect of Deventer. And so signed by the mandate of the aforesaid most honourable Lord Archbishop.

units.la: HENRICUS ZONNIUS, Not. Pro suâ & Reverendiss. specialiter deputatus.
units.tr: Henricus Zonnius, notary, specially deputed for himself and the Most Reverend (Archbishop)

units.la: Quare repetito exasperatoq; Ultrajectini edicto conventus cleri Leovardiæ habitus, decretumq;, ut ad declinandam contumacis silentij invidiam Archi-Episcopo responderetur, mitterenturq; Ultrajectum Ghysbertus Arnoldinus, actuarius publicus, cum Arnoldo Harderviceno, qui litteras perferrent, sub hac formulâ. Allatæ sunt ante paucos dies.
units.tr: Therefore, after the Utrecht edict had been repeated and made more severe, a meeting of the clergy was held at Leeuwarden. It was decided that, to avert the odium of silent contumacy, a reply should be made to the Archbishop, and that Ghysbert Arnoldinus, public notary, and Arnold Harderwijck should be sent to Utrecht to carry the letters, in the following form. They were delivered a few days ago.

units.la: Reverendissime atque Illustrissime Domine, nobis per quendam, qui se cursorem juratum asserebat, littera tuæ Rev. Celsit. perlatæ sunt, quibus tua Rev. Celsit. nos contumaciæ accusabat, & denuo ad diem duodecimum post earum receptionem vocabat, ut Trajectum veniremus.
units.tr: Most Reverend and Illustrious Lord, your Reverence's letters were brought to us by a man who declared himself a sworn courier. In them your Reverence accused us of contumacy and summoned us again, to come to Utrecht on the twelfth day after their receipt.

units.la: Atqʒ in ÿsdem Rever. tua Celsit. affirmabat sese destinasse nos competenti pœnâ afficere, quod omnino factum fuisset, nisi tuæ Rever. Celsitud. præstabilius visum fuisset, de nimiâ misericordiâ quam rigore argui. Nos ut laudamus, quod insontes non punieris, ita summopere admirati sumus, quæ res effecerit, ut tam sinistram de nobis opinionem conceperis, cum ante hac nunquam citati fuerimus. Sed tamen cum huiusmodi evocatio, extra fines huius nostræ regionis fiat, contra antiquas atqʒ approbatas consuetudines atqʒ privilegia nostra, re deliberatâ cum Deputatis Ordinum huius regionis, quos Status vocant, atqʒ Senatu Leovardiensi, scripsimus tuæ Rever. Celsit. excusationes nostras, idqʒ linguâ vernaculâ, propterea, quod Deputati Senatusqʒ nobis socy sint in privilegys atqʒ consuetudinibus patriæ defendendis. Nos etsi non dubitamus, quin rationibus allegatis, etiam secundum sacros Canones, excusemur, quo minus eo venire cogamur, tamen & privatim volumus testari nostri animi erga tuam Rever. Celsit. benevolentiam atque promptam obedientiam in ÿs, quibus consuetudinibus nostraqʒ regionis privilegys nihil derogatur. In his autem, quamvis maximè velimus; non est nobis integrum, neqʒ in nostrâ manu, quicquam absqʒ aliorum Ordinum consensu tentare. Is est enim, semperqʒ fuit omnium Ordinum nexus, ut unus absqʒ alio in ÿs, quæ publicam utilitatem concernant, nihil queat efficere. Quare cum nos tantum unius Ordinis, Ecclesiastici, scilicet pars aliqua simus, & frustra non habentes aliquam potestatem quidquam decernendi in aliorum præjudicium, veniremus, idqʒ instante jam hyeme atqʒ tempore, quo secundum probatos autores maria clausa censentur, non sine summo discrimine, petimus unanimes ut tua Rever. Celsit. nos excusatos habere dignetur. Offerimus in alÿs omnibus, in quibus & possumus & debemus, promptam obedientiam. Rogamus clementissimum atqʒ omnipotentem Deum, ut tuam Reverendiss. Celsit. quam diutissimè servet incolumem, atqʒ depulsis tenebris atqʒ erroribus, restituat Ecclesiæ suæ serenitatem, atqʒ fidei unitatem, nosqʒ tuæ Rev. Celsit. quam humillimè commendamus. Leovardiæ 8. Novembris, 1565. Nicolaus Landensis, Abbas Stauriæ in Hemelis; Petrus, Abbas in Fosuert; Eyso Wiltink, Abbas Clarecampi; Henricus Steenwyck, Abbas Floridi Campi; Everardus Dotechem, Abbas Gerricomius; Isbrandus Harderwyck, Abbas in Lidlum; Henricus Kesselt, Abbas in Dockum.
units.tr: In the same letters your Reverence affirmed that you had resolved to punish us with a fitting penalty, which would certainly have been carried out, had it not seemed better to your Reverence's most generous mercy than to rigour. We praise you for not punishing the innocent, but we are greatly surprised what has caused you to form so unfavourable an opinion of us, since we had never been summoned before. Nevertheless, since this kind of summons is issued beyond the bounds of our region, contrary to ancient and approved customs and to our privileges, we have, after deliberation with the Deputies of the Orders of this region, whom they call the States, and with the Leeuwarden Senate, written our excuses to your Reverence in the vernacular, because the Deputies and the Senate are our partners in defending the privileges and customs of the country. Although we do not doubt that, on the reasons alleged, and also according to the sacred canons, we shall be excused from being compelled to come, we nevertheless wish to testify privately to our goodwill towards your Reverence and our ready obedience in those matters which do not detract from the customs and privileges of our region. In these matters, however much we desire to act, it is not within our power to attempt anything without the consent of the other Orders. For it is and always has been the bond of all the Orders that none can accomplish anything, in matters concerning the public good, without the others. Therefore, since we are only a part of one Order, the ecclesiastical, and would be coming in vain, having no power to decide anything to the prejudice of the others, and since winter is now upon us, and the season in which, according to approved authors, the seas are considered closed, we petition unanimously, not without great danger, that your Reverence will deign to hold us excused. In all other matters, in which we can and ought, we offer ready obedience. We pray the merciful and almighty God to keep your Most Reverend Lordship safe for as long as possible, and, with the darkness and errors dispelled, to restore to His Church its serenity and the unity of faith; and we most humbly commend ourselves to your Reverence. Leeuwarden, 8 November 1565. Nicolaus Landensis, Abbot of Stavoren in Hemelum; Petrus, Abbot in Vosswert; Eyso Wiltink, Abbot of Clarenkamp; Henricus Steenwyck, Abbot of Floridus Campus; Everardus Dotechem, Abbot of Gerkesklooster; Isbrandus Harderwyck, Abbot in Lidlum; Henricus Kesselt, Abbot in Dockum.

units.la: Quo die juxta nominatos Præsules, Ordinum quoqʒ Frisiæ Delegati, una cum Magistratu Leovardiensi, litteras ad Archi-Episcopum Ultrajectum miserunt, expositâqʒ Belgico idiomate juris antiqui consuetudine, hoc modo responderunt.
units.tr: On the same day, the abovementioned prelates, together with the delegates of the Frisian Orders and the Leeuwarden magistracy, sent letters to the Archbishop of Utrecht. Setting out their case in the Dutch language, following the custom of ancient law, they replied in this manner.

units.la: Reverendissime in Christo Domine & Pater,
units.tr: Most Reverend Lord in Christ and Father,

units.la: Paucos ante dies Præsules nostros Ultrajectum evocasti ad Concilium. Ad quod, etsi sub interminatione pœnarum, cum non iverint, denuò citari ad tuum judicium fecisti. Quo ipso cum jura, privilegia, & exemptiones gentis nostræ tollantur, quæ auferri non expedit, & quæ neque pro affectu tuo in Frisios imminuta voles, ita scies longa libertatis possessione nos gaudere. Quam neque per illos etiam Principes infirmari volumus, quibuscum contraximus, ut neque belli tempore, neque ex alia causa, finibus nostris extrahEremur. Hoc ipsum Saxonica dominatione, hoc conventione regiâ & Carolinâ cavimus, ac ut ipsi religione juris-jurandi nostra sacra, nostras leges ges confirmarent. Sic anno quadringentesimo nonagesimo octavo Saxonem, anno millesimo quingentesimo Carolum Principem obstrinximus, ne provincia evocaremur, cuius pacti fructum, & Caroli Caesaris, & Philippi filij durante imperio, retinuimus. Et quoniam Ecclesiasticus ordo nobiscum communem Remp. constituit, ex indissolubili nexu, quo invicem obligamur, ita separari disjungique non possunt, quae longis temporum spatijs coaluere. Tanto minus in praejudicium alicuius statui poterit, praesertim cum sine conventu Ordinum, sine relatione ad populum Ordinesque institutâ, nihil agi gerique possit. Praeterea ad vos ire, nec anni tempus, nec clausum navigantibus mare permittet, neque censemus Praesules nostros (quod in Concilio Turonico factum) ad hoc teneri, imprimis cum ex praeceptione regiâ ab isto onere liberentur. Quare excusabis absentiam illorum, dabisque veniam illorum libertati, cuius argumentum hoc in casu allegandum est. Quod si feceris, beneficia, quae nostrae potestatis erunt, à nobis expectabis, habebisque caeteris in rebus nos dignitatis tuae reverentes. Ita à Nicolao Landensi, Petro Fosuerdico, Eysone Wittinghio, Henrico Steenuicano, Everardo Dotechemio, Isbrando Harderuiceno, Henrico Kesselio, Ruardo Roorda, Haringio Glinsio, Valerio Cammingha, Doeone Martna, & Hesselo Aysma signatum.
units.tr: A few days ago you summoned our prelates to Utrecht to a council. Although they did not go, under threat of penalties, you have made a further summons to your judgement. By this very act, the rights, privileges and exemptions of our people, which it is not expedient to remove and which you would not wish to diminish out of your hostility towards the Frisians, are being abolished; and you will know that we enjoy the long possession of our liberty. We do not wish this to be weakened even by those princes with whom we have made treaties, so that we shall not be dragged out of our territory, neither in time of war nor for any other cause. We secured this under Saxon rule, and by the royal and Carolingian agreement, and we had them confirm by the religion of an oath our sacred rites and our laws. Thus in the year 1498 we bound the Saxon, and in the year 1500 the Prince Charles, that we should not be summoned out of the province; and we have kept the fruit of that pact during the reign of Charles Caesar and of his son Philip. And since the ecclesiastical order shares the common commonwealth with us, and by the indissoluble bond by which we are mutually obligated, things which have grown together over long spans of time cannot be so separated and disjoined. Still less can this be done to the prejudice of any estate, especially since nothing can be transacted or carried out without the assembly of the Orders, and without reference to the people and the Orders. Moreover, neither the season of the year nor the sea, closed to sailors, will permit us to come to you; nor do we think our prelates are bound to this (as happened at the Council of Tours), especially since they are freed from this burden by royal precept. Therefore you will excuse their absence and grant pardon to their liberty, the proof of which must be alleged in this case. If you do so, you may expect from us the benefits which lie in our power, and in other matters you will have us reverent of your dignity. Signed thus by Nicolaus of Leeuwarden, Petrus of Vosswert, Eyso Wittinghius, Henricus Steenuicanus, Everardus Dotechemius, Isbrandus Harderwicensis, Henricus Kesselius, Ruardus Roorda, Haringius Glinsius, Valerius Cammingha, Doeo Martna and Hesselus Aysma.

units.la: Quorum postremi ad Arembergium Praefectum, Senatumque regium postero die ablegati, auxilium intercessionemque apud Philippum aut Archi-Episcopum oravere.
units.tr: The last of these were sent the following day to the Governor Arenberg and the royal Senate, to beg for their help and intercession with Philip or with the Archbishop.

units.la: Reperio in actis, Ghysbertum Grotium actuarium publicum, Frisiorum nomine, litteras provincialium decimo quarto Novembris die Durestedum pertulisse, admissumque ad colloquium aulicorum Mindani, & Wingardij perhumaniter exceptum. Ipsum quoq; Archi-Episcopum, quasi suo consilio tota res non ageretur, se modeste excusasse, Suffraganeisq; suis atque provincialibus Episcopis partem istius invidiae imputavisse. Mandatum quoq; Margaretae Gubernatricis obtendisse, apud quam, si excusari contumacia Praesulum posset, quorum litteras ad Margaretam missurus foret, se de severitate consilij facile remissurum. Haec v. Id. Nov. Durestadi acta, ac Ghysberti Grotij manu signata. Caeterum Philippi animus propositi tenax, ne aut regno suo, quod moliebatur, quid decederet, & ne gentis obsequium minueretur, severioribus decretis negotium religionis exasperavit, immaniumque edictorum rigorem majore acerbitate tutatus est.
units.tr: I find in the records that Ghysbert Grotius, public notary, on behalf of the Frisians, carried the provincials' letters to Duurstede on 14 November, and that he was admitted to an audience with the courtiers Mindanus and Wingardius and very courteously received. The Archbishop himself, as though the whole business were not being carried out on his own counsel, modestly excused himself and laid part of this odium on his suffragans and the provincial bishops. He also put forward the mandate of Margaret the Regent, before whom, he said, if the contumacy of the prelates could be excused (whose letters he would send to Margaret), he would readily relax the severity of the council. These things were done at Duurstede on the fifth day before the Ides of November, and were signed by the hand of Ghysbert Grotius. Moreover, Philip, tenacious of his purpose, so that nothing should be taken from his kingdom, which he was striving to build up, nor from the obedience of his people, exacerbated the matter of religion with harsher decrees, and maintained the rigour of his monstrous edicts with greater bitterness.

units.la: Addit Borraeus atrocius quiddam, Philippumque prodito immanis sevitiae consilio horrendam hanc Legem edixisse: Malle se multorum millium sanguinem profusum, quam suis de Religione, Carolique patris Edictis, quid decedere. Mandasse quoque, ut Anabaptistae, quotquot vinculis dati essent, per omnes Provincias nullâ miseratione, aut conniventiâ Iudicum necarentur, statuerenturque exempla deterreundis populi ingenijs valida. Ita recens gaudium maerore conversum, aegerrimè ferente Egmondano Principis animae, & legationis suae fidem contrarijs decretis subverti. Quare immodicus affectuum, probra in Philippum, etiam in ipso procerum consessu, effudit, questusque de fluxâ fallacis regni conditione, fraudem legationi suae fa-ctam temperandis inimicorum aemulationibus asseruit. Quae res, quia secresecreto silentio ægrius obsignabatur, sparsa in populum, venerationem Regis, auctis econtra odijs, minuebat. Itaq; nobilissimi quique, velut prævisa formidabili tempestate, in cætus coire, & communicare consilia, ut si plebes tumultuaretur, communis auctoritas tempestatem sedaret, si Philippus desæviret, concordia opponeretur. Philippus namque ut suo in exitium populo uteretur, Edicto Leovardiæ publicato caverat: Ne extra Provinciam Frisij stipendia facerent, commeatumve bellicum vicinis regnis Provincijsque præstarent. Quare & externa Principum arma secutos, eodem edicto revocari jussit, ipseque mentis metusq; sui detector conciliabula cætusq; populi prohibuit, ad quos per exceptas immodestius virorum Principum legationes amor vacillantis patriæ populum, Principesq; haud iniquis desiderijs impellebat.
units.tr: Borrhaeus adds something more savage: that Philip, betraying a monstrous plan of cruelty, decreed this dreadful law: that he preferred the blood of many thousands to be shed rather than anything be taken away from his edicts on religion and those of his father Charles. He also ordered that the Anabaptists, as many as had been put in chains, should be put to death throughout all the provinces without any pity or connivance of the judges, and that examples should be set, strong enough to deter the minds of the people. Thus the recent joy was turned to grief, Egmont taking it very badly, as the spirit of the Prince and the faith of his embassy were subverted by contrary decrees. Therefore, in an immoderate outburst of feeling, he poured out reproaches against Philip, even in the very assembly of the nobles, and complained of the unstable condition of a deceitful kingdom, asserting that the fraud practised on his embassy had been arranged to placate the rivalries of his enemies. This matter, since it was sealed with a secret silence with more difficulty, was spread among the people, and it diminished reverence for the King, while hatreds increased in return. And so the most noble men, as if a dreadful storm had been foreseen, began to gather in groups and to share their counsels, so that if the common people should riot, their common authority might calm the tempest, and if Philip should rage, concord might stand against him. For Philip, in order to use the people for their own destruction, had provided by an edict published at Leeuwarden: that the Frisians should not serve for pay outside the province, nor furnish military supplies to neighbouring kingdoms and provinces. Therefore he also ordered that the foreign forces of the princes who had followed them should be recalled by the same edict; and he himself, betraying the fear of his own mind, forbade the assemblies and gatherings of the people, to whom, through the more immoderately received embassies of the leading men and princes, love of their wavering country was driving the people and the princes to desires that were not unreasonable.

units.la: Quamobrem oblatâ nuptiarum opportunitate, quas Alexander Farnesius Octavij, & Margaretæ Gubernatricis filius, cum Mariâ Portugallicâ celebrabat, colloquia Principum, Belgicæque Nobilitatis instituta, consultatumq; de fœdere, quod solemnibus sanctientium votis post ictum retundendæ peregrinorum in aulâ Philippi, & Senatu regio potentiæ, submovendisq; omni Provinciâ Inquisitoribus fuit. Formula fœderis hæc erat:
units.tr: Therefore, seizing the opportunity of the wedding that Alexander Farnese, son of Octavio and Margaret the Governess, was celebrating with Maria of Portugal, the princes and the Belgian nobility held conferences and arranged a consultation about a covenant. After solemn vows by those who swore it, it was to be used to break the power of the foreigners at Philip's court and in the royal Council, and to remove the Inquisitors from every province. The form of the covenant was this:

units.la: Vandoquidem pro vero accepimus, peregrinos quosdam alienis à Belgicâ animis sepositâ gloriæ divinæ, ac salutis publicæ cura, privatâ ambitione, & avaritiâ compulsos, regio, & Provincialium censui inhiare, eosdemque peregrinos fucatâ pietatis specie, & simulato in concordiam, pacemque publicam affectu, eò Philippum Regem compulisse, ut, spreta juris-jurandi, quo se obstrinxerat, religione, exasperandis Edictis incumbat, Inquisitionemq; omni divino humanoq; juri adversam, ac omnium temporum memoriam superantem Belgica interqueat. Ipsi vero sanctimoniæ prætextu id tantum curent, ut Ordinum, Magistratuumq; auctoritatem, legum, consuetudinum, immunitatumq; à majoribus traditarum vim atque efficaciam conculcent, potestatemque legitimis administratoribus ereptam in se suosq; transferant, habitisque per Inquisitionem in modum mancupiorum Provincialibus ea moliantur, quibus patriæ periculum, Deo, Religioni atq; Regi, cultus, honos, obsequium minuatur, inferaturque Provinciys ut solitudo, ita vastitas & confusio. Ita nos officij Legisq; nostræ, quâ Regi obstringimur, non ignari perseverare volentes in fide & obsequio erga Regem, & à sacris rebusque nostris vim omnem atq; miseriam avertere, sanctum & religione jurisjurandi firmatum fœdus iniimus, eo maxime consilio ut Inquisitio cesset, ipsaque ut omnium malorum fons & origo, prout in regno Neapolitano, aboleatur, extirpeturque. Præmissa obtestatione Deo coram & omnibus gentibus terrarum, nos nihil adniti contrarium gloriæ Dei, aut repugnans Regiæ Majestati, cæterum id curare ut Regi suos honos, legibus institutisque majorum, sua vis atque integritas constet, arceanturque seditiones & turbæ nostræ patriæ exitiales. Quod idcirco Fœdus juravimus validum, atque perpetuum fore, advocantes ad hoc Deum Opt. Max. & conscientias nostras nullâ ratione aut causa nos illud infracturos, transgressurosque esse, neque laturos ut cuiquam nostrum vis aut injuria ex hoc ipso fiat, eoque ipso semel obligatus, quocunq; etiam casu, aut tempore eximatur, ita tamen ut officium omne conforme sit nostro fœderi aut sociorum arbitratui. In testimonium fidemque rei supra scripta pta advocavimus aternum numen, quod animis atque conscientiis nostris praesit, ut benedicat fœderi, sapientiaq, & prudentia spiritum nobis det, quo omnes nostræ actiones ad nominis divini gloriam, regis commodum, concordiam pacemque publicam, ac salutem nostrarum animarum dirigantur.
units.tr: Since we have learned as true that certain foreigners, estranged from Belgian feelings, driven not by care for God's glory or the public safety but by private ambition and greed, are aiming at the royal and provincial revenues, and that by a counterfeit show of piety and a pretended desire for concord and public peace they have brought King Philip to the point where, disregarding the religion of the oath by which he bound himself, he sets to work to sharpen the edicts and to introduce into Belgium an Inquisition hostile to all divine and human law and surpassing the memory of every age. They, under the pretext of holiness, take care only to trample down the authority of the estates and magistrates, and the force and efficacy of the laws, customs and immunities handed down by our ancestors, and to snatch the power from the lawful administrators and transfer it to themselves and their own people. And, having the provincials held by the Inquisition as if they were slaves, they undertake measures by which danger to the country, and worship, honour and obedience to God, religion and the King, are diminished, and by which desolation and, as it were, waste and confusion are brought upon the provinces. Therefore we, not unaware of the duty of our office and of our law, by which we are bound to the King, wishing to persist in faith and obedience towards the King, and to avert all violence and misery from our sacred things and affairs, have entered into a holy covenant, confirmed by the religion of an oath. Our chief aim in this is that the Inquisition may cease, and that it, as the source and origin of all evils, may be abolished and rooted out, as it was in the kingdom of Naples. With God called to witness before all the nations of the earth, we declare that we strive for nothing contrary to the glory of God or repugnant to the Royal Majesty, but rather that we take care that honour, the laws and institutions of our ancestors, and their strength and integrity, may stand for the King, and that seditions and the tumults that are destructive to our country may be warded off. We have sworn that this covenant shall therefore be valid and perpetual, calling God, the best and greatest, to witness, and our consciences, that we will by no reason or cause break or transgress it, nor will we allow any violence or injury to be done to any of us because of it. Once bound by it, a man shall be released from it in no case or at no time, except that every duty must accord with our covenant or with the judgement of our allies. In witness and in faith of the matters written above, we have called upon the eternal Deity, who presides over our minds and consciences, that He may bless the covenant, and give us a spirit of wisdom and prudence, by which all our actions may be directed to the glory of the divine name, the advantage of the King, the concord and public peace, and the salvation of our souls.

units.la: Cuius Tabulæ per Provincias sparsæ, ac ad Maximilianum II. Imperatorem Philippi patruelem, qui Augustæ in Vindelicis comitia Imperij tum agebat, missæ, Romani Imperij intercessionem implorabant. Sperabant namque fœderati, ut Germania, partâ in invidiam Caroli Cæsaris religionis libertate, communione juris antiqui, & memoriâ veterum coloniarum, tum fœderis Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xlix. icti, sociæ gentis miseresceret, asserendæque libertati Belgicæ intercessionem potentis Imperij apud Philippum commodaret. Maximilianus Cæsar mitis ingenij Princeps propinquitate sanguinis, & ductâ in matrimonium Mariâ Philippi sorore per affinitatem Hispanicæ domui innexus optimo & amantissimo pacis ingenio ad conciliandum cum Philippo Belgicæ populum uteretur. Itaque vulgatâ per Provincias ac omne confinium fœderis famâ magnus horror atque trepidatio fuit, ac si isto nobilitatis fœdere extrema secessio, & rerum omnium certissima confusio pararetur. Emissæ in publicum turbidæ voces, criminantium, pollutas civilibus armis infælices dexteras esse, legiq; per Provincias militem alio à Principis sacramento autoratum. Cæteri censebant religioni Pontificiæ discrimen impendere, non alio coeuntium in fœdus consilio, quam ut populus asperè habitus durioris imperij sortem, cum licentiæ regno commutaret. Magnam verò illam rerum conversionem sine tempestate perfici non posse, valido & inexorabili rege, & fœderatâ Nobilitate tuendæ libertatis percupidâ. Eam quippe juris sui defensionem à fœdere orsam, Bruxellas Brabantiæ urbem, sedem Principis habendo conventui, & maturandis consilijs destinasse. Quæ omnia, senescentibus nusquam rumoribus, mobilitate velocis famæ tamquam præcipiti turbine ferebantur. Neq; Margaretæ Gubernatricis animus idem, ceterum pro disceptantium opinione, ut solet rebus turbidis, muliebri quoque fragilitate fluctuabat. Quare increscente per aulam metu, vehementi sollicitudine implexa de detegendo rerum per Provincias statu, & scribendis ad Philippum litteris agitavit. Metuebat namque Margareta, ne infirmitate sexus sui, aut publici commodi respectu, commotæ nobilitati equior facta lenitatis apud Philippum regem incusaretur, incerta famæ pro veris sæpe haurientem. Econtra assertâ Edictorum asperitate & mandatis Philippi oblecuta, infidam nobilitatem, & jam novæ societatis consilia professam acerbioribus odiis irritaret. Itaque litteras in Hispaniam ocyus dedit, quo omne adhibendi robusto malo remedij discrimen in ipsum Regem reclinaret. Iis litteris docebat.
units.tr: Copies of this document were scattered through the provinces and sent to the Emperor Maximilian II, Philip's cousin, who was then holding the Diet of the Empire at Augsburg in Vindelicia, and they implored the intercession of the Roman Empire. For the confederates hoped that Germany, having been moved to envy by the religious liberty which Charles the Emperor had granted, by the shared ancient law, and by the memory of the old colonies, and also by the covenant struck in the year 1549, would take pity on a kindred nation, and would lend the intercession of the powerful Empire to Philip, in defence of Belgian liberty. Maximilian, a prince of gentle disposition, related by blood and, through his marriage to Maria, Philip's sister, bound to the Spanish house by kinship, would use the best and most loving temper of peace to win the Belgian people back to Philip. And so, once the news of the covenant had spread through the provinces and all the neighbourhood, great horror and alarm arose, as if by this noble covenant a final secession and the most certain confusion of all affairs were being prepared. Angry voices were raised in public, accusing the men who had joined in the covenant of having unlucky right hands polluted by civil arms, and of enlisting soldiers through the provinces, sworn to someone other than the Prince. Others thought that danger hung over the Papist religion, since those who came together in the covenant had no other plan than that a people harshly treated would exchange the lot of a harder rule for licence. A great change of this kind, they said, could not be brought about without a storm, with a strong and inexorable king and a nobility united and eager to defend its liberty. For the defence of their rights, which had begun with the covenant, they had apparently chosen Brussels, a city of Brabant and the Prince's seat, as the place for their assembly and for speeding their plans. All these things, with the rumours never growing old, were carried along by the swift mobility of fame, like a headlong whirlwind. Nor did Margaret the Governess remain of one mind; rather, according to the opinions of those who disputed about it, as usually happens in troubled times, her spirit wavered with womanly frailty. So, as fear grew through the court and anxious concern for discovering the state of affairs in the provinces took hold of her, she turned over in her mind the writing of letters to Philip. For Margaret feared that, through the weakness of her sex, or out of regard for the public good, she might be blamed before King Philip for having been too mild towards the stirred-up nobility, since she was often drinking in uncertain rumours as if they were true. On the other hand, by insisting on the harshness of the edicts and the commands of Philip, she would provoke the untrustworthy nobility, which had already declared the plans of a new association, to still bitterer hatred. So she quickly sent letters to Spain, so that the whole decision about applying a strong remedy to the evil might rest upon the King himself. In these letters she taught the following:

units.la: Populum Belgicum Edictis offensum magnâ inquietudine ferri, & turbis ciendis proxumum perniciosa quieti publicæ consilia meditari. Ita nobilitatem in fœdus pertractam stabili concordiâ coaluisse, facturam haud dubiè majora, nisi istiusmodi pactiones aut effecta fœderum prudentiâ Regis cohibeantur. Clementiâ, & moderato imperio opus esse. Saltem cavendum ne quid ipsâ mali exacerbatione, aut vigore præ-
units.tr: The Belgian people, offended by the edicts, bear it with great restlessness, and are meditating plans harmful to public quiet, close to stirring up tumults. Thus the nobility, drawn into the covenant, has united in firm concord, and would undoubtedly do greater things, unless such pacts, or the effects of covenants, were restrained by the prudence of the King. Clemency and moderate government are needed. At least care must be taken that nothing is prescribed by the very exacerbation of evil, or by severity,

units.la: Ioan. Ier. Regem. cIↄ .Iↄ praescribatur, praeterquam quod Rex judicaverit rei suae & juxta subditorum expedire. Interim rogare se Regem mitigari quam primum Edicta curet, leniatq; imperium, & cum eo animos novitate rerum effrenes.
units.tr: except insofar as the King shall judge it to be to his own advantage and that of his subjects. Meanwhile she asks that the King take care to soften the edicts as soon as possible, and to relax his rule, and with it the minds made unbridled by the novelty of affairs.

units.la: Tum Margareta Gubernatrix ut Frisios à societate foederis deterreret, & ne oppida per Provinciam, velut robur regij imperij in partem adversam transirent, foederatique juris fierent, litteras ad Senatum Leovardiae urbis VI. Kal. April. istiusmodi misit:
units.tr: Then Margaret the Governess, in order to deter the Frisians from the confederacy, and so that the towns throughout the province, like the strongholds of royal power, would not pass to the opposing side and become parties to the covenant, sent a letter to the Senate of the city of Leeuwarden on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, of the following kind:

units.la: Nisi certa essem instantis periculi, meâ admonitione vestrae res non eguissent. Nunc autem quia fide non vanâ accipio homines quosdam clandestinis conventibus, dein conspirationibus subnixos Provincijs exitium, Philippo Regi, cuius sacramento obligantur, vim, atque bellum machinari, ac jam militem autorasse, majoris mali metu deterrita, ut illorum consilij certiores vos facerem, mei muneris esse duxi. Cum enim hoc tantum agere in animum inducant, ut cuncta misceant, ac turbent, parandarumq; per vim opum avidi, civitates, honores, aeraria & privatorum fortunas suas faciant, occurrendum veteri medicina censeo, quâ in ipso civilium furorum ortu cautum semper fuit, ne invalescerent. Quapropter vestro, & maxime publico bono agetis, ut fomenta malo dematis, providique & perspicaces rerum curetis ne illorum societas novâ mobilis populi accessione augeatur. Quin Philippi Regis nomine mando vobis, ut urbis vestrae, portarumq; decentem curam custodiamque habeatis, faciatisque ea omnia, quae impediendis foederatorum machinationibus, & vestrae securitati conducere censebitis. Vigilantibus, & in commune consulentibus cuncta prosperè evenient, ignavos ac suarum rerum incuriosos fortuna destituet.
units.tr: If I were not certain of the danger that threatens, your affairs would not have needed my warning. But now, since I receive from trustworthy sources that certain men, relying first on secret meetings and then on conspiracies, are plotting destruction for the provinces, violence and war against Philip the King, to whose oath they are bound, and have already enlisted soldiers, I, frightened by the fear of a greater evil, have thought it my duty to inform you of their plans. For since they intend nothing else than to throw everything into confusion and disorder, and, greedy for seizing wealth by force, to make cities, offices, treasuries and private fortunes their own, I think we must meet them with the old remedy, which was always kept in place at the very birth of civil frenzy, so that it does not grow strong. Therefore you will act for your own good and especially for the public good, if you remove the fuel of the evil, and if you, prudent and far-sighted in your affairs, take care that their society is not increased by the new addition of a restless people. Indeed, in the name of King Philip I charge you to keep a fitting care and watch over your city and its gates, and to do all those things which you judge conducive to hindering the machinations of the confederates and to your own security. For those who are watchful and give counsel for the common good, all things will turn out well; fortune will abandon the idle and the careless about their own affairs.

units.la: Quae Leovardiam Bruxellis perscripta, ac in primarias Belgicae urbes transmissa foederatam pessime nobilitatem habuere. Et quemadmodum impuris corporibus ingesta supra modum alimenta quam maxime nocent, ita adactum jam ante civili concordiae vulnus atrocis injuriae faeditate, tanquam faecundâ mali materiae, intumuit. Iniquum namq; erat, homines praeter majorum decora, & gentilitias imagines, tot Principum affinitatibus, & suâ gloriâ claros conjurationis infamiâ gravari, Margaretamq; Gubernatricem extra matrimonium Caesaris natam faeminam, tam enormem calumniam clarissimis Belgicis familijs imponere. Quapropter foederata Nobilitas suam juxta & publicam causam actura, ne quid morae interveniret, die Bruxellis conducto coram Margaretâ Gubernatrice voce, & scripto, verba faciente Henrico Brederodio, hunc in modum disseruit:
units.tr: When this letter had been written at Brussels, sent to Leeuwarden, and circulated to the chief cities of Belgium, it gravely offended the confederate nobility. And just as foods taken beyond measure do the greatest harm to impure bodies, so the wound already inflicted on civil concord swelled, as if into a fertile matter of evil, through the foulness of an atrocious insult. For it was unjust that men who were distinguished by the honours of their ancestors, by their family images, by so many alliances with princes, and by their own glory, should be burdened with the infamy of conspiracy, and that Margaret the Governess, a woman born outside marriage to the Emperor, should impose so monstrous a calumny on the most illustrious Belgian families. Therefore the confederate nobility, about to act for its own cause and the public cause alike, so that no delay should intervene, having hired a day at Brussels, spoke before Margaret the Governess, by voice and in writing, Henry Brederode speaking, and argued in this manner:

units.la: Libellum, quem vides, supplicem exhibemus tibi Margareta, ut apud te more antiquo scripto ageremus, ac de nostro in Philippum regem affectu propalam testaremur. Cui legitima obsequia conferre, more majorum nostrorum qui hac laude omnes terrarum nationes provocavere, gloria quoq; nostra, & incolumitas est. Itaque illi olim fortunas suas, corpora, atque animas periculis objecere, ut in tuto Principum suorum, & simul res patriae essent, quas hoc ipso tempore Philippi Regis Edicta non parum conturbavere. Cui etsi Caroli patris decreta tolli durum atque profanum videatur, tamen in acta eius Edictaque nos jurare manifestae civilium animorum perturbationes non sinunt. Quas etiam ipsas severa Philippi jussa ac imperia augebunt potius, quam sedabunt. Ita vides concitatum populum haud ob-scura affectarum mentium signa praeferre, nihilq; instare, quam ut captâ seditione, praeceps ruina sacra omnia atque profana commisceat. Quare satius erit, inquietis, & nisi sistas, mox efferis futuris animis, amovere aut in aliud tempus rejicere Inquisitionem, fontem omnium malorum ut vides, quam optimi cuiusque civis fortunam, sanguinem atq; famam levissimorum hominum delationibus, accusationibus, atq; sententiis subjicere. Quarum certe rerum vel solus metus turbas, & seditiones exitabit, quae si ingruant, Margareta Princeps, reputabis nostrorum omnium, quos vides, conditionem miserrimam fore, dum urbibus munitionibusq; exclusi, ac per plana agrorum divisim sparsi, primam furentium insolentiam, & cum eâ terrima quaeque sufferemus. Spectabimus direptionem nostrarum rerum, & possessionum vastationem, ne quid dicamus de liberorum, ac conjugum statu, quas pro arbitrio victoris impudicus furor, aut hostiles manus temerabunt. Quare habendum Margareta, clementius imperium, sine quo integritati, securitatique nostrae locus esse non potest. Edicta mitigari, aut aboleri è re Philippi regis, & simul nostrâ erit. Quare hoc imprimis necessarium judicamus, ut Legatum in Hispaniam mittas ocyus, moneasque Philippum praesentium rerum & impendentis exitij. Non quod regiî imperiî majestatem nostro praescripto aut consilio stare velimus, sed ut nostrae fidei publicum hoc & illustre documentum rex accipiat, omniaque paci ac fortunae publicae adversa clementiâ hac de re commomiti Regis, & de consilio Ordinum amoveantur. Rogamus interim Margareta, ut omnis actio Inquisitionis religionisve in suspenso sit, dum Rex alter decernat, & consilium hoc nostrum, quod publicae salutis cura nostris mentibus atq; pectoribus extorsit, à Philippo Rege in ipso rerum secreto expendatur. Quod si fiat, satisfactum nostris desideriis, & in patriam affectui erit: sin minus obtestamur, Deum, Regem, & te Principem Margareta, dein nostras conscientias, publici exitij consilium aliis autoribus stetisse. Quin scias non Gallorum nos foedera, non Germaniae societates quaerere, sed ut exasperatus seductusque Philippi Regis animus ad se redeat, misereaturque innocentiae illorum, qui sanguinem suum, atque gloriosa funera, regiis imperiis sacraturi essent. Tantum abest nos vetus sacramentum exuere, aut à rege desciscere, (quo piaculo non nisi aulae satelles, & vanus delator nos adstringet) caeterum volumus ut patriae quies, Regi bonos atque autoritas sit, sileantque in posterum Edicta libertati, & conscientiis hominum adversa.
units.tr: We present to you this petition, Margaret, so that, in the old manner, we may plead our cause before you in writing and openly declare our attitude towards King Philip. To render him lawful obedience is, as our ancestors did, who challenged all the nations of the earth with this praise, also our glory and our safety. Our forefathers once exposed their fortunes, bodies and souls to danger, so that their princes and the affairs of the fatherland might be secure, and at this very time the edicts of King Philip have greatly disturbed those same affairs. Although to annul the decrees of his father Charles may seem harsh and impious to him, nevertheless the manifest disturbances of men's minds do not allow us to swear to his acts and edicts. These very disturbances the harsh commands and orders of Philip will increase rather than calm. Thus you see the aroused people showing clear signs of inflamed minds, and nothing threatens but that, once sedition has been seized, headlong ruin will throw everything sacred and profane into confusion. It would therefore be better, lest men's spirits soon rise up in fury, to remove or postpone the Inquisition, the source of all these evils, as you see, which subjects the fortune, blood and reputation of every good citizen to the denunciations, accusations and sentences of the most worthless men. The mere fear of these things will stir up tumults and seditions, and if they break out, Princess Margaret, you will consider how wretched the condition of all of us here will be. Shut out of the cities and fortified places, and scattered separately over the open fields, we shall first endure the insolence of the raging mob, and with it every kind of terror. We shall witness the plundering of our goods and the devastation of our estates, not to mention the state of our children and wives, whom the shameless fury or hostile hands of the victor will defile at will. Therefore, Margaret, you must hold a milder rule, without which there can be no place for our integrity and security. To mitigate or abolish the edicts will serve the interest of King Philip and at the same time our own. We therefore judge it especially necessary that you send an envoy to Spain at once, to inform Philip of the present state of affairs and of the impending ruin. We do not wish to prescribe to the majesty of the royal authority by our demand or counsel, but that the king may receive this public and clear proof of our loyalty, and that, once the king has been informed of these matters with clemency and by the counsel of the Estates, all things adverse to public peace and welfare may be removed. Meanwhile we ask you, Margaret, that every action of the Inquisition or of religious matters be suspended until the king decides otherwise, and that this our counsel, which concern for the public safety has wrung from our minds and hearts, be weighed by Philip the King in the secrecy of his own deliberation. If this is done, our desires will be satisfied and our affection for the fatherland fulfilled; if not, we call to witness God, the King, and you, Princess Margaret, and then our own consciences, that the plan of public ruin stood on other authors' initiative. Know, moreover, that we do not seek alliances with the French or confederacies with Germany, but that the spirit of the King, exasperated and misled, may return to itself and take pity on the innocence of those who would consecrate their blood and glorious deaths to royal commands. We are so far from renouncing our ancient oath or revolting from the king (a sin into which only a courtier's lackey and a worthless informer would draw us) that we wish rather that the quiet of the fatherland, goodwill and authority may belong to the king, and that in future no edicts hostile to liberty and men's consciences may be heard.

units.la: Ad haec Margareta: Accepisse se supplicationem, atturamq; ut ea ad Philippum Regem ocyus mittatur. Se quidem jam diu consilium cepisse intercedendi apud Regem pro leniendis Edictis, idque cum Ordine Aurei Velleris Provinciarum Praefectis, tum Status Belgici, Regioque Senatu communicasse. Caeterum suae potestatis non esse, quod delegatam tantum haberet, statuere pro arbitrio, aut mederi malis temporum sine Regis rescripto, quod interponi debere ipsi foederati non ignorarent. Curaturam interea, ut (dum rex decernat) quies Provinciis sit, Magistratuumque ac Inquisitorum potestas cum temperamento exerceatur. Haec postridie, Non. April. perscripta.
units.tr: To these things Margaret replied: she had received the petition and would take care that it be sent to King Philip at once. She had indeed for a long time resolved to intercede with the King for the softening of the edicts, and had communicated this both to the Provincial Governors of the Order of the Golden Fleece and to the Estates of Belgium and the Royal Council. Otherwise it was not within her power, since she held only a delegated authority, to decide at her own discretion or to remedy the evils of the times without the King's rescript, which the confederates themselves knew must be interposed. Meanwhile she would see to it that, until the king decided, there be quiet in the provinces, and that the power of the magistrates and inquisitors be exercised with moderation. This was written out the day after the Nones of April.

units.la: Ita Margareta Gubernatrix muliebri astutiâ, & ex Italiae suae disciplinâ velum Edictis obducere, praeferre moderamen, metu foederatae Nobilitatis & civilium armorum, quod ijs resistendis par non esset, debili cIↄ. Iↄ. debili urbium præsidio, & solis prætorianis ad corporis custodiam delectis. Quare crudis adhuc per Hispaniam quoque rebus, & mobili per Belgicam populo remedium ab ostentatione clementiæ quæsivit, factaque lenioris imperij fide exacerbatas mentes demulsit. Tum federati lenocinio verborum Margaretæ Gubernatricis, verspellis fæminæ, ac fiduciâ restitutæ quietis in sua redire. Scribit Demetrius finitâ Nobilitatis cum Margaretâ actione simplicem populum, & morum aulæ rudem suis commercijs, ac diurnis operis mox usum, intermissa turbidis rebus negotia velut compositâ tempestate continuasse. Caeterum ut spes mortalium lubricæ, ut plurimum, & fallaces esse solent, ita fœderatæ Nobilitatis, populiq; incerta & eventu inrita fuit. Perlato namque in Hispaniam ícti fœderis, mox Philippi aulam nuntio, regium animum primo consternatio, post ira, & abolendi fœderis studium occupavere. Constat certe ab illo tempore alieno magis à Belgicâ animo Philippum fuisse, subsecutasque res, ut aulicâ simulatione, ita revera secretis & infestis odijs obductas. Populum quoque suæ servitutis, & fluxæ per aulam Principis fidei pertæsum majore desiderio fœderis flagrasse, respuentemq; Edicta, ac velut spatia laxantem libertati, arcana conscientiarum professum. Criminabatur namque Margaretam Gubernatricem pactis conventis vim derogare, ac datam publicè Nobilitati fidem aulæ artibus deludi. Philippum ipsum, adhibendo deploratis rebus remedio tardum, lenta consilia trahere, differreque illius vulneris curationem, quod moræ impaticns esset, &, cuius notæ, necdum coalitâ cicatrice, conspicerentur. Cavisse enim fœderatam Nobilitatem, ut rescriptum Margaretæ libello Brederodij subscriptum efficax esset, minimoq; temporis spatio interjecto Philippi regis ratihabitione firmaretur. Ordinum quoque, (penes quos pace, bellog; administratio rerum, & jus publici consilij fuisset) conventus intra Provincias de voluntate Regis haberetur, statuereturque quiddam tollendis civilis dissidij fomentis opportunum.
