Itaque debili Philippi ac Margaretæ Principum fide, & quod Ordinum convocatio illâ rerum desperatione præpediretur, offensa multitudo velut ad mores, ac ingenium rediens rursum in cætus coïvit, communemque concordiam, ut munimentum retinendi juris durioribus dominantium imperijs objecit.
units.tr: Thus Margaret the Governess, with womanly cunning and after the discipline of her Italy, sought to draw a veil over the edicts and to put forward a show of moderation, out of fear of the confederate nobility and of civil arms, which she was not equal to resisting, the cities being weakly garrisoned and only the praetorians chosen for the guard of her person. Therefore, since affairs were still unsettled in Spain too, and the people in Belgium restless, she sought a remedy in a display of clemency, and by promising a gentler rule she soothed the exasperated minds. Then the confederates, won over by the flattering words of Margaret the Governess, a woman of slippery faith, and trusting in the restored quiet, returned to their own affairs. Demetrius writes that, once the nobility's action with Margaret was finished, the simple people, unskilled in the manners of the court, resumed their trade and daily work, and that business interrupted by troubled times went on as if the storm had been calmed. But as the hopes of mortals are usually slippery and deceptive, so the hope of the confederate nobility and the people proved uncertain and, in the outcome, vain. For when the agreement made was carried to Spain, the news reached Philip's court, and first dismay, then anger and the desire to abolish the covenant seized the royal mind. It is certain that from that time Philip was more estranged from the Belgian spirit, and the events that followed were shrouded, as much in courtly pretence as in truth, in secret and hostile hatreds. The people, too, weary of their servitude and of a prince's faith that was slippery through the court, burned with a greater desire for the covenant, and rejecting the edicts, which seemed to restrict liberty, they professed the secrets of their consciences. For they charged Margaret the Governess with weakening the agreed terms by force, and with the court's arts deceiving the faith publicly pledged to the nobility. They charged Philip himself with being slow to apply a remedy to desperate affairs, drawing out his sluggish counsels and delaying the cure of a wound which, since he could not bear delay, was still visible, its scar not yet healed. For the confederate nobility had taken care that Margaret's rescript, subscribed to Brederode's petition, should be effective, and should be confirmed by King Philip's ratification within a very short time. Also, an assembly of the Estates (in whose hands the administration of peace and war and the right of public counsel had rested) was to be held within the provinces with the King's consent, and something was to be decided that would be useful for removing the fuel of civil discord. Thus, with the faith of Philip and of the princess Margaret weakened, and because the convening of the Estates was hindered by that despair of affairs, the offended multitude, as if returning to its customs and disposition, came together again in assemblies, and opposed its common concord as a bulwark for maintaining its right against the harsher rule of its masters.

units.la: Quapropter Margareta periculi metuens, & ut sponsioni suæ, quâ Nobilitati se obligaverat, robur adfingeret, de suo & Senatus Belgici Consilio, Ioannem Marchionem Bergæ, & Florentium Montmorentium Moutinium in Hispaniam ablegavit, ijsq; potestatem fecit, ut de mitigandis Religionis Edictis, ac auferendâ Inquisitione coram Philippo agerent, veniamq;' præteritorum orarent. Additum quoque de maturando Ordinum Belgicæ conventu, quod sinillo subortam tempestatem sedari non posse consentiens hominum fama testaretur. Quas mandata in ipso regij Senatus consessu à Legatis exposita, plus invidiæ suis autoribus, quam adjumenti rebus Belgicis attulere. Creditum fuit, eosdem Legatos longioris in aulâ moræ pertæsos, ac jure suo immodestius, quam consuetudo regni ferret, usos, pro gratiâ odium, & ex eo contumaciam audientium reperisse. Alij addunt, conventum omnium Belgicæ Ordinum urgentes ferventius, & de contumelijs ac inrisu
units.tr: Therefore Margaret, fearing danger, and so as to give strength to her promise by which she had bound herself to the nobility, with the advice of herself and of the Belgian Council sent John, Marquis of Berghes, and Florent de Montmorency, Lord of Montigny, into Spain, and empowered them to treat before Philip about moderating the edicts on religion and removing the Inquisition, and to beg pardon for past offences. It was also added that the assembly of the Belgian Estates should be hastened, since the common report of men bore witness that the storm which had arisen could not be calmed without it. These instructions, set out by the envoys in the very council of the royal Senate, brought more odium upon their authors than help to Belgian affairs. It was believed that the same envoys, weary of a longer stay at court, and using their right more arrogantly than the custom of the kingdom allowed, found hatred instead of favour, and from this the obstinacy of their hearers. Others add that they, pressing the assembly of all the Belgian Estates more fervently, and [complaining] of the insults and mockery...

units.la: Philippus à fœderefacto Belgis iniquior.
units.tr: Philip more hostile to the Belgians after the covenant was made.

units.la: Margareta mitigationem Edilorum promittit.
units.tr: Margaret promises a mitigation of the edicts.

units.la: Legati à Margareta in Hispan. missi. inrisu Hispanicæ gentis, haud vana suæ Belgicæq; nobilitatis fiducia, cIↄ. Iↄ. questos, instructuosam legationem, & post mercedem tristis officij LXVI. accepisse. Quorum omnium, ut nihil fœderatos fallebat, quod secretis epistolarum commercijs & fido interprete res gererentur, ita in populum ferente ocyus famâ divulgatum, infidam jam ante Belgicæ quietem abrupit. His accedebat, quod exules fœderati excedere ditionibus Edicto juberentur, disturbatisque per arma, aut vim, populi conventibus, reformata, ut vocabant, religio novis supplicijs, & piorum sanguine coërceretur. Suspectæ namq; Margaretæ Gubernatrici ad populum conciones erant, & divino cultui securitas armis quæsita. Quæ propterea ne odia fœderatæ Nobilitatis, & conglobatæ multitudinis in se derivaret, longarum precum continuatione tantum profecit, ut lenito, prout videbatur, Philippi regis animo cum fœderatâ & jam mobili Nobilitate in reciprocam conventionem descenderit. Eâ perscrip-tum fuit, ut Inquisitio cessaret, novoque ac mitiore Edicto antiquatis superioribus, supplici Nobilitati litteræ traderentur, quibus de FIDE PUBLICA caveretur. Nobilitas quoq; legis, ac officij memor, justum Philippo obsequium præstaret, provideretque in posterum, ne sacrorum locorum vastatio, arma, aut vis ulla, fœdera quoq; aut societates haberentur, regio juri publicæ tranquillitati adversæ. Id Pactum IX. Kal. Sept. tabulis signatum, ac in Frisios eodem Augusto inclinante perlatum. Itaq; tum arma posita, ac conciones (quod jam ante Margareta indulserat) per Provincias restauratæ, populusque, ut fere solet, facilè affectuum imperio parens priorum criminationum materiem per subsecutam felicitatem excussit. Nobilitas quoque fœderis auspex velut restituto jure patrio secura, secreto suo se clausit, Præfectiqúe à pactionis formulâ Provincias ordinavere. Cæterum affulgentis fortunæ, & quietis splendor durabilis non fuit, quod armorum apparatum fama nuntiaret, & quod pactionis ratihabitio præter expectationem tardius ex Hispaniâ mitteretur. Quare diffidentiâ Principum, civiliumq; animorum subdola omnia, atque involuta suspicionibus mansere, animiq; mobiles, velut impellente vento, huc illuc in spem publicæ securitatis acti varias rerum species, & imagines circumtulere. Ea per superiores Belgicæ Provincias, & in Philippi aulâ rerum facies, tum erat. Neque per Frisiam, quam Lavica Flevusque lato alveo disterminant, melioribus fatis res agebantur.
units.tr: The envoys sent by Margaret into Spain. ...of the mockery of the Spanish people, complaining that their confidence in themselves and in the Belgian nobility, which was not vain, had been met with insults, that their embassy was fruitless, and that after the reward of their sad office they received [a sentence]. Of all these things nothing escaped the confederates, since the affairs were conducted by secret exchanges of letters and a trusty interpreter; so, as the report spread quickly among the people, it broke the already unreliable quiet of Belgium. To this was added that the exiled confederates were ordered by edict to leave the territories, and that the gatherings of the people, disturbed by arms or force, and the so-called reformed religion, were held in check with new punishments and with the blood of the pious. For sermons to the people were suspect to Margaret the Governess, and security for divine worship had been sought by arms. Therefore, so that she might not draw upon herself the hatred of the confederate nobility and the banded multitude, she gained so much by a long continuance of prayers that, the mind of King Philip being softened, as it seemed, she came to a mutual agreement with the confederate and now restless nobility. By this agreement it was written down that the Inquisition should cease, and that, with the earlier edicts annulled by a new and milder edict, letters should be handed to the suppliant nobility concerning PUBLIC FAITH. The nobility also, mindful of the law and of its duty, should render just obedience to Philip, and should take care in future that no devastation of sacred places, no arms or violence, and no covenants or associations contrary to royal right and public tranquillity be maintained. This pact was sealed in documents on the 9th day before the Kalends of September, and was carried into Friesland at the end of August. Therefore the arms were laid down, and the sermons (which Margaret had already permitted earlier) were restored throughout the provinces; and the people, as usually happens, easily obedient to the rule of their emotions, shook off the matter of former accusations through the good fortune that followed. The nobility too, the sponsor of the covenant, as if its ancestral right had been restored, shut itself up in its own privacy, and the governors arranged the provinces according to the form of the agreement. But the splendour of the fortune that was shining and of the quiet was not lasting, because rumour reported an assembly of arms, and because the ratification of the agreement was sent from Spain more slowly than expected. Therefore, through the distrust of the princes and the deceitful and entangled suspicions of the civil minds, everything remained, and the restless spirits, as if driven by a wind, were carried hither and thither in hope of public security, and bore about various appearances and images of affairs. Such was the state of affairs in the upper Belgian provinces and at Philip's court at that time. Nor were things going on with better fortune in Friesland, which the Lauwers and the Vlie divide with their broad channel.

units.la: Postquam enim libellus supplex (quem Henricus Brederodius fœderatorum nomine Margaretæ Gubernatrici obtulerat) Leovardiæ circa Kal. Iun. vulgatus, ingenia procerum, populiq; non parum is affecit. Reputantibus prudentioribus non sine gravi causâ sociatam fœdere Nobilitatem fœminæ Principi supplicasse. Eam namque optimo jure de confractis patriæ suæ legibus questam non temerario nexu, non fortuito concursu convenisse. Æternum rerum ordinem istiusmodi consilia sequi. Gentes quippe ab initio faciundæ societatis causâ congressos, post dominantium lubidine oppressos, mutuæ defensionis auxilium, odio ac infamiâ pravorum principum à communi concordiâ petijsse. Ita pacatos ante Belgas, & suorum Principum reverentes, secessionem non nisi ab oppressione fecisse, & quod interesse censerent liberum an man-cipem cipem Spiritum sub patrio cælo traherent. Hoc modo ne cum lucis usurâ inauditæ servitutis legem acciperent, Edictis atq; Inquisitoribus, dein Episcopis obstitisse, advocatâ juris patrij, & antiquarum conventionum fide, quas teredo annosæ vetustatis & potentia regnantium necdum sustulisset. Extare adhuc homines memoriam temporum repetentes, qui obsequium Principi debitum confundi cum servitute, & infælicem Patriam exponi periculis indignentur. Pressisse interea generosos Spiritus, & ne causam exitio darent, supplices Principi factos, turbidis temporibus usitata remedia, conventum Ordinum orasse. Æquum scilicet fuisse, ut inter Regem populumque ortæ lites, intercessione Optimatum sternerentur, sanaretuŕq; omne malum, à motu ac licentiâ populi, aut ambitione Principis profectum. Id recusanti inimicam pacem videri. Esse Margaretam versipellem fœminam, & vota Nobilitatis fœderatæ aulicis artibus trahentem, tum Philippum Hispaniâ sua septum falsis rerum testimonijs inturgescere. Alterutrum eligendum esse, aut coëundum in fœdus, aut turpiter serviendum. Hæc in secreto per Frisiam agebantur.
units.tr: For once the petition (which Henry Brederode had presented to Margaret the Regent on behalf of the confederates) was published at Leeuwarden around the first of June, and it stirred the minds of the nobles and the common people no little. More prudent men reflected that the Noblemen, bound together by their covenant, had not petitioned the princess without serious cause. She had been justly complaining that the laws of her country had been broken, and they had not come together by a rash bond or a chance gathering. Such plans always follow the eternal order of things. From the beginning, peoples had joined together for the sake of forming a society, and afterwards, when they were oppressed by the lust of rulers, they had sought the aid of mutual defence and of common harmony against the hatred and infamy of wicked princes. In the same way the Belgians, who had been peaceful and respectful of their own princes, had seceded only from oppression, and they judged it important whether they drew free breath or breathed as slaves under their native sky. For this reason, so that they would not accept the law of an unheard-of servitude at the cost of losing the light of liberty, they had resisted the edicts and the inquisitors, and then the bishops, appealing to the faith of their national law and of their ancient agreements, which the worm of long antiquity and the power of rulers had not yet destroyed. There were still people, recalling the times past, who were indignant that the duty owed to a prince should be confused with servitude and that an unhappy country should be exposed to dangers. Meanwhile, the nobles had restrained their high spirits, and, lest they give their cause over to ruin, they had made humble petitions to the prince, and in these troubled times they had asked for the usual remedy, a meeting of the Estates. It was only fair, they said, that disputes arising between king and people should be settled by the intervention of the nobles, and that every evil arising from the movement and licence of the people, or from the ambition of the prince, should be cured. To refuse this, they said, looked like hostility to peace. Margaret was a shifty woman who drew the wishes of the confederated nobility to herself by courtly arts, while Philip, hemmed in by his Spanish counsellors, swelled with false reports of affairs. One of two courses had to be chosen: either to join the covenant or to serve shamefully. These matters were being discussed in secret throughout Frisia.

units.la: Quamobrem fœderati sparsis per omnem Provinciam socijs, perceptâq; populi Frisici in fœdus inclinatione, Herbertum Raephorstium, Fredericum Egmondanum, & Albertum Huchtenbroeckium, clarorum natalium viros, in Frisiam ablegavere: Mandata eorum hæc erant, ut de fœdere, & rebus cum Margaretâ Gubernatrice Bruxellis, tum cum ipso Philippo Rege in Hispaniâ gestis ad Frisios referrent, ijsque copiam scripti fœderis & suorum simul mandatorum facerent. Curarent quoque, ut, factâ regiæ iræ, & ruentium indies in peius rerum obnuntiatione, repellendis à Patriâ periculis in eandem societatem Frisij condescendant, spretâque Margaretæ Gubernatricis monitione, & fallacibus litteris, commune libertatis studium, & simul discrimen amplectantur. Ita acceptis mandatis Legati in Frisiam profecti, Leovardiam Provinciæ metropolim pervenere. Famâ ferunt Legatos candidis equis vectos, vestesque cinericei coloris indutos, ligneumque poculum argenteis laminis obductum, præferentes, multorum hominum affectus commovisse, formatoque præter morem habitu, servile etiam in Regem obsequium, & patientiam insontis ludibrij signasse. Immania namq; à Pontificijs in Legatos convitia jaciebantur, effrænisque ac maledici oris licentia integritatem fœderis, & simul existimationem Legatorum impetebat. Notat Antonius Iodocius, actuarius publicus, Herbertum Raephorstium unum Legatorum, diem ut plurimum somno, noctem oblectamentis vitæ, & exercitijs libidinum egisse, dignitatemque Legati turpi ignaviâ & nocturnis fœminarum amoribus attaminasse. Alij in atrociores calumnias, prout pravus cuiusque animus, aut ingenium dictabat, invidiâ fœderis effundebantur. Quamobrem Legati ne illa temporum partiumq; dissensione in discrimen traherentur, Delegatis Ordinum Frisiæ Leovardiam evocatis, istiusmodi litteras exhibuere:
units.tr: Therefore the confederates, having scattered their allies throughout the whole province and having noted that the people of Friesland were inclined to join the covenant, sent Herbert Raephorst, Frederick of Egmond and Albert Huchtenbroek, men of distinguished birth, into Friesland. Their instructions were these: they were to report to the Frisians about the covenant and about what had been done at Brussels with Margaret the Regent, and also about what had been done in Spain with King Philip himself, and to give them a copy of the written covenant along with their own mandates. They were also to see to it that, since the king's anger had been aroused and the news of a situation that was daily getting worse had been announced, the Frisians would come down into the same society in order to ward off the dangers threatening the country, and that, scorning the warnings of Margaret the Regent and her deceptive letters, they would embrace the common zeal for liberty and at the same time its peril. So, having received their mandates, the envoys set out for Friesland and arrived at Leeuwarden, the metropolis of the province. Report has it that the envoys, riding on white horses and dressed in clothes of ash-grey colour, carrying a wooden cup covered with silver plates, stirred the feelings of many people; and that, since their dress was unusual, they also displayed a servile obedience toward the king and a patient endurance of an innocent mockery. For the Papists were hurling monstrous insults at the envoys, and the unbridled licence of a slanderous tongue attacked both the integrity of the covenant and at the same time the reputation of the envoys. Anthony Jodocius, the public notary, notes that Herbert Raephorst, one of the envoys, spent the day mostly in sleep and the night in the pleasures of life and in exercises of lust, and that he had stained the dignity of an envoy with shameful idleness and nightly love affairs with women. Others, as the depraved disposition or talent of each dictated, poured out in envy of the covenant more atrocious calumnies. Therefore, lest the envoys be dragged into danger by that dissension of parties and of the times, they summoned the deputies of the Estates of Friesland to Leeuwarden and presented letters of this kind:

units.la: Q Vanquam graves causæ nos impulerint, Ordines, ut in Frisiam vestram profici scneremur, ita pro vero accepimus, esse quosdam qui afferant speciali nos manmandato instructos ad pertrahendam clandestinis modis in fœdus nostrum Frisicam Nobilitatem advenisse. Quæ calumnia ne famæ, ac existimationi nostræ aliquid credulas mentes quidquam derogaret, ac ne haberemur pro iis, quos pudere suæ Legationis & officij posset, vestro in cœtu Ordines nos sistimus, fidemque facimus nullis secretis mandatis nos munitos esse, cæterum adferre tabulas Sanctissimi Fœderis, & honestissimæ societatis Principum nobiliumque virorum manu obsignatas. Tantum abest homines nos esse malis artibus, consiliisque instructos. A quibus etiam ut longius nos abesse probemus, exhibemus propalam easdem tabulas, obtestamurque; nostrum ac majorum decus, non aliam Legationis nostræ causam fuisse, quam ut de honesto sanctoque fœdere certiores vos faceremus. Vestri arbitrii erit, hoc approbare aut rejicere. Nobis satis erit, nostræ Legationi satisfecisse, ac nos ipsos populum Frisicum, Ordines, à communione ejusdem fœderis excludere noluisse.
units.tr: Although serious causes have moved you, the Estates, to send us into your Friesland, yet we have learned for a fact that there are some who assert that we have come instructed by a special mandate to draw the Frisian nobility secretly into our covenant. Lest this calumny lessen anything in the eyes of credulous minds, and lest we be regarded as men whom shame at their own embassy and office could affect, we present ourselves before your assembly of the Estates, and we give our assurance that we are furnished with no secret mandates; on the contrary, we bring the tablets of the most holy covenant and of the most honourable society of princes and noblemen, sealed with their hands. So far are we from being men equipped with wicked arts and plots. To prove that we are far from these things, we openly display the same tablets, and we call to witness our own honour and that of our forefathers that the only reason for our embassy was to inform you about an honest and holy covenant. It will be for your judgement to approve or reject this. It will be enough for us to have satisfied our embassy and to have shown that we did not wish to exclude the Frisian people, the Estates, from fellowship in this same covenant.

units.la: Cui Orationi ut fides adstrueretur, & ne quid Legatorum officijs, illà partium per Provinciam, & simul civitatem æmulatione, affingi posset, testimonij publici dictionem petiere, ac ut rei apud Frisios gestæ memoria actis mandaretur. Igitur Ordinum Delegati, quò facili, & quod metuebant, instanti calumniæ occurreretur, & ne plebs seditionem ex vanis acribusque rumoribus agitaret, ita perscribi curaverunt.
units.tr: So that faith might be added to this speech, and lest anything be attributed to the offices of the envoys, in the rivalry between the parties across the province and the city, the envoys sought a public attestation and asked that a memorial of the affair done among the Frisians be recorded in the acts. Accordingly, the deputies of the Estates, in order to meet the calumny that was easy and, as they feared, pressing, and so that the common people should not stir up sedition from vain and sharp rumours, took care to have it written out as follows.

units.la: Venere ad nos VV. Nob. ALBERTUS HUCHTENBROECKIUS, & FREDERICUS EGMONDANUS, formulam Fœderis adferentes. Præter hoc verba in nostro conventu habuere non alium, ut profitebantur, in finem, quam ne clandestinæ conjurationis insimularentur, & ut evulgaretur justissimum sanctissimumque Fœdus, quod nostræ quoque genti, si retinere libertatem vellet, offerri desiderabant. Neque enim Legatos arcere provinciâ licuit, quos gentium jus inviolabiles fecisset, & qui ex uxorum suarum dotibus prædia & possessiones per Frisiam tenerent. Ut certè ne in mali quidem consilij, aut fabricatæ conspirationis suspicionem apud nos venirent, quæ plerumque imbecilla, ex animi livore atque odio, aliquid injuriæ, etiam bonis, afformat. Ita enim fit, ut qui timeri volunt ex suâ, alienam potentiam formident, credantque vero proxima, quæ ipsi finxere. Nos testimonium, quale debuimus illorum integritatis innocentiæque dandum duximus, ne videamur ex iniquo quid egisse. Hoc à Ruardo Roorda, Haringio Glinzio, Valerio Cammingha, Docome Martna signatum.
units.tr: There came to us, your most noble men, Albert Huchtenbroek and Frederick of Egmond, bringing the formula of the covenant. Besides this, they spoke words in our assembly, with no other purpose, as they professed, than that they should not be accused of secret conspiracy, and that the most just and most holy covenant, which they wished to be offered also to our nation, should be made known, if it wished to keep its liberty. For it was not lawful to exclude from the province envoys whom the law of nations had made inviolable, and who held farms and estates throughout Friesland by the dowries of their wives. Certainly they did not come under suspicion among us even of a wicked plan or of a fabricated conspiracy, which, for the most part, are feeble, and which, arising from the spite and hatred of the mind, attach some injury even to good men. For it happens that those who wish to be feared fear the power of others as if it were their own, and they believe the near things to be true which they themselves have invented. We have thought it right to give such testimony of their integrity and innocence as we owed, lest we seem to have acted unjustly. Signed by Ruard Roorda, Haring Glinzius, Valerius Cammingha, Docome Martna.

units.la: Ut mirari liceat, lœsæ libertatis Belgicæ concors documentum non inerudițis alias ingenijs & huius sæculi scriptoribus conjurationis titulo traduci, ipsosque suorum Pontificum, aut Principum assentatores juris aboliti vindicias pessimi criminis enormi infamiâ velare. Quod equidem illis familiare deprehendo, qui in regno, aut Principatu nati, educatiq; suæ tantum servitutis conscientiâ, ad defensam armis nobilissimarum gentium libertatem, ex consuetudine crudi, atque infælicis obsequij non assurgunt. Ut ut sit, hoc saltem incomperto est, invalidi Fœderis initium fato quodam regnanti Philippo obiectum, magna & quidem terrarum orbi formidolosa incrementa inter continuas belli tempestates, & variantis fortunæ asperitatem traxisse, nobilitatemque
units.tr: One may well wonder that a united evidence of a wronged Belgic liberty should be branded by writers of this age, not otherwise unlearned in their talents, with the name of conspiracy, and that the defenders of abolished law, flatterers of their own Popes or princes, should veil the rights of this liberty with the enormous infamy of the worst crime. This indeed I find to be a habit of those who, born and bred in a kingdom or principality, aware only of their own servitude, do not rise, from the custom of a raw and unhappy obedience, to defend with arms the liberty of the most noble nations. However that may be, this at least is certain: the beginning of a weak covenant, opposed by fate to the reigning Philip, brought about great increases, indeed increases frightening to the whole world, amid continual storms of war and the harshness of changing fortune; and the nobility

units.la: ac populum Belgicum in vindicandâ dominantium immanitate terrarum gentibus ex divinæ benignitatis indulgentiâ præluxisse.
units.tr: and the Belgic people, in vindicating themselves against the cruelty of their rulers, shone forth to the nations of the earth by the indulgence of divine kindness.

units.la: Invenio in actis istorum temporum, magnam de Fenis Bantianis Scoterlandiisq; inter Petrum Dekama Equitem, Antonium del Vailium, Baldvinum Loæum cum socijs, & quosdam nobilium, super aquâ istarum paludum deducendâ controversiam fuisse, litemq; modo ad Senatum regium, modo ad legatos Ordinum remissam, magná acerbitate partium animos inritasse. Quippe Dekamæ inveteratum sedecim annorum jus, & intemeratam possessionem obtendebant, eq; Fenorum fossurâ (quos insularum natantium instar Frisicis terris stagnisque se superfudisse creditum est) magnum operariorum multitudini, tum totiprovinciæ commodum obvenire. Quippe egestati istos bituminosos agros tractantium subveniri, & evocari in provinciam vicinos, è fossurâ cespitum se sustentantes, quos in omnem regionem devehi gentis interesset. Econtra nobiliras istis paludum ac bituminosis aquis suos agros ingenio suo depressos, & humentes oppleri criminabatur, agrisq; fertilibus ex vitiatæ corruptæque aquæ inundatione sterilitatem induci. Ne ipsa quoq; regis domania ab hoc malo exempta esse, consulendumq; esse æquitati, quæ non ferret, ex unius paucorumq; commodis, inreparabile damnum detrimentumq;, nisi subveniatur, Frisicis agris terrisque accedere. Cæterum causæ ex se justæ patronos atque advocatos deesse, potentiâq; adversariorum perterritos officia sua, & clientum fortunas negligere. Hæc à Douwone Douma, Tito Hettingha, Erasmo Douma, Florentio Abbema, Horatio Oeningha, Onnone Grovenstenio signata, 28. Iun. & Deputatis exhibita. Ita factum est, ut tarditate judicum, majora odia accenderentur, spretâq; judicij autoritate, prædicta nobilitas, coactâ plebis rusticæ manu, catarractas rivosque devehendo cespiti factos injectâ terrâ oppilaverit. Quo tempore metui poterat, ne futura civilis belli fax se ostenderet, latensque inter regios & libertatis patriæ amantes, odium ex violentis iustiusmodi actionibus, turbisq; se aperiret. Cæterum interventus Sibrandi Hettingha Prætoris Scoterlandici, & Hansonis Gelij actuarij, negotium Eelkoni Haulæo advocato Curiæ disceptandum in foro demandavit, actionemq; in judicio persequendi potestatem fecit. Hoc etenim Scoterlandi volebant, ut Drachtana fossa, qua Drachtanis in orientem est, juxta viam publicam repurgaretur, oppilatusq; paulò ante rivus omnem paludum agrorumq; eluviem sine ullo obstaculo exoneraret. Itaq; litis contestatio in judicio regij Senatus facta, omnem occultioris dissidij vim amovit. Gemma notat paulo ante Iconomachiam, quæ per omnem Belgicam mox secuta, horrendæ nubis imaginem in cælo, mense Iulio conspectam, ingentia fulgura cum grandine ejaculasse, flammeoq; colore, quasi universi conflagrationem minaretur, non nihil remisso, in ventos pluviasq; abijsse. Magnam etiam tempestatem fulminum, una cum nubium fragoribus Leovardiæ auditam, ex incerti notis observo, illamq; cælestis oræ conturbationem secuturis populi motibus assimilatam.
units.tr: I find in the records of these times that there was a great controversy between Peter Dekama, a knight, Anthony del Vaille, Baldwin Loo with his associates, and certain noblemen, concerning the draining of the water from the Fens of Bant and Scoterland; and the lawsuit, now sent to the royal Senate and now to the envoys of the Estates, roused the minds of the parties to great bitterness. For Dekama put forward a right of sixteen years' standing and an unbroken possession, and he argued that by the digging of the Fens (which were thought to have spread over the Frisian lands and pools like floating islands) a great benefit would come to the multitude of workmen and to the whole province. For, he said, the poverty of those who worked these bituminous lands would be relieved, and neighbouring men who supported themselves by digging turf would be called into the province, and it was in the nation's interest that they be carried into every region. On the other hand, the noblemen accused Dekama of having lowered their fields by his device, and of filling them with these marshy and bituminous waters, and of bringing barrenness upon fertile fields by the flooding of polluted and corrupted water. They added that even the king's own domains had been spared from this evil, and that equity had to be consulted, which would not tolerate that irreparable loss and damage should come to the Frisian fields and lands from the advantage of one or a few, unless help were given. Otherwise, they said, the just cause lacked its own patrons and advocates, and, frightened by the power of their opponents, the men of office neglected their duties and the fortunes of their clients. These matters were signed by Douwe Douma, Tito Hettinga, Erasmus Douma, Florentius Abbema, Horatius Oeninga, Onno Grovenstein, on the 28th of June, and were presented to the deputies. So it came about that, through the slowness of the judges, greater hatreds were kindled; and the noblemen, scorning the authority of the court, with a band of rustic people forced together, by carrying cataracts and streams to the turf that had been made, blocked them by throwing in earth. At that time it could be feared that the torch of a future civil war might show itself, and that hatred, lurking between the royalists and the lovers of their country's liberty, might reveal itself through such violent actions and disturbances. However, the intervention of Sibrand Hettinga, the praetor of Scoterland, and of Hanso Gelius, the notary, handed the matter over to Eelko Haulaeus, an advocate of the court, to be disputed in the forum, and gave him the power of pursuing the action in court. For the Scoterlanders wanted this: that the Drachten ditch, which runs eastward from Drachten, be cleared out along the public road, and that the stream blocked a little earlier should discharge, without any obstacle, all the flood of the marshes and fields. So the joining of issue was made in the judgement of the royal Senate, and this removed all the force of the hidden dissension. Gemma notes that shortly before the Iconoclasm, which soon followed throughout the whole of Belgium, a terrible cloud was seen in the sky in July, and it hurled huge lightning bolts with hail, and with a flame-coloured hue, as if threatening the burning of the whole world, and then, somewhat lessened, it went away into the winds and rains. I also observe from the notes of an uncertain writer that a great storm of thunderbolts, together with the crashing of clouds, was heard at Leeuwarden, and that this disturbance of the sky was compared to the coming movements of the people.

units.la: Reperio in notis ejusdem Iodocij, famosos libellos odio Inquisitorum Leovardiæ tum sparsos, gratumq; eâ tempestate Brederodij nomen men publico præconio celebratum. Autores quoq; famosorum carminum de Sententiâ regij Senatus virgis cæsos, proscriptosque, immodesti laboris mercedem præter cruciatum saucij per flagra corporis, pœnam exilij accepisse. Idem Iodocius addit, crescente per exemplorum fæditatem populi audaciâ, Regem quoque ipsum diris opprobrijs impetitum, Margaretamque Gubernatricem, tum Præfectum Senatumque per Frisiam regium haud absimili criminatione, & acerbis dicteriis exceptum. Itaque exasperatis judicijs, animi concivium, quos miseratio atrocis spectaculi, aut propinquitas movebat, majoribus in regios odijs ferbuere, quibus fomentum Gabinius Selsma vir audacis ingenij, & juxta liberrimi oris, (apud quem Legati diverterant) novo commento subministrabat.
units.tr: I find in the notes of the same Jodocius that famous libels were then scattered at Leeuwarden out of hatred for the Inquisitors, and that Brederode's name was celebrated by public proclamation that season as a welcome one. The authors of the famous verses, by the sentence of the royal Council, were flogged and banished, and besides the torment of the lash on their bodies they received the penalty of exile as the wages of their immoderate labour. The same Jodocius adds that, as the people's boldness grew with the foulness of these examples, the King himself was assailed with dreadful reproaches, and Margaret the Regent, the Governor, and the royal Council throughout Friesland were met with a charge hardly different and with bitter gibes. So the judgments were exasperated, and the minds of fellow citizens, whom pity for the savage spectacle or kinship moved, boiled over with greater hatred against the royalists. Gabinius Selsma, a man of daring genius and of an equally free tongue, with whose household the envoys had lodged, supplied fuel for this with a new contrivance.

units.la: Is namq; clam per urbem cives convocare, deprædicare periculum, quod à Pontificijs immineret, qui infidis animis publicè familiares, intra se cædes, & excidium fœderati populi agitarent. Ideò scilicet in socios, ac concives statutum asperius, regiumque Senatum in corpora liberorum, ingenuorumq; civium sævijsse. Aggestas in supplicij loco tristes virgas, & avidum libertatis avitæ sanguinem manu carnificis expressum. Parari adhuc majora socordibus fœderatis. Commeare namque ad Arembergium internuncios, eosque noctu intromitti, insció inconsultoque cive, cujus interfit urbem in tuto esse, & non introire clam homines infesta aut saltem suspecta consilia perferentes. Quin demandandam potius civi urbis custodiam, ut per omnium curam, omnium quoque securitas habeatur. Hæc ab eodem Gabinio in Curiâ oppidanâ cum vehementiâ dicta. Quare Decreto Magistratus claves portarum civibus traditæ, Sagittariorumq; collegium agendis excubijs præfectum. Additi his diurni vigiles, quibus mandatum erat, ne militem intromitterent, quem ad firmandam majore præsidio regiam arcem, alijs è locis Arembergius evocaverat. Qui comperto regium militem portâ prohiberi (quam D. Iacobo sacram illorum temporum religio, Carolo v. Cæsare sub Maximiliano Burano Frisiæ Præfecto extruxerat) arce regiâ cum paucis stipatoribus descendit, Vibiumque Allartium primipilarem asperè adlocutus, iræ plenus in arcem se recepit. Addit Iodocius, Arembergium prehensâ viri barbâ comminatum extrema; Magistratus, quod Allartius obtendebat, imperium contemptim habuisse. Itaque Magistratus robur imperio daturus Kal. Sept. primipilares civicarum cohortium ad se vocavit, ac pro defensione urbis sacramentum accepit. Alij putant defendendis reformatis concionatoribus id factum, quos durante Inquisitorum & Gulielmi Lindani dominatu per Leovardiam urbem sacris domesticisq; ministerijs liberiores conscientias clàm delegisse jam diu Arembergius indignabatur. Itaq; illum nimia & imperiosa populi libertas, Magistratum importuna Arembergij consilia, & sinistræ machinationes urebant. His accedebat, quod Philippum Segoviæ è febre lecto affixum conventio Margaretæ, & fœderatæ Nobilitatis offendisse diceretur, Philippusq; displicitæ pactionis ægritudinem aulicâ simulatione, & fucatis in Principes blandicijs velaret. Quapropter Magistratus ne discordi cive aut multitudine quid tentaret, frequentissimo conventui in Curiâ habendo v111. Eid. Sept. dicm
units.tr: For he secretly summoned citizens throughout the city and proclaimed the danger that threatened from the Papists, who, though publicly familiar with the disloyal party, were plotting among themselves the slaughter and destruction of the confederated people. For this reason, they said, the Council had dealt more harshly with allies and fellow citizens, and the royal Senate had raged against the persons of free-born and native citizens: sad rods had been piled up in place of punishment, and the blood of their ancestral liberty, greedy for it, had been wrung out by the executioner's hand. Still greater things were being prepared against the careless confederates. Messengers were going back and forth to Arenberg, and were admitted at night without the knowledge or consent of the citizen whose concern it was that the city be safe, and men carrying hostile or at least suspicious plans were secretly let in. Rather, the guarding of the city should be entrusted to a citizen, so that by the care of all, the safety of all might also be secured. These things were said with vehemence by the same Gabinius in the town hall. Therefore, by decree of the Magistrates, the keys of the gates were handed over to the citizens, and the college of archers was put in charge of carrying out the watches. To these were added daily watchmen, who were ordered not to admit soldiers, whom Arenberg had summoned from other places to strengthen the royal citadel with a larger garrison. When Arenberg learned that the royal soldiers were being kept from the gate (which, in those times, the religion of the people had built for St James, under Charles V, while Maximilian Buren was governor of Friesland), he came down from the royal citadel with a few attendants, addressed Vibius Allartius, the centurion, harshly, and returned to the citadel full of anger. Iodocus adds that Arenberg, seizing the beard of a man, threatened him with the worst, and that the Magistrates had treated the authority of the Council with contempt, as Allartius alleged. Therefore, intending to give strength to the Magistrates' authority, on the first of September he summoned the centurions of the civic cohorts to himself and took an oath from them for the defence of the city. Others think this was done for the defence of the Reformed preachers, whom Arenberg had long resented, for during the domination of the Inquisitors and of William Lindanus, they had secretly chosen, through the city of Leeuwarden, to hold freer consciences in sacred and domestic ministries. So the excessive and imperious liberty of the people, the troublesome plans of the Magistrates, and Arenberg's sinister machinations were inflaming them. To this was added the report that the agreement of Margaret, and of the confederated nobility, had offended Philip, who was fixed to his sickbed at Segovia by fever, and that Philip concealed the sickness caused by his displeasure with the agreement under a courtly pretence and flattering endearments toward the princes. Therefore, so that the Magistrates might not attempt anything through a divided citizenry or the crowd, they appointed the most crowded assembly to be held in the town hall on the eighth day before the Ides of September, 1566, and ordered a sworn council to be convened, and the tribunes of the cohorts and the captains of the archers to attend the Senate.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. diem dixit, Conciliumq; juratum, ut & Tribunos cohortium, lxvi. ac sagittariorum Præfectos adesse in Senatu jussit. Ibi Tarquinius Vallesius Consulatum tum gerens, & qui in Senatu præsidebat, verba in hunc modum fecit:
units.tr: 1566. He appointed the day, and ordered the sworn council, along with the tribunes of the cohorts and the captains of the archers, to be present in the Senate. There Tarquinius Vallesius, who was then consul and presided in the Senate, spoke as follows:

units.la: COnvenimus in hunc locum P. C. ut de formandâ civitate nostrâ cogitaremus, prospiceremusque conscientijs, legibus, atque fortunis nostris, quas regij imperij importunus rigor, & soluti dominantium mores fermè oppressere. Ut ea singula restituamus parabili medicinâ, & non longâ curatione egemus. Ab animarum nostrarum curâ, tanquam praecipuo mortalium bono, ut incipiamus censeo, ac ut diu sacra nostra clàm & in secreto professi submoto potentium metu profiteamur publicè. Quapropter templa ab imaginum idolorumq; cultu repurganda, ut Deum ex præscripto nostrarum mentium, & divinæ legis cultui, locum habeamus superstitione vacuum, & nullâ sacerdotum illuvie deformem. Occasionem absentia Præfecti, qui in Trans-Isulaniam concessit, & noster zelus dabit. Neque enim grave nobis præsidium, quod portis nostris exclusimus, neque alieni à nobis, quos exploravimus, civium animi sunt. Paucis adversarijs nostræ vires aultæ meo consilio pares sunt, modò moræ rumpantur, & opportunitate commodi temporis utamur. Quamobrem censeo primâ nocte id faciendum, ac depurgandis fanis, ne quid promiscuus plebis turbevè furor peccet, sagittarios adhibendos. Opificum collegia, quæ templis dicavere auferant, cætera amoveantur pro arbitrio eorum, quibus negotium demandabitur. Hæc Vallesius:
units.tr: We have come together in this place, Fathers of the city, to consider how to shape our commonwealth, and to provide for our consciences, our laws and our fortunes, which the harsh rigour of royal rule and the lawless conduct of those in power have nearly crushed. To restore each of these we need a ready remedy and no long treatment. I propose that we begin with the care of our souls, as the chief good of mortals, and that we who have professed our sacred faith secretly and in hiding, now that the fear of the powerful is removed, profess it openly. Therefore the temples must be cleansed of the worship of images and idols, so that we may have a place for God, according to the rule of our minds and the worship of the divine law, free of superstition and not defiled by any filth of priests. The absence of the Governor, who has withdrawn into Trans-Isulania, and our zeal will give us the opportunity. For the garrison which we have shut out of our gates is no serious threat, and the minds of the citizens whom we have sounded are not alien to us. Our forces, with my plan, are equal to the few opponents we have, provided that delays are broken off and we make use of the opportunity of a convenient time. Therefore I propose that this be done on the first night, and that archers be employed to purge the shrines, so that the indiscriminate fury of the common people may not commit any offence or disorder. Let the guilds of craftsmen which have dedicated themselves to the temples remove them, and let the rest be removed at the discretion of those to whom the business is entrusted. So spoke Vallesius.

units.la: Mox decretum Senatus eâ de re perscriptum, Edictumque per præconem; Ne qui nocte proxumâ in publico præterquam Sagittarij, illivè essent, quibus potestatem prodeundi Senatus fecisset. Cæteri dubia civitate aut triste silentium, aut mæstam solitudinem, omnes varias rerum spes, atque eventus exercebant. Itaque Sagittarij mandato Senatus accepto, adultâ nocte in unum convenere, progressique in templa, præter Nyehovam, D. Vito & Catharinæ sacra, subversis aris omne Pontificijs ceremonijs ante subserviens, quod per omnem Belgicam jam ante factum erat, submoveri spectantium oculis fecere. Iodocius notarum autor, etsi affectibus indulgens, tradit omnem sacram supellectilem fædè confractam atque disjectam jacuisse, octenosque sagittariorum manipulos isti negotio destinatos mandatum Senatus perfecisse: Tum Edictum ab eodem Præcone pronuntiatum, quod turbandæ quieti nocturnæ aut vastandis ultra sacris vim omnem atqj; insolentiam vetabat. Hoc modo immutato civitatis statu postero die (qui v. Eid. Sept. fuit) exercitia reformatæ religionis cæpere, sacra facturis Antonio Nicolao & Martino Elio, quos magno numero ad fanum D. Vito sacrum, armati cives sequebantur. Tarquinius verò Vallesius, Consul, cum Henrico Albertio Senatorij ordinis viro stipati satellitio suorum, & insignia imperij præferentes, totum ordinem procedentium antecedebant, omneq; negotium, quod invidiâ non carebat, & simul securitatem docentium gravi autoritate tuebantur. Tum Res divina primum ab Antonio Hogebeintano nuper sacerdote, post à Martino presbytero Tjumano, facta. Scribit Iodocius eos depositò sacerdotali habitu ædem ingressos, mox pileis pallijsque concontedtos, in suggestum ascendisse, populumq; praesidio armorum subnixum, ab ore differentium, tanquam oraculi voce pependisse, Itaq; Senatus regius peractam concordibus animis rem divinam aegrè ferens, metuensque ne caeteri ad exemplum desciscerent, trium Ecclesiarum pastores Ivonem Joannis, Sixtum Abbaeum, & Douwonem, Oldehovios; Adrianum Vernerum, Nyehovium; & Douwonem Jouckenium, cum Petro Jacobaeo, Vicario ad Catharinae, in Regiam Curiam ad III. Eid. Septemb. evocavit. Ibi Carolus Nitzenius Praeses, in haec verba erupit:
units.tr: Soon afterwards a decree of the Senate was drawn up on this matter, and an edict was proclaimed by the herald: that no one should be in public during the coming night except the archers, or those to whom the Senate had given power to go out. The rest, with the city in doubt, were troubled by either a grim silence or a sad solitude, and all sorts of hopes and outcomes of events. So the archers, having received the Senate's order, gathered together late at night, went into the churches, and, except for the Nieuwe Kerk and the churches of St Vitus and St Catherine, overturned the altars and caused everything that served the Papist ceremonies, as had already been done throughout the Netherlands, to be removed from the sight of onlookers. Jodocius, the author of the notes, though he indulges his feelings, reports that all the sacred furniture lay shamefully broken and scattered, and that eight companies of archers appointed for this business carried out the Senate's order. Then an edict was announced by the same herald, forbidding every violent act that disturbed the night's quiet or wasted the sacred things beyond measure. With the state of the city changed in this way, on the following day, which was the fifth before the Ides of September, the exercises of the Reformed religion began, with Antonius Nicolaus and Martinus Elius about to perform the sacred rites, and armed citizens followed them in great numbers to the church of St Vitus. Tarquinius Vallesius, the consul, with Henricus Albertius, a man of the senatorial order, attended by a bodyguard of his own men and carrying the insignia of office, went before the whole procession, and guarded the whole undertaking, which was not free from odium, and at the same time protected the safety of the teachers with his grave authority. Then the divine service was first performed by Antonius Hogebeintanus, lately a priest, and afterwards by Martinus Tjumanus, an elder. Jodocius writes that they, having laid aside priestly dress, entered the church, and soon, with caps and cloaks taken off, mounted the platform, and that the people, supported by the protection of arms, hung upon the speakers' words as upon the voice of an oracle. Therefore the royal Council, distressed that the divine service had been completed with one accord, and fearing that the others would follow the example, summoned the ministers of three churches, Ivo Joannis, Sixtus Abbaeus and Douwo Oldehovius; Adrianus Verner, Nieuwe Kerk; and Douwo Jouckenius, together with Petrus Jacobaeus, vicar at St Catherine's, to the royal court on the third day before the Ides of September. There Carolus Nitzenius, the president, burst out in these words:

units.la: Etsi de integritate vestrâ non dubitemus, quin de Romanâ Ecclesiâ Catholicâ optimè sentiatis, tamen quia pericula nos urgent, voluimus, ut testimonium vestrae fidei nostro in Senatu diceretis. Idcirco per salutem animarum vestrarum, per conscientias vestras, & jusjurandum quod Philippo Regi praestitistis, vobis deferimus, ut id nobis audientibus dicatis, adprobetisve religionem Romanam Catholicam, aut significetis eam animis mentibusque vestris adversari. Nolumus equidem ut vera rerum judicia falsis involvantur, ac vos videamini simulatam pietatem metu periculi, & pro conditione temporum professi.
units.tr: Although we do not doubt your integrity, and that you think well of the Roman Catholic Church, nevertheless, because dangers press upon us, we wish you to bear witness to your faith in our Senate. Therefore, by the salvation of your souls, by your consciences, and by the oath you swore to King Philip, we charge you to say in our hearing and to declare whether you approve the Roman Catholic religion or signify that it is opposed to your minds and hearts. Indeed we do not wish true judgments of things to be wrapped up in false ones, nor that you should seem to profess a feigned piety out of fear of danger and according to the conditions of the times.

units.la: Refert Iodocius, Sixtum Abbaeum Oldehovium, omnium nomine, Senatui regio respondisse, eundemque adprobatâ in Senatu Romanâ religione postridie inversâ mente reformatae apertam confessionem fecisse. Quamobrem Senatus Regius ijs mandavit, ut, non obstante locorum sacrorum vastitate, ac turbatissimi temporis injuriâ, officia, atque conciones continuarent; subnixiq; conscientijs in arduâ, ac concreditâ sibi presbyterij vocatione persisterent. Edictum quoq; VIII. Kal. Sept. Bruxellis à Margaretâ Gubernatrice in templorum, sacrorumque violatores perscriptum, publicari ocyus Leovardiae & per omnem Frisiam jussit, suumq; graviore sub poena prid. Kal. Sept. factum addi, vulgarique fecit. Ijs cautum erat: Ne quis templa, sacravè loca, rituales libros, aras, imagines, statuasvè confringeret, auferretvè, sub poenâ suspendij, & bonorum confiscationis. Sanxit quoq; ut in talium reos, velut sacrilegos, Dei hominumque hostes & contemptores, jus necis cuivis esset, impunitate non tantum caedis, sed & mercede promissa. Magistratus quoque oppidorum conniventes, &, quo minus istiusmodi puniantur, praepedientes, pro fautoribus talium habendos edixit, ac ut Oppida, Universitatesq; per Magistratus populivè delictum omni jure, ac immunitate excsiderent. Famosi quoque carminis crimen, modo in Religionem, Pacem publicam, Regem, Gubernatricem, Rectoresve Provinciarum commissum esset, eâdem laqueï poenâ corrigi jusit, eandemque Flevum inter Amasumque copias conscribentibus, autorantibusvè denuntiavit.
units.tr: Jodocius reports that Sixtus Abbaeus Oldehovius, on behalf of all, answered the royal Council, and that the same man, having approved the Roman religion in the Senate, the next day with a changed mind made an open confession of the Reformed faith. Therefore the royal Council ordered them that, despite the devastation of the holy places and the injury of a most troubled time, they should continue their duties and sermons, and, supported by their consciences, persist in the difficult calling of the eldership entrusted to them. Margaret the Regent also ordered an edict, drawn up at Brussels on the eighth day before the Kalends of September against violators of churches and sacred things, to be published at once at Leeuwarden and throughout Friesland, and had it added under heavier penalty what had been done the day before the Kalends of September, and made it public. By this it was provided that no one should break, carry off or deface churches, sacred places, ritual books, altars, images or statues, under penalty of hanging and confiscation of goods. It also decreed that against the guilty of such acts, as sacrilegious persons, enemies and despisers of God and men, the right of killing should belong to anyone, with impunity not only for the slaughter but also with a promised reward. It further declared that the magistrates of towns who connived at these things, or hindered their punishment, should be held as supporters of such men, and that towns and corporations should lose all right and immunity on account of an offence by the magistrates or the people. She also ordered that the crime of a libellous verse, if it were committed against religion, public peace, the King, the Regent or the governors of the provinces, should be punished with the same penalty of the noose, and announced this to those enrolling troops at Vlieland between Amsum and the others, and to those who gave the orders.

units.la: Mox Arembergius xvi. Kal. Octob. quatuor civitatis Consules ad se vocavit: missionemq; quanto ocyus reformatae religionis ministris postulavit. Templis quoq; fanisq; veterem ornatum reddi petijt, omnemq; deformatae civitatis statum mutari antiquo jusit. Ad quae Consules.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Aremberg, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, summoned the four consuls of the city to his presence and demanded that the ministers of the reformed religion be dismissed as quickly as possible. He also asked that the churches and shrines be restored to their former ornament, and ordered that the whole deformed state of the city be changed back to its old condition. To this the consuls replied.

units.la: Convocavimus, Scabinos, concilium juratum, cohortium Praefectos & vexilliferos, praeterea manipulares sagittariorum, & honestissimorum civium primos, ut postulatis tuis, Praefecte, responderemus. Quo tempore decretum est
units.tr: We have convened the aldermen, the sworn council, the prefects of the cohorts and the standard-bearers, as well as the file-leaders of the archers and the foremost of the most honourable citizens, so that we might answer your demands, Prefect. At this meeting it was decided

units.la: (quod ante triduum te præsente professi sumus) reformatos pastores dimitti non posse, neq; ornamenta templis restitui, cæterum volumus ut in præsenti statu civitas permaneat, dum aliter à rege, aut Ordinibus generalibus totius Belgicæ statutum sit. Nihilominus, fidem Regi datam servabimus, petimusq; ut odio, aut gratiâ sepositis, regi omnia transcribas prout actasunt. Itaque pastores reformatos admisimus, ornamenta templorum amovimus, averruncandis majoribus malis, & ne in publicam seditionem iste civitatis motus erumperet. Quamobrem petimus, ne sinistre hoc interpretari velis, omnemq; rerum gestarum seriem bonâ apud regem aut Gubernatricem fide exponere. Quam eum in acta redigi petieris, ut Rex, aut Gubernatrix de toto negotio cognoscat, ita censuimus mittendos ad te ex primariâ nobilitate, qui conventionem honestam offerant, ut utriusque religionis exercitia in fanis, templisq; indulgeas. Nos, si id permittas, cives nostros inducemus, ut sacramentum regi dictum renovent, & ut regiæ arci, tuæ personæ, & Senatui regio securitas sit. Hoc saltem præcaveri volumus, ne præsidium arcis novo externoq; milite adaugeas, cum nostrorum civium fide tutus esse queas. Et quoniam mandatum Regis desiderari obtendis, neq; conventionem institui super his rebus posse, ita actis comprehensa tibi tradimus, ne istorum, quæ evenere, memoriam prægraves. Neq; enim religiosorum tuorum exercitia turbavimus, cæterum hoc egimus cavimusq;, ut tutè Pontificiorum sacra fierent. Quæ si ipsi continuare volent, per nos licebit, obeant.
units.tr: (as we declared in your presence three days ago) that the reformed ministers cannot be dismissed, nor can the ornaments be restored to the churches. Rather, we wish the city to remain in its present state until the King or the General Estates of all Belgium decide otherwise. Nevertheless, we will keep the faith given to the King, and we ask you, setting aside hatred and favour, to report everything to the King just as it has been done. Therefore we have admitted the reformed ministers and removed the church ornaments, in order to avert greater evils and to prevent this disturbance in the city from breaking out into public sedition. Wherefore we ask that you not wish to interpret this unfavourably, and that you set out the whole course of events before the King or the Governess in good faith. When you have asked that it be recorded in the acts, so that the King or the Governess may learn the whole affair, we have resolved to send to you men from the leading nobility, who will offer an honourable agreement, that you may grant the exercise of both religions in the shrines and churches. If you permit this, we will bring our citizens to renew the oath sworn to the King, so that there may be security for the royal citadel, for your person and for the royal Senate. This above all we wish to be guarded against: that you should strengthen the garrison of the citadel with new and foreign soldiers, since you can be safe with the loyalty of our citizens. And since you object that the King's mandate is lacking and that no agreement can be made on these matters, we hand over to you what is contained in the acts, so that you do not burden your memory with what has happened. For we have not disturbed the exercises of your religious people; rather we have arranged and ensured that the Papist rites may be carried on safely. If they themselves wish to continue these, let them do so through us.

units.la: Deïn Deputati quoq; Ordinum Arembergio libbellum hunc obtulere.
units.tr: Then the deputies of the Estates also presented this little book to Aremberg.

units.la: NOn hanc tantum per civitatem, Præfecte, sed populum per reliquas oppida agrosq; conturbatum vides. Omnia quoq; angore, metu atq; tumultu agitari, non aliâ ex causâ, quam quod militem conscribas, arcemq; regiam majore præsidio obfirmes. Et quamvis propter merita tua, etiam ab illis annis, quibus Frisiam cum laude rexisti, sinistræ suspiciones de te concipi non possint; & quidem eo magis, quod neq; mandatum à rege Philippo autorandi armatos, coram Valerio Cammingha, & Ruardo Roorda, pridem sis professus, tamen sedari efferatæ plebis mentes nequeunt, & fiduciam reconcipere, quam minuerunt. Nam unam cohortem & quidem in corporis tui arcisq; custodiam tibi non invident, modo fidem securitati nostræ des, bonaq; ac corpora nostra à vi & incursu militum tuta fore. Cuius animi fisis, Præfecte, colluviem otiosorum per agros ac cænobia se spargentem, ad disciplinam revoca, & exonera sacra profanaque loca isto metu, qui infidus ut plurimum, concordiæ pacisq; custos est. Quod si feceris, Præfecte, perseverabimus in fide regi datâ, pacem pro bello habituri. Hæc ab Isbrando Herderviceno, Præsule Lidlumano; Sceltone Liauckama, Petro Cammingha, Amelandiæ Domino; Gemma Burmania, Iulio Dekama, Sixto & Siricio Donia, Epone Douma, Sceltone Tiaerda, Serapio Galama, Hartmanno Galama, Edone Heringha, Wilcone Holdingha, Erasmo Douma, Sibæo Sceltema, Gabinio Sceltama, Vigero Sitsma, Alepho Aggema, Ottone Herama, Hesselo Oosthemio, signata.
units.tr: You see, Prefect, that not only this city but the people throughout the remaining towns and countryside are thrown into confusion. Everything is also stirred up with anxiety, fear and tumult, for no other reason than that you are raising soldiers and fortifying the royal citadel with a larger garrison. And although, on account of your merits, even from those years when you ruled Friesland with distinction, no sinister suspicions can be entertained about you, and all the more so because you once declared before Valerius Cammingha and Ruard Roorda that you had no mandate from King Philip to arm men, nevertheless the minds of the enraged common people cannot be calmed, and they cannot recover the trust which has been diminished. For they do not begrudge you a single cohort, indeed for the guarding of your own person and the citadel, provided you give assurance for our safety, and that our goods and bodies will be secure from the violence and attacks of soldiers. Prefect, with this disposition of mind, call back to discipline the rabble of idlers scattered through the fields and monasteries, and free the sacred and profane places from that fear which, being for the most part faithless, is the guardian of discord rather than of concord and peace. If you do this, Prefect, we will persevere in the faith given to the King, regarding peace as a substitute for war. These things were signed by Isbrand Herderviceno, Provost of Lidlum; Sceltone Liauckama, Peter Cammingha, Lord of Ameland; Gemma Burmania, Julius Dekama, Sixtus and Siricius Donia, Epo Douma, Sceltone Tiaerda, Serapio Galama, Hartmann Galama, Edo Heringha, Wilco Holdingha, Erasmus Douma, Sibo Sceltema, Gabinius Sceltama, Vigerus Sitsma, Alepho Aggema, Otto Herama, Hessel Oosthemius.

units.la: Post Kalend. Octobrib. alio Edicto Senatus cavit: Ne per presbyteros, Pastores, vicarios cæterosve beneficiarios, in Religione quid novaretur, cæterum res divina, more prisco, sub pænâ amissionis beneficij, exerceretur. Sed novæ Veritatis desiderio incalescens ministrorum zelus, alia meditabatur. Itaque factum est, ut finità Anthonij concione (solis Ivone & Douwone Oldehovio exceptis) caeteri priore habitu excusso, reformatis se sociarent, spretisque temporum periculis secreta animorum profiterentur. Tum Sixtus Abbaeus vir magnae facundiae pro concione verba fecit, praemissaque Fidei confessione multa de institutis, erroribusque Pontificum, ac regno Antichristi disseruit. Quare gratulari non parum sibi ac symmistis suis quod à tanta saeculorum caligine sacrario veritatis recepti ad veros divini numinis cultus redijssent. Petere se D. O. M. misereatur caecitatis tam diuturnae (cuius omnes singulosq; certo conscientiae testimonio puderet) ac firmandis in fide mentibus Spiritum det sanctioris sapientiae autorem. Tum cessantibus edicto Magistratus Pontificiorum exercitijs, templa reformatae Religioni assignata.
units.tr: After the Kalends of October the Senate issued another edict, providing that nothing be changed in religion by the elders, ministers, vicars or other beneficed men, but that divine service be conducted in the ancient manner, under penalty of loss of benefice. But the zeal of the ministers, inflamed by desire for the new truth, was devising other things. So it came about that, when Anthony's sermon had ended (only Ivo and Douwo Oldehovius excepted), the rest cast off their former habit, joined themselves to the reformed, and, despising the dangers of the times, openly professed what they had kept secret in their minds. Then Sixtus Abbaeus, a man of great eloquence, spoke in place of a sermon, and after a preliminary confession of faith he discoursed at length on the institutions and errors of the Pontiffs and on the kingdom of Antichrist. He therefore congratulated himself and his fellow ministers no little that, having been received from such great darkness of the ages into the sanctuary of truth, they had returned to the true worship of the divine majesty. He prayed that the Lord, the Best and Greatest, would have mercy on such long-lasting blindness (of which everyone, each one of them, ought to be ashamed by the sure testimony of conscience), and that he would give the Spirit, the author of holier wisdom, to strengthen minds in the faith. Then, the Papist services having been suspended by the magistrates' edict, the churches were assigned to the reformed religion.

units.la: Igitur velut fatis concordiam pacemq; publicam revellentibus, & religionis dissensione simul cum metu regio aucta, Ordinum Deputati conventum Praesulum, Nobilitatis, & agrariorum indixere, omnesque citati, quasi de re ponderosa consultaturi ad diem xiv. Kal. Decembrium adesse Leovardiae jussi. Ex Ooftergois, Petrus Trajectensis; Mosanus, Abbas Fosuerdicus; Gerardus Dotichemus, Praesul Gerricomius; Petrus Camminga, Amelandiae Dominus; Suffridus Heemstra, Epo Douma, Gemma Burmania, Tetardus Holdingha, Ritsco Eysingha, Hector Abingha, Sixtus Emingha, Bennertus Hillingha, Ritsco Dyxtra: Ex Westergois, Isbrandus Hardervicenus, Praesul Lidlumanus; Henricus Steenvicensis, Abbas Floridi-Campi; Hector Hemmema, Edzardus Grouftins, Iarichius Botnia, Oldermannus Franequerensium; Scelto Liauckama, Dominicus Hottingha, Oldermannus Bolsuerdiensium; Hero Ockingha, Sixtus Donia, Serapius Galama, Vibius, pastor Cubardius; Godicalcus Hiddema, Renicus Gerlacius; Ex Sylvestribus, Ioannes Harmannus, Prior Hafcheranus, Auco, pastor Sindelius; Douvo Douma, Iulius Dekama, Foppo Douma, Meinius Lyclesius, juris Licentiatus, Iouco Oenius, Edo Auconius, Florentius Abbema, Poppo Pierius, Andreas Mirica, Medicus; Quo die, cum Deputatis congregati Ordines de negotio religionis deliberavere, non sine animorum perturbatione, quod Margareta Gubernatrix litteras comminationis & acerbitatis plenas ad Arembergium, Arembergius ad Senatum regium misisse, nec inveris rumoribus, diceretur. Unde Delegati Ordinum, mox in Curiam citati, praelectaq; Gubernatricis litterae, quibus Magareta jubebat; Nihil in religione, sacrisque ritibus mutari Regem velle, neque dandum esse tempus postulatis foederatorum Nobilium, cavendumque imprimis Senatui, ut omne Foedus, omnem societatem, omnes conventus disturbet. Haec Leovard. xiv. Kal. Dec. acta.
units.tr: Thus, as if the fates were tearing up concord and public peace, and dissension in religion grew together with royal fear, the deputies of the Estates called a meeting of the prelates, the nobility and the landowners. All were summoned, as if to deliberate on a weighty matter, and were ordered to be present at Leeuwarden on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December. From Oostergo: Peter of Utrecht; Mosanus, Abbot of Vosswerd; Gerard Dotichemus, Provost of Gerkesklooster; Peter Cammingha, Lord of Ameland; Suffridus Heemstra, Epo Douma, Gemma Burmania, Tetardus Holdingha, Ritsco Eysingha, Hector Abingha, Sixtus Emingha, Bennert Hillingha, Ritsco Dyxtra. From Westergo: Isbrand Herderviceno, Provost of Lidlum; Henry Steenvicensis, Abbot of Florikamp; Hector Hemmema, Edzard Grouftins, Jarichius Botnia, Oldermann of the Franekers; Scelto Liauckama, Dominicus Hottingha, Oldermann of the Bolswarders; Hero Ockingha, Sixtus Donia, Serapius Galama, Vibius, pastor Cubardius; Godocalcus Hiddema, Renicus Gerlacius. From the Sylvestres: John Harmannus, Prior of Hasselt; Auco, pastor Sindelius; Douvo Douma, Julius Dekama, Foppo Douma, Meinius Lyclesius, Licentiate in law, Jouco Oenius, Edo Auconius, Florentius Abbema, Poppo Pierius, Andreas Mirica, physician. On that day, when the Estates met with the deputies and deliberated on the matter of religion, there was no little disturbance of minds, because it was said that Margaret the Governess had sent letters full of threats and bitterness to Aremberg, and Aremberg to the royal Senate, and these reports were not unfounded. Whereupon the delegates of the Estates, soon summoned into the court, had the Governess's letter read aloud, in which Margaret ordered: that the King wishes nothing to be changed in religion or in sacred rites, that no time should be given to the demands of the confederated nobles, and above all that the Senate must take care to break up every league, every association and every assembly. These things were done at Leeuwarden on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December.

units.la: Itaq; magna in conventu Ordinum consternatio orta, qui ut instantibus malis mederentur, Delegati ad Arembergium, & simul Margaretam Gubernatricem, Doco Martna, Barthius Idzaerda, Dominicus Hottingha, Oldermannus Bolsuerdiensium; qui dilationem publicando Philippi Edicto postularent, ac ut Praefectus Arembergius apud Gubernatricem, Gubernatrix apud Regem pro Frisiis, datis fiduciarijs legatorum litteris intercederet. Hoc etiam additum, ut, dum rex decretum religionis cum Ordinibus Belgicae fecisset, toti Belgicae populo, & eius supplicationibus Legati se afformarent, & ut remedia minuendis Philippi exacerbationibus, & restituendae per provincias paci quaererentur. Caeterum an institutae legationi eventus responderit, non reperio, hoc saltem constat, Philippi animum ex se immanem mitiora decreta tum respuisse, anniq; sequentis discordias majoribus odijs repetitas.
units.tr: Thus great consternation arose in the assembly of the Estates, and in order to remedy the impending evils they sent delegates to Aremberg and at the same time to Margaret the Governess: Doco Martna, Barthius Idzaerda, Dominicus Hottingha, Oldermann of the Bolsward men. They were to request a postponement by publishing Philip's edict, and that Prefect Aremberg should intercede with the Governess, and the Governess with the King, on behalf of the Frisians, the envoys' letters being given as sureties. It was also added that, while the King made a decree on religion with the Estates of Belgium, the envoys should present themselves to the whole people of Belgium and to its supplications, and that remedies be sought for lessening Philip's exasperations and for restoring peace throughout the provinces. However, whether the outcome answered to the mission undertaken, I do not find. This at least is certain: Philip, of his own savage nature, then rejected milder decrees, and in the following year the discords were renewed with greater hatreds.

units.la: Quas populares turbas & mutationem rerum aegre ferens Arembergius, qui in Transisulaniam profectus erat, iv. Eid. Decemb. litteras ad Magistratum dedit, quibus fidem faciebat; Non placere sibi istam actionem, quin monere Magistratum, ut habita quietis publicae cura, modum ponat fervidis studijs, sinatq; religionem Romanam restitui tot saeculis usurpatam. Se propediem adfore, conciliandis divulsis mentibus, daturumque operam ut sopiatur auferaturque omne civilis discordiae fomentum. Reperio in notis Iodoci, litteras Arembergij non multum ponderis habuisse, Magistratumq; oppidanum prioris constantiae documentum tam diu dedisse, donec Phillippi regis asperius Edictum postrid. in secreto Senatus recitaretur. Itaque tum, ne adspernari Philippi Imperium, & excusisse legitimum obsequium per desideria novae pietatis foederisque videretur, Proprid. Eid. Decemb. collegium Sagittariorum in templum D. Viti convocavit, communicatoq; edicto (quod, restitui Romanam religionem, & autoritatem Praefecti volebat) super eo publicando longum consultavit. Erant namque in collegio sagittariorum, qui procacibus, servilibusque studijs Philippum sectabantur, sacrisque ac ceremonijs Pontificijs impensius dediti, gloria etiam faedissimae servitutis se placarent. Qui propterea, ne pro supprimendo Philippi Edicto stetisse viderentur, dubijsque temporibus suffragiorum libertate in discrimen venirent, fano D. Viti excessere, relicta multorum civium multitudine, quam Dionysius Wingia, qui Magistratui a secretis erat, in hunc modum allocutus fertur:
units.tr: Aremberg, who was grieved by these popular disturbances and this upheaval, and who had set out for Transisulania, on the fourth day before the Ides of December sent a letter to the Magistrate, by which he assured them that this action did not please him, and warned the Magistrate that, having regard for public peace, it should set a limit to its fervent zeal and allow the Roman religion, used for so many centuries, to be restored. He would shortly be present to reconcile the divided minds, and he would take care that every fuel of civil discord be put out and removed. I find in the notes of Jodocus that Aremberg's letters carried little weight, and that the town magistracy gave proof of its earlier constancy for as long as it could, until Philip's harsher edict was read in a private session of the Senate on the following day. Then, so as not to seem to spurn Philip's rule and to have thrown off lawful obedience through desires for a new piety and a new league, on the day before the Ides of December the magistrates summoned the company of archers into the church of St Vitus. After the edict (which demanded the restoration of the Roman religion and the authority of the Prefect) had been communicated to them, they deliberated at length on publishing it. For there were in the company of archers some who followed Philip with shameless and servile zeal, more devoted to Papist rites and ceremonies, and who sought to win favour through the glory of the most shameful slavery. These men, so as not to seem to have stood for suppressing Philip's edict, and so as not to be put in peril of their freedom of voting in such dangerous times, left the church of St Vitus, leaving behind a great multitude of citizens. To them Dionysius Wingia, who was secretary to the Magistrate, is reported to have spoken in this way:

units.la: Quod verba apud vos faciam, Concives, non de nihilo est, posteaquam in magnum discrimen Philippi regis exacerbatio, & nostra innocentia nos perduxit. Qui ut vivere optaveramus more felicium majorum, quibus omnia secura, inturbataque etiam Carolo Caesare fuere, ita nos nepotes fortunatorum patrum Philippi filij asperitas exercet. Cuius etiam imperium ut omni lege ac exceptione careret, & ut minimum haberemus, quod intactum servitute esset, conscientias quoque nostras paucorum hominum inspectionibus subjicere conatus est. Vidimus quippe jam diu oberrantem Gulielmum Lindanum Inquisitorem, hominem peregrinum, & praeferocem, istiusmodi imperia exercentem, quae pati fortium, & liberorum hominum non est. Quorum majores ut Normannicam servitutem, ac Hollandicam dominationem excussere, ita nos soli degeneres huc usque, ignobiles animos inhonestaq; pectora novis istis vilissimisq; censoribus mancipavimus. Reliqui vero vicini, sociisq; nostri, ne ista turpia, & horrenda paterentur, in foedus coivere, gnari concordia res parvas crescere, discordia dilabi & concidere. Atqui ipsius foederis copiam miseratione sociorum accepimus; ut sepulta virtus nostra se erigeret, ac nos semel memores patriae vacillantis, omnemque ignaviam, metumque generosis annianimis excuteremus. Ratum quoque idipsum fœdus fecimus, quantum in no-bis fuit, & æquissimam censuimus supplicationem, quam Henricus Bredero-dius Margaretæ Gubernatrici obtulerat. Eâ opinione submixi populum in justos cætus convocavimus, & ne superstitionum servi essemus, templa à sordibus depurgavimus, stabilïmusq; religionem nostris congruam. Vt paucis dicam, Libertatem nobis, aut saltem imaginem, eius paravimus, istorum hominum machinationibus adversam, qui in ultimam servitutem protrusos nos vellent. Inde Arembergij minates litteras, & hesterno die Philippi Edictum accepimus, jussisque sumus ea dimittere, quæ magno constiterunt. Redonare hostibus inimicisque nostris templa, Curias, Collegia, Magistratus, dignitates, & opes, & brevi omnia ista, quæ justis titulis possidemus, nobis econtra reservare contemptum, infamiam, egestatem, exilium, mortem, & hac ipsâ peiorem æternam servitutem. Id namque necessario eventurum est, si Edictum hoc publicemus, quod ego, salvis circumstantis coronæ judiciis, supprimendum censeo. Quin suadeo potius, Concives, ut memores fœderis, & sanctissimi nexus, quo nos invicem obligavimus, perseveremus in propositio, parati res nostras atque sanguinem consecrare Libertati, quam recidere in sortem fortibus egregijsque viris non tolerandam.
units.tr: Fellow citizens, I speak to you now because King Philip's anger and our own innocence have brought us into great danger. As our forefathers, the fortunate ones, wished to live, when everything was secure and untroubled even under Charles Caesar, so now we, the grandchildren of fortunate fathers, are harassed by the harshness of Philip, the son. He has tried, moreover, to make his rule free of all law and restraint, and to leave us not even the smallest thing untouched by slavery; he has tried to subject our consciences to the scrutiny of a few men. For we have long seen Willem Lindanus the Inquisitor wandering among us, a foreigner and very arrogant, exercising a rule such as brave and free men cannot endure. Our ancestors threw off the Norman servitude and the Hollandic domination, but we alone, degenerate until now, have handed over our ignoble spirits and dishonourable hearts to these new and most worthless censors. The rest of our neighbours and allies, however, so that they would not suffer these shameful and dreadful things, have bound themselves in a league, knowing that small things grow by harmony and fall apart and collapse by discord. And indeed, through the kindness of our allies we have received the opportunity of that league, so that our buried courage might rise up and we, mindful at last of our wavering country, might shake off all cowardice and fear with noble spirits. We have also ratified that same league as far as lay in us, and we have judged just the petition which Henry Brederode offered to Margaret the Governor. Encouraged by that opinion, we have summoned the people to lawful assemblies, and so that we might not be slaves to superstitions, we have cleansed the churches of their filth and established a religion suited to ourselves. To put it briefly, we have won for ourselves liberty, or at least its image, opposed to the schemes of those men who wished to thrust us into utter servitude. Then we received the threatening letters of Aerschot and, yesterday, Philip's edict, and we have been ordered to give up what has cost us so dearly: to restore to our enemies the churches, courts, colleges, magistracies, dignities and wealth, and soon all those things which we hold by just title; and in return to reserve for ourselves contempt, infamy, poverty, exile, death, and eternal servitude worse than death itself. For this will certainly happen if we publish this edict, which I, saving the judgement of the assembled council, think must be suppressed.
