Indeed, I rather urge you, fellow citizens, to remain mindful of the league and of the most sacred bond by which we have bound ourselves to one another, and to persevere in our purpose, ready to consecrate our property and our blood to liberty, rather than fall back into a lot which brave and excellent men cannot tolerate.

units.la: Tum cricumstantes dexteras erexere, perorantiq; Dyonisio pronis vultibus assensum est. Cæteri qui cætui se subtraxerant, postridie eodem in loco se sistere jussi, multâ, nisi præsto essent, Carolini aurei indictâ. Ibi perrogatis populi suffragijs iterum de supprimendo Edicto decretum factum, proficiente nequicquam illorum secessione, qui isti rei vehementibus studijs adversabantur. Itaque Hector Æbinga vir nobilis, & ab illo decreto alienior, etsi in ordinem sagittariorum cooptatus, Hallemum se conferre jussus est, ac curare amplissimas possessiones, quas illo in districtu plurimas hæreditario jure tenebat. Non egere quippe libertatem populi istiusmodi defensoribus dicebant, quibus periculum creare crudis illis civilium furorum temporibus, immodestæ locutionis præceps temeritas posset. Tum xvii. Kal. Ian. magnum illud Dominicæ cœnæ mysterium Leovardiæ administratum est, accipiente illud è primis Tarquinio Vallesio Consule. Cæteris longo ordine accedentibus, ut magnum Ecclesia incrementum senserat, eadem communio facta. Nec multum post quatuor Curijs populi, etsi seorsim, convocatis (quas Hoecani, Kempemani, Mennemij & Oldehovij constituebant) Magistratus creandis tribunis cohortium sededit, ne illâ teneritudine ac infantiâ libertatis publica quies occultis machinationibus obturbaretur. Urgebat namq; Magistratus, ut Sagittarij, penes quos jus eligendorum Tribunorum erat, ijsdem Tribunis potestatem facerent cum Senatu urbis agendi, consulendi, statuendique quod è re civitatis esset, tabulæque mandatorum, & procurationes Tribunorum ad arbitrium Senatus formarentur. Sed divisâ urbe, & sagittariorum collegio in diversa scisso, paucorum contumacia Senatus consilijs obstitit. Hoc quippe cavebant Sagittarij partis adversæ, ne quid juramento Philippo regi præstito decederet, omneque civitatis commodum, & actiones Senatus, cum sacramento populi, & Philippi imperio convenirent. Ita Paulus Breckerus rus, Henricus Tarquinius, Bernardus Sirxma, Thecdorus Haringius, & Nicolaus Stasius intercessere. Alij immodestius pro affectuum lubidine agebant. Neque enim deerant, qui scriptis clam protestationibus libellisque criminationum (conciliandæ apud Arembergium ac Margaretam Gubernatricem gratiæ) populum divellerent, publicèq; confidentes & turbulenti, violatam à fœderatis jurif-jurandi religionem clamitarent. Sibi quippe Philippo Caroli Cæsaris filio & hæredi Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. L. & post Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LV. Regi Principique præstitum jurif-jurandum, integrum, intemeratumque fuisse, neque miscuisse se turbulentis eorum consilijs, quorum manus intactæ sacrilegijs non essent. Quæ res cum seditionibus datura causam videretur, Magistratus Henricum Tarquinium, tanquam incentorem turbarum in custodiam dari jussit, quo cæteros ab effræni licentiâ commodius deterreret. Reperio Antonium Iodocium notarum autorem, Consuli Allæo Teresio de sistendo cavisse, Magistratumque, ne quid in innoxios statuisse videretur, acta protestantium Pontificiorum in populum vulgasse. Paulum quoque Breckerum hominum peregrinum, & quod in matrimonio nobilem fœminam teneret, ad dignitatem Præturæ evectum, à Suffrido Bejemo viro nobili in regio Senatu frustra accusatum, materiem suæ defensioni à vehementibus in Philippum, & Romanam religionem studijs mutuasse. Ita sursum deorsum magnâ dissensione animorum res Leovardiensium volutabantur, donec Arembergius è Transisulaniâ redux (in quam sedandis motibus cum quatuor Germanorum peditum cohortibus, & aliâ Equitum levis armaturæ profectus erat) suo in Bergumanos adventu, Pontificiorum animos, & juxta fortunam erigeret. Qui vocatis ad se confestim militarium copiarum tribunis, Iacobo Husingio, Quirino Laccelo Burano, Ernesto Mulartio, Foxio Hasseltano, & Ioanne Splinterio, parari ultionem nuperis seditionibus non obscuris indicijs innuebat. Cui, etsi salubrius remedium ordinare Margareta, adjuta Belgici regijq; Status concilio, potuisset, sopiendis coercendisq; turbis validum, ita econtra muliebri temeritate, aut magnitudine periculi perculsa litteras in Hispaniam ad Philippum dedit, quibus civilium motuum seriem exponebat. Vastata templa, innovatos divini numinis cultus, oppressam autoritatem regnantium, & quidem de eorum consilio, quos olim Carolus Cæsar, aut Philippus filius sui imperij exordio, dignitate Equestri, Aureiq; Velleris insignibus ex instituto Burgundicæ domus donaverat. Rogare itaq; Philippum, ut rerum per Provincias suas nutantium misertus, ex Hispaniâ in Belgicam properet, mobilem facile populum suâ majestate ac præsentiâ compressurus. Quod Margaretæ consilium expendens secum Philippus, convocatis regni proceribus, de componendis Belgicæ turbis consultavit. Erant, qui popularem illum morbum, (quem ex immodestâ potentum dominatione ortum non ignorabant) lenioribus medicamentis curandum censerent, persanandisque tumoribus optumum semper remedium Quietem fuisse. Parum gloriæ ex civili bello sperandum, multum periculi. Hostem autem, si bellum rex velit, non longè quærendum importunis adhuc Othomannorum furoribus & Africæ orâ nuperis etiamnum bellis, & insidijs dijs Maurorum infidâ. Belgas enim peculiari Principum reverentiâ, velut religione quadam numinis, ad obsequia redituros, si recludi clementiæ secretum spectent, & regiæ iræ impetum lenitate fractum. Alij verò bellum & arma suadebant, respuentibusque velut medicinam malis, ferro atque cauterio utendum. Animum quippe Belgici belli Philippo, jam dudum, nunquam causam fuisse, quam nova populi fœdera, & defectiones, turbæ nunc & sacrilegia suppeditarent. Auferendam itaque libertatem, omnis licentiæ fomitem & Remp. regno per bellum mutandam, quod solo etiam sici nervo trahi queat. Ita decretum de inferendo Belgicæ bello Madriti in Hispaniâ perscriptum, autore præcipuo Antonio Perennotto Episcopo nuper Atrebatense ac Cardinale Granvellano, quem ut Belgicæ libertati gravem, querimoniis Principum Aurei Velleris inductus, Philippus in Burgundiam post Hispaniam sevocaverat. Ipse verò Philippus curam administrationemque gerendi belli in se recepit, ordinatâque per Sábaudos, Burgundos, & Lotharingiam profectione litteras in Frisiam præmisit, quibus ut sui adventus, (quod postremo Gandavensi conventu Ordinibus Provinciarum promiserat) certiores Frisios faciebat, ita ad pacis concordiæq; studia illius oræ populum hortabatur. Dies quoque supplicationum isti rei prosperandæ ordinatione Philippi ac Pij iv. Pontificis per Frisios indicti, ne adversitate votorum auspiciorumque magnos armorum apparatus, & longinquum ex Hispaniâ itinerl Philippus inchoaret. Quod propositum alij dissuadere, commodo, aut ambitione, allegare domesticas imperij curas regnumque rectore vacuum relinqui non posse. Fore namq;, ut Philippo externis bellis occupato, interna per Hispaniam resurgant, breves intra annos repressa, sed quorum vulnera, aut saltem sensus in illustribus familijs extaret. Præter hoc arma, & eventus bellorum volubili fortunæ subjacere, cui committendum augusti capitis pignus non sit, in quo tot nationum, populorumque salus versetur. Esse mare vastum & turbidum, aut intermedios hostiles agros, tum adventurum Regem eo locorum, ubi omnia infida, & popularium tumultuum plena sint.
units.tr: Then those standing about raised their right hands, and while Dionysius was finishing his speech they assented with bowed faces. The others who had withdrawn from the assembly were ordered to present themselves the next day in the same place, on pain of a fine of Carolus gold coins unless they were present. There, the votes of the people having been asked again, a decree was passed once more for the suppression of the edict, though the secession of those who had strongly opposed this measure achieved nothing. And so Hector Aebinga, a nobleman who was more opposed to that decree, although he had been enrolled among the archers, was ordered to betake himself to Hallem and to look after the very large estates which he held there by hereditary right. For they said that the liberty of the people did not need defenders of that kind, by whose rash and immoderate speech danger might be created in those raw times of civil fury. Then, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, that great mystery of the Lord's Supper was celebrated at Leeuwarden, the first to receive it being Tarquinius Vallesius, the consul. The others approached in a long line, and as the Church had perceived a great increase, the same communion was held. Not long after, the magistrates sat to appoint tribunes of the cohorts, the people having been summoned to four separate courts (those of Hoecama, Kempema, Menninga and Oldehove), so that public quiet should not be disturbed by hidden schemes during that tender and infant stage of liberty. For the magistrates were pressing that the archers, who held the right of electing the tribunes, should give these same tribunes power to act, consult and decide with the Senate on whatever was for the good of the city, and that the instruments of commission and the powers of the tribunes should be drawn up at the discretion of the Senate. But the city was divided, and the college of archers was split into opposing parties, so the obstinacy of a few stood in the way of the Senate's plans. For the archers of the opposing side were taking care that nothing should be lost of the oath sworn to King Philip, and that all the advantage of the city and the acts of the Senate should agree with the oath of the people and with Philip's rule. Thus Paulus Breckerus, Henricus Tarquinius, Bernardus Sirxma, Theodorus Haringius and Nicolaus Stasius interceded. Others acted more immoderately, according to the desire of their passions. For there were not lacking men who, by secret written protests and libels of accusation (to win the favour of Aerschot and Margaret the Governor), split the people, and, openly confident and turbulent, cried out that the oath of the confederates had been violated. For they themselves, they said, had kept their oath to Philip, son of Charles Caesar and heir, sworn in the year 1550 and again in the year 1555 to him as king and prince, whole and inviolate, and that they had not mixed themselves with the turbulent plans of men whose hands were not free from sacrilege. Since this matter seemed likely to give cause for sedition, the magistrates ordered Henricus Tarquinius to be put in custody as the instigator of the disorders, so that they might more conveniently deter the others from unbridled licence. I find that Antonius Jodocius, the author of the notes, had taken care to appear before the consul Allaeus Thesius, and that the magistrates, so as not to seem to have decided anything against the innocent, had made public the proceedings of the Papist protesters against the people. Paulus Breckerus too, a foreigner who, because he kept a noblewoman as his wife, had been raised to the dignity of praetor, was accused in vain before the royal Senate by Suffridus Bejema, a nobleman, and borrowed material for his defence from the vehement zeal against Philip and the Roman religion. So the affairs of Leeuwarden were tossed up and down with great dissension of minds, until Aerschot, returning from Overijssel (whither he had set out to quell the disturbances with four cohorts of German foot soldiers and another force of light-armed horsemen), by his arrival among the people of Bergum raised the spirits of the Papists and their fortunes too. Having at once summoned to himself the tribunes of the military forces, Jacobus Husingius, Quirinus Laccelus Buranus, Ernestus Mulartius, Foxius Hasseltanus and Joannes Splinterius, he gave clear hints that vengeance was being prepared for the recent seditions. Margaret could have ordered a more wholesome remedy, with the help of the council of the Belgian and royal estates, for quelling and restraining the disturbances, but instead, struck by womanly rashness or by the magnitude of the danger, she wrote a letter to Philip in Spain, in which she set out the series of civil disturbances: the churches laid waste, the worship of God renewed, and the authority of the rulers oppressed, and indeed by the counsel of those whom Charles Caesar long ago, or Philip at the beginning of his rule, had honoured with knightly rank and with the insignia of the Golden Fleece, according to the custom of the Burgundian house. She therefore asked Philip to take pity on his provinces, which were wavering, and to hasten from Spain to Belgium, to restrain the easily moved people by his majesty and presence. Philip, weighing this advice of Margaret's with himself, summoned the nobles of the kingdom and consulted about settling the Belgian troubles. Some thought that this popular disease, which they knew arose from the immoderate domination of the powerful, should be treated with gentler remedies, and that quiet had always been the best remedy for healing swellings. Little glory was to be hoped for from civil war, and much danger. If the king wished for war, the enemy need not be sought far off, given the still troublesome fury of the Ottomans and the recent wars on the African coast, and the faithless tricks of the Moors. For the Belgians, by a peculiar reverence for princes, as by a kind of religious awe of divinity, would return to obedience if they observed the secret of clemency, and the force of the king's anger were broken by mildness. Others, however, urged war and arms, and that, since they refused remedies like medicine, the evils must be treated with iron and cautery. For, they said, Philip had long had no intention of a Belgian war, except that new alliances of the people, defections, disorders now and sacrileges supplied him with a cause. Liberty must therefore be taken away, the fomenter of all licence, and the state changed by war into a kingdom, which could be drawn even by the sinew of a dry thread. So a decree for waging war in Belgium was drawn up at Madrid in Spain, the chief author being Antonius Perrenotus, lately bishop of Arras and cardinal Granvelle, whom Philip, moved by the complaints of the nobles of the Golden Fleece, as one burdensome to Belgian liberty, had called away to Burgundy after Spain. Philip himself took upon himself the care and conduct of the war, and, after arranging his departure through Savoy, Burgundy and Lorraine, sent letters ahead into Friesland, by which he informed the Frisians of his coming (as he had promised the estates of the provinces at the last assembly at Ghent), and encouraged that region's people toward the pursuit of peace and concord. A day of supplications was also appointed by the Frisians, by the order of Philip and Pope Pius IV, to prosper this business, lest Philip should begin, through the adversity of prayers and omens, the great preparation of arms and the long journey from Spain. Others argued against this plan, saying that for the sake of convenience or ambition, and for domestic cares of the empire, the kingdom could not be left without a ruler. For, they said, while Philip was occupied with foreign wars, internal troubles would rise up again in Spain within a few years, troubles that had been suppressed but whose wounds, or at least whose feeling, remained in the illustrious families. Besides this, arms and the outcomes of wars are subject to the fickle fortune, and the pledge of the august head, on which the safety of so many nations and peoples depends, should not be entrusted to it. The sea is vast and turbulent, and the intervening lands are hostile, and then the king would arrive in places where everything is untrustworthy and full of popular tumults.

units.la: Quare satius esse cum imperio, ac exercitu in Provincias Belgicæ Legatum Præfectumq; mitti, facturum quæ rex jusserit, & minore infamiâ decretâ sævitiæ usurum. Sic mutato Philippi consilio, supremum belli imperium in Ferdinandum Albanum devolutum fuit, æmulo nequicquam Carolo Principe Philippi primogenito, quem Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xlv. è Mariæ Portugallicæ priore matrimonio susceperat. Is namqne regiæ indolis vigentiumq; annorum Princeps, gerendo bello, aut administrando per ætatem imperio capax, in hoc maxime adnitebatur, ut repressâ inimicorum aulicorumq; potentiâ, Belgicæ præficeretur, suaeque apud populum illum gratiæ non vanus æstumator, nullo sanguine, cæterum vacuum sibi dissensione imperium assereret. Sed civile Carolo ingenium, & stabiliendæ, ut creditum fuit, Belgicæ Libertati pronum, Philippo patri displicebat, cuius animus per icti fœderis & infælicium turbarum recentem memoriam, tristes civilis licentiæ vindicias per Præfectos meditabatur. Quare Leovardij, ne studia quærendæ libertatis, & nupera urbis tempestas in exitium suum vertereteretur, Serapium Hania Iure-Consultum, Consulatum tum gerentem, & Allardum Iacobæum Senatorem oppidanum, una cum Gisberto Aernsma, ac Frederico Inthima in suprema Curia causarum patronis ad Arembergium misere, ne in causa reformatae Religionis, quid novaretur, sed eadem permissa, omnibus singulisq; publicae pacis beneficium esset. Caeterum Arembergius conte&tam animo offensam aegre occulens, severius rescripsit, statuitque ut reformati ministri ad iii. Eid Ianuar. ante Solis occasum Leovardia excedant, neque recipiantur in posterum, sub poena regiae indignationis, & publici judicij. Rescripsit quoque ut Ædilitiae potestati, quos comites aggerum vocabat, omnem templorum ornatum, cultumque numinis veterem restituant, curentque ne quid discrepans contrariumve moribus ceremoniisque antiquis intra urbem habeatur. Hæc vi. Eid. Ian. in coenobio Bergumano acta. Tum ipsi etiam Pontificij, sui metuentes veniam Arembergium orarunt, testati propalam.
units.tr: It was therefore better to send a legate and prefect with an army into the Belgic provinces, one who would do what the king ordered and would use severity with less infamy. Philip changed his plan accordingly, and supreme command of the war passed to Ferdinand of Alva, though Charles, Philip's eldest son by his first marriage to Maria of Portugal, whom he had had in 1545, was a rival for it to no avail. This prince, of royal character and in the vigour of youth, was capable of conducting a war or administering government by reason of his age, and he strove above all to be placed over the Netherlands, once the power of the enemies and courtiers had been checked. He was not a vain judge of his own popularity with that people, and he claimed for himself an empire free of bloodshed and free of dissension. But Charles's civil temperament, which was believed to incline towards securing Belgian liberty, displeased his father Philip, whose mind, mindful of the recent treaty and the unhappy disturbances, was planning harsh punishments through prefects for civil licence. Therefore, lest the efforts to seek liberty and the recent storm in the city turn to their own ruin, the people of Leeuwarden sent Serapius Hania, a jurist then serving as consul, and Allardus Jacobaeus, a town senator, together with Gisbertus Aernsma and Fredericus Inthima, advocates in the supreme court, to Aremberg, so that nothing new might be introduced in the matter of the reformed religion, but that the same concessions be granted, and the benefit of public peace extended to all and each. Aremberg, however, hardly concealing the offence he had conceived in his mind, replied more severely, and decreed that the reformed ministers should leave Leeuwarden before sunset on the 11th of January, and not be received again in future, under penalty of the royal displeasure and public judgment. He also replied that the aediles, whom he called the commissioners of the dykes, should restore all the ornament of the churches and the ancient worship of the deity, and should take care that nothing discordant or contrary to ancient customs and ceremonies be tolerated within the city. These things were done on the 8th of January in the monastery at Bergum. Then the Papists themselves, fearing for their own safety, also begged pardon of Aremberg, openly declaring their attestation.

units.la: Vpero illo urbis motu ijsdem animis erga regiam Majestatem se affectos fuisse, quos quinquagesimo, & dein quinto post anno solemni illa Philippi Principis inauguratione professi essent. Quale nec in partes factionum pertractos sacramentum variasse, caeterum abstinuisse facinoribus, quae praeceps furor paucorum, spreta regnantis Majestate suasisset. Qui propterea etsi jure statuere quid posset istis furoribus & insolentia dignum, tamen non dubitare se, quin pro clementia sua daturus veniam sit Philippus Rex, & quidem iis praesertim, in quorum animis ac conscientiis incorrupta fides habitaret. Paratos se etiamnum esse, sacramentum dicere ad arbitrium Praefecti, modo ne publico civitatis juri quid decedat.
units.tr: In that recent movement of the city, they had been disposed towards the royal majesty with the same feelings that they had professed in the solemn inauguration of Prince Philip fifty years earlier, and again five years after that. Their oath had not been varied by being drawn into the parties of the factions; rather, they had abstained from the crimes that the headlong fury of a few had prompted, scorning the majesty of the reigning sovereign. Therefore, although he might rightly decide what punishment such frenzies and insolence deserved, nevertheless he did not doubt that King Philip, in his clemency, would grant pardon, and especially to those in whose minds and consciences unbroken loyalty dwelt. They were still ready to take the oath as the prefect might direct, provided nothing was taken from the public right of the city.

units.la: Tradit Iodocius, Magistratus oppidani Legatos eodem die cum Pontificijs Bergumi convenientes, inspecto Pontificiorum libello supplice ejusdem subscriptionem obtulisse , Pontificiosq;. suâ innocentiâ subnixos, & seorsim patrocinio suæ causæ usos , id modeste recusasse. Itaque Arembergius loquendi copiâ Tarquinio Vallesio, & Allæo Te- jesio Legatis Magistratus factâ , dimissis repente Pontificijs, postulata quædam exhibuit, quæ suppleri ocyus, non falso perturbatæ mentis indicio flagitabat. Ea hæc erant.
units.tr: Iodocius relates that the town magistrates' envoys, meeting at Bergum on the same day as the Papists, having inspected the Papists' supplicating petition, offered their signature to it; but the Papists, relying on their innocence and having used patronage for their cause separately, modestly declined this. Therefore Aremberg, having granted the envoys of the magistracy, Tarquinius Vallesius and Allaeus Tejesius, an opportunity to speak, suddenly dismissed the Papists and presented certain demands, which he urged should be fulfilled quickly, as no unfair sign of a disturbed mind. These were the following.

units.la: Senatus populusque Leovardiæ urbis mandato viii. huius mensis die facto ( de exterminandis scilicet Ministris ) pareto.
units.tr: The senate and people of the city of Leeuwarden are to obey the command made on the 8th day of this month (namely, concerning the expulsion of the ministers).

units.la: Novam Religionem aut fædera non habeto, facitovè; si quæ facta sint, rescindito.
units.tr: They are not to hold a new religion or covenants, and are to annul any that have been made.

units.la: Decreta Philippi Regis pro more publicato.
units.tr: The decrees of King Philip are to be published in the customary way.

units.la: Tor.
units.tr: Tor.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. Tormenta, pulverem, omniaq; instrumenta Belgica, Arembergio LXVII. permittito.
units.tr: The cannon, gunpowder and all Belgian equipment are to be handed over to Aremberg, 1567.

units.la: Ruardum Roordam, Valerium Cammingham, Douwonem Doumam, Goffonem Ebingam, Serapium Haniam, Tarquinium Vallesium, Allæum Tejesium, Wibrandum Elconium, Sibrandum Sibrandium sponsores obsidesve dato, si recusent, alios substituito.
units.tr: They are to give as sureties or hostages Ruardus Roordam, Valerius Cammingha, Douwo Douma, Goffo Ebinga, Serapius Hania, Tarquinius Vallesius, Allaeus Tejesius, Wibrandus Elconius, Sibrandus Sibrandius; if they refuse, substitute others.

units.la: Ab Inquisitione, Ediƈtisque nuperis, ut & militum præsidio, immunis esto:
units.tr: Let them be exempt from the Inquisition, from recent edicts, and likewise from the garrison of soldiers.

units.la: Concordiam pacemq; publicam curato, eâ servatâ, sponsores obsidesve post annum liberi sunto, veniaque esto.
units.tr: Let them take care of concord and public peace; if this is kept, the sureties or hostages are to be free after a year, and there is to be pardon.

units.la: Margareta Gubernatrix (à cuius voluntate totum negotium, dum aliter de consilio Ordinum Belgicæ, rex decernat, pendebit) si approbaverit, omnia rata firmaque sunto.
units.tr: If Margaret the governor (on whose will the whole matter will depend, until the king decrees otherwise on the advice of the Belgian estates) approves, all things are to be ratified and confirmed.

units.la: Quæ ab Arembergio IIII. Eid. Ian. in Bergumanis signata, ac Leovardiam à Legatis perlata.
units.tr: These things were sealed by Aremberg at Bergum on the 10th of January, and were carried by the envoys to Leeuwarden.

units.la: Ibi coacto confestim Senatu, cæterisque de quorum securitate ac periculo agebatur in consilium adhibitis, mandata Arembergij Legati exposuere, ad quorum ratihabitionem offensi regis potentia, & indignatio Præfecti, tum maxime civiles discordiæ stimulabant. Ab alia parte, quo minus Arembergij mandatis obsequerentur, sacramentum fœderis, & clam initæ societatis, tum, quæ magnum in animos hominum jus atque imperium habet, libertatis cupido dubium Senatum remorabantur. Cæterum suspensa & ardua consilia formido imminentium, & domestici cujusque pignoris cura, & simul miseratio abrupit. Itaque decreto Senatus ratihabitio perscripta, sponsoresque in Senatum evocati fidejussoriam cautionem præsentaneis periculis interposuere. Tabulæ eâ de re xix. Kalend. Febr. scriptæ, & Ruardi Roordæ, Valerij Cammingæ, Douwonis Doumæ, Goffonis Ebinghæ, Serapij Haniæ, Tarquinij Vallesij, Allæi Tejesij, Wibrandi Elconij, & Alberti Iacobæi manu figuatæ. Tum à Senatu primoribusque civium, quos jam ante communio juris, fæderisvè obligaverat, sponsorum indemnitati prospectum, actaque ea de re confecta Serapius Hania, Tarquinius Vallesius, Allæus Tejesius, Albartus Iacobæus, B. Ioannis, Ioannes Symonius, P. Petræus, H. Aythma, G. Florentius, Ioannes Francifcius, Wibrandus Elconius, Hector Sixtinus, Franciscus Gerritius, W. Arnoldius, Nocolaus Ioannis, Franciscus Regnerius, Cornelius Gellius, F. Amckius, Cornelius Florentius, Elco Valerius, Ioannes Lambartus Senior, Suffridus Gerbrandius Beima, Heffelus Tarquinius.. T. Petræus Teetlum, Leo Petræus, Ioannes Gommartius, Arnoldus Everardus, Michaël Melius, Eilardus Meinardus, Abbæus Udius, Iarichus Wopconius, Henricus Iarichius,. Wibrandus Wibrandius, Petrus Arnoldius, Auco Emius, Petrus Tevius, Ielbo Iacobus, Iacobus Sibrandius, Ioannes Wilhelmi Velsius, & Dyonisius Wingia confirmavere. Dein Arembergius ne conventio vacillaret, & ne potens civitas ad capessendam per arma defensionem accenderetur, veniam anteactorum fecit, nihilq; in corpora, ac res fortunasq; civium & Senatus è causa innovatæ religionis, anteactarumq; turbarum se statuturum fidem dedit, scriptoq; comcommunijt. Hoc tantum cavit, ut pro præsidio justo comitatui, & Prætoriæ equitum alæ intra urbem locus esset, quam Leovardij non ignorarent custodiæ corporis deberi. Spondebat præterea, si forte Margatæ Gubernatricis assensus non subsequeretur, se daturum operam, ut urbe, ac Provinciâ excessuri periculi præmoneantur, justumque fugæ spatium deserturis patriam assignetur. Quæ ad Margaretam Gubernatricem transmissa, magnis negotijs tum implicitam, & sui metuentem, tamdiu efficacia fuere, donec adultis viribus & circumfusâ nihil sinistri metuentibus infidi Regis potentiâ, clarorum civium exilijs fortuna, & vanitas fallacis aulæ probaretur. Quapropter Margareta, ut animum ostenderet ab extremis consilijs, & subjugando per vim populo non abhorrere, hoc etiam caverat: Ne, quod inter Leovardios, & Arembergium de præsidio actum erat, exemplo esset, cæterosque Præfectos Arembergio successuros obligaret. Itaque fide publicâ, aut saltem eius imagine per Legatos acceptâ, omnia securitatis plena videbantur, nisi quod ministri statò die Prid. Eid. Ian. urbe ejecti magno & velut domestico luctu totam urbem complevere. Scribit Iodocius, eos à Tarquinio Vallesio cæterisque fœderatis inclinante die deductos, ac in exilium prægressos mutuis solatijs tædia temporis, & molestiam instantis fugæ levasse. Fæminas quoque consulares, & patritias ut mollitie sui sexus, ita miseratione abeuntium correptas profusis in sinum lachrymis, & illuvie corporum squallentes, importuno dolori succubuisse. Tum xii. Kal. Febr. fana refecta, omnique templorum ornatu ex pacto restituto, Pontificij ad intermissa divini cultus exercitia rediere. Supellex quoque sacra & æs signatum, (quod elapso autumno antistites cænobiorum extra Provinciam non tam direptionis metu quam explendæ avaritiæ ablegasse Senatus regius criminabatur) cænobijs tum restitutum, cumque injuriæ crimen, & religionis edictum, ut oblivione præteriti temporis obductum, ita concordi amicitiâ penSatum est. Mox armamentario urbis reserato pulvis tormentarius, globique ferrei in arcem comportati, æneaque machinæ sumptu civitatis, intestino, & factionum bello fusæ Arembergij usibus cesserre. Qui compositâ cum Leovardijs lite, ut omnem intra Flevum Lavicamque Provinciam ad exemplum compressæ urbis formaret, ad præTores Grietmannosvè litteras dedit, quibus statuebat: Ut reformati ministri intra triduum provinciâ, sextiduum vero ditionibus Philippi, sub pænâ capitis excederent, redintegratisque per Frisiam sanis sacrisque locis ijdem Prætores Romanam Religionem restitui curarent. Dein convocato Senatu Regio de habendo Leovardiæ Comitio proposuit, sextumque Kal. Febr. diem conventui Ordinum in æde (quam circa annum cIↄ. IIII. LXXXVII. fundatam in archivis Leovardiæ urbis reperio) Iacobæorum designavit. Ibi per Carolum Nitzenium præsidem Senatus eadem fere cum ijs, quæ Leovardijs obtulerat, postulata exhibuit. Hoc verò maxime urgebat, Ne quod fœdus Ordines facerent, nuperèque inito, nisi excludi à conventione vellent, renuntiarent ocyus. Ratihabendis quoque postulatis idoneos ex Ooftergois, Weftergois, Sylveftribus, & Oppidanis sponsores dari sibi petijt, totamque actionem arbitratui Regis, aut Margaretæ Gubernatricis permisit.
units.tr: There, the Senate was at once called together, and the others whose safety and danger were at stake were brought into the council. The commissioners of Aremberg set out their instructions; in considering whether to ratify them, the king's power and the prefect's indignation, and above all the civil discord, spurred them on. On the other side, the oath of the covenant and the secretly formed association, together with the desire for liberty, which holds great sway and authority over men's minds, held the wavering Senate back from obeying Aremberg's instructions. Yet fear of impending events and concern for each man's own dear ones, together with pity, broke off their uncertain and difficult deliberations. So by decree of the Senate the ratification was drawn up, and the sureties were summoned before the Senate and gave bonds of surety against the immediate dangers. The documents on this matter were written on the 19th day before the Kalends of February and signed by the hands of Ruardus Roorda, Valerius Camminga, Douwo Douma, Goffo Ebinga, Serapius Hania, Tarquinius Vallesius, Allaeus Tejesius, Wibrandus Elconius and Albert Jacobaeus. Then the Senate and the chief citizens, whom a common law or covenant had already bound, provided indemnity for the sureties; and the act drawn up on this matter was confirmed by Serapius Hania, Tarquinius Vallesius, Allaeus Tejesius, Albartus Jacobaeus, B. Joannis, Joannes Symonius, P. Petraeus, H. Aythma, G. Florentius, Joannes Franciscus, Wibrandus Elconius, Hector Sixtinus, Franciscus Gerritius, W. Arnoldius, Nicolaus Joannis, Franciscus Regnerius, Cornelius Gellius, F. Amckius, Cornelius Florentius, Elco Valerius, Joannes Lambartus Senior, Suffridus Gerbrandius Beima, Heffelus Tarquinius, T. Petraeus Teetlum, Leo Petraeus, Joannes Gommartius, Arnoldus Everardus, Michael Melius, Eilardus Meinardus, Abbaeus Udius, Iarichus Wopconius, Henricus Iarichius, Wibrandus Wibrandius, Petrus Arnoldius, Auco Emius, Petrus Tevius, Ielbo Jacobus, Iacobus Sibrandius, Joannes Wilhelmi Velsius and Dionysius Wingia. Then Aremberg, so that the agreement might not waver, and so that the powerful city would not be stirred to take up defence by arms, granted a pardon for past deeds, and pledged his good faith in writing that he would take no action against the bodies, property, fortunes or citizens, nor against the Senate, on account of the innovated religion or the earlier disturbances. He required only this: that a place within the city be set aside for his escort and a wing of the praetorian cavalry, which the people of Leeuwarden did not fail to understand was owed as protection for the person of the governor. He further promised that, if by chance the consent of the Governess Margaret did not follow, he would take care that those leaving the city and province were warned of the danger, and that a fair span of time for flight would be assigned to those departing the fatherland. These terms, sent to the Governess Margaret, who was then much entangled in affairs and fearful for herself, remained effective for so long as the power of the faithless king, now grown in strength and surrounded by men fearing no mischief, and the fortunes of exile for distinguished citizens, and the emptiness of a deceitful court, proved themselves. Therefore Margaret, to show that she shrank from no extreme measures and from subjugating the people by force, also provided this: that what had been agreed between the people of Leeuwarden and Aremberg concerning the garrison should not become a precedent binding the other prefects who would succeed Aremberg. So, with public faith, or at least its image, received through the commissioners, all seemed full of security, except that the ministers, expelled from the city on the appointed day, the day before the Ides of January, filled the whole city with great grief, as though it were their own. Iodocus writes that they were escorted out by Tarquinius Vallesius and the other confederates as the day declined, and that, going into exile before them, they relieved the tedium of the time and the distress of the impending flight with mutual consolations. The women too, both of consular and patrician rank, were seized, as their sex's softness and their pity for those departing prompted, with tears poured into their bosoms, and, squalid with the dirt of their bodies, gave way to unseasonable grief. Then, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, the temples were repaired, and with all the ornament of the churches restored under the agreement, the Papists returned to the practice of divine worship that had been interrupted. The sacred furniture also, and the coined money (which the Senate of the king accused the abbots of the monasteries, in the past autumn, of having sent out of the province, not so much from fear of plunder as to satisfy their greed), was then restored to the monasteries; and the charge of wrong and the edict on religion were, as if covered by oblivion of the past time, so too weighed down by a harmonious friendship. Soon afterwards, the city's arsenal was opened, and the gunpowder and iron cannonballs were carried into the citadel, and the bronze engines, cast at the city's expense, were given over to the use of Aremberg, who had been defeated not by the war of factions but by the internal strife of the city. Having settled the dispute with Leeuwarden, so that he might shape the whole province between the Flie and the Lauwers after the example of the subdued city, he sent letters to the praetors and the Grietmanns, by which he decreed that the reformed ministers should leave the province within three days, and the ditions of Philip within six days, under penalty of death; and that the same praetors should take care that, with the sound and sacred places restored throughout Friesland, the Roman religion be re-established. Then, having called together the royal Senate, he proposed holding a diet at Leeuwarden, and he appointed the sixth day before the Kalends of February for the assembly of the Estates in the church of the Jacobins (which I find in the archives of the city of Leeuwarden was founded about the year 1487). There, through Charles Nitzenius, president of the Senate, he put forward nearly the same demands he had presented at Leeuwarden. Above all he pressed this: that the Estates should not make any covenant, and should renounce, as quickly as possible, any recently made, unless they wished to be shut out of the assembly. He also asked that suitable sureties from the Oostergo, Westergo, the Sylvestrians and the townsmen be given to him for ratifying these demands, and he left the whole action to the discretion of the king or the Governess Margaret.

units.la: L misit. Voluit quoque, ut Ordines Frisiæ, quod numero plures essent, triginta aut circiter Delegatos è suo cætu ederent, ijsq; potestatem amplam facerent secum, & Senatu regio de rebus controversis agendi. Ordines verò, etsi in constituendo certo Delegatorum numero minima difficultas esset, pessime habebat, quod actioni incho-andæ universum Senatum Arembergius destinaret, ac quibusque peregrinis (qui ex instituto Burgundicæ Curiæ in istum Ordinem cooptabantur) arcana reipub. & jus partium tanquam suspectis arbitris committeretur. Quare Valerium Cammingam, & Doconem Martnam, viros è primariâ Nobilitate, & scientiâ rerum claros ad Arembergium misère, qui de eo referrent, ac ut soli inquilini Senatores actioni comitioque pro more patrio interessent, postularent pertinacius. Quod etsi Arembergius ferret ægrius, ita morem petentibus gessit, binosque Senatorij ordinis, & nobilis prosapiæ viros, Tiallengum Eysingam & Petrum Frittemam, faciendis actorum relationibus delegit. Tum Frisiæ Ordines ab Arembergij postulatis orsi grates ei egere, quod ut ante Leovardios, ita tum Frisios quosque Edictorum asperitati, & durioribus Inquisitorum imperijs exemisset, Friscæque genti cum cæteris Philippi Provincijs jus indivisum fore in ijsdem postulatis declarasset. Hoc tantum volebant Ordines; Ne cui Frisio in causâ Religionis vis fieret, & ne in corpus liberi hominis, aut etiam fortunas asperiore judicio sæviretur. Censebant quippe illâ Margaretæ Gubernatricis cum fœderatâ Nobilitate pactione licentiam immodestæ coercitionis imminutam, & duriorum Iudicum officia per vim conventionis refrænata. Ea propter asserebant, Arembergium veniam anteactis inconsultâ Margaretâ Gubernatrice pro jure Præfecti largiri posse, sociosque suæ imbecillitatis pænitentiam professos illustri clementiæ exemplo donare. Quod verò ad publicationem Edictorum Philippi attineret, eam se facturos more usitato, modo ne Edicta conventioni inter Margaretam fœderatosque initæ, aut juri patrio adversarentur. Sponsionem verò pro exequendis postulatis præstare, ut nec juris, ita nec potestatis suæ esse, lubricis in lapsum mortalium ingenijs, & unius crimine per alterius innocentiam non expiando. Itaque patrijs legibus etiam ante Saxonum tempora validâ libertate, post etiam Carolo Cæsare Anno clo. Io. xxiv. & dein Anno cIo. Io. xlv. sancitum fuisse, ne ex alterius delicto quis conveniretur, & ne paucorum culpa in omnium pænam excurrat. Posse Arembergium subsidio juris adversus ruptores pactionum uti, ac vi tacitæ obligationis, quâ delinquentium bona fisco subjacent, injuriam spretæ, ac violatæ legis vindicare. De Fœdere ajebant Ordinis, id ad se non spectare, & ex veteri juris formulâ ab alijs ictum, per alios dissolvi debere. Rogare itaque Arembergium, ut militem quietis securitatisque publicæ perturbatorem finibus amoveat, præstetque Provinciam ab omni violentiâ militum, grassatorumque immunem. Hæc Ruardus Roorda, Douwo Douma, Iulius Dekema, Hero Ockingha, & Douwo Roorda postulatis Arembergij responderunt. Fæderati verò seorsim. Qui ne rerum suarum, ac famæ discrimen facerent, & ut defensione sione communium Provinciae Ordinum se munirent, Prid. Kal. Febr. cIↄ. Iↄ. Nicolaum Cleutingium, & Arnoldum Albartum Hardervicenum in LXVII, confessum Ordinum cum hac obtestatione ablegavere: Non censere se, Arembergium alia adversum se actione uti posse, quod renuntiatio foederis per conventionem Margaretae, ac foederatorum facta videretur, & quod eadem conventio omnem societatem, & cum ea, si quae fuerit, noxam sustulisset. Ideo scilicet eandem conventionem de voluntate Margaretae Gubernatricis per Frisios publicatam, ne priorum memoria extaret, & ut omnium offensionum materies aeterna oblivione sepeliretur. Et quoniam Arembergius exemplar foederis, sociorum nomina, & novam renuntiationem flagitaret importunius, eosdemq; foederatos autores publicae calamitatis, & evocati in Frisiam militis praedicaret, ita Foederati coram Ordinibus eorumque Delegatis fidem faciebant, Arembergij accusationes falsis rerum testimonijs inniti. Nullo quippe tempore adversus Philippum consilia cepisse, non legisse militem, aut in usum stipendiorum tributa cumulasse, caeterum ea fecisse, quae fidelium subditorum officia, & sacramenti lex postularet. In eo proposito persistere paratos esse, modo ne publicae pacis beneficium sibi adimatur, & in ipsa patria ac natali sede, cujus sanctissimum affectum in omni actione praeferrent, aetatem agere iniqui temporis fortuna, & inimicorum invidies non vetaret. Daturos interim operam, ut copiam Foederis Ordines habeant, experianturque ab omni malititi, ac flagitio alienos, ipso Foederis consilio nihil aliud, quam Divini nominis gloriam, Regis, & Patriae commodum quaesivisse. Ista Epaei Doumae, Suffridi Bejemi, Renici Gerlacij, Hartmanni Galamae, Wilconis Holdinghae, Sibonis Sceltamae, & Edonis Heringhae caeterorumque Foederatorum nomine a Nicolao Cleutinghio, & Arnoldo Albarto Harderviceno actuarijs perscripta, ac Ordinibus Provinciae exhibita. Hoc vero maxime spem conciliandarum partium, & captae conventionis praepediebat, quod Arembergius in perferendis rescriptis apparitore, homine importuno uteretur, & quod Iacobum Elpendamum (is Brederodio a secretis) virum nobilem, & faderi socium, Suffridi Beyemi domo extractum in custodiam, mox publicum carcerem dedisset. Metuebant namque Ordines, ut idem non semel religionem Foederis professis accideret, & ut ipsi cura aut miseratione propinquorum, affiniumque periculosis intercessionibus involuti, eiusdem discriminis, & juxta invidiae magnitudinem sentirent. Quapropter missis ad Arembergium Docone Martena, & Ruardo Roorda fidei publicae cautionem poposcere, ne, dum lege & ex aequo agerent, Arembergius dolosis artibus, & insperatis insidijs securos circumveniret. Qua accepta, hoc etiam foederatorum nomine proposuere, ut quoniam exhibi tabulas foederis urgeret Arembergius, faederatis ad socios eundi potestatem faceret, ut de rescindendo faedere consultarent, quo solvi se non posse sine assensu sociorum, & laesione famae Faederati aiebant. Neque enim violati foederis macula adspergi se velle, aut descisere a socijs impendentis periculi metu: semel quippe fidem foederi datam, miseratione infaelicis patriae, ne ferret dominos libertati graves, & ipsi Philippo minus aequos, cui parere e formula
units.tr: Margaret sent him the same demand. He also wanted the Orders of Friesland, who were the more numerous, to name about thirty delegates from their own body and to give them full power to treat with the royal Senate on the disputed matters. The Orders, although choosing a fixed number of delegates would be no great difficulty, took it very badly that Arembergius was assigning the whole Senate to begin the proceedings, and that the state's secrets and the question of rights were to be entrusted to outsiders, as suspect arbiters, who were admitted to that Order by the custom of the Burgundian Court. So they sent Valerius Cammingha and Doco Martna, men of the first nobility and distinguished in public affairs, to Arembergius to report on this and to insist more firmly that only the resident senators, according to the custom of the fatherland, should take part in the proceedings and the assembly. Although Arembergius bore this less easily, he yielded to their request and chose two men of senatorial rank and noble family, Tiallengus Eysinga and Petrus Frittema, to make the reports of the proceedings. Then the Orders of Friesland, beginning from Arembergius's demands, thanked him, because, as he had earlier freed the Leeuwarders, so now he had spared all the Frisians from the harshness of the edicts and the harsher commands of the Inquisitors, and had declared in those same demands that the Frisian people would share an undivided right with the other provinces of Philip. The Orders wanted only this: that no Frisian be coerced in matters of religion, and that no free man be punished in his person or property by harsher judgment. For they held that by the agreement of Margaret the Regent with the confederated nobility the licence of excessive coercion had been diminished, and the duties of the harsher judges had been checked by the force of the compact. Therefore they claimed that Arembergius, by the right of his office, could grant pardon for past acts without consulting Margaret the Regent, and could forgive his associates, who professed repentance for their weakness, as an example of illustrious clemency. As for the publication of Philip's edicts, they said they would carry it out in the usual way, provided that the edicts did not conflict with the agreement made between Margaret and the confederates, or with the ancestral law. But they said that a guarantee for the carrying out of the demands was neither within their right nor their power, since human minds are prone to slip and the guilt of one man cannot be expiated by the innocence of another. Thus, by the laws of the fatherland, which held firm liberty even before the time of the Saxons, and afterwards were sanctioned under Charles Caesar in the year 1524 and again in the year 1545, no one may be sued for another's crime, and the fault of a few must not be extended to the punishment of all. Arembergius might use the aid of the law against breakers of agreements, and by the force of the tacit obligation, by which the goods of offenders are liable to the treasury, avenge the injury of a spurned and violated law. Concerning the Confederacy, the Orders said that it did not concern them, and that what had been struck by some under the old formula of law ought to be dissolved by others. They therefore asked Arembergius to remove from the borders the soldier who disturbed the public peace and security, and to keep the Province free from all violence of soldiers and marauders. Ruardus Roorda, Douwo Douma, Julius Dekema, Hero Ockinga and Douwo Roorda answered these demands of Arembergius. The Confederates, however, answered separately. Lest they expose their own affairs and reputation to danger, and so that they might protect themselves with the common defence of the Provincial Orders, on 31 January 1566 they sent Nicolaus Cleutingius and Arnoldus Albartus of Harderwijk to the assembly of the Estates, LXVII, with this protest: that they did not think Arembergius could use any other action against them, since the renunciation of the Confederacy seemed to have been made through the agreement of Margaret and the confederates, and since that same agreement had removed all association, and any harm that might have come from it. They explained that this agreement had been published by the Frisians with Margaret the Regent's consent, so that the memory of earlier events should not survive, and so that the matter of all offences should be buried in eternal oblivion. And since Arembergius was urging more insistently for a copy of the Confederacy, the names of the associates and a new renunciation, and was calling these confederates the authors of the public calamity and the soldier summoned into Friesland, the Confederates assured the Orders and their delegates before them that Arembergius's accusations rested on false testimony about the facts. They had never at any time taken counsel against Philip, nor had they levied soldiers or piled up taxes for the use of the pay; rather, they had done what the duty of loyal subjects and the law of their oath required. They said they were ready to persist in that purpose, provided that the benefit of public peace was not taken from them, and that the misfortune of an unjust age and the envy of enemies did not forbid them to spend their life in their own land and native home, whose most sacred affection they put first in every action. Meanwhile they would take care that the Orders might have a copy of the Confederacy, and they would test whether men free from all malice and wickedness had sought, by the very purpose of the Confederacy, nothing but the glory of the divine name, the good of the King and of the fatherland. These things were written down by the clerks Nicolaus Cleutinghius and Arnoldus Albartus of Harderwijk in the name of Epaeus Douma, Suffridus Beyemus, Renicus Gerlacius, Hartmannus Galama, Wilco Holdingha, Sibo Sceltama, Edo Heringha and the other Confederates, and were presented to the Orders of the Province. What chiefly hindered the hope of reconciling the parties and the agreement they had reached was this: Arembergius used in delivering his rescripts an officer, an importunate fellow, and he had dragged Jacobus Elpendamus, a noble man, secretary to Brederode and an associate of the Confederacy, from the house of Suffridus Beyemus into custody and soon into the public prison. For the Orders feared that the same thing would happen, as it had more than once to those who professed the Confederacy's cause, and that they themselves, entangled by the care or pity of relatives and the dangerous intercessions of kinsmen, would feel the same peril, in proportion to the magnitude of the odium. Therefore, having sent Doco Martena and Ruardus Roorda to Arembergius, they asked for a guarantee of public faith, lest, while they acted lawfully and fairly, Arembergius should entrap them, secure as they were, by deceitful arts and unexpected snares. Having received this, they also proposed in the name of the Confederates that, since Arembergius was insisting on the production of the tablets of the Confederacy, he should give the Confederates the power to go to their associates, so that they might consult about rescinding the Confederacy, since they said they could not be released from it without the consent of their associates and without injury to the Confederates' reputation. For they did not wish to be stained by the blot of a violated agreement, nor to desert their associates out of fear of impending danger: once faith had been given to the Confederacy, out of pity for their unhappy fatherland, lest it bear masters burdensome to liberty and not very fair to Philip himself, whom it was in the spirit and nature of the old conventions to obey.

units.la: { } Federatorum acta.
units.tr: Acts of the Confederates.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. mulâ antiquarum conventionum animus adhuc, atque ingenium esset. Volebant interea tam Ordines, quam Foederati, ut venia anteactis esset, ac ut Arembergius ad Gubernatricem eâ de re scriberet, potestatemque impetraret condonandis offensis validam. Hæc Ruardus Roorda, Doco Martna, Edsardus Grovensteinius, Hesselus Mockama, Hesselus Feitzma, Siuckius Emingha, & Ioannes Aylva, cæterique; Ordinum, Foederatorumque, retulere. Cæterum Arembergius liberiore response excandescens Federatis objecit. Non potuisse eos in nova foedera coïre, obligatos adhuc Philippo regi, cuius obsequium, nec apud Margaretam. Gubernatricem, aut se Præfectum exuissent. Itaque geminasse jus-jurandum, quod ij facere solent, qui venales animas Principum imperiis professi antiquam fidem novâ eluunt. Quin recordarentur à Rege ac Principe suo descivisse ligatos adhuc veteris obsequij lege, neque protestatione apud quenquam usos, consilium secutos fuisse licentiæ, & fæditatis plenum. Quare militem exautorare, ac præstare intactam præsidio Provinciam non posse, nisi ad sanas mentes Ordines, Foederatique redeant, deprecatique veniam enormium, offensi Regis gratiam exorent.
units.tr: 1566 Meanwhile both the Orders and the Confederates wished that pardon be given for past acts, and that Arembergius write to the Regent about this matter and obtain from her power to remit offences effectively. Ruardus Roorda, Doco Martna, Edsardus Grovensteinius, Hesselus Mockama, Hesselus Feitzma, Sjuckius Emingha, Joannes Aylva and the other delegates of the Orders and of the Confederates reported these things. But Arembergius, growing angry at their rather free reply, objected to the Confederates that they could not join new confederacies while still bound to King Philip, whose obedience they had not cast off, either before Margaret the Regent or before himself as Governor. Therefore they had doubled the oath that those do who, having sold their souls to the commands of princes, wash away their old fidelity with a new one. Moreover, they should remember that they had revolted from their King and Prince while still bound by the law of their old obedience, and had used no protest before anyone, but had followed a counsel full of licence and disgrace. Therefore the soldier could not be dismissed, nor could the Province be kept free and untouched by a garrison, unless the Orders and the Confederates came back to sound minds, and, having begged pardon for their great offences, won back the favour of the offended King.

units.la: Quâ longâ & acri contentione factum est, ut Frisiæ Ordines pro se & Foederatis propalam testarentur; Approbare se jam ante dicta factavè, neque spe impetrandi favoris, aut metu imminentium periculorum recessuros à jure suo, quin daturos potius illustre constantiæ documentum, quo jus patriæ retinendum, aut simul cum eo subeundum discrimen decernant. Pereunte patria periculo solatium fore, vana jam dudum ad avitas leges, & Principum fidem provocatione, cujus fructum adulta potestas, & novi dominatus insatiabilis cupido sustulisset. Ita namque Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xv. ipsâ Caroli per Frisiam inauguratione conventum fuisse:
units.tr: After a long and bitter dispute it came about that the Orders of Friesland openly declared, on their own behalf and on behalf of the Confederates, that they approved of what had been said and done before, and that neither by hope of obtaining favour nor by fear of impending dangers would they depart from their right; rather they would give a notable proof of constancy, and decree that the right of the fatherland be retained, or else that the danger be undertaken together with it. With the fatherland perishing, they said, it would be a comfort to appeal, long since in vain, to the ancient laws and the faith of princes, a appeal whose fruit the grown power and the insatiable desire of a new domination had taken away. For thus, in the year 1515, at the very inauguration of Charles in Friesland, it had been agreed:

units.la: VTomnis, si quæ obveniret, Carolum inter, populumque Friscum, Dissensio, per quatuor Arbitros componeretur; judicandæque liti bini è Frisijs, totidemque pro Principe ederentur. Carolus quoque in fines Provinciæ militem non induceret, omneque controversum ex pactione Anni cIↄ. Iↄ. xxxi. Præfecto, Senatuique suo decidendum daret.
units.tr: Thus, if any dispute should arise between Charles and the Frisian people, it would be settled by four arbiters; two Frisians and two on the Prince's side would be named to judge the case. Charles, too, would not bring soldiers into the borders of the province, and he would leave every point in dispute to be decided by his Prefect and Senate under the agreement of the year 1531.

units.la: Ita Ruardus Roorda, Doco Martna, Valerius Camminga, Dominicus Hottinga, Barthius Idzarda rescripsere. Creditum fuit, Arembergium spectatâ Ordinum pro tuendo patrio jure, fide, atque constantiâ, implacabilem tum animum induisse, spretâque nuperâ pactione cum Leovardijs initâ, pejora, &, concordiæ infesta consilia cæpisse. Itaq; dimissis præfractè Delegatis, conventus quoque ipsoipsorum Ordinum Leovardiæ solutus est, cursuque præcipiti, velut flexu syderum solet, cum fragore se aperiens futura tempestas procerum ingenia dissociavit. Scribit Iodocius, isto conventu de rescindendo præsertim fœdere Arembergium egisse, Delegatisque Ordinum, modo renuntiatum fœderi foret, læsi regis gratiam, & restitutionem in integrum addixisse. Cæterum mihi res patriæ evolventi penitius, secus notatum, Arembergiumq; nullo pacis consilio, militem hoc tempore clàm collegisse, eundemq; adultâ demum ætate in speciem dimissum, ac edicto Senatus regij coërcitum, Provincialium rebus damna, atq; molestiam dedisse.
units.tr: So Ruardus Roorda, Doco Martna, Valerius Camminga, Dominicus Hottinga and Barthius Idzarda wrote back. It was believed that Aremberg, seeing the Estates' resolve to defend the national right with loyalty and steadfastness, then took on an implacable spirit; scorning the recent agreement made at Leeuwarden, he began to plan worse things, hostile to harmony. Accordingly, the delegates having been dismissed with obstinacy, the assembly of the Estates themselves was also dissolved at Leeuwarden, and the coming storm, breaking out with a crash just as the stars are wont to change their course in a headlong rush, divided the minds of the nobles. Iodocius writes that at that assembly Aremberg argued especially for rescinding the covenant, and that he assigned to the delegates of the Estates, provided it were announced that the covenant was renounced, the king's favour toward the injured parties and restoration to their former state. For my part, however, in unrolling the affairs of the homeland more thoroughly, I have noted otherwise: that Aremberg, with no thought of peace, secretly gathered soldiers at this time, and that he, only when grown to adulthood, dismissed them in appearance, and, being restrained by the edict of the royal Senate, caused losses and trouble for the affairs of the provincials.

units.la: Finis Libri Primi.
units.tr: End of the First Book.

units.la: P. WINSEMII Historiarum
units.tr: P. Winsemius, Histories

units.la: MDLXVII.
LIBER SECUNDUS.
units.tr: BOOK TWO.

units.la: TAQVE dubiâ per Frisiam pace, & Ordinum Arembergijq; conventu dirempto, ac si longius à concordiâ mortalium mentes occulta fatorum vis, nexusque causarum latentium abduceret, manifesta mox graviorum dissensionum signa se ostendère. Populus namque læsi juris, & oppressæ libertatis sarcinam, & simul infamiam ferens ægrius, novis conciliabulis se immiscuit, effususque in publicum communicati doloris sensum, tacitâ indignatione, & secreto murmure expressit. Plebs verò suarum perturbationum & simul potentiorum civium manceps, incondito ac dissono clamore omnem Leovardiæ urbis angulum complebat. Ea vociferari amissam libertatem, oppressos sanctissimi fœderis socios, Arembergium commissæ sibi genti iniquum nova, & servilia obsequia per nudatam munimentis urbem sperare. Eiectos in exilium ministros, abducta in arcem tormenta ac pulverem, nihilque aliud superesse, quam ut patientiam minuant, instarque servorum compediti ruptis ergastulis in libertatem se vindicent, cum ipso sanguine, ac vitâ à laudatis majoribus relictam. Paucis quippe consiliorum fabricatoribus omnem calamitatem stare, esseque in Senatu urbico tuendæ plebi creatos, ministeria sua Præfecto Senatuque regio venditantes, Præcipuè verò in Matthiam Rommartium civitatis Syndicum mordacibus odijs invehebatur. Itaq; factum est ut eidem Rommartio vii. Kal Mart. oppidanâ Curiâ, pro more egresso, & domum eunti periculum strueretur, populusque confertim confluens eundem Rommartium, velut piacularem læsæ libertati victimam, trucidandum clamitaret. Cæterum Rommartius ut vitæ consuleret, secreto domus suæ derepente se abdidit, tnrbaque æstuantis impetum honesto perfugio declinavit. Quâ re perceptâ Arembergius, sedandis exulceratis civium animis arce regia p opere descendit, pultatisq; Rommartij foribus intromissus, eundem in arcem regiam, quærendæ securitati duxit, quam publico illo motu rerum, adscitis in comitatum quinquaginta stipatoribus, ipsi sibi Arembergius parabat. Tradit Iodocius isto motu populi vix repressó, inclinante in vesperam die novum cæpisse, civiumq; multitudinem in foro conglobatam, Abbæo Udio & Theodoro Guliel-
units.tr: With peace in Friesland uncertain and the assembly of the Estates of Aremberg broken up, as if the hidden force of fate and the concealed chain of causes were drawing men's minds further from concord, clear signs of more serious discord soon appeared. The people, bearing with difficulty the burden of a wronged right and a suppressed liberty, and the disgrace along with it, joined in new gatherings, and, pouring out into public, expressed their shared grief in silent indignation and secret muttering. The common people, the tools of their own disorders and of the more powerful citizens, filled every corner of the city of Leeuwarden with a disordered and discordant clamour. They cried out that their liberty was lost, that their allies in the most holy covenant had been crushed, and that Aremberg, unjust to the people entrusted to him, hoped to win new and servile obedience through a city stripped of its defences. The ministers had been driven into exile, the artillery and powder had been carried off into the citadel, and nothing remained but to wear down their patience until, like slaves in chains who break out of their prisons, they might assert their liberty with their own blood and life, which had been handed down by their praised ancestors. Almost the whole calamity, they said, rested on a few makers of these plans, and the men appointed in the city Senate to protect the people were selling their services to the Prefect and the royal Senate. Their bitter hatred was directed especially at Matthias Rommartius, the syndic of the city. Thus it came about that on 22 February, when Rommartius was leaving the town hall as usual and going home, a danger was prepared against him, and the people, flocking together, shouted that he should be slaughtered as a victim to expiate the violated liberty. Rommartius, however, to save his life, suddenly hid himself in a secret part of his house, and by this honourable refuge escaped the rage of the seething crowd. When Aremberg learned of this, he came down from the royal citadel to calm the inflamed minds of the citizens. He knocked at Rommartius's door, was admitted, and led him into the royal citadel to seek safety there. Aremberg himself prepared this safety amid the public disturbance by taking fifty armed attendants with him. Iodocus relates that when this movement of the people had scarcely been checked, and as the day was drawing toward evening, a new disturbance began, and that the crowd of citizens gathered in the market place, with Abbaeus Udius and Theodorus Gulielmius as, he adds, the instigators, had used violence against Pierius Telgerhusius, a Papist. Telgerhusius, going out in public and hiding himself in a private house, escaped the danger to his life and imminent death.

units.la: Vrbis Leovardiestanus. cIↄ. Iↄ. Gulielmio, ut idem addit, autoribus, Pierio Telgerhusio homini Pontificio vim intulisse, eundemq; Ielgerhusium publico digressum, & in privati domum se abdentem vitae discrimen, & praesentaneam mortem evasisse. Quare Arembergius ne illa civilium animorum effervescentia continuis periculis exponeretur, consiliorum Philippi haud ignarus, Martij mensis initio duas militares cohortes in urbem evocavit, quas Quirinus Laceius Buranus, & Ernestus Mulartius certis sub signis ducebant. Snecensibus quoque (quorum res elapso Septembri ut & Franequeranorum infidas fuisse Borraeus notat) duarum cohortium praesidium imposuit, quibus Iacobum Husingium, & Ioannem Splinterium praefecerat. Quare ut ante edictis, ac severitate legum, ita tum popularis licentia armis frenabatur, duriorisque imperij impatientiam duriora remedia sequebantur. Philippus namq; Edicto in Frisiam transmisso, jam ante sanxerat; Utij, apud quos veteris jurisjurandi religio valeret, turbandis defectorum conventibus se darent, eosq; & cum ijs crescentem licentiam poenâ capitis, aut etiam graviore coercerent.
units.tr: Leeuwarden city, 1567. Therefore, so that such an effervescence of civil minds should not expose the city to constant dangers, Aremberg, not ignorant of Philip's plans, at the beginning of March summoned two military cohorts into the city; Quirinus Laceius of Buren and Ernestus Mulartius led them under their own standards. He also placed a garrison of two cohorts in Sneek (whose affairs, as Borrhaeus notes, were unreliable after the past September, as were those of the people of Franeker), and he set Jacobus Husingius and Joannes Splinterius over them. Thus, just as the people's licence had earlier been restrained by edicts and the severity of the laws, so now it was restrained by arms, and harsher remedies followed the impatience with harsher rule. For Philip had already, by an edict sent into Friesland, decreed that the Utians, among whom the sanctity of the old oath still prevailed, should be prevented from disturbing the assemblies of the rebels, and that they should punish, with death or even with something more severe, those who joined them and their growing licence.

units.la: Qua lege omnes armorum crimine pollutos, aut populi seductores puniri, eorumq; bona fisco addici praeceperat: Itaque tum Arembergius spreta, quam cum Leovardijs inierat, pactione, & praesidio urbi inducto, velut securum imperium adeptus, adhibito in consilium regio per Frisiam Senatu, de pellendis Frisiâ reformatis ministris decretum executus est, eq; territorio Leovardiensi Andreas Husumanus, Aggaeus Hempenius, Gellius Fintzumanus, Joannes Corniumanus, Michael Leckumanus, Eco, & Henricus Stenani, è Ferverdico Petrus, & Rodmarus Ferverdij, Tiebbo Marrumanus, Focco Blyensis, Bernardus & Ioannes Wansuertij, Valerius Hallemius, è Menaldumaeo Gysbertus Deinumanus, Iacobus Marsemius, Fredericus Menaldumaeus, Edo Schingensis, Fecco Vierius, è Wonserano Iacobus Arumaeus, Sibrandus Kimsuartius, Sixtus Burguartius, Ioannes Pingumanus, Arnoldus Dedgumanus, è Winbritserano Feito Osthemius, Gellius Smallebruggius, Sibo Santfortius, Andreas Snecanus, Suffridus Hegius, è Lemsterano Ioannes Lemmarius, è Franequerano Egbertus, & Henricus Tjumani, Cyprianus Buranus, Wigerus Scalsemius, è Tietzerckio Gerardus Wijnsius, Sixtus Oedkerckius, Gellius Tietzerckius, Nicolaus Eeftrumanus, è Baerderano Tyallengus Huynsius, Abbaeus Weidumanus, Ioannes Bofumanus, ex Hennardaeo Vibius & Wiardus Cobardij, è Biltano Ioannes duo Mariae, & Annae Parochi, è Dantumano Wilco Ianumius, Regnerus Rinsmageestanus, è Dongerano Joannes Bornuerdius, Folcardus Morraeus, duo Butenpostij, Collumanus, & Olduoldius pastores Provinciâ eiecti.
units.tr: By this law he had ordered that all who were tainted with the crime of taking up arms, or who seduced the people, should be punished, and that their goods should be forfeited to the treasury. Accordingly, Aremberg, having set aside the agreement he had made with Leeuwarden and having brought a garrison into the city, and having obtained, as it were, a secure government, and with the royal Senate for Friesland taken into council, carried out his decree concerning the expulsion of the reformed ministers from Friesland. From the territory of Leeuwarden were expelled: Andreas Husumanus, Aggaeus Hempenius, Gellius Fintzumanus, Joannes Corniumanus, Michael Leckumanus, Eco, and Henricus Stenani; from Ferwerd, Petrus and Rodmarus of Ferwerd; Tiebbo Marrumanus, Focco of Blija, Bernardus and Joannes Wansuertius, Valerius Hallemius; from Menaldumadeel, Gysbertus Deinumanus, Jacobus Marsemius, Fredericus Menaldumaeus, Edo of Schingen, Fecco Vierius; from Wonseradeel, Jacobus Arumaeus, Sibrandus Kimsuartius, Sixtus Burguartius, Joannes Pingumanus, Arnoldus Dedgumanus; from Wymbritseradeel, Feito Osthemius, Gellius Smallebruggius, Sibo Santfortius, Andreas Snecanus, Suffridus Hegius; from Lemsterland, Joannes Lemmarius; from Franeker, Egbertus and Henricus Tjumani, Cyprianus Buranus, Wigerus Scalsemius; from Tietjerksteradeel, Gerardus Wijnsius, Sixtus Oedkerckius, Gellius Tietzerckius, Nicolaus Eeftrumanus; from Baarderadeel, Tyallengus Huynsius, Abbaeus Weidumanus, Joannes Bofumanus; from Hennaarderadeel, Vibius and Wiardus Cobardius; from Bildt, Joannes, the two Marias, and the parish priest Anna; from Dantumadeel, Wilco Ianumius, Regnerus Rinsmageestanus; from Dongeradeel, Joannes Bornuerdius, Folcardus Morraeus, the two Butenpostii, Collumanus, and Olduoldius, ministers, were driven out of the province.

units.la: Reperio in armario Biltano praeter hos à Iodocio nominatos Ioannem Sichemensem Coudumanum, Sceltonem Aitzema Lutkepostium, Iacobum Galmerium, Betsterfuagium, Iacobum Abbaeum Vreterpium, & Joannem Joannis Norderdrachtanum fuisse, eosdemque purioris doctrinae professione facta fatalem illa tempestate clarissimis optimisque viris exilij fortunam domestico otio, & non spernendis conditionibus praetulisse. Unde miseratio sociorum, metus verò sui, populum pulum, atque Nobilitatem pervasit, haud inani conjectura præsidium militare ignaris Provinciæ Ordinibus clàm collectum, & tot innocentium capitum exilia stabiliendo irati Regis imperio, & exitio libertatis decerni. Itaque Ordinum Frisiæ Delegati suspectà Margaretæ Gubernatricis, & Præfecti actione, in Hispaniam ad ipsum Regem libellum supplicem hunc in modum misere.
units.tr: I find in the Bildt archive that, besides those named by Iodocus, Joannes Sichemensis Coudumanus, Scelto Aitzema Lutkepostius, Jacobus Galmerius, Betsterfuagius, Jacobus Abbaeus Vreterpius, and Joannes Joannis Norderdrachtanus were also there, and that these men, by professing a purer doctrine, preferred exile, which fate imposed in that troubled time on the most distinguished and best men, to domestic leisure and to conditions that were not to be despised. Hence pity for their companions, and fear for themselves, spread through the common people and the nobility, not without good reason to suspect that a military garrison was being secretly gathered by the Provincial Estates, who knew nothing of it, and that the exile of so many innocent persons was being decreed by the command of the angry King and for the destruction of liberty. Therefore the deputies of the Estates of Friesland, distrusting the actions of Margaret the Governess and of the Prefect, sent a supplication to the King himself in Spain, in the following manner.

units.la: CAROLUS CAESAR pater tuus, Philippe Rex, primâ Principatus sui per Frisiam ætate id majoribus nostris insuper dulserat, ut à militum bellicâ onere immunes essent, & ne ex alieno errore dicto corrigerentur. Posterius indultum agente adhuc in terris CAROLO patre tuo repetitis Anno clo. Io. xxxix. & xlv. pactionibus tamdiu integrum servavimus, donec te Principe de vigore legis & integritate simul prioris beneficij dubitaremus. Postquam enim extitere, qui jure Ecclesiasticarum collationum nec immodestè usi religionem delegere suis conscientiis congruam, ita ab eo tempore paucorum actio nos omnes suspectos fecit, ac si offensus universæ gentis, & communis suffragatio eorum consiliis intervenisset. Quorum memoriam etsi conventio MARGARETAE Gubernatricis & fœderatæ Nobilitatis haud dubiè aboleverit, ita non vano metu percellimur, ultionem recentium turbarum autoribus facinorum, nobis verò omnibus periculum, atque discrimen parari. Ut istud averruncemus, offerimus obsequium, & si poposcerit, Rex, corpora, atq; sanguinem, modo sinas nos publicâ pace frui, & in tutâ possessione, ac nostrarum rerum usu consenescere. Si namque, quod fore prævidemus, bellum & militem terris nostris induxeris, subvertes fortunas nostras, rescindesq; conventionem Anni clo. Io. xxxiv. & cum eâ patris tui Caroli Cæsaris memoriam. Utraque verò cultâ tibi firmum imperium, nobis securitatem præstabis. Hoc tantum subiunge pro clementiâ tuâ, ut, quoniam in pristinum statum, incompositis adhuc per Frisiam & lubricis rebus, doctrina Pontificum restitui nequit, libertatem conscientiis habeamus, finasq; nos profano loco sociari, quem ipsi nostrâ religione imbuamus. Templa, & fana à majoribus nostris rei divinæ dedicata, Pontificijs cedent, nobis satis erit privato tecto fortunam, & simul exercitium nostræ fidei clausisse. Hæc Delegati.
units.tr: CHARLES CAESAR, your father, Philip the King, in the first years of his rule over Friesland, had additionally granted this to our ancestors: that they should be free from the burden of soldiers' warfare, and that they should not be corrected for another's error. We have kept this later indulgence, granted while your father Charles was still living on earth, intact, and renewed by the agreements of the years 1539 and 1545, for so long as we did not doubt, while you were prince, the force of the law and the integrity of the earlier favour. For after there arose men who, using the right of ecclesiastical appointments not immodestly, chose a religion congruent with their consciences, from that time the actions of a few have made us all suspect, as if the anger of the whole nation and the common assent had joined their counsels. Although the agreement of Margaret the Governess and of the confederated nobility has doubtless abolished the memory of these things, we are struck with no idle fear that vengeance for the recent disturbances will be prepared against the authors of those deeds, and danger and peril against all of us. To avert this, we offer obedience, and if the King should demand it, our bodies and our blood, provided you allow us to enjoy public peace and to grow old in secure possession and use of our own property. For if, as we foresee will happen, you bring war and soldiers into our lands, you will overthrow our fortunes and annul the agreement of the year 1534, and with it the memory of your father Charles Caesar. By honouring both, you will secure for yourself firm rule and for us safety. Add only this, in your clemency: since, while affairs in Friesland remain unsettled and unstable, the teaching of the Papists cannot be restored to its former state, let us have liberty of conscience, and allow us to be joined in a profane place, which we ourselves may imbue with our religion. The churches and shrines dedicated to divine worship by our ancestors will yield to the Papists; it will be enough for us to shut up our fortunes and at the same time the exercise of our faith within private roofs. So the deputies.

units.la: Cui supplicationi Bruxellis interceptæ Margareta respondit: Querimonias Ordinum Frisiæ sæpe ex Arembergio Præfecto auditas, nunc scripto comprehensas, ac mittendas ad Philippum Regem in suas manus incidisse. Qua ex re occasionem nacta esset propensum in Frisicam gentem animum ostendendi, ratihabitione pactorum, conventionumq;, quas Carolus pater divæ memoriæ cum isto populo inijssset. Interim muliebri etiam patientiâ ferre se non posse, paucos Philippi Regis, & sui oblitos inquieta ingenia novandis rebus admovisse, spretis Edictis, quibus Carolus Philippusq; Reges antiquarum traditionum, & Romanæ Sedis fidelem observantiam præcepissent. Quod ne fiat in posterum, atrociores pœnas delinquentibus decrevisse, quibus optimos in fide, pessimos in metu contineret. Nam promiscuam religionem pro captu, ac temperie ingeniorum variam per Frisiam tolerare, nec fas sibi, nec honestum videri, Romanorum Pontificum, & Caroli PhilipPhilippique Regum infamiâ, qui majorum ritus reverenter habuissent, velut retinendo imperio, & ordini rerum utiles. Quibus attemperandis adfuturus propediem ex Hispaniâ Philippus fit, daturus operam, ut indicto Ordinum totius Belgicæ conventu, decernantur, statuanturque Regi & juxta subditis salutaria. Monere interim ac hortari Frisios, in fide erga Philippum Regem persistant, dentque operam quam maximè ut pravitate temporum aut erronbus imbuti in viam redeant, justitiæque ac pacis officina culto servatoque sacramento regio habeatur. De collatione beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum, & eorum jure, addebat Margareta, dependere illud à Philippo Rege, & institutione Archidiaconorum, si quid verò patrij juris hac in re fuisset, id defectione eorum amissum esse, quos incapaces beneficij in regem rebellio, & reatus teterrimi criminis fecisset.
units.tr: Margaret answered this supplication, which had been intercepted at Brussels, as follows: that the complaints of the Estates of Friesland, often heard from Aremberg the Prefect and now put in writing to be sent to King Philip, had fallen into her hands. From this she had taken the opportunity to show her favourable disposition toward the Frisian people, by ratifying the agreements and covenants which Charles her father, of divine memory, had made with that people. Meanwhile, she said, although she could not bear it even with womanly patience, a few men, forgetful of King Philip and of herself, with restless dispositions had turned to revolution, scorning the edicts by which the kings Charles and Philip had enjoined faithful observance of ancient traditions and of the Roman See. Lest this happen again, they had decreed harsher punishments for offenders, by which they might keep the best in loyalty and the worst in fear. For it seemed right and proper to her neither to tolerate in Friesland a mixed religion, varying according to each person's understanding and temperament, nor to dishonour the Roman Pontiffs and the kings Charles and Philip, who had reverently observed the ancestral rites as useful for maintaining rule and the order of affairs. Philip was soon to come from Spain to moderate these matters, and he would take care that, by summoning an assembly of the Estates of all Belgium, decisions should be made and settled that were both useful to the King and salutary for the subjects. Meanwhile she advised and urged the Frisians to persist in loyalty to King Philip, and to take the greatest pains that, having been led astray by the wickedness of the times or by errors, they might return to the right path, and that the workshop of justice and peace might be kept, with the royal oath cultivated and preserved. Concerning the bestowal of ecclesiastical benefices and the right to them, Margaret added, that this depended on King Philip, and on the institution of the archdeacons; and if any hereditary right had existed in this matter, it had been lost through the defection of those whom rebellion against the King and the guilt of the most foul crime had made incapable of holding a benefice.

units.la: Tum Flos Frisicæ, fœderataque Nobilitatis in exilium per injuriam temporum pulsus, exterminatusque; patriâ ac possessionibus suis Rhenum Amasumque ultra recessit, invictisque animis libertatem suam, & simul fortunam exilij professus est.
