Quod ipsum Hartmannum Galamam, & Franciscum Eysingham Wirdumanos, Hesselum Feitzmam Husumanum, Siuckium Emingham Cornjumanum, Suffridum Beiemum, & Ottonem Haniam Leovardios, Oenonem Heringham Hyemanum, Epæum Doumam Seniorem, & Menenium Scheltemam Hallemios, Deitzium Wingiam Blyensem, Wilconem Holdingham Angjumanum, Pibonem Haerdam Tennartium, Douwonem Glinzium Dronrijpium, Oenonem Grovensteinium & Edonem Heringham Marsemios, Foppium Camstram Deinumanum, Sibethum Scheltamam Boxemium, Scheltonem Roordam Beilicomium, Hommium Hettingham Prætorem Baerderanum, Hesselum Oosthemium Prætorem Idardium, Hesselum Feitmam Peynsium, Ieltonem Eelsmam Sexbyrumanum, Edonem Gerbrandam Harlinglum, Gulielmum Bumam Dresumanum, Franciscum Leonardum Hugenium Collumanum, Tarquinium Vallesium, & Allæum Teiesium Consules Leovardios, Focconem Aysmam, Henricum Allartium, Gerardum Florentium Scabinos, Franciscum Hemmium, Iureconsultum, Gabinium Selsmam Iuniorem, Ioannem Simonium, Everardum Arckenium, Siboldum Aysmam, Sibrandum Sibrandium, & Renicum Gerlachum Hotzemanum, nullâ tum adhuc judicis sententiâ sponte, & sagaci imminentium formidine compulsos delegisse, in actis illorum temporum reperio. Hesselum quoque Haitzma virum nobilem, & Simonem Longobardum à Foxio Hasseltano qui præsidium Slotæ agebat, prope Lemma iam captos, Leovardiamq; abductos. Iam enim circa portus & catarractas fluminum, rivorumq; miles, aut grassator regius oberrabat, locaq; fugæ gentis commeda militaritus stationibus exponebantur. Ne scilicet discrimen, quod parabatur, nobilitas populusque declinaret, & ne gentium per Hollandiam vicinaq; loca commercijs conciliabulisq; Frisij libertatis percupidi, communicatis in regem odijs juvarentur. Septuaginta Nobiles fuisse, autor tradit, eosque suspecto Arembergij ingenio, & aulæ moribus, triste exilium domestico discrimini prætulisse. Quare plurimi Groningam urbem validam & præpotentem se contulere, ut illa civitate, tanquam tutâ fugæ suæ sede recíperentur, utq; civitatem partium foecundam, aucta exulantium multitudine, a regia magis dominatione alienarent. Quod in medijs aulae pavoribus, ne Transrhenana Frisiorum ora deficeret, observans Margareta perspicax faemina, Arembergium Leovardiae agentem secretionibus litteris hortata est, ut praesidium, si fieri posset, urbi inducat, populiq; libertatis superbia ferocis infida obsequia militari manu coërceat. Quare Arembergius inter blandimenta, & minas regiae indignationis ope Mepschij, qui vicarium ista in urbe rectoris imperium tenebat, tantum profecit, ut collegia opificum, civitatis robur, Philippo assereret, multisque reluctantibus, de recipiendo regis praesidio decerneretur. Qua pactione firmata, Margareta Gubernatrix e legione Scombergica quatuor peditum cohortes, ductore Blasio Vegersen.io, homine Germano, urbi induci curavit, non sine magna criminatione illorum, qui potiundae libertati destinata, praesidiario milite interversa querebantur. Econtra Margareta laetabatur Groningam Philippo regi assertam, dubiumq; & nutantem populum armorum vi, & terrore praesidij coërcitum.
units.tr: Then the Flower of Friesland and the confederated nobility, driven out of their homeland by the injustice of the times, withdrew beyond the Rhine and the Ems, professing with unbroken spirit their liberty and, at the same time, the fortune of exile. I find in the records of those times that the following men chose exile of their own accord, compelled by the sharp fear of impending danger, though no judicial sentence had yet been passed against them: Hartmann Galama and Franciscus Eysinga of Wirdum, Hessel Feitzma of Hus, Siuck Emingha of Cornjum, Suffridus Beiema, and Otto Hania of Leeuwarden, Oeno Heringa of Hijum, Epaeus Douma the Elder and Menenius Scheltema of Hallum, Deitzius Wingia of Bolsward, Wilco Holdinga of Anjum, Pibo Haerda of Tennard, Douwo Glinzia of Dronrijp, Oeno Grovensteinius and Edo Heringa of Marssum, Foppius Camstra of Deinum, Sibetus Scheltama of Boxum, Scheltus Roorda of Beilum, Hommius Hettinga, praetor of Baarderadeel, Hessel Oosthemius, praetor of Idaarderadeel, Hessel Feitema of Pingjum, Jeltus Eelsma of Sexbierum, Edo Gerbrandi of Harlingen, Gulielmus Buma of Dressum, Franciscus Leonardus Hugenius of Collum, and Tarquinius Vallesius and Allaeus Teiesius, consuls of Leeuwarden; Focco Aysma, Henricus Allartius, and Gerardus Florentius, aldermen; Franciscus Hemmius, jurist; Gabinius Selsma the Younger, Joannes Simonius, Everardus Arckenius, Sibaldus Aysma, Sibrandus Sibrandius, and Renicus Gerlachus of Hotzum. Likewise, Hessel Haitzema, a nobleman, and Simon Longobardus were seized by Foxius of Hasselt, who commanded the garrison at Sloten, near Lemmer, and were led away to Leeuwarden. For by now royal soldiers and marauders were roaming about the ports and sluices of the rivers and canals, and the routes of escape were watched by military posts. The purpose was that the nobility and the people should not evade the danger that was being prepared, and that the people of Holland and the neighbouring regions, eager for Frisian liberty, should not be helped by meetings and dealings with them and by a shared hatred of the king. The author records that there were seventy nobles, and that, distrusting the character of Arenberg and the manners of the court, they preferred a bleak exile to the danger at home. Therefore very many betook themselves to the strong and powerful city of Groningen, so that they might be received there as in a safe refuge for their flight, and so that they might turn that city, rich in factions, away from royal domination by the increased number of exiles. Margaret, a shrewd woman amid the court's alarms, anxious that the Frisian coast beyond the Rhine should not fail, urged Arenberg, who was at Leeuwarden, by secret letters to bring a garrison into the city, if it could be done, and to restrain by military force the arrogant and fierce loyalty of the people to liberty. Accordingly, Arenberg, by means of flattery and threats of royal displeasure, with the help of Mepschen, who held the deputy command in the city as vice-governor, gained so much that he assured Philip that the guilds of craftsmen, the strength of the city, were on his side; and, though many resisted, it was decreed that the king's garrison should be received. With this agreement confirmed, Margaret, the governor, took care that four companies of infantry from the Schomberg regiment, under the leadership of Blasius Vegersen, a German, should be brought into the city, not without great accusation from those who complained that the soldiers stationed there had frustrated the plan intended for winning liberty. On the other hand, Margaret rejoiced that Groningen had been secured for King Philip and that a wavering and hesitant people had been brought under control by the force of arms and the terror of the garrison.

units.la: Ita depresso per Frisiam faedere, Arembergius Maij mensis initio Harlingam properavit, stipatusque ala equitum levis armaturae, Ernestum quoq; Mulartium cum cohorte pedestri cito isthuc agmine ire jussit. Iam enim non inanis famae rumoribus narrabatur, Faederatos exules mari se commisisse, fideq; publica nequicquam per Arembergium data, patrijs terris ejectos, Transmalanam Frisiam cogitare, quam Edzardus II. Ennonis II. & Annae Oldenburgicae filius, paterni Comitatus haeres tum moderabatur. Quorum exulum consilia, ut everteret Arembergius, instructissimam triremem (cui Mulartius cum imperio praerat) latissimis Flevi aestuarijs immisit, ut de exulum adventu cognosceret, quos Jacobus Donckerus Harlinganus onerariâ navi vectabat. Qui enavigato Austrino sinu, dein Flevi (tertium & Boreale Rheni ostium est) aestuario, quod minores majoresque Frisios interluit, navem eandem (cui Batenburgici fratres, profugaque nobilitas alijque se commiserant) ad vadum adegit, quod non longo intervallo a littore discretum in ora praeterfluentis Flevi exsurgebat. Quare Mulartius valida remigum manu eandem navem assecutus suam fecit, proditosque Donckeri scelere ac perfidia Gysbertum & Theodoricum Batenburgicos Harlingam in arcem abduxit, in qua ipse Arembergius apud Satrapam Espelbacchum, cuius infantem in lavacro susceperat, geniali tum festivitate agebat. Itaq; is velut de Belgica Frisicaque nobilitate triumphaturus, (in qua Hartmannus Galania, Suffridus Beiemus, & (quem tertium in annalibus Franckenae reperio) Gulielmus Buma erant, captivorum sorti illusit, minacemque vultum, ac torvitate horridum interpositis acribus verbis, in Suffridum praecipue Beiemum detorsit. Caeterum is spretis comminationibus masculo responso in Ioannem Lignaeum (ita enim contemptim indigetabat) invectus, insolentiam Arembergij praeclara voce, & illustri constantiae elogio rerudit. Ostendebat quippe Beiemus, non faedi carceris, aut instantis leti metum generosam mentem labefactasse, sed superesse etiam compedito libertatem, qua testimonium sanctissimo foederi daret.
units.tr: Thus, with Friesland subdued by the treaty, Arenberg hastened to Harlingen at the beginning of May, and, attended by a wing of light-armed horsemen, ordered Ernst Mulart with an infantry cohort to go there quickly. For now reports were being spread, not without foundation, that the exiles who had sworn allegiance had put themselves to sea, and that, driven from their native lands though public faith had been given in vain by Arenberg, they were planning to go to Ostfriesland beyond the Lauwers, which was then governed by Edzard II, son of Enno II and Anna of Oldenburg, heir to his father's county. To thwart the plans of these exiles, Arenberg sent a well-equipped trireme, under the command of Mulart, into the broad estuaries of the Vlie, to learn of the exiles' arrival, whom Jacob Donckerus of Harlingen was carrying in a transport ship. This ship, having sailed across the Austrian bay and then into the Vlie estuary (the third and northern mouth of the Rhine, which separates the Lesser and Greater Frisians), drove aground on a shoal that rose not far from the shore, at the edge of the flowing Vlie, the same ship in which the Batenburg brothers, the fleeing nobility, and others had entrusted themselves. Therefore Mulart, reaching it with a strong crew of rowers, seized it, and, through the treachery and perfidy of Donckerus, led the Batenburg brothers, Gijsbert and Dirk, to Harlingen, into the citadel, where Arenberg himself was feasting in festive mood at the house of the governor Espelbacht, whose infant son he had held at baptism. And he, as if about to triumph over the Belgian and Frisian nobility, in which were Hartmann Galama, Suffridus Beyma, and (whom I find third in the annals of Francker) Gulielmus Buma, mocked the lot of the captives, and turned a menacing face, horrid with fierceness, with sharp words interposed, chiefly against Suffridus Beyma. But he, scorning the threats, rounded on Johannes Lignaeus (for so he was contemptuously called) with a manly reply, and with a clear voice and illustrious praise of constancy rebuked the arrogance of Arenberg. For Beyma showed that neither the fear of a foul prison nor of impending death had shaken his noble mind, but that even in fetters liberty remained, by which he might bear witness to the most sacred treaty.

units.la: Captivi nobiles in arcem Rupelmondanam ditionis Flandricæ post du-cti, annuæ custodiæ tædium, glorioso vitæ exitu, & memorabili morte finierunt. Tradit V. Cl. Abelus Franckena in Historicis suis commentarijs, Donckerum nautam ære corruptum, cuidam nobili, (sed obscuræ originis regiæque factionis, per scelus istud ad Prætoram post evecto) hac in re servijsse, ipsumq; Donckerum à perpetrato facinore Deo, hominibusq; invisum, commissum crimen perpetuo contemptu & egestate suorum quasi fatalibus pænis expiasse. Tum nomen Prætoris memoriâ temporum, fastisque indignum annales doctorum virorum censuere. Quod Arembergij facinus Frisios certè pessime habuit, qui posthabitis majorum immunitatibus extrahi patriâ suâ indigetes non inritis querimonijs criminabantur. Nullos quippe avorum suorum à Francorum per Frisiam dominatione indulto Pipini Regis Flevum ultra & Visurgum flumina, patrijs terris evocatos, domesticamq; militiam & suum forum semper secutos, aliena judicia non pertulisse. Itaque Carolo V. Cæsare cautum fuisse: Ne quis nobilis, aut in dignitate, constitutus, ratione delicti Provinciâ evocaretur, ipsique etiam perduelles non nisi binis è Nobilitate, binis è populo Oppidano delatâ criminis cognitione, damnarentur. Nunc verò nobilissimi sanguinis viros (quos ex ipso quoque Caroli Cæsaris rescripto coràm Frisiæ Ordinibus, aut eorum arbitris sisti oportebat) alio terrarum captivos abduci, nulliusq; manifesti in Principem criminis convictos remotæ custodiæ & peregrinis carceribus mancipari. Hæc præmia sui in Burgundicam Austriamq; domum affectus, & in Principem fidei esse, ut habi am religiosè, Carolo etiam Cæsare, populi libertatem adolescens dominatio & potentia in summum, & mox ruiturum fastigium adducta subverteret? Itaque duorum sæculorum & ultra factionibus fessos ac mutuo sanguine madentes ad imperium principis tanquam portum quietis perfugisse, ut vix detersâ aviti sanguinis adspergine, suo quoq; imbuerentur, & non in acie, aut armis, ut majores, cæterum inter vincula, & pædorem carcerum per tormenta & carnificum manus perirent? Ideone sub Georgio Saxone Gerbrandum Mockamam, & Gemmam Ioufmam viros Nobiles, templis ac asylis extractos & gladio percussos, post Carolo Cæsare, Ianconem Doumam invicto supra fortunam animo patriæ libertatis defensorem acerrimum accusatione inimicorum, & si retâ in Cæsarem adulatione oppressum, in peregrino carcere & octenni custodiâ extinctum, ut in exemplum sævitia iret, & omnis patriæ defenso odium, & mox damnationem irati Principis acciperet? Hac de causâ Arembergium nupero conventu certum datæ fidei publicæ tempus assignasse, ut eo evoluto securitas coëuntium procerum, & patriæ tranquillitas terminum haberet, sociosq; fæderis & propinquitate sanguinis sibi junctos in longinqua terrarum salubris consilij victrix necessitas, & vis major dispargeret? Scribit Jodocius præter vestes sacerdotales, hierothecas, infulas, aureos cælatosq; calices, captivorum numerum centenarium fuisse, eorumq; plurimos in campi planitie haud procul agere, & marino littore, quod urbi in Austrum est, morte affectos triste aditi fæderis præmium tulisse. Septem quoque ex ijsdem captivis, & in ijs nobilissimæ familiæ adolescentem suspendio necatum. Cla-
units.tr: The captive nobles, led after this into the citadel of Rupelmonde in the territory of Flanders, ended the tedium of a year's confinement by a glorious end of life and a memorable death. The most distinguished Abel Franckena, in his historical commentaries, relates that Donckerus, a sailor bought with money, served a certain nobleman, of obscure origin and of the royal faction, who was afterwards raised to the praetorship through this crime, and that Donckerus himself, hated by God and men for the deed he had committed, atoned for his crime by perpetual contempt and the poverty of his own people, as by fated punishments. The annals of learned men have judged the name of the praetor unworthy of memory of the times and of the records. This deed of Arenberg certainly grieved the Frisians most grievously, who, disregarding the immunities of their ancestors, complained with no idle protests that they were being dragged out of their country and summoned to foreign trials. For, they said, none of their forefathers, since the indulgence of King Pepin under Frankish rule over Friesland, when summoned beyond the Vlie and the Weser from their native lands, had ever submitted to foreign judgments, but had always followed their own domestic military service and their own court. Therefore, they said, it had been provided under Emperor Charles V that no nobleman, or one holding office, should be summoned out of his province on account of an offence, and that even traitors should not be condemned unless the cognizance of the charge had been referred to two nobles and two townsmen. But now men of most noble blood (who, by the emperor's own rescript, ought to be brought before the Frisian Estates in person, or before their arbiters) were being led as captives to another part of the world, and those convicted of no manifest crime against the prince were being consigned to remote custody and foreign prisons. Are these the rewards of loyalty to the house of Burgundy and Austria, and of faith toward the prince, which, if they had been religiously observed even under Charles the Emperor, would have overturned the liberty of the people, since a youthful domination and power, raised to the highest point, was destined soon to fall? Therefore, after two centuries and more, wearied by factions and drenched in each other's blood, they had fled to the command of the prince as to a harbour of quiet, only to be imbued, scarcely cleansed of the stain of their ancestors' blood, with their own, and to perish not in battle or in arms, as their forefathers did, but in chains and the stench of prisons, through torture and the hands of executioners? Was it for this that under George of Saxony Gerbrand Mockema and Gemma Joufma, noble men, were dragged from temples and asylums and struck down with the sword, and afterwards, under Charles the Emperor, Jancko Douma, an invincible defender of the country's liberty, beyond his fortune, was accused by enemies and oppressed by a feigned adulation toward the emperor, and was extinguished in a foreign prison by eight years of custody, so that his cruelty might serve as an example, and every defender of the fatherland might receive hatred and soon the damnation of an angry prince? For this reason, they said, Arenberg had at the recent assembly fixed a definite time for the public faith to be given, so that when it had run out the safety of the assembled nobles and the tranquillity of the country might have an end, and that the victorious necessity and superior force of a salutary council might scatter across distant lands the allies of the treaty and those joined to them by kinship of blood? Jodocus writes that, besides priestly vestments, reliquaries, mitres, and golden, chased chalices, the number of captives was a hundred, and that most of them were brought to death in the open plain not far from the shore of the sea, which lies to the south of the city, and so received the bitter reward of the broken treaty. Seven of the same captives also, and among them a youth of a most noble family, were put to death by hanging. Cla-

units.la: Clariff. Franckena notat, quod interrogatus an perpetrati per Frisiam sacrilegij, violatorumq; templorum reus esset, longo annorum spatio, se sacris non interfuisse liberius, aut forte incautius respondisset. Id certè si non causam, pondus saltem addidit, ut præter dignitatem natalium violento, & ignobili fato tolleretur. Addit idem scriptor, eorundem neces repentinâ Inquisitoris morte velut divinitus signatas, Ioannemq; Carolum, advocatum, & Levinum Everardum Curiæ Mechlinien-sis Senatorem, à Margaretâ Gubernatrice in Frisiam tum missos, patrimonia exulum fisco regio applicasse. Iodocius subjungit, eosdem Margaretæ Delegatos, ut capitalium rerum quæsitores cognitionibus captivorum Harlingæ præsedisse, Focconemque Romartium Senatorem Regium una cum Iulio Gelio fisci regij per Frisiam Patrono prioribus additum examini reorum, & mox ferendis sententijs præfuisse. Batenburgici fratres jussu Margaretæ per Ernestum Mulartium Vilvordam ducti, per studia libertatis & quærendi suffugij suo post sanguine infælicem patriam inbuêre. Alij narrant ex captivis viginti quatuor à delegatis Curiæ, aut regij senatus ad triremes damnatos, pauciq; suspendio necatis, quosdam intercessione virginum, quæ Harlingæ Arembergio supplices factæ erant, à custodiâ & simul periculo mortis liberatos, inter aliorum aspera clementiæ beneficium & gratiam vitæ accepisse. Partem quoq; prædæ inter Mularti milites distributam, partemq; illius occultatam sectoribus profuisse.
units.tr: The distinguished Franckena notes that when he was asked whether he was guilty of the sacrilege committed throughout Friesland and of violating churches, he answered rather freely, or perhaps rashly, that he had not attended religious services for a long span of years. Certainly this did not cause his death, but it at least added weight, so that, apart from his noble birth, he was removed by a violent and ignominious fate. The same writer adds that the sudden death of the Inquisitor seemed, as it were, a divine sign of their executions, and that John Charles, advocate, and Levinus Everardus, a senator of the Mechlin court, who had then been sent into Friesland by Margaret the Regent, applied the exiles' estates to the royal treasury. Jodocius adds that the same deputies of Margaret presided over the trials of the prisoners at Harlingen as inquisitors of capital cases, and that Focco Rommartius, a royal senator, together with Julius Gelius, patron of the royal treasury in Friesland, who had been added to the earlier judges, presided over the examination of the accused and the later pronouncement of sentences. The Batenburg brothers, led by order of Margaret by Ernestus Mulartius to Vilvoorde, imbibed with their blood, in their last hours, a love of liberty and a longing for refuge for their unhappy country. Others relate that of the prisoners, twenty-four were condemned by the deputies of the court or the royal senate to the galleys, and a few were hanged; that some, through the intercession of virgins who had come as suppliants to Aremberg at Harlingen, were freed from custody and from the danger of death, and received, amid the harshness of the others, the favour of clemency and the gift of life. Part of the booty, too, distributed among Mulartius' soldiers, and part of it hidden away, benefited the plunderers.

units.la: Mox regressis Leovardiam Rommartio & Gelio Senatoribus, Abbæus Udius civis primarius, vinculis datus, Theodorusq; Gulielmius exilio multatus est. Creditum fuit eisdem civibus nuperæ seditionis suspicione, & per intentatam Rommartio, ac Ielgerhusio vim id mali obvenisse, Focconemq; Rommartium Senatorem regium illatam Matthiæ fratri injuriam honestâ ultione & prætextu juris vindicasse. Tum Iacobus Elpendamus Leovardiâ Harlingam, Gulielmus Buma Harlingâ Leovardiam perductus, Everardusque Enfius Coverdiæ Satrapa, in arce regiâ acuto morbo extinctus, deducente funus ipso Arembergio, honoratis exequijs Oldchovæ humatus est. Reperio in libris Edictorum Margaretam Gubernatricem, etiam gerendi belli potestate Ferdinando Albano clàm commissâ, de regis adventu ad Senatum Leovardiæ urbis hoc tempore scripsisse, populumque illius loci ad concordiam & obsequium hortatam de resarciendis sacrarum ædium damnis atque dispendijs monuisse. Mandasse quoque, ut Senatus profugorum civium nomina in indicem referret, fugæq; proxumorum consilia denuntiata bonorum confiscatione, & post Edicto xviii. Kal. Octob. vulgato, pænâ capitis præpediret. Ubi namq; certis rumoribus nuntiatum, Præfecturam Belgicæ Ferdinando Albano demandatam formidati nominis, (quod immanitatis suæ famâ Pyrenæos Alpiumque juga jamdudum transcenderat) & simul prævisæ tempestatis horror Frisios, & in ijs Leovardios concussit, quod in eius adventu oppressas leges, temeratos penates, cruentata parentum ac liberorum ora, denique polluta divina, atq; humana jura intuerentur. Itaque factum est, ut plurimæ familiæ per tutiores domesticis malis fugas rebus suis consulerent, ligneisque muris clausa libertas, & portis con-sepcIↄ. Iↄ. septisque urbium ac infidæ continentis effusa, ventis marique se committeret. Tum Amasus, ac Visurgis fluvij classe frequentati, exulesque aut ultrò profugi metu instantium bellorum apud Bremenses Embdanosque consederunt, quod ijs in locis, etiam ante Ioannis Lasci adventum, reformata religio, connivente Germaniâ, & oræ istius rectoribus haberetur. Ita nissis in exilium fœderatis, Arembergius compositam, ordinatamq; Provinciam ratus, circa Kal. Iul. in Transisulaniam & post Brabantiam profectus est, quo loci Ferdinandus Albanus regio cum exercitu expectabatur. Bellum namque infælici Belgicæ parari, novi quoque jam ante per Germaniam, & Burgundiam delectus, tum Francisci Avilani regij apud Carolum Gallorum regem Legati interceptæ litteræ adstruebant. Erant quoque qui ante biennium restauratum Baionæ inter Galliæ, ac Hispaniæ reges fœdus non ignorarent, Carolumq; Galliæ regem impuberem, & adhuc regni incapacem per limitanea Galliæ à Catharinâ Medicææ matre specie lustrandorum finium circumductum, curante eâdem matre cum sorore Elisabethâ Vallesiâ Philippi conjuge, & (ut Reidanus tradit) auspice fœdeis Albano, novam societatem opprimendæ religionis & auxiliorum mutuorum inijsse. Quare Ferdinandi Albani, & surgentis belli terrore, Principes quoq; Aurei Velleris perculsi habitis conventibus, de summâ rerum, & periculi consultavere. Non defuerunt, qui inter arma, & minacem cædis Philippum (id namque ad Margaretam Gubernatricem clàm perscriptum erat) etiam de veniâ cogitarent, parciturumque subditis Regem pro agnatâ clementiâ opinarentur. Ita Egmondanum ne Belgicâ excederet, amplæ possessiones, conjugis, ac liberorum cura, tum vana, & imaginaria conciliandæ securitatis spes occupaverat. Præterea favor militum, partæque gloriæ decus obvium, velut intercessuræ pro eo legiones essent, cuius imperia & simul victorias Gallico bello adorassent. Aurantius verò providens casuum circumstrepentibus periculis tutiorem fugam censebat, & ut innocentiæ asylum per Germaniæ imperium quæreretur. Esse in eo Principes propinquos, quibus post exacta Germaniæ bella, diuturnum pacis tempus adfluentiam opum, commodum amicis subsidium, dedisset. Neque in Galliæ regno intutas sedes, aut minora auxilia fore, quod in eo Condæus & Amiralius rerum potiantur, & quod laboranti nuper ijsdem de causis Germaniæ vires suas suppeditaverit. Tum Carolum Cæsarem Gallicis armis ad æquas conditiones compulsum, integrâ manente Germaniæ libertate, quam à Philippo per Belgicam non temerari, maximè etiam Galliæ interfit. Idcircò satius esse obsequi necessitatibus temporum, ac impetrandis Germaniæ Galliæve subsidijs locum quærere securitati, quam habere in infælici Belgica per advolantia Hispanorum agmina non possent. Cæteri autem Principum opponenda Philippo arma, & commune auxilium judicabant, quod stabiliendæ patriæ libertati Henricus Brederodius per ditiones suas alijq; è Nobilitate Belgicâ parabant. Sed omne negotium per contraria Principum virorum consilia improsperis auspicijs procedebat. Ex quo evenit, ut sparsis dissipatisque fœderatorum copijs Margareta Gubernatrix vergente Præfecturæ suæ tempore, omnem fere Belgicam regi asseruerit, Romanâ religione, una cum
units.tr: Soon afterwards, when the senators Rommartius and Gelius had returned to Leeuwarden, Abbaeus Udius, a leading citizen, was put in chains, and Theodorus Gulielmius was punished with exile. It was believed that these citizens were under suspicion of the recent sedition, and that the harm had come upon them through the violence threatened against Rommartius and Jelgerhusius; and that Focco Rommartius, a royal senator, avenged the injury done to his brother Matthias with an honourable retribution and under the pretext of law. Then Jacob Elpendamus was taken from Leeuwarden to Harlingen, William Buma from Harlingen to Leeuwarden, and Everardus Enfius, governor of Coeverden, died of a sharp illness in the royal citadel. Aremberg himself conducted the funeral, and he was buried with honourable rites at Oldeholtpade. I find in the books of edicts that Margaret the Regent, to whom the power of waging war had been secretly entrusted with Ferdinand of Alva, wrote at this time to the senate of the city of Leeuwarden about the king's coming, urged the people of that place to concord and obedience, and advised them about making good the losses and expenses of the sacred buildings. She also ordered that the senate should draw up a list of the names of the exiled citizens, and, by an edict published on the 14th day before the Kalends of October, she forbade, under pain of death and confiscation of goods, the plans of those closest to them for flight. For when it was announced by certain rumours that the governorship of the Netherlands had been entrusted to Ferdinand of Alva, a man of dreaded name (whose reputation for savagery had long since crossed the Pyrenees and the ridges of the Alps), and at the same time the horror of the coming storm shook the Frisians, and among them the Leeuwardeners, because they looked to his arrival as the trampling of laws, the defiling of household gods, the bloodying of the faces of parents and children, and, finally, the violation of divine and human rights, it came about that many families, with greater safety than their domestic troubles allowed, looked to their possessions by flight; and liberty, shut up behind wooden walls, and poured out from the gates and barriers of cities and from the untrustworthy mainland, committed itself to the winds and the sea. Then the Ems and the Weser rivers, crowded with fleets, and exiles, some voluntarily fleeing from the threat of impending wars, settled at Bremen and Emden, because in those places the reformed religion, with Germany conniving and the rulers of that coast permitting it, was held, even before the coming of John à Lasco. Thus, with the confederates driven into exile, Aremberg, thinking the province settled and ordered, set out around the Kalends of July for Transisulania and afterwards for Brabant, where Ferdinand of Alva was expected with the royal army. For the war was being prepared against the unhappy Netherlands; new levies were already under way throughout Germany and Burgundy, and the letters of Francis Avilanus, the royal envoy, intercepted at the court of Charles, king of the French, confirmed this. There were also those who did not ignore that two years earlier, at Bayonne, a treaty between the kings of France and Spain had been renewed; and that Charles, king of France, still a minor and not yet fit to rule, had been taken around the frontier of France, under the pretext of inspecting the boundaries, by his mother Catherine de' Medici, who, with her sister Elisabeth, wife of Philip, arranged the matter, and (as Reidanus relates) under the auspices of the confederate Alva, had entered a new alliance for the suppression of the religion and for mutual aid. Therefore, struck by the terror of Ferdinand of Alva and of the rising war, the princes of the Golden Fleece also held meetings and consulted about the sum of affairs and the danger. There were not lacking those who, amid the arms and the threatening slaughter (for this had been secretly written to Margaret the Regent) even thought of pardon, and judged that the king, out of his kinsmanly clemency, would spare his subjects. Thus the fear that Egmont might leave the Netherlands was occupied by ample possessions, care for his wife and children, and then by a vain and imaginary hope of winning security. Besides, the favour of the soldiers and the glory of the reputation he had won stood in his way, as if the legions would intercede for the man whose commands and victories they had admired in the French war. Orange, however, foreseeing the chances, as dangers crowded round, advised a safer flight, and that a refuge of innocence be sought within the empire of Germany. He had relatives among the princes there, to whom, after the wars of Germany had ended, a long period of peace had given abundance of wealth and convenient help for friends. Nor would there be safe seats or lesser aid in the kingdom of France, since Condé and Coligny held power there, and since Germany had lately supplied its own forces to the same men when they were in difficulties for the same reasons. Then Charles the Emperor, forced by French arms to fair terms, would keep Germany's liberty intact, which it was especially in the interest of France that Philip should not disturb through the Netherlands. Therefore it was better to yield to the necessities of the times and to seek, by obtaining aid from Germany or France, a place of security, than to have one in the unhappy Netherlands, where the Spanish columns were flying in. The other princes, however, judged that arms must be opposed to Philip and a common help raised, which Henry Brederode was preparing through his lordships and other men of the Belgian nobility, to establish the liberty of the fatherland. But the whole undertaking, through the conflicting counsels of the leading men, went forward under unfavourable auspices. From this it came about that, with the forces of the confederates scattered and dispersed, Margaret the Regent, as her governorship was drawing to a close, declared almost all the Netherlands to be subject to the king, and the Roman religion, together with

units.la: Arembergius in Brabantiam.
units.tr: Arembergius into Brabant.

units.la: Principum Aurei Velleris consultatio. cum ornatu templorum reducta. Quæ causa fuit, ut Aurantius magno comitatu Bredam, deìn Dillenburgum concesserit, Henrico Brederodio Principe fœderis Embdam, & deìn Gemam comitatus Scouwenburgici avecto. Quo in loco velut decretâ fugæ, & morti sede post annum nullo hærede extinctus est. Tradit præclarus scriptor Everardus Reidanus, Ioannem Bergæ Marchionem, & Florentium Montmorentium, Montinium, intellecto Ferdinandi Albani adventu, deprecandæ culpæ privatâ legatione in Hispaniam profectos, omnem turbatæ Belgicæ causam in Gulielmum Nassovium Principem Aurantium rejecisse. Tum Segerus Grosbecius, agente per Brabantiam Arembergio, omni intra Flevum Amasumq; Frisiæ regendæ datus, quæsitoresque rerum capitalium Prid. Non. Iul. Leovardiam advenere, ubi tum de more solenne ambubium nundinalibus ferijs habebatur. Scribit Iodocius eosdem cognitores una cum Foccone Rommartio, & rerum criminalium per Brabantiam Prætore isti processui interfuisse, severitatemq; capitalium judiciorum Harlingæ exercitam publicâ religione expiasse. Frieltum quoq; Mularum, & Quirinum Laceium Buranum, toto mundinarum tempore cum cohortibus per urbem præsidio stetisse, quæ rudiore illorum temporum disciplinâ, multis tum ac seditiosis discordijs exponebantur. Quare Grosbecius propè regiam arcem Leovardiæ prætorium erexit, adscitisque in consilium Iacobo Husingio, Foxio Hasseltano, Ioanne Splinterio, Quirino Laceio, cæterisq; militaribus viris, per Henricum Stellinguerfium Prætorem partium litem dirimit. Tum Foxius Hasseltanus, qui Harlingæ præsidium egerat, cohortem suam Bolsuardiam, & post Oldenzelam antiquam Saliorum in Tubantibus sedem ducere jussus, ac Grosbecius cum Petro Dekama habendæ militum recensioni, Groningam profectus est, cui urbi Arembergius, ut antè dixi, sollicitâ ac urgente Margaretâ Gubernatrice, ope Ioannis Mepschij, quatuor Germanicarum cohortium præsidium imposuerat. Quo armilustrio peracto Grosbecius Leovardiam se recepit, convocatoq; de more Senatu bellico duos militum Gerarduni Stuferium, & Beilanum quendam, capitis damnatos vitæ servavit. Mox profectione in Transfulaniam parata Snecam transiens urbem partibus infidam, ubi præsidium jam ante locaverat, tribunos cohortium in Xenodocheium convocavit, expositisq; clàm quæ fieri vellet, navem ingressus & relicto ad lævam lato Vidri ostio sinum Austrinum emensus Campos pervenit, quod oppidum in orâ Isalæ fluminis situm, fatales isti temporum ætati discordiæ agitabant. Credebant Snecenses Grosbecium civilibus ingenijs diffisum, majores copias per Transfulaniam paraturum, grave præsidium, & turbidæ civitati asperius remedium minari. Iam enim civis societate fœderis ardescebat, militem æris egentem insolentia sequebatur. Itaque vulneratis per eum centurionibus & (ut Cl. Franckena tradit) omni lege per inopiam stipendij spreta, factum est, ut Grosbecius compositis per Transfisulaniam rebus festinantius Snecam rediret, nulloque tumultuario milite stipatus & suspicione civium animis exemptâ, è veteri disciplinæ militaris instituto unius facinorosi gregarijque militis sanguine periculosam seditionem componeret. Neq; modestioribus animis per omnem Provinciam ista multitudo utebatur. Ea rapere, auferre, caedes, & juxta incendia dare, odio foederis, ac popularium turbarum, quibus rependi istud enormis praemij debere non dissimulatâ mente, Arembergius judicaverat. Quo Bruxellis agente, continuis agrariorum apud Senatum regium querimonijs, effectum est, ut insolens miles, quem tumultuariè Arembergius reprimendis foederatis collegerat, sacramento cederet, turpiterque & ex flagitio dimissus, Senatus regij lege, & post Edicto Margaretae coërceretur. Ita fluitantibus per Frisiam caeterasque provincias rebus de maturando bello Philippus cogitavit, cuius apparatu Hispania etiam, & Sicilia caeteraeq; Philippi ditiones perstrepebant. Quare veteranae legiones omni ferè Italiae orâ insulisque mediterranei maris evocatae, quas in usum Turcici belli, aut retinendi per ea loca dominatus Carolus Philippusq; reges conscripserant. Tum Insubrum agros lustrandis copijs Ferdinandus Albanus (qui Barcelonâ Genuam Ligustici maris emporium cum triremibus adpulerat) designavit, parumq; à quartanae paroxysmis, doloribusq; articulorum convalescens in Sebaudos, ac Allobroges, dein Burgundiam, & Lotharingos progressus, omnem exercitum (in quo decem Hispanorum millia fuisse Everardus Re danus notat) in agrum Luxemburgicum ditionis Belgicae effudit, tabulasque mandatorum suorum flagitante Margaretâ exhibuit.
units.tr: Consultation of the Princes of the Golden Fleece; with the adornment of the churches restored. This was the reason why Orange departed with a large retinue for Breda, and then for Dillenburg, while Henry Brederode, leader of the confederacy, was carried off to Emden and then to Gemen, in the county of Schaumburg. There, as if in a place decreed for flight and death, he died a year later without an heir. The distinguished writer Everardus Reidanus relates that John, Marquis of Berg, and Florence of Montmorency, lord of Montigny, when they learned of Ferdinand of Alva's arrival, set out for Spain on a private embassy to plead for pardon, and laid the whole cause of the troubled Netherlands on William of Nassau, Prince of Orange. Then Segerus Grosbecius, with Aremberg acting through Brabant, was given authority over the whole of Friesland between the Vlie and the Ems, and the judges of capital cases arrived at Leeuwarden on the day before the Nones of July, when, according to the solemn custom, the fair of the mummers was being held in the festival days of the market. Jodocius writes that these investigators, together with Focco Rommartius, and the praetor of criminal affairs throughout Brabant, took part in that proceeding, and that the severity of the capital judgments exercised at Harlingen was atoned for by public religious rites. He also says that Frieltus Mularus and Quirinus Lacius of Buren had stood with their cohorts as a guard throughout the city for the whole time of the fair, which in that rougher discipline of those times was exposed to many quarrels and seditious disputes. Therefore Grosbecius erected a praetorium near the royal citadel at Leeuwarden, and, taking into council Jacob Husingius, Foxius of Hasselt, John Splinter, Quirinus Lacius, and other military men, settled the dispute of the parties through Henry Stellingwerf, the praetor. Then Foxius of Hasselt, who had commanded the garrison at Harlingen, was ordered to lead his cohort to Bolsward, and afterwards to Oldenzaal, the ancient seat of the Salii among the Tubantes; and Grosbecius, with Peter Dekama, set out for Groningen to hold a review of the soldiers, a city to which Aremberg, as I said above, at the urgent request of Margaret the Regent, had assigned a garrison of four German cohorts through the help of John Mepschius. When this review of arms was finished, Grosbecius returned to Leeuwarden, and, the war-senate being convened according to custom, he spared the lives of two soldiers, Gerard Stufferius and a certain Beilanus, who had been condemned to death. Soon afterwards, as the departure for Transisulania was being prepared, he crossed to Sneek, a city hostile to his party, where he had already placed a garrison, and summoned the tribunes of the cohorts to the hospice; and, having explained secretly what he wished to be done, he boarded a ship, left the wide mouth of the Vlie to the left, sailed through the southern bay, and reached the Campen, a town situated on the bank of the river Isala, which the fatal discords of that age were troubling. The people of Sneek believed that Grosbecius, distrusting the civil temperament, would bring greater forces through Transisulania, and threatened a heavy garrison and a harsher remedy for the disturbed city. For already the citizens were burning with the confederacy's association, and insolence followed the soldier who lacked pay. Therefore, after the centurions had been wounded by his men, and (as Cl. Franckena relates) every law had been disregarded because of the lack of wages, it came about that Grosbecius, having settled matters throughout Transisulania, returned more quickly to Sneek, and, accompanied by no tumultuous soldiers, and with the suspicion of the citizens removed from their minds, by the ancient military custom of putting one criminal and common soldier to death, he quelled the dangerous sedition. Nor did this multitude behave with more moderate spirits throughout the whole province. Aremberg had judged that they seized, carried off, murdered, and at the same time set fires, from hatred of the confederacy and of the popular disturbances, by which, as he did not conceal in his mind, this enormous reward ought to be repaid. While he was acting at Brussels, the constant complaints of the farmers before the royal senate brought it about that the insolent soldiers whom Aremberg had gathered in disorder to repress the confederates were discharged from their oath, and, dismissed with disgrace and infamy, were restrained by the law of the royal senate and afterwards by an edict of Margaret. Thus, with affairs wavering throughout Friesland and the other provinces, Philip thought of hastening the war; and by his preparations Spain as well as Sicily and the other lordships of Philip resounded. Therefore the veteran legions were called from almost the whole coast of Italy and the islands of the Mediterranean, which Charles and Philip, the kings, had enrolled for use in the Turkish war or for keeping their dominion in those places. Then Ferdinand of Alva, who had brought triremes from Barcelona to Genoa, the emporium of the Ligurian sea, appointed the fields of the Insubrians for the review of his troops; and, scarcely recovering from the fits of the quartan fever and the pains of his joints, he advanced into Savoy and the Allobroges, then into Burgundy and Lorraine, and poured his whole army (in which Everardus Reidanus notes there were ten thousand Spaniards) into the Luxembourg territory of the Belgian lordship, and at Margaret's demand displayed the tables of his orders.

units.la: Strada notat in exercitu Albani octo peditum millia, & septingentos, equites mille & ducentos fuisse, Margaretamq; Duci adhuc per Insubriam agenti de attenuando exercitu scripsisse, minuendo terrori, & ne partes jam pacatis & resumptis obsequijs mites ad virtutum sicuti mos est, aut propellendam immanissimi ducis asperitatem resuscitaret. Hoc quoq; creditum fuit, metuisse Margaretam imperij sui & plus quam muliebris prudentiae fructum periturum, si ferox Dux, & mandato, quod dedisse fratrem inconsulto impetu arguebat, subnixus atq; superbiens tantis cum copijs Alpium summitate descendens, Belgarum fines ac provincias ingrediatur, destructurus per vim & arma, quicquid illa consilio, & sagacitate profecisset. Neq; enim alia sperari posse, quam quod praeter colluviem, quae castra sequi solet, nobilium scortorum lixarumq; peritissimos belli, & clarissimos omnium gentium Duces, militesq; severitati admoturus sit, surrepturus sibi omnem gloriam, quâ fratri, & ut tacitè in litteris arguebat, ingrato provincias asseruisset. Igitur Margareta, etsi omnia, sicut in aulâ fieri solet, simulatione tegerentur, quo Caroli V. filiae, & sorori regiae quid honoris daret, in palatio regio salutatâ veteranos, quos Provincijs induxerat, per praesidia dispos​uit, indignantibus civitatum rectoribus ac legatis, tam aspera Praefecturae initia, & invidiosam autoritatem, etiam gratulantibus assentantibusq; ex metu se ostendere. Ferunt duras superbasq; voces ex ipsius ore auditas, omnium rerum, quae eminentissimae dignitatis forent, arbitrium protulisse, traditumq; sibi à Philippo per Belgicam Frisiosq; summum imperium haud obscuris indicijs declarasse Bruxellis. Traditumq; sibi à Philippo summum rerum per Belgicam Frisiosq; imperium haud obscuris indicijs ostendit. Margaretam quippe dominatus exsortem modicis tantum vulgaribusq; negotijs praefuturam solam imperij umbram, atq; imaginem retinuisse. Sibi curam Magi-strastratuum civiliumq; functionum commissam, quibus privare modicè suspectos queat, facili censurâ, sed quæ vitæ necisque potestatem includat. LXVII. Ad hæc urbes infidas & rebellium exemplis inhærentes arcibus armisq; coërcere, omniaq; posse facere, quæ retinendam ad pacem regisq; sui jus tutandum conducerent.
units.tr: Strada notes that Albano's army had eight thousand seven hundred infantry and twelve hundred cavalry. He also writes that Margaret, while the Duke was still travelling through Insubria, had written to him about reducing the army, so as to lessen alarm and to keep the provinces, now pacified and back in obedience, from being stirred up again, as is customary, or from reviving the harshness of that most savage duke, which they had only just thrust off. It was also believed that Margaret feared that the fruit of her rule, and more than womanly prudence, would perish if the fierce Duke, relying on his commission, which her brother had given him in what she charged was a rash impulse, and puffed up with pride, came down from the crest of the Alps with so great a force and entered the frontiers and provinces of the Belgians, to destroy by force and arms whatever she had achieved by counsel and shrewdness. For nothing else could be expected, since he would bring to bear on his severity, besides the rabble that usually follows an army, the most skilled nobles, prostitutes and camp-sutlers, and the most famous generals and soldiers of every nation. He would snatch for himself all the glory which, as she hinted in her letters, he had won for her brother, an ungrateful man, in the provinces. Therefore Margaret, although everything was concealed by pretence, as is usual at court, in order to show what honour she gave to the sister of Charles V and daughter of the king, greeted him in the royal palace. She posted the veterans whom she had brought into the provinces through the garrisons, while the magistrates and envoys of the cities were indignant at such harsh beginnings of the governorship and at its hateful authority, and showed themselves to be congratulating and fawning only out of fear. They report that harsh and proud words were heard from her own mouth: that the decision on all matters of the highest dignity rested with her, and that the supreme power over the Netherlands and Frisia had been handed over to her by Philip, which she declared at Brussels by no obscure signs. The supreme power over the Netherlands and Frisia, handed over to her by Philip, she showed by no obscure signs. For Margaret, excluded from the exercise of rule, would preside only over minor and ordinary business, and would keep only the shadow and image of power. The care of the magistrates and civil offices was committed to her, by which she could remove those moderately suspected, with an easy censure, yet one which would embrace the power of life and death. Moreover, she could restrain by fortresses and arms the cities that were faithless and clung to the examples of the rebels, and could do everything that would serve to keep the peace and to defend the right of her king.

units.la: Dein sub exitum mensis Septembris Ioannes Carolus Antverpius, & Levinus Everardus in suprema Mechliniensi Curiâ Senator, Leovardiam iterum à Margareta missi. Iis datum in mandatis erat, Se- natum per Frisiam regium secretum sui officij commonefaciendi, quo in exules, profugosque & eorum bona è decreto regis statueretur. Alij credidere, progresso jam in Belgicam cum exercitu Albano, eos copiam mandatorum, quæ à Philippo rege Ferdinandus Albanus acceperat, clàm attulisse, litterisque Margaretæ munitos durius administrandi per Frisiam imperij præscriptum regio Senatui exhibuisse. Ioannes Carolus vir ob peritiam legum à morte Iulij Gelij (qui tum vitâ concesserat) procuratoris fisci, eidem tum Gelio surrogatus est. Qui annus ut Frisicæ libertati maximè climactericus, ita annonæ exitialis fuit. Quippe Sole Tropicum Cancri ingresso, post Caniculæ exortu effervescens aër, tantâ, & tam continua siccitate attactus est, ut tostæ per ardorem fruges uredine syderis marcescerent, ruptâque velut naturæ lege nullo fere imbre, aut pluviâ fluens æstas annonæ proventum accideret. Quamobrem Margareta Gubernatrix spreta & seposita Agrariorum Oppidanorumque lite postremo (quod in Frisiam misit) Edicto, asservari per Provinciam frumenta jussit, ne patente in vicina loco commercio, ut ante inclementiam cæli, ita caritatem frugum inops & egena plebes sentiret. Jam enim Ferdinandus Albanus crudele, & præterox imperium gerendis rebus applicabat, instarq; feræ Belgicam velut saltum prædæ fæcundum ingressus, rudimenta durioris virilisq; imperij mulicbribus lenbusque Margaretæ consilijs obtendebat. Molles quippe à sexu fæminarum animos esse, pace aut secundis rebus nonnunquam imperio pares, ingruente verò procellâ rerum oneri & periculis succumbentes. Nunc verò exedentibus viscera ulceribus asperam manum admovendam, depurgandamq; impuri corporis sentinam validiore cataræctico, ut integris adhuc partibus vigor suus, & vis spirantis moventisque animæ constet, cæteras malo contactas, & vitiatas per consensum ignis, aut ferrum absumat. Adultos Belgicæ morbos extrema remedia exposcere. Id Philippo Regi, id sanctissimæ Inquisitioni placuisse, quorum uni parere majestas veri legitimiq; Principis, alteri verò veneratio numinis compellat. Itaq; Ferdinandus Albanus à restaurandis (quæ Carolus Philippusq; Reges sanxerant) Edictis, im- perium orsus, Senatum quoque capitalium rerum constituit, istiqueiudicum consessui Præsidem se designavit. Post Lamoralium Egmondanum, & Philippum Montmorentium Hornanum velut ad consilium vocatos, in secretum conclave sevocari, discinctosque contra jus Ordinis & inani obtestatione usos in custodiam dari jussit. Traditum litteris est Albanum invidiâ gloriæ (quam Lamoralius Egmondanus Gallico bello sibi pepererat,) correptum, id mandati à Philippo rege clam accepisse, eidemq; Egmondano, (ut & Aurantio ac Hornano)
units.tr: Then, toward the end of September, John Charles of Antwerp and Levinus Everardus, a senator of the supreme Court of Mechlin, were sent again to Leeuwarden by Margaret. They were instructed to remind the Frisian royal Senate of its duty concerning the decree of the king, by which the exiles and fugitives and their goods were to be dealt with. Others believed that, since Albano's army had already advanced into the Netherlands, these men had secretly brought the copy of the commissions which Ferdinand of Alva had received from King Philip, and, armed with Margaret's letters, had shown the royal Senate the more severe regulations for governing Frisia. John Charles, a man famed for legal skill, was put in place of Julius Gelius, the fiscal procurator, who had died at that time; he was appointed to succeed Gelius. That year, the most critical for Frisian liberty, was also deadly for the grain supply. For when the sun entered the tropic of Cancer, and the air grew hot after the rising of the Dog Star, it was struck by such a dry and continuous drought that the grain, scorched by the heat, withered from the burning of the star, and, as if the law of nature had been broken, the summer, almost without rain or showers, brought a poor harvest. Therefore Margaret, the Governess, setting aside and putting off the quarrel between the landowners and the townsmen, at last sent an edict into Frisia ordering that the grain be kept back within the province, so that, with trade opened to neighbouring places, the poor and needy common people should not feel the dearth of food as they had felt the harshness of the weather. For Ferdinand of Alva was already applying a cruel and premature rule to affairs, and, entering the Netherlands like a beast into a fruitful forest of prey, he put forward the beginnings of a harsher and manlier rule as an excuse for the soft counsels of Margaret and women. Women's minds, they said, are soft by nature, and in peace or prosperity sometimes equal to rule, but when a storm breaks they yield under the burden of affairs and its dangers. Now, however, with ulcers eating into the vitals, a rough hand must be applied, and the filth of the impure body must be purged with a stronger caustic, so that its vigour and the force of the breathing and moving soul may remain in the parts still whole, while the others, touched and corrupted by contagion, are consumed by fire or iron. The grave diseases of the Netherlands, he said, demanded the last remedies. This had pleased King Philip and the most holy Inquisition, of whom the one compels obedience by the majesty of a true and lawful prince, and the other by reverence for the divine power. So Ferdinand of Alva, beginning his rule by restoring the edicts which Kings Charles and Philip had enacted, also set up a senate for capital cases, and he appointed himself president of the assembly of these judges. After Lamoral of Egmont and Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn, had been summoned as if to a council, he ordered them to be called aside into a private chamber, and, stripped of their swords, contrary to the law of the Order and after using a useless protest, to be placed in custody. It is recorded that Alva, seized with envy at the glory which Lamoral of Egmont had won in the French war, had secretly received an order from King Philip, and had brought from Spain the sentence of death for Egmont, as well as for Orange and Horn, and the chosen executioner.

units.la: N nano) ex Hispania sententiam mortis, & destinati percussoris attulisse. LXVII. Igitur Margareta Gubernatrix sagax faemina, & ut ex Albani odio gratiam captaret, mense Sept. de assignatâ Ferdinando Albano potestate latius apud Frisios per litteras expositi, ipsaque aemulatione, ut Demetrius tradit, ergà Ferdinandum Albanum, aut taedio imperij ducta, missionem flagitavit. Quâ post impetrata, ne insalutatis provincialibus Italiani reviseret, v. Eid. Decemb. ad Ordines, Senatumque per Frisiam regium litteras misit, quibus seriem, molestiamque gestarum à se rerum exponebat: A pacis quippe, foederisque Gallici pactione Belgicae Frisiisque se praefuisse, veteri Principum faeminarum exemplo, quas aetate, aut bello olim compeditus Carolus Caesar moderamini rerum admovisset. Ita primis Caroli annis Margaretam amitam, dein adulto jam Principe, & Germaniae Imperium adepto Mariam sororem Provincijs praefectas magnarum etiam rerum capacem muliebrem sexum ostendisse. Caeterum omne imperij onus in spem Regij adventus à se susceптum, quem in Belgicam suam celerare primo, quo ipsa voluisset, tempore, Turcarum arma, ac infidae Maurorum per Hispaniam res vetuissent. Istâ occasione usurpatum sibi diuturnius imperium, quo, etiam surgente per Belgicam tempestate, se non abdicasset, adjuta quam maximè eorum consilijs, qui in partium novarum societates aegrius pertrahebantur. Quare nec spes suas redeundi in Italiam, nec Octavij mariti desideria explevisse, quin curasse potius, ut ad Ecclesiam Romanam, ac reverentiam regis licentiosa nonullorum ingenia redirent. Hoc modo bonum publicum domesticâ consuetudine ac matrimonij dulcedine sanctius habitum opimos post imperio suo fructus sedatam Belgicam attulisse. Quâ ipsâ quoque excedere medio in cursu rerum mens adhuc, neque consilium fuisset, nisi praeter fragilitatem sexus continua invaletudo infirmum corpus labefactaret. Hanc causam maturati discessus, & longarum apud Philippum precum fuisse, quae multo post tempore tantum valuissent, ut secuturus propediem Rex Ferdinandum Albanum in provincias cum imperio praemiserit, quod hac significatione, dum in consessu Ordinum non liceret, se deponere testaretur. Ita valere Frisios jussit, ac III. Kal. Ian. Belgicâ excessit octennis imperij, & compositae fermè tempestatis gloriam suo Octavio reportans. Mox à discessu Margaretae, velut amotâ consorte rerum, Ferdinandus Albanus in promiscuam saevitiem effusus, publica loca civili foederatoq; sanguine implevit, nefariumq; excindendae reformatae multitudini faedus, ut ante Cambresij, ita postmodum Baionae ictum optimus istiusmodi rerum minister executus est. Quare ne per Galliam, intestino bello tum flagrantem exules Belgae cessante domestico questu foris sustentandae vitae stipendia facerent, omnes Condaei militiam secutos edicto revocavit, auxiliaq; insuper è Baionae pacto promissa Catharinae Medicae addixit, quae Florentinae gentis faemina, per aetatem impuberis filij in procuratione regni tum erat. Tum ut melius res per Galliam procederent, ipse Albanus ducturum se auxilia promisit, quae nec tanta in Galliae regnum simul effundi, nec tam validò, & ambitioso exercitus Duce Catharina Medicaea verspellis faemina volebat. Hoc modo modestè repulsus Albanus, Ioanni Lignaeo Arem-
units.tr: Therefore Margaret, the Governess, a shrewd woman, and, in order to win favour by Alva's hatred, in September requested her release from the power assigned to Ferdinand of Alva, which she set out at greater length in letters to the Frisians, and which was driven either by rivalry with Ferdinand of Alva itself, as Demetrius reports, or by weariness of rule. When this was granted, so that she would not return to Italy without bidding farewell to the provincials, she sent on the 5th day before the Ides of December letters to the Orders and to the royal Senate in Frisia, in which she set out the course and the troubles of the affairs she had handled. For she had presided over the Netherlands and Frisia since the treaty of peace and the French alliance, after the manner of the earlier princesses whom Charles Caesar, when hindered by age or by war, had put in charge of government. Thus in the early years of Charles, she had shown his aunt Margaret, and later, when the prince had grown up and obtained the empire of Germany, his sister Mary, set over the provinces, a woman's sex capable of great affairs. Moreover, she said, she had taken up the whole burden of rule in hope of the king's arrival, which the Turkish arms and the faithless Moors in Spain had prevented him from hastening to his Netherlands at the time she herself would have wished. On that occasion, she said, she had assumed a longer rule, which she would not have laid down even when a storm had risen in the Netherlands, aided as she was by the counsels of those who were more reluctantly drawn into the associations of the new parties. Therefore, she said, she had satisfied neither her hopes of returning to Italy nor the longings of her husband Octavio; rather she had taken care that the licentious minds of some would return to the Roman Church and to reverence for the king. In this way, she said, by holding the public good more sacred than domestic habit and the sweetness of marriage, she had brought Belgium, now calmed, the rich fruits of her rule. Even in this course of affairs her mind had not yet, nor had her purpose, been to withdraw, had not the constant ill health, beyond the weakness of her sex, weakened her infirm body. This was the reason for her hastened departure, and for her long prayers to Philip, which after a long time prevailed so far that the king, about to follow shortly, sent Ferdinand of Alva ahead into the provinces with the command, by which she declared that she would lay down her office, since it was not permitted to do so in the assembly of the Orders. Thus she bade the Frisians farewell, and on the 3rd day before the Kalends of January she left Belgium, after eight years of rule, bearing away for her Octavio the glory of a tempest now almost quieted. Soon after Margaret's departure, as if a partner in affairs had been removed, Ferdinand of Alva poured himself out in indiscriminate cruelty, filling public places with civil and confederate blood. He carried out, as the most excellent minister of such deeds, the impious league for the destruction of the reformed multitude, which had been struck at Cambrai before and afterwards at Bayonne. Therefore, lest the Belgian exiles, while there was no longer domestic complaint, should earn their living abroad through France, then aflame with civil war, he recalled by an edict all who had followed Condé into the army, and he pledged the auxiliaries, promised by the Bayonne agreement, to Catherine de' Medici, who, a woman of the Florentine people, was then managing the kingdom during the minority of her son. Then, so that affairs might go better in France, Alva himself promised that he would lead the auxiliaries; yet Catherine de' Medici, a woman, did not want so great a force poured into the kingdom of France at once, nor one led so powerfully and ambitiously by a general. Thus Alva, modestly rebuffed, entrusted to John Ligne, Count of Aremberg, the prefect of Frisia, the leading of the auxiliaries into France, in which there were two thousand infantry and fifteen hundred cavalry.

units.la: Arembergio Frisiæ Præfecto, ducenda in Galliam auxilia demandavit, in quibus duo peditum millia, equitum mille & quingenti habebantur. Quæ expeditio ne improsperè succederet, Prid. Non. Ian. triduanæ supplicationes, & amburbiorum ritus Leovardiæ instituti, ut solennium votorum nuncupationibus repurgando à reformatis Galliæ regno, susceptum negotium promoveretur. Neque minoribus erga fœderatos odijs per ipsam etiam Frisiam Ferdinandus Albanus grassabatur. Is namque datis ad Senatum regium litteris, omnes singulosque exulum (quorum nomine consulares viros, & profugam præcipuè Nobilitatem censebat) Bruxellas ad iii. Eid Febr. evocavit, ac ad dicendam causam adesse Educto jussit, quod v. & iv. Eid. Ian. ad campani æris sonum pro rostris recitatum concivium animos non parum commovit. Eo comprehensum erat, ut citati, nisi se sisterent, pro convictis haberentur, contumaciumque ac profugorum bona publicæ auctioni, & Fisco regio subessent. Idem dies xii. Kalend. Febr. per Benedictum Francetum apparitorem regij Senatus, viro Nobili Edoni Heringa, & Cornelio Fouckio Tribuno nuper ærarij dictus, locandarumque ædium potestas, quibus exules Leovardij profugerant, Thesaurario per Frisiam regio data. Tum stipendia per Hispanum quendam à Ferdinando Albano Leovardiam missum, militi assignata, militariumq; cohortium recensio Oldehovæ facta. Scribit Iodocius earundem cohortium tribunos à peculatu immunes non fuisse, multosq; per egestatem, & penuriam æris nomina professos, isti recensioni interfuisse. Idem tradit, circa ea tempora militem quendam, qui Arembergium Præfectum glande in Galliâ ictum nuntiabat, à Quirino Laceio captum, ac de sententiâ regij Senatus virgis cæsum, validumq; incendium non procul Hoca ac Haionis Cammingani domo subortum ope civium militumque; qui in armis erant, repressum fuisse. Dein postrid. Non. Mart. Leovardiæ Tarquinij Vallesij viri Consularis nomen ex oppidanâ Curiâ per Edictum recitatum, quo noxij turbatæ civitatis motus, & receptio novi fæderis, ac simul religionis, ilti viro tanquam moderatori omnium rerum imputabantur. Per eum conciliabula populi imperata, conventusque collegiorum instituros, ut consilium facilegio commodaret, templaque ac cœnobia nefandà civilium furorum intemperie vastarentur. Prohibitum urbe regium militem, spectante & indignante ipso Arembergio, & portarum custodiam militi extortam, ac seditioso civi commissam. Ductos in subsellia novos sacrorum Doctores, & arma ipsis quoq; templis inlata, quæ non nisi jussu Principis, & pro eius defensione haberi possent. Illi semel sacramenta dicta, illi nuncupatas supplicationes, ne desciscere quis à Philippo præterquam perduellis posset. Quapropter mandare ut Tarquinius Vallesius ad iii. Kal. Aprîl. dein vii. & xiv. diem Bruxellis coram Ferdinando Albano compareat, rationem suorum factorum redditurus. Reperio in Historicis fragmentis clarissimi scriptoris A: Franckenæ, ijs ferè temporibus fœderatos nonnullos, & seorsim Anabaptistas (quod Anno 1565. etiam evenerat) supplicijs affectos, aliosq; squallore funesti carceris aut metu mortis absumptos, vitam finisse. Inquisitores quoque ante ex pacto ablegatos, in Provinciam tum reductos, ctò. Io. ductos, asperisq; edictis annuos exulum reditus interceptos. Horren-da quoque proscriptionis perduellionisque vocabula per Frisiam audita, durante avitâ libertate, à Francorum quoque temporibus, nostris majoribus ignorata, & cum robusto Principis imperio introducta, repertis ingenijs, quae curas patrum, & sanctissimas pro retinendâ libertate sollicitudines, calumniâ teterrimi criminis fœdarent. Unde in vicinis cæterisque locis factum est, ut summâ velut animorum desperatione (cum innocens quisque à supplicio, aut saltem eius metu immunis vix haberetur) relictâ domo, ac familiâ, urbibus pagisque excederent, agrestiumque ac barbarorum more, sylvis clausi ferinam belluinamque vitam latrocinijs simul ac flagitijs sustentarent. Quod ne per Frisiam fieret, quæ magnis arboretorum spatijs in Austrum se effundit, Edicto Albanus cavit, hominesque vitæ ac fortunarum incertos, à vindicandâ temporum iniquitate revocare conatus est. Quamobrem & Edicto Anni MDLXVI. xii. Kal. Maii. renovato, ullas copias intra Flevum Amasumq; flumina colligi, autorarique sub pænâ capitis vetuit, exulumque ac profugorum bona per Ioannem Carolum Senatorem fisco adjudicavit. Iussit quoque ut exulum cognati, propinquiq;, tum actuarij publici apud Prætorem Judicemvé, omnium bonorum, actionum, obligationum, pignorum, redituumq; profcsionem, sub pænâ legis, facerent, deque exulum statu ac conditione, Martinum Bergium fisci quæstorem docerent. In sacerdotum quoque religionem, mores, atque vitam asperè inquiri fecit, interdictâque ijs matrimonij societate, & omni quoque concubinatu damnato, cælibatus & continentiæ legem inculcavit. Id verò asperrimè vetabat; Ne cum perduellibus (ita enim Edictum habebat) ullum commercium esset, & ne mariti patrijs terris extrusi onera exilij solatijs conjugum levarent. Quapropter fœminas ad maritos commeare, sub pænâ fustigationis, prohibuit, deprehensosq; exulum custodiæ dari, & puniri ex Edictis præcepit. Sic ut domi oppressâ per vim patriâ intuta mansio, ita deligentibus exilia mutationes sedium, aditus atque itinera præcludebantur. Jumenta quoq;, navigia, & currus infpectoribus expositi, quo deferentium patriam consilia Senatus regius perverteret, & ne fœviendi materies multitudine fugientium minueretur. Mare etiam navigantibus invium quod præsidiariæ naves, aut plurimæ triremium per æstuaria vicini maris, aut ostia fluminum spargerentur. Quare & per omne Frisiæ confinium sparsi exules, præclusâ veniæ spe, rati, quod res erat, gloriosius fore bello miseriam finire, quam æternâ exilij sorte multari, divisi ante & palantes multis in locis confertim confluxere, communicatisque consilijs retundendam Philippi, præfectorumq; sævitiem, justis armis decrevere. Neque enim de jure armorum longum differebatur, apud homines gnaros, in quâ nati essent, suæ libertatis, & juxta immanis injuriæ, quâ peregrinis in terris inter ignotas facies trahere vitam cogerentur, honestâ fere morte peiorem. Idcircò Legatos ad Aurantium Dillenburgum mittere, ut bellum paret, promittere subsidia, & residuas adhuc in exilio vires, modo fœderatis socijsque Ducem se præbeat, quibus placuisset, aut fortiter in armis occumbere, aut dulcissimam patriam semel videre à tyrannis liberatam. Sed Principem Auran-
units.tr: He entrusted to Arenberg, governor of Friesland, the leading of auxiliary troops into France. Among them were two thousand foot and fifteen hundred horse. So that this expedition would not turn out unsuccessfully, three days of supplications were ordered on the 4th of January, and a rite of processions around the walls was instituted at Leeuwarden, so that by solemn vows the kingdom of France might be cleansed of the Reformed and the undertaking begun might be advanced. Nor did Ferdinand Alva rage with lesser hatred against the confederates, even throughout Friesland itself. For by letters sent to the royal Council, he summoned all and each of the exiles (among whom he counted men of consular rank, and above all the fugitive nobility) to Brussels by the 3rd of the Ides of February, and by edict ordered them to appear to plead their case. This, read out from the rostra at the sound of the bell on the 5th and 4th of the Ides of January, stirred the minds of the citizens not a little. It was included in the edict that those summoned, unless they presented themselves, would be held as convicted, and that the goods of the contumacious and the fugitives would be liable to public auction and to the royal treasury. On the same day, the 12th before the Kalends of February, through Benedict Francetus, attendant of the royal Council, it was declared to the noble Edo Heringa and to Cornelius Fouck, recently tribune of the treasury, and the power of letting the houses from which the exiles had fled at Leeuwarden was granted to the royal treasurer for Friesland. Then pay was assigned to the soldiers through a certain Spaniard sent to Leeuwarden by Ferdinand Alva, and a review of the military cohorts was held at Oldehove. Jodocus writes that the tribunes of these cohorts were not free from embezzlement, and that many, through poverty and lack of money, having given in their names, took part in that review. He also relates that about this time a certain soldier, who announced that the governor Arenberg had been struck by a bullet in France, was seized by Quirinus Laceius and, by sentence of the royal Council, beaten with rods; and that a violent fire which broke out not far from Hoca, at the house of Haio Cammingha, was suppressed by the help of the citizens and the soldiers who were under arms. Then, on the day after the Nones of March, at Leeuwarden, the name of Tarquinius Vallesius, a man of consular rank, was read out from the town hall by edict, by which the harmful disturbances of the commonwealth, the admission of the new covenant and at the same time of the new religion, were imputed to that man as the director of all affairs. It was charged that through him meetings of the people were ordered and assemblies of the guilds were to be set up, so that he lent his counsel to sacrilege, and that churches and monasteries were laid waste by the unspeakable excess of civil frenzy. The royal soldiery was barred from the city, while Arenberg himself looked on indignantly, and the guard of the gates was wrested from the soldiers and entrusted to a seditious citizen. New teachers of sacred things were led to the benches, and arms were brought into the churches themselves, which could be held only by the prince's order and for his defence. Those men once took oaths, those men pronounced vows of supplication, so that no one could revolt from Philip except as a traitor. Wherefore he ordered that Tarquinius Vallesius should appear at Brussels before Ferdinand Alva on the 3rd before the Kalends of April, and again on the 7th and 14th days, to render an account of his deeds. I find in the historical fragments of the most distinguished writer A. Francken that about these times some of the confederates, and separately the Anabaptists (which had also happened in the year 1565), were put to death with torments, and others were worn away by the squalor of a deadly prison or by fear of death, and ended their lives. Inquisitors, too, who had previously been sent away under the agreement, were then brought back into the Province and led (...), and by harsh edicts the yearly returns of the exiles were cut off. The dreadful words of proscription and treason also began to be heard throughout Friesland. These words were unknown to our ancestors while their ancestral liberty endured, nor were they known from the time of the Franks; they were introduced together with the robust rule of the prince, and devised by inventive minds, which would defile the cares of the fathers and their most holy anxieties for preserving liberty with the calumny of the foulest crime. Whence it came about in neighbouring and other places that, in a kind of utter despair of mind (since scarcely anyone innocent was thought free from punishment, or at least from fear of it), they left home and family, departed from towns and villages, and, after the manner of rustics and barbarians, shut up in the woods, sustained a brutish and beast-like life by robbery and crime alike. To prevent this from happening in Friesland, which stretches southward over wide tracts of woodland, Alva provided by edict, and he tried to recall men uncertain of their life and fortune from avenging the injustice of the times. Therefore, renewing the edict of the year 1566 on the 12th before the Kalends of May, he forbade any troops to be gathered or hired between the rivers Flie and Ems, under pain of death, and he adjudged the goods of the exiles and fugitives to the treasury through the councillor Johannes Carolus. He also ordered that the relatives and kinsfolk of the exiles, and then the public clerks before the praetor or judge, should make a declaration of all goods, actions, obligations, pledges and revenues under penalty of law, and should inform the treasury quaestor Martin Bergius about the status and condition of the exiles. He also had the religion, morals and life of the priests strictly examined, and, forbidding them the fellowship of marriage and condemning every concubinage, he enforced the law of celibacy and continence. But he most harshly forbade that there should be any dealings with traitors (for so the edict called them), and that husbands driven out of their native lands should lighten the burden of exile with the comfort of their wives. Wherefore he forbade women to go to their husbands, under penalty of flogging, and ordered that those caught be handed over to custody and punished under the edicts. Thus, as the homeland was oppressed by force and staying at home was made unsafe, so for those choosing exile, changes of residence, approaches and roads were closed off. Beasts of burden, boats and carts were also put under inspectors, so that the royal Council might defeat the plans of those who would carry people out of the country, and so that the material for cruelty would not be lessened by the multitude of fugitives. The sea, too, was made impassable for sailors, since guard ships, or many galleys, were scattered through the estuaries of the neighbouring sea or at the mouths of rivers. Hence the exiles, scattered through every border of Friesland, with the hope of pardon shut off, judging (as was the case) that it would be more glorious to end their misery by war than to be punished with the eternal lot of exile, having been divided and wandering in many places, flocked together in crowds, and, having shared their plans, resolved to repress the cruelty of Philip and his governors with just arms. For among men who knew into what liberty they had been born, the right of arms was not long deferred; close to it lay the monstrous injustice by which they were forced to lead, in foreign lands among unknown faces, a life almost worse than an honourable death. Therefore they resolved to send envoys to Orange at Dillenburg, to prepare for war, to promise help and the forces still left in exile, provided he would show himself leader to the confederates and allies, who had resolved either to fall bravely in arms or to see their dearest country, once freed from tyrants, one time more. But the Prince of Orange

units.la: Legati ad Aurantium ultrò circumspectum & onera bellorum serio expendentem, multæ causæ, & inter has magnitudo hostium, & infirmitas oppressæ patriæ remorabantur. Adhæc imperium Germaniæ dubium, Cæsarem Maximilianum naturâ mitem, & nuper in Philippi aulâ missō in Hispaniam Carolo fratre male exceptum, Principes propinquos communis periculi metuentes, & impulsas magnopere exulum res criminabatur. Quin prolatandum potius bellum esse, dum defectio urbium quarundam Belgicæ habeatur, surgantque in ipsis patriæ visceribus validæ partes Philippi imperijs adversæ. Tum quippe opportuna exulum sociorumque auxilia fore, si domesticis populi armis externa se junxerint, omnesque confestim robur se aperiat geminatis viribus pugnaturum. Quo Aurantij consilio belli quoque apparatus tam diu protractus est, donec inritâ omni, etiam Cæsaris Electorumque Imperij intercessione, post Philippum filium Secreto literarum extractum, & in Hispaniam abductum, ipse Bruxellas cum cæteris proceribus ab Albano evocatus, proscriptusque, suarum rerum & principis famæ, iteratisque exulum precibus motus, bellum decerneret. Quare Principum propinquorumque societatibus subnixus, Ioanneque Nassovio fratre, & ærario exulum (qui Embdam, Bremam atque Vesaliam Clivorum plurimi è Frisiâ profugerant) adjutus armis experiri statuit, Ludovicumque Nassovium fratrem, ac Gulielmum Bergensem habendis delectibus militum præfecit, quos Bergensis per Geldriam ac vicina loca, Ludovicus in superiore Germaniâ autorabat. Ita coactas tumultuariè copias expediri per Hasiae, ac Westphaliae fines jussit, Ludovicumque fratrem in Transamasanos Frisios amandavit, certus è majoribus Frisijs (qui Flevo Lavicâque terminantur) prompta auxilia adfore, & istius orae nobilitatem ultrò mobilem in partem resurgentis iterum fœderis concessuram. Quare Ludovicus Embdam, urbem in ripâ Amasi fluminis sitam, ingressus, commeatum sibi paravit, copiasque Amasum fluvium transvexit, quem orto etiam Æquinoctij verni fydere, ac primo quoque Aprili (ut & per Frisiam lacus ac incilia) glacie obtectum fuisse, in notis suis Ioannes Tiara Iureconsultus annotavit. Fossam quoque Leovardiæ urbis ternis quaternisq; viris transitum dedisse, absumptisque pecorum pabulis, magnâ fæni penuriâ & simul caritate Frisiam laborasse. Sic traducto per Amasum milite, & in Reiderium agrum expositō, magna per urbem Leovardiam civilium animorum trepidatio fuit. Nam Pontificius quisque deprædicare periculum, ac non obstantibus Paschalibus feriis (quæ in vigesimum April. diem tum incidebant) sarcinas, ac vasa colligere, & mox fugam parare, quam solæ stationes militum ad portas excubantium præpediebant. Illi confirmare animos, promittere securitatem, non esse eam fœderati exercitus magnitudinem, ut ad urbem adventurus sit, tot passuum mill. & intervallis locorum à Ludovico discretam. Intermediam adhuc Groningam urbem validam, & præsidio regio firmam, superandos Ludovico amnes, & locorum difficultates esse, quæ regijs adhuc copijs teneantur. Manendum itaque intra conseptum urbis, & rejecto levi periculo, imitandum esse exemplum fortibus viris semper usitatum, qui corpora & dexteras suas telæ
units.tr: The envoys found Orange cautious and seriously weighing the burdens of war; many reasons delayed him, among them the greatness of the enemy and the weakness of the oppressed homeland.
