Besides, the empire of Germany was uncertain: Emperor Maximilian was gentle by nature, and his brother Charles, recently sent into Spain from Philip's court, had been badly received; the neighbouring princes feared the common danger; and the exiles' affairs, though pressed forward eagerly, were denounced as criminal. Rather, he argued, the war should be deferred while the revolt of certain Belgian cities was awaited, and strong factions opposed to Philip's rule rose in the very heart of the country. For then the help of the exiles and allies would be timely, if foreign forces joined themselves to the domestic arms of the people, and all at once the strength would reveal itself, about to fight with doubled forces. By this counsel of Orange, the preparation of war was also delayed for so long, until all intercession, even that of the Emperor and the electors of the Empire, proved vain; and after Philip's son had been taken away by secret letters and led off into Spain, he himself, summoned to Brussels by Alva with the other nobles and proscribed, moved by regard for his own affairs and the prince's reputation and by the repeated prayers of the exiles, decided on war. Wherefore, supported by the alliances of princes and kinsmen, and aided by his brother John of Nassau and by the exiles' treasury (many of whom from Friesland had fled to Emden, Bremen and Wesel in Cleves), he resolved to try arms, and he set his brother Louis of Nassau and William of Berg over the levying of soldiers: Berg was to recruit through Gelderland and the neighbouring places, Louis in Upper Germany. Thus he ordered the hastily gathered forces to be sent through the borders of Hesse and Westphalia, and sent his brother Louis to the Frisians beyond the Ems, certain that ready help would come from the greater Frisians (who are bounded by the Flie and the Lauwers), and that the nobility of that shore would of its own accord, moved to the side of the renewed covenant, yield. So Louis entered Emden, a city on the bank of the river Ems, provided supplies for himself, and carried his forces across the river Ems, which, as John Tiara the jurist noted in his commentaries, was covered with ice even when the star of the spring equinox had risen and at the very beginning of April (as were the lakes and marshes of Friesland). The moat of the city of Leeuwarden, too, allowed passage to men three or four abreast, and with the fodder of the cattle used up, Friesland suffered from a great scarcity of hay and at the same time high prices. So, with the soldiers led across the Ems and landed in the district of Reiderland, great alarm arose in the minds of the citizens throughout the city of Leeuwarden. For every Papist proclaimed the danger and, despite the Paschal holidays (which then fell on the 20th of April), gathered up their baggage and goods and soon prepared to flee, which only the posts of soldiers keeping watch at the gates hindered. Others steadied their minds and promised safety: the army of the confederates was not so great as to come to the city, which was separated from Louis by so many thousands of paces and such intervals of places. Groningen, a strong city and secured by a royal garrison, still lay in between; Louis had rivers to cross and the difficulties of places, which were still held by royal forces. They should therefore remain within the enclosure of the city and, dismissing the slight danger, imitate the example always used by brave men, who had thrown their bodies and right hands in the way of the weapons

units.la: Aurantij res. telæ liberorum, atque conjugum objecissent, & si res poposcisset, gloriosa funera turpi effugio antehabuissent. Istis rationibus inducti cives qui Pontificij erant, domum ivere. Cæteris fœderi clàm adscriptis, (qui huc usque latuerant) excedendi urbe potestas facta, ne, si quando cum copijs ad portam Ludovicus, civitatis periculum duplicato hoste geminaretur. Tum in Frisiâ quæ Amaso Flevoque clauditur, multa prodigia, ac horrendæ species præliantium in aëre armatorum apparuere.
units.tr: The affairs of Orange. They had objected to the children and spouses, and if the situation had called for it, they would have preferred a glorious death to a shameful escape. Moved by these considerations, the citizens who were Papists went home. The others, who had been secretly enrolled in the covenant and had lain hidden until then, were given permission to leave the city, so that if Ludovico ever came to the gate with his forces, the city's danger would not be doubled by a double enemy. Then in Friesland, which is bounded by the Ems and the Flie, many portents and dreadful sights of armed men fighting appeared in the air.

units.la: Notat quippe Andreas Gryphius prætor Utingeranus, vergente Augusto paulum à medio noctis cælum velut colore sanguinis rubuisse, versusque ortum Solis æstivum, partes in justâ quadam planitie concurrisse. Copias quoque militares à cæteris discretas, seorsim tanquam auxiliares stetisse, aciemque exercitus, ab ortu venientis primam inclinasse. Tum agmen ab occasu descendens, terga fugientium ferijsse, ac victoriâ potitum. Itaq; tum primum funestæ partes per Frisiam cis ac trans Lavicam se aperuere, populique secessio, & rerum omnium apparatus instans bellum spectavit. Quare annonæ reique frumentariæ extemplo provisum, cautumque edicto; Ne quid frumenti aliudvè bello necessarium, Provinciâ exportaretur. Tum navigia, currus, equi undique per Grosbecium conquisiti, educique præsidijs milites per finitima Leovardiæ loca & circa Bergumanos oberravere. Grosbecius namque decem & quatuor schlopetariorum manipulos, & sexaginta ex principijs delectos milites, Bergumum VIII. Kal. Majas ablegaverat, ne fœderati per ista loca provinciales armarent, ijsque copijs adscriberent, quas Hylco Martinius, vir magni animi, pro Ludovico Nassovio velut nomine Imperij autorabat. Ducenti quoq; milites, ductore Quirino Laceio Burano, Snecâ Columum missi, ut littore prætersluentis æstuarij, ac ingressu istorum locorum fœderatas copias prohiberet, quæ circa Doccomium & per Dongrios, ab Hommio Hettingha, viro è Frisicâ nobilitate, & assertore fœderis contrahebantur. Cæterum arce Weddanâ, expeditâ militum delectorum manu per Ludovicum Nassovium occupatâ, vulgatâque per Frisios istius rei famâ, altior adhuc metus Pontificiorum animos, & ipsum quoq; Grosbecium invasit. Qui propterea, ut dubiâ temporum fortunâ, procerum ingenia atq; voluntates introspiceret, Kal. Maijs vicinam nobilitatem ac primarios Leovardiæ viros, quos aut honor Magistratus, aut forensis eloquentia commendabat, in Curiam regiam convocavit, universosq; velut pro concione, hunc in modum adlocutus est.
units.tr: Andreas Gryphius, praetor of Uithuizen, records that as August drew on, a little after midnight, the sky grew red as if with the colour of blood, and toward the summer sunrise, armies came together on a certain level plain. A military force, separate from the rest, stood apart like an auxiliary body, and the battle line of the army coming from the east first gave way. Then the column descending from the west struck the backs of the fleeing and gained the victory. Thus for the first time the deadly parts of the war appeared throughout Friesland on both sides of the Lauwers, and the people's secession and the preparations for everything foresaw imminent war. Hence provision was made at once for the grain supply, and it was ordered by edict that no grain or anything else needed for war be exported from the province. Then ships, carts and horses were requisitioned from everywhere through Grosbeek, and soldiers led out of the garrisons roamed the neighbouring places around Leeuwarden and about Bergum. For Grosbeek had sent fourteen companies of musketeers and sixty picked soldiers from the principal men to Bergum on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, so that the confederates would not arm the provincials in those parts and enlist them in the forces which Hylco Martinius, a man of great spirit, was commanding for Ludovico of Nassau, as if in the name of the Empire. Two hundred soldiers also, under the leadership of Quirinus Laceius Buranus, were sent from Sneek to Kollum, to block the confederate forces which were gathering around Dokkum and through Dongeradeel under Homme Hettinga, a man of the Frisian nobility and a champion of the covenant; they were to guard the shore of the flowing estuary and the entrances to those places. Moreover, when the fortress of Weddan had been seized by a picked band of soldiers under Ludovico of Nassau, and the report of this had spread among the Frisians, an even greater fear invaded the minds of the Papists and Grosbeek himself. Therefore, in order to look into the dispositions and wills of the nobles while fortune in the times was uncertain, on the Kalends of May he summoned the neighbouring nobility and the leading men of Leeuwarden, whom either the honour of office or skill in public speaking recommended, to the royal court, and addressed them all together, as if from a pulpit, in this manner.

units.la: Oratio Grosbecij.
units.tr: Grosbeek's Speech

units.la: NON ignorare vos puto, Frisiam vestram post factionum tempora, Carolo Cæsare armis, aut bellis intactam, mutuâ populi concordiâ floruisse. Quâ ipsâ ut etiamnum viveretis, diu in votis habui, operamque, absente Arembergio, omnem impendi, ut fomes ulterioris dissidij tolleretur, ac Provinciam intra hanc omnia moderata, & quam longissime ab omni violentiâ essent. Cæterum, quia supra modum periculum excrevit, & commune concordiæ vinculum eorum defectione ruptum est, qui armis uti, quam parere regi suo malebant, restaurare hoc, quod datum mihi est, imperij validius cogor, cuius robur, lenitate & patientiâ fermè amissum erat. Quare volo ut sacramentum auctius, quam quod professi estis, Philippo regi praestetis, juretisque universi & singuli, non defecturos vos unquam à Philippo rege vestro, quacumque etiam de causa, daturosque operam ut Praefectorum ac Senatus imperijs abunde satisfiat. Et quia metui potest, ut Ludovicus Nassovius Reiderios jam ingressus ac tert. vix lap. à Groninga castra tenens nobis, & urbi huic periculum creet, censeo concordia opus esse (sine quâ propulsari nulla vis unquam potuit) & Leovardiam urbem communibus viribus propugnandam. Hoc ut faciatis, praestari fidem mihi hoc ipso conventu volo, ut in bellum iturus omnia hic composita habeam, & securitatis plena. Si qui vero sint, quibus id factu grave videatur, eos secedere jubeo, ac sua simul consilia & pericula expendere.
units.tr: I suppose you are not unaware that your Friesland, after the times of faction, untouched by arms or wars under Emperor Charles, flourished through the mutual harmony of its people. I have long hoped that you might still live in that state, and while Arenberg was absent I took every pains that the seed of further discord should be removed, and that in this province all things should be moderate and as far as possible free from all violence. But since the danger has grown beyond measure, and the common bond of concord has been broken by those who preferred to use arms rather than obey their king, I am compelled to restore with greater strength the authority that has been given to me, whose strength had nearly been lost through leniency and patience. Therefore I want you to give King Philip a more binding oath than the one you have professed, and to swear, all of you and each of you, that you will never fall away from Philip your king, for whatever cause, and that you will take care that the commands of the governors and the Senate are fully obeyed. And since it may be feared that Ludovico of Nassau, who has already entered Reiderland and is camped barely three leagues from Groningen, may create danger for us and for this city, I judge that concord is needed (without which no force could ever be repelled), and that Leeuwarden must be defended by our common strength. That you may do this, I want my faith to be pledged at this very assembly, so that when I go to war I may have everything settled here and be free of anxiety. If there are any who find this burdensome, I order them to withdraw and weigh their own counsels and dangers at the same time.

units.la: Tum secedens nobilitas, in quâ Doco Martna, Hector Dekama, Hector & Goffo Abingha, Renicus & Vitus Cammingha, tum Siricius Donia erant, communicato cum Gysberto & Christophoro Aernsma, Feccone Rhala, & Ioanne Tiara Iurisconsultis, consilio, per eundem Tiaram Grosbecio respondit. Majores suos à multis annis, & deïn se ipsos Carolo ac Philippo regibus fidem obsequio fecisse. Itaque novo sacramento, dum vetus adhuc obstringat, obligare se non posse, facturos interim ad quae teneantur è jure formulaque pactorum, quae Carolus Caesar & majores sui injissent. Tum Curijs populi in Minoritarum templum evocatis, per Grosbecium, ore Graphiarij regij eadem, sed nulla successu, repetita. Quippe magnum murmur secedentis mox turbae ortum, alienos à Grosbecij propositio animos ostendebat. Quare contegendae irae vix par, caetu effusus in arcem regiam se contulit, reducemqʒ; post è Gallia Arembergium, in ultionem contumacis populi instigavit. Refert Iodocius, nonnullis causarum in regio Senatu patronis, quod à dictione novi sacramenti abhorruissent, foro interdictum, & Hylconem, de quo dixi, Martinium, militum apud foederatos conquisitorem, in caenobio quodam captum, una cum sex captivis Leovardiam abductum. Interim ne res per Leovardiam in incerto essent, & ne civitas foris cum Ludovico Nassovio, domi cum inimico cive certaret, Senatores regij firmandis populi in regem obsequijs privatorum domos adiere. Eos monere ac hortari, manerent in fide Philippi, inveteratumqʒ; Austriae Principum jus integrum illaesumque curent, fore alias, ut, cum novarum partium professione, fructum quoque delibent, novae & non speratae calamitatis. Spargi quidem Ludovicum tumultuariâ manu circa Amasi ripam per Provinciae fines, caeterum facile debellandum, si concordes coëant cives, ac regis sui observantes, commune auxilium in exitium hostium vertant. Cogitarent Leovardiam Provinciae metropolim vallo, ac fossâ circumductam sedem Senatus, & publicorum munimentorum vastationibus, ac rapinis exponendam non esse. Quin expenderent potius liberos, conjuges, omniaque divina ac humana concordiam & commune sacramentum implorare, quo salvo everti neqeat tot carorum pinorum incolumitas. Sed dubiâ & divisâ civitate parum profectum. Itaque Grosbecius Non. Maij. Groningam celeravit, lustratoque, quod Arembergius in Galliam iturus ibi poluerat, praesidio, quadringentorum rum manum in cænobium Wittewerumanum duxit, ut Ludovicum ulteriore in Provinciam ingressu prohiberet. Cæterum territus Ludovici copiis pedem retraxit, relicto interea Groningæ Ioachimo Pansero, qui regio nomine delectum ageret, tutandisq; Translavicorum finibus plures copias conscriberet. Quas ipsas per eundem Ioachimum Pansernum Marnium, in Harenum pagum post eductas ipso noctis obscuro à præsidio, quod Ludovicus Dammonae locaverat, cum præfectis, primipilaribusque cæsas deletasque in fragmentis suis Historicis Cl. Franckena annotavit. Ludovicus namque redacto in potestatem Weddæ castello partem exercitus Dammonam miserat, ut propius Groningam suggressus, præsidiarios ad velitandum eliceret, metuque sui majore omnem Provinciam impleret. Itaque convocatis Dammonæ Translavicanorum Ordinibus, per Tiallingum Eysingham virum è Frisica nobilitate, & juris scientissimum, commeatum atq; pecuniam recensendis copiis imperavit. Instare quippe alias militarium seditionum discrimen ostendebat, ac metuendum esse, ut miles è rapto stipendia faciat, magno Provincialium incommodo, quibus opprimendis non venisset. Solam enim populi libertatem sibi curæ esse, & non alio fine arma sumpta, quam ne Hispanus oppressum iret Provincias sanguine suorum madentes. Cuius furori ut modus ponatur, militem è Germania in Frisios duxisse, sed qui retineri in officio sine stipendijs non posset. Itaque militi stipendium, stipendio tributum deberi, ut disciplinæ militari locus sit, & intacti maneant eorum agri & possessiones, quorum interesset; Ne quid detrimenti. Tum petito deliberandi spacio Translavicani Ordines Groningam ad Grosbecium profecti, mandata Ludovici exposuerunt, quibus tributa per Provinciam eum flagitare fidem faciebant. Quare Grosbecius Translavicanorum Legatos in castra Ludovici se recipere, ac redimere pecuniâ periculum jusit, quod isti amovendo non aliud remedium superesset. Parvas quippe sibi copias & Harenâ clade accisas, tum infidum omne per utramq; Provinciam imperium expendebat. Itaq; Legati ad Ludovicum reversi, coacto repente per agrarios tributo, pecuniam assignavere, omniqué insolentiæ parcitum est. Mox Groningani metu obsidionis ad Ferdinandum Albanum Legatos Bruxellas misere, qui auxilia rogarent, debili intra urbem præsidio, & maxumâ Translavicani agri parte hostium copijs expositâ. Igitur Ferdinandus Albanus proclamata Carolum inter 1 x. Galliæ regem, & Condæum, Amiraliumq; pace, Ioannem Lignæum Arembergium Galliâ evocavit, ducendaque ei in Frisios auxilia commisit. Tum Carolus Brimæus Comes Meganus, qui mille, & quingentos peditum, equitum quadringentos ducebat, subsequi jussus, ac præsidia pleraq; Cislavicanarum civitatum Groningam amota, quo Grosbecius, Non. Maij mensis absente adhuc Arembergio, præcesserat. Qui mox Gallico bello defunctus è Brabantiâ in Transfisulaniam, post Frisios maturans 1 v. Eid. Maij Bergumanos, ac mox sex navigijs vergente in occasum die Leovardiam advenit, communicatoq; cum regio Senatu consilio, Grosbecium Groningâ per litteras acciri jusit. Is acceptis Prid. Eid. mandatis Groningam se recepit, ipseque Arembergius etsi affectâ valetudine, præpræpediretur, salutato quoq; Senatu in Bergumanos, & post Groningam profectus est, decem Hispanorum, & post duabus cohortibus Quirini Lacei Burani, & Ernesti Mulartij in eandem urbem præmissis. Ubi conpositâ, ut Cl. Franckena notat, militari seditione, nihil cunctandum ratus, exercitum omnem, sex tormentis campestribus instructus, Dammonam ducere constituit, quàm Ludovicus Nassovius, ut ante dixi, plerisque cum copijs tuebatur. Quorum certior factus Ludovicus castra Dammonâ Slochterum movit, non metu, ut quidam voluere, sed ut sparsas istam per oram copias conjungeret. Quare Ludovici recessum, fugam ratus Arembergius, ocyus exercitum pergere jussit, compertoque è captivis (quos Ludovicus Harenâ pugnâ captos dimiserat) magnam in exercitu Ludovici commeatus penuriam esse, decertare prælio constituit, ad quod Hispani sive insito calore, sive pugnandi occasionem speculati, præfervidis studijs incendebantur. Sed instans & illunis nox castra diremit. Igitûr, postero die, curatis militum corporibus Arembergius castra propius adduxit, exercitumque magno cæli ardore, adultum enim ver erat, ac armorum juxta pondere defatigatum apud Winschotum stare parumper jussit, præmissis confestim exploratoribus, qui de Ludovico cognoscerent, ac de situ Castrorum nuntiarent. Ubi verò per eosdem speculatores cognitum, Ludovicum nullo fugæ, ut rati erant, consilio, decertare prælio constituisse, animus Arembergij velut eventuri mali præsagio non parum elanguit. Quapropter differendum diem pugnæ ratus, moræ ac tarditatis suæ causam, tanquam apud milites concionatus in absentem Carolum Brimæum Comitem Meganum rejecit. Illum quippe vix diei itinere castris abesse, & postero die cum auxilijs adfore, quo cum Ludovico confligere auctæ vires & vegetior miles suaderent. Sed Hispanus præconceptæ victoriæ fiduciâ præceps, tum gloriæ ac prædæ juxta avidus, conferendas cum Ludovico manus incondito clamore vociferabatur. Quare Arembergius importuno militi obsecutus, confertam simul aciem in Ludovicum duxit, qui mediâ & arbustis circumseptâ camporum planitie tripartitum jamdiu exercitum justis ordinibus instruxerat. Schlopetarij etiam quadringenti per insidias positi, quibus mandaverat Ludovicus, ut sponte recedentes suos exciperent, insequentemq; festinantius hostem ex insidijs adorirentur. Quod consilium magnum pondus subsecutæ victoriæ attulit. Itaque Nassovij, & in ijs Ludovicus, & Adolphus fratres, impressione in equitum turmas, quæ paucæ circa Arembergium erant, factâ, mox volentes pedem retulere, donec constituto loco machinæ, & ingruens equés, tum locati per insidias schlopetarij Arembergici exercitus ordines conturbarent. Quibus luxatis versi in fugam Hispani promiscuâ cæde ceciderunt. Arembergius ipse, levi primum capitis vulnere accepto, mox equo, quo vehebatur, deturbatus, fortiter adhuc pugnans, ac nequicquam hostilis post dexteræ misericordiam implorans à gregario Ludovici milite, textore, ut tradunt, Bosumano, vel ut alij asserunt, à ligulario Franequerano, Zeugma dicto, confossus est. Cæteros frequens ijs locis uligo, altissimæque paludes absorpserunt, mille, & octingenti, una cum ipso Arembergio, in cæsorum numerum
units.tr: Then the nobility who had seceded, among whom were Doco Martena, Hector Dekama, Hector and Goffo Abingha, Renicus and Vitus Cammingha, and Siricius Donia, having taken counsel with Gysbert and Christoph Aernsma, Feccone Rhala, and John Tiara, jurists, replied through the same Tiara to Grosbeck. Their ancestors, and they themselves, had for many years shown loyalty and obedience to Charles and Philip as kings. Therefore they could not bind themselves by a new oath while the old one still held them. In the meantime they would do what they were bound to do by the law and by the form of the agreements which Charles the Emperor and their ancestors had entered into. Then the citizens were called by the curia to the Minorite church, and the same demand was repeated through Grosbeck, with the royal secretary reading it out, but without success. Indeed a great murmur soon rose from the seceding crowd, which showed that their minds were turned against Grosbeck's proposal. Scarcely able to restrain his anger, he withdrew from the assembly into the royal citadel. Afterwards, bringing Arenberg back from France, he urged him to take vengeance on the obstinate people. Iodocius reports that some of the advocates in the royal Senate, who had refused to take the new oath, were barred from the courts, and that Hylco, whom I mentioned, Martinius, a recruiter of soldiers for the allied provinces, was captured in a certain monastery and led to Leeuwarden together with six prisoners. Meanwhile, so that matters would not remain uncertain in Leeuwarden, and so that the city would not contend with Louis of Nassau abroad and with a hostile citizen at home, the royal senators went to the private houses to secure the people's submission to the king. They warned and urged them to remain loyal to Philip, and to keep the ancient rights of the Princes of Austria whole and unharmed; otherwise, by joining the new party, they would also taste the fruit of a new and unexpected calamity. It was true, they said, that Louis was scattering a tumultuous band around the banks of the Amasis, within the borders of the province, but he could be easily crushed if the citizens united in harmony, and, obeying their king, turned their common aid to the destruction of the enemy. They should consider that Leeuwarden, the metropolis of the province, enclosed by a rampart and ditch, was the seat of the Senate, and should not be exposed to the devastation and plunder of public fortifications. Rather, they should weigh that they ought to implore, with their children, their wives, and all things divine and human, concord and common allegiance, by which, if preserved, the safety of so many dear ones could not be overthrown. But the city, divided and uncertain, achieved little. Therefore Grosbeck hurried to Groningen on 5 May, and, having reviewed the garrison which Arenberg had left there when he was about to go to France, he led a force of four hundred men into the monastery of Wittewierum, to prevent Louis from entering the province further. But, frightened by Louis's troops, he drew back, leaving Joachim Panser at Groningen in the king's name to raise a levy and to enlist more troops to defend the borders of the Trans-Lauwers region. These same troops, after being led out by the same Joachim Panser to the village of Harenum near Marne, were cut down and destroyed, in the dark of night, by the garrison which Louis had placed at Dammona, together with their commanders and centurions; Franckenus recorded this in his historical fragments. For Louis, having taken the castle of Wedde, had sent part of his army to Dammona, so that, advancing nearer to Groningen, it might draw out the garrison to skirmish and fill the whole province with greater fear of himself. Therefore, having summoned the Trans-Lauwers estates at Dammona, he ordered, through Tiallingius Eysinga, a man from the Frisian nobility and most learned in law, that provisions and money be provided for reviewing the troops. He pointed out that the danger of other mutinies among the soldiers was impending, and that it must be feared that the soldiers would support themselves by plunder, to the great harm of the provincials, whom he had not come to oppress. For, he said, the liberty of the people alone was his concern, and he had taken up arms for no other purpose than to prevent the Spaniard from overrunning the provinces, which were soaked in the blood of their own people. To put an end to that fury, he had brought soldiers from Germany into Friesland, but these could not be kept under discipline without pay. Therefore pay was owed to the soldiers, and the tax was owed for the pay, so that there might be room for military discipline, and so that the fields and possessions of those whose interest it was would remain untouched, lest any harm be done. Then, having asked for time to deliberate, the Trans-Lauwers estates went to Grosbeck at Groningen, and set out the commands of Louis, by which they showed that he was demanding taxes throughout the province. Therefore Grosbeck ordered the Trans-Lauwers envoys to betake themselves to Louis's camp and to buy off the danger with money, since no other remedy would remain once he had removed them. For he weighed that his own forces were small and had been weakened by the defeat at Harenum, and that all government in both provinces was unreliable. So the envoys returned to Louis, and, a tax having been suddenly levied through the farmers, they handed over the money, and his insolence was spared. Soon the Groningers, in fear of a siege, sent envoys to Ferdinand of Alba at Brussels to ask for aid, since the garrison within the city was weak and most of the Trans-Lauwers countryside lay open to the enemy's forces. Therefore Ferdinand of Alba, having proclaimed peace between Charles, king of France, and Condé and Admiral Coligny, summoned John of Ligne, Count of Arenberg, from France, and entrusted to him the leading of auxiliary troops into Friesland. Then Charles Brimaeus, Count of Megen, who led fifteen hundred foot soldiers and four hundred horse, was ordered to follow, and most of the garrisons of the Cis-Lauwers cities were withdrawn to Groningen, whither Grosbeck had gone ahead on 5 May, while Arenberg was still absent. Megen, having finished with the French war, hastened from Brabant into Transisulania, and after Friesland, by way of Bergen, he came on 11 May, and soon after, with six ships, as the day was sinking into the west, he arrived at Leeuwarden. Having communicated his plan to the royal Senate, he ordered Grosbeck to be summoned from Groningen by letter. Grosbeck, receiving the orders on the day before the Ides, withdrew to Groningen; and Arenberg himself, although his health was weakened and he was hindered, after greeting the Senate, set out for Bergen and afterwards for Groningen, having first sent ahead into that city ten Spaniards and afterwards two cohorts under Quirinus Lacey, Buran, and Ernest Mulartius. When, as Franckenus notes, the military mutiny there had been quelled, thinking there was no time for delay, he decided to lead the whole army, equipped with six field guns, to Dammona, which Louis of Nassau, as I said before, was holding with most of his forces. Louis, informed of this, moved his camp from Dammona to Slochteren, not from fear, as some have wished, but in order to join his scattered forces along that shore. Therefore Arenberg, thinking that Louis's withdrawal was a flight, ordered the army to advance more quickly; and, having learned from prisoners (whom Louis had released after the battle at Harenum) that there was a great shortage of supplies in Louis's army, he resolved to fight a battle, for which the Spaniards, whether from their natural heat or having seized the chance to fight, were fired with eager zeal. But the approaching night, dark and gloomy, separated the camps. Therefore, on the next day, after the soldiers' bodies had been refreshed, Arenberg brought the camp nearer and, since the army was worn out by the great heat of the sky (for it was now the full spring) and by the weight of its arms, he ordered it to halt for a while at Winschoten, sending scouts ahead at once to learn about Louis and report on the position of the camps. But when the scouts reported that Louis had resolved to fight a battle, having no plan of flight, as they had supposed, Arenberg's spirit, as if sensing an impending evil, grew not a little faint. Therefore, thinking the day of battle should be postponed, he gave as the cause of his delay and sluggishness, as if preaching to the soldiers, the absent Charles Brimaeus, Count of Megen. For Megen, he said, was scarcely a day's journey from the camp and would arrive with reinforcements the next day, and it would be wiser to meet Louis with increased strength and a more vigorous soldiery. But the Spaniard, rash through confidence in a victory already conceived, and as eager for glory as for booty, shouted in disorderly clamour that hands should be joined with Louis at once. Therefore Arenberg, yielding to the troublesome soldiery, led his massed line against Louis, who had long since drawn up his army in three divisions in good order across the middle of a plain enclosed by trees. Four hundred musketeers had also been posted in ambush, whom Louis had ordered to receive his men as they retreated voluntarily and to attack the enemy from ambush as he followed too eagerly. This plan brought great weight to the victory that followed. So the Nassau brothers, and among them Louis and Adolphus, made an attack on the squadrons of horse, which were few around Arenberg, and soon, willingly giving ground, they halted at a place of their choosing, while the artillery and the advancing cavalry, and the musketeers placed in ambush, threw the ranks of Arenberg's army into disorder. With these broken, the Spaniards turned in flight and fell in a mass slaughter. Arenberg himself, first wounded slightly in the head, soon thrown from the horse he was riding, still fighting bravely and in vain begging the mercy of the enemy, was stabbed by a common soldier of Louis, a weaver, as they report, from Bosum, or, as others assert, by a ribbon-maker from Franeker, called Zeugma. The rest were swallowed up by the frequent marsh in those places and by the deepest bogs, eight hundred and a thousand, together with Arenberg himself, among the number of the slain

units.la: Orum relati incruentam Ludovico (sexaginta enim tantum desiderabantur) victoriam reliquêre. Solus Adolphus, Ludovici frater, fortiter rem gerens inter Principes viros gloriosâ morte exspiravit, suique desiderium luctuosæ Nassoviorum domui reliquit. Cadaver eius Weddæ, ut & Arembergij fano cænobij Heiligerlæi, militaribus exequijs inlatum. Ita primam fœderati belli, ac Ludovici fœlicitatem fratris morte acerbior Fortuna pensavit. Tum ex Hispanis captivi laqueis enecti, communem adversi sortem pertulere. Reperio in notis A. Franckenæ, finito prælio Germanis parcitum fuisse, trecentosque captivos, qui post id temporis stipendia se apud hostem non facturos, Ludovico depacti erant, singulari clementiâ dimissos. Aberat non procul eo loco cum quinque cohortibus, paucisque equitum turmis Carolus Brinæus Comes Meganus, qui perceptâ Arembergij ac suorum clade celerrimâ fugâ Groningam abreptus civitatem, in quam ægre intromissus erat, exarmari fecit, veritus haud dubio ne adversâ Arembergicæ pugnæ fortunâ animi civium, novarum, ut solent, rerum ultrò avidi Fœderatis partibus se adjicerent. Iam enim illius cladis reliquiæ sine ullo ordine palantes, ac inermes circum urbem Groningam & per universam Frisiam spargebantur. Unde castrorum fusique exercitus opes, aurum atque argentum omne, tum arma, vestes, equi, trecentique currus vehendis machinis, cæterisq; rebus facti, victoribus cessere. Ludovicus victor, more bellicis Imperatoribus recepto, postquam locum pugnæ, sed sanguine hostium cruentatum spatio tridui insedisset, Dammonam se recepit, portumque Delphzilanum munijt. Tum Tiallengium Eysingham Iureconsultum, qui verba apud Translavicanos nuper fecerat, ac in comitatu Ludovici tum erat, domestico malo multatum fuisse reperio, omniaque eius bona immissis in domum militum manipulis, commentario perscripta. Notat Iodocius sex campestria tormenta, quæ Arembergius Groningâ abduxerat, Ludovico quoque obvenisse, ac quatuor cohortes peditum III. Kal. Iun. sparsas, & inermes Leovardiam profugas advolasse. Duas quoque cohortes, Snecâ prohibitas, ipsumque Grosbecium festino itinere modo Groningâ Leovardiam, deinde Leovardiâ Groningam revectum, reparandis per Frisiam rebus incubuisse. Idem Iodocius notat, clerum Leovardiæ hoc tempore ex omni inter Flevum, Lavicamque Frisia convenisse, ac de mittendis Ultrajectum Delegatis consultasse, quos Fredericus Scencus Teutoburgius, Archiepiscopus Ultrajectinus de mandato Ferdinandi Albani, promulgandis per omnem Diocæsin Concilij Tridentini Decretis Ultrajectum evocaverat. Litteræ x x ii. Aprilis Ultrajecto datæ. Quibus responsum ab Abbatibus hunc in modum reperio.
units.tr: Those who were brought back left Louis a bloodless victory, for only sixty were reported missing. Adolphus alone, Louis's brother, fighting bravely among the princes, died a glorious death and left the house of Nassau grieving for him. His body was carried to Wedde and to Aremberg's chapel at the monastery of Heiligerlee, and received military funeral rites. Thus a harsher Fortune balanced the first success of the allied war and of Louis by the death of his brother. Then the Spanish captives were strangled in nooses and suffered the common fate of the defeated. I find in the notes of A. Franckena that once the battle was over the Germans were spared, and three hundred captives who had agreed with Louis that they would not serve the enemy again were released with singular clemency. Not far from that place, with five cohorts and a few troops of cavalry, was Count Charles Brienne of Megen. On hearing of the defeat of Aremberg and his men, he fled very swiftly to Groningen, where he was admitted with difficulty, and had the citizens disarmed, fearing without doubt that, with the fortunes of the Aremberg battle going against him, the citizens, always eager for revolution, would join the allied side. For the remnants of that defeat were scattered around the city of Groningen and throughout all Friesland, wandering without order and unarmed. Hence the camp's wealth and that of the routed army, all the gold and silver, the arms, clothing, horses, three hundred wagons for carrying siege engines, and the rest, fell to the victors. Louis, the victor, following the custom of commanders, after occupying for three days the field of battle, stained with the blood of the enemy, withdrew to Damme and fortified the harbour of Delfzijl. I find that Tjallingius Eysinga, a jurist who had recently spoken before the men of Overijssel and was then in Louis's train, was punished through a misfortune in his own household; all his goods were recorded in an inventory after bands of soldiers were sent into his house. Jodocus notes that six field guns, which Aremberg had taken from Groningen, also fell to Louis, and that four cohorts of infantry, scattered and unarmed, fled to Leeuwarden on 30 May. Two cohorts, held back at Sneek, and Grosbeek himself, hurrying back and forth from Groningen to Leeuwarden and then from Leeuwarden to Groningen, set to work repairing affairs throughout Friesland. The same Jodocus notes that the clergy of Friesland, from the region between the Zuider Zee and the Lauwers, had gathered at Leeuwarden at this time and consulted about sending delegates to Utrecht. Frederick Schenck of Toutenburg, Archbishop of Utrecht, on the orders of Ferdinand of Alva, had summoned them there to publish the decrees of the Council of Trent throughout the diocese. The letter was given at Utrecht on 22 April. I find the abbots' reply to it was in this manner.

units.la: Illustriss. ac Reverendiss. citari nos denuò coram Metropolitana fecisti, & quidem, ut profiteris ex mandato Ferdinandi Albani, ut voluntatem regis cognosceremus, ac quid de Concilio Tridentino per Frisiam & Diocæsin publicando decreverit.
units.tr: Most illustrious and most reverend sir, you have summoned us again before the Metropolitan, and indeed, as you declare, on the orders of Ferdinand of Alva, so that we may learn the king's will and what he has decided about publishing the Council of Trent throughout Friesland and the diocese.

units.la: Quæ evocatio etiamsi legitima foret, neque derogaret privilegijs nostris, & integrum nobis commodumq; foret ire, tamen non possumus hac in re imperio tuo ac mandato obsequi, cum sine totius provinciæ, cui innexi sumus, consensu nihil agi queat, quod ad plurium, imo ad omnium commodum atque utilitatem spectat. Tempus præterea breve, & per quam quam augustum nobis praescriptum. Addimus vias ipsas, hostium copijs, quae non longè absunt intutas impeditasq; esse, nosque in perpetuo metu futurae vastitatis, versari. Itaque extra fines regionis hoc tempore ire, & à monasteriis nostris abesse, valde grave & molestum nobis erit, quod ijs evenire solet, quibus de securitate praestari cautio, etiam per autoritatem judicij, non potest. Et quia tertio tantum Ordinum Frisiae membro censemur, neque in fraudem sociorum nostrorum quid statuere possumus, petimus ut excusari nos sinas, quos alijs in causis reverentia tuae Sedis obligavit.
units.tr: Even if this summons were lawful, and did not infringe our privileges, and it were open to us to go, still we cannot in this matter obey your command and order, since nothing can be done without the consent of the whole province to which we are bound, nothing that concerns the advantage and utility of many, indeed of all. Moreover, the time set for us is short and most very inconvenient. We add that the roads themselves, not far from the enemy's forces, are unsafe and obstructed, and that we live in constant fear of devastation. Therefore to go beyond the borders of the region at this time, and to be away from our monasteries, will be very burdensome and troublesome to us, as it usually is for those whose safety cannot be guaranteed even by the authority of a court. And since we are counted only as the third estate of the Frisian orders, and cannot decide anything to the prejudice of our fellows, we ask that you allow us to be excused, since in other matters we are bound by reverence to your See.

units.la: Post exequias Arembergio xv. Kal. Iul. Leovardiae factae magnoq; funebri apparatu praemisso, Pontificiorum praesertim in defunctum suprema officia eluxerunt. Caeteri credebant quod iniquior foederi, & tot exulum conscientijs fuisset, divinâ ultione sublatum digno factis luctu prosequendum esse. Recordabantur quippe Arembergium eodem die, quo expeditionem molitus erat, viginti & octo cives exilio multasse, horaeq; tantum spatium urbe excessuris singulari saevitiâ indulsisse. E Minnemijs Andream Wibrandium, Abbeaeum Udium, cum filio, Vibium Allartium, ex Oldehovijs Elconem Valerium, Philippum Ioannis, Franciscum Capsarium, Douwonem Symonium, Witzonem Pistorium, Ioannem Thomaeum, Riemerum Fabrum, Joannem Sagittarium, Petrum Stroierum, Sibrandum Tetardum, Heronem Hottingha, Cornelium Scandularium, Gabbeum Vitriarium, Henricum Clyncbylium, Buwonem Ielmerium, ex Hoecanis Ioannem Ieppenium, Franciscum Ioannis, Paulum Ægidium, Ioannem Æmylium, Thomam Thomaeum, Siouckonem Fabrum, Elconem Leoninum, Ludolphum Nautam fuisse in horrendae proscriptionis tabulis xiv. Kal. Iun. signatis reperio. Quorum exilijs justa propterea caede satisfactum, illi interpretabantur, qui non ignorabant, saevos Principes vitae suae spatia ut plurimum infaelici exitu clausisse. Post senescente Iunio mense, inermibus, quae Leovardiae oberrabant, à clade Heiligerlaeâ copijs arma Antverpiâ suppeditata, ac quatuor cohortes (etsi dubijs animis, ac vultu contumaciae propiores essent) Groningam praemissae, subsequente ocyus Grosbecio, ut ulteriorem Ludovici progressum, & secundos rerum cursus remoraretur, quae prosperis tum fatis in continente non tantum, sed in ipso quoque mari, & aestuario Amasi fluminis agebantur. Didericus namque Sonnoius acceptâ famâ Franciscum Boshusium Classi regiae praefectum eadem classe Amasium flumen ingressum (ne commeatus in castra Ludovici Embdâ, aut è vicinis Frisijs perferretur) sociorum ope multas naves adornaverat, marique Frisico immissus onerariam quandam in anchoris stantem suam fecerat, fugatoque Boshusio ac directâ hostium classe victor foederatae per Oceanum expeditionis primus gloriam reportaverat. Quibus rebus, etsi maxumè Arembergicae cladis dolore, commotus Albanus captivae Nobilitatis supplicia maturavit, animumque ultrò immanem, sed Ludovici Nassovij fortunâ efferum, Nobilitatis Belgicae, Principumque virorum sanguine placare adnixus est. Quare ad Kal. Iun. pegmata Bruxellis extructa proclamatisq; in Curiâ feralibus sententijs, Batenburgici, reliquiq; Nobiles (inter quos è Frisijs Hartmannus Galama,
units.tr: After Aremberg's funeral rites were held at Leeuwarden on 17 June, with a great funeral display sent ahead, the last honours to the dead man shone out, above all from the Papists. Others believed that, since he had been hostile to the confederacy and to the consciences of so many exiles, and had been removed by divine vengeance, he should be mourned with the grief his deeds deserved. For they recalled that Aremberg, on the very day he set out on the expedition, had banished twenty-eight citizens and granted those leaving the city only an hour, with exceptional cruelty. I find that the following were named in the dreadful lists of proscription, signed on 19 May: from Minnema, Andreas Wibrandus, Abbe Udius with his son, Vibius Allartius; from Oldehove, Elco Valerius, Philip John, Francis Capsarius, Douwo Symon, Witzo Pistorius, John Thomas, Riemer Faber, John Sagittarius, Peter Stroier, Sibrand Tetardus, Heron Hottingha, Cornelius Scandularius, Gabbe Vitriarius, Henry Clyncbylius, Buwo Ielmerius; from Hoeck, John Ieppenius, Francis John, Paul Aegidius, John Aemylius, Thomas Thomas, Sioucko Faber, Elco Leoninus, Ludolph Nauta. Those who did not forget that cruel princes had mostly ended their lives in an unhappy death interpreted it so: by the exile of these men a just slaughter had been made satisfaction. Later, as June wore on, arms were supplied from Antwerp to the unarmed men who wandered around Leeuwarden after the defeat at Heiligerlee, and four cohorts (though of doubtful minds, and nearer to defiance in their looks) were sent ahead to Groningen, with Grosbeek following more quickly, to delay Louis's further advance and his successes, which were then going well not only on the mainland but also at sea and in the estuary of the Ems. For Dirk Sonoy, on hearing the news that Francis Bossu, prefect of the royal fleet, had entered the Ems with that fleet (to stop supplies reaching Louis's camp from Emden or the neighbouring parts of Friesland), had with the help of his allies fitted out many ships. Sending them out onto the Frisian sea, he seized a merchant vessel lying at anchor as his own, routed Bossu, and destroyed the enemy fleet, and as victor he gained the first glory of the allied expedition over the ocean. Moved by these events, and above all by grief over the defeat at Aremberg, Alva hastened the execution of the captive nobles and strove to appease, with the blood of the Belgian nobility and of princely men, a spirit savage of its own accord but made fiercer by the fortune of Louis of Nassau. Therefore, by 1 June, scaffolds were built at Brussels, fatal sentences were proclaimed in court, and Batenburg and the other nobles (among whom from Friesland were Hartmann Galama,

units.la: Suffridus Beiemus, & Gulielmus Buma erant) capite plexi optumos in patriam affectus tristi eventu expressere. Capita, truncaq; corpora pinnis passim suffixa, & nobili patritioq, sanguine stillantia sepulchri quoque honore carere.
units.tr: Suffridus Beiemus and Gulielmus Buma) were beheaded, and by their sad end expressed the best feelings towards the fatherland. Heads and trunks, fixed here and there on spikes, dripping with noble and patrician blood, were denied even the honour of a tomb.

units.la: Ita Ferdinandus Albanus, qui vitae beneficium nobilissimis viris ademerat, communem quoque mortalibus terram eorum corporibus invidit, fædusque naturæ hostis, superesse odium, etiam amoto furoris sui pabulo professus est. Tum in Amoralium Egmondanum, & Philippum Montmorentium Principes viros, & Equites Aurei Velleris conversus ultimam ijs necessitatem denuntiari fecit, sententiamque mortis, quam clam ex Hispania attulisse credebatur, sua manu perscripsit. Egmondanus terror fulmenque Galliæ (prædicante id Mondulceto Caroli IX. Gallorum Regis Legato) primus cervicem gladio præbens, omne etiam moribundus fati solatium in gratia Philippi reponebat. Itaque orare eum, miseretur mæstissimæ viduæque conjugis, & undecim liberorum, numerosæque prolis fortunam, denique principis, sed miserrimæ domus sortem regia clementia levet. Se jam morti proximum, neque ferendis extremis imparatum, hoc solo voto preces, & desideria finire. Ea codicillis signata, ac in Hispaniam transmissa, ultimæ sollicitudinis fidem implevere. Cornelius Gemma scribit, illum, qui dextrum sæpe Philippi latus clauserat, regij nominis imperio raptum laudabilique patientia in extremis usum, regiæ voluntati tanquam fato ac providentiæ se subjecisse. Tum Philippum Montmorentium Comitem Hornanum idem exitus abstulit. Capita fortissimorum Heroum truncis recisa, ferreisque pilis impositæ triste spectaculum, odiaque populi, & cricumstantium militum in Albanum auxere. Erant, qui meminissent post victorias Gallicis alijsque bellis partas eo in loco triumphales arcus inter applausus populi, sonantiumque cuneorum victoribus erectos fuisse. Nunc trophæa ipsa cæsorum debellatorumque hostium monumenta in usum fædissimi spectaculi conversa. Is exitus Egmondani Hornijque Comitum fuit, quos summis olim honoribus decoratos, Carolique ac Philippi militiam à triginta annis per Africam & mediterraneum mare secutos autores tradidere. Addunt ijdem Gulielmum Nassovium Aurantium Principem, Willebrocano conventu eum eventum rerum Egmondano prædixisse; ac Gemmam Frisium Mathematicum eà ætate celeberrimum, in Hornani Genetliaco fatalem illum casum è cæli constitutione, ac concurrentium syderum posituris observasse. Itaque eundem Montmorentium præmonuisse, præsentiam Albani, & forum declinaret, subductusque periculis pari cum socijs exilio privatæ securitati, & simul publicæ causæ consuleret. Cæterum mihi memoriam temporum revolventi observatum ut plurimum fuit, Tyrannorum sævitiem, & optimis quibusque imperatas mortes ab æternâ & immutabili providentiâ esse, fereque gentium libertatem, velut fato præfinitam, crebra supplicia, virorumque Principum neces tanquam tempestates venturæ serenitatis antecessisse. Quamobrem vindictâ ulteriore Arembergicæ cædis exardescens Albanus, sparsum per omnem oram militem colligi imperavit, Carolumque Brimæum Meganum ab excessu Ioannis Lignæi Arembergij Præfectura Frisiæ omniumque intra Flevum Amasumq; ditionum cIↄ. Iɔ. donatum, Groningam mox cum copiis ablegavit. Erico quoque LXVIII. Brunsuigio duo millia equitum levis armaturæ conscribendi potestatem fecit, navesque plurimas commeatu onustas prope Delphzilam stare jussit. Ludovicus vero castra ad Groningam metatus, copiarum partem in cænobio Selverdico locaverat, victoriaque velut uti nescius, otio, & insumendis stipendijs militem alebat. Unde factum est, ut gerendarum rerum magnæ occasiones elaberentur, ipseque Ludovicus, etsi Hoogstratani auxilijs adjutus, levibus tantum velitationibus cum Carolo Megano certaret. Adeò verum est adversa tolerari, prosperis vero corrumpi ingenia Principum, & fælicitate insolescere.
units.tr: Thus Ferdinand of Alva, who had taken life from the noblest men, also begrudged them the earth common to mortals for their bodies, and, like a foul enemy of nature, declared that hatred survived even when the fuel of his rage was removed. Then, turning on Lamoral of Egmont and Philip of Montmorency, princes and Knights of the Golden Fleece, he had their final fate announced to them, and wrote the death sentence with his own hand, though it was believed to have been secretly brought from Spain. Egmont, the terror and thunderbolt of France (as Mondoucet, envoy of Charles IX, King of the French, proclaimed), was the first to offer his neck to the sword, and even while dying he placed all his solace for his fate in King Philip's favour. So he begged that the king would have pity, and by royal clemency relieve the lot of his most sorrowful widowed wife and eleven children, the numerous offspring, and finally the fortune of a princely but most wretched house. Now near death, and not unprepared to bear his last moments, he ended his prayers and desires with this one vow. These requests, sealed in a codicil and sent to Spain, fulfilled the trust of his last anxiety. Cornelius Gemma writes that he, who had often guarded the right side of Philip, was seized by the command of the royal name, and, using laudable patience at the end, submitted himself to the royal will as to fate and providence. Then the same end carried off Philip of Montmorency, Count of Horn. The heads of these bravest heroes, cut from their trunks and set on iron spikes, made a sad spectacle, and increased the hatred of the people and of the soldiers standing about against Alva. There were those who remembered that after victories won in the French and other wars, triumphal arches had been erected in that place for the victors, amid the applause of the people and the sounding of trumpets. Now the very trophies, the monuments of the slain and defeated enemies, had been turned to the use of a most foul spectacle. This was the end of Counts Egmont and Horn, who, once decorated with the highest honours and having followed the military service of Charles and Philip for thirty years across Africa and the Mediterranean, are recorded by writers. The same writers add that William of Nassau, Prince of Orange, had foretold this outcome for Egmont at the meeting at Willebrord, and that Gemma Frisius, the most celebrated mathematician of his age, had observed in Horn's horoscope that fatal fall from the arrangement of the heavens and the positions of the converging stars. So he had also forewarned Montmorency, that he should avoid the presence of Alva and the court, and withdraw with his companions into exile, from dangers, to provide both for his private safety and at the same time for the public cause. But, as I go back over the memory of these times, I have mostly observed that the cruelty of tyrants and the deaths imposed on the best men come from eternal and unchangeable providence, and that the liberty of nations, as if fated beforehand, has been preceded by frequent executions and the murders of princely men, as storms precede the coming calm. Therefore, inflamed to further vengeance for the Aremberg slaughter, Alva ordered soldiers scattered along the whole coast to be gathered, and soon sent Charles Brienne of Megen, who had been granted the prefecture of Friesland after the death of John Ligne of Aremberg, and all the lands between the Zuider Zee and the Ems, off to Groningen with troops. He also gave Eric of Brunswick power to enlist two thousand light-armed horsemen, and ordered many ships laden with supplies to lie near Delfzijl. Louis, however, had pitched camp at Groningen, had quartered part of his troops in the monastery of Selwerd, and, not knowing how to use his victory, kept the soldiers idle and consumed their pay. Hence great opportunities for action slipped away, and Louis himself, though aided by the troops of Hoogstraten, contended with Charles of Megen only in light skirmishes. So true it is that adversity is endured, but prosperity corrupts the minds of princes and makes them arrogant with good fortune.

units.la: Albanus verò serio rerum apparatu occupabatur. Quippe præmisso in Frisiam Chiappino Vitellio cum decem cohortibus peditum, mille & quingentos Germanos, & Casparum Roblesium cum sex signis subsequi jusserat, præter eas pedestres copias quas Ægydius Barlamontius Hyergius ducebat. Quibus de rebus certior factus Ludovicus metuensque ne cum majoribus auxilijs Albanus succederet, misso præcone Chiappinum Vitellium ad conflictum provocavit, qui diem pugnæ necdum effluxisse mordacibus verbis respondebat. Innuebat quippe Vitellius Ferdinandum Albanum, mox cum valido exercitu adfore, & Arembergij manibus adhuc inultis opportunas inferias decerni. Quare Ludovicus qui circumdare urbem Groningam præ paucitate copiarum non poterat, Reiderio tantum & Dammonensi rivis obseptis, misso longæ obsidionis consilio, ut urbe potiretur, ad dolum conversus est. Itaque decem & sex milites, apud quos vitæ ac mortis nullum discrimen, & facile paratu omne etiam facinus videbatur, è toto exercitu delegit, qui armata corpora lineis camisijs contegentes, ac ii e lectis dormitoriisque à milite Ludovici proturbati essent, ad portam urbis se contulere. Constituerant enim trucidatis vigilibus per vim portam occupare, & Ludovicum proxumè secuturum suis cum copiis intromittere. Sed sive fato, sive quod Ludovicus tardius cum auxilijs progrederetur, detecta res, Ludovicum successu consilij, fortissimum militem & animæ prodigum vita privavit. Pauci capti, Ludovicusque incertos rerum eventus animo volutans exercitum reduxit, quem Justi post Scouwenburgij, ( qui mille schlopetarios, & quadringentos equites ductabat ) diu sperata auxilia non parum roboravere.
units.tr: Alva, meanwhile, was busy with serious preparations. He had sent Chiappino Vitellio ahead into Friesland with ten cohorts of infantry, and had ordered Caspar Robles to follow with six companies, as well as the foot soldiers led by Egidius Barlaymont and Hierges. Informed of this, Ludovicus feared that Alva would come up with larger reinforcements. He sent a herald to challenge Chiappino Vitellio to battle, and Vitellio replied with biting words that the day of the fight had not yet passed. He hinted that Ferdinand Alva would soon arrive with a strong army, and that funeral rites were being prepared for the still unavenged shades of Aremberg. Ludovicus could not surround the city of Groningen because his forces were too few, and he had only blocked the Reiderland and Damme waterways. He therefore gave up the plan of a long siege and turned to a trick to take the city. He chose sixteen soldiers from the whole army, men for whom life and death made no difference and to whom any deed seemed easy to carry out. They covered their armed bodies with linen shirts, as if they had been driven out of their beds and dormitories by Ludovicus's soldiers, and made their way to the city gate. They planned to kill the watchmen, seize the gate by force, and let Ludovicus, who would follow close behind with his troops, come in. But whether by fate, or because Ludovicus advanced with the reinforcements too slowly, the plot was discovered. It deprived Ludovicus of the success of his plan and deprived him of his bravest soldiers, men who had been prodigal with their lives. A few were captured. Ludovicus, turning over in his mind the uncertain outcome of events, led the army back. Justus Scouwenburgius, who led a thousand harquebusiers and four hundred horsemen, strengthened it considerably with the reinforcements that had long been hoped for.

units.la: Tum Ferdinandus Albanus collecto ex Italis, Hispanis, & Burgundionibus exercitu, xvii. tormentis instructus, è Brabantiâ, post Geldriam Transisulaniamq; peragratas, Covardiam, deïn Groningam advenit, multosque pontes traijciendo amni factos secum duxit. Quarum rerum famâ excitus Ludovicus castra Slochterum movit, multoque conflictu, cum Epirotis, qui eum ocyus insequebantur, equitibus, habito, etsi suffosso equo alterius beneficio servatus est. Itaque pugnæ instantis discrimen expendens relicto Slochtero Iemmingam in Reiderios duxit, castraque in Amasi ripa metatus, opperiri hostem constituit. Deïn catarractas fluminis laxandis per agrum aquis aperiri jussit, ijsque intra alveum compressis (propterea quod flumen non nisi tempestate, aut æstu motum exundaret) à speculatorijs cohorcio. Io. tibus, quas Albanus praemiserat, sed maxime ignavia militum circumventus est.
units.tr: Then Ferdinand Alva, having gathered an army of Italians, Spaniards and Burgundians with seventeen cannon, came from Brabant. After passing through Gelderland and Overijssel, he reached Coevorden and then Groningen, and he brought with him many bridges built for crossing rivers. Roused by the news of these things, Ludovicus moved his camp to Slochteren. In a fierce skirmish with the Epirots, who pursued him more swiftly, and with the cavalry, he was saved, though his horse was stabbed under him, by the help of another horse. Therefore, weighing the danger of the impending battle, he left Slochteren, led his men to Jemgum in the Reiderland, and pitched camp on the bank of the Ems, resolving to wait for the enemy there. Then he ordered the sluices of the river to be opened so that the water would spread over the fields. But the water was held within the channel, because the river only overflowed when it was moved by a storm or by the tide. He was caught out by the scouting cohorts that Alva had sent ahead, but above all by the cowardice of his soldiers.

units.la: Illi namque in ipso discrimine, aleam jacere, canere, potare, bellum lusu, periculum securitate miscere, lacerare signa, aut pro libitu deserere, eaque facere, quae maturando exitio erant. Econtra celerare praelium Albanus, instigare Praefectos, hortari milites periculum in mora esse, ne firmiore opere Ludovicus se circumdet, aut patente post tergum Amaso majora auxilia accipiat. Ita velitatione praemissa graviore mox praelio partes concurrerunt, in quo schlopetarij fere omnes (quos ad prohibendum ponte hostem a Ludovico missos Cl. Franckena tradit) fraude ac perfidia rustici cecidere. Is namque sexcentos tantum Hispanorum, cum jam tota acies instaret, ponti imminere, ac expedita paucorum manu repelli posse falso nuntiaverat. Quare ad mandatum Ludovici progressi schlopetarij fraude decepti, & sustinendis exercitus universi viribus impares, accedente nitrosi pulveris defectu faeda internecione deleti sunt. Nihilominus Ludovicus ordines instruere, monere militem sacramenti, iret in hostem jam in acie stantem, efferum sociorum sanguine, mox, nisi pugnarent, suo se pasturum.
units.tr: For at the very moment of danger, they threw dice, sang, drank, played at war, mixed peril with carelessness, tore up their standards, or abandoned them at will, and did whatever hastened their ruin. On the other side, Alva hurried the battle along, urged on the commanders, and encouraged the soldiers that delay was dangerous, lest Ludovicus should fortify himself with stronger works, or receive larger reinforcements through the open ground behind the Ems. So after a skirmish had been sent forward, the two sides joined in a fiercer battle. In it nearly all the harquebusiers, whom Ludovicus had sent to hold the bridge against the enemy (as Franckena reports), fell through the trickery and treachery of a peasant. For this man had falsely reported that only six hundred Spaniards were pressing upon the bridge, and that they could be driven back by a small band of light troops, although the whole enemy line was about to attack. Therefore the harquebusiers advanced at the order of Ludovicus, deceived by the trick. Being unequal to holding out against the full strength of the army, and with the supply of gunpowder failing, they were destroyed in a shameful slaughter. Nevertheless Ludovicus tried to draw up his battle lines and warned the soldiers of their oath: they should go against the enemy already standing in battle order, and he said that, unless they fought, he would feed the savage ones with the blood of their comrades.

units.la: Cogitaret illum, patriae vastitiem, genti excidium, uxoribus liberisque (quos impotentia sexus aetatisque domi reliquerat) pejorem morte servitutem minari. Pugnarent itaq; quo solo praesens periculum vitari posset; aut gloriosa morte, adversisq; vulneribus confossi instar fortium virorum cruentam hostibus victoriam relinquerent. Sed spreta sacramenti religione contumax miles, (quem ex Oldenburgicis conscriptum fuisse, fidus autor notat) praelij puncto Ludovicum stipendia poscens pugnam detrectavit, caesusq; aut Amaso flumini immersus interijt. Ludovicus post praestitum optimi fortissimiq; Ducis exemplum faede a commilitonibus tandem derelictus, scaphaque Amasum transvectus in Transamasanos secessit. C. Gemma tradit, Germanos ipso instantis pugnae tempore, stipendia importune postulantes, fere ipsum Ludovicum prodidisse, eundemq; nudum vicinum flumen, istius artis peritia enatasse. Tradunt annales tantam in castris Ludovici insolentiam fuisse, ut miles majore flagitio dubium arma projecerit, an vexilla legionum discerpserit. Nonnulli beneficio fossarum inciliumqueservati triduo post Embdam devenere. Justus quoque Scouwenburgius cum ducentis equitibus pugnae subductus Bondam evasit.
units.tr: Let them consider, he said, the devastation of their fatherland, the destruction of their people, and the slavery, worse than death, that threatened their wives and children, whom the weakness of sex and age had left at home. Let them therefore fight, the only way by which the present danger could be avoided, or else, dying a glorious death, pierced by wounds received in the front, like brave men, leave the bloody victory to the enemy. But a stubborn soldier, scorning the sanctity of his oath (a trustworthy authority notes that he was enlisted from the Oldenburg region), demanded his pay at the crucial moment of the battle, refused to fight, and was either cut down or drowned in the Ems and perished. Ludovicus, after setting the example of an excellent and most brave leader, was at last shamefully abandoned by his fellow soldiers. He was carried across the Ems in a boat and withdrew to the people beyond the Ems. C. Gemma reports that the Germans, who at the very time of the battle importunately demanded their pay, almost betrayed Ludovicus himself, and that he, stripped naked, swam across the neighbouring river by the skill of that art. The annals relate that there was such insolence in the camp of Ludovicus that a soldier, in a greater disgrace, threw down his weapons in doubt whether he should tear up the standards of the legions. Several, saved by the help of ditches and hiding places, reached Emden three days later. Justus Scouwenburgius also withdrew from the battle with two hundred horsemen and escaped to Bunde.

units.la: Reperio in historicis narrationibus A. Franckenae, D. Galama Frisicae gentis virum nobilem, cum paucis fugientem plurimos hostium, qui acrius Ludovicum insequebantur; a suis disjunctos interemisse, refertumq; spolijs vitae servatum. Ludovicus collectis sparsi exercitus reliquijs ad fratrem Gulielmum Nassovium Aurantium Principem se contulit. Duo millia illo praelio caesa, praedaq; ingens victoribus concessa. Tum in victore exercitu stupra matronarum ac virginum omnisque insolentiae exempla viguere, abactis e Reiderio agro xviii. pecorum millibus. Annotatum quoque invenio x. Kal. Aug. (qui dies Jemminganae pugnae postridianus fuit) Leovardios comparatis ad hoc curribus commeatum atque annonam Ferdinando Albano procu, rasserasse, eundemque Albanum victoriâ potitum vii. Kal. in Heilegerlaeum caenobium, post Delphzilam atque Dammonam redijsse, quarum priorem deumbratâ novae urbis formâ commutare velle impositò Marspurgi nomine credebatur. Isti namque rei Chiappinum Vitellium, & Paciottum Antverpianae nuper arcis architectum, tum Iohannem Knijssium Groningensium Praesulem, consecrando templi loco delegaverat. Sed Groningensium precibus, ac Caroli Brimaei Frisiae Praefecti intercessione condendae urbis negotium omissum est. Quo tempore Margareta Marchica ab Arembergij mariti morte Bruxellis agens, ut defuncti memoriam innovaret, litteras in Frisiam dedit, proceresque eius populi hoc modo salutavit.
units.tr: I find in the historical narratives of A. Franckena, that D. Galama, a noble man of the Frisian people, killed with a few men many of the enemy who were pursuing Ludovicus more fiercely, after they had been cut off from their own; and that he was saved, laden with spoils. Ludovicus, gathering the remnants of his scattered army, went to his brother William of Nassau, Prince of Orange. Two thousand men were killed in that battle, and great booty was given to the victors. Then in the victorious army the rapes of matrons and virgins and every example of insolence flourished, after eighteen thousand head of cattle had been driven out of the Reiderland. I also find it noted that on the tenth day before the Kalends of August (which was the day after the battle at Jemgum), Ferdinand Alva arranged for provisions and grain to be brought to him from Leeuwarden by carts prepared for the purpose. And that the same Alva, having gained the victory, returned on the seventh day before the Kalends to the monastery of Heiligerlee, and after that to Delfzijl and Dam. It was believed that he wanted to change Delfzijl, its old form hidden, into a new city, to be called Marsburg. For this purpose he had appointed Chiappino Vitellio, and Paciotto, recently architect of the citadel of Antwerp, and also John Knijssius, bishop of Groningen, to choose the site for the temple. But at the request of the people of Groningen, and through the intercession of Charles Brimaeus, prefect of Friesland, the project of founding the city was dropped. At this time Margaret of Melen, living at Brussels after the death of her husband Aremberg, wrote a letter to Friesland to renew the memory of the dead man, and greeted the nobles of that people in this way.

units.la: LVCTVOSISSIMVM casum, quì mihi domuiqne meae evenit, non ignorare vos puto, erepto terris Arembergio marito meo & vitae fortunarumq; consorte. Qui cum pro PHILIPPO rege, pro tuendis agris finibusq; vestris, ut egregij exercituum Duces solent, mortem oppetierit, ita recordari vos credo quâ laude Praefecti imperium Carolo Philippoq; rerum potiuntibus gentem apud vestram obiverit. Quâ ex causâ sibi aeternum decus peperit, secitque, ut vos magno affectu vivum amaretis, quem mortuum desideratis. Itaq; & ego, dum in provinciâ vestrâ substiti, communem cum marito fortunam, & sortem experta, propensos in me animos vestros sensi, quos ut servetis etiam erga me absentem, & orbitate miseram obnixe peto. Ego certe, quae maximam aetatis meae partem vestro in solo, vestris in terris cum desideratissimo marito exegi, vos jure meritoque amavi, & ita quidem ut à sororis conditione non absuerim. Quin omne officium à primogenito filio, à reliquis liberis pignoribusque meis, paternae, ut auguror, virtutis vestigia pressuris, expectate, ac pro certo habete Arembergicam domum, etsi tristissimo hoc casu infelicem, vobis addictam fore. Idem ut faciatis mihi liberisque meis, impense oro. Litterae prid. Kal. Aug, Bruxellis datae.
units.tr: I suppose you are not unaware of the most grievous misfortune that has befallen me and my household: my husband Aremberg, who was snatched from the earth, my companion in life and fortunes. Since he met his death for King Philip, and to defend your fields and borders, as excellent commanders of armies usually do, I believe you remember with what praise he discharged the office of prefect among your people while Charles and Philip were in power. For this reason he won for himself eternal honour, and made you love him living with great affection, the very man whom you now miss dead. And so I too, while I stayed in your province, having shared the common fortune and lot with my husband, have felt your minds well disposed towards me. I earnestly ask you to keep these feelings towards me even now that I am absent and wretched in my bereavement. Indeed I, who spent the greater part of my life on your soil and in your lands with my most beloved husband, have loved you justly and deservedly, and indeed so much that I have not been far from the condition of a sister. Moreover, look for every service from my firstborn son and from my other children and pledges, who, I trust, will follow the footsteps of their father's virtue. And be assured that the house of Aremberg, though unhappy in this most sorrowful event, will be devoted to you. I earnestly beg you to do the same for me and my children. Letter dated Brussels, the day before the Kalends of August.

units.la: Similes litterae à Johanne Roorda juris perito, qui in Comitatu ac aulâ Margaretae Marchicae fuerat, & tum caesarum patronum in supremo Senatu Mechlinienfi agebat, ad Deputatos Ordinum missae, quae Arembergij laudes prolixe enarrabant, & quantum doloris ex ipsius insperatâ morte Rex simul & provinciae hausissent. Hoc etiam petebat, ut si forte ab Albano Philippi prorege, populus Friscus ad comitium vocaretur, Frisij de defuncti justo temperatoq; regimine apud Albanum testarentur, eundemque Arembergium turbatissimis temporum, Philippi hostibus armatâ manu, atq; fortissimo exemplo restitisse. Tum de successione filij mentio injecta, petitumq; ut proximo comitio, quod Frisij habituri forent, eius ratio haberetur. Hoc verò dolebat Margareta, omissam esse à Frisijs doloris publici, quem ex morte praefecti sui facere debuissent, testificationem, Frisioq; neglecto more, regis Gallorum, Bavari ac Lotharingi, tum Traufisulaniae, Translavicanorumq; officia in complorando funere neglexisse. Non misisse legatos, nec expedivisse litteras solemnium testes, quod in illorum exequijs fieri soleret, qui praeclaras bello paceque res gesissent, & qui laudabidabilis imperij finem egregiâ morte, & imitando posteris exitu cohonestassent. Ad quas Iohanni Roordæ respønsum.
units.tr: Similar letters were sent to the deputies of the estates by John Roorda, a lawyer who had been in the service and household of Margaret of Melen, and who then acted as advocate for the Crown in the supreme senate of Mechelen. These letters spoke at length of the praises of Aremberg, and of how much grief the King and the provinces had drunk in from his unexpected death. He also asked that, if perhaps the Frisian people were called to an assembly by Alva, the viceroy of Philip, the Frisians should bear witness before Alva to the just and moderate rule of the dead man, and that Aremberg had resisted with armed force, and with a most brave example, the enemies of Philip in the most troubled times. Then mention was made of the succession of his son, and it was asked that his claim be taken into account at the next assembly the Frisians were to hold. Margaret was indeed distressed that the Frisians had omitted the public testimony of grief that they should have made at the death of their prefect. And, neglecting the custom, they had failed to perform the duties of mourning at his funeral, as the King of the French, the Bavarians and the Lorrainers, and also the peoples of Trans-Ems and Trans-Lauwers, had done. They had not sent envoys, nor dispatched letters as witnesses of the solemn rites, as was customary at the funerals of those who had done splendid deeds in war and peace, and who had graced the end of a praiseworthy rule with a noble death and an example for posterity to imitate. To these letters John Roorda gave a reply.

units.la: Litteræ tuæ nobis bene traditæ sunt, ex quibus desideria Margaretæ Marchicæ Arembergÿ viduæ cognovimus. Cuius memoriam ex gloriâ gestarum apud nos rerum sub Carolo Philippoq; quia amoveri non sinemus, ita testamur gravem nobis luctum acerbissimumque mærorem ex illius excessu obvenisse. Cui quoque condolere in animo habuimus, nisi incertis rumoribus evulgata mors fuisset, & nisi formidaremus Margaretæ luctum lugubri officio geminare. Caeterum, ut testemur de affectu nostro, quo orbam Marito Margaretam prosequimur, dabimus operam, ut apud Albanum, si conventum populi Frisici indixerit, & Præfecti nostri memoriam, attamq; cum laude ætatem, & juxta liberos superstites commendemus, ac ut filium paternæ laudis & imperij heredem habeamus. De reliquis petimus, ut mæstæ desolateque viduæ, liberisq; nostro nomine omne officium promittas, fidemq; facias, nos Arembergÿ etiam à morte cultores filium liberosq; in spem futuræ successionis salutare. Neq; omittemus Ferdinando Albano nostrum desiderium exponere, quo favoris nostri amplissimum documentum extet. Litteræ Leovard. xv. Kal. Septemb. datæ.
units.tr: Your letter has been duly delivered to us, and from it we have learned the wishes of Margaret, Marchioness of Aremberg, widow. We testify that her memory, which we will not allow to be erased, along with the glory of the deeds done among us under Charles and Philip, has brought us a heavy grief and most bitter sorrow at her passing. We also intended to offer our condolences to her, had not the news of his death been spread by uncertain rumours, and had we not feared to double Margaret's grief with a mournful duty. Moreover, so that we may show our feeling toward Margaret, bereaved of her husband, we will take care that, if Alva calls an assembly of the Frisian people, the memory of our prefect is commended there, along with his life, worthy of praise, and his surviving children, so that his son may be the heir of his father's praise and rule. As for the rest, we ask that you offer every service on our behalf to the sorrowing and desolate widow and her children, and assure them that we, even after his death, still hold Aremberg in honour, and that we keep the son and children in hope of a future succession. Nor will we fail to set out our wish to Ferdinand Alva, so that a most ample proof of our favour may exist. Dated at Leeuwarden, xv Kal. Septemb.

units.la: Quibus confirmandis missi sub exitum Augusti ad eandem Margaretam Marchicam Ruardus Roorda, & Hero Ockingha, quo ægritudinem Margaretæ ex mariti morte conceptam, honesto alloquio levarent, opeq; Viglij Præsidis idoneum, si res adhuc integra foret, successorem Arembergio peterent. Quod in gratiam Margaretæ ab Ordinibus Frisiæ factum facile crediderim, quo filius, quem primo partu enixa erat, per Viglium & Legatos, paternam in dignitatem succederet. Quibus & hoc in mandatis datum; ut apud eundem Præsidem, de immoderatis fisci regij actionibus quererentur, nobilitatemque & simul locupletiores fiscali actione non in judicio regio, caeterum coram Albano conveniri.
units.tr: To confirm these things, Ruardus Roorda and Hero Ockingha were sent toward the end of August to the same Margaret Marchica, to relieve her grief, conceived from her husband's death, by a respectful address, and to seek, with the help of Viglius the President, a suitable successor to Aremberg, if the matter was still open. I readily believe this was done by the estates of Friesland for Margaret's favour, so that her son, whom she had borne in her first delivery, might succeed to his father's dignity through Viglius and the envoys. They were also given this instruction: that they should complain before the same President about the immoderate actions of the royal treasury, and that the nobility, and at the same time the wealthier men, should be sued not in the royal court by a fiscal action, but before Alva.

units.la: Tum Albanus Groningæ (quam v. Kal. August. pro more victoris à clero universoque Senatu magnâ pompâ exceptus intraverat) suspectâ civium fide validam arcem munimentum durioris imperij decrevit, locatoque ibidem valido præsidio, ordinatisque per Provinciam rebus Ultrajectum, & dein in Brabantiam properavit, cui imminere magno cum exercitu quem in Treviris lustraverat, Gulielmus Nassovius, Princeps Aurantius dicebatur. Qui Trajecto post Rheno, dein Mosa flumine, ut fraternæ ad Iemmingham cladis infaelicitatem vindicaret, Ferdinandum Albanum apud Trajectum Mosæ loricâ castrorum clausum ad pugnam nequicquam evocavit, consumptus morâ, & annonæ penuriâ, post seditione militum, (qui praefecti caede nefarias manus imbuerant) fractus, in Germaniam se recepit, suamque & Ludovici fratris fortunam principis animi constantiâ toleravit. Dein peracto Iemmingano prælio copiæ iterum in præsidia reductæ, ac decem cohortes peditum, quibus Ægydius Barlamontius Hyergius cum imperio præerat, per Leovardiam urbem, & suburbana loca iter fecere. Tres quoque cohortes è Valonum gente Leovardiæ noctem egere, posteroque die in Transfisulaniam ablegatæ propriam illis temporibus sollicitudinem dubiæ biæ urbi excussere. Tum Prid. Non. Augusti, ob Iemminganam Albani victoriam supplicationum dies, per omnem Frisiam institutus, eorumque nomina, qui Ludovici Nassovij partes illo bello secuti erant, ad Senatum regium perlata. Ita sursum ac deorsum prosperis juxta & adversis immistæ res per Frisiam fluebant, robustioribusque sensim nervis mutabile, & incertum eventibus bellum trahebatur. Pro cuius mole animum quoque Philippi jam diu exasperatum majora odia induisse, per ipsam quoque Hispaniam tristissima exempla & imperatæ Legatorum mortes docuere. Ioannem quippe Bergæ Marchionem, carcere, & ægritudine mentis ferme absumptum, post veneno extinctum, omnis fama asseruit; Florentiumque Montmorentium tentato nequicquam effugio apud Segoviam gladio percussum, infælicem Legati sortem explevisse. Quod factum pessimæ per omnem Europam aulasque regum famæ fuit. Hoc scilicet unum Philippo superfuisse, ut tot millium per Provincias sanguini fuso, & Principum cædibus, omni jure, mox etiam gentium violato, ipsorum quoque Legatorum necs adjiceret. Mox percrebescens per Frisiam rumor tot tristium rerum famæ superaditus Caroli Hispaniæ Principis mortem nuntiavit. Creditum fuit, eum secretis novercæ conloquiis, deïn consuetudine Belgicorum Legatorum Marchionis Bergæ, & Montinij usum familiarius, suspicionem proni in Belgicam affectus dedisse, & ab illo duriore Philippi patris imperio alienum, tutius mitiusq; remedium componendis civilibus turbis destinasse.
units.tr: Then Alva, who had entered Groningen toward the end of July, received with great pomp by the clergy and the whole senate, as is the custom for a victor, decided, since he distrusted the loyalty of the citizens, to build a strong citadel as a bulwark of harsher rule. After placing a strong garrison there and putting affairs in the province in order, he hastened to Utrecht and then into Brabant, where William of Nassau, called the Prince of Orange, was threatening with a great army which he had mustered in Trier. Crossing the Rhine and then the Meuse, so as to avenge the unhappy defeat at Jemmingen of his brother, he called Ferdinand Alva out to battle in vain, when Alva had shut himself within the fortified camp at Maastricht on the Meuse.
