Ut ea impetraremus, Caesar Principesq;, supplices hoc in loco apud vos devolvimur, oramusque exules, ut quoniam divini nominis, & sola Evangelicae veritatis professione munimur, omnem sinistram de nobis suspicionem amoveatis, deque consilio Principum, procerumque vestrorum ea de re cognoscatis, succurratisque interim nobis, omnibus & singulis, qui innocentiae nostrae perfugium vestram Germaniam delegimus. Quod si faciatis, Caesar, Principesque, pollicemur digna nostro nomine, & vestro simul imperio, precabimurque Deum Opt. Max. ut rebus consiliisque vestris interfit.
units.tr: We have come to you, Emperor Maximilian, and to the Electors and Princes, because we have been driven out by the horrible tyranny of Ferdinand of Alva. Stripped of our goods and exiled from our country, we are asking for your help and that of the most merciful Princes, and we want to defend our cause against those who, pretending to religion and holiness and relying on the ambitious cleverness of the Roman Pontiffs, have insinuated themselves into the counsels of kings and princes. It was from them that the Inquisition, devised for correcting Jews and pagans, was turned against Christians and today against us Frisians. The same institution, introduced under Emperor Charles V and afterwards under his son Philip, has brought us every misery and calamity. We had hoped for life and liberty, and to profess our sacred rites and religion without distinction, as your Germans or the French people do. Instead we have fallen into such slavery that our consciences are assailed, and we have been proclaimed heretics, rebels and seditious persons, so that not one crime but many is charged against our innocence. Then they raged against our goods and fortunes. Lest the fury of this insatiable cruelty stop at these limits, after we saw our belongings plundered, the blood of innocent fellow citizens poured out, and finally divine and human law violated, we pulled our necks from the still bloody sword of the tyrant, and we have preferred this exile, which you see, Caesar and Princes, to our dearest fatherland. We have borne this exile too with singular patience up to now, and only in the trust that it comes to us by the eternal ordering of God's providence, and that God will at some time give our affairs an outcome, and that in this very exile he will give solace for the adversity we endure. So that we may obtain these things, Caesar and Princes, we prostrate ourselves as suppliants before you in this place, and we beg you: since we are fortified by the name of God and by the sole profession of Evangelical truth, remove every sinister suspicion of us, take cognizance of this matter by the counsel of your Princes and nobles, and meanwhile come to the aid of us, each and all, who have chosen your Germany as a refuge for our innocence. If you do so, Caesar and Princes, we promise things worthy of our name and of your empire at the same time, and we will pray to God Most High that he may be present to your affairs and counsels.

units.la: Caeterum tota exulum Legatio, etsi prono, ut creditum fuit, Maximiliano Caesare, ac quibusdam Electorum, per Legatos Ferdinandi Albani inrita ac infructuosa fuit. Qui vergente mense Iulio de mandato Philippi, quod Madriti in Hispania Anno cIↄ Iↄ. xxix. xvi. Kal. Decemb. factum erat, edictum Veniae regio apparatu ac magnificentia publicavit, exulesq; per Germaniae Imperium, & confinia Frisiae sparsos, speciosa clementiae praetextu revocare conatus est. Sed diffidentiae vitio, & quod ministros reformatorum Ecclesiarum, federatam Nobilitatem, tum Magistratus quosdam & collegia civium excluderet, nullius fermè efficaciae fuit. Hoc tantum memoriae traditum est, exules paucos & quidem è plebe, nullo vitae, aut suarum rerum metu, relictâ Embdâ, Leovardiam remigrasse, nullumque fidei datae discrimen, atque periculum pertulisse.
units.tr: The whole embassy of the exiles, though, as was believed, Emperor Maximilian and some of the Electors were favourably inclined, came to nothing and was fruitless, through the envoys of Ferdinand of Alva. Toward the end of July, by the command of Philip, which had been given at Madrid in Spain on 16 November 1579, he published a pardon with royal pomp and magnificence, and tried, under the pretext of clemency, to recall the exiles who were scattered through the Empire of Germany and the borders of Frisia. But because of the defect of distrust, and because it excluded the ministers of the reformed churches, the confederated nobility, certain magistrates and colleges of citizens, it was almost without effect. It is only recorded that a few exiles, and indeed from the common people, left Emden and went back to Leeuwarden with no fear for their life or property, and suffered no breach or danger of the faith that had been given.

units.la: Illo quoq; tempore Stellinguerfios occidentales, quorum agri juxta
units.tr: At that same time the western Stellingwerfs, whose fields lie alongside

units.la: Lindam flumen ad Cunerae fines procurrunt, de magnis impendijs questos libellum supplicem Senatui regio obtulisse; rejectosque ad Praefectum sub hac formula (fiat sermo Gubernatori) inrita vota ac desiderata reparandis damnis iterasse. Volebant namq; Stellinguerfij, ut ab Haskeranis & Auguerdijs, quorum fines contigui sunt, parte onerum levarentur, aut detrimenta ex commeatibus militum copiarumque illata aerarium provinciae resarciret. Quod ipsum utrosque Dongrios cis ac trans Palenum rivum sitos, Dantumanos, Collumanos, Octopagicos, Raverdios, Tietzerkios, Wonseranos, Baerderanos, Barranos, Utingeranos, Haskerios fecisse in actis illorum temporum invenio. Hoc namque periniquum dicebant, praeter annonam commeatumq; militarem currus, equos, navigia, dein ipsa quoque cohortium stipendia ex florenis aureis praestari, vastatisq aut direptis per militem agris, pauperum quoq; egestati & tenuiori fortunae sumpto in usuras aere subveniri. Adeo verum belli initia incrementis saepe graviora esse, populumq; militaribus insolentijs tributisque stipendiorum assuetum consuetudine, sicuti mos est, facilem patientiam induere. Itaque Albanus, ut aerario Philippi, quod jam mole belli impellebatur, prospiceret, autut enervem populum immani exactione redderet dubium, omnium Frisiae Ordinum conventum (quos centenarium numerum excessisse ex archivis constat) indici ad iv. Eid. Ian. per Praesidem Senatumque regium fecit, eundemque hoc modo verba facere jussit.
units.tr: the river Linda, running out to the borders of Cuinera, complained of great expenses and presented a supplicating petition to the royal Senate. Sent back to the governor under this formula (let the matter be spoken to the governor), they repeated their fruitless prayers and desires for the repair of their losses. For the Stellingwerfs wanted part of their burdens relieved by the Haskerans and the Auguerds, whose territories are adjoining, or else the provincial treasury to make good the damage done by the movement of soldiers and the supplies of the troops. I find in the records of those times that the Dongrians on both sides of the river Palen, the Dantumans, Collumans, Octopagicans, Raverds, Tietzerks, Wonserans, Baerderans, Barrans, Utingerans and Haskers did the same thing. They said it was most unjust that, besides provisions and military transport, carts, horses, ships and then the pay of the cohorts were furnished from gold florins, and that, when fields were laid waste or plundered by soldiers, even the poor and those of meagre fortune had to be helped by money borrowed at interest. So true it is that the beginnings of war are often more burdensome than its increase, and that a people accustomed to the insolence of soldiers and the taxes for their pay, as usually happens, puts on an easy patience. Therefore Alva, either to provide for Philip's treasury, which was already being pressed by the weight of war, or to wear out a weakened people by an enormous exaction (it is doubtful which), ordered a meeting of all the orders of Frisia to be summoned by the President and the royal Senate for 10 January. (It is recorded from the archives that they numbered more than a hundred.) He ordered this meeting to be addressed in the following way.

units.la: Missum in Belgicam Albanum, Frisij, à Philippo rege nostris sedandis componendisq; turbis, quae tempestiva remedia, amovendis gravioribus flagitabant. Is vero negotium à judicio orsus in autores tumultuum animadvertit, ut regio quanto ocyus satisfaceret mandato, & ut veniam pro ijs à Rege impetraret, qui à turbarum autoribus concitati, & seducti propositum Ducis subverterunt. Tantum namque molestiae ipsi Duci ab illis creatum est, ut maximam anni partem in castris agere coactus sit, donec hostes regis, partimque Duces magnâ illorum infamiâ agris finibusq; Belgicae victricibus armis expulerit. Et quoniam motuum turbarumque incentores ab innovatâ religione consilia sua capere, quae semel polluta omnem licentiam inducere solet, prima Duci cura fuit, ut Catholica religio restitueretur, & ut legibus Philippiq; editis robur accederet. Quae res cum regis valde aerarium infirmaverit, metuendumq; sit, ne à seditiosâ & perduelli multitudine nova pericula, atq; arma patiamur, omnino necessum est, ut gerendarum rerum subsidia à fidelibus Philippi subditis petamus. Quos ad conferendum regijs armis tributum Caroli Caesaris, Philippiq; in vos merita impellent, si memoriâ repetatis, quantis impendijs externa bella, pro aris focisque vestris gesserint. Ex eo namque evenit, ut domania, sicuti vocant, regia creditorum aere gravata, & simul pignori data sint, rogaque quoque & honoraria subsidia Regi praestita cessaverint, nihilq; ad manum sit, quo turmarum equestrium, praesidiorumque stipendia habeantur. Mitto tormenta, & omnem belli commeatum requiri, solvenda militi stipendia, & crediti per mercatores aeris magnitudinem, quam Philippus à postremo in Hispaniam discessu salutiv estrae impendi fecit. Consideratē praeterea, quantis itinerum molestiys sumptibusque Albanus in Belgicam venerit, quantos exercitus aluerit, impediendis rebellium conatibus, & ne amota religione, quae in discrimen trahebatur, ex-torres patriâ viveretis. Ea propter cum ex domanijs regijs, ex transmari-nis regnis ac provincijs Philippi subsidia haberi non possint, excogitanda sunt nova, quibus vos ipsi juvemini. Idcircò placuit ut aes creditum tempestivâ pe-cuniæ corrogatione minuatur, perque speciem rogarum, aut honorariæ oblationis, quo minus populum laedamus, desiderata militi stipendia solvantur. In usum verò belli ordinarium tributum habendum erit, ne aeterna debiti aeris obligatio sit. Praeterea hoc etiam necessarium est, ut sacrum aerarium habeatis sepositum ultimæ necessitati, quæ, quemadmodum in omni re mortalium, ita maxime in bello se interponit. Quod ut obtineamus, nullum consilium aptius, nullum salubrius Duci visum est, quam, quod Philippo regi primo in Belgicam ingressu placuit, ut decimæ omnium bonorum praestarentur, & ut ex aequalitate opum tributi quoq; aequalitas nasceretur. Et Rex quidem isti consilio modum praescripserat, quem quia aut aliqui aversabantur, aut imperiti non capiebant, egentiæ publicæ salubre remedium omissum est. Nunc autem quoniam Albanus singulari curâ isti rei prospexit, ne quæ confusio oriatur, concepto hunc in finem edicto, quod videtis, inveniri impulsis Philippi rebus praesentius remedium non potuit, quam si ex mobilium venditione decima, ex immobilium vigesima praestetur. Consensum huic rei reliquæ provinciæ adhibuere, idem rogo ut Regi praestatis; vosq; oppidani concivibus vestris persuadeatis, nullum retinendis in ordine rebus praestantius decentiusq; vinculum fore. Ad haec si pareatis, veniam Philippi & gratiam impetrabitis, facietisque quod vestra in Regem fides, vestrum sacramentum exigit.
units.tr: Frisians, King Philip sent Alva into the Low Countries to calm and settle our disorders, which called for timely remedies to remove the more serious troubles. He began this business with judgment against the authors of the tumults, so that he might the sooner satisfy the royal command, and obtain pardon from the King for those who, stirred up and seduced by the instigators of the disturbances, subverted the Duke's purpose. So much trouble was caused to the Duke himself by them that he was forced to spend the greater part of the year in camp, until he drove the King's enemies, and partly their leaders, to great disgrace from the fields and territories of Belgium with victorious arms. And since the instigators of the movements and disturbances take their plans from the renewed religion, which, once polluted, usually brings in every licence, the Duke's first care was that the Catholic religion be restored, and that the laws and the edicts of Philip gain strength. Since this business has greatly weakened the King's treasury, and since we must fear that new dangers and arms come upon us from a seditious and rebellious multitude, it is absolutely necessary that we ask for the means of carrying on affairs from Philip's faithful subjects. The tribute of Charles Caesar and Philip's services toward you should move them to contribute to the royal arms, if you call to mind how great the expenses were that they bore in foreign wars for your altars and hearths. For from this it came about that the royal domains, as they are called, burdened with debt to creditors and at the same time pledged, and the gifts and honorary aids given to the King have ceased, and there is nothing at hand from which the pay of cavalry squadrons and garrisons can be met. I pass over the fact that artillery and all supplies of war must be sought, that the pay owed to soldiers must be settled, and the size of the money borrowed from merchants, which Philip caused to be spent for your safety since his last departure for Spain. Consider besides with what troubles of travel and expense Alva came into Belgium, how many armies he has fed, to hinder the attempts of the rebels, and so that, religion having been removed, which was being brought into danger, you should not live as exiles from your country. Therefore, since subsidies cannot be had from the royal domains or from Philip's transmarine kingdoms and provinces, new means must be devised by which you yourselves may be helped. It has accordingly been decided that the borrowed money be reduced by a timely collection of cash, and that, under the appearance of a gift or honorary offering, so that we do not burden the people, the pay desired by the soldiers be paid. For ordinary war a tax is to be kept, so that there is not an eternal obligation of debt. Besides this it is also necessary that you keep a sacred treasury set aside for the final necessity, which, as in every human affair, so especially intrudes itself in war. To secure this, no plan seemed more suitable or more wholesome to the Duke than the one that pleased King Philip at his first entry into Belgium: that a tenth of all goods be paid, and that from equality of wealth equality of taxation also arise. Indeed the King had prescribed a measure for that plan, which, because some either disliked it or did not understand it, was dropped, a healthy remedy for public want. Now, since Alva has looked after this matter with special care, so that no confusion arises, a decree drawn up to this end, which you see, has been issued. For Philip's affairs, when pressed, no more immediate remedy could be found than that a tenth be paid from the sale of movables and a twentieth from immovables. The other provinces have given their consent to this; I ask you to give the same to the King, and to persuade your townsmen that nothing will be a more excellent or fitting bond for keeping affairs in order. Moreover, if you obey, you will obtain Philip's pardon and favour, and you will do what your loyalty to the King and your oath demand.

units.la: Quâ Oratione habitâ, Senatus per Frisiam regius, more consueto, Deputatis Ordinum se adjunxit, ipsiq; Ordines nomina sua, ne quid solemnibus deesset, professi sunt. Tum ne multitudo ex se discors regis edicto impedimentum afferret, pauciores delecti èq; oppidanis Nicolaus Hansonius, Matthias Rommartius Jure-consulti, Gerardus Vibius, Haringus Andringha, & Ruardus Vibius L. Doctores, qui cum agrarijs conferrent, locoq; tantæ multitudini angusto, divisis secessibus secretisq; uterentur. Invenio in actis promovendis comitij rebus Senatores quoq; adhibitos, ne in tam gravi deliberatione, aut Regis auctoritas, aut patriæ salus periclitaretur. Itaq; postero (qui fuit v. Iun.) cum Iacobo Rouffellio Ooftergoo, Iulio Dekama Westergoo, Idzardo Sickinga è Sylvestri tractu delegato, communicatione habitâ, hunc in modum responsum.
units.tr: After this speech, the Frisian Senate, as is customary, joined the deputies of the Orders, and the Orders themselves declared their names so that nothing required by the ceremony would be missing. Then, so that the crowd, being divided among itself, would not hinder the king's edict, a smaller group was chosen from the townsmen: Nicolaus Hansonius, Matthias Rommartius, jurists, and Gerardus Vibius, Haringus Andringha and Ruardus Vibius, doctors. They were to confer with the country representatives, using divided rooms and private corners, since the place was too cramped for so great a crowd. I find in the records of the assembly's business that senators were also admitted, so that in so grave a deliberation neither the king's authority nor the safety of the country would be put at risk. Therefore, on the following day (the 5th of June), after a joint discussion with Jacobus Rouffellius for Oostergo, Julius Dekama for Westergo, and Idzardus Sickinga, delegated from the Sylvester district, they gave this answer.

units.la: PEtitioni regiæ & Ferdinandi Albani, neq; agrarij, neque oppidani pares sumus. Provincia nostra ut ambitu parva, septem tantum miliarium longitudinem latitudinemq; complectens, ita ad egestatem redacta est. Quamvis enim fertiles in eâ agros habeamus, & aut pascendo pecori, aut habendæ messi commodos, ita bonis quoq; arenosi ac palustres immisti sunt. Et quidem ita, ut omni apud nos solo non idem ingenium, non eadem natura sit, cuius fæcundissima pars magnis marinorum aliorumq; aggerum impendijs retinenda est. Præter ipsum, quoq; mare littori nostro infectum, à piratis praedonibusq; damna sensimus à quibus immunes tutosq; nos praestare rex Philippus ex Carolinâ conventione, tum etiam suâ, debuisset. Neque enim rogas (bono.
units.tr: We are not equal to the king's petition and to that of Ferdinand of Alba, neither the country representatives nor the townsmen. Our province, as it is small in extent, embracing only seven miles in length and breadth, has also been reduced to poverty. For although we have fertile fields in it, suited either to pasturing herds or to producing a harvest, sandy and marshy tracts are mixed in with the good land as well. Indeed the soil among us is not of one kind or one nature throughout, and its most fertile part must be kept by great expenditure on sea dikes and other embankments. Besides, the sea itself has done damage to our shore, and we have suffered losses from pirates and robbers, from which King Philip ought to have kept us free and safe, by the Carolinian convention and also by his own. For you do not ask (for the good.

units.la: {a} cIↄ. Iↄ. LXX. (honorarium Principis tributum) alium in finem elargiti sumus, quam ut omnis externa vis atq; armatorum incursus averteretur, nostroq; are, aut donativo pax terris nostris atq; securitas foret. Fidem tam subdito, quam Principi da tam servandam esse.
units.tr: We paid the 100,000 (the honorarium, a tribute to the Prince) for no other purpose than that every external force and every incursion of armed men might be turned away, and that peace and security for our lands might come from our own money or gift. Faith must be kept as much by the subject as by the Prince.

units.la: His addebant, magna Caesarem beneficia à Frisijs accepisse, subactâ domitaq; Groningâ, ac Omlandiâ, dein Drentiâ Coverdiâq; in fidem receptis, quadraginta aureorum millia Caesari concessa, assignatos agros Biltanos, caeteraq; Caesaris aerario attributa, laudabili liberalitate, quò conventiones antiquæ inviolabiles forent, quas Philippus Anno I. per Arembergium & post quinquennium coram ipsâ inauguration is festivitate principali voce firmassset. Quæ cum ita se habeant, mirari Frisios novis & non ferendis exactionibus se gravari. Nam agros inundationibus sæpe oppressos, arva ac pascua salsedine aquarum corrupta, annonæ penuriam, mortes animalium, & omnem miseriam induxisse. Adhoc vagari per agros mendicantium greges, vim atq; injuriam colonis facere, habendas esse noctu marinum per aggerem excubias, quo prædonum piratarumq; incursionibus occurratur; Quæ quanquam populum premant, eiusq; opes facultatesq; exhauriant, tamen testari se amore & fide in Regem ductos, quo provinciam ab omni armorum vi immunem præstet, daturos septuaginta quinq; aureorum millia, certis æquisq; sex annorum pensionibus exsolvenda, sub hac tamen cautione, ut conventionibus pactisq; antiquis stetur. Ea propter rogabant, regem, ut veteris clementiæ retinens à centesimæ, vigesimæ, decimæq; exactione abstineat, populumq; jure suo & immunitate non privet. His, de inquilinis, quod in Brabantiâ ac Flandriâ fieri dicebant, extraneo præferendis, beneficijsque Ecclesiasticis addita. Quæ x v. Iun. actis concepta comitium populi extraxere. Itaque Kal. Iul. instigante & urgente Carolo Brimæo conventus Ordinum repetitus, oblatisque per Frisios centum aureorum millibus tandem conventio facta, ut quaternis pensionibus ad Odulphi diem centum & viginti octo millia præstarentur, & centesimæ, vigesimæ, decimæque exactio cessaret. Quod ab oppidanis, (nam agrarij id stipulati erant) post approbatum, Westergoos ante discordes Sylvestribus conciliavit. Hoc verò contractui suberat, ut Albanus Philippi nomine approbaret, publicâque ac solemni ratihibitione vim ac robur confecto instrumento adjiceret. Quod ipsum quoque tardius factum, ob infectam pestilentiâ Bertij, qui Albano à secretis erat, domum, in litteris Caroli Brimæi Id. Iul. Zuollâ datis reperio.
units.tr: To these points they added that Caesar had received great benefits from the Frisians: after Groningen and Omland had been subdued and conquered, and Drenthe and Coevorden received into allegiance, forty thousand gold pieces were granted to Caesar, together with the assigned lands of Bilt and other things given to Caesar's treasury, in a praiseworthy generosity, so that the old conventions would remain inviolable, which Philip had confirmed in the first year through Aremberg, and five years later in person, by a solemn voice, at the principal festivity of his inauguration. Since these things stand thus, the Frisians marvel that they are burdened with new and intolerable exactions. For, they said, these had brought to fields often overwhelmed by floods, to arable and pasture land corrupted by salt water, a shortage of grain, the deaths of livestock, and every kind of misery. Moreover, herds of beggars wandered through the fields, using force and injury against the farmers; night watches had to be kept along the sea dike, so that the raids of robbers and pirates might be met. Although these things weigh upon the people and drain their resources and means, they nevertheless testified that, moved by love and loyalty toward the King, so that he might keep the province free from all armed force, they would give seventy-five thousand gold pieces, to be paid in fixed and equal instalments over six years, on the condition, however, that the old agreements and pacts be upheld. For this reason they asked the King, keeping his former clemency, to abstain from the exaction of the hundredth, the twentieth and the tenth, and not to deprive the people of their right and immunity. To these they added complaints that, as they said was done in Brabant and Flanders, foreigners were preferred to native residents, and ecclesiastical benefices were added to this. These matters, recorded in the minutes on the 15th of June, drew out the assembly of the people. So on the 1st of July, at the urging and pressure of Carl Brimaeus, the meeting of the Orders was resumed, and when the Frisians offered one hundred thousand gold pieces, an agreement was finally reached: 128,000 were to be paid in four instalments up to the feast of St Odulphus, and the collection of the hundredth, the twentieth and the tenth would cease. The townsmen (for the country representatives had stipulated this) approved it, and this won over the Westergo men, who had earlier been at odds with the Sylvester men. Moreover, this contract rested on the condition that Alba, in Philip's name, should approve it and add force and strength to the completed document by a public and solemn ratification. I find in a letter of Carl Brimaeus, written at Zwolle on the 13th of July, that this too was done more slowly, because of the plague that had infected the house of Bertius, who was Alba's secretary.

units.la: Mox perlatis in Frisios Ferdinandi Albani litteris Antverpiâ XIII. Kal. Aug. datis, de Annæ Austriacæ Maximiliani II. Imperatoris filiæ, quæ in Philippi domum indulto Romani Pontificis, extinctâ Elisabethâ Vallesiâ denupserat, in Belgicam adventu, Carolus Brimæus Præfectus delegari petijt, qui designatam ex novo matrimonio Principem, Neomagi ad Vahalim salutarent, oblatisq; ut in novâ regnatrice fieri solet, donarijs, infensiorem Belgis Philippi animum emollirent. Quæ cum in signato ære præstari Albanus nollet, quasi infra reginæ dignitatem foret, tanti Regis, qui non unius orbis gazâ superbiret, sponsponsam vili & non facturo ad memoriam temporum donario adiri, pretiosos tapetes insignibus provinciarum notatos offerri voluit; Carolique, ut innuebat, maximi Caesarum neptem, more gentibus recepto, salutari. Modum quoq; conferendi aeris provincijs praescripsit, Frisiosq; sexcentos florenos, ut & Transisulanos, coemendis donarijs, corrogare jussit. Reliquis Groningensium, Drentinorum ac Lingensium provincijs Caroli Brimaei praefecturae subjectis, pro cujusque statu ac opulentia contributionem imperavit, omniumq; gentium, quae inferiorem Germaniam Belgicae appellatione constituunt Neomagi ad Rhennm ad v. aut sextum Iduum Augusti adesse voluit. Quare per eundem Brimaeum conventu in Aede praedicatorum ad iv. Non. Iul. indicto obeundae legationi delecti ex Oostergois Hero Burmania, è Westergois Iulius Dekama, è Sylvestribus Idzardus Sickingha, ex Oppidanis Petrus Boimerus Iure-consultus, & Oldermannus Franequerensium, qui juxta Carolum Brimaeum, legationis principem, Annae Austriacae congratularentur, deque Frisici in Regem Reginamque populi affectu nomine Ordinum hoc modo edocerent:
units.tr: Soon after, letters from Ferdinand of Alba, written at Antwerp on the 19th of July, were brought to the Frisians concerning the arrival in Belgium of Anne of Austria, daughter of the Emperor Maximilian II, who had been married into Philip's house by dispensation of the Roman Pontiff, after the death of Elizabeth of Valois. Carl Brimaeus, the prefect, asked to be appointed to greet the Princess designated by the new marriage at Nijmegen on the Waal, and, as is customary with a new queen, to offer gifts, so as to soften Philip's more hostile feeling toward the Belgians. Since Alba did not want these gifts given in coined money, as if this were beneath the dignity of a queen, and as beneath the greatness of a king who did not pride himself on the wealth of one world only, he wished that a bride should be approached with a cheap gift that would not keep the memory of the times; he wished costly carpets marked with the emblems of the provinces to be offered, and that she be greeted, as he hinted, as the granddaughter of Charles, the greatest of the Caesars, in the manner received among the nations. He also prescribed the manner of raising money from the provinces, and ordered the Frisians to collect six hundred florins for buying the gifts, and likewise the Transisulani. For the rest of the provinces of Groningen, Drenthe and Lingen, which were subject to the prefecture of Carl Brimaeus, he ordered a contribution according to each one's rank and wealth, and he wished all the peoples who make up Lower Germany under the name of the Netherlands to be present at Nijmegen on the Rhine by the fifth or sixth of the Ides of August. Therefore, at a meeting called by the same Brimaeus in the church of the preachers on the 4th of July, the following were chosen to carry out the embassy: from Oostergo, Hero Burmania; from Westergo, Julius Dekama; from the Sylvester district, Idzardus Sickingha; from the townsmen, Petrus Boimerus, jurist, and Oldermannus of Franeker. They were to congratulate Anne of Austria, together with Carl Brimaeus, the head of the embassy, and to make known, in the name of the Orders, the feeling of the Frisian people toward the King and Queen, in this way:

units.la: Mittimus ad te Regina Legatos nostros, qui in exoptato tuo in Belgicam ingressu, te adirent, teq; pro dignitate futurae Belgarum Principis exciperent. Regi nostro quaedam à te proponi petimus, ac ut clementem bonumque Principem nobis praestes, legatisque nostris plenam fidem adhibeas. Nos in fideli majestatis tuae ac Philippi reverentiâ perstabimus, liberisque ac nepotibus vestris ad quos tantarum rerum successio perveniet, omne officium, omne obsequium deferemus.
units.tr: We send to you, Queen, our envoys, who will approach you at your longed-for entry into Belgium and receive you in a manner worthy of the future Princess of the Belgians. We ask that you put forward certain matters to our King on our behalf, and that you show us a merciful and good Princess, and give full credence to our envoys. We will remain steadfast in faithful reverence toward your majesty and Philip, and we will offer every duty and every obedience to your children and grandchildren, to whom the succession of such great affairs will come.

units.la: Haec iv. Non. Iulij per Valerium Cammingha, Bennertum Roorda, Heronem Ockingha, Barthium Idzarda, Ruardum Roorda, Gellium Roorsma, Matthiam Rommertium signata. Invenio in litteris Caroli Brimaei Antverpiae datis sexcentos, quos Albanus ordinaverat, florenos, sex aureorum millibus in gratiam reginae, sive ad provincialis opulentiae ostentationem, auctos, Frisiorumque legatos curante Brimaeo binos aureos crateres sex millium aureorum pretio à Conrado Scettio Antverpiano emptos, Annae Austriacae una cum litteris secretioribus obtulisse. Legatos quoque medio Septembri cum litteris reginae reversos, plenam rerum Neomagi gestarum relationem enarrasse.
units.tr: These were signed on the 4th of July by Valerius Cammingha, Bennertus Roorda, Hero Ockingha, Barthius Idzarda, Ruardus Roorda, Gellius Roorsma and Matthias Rommertius. I find in a letter of Carl Brimaeus, written at Antwerp, that the six hundred florins which Alba had ordered, increased to six thousand gold pieces for the queen's favour, or to display the wealth of the province, were offered to Anne of Austria by the Frisian envoys, who, through Brimaeus's care, bought two gold cups for six thousand gold pieces from Conrad Scettius of Antwerp, together with more private letters. I also find that the envoys returned in the middle of September with letters from the queen, and reported a full account of what had been done at Nijmegen.

units.la: Classi quoque Aurantiae, quae Germanico Caledonioque mari volitabat, mandatum reperio, ne molestiam ei crearet, si forte novi matrimonij dulcedine, aut intercessione sponsae Principis Philippi animus leniretur.
units.tr: I also find an order to the fleet of Orange, which was flying over the German and Caledonian seas, not to cause trouble for it, in case by chance the sweetness of the new marriage, or the mediation of the Prince's bride, should soften Philip's mind.

units.la: Itaq; valida faederatarum partium classe, quâ mare ipsum & aestuaria florebant, de re navali quoque in Frisiâ cogitatum, factâ Segero Grosbeccio potestate, ut apud Carolum Brimaeum cui vicarius erat, pro reparandis Praesidiarijs navigijs ageret, curamque maris & commerciorum eidem Brimaeo commendaret. Caeterum tenue regis aerarium, & praefecti sollicitudo alijs rebus incumbens purgandi tutandiq; maris consilia tardavit. Quae ipsa quoque etsi à tanto rege profecta, tamen contumacis populi, quae per omnes provincias visebatur, subsidijs destituebantur, quae armandis utrinque partibus destinata, publicas provincia-rum rum opes & affecta ex se æraria enervabant.
units.tr: Therefore, with a strong fleet of the allied provinces, by which the sea itself and its estuaries flourished, the naval question was also considered in Friesland: Segerus Grosbeccius was given authority to act with Carl Brimaeus, of whom he was deputy, for repairing the guard ships, and the care of the sea and of commerce was committed to the same Brimaeus. However, the king's slender treasury, and the prefect's anxiety, which lay upon other business, delayed the plans for clearing and defending the sea. These plans, though they came from so great a king, were nevertheless starved of the subsidies needed by the stubborn people, which were visible in all the provinces; the sums set aside for arming both sides drained the public resources of the provinces and the treasuries they had been drawn from.

units.la: Mox Kalend. Novemb. enormis calamitas, quam gravissime, Frisios adflixit. Præterquam enim quod odia partium, ut dixi, & grassantia arma spectarent, ita stupendi elementorum furores civilem quoq; discordiam castigavere. Surgens enim ab extremo Occasu, deïn in Corum se deflectens tempestas adeò desævijt, ut intumescens Oceanus ruptis perforatisque aggeribus, sui alvei quasi ac legis oblitus, universam provinciam, quà ostia fluminum, aut depressa littorum spectat, invalidis fluctuum obijcibus inundaverit. Neque defuere, qui inguentibus atrocissimis, & supra hominum memoriam procellis, seseque Oceano supra ordinarios æstus, & legem moti syderis efferente gentis excidium formidarent. Flans enim Corus tum tumidum ultrò mare, non maritima tantum & littoralem tractum, sed meditullia quoque Provinciæ obtexerat. Dongrij quoque, & præturæ per Oostergoam, quæ in Boream excurrunt, profundissimis aquis innatavere, undarum mole in undecim pedum altitudinem provectâ. Quare, si monumento, quod in templi limine apud Metselvíranos visitur, fides, in Dongriæ Prætura, quæ orientem spectat, mille & octingenti submersi, ijs etiam exceptis, qui recedente unda in Oceanum devecti, propulsique sunt. Neque absimilis in Austrum fluctuum furor fuit, qui per universam Westergoam, partemque post Sylvestris oræ sparsi villas, domos, aggeres disjecere, abreptis etiam per vim aquæ integris familijs, quas concubia, & illunis nox, tum altus sopor, & prima quies in lectis dormitorijsque oppresserat. Itaque conjuges, liberi, tum in cunis positi infantes, cum supellectile domorum, rusticisque instrumentis acti, non sine damno annonæ, & perditione frugum, quas effractis horreis assilieus mare eluebat. Notat Andræas Gryphius PræTor Utingeranus, solos Utingeranos reliquosque Sylvestres, umbilico velut Frisiæ clausos, minoribus undis expositos fuisse, omnemq; dulcis aquæ molem confertim aggestam, & salsedine sensum tinctam centenos fabarum fasciculos penetralibus editioribusque domorum locis apud Bornenses adjecisse. Signa quoque huius inundationis, à Feicone Siboldio Nessano, jam ante per aërem notata, domumque Focconis Leppij apud Haskerios altissimis aquis innatare visam, Kal. Nov. solam in isto districtu ijdem obrutam fuisse. Mense quoque Septembri qui malum hoc præcessit, multos glires, muresque aquatiles, metu, ut creditum fuit, futuræ tempestatis examinatos, in corde brassicæ desedisse, ac non vanum isti rei prodigium fecisse. Hoc saltem Bornensium seniores longâ temporum memoriâ observatum annotaverant, mures in arundinetis calamorum summitatem petentes, ibique nidulos suos struentes, graves ut plurimum terrarum inundationes significasse. Relatum in fidem annalium est, navem onerariam cum mercibus Hamburgo venientem, supra altissimos aggeres sublatam in mediterraneis consedisse, multaque octo aut circiter pedum altitudine, totum quod Cuneram Snecamq; interjacet, terrarum spatium, oceano opertum enavigasse. Victoriam quoq; aliam, quæ Amstelodamo solverat, medio in Flevo cum centum hominibus demersam. Itaq; tum ejulatus, ac lamenta vagientium flentiumq;, liberorum ac conju-
units.tr: Soon after the Kalends of November, a huge calamity struck Frisia with great severity. For, as I said, the hatreds of the parties and the arms that were raging had already been at work, and the astonishing fury of the elements also punished the civil discord. A storm rose from the far west and, turning toward the northwest, raged so fiercely that the ocean swelled, broke through and pierced its dikes, and, as if forgetting its bed and its law, flooded the whole province that lies where the river mouths or low shores face the sea, with the weak barriers of the waves giving way. Some men, terrified by the most dreadful gales, beyond the memory of humankind, and by a sea that rose above its ordinary tides and the law of the moon, feared the destruction of the nation. For the northwest wind, driving the sea before it, had covered not only the coast and the shoreline but also the inland parts of the province. The Dongeri and the marshes through Oostergo, which run toward the north, were also submerged in very deep waters, the mass of the waves rising to a height of eleven feet. Therefore, if the inscription that is seen at the threshold of the church at Metselvir can be trusted, in the district of Dongeria, which faces the east, 1,800 were drowned, not counting those who were carried out to sea when the water receded and were driven away. The fury of the waves in the south was not unlike this. It spread over the whole of Westergo and part of the coast beyond Sylvestris, and tore down the villages, houses and dikes. Whole families, whom the night and the deep sleep and first rest had overtaken in their beds and bedrooms, were also seized and carried off by the force of the water. Thus wives, children, and infants still lying in their cradles were swept away together with household goods and farm tools, and not without loss to the food supply and destruction of the crops, which the sea washed over after breaking open the granaries. Andreas Gryphius, the magistrate of Utinga, records that only the people of Utinga and the rest of Sylvestris, as if shut in by the navel of Frisia, were exposed to the smaller waves, and that all the great mass of fresh water, heaped together and tinged with salt, had reached the inner rooms and the upper parts of the houses at Borne, and had reached the level of a hundred bundles of beans. Signs of this flood were also noticed beforehand in the air by Feico Siboldus of Ness, and the house of Focco Leppius at Haskerie was seen floating in very deep water. Only in this district, they say, was it submerged on the Kalends of November. In the month of September, which preceded this disaster, many dormice and water mice, as was believed, driven out by fear of the coming storm, settled in the heart of a cabbage, and this was no empty portent for the matter. The elders of Borne had at least noted this, observed over a long span of time: mice seeking the tops of the reeds in the marshes and building their little nests there usually signified severe floods of the land. It is reported, on the authority of the annals, that a cargo ship coming from Hamburg with its goods was lifted over the highest dikes and came to rest inland, and that it sailed over the whole stretch of land lying between Cunera and Snecka, covered by the ocean, for a distance of about eight feet in depth. Another ship, which had sailed from Amsterdam, was also sunk with a hundred men in the middle of the Flevo. And so, through the whole province, the wailing and laments of infants and weeping children and wives were heard, while the people were still often in doubt, with minds in suspense, whether they were hearing the truth about the dead or only rumours.

units.la: conjugum per universam Provinciam audiebantur, dubijs adhuc saepe clo. Io. suspensisque animis vera an incerta funerum flerent. Sed recedens sen-sim mare vera rerum nuntia, & Provincialium calamitates detexit. Tum quisque orbitates suas ac desideria exponere, queri turbatas domos, ac patrimonia, neque propinquorum allocutiones morientibus fuisse, aut voluntatis ultimae testationem supremâ voce obsignatam. Vastatam & obrutam velut uno fluctu Provinciam, novâq, solitudine non aliam rerum imaginem, quam pereuntis generis humani spectari. Nonnullorum cadavera circa ostia fluminum, aut in limo, quem aestus, reliquerat, reperta, agnitaque propinquis solemni funerum decorata sunt. Caetera per Oceanum sparsa (quia sepulturae honos ijs non concessus) caelo contecta fluctuavere. Tradunt autores in utraque Dongria tum Doccomio urbe quinque millia hominum, & ducentos, caeterum in universâ Frisiâ, (quae Flevo Lavicaque continetur) ultra viginti millia perijsse.
units.tr: But as the sea gradually receded, it revealed the true news and the misfortunes of the people of the province. Then each man set forth his own bereavements and losses, and complained that their homes and patrimonies were ruined, and that the dying had not been able to speak words of farewell to their kinsfolk, nor to attest their last wishes with a final voice. The province, laid waste and overwhelmed as if by a single wave, and in its new desolation, presented no other picture than that of a perishing human race. The bodies of some were found near the river mouths or in the mud left behind by the tide; these, when recognised by their relatives, were honoured with solemn funerals. The rest, scattered across the ocean (since the honour of burial was not granted to them), drifted, covered by the sky. Authors report that in both Dongeria and the town of Dokkum there perished five thousand two hundred people, and that in the whole of Frisia (which is bounded by the Flevo and the Lauwers) more than twenty thousand perished.

units.la: Quae quanquam apud illos ex magnitudine tantae cladis aucta, tamen ex actis postmodum repertis constat, multa, & ex tantâ confusione incerta hominum millia inruentibus cum impetu aquis abrepta. Hoc tantum addam, Senatum regium in inquirendo submersorum numero, ex notitiâ mali sagacem, commentarios quorundam per Provinciam praetorum exegisse, infraque vulgarium autorum, qui plus famae dederunt, fidem, inundationis istius, sive diluvij ferociam stetisse.
units.tr: Although these figures were increased among those people by the magnitude of so great a disaster, it is nevertheless clear from the records found afterwards that many thousands of people, uncertain in such great confusion, were carried off by the waters rushing in with force. I will add only this: the royal Senate, shrewd in judging the evil from its knowledge, required written reports from certain magistrates throughout the province in order to inquire into the number of the drowned. It was found that the account of the ordinary writers, who gave more weight to rumour, was less reliable, and that the violence of this inundation, or deluge, stood below their estimates.

units.la: Repertorum quoque miram in facie deformitatem fuisse, caeterum pulcherrimos habitus more majorum nostrorum, aureis argenteisque lamellis interstinctos in mortuorum cumulis notatos. Invenio Geesterlandos, quod illorum agri clementibus jugis adsurgant, periculi immunes fuisse, ac infantem una cum fele cunis impositum, Snecam ap-pulisse, prodigiosèque servatum. Frisiam quoque toto decemdio profundisimis aquis obtectam stetisse, ac restagnantem velut undam, & continuis exhalationibus frigeratum aërem, asperum gelu, prima etiam brumà peperisse.
units.tr: The drowned were also strangely disfigured in their faces, but their clothing, in the manner of our ancestors, decorated with little golden and silver plates, was noted among the heaps of the dead. I find that the people of Geesterland were free from danger, because their fields rise up in gentle ridges, and that an infant placed in a cradle along with a cat was carried ashore at Sneek and miraculously saved. Frisia also stood covered for ten days by very deep waters, and the air, cooled by the standing water as if by a wave and by continuous exhalations, brought forth a harsh frost even at the start of winter.

units.la: Quod incommodum prioris anni, qui Novembri mense apparuerat Cometæ, velut evoluto jam motus annui circulo à Cornelio Gemma insigni istorum temporum Mathematico imputatum reperio;tantumq; virum cæli peritum, non terrarum tantum mala, sed maris quoque injurias & feroces æstus efficaciæ crinitorum siderum, etiam inclinantium, ascripsisse. Cui provincialium infelicitati & hoc accessit, quod quæstores ærarijq; tribuni illorum, quos Philippus ab edicto Veniæ exclusserat, reditus strangularent, objectoq; majestatis crimine, quod illis temporibus nullâ judicij sed Edicti formula intentabatur, vitæ subsidijs non profugos tantum & exules, sed promiscuam multitudiem exuerent. Qua ex re, cum obligationum, quibus domania, ut vocant, regia premebantur, vis cessaret, creditoribusq; jus suum in foro persequendi adimeretur, cavit edicto Albanus, ut creditores intra trimestre, tabulas æris crediti exhiberent, illisq; modo Præfectus Senatusq; approbasset, annuorum reddituum pensiones præstarentur. Quod sive pungente Albanum conscientia, sive miseratione cladis factum, in dubium relinquo. Hoc saltem verisimile est tantam calamitatem, etiam obdura-tum tum ad quælibet Albani pectus movisse, communemque mortalium ingenijs affectum, etiam in ipsâ Ducis exulceratâ inexpiatâque cædibus mente excitasse. Mox Anna Austriaca fælici navigatione, in Hispaniam provecta, exhibitisque Philippo Frisiorum litteris de iltius gentis eximiâ humanitate apud sponsum Regem commemoravit. Donaria quoque mitigando Philippi ingenio exhiberi fecit, ipseq; Philippus amore sponsæ orantis deflagrans Albano, Frisiorum genti, ut grates ageret, binis litteris imperavit. Tum ne quid officij regij erga Frisios omitteretur, & ut honorario æri, quod Philippo præterito mense Iulio concessum erat, regiæ gratitudinis signum reponeret, litteras suâ manu Madriti xi. Kal. Febr. scriptas, in Frisiam misit, populumque in fide regis adhuc perstantem, singulari benevolentiæ regiæ argumento complexus est. Hoc verò imprimis Philippum indoluisse reperio, quod mare insolito æstu tumefactum fertilem provinciam inundasset, præterque pecora, domos, villas, hominum quoque millia abstulisset. Quapropter litteras ad Archiepiscopos, Episcoposque dari præcepit, expiandisq; provincialium noxis, placandæq; cælesti iræ per oppida ac in cænobijs amburbiorum, supplicationumq; ritus instituí jussit. Cæterum omnem regiæ mentis affectum ingruens rumor discusit, quo Gasparus Roblesius, coactâ Groningæ militum manu, per Translavicanos, & ipsam quoque Frisiam, vim colonis agrorum intulisse dicebatur. Quæ etsi Igramus Achlemius Frisici Senatus Præses datis Groningâ xi. Kal. Feb. litteris elevaret, ita fidem faciebat Roblesium occupandæ, (ne fæderata classis mari oberrans, in insulam inrueret) Amelandiæ consilio capto, severis mandatis militem instruxisse. Eundem quoque Roblesium frænandæ militum licentiæ stipendia exsolvisse, quæ opportuno tempore pensitata omnem etiam laxiorem disciplinam castrensi moderatione composuissent. Cæterum regius miles, etsi ære accepto, ultro insolens omne delicatum immodesto ori exigebat, vinoque ac epulis indulgens, pecuniam quoque colentibus agros extorquebat. Quare Senatus Regius, petentibus agrariorum Delegatis ad Achlenium Vastartiumq; Senatores, qui Groningæ agebant, litteras dedit, utque remedium insolentiæ militari orarent, commonuit. Cæterum rudis armorum, & disciplinæ ingnara multitudo primis militiæ rudimentis, velut laxatis prioris vitæ frænis agebatur, licentiamq; belli legem interpretata raro centurionum imperio per vicos agrosque discurrebat. Ita factum est, ut habitis per provincias & confinia delectibus, Carolus quoq; Brimæus tertium quemque è rusticâ plebe ad militiam evocaret, stipendiaq; tyronibus privato ex ære deficiente regis ærario poscceret. Quæ res ut cum severitate & imperio agebatur, ita nobilitatem populumque agrarium magis magisq; à Carolo Brimæo, dein ipso quoq; Philippo alienavit. Quare omnia acerbius ad bellum spectabant, cujus prodigium, si Cornelio Gemmæ fides, in quodam Frisiæ tractu depluens sanguis confirmavit.
units.tr: I find that this misfortune of the previous year, which followed the comet that had appeared in November, was ascribed by Cornelius Gemma, the distinguished mathematician of those times, as if the annual circle of motion had now been completed, and that he attributed to the efficacy of the hairy stars, even of those inclining, not only the evils of the lands but also the injuries of the sea and its savage tides. To the misery of the people of the province this was also added: their quaestors and tribunes of the treasury, whom Philip had excluded from the edict of pardon, were strangling the revenues. Charging them with treason, a charge which at that time was brought not by the form of a judicial process but by a mere edict, they stripped of the means of life not only the fugitives and exiles but the general multitude without distinction. For this reason, since the force of the obligations by which the royal domains, as they are called, were burdened had ceased, and creditors were deprived of their right to pursue their claims in court, Alva provided by edict that the creditors should present their registers of debt within three months, and that payments of annual revenues should be made to them only if the Governor and the Senate approved. Whether Alva did this from a stinging conscience or from pity for the calamity, I leave in doubt. This at least is likely: so great a calamity moved even Alva's hardened heart, which was harsh toward everything, and awakened in his mind, ulcerated and unatoned by slaughter, the feeling common to human nature. Soon afterward Anna of Austria, having reached Spain by a fortunate voyage, presented to Philip the letters of the Frisians and spoke to her betrothed king of that nation's remarkable humanity. She also had gifts brought to soften the temper of Philip, and Philip himself, burning with love for his bride who was pleading for them, ordered Alva by two letters to give thanks to the Frisian people. Then, so that nothing of royal duty toward the Frisians should be omitted, and so that he might give a sign of royal gratitude for the honorary sum that had been granted to Philip in the previous July, he sent a letter written in his own hand at Madrid on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February into Frisia, and embraced the people, who still remained steadfast in the king's allegiance, with a singular proof of royal goodwill. But I find that Philip was especially grieved by this, that the sea, swollen by an unusual tide, had flooded a fertile province and had carried off, besides livestock, houses and farms, also thousands of people. Therefore he ordered letters to be sent to the archbishops and bishops, and commanded that to expiate the sins of the provincials and to appease the heavenly anger, rites of supplication and prayers should be instituted in the towns and in the monasteries around them. But a rumour that was spreading broke up the whole royal feeling: it was said that Gaspar Robles, having gathered a force of soldiers at Groningen, had inflicted violence on the farmers throughout the lands beyond the Lauwers and Frisia itself. Although Igram Achlema, president of the Frisian Senate, by letters sent from Groningen on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, lightened this charge, he nonetheless made it credible that Robles had equipped the soldiers with strict orders, having decided on Ameland, in order to occupy it (lest the allied fleet, wandering over the sea, should rush upon the island). The same Robles had also paid the soldiers' wages to curb their licence, which, paid at the proper time, would have restrained even a looser discipline by military moderation. But the royal soldier, although he had received his pay, insolently demanded every delicacy with his immodest mouth, and, indulging in wine and feasts, extorted money also from those who cultivated the fields. Therefore the royal Senate, at the request of the delegates of the farmers, gave letters to Achlenius and to the senators Vastartius, who were acting at Groningen, and reminded them to seek a remedy for this military insolence. But the crowd, rough in arms and ignorant of discipline, was driven in its first military rudiments as if the reins of its former life had been loosened; interpreting the licence of war as its law, it ran through the villages and fields with little obedience to the centurions. And so it came about that, after levies had been held throughout the provinces and their borders, Charles Brimaeus also called every third man of the rustic commons to military service, and demanded wages for the raw recruits from the royal treasury, which was failing because of private expense. This matter, pursued with harshness and command, alienated the nobility and the agrarian people more and more from Charles Brimaeus, and afterward from Philip himself. Therefore everything looked more bitterly toward war, and a portent of this, if we trust Cornelius Gemma, was confirmed by blood raining down in a certain district of Frisia.

units.la: Quo inundationis malo Saxonum olim & Burgundionum temporibus motal is ac controversia recruduit. Præterquam enim quod damna passis omnia gravia & per funera, ac orbitates tristitia essent, ita tum reparationem aggerum non sustinebant, exhausti communi malo littorales, recenti inundatione fracti. Itaque illi Carolum Brimæum Comitem Meganum orare, miserceatur nuperæ calamitatis, & publico dispendio publicum subsidium decernat. Suæ potestatis non esse privatis opibus averruncare commune Provinciæ discrimen, omniumque incolumitatem emere suarum rerum jactură & paratissimâ egestate. Subveniendum potiùs communibus iris, ac inclementijs naturæ, ne parte terræ Frisicæ incendio exustâ, aut aquarum vi absorptâ, toti Provinciæ quid decedat, quæ stare abreptis partibus non possit. Idcirco olim aggerum neglectu maxuma terrarum, ac continentis spatia, aut Oceano contecta, aut seorsim avulsa per circumfluum mare formam insularum induisse. Neque enim hoc in Frisiâ infrequens, cum urgentibus agrorum possessoribus (qui tum palustria, ac depressa locorum inhabitabant) invalido aggere ducti in Oceanum Germanicum rivi viam sævissimo elemento aperuere. Flevo fluvio marinis aquis in latissima æstuaria effuso. Caveret ergo Brimæus quam maxumè, ne dum de aggerum lite Provinciales contenderent, altercantium controversiam importunum & præceps mare dirimat. Tum componendæ liti è regio Senatu Igramus Achlemius Præses, & Petrus Frittema Iureconsultus designati, qui discordibus agrariorum animis, etiam durante diario maris influxu, nihil profecere, quod parum miserationis in animis hominum tanta vastatio, & calamitas reliquisset. Quare littorales Westergoï ad Ferdinandum Albanum mittere Legatos decrevere, publicaq; cæterorum ignavia maturare negotium opprimendæ Provinciæ validum. Res Cunero Episcopo, & Petro Medenblicano Præsidi Achlemio, Sceltoni Lyauckamæ, Dothiæ Bongæ, Ulpio Hiddamæ, & Cronenburgio ut maritimis Westergois commissa. Qui, ne quid in morâ majoris periculi, libellum mox supplicem ad Ferdinandum Albanum per delegatos è nobilitate Heronem Ockinga, & Valerium Camminghamitti fecerunt, in quo disjectos aggeres, & damna agris possessionibusque suis illata exponebant. Non esse suarum virium id reparare, quod vis marinorum fluctuum abstulisset, aut pendere ulterius tributum, quod huc usque gerendo pro Rege bello impendissent. Agros quippe sibi, non magnis latifundijs turbido & procelloso mari adjectos, eosdemque sterilitate novæ salsedinis incultos ferendis aggerum, belliqueoneribus pares non esse. Rogare igitur Ferdinandum Albanum, ut tot damna passos tributo levet, statuatq; modum, & subsidia, quibus servari Frisia queat, marinis etiamnum aquis obtecta.
units.tr: This flood disaster revived an old dispute, as it had in the days of the Saxons and Burgundians. Apart from the grievous losses, with deaths and bereaved families, the coastal people, exhausted by the common calamity and broken by the recent inundation, could not afford to repair the dykes. They therefore begged Count Charles Brimaeus of Megen to take pity on their recent misfortune and to decree public aid from the public purse. It was not in his power, they said, to avert with private resources a danger that threatened the whole province, nor to buy the safety of all with the loss of their own property and utter poverty. Aid should rather be given against the common calamities and the harshness of nature, so that if a part of Friesland were burned or swallowed up by the force of the waters, the whole province would not suffer loss, since it could not stand once its parts were torn away. For this reason, when the dykes had long been neglected, the greater part of the land and the continent had either been covered by the ocean or, cut off in sections, had taken the shape of islands surrounded by the sea. Nor was this uncommon in Friesland: when the landowners, who then inhabited the marshy and low-lying places, pressed on, weak dykes gave the streams a way into the German Ocean, and the most savage element was let loose. The river Flevo, with the sea water poured into vast estuaries. Brimaeus should therefore take the greatest care that the sea, rushing in headlong and untimely, does not break off the quarrel of the provincials contending over the dykes. Then Igram Achlenius, the president of the royal Senate, and Peter Frittema, a jurist, were appointed to settle the dispute. But with the minds of the landowners still hostile, and even while the sea continued to flow in daily, they achieved nothing, since such great devastation and calamity had left little pity in men's hearts. Accordingly the coastal Westergoers resolved to send envoys to Ferdinando Alvarez, the Duke of Alba, and, because of the public indifference of the others, to hasten the business of crushing the province. The matter was entrusted to Bishop Cunerus, Peter Medenblicus, the president Achlenius, Scelto of Lyauckama, Dothia of Bonga, Ulpius of Hiddama and Cronenburgius, as those responsible for the maritime Westergoers. Lest anything be delayed to their greater peril, they soon drew up a humble petition to Ferdinando Alba, through the delegates from the nobility, Heron Ockinga and Valerius Camminghamitti. In it they set out the broken dykes and the damage done to their fields and estates. They said it was not within their power to repair what the force of the sea waves had carried away, nor to go on paying the taxes they had contributed to the king's war up to now. Their fields, added by no great estates to the stormy and turbulent sea, and made barren by the fresh salt, were not equal to the burdens of dyke-building and war. They therefore asked Ferdinando Alba to relieve these men, who had suffered so much damage, from taxation, and to set a limit and supply the aid by which Friesland, still covered by sea water, might be preserved.

units.la: Cæterum Albani animus alijs negotijs & mole belli æstuans, amotâ Frisicæ securitatis curâ Legatum dimisit, ac apud Carolum Brimæum Frisiæ Præfectum agere jusit. Ita res moræ impatiens maguo Provincialium damno protracta, disjectaque per vim aquæ piscatorum tugurias, quæ marino aggeri rursum adstrui Senatus regius vetabat, vacua habitatoribus manserc. Incolæ ipsi aut undis submersi, lati, aut, qui superstites fuere, laris incerti per universam Provinciam fædo spectaculo circumacti. Quorum miseratione, & suo quoque periculo adducti Westergoï, qui maritima tenent, Carolum Brimæum Frisiæ Præfectum rogarunt, ut conventum omnium Frisiæ Ordinum cogeret, deque lite aggerum cognosceret quàutò ocyus. Itaq;
units.tr: Meanwhile Alba's mind, seething with other business and the burden of war, set aside his concern for Frisian safety, dismissed the envoys and ordered them to deal with Charles Brimaeus, the governor of Friesland. So the matter, impatient of delay, was prolonged to the great loss of the provincials. The waters, driven by force, scattered the fishermen's huts, which the royal Senate forbade to be rebuilt against the sea dyke, and they remained empty of inhabitants. The inhabitants themselves were either drowned by the waves or, those who survived, wandered without a home through the whole province, a sad spectacle. Moved by their pity and by their own danger too, the Westergoers who hold the coast asked Charles Brimaeus, governor of Friesland, to summon a meeting of all the estates of Friesland and to take cognizance of the dispute over the dykes as quickly as possible. And so:

units.la: Discepratio de aggere marino.
units.tr: Dispute concerning the sea dyke.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. Carolus Brimæus ad xiv. Kal. Iun. diem Ordines tum Westergoos LXXI. Frisiae, ac Sylvestres, quorum agri mari praetexuntur adesse Leovardiae jussit, Igramumque Achlenium Senatus Praesidem collegarum suffragijs novo more, à morte Caroli Nitzenij ad clarissimam dignitatem evectum perorandae causae designavit. Ibi Achlenius.
units.tr: On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 1550, Charles Brimaeus ordered the estates to appear at Leeuwarden: the seventy-one Westergoers of Friesland, and the Sylvestres, whose lands lie along the sea. He appointed Igram Achlenius, president of the Senate, who had recently been raised to that most distinguished office after the death of Charles Nitzenius, by the votes of his colleagues in a new manner, to plead the case. There Achlenius spoke.

units.la: CONVOCAVIMUS vos, Ordines & Delegati, ut litem vestram, quam majores & vos ipsi tot annis magno Provinciae detrimento exercetis, componamus celerius. Et quoniam metuendum est, ut recrudescens mare, Lunae, quod in maria dominatur, sydere, aut procellâ actum majus terris vestris periculum creet, ita aequum censuimus suspenso ad tempus partium jure aggeres marinos communibus impendijs reficiendos. Hoc verò curavimus; Ne exemplo esset, nostrâque interpositione cujusq; jus aut immunitas subverteretur. Securitate Provinciae & vestris agris, villis, atq, familijs partâ differetis in foro nostro commodius. Nunc manus, impendia, operae exiguntur, & pro periculi magnitudine provida festinatio, ne vestrâ cunctatione mare nos obruat, aut graviore saltem damno omnem Provinciam adfligat.
units.tr: We have called you together, estates and delegates, so that we may settle more quickly the dispute which your forebears and you yourselves have carried on for so many years to the great harm of the province. Since it is to be feared that the sea, once stirred up again, by the influence of the moon, which rules the seas, or by a storm, may create a greater danger for your lands, we have judged it fair that, for the time being, the rights of the parties be suspended and the sea dykes be repaired at common expense. We have taken care, moreover, that this should not become a precedent, and that no one's right or immunity be overturned by our intervention. Once safety has been secured for the province and for your fields, farmsteads and families, you will dispute more conveniently in our court. Now hands, money and labour are demanded, and in view of the greatness of the danger we need prudent haste, lest the sea overwhelm us through your delay, or at least afflict the whole province with greater loss.

units.la: Quâ praesidis oratione audità, Wonserani qui in mediterraneis septem pagos constituunt, asserendo juri suo allegabant magna aggerum spatia & simul onera à Maccomio in Austrum suis pagis assignata, eaque vi aquae rupta, aut profunditate gurgitum excavata modico sumptu non reparari. Damnum quippe aggeri inlatum viginti quinque carolaeorum millibus, ducentis, & nonagenta aestumari, elisaque insuper fluctibus tabulationes, & emissaria laxandis reprimendisque aquarum molibus inventa, loco mota dispendium geminasse. Quod ad Wonseranos maritimos spectaret, discretos sibi ab ijs aggeres esse, quos confundi non oporteret, & quorum oneribus ipsi maritimi pares essent, non minore soli facunditate, & paribus agrorum locarijs faelices. Rogare itaq; Carolum Brimaeum iniquis maritimorum Wonseranorum studijs prospiciat, beneficiumq; juris implorantibus ex aequo subveniat. Ita Petrus Aggema, Matthias Livius, & Theodorus Ioannis xii. Kal. Iun. signavere. Eadem feré Wonserani maritimi, nisi quod damni ex inundatione terrarum dati aestumationem viginti & trium millium carolaeorum facerent, suaeque impotentiae causam obtexentes, commune reparandis aggeribus, & aequale subsidium ex arbitrio Praefecti & Senatus regij flagitarent. Sylvestres verò respondebant: Sterilius sibi prae Westergoïs solum esse, multorumque annorum infæcunditate pressos, resarciendis aggerum damnis invalidos esse. Ita Donieverstallaeos, Geesterlandos, Lemsteranos, Schoteranos, & Engwirdios aggerum sumptus à Feenhusâ ad Cliffam promontorium (quod intervallum quatuor miliaria comprehendit) sustinere; ipsisque Stellinguerfijs praeter marinos aggeres alios quoque impendia creare, divertendis, quae è Drentiae, Frisiaeq, bituminosis agris per Stellinguerfiam labuntur, aquis extructos. Utingeranos verò quinque milliaribus à Stauri co littore discretos, aggeres Stauriae vicinos curare, cuius mali ea ratio sit, quod Westergoi confusis usibus aggerum jure se muniant, ac vix tertiam sumptuum partem, quam è tributo pagorum petunt, eorundem aggerum, & fulciendis fluctuum obicibus impendant. Postremò Westergoï, qui in memediterraneis quinque prætoras aut jus suffragiorum tenent, quales sunt Franequerani, Menaldumæi, Baerderaui, Hennardij, & Minnertsgæi id responsi attulere. Ut, quamvis ab omni marinorum aggerum onere ipso jure immunes essent, velut longius à mari dissiti, & privatis agrorum munimentis conscepti, tamen, quia pronuntiatum à regio Senatu esset, Georgium Scencum Præfectum quondam, & Senatum Cæsaris ritè judicasse, ac ex æquo ad eos aggerum onera devoluta videri, obtemperasse judicio Senatus. Hoc vero ægrius se ferre, Westergoos maritimos non acquiescentes rei judicatæ, velut gravatos, nova statuta Senatum Regium orasse, ac in fraudem juris sui obtinuisse. Ideo se ad Ferdinandum Albanum spe restitutionis in integrum perfugisse, rejectosque ab eo ad Senatum per Frisiam regium præsidium juris rogare. Interim ne videantur omnem humani affectum exuisse, miseratione infælicium temporum, subsidia maritimis Westergoïs offerre, sed hac cautela, ne officium exemplo sit, ac ne videatur jus suum ratione beneficij imminutum.
units.tr: When this speech of the president had been heard, the Wonserani, who occupy seven villages in the interior, asserted their right by arguing that the large stretches of dykes and the burdens assigned to their villages from Makkum southward had been broken by the force of the water, or hollowed out by the depth of the currents, and could not be repaired at small cost. They estimated the damage done to the dyke at two hundred and ninety-five thousand carolus-guilders, and said that the tiled tracts and outlets, devised to loosen and restrain the masses of water, had been displaced and had doubled the loss. As for the coastal Wonserani, they said the dykes which belonged to them were separate from those, which ought not to be confused, and that the coastal men were equal to their burdens, being no less fortunate in the fertility of the soil and in the equal extent of their fields. They therefore asked Charles Brimaeus to look after the unfair zeal of the coastal Wonserani, and to bring equal help to those who implored the benefit of the law. So Peter Aggema, Matthias Livius and Theodorus Ioannis signed on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June. The coastal Wonserani said much the same, except that they put the compensation for the land lost to inundation at twenty-three thousand carolus-guilders, and, pleading their own inability, they asked that the cost of repairing the dykes be shared equally, at the discretion of the governor and the royal Senate. The Sylvestres, however, replied that their soil was poorer than that of the Westergoers, that they were oppressed by the barrenness of many years, and that they were unable to pay for the repair of the damage. Thus the Donieverstallaei, Geesterlandi, Lemsterani, Schoterani and Engwirdii bore the cost of the dykes from Feenhusa to the promontory of Cliffa, an interval of four miles; and the Stellinguerfii themselves, besides the sea dykes, incurred other expenses, for sluices built to divert the waters that flow through Stellinguerfia from the bituminous fields of Drenthe and Friesland. The Utingeri, separated by five miles from the shore of Stauria, looked after the dykes near Stauria. The cause of this trouble, they said, was that the Westergoers, by confusing the uses of the dykes, protected their rights and spent scarcely a third of the costs, which they exact from the taxes of the villages, on the same dykes and on the barriers against the waves. Finally, the Westergoers who live in the interior and hold five praetorships or the right of voting, such as the Franequerani, Menaldumaei, Baerderauni, Hennardii and Minnertsgaei, gave this answer: although they were by law wholly exempt from the burden of sea dykes, as lying too far from the sea and having their own protections for their fields, yet, since the royal Senate had pronounced that Georgius Scencus, the former governor, and the Senate of the Emperor had judged rightly, and that the burdens of the dykes seemed to have been transferred to them equally, they had obeyed the Senate's judgment. But they bore it with greater reluctance that the maritime Westergoers, not content with a matter already adjudicated, as if burdened, had petitioned the royal Senate for new statutes and had obtained them to the fraud of their own rights. For this reason they had fled to Ferdinando Alba, in hope of restoration to their former state, and, rejected by him, they asked the royal governor of Friesland to refer the matter back to the Senate. Meanwhile, lest they seem to have put off all human feeling, out of pity for the unhappy times they offered aid to the maritime Westergoers, but with this caution, that the act should not become a precedent, nor that their own right seem diminished on the ground of a benefit.

units.la: Quamobrem Carolus Brimæus tam mediterraneis quam maritimis Westergoïs mandavit, ut scripto jus suum ad xxiv. Maii diem, exhiberent, quo deferri ad Ferdinandum Albanum, Senatum secretiorum, aut Curiam Mechlinienfem curet, ac lis definiatur, toti Provinciæ damnosa. Ubi cum res tardius procederent, suspectaq; maritimis Westergoïs, quos periculum premebat, comperendinatio litis esset, iii. Eid Jun. Carolo Brimæo hanc supplicationem exhibuere:
units.tr: Therefore Carolus Brimaeus ordered both the inland and the maritime Westergoi to present their claim in writing by 24 May, so that it could be referred to Ferdinand of Alba, the Council of Secrets, or the court at Mechlin, and the suit, ruinous to the whole province, could be decided. When matters moved too slowly, and the maritime Westergoi, pressed by danger, suspected that the suit was being adjourned, they presented this petition to Carolus Brimaeus on 11 June:

units.la: QVandoquidem Carole Præfecte, præcedens annus ipsis Kal. Nov. enormi tempestate funestus rebus nostris commune exitium, universis periculum attulit, jamdudum animo consilia agitavimus, quibus (quantum humana ope fieri potest) Oceani injurys, atque inundationibus nostrorum agrorum subveniremus. Ita tibi jam ante querimonias nostras aperuimus, post ad Ferdinandum Albanum supplices devoluti rogavimus subsidia nostræ calamitati, & ut ipse summum Philippi nomine his in Provincijs imperium gerens, spretis discordijs nostris publica autoritate remedium præscriberet coercendo mari oppertunum. Quem ipsum, quia aliæ tum curæ exercebant, jussit, ut te arbitro nostrarum rerum uteremur, ac tu demandatâ potestate instructus, litem dirimeres à nostris quoque majoribus institutam. Quæ tes, quia multis magnisque difficultatibus implexa, huc usque longi temporis determinatione egebit, rogamus demisse, ut nos ipsos privato sumpta & consilio, aggeres eos, qui nostris possessionibus prætexuntur, reficere sinas, prætermisis eis, aut eorum consensu non adhibito, quorum officia sine magno impendio, ac longiore morâ haberi non possunt. Per eos namq; sæpe factum est, ut tributum muniendis aggeribus destinatum, in alios usus vertatur, ac nos expositi ijsdem & quidem gravioribus periculis, agros & prædia maris æstui nudemus. A quo ut tuti magis post hac simus, dabimus operam privato, si ita decernas, impendio, ut aggerem validum habeamus, & nostræ calamitati, ac simul juri publico satisfiat. Quod nisi præstemus parati erimus subire judicium, & sentire multas ifriusmodi ante rebus irrogatas. Tuum erit, Carole Brimæe, viduarum, & orphanorum subsidia implorantium querimonijs, & incolumitati prospicere, ac in universum consulere Provinciæ, tuæ fidei commissa.
units.tr: Since, Carolus, our Prefect, the year before, on the Kalends of November, a dreadful storm brought ruin to our affairs and danger to all, we have long been turning over in our minds plans by which we might help (as far as human effort can) against the injuries and inundations of the ocean on our lands. We have already laid these before you in our complaints, and afterwards, as suppliants, we appealed to Ferdinand of Alba for aid in our calamity. We asked that he, who exercises the supreme power in these provinces in Philip's name, should, setting aside our disputes, prescribe by public authority a remedy, namely a dyke suited to restraining the sea. But because he was then occupied with other cares, he ordered that we should use you as arbiter of our affairs, and that you, invested with the power entrusted to you, should settle the dispute begun by our ancestors as well. Since this matter is entangled in many great difficulties and so far will need a long period to decide, we humbly ask that you allow us, acting on our own authority and at our own counsel, to repair the dykes that stretch before our holdings, passing over those who have no part in this work, or whose consent is not sought, since their services cannot be had without great expense and long delay. For it has often happened through them that the tax set aside for building the dykes has been diverted to other uses, and we, exposed to the same and even graver dangers, have seen our lands and estates stripped bare by the tides of the sea. So that we may be safer from this in future, we will, if you so decree, spend our own money to have a strong dyke, and thus both our calamity and the public right will be satisfied. If we do not do this, we are ready to submit to judgment, and to suffer the many penalties of this kind that have been imposed on such people before. It will be your duty, Carolus Brimaeus, to look to the safety of widows and orphans who implore your help, and generally to take thought for the province, which has been entrusted to your good faith.

units.la: Ita
units.tr: Thus.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXI. Ita manifestâ temporum calamitate, Frisia inclementiis naturæ, & simul exactionibus Albani lacerabatur. Is namque elapso Octobri, quod decimæ centesimæque suæ adversari Frisios intelligeret, enormè Tributum imperaverat, obluctantemque consilijs suis populum non disparia à priore poposcerat. Quare oppresso per arma juie, & legum autoritate, per metum sublatâ factum est, ut Frisij talium rerum non ignari, Honorarium Duci decernerent, centumque & viginti octo aureorum millia, ut ante dixi, gerendis pro Philippo rebus assignarent. Hoc verò caverant Frisij, ut Honorarium statò die in ærarium Provinciæ inferretur, asservatumque ad ingruentia temporum ultimæ necessitati & usui regis serviret. Quod etsi Albanum præter violentiam & minas nihil sedatum, aut lenè spirantem pessime haberet, ita decreto gentis obsecutus est, suâque manu confectas eâ de re tabulas Ix. Kalend. Novemb. obsignavit. Reperio in actis originalibus, hoc ipso (de quo mensibus Junio & Julio disceptatum fuit) Frificæ gentis tributo ulterioribus Philippi Albaniq; exactionibus occursum, & centesimam, vigesimam, decimamque bonorum, quas Albanus exegerat summâ istius æris redemptam. Sic grassante per omnem Provinciam Albano pro imperij atrocitate, exulum quoque civiliumque animorum virtus se asperavit, validæque classes, infidâ per Ducem continente, Frificis æstuarijs immissæ toto mari volitavere. Tum Amelandiæ insula, quæ in Boream Frisico littori objecta, ab ijsdem sederatis occupata, ipsaque arx, quam Petrus Cammingha vir Nobilissimus cum imperio tum tenebat, à Bartoldo Entenio homine nobili & Translavicano cæterisque fœderatis direpta. Mox ab ijsdem in interius Flevi æstuarium cum classe regressis Worcomium quoque urbs, quod nullo præsidio teneretur, fœde vastata, abductique magno numero cives suam & juxta patriæ fortunam doluere. Quæ res Edzardum Transamasanæ Frisiæ Comitem, quod circâ Amasum fluvium non minore vi agerent, haud parum affecit. Itaque intutos reddi portus, totumque quod ditioni suæ obtenditur littus ægrè ferens, Aurantij naves detinuit, in quibus Ioannes Mepschius & Rembertus Iensma è Translavicanis, & Antistes Hemelumanus propè Staurios captivi asservabantur. Quod factum declinandæ apud Aurantium invidiæ mandatis Imperij Edzardus velabat, velut Cæsaris interesset Germaniæ limitem peregrinis armis non infestari. Econtra Aurantius naves reposcere, excusare suorum facta, ac testari propalàm, dandum quid esse moribus belli, quod pro libertate oppressi populi suscepisset. Constituisse se interea liberandæ oræ Frisicæ classem suam in Norvegiam, aut Britanniam expedire modo per anni tempus, & continuas asperioris cæli inclementias liceret. Ita Edzardi offensæ ad tempus occursum, cujus animus suo sive incommodo, quod ex Aurantij armis sentiebat, sive adversâ Principis fortunâ, pro more hominum iniquior, retardandæ navalium expeditionum, rei Occone Frisio homine fœderi inimico utebatur. Per eum namque factum est, ut navis, quæ in Amaso stabat, omni genere armorum per Pompeium Ufkenium Translavicanum instructa diriperetur, tardiusq; procederent negotia secretis consilijs subnixa. Id namque moliebatur Aurantius, ut limitaneas, maritimasque urbes in societatem fœderis solertiâ Legatorum perduceret, suisque rebus, & gerendo in Albanum bello, (Philippi enim nomen dissimulabat) firmam sedem pararet. Sed flans Subsolanus, continuique post Aquilones, dein asperrimum gelu invia omnia atque impervia navigantibus faciebant, Legatorumque negotia, & simul publicæ prosperitatis cursum, velut conspirantibus elementis, remorabantur. Borræus scribit stupendam tempestatem Kalend. Nov. ortam Aurantij quoque consiliis non parum obstitisse, Principemque magnarum rerum fortunam per minores Frisios, & confinem Trans-Isulaniam animo versantem importuno maris æstu retardasse.
units.tr: In 1571, amid this manifest calamity of the times, Friesland was being torn apart both by the harshness of nature and by the exactions of Alba. For in the past October, learning that the Frisians opposed his tithe and his hundredth penny, he had imposed an enormous tax, and against a people resisting his plans he had demanded not much less than the earlier one.
