Hence, with justice overpowered by arms and the authority of the laws taken away by fear, the Frisians, who were not unaware of such things, decreed a gift for the Duke and assigned him one hundred and twenty-eight thousand gold pieces, as I said before, for carrying on affairs on Philip's behalf. The Frisians, however, took care that this gift should be paid into the provincial treasury on a fixed day, and kept there to serve the king's last necessity and use in the pressing times. Although Alba, who was not calmed by anything but violence and threats, and who treated with contempt anyone who breathed a mild word, nevertheless yielded to the people's decree, and on 23 October he sealed the documents concerning this, written out by his own hand. I find in the original records that by this very sum (over which the discussion was held in June and July) the Frisian tax was redeemed, and the further exactions of Philip and Alba were met, and the hundredth and twentieth penny of goods, which Alba had levied, was paid off. Thus, while Alba raged throughout the whole province with the cruelty of his rule, the courage of the exiles and of the citizens also grew fierce, and strong fleets, sent into the Frisian estuaries against the Duke's wishes, sailed across the whole sea. Then the island of Ameland, which lies opposite the Frisian coast to the north, was seized by the same confederates, and the fortress itself, which the most noble Petrus Cammingha then held with authority, was plundered by Bartoldus Entenius, a nobleman from across the Lauwers, and the other confederates. Soon afterwards, the same men, returning with their fleet into the inner estuary of the Vlie, foully devastated the town of Workum as well, which was held by no garrison, and the citizens who were carried off with great numbers grieved for their own fortunes and those of their homeland alike. This affected Edzard, Count of East Friesland, not a little, because they were acting with no less force around the river Ems. Therefore, ill-pleased that the harbours were being made unsafe and the whole shore that lies under his rule was being exposed, Edzard detained the ships of Orange, among which John Mepschius and Rembert Iensma of the Lauwers, and the minister of Hemelum, were held captive near Stavoren. Edzard covered this act, done to avoid Orange's ill will, by the commands of the Empire, as though it were the Emperor's concern that the frontier of Germany should not be harassed by foreign arms. On the other side, Orange demanded the ships back, excused the deeds of his men, and openly declared that something must be granted to the customs of war, since he had undertaken it for the freedom of an oppressed people. He had meanwhile resolved to send his fleet to Norway or Britain to free the Frisian coast, provided the season of the year and the continual harshness of the rougher sky allowed it. Thus, Edzard's offences were met for the time being; but his mind, less fair than men usually are, either because of his own loss, which he felt from Orange's arms, or because of the adverse fortune of the Prince, used Occo Frisius, a man hostile to the alliance, to hinder the naval expeditions. For through him it came about that a ship which stood in the Ems, fully armed by Pompeius Ufkenius of the Lauwers, was plundered, and affairs that rested on secret counsels went more slowly. For Orange was aiming to bring the border and maritime towns into partnership with the confederacy by the skill of his envoys, and to establish a firm base for his own affairs and for waging war on Alba (for he concealed Philip's name). But the east wind blowing, and after it the north winds, and then the sharpest frost, made everything impassable and inaccessible to sailors, and, as though the elements conspired, delayed the envoys' business and the course of public prosperity at once. Borrhaeus writes that the amazing storm which arose on the Kalends of November had not a little hindered Orange's plans too, and that it had delayed the Prince, who was bent on great things, with its untimely tide of the sea, in the minor Frisians and in the neighbouring Trans-Isulania.

units.la: Sic fœderis rebus dubio aut infælici fato actis, Præfectus Senatusq; per Frisiam regius de perficiendâ Iustitiæ Æde velut partæ pacis monumento cogitavit, cuius fundamentum à Carolo Nitzenio Præside de consilio Præfecti, & collegarum magno sumptu iactum, tot annorum impendia trahebat. Quamobrem sumptuoso & admirando opere, ad finem perducto, ne sacrum loci votorum solemnibus vacaret, Senatus regius votivum Ædi præfixit, monumentumque signandæ temporum Æræ istiusmodi statuit.
units.tr: With the affairs of the confederacy thus conducted under a doubtful or unlucky fate, the royal Prefect and Senate for Friesland thought of completing the House of Justice, as a monument of peace won, the foundation of which had been laid at great expense by Carolus Nitzenius, the President, with the advice of the Prefect and his colleagues, and which had already cost many years. Therefore, so that the sacred place should not lack the solemnities of vows, once the splendid and admirable work had been brought to its end, the royal Senate attached a votive inscription to the building and decided to mark it with a monument of this kind dating the era of the times.

units.la: Redemptoris Incarnati ANNO CIↃ. IↃ. LXXI. VII. EID. NOVEMB.
units.tr: In the year of the Incarnate Redeemer 1571, on the seventh day before the Ides of November

units.la: DIVO PHILIPPO HISPANIARUM REGE CATHOLICO, ET FRISIÆ DOMINO REGNANTE, CAROLO DE BRIMÆU COMITE DE MEGEN, EIUSDEM REGIS NOMINE FRISIAM GUBERNANTE, SS. HANC IUSTITIÆ ÆDEM OPERAET SOLLICITUDINE CAROLI NITZENII QUONDAM PRÆSIDIS INCHOATAM, PIIS VOTIS, ET CONCORDIBUS ANIMIS IGRAMUS AB ACHELEN PRÆSES, IACOBUS ROUSSEL, VALERIUS AB OCKINGA, ADRIANUS VASTAERTS, ANTONIUS LOPES DEL VAILE, BOUDEVINUS À LOO EXQVÆSTOR, IDZARDUS À SICKINGA, PETRUS À FRITTEMA, FOCCO ROMMARTS,
units.tr: To the divine Philip, Catholic King of Spain and reigning Lord of Friesland; Charles de Brimeu, Count of Megen, governing Friesland in the name of the same king; this Hall of Justice, begun under the care and labour of Charles Nitzenius, formerly President, was undertaken with pious vows and united hearts by Igramus ab Achelen, President; Jacob Roussel, Valerius ab Ockinga, Adrianus Vastaerts, Antonius Lopes del Vaile, Boudevinus à Loo, treasurer; Idzardus à Sickinga, Petrus à Frittema, Focco Rommarts,

units.la: Basilicæ regiæ monumentum.
units.tr: A monument of the royal basilica.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXXI. IOANNES CAROLUS PROCURATOR REGIUS, IULIUS À DEKAMA, HYERONIMUS AB HANIA, ET HECTOR AB AYTA, CONSILIA- RII, SOLENNI PER ACTO SACRO, PRIMUM IURIS DICENDI CAUSA, COLLEGIATIM CUM PETRO AB EMSKERCK GRAPHAEO IN- GRESSI, HOC MONUMENTUM PERPETUAE MEMORIAE ERGO POS.
units.tr: In the year 1581, John Charles, royal procurator, Julius of Dekama, Hieronymus of Hania, and Hector of Ayta, councillors, entered together for the first time to exercise their judicial office, with solemn sacred ceremony, with Peter of Emskerck, the clerk. They set up this monument for lasting remembrance.

units.la: Reperio in vitis Antistitum Lidlumanorum, Senatum regium, Praepositurae Bolsuerdiensis administratione Isbrando Herderviceno Praesuli Lidlumano ademptâ, ejusdem Praepositurae reditus toto quinquennio extruendae Ædi applicasse. Hoc verò regij Senatus securitati adhuc deerat, quod exules proscriptiq; per æstuaria, & vicinum mare sparsi Provinciae incumberent, subvectiq; in portus, aut profunda littorum mediterraneis imminerent. Quare Senatus regius xiv. Kal. Maii ad Ferdinandum Albanum litteras dedit, eumq; periculi certiorem fecit, ac suppetias rogavit. Is verò, velut fortunae, quam immodestè haberat, ludibrium debens, ratus jam ante debellatas partes vires animosq; non resumpturas, suam tum demum intra se vecordiam, simul imbecillitatem expendit, litterasque impotentiae suae testes viii. Kal. ejusdem Maii Leovardiam dedit. Eæ habebant:
units.tr: I find in the records of the Lidlum prelates that the royal Senate, when the administration of the provostry of Bolsward had been taken from Isbrand Herderviceen, prelate of Lidlum, had assigned the revenues of that provostry for the whole of five years to the building of the church. But the royal Senate still lacked security in one respect: exiles and outlaws, scattered along the estuaries and the nearby sea, were threatening the province, sailing into harbours and lurking off the coasts and inland. So on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May the royal Senate wrote to Ferdinand of Alba, warned him of the danger, and asked for help. He, as if paying the price for the mockery of fortune which he had treated so arrogantly, thought that the parties had already been crushed and would not regain their strength or spirits. Only now did he weigh his own folly and weakness within himself. On the eighth day before the Kalends of May he sent from Leeuwarden a letter that bore witness to his helplessness. It read:

units.la: Omne littus peiratis infestum, cæterum Harlingios mari objectos, ac regi fidos operam suam parandæ classi addixisse, modo agrarij, caeterique Provinciales justa subsidia, instruendis triremibus præstent. Se verò renascentium bellorum moli expositum suppetias ferre non posse, aut ex Hollandia Zelandiâque submin istrare triremes regias, quod ijs in locis acrius bellum exardescat. Interim daturum se operam, ut Gasparus Roblesius legionis Praefectus, ac praesidium Groningae agens, classem milite instruat; modo Ordines Frisiae regis, & simul suo commodo apparatum, simul & pecuniam isti negotio decernant. Quae litterae à Senatu regio Deputatis Ordinum nullo fructu communicatae, quod hi ex omni provinciâ convocandos Ordines censerent, ut cogendo tributo eorum consensus interponeretur. Itaque in omnem provinciae oram missae litterae, quibus singulae Præturae Oppidaq; non binos pro more, caeterum unum tantum delegatum edere minuendis Provinciae impendijs, jubebantur. Dies quoq; Prid. Non. Maii Comitio dictus. Quo conventu, etsi verba speciosè faceret Achlenius Praeses, vir facundus, & solertis ingenij, tamen contumaciâ Ordinum evenit, ut nihil subsidij adornandis triremibus decerneretur. Ordines namque re Quatuor-viris demandatâ respondebant. Potestatis suae non esse ulterius tributum pendere recenti inundatione obrutis agris, & aerario per continuas exactiones exhausto. Ita centum & viginti octo aureorum millia ante annum regi depactos, non eâ mente ut tributum tributo cumularetur, sed ut sanctius aerarium ultimis necessitatibus, & publicae imbecillitati subveniret. Eam verò interea temtemporum fortunam fuisse, ut promissa praestari vix queant, omni fru-mento salsedine aquarum corrupto, & annonae caritate per Provinciam obvia. Adhaec nulla commercia, aggeres disjectos, ac solo aequatos, quos bono regis refici maxime expediat, Biltanis agris & vectigali regis ora magnis periculis exposita. Interim duo millia Carolaeorum se offerre, sed hac lege, ut in solutum proxumae pensioni cedant. Ea ad Ferdinandum Albanum perscripta Ordinum nomine, pro Ooftergois Ulpius Aylva, pro Westergois Tarquinius Haytsma, pro Sylvestribus Tinco Andringha, pro Oppidanis Matthias Rommartius VIII. Eid. Mai signavere. Hoc modo Albani exactiones Ordinum Frisiae populiq, frequentes querimonias trahebant, exulumq; mentes fæditate regnantium in spem reviviscentis patriae erigebantur. Quare & eorum plurimi prosperitate quoq; rerum impulsi, quas per Hollandiam Gulielmus Lumaeus, per Geldriam & Transisulaniam Bergensis non longe Frisiorum finibus gerebant, arma sumpsere, quorum apparatum per Germaniam rursum agitare Princeps Aurantius ferebatur. His accedebat quod Carolus IX. Galliae rex, Elisabethae Vallesiae sororis suspecta morte, sive aliis de causis Hispano infensus, studia & affectum asserendae Belgarum libertati praeferret, Principique Aurantio auxilia clam depactus occulta in Philippum aemulatione diceretur. Reidanus scribit, connivente tantum Carolo rege Gallicae Nobilitatis auxilia Aurantio decreta, Carolumque regem, sive Philippi potentiae iniquum, sive nefarij furoris (quo post Galliam reformatorum sanguine implevit) consilium agitantem, suspecti ac vere infidi favoris argumentum Principi Aurantio, & reformatae per Galliam Nobilitati fecisse. Neq; per Frisiam ingenia servilibus temporum conditionibus acquiescebant, cum essent qui domesticam pacem haberi non posse praeterquam restituta Libertate, & reparatis exulum rebus censerent. Quamobrem Doco Martna vir primariae Nobilitatis, (cujus majores Anno cIo. iii. c. ix. memorabili adversus Gulielmum iii. victoriâ Hollandicum quoq; jugum excusserant) dissimulatâ Fæderis prosessione, qua plurimae nobiles familiae exilium tum sustinebant, & privatam vitam secretis in patriam officijs obtendens, cum Aurantio Principe, ut Borraeus scribit, occupandae Leovardiae consilium communicavit, nactusque ejus rei diploma ope sociae Nobilitatis, in quâ Sixtum Botniam, Titum Hettingham, Serapium Galamam, Petrum Cammingham, Augustinum Oedsinam, Praetorem Dantumanum, Scipionem Sceltamam, Edonem Abbemam, Haringij Haersmae filios, Vibium Grovensteinium, Praetorem Menaldumaeum, & Siccononem Tyeffenium caeterosque fuisse Demetrius tradit, idipsum execqui conatus est. Quare ad Didericum Sonnoium (qui minoribus Flevum inter & Kennemarios Frisijs Aurantii nomine tum praerat) litteras dedit, pedestriumque copiarum auxilia rogavit. Sonnoius vero, ne lubricis adhuc & infidis per minorem Frisiam rebus, latera recentis imperij nudaret, & quod Gulielmo Bergensi auxiliares copias non ita pridem suppeditaverat, Horatium Bumam Tribunum Frisicae cohortis, virum militarem in Frisiam ire jusit, in quam Gulielmus quoq; Bergensis, Didericum Bronchorstium, hominem Batenburgicae gentis, cum imperio cIↄ. Iↄ. imperio amandaverat. Is namque velut propinquorum, quos Albani furor Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LXVIII. hauserat, caedem ulturus, acceptâ potestate militares copias conscribendi, designatis cohortium tribunis militem mox collegit, expugnatâque Cunera Comitum olim sede (qui in Hermanno ultimo eius gentis, sterilitate conjugalis lecti defecerant) ejecto munitione istâ Valonum praesidio, in Sylvestres Frisios se effudit. Cuius rei famâ perculsus regius Senatus, & quod Aegydius Barlamontius, qui Carolo Brimaeo vi. Eid. Ian. Swollis (ut nobilissimus Hemmingha in genituris suis tradit) ex apoplexiâ, cum liberalius festum magorum celebrasset, extincto iii. Eid. Maii successor datus erat, apud Geldros tum ageret, Gasparum Roblesium gente Lusitanum, Legionis Valonicae Praefectum, Groningâ cum copijs evocavit. Qui mox de consilio regij Senatus, (is namque absente Barlamontio rerum potiebatur) vicarium per Provinciam imperium adeptus, sedem sibi in arce regiâ apud Leovardios destinavit, amotoque Germanorum praesidio, ne quid foederati molirentur, legionis suae copias arci pro praesidio imposuit. Mox urbe novo opere firmatâ, ac stipendio, quas Adolphus Holsatus circâ Frisiorum fines ducebat, auxiliaribus copijs asignato, prohibendis, ulteriore in Provinciam ingressu, foederatis incubuit. Iam enim intellexerat Bronchhorstium Cuneræ potitum copias parare, dubiâque quarundam civitatum fide, Snecensem populum sociorum exilijs, & aspero dominantium imperio offensum adipiscendae libertatis consilium agitare. Igitur comparatis, quibus militem vehebat, undecim curribus, adscitoq; in comitatum, & mox Snecam praemisso Petro Frittema Senatore regio, ut primarium civitatis Consulem sui adventus clàm certiorem faceret, transitum sibi per urbem dari petijt, minuendaeque suspicioni sinistrae, suburbanis interea arundinetis militem occultavit. Sed contecta res non mansit. Avocato namque ad captandum secretum Consule, (qui cum praefectis forte civicarum copiarum diem conloquio trahebat) ijdem tribuni subesse, ut erat, dolum rati, totam per urbem magnâ celeritate se sparserunt, compertoq; Gasparum Roblesium sub ipsa maenia suggressum, dato signo ad arma conclamarunt. Unde clerus periculi metuens, arma, quae clam pro Roblesio paraverat, omnemque nitrosum pulverem in Curiam portavit, veniamque deprecatus est. Roblesius ipse, schlopo, ut ferunt, petitus fremens nequicquam & indignabundus contectam animo iram vultu expressit. Petrus Frittema Senator, velut vitae exspes, magno animi angore diu pressus, periculum tandem evasit, occupandaeque, quod dedisse ferebatur, urbis consilium, magno suarum rerum impendio mercatus est.
units.tr: Every shore is exposed to pirates, and as for the towns that lie on the sea, Harlingen and the others, they have pledged their support to the king and to preparing a fleet, provided that the landowners and the other provincials furnish the due subsidies for equipping the warships. He himself, exposed to the mass of renewed wars, cannot bring help, nor can he supply royal warships from Holland and Zeeland, since the war is blazing more fiercely in those places. Meanwhile he will see to it that Gaspar Robles, prefect of a legion and commander of the garrison at Groningen, equip the fleet with soldiers, provided that the Estates of Friesland decree the king's money, and at the same time the equipment and the cash for this business. This letter was communicated by the royal Senate to the deputies of the Estates, but to no effect, because they thought the Estates should be summoned from the whole province, so that by compelling a tax their consent could be interposed. Accordingly letters were sent to every part of the province's coast, ordering that each district and town should send, not two delegates as usual, but only one, to reduce the expenses of the province. The meeting was also called for the day before the Nones of May. At that assembly, though Achlenius the president spoke in fine terms, being an eloquent man of quick wit, the obstinacy of the Estates meant that nothing was granted for the fitting out of warships. For the Estates, when the matter was entrusted to the Four-men, answered that it was not in their power to pay any further tax, since their fields had been overwhelmed by a recent flood and the treasury had been drained by constant exactions. They had agreed with the king a sum of one hundred and twenty-eight thousand gold pieces the year before, not so that tax should be piled on tax, but so that the treasury might be the more securely relieved in its extreme needs and in the public weakness. In the meantime, they said, the state of affairs was such that promises could scarcely be kept: all the grain had been spoiled by salt water, and there was dearth of food throughout the province. Moreover, there were no trade routes; the dikes had been broken and levelled to the ground, which it was most advantageous to repair for the king's good; and the coast, with the fields of Biltan and the king's revenue, lay exposed to great dangers. Meanwhile they offered two thousand Carolus guilders, but on the condition that they be set off against the next instalment. This reply was drawn up for Ferdinand of Alba in the name of the Estates, and was signed on the eighth day before the Ides of May by Ulpius Aylva for Oostergo, Tarquinius Haytsma for Westergo, Tinco Andringha for the Sylvestrine district, and Matthias Rommartius for the towns. In this way Alba's exactions and the frequent complaints of the Frisian Estates and people dragged on, and the minds of the exiles were roused, by the foulness of their rulers, to hope for a revived homeland. Therefore many of them, also stirred by the state of affairs, which William of Lumey was pursuing in Holland and Bergen was pursuing in Gelderland and Overijssel, not far from the borders of Friesland, took up arms; and the Prince of Orange was said to be again stirring up their preparations throughout Germany. To this was added that Charles IX, king of France, whose sister Elisabeth of Valois had died under suspicion, or hostile to Spain for other reasons, preferred the cause of asserting the liberty of the Netherlanders, and was said to have secretly promised auxiliary troops to the Prince of Orange out of a hidden rivalry with Philip. Reidanus writes that the French nobility's auxiliaries were granted to Orange with only the tacit connivance of King Charles; and that King Charles, either hostile to Philip's power or meditating the wicked plan of his frenzy (with which he afterwards filled France with the blood of the Reformed), gave the Prince of Orange and the reformed nobility of France a sign of a suspected and truly faithless favour. Nor in Friesland were minds content with the servile conditions of the times, since there were men who thought that domestic peace could not be had unless liberty were restored and the fortunes of the exiles repaired. Therefore Doco Martna, a man of the first nobility (whose ancestors in the memorable year 1572, the ninth day of the month, had also shaken off the Hollandic yoke by a victory over William III), concealing his profession of the faith, for which many noble families were then enduring exile, and pretending a private life with secret services to the homeland, communicated to the Prince of Orange, as Borraeus writes, the plan of seizing Leeuwarden. Obtaining a commission for this, with the help of the allied nobility, among whom Demetrius records Sixtus Botnia, Titus Hettinga, Serapius Galama, Peter Camminga, Augustine Oedsma, the praetor of Dantumadeel, Scipio Sceltema, Edo Abbema, the sons of Haring Haersma, Vibius Grovenstein, the praetor of Menaldumadeel, Siccco Tyeffenius, and others, he tried to carry this out. Therefore he wrote to Diederik Sonoy (who at that time commanded for Orange in Minor Friesland, between the Vlie and the Kennemers) and asked for infantry auxiliaries. Sonoy, however, so as not to leave the flank of his newly established rule exposed while affairs in Minor Friesland were still slippery and untrustworthy, and because he had not long before supplied auxiliary troops to William of Bergen, ordered Horatius Buma, tribune of a Frisian cohort, a soldier, to go into Friesland, the place into which William of Bergen had also sent Diederik Bronchorst, a man of the Batenburg family, with command. For Bronchorst, as if to avenge the slaughter of his kinsmen, whom Alba's fury had devoured in the year 1568, having received power to levy military forces, soon gathered soldiers from the appointed tribunes of the cohorts. Having taken Coevorden, the former seat of the counts (who had died out in Hermann, the last of that family, through the barrenness of his marriage bed), and having driven out the Walloon garrison from that fortress, he poured himself out among the Sylvestrine Frisians. Alarmed by the report of this event, and because Egidius Barlaymont, who had been appointed successor to Charles of Brimeu at Sweollis (as the noble Hemminga records in his genitures) after Charles died of apoplexy on the third day before the Ides of May, when he had celebrated the feast of the magi too lavishly, and who was at that time in Gelderland, the royal Senate summoned from Groningen, with troops, Gaspar Robles, a Portuguese by birth and prefect of the Walloon legion. He soon, on the advice of the royal Senate (for Barlaymont being absent, the Senate held the power), obtained the office of vicar throughout the province, appointed for himself a seat in the royal citadel at Leeuwarden, removed the German garrison so that the allies could not plot anything, and placed the troops of his legion in the citadel as a guard. Soon, having strengthened the city with new works and assigned to the auxiliary forces that Adolf of Holstein was leading around the borders of Friesland, a stipend, he turned his efforts to preventing the allies from advancing further into the province. For he had already learned that Bronchorst, having seized Coevorden, was raising troops, and that the faith of some cities was doubtful, and that the people of Sneek, offended by the exile of their allies and by the harsh rule of their masters, were considering a plan to win their liberty. Therefore, having prepared eleven wagons to carry the soldiers, and having taken a retinue, and having sent ahead Peter Frittema, royal senator, so that he might secretly inform the chief magistrate of the city of his coming, he asked for passage through the town. To lessen sinister suspicion, he hid the soldiers meanwhile in the reed beds outside the walls. But the matter did not remain hidden. For the consul was called away to deal with the secret, and while he was delaying the talk with the commanders of the civic forces, the tribunes, thinking that a trick lay behind it, as it indeed did, scattered themselves with great speed through the town, and having learned that Gaspar Robles had approached right up to the walls, gave the signal and raised the cry to arms. Then the clergy, fearing danger, carried into the court the weapons which they had secretly prepared for Robles, and all the saltpetre powder, and begged pardon. Robles himself, as they say, was fired on with a schlopo, and fuming in vain and indignant, expressed on his face the anger he had hidden in his heart. Peter Frittema, the senator, as if despairing of his life, long oppressed by great anguish of mind, at last escaped the danger; and the plan of occupying the city, which he was said to have given away, he bought at the great expense of his own fortunes.

units.la: Mox Gasparus Roblesius Sneca exclusus, caenobium Floridi Campi se contulit, datisque ad Bolswerdios confestim litteris locum praesidio regio modestè rogavit. Quibus acceptis Magistratus oppidanus cohortium urbicarum praefectos in aedicula Mariae Virginis convocavit, litterasque Roblesij exhibuit. Caeterum tribuni copiarum, Paulus Symonius, Romko Vibenius, Vibius Mollius, & Bernardus Vietor quod ipso noctis meridie capiendum consilium non esse dicerent, postero die se responsuros ad postulata Roblesij fidem fecere, obseptisq; interim terim per manipulos armatorum civium portis, pueros, faeminas, re- liquamque imbellem turbam abstinere publico jusserunt. Quae res quia ad Roblesij propositum non erat, qui patere urbem sibi ac juxta praesidio voluerat, Magistratus consumpta per curas nocte, ipso lucis ortu ad Roblesium Legatos misit, qui referrent: Praevalere intra urbem foederatos, neque suis erga Philippum studijs reprimi potuisse civilium animorum motus. Duplicatos quippe vigilum ordines, ac portas manipulis obseptas, ne quis intrare cum milite queat, praeterquam assensu populi, cuius in infaelici urbe per discordias imperium sit. Tradunt alij, Magistratum oblatum a Roblesio praesidium tacitè respuisse, animisq; in foedus propensum, concordiam civium parem suae defensioni respondisse.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Gaspar Robles, shut out of Sneek, withdrew to the monastery of Floridus Campus and at once sent letters to Bolsward, modestly asking for a place for the royal garrison. When these were received, the town magistracy summoned the prefects of the city cohorts to the little shrine of the Virgin Mary and showed them Robles's letter. The tribunes of the troops, however (Paulus Symonius, Romko Vibenius, Vibius Mollius and Bernardus Vietor), said that no decision should be taken at midday that very night, and promised to give their answer to Robles's demands the next day. Meanwhile they had the gates blocked by squads of armed citizens and ordered boys, women and the rest of the unwarlike crowd to keep away from public places. As this did not suit Robles's purpose, since he had wanted the town opened to him and his garrison, the magistracy, having spent the night in anxious debate, at sunrise sent envoys to Robles to report: the confederates prevailed within the town, and the movement of the citizens' minds could not be restrained by their sympathy for Philip. The ranks of the watch had been doubled and the gates blocked with squads, so that no one could enter with soldiers except by the consent of the people, whose authority in that unhappy town rested on its dissensions. Others relate that the magistracy silently rejected the garrison offered by Robles, and that, inclined in spirit towards the confederacy, the harmony of the citizens answered for its defence.

units.la: Ita Roblesius simul Bolsuerdia prohibitus irâ tumens, tamen secreto odio injuriam tegens, per plana agrorum se & militem sparsit. Tum Leovardiam xvi. Kal. Sept. regressus, minax foederi, & jam animo ultionem expendens in Senatu regio de mittendis Franequeram Legatis consultavit, quâ in urbe, nihil caeptandum esse, praeterquam praetentatis civium animis, Senatus regius censebat. Quare Roblesius Leovardiam, velut sedem bello habiturus, commeatu atque annonâ instruxit, Praetoresque per utrosque Stellinguerfios, curare fines suos, ac de adventu Foederatorum, qui circa Cuneram denuò congregabantur, certiorem facere Senatum regium jussit. Constitutis quoque exploratoribus, qui actiones consiliaque foederatorum specularentur, ad caenobiorum antistites litteras dedit, quibus de subministrandâ annonâ hortabatur. Populum etiam Leovardium, ut M. Heymannus notat, novo sacramento obstrictum, armari recenseriqe fecit, conscriptisque quatuor Germanorum cohortibus tributum imperavit. Adeò adventantium foederatorum fama omnem Provinciam impleverat. Quare Valones qui Stauriae ac Maccomij praesidia agebant, adesse foederatos rati, Stauriam ac Maccomium deseruere, abductoque secum Henrico vectigalium Conductore, homine opulento, Leovardiam fugerunt, quo & Floridi Campi Antistes sacri aerarij gazam, aurum atque argentum omne, tum pretiosissimam supellectilem transmiserat. Metuebat namque ne Snecenses publicè infidi, & novarum partium professione ferventes, excursionem facerent, caenobiumq; caeteris ferè opulentius, ac magno rerum paratu famosum, cupidine praedae expilarent.
units.tr: Thus Robles, barred also from Bolsward, swelled with anger, yet hid his injury under secret hatred, and spread himself and his soldiers over the open fields. Then, returning to Leeuwarden on 16 Kal. Sept., threatening the confederates and already weighing his revenge, he consulted the royal Council about sending envoys to Franeker. The royal Council judged that nothing should be attempted in that town except after first sounding the minds of the citizens. Therefore Robles provisioned Leeuwarden with supplies and food, as if he meant to make it his base for war, and ordered the magistrates of both Stellingwerfs to guard their borders and to inform the royal Council of the arrival of the confederates, who were again gathering around Cunera. He also set up spies to watch the actions and plans of the confederates, and he wrote to the heads of the monasteries urging them to supply provisions. He further had the people of Leeuwarden, as M. Heymann notes, bound by a new oath, armed and enrolled, and imposed a tax on them, while four companies of Germans were levied. So completely had the report of the approaching confederates filled the whole province. Therefore the Walloons who held the garrisons of Stavoren and Makkum, thinking the confederates were near, deserted Stavoren and Makkum and fled to Leeuwarden, taking with them Henry, a wealthy collector of the revenues. The abbot of Bloemkamp had also sent there the sacred treasury, all the gold and silver and the most precious furnishings. For he feared that the men of Sneek, openly disloyal and fervent in their new allegiance, would make a raid and plunder the monastery, which was richer than most others and famous for its great store of goods, out of desire for booty.

units.la: Ubi verò cognitum Ioannem Bongam virum natalibus, & bello clarum, trajecto navigijs quibusdam Austrini maris sinu Snecam appulisse, intraque urbem magnâ civium concursatione & applausu admissum esse, altior adhuc metus omne confinium pervasit. Igitur per agros fuga & desertio palam caepta, caenobiorumque antistites extremo pavore correpti, rebus suis asylum quaesivere. Bonga verò ordinato Snecae praesidio, ac oppido multo opere, effossis Frittemanis praedijs, munito, vastandis caenobijs militem admovit, stipatusque trecentorum cohorte Bolswerdiam progressus, deditionem urbis postulavit, in qua Hobbo Ottonius vir impensè Pontificijs addictus, inter caeteros consulatum, & cum eo imperium gerebat. Qui repulsum nuper Sneca Roblesium vehementer criminatus, pensandae velut injuriae, Bongam quocIↄ. Iↄ. que militemque eius arcendum urbe censuit, dispositisque ad portas LXXII. vigilijs defensioni se paravit. Tum formula novi quoque juris jurandi perscripta, quâ mobilem dubiamque civitatem arctiore sacramenti religione Philippo obligaret. Quare Bonga prolato oppugnandæ Bolsuerdiæ consilio omni circum pecore abacto, ac Oegano, Ioannitarum & Groendiceno cænobijs exustis, Snecam regressus est, quod oppidum præfervidis in libertatem studijs istius parandæ diu consilium inierat.
units.tr: When it became known that John Bonga, a man distinguished by birth and in war, had crossed the bay of the Eastern Sea in some ships and put in at Sneek, and had been admitted into the town amid great crowds and applause, a deeper fear spread through all the neighbourhood. So flight and desertion of the fields began openly, and the heads of the monasteries, seized with extreme panic, sought safety for their goods. Bonga, having posted a garrison at Sneek and fortified the town with much labour (the Frittema estates having been dug up for the purpose), moved soldiers against the monasteries to lay them waste. Escorted by a cohort of three hundred, he advanced to Bolsward and demanded its surrender. There Hobbo Ottonius, a man strongly devoted to the Papists, held the consulship among the others and, with it, the government. He bitterly accused Robles, who had recently been driven from Sneek, and, wishing to avenge the insult, decided that Bonga and his soldiers should be kept out of the town. Having posted watches at the gates, he made ready for defence with seventy-two guards. Then a formula of a new oath was also drawn up, by which he would bind the fickle and doubtful citizens more tightly to Philip by the sanctity of an oath. Therefore Bonga, abandoning the plan of attacking Bolsward, drove off all the livestock in the neighbourhood and burned the monasteries of Oegaa, the Johannites and Groenedijk, and returned to Sneek, a town which had long been planning, out of fiery zeal for liberty, to secure that liberty.

units.la: Idcirco enim mense Aprili auxilia Principem poposcerat, misso Dilenburgum Tito Hettingha viro nobili, qui conscribendi militem, ac occupandæ urbis potestatem acceperat. Diploma quod apud gentiles asservatur, xvi. Kal. Maij signatum. Dein Bolsuerdij animis jam diu à Magistratu alieni, & dolore repulsorum auxiliorum concitati, ut exemplum Snecensium imitarentur, formulam regij juramenti publico igne combussere. Horatiumque Buma, & Gosuinum Allartium Staurium, tribunos pedestrium copiarum, ut caduceatores evocavere, ut de modo dedendi ageretur. Res in biduum protracta. Itaq; caduceatoribus Slotam regressis, qui locus præsidio erat, Ioannes Bonga, eorum, quæ evenerant, ignarus, eadem postulata fecit, Bolsuerdijque invito etiam, ut creditum fuit, Magistratu urbem Aurantio permisere.
units.tr: For in April he had asked the Prince for help, sending Tito Hettinga, a nobleman, to Dillenburg, who had received authority to raise soldiers and to seize the town. The diploma, which is kept in the family papers, is dated 16 Kal. May. Then the men of Bolsward, long estranged from the magistracy and stirred up by the grief of their rejected aid, imitated the example of Sneek and burned the formula of the royal oath in a public fire. They also summoned Horatius Buma and Gosuinus Allartius of Stavoren, tribunes of the foot soldiers, as heralds, to discuss the terms of surrender. The matter was dragged out for two days. Then, when the heralds had returned to Sloten, which was a garrison post, John Bonga, unaware of what had happened, made the same demands. The men of Bolsward, with the magistracy unwilling too, as was believed, surrendered the town to Orange.

units.la: Ita Bolsuerdia, cujus cives clàm cum Snecensibus inijsse societatem dicebantur, in fœdus adscita, cadùmque vini Diderico Bronchorstio, qui Balckij apud Geesterlandos agebat, missum est. Mox pultato campano ære, & omni cive in fanum, quod Martino sacrum est, evocato, populus Bolsuerdicus cum Magistratu portâ Snecanâ effusus, Bronchorstium recepit, verba faciente Regnero Annio viro Consulari:
units.tr: Thus Bolsward, whose citizens were said to have secretly entered into an alliance with the Sneek men, was received into the confederacy, and a cask of wine was sent to Dirk Bronchorst, who was at Balk among the Geesterlanders. Soon the Campanian bell was rung, and every citizen was summoned to the temple dedicated to Martin. The people of Bolsward then poured out with the magistracy through the Sneek gate and received Bronchorst, Regnerus Annius, a man of consular rank, making the speech.

units.la: EX quo, Diderice Bronchorsti, cum famâ Albanæ sævitiæ, bellum simul, & periculum accepimus, eius etiam imperij fastidium ad nos devolutum est, quod reverenter habere, quamdiu à tyrannide integrum fuit, nostri majores consueverant. Vbi verò servire, & pati immoderata, inglorium & turpè nobis visum, consilia inijmus, quomodo in libertatem restituteremur, & nos ipsi uxoribus, liberisque securitatem pararemus. Cujus spem quia in te nobis fecimus, tradimus tibi urbem, non inconsulto impetu, sed sacrâ æde, & communibus suffragijs connexi. Itaque, quæ nostræ potestatis erunt, subsidia, munimentà urbis, muros, arma &c, si pro libertate sit, corpora ac sanguinem habebis, modo ea integra pro virili cures, quæ Philippi Præfectorum vis, atque insolentia adulteravit. Virtute ac constantiâ tuâ multum proficies, cætera à Deo sperabis.
units.tr: Dirk Bronchorst, since with the report of Alban cruelty we have received war and danger together, and the arrogance of that rule has also been handed down to us, which our ancestors were used to regard with reverence as long as it was free from tyranny: but when we judged it inglorious and shameful to serve and to suffer immoderate things, we planned how we might be restored to liberty and secure safety for ourselves, our wives and our children. Since we have placed this hope in you, we hand over the town to you, not by a rash impulse but bound together by a sacred oath in the temple and by common votes. Therefore, whatever is in our power, the aids, the defences of the town, its walls, arms and so on, you shall have, and our bodies and blood too, if it is for liberty; provided only that you put right what the force and insolence of Philip's prefects have corrupted. By your courage and constancy you will achieve much, and the rest you will hope for from God.

units.la: Ita Bronchorstius multo nobilium comitatu urbem ingressus, lætissimi introitus pompam exercuit. Bonga cum trecentorum militum manu pro præsidio admissus, & Horatius Buma Harichius actâ apud Scettanos nocte, postridie urbi quoque inductus est. Tum reformata religio invecta, depurgatoque ab imaginum ornatu Minoritarum fano Ioannes Ianssonius rem divinam fecit. Magistratus quoq; novus, vetere abrogato urbi datus, in quem à Bronchorstio Geroldus Herama Oldermannus, Dominicus Hottingha, Iacobus Symonius, Petrus Vibenius, Regnerus Annius, Iacobus Iacobæus, Dominicus Tiallengius, Theodorus Occonius, & Paulus Symonius cooptati. Post collegij jurati mutatio secuta, omnisque ordo in verba Bronchorstij juravit. cIↄ. Iↄ. Idem Snecæ factum. Tum Pontificij plerique desertis conjugibus, liberisque Leovardiam concessere. Quos ut revocarent fœderati, profugorum uxores liberosq; in custodiam dedère, velut animo præconciperent redimendis carissimis pignorum, perfugas maritos honesta per conjugum desideria secessionem à Roblesio facturos. Ubi verò regium sacramentum matrimonij fide sanctius cariusq; deprehensum est, conversi ad exactiones fœderati, grande tributum captivas poposcêre. Sed rigidum illud, & proclamatæ libertati minus congruum interveniente propinquorum fidejussione sanatum est. Douwonis Heramæ, quod is urbe excessisset, bona commentario perscripta. Sacrarum quoque ædium supellex longâ annorum serie intacta, in tabulas tum redacta, censusque sacer detectus, religiosi ordinis opes, & simul luxum aperuit. Floridi etiam Campi cænobium tum vastatum, in actis reperio, præterque abacti pecoris damna, omne utensile Bolsuerdiam comportatum. Thomam Groningensem loci antistitem in possessionem muneris mense Iulio immissum, uno suorum fugæ comite adscito Leovardiam se contulisse, questumq; de vi illatâ, apud Senatum regium juris subsidium adversus autores damni dati nequicquam implorasse. Ita grassantibus Bolsuerdijs, multi familiarium rerum jacturâ impulsi, exitiosa clàm consilia, & simul incendia miserae urbi parabant. Quod propositum cum ægrius dissimularent homines, quibus animi secretum præceps ultionis cupiditas depromebat, Leovardiæ vulgatum, ad Franequeranos jam pervenerat. Qui propterea datis ad Bolsuerdios litteris de instantibus monebant, & esse intra oppidum, qui proditionem & incendia occultis artibus moliantur. Similes litteræ ad Bronchorstium datæ. Quare is relictâ confestim Snecâ Bolsuerdiam advolavit, arctâque custodiâ per excubias vigiliasque militum amovendis malis urbem sepsit. Reperio Leovardios Snecensibus hoc tempore infestos, suburbanum pecus abegisse, ipsosq; Worcomios dissimulata partium fide, Bolsuerdiâ urbe tanquam asylo usos, sua erga fœderatos odia falsis affectibus velasse. Arces quoque ac domos nobilium familiarum Pingumi, Oosterendæ, Elosti alijsque in locis disjectas, fœderatumque militem colonis cænobitarum vim & incendia comminatum agrorum locaria, & sacri ærarij proventus intercepisse. Eundem quoque Slotam progressum, nominis sui terrore Lemmariâ hostem submovisse, ac Coudumum non procul Stauriâ regressum præbyterum sacra, de more, facientem æde exturbasse. Adeò bellum lege adhuc, & disciplina vacuum, omnem secum insolentiam trahebat.
units.tr: Thus Bronchorst entered the town with a large retinue of nobles and held a most joyful procession of entry. Bonga, with a band of three hundred soldiers, was admitted as a garrison, and Horatius Buma Harichius, after spending a night at Scettens, was likewise brought into the town the next day. Then the reformed religion was introduced, and the Minorites' church, cleansed of its decoration of images, was used for divine service by John Janssonius. A new magistracy was also given to the town, the old one having been abolished. Into it Bronchorst co-opted Gerold Herama as Oldermann, with Dominicus Hottinga, Jacobus Symonius, Petrus Vibenius, Regnerus Annius, Jacobus Jacobaeus, Dominicus Tiallingius, Theodorus Occonius and Paulus Symonius. After that the sworn council was changed, and the whole body swore to Bronchorst's terms. The same was done at Sneek. Then many Papists, leaving their wives and children behind, withdrew to Leeuwarden. To bring them back, the confederates put the wives and children of the fugitives into custody, supposing, as it were, that the husbands who had deserted would, out of honourable longing for their wives, and to redeem their dearest pledges, secede from Robles. But when the royal oath was found to be more binding and dearer than the bond of marriage, the confederates turned to exactions and demanded a large tax for the captives. That harsh measure, however, which was less fitting for the liberty they proclaimed, was remedied by the surety of the relatives who intervened. The goods of Douwo Herama, because he had left the town, were set down in a written account. The furnishings of the sacred buildings, untouched through a long series of years, were then also entered in lists, and the church's wealth was disclosed, revealing at once the riches and the luxury of the religious order. I find in the records that the monastery of Bloemkamp was then also laid waste, and that, besides the losses of driven livestock, all its equipment was carried to Bolsward. Thomas of Groningen, the abbot, who had been put into possession of his office in July, went to Leeuwarden with one companion of his flight, complaining of violence, and vainly implored the royal Council for legal help against the authors of the damage. Thus, with Bolsward running wild, many men driven by the loss of their property were secretly preparing deadly plots and fires for the wretched town. When men whose desire for headlong vengeance drew the secret out of them could hardly keep this plan hidden, it was made known at Leeuwarden and had already reached the Franekers. They therefore sent letters to the men of Bolsward giving warning of the danger, and saying that there were persons within the town who were contriving treachery and arson by hidden arts. Similar letters were given to Bronchorst. Accordingly he at once left Sneek and flew to Bolsward, and by strict guard, with watches and sentries of soldiers, he fenced the town against these evils. I find that at this time the Leeuwarders were hostile to the Sneekers, and drove off the livestock of the suburbs; and that the men of Workum, having disguised their party loyalty, used Bolsward as a refuge and veiled their hatred of the confederates under false pretences. Also the castles and houses of noble families at Pingjum, Oosterend, Elst and other places were scattered, and the soldiers of the confederates threatened the tenants of the monks with violence and fire, and intercepted the revenues of the sacred treasury. The same man, having also advanced to Sloten, drove the enemy away from Lemmer by the terror of his name, and expelled an elder who, as was customary, was performing the sacred rites in the church at Koudum, not far from Stavoren. So far did a war still lacking law and discipline carry all its insolence with it.

units.la: Quo animorum civilium æstu per Frisiam durante, & , ut solet, ex secundis concitatiore Ferdinandus Albanus gestarum rerum seriem Philippum ad Regem perscripsit, regiqué fiduciâ suarum virium paulò ante elato, majorem sollicitudinem incussit. Quare Philippus Madrito xiii. Kal. Iul. ad Frisios scripsit, subsidiaque ardenti jam bello, & simul auxilia poposcit.
units.tr: While the agitation of civil feeling continued throughout Friesland, Ferdinand Alba, as usual more excitable after success, wrote a full account of the course of events to King Philip. Having been somewhat lifted up beforehand by the king's confidence in his own forces, he also caused greater anxiety. Therefore Philip wrote from Madrid on 19 June to the Frisians, and at once sought subsidies and help, since the war was now blazing.

units.la: Intellexi ex Albano prorege meo , quosdam ex rebellibus & imperio meo contumacibus multitudinem coegisse, turbandaque paci oppida quaedam per
units.tr: I have learned from Alba, my viceroy, that certain men, rebellious and obstinate against my rule, have gathered a multitude and have seized certain towns throughout

units.la: Frisiam occupasse. Ea ipsa quoque oppida & municipia igne passim ac ferro vastasse, nihilque omisisse, quod ad explendam sceleris atrocitatem spectaret. Cui rei cum remedium in tantâ rerum perturbatione quærendum sit, faciam boni Principis officium, daboque operam, ut, quantum res meae ferent, tantum utilitati vestrae impendam. Hoc tantum peto, ut impulsas res meas subsidiis viribusq; vestris juvetis. Quod si faciatis, clementiae exemplum, more antecessorum apud vos edam.
units.tr: Friesland. They have also laid waste those same towns and municipalities everywhere with fire and sword, and have left nothing undone that would serve to complete the atrocity of their crime. Since a remedy for such a disturbance must be sought in so great a confusion of affairs, I will perform the duty of a good prince, and I will take care to devote to your advantage as much as my resources allow. I ask only this, that you help my troubled affairs with your aid and forces. If you do so, I will show the example of clemency, as my predecessors did among you.

units.la: Tum Bronchorstius more mortalium, prospero fortunae cursu huc usque usus, de adjiciendâ victorijs suis Franequerâ cogitavit, quam etiam urbem illorum temporum fato, vehementia partium odia adfligebant. Vulgus ut ferè novis rebus facillimum, & quod vento velut ferente cum impetu agebatur, à Philippo animis discretum, Magistratum verò & primos ferè civitatis veteris sacramenti memoria, & parti sub Philippo honores occupaverant. Ita discordi civitate capescendam consilij sui occasionem ratus Bronchorstius, trecentorum militum cohortem isthuc ire, & mox Campanellam Spaniumque copiarum ductores subsequi jussit, castraque medio Tzumam inter & oppidum loco metatus, Delegatos in urbem misit, quibus Magistratum sui adventus, & juxta consilij certiorem faciebat. Qui metuens ne honoribus dignitatibusque primum, post bonis, ac facultatibus exueretur, recipiendi Bronchorstij consilium meditatâ cunctatione trahebat. Itaque plebs morae impatiens, & suspectam Magistratus tarditatem ducens, totam per urbem se sparsit, effractisque per vim portarum seris Didericum Bronchorstium cum copijs intromisit. Bronchorstius Franequerae locato modico praesidio, & frumentatione per vicinos agros imperatâ annonam procuravit latisque quibusdam statutis, quae ad continendum in fide & modestiâ, populum facere videbantur, Bolsuerdiam revertit, ac de mittendis, quam foederati ix. Kalend. Sept. occupaverant, Stauriam, auxilijs deliberavit. Enchusâ quippe foederi adjectâ, submotisque jam ante proxumo Flevi aestuario per Titum Hettingham, Vibium Siurtenium ceterosque classium praefectos regijs triremibus, hoc maxumè, neque imprudenter curabat Bronchorstius, ut tuti in utrosq; Frisios trajectus essent, maritimisque ac limitaneis locis in potestatem redactis, omni ex orâ commodè auxilia haberentur. Quare Stauriam vetus oppidum, Ducum olim Regumque Frisiae sedo, nostrâ memoriâ Anseatico foedere, & veteris fortunae famâ clarum, fugâ regij praesidij desertum, suam fecerat, ac in oppugnando castello, quod in Boream portui imminebat, & Valonum praesidio tenebatur, omnem operam collocabat. Unde praeter tres cohortes, quas è Transflavicanis militares viri ducebant, plures copias expedijt, tormentaque muralia è foederatis oppidis, Sneca, Bolsuerdiâ, & Franequerâ advehi jussit. Quae cum nullo fere usui essent, quod cicumducti operis murorumque magna crasities, & firmitudo obstaret, obseptis vijs locisque, quibus commeatus ac annona subministrabatur, morâ ac juxta fame consumere praesidium constituit. Quare Roblesius etsi lecto apud Leovardios affixus, regium in arce Senatum habuit, multaq; de solvenda obsidione ac mittendis ocyus auxilijs proposuit. Interesse namque regis Philippi quam maxumè, ne eâ fæderati munitione potiantur, quam Carolus Cæsar magno sumptu ex- trui curasset, & quæ magnum Philippi imperio stabilimentum adferre posset. Reputaret Senatus minores Frisios gentem adverso littori objectam Aurantio se permisisse, majusque in hac ipsâ Provincia post discrimen fore, si claustrum illud æstuario Flevi, & simul continenti impositum fœderati occupent, transitum in minorem Frisiam ad evo-candâ Aurantij auxilia hac occasione habituri. Ut ea intercipiantur, & ne præsidium fidei tenax, illustre exemplum virtutis professum, inediâ aut famè fractum in manus hostium veniat, mittenda auxilia esse, vel se ipso Duce, apud quem publici commodi potior cura, quam privatæ valetudinis sit. Cæterum regius Senatus, qui imbecillitatis ra-tionem, ac hoc ipso rerum incendio Præfectum morbo attritum extrà discrimen haberi volebat, alium copijs ductorem ordinavit, comparatisq; quinquaginta onerarijs navigijs, quibus cespitum vectura fieri solet, militem imposuit. Quibus de rebus certior factus Bronchorstius, qui Bolsuerdiæ otium inter & segnitiem agebat, leve quoque Schlopetariorum auxilium Stauriam confestim ablegavit, ut hostem anteveniret, & ad oppugnandum castellum cæteris cum copijs se pararet, quod præsidiarij Valones nullo adhuc dedendi consilio tuebantur. Illi namque perceptâ auxiliorum adventantium famâ, sociosq; ac commilitones proximos lacus navibus eminensos ac in terram jam expositos, castello se effudere, atque per subjectam urbem agmine, cum fæderatis congressi sunt. Quorum terga cum auxiliares hostium copiæ ferirent, quas Roblesius Leovardiâ miserat, & plures numero esse fœderati autumabant, errore decepti, & simul imbelles in fugam se dedere. Tum strages edita, totaque ferme urbs referens rudera, & imaginem adhuc ostendens antiqui splendoris miserabili incendio conflagravit. Fugientium pars Lemmariam ac Vollenhoam, pars Coudumum se recepit, quod à Valonibus una cum Stauriâ urbe opulentâ direptum prædam victoribus opimam attulit. Tormenta fœderatarum urbium in castellum devecta. Reperio in notis illorum temporum, omne illud incommodum Nicolao cuidam Bremensi, quod Ordines suorum fœditer deseruisset, imputatum, eundemque vinculis datum, nullâ ferè aut rudi illorum temporum disciplinâ, impunè dimissum. Alij verò in Diderici Bronchorstij socordiam, & quod omne fœderatarum copiarum robur simul castello non admovisset, rejecere. Cives plurimi è ligneis pontibus penduli fædâ morte strangulati sunt. Notat M Heymannus, quadringentos quoque fœderatos etiam desertâ Stauriâ predæ hostium imminentes ad Galedamum cæsos, Valonesq; paucis desideratis, & inter eos signifero Wibij Gerritij, cuius pectus glande transverberatum erat, Leovardiam ovantes redijsse.
units.tr: Then Bronchorstius, as men do, having used good fortune's course until now, thought of adding Franeker to his victories. That town too was being struck in those times by the fate of its divided factions, and the hatred between the parties was violent. The common people, as nearly always eager for revolution and carried along as if by a driving wind, had been separated in spirit from Philip; but the magistrates and almost the leading men of the old city, mindful of the oath of allegiance, and of the party that held office under Philip, had taken the offices. Bronchorstius, judging that the discord in the city offered him an opportunity for his plan, ordered a cohort of three hundred soldiers to go there, and soon Campanella and Spanius, the commanders of the troops, to follow. Pitching camp midway between Tzum and the town, he sent envoys into the city, by whom he informed the magistrates of his arrival and of his plan. The magistrates, fearing that they would first be stripped of their honours and offices and afterwards of their goods and property, dragged out the decision on whether to admit Bronchorstius with deliberate hesitation. So the common people, impatient of delay and thinking the magistrates' slowness suspicious, spread through the whole city, broke the gate bolts by force, and admitted Didericus Bronchorstius with his forces. Bronchorstius, leaving a small garrison at Franeker and ordering the collection of grain from the nearby fields, provided for the food supply, and after issuing certain regulations which seemed likely to keep the people in loyalty and good order, returned to Bolsward. There he deliberated with the allies about sending help to Stavoren, which they had occupied on 24 August. Indeed, having added an alliance with Enkhuizen, and having already earlier removed the royal triremes from the nearby Vlie estuary through Titus Hettingh, Vibius Siurtenius and the other commanders of the fleets, Bronchorstius took most care, and not without foresight, that crossings to both Frisias be secure, and that, with the maritime and border places brought under control, aid could be obtained conveniently from every shore. Therefore he had made Stavoren, an old town, seat of the dukes and former kings of Friesland, famous in our time for its Hanseatic alliance and the fame of its old prosperity, his own, after the royal garrison had fled and deserted it. He devoted all his effort to attacking the castle, which overhung the harbour to the north and was held by a Walloon garrison. From there, besides three cohorts which the military men from beyond the Vlie were leading, he sent out more troops, and ordered wall artillery to be brought from the allied towns of Sneek, Bolsward and Franeker. As these were of almost no use, because of the great thickness and strength of the walls and the great extent of the work, he resolved to block the roads and places by which supplies and food were provided, and to wear the garrison down by delay and thereby by hunger. Roblès, though confined to bed at Leeuwarden, therefore held a royal council in the castle and proposed many measures for lifting the siege and sending help more quickly. It was greatly in the interest of King Philip, he said, that the allies not gain possession of that stronghold which Charles Caesar had had built at great expense, and which could bring great strength to Philip's rule. The council should consider that the Lesser Frisians, a people placed on the opposite shore, had surrendered themselves to Orange, and that in this very province the position would be more serious after the loss, if the allies seized that barrier on the Vlie estuary, which was also placed on the mainland, and so would have the opportunity of passing into Lesser Friesland to summon Orange's help. To prevent this, and so that a garrison faithful to its allegiance, which had shown a famous example of courage, should not come into the hands of the enemy broken by starvation or famine, help must be sent, even if he himself led it, since for him public advantage matters more than private health. But the royal council, which wanted to keep the Prefect, who was worn out by sickness and by the very fire of these events, out of danger, on account of his weakness, appointed another commander for the troops. It fitted out fifty transport ships, which were usually used for carrying turf, and put soldiers aboard. Bronchorstius, informed of these matters and spending his time at Bolsward in idleness and sloth, at once sent a light force of musketeers to Stavoren to forestall the enemy, and prepared himself with the other troops to attack the castle, which the Walloon garrison still held without any intention of surrendering. For they, having heard the rumour of the approaching help, poured out of the castle, their nearby comrades and fellow soldiers having already disembarked on land from the ships on the lake, and met the allies in a body through the city below. When the auxiliary forces of the enemy, which Roblès had sent from Leeuwarden, struck their rear, and the allies thought them more numerous, the men, deceived by the error and at the same time unwarlike, turned to flight. Then a slaughter followed, and the whole town, showing hardly more than ruins and still displaying the image of its former splendour, was burned in a wretched fire. Some of the fugitives retreated to Lemmer and Vollenhove, others to Kuinre, which, having been plundered by the Walloons together with the wealthy town of Stavoren, offered rich booty to the victors. The artillery of the allied towns was carried into the castle. I find in the records of those times that all this disaster was blamed on a certain Nicolaus of Bremen, because he had shamefully deserted his own comrades, and that he was put in chains, and then, given the almost nonexistent or crude discipline of those times, was released unpunished. Others, however, put the blame on the sloth of Didericus Bronchorstius, and on the fact that he had not brought the whole strength of the allied forces to the castle at the same time. Many citizens were strangled in a foul death, hanging from the wooden bridges. M. Heymann notes that four hundred allied soldiers also, when Stavoren was abandoned, were cut down at Galedamum while pressing on the enemy's booty, and that the Walloons returned to Leeuwarden in triumph, with few missing, among them the standard-bearer of Wibius Gerritius, whose chest had been pierced by a sling-bullet.

units.la: Bronchorstius interea durante Stauricæ arcis obsidione, ut mari dominaretur, classem adornari fecit, eâq; latissimis, quæ Frisiam lambunt æstuarijs immissus, regias naves commeatu atq; annonâ instructas expugnavit, classiariocq; milite in proximum littus exposito obsidere Doccomium constituit, quod Philippi nomine Renicus Dekama & Cruningius nobiles viri, duabus cum cohortibus præsidio tenebant. Quod etiam cIↄ. Iↄ. etiam oppidum ad Eam flumen in Ooftergoâ situm, varia & mutabili LXXXII. fortunâ jactatum castelli formam sub Ubbone II. accepisse patrij annales memorant, auctisq; per Lavicam, Eamq; flumina commercijs opibusq; sub Adgillo I. in urbem conversum regalium jus ac praesertim cudendae monetae usurpasse. Tum à quadringentis & ultra annis, factionum tempore majore curà munitum, ac post à Geldris, dein Burgundis recuperatum, ab Anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxi. justâ pace floruisse, donec orto Philippum inter, & Provinciales formidabili bello, de eo oppugando, etsi, inrito conatu, Didericus Bronchorstius agitaret. Per Gasparum namque Roblesium Groningâ, ut dixi, evocatum, qui signa per Dongrios tractumque littoralem circumducebat, accessu littorum prohibitus, ventis velisq; fortunam recommisit, ac mutare consilium coactus est. Ex quo factum est; ut depulso Bronchorstio, Gasparus Roblesius (absente ut dixi Barlaemontio vicarium per Frisiam imperium gerens) omnem illum agrum vastaverit, opprimendaeque per oram illam Nobilitatis clandestinum consilium caeperit. Caeterum detecto consilio parum profectum, nisi quod arces per Dongriam direptae, omnisque fere ornatus nobilium familiarum, tum aurum & argentum à praedonibus devectum. Scipio Sceltama & Sicco Tyesseuius, qui in iltius orae Nobilitate tum censebantur, periculis subducti, primo eorum in Amelandiae insulam, altero Franequeram amoto, quae urbs, ut ante memoravi, spreto Albani imperio, quod pro Philippo gerebat, partes libertatis sequebatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, while the siege of the Stavoren castle continued, Bronchorstius, to gain command of the sea, had a fleet fitted out, and with it, sent into the widest estuaries that wash Friesland, he attacked the royal ships, which were equipped with supplies and provisions, and having landed the marines on the nearest shore, he resolved to besiege Dokkum, which was held in the name of Philip by the noblemen Renicus Dekama and Cruningius with two cohorts as garrison. Chronicles of the country also record that this town, situated on the river Ee in Oostergo, which had been tossed about by changing fortunes, had received the form of a castle under Ubbo II, and was converted into a town under Adgillus I, its commerce and wealth increased through the rivers Lauwers and Ee, and had assumed royal rights, especially the right to coin money. Then, for more than four hundred years, being fortified with greater care in the time of the factions, and afterwards recovered first by the Gelderlanders and then by the Burgundians, it flourished in just peace from the year 1531 until, a dreadful war having arisen between Philip and the Provincials, Didericus Bronchorstius was planning to attack it, though with an unsuccessful attempt. For Gaspar Roblès, who, as I said, had been summoned from Groningen, was leading the standards through the Dongeradeel district and the coastal tract, and, prevented from approaching the shores, he trusted his fortune to the winds and sails and was forced to change his plan. As a result, Bronchorstius was driven off, and Gaspar Roblès (Barlaymont being absent, as I said, and he exercising the viceroy's command through Friesland) laid waste all that countryside and began a secret plot to crush the nobility along that coast. But the plot, once discovered, achieved little, except that the castles in Dongeradeel were plundered, and nearly all the ornaments of the noble families, and gold and silver, were carried off by the plunderers. Scipio Sceltema and Sicco Tjessens, who were then counted among the nobility of that shore, were withdrawn from danger: the first went to the island of Ameland, the other, as I said earlier, was taken to Franeker, a town which, having scorned the authority of Alba which he exercised for Philip, was following the side of liberty.

units.la: Stabat tum in anchoris apud Amelandos praesidiaria navis, cui Gisbertus vir Hollandicae gentis cum imperio praerat, & qui sexaginta armatos, nomine Gulielmi Aurantij ducebat. Is rejectum Dongrico littore Bronchorstium aegrè ferens, Scipionem Sceltamam, qui, ut dixi, apud Amelandos perfugerat, ad reparandum Doccomij obsidium speciosis rationibus hortatus est. Amotum namq; in mediterranea Roblesium, littusque patère ascensui obvium, neque quidquam deesse, praeter animum gerendis festinanter rebus paratum. Reputaret Sceltama vastatam arcem suam, expilatum omne avitae domus ornamentum, cuius injuriae ultionem à pulcherrimi facinoris caepto habere posset. Modicum namq; intra urbem praesidium, quod infensos etiam cives haberet, faederi pronos, & novis rebus (ut fluxum vulgus est) se facile daturos, si ducem partium viderint, & qui suâ ac majorum claritudine imperium cum autoritate gerat. Intus civium, foris Provincialium auxilia fore, quae si paria negotio non sint, sibi militem, & classiarium esse, quorum operâ uti queat. Non submin-istraturum se inermium gregem, sed viros fortes; ac periculis suetos, & qui ardua quaeque ac molesta pro patriâ, & faedere non recusent. Ita Sceltamae animus evictus, de occupando Doccomio cogitavit. Quare levatis confestim anchoris, secundante Coro, praesidiaria navis Oostmahornam advecta. Ubi triginta classiarijs militibus in terram expositis, plebs rustica per Dongrios & è vicinis locis, ad eius rei famam excita turmatim confluxit, sacramentumque dixit. Dein coactore agminis ordinato mistum Provincialibus militem non lente itinere Doccomium duxit, habitoque ad portam cum praesidiarijs conflictu, quo superior Scel-
units.tr: There lay at anchor off Ameland a garrison ship, commanded by Gisbert, a man of Holland stock, who led sixty armed men in the name of William of Orange. Taking it badly that Bronchorst had been driven from the Dongeradeel coast, he urged Scipio Sceltama, who, as I said, had taken refuge on Ameland, to retake the siege of Dokkum, citing plausible reasons. For Roblesius had withdrawn inland, leaving the shore open for landing, and nothing was lacking except the will to act quickly. Sceltama should consider his ruined stronghold and the plundering of all his ancestral household treasures; he could take vengeance for those wrongs by beginning this most glorious enterprise. A small garrison inside the town, which also had citizens hostile to the Spanish, would find them ready to side with the treaty and to revolt (since the common crowd is fickle), if they saw a leader of their party, one who held authority by his own renown and that of his forebears. Help would come from the citizens within and the Provincials without; and if these did not match the task, Sceltama would have soldiers and sailors at his disposal, whose services he could use. He would not lead an unarmed crowd, but brave men, practised in dangers, who would not refuse arduous and troublesome tasks for their country and the treaty. So Sceltama's mind was won over, and he planned to seize Dokkum. Accordingly the anchors were weighed at once, and with a fair wind from the south the garrison ship was brought to Oostmahorn. There thirty sailor-soldiers were put ashore, and the country folk from Dongeradeel and the neighbouring places, roused by the news of this affair, flocked together in troops and took the oath. Then, having organised the column under a leader, he led the soldiers, mixed with Provincials, to Dokkum by no slow march, and at the gate, after a fight with the garrison, in which the upper hand was Sceltama's,

units.la: Roblesius vastat Dongriae tractum.
units.tr: Roblesius lays waste the district of Dongeradeel.

units.la: Doccomium Federati invadunt. Sceleratma fuit, propiùs cum copijs suggressus urbem occupavit. Præsidia- rij è quibus novem desideratos Heymannus Graph. scribit, partim celer- rimâ fugâ Leovardiam, ubi Roblesius tum erat, partim in turrim Bo-nifacij martyris cænobio proxumam spe novorum auxiliorum se contulere. Tum in signum victoriæ machinæ laxatæ, potiorque civitatis pars, quod ante non licebat, amotis obstaculis secretum suum profes- sa in verba victoris juravit. Sacra quoque ac profana loca, quibus mul-ti se occultaverant, curiosè perlustrata, milesque hostilis suo latibu-lo extractus, arbitrio æqui victoris se permisit. Tradunt alij, qui tam iniquis turbatisque temporibus commentarios confecere, eam victo-rum insolentiam fuisse, ut nec donarijs templorum abstinuerint. Cæ-terum mihi alia vivorum testimonia suppeditata, fæderatosque omni moderatione usos, magnam etiam hostium partem clementiâ in victos pellexisse. Itaque in turrim receptis, monachus (is solus ex illo ordine in oppido permanserat) caduceator missus, qui veniam præferret. Postquam ea ipsa; ac juxta periculum contemptui, præter admotas turri machinas, materies omnis concremandæ altissimæ crassissimæque moli aggesta, ut metu instantium extremorum, ad faciendam loci de-ditionem, obsessi compellerentur. Cæterum infracta militum virtus, & cedere periculis nescia, in ferventissimis etiam caloribus perstitit. Turris quoq;, etsi à Solis ortu in medium diei arderet, defensioni servata, è quâ obsessi missis desuper in fæderatos dicterijs saxa quoque immania, schlopofque jaculabantur. Eo rerum statu metuens Sceltama', ne quod post evenit, tumultuaria agrariorum manus fugæ se daret, recitato per Præconem edicto cavit; Ne quis, nisi de voluntate Tribunorum Centurionumque urbe egrederetur. Litteras quo-que ad Didericum Bronchorstium Franequeram dedit ocyus, in quibus de auxilijs monebat: Subesse quippe periculum negotio, & præter infidas multorum civium mentes, non magnum & fere inerme præsidium. Triginta quippe tantum classiarios, &dein è Dongrijs tumultuariam manum accitam, nesciam disciplinæ, & armorum rudem.
units.tr: The Federated troops attack Dokkum. Sceltama approached the city with his forces more closely and took it. The garrison, of whom Heymann the chronicler records nine as missing, partly by swift flight to Leeuwarden, where Roblesius then was, and partly by taking refuge in the tower of the monastery of Boniface the martyr nearby, in hope of new reinforcements. Then, as a sign of victory, the engines were loosed, and the greater part of the town, which before had not been permitted, having removed the barriers, professed its secret allegiance and swore in the words of the victor. The sacred and profane places, where many had hidden themselves, were searched with care, and the enemy soldier, dragged from his hiding-place, submitted himself to the judgement of the fair victor. Others who compiled accounts in such unjust and troubled times relate that the victors were so insolent that they did not refrain from the gifts of the temples. But I have been supplied with other testimonies from living people, and that the Federated men used all moderation, and by clemency towards the vanquished drew over a large part of the enemy. Thus the men who had been received into the tower, the monk (he alone of that order had remained in the town) was sent as herald to offer pardon. After this had been done, and the danger was to be despised, besides the engines brought up against the tower, all sorts of combustible material were heaped against its very high and very thick mass, so that the besieged might be compelled, by fear of the imminent extremity, to surrender the place. But the soldiers' courage, unbroken and unaccustomed to yield to dangers, persisted even in the fiercest heat. The tower too, though it burned from sunrise to midday, was kept for defence, from which the besieged hurled down upon the Federated men insults, and huge stones, and missiles. In this state of affairs Sceltama, fearing lest what happened afterwards should come about, that the tumultuous band of country folk would take to flight, had a proclamation read out by a herald: that no one should leave the town except by the will of the tribunes and centurions. He also sent a letter quickly to Diederik Bronchorst at Franeker, in which he warned about reinforcements: there was danger in the enterprise, and besides the unreliable minds of many citizens, the garrison was not large and almost unarmed. For there were only thirty sailor-soldiers, and then a tumultuous band summoned from Dongeradeel, ignorant of discipline and untrained in arms.

units.la: Econtra Roblesium in propinquo, sparsos per Provinciam & in ipsâ urbe superbos hostes editissimâ turre defendi, non periculis, non terroribus fractos. Perseverasse quippe in ipsis flammis, ac ardore igni-um, animas citius, quam arma posituros naturali pectorum robore, & quod abesse non procul auxilia præsumant. Quare nectendas moras non esse, cogitaret Bronchorstius, omnemque prolationem paratis semper rebus inimicam, vel hoc ipso discrimine maximè nociturum fore. Quæ litteræ dum ad Bronchorstium mittuntur, qui intra oppidum, mu-nire loca, vallum roborare, crates præstruere, tantâ laborantium ala-critate, ut imbeliis etiam sexus, necessario operi industriam commo-daret. Neque enim pueris fæmellisque largius otium, quin invalidâ etiam manu, sudes, ligna, comportarent, canoræque voce velut classico, virorum mentes accenderent. Interim Roblesius eorum, quæ evenerant certior factus, expedire Doccomium copias, totâque le-gione quam ex Valonibus conscripserat, urbem circumvenire consti-tuit, de cuius quoque excidio cogitare nec inveris rumoribus ferebatur. Qui ubi Doccomium perlati, tanta consternatio oppidanos, ac cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXII. juxta plebem rusticam occupavit, ut de deserendâ urbe cogitaturi suissent, nisi solatia quædam inanium litterarum eorum fugæ Bronchorstius interposuissel. Istæ habebant Ioannem Bongam, & Sicconem Tyessenium cum suis cohortibus iter ingressos, citum agmen ducere, adturos propediem.
units.tr: On the other hand, Roblesius was near, the enemy, scattered through the Province and proud within the town itself, defended in the very high tower, not broken by dangers or terrors. For they had persisted even in the flames and the heat of the fire, and would sooner give up their lives than their arms, through the natural strength of their hearts, and because they presumed that help was not far off. Therefore, Bronchorst should consider that there was no delay to be made, and that every postponement, always hostile to ready affairs, would do the greatest harm in this very crisis. While this letter was being sent to Bronchorst, they fortified the places within the town, built up the rampart, and laid down hurdles, with such eagerness of those labouring that even the sex unfit for war lent its diligence to the necessary work. Indeed boys and girls had no more leisure, but even the weak hands carried stakes and wood, and with clear voices, as if at a trumpet call, inflamed the minds of the men. Meanwhile Roblesius, having been informed of what had happened, decided to send troops from Dokkum and to surround the town with his whole legion, which he had enlisted from the Walloons; and it was reported that he was also thinking of its destruction, with unfavourable rumours. When these reports reached Dokkum, such consternation seized the townsfolk, together with the country folk, that they would have thought of abandoning the town, had Bronchorst not interposed some comfort in the form of empty letters for their flight. These said that John Bonga and Sicco Tyessenius had set out with their cohorts, leading a swift column, and would arrive shortly.

units.la: Quare tum pavor in fiduciam, mæror in gaudium conversus, quo ignaræ futurorum mentes nullo discriminis metu se compleverant. Cæterum postriduanus dies securitatem fæderati populi, & simul fortunam urbis invertit. Postquam enim tardius, quæ Bronchorstius prommiserat, auxilia adfuere, quingenti pedites ipso noctis obscuro Leovardiâ emissi, Doccomium perrexere, positisque ad emissarium vetus, per quod Ea flumen aquas laxat, castris, tormenta mox in urbem laxavere. Tum timor ingens oppidanis incussus, fletusque ac ejulatus muliebres compressò gaudio auditi. Quare ne planctus fœminarum puerorumque viris obesset, calorq; in pugnam ardescentium, miseratione prostrati in terram sexûs languescerent, fœminæ omnes domum abscedere jussæ, amotâque imbelli turbâ, civis milesq; defensioni urbis se paravit. Ita ad manus ventum, cominusque acri pugnâ certatum, tam egregio virtutis per oppidanos experimento dato, ut hostes pedem referrent, esseque in tuto fœderatorum res viderentur. Postquam verò urbis ac portarum custodia laxior, tum agrarij quique per temulentiam socordes, & ad pericula pavidi duarum partium, & tacitis odijs gravem urbem reliquere, prospera omnia fœdissimus signorum desertor invertit. Occupatâ namque, quâ plebes rustica profugerat, per hostem portâ, civium quoque acies inclinavit. Quæ tepidiore sensim sanguine ubi in fugam abreptos socios intellexit, spem servandæ urbis excussit, ordinesq; deseruit.
units.tr: Therefore fear was turned into confidence, and mourning into joy, so that minds ignorant of the future filled themselves with no fear of danger. But the following day overturned the security of the Federated people and at the same time the fortune of the town. For when the reinforcements that Bronchorst had promised arrived rather late, five hundred foot soldiers, sent out from Leeuwarden in the dark of night, marched on Dokkum, and, pitching camp by the old outlet through which the river Ee lets out its waters, soon unleashed their artillery upon the town. Then great fear struck the townsfolk, and the weeping and wailing of women were heard, mingled with joy. Therefore, lest the lamentation of women and children should harm the men, and lest the heat of those kindling for battle should be weakened by pity for those prostrated on the ground, all the women were ordered to go home, and with the unwarlike crowd removed, citizen and soldier prepared themselves for the defence of the town. So they came to hand-to-hand fighting, and fought at close quarters with a fierce battle, the townsmen having given such an excellent proof of courage that the enemy gave ground, and the affairs of the Federated men seemed safe. But when the guard of the town and its gates became more lax, then the country folk, who were careless through drunkenness and fearful of danger, and the men of both parties, who were hostile in secret, abandoned the grave town; and the most shameful deserter of the standards overturned all their success. For, the gate through which the country folk had fled having been seized by the enemy, he also turned the line of the citizens. When this citizen line, its blood gradually cooling, understood that its comrades had been carried off in flight, it lost hope of saving the town and deserted its ranks.

units.la: Tradit Henricus Bra milites illos, qui in turrim, ut ante memoravi, se receperant, commilitonibus suis indicium fugæ rusticæ fecisse, visoque civium languore destertâ turre victoribus se sociasse. Tum straminea fascia pileo adfixa, tessera cædi data, quam sexaginta equites, qui cito agmine Groningâ advenerant, enormi sævitiâ auxere. Trucidatis namque plurimis, qui arma ferebant, ætati quoque nec sexui ferè parcitum, saucio truncatoq; corpore per vicos sparso, & multo sanguine in præfluentem Eam effuso. Tum cæde ipsâ pejus incendium eluxit, multique, qui fugiendo ferri periculo, in domorum culmina se contulerant, nidoribus fumisque subtus ardescentium ignium depulsi in manus crudelissimorum hostium venerunt. Ferunt seminudos adhuc & valetudine languidos, tum puerperas cum infantibus in publicum productas, communis periculi fortem expleviSse, ipsumque Roblesium, iræ immodicum de delendâ ferro, ac flammis urbe cogitasse.
