units.tr: I find in the records that the Hemelumolpherdi and the Nordvoldi, allied with the maritime Westergoi, had at that time likewise brought the same suit against the Sylvestres, and that those maritime parties, having rashly begun the suit and relying both on their case and on hope of a good outcome, had lost by the decision of the same arbiters. This was confirmed by Philip in a solemn edict in the years 1533 and 1550 and remained in use. These things were written out in the royal citadel at Leeuwarden and signed by the hands of Gaspar Roblès, Igram Achlenius, Baldwin Ronius, Gerard Ostendorp, and Johannes Fonck. With the dyke dispute, which we have joined together, thus concluded, Gaspar Roblès ordered that the royal charter, which Philip had issued for the building up and repair of the sea dyke, be ratified and made effective; and, since the people, still obstinate, were neglecting the dykes and bringing ruin both upon themselves and upon the public, he proceeded against them with sterner commands.

units.la: Tum ut regiae, & simul suae dominationi consuleret, conventum quoque denuo Leovardiae habuit, instruendisq; quatuor pro rege trirem ibus subsidia popposcit. Quippe plerosque maris sinus hostium classibus obseptos, & praepedita commercia querebatur, foederatosque per proscriptiones, aut arma submotos, terrestre bellum exitiali peiraticâ commutasse. Sic istis amphibijs aliud suffugium malitiae quaesitum, non alio consilio, quam ne commeatum regijs copijs transmarinae provinciae praestarent, & ut proxuma littorum foedis incursionibus infestarentur. Sic foederatos sagaces, & nocendi peritos omnem maritimam oram scaphis, lintribusq; legere, diurnique aestus observatione, quem ex Lunae sydere metiantur, superatis brevibus levia navigia, classiario milite completa, extimum ad littus adigere.
units.tr: Then, in order to look after the royal interests and at the same time his own rule, he again held a meeting at Leeuwarden and demanded funds for equipping four triremes for the king. Indeed, he complained that most of the bays of the sea were blocked by enemy fleets and that trade was hindered, and that the outlawed and driven-off confederates had exchanged land warfare for deadly piracy. In this way these amphibious men sought another refuge for their malice, for no other purpose than to keep the royal forces from receiving supplies from the overseas province, and so that the nearest shores might be harassed by foul raids. Thus the shrewd confederates, skilled in harm, gathered in every coastal region small boats and skiffs, and, by watching the tides which they measure by the moon, they overcame the shallows and brought light ships, filled with marines, up to the outermost shore.

units.la: Mox ascensu in continentem facto, silente Lunâ, aut opaco noctis per eos villas vastari, exuri fana, liberos & ingenuos homines, instar pecorum, contrucidari, aut abduci, esseque metuendum, si progressus fecerint, ut pejora furoris sui exempla edituri sint. Itaque quaerendum ocyus malis remedium, & aestuaria maris validâ classe, aut multo remige purganda. Ut ij habeantur, instruanturque triremes, pecuniâ opus esse, quam hoc ipso tempore ex publico haberi Regis simul, & provinciae interfit. Haec à Roblesio in consessu regij Senatus, coram Ruardo Roorda, Valerio Cammingha, & Herone Ockingha Deputatis Ordinum, praefervidis in Regem studijs dicebantur. Quamobrem Deputati, corrogandi aeris difficultate moti, convocandorum ocyus Ordinum spem fecere, quo assensu populi, aut eorum, ad quos jus & simul summa reip. pertineret, gerendis pro Philippo justum rebus tributum decerneretur. Interim obtestabantur se Regis & provinciae commodis non defuturos, daturosque operam, ut necessarij, & prudentis consilij fructum ferat Roblesius, publicâque liberalitate, etiam extenuato aerario, & distractis provincialium fortunis, tam utile negotium juvetur. Posse pensiones vectigalium agrorum, & semestres aerarij reditus anticipari, aut supplendae aeris inopiae aliud subsidium decerni, cujus copiam propediem Praefectus Senatusque regius habituri essent.
units.tr: Then, having landed on the mainland while the moon was silent or in the dark of night, they laid waste the villages, burned the temples, and slaughtered or carried off free-born men like cattle; and it was to be feared that, once they had advanced, they would produce still worse examples of their madness. Therefore a remedy for the evils must be sought quickly, and the estuaries of the sea must be cleared with a strong fleet or many oarsmen. To have these triremes provided and equipped, money was needed, which at this very time it was in the interest of both the King and the province to obtain from the public purse. This was said by Roblesius in the assembly of the royal senate, in the presence of Ruardus Roorda, Valerius Cammingha and Hero Ockingha, deputies of the Orders, who were very zealous for the King's cause. Therefore the deputies, moved by the difficulty of raising money, held out hope that the Orders would soon be summoned, so that with the consent of the people, or of those to whom the right and the chief authority of the commonwealth belonged, a tax might be decreed for carrying out what was just on behalf of Philip. Meanwhile they pledged that they would not be lacking in the advantages of the King and the province, and that they would take care that Roblesius should reap the fruit of a necessary and prudent plan, and that such a useful undertaking should be aided by public generosity, even though the treasury was reduced and the fortunes of the provincials were scattered. The payments due from the land taxes and the half-yearly revenues of the treasury could be paid in advance, or some other aid be decreed to make up for the lack of money, the supply of which the Prefect and the royal senate would soon have.

units.la: Quare Senatus regius missis extemplo in omnem provinciae oram litteris, diem comitio ad xviii. Aug. dixit, delectosque Ordinum praestituto die adesse jussit. Ibi ex Oostergois Cunerus Episcopus, Gerardus Jacobus Antistes Clarecampensis, Scelto Sceltama, Hero Burmania, & Hector Vibenius Wirdumanus. E Westergois Praesul Lidlumanus, Petrus Frittema Jureconsf. & Senator regius, Goslicus Herama Jure-Conf. Petrus Widmarsius Buranus. E Sylveftribus Commendator Neffanus, Idzardus Sickingha, & Julius Dekama Senatores, Tarquinius Annius, & Meinius Lyclefius Nyholtius comparuere. Quo conventu, etsi effent, qui discordem provinciam, & inops aerarium obtenderent, tamen plerique publico discrimini subveniendum privatis impendijs censuēre. Itaque sestertius singulos in florenos aureos, adornandis triremibus, ex eorum bonis decretus, mandatumque praetoribus, ut per territoria ac districtus tributum cogant ocyus, pendantque Heroni Burmaniae erogandis pecunijs delegato.
units.tr: Therefore the royal senate, having at once sent letters throughout the whole coast of the province, fixed the assembly for the eighteenth day of August, and ordered the chosen delegates of the Orders to be present on the day appointed. There appeared from the Oostergoers: Cunerus, Bishop; Gerardus Jacobus, abbot of Clarecamp; Scelto Sceltama; Hero Burmania; and Hector Vibenius of Wirdum. From the Westergoers: the Prelate of Lidlum; Petrus Frittema, jurisconsult and royal senator; Goslicus Herama, jurisconsult; and Petrus Widmarsius of Bura. From the Sylvestri: the commendator of Nes; Idzardus Sickingha and Julius Dekama, senators; and Tarquinius Annius and Meinius Lyclefius of Nyholt. At this assembly, although there were some who put forward the discord of the province and the poverty of the treasury, most of them judged that the public danger should be met by private expenditure. Therefore, out of their goods, a sestertius on each gold florin was decreed for fitting out the triremes, and the magistrates were ordered to collect the tax quickly through their territories and districts, and to pay it to Hero Burmania, who had been appointed to disburse the money.

units.la: Mox Roblefius, quo triremes regias, quas Groningae clam fieri curaverat, commeatu ac annonā instrueret, Harlingam profectus est, maritimaeque expeditioni necessaria paravit. Igitur adornatae triremes Reideiium in sinum immissae, qui in Lavicae aestuarium influens Groningam urbem modico & navigabili alveo adlabitur. Caeterum enormi tempestate mox disjectae, aggeresque marini, ultro quoque infirmi, & sustinendis fluctibus invalidi, intumescentibus aquis patuere. Itaq; omnis Frisia, qua Flevum, Lavicam, Amasum flumina latissimis ostijs exonerat, aquis obruta, mareque, velut novis cladibus consilia mortalium provocaret, aut eluderet, per lata continentis spatia se effudit. Unde jumenta & homines undis hausti, frequentiam incolarum, & fortunam simul provinciae minuerunt. Tum praeter navem praesidiariam, cui Joannes Andreas vir fortis, nomine foederatae societatis praefectus erat, cum decem & quatuor classiarijs undis datam, triremis quoque regia continuis Cori, qui Frisico litori infestissimus est, procellis, & vehementiā brevium subversa. Ibi Siricius Donia vir nobilis, & juxta eum octoginta classiarij desiderati. Reliquae triremes non meliore fortunā per intumescentia aestuaria circumductae, diversis littorum vadis illisae. Unam tradit M. Heymannus, superatis aestuarijs sinu Amelandico in mare magnum, & quod veteres novissimum credidere, actam, reciprocante aestu, post introrsum vi fluctuum pulsam, in TransLavicanis haud procul Groningano littore desedisse. Reliquae duae diu alto jactatae Holverdicum in littus ejectae, consilia Roblesij non parum retardavere.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Roblefius, to provision the royal triremes, which he had secretly had built at Groningen, with supplies and grain, set out for Harlingen and made the necessary preparations for the naval expedition. The ships, once fitted out, were brought into the Reideiium inlet, which flows into the estuary of the Lauwers and glides up to the city of Groningen by a narrow but navigable channel. But they were soon scattered by an enormous storm, and the sea-dykes, weak of themselves and unable to withstand the waves, gave way as the waters swelled. So all Friesland, where the Vlie, the Lauwers and the Ems discharge through very wide mouths, was overwhelmed by the waters, and the sea, as if to challenge or mock human plans with fresh disasters, poured across the broad stretches of the mainland. Beasts and men were swallowed by the waves, diminishing both the number of inhabitants and the wealth of the province. Then, besides the guard ship, under the command of Johannes Andreas, a brave man appointed by the allied states, with fourteen sailors given to the waves, the royal trireme too was wrecked by the constant storms of the Cor, which is most dangerous to the Frisian coast, and by the violence of the shallows. There Siricius Donia, a noble man, and with him eighty sailors, were lost. The remaining triremes, no more fortunate, were carried round through the swollen estuaries and dashed against the various shoals of the shore. M. Heymannus reports that one, having passed the estuaries by the Ameland channel into the open sea, and sailed where the ancients thought the world ended, was driven back inland by the force of the waves when the tide turned, and came to rest on the Trans-Lauwers shore not far from Groningen. The other two, long tossed on the deep, were cast ashore at Holwerd, and considerably delayed Roblesius's plans.

units.la: Quorum conatus ne irritus esset, idem Roblesius triremem regiam, cui Siricius Donia cum imperio praefuerat, à Biltanis in continentem subductam refici ocyus curavit, novoque classiario milite complevit. Tum novem ex foederatis classiarijs, qui nando in littus evaserant, naufragi & fati inclementiā infaelices Leovardiam abducti, vinculisq; dati sunt. Itaque tum serio provincialium, procerumque animos desperatio pervasit, credentium irascentem fortunam, non solā civilium bellorum calamitate satiatam, anniversarias inundationes, perdendae genti, intestinis armis adjicere. Efferari coelum & sydera, ac non tantis aestubus concitata maria fortunatos majores afflixisse. Omne adversum infoelicibus posteris reservari, locum aliquando non habituris in quo spiritum trahant, nisi confusione quadam gentium priscis aetatibus assimilatā, infestent occupentque aliena.
units.tr: To keep their attempt from being fruitless, the same Roblesius took care that the royal trireme, which Siricius Donia had commanded, should be hauled from Bildt onto the mainland and quickly repaired, and he filled it with fresh sailors. Then nine of the allied sailors, who had swum to shore, shipwrecked and unhappy at the harshness of their fate, were taken to Leeuwarden and put in chains. So despair seized the minds of the provincials and the nobles in earnest, as they believed that an angry fortune, not satiated by the calamity of civil wars alone, was adding to the armed strife the annual floods, to destroy the people. The sky and the stars, they said, were growing savage, and seas stirred by such great tides had afflicted our fortunate ancestors. Everything adverse was being reserved for unlucky posterity, which would one day have no place in which to draw breath, unless, in some confusion of peoples like the ancient ages, they attacked and seized the lands of others.

units.la: Roblesius quoque, Harlingae tum agens, saevientis Oceani spectaculo, velut provinciae imperium amissurus, non levi sollicitudine attinebanebatur. Quamobrem missis Leovardiam litteris Igramum Achlenium Praesidem, Balduinum Loaeum, Idzardum Sickingam, & Petrum Fritemam Senatores Harlingam vocavit. Ibi Senatui regio Praefectos aggerum Leovardiam ex omni provincia evocandi potestatem fecit, tertiumque Sept. diem habendo conventui praefinivit. Igitur Senatus regius Leovardiam, salutato Roblesio, regressus Dodonem Syrxmam & Paulum Breckerum aggerum Dongriae cis ac trans Pasenum fluvium, Praetorem Ferverdium, Rolandum Achlenium Dantumanorum, Andream Haringium Collumanorum, Fredericum Hornium Hemelolpherdae & Nortvoldae, Douwonem Heramam Wonseranorum, Sicconem Albadam Winbritseranorum, Idzardum Stientjemam a Feenhusa ad Clifsum promontorium, marinorum aggerum Praefectos ad III. Septemb. adesse Leovardiae jussit. Quae urbs, etsi meditullio provinciae, & non uno aggere clausa, novae tum tempestatis acerbissimae calamitate jactabatur. Itaque aeris campani per urbem ac municipia pultatio imperata, colonique agrorum suburbanorum cum instrumentis rusticis Suettanuum in aggerem evocati, quo novo & fosili opere impetum aquae morarentur. Flante Africo illam tempestatem evenisse autores tradidere. Quamobrem Roblesius, ne quid temporis & consilij elaberetur, & ne diurnis tempestatibus per omnem provinciam agperes eluerentur, curatis Harlingae rebus, Prid. Kal. Sept. Leovardiam se recepit. Mox condicto die haberi Senatum jussit, Praefectosque aggerum in Curiam regiam citatos per Achlenium Praesidem hunc in modum allocutus est.
units.tr: Roblesius too, then at Harlingen, was not without considerable anxiety as he watched the raging Ocean, as if he were about to lose his authority over the province. Therefore, sending letters to Leeuwarden, he summoned to Harlingen Igramus Achlenius the President, Balduinus Loaeus, Idzardus Sickingha and Petrus Fritema, the Senators. There he gave the royal Senate the power to summon the prefects of the dykes from the whole province to Leeuwarden, and fixed the third day of September for the meeting. So the royal Senate returned to Leeuwarden, having paid its respects to Roblesius, and ordered the prefects of the dykes to be present at Leeuwarden on the third of September: Dodo Syrxma and Paulus Brecker, of the dykes of Dongeradeel on both sides of the river Pasen; the praetor Ferverdius; Rolandus Achlenius of Dantumadeel; Andreas Haringius of Kollumerland; Fredericus Horn of Hemelumer and Noordwolde; Douwo Herama of Wonseradeel; Siccho Albada of Wymbritseradeel; and Idzardus Stientjema, from Feenhuizen to the promontory of Clifsum, prefect of the sea-dykes. This city, though in the middle of the province and enclosed by more than one dyke, was then troubled by the bitter calamity of a new storm. So the bronze bells were ordered to be struck throughout the city and the towns, and the farmers of the suburban lands, with their farm tools, were called out to the dyke at Suettanuum, so that by this new and hastily built work they might check the force of the water. Authors have recorded that the storm came with the south-west wind. Therefore Roblesius, lest any time or counsel be lost, and lest the lands be laid waste by continual storms throughout the province, having settled matters at Harlingen, withdrew to Leeuwarden on the day before the Kalends of September. Soon afterwards he ordered the Senate to meet on an appointed day, and, with the prefects of the dykes summoned to the royal court, he addressed them through President Achlenius in this manner.

units.la: NOn alio consilio convocavimus vos Praefecti, quam ut de remedio istius mali consultaremus, quod tot annorum inclementia ferociens continuis furoribus non publico tantum littori, sed agris, ac ipsis etiam incolentibus injurium est. Ita tot funerum strage nuper edita, velut novissimum diem bis terris decerneret, paucos ante dies periculose desaevit, ac si nostris, de quibus deliberavimus, remedijs auxilium per intervalla malitiem opponeret. Quare ne rupta natura lege terram, quam incolimus, mare bauriat, & ne vivi transfire in se invicem elementa spectemus, censeo rumpendas moras esse, ac naturae iras nostra ope ac solertia reprimendas. Spectate corruptam annonam, dissectas villas, abacta pecora, & tantam carissimorum pignorum multitudinem iratis fluctibus absorptam. Adeo quidem ut nos vivere, aut mori, non naturae, aut fati, sed beneficio fere ambientis Oceani videamur. Quare volo ut de statu aggerum, qui agris finibusque vestris praetexuntur, ad Senatum hunc referatis, perscribatisque ocyus, quid erigendo reficiendoque aggeri factu utile, ultima rerum desperatione censeatis. Nos vestris consilijs ac arbitrijs regis nomine auctoritatem commodabimus, ne videamur conscientiae fidem, & publicum bonum neglexisse, cui solenni sacramento nos obligavimus.
units.tr: We have called you, prefects, for no other purpose than to consult on a remedy for this evil, which, raging with the savagery of so many years in continual fury, is harmful not only to the public shore but to the fields and to the very inhabitants. Thus, after the recent slaughter of so many lives, as if it would decree the last day for the lands, it has lately raged dangerously for a few days, and, as if to oppose malice at intervals to the remedies we have discussed, it has come to our aid. Therefore, lest nature, its law broken, should see the sea swallow the earth we inhabit, and lest we watch the elements pass into one another alive, I hold that delays must be broken and the wrath of nature restrained by our power and skill. Look at the ruined crops, the farmsteads torn apart, the cattle driven off, and so great a multitude of our dearest pledges swallowed by the angry waves. Indeed we seem to live or die not by nature or fate, but almost by the favour of the encroaching Ocean. Therefore I want you to report to this Senate on the condition of the dykes which run before your fields and lands, and to set down quickly what, in this utmost despair of affairs, you judge useful for raising and repairing the dyke. We will lend the authority of the king's name to your counsels and judgements, so that we may not seem to have neglected the trust of our conscience and the public good, to which we have bound ourselves by the solemn oath.

units.la: Sic Praefecti aggerum imperata facturi a Praefecto Senatuque regio dimissi. Mox ne, pervio per inundationes littore, provincialibus periculum ex annona esset, omne frumentum, quod ex injuria atrocissimae tempestatis reliquum erat, exportari edicto, praeterquam in castra regia vetuit, faenumque pecori pabulum, quod agrarij, penuria graminis, ante
units.tr: Thus the prefects of the dykes were dismissed by the prefect and royal Senate, to carry out what had been ordered. Soon afterwards, lest the shore, open to the floods, become a danger to the provincials through want of food, he ordered by edict that all grain left over from the injury of the most savage storm should not be exported, except to the royal camps. He also ordered that the hay, which the farmers, in the scarcity of grass, had shut up in their stalls before the autumn equinox as fodder for the cattle, should be collected and stored throughout the province.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. ante æquinoctium autumnale stabulis clauserant, cogi asservarique per provinciam jussit. Aquæ quoque erosis salsedine agris superfluæ solitis vijs ductibusq; laxatæ, cataractæq; & emissaria pro ratione diurni æstus, & spirantium ventorum clausa, ac reclusa inundationibus incrementum ademere. Reperio in actis illorum temporum, subversis Dongriæ circa Pasenum fluvium aggeribus, omnique pecore ac supellectile undis haustâ, multos beneficium cessionis bonorum Senatum regium orasse, exutosque fortunis ac possessionibus incerta sedium miserando spectaculo quæsivisse. Rex Philippus quoq; ut, attenuato per provinciam victu, negotiantium fraudibus mederetur, frumentarias leges, reprimendis coemptionibus, tulit, contractusque & actiones, ex ijs natas, nascendasve rescindi, abolerique fecit. Post nullo veteris discordiæ respectu, quæ de exportandis provinciâ frumentis, Carolo Cæsare sub Mariâ Gubernatrice, dein se Principe sub Margaretâ, exarserat, structores annonæ, coemptionum reos, poenâ suspendij puniri jusit, publicamq; populi inopiam novâ legis severitate ulcisci conatus est. Quare Prætoribus quoq; per provinciam, quovis modo, annonæ consulendi potestatem fecit, quo, ut olim sub Burgundicâ domo, procul angustiâ rerum, & damnatis coemptionibus ubere alimoniâ foelices subditi victitarent.
units.tr: The waters, which had been let out by the usual channels and sluices, and by the floodgates and outlets, according to the state of the daily tide and the winds blowing, and which were now superfluous over fields eroded by salt, took away the means of increase when the floodgates were shut or opened by the inundations. I find in the records of those times that, when the dykes around the river Pasen in Dongeradeel had been overthrown and all the cattle and household goods swallowed by the waves, many begged the royal Senate for the benefit of cession of goods, and, stripped of their fortunes and possessions, sought uncertain dwellings in a pitiable spectacle. King Philip, too, so that food was scarce throughout the province and the frauds of traders might be remedied, enacted grain laws to check monopolies, and caused contracts and actions arising from them, or to arise, to be annulled and abolished. Afterwards, with no regard for the old quarrel which had flared up under Charles the Emperor, under Mary the Regent and later under Margaret as Princess, over exporting grain from the province, he ordered the engineers of the food supply and those guilty of monopolies to be punished with the penalty of hanging, and tried to avenge the public want of the people with the new severity of the law. Therefore he also gave the praetors throughout the province the power to provide for the grain supply in any way they could, so that, as once under the house of Burgundy, far from scarcity and with monopolies condemned, the happy subjects might live on abundant sustenance.

units.la: Dein dubiâ armorum fortunâ, per Ferdinandum Albanum, & civitates ejus imperio parentes, sociæ foederi urbes ad defectionem sollicitatæ, velumque clementiæ, & fidei regiæ, speciosis ultro pacis consilijs, obductum est. Itaque, mite regis ingenium, & paterni affectus documenta exponebantur, velut non aliâ sollicitudine Philippi animus attineretur, quam, ut populus persuasionibus pravorum, aut suâ imbecillitate seductus, ac à majoribus degener, ad imperium clementissimi Principis rediret. Inde veniæ spes, & omnium rerum oblivia redeuntibus ad regem, perseverantibus in foedere effrænis saevitiæ comminatio, & excidia gentium denuntiabantur. Adhæc magni armorum apparatus ostentatio regiæ potentiæ magnitudinem circumferebat, fiduciamque fortunæ, velut tot regnorum regem non desertûræ certo bellorum successui augurabatur.
units.tr: Then, as the fortune of arms was uncertain, through Ferdinand of Alva, cities obedient to his rule and allied to the league were tempted to defect, and the veil of royal clemency and good faith was drawn over them, with specious proposals of peace offered freely. So the mild disposition of the king and proofs of paternal affection were displayed, as if Philip's mind were concerned with no other anxiety than that the people, led astray by the persuasions of wicked men or by their own weakness, and degenerate from their ancestors, should return to the rule of the most merciful Prince. Hence hopes of pardon and the forgetting of everything were held out to those returning to the king, while threats of unbridled cruelty and the destruction of peoples were proclaimed to those who persisted in the league. Besides, the great display of armaments carried about the magnitude of royal power, and, confident in its fortune, augured certain success in the wars for a king who would not be deserted by so many kingdoms.

units.la: Econtra Albanus fastidio foederis non duraturæ societati, & infaustis coitionibus breves terminos, & funestum exitum, velut ilicia ad defectionem, ominabatur, dolosisque actionibus subnixam perfidiem aulicis artibus, & peritiâ simulandi venditabat. Itaque inritâ foederatarum urbium defectione, postquam dolosæ artes non procederent, bello domitandum populum ratus, ad exactiones conversus est, impulsoque regis aerario Ordines provinciarum vicies centena aeris millia annuum tributum poposcit. Ita enim, datis ex Hispaniâ litteris, jusserat Philippus, ut affectis regni rebus, & accisis Hispaniæ opibus ordinaria subsidia gerendo bello peterentur, populusque suo exitio alimenta praestaret. Quare foederati ad socios Belgicæ Ordines, ne per assentationem, aut metum quid statueretur, litteras dedere: Ijs monebant.
units.tr: On the other hand Alva, with a disdain for the league which would not last, foretold brief limits and a disastrous end for an alliance and unlucky unions, as if they were holm-oaks destined for defection, and he boasted of a faithlessness resting on deceitful dealings, with courtly arts and skill in dissimulation. So, the attempted defection of the allied cities having come to nothing, since deceitful arts did not succeed, he judged that the people must be subdued by war, and turned to exactions. Draining the royal treasury, he demanded from the orders of the provinces an annual tribute of two thousand thousand florins. For Philip had ordered, by letters sent from Spain, that since the affairs of the kingdom were in a bad way and the resources of Spain were cut back, ordinary subsidies should be sought for waging war, and that the people should supply sustenance to their own ruin. Therefore the allied states of the Netherlands sent letters to the allied orders, so that nothing should be decided through flattery or fear: they warned them of these things.

units.la: INtellexisse se Ferdinandus Albanum suppetias gerendis rebus postulare, & jam convenjua indixisse. Etsi vero ad se id postulatum non spectet, quos à cæteris provinciis sua infœlicitas secrevisset, tamen amore patriæ com-pulsos, quam ortu legibusque coaœunev habērent, celare consilia sua non posse. Placitum scilicet maioribus fuisse, tuendæ adversum externam vim mutuæ societati, non arma tantum, sed consilia commodare, quo sociæ gentis consensu & concordiâ, publicæ provinciarum res pace ac bello, domi & foris constarent. Tantum abfuisse, libertatem unquam peregrini dominatus capacem fuisse, non semel assertam maiorum sanguine, quibus infra servitutem mors fuisset. Nunc vero peregrinos, ex obscuris initiis ad eminens aulæ fastigium per malas artes, & seda consilia evectos, nihil aliud moliri, quam ut, procuratis gentium secessionibus, mutuum in exitium provinciæ conspirent, attritisque provinciarum opibus, tyranni & exteræ secis imperium stabiliatur. Inde annuum tributum subvertendis socijs peti, quos in arma, ac bellum, more maiorum, non aliud incitamentum quam tutela patriį juris impullisset. Quo-rum nomine cum Belgicæ Principes majestatis jura usurpaverint, insolens esse se servos illius potentiæ facere, cujus vis ac dignitas à populo sit. Neque enim Philippi maiores, Burgundiæ Duces, belli aut pacis, signandi æris, aut sanciendarum legum jus, præterquam assensu Ordinum habuisse, quo ostenderent Ordines Principatum eos tenere à rep. non disformem. Itaque communis concordia reprimendæ exterorum dominationi, & mutua subsidia flagitabantur, arguentibus insuper fœderatis, divulsis provinciis firmari imperia hostium, do-mesticam libertatem subverti. Eam ipsam quoque restitui terris patriis posse, si in fœdus provinciæ coëant, regi principatum, populo jus, hostibus fugam & ludibria asserturæ. Prospectum quippe satis esse internæ potentiæ, neque aliud desiderari, quam ut magnarum virium documenta sint, & generosam posteritatem majorum decora irritent.
units.tr: Ferdinand of Alva, it was said, had learned that Roblès was asking for help in carrying on the war and had already called assemblies. Although that demand did not concern the Frisians, whom their misfortune had separated from the other provinces, they could not keep their plans hidden, since they were moved by love of their country, which they shared with the other provinces by birth and by its laws. It had been the settled policy of their ancestors to lend the allied provinces counsel as well as arms in defence against foreign force, so that the public affairs of the provinces, in peace and in war, at home and abroad, might stand firm through the agreement and harmony of the allied nations. Liberty had never been able to endure foreign domination; it had been claimed more than once with the blood of their forefathers, for whom death was preferable to servitude. But now foreigners, raised by wicked arts and dark counsels from obscure beginnings to the high summit of the court, were plotting nothing else than to foment secessions among the peoples and so conspire to the ruin of the provinces, and, once the resources of the provinces were worn down, to establish the rule of a tyrant and of a foreign faction. Hence the yearly tax was demanded in order to overthrow the allies, whom, after the manner of their ancestors, no motive but the defence of their country's rights had urged to arms and war. Since the princes of the Netherlands had usurped the rights of sovereignty in their name, it was insolent to make them slaves of that power whose strength and dignity come from the people. For the ancestors of Philip, the dukes of Burgundy, had not held the right of war or peace, of coining money, or of enacting laws, except with the assent of the Estates, which showed that the Estates held their princely authority from a commonwealth that was not unlike their own. Therefore common concord was urgently demanded, to check foreign domination and to provide mutual aid, the confederates adding that the enemy's power would be strengthened and domestic liberty overthrown if the provinces were divided. That liberty itself could be restored to the native lands if the provinces united in a league: the prince would keep his principality, the people their right, and the enemy would be put to flight and mocked. For there was surely enough of internal strength; nothing else was wanting but that there should be proofs of great powers, and that they should rouse the noble posterity to emulate the honours of their ancestors.

units.la: Mox supplicationes per omnem Frisiam imperatæ, quod Anna Au-striaca regi avunculo primogenitum filium Carolo Cæsari cognomi-nem fœlici partu edidisset. Vota quoque omni clero seorsim injuncta, quo propitio numine in nepotem Cæsaris fortuna simul & virtus clarissimi Imperatoris transfunderetur. Tum Roblesius, ut pellendis mari fœderatis classiarium militem suppleret, sestertium, quem è sin- gulis florenis aureis Delegati Ordinum colligendum decreverant, in consessu Senatus cogi per provinciam postulavit.
units.tr: Soon thanksgivings were ordered throughout Friesland, because Anna of Austria had brought forth a firstborn son, a happy birth, to the king her uncle, to be named after Charles the Emperor. Prayers were also enjoined on the whole clergy separately, that by the favour of God the fortune and the virtue of the most illustrious Emperor might pass at the same time into his grandson. Then Roblès, in order to supply soldiers for the naval forces to drive the confederates from the sea, demanded in the assembly of the Senate that the sestertium, which the deputies of the Estates had decided to collect from each gold florin, be levied throughout the province.

units.la: CVnctando quippe salubria consilia subverti criminabatur, & increscere potentiam hostium, qui peiraticæ beneficio imperium ferme maris adepti essent. His addebat infidos contumacis populi affectus esse, & maltos ore tenus sacramenta regia professos occulta fœderi fomenta commoda-re. Adornatis quoque triremibus nullum usum fore, nisi commeatu & justo mi-lite instruantur, promissoque are per provinciam corrogato, armis Philippi per Hollandiam Zelandiamque sparsis, trans Rhenum & in maioribus Frisijs re-gi subsidium præstetur. Navali expeditione imprimis opus esse, ut bellum nu-per in continente gestum, mari finiatur.
units.tr: They charged, of course, that wholesome counsels were being undermined by delay, and that the power of the enemy was growing, since by the advantage of piracy they had gained almost control of the sea. To this he added that the disloyal were the feelings of a stubborn people, and that many who had professed the royal oath with their lips were supplying secret fuel to the league. Moreover, the armed triremes would be of no use unless they were equipped with supplies and with proper soldiers; and with the money collected through the province, and with the arms of Philip spread through Holland and Zeeland, aid should be given to the king across the Rhine and in the Further Frisia. A naval expedition was above all needed, so that the war recently waged on the mainland might be ended at sea.

units.la: Ad quæ IDZARDUS SICKINGHA, Senator regius.
units.tr: To these things IDZARD SICKINGA, royal Senator, replied.

units.la: EVm à majoribus morem se accepisse, ut tributum cogi sine assensu populi per provinciam nequeat. Delegatos quidem Ordinum pendendum instruendis triremibus sestertium in singulos florenos annuos decrevisse, caterum nullà relatione ad populum factâ. Se suaque tantum obligasse privato affectu in Regem, cujus ærarium sublevari communi liberalitate, & contribuentium consensu debuisset. Non posse Senatum regium cogendis pecuniis mandatum interponere, nisi solenni comitio referibatur decretum, nomine populi ab ipsis Ordinibus confirmatum.
units.tr: He had received this custom from his ancestors: that a tax could not be levied throughout the province without the consent of the people. Indeed, the deputies of the Estates had decided that a sestertium a year should be paid from each florin for equipping the triremes, but without any report made to the people. He had bound only himself and his own property through private affection for the King, whose treasury ought to be relieved by the common generosity and the consent of those who paid. The royal Senate could not issue a command for raising money unless the decree, confirmed in the name of the people by the Estates themselves, had been referred to a solemn assembly.

units.la: Itaque in suspenso negotium mansit, Roblefiusque, etsi animo dissimularet, aliud subsidium instruendis triremibus quærere coactus est. Ferunt eundem Senatorem libertate fandi, & simul publicâ, usum, à Præfecto & Senatu regio malè exceptum, damnatumque privatæ & domesticæ vitæ, ac publico semotum, ex ægritudine animi, velut optumè sibi conscij, & ad injuriam impatientis, morbum, & ex eo causam mortis contraxisse. Eâ quoque intentatæ à Joanne Carolo, fisci regij patrono, litis eventum prævenisse, corporeque, supra modum obæso sensim mærore, & mox tabe extenuato, regiæ indignationis, & simul legem pessimi temporis effugisse. Adeo verum est, egregijs viris ut gloriam, ita odia & simul pericula crescere, ne hoc quidem indulgente Principis imperio, ut inter oppressi juris ludibria patriæ defensor libertate vocis, exuto, & quidem citra immodestiam, silentio frueretur. Hoc namque ægrius à provincialibus ferebatur, Roblefium, expulsis etiam provinciâ partibus, militem suum planos per agros exigendis stipendijs sparsisse, Josephumque Talimerium, triremi regiæ apud Stauríos præfectum immani sævitiâ famosum, nullo delectu hostium an provincialium fortunis ferocem animum explere. Quare Roblefius datis III. Sept. in arce regiâ ad Pastranam Hispanicæ cohortis tribunum, qui castellum Stauriæ cum præsidio tuebatur, litteris, Josephum Talimerium custodiæ dari, neque ante dimitti jussit, quam dilutis accusationibus, & evictâ scelerum fama, rationem turpium factorum, & exercitæ immanitatis reddidisset. Hoc vero cavebat Roblefius, ne quid ignominiæ molestiæque per irreverentiam Hispanici sanguinis sævissimo hominum fieret, proculque vinculis, & squallore carceris leni custodiâ haberetur. Mox quo agrariorum querimonias sanaret, militem per provinciam sparsum in præsidia revocavit, ac adesse ad signa jussit. Scilicet ne populus impendia maris, aggerum, & belli ferens, mox graviora laturus, exactionibus insuper discurrentium militum attereretur, dissolutusque belli ordo inopiam æris, & ultimam egestatem adflictis terris inducerêt. Quare & à signis abeundi, præterquam veniâ à seipso aut Bustamantio Tribuno cohortis impetratâ, nulli potestatem fecit, vagantesque & colonis agrorum molestos capi abducique Leovardiam, punirique ex instituto militaris disciplinæ imperavit. Arctandæ quoque militum licentiæ, & cohibendis excursionibus stipendia petijt, ordinarioque tributo in quemque florenum aureum quatuor per provinciam sestertios exegit. Tum de pensione viginti octo millium ex pacto regi præstanda commonuit, partemque copiarum suarum, sub quinque signis, Alcmariam in castra Frederici Albani ablegavit, partem in praesidijs retinuit. Triremes quoque regiae quas Roblesius milite & commeatu impleri fecerat, in aestuaria missae, quo Flevum fluvium, latissimo ostio in mare se effundentem, classe occuparent, minoribusque Frisijs auxilia simul, & commercia praecluderent. Caeterum Doconis Martnae nobilis Frisij, cui ab Aurantio Principe Frisici maris imperium commissum erat, & qui ostium fluminis anteceperat, rejectae, dubio flexu per infida aestuaria se sparsere. Hoc vero maxime Roblesius ac Trierarchae moliebantur, ut triremes classi regiae, cui Maximilianum Heninium Bossuvium Albanus praefecerat, se jungerent, foederatorumque naves à minoribus Frisijs instructas, sociatis viribus Austrino in sinu disiparent.
units.tr: So the matter remained in suspense, and Roblès, though he concealed his feelings, was compelled to seek another aid for equipping the triremes. They say that this same Senator, having used freedom of speech, and at the same time public freedom, was received badly by the royal prefect and Senate, and condemned to a private and domestic life, removed from public affairs; and that from the distress of his spirit, as one who was very conscious of his own integrity and impatient of injury, he contracted an illness and from it the cause of his death. Having been threatened also with a lawsuit by John Charles, advocate of the royal treasury, he forestalled the outcome of the case; and his body, gradually made excessively fat by grief, and soon wasted by decay, escaped both royal indignation and the law of that wicked time. So true it is that for distinguished men, as glory grows, so do hatred and at the same time dangers, and that not even by the indulgence of the prince's command could the defender of the country, in the mockery of oppressed right, enjoy silence, stripped of the liberty of his voice, and that without any intemperance. For the provincials took it more grievously that Roblès, after even the parts of the province had been expelled, had scattered his soldiers through the open fields to exact pay, and that Josephus Talimerius, the prefect of the royal trireme at Stavoren, notorious for his monstrous cruelty, indulged his fierce spirit without any choice of enemy or of provincials' fortunes. Therefore Roblès, by a letter given on 3 September in the royal citadel at Pastrana, to the tribune of the Spanish cohort who guarded the fortress of Stavoren with its garrison, ordered that Josephus Talimerius be put under custody, and not released until, the accusations being refuted and the reputation for crimes overcome, he had given an account of his shameful deeds and of the savagery he had practised. Roblès took care, however, that nothing of disgrace or hardship should be inflicted through disrespect for Spanish blood on so cruel a man, and that he be held under a light guard, far from chains and the squalor of a prison. Then, to heal the complaints of the farmers, he recalled the soldiers scattered through the province to their garrisons and ordered them to report to their standards. Of course, lest the people, bearing the expense of the sea, the dikes and the war, and soon to bear heavier burdens, should be worn down further by the exactions of soldiers roaming about, and lest the disorder of the army bring want of money and utter destitution upon the afflicted lands. Therefore he permitted no one to leave the standards, except by leave obtained from himself or from Bustamante, tribune of the cohort; and he ordered that the wandering soldiers, who were troublesome to the tenants of the fields, be seized, led away to Leeuwarden, and punished according to the established discipline of military order. To restrain the licence of the soldiers and to check their raids, he also demanded pay, and collected from the ordinary tax four sestertia from each gold florin throughout the province. Then he reminded them of the pension of twenty-eight thousand due to the king by agreement, and sent part of his troops, under five standards, to the camp of Frederick of Alva at Alkmaar, keeping part in the garrisons. The royal triremes also, which Roblès had had filled with soldiers and supplies, were sent into the estuaries, to occupy with their fleet the River Vlie, which pours into the sea by a very wide mouth, and to cut off at once the aid and the commerce of the Lesser Frisia. But the triremes, driven back from the mouth of the river by Doco Martena, a noble Frisian to whom the command of the Frisian sea had been entrusted by the Prince of Orange, and who had got ahead to the mouth, scattered by a doubtful course through the treacherous estuaries. Roblès and the trierarchs had been especially striving for this, that the triremes should join the royal fleet, which Alva had placed under the command of Maximilian Henin, Count of Bossu, and that they should with combined forces scatter the confederates' ships, fitted out by the Lesser Frisians, in the Zuiderzee.

units.la: Caeterum Aurantius etsi de liberanda obsidione Alcmariâ animo agitaret, Sonnoium minori Frisiae Praefectum, speculatorijs navigijs curare Roblesij consilia jusserat. Sic factum est, ut Sonnoius fretum, quod majores minoresque Frisios interluit, obseptum classibus redderet, hostiumque expeditiones & auxilia triremium, compedito velut mari, moraretur. Itaque navali pugnâ haud procul Muda oppido, Austrino in sinu commissa, regiâque classe per adversitatem fatorum foederatorum armis fugatâ, triremes quoq; & regiae naves, infidis aestuarijs, Harlinganum in portum subductae, moerorq;, & trepidatio, ut regium exercitum, qui Alcmariâ castra moverat, ita omnem majoris Frisiae provinciam pervasit. Adeo verum est mortalium mentes fortunae imperijs regi, infaustosque magnarum rerum exitus, fiduciam animorum adversitate casuum confundere. Idcirco fuere, qui perculsis navali clade, & capti-vitate Maximiliani Heninij Bossuvij, hostibus, de oppugnandis, exurendisq; in ipso Harlingano portu triremibus cogitarent, caecoque fortunae impetu utendum rati arduis ac difficilibus consilijs occuparentur. Caeteris placebat mediocritatem rebus quoque proisperis tutissimam esse, & instabile caducumque fortunae providentiâ futuri discriminis metiendum. Non semper quippe eodem ordine res humanas ferri, caeterum reciproco aestu se vertentem fortunam modo fluxâ benignitate, modo importunis odijs exorbitare. Ita grande consilium oppugnandarum triremium, cujus Doconem Martnam maris Praefectum autorem fuisse aunalibus proditum est, magnitudine periculi omissum, & quod classiarij militis justa supplementa desiderarentur.
units.tr: But the Prince of Orange, though he was concerned about freeing Alkmaar from siege, had ordered Sonnoy, prefect of Lesser Friesland, to watch Roblès' designs with scouting vessels. So it came about that Sonnoy made the strait which divided Greater and Lesser Friesland closed off by fleets, and held up the enemy's expeditions and the supply of the triremes, as if the sea were shackled. Therefore, in a naval battle fought not far from the town of Muiden, in the Zuiderzee, and the royal fleet being put to flight by the arms of the confederates through the adversity of fortune, the triremes and the royal ships, driven by the treacherous estuaries, were drawn into the harbour of Harlingen; and grief and alarm spread through the whole province of Greater Friesland, just as they had through the royal army which had moved its camp from Alkmaar. So true it is that men's minds are governed by the rule of fortune, and that the unlucky outcomes of great affairs confuse the confidence of spirits by the adversity of events. Hence there were those who, shaken by the naval defeat and the capture of Maximilian Henin, Count of Bossu, began to plan that the triremes, in the very harbour of Harlingen, should be attacked and burned by the enemy; and thinking that the blind rush of fortune should be used, they busied themselves with bold and difficult plans. Others were pleased that moderation is the safest course even in prosperous affairs, and that fortune, being unstable and fleeting, should be measured by foresight of the danger to come; for human affairs do not always move in the same order, but fortune, turning like a returning tide, swings now with a flowing kindness, now with cruel hatreds. So the great plan of attacking the triremes, of which Doco Martena, prefect of the sea, is recorded in the annals as the author, was abandoned because of the magnitude of the danger, and because the proper reinforcements of the naval soldiers were needed.

units.la: Ferunt Philippum inaugurationis tempore lustrandis provincijs, & urbium magnificentiae intentum, Harlemumque provectum, de visendâ quoque Alcmariâ cogitasse, invitatumque, quo id honoris civitati & populo daret, certam sui adventus spem legatis Alcmarienfium fecisse. Caeterum persuasum à purpurato, obscurae urbis famam infra majestatem ac fortunam tanti Principis esse, consilium mutasse, elusoq; populo, & omnium rerum apparatu in contumeliam, ludibriumq; verso, negletâ urbe, & minoris Frisiae provinciâ Amstelodamum perrexisse. Quâ in re mirari prudentiam & aequitatem fati lubet, fore aliquando, ut tantae potentiae, & ex hac legis sui oblitus Princeps, idem, interruptâ obsidione, inglorij contemptus exemplum ab illâ urbe acciperet, totque regnorum coeuntium vis, in medio victoriarum cursu, cuʃu, ad ignobiles opinione Principis muros sisteretur. Bossuvius quo-que regiæ classi Præfectus, à minoris Frisiæ despecta gente vinceretur, doceretúrque Philippus, magnitudinem regiam tot terras, & maria possessione, & plus animo ac spe complexam, summa destruentis fortunæ ludo includi.
units.tr: They say that Philip, intent on touring the provinces and admiring the magnificence of their cities at the time of his inauguration, advanced to Haarlem and also thought of visiting Alkmaar. He invited the envoys of the Alkmaarians, so as to give that honour to the city and its people, and led them to hope for his coming. But he was persuaded by the purple-clad cardinal that the fame of an obscure town was beneath the majesty and fortune of so great a Prince. He changed his plan, mocked the people, and turned all the preparations into insult and ridicule. Neglecting the city and the province of West Friesland, he went on to Amsterdam. In this matter it is good to marvel at the prudence and the fairness of fate: that one day this Prince, so mighty and forgetful of his own law, would, with the siege broken off, receive from that city an example of inglorious contempt; and that the force of so many united kingdoms, in the midst of its course of victories, would be halted before walls that were ignoble in the Prince's opinion. Bossu too, prefect of the royal fleet, would be defeated by the despised people of West Friesland, and Philip would learn that royal greatness, which embraced so many lands and seas in possession and even more in mind and hope, is enclosed within the game of a fortune that destroys all things.

units.la: Igitur Ferdinandum Albanum, qui jam ante prosperà fatorum in lasciviem superbiamque converterat, adversitate fortunæ dejectum mæror, & consternatio occupavit. Quippe impurus Ducis animus, per tormenta pectorum, omne adversum irascentem fortunam robur amiserat, pociitudineque anteactarum rerum, velut interno vulnere, debilitabatur. Ita reputabat in Hispaniâ & Philippi aulâ pacem, quietemque optuma sedandæ Belgicæ remedia suadentibus se opposuisse, submotâque principatu Margaretâ Gubernatrice, optimum solertis fæminæ imperium cum asperrimo & insolenti commutasse. Inde fomentum bello, causam tastis provincialium miserijs se dedisse, quo minus placare animum possit utriusque fortunæ non capacem, & tantum prosperis assuetum. Refluentibus adversis, ut ante soelicibus rebus temperamentum, ita nunc remedia sedandæ menti deesse. Sic rudimenta dominatus prospere acta, velut non alia rerum lege, quam ut summam imperij maturitatem, & simul statuæ beneficio monumentum famæ adeptus, instabili & res cunctas vertente fortunæ invidia exerceretur. Incerto loco res mortalium positas tunc maximè deficere cum ad fastigium pervenere. Librari namque dubijs eventibus per Zelandiam bellum, & Alcmariâ minoris Frisiæ urbe per Fredericum filium, velut constituto prosperis termino, desertâ, classem regiam non uno loco improsperis naumachijs disjectam. Adhæc omnem fere Hollandiam in partibus, & per omnem provinciam infidas res, aperta arma aut defectiones agitare. Ita non missum in principijs sanguinem, non depurgatas proscriptionibus urbes securum adhuc imperium polliceri, cæterum extare publicæ cladis aut iræ reliquias, nova consilia in Philippum, & maxume se Proregem fabricantes.
units.tr: Therefore grief and consternation seized Ferdinand of Alva, who had already before been turned to wantonness and pride by his prosperous fortunes, now cast down by adversity. Indeed his unsound spirit, through the torments of his breast, had lost all its strength against a fortune that raged against him, and was weakened, as by an inward wound, by the memory of past successes. He reflected thus: in Spain and at Philip's court he had opposed those who advised peace and quiet, the best remedies for calming the Belgic troubles; and, with Margaret the regent removed from power, he had exchanged the excellent rule of a skilful woman for a most harsh and insolent one. Hence he had given fuel to the war and a cause for the miseries of the provinces, so that he could not appease a mind incapable of either fortune, accustomed only to prosperity. Now that adversity was flowing back, there was no moderation in his prosperous days, and now there were no remedies to calm his mind. Thus the beginnings of his rule, carried out successfully, as though by no other law of affairs than that he should gain the highest maturity of power and, at the same time, a monument of fame through the favour of a statue, were now to be harassed by the envy of a fickle fortune that overturns all things. Human affairs, placed in an uncertain position, fail most of all when they have reached their height. For, with the war in Zeeland going on with doubtful outcomes, and Alkmaar, a town in West Friesland, abandoned to Frederick, the son of Alva, as if a limit to prosperity had been set, the royal fleet was scattered in unlucky sea-battles in more than one place. Besides, almost all of Holland was in revolt, and throughout the whole province disloyal affairs were stirring up open arms or defections. Thus the blood shed at the beginning, and cities not yet purged by proscriptions, promised no secure rule; rather, there remained the remnants of public ruin and anger, forming new plans against Philip and especially against himself as viceroy.

units.la: Quare inclinante fortunâ, & efferato magis per provincias populo, tutissimam missionem esse, ne quæsita secundis gloria per adversa obscuretur. Posse adhuc, necdum collapsis Philippi rebus gratiam regiam, & inconstantis aulæ promereri. Neque enim sævitiem suam regi culpabilem fore, & professuros silentium ætmulos, si viderint Philippum, non verso in odia affectu, ministeria exerciti furoris, & simul patienter adversitatem fortunæ ferre, suo more documenta casuum, & fluxæ sortis edentem. Sic expeditis in Hispaniam, præmisso jam ante, ut Thuanus tradit, Bernardino Mendoza, ad Philippum regem litteris, excusatione diuturnæ valetudinis, & imbecillium annorum usus, missionem oravit, animoque immani, etsi otia ac vacationes suopte ingenio fastidienti, secessum paravit. Erant qui crederent, Philippum regem adversâ Ducis fortunâ alium, suis etiam mandatis in perniciem ministri usurum fore, Ferdinandumque Albanum à fortunâ destitutum, regis quoque, velut fastidientis infœlicem indignationem & odia sensurum. Militarium quippe Ducum prospera regum gloriæ ut plurimum cedere, adversa privatis imputari. Esse haud dubie, quæ Philippi ingenio, ultro crudeli, materiam offensæ ᴄIↄ Iↄ afferre queant, & ut aliud incitamentum non sit, solius superbiæ esse. LXXIII. Ita Belgicæ solium, quod Principi reverentia majestatis reservaverat, ab eo in conspectu Ordinum, populique occupatum, & insigni arrogantiâ, moderatis antecessoribus damnatâ, Trophæum, fallaci famæ erectum. Regiæ aut imperatoriæ fortunæ ista decora esse, privatis, & Principum suorum æmulis semper incommodo cesisse.
units.tr: Therefore, with fortune declining and the people, now more savage, growing fiercer throughout the provinces, the safest course was to be dismissed, lest the glory won by his successes be obscured by his reverses. He could still, while Philip's affairs had not yet collapsed, earn the royal favour of an inconstant court. For they would not hold his cruelty against the king, and his rivals would keep silent, if they saw that Philip, with his feeling not turned to hatred, was bearing patiently the adversity of fortune, as the ministers of his savage rage, and was offering, in his customary way, lessons of chance and of a changing lot. So, having sent ahead to Philip, as Thuanus relates, letters to King Philip through Bernardino de Mendoza, Alva, with the excuse of long illness and the infirmity of his years, asked for his dismissal, and, though his nature despised leisure and idleness, he prepared for retirement with a savage spirit. There were those who believed that Philip the king, with Alva's fortune against him, would use another minister for his purposes, even for destruction, and that Alva, abandoned by fortune, would feel the king's indignation and hatred as towards one who had become unfortunate and was now despised. For the successes of military commanders mostly redound to the glory of kings, and their failures are imputed to private individuals. There were undoubtedly things which, in Philip's nature, which was ready to be cruel, could supply the matter of offence; and that there is no other incentive than pride alone. LXXIII. Thus the throne of Brabant, which he had kept for the Prince out of reverence for majesty, was seized by Alva in the sight of the Estates and the people, with conspicuous arrogance, condemned by his moderate predecessors, and a trophy was raised upon a deceitful fame. Such honours belong to the fortune of kings and emperors, but for private men and the rivals of their princes they have always turned out to be a disadvantage.

units.la: Cambdenus Britannicarum rerum Historicus notat, aulæ regiæ magnates, & in ijs Cardinalem Granvellanum, ac Gomesium de Sylva, ut in Hispaniam ocyus revocaretur, Philippum apud regem intercessisse, ne crudele, & haud multum infra Principem imperium, desperationem civilium animorum, & simul defectionem universæ gentis irritaret. Augustus scriptor Thuanus addit, Philippum sinistris de Albano rumoribus jam ante instructum, id paci Belgicæ, & simul dignitati viri largitum, Joannemq; Cerdam Medinacœlium natalibus clarum, cæterum suâ virtute & gestarum rerum fama obscurum, in regenda ei Belgica sufficiisse. Eundem Cerdam quoque, Albani æmulatione diu flagrantem, metu defectionis, oblatam à Philippo dignitatem asperna-tum, odiosi muneris molem, & cum tacita velut exprobratione, fœdæ dominationis invidiem in eundem Albanum rejecisse. Itaque Fœderati, quo ituro in Hispaniam Albano invidiem crearent, & ne Albanus falsò refricata contumacis populi rebellione, regium animum majore irâ accenderet, supplicationem hac forma ad PHILIPPUM Regem misere.
units.tr: Camden, the historian of British affairs, notes that the magnates of the royal court, among them Cardinal Granvelle and Gomez de Silva, interceded with the king that Alva be recalled to Spain more quickly, lest a cruel government, not far below the rank of a prince, should provoke the despair of civil minds and at the same time the defection of the whole nation. The august writer Thuanus adds that Philip, already prepared by unfavourable rumours about Alva, granted this to the peace of Brabant and at the same time to the dignity of the man, and that Juan de la Cerda, Duke of Medinaceli, famous for his birth but obscure in his own virtue and the fame of his deeds, was sufficient to govern Brabant for him. He adds that the same Cerda, long burning with rivalry against Alva, refused out of fear of revolt the dignity offered him by Philip, and, with a tacit reproach, threw the burden of the hateful office and the odium of shameful domination back upon the same Alva. Therefore the Confederates, so that Alva, when he went to Spain, would be the object of hatred, and so that Alva, by falsely reviving the rebellion of a stubborn people, would not kindle the king's spirit with greater anger, sent a supplication to King Philip in this form.

units.la: QVotiescunque in clementiam tuam PHILIPPE Rex, (postquam CAROLO patre imperio se abdicante principatum Belgicæ jumpsisti) cogitationes nostræ defiguntur, toties in spem ac fiduciam erigimur, te miseratione querimoniarum nostrarum & ultimæ calamitatis, in quam FERDINANDI ALBANI proregis tui immanis ac superba dominatio nos detrusit, remedia nostris malis daturum. Ut, quoniam majoribus tuis fidem nostram, obsequia & officia pignoravimus, quo Burgundicæ domus fortuna ad destinatum magnitudini suæ fastigium exsurgeret, ita te laturum non speravimus, ut religionis prætextu patriæ jura, ac immunitates ab immanissimo hominum opprimerentur. Et spes quidem nostræ tanto certiores fuere, quod ijdem legibus & privilegijs nostris sacramento te obligaveris, ne quid ijs te Principe decederet, &, ut omne sacrum, quod in his terris possidemus, tuâ protectione & potentiâ incolume esset. Caterum quoniam in comperto est, nostras querimonias, quas non semel Majestati tuæ obtrusimus, & simul fructus nostrarum supplicationum, quibus intercessionem Principum quærebamus, subverti, ita non dubitamus quin nostræ calamitatis & miseriæ documenta fraude & prævaricatione nostrorum inimicorum intercipiantur. Ita fit, ut qui malis levamenta poposceramus, contumaciam experiamur, præcludique ad clementiam tuam omne suffugium, quod à naturâ sanctissimâ rerum parente patere nostræ innocentiæ debebat. Itaque inritis querimonijs nostris illustrem patientiam profiteri destinavimus, si forte fatalis, & definitus clementiæ tuæ dies nostris miseriis illuceseret. Sed magnitudo urgentis exitij, & ruina metus legem patientiæ abrupit, adeo ut moram ferre curatio nostrorum rum vulnerum nequeat. Nec nostra tantum bona, corpora, ac res in discrimen adductæ, cæterum ditionibus quoque tuis, quas hæreditate in te volutas accepisti, proxima & vicina pernicies est. Vt ea amoveatur terris & principatui tuo, iterum obtestamur, Clementissime Rex, nostra obsequia, rogamusque ut populi tui misertus, justi Principis officium expleas, tuterisque leges nostras, quas, divisis olim provincijs sancitas, majores tui tantarum rerum ditionumque hæredes asserendas suscēpere. Ita recordare CAROLUM Cæsarem patrem tuum more majorum, tuâ etiam inauguratione, (quâ hæredem Cæsaris, post successorem te declaravimus) solenni sacramento provincijs se obstrinxisse, quo inter Principem populumque nexus constaret, mutuâque societate concordiam aleremus. Ea certe majoribus tuis, Clementissime Rex, potentiam, subditis opes, & affluentiam rerum peperit. Inde subsidia bellorum in CAROLUM patrem erogata, quorum, ne publice dissimularet, te principatum inchoante, in consessu Ordinum imperatoriâ voce fidem fecit. Itaq; voluit, ut, ratione fidi potentisque populi habitâ, moderato imperio provincijs præesses, disceresque & tuæ potentiæ modum ponere, & illorum obsequia revereri. Per ea fuit, ut auxilia primis principatus tui annis acciperes, metumque hostibus, tibi potentiæ incrementum & gloriam, subditis tuis securitatem dares. Et floruerunt stante Principis populiqué concordiâ res nostræ, postquam intra aulam & secretum regni admissi homines nostræ simul & tuæ fortunæ insidiosi, in deterius ivere. Quorum cupiditatibus cum patriæ leges obstarent, quibus integris nec illorum ambitio quid assequi, nec pati nostra libertas poterat, alio commento te circumvenere, velut nostra obsequia tuo imperio, nostræ leges tuæ potentiæ obessent. Nefarijs consilijs velum religionis obductum est, quo improbam ambitionem vis ac autoritas Pontificum muniret, & serendis discordijs dissidia sacrorum obtexerentur. Itaque ut in penetrale Reipub. pervaderent, suisque arbitrijs regnandi licentiam afformarent, sinistris accusationibus nos apud te Principem aggressi civiles discordias sevère, quibus in ultimam confusionem res irent, convulsisque patrijs legibus dominationem apiscerentur. Ita Inquisitio & novi Episcopatus, nostris legibus, ac immunitatibus infesti, illorum importunitate introducti, ac si paganis, barbarisque gentibus assimilandi essemus, publicamque impietatem divino cultui obtenderemus. Inde tot millium sanguine illorum consilijs litatum, tantos progressus faciente sævitiâ, ut excīsa per solitudinem gente defuturi Principi cives viderentur. Quibus præpediendis ad te Principem læsi confugimus, ut ostenderemus, quantum inter illorum consilia, & nostram salutem interesset. Itaque severitatem edictorum, quæ stabiliendæ Romanæ religioni, per Belgicam, Frisiosque scripseras, sub Margaretâ Gubernatrice mitigasti, fidemque Præfectorum tuorum, ac Principum Aurei Velleris interposuisti, nihil novum, insolensque te moliri, rescissoque Inquisitionis decreto, paci tranquillitatique publicæ, & desiderys populi consulere. Cæterum tuâ cum lenitate, clementissime Rex, illorum furor increvit, postquam infra Majestatis tuæ magnitudinem habuerunt, semel placitis aliud decretum interponere. Itaque persuasus ab ijs FERDINANDUM ALBANUM ferocis ingenij virum, & veteri odio Belgicæ infensum cum imperio in provincias missisti, ut populum suis erga te obsequijs certantem, bello & armis perderet. Quem ipsum, utpote nec tuo, nec Belgico sanguini innexum, etsi prohibere finibus nostræ vires quivissent, tamen tuæ venerationi id dedimus, & ne videremur cuiuspiam iustiam mali testem conscientiam possidere. Ita portas reclusimus, praesidia accepimus, non alio consilio, quam ut de fide nostra constaret, & ne cultum obsequij cum armorum necessitate mutaremus. Ab eo tempore pactis, & conventionibus omne robur demptum, tuque, PHILIPPE Rex, sacramento, quod in coetu Ordinum Belgicae praestiteras, à Ferdinando Albano non semel illusum est. Sic ruptae violatequae pactiones oppressionem secum legum traxere, clausoque per iustitium omni foro, non alio loco habiti fuimus, ac si armis, instar mancupiorum, subjugati, omne beneficium majorum probrosa rebellione perdidissemus. Unde ALBANUS in omnem immodestiam, & professionem sacrilegissimi sceleris effusus sacrum omne atque profanum attaminavit. Rapiendo, vastando, proscribendo imperium exercuit. Villae aut agri direpti, patrimonia divitum expilata, & innocentium sanguis promiscuâ caede, aut per supplicia fusus. Tum virginum ac matronarum pudicitia stupris corrupta, & infantes cum profugis parentibus in exilium acti. Fœtus quoque ipsi praegnantium uteris extracti, nihilque tam sacrum sanctumque, quod Sol & sydera illustrant, quin immanitatem execrandi capitis pertulerit. Matrimonia ipsa, societatis humanae vincula, aut rescissa, aut divortiis foedata. Cadavera in sinum naturae recepta, & quieti reddita sepulchris educta, ne mors omnis miseriae levamentum saevitiam Ducis, & horrorem supplicij finiret. Dein immodicis exactionibus imminuta provinciarum commercia, & centesimae, vigesimaeque decima bonorum adjecta. Insolentiâ praesidiorum exhaustae urbes, nullaque disciplinâ solutus miles extorquendo aeri, & atterendis civium facultatibus diurna flagitia exercuit. Haec FERDINANDI ALBANI, Clementissime Rex, consilia, haec imperia fuere. Qui ut animum supra quam ambitiosum ostenderet, foeditati suorum scelerum indulgens, aereum monumentum ignobili famae insuper erexit, quo fortunâ suâ & tuo imperio male usus, turpitudine exercitae dominationis apud suas, exterasque gentes serae posteritati redderetur. Solium quoque tuum pacis bellicque arbiter insedit, velut, solo nomine dissimulato, à potentiâ parum Principis abesset. Hoc modo tibi contemptum, sibi ipsi ludibrium, nobis imaginem servitutis locavit. Quarum rerum immanitas, quia clementiae tuae convenire non potest, moribus Tyranni imputatur. Qui etsi regio & sumptuoso paratu in Theatro se ostentans veniam, pacemque proclamet, quasi condonare innocentiae nostrae quid possit, ita testamur denuo erga te Regem, nostrae fidei nihil decessisse, caeterum nos consilia & arma nostra solis Albani violentiis opponere. Cui non aliud quoque propositum est, quam ut regnum, aut dominationem regno proximam spirans, cum bello nequeat, umbra fallacis clementiae nos expugnet, agnitique criminis confessione reos faciat majestatis, cujus venerationem nunquam exuimus. Ut faciamus fidem dictis nostris, Clementissime Rex, testamur Deum conscientiis nostris praesidem, puros illius sceleris nos esse, quod expiari alias à nocentibus ultimo exitio, ac cruciatu debebat. Quare divinum numen, & te, PHILIPPE Rex, reveriti, captae pietatis incrementa nostro sanguine, opprobrio Ducis tutabimur. Qui quoniam, silentibus per justitia legibus, omne forum, ac tribunal nostris querimoniis occlusit, arma capere coacti sumus, quibus patriam continuis cladibus, & praesentaneae servityти subduceremus. Parati potius honestâ morte velut victimas immolare corpora nostra, quam spectare feram belluam sacra nostra continuis sacrilegiis foedantem. Effundemus tutelae conjugum, liberorumque novissimum spiritum, quo libertatem à majoribus in nos trans-
units.tr: Whenever our thoughts turn to your clemency, King Philip (since you took up the government of the Netherlands after Charles, your father, abdicated his rule), we are lifted up with hope and trust that you will, out of pity for our complaints and for our utter distress, into which the cruel and arrogant rule of Ferdinand Alva, your governor, has thrust us, provide remedies for our troubles. We did not expect that you, whose forefathers we pledged our loyalty, service and duty to, so that the fortune of the house of Burgundy might rise to the height of greatness it aimed at, would allow the rights and privileges of our country to be oppressed by this most savage man under the pretext of religion. Our hopes were all the more certain because you had bound yourself by oath to our laws and privileges, that nothing should be taken from them while you were prince, and that all the sacred things we possess in these lands should remain intact under your protection and power. But since it is known that our complaints, which we have more than once laid before Your Majesty, and with them the fruit of our petitions, by which we sought the intercession of princes, have been overturned, we do not doubt that the evidence of our calamity and misery is being intercepted by the fraud and prevarication of our enemies. So it happens that we, who asked for remedies for our troubles, meet with refusal, and every refuge to your clemency is shut off, though nature, the most holy parent of all things, ought to have kept it open to our innocence. Therefore, with our complaints ignored, we had resolved to show a noble patience, should the appointed and fixed day of your clemency dawn upon our miseries. But the magnitude of the approaching ruin and the collapse of our fear have broken the rule of patience, so that the cure of our wounds cannot bear delay. Not only our goods, bodies and property have been put in peril, but a near and neighbouring destruction also threatens your dominions, which you received by inheritance from your forefathers. So that this may be averted from the lands and from your principality, we once more beseech you, most merciful King, we offer our obedience, and we ask you, as a just prince, to take pity on your people and perform the duty of a prince, and to protect our laws, which were ratified long ago when the provinces were divided, and which your forefathers, the heirs of such great realms and dominions, took up to uphold. Remember that Charles the Emperor, your father, following the custom of our ancestors, bound himself to the provinces by solemn oath at your inauguration (when we declared you heir of the Emperor and his successor), so that a bond might exist between prince and people, and we might nourish concord by mutual fellowship. Certainly this has brought your forefathers power, your subjects wealth, and abundance of goods. From this came the funds spent on wars against your father, which, so that he should not conceal it publicly, he acknowledged with imperial voice in the assembly of the Estates when you began your rule. Therefore he wished that, with regard to a loyal and powerful people, you should rule the provinces with moderate authority, learn to set limits to your power, and respect their obedience. By these means you received aid in the first years of your reign, and you gave fear to enemies, increase of power and glory to yourself, and security to your subjects. Our affairs flourished while the concord of prince and people stood firm, until men admitted into the court and the secret councils of the realm, treacherous to our affairs and yours alike, turned for the worse. Since the laws of our country stood in the way of their desires, and while they were intact neither their ambition could gain anything nor our liberty endure it, they deceived you by another device, as if our obedience were a hindrance to your rule and our laws to your power. The veil of religion was drawn over wicked plans, so that the power and authority of the Pontiffs might fortify their shameless ambition, and quarrels over sacred things might cover the sowing of discord. Thus, in order to penetrate to the inner core of the commonwealth and to frame for themselves a licence to rule as they pleased, they attacked us before you, the Prince, with sinister accusations, and they stirred up civil dissensions so severely that affairs would fall into utter confusion, and by overturning the laws of our fathers they might seize domination. So the Inquisition and the new bishoprics, hostile to our laws and immunities, were introduced at their importunity, as if we were to be classed with pagan and barbarous peoples, and they put up public impiety as a cover for divine worship. From this, sacrifices of the blood of countless thousands were offered to their plans, and cruelty advanced so far that the nation seemed about to be cut down throughout its wilderness and left without citizens for the prince to rule. To hinder these things we, the injured, have fled to you, the Prince, so that we might show how much our safety differed from their designs. Therefore you softened, under the governess Margaret, the severity of the edicts which you had written to establish the Roman religion throughout Belgium and Friesland, and you pledged the faith of your officers and of the Knights of the Golden Fleece, promising that you were attempting nothing new or unusual, and that, by rescinding the decree of the Inquisition, you were providing for the peace and tranquillity of the public and the wishes of the people. But under your gentleness, most merciful King, their fury grew, since they thought it beneath the greatness of Your Majesty to let their wishes be overruled by any other decree once they had been given. So, persuaded by them, you sent into the provinces Ferdinand Alva, a man of fierce temper and long hostile to Belgium, with command, so that he might destroy with war and arms a people striving in their obedience to you. We, although our forces could not have kept him out of our borders, nevertheless gave him this honour out of reverence for you, and so that we would not seem to possess a conscience that is a just witness of wrong. Thus we opened the gates, received garrisons, with no other purpose than that our loyalty might be established, and so that we would not exchange the cult of obedience for the necessity of arms. From that time all strength was taken from pacts and agreements, and you, King Philip, by the oath you had sworn in the assembly of the Belgian Estates, have been mocked more than once by Ferdinand Alva. Thus pacts were broken and violated, and oppression followed in their train; with all justice shut down and every court closed, we were treated as nothing else than men subdued by arms, like slaves, and we lost every benefit of our ancestors through a shameful rebellion. Hence Alva, poured out into every kind of insolence and into the open profession of most sacrilegious crime, has defiled everything sacred and profane. He exercised his rule by plunder, devastation and proscription. Villages and fields were looted, the estates of the rich were stripped, and the blood of the innocent was spilled in indiscriminate slaughter or by executions. Then the chastity of virgins and matrons was corrupted by rapes, and infants were driven into exile with their fleeing parents. Even unborn children were torn from the wombs of pregnant women, and there was nothing so sacred or holy, on which the sun and stars shine, that did not suffer the savagery of that accursed head. Marriages, the very bonds of human society, have been either dissolved or defiled by divorces. Corpses, received back into the bosom of nature and given rest, were dragged out of their graves, so that death itself might not end all miseries as a relief, nor the cruelty of the Duke and the horror of execution. Then the trade of the provinces was diminished by excessive exactions, and the tenth, the twentieth and the hundredth penny of goods were added. The cities were drained by the insolence of garrisons, and soldiers, released from all discipline, practised for a long time extortion of money and the wearing down of the citizens' resources. These, most merciful King, were the designs and commands of Ferdinand Alva. And so that he might show a spirit beyond what is ambitious, indulging the foulness of his crimes, he erected a bronze monument to his ignoble fame besides, by which, having abused his fortune and your rule, he might hand down to distant posterity the shame of his tyranny practised among his own people and foreign nations. He has also seated himself as arbiter of peace and war on your throne, as if, while the name alone was concealed, he were scarcely distant from the power of the Prince. In this way he has placed you in contempt, himself in mockery, and us in the image of slavery. Since such enormity cannot agree with your clemency, it is imputed to the character of a tyrant. Although he, displaying himself in a royal and sumptuous show on the stage, proclaims pardon and peace, as if he could grant anything to our innocence, we testify again, King, toward you, that nothing has diminished in our loyalty, but that we oppose our plans and arms only to the violence of Alva alone. For him there is no other aim than that, breathing after a kingdom or a domination near to kingship, since he cannot gain it by war, he may overcome us with the shadow of a false clemency and, by a confession of a crime we acknowledge, make us guilty of treason, whose reverence we have never laid aside. To make our words credible, most merciful King, we call God, the guardian of our consciences, to witness that we are clear of that crime, which the guilty ought otherwise to expiate by the utmost destruction and torture. Therefore, reverencing the divine power and you, King Philip, we will defend the growing piety we have taken up with our blood, and the disgrace of the Duke. Since, with the laws of justice silenced, he has shut every court and tribunal against our complaints, we have been compelled to take up arms, by which we may withdraw our country from continual disasters and from present slavery. We are ready, rather, to offer up our bodies as victims in an honourable death, than to watch a savage beast defiling our holy things with continual sacrileges. We will pour out the last breath of our wives and children in defence of their safety, so that we may not exchange for base servitude the liberty that is a just witness of wrong, and a conscience that possesses, and that we opened the gates, received garrisons, with no other design than that our loyalty might be established, and that we might not change the cult of obedience for the necessity of arms. From that time all strength was taken from pacts and agreements, and you, King Philip, were mocked more than once by Ferdinand Alva, by the oath you had sworn in the assembly of the Belgian Estates, handed down to us from our ancestors.

units.la: LXXIII. dei nos permittere ruptarum factionum exempla, excidia urbium, & fecundae strages non sinunt. Itaque horror enormiter saevientis diffidentes, & bonae ad concordiam spei vacuos nos fecit, nisi clementia tuae secretum, REX, aperias, utilique correctione frenes immodestiam regnantis. Interim rogamus, Clementissime REX, ut querimoniis nostris auscultes, praestesque integra illaesaque majorum jura, quorum haeredes sumus, & quae CAROLUS Caesar, & tu, PHILIPPE Rex, sacramento firmavistis. Id si facias, non arma tantum, quae sumpsimus, ponemus, caeterum omnia, quae potestatis nostrae, aut juris fortuna esse voluit, cum obtestatione sanctissimi numinis, tuae potentiae, & Principatui sacrabimus.
units.tr: LXXIII.
