Therefore we, distrustful of the horror of his savage rule and left without any hope of a good settlement, have been driven to this, unless you, O King, in your clemency open the way to a secret remedy and by a useful correction restrain the excesses of the ruler. Meanwhile we beg you, most merciful King, to hear our complaints and to grant the whole and unharmed rights of our ancestors, whose heirs we are, and which Charles Caesar and you, King Philip, confirmed by oath. If you do so, we will not only lay down the arms we have taken up, but will also dedicate to your power and to the Principate, with an oath calling on the most holy divinity, everything that fortune has willed to be within our power or right.

units.la: Intercessiones quoque Regum Principumque imploratae, ut, si forte populi sui precibus emolliri regius animus nequiret, affinium proq pinquorumque procerum desiderijs leniretur. Creditum fuit in Maximilianum Caesarem, & Imperij Principes, foederatos tum respexisse, recente adhuc Gallici furoris memoria, & veteri Anglici regni cum Hispania societate nuperis inducijs restituta. Igitur profuturam auctoritatem, aut reverentiam Imperij, si non paci procurandae, saltem ut exulum suffugijs Germania pateret, leniusque proscripti, aut extorres ijs in terris haberentur. Caeterum Philippi animus, sive cupidine majoris duriorisque per Belgicam imperij distortus, sive fatali odio gentis pervicax, omne etiam Albani immoderatum, velut retinendo principatui utile, interpretabatur. Quare missionem petenti Ludovicum Requesentium Insubriae Proregem, successorem dedit, eidemque Albano, perseverante fluxae, & fallacis aulae gratia, usque in supremum vitae diem continuos honores, velut praemia rite administratae Belgicae, indulsit. Adeo verum est aequam ut plurimum improbis aulae fortunam esse, & asperrimum regnandi modum, ab Albano per provincias institutum, a secretis Philippi consilijs non abhorruisse.
units.tr: Intercessions of kings and princes were also sought, so that if the royal mind could not be softened by the prayers of its people, it might be moved by the desires of related and kindred nobles. It was believed that Maximilian Caesar and the princes of the Empire, who were then allied, would look to this, the memory of the French fury being still fresh and the old alliance of the English kingdom with Spain having been lately restored by a truce. Therefore the authority or reverence of the Empire would be of help, if not in securing peace, at least so that Germany might be open as a refuge for exiles, and that the proscribed or banished might be treated more mildly in those lands. But Philip's mind, either bent by a desire for a greater and harsher rule through the Netherlands, or stubborn with a fatal hatred of the nation, interpreted all of Alba's excesses as useful for maintaining his power. Therefore, when Requesens, who asked for his dismissal, was given as successor Ludovicus, Viceroy of Lombardy, he also granted to the same Alba, who persisted in the favour of a fleeting and deceptive court, continual honours until the last day of his life, as rewards for administering the Netherlands properly. So true it is that a fair fortune for the most part belongs to the wicked at court, and that the harshest manner of ruling, instituted by Alba throughout the provinces, did not shrink from Philip's private counsels.

units.la: Reperio in V. Clar. Cornelij Gemmae Mathematicis commentarijs, mense Octobri deformem partum alibi editum, Lunaeque enormem defectum ad v. Eid. Decemb. observatum, magnitudine sua, obscurationem sub initia Philippici principatus anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LV. factam, neque absimili prodigio, adaequasse. Mihi verisimile est, naturam, in evolvendo coelestium corporum motu, id laborantibus provincijs tum dedisse, tacito indicio, sumptum diris auspicijs imperium non melioribus procedere, redarguendisque dominantium noxis, eadem luminum deliquia mutatis temporum aetatibus assimilari. Thaddaeus Hagecius aulae Caesareae Maximiliani II. medicus in sua Apodixi tradit, Novam Stellam, quae designatura mortem Regis circa hoc temporis observantibus coelestia credebatur, manifesto luminis sui decremento sensim tum attabuisse, mensemque, quem excessui regnantis, ac mutandis rebus curiosa speculatione Mathematici assignaverant, disparitioni lucidissimi corporis inservijsse. Etsi sciam, alios in annum sequentem, conspectum, & vim novi syderis protraxisse, ominatosque, ut post memorabo, sinistra, Cornelij Gemmae praedictionibus pondus ac robur addidisse,
units.tr: I find in the mathematical commentaries of the most distinguished Cornelius Gemma that a misshapen birth, reported elsewhere in October, and an enormous eclipse of the Moon observed on the fifth of the Ides of December, equalled in its magnitude the darkening that occurred at the beginning of Philip's reign in the year 1555, and a prodigy not unlike it. It seems probable to me that nature, in unrolling the motion of the heavenly bodies, gave at that time to the afflicted provinces a silent sign that an empire assumed under evil auspices would not proceed for the better, and that these eclipses of the lights, when the ages of the times change, are comparable for the purpose of exposing the crimes of rulers. Thaddaeus Hagecius, physician to the Caesarean court of Maximilian II, reports in his Apodixis that the New Star, which those observing the heavens at that time believed was foretelling the death of the King, gradually waned with a manifest decrease of its light, and that the month which the mathematicians, through curious observation of the changing times, had assigned to the king's departure and the change of affairs, coincided with the disappearance of that most bright body. Although I know that others extended the sight and power of the new star into the following year, and, as I will relate later, gave omens of misfortune, and added weight and strength to the predictions of Cornelius Gemma,

units.la: Tum
units.tr: Then

units.la: Historiarum Lib. III. 185
units.tr: Histories, Book III, 185

units.la: Tum omni æstuario classibus obsepto, omne Frisiæ littus prædonibus ac peiratis infidum, quos aut exilij vindicta, aut appetitus alieni per periculosa syrtium vada, & infidum mare circumterebat. Geesterlandia vero, & quicquid terrarum minoribus Frisijs objacebat, regia & simul fœderata classe infestabantur. Itaque nec Elahusij tantum, aut Harichij, quorum agros latissimi lacus alluunt, cæterum Wikelij, & mediterranea incolentes prædonum incursionibus patuere.
units.tr: Then, with every estuary blocked by fleets, the whole Frisian coast was unsafe, given over to pirates and sea-robbers, whom either the desire for revenge for exile or greed for others' property, through the dangerous shallows of the sandbanks and the treacherous sea, kept circling about. Geesterland, and whatever lands lay opposite the Lesser Frisians, were harassed by the royal fleet, which was also allied. So not only the people of Elahusij and Harichij, whose fields the broadest lakes wash, but also the Wikelij and those living inland lay open to the raids of the pirates.

units.la: Notat M. Heymannus, Regneri Wibrandij, qui apud Wikelios prædium tenebat, domum ab ijsdem prædonibus incensam, ipsumque Wibrandum glande trajectum lætali vulnere exspirasse. Mox conjugem ejus Dodam unâ cum filiâ Bauciâ ferro percussoris necatas, alteramque ex filiabus Fokelam cum uno filiorum Enchusam in captivitatem abductam. Tertiam quoque è fenestrâ præcipitem datam, filiumque Hansonem è lecto prosilientem, & nullâ veste flammis subductum, ab ambienti fermè frigore exanimatum, fugæ beneficio, & per admota corpori fomenta vitæ servatum. Sic tabescente justo per Frisiam bello latrocinia, ac cædes exercebantur, infœlicisq; provinciæ fortunam, aut egestas regij militis, aut vis piratarum adfligebat, non ante reperto sceleribus remedio, quam Ludovicus Requesentius, à discessu Albani impetium capescens, promerendis provincialium animis, lenem medicinam inveteratis militiæ flagitijs præscriberet.
units.tr: M. Heymann records that Regner Wibrand, who held an estate among the Wikelians, had his house burned by these same pirates, and that Wibrand himself, struck by a sling-bullet, died of a deadly wound. Soon his wife Doda, together with her daughter Bauca, was killed by an assassin's sword, and another of the daughters, Fokela, was led into captivity with one of the sons, Enchusa. A third daughter was also thrown headlong from a window, and the son Hanso, leaping from his bed and rescued from the flames with no clothing on, was almost dead from the cold of the surrounding air, and was saved by flight and by warm compresses applied to his body. Thus, while the just war was wasting away, robberies and slaughters went on throughout Friesland, and the misfortune of the unhappy province was afflicted either by the poverty of the royal soldiers or by the violence of the pirates. No remedy for these crimes was found until Luis de Requesens, taking up power after Alba's departure, set out to win the provincials' minds with a gentle remedy for the long-established abuses of the soldiery.

units.la: Tum Ferdinandus Albanus Philippi gratiæ, & successoris Ludovici Requesentij certus, profectionem adornavit, cumulatasque egestate provinciarum, aut infamiâ exactionum, opes, dubium suæ an regiæ gazæ administer, in Hispaniam præmisit. Mox Ludovico Requesentio, magnifico rerum apparatu, Bruxellas ingresso, comitatus Frederico filio, Italiam versus iter instituit, turbidamq; & cruentatam Belgicam, sibi ipsi acerrimum conscientiæ vulnus, & ex ignobili sævitiæ famâ æternum in animis hominum dedecus reliquit. Relatum in fidem annalium est, supra octodecim hominum millia sexcentos insuper fœderatos suo jussu manu carnificis sublatos, ipsumque Ducem, exerciti furoris infamiâ superbum, recordatione suorum scelerum infœlicem animum pavisse. Tradit Reidanus florentissimus rerum Scriptor, per confinia Germaniæ iter capienti pernoctantique apud Ludovicum Cunisteinum Comitem, imprudentem & superbam vocem excidisse, eundemq; Albanum suo tum demum è Belgica discessu, non tam provincialium odia, quam insidias quoque & pericula effugisse. Scribit idem autor quadragesimali jejunio, haud procul Bruxellis, in coenobio quodam sacra sumpturo destinatos percussores fuisse, monitoque, ne publico se daret, vitæ beneficium concessum. Addit Reidanus Noviomagi agentem, & concamerato dormitorio, quod multo tormentario pulvere suffertum erat, usum magnum in discrimen incurrisse, desiderato è conjuratis, qui ministerium, tyranno decretum, admoto igne, aut stupâ exequeretur. Carolum quoque Brimæum Geldriæ, & post majoris Frisiæ Præfectum, indicendi apud Noviomagenses comitij consilium coepisse, eidemque Albano, quem isthic evocare ordinandis provinciæ rebus constituerat, velut popularis gratiæ ex odio Ducis certum, injectionem manuum destinasse. Litteras quoque, quibus facti rationem daret, Philippum ad regem, praeveniendis Hispanorum criminationibus, paravisse, arduaque res agitantem syderatione tactum, & mox morte praeventum, Profutura libertati consilia non explevisse. Innuente velut fato, Ducem sævitiæ & effundendi sanguinis immodicum, expiandis provincialium noxis, longiori vitæ, & simul poenæ reservari.
units.tr: Then Ferdinand Alba, sure of Philip's favour and of Luis de Requesens as his successor, prepared his departure. He sent ahead to Spain his wealth, heaped up from the poverty of the provinces or from the infamy of the exactions, and it was doubtful whether it was his own treasure or the royal treasury he was administering. Soon Luis de Requesens entered Brussels with a splendid display of affairs, and Alba, accompanied by his son Frederick, set out on a journey towards Italy. He left Belgium troubled and bloodied, a most bitter wound to his own conscience, and from his ignoble reputation for cruelty an everlasting disgrace in the minds of men. It is recorded in the trustworthy annals that, at his command, more than eighteen thousand men, and six hundred more confederates besides, were removed by the executioner's hand, and that the Duke himself, proud of the infamy of his raging army, fed his unhappy mind on the memory of his crimes. The most distinguished writer of affairs, Reidanus, relates that when Alba was passing through the borders of Germany and spent the night with Count Ludwig of Cunstein, he let slip an imprudent and proud remark. The same Reidanus says that Alba, on leaving Belgium at last, escaped not only the hatred of the provincials but also ambushes and dangers. The same author writes that during the Lenten fast, not far from Brussels, in a certain monastery where he was to receive the sacrament, assassins had been appointed for him, and that he was granted his life on condition that he not show himself in public. Reidanus adds that when Alba was staying at Nijmegen, in a vaulted dormitory filled with much gunpowder, he was in great danger, since one of the conspirators who was to carry out the tyrant's decree, by applying fire or tinder, was missing. Charles Brimaeus also, governor of Guelders and afterwards of Frisia Major, began a plan to summon an assembly at Nijmegen, and intended to lay hands on Alba himself, whom he had decided to summon there to settle the affairs of the province, being sure of popular favour from hatred of the Duke. He had also prepared a letter to King Philip to give an account of the deed, to forestall the Spanish accusations. But while pursuing this difficult enterprise he was struck by a stroke, and, soon prevented by death, did not carry out plans that would have benefited liberty. As if fate were nodding assent, the Duke, given to cruelty and to the immoderate shedding of blood, was reserved for a longer life, and at the same time for punishment, so that the provincials' wrongs might be expiated.

units.la: Unde in Requesentium certæ spes, velut dura antecessoris imperia attemperaturum, nisi Hispanicæ suspectæque indolis metus fiduciam popularium animorum minuisset. Credebatur quippe naturæ diversitas Belgicis Hispanicisque ingenijs subesse, immiteque ardoribus Hispaniæ cœlum, gentis suæ consilia peculiari syderum influxu efferare. Itaque innuebant Philippi & provinciarum rebus melius prospectum fore, si Belgici sanguinis Principem moderamini rerum Philippus admovisset, datusq; Ferdinando Albano alius successor, flectendis, quæ iniquitas exterorum movisset, ingenijs, domesticæ pacis desideria applicâsset. Hoc modo ortis diu turbis remedium adhibere, percuraque grave vulnus potuisse, velut quodam intermedio coituru m. Sic ruptam ossium in humano corpore compagem restitui, ut, quoniam extrema jungi per naturam nequirent, solertia artis coalescerent. Satis exempli apud Regem esse, invisum gentis suæ nomen civili concordiæ obstare, requirique Belgicæ Præsidem æqua imperia libertati assimilantem. Sic in Margaretâ Gubernatrice dubios natales, & versatile peregrinæ fœminæ ingenium, in Albano externum sanguinem & foeditatem imperij patribus displicuisse. Esse Requesentium Hispanicæ originis, & apud Insubres diu Italiæ artibus excultum, ijsdem moribus acturum. Quippe ab Albano præcepta administrandæ Belgicæ clam & in secreto accepisse, haud dubiè edoctum, Philippum regem sua in Belgas odia externis dominationibus nutrire.
units.tr: Hence there were firm hopes in Requesens, as if he would temper the harsh commands of his predecessor, had not the fear of his Spanish and suspected character diminished the people's confidence. For it was believed that a difference of nature lay in Belgian and Spanish dispositions, and that the harsh heat of the Spanish sky made its nation's plans fierce by a peculiar influence of the stars. Accordingly, it was hinted that there would be better provision for the affairs of Philip and of the provinces if Philip had placed a prince of Belgian blood in charge of government, and had given Ferdinand Alba another successor, one who would bend minds, moved by the injustice of foreigners, towards a desire for domestic peace. In this way, the disturbances that had long arisen could be remedied and the grave wound healed, as if the two parts were joined by some intermediate means. Thus the bone broken in a human body is restored, so that, since the extremities cannot be joined by nature, they grow together by the skill of art. It was enough of an example for the King that the hated name of his nation stood in the way of civil concord, and that a governor of Belgium was needed who would match fair rule with liberty. So in Margaret, the governess, her doubtful birth and the changeable temper of a foreign woman had displeased the senators, and in Alba, foreign blood and the foulness of his rule. Requesens was of Spanish origin, and, having long been trained in Italian ways among the Insubres, would act by the same customs. Indeed, having secretly received from Alba, in private, the precepts for governing Belgium, he had no doubt been taught that King Philip nourished his hatred of the Belgians through foreign domination.

units.la: Igitur Philippus, quo Requesentium Belgicæ Friscaeque genti commendaret, litteras Madriti perscriptas ex Hispaniâ in Frisiam dedit, populumque ad novas spes, & imperia suspensum hoc modo edocuit.
units.tr: Therefore Philip, in order to commend Requesens to the Belgian and Frisian peoples, drew up a letter at Madrid and sent it from Spain to Friesland, and thus informed the people, who were held in suspense between new hopes and new commands.

units.la: {R}Egredi ad vos, Ordines, jam diu animus ac consilium mihi fuit. Caeterum quoniam regnorum meorum moles, ac difficile multa regendi onus mihi hoc tempore incumbunt, Hispaniâ meâ attinere me cogor. Vbi vero concurrentium negotiorum cura remiserit, daturus sum operam, ut, quod maxime expeto, ad vos redeam. Et quoniam missione FER- DINANDO ALBANO certis de causis factâ Medinacœlium ei successorem destinaveram, ita mutato consilio hocipso LUDOVICUM REQUESENTIUM eidem Albano substituo, virum fide & officijs de me optime meritum. Neque dubito quin eodem affectu res quoque, & incolumitatem vestram meo nomine curaturus sit. Rogo itaque & mando, ut eundem REQUESENTIUM Belgicæ Proregem recipiatis, præstetisque ei obsequia nostra per provincias imperia gesturo. Hoc etiam addo, ut res consiliaque vestra ei commodetis, reputetisque omne, quod ei præstaturi eritis, officium nobis gratum fore. Hæc PHILIPPUS.
units.tr: I have long had the intention and desire to come out to you, Estates. But since the weight of my kingdoms and the difficult burden of ruling so many things now rest upon me, I am compelled to remain in my Spain. When, however, the care of pressing business has eased, I will take pains to return to you, which is what I most earnestly desire. And since, for certain reasons, I had designated Medina Celi as successor when Ferdinand Alba was dismissed, I have now changed my plan and substitute Luis de Requesens in Alba's place, a man who has deserved very well of me through his fidelity and services. Nor do I doubt that with the same goodwill he will also look after affairs and your safety in my name. I therefore ask and command you to receive the same Luis de Requesens as Governor of Belgium, and to render him the obedience you owe us, since he will govern the provinces. I add also that you should assist him with your affairs and counsels, and consider that whatever service you render him will be pleasing to us. Philip.

units.la: Mox regijs à Requesceptio additæ litteræ: Istæ habebant.
units.tr: Soon after, letters from Requesens were added to the royal ones. These were their contents:

units.la: Placuisse PHILIPPO regi, revocato in Hispaniam FERDI-NANNANDO ALBANO, moderamen Belgicarum provinciarum Frisiaq; ditionum in se devolvere. Et quoniam Regis sui imperio parere aequum esset, ita orare sanctum aeternumque numen mentem sibi det turbidis temporibus librandae tantae moli capacem. Non alium scilicet votorum suorum finem esse, quam ut, fato rerum Philippi arbiter ac moderator datus, reducendae civili & inter Principem concordiae destinetur. Ut ea habeatur consiliorum communione opus esse, & ut sua a patrum secretis indivisa sint.
units.tr: It has pleased King Philip, with Ferdinand Alba recalled to Spain, to take upon himself the government of the Belgian provinces and the Frisian lordships. And since it is right to obey the command of one's King, may the holy and eternal God give me a mind capable of bearing so great a burden in troubled times. My only aim in my prayers is that, appointed by the course of events as the arbiter and governor of affairs under Philip, I may be destined to restore civil concord and peace between the Prince and his subjects. There is need of a common counsel to this end, and my own actions should not be separated from the secrets of the senators.

units.la: Haec litteris signata.
units.tr: These things were stamped into the letter.

units.la: Caetera quae ducendis validius animis erant in consessu Ordinum provinciarum speciosis verbis a perito fandi differebantur.
units.tr: The rest, which was meant to stir their spirits more strongly, was set out in fine words by a skilled speaker in the assembly of the Estates of the provinces.

units.la: Se paci ab ingenio proclivem fastidio civilium, infaliciumque bellorum desideria quietis ac concordiae diu intra animum aluisse. Neque aliud PHILIPPI REGIS votum esse, quam ut provinciae nuper CAROLO Caesare felices, tot annorum discordiis fessae, vetere fortuna reflorent. Satis scilicet sanguinis fusum, & exercitos abunde furores, quos aequum sit remissione quadam, adinstar febrium, leniri. Non semper quoque caelum infausto sydere ardescere, aut circumagi maria procellosis aestibus, caeterum definitas esse rerum omnium exacerbationes, quas sisti oporteat ad naturae ordinem statas per vices servandum.
units.tr: That he, inclined to peace by nature and weary of the strife of civil wars and of unhappy wars, had long nourished in his heart a longing for quiet and concord. The wish of King Philip is no other than that the provinces, once happy under Emperor Charles and now worn out by the discords of so many years, should flourish again in their former fortune. Surely enough blood has been shed and enough armies' rage has been let loose, which it is fitting to soothe by some remission, like fevers. The sky does not always blaze with an unlucky star, nor do the seas always churn with stormy tides; rather, the exacerbations of all things are finite, and ought to be halted, set by the order of nature to be kept in their turns.

units.la: Quae omnia tacite & secretis indicijs, demulcendis Ordinum ingenijs, non cauta simulatione innuebantur. Quare evenit, ut vagae, & velut fortuna temporum lubricae provincialium mentes, novas in Requesentio spes collocarent, odioque superbi ac damnati antecessoris novi dominantis imperium, tanquam benignius, amplecterentur.
units.tr: All these things were hinted at secretly and by private signs, to soothe the spirits of the Estates, not by cautious pretence. Hence it came about that the wandering minds of the provincials, slippery as the fortune of the times, placed new hopes in Requesens, and, with hatred of their proud and condemned predecessor, embraced the rule of the new governor as the kinder.

units.la: His accedebat, quod Joachimus Hopperus vir perantiquae apud Frisios gentis (quem ob peritiam rerum per lentos, & continuos honores arcanis consilijs & sigillo regni Philippus praefecerat) datis ad Cornelium Wellemannum Ordinum Brabantiae Graphiarium litteris, singulare Philippi regis in provincias studium, & Ludovicum Requesentium, velut gerendis rebus parem, non mediocribus laudationibus extulisset.
units.tr: Added to this was that Joachim Hopper, a man of a very ancient family among the Frisians, whom Philip had placed over his secret counsels and the royal seal because of his skill in affairs gained through slow and continuous offices, had written to Cornelius Wellemann, clerk of the Estates of Brabant, praising Philip's singular zeal for the provinces and Ludovicus Requesens, as an equal in managing affairs, with no small praise.

units.la: Esse scilicet REQUESENTIUM conscientia probata, circumspectaque mente res cunctas metientem, trahentemque annos & praeclaras dignitates procul malis artibus per virtutem actas. Sic Insubriam pro Philippo, sic Longobardos Subalpinas gentes rexisse, ut dignum judicaverit Philippus, cui provincia Belgicae Frisiorumque, regiae hereditatis, & opulentiae non minima portio, & difficile grassantibus armis imperium, committeretur. Itaque sperari posse, ut per eum laesae aut oppressae leges revivisc ant, restitutisque in integrum judicijs, & Magistratuum autoritate, civile bellum concordi pace mutetur.
units.tr: Namely, Requesens's conscience is proven, and his mind weighs all things with circumspection. He has spent his years and distinguished dignities, far from wicked arts, through virtue. He ruled Insubria for Philip, and the Lombard peoples of the Alps, so that Philip judged him worthy to be entrusted with the province of Belgium and Friesland, a not least part of the royal inheritance and wealth, and with an authority difficult to exercise amid raging arms. It could therefore be hoped that through him laws that had been injured or oppressed would revive, and that, with judgments restored to their integrity and the authority of the magistrates, civil war would be exchanged for concord and peace.

units.la: Ita Requesentius Praefecturam Belgicae exorsus dubias provincias, exercitum seditionibus proxumum accepit. Quippe deficientibus tot mensium stipendijs sacramenta militum nutabant, praeterque inopiam aeris, exercita sub Albano licentia, & corrupti mores fidem dissolverant. Ita verum est concessam scelerum impunitatem pro exemplo esse, cIↄ. Iↄ. esse, & revocare ad veterem disciplinam aegrius posse conniventia Du- LXXIII. cum semel flagitia professos. Tum quod jam ante per Heronem Ockingha & Heronem Burmania legatos Bruxellis coram Albano actum erat sub Requesentio repetitum, missusque provinciae nomine ex Ordinum Deputatis Valerius Cammingha, qui Requesentio Frisiorum praefecturam una cum Belgicae, auspicanti Caroli Philippique cum Frisijs conventiones, & modum egressam dominationem aperiret.
units.tr: Thus Requesens, beginning his government of Belgium, received provinces of doubtful loyalty and an army nearest to mutiny. Indeed, with pay failing for so many months, the soldiers' oaths were wavering, and, besides the lack of money, the licence practised under Alba and corrupted morals had dissolved their loyalty. It is true that impunity granted for crimes becomes a precedent, and that a tolerance once extended to those who openly professed wickedness is harder to recall to the old discipline. There was also the matter that had already been raised before Alba at Brussels through the envoys Heron Ockinga and Heron Burmania, and was now repeated under Requesens. Valerius Cammingha was sent in the name of the province from the deputies of the Estates, to lay before Requesens, at the start of his command over Belgium and Friesland, the agreements made by Charles and Philip with the Frisians, and the excessive domination that had overstepped its bounds.

units.la: Carolus, inquit, Caesar Saxoniae Ducum exemplo reflurum se nos Frisios, omneq; jus nostrum ratum firmumque fore fidem dedit. Clementiam Saxonicâ majorem & juris nostri auctum huic genti promisit, quae verborum solennia à Principe prolata oraculo numinis adaequavimus.
units.tr: Charles, he says, Caesar, following the example of the Dukes of Saxony, gave us Frisians his pledge that he would restore us, and that all our right would be ratified and secured. He promised this people a clemency greater than that of Saxony and an increase of our right. We have held the solemn words spoken by the prince to be equal to an oracle of the divine will.

units.la: Conventione non unâ data fides, velut obsignatione sacrae vocis, firmata est. Nos vero Frisij, quae Carolo concessimus rata servavimus, fecimusq; ut ordinarios ex Provinciâ nostrâ reditus continua rogarum subsidia acciperet. Ante triennium viginti & octo aureorum millia Philippo depacti sumus, quo pacem armorum loco haberemus, & ut sacrum quoq; aerarium fortuitis casibus inserviret. Quo tempore quoq; cavimus ut si damna agri nostri ac possessiones paterentur honorarium tributum levaretur, & ne parte provinciae affectâ paucorum calamitatem publica tributa resarcirent. Caeterum milites nostros per agros sparsus, tum terrarum nostrarum inundationes & marinis aquis corrupta fruges desperationem nobis incussere. Praeter hoc cottidianae exactiones & aris extorsio invitis molesta quae adornandis instruendisq;, regijs triremibus navibusq; bellicis postulatur. Adhaec miles in diversa praesidia deducendus, pabula equis, & commeatus militi praestandus est. Mitto tertium quemq; è gente nostrâ armandum, & stipendio juvandum esse. Adeo, ut regi quoq; ipsi in capiendis ordinarijs subsidijs detrimentum hac calamitas allatura sit. Et quoniam Albanus praedecessor tuus aliquid favoris ac gratiae, propter promptu in Philippum officia, se daturum huic genti affirmavit, in hac ultimâ calamitate & egestate nostrâ constituti, ut nos malis istis leves, donec melior fortuna terris nostris illuxerit.
units.tr: The pledge given not once but in agreement after agreement was confirmed as if by the sealing of a sacred word. We Frisians indeed kept as valid what we granted to Charles, and we ensured that he received from our province continual aid in levies, over and above the ordinary revenues. Three years ago we were bargained to Philip for twenty-eight thousand gold pieces, so that we might have peace in place of arms, and so that the sacred treasury might serve in chance misfortunes. At that same time we also took care that, if our fields and possessions suffered damage, the honorary tax would be lightened, and that public taxes would make good the calamity of a few when a part of the province was affected. Besides this, our soldiers, scattered through the fields, and the inundations of our lands, and crops spoiled by sea water, struck despair into us. Beyond this come daily exactions and the extortion of money, burdensome to the unwilling, demanded for equipping and fitting out the royal triremes and warships. Soldiers must also be led to different garrisons, and fodder for horses and provisions given to the soldier. I say nothing of every third man of our people having to be armed and paid. So much so, that this calamity will bring loss even to the king himself in raising his ordinary subsidies. And since your predecessor Alba affirmed that he would grant some favour and grace to this people on account of its prompt services to Philip, we, placed in this final calamity and destitution, beg you to lighten these evils for us, until better fortune shines upon our lands.

units.la: Hoc etiam addimus Frisij, ut ex conditio pacem nobis ac securitatem praestes, & ut jure nostro sancte servato, nobis iniquâ exactione gravandis abstineas. Quae ad Requesentium per Legatum perlata, statum illi provinciae & civilium animorum aperuere.
units.tr: We Frisians add this also: that on this condition you grant us peace and security, and that, with our right sacredly kept, you refrain from burdening us with unjust exactions. These things were carried to Requesens through our envoy, and they revealed to him the state of the province and of the civil minds.

units.la: Invenio in archivis, Requesentium Frisiorum calamitati ex inundatio- ne terrarum natae serio condoluisse, litterisq; xiii. Dec. Bruxellis datis, omnem benevolentiam, omnem opem, omne auxilium annuntiasse. Facturum se quoque, ut, quoniam militaribus cohortibus agri, oppida, arces ac castella tenerentur, miles disciplinae vacuus non sit, & ut memoratis ab afflictâ gente terrâ marique malis, quantum quidem regiae vires ferrent, remedia reperiantur. Quae etsi speciose dicerentur, etiam Albano regnante, tamen illa temporum aetas vidit, quid primum in irâ & crudelitate dominantis, & postremum in impatientiâ servitij foret. Mox, ne quid morae interveniret, ampliores ad Requesentium litterae datae, additisque Viglium ad Praesidem, tantâ gratiâ apud regem florentis viri intercessionem oravere, ac ut difficillimis mis patriæ suæ temporibus, novum Gubernatorem Frisico populo conciliaret.
units.tr: I find in the archives that Requesens sincerely grieved over the calamity of the Frisians arising from the inundation of their lands, and that in letters dated at Brussels on 13 December he announced all goodwill, all help and all aid. He would also see to it that, since the fields, towns, citadels and castles were held by military cohorts, the soldier should not be without discipline, and that remedies for the evils suffered by the afflicted people by land and sea should be found, as far as the royal resources could bear. Though these things were said handsomely, even under Alba's rule that age saw what came first in the anger and cruelty of the ruler, and what came last in the impatience of servitude. Soon, lest any delay intervene, fuller letters were sent to Requesens, and with Viglius added to the president, they begged his intercession with the king, a man flourishing in such great favour, so that in the most difficult times of their country he might win the new governor to the Frisian people.

units.la: Quare Requesentius ne, primo imperij sui per Belgicam Frisiosque initio, animos provincialium & simul curam militaris disciplinæ negligeret, edictum frænandæ militum licentiæ in Frisiam misit, quam Gasparus Roblesius, qui, pro Ægydio Barlamontio Hyergio in id temporis imperium gesserat, oppressis Scouwenburgicis partibus, fatali istorum temporum severitate moderabatur.
units.tr: Therefore Requesens, so that at the very beginning of his rule over Belgium and the Frisians he would not neglect the spirits of the provincials and at the same time the care of military discipline, sent to Friesland an edict for restraining the licence of the soldiers. Gaspar Robles, who had held command at that time in place of Egidius Barlaymont of Hierges, enforced it with the fatal severity of those times, after the Schouwenburg party had been crushed.

units.la: Itaq; Præfectura trium ditionum, quas Amasus Flevusque latissimis alveis claudunt, rescripto Philippi, & mox Senatusconsulto ei delata, ipseque probatæ in regem fidei illustre præmium, & simul splendorem ignobili familiæ adeptus est. Matre quippe Philippi regis nutrice editum communis fama asseruit, creditusq; fuit obscuros, & spretos magnatibus natales, non per aliena decora, sed propriam virtutem promovisse. Thuanus addit eum à puero in aulâ Gulielmi Nassovij Aurantij Principis educatum, eximiâq; morum venustate, & gratiâ præditum favore, ac commendatione Aurantij ductâ nobili & dotatâ virgine, rebusque præclare sub Joanne Lignæo Arembergio, & Carolo Brimæo gestis, ad legionis Belgicæ Tribunatum, & post Præfecturam provinciæ pervenisse. Eundem quoque Roblesium extructis per Frisiam munitionibus, & validâ arce jussu Albani Groningæ, ut memoravi, aliquod ante annos extructâ, velut fortunæ insolentem se gessisse, Comitisque titulum, intercessione amicorum, obscurae domui orâsse. Cæterum à Philippo Rege superbiam ejus perosō, ne sui oblivisceretur, monitum, altam & destinatam magnis rebus indolem vix repressisse, provinciâque, qua mari objacet, aggeribus circumductâ, invisam dominationem illo laudabili consilio attemperasse. Sic quod Iselsteinij, Egmondani, Lignæi, Brimæi speciosis majoribus orti pro Carolo Philippoq; regibus per Frisiam tenuerant, in Roblesium devolutum est, cujus aspero imperio, & solutis militum moribus provincialium hoc tempore res & fortunæ atterebantur.
units.tr: Thus the prefecture of the three districts which the Ems and the Flevo enclose with very broad channels was conferred on him by a rescript of Philip, and soon after by a decree of the Senate. He himself obtained both an illustrious reward for proven loyalty to the king and at the same time lustre for an ignoble family. For it was put about by common report that he had been suckled by the king's nurse, and it was believed that, having obscure birth and being despised by the magnates, he advanced himself not through others' honours but through his own virtue. Thuanus adds that from boyhood he was brought up at the court of William of Nassau, Prince of Orange, and, endowed with exceptional charm of manners and favour, through the recommendation of Orange he married a noble and well-dowered maiden, and, with affairs successfully conducted under John of Ligne, Count of Aremberg, and Charles de Brimeu, he rose to the tribunate of the Belgian legion and afterwards to the prefecture of the province. The same Robles, after fortifications had been built throughout Friesland and a strong citadel at Groningen by Alba's order some years before, as I have mentioned, behaved as one elated by fortune, and, through the intercession of friends, begged the title of Count for his obscure house. But Philip the king, hating his pride, warned him lest he forget himself. He scarcely restrained a high spirit destined for great things, and by that praiseworthy design he tempered the hated domination over the province that lies open to the sea, by surrounding it with embankments. Thus what the Isselsteins, Egmonts, Lignes and Brimeus, sprung from illustrious ancestors, had held through Friesland on behalf of the kings Charles and Philip, devolved upon Robles. Under his harsh rule and the loose morals of the soldiers, the affairs and fortunes of the provincials were worn down at this time.

units.la: Quippe regio militi per agros & municipia agenti omnis licentia dabatur, & quidem tacito illorum assensu qui regundis legionibus & administrando Philippi judicio delecti, pacem non nisi stabilito regis & suo imperio, attritisque provincialium opibus augurabantur. Itaq; Roblesius excussâ omni miseratione, & cum Senatu Philippi in omnem immodestiam effusus, præter ordinarium tributum quod cogendo honorario dictum erat, quatuor stuferos in florenum quemque aureum exigi jussit, eque singulis præturis, mutato veteri more, Legatum evocavit. Ibi fremens & indignabundus, ut stipendia militi quanto ocyus parerent legatos Ordinum allocutus est, moraeq; omnis impatiens executionem tributi militaris per armatos denuntiavit. Jam enim sclopetariorum equitum turmam colligi fecerat, instructosq; velut ad prælium, præcinentibus tubis per pagos, atque municipia ostentabat. Igitur tardioribus ex rei, quam tractabant, magnitudine in decernendo legatis equites triginta Wirdumum ablegavit, minatusque Valerio Camminghæ domus subversionem rusticæ plebi enorme tributum extorsit. Dein pedestri milite Arumum in Westergoam misso, quo loci
units.tr: For to the royal soldier moving through the fields and towns every licence was given, and indeed with the tacit assent of those chosen to govern the legions and administer Philip's judgement. They expected peace only from the fixed rule of the king and their own command, and with the resources of the provincials worn down. So Robles, shaking off all compassion and given over with the Senate of Philip to every excess, besides the ordinary tax which had been called honorary by compulsion, ordered four stuivers to be exacted on each gold florin. Changing the old custom, he summoned the envoy from each prefecture. There, fuming and indignant, that the pay might reach the soldier as quickly as possible, he addressed the envoys of the Estates, and, impatient of any delay, announced the execution of the military tax by armed men. For he had already caused a troop of carbineer horsemen to be gathered, and displayed them drawn up as if for battle, with trumpets sounding through the villages and towns. Therefore, since the envoys were slow in deciding, owing to the magnitude of the matter they were treating, he sent thirty horsemen to Wirdum. Threatening the overthrow of Valerius Cammingha's house, he extorted an enormous tax from the rustic people. Then, sending foot soldiers to Arum in Westergo, where Livius Beyemus, the province's accountant, held an estate, he displayed every insolence. With the most foul examples of conduct and no discipline of soldiery, he oppressed the farming people.

units.la: cI͞ↄ. Iↄ. LXXIV. Livius Beïemus provinciæ à rationibus, prædium tenebat, omnem insolentiam exercuit, sædissimisq; factorum exemplis, nullâ militiæ disciplinâ, agrarium populum oppressit. Quæ ad Philippum, aut Proregem perscripta, ut tum ferebant tempora, nullius efficaciæ fuere. Reperio in notis triginta istos equites sclopetarios Wirdumi in otio ac luxu atterendæ rusticæ plebi agentes, exceptis equorum, quæ trecentos faciebant aureos, mille octoginta novem aureos intra decendium insumpsisse, præterq; stipendia, quæ nongentis triginta quatuor aureis censebantur, omnium rerum paratissimam egestatem isti municipio induxisse. Itaq; Ordines per Epistolam apud Regem de enormi Roblesij imperio conquesti, & quod linguæ Frisicæ Belgicæq; imperitus, rejectis supplicationibus, omnem querelam, velut non intelligendo, dissimularet. Hoc scilicet contra privilegia, contra fidem conventionis Caroli Cæsaris esse, quâ cautum fuit, ut provinciæ Præfectus Belgici sanguinis, & magnarum opum foret, & ne peregrini sermonis interventu præfectorum indigenarumque colloquia & actiones impedirentur. Hoc etiam criminatos Ordines reperio, quod classiarius miles magna ex ærario stipendia præter commeatum traheret, prædaq; nonnunquam dives spolia maris in luxuriem privatosq; usus converteret. Tum de locarijs centurionum, servitia vocant, quæ per absentiam maritorum in castris domi relictæ uxores exigebant additum, militesque legionis Valonicæ per oppida distributos, civium opes atque facultates exhaustisse. Quæ omnia singulaq; cum perdundis provinciæ rebus forent, hoc etiam accedere, quod Episcopus Cunerus inordinatis exactionibus provinciales gravaret, neglectisq; Sacris, aut ex receptis fœderatis, aut adulterijs vitæque incontinentiâ notatos, supellectile domesticâ & gravi ære multaret. Hoc, certe reperio, ex agrarijs, quod Martinalium festo non interfuissent, per Fiscum, qui domatim discurrebat, Episcopali multâ affectos, ipsumq; Episcopum, etsi sacra, profanaq; distrahentem, odio Ordinum, regij Senatus gratiâ floruisse. Hæc in Prædicatorum Cænobio IX. Kalend. April. acta, ac ad regem expedita. Quo die conventum inter Ordines & Roblesium invenio, ut bini stuferi in florenos aureos retinendo, in Frisiâ præsidiario militi præstarentur, sed hac cautione, ut, si eos ex pensione proximâ regi danda deduci non pateretur Requesentius, ex ipso regis ære militibus munerando per Frisios repeterentur. Quorum omnium ignarus, etsi Hispaniâ attineretur, rex non foret, ita in Frisiam VIII. Eid. Madrito litteras dedit.
units.tr: Which complaints, written to Philip or to the viceroy, were, as the times then went, of no effect. I find in my notes that those thirty carbineer horsemen at Wirdum, living in idleness and luxury at the expense of the rustic people, consumed, apart from the horses' keep, which came to three hundred gold pieces, one thousand and eighty-nine gold pieces within ten days. Besides their pay, which was reckoned at nine hundred and thirty-four gold pieces, they brought that town into the most complete destitution of everything. Therefore the Estates complained by letter to the king about Robles's enormous rule, and that, being ignorant of the Frisian and Dutch tongues, he rejected their supplications and, as if not understanding, ignored every complaint. This, of course, was against their privileges and against the faith of the convention of Charles Caesar, by which it was provided that the prefect of the province should be of Belgian blood and of great wealth, and that conversations and dealings between prefects and natives should not be hindered by the intervention of a foreign tongue. I also find the Estates accusing him of this: that the naval soldiery drew large pay from the treasury beyond provisions, and that, rich in booty, he often turned the spoils of the sea to luxury and private use. Then there were the lodgings of the centurions, which they called services, which the wives left at home demanded during their husbands' absence in camp, and the soldiers of the Walloon legion, distributed through the towns, had drained the wealth and resources of the citizens. All these things, each of them ruinous to the province's affairs, were joined by this: that Bishop Cunerus burdened the provincials with disorderly exactions. Having neglected sacred duties, he fined those marked either for confederate sects, or for adultery and incontinence of life, with household furniture and heavy sums of money. This, certainly, I find: that rustics who had not been present at the feast of Martinmas were visited with an episcopal fine by the fiscal officer who ran from house to house, and that the bishop himself, though mixing sacred and profane things, flourished through the hatred of the Estates and the favour of the royal Senate. These things were done in the Dominicans' convent on 24 March and reported to the king. On that day I find an agreement between the Estates and Robles that two stuivers per florin should be retained and paid to the garrison soldiers in Friesland, but with this caution: if Requesens did not allow them to be deducted from the next payment to be made to the king, they were to be recovered from the king's own money through the Frisians, to be paid to the soldiers. The king, though kept in Spain, was not unaware of all these things, and so he wrote a letter to Friesland from Madrid on the eighth day before the Ides.

units.la: Omnium rerum, quæ in provincijs meis gestæ sunt, cum notitia ad me pervenerit adhibito purpuratorum & Senatus mei consilio, de modo cogitavi quo Catholicæ Romanæ religioni, & juxta provinciarum mearum commodis prospicerem. Et quia subditorum meorum animos turbatos deprehendo, quo illis tranquillitatem redonem, pacis ac Veniæ communis edictum concepi. Quare vos moneo hortorque, ut isti negotio fideliter incumbatis, ne consilia mea ac decreta, quæ ex Protege meo plenius intelligetis, suo & quidem felici exitu destituantur.
units.tr: I have considered, once news of everything done in my provinces reached me, and after taking counsel with my nobles and my Senate, how I might provide for the Catholic Roman religion and for the welfare of my provinces. Because I find that the minds of my subjects are troubled, I have drawn up an edict of peace and general pardon to restore their tranquillity. I therefore advise and urge you to apply yourselves faithfully to this business, so that my plans and decrees, which you will understand more fully from my Protector, do not fail of their happy outcome.

units.la: Invenio in actis Salencincum cohortis, quæ Franequeræ agebat, vexillixilliferum publicæ tum licentiæ fædum exemplum edidisse, Æmyliumq; Adamam legum doctorem, & consulatum tum gerentem, injuriosà primum voce, post vi infestasse. Isti quoque delicto, reprimendæ militum proterviæ, testimonia in senatu dicta, delectis qui ad Roblesium perferrent, violatæque militari disciplinæ edicta, ac damnationem postularent. Ipsum quoque Roblesium Harlingæ agentem, quo marino æstui disiecta adhuc littorum eruenti provideret, v. Id. April. Ruardum Roorda Harlingam evocasse, eiq; jussisse, ut Delegatorum Ordinum conventum ad xviii. Kal. Mai diem indiceret, & ut interea Martini Nitzenij legatio, quæ Bruxellas decreta erat, dum stipendijs suorum militum prospectum foret, protraheretur. Hoc namque in votis habebat Roblesius, ut regiæ suæque securitati consuleret, ærisque militaris subsidio adjutus mixtam superbiâ avaritiaque, dominationem intenderet. Itaq; in conventu Ordinum, ubi jus magis, quam arma expendi decentius erat, edixit.
units.tr: I find in the records that a company of Salencincum, which was serving at Franeker, gave a shameful example of public licence. Its standard-bearer, and Emilius Adama, a doctor of laws who was then also holding the consulship, were first assailed with insulting words and afterwards with violence. For this offence, and to check the insolence of the soldiers, testimonies were given in the Senate, chosen men were sent to carry them to Robles, and they demanded edicts condemning the violation of military discipline. Robles himself, who was at Harlingen so that he might provide against the coasts, still being dug out from the damage of the sea's tide, summoned Ruard Roorda to Harlingen on 9 April. He ordered him to fix the day of the assembly of the deputies of the Estates for 18 April, and meanwhile to hold back the embassy of Martin Nitzen, which had been decided upon for Brussels, until provision was made for the pay of his soldiers. For Robles had this aim: to look after his own security and the king's, and, aided by the money for the army, to extend a domination mixed with pride and greed. Therefore, in the assembly of the Estates, where it was more fitting to weigh law than arms, he issued this decree:

units.la: Nisi Ordines parerent se equitem militemque plana agrorum ut vastaret, missurum plusque damni, si stipendia non velint, uno septiduo, quam alias pensitatis stipendijs toto mense daturum.
units.tr: Unless the Estates obey, he will send horsemen and soldiers to lay waste the flat fields, and he will do more damage in one week, if they refuse the wages, than he would otherwise do in a whole month if the wages were paid.

units.la: Quæ arrogantiæ ac immodestiæ plena, etsi ad Proregem perscriberentur, ita testabantur Frisij (in litteris ad Viglium viii. Id. April. datis) Albani ac Requesentij rescripta nihil ponderis habuisse, eoq; more aulæ speciosa verba professos integritatem fidemq; optumæ gentis elusisse.
units.tr: These things, full of arrogance and insolence, were reported to the Proregent. Yet the Frisians testified, in letters to Viglius dated 6 April, that the replies of Alba and Requesens had no weight, and that, in the manner of the court, they had professed fair words and so mocked the integrity and loyalty of a most excellent people.

units.la: Nihil dicebant nisi lustralem regalis Curiæ aquam, aut speciosa poma, ac ciborum condimenta porrexisse in exitium populi destitura, qui si ducenta aureorum millia præstare largientibus futilia posset, majora vani favoris gratiaque documenta habituram fore.
units.tr: They said nothing but that the royal court had offered lustral water, or showy apples and seasonings for food, all of which were destined to ruin the people. If the people could pay two hundred thousand gold pieces to those who lavished such gifts, they would have greater proof of empty favour and grace.

units.la: Igitur conventus Delegatorum Frisiæ ipsis Idib. April. Leovardiæ coeptus, decretumque ut sublevandæ provincialium egestati inductiones ante triennium institutæ, repeterentur, commercioque omni ac rebus, quas usus consumeret, onus tributumq; imponeretur. Cæterum hac cautelâ ut cogendo per provinciam æri inquilini præessent, rationibusq; reddendis quovis tempore obligarentur. Ita Hero Ockingha, Douwo Roorda, Hector Dekama, R. Dekama, Ruardus Roorda, Vitus Cammingha, Lollius Ockingha, Livius Beiemus, Iulius Dekama, Siricius Donia, Edo Gerbranda, Petrus Abbas in Fosewert, Titus Canmingha, Hesselus Hania, Scelto Liaukama, Hero Burmania, Upco Burmania, Hubertus Schooff, Joannes Witte prior Haskeranus, censuere. Econtra pars nobilitatis, populiquemagnis acribusq; obtestationibus se tuebantur, indictionesq; quod Caroli Brimæi ætate factum erat, velut libertati gentis adversas asperioribus decretis amovendas. Ita quippe fœlicius Frisios Carolo sub Cæsare vixisse, assertis privilegijs immunitatibusq; quarum umbram, aut speciem ne minuere quidem paucorum assensus queat. Itaq; corrigendos censorum ope, quos ideo provincia Caroli Cæsaris Philippique ætate delegisset, ne quid incommodi patriæ leges ferrent, & ne illorum malis consilijs servitium introdutroduceretur, quorum officij esset, intactam novis rogationibus libertatem populo praestare. Hoc tamen additum, velle se rebus facultatibusq; suis regem juvare, insigni aemulatione, ut, quod antiquis temporibus factum & Philippi imperium, & populi libertas per aeris subsidia retineretur. Quare populi Frisij Aegydium Barlamontium Hyergium Geldriae, Zutphaniae & Frisiae praefectum, magnis laudibus efferebant, quod alius a Roblesio, qui Praefecti nomen superbo & quidem falso, ut aiebant, titulo usurpabat, egregia animi exactionumq;, moderatione provinciam administraret. Econtra Roblesium repetitis criminationibus sectabantur, quod animi ac imperij juxta immodicus Frificum populum, a mari damna passum, armatorum insolentia & exactionum gravitate exhauriret. Unde missus pro legato Bruxellas Martinus Nitzenius, Caroli Praesidis filius, qui Proregi Requesentio hunc libellum Frisiorum nomine offerret.
units.tr: Thus the assembly of the deputies of Friesland began at Leeuwarden on 13 April. It decided that the levies instituted three years earlier to relieve the provincials' poverty should be called back, and that a burden of tax should be laid on all trade and on the goods that daily use consumes. However, this was on the condition that they should preside over the collection of money through the province, and be bound to render accounts at any time. So voted Hero Ockinga, Douwe Roorda, Hector Dekama, R. Dekama, Ruard Roorda, Vitus Cammingha, Lollius Ockinga, Livius Beyma, Julius Dekama, Siricius Donia, Edo Gerbrands, Peter, abbot of Vosswerd, Titus Cammingha, Hessel Hania, Scelto Liauckama, Hero Burmania, Upco Burmania, Hubert Schooff, and John Witte, prior of Haskerland. On the other side, a part of the nobility and the people defended themselves with loud and vehement protests. They argued that the taxes, as had been done in the time of Charles Brimaeus, were hostile to the liberty of the nation and should be removed by sterner decrees. Under Emperor Charles, they said, the Frisians had lived more happily, with their asserted privileges and immunities, of which not even the shadow or appearance could be diminished by the consent of a few. So they demanded that the censors, whom the province had chosen in the time of Charles the Emperor and Philip for this very purpose, should be restored by their help, so that the laws would bring no harm to the homeland and servitude would not be introduced through the evil counsels of those whose duty it was to keep liberty intact for the people against new proposals. Yet this was added: they were willing to help the king with their resources and goods, with remarkable zeal, so that, as had been done in ancient times, both Philip's rule and the people's liberty might be preserved by means of money-aid. Hence the Frisian people greatly praised Giles de Barlaimont, Lord of Hierges, prefect of Guelders, Zutphen and Friesland, because he governed the province with outstanding moderation of spirit and of exactions, unlike Robles, who, as they said, usurped the title of Prefect with a proud and indeed false name. On the contrary, they pursued Robles with repeated accusations, because his spirit and power, excessive toward the Frisian people, who had already suffered losses from the sea, drained them through the insolence of armed men and the heaviness of exactions. Whence Martin Nitzen, son of the President Charles, was sent as envoy to Brussels, to offer this petition of the Frisians to the Proregent Requesens.

units.la: INtellexi Prorex, a Roblesio litteras ad te missas, quo nova tributorum ope copijs suis, quas per Frisiam distributas in praesidijs habet, stipendia procuraret. Nos vero econtra supplices petimus, ut ab honorario aere regi praestando & simul militaribus praesidijs liberaremur. Is enim nostrarum rerum status est, ut ijs ferendis pares non simus. Praeter maris inundationes & anniversarios velut fluctuum aestus supra littus aggeresq; elatos, alias quoque caeli & naturae injurias accipimus. Agros quippe nostros, arvaque seminibus consita salsedo aquae, & eam secuta trimestris siccitas corrupit. Unde annonae apud nos metus, & ut Oceanus nullo aggere coercitus nostros in agros, & depressa terrarum se refundat. Atq; hoc malum a praediis ac possessionibus nostris amovere non poterimus, nisi aggere repellendis aestubus erecto, qui senos pedes tantum habens sedecim pedum altitudine firmandus est. At hoc praestare nostrae facultates non sinunt, nisi condonata honorarij portione militem amoveas. Adhaec bona provincialium passim cessionibus gravata; aut per venditiones alienata, aut pro derelictis haberi vides. Denique praeter tributum reficiendo aggeri decretum, novis operum molibus adstruendis gravamur, quorum impendia centum & nonaginta sex millibus aureorum aestumantur. Nisi levemur subsidio, aut remissicre tributo habeamur, nec nos patriam, nec rex provinciam habiturus erit.
units.tr: I understood, Proregent, that letters were sent to you from Robles, so that new tax-money might pay the wages of his troops, who are distributed through Friesland and held in garrisons. We on the contrary humbly beg that we be freed from paying the honorary money to the king and at the same time from the military garrisons. For such is the state of our affairs that we are not equal to bearing them. Besides the floods of the sea and the yearly surges of the tides, as if of waves, driven over the shore and the dikes, we suffer other injuries from the sky and from nature. For salt water has spoiled our fields and seed-sown lands, and a three-month drought has followed it. Hence there is fear of food shortage among us, and the ocean, not restrained by any dike, pours itself over our fields and sunken lands. Nor can we remove this evil from our farms and holdings unless a dike is raised to repel the tides, which, being only six feet high, must be strengthened to a height of sixteen feet. Our resources do not allow us to do this, unless you remit the part of the honorary money and remove the soldiers. Besides, you see the goods of the provincials everywhere burdened by cessions, either alienated by sales or regarded as abandoned. Finally, besides the tax decreed for repairing the dike, we are burdened with building new works, whose expenses are reckoned at one hundred and ninety-six thousand gold pieces. Unless we are relieved by aid, or the tax is remitted, you will have neither a homeland left to us nor a province for the king to hold.

units.la: Quae omnia, etsi in apertum producta, cunctatione tamen, aut supespecto silentio trahebantur. Quare Nitzenius litteras 1 v. Id. Mai in Frisiam Bruxellis dedit, quibus de regij Senatus Ordinumque Belgicae infida aemulatione commonebat, Viglioque praesidc, Fonckio, Assonvilio, & Schetzio a promovendis Frisiorum rebus non alienis, Barlamontium Bertiumque Requesentij actuarium actionibus Friscis infestos habuisse. Caeterum se per adventum Margaretae Marchicae Arembergij viduae, meliora sperare quae Friscae genti, quam maritus rexisset, imprimis aequa; plus quam, qua polleret, muliebrem prudentiam interpositura pro Frisijs foret. Hoc etiam suggerebat Roblesium, de cujus imperio queri tutum non esset, eminentis apud aulicos gratiae esse, eumq; actionem publicam jam inclinantem & fessam, deniq; ossicia legati missis Bruxellas litteris praejuvisse. Itaq; metuendum non esse ut, in tanto etiam regij aerarij defectu, quem suppleri rex, & senatus Belgicae velit, Frisij majore in posterum exactione premantur Quod captata temporum opportunitate calamitates suas terrâ marique cIↄ. Iↄ. enatas, non dissimulatâ malorum magnitudine exposuissent.
units.tr: All these things, though brought out into the open, were nonetheless delayed by hesitation or by a suspicious silence. Therefore Nitzenius, on 11 May, sent letters from Brussels to Friesland in which he warned them of the treacherous rivalry of the royal Council and the States of Belgium, and said that Viglius, as president, along with Fonck, Assonville and Schetz, who were not unconcerned with advancing the affairs of the Frisians, had kept Barlaimont and Bertius, Requesens's secretary, hostile to the Frisians through their proceedings. Moreover, he said that by the arrival of Margaret of Mark, widow of Aremberg, he hoped for better things for the Frisian people, above all fair treatment, which her husband had not given, and that she would bring to bear on behalf of the Frisians whatever womanly prudence she possessed. He also suggested that Robles, whose rule it was unsafe to complain of, had great favour at court, and that he had already eased the public business, which was tilting and worn out, and had at last, by letters sent to Brussels, furthered the duties of an envoy. Thus there was no need to fear that, in such a great shortage of the royal treasury, which the king and the Senate of Belgium wished to make good, the Frisians would be burdened with heavier exactions in future. They should seize the opportunity of the times, and in 1568 they had set out their calamities, arising by land and sea, without hiding the magnitude of their misfortunes.

units.la: Quare ego suadeo, inquiebat, ut, si Roblesius denuo res vestras ex se impulsas gravet, viâ facti occurratis, extremisque miseriis extrema quoque remedia libertati usitata decernatis.
units.tr: Therefore I advise, he said, that if Robles again burdens your affairs, pushed on by himself, you meet him by force, and that, against the extremest miseries, you decree the extreme remedies customary for liberty.

units.la: Ex quo etiam factum est, ut in ipso, quod tum agebatur, comitio liberæ consultantium voces audirentur, indictionumque vis atque efficacia obloquijs agrarij populi solveretur.
units.tr: From this it also came about that, in the very assembly then being held, the free voices of those deliberating were heard, and the force and effect of the levies were undone by the objections of the country people.

units.la: Invenio in actis Valerium Cammingha à Roblesio Harlingam ratihabendis indictionibus evocatum profectionem declinasse, missoque illico huc loci Jacobo Bouricio Jureconsulto, infensam novandis rebus obtestationem succensenti Roblesio obtulisse. Quod à Leovardiensibus & Oostergois, Collumanis, Menaldumæis, Barderanis, alijsque Westergois tum Sylvestribus factum in actis illorum temporum deprehendo. Igitur petente Nitzenio, qui Bruxellis adhuc agebat, decreta nobilitatis populique Frisici ad legatum transmissa animos regij Senatus alienavere, indignantibus plerisque Frisios juris sui fiduciâ lubnixos, cum invidiâ cæterarum provinciarum, odio Roblesij, & Senatus regij institutas indictiones, firmamenta regij imperij & militaris disciplinæ subvertisse. Quæ etsi dicerentur scriberenturque, fidem quoq; Legati minuebant, donec illa Roblesij litteris ex ipsa Frisiorum provinciâ stabiliretur. Igitur tum odio Frisicæ immunitatis, quasi communes Belgicæ res turbaret, multa in secretiore Senatu rescissa, retractatac, prima quoque in tanta rerum perturbatione partium studia & æmulationes aperuere, volentibus reliquarum Belgicæ gentium legatis, ut Frisia æquali jure ac simul servitio in causis Philippi haberetur.
units.tr: I find in the records that Valerius Cammingha, summoned by Robles to Harlingen to ratify the levies, declined the journey. He at once sent Jacob Bouricius, a jurist, to this place, and offered the protest against innovation to Robles, who was angered. The people of Leeuwarden, Oostergo, Kollum, Menaldum, Barderad, and the others of Westergo and of the Sylvestrine district, did the same, as I find in the records of those times. Therefore, at the request of Nitzen, who was still at Brussels, the decrees of the nobility and of the Frisian people, sent to the envoy, alienated the minds of the royal Senate. Most were indignant that the Frisians, relying on the confidence of their right, and with the envy of the other provinces and the hatred of Robles and of the royal Senate, had overturned the levies instituted, the supports of royal rule and of military discipline. Although these things were said and written, they lessened the envoy's credibility too, until those matters were confirmed by Robles' letters from the province of Friesland itself. Therefore, then, out of hatred for Frisian immunity, as if it disturbed the common affairs of Belgium, many things were rescinded and reconsidered in the more secret Senate. Also, in so great a disturbance of affairs, the rivalries and jealousies of the parties were first revealed, the envoys of the remaining Belgic nations wishing that Friesland be held, with equal right and at the same time equal service, in the causes of Philip.

units.la: Invenio in secretis Antistitis Clarecampij ad Viglium litteris, illud sanciendarum indictionum negotium extraneos quosdam Abbates ursisse, metuque regis perculsos, aut falso persuasos indigenarum Præsulum & imprimis Clarecampij, qui in arcem Leovardiæ evocatus libertati patrocinabatur consilia suspectasse. Scribit Nitzenius rejectis per Frisiam indictionibus non leves procerum offensas Bruxellis subortas fuisse, Belgicæque & regis Senatum de mittendis in Frisios, quo vastarent, equitum copijs deliberavisse. Itaque Nitzenius autoritate Legati munitus Ottonem Scouwenburgium, qui iturus cum equitatu Sylvestrem in tractum dicebatur, compellavit, cognitisque quæ ad hæc pertinebant, in provinciam rescripsit comminationibus sociorum expositam.
units.tr: I find in the private letters of the Abbot of Clarecamp to Viglius that certain foreign abbots had taken up the business of enacting the levies. The native prelates, and above all Clarecamp, who had been summoned to the citadel of Leeuwarden and was championing liberty, were struck with fear of the king or falsely persuaded, and came to suspect their plans. Nitzenius writes that, once the levies were rejected throughout Friesland, no slight offence arose among the nobles at Brussels, and that the Council of the Belgic provinces and of the king discussed sending troops of cavalry into Friesland to lay it waste.

units.la: Quare animorum audaciâ ex periculo auctâ, decretum de abolendis indictionibus scriptum, quas patrio juri adversas & destruendis Caroli Philippique conventionibus repertas masculâ virtute & majorum æmulâ D. Petrus Abbas Fosuerdicus, Thomas Groningensis Antistes Floridi campi, Hector Abingha, Ruardus Roorda, Livius de Bejem, Hero Ockingha, Petrus Boimerus, Oedsma, Meinius Lyclesius Nyholtpadius, Bernardus Romkenius, Jacobus Idsius, Titus Hajonius, Vitus Heinama signavere. Quæ cum militum animos accenderent, quod stipendiorum incerta à fundamentis convellerentur, omni licentiæ frænos laxavere, direptisque privatorum bonis querimoniæ apud Requesentium instituendæ occasionem commodavere. rens furor contumacem populum deligendos ad arbitros compulisset, à Philippo Rege, Ferdinando Albano, & Senatu regis potestate judicandi instructos. Itaque eludi majestatem regnantis & autoritatem judicij non posse. Quin admovendas confessim manus isti operi, quod securitatem & fortunam terris Frisicis, æternitatem famæ sui autoribus daturum sit.
units.tr: Therefore Nitzenius, armed with the authority of the Legate, summoned Otto Scouwenburgius, who was said to be about to march into the district with cavalry against Sylvester. Having learned what pertained to these matters, he wrote back to the province, which was exposed to the threats of its allies. Consequently, with the audacity of their spirits increased by the danger, a decree was drawn up for abolishing the levies. The men who with manly courage, and emulating their ancestors, had found these levies contrary to the native law and destructive of the agreements of Charles and Philip, signed it: D. Petrus, Abbot of Fosuerdicus; Thomas, Bishop of Groningen, of Floridus Campus; Hector Abingha; Ruardus Roorda; Livius de Bejem; Hero Ockingha; Petrus Boimerus; Oedsma; Meinius Lyclesius Nyholtpadius; Bernardus Romkenius; Jacobus Idsius; Titus Hajonius; Vitus Heinama. Since these acts inflamed the minds of the soldiers, because the uncertain pay was being overthrown from its foundations, they loosened every rein of licence, and, with private property plundered, they gave occasion for complaints to be lodged before the Requesens. When the raging fury had compelled the stubborn people to appoint arbiters, who were furnished with the king's power of judging by King Philip, Ferdinand of Alba and the king's Council, so the majesty of the reigning king and the authority of the court could not be mocked. Rather, hands should at once be set to this work, which would give security and fortune to the Frisian lands and eternal fame to its authors.

units.la: Mandatum quoque Ioanni Carolo fisci regij Advocato, ut ad Westergoos scribat ocyus, regisque sui nomine agat, cujus interfit annuis eluvionibus Frisiorum agros non absumi. Quod si fiat, magnum regi detrimentum creari, qui unice velit suo patrimonio ac fisco nihil decedere. Quare nec crebras inundationes aut ultimam egestatem pertinacibus ad excusationem apud regem profuturas, publica ac sua, si posthac ingruant, damna contumaci discordiæ, non divinis iris imputaturum. Tributa quoque extra ordinem maturando operi Roblesius poposcit, diemque auspicandæ moli præfinitum negligi vetuit. Mox conficiendis tabulis Gasparus Roblesius Præfectus, Igramus Achlenius Præses, Adrianus Vastartius, Petrus Frittema, & Ioannes Carolus Senatores delegati, modicque dimensionum Harlingæ in arce regiâ scripti. Operariorum quoque vacationibus prospectum, quo duri operis molestiam interjuncto otio dispungerent, viriumque fomentis laborantium corpora refocillarentur. Disciplinæ quoque leges continendæ in officio multitudini scriptæ, cautumque severe, ne quis à diurnis operis cessaret, festinandique laboris assiduitatem insolentiâ aut ignaviâ interverteret. Itaque die condicto per omne littus tot millium inconditus clamor & dissonæ voces, velut in castris aut exercitu edebantur. Quippe diversis ministerijs occupata multitudo materiem operi aut consilia poscebat, streperoque murmure silentia littoris & inspicientium imperia morabatur. Quare distinguendis temporum intervallis, quæ longior ab Æquinoctio dies præstabat, signum ex edito datum vacationum, aut operarum statas vices designabat. Sic jacta magnæ & stupendæ molis fundamenta, populusque agrarius sævienti elemento compedem injecturus, importunum mare tumultuario primum opere coercuit. Inde aquæ, fœcundis agris jam ante superfusæ, sensim repressæ, fluctusque diurnis quondam æstubus per lata terrarum littorumque spatia se laxantes solertiâ hominum deledere. Tum sequens annus perducendo ad finem operi dictus, cautumque Senatusconsulto, ut eo anno in denos pedes agger marinus exsurgeret, impendiaque tabulationum arbitrio Præfecti & Senatus Regij starent. Injunctum quoque mediterraneis Westergois Heroni Ockinghæ, & Hesselo Haniæ, ut veteri marino aggeri necessarias reparationes præstent dentque effectum, ne quid damni resp. per socordiam & neglectum publici operis patiatur. Hæc Jani Gulielmij aggerum Scribæ manu signata. Sic aggeres quique, qui aut extimo littori, aut introrsum disjunctis à mari agris prætexuntur, novis molibus firmari, protractaque per tot annorum dissensiones & socordiam Præfectorum provinciæ incolumitas unius Roblesij severo & aspero per Frisiam imperio stabilita. Creditum fuit Gasparum Roblesium ex imo per egregia facinora ad amplissimam Præfecturam evectum, tam suo quam populi bono sumptuosi operis consilium cum vehementiâ ursisse, quo soli ubertate fœlicissimas ditiones nacIↄ. Iↄ. LXXIV. nactus, præducto terris aggere, suæ dominationi & simul bello certiora subsidia apisceretur. Cæterum sternendo aggere occupatum, & glo-riæ suæ è pacis negotio indulgentem belli mox ardescentis rumor perculit. Quippe Ludovicus Nassovius, qui jam ante utriusque fortunæ documenta in Frisijs fecerat, adventare cum exercitu ferebatur, Gulielmoque Nassovio Aurantio Principi, res per Hollandiam, Zelandiamque gerenti, auxilia parare. Jam enim Ludovicus post occupatos & mox desertos Hannoniæ Montes, per Germaniam Galliasque fœdera ac societates agitaverat, credebaturque Carolum ix. Gallorum Regem, velut pœnitudine exercitæ per regnum coœdis ductum, tum ipsos quoque Romani Imperij Principes in socia arma secretis legationibus traxisse.
units.tr: A mandate was also given to John Charles, advocate of the royal treasury, to write at once to the Westergoers and act in the king's name, since it was in the king's interest that the fields of the Frisians should not be consumed by yearly floods. If this came about, a great loss would be created for the king, who wished that nothing should be taken from his patrimony and treasury. Therefore, if these floods, or their ultimate poverty, which would be advanced before the king as an excuse by the stubborn, should press again hereafter, he would not impute the public and private damages to divine wrath, but to stubborn discord. Roblesius also demanded extraordinary taxes to be hastened for the work, and forbade neglect of the day appointed to begin the project. Soon Gaspar Roblesius, the Prefect, Igram Achlenius, the President, Adrian Vastartius, Peter Frittema and John Charles, Senators, were appointed to draw up the plans, and the measurements were written out at Harlingen in the royal citadel. Provision was also made for the rest of the workers, so that the weariness of hard labour might be relieved by intervening leisure and the bodies of those toiling might be refreshed with supports of strength. Rules of discipline were also written out for the multitude, to keep them in their duty, and it was strictly provided that no one should cease from the daily work, and that insolence or idleness should not overturn the constant haste of the labour. So on the appointed day, throughout the whole shore, the disorderly shouting and discordant voices of so many thousands rose up, as if in a camp or army. Indeed the multitude, occupied with various services, demanded materials for the work or counsels, and with noisy murmur delayed the quiet of the shore and of those who were overseeing the orders. Therefore, distinguishing the intervals of time, which the longer days after the equinox allowed, a signal given from a raised place marked the breaks from work or the turns of the workmen. Thus were laid the foundations of a great and astonishing mass, and the agrarian people, about to fetter the raging element, first restrained the troublesome sea with a hasty work. Then the waters, already poured over the fertile fields, were gradually held back, and the waves, which once spread over the broad expanses of lands and shores with daily tides, were beaten down by human skill. Then the following year was appointed for bringing the work to completion, and it was provided by decree of the Senate that in that year the sea dyke should rise ten feet, and that the expenses of the boards should depend on the judgement of the Prefect and the royal Senate. It was also enjoined on the inland Westergoers, to Hero Ockingha and Hesselo Hania, that they should make the necessary repairs to the old sea dyke and carry them out, so that the public should suffer no damage through carelessness and neglect of the public work. These things were sealed by the hand of Jan Gulielmius, clerk of the dykes. Thus the dykes, whether they stretch along the outer shore or along the fields lying inland and separated from the sea, were strengthened with new mounds; and the safety of the province, which had been neglected through so many years of dissension and the sloth of the Prefects, was secured by the stern and harsh rule of Roblesius alone over Friesland. It was believed that Gaspar Roblesius, raised from the bottom to the highest Prefecture through outstanding deeds, had with vehemence devised this costly work for his own good and that of the people, so that by means of the fertility of the soil he might gain for his own dominion, and at the same time for the war, more certain resources. Meanwhile, occupied with laying the dyke, and indulging his glory in the business of peace, he was struck by the rumour of war soon to blaze up. For Ludovicus Nassovius, who had already given proofs of either fortune in Friesland, was reported to be approaching with an army, and to be preparing aid for William of Nassau, Prince of Orange, who was conducting affairs in Holland and Zeeland. For Ludovicus, after occupying and soon abandoning the mountains of Hainaut, had been negotiating alliances and confederacies through Germany and France, and it was believed that Charles IX, King of the French, drawn by regret for the slaughter carried out throughout the kingdom, and even the princes of the Holy Roman Empire, had been drawn into joining arms by secret embassies.

units.la: Tradit Thuanus à Carolo Rege, quo foedissimi facinoris infamiam elevaret, Gasparum Scombergium in Germaniam ad Principes imperij missum, eundemque Francofurti ad Moenum, Galeacio Fulgosio reginæ legato intercessore, cum Ludovico Nassovio nomine Aurantij fratris arcanam pactionem inijsse. Eádem cautum fuisse, ut si bellum His-pano, aut trecentorum millium carolæorum mutuum foederatis in subsidium Rex Carolus præstaret, Hollandiam ac Zelandiam, fidejussore Romani Imperij Principe, accipiat, oppidaque, si quæ adjici fœderatis bello eveniat, Regi cedant, secus Hollandiam Zelandiamque ex pacto teneat. Quæ in acta relata pro ingenijs partium fiduciam, aut metum dedere. Itaque Ludovicum Requesentium Belgicæ Præsidem pavor invasit, progresso jam in interiora provinciarum Ludovico, & exercitu regio per inopiam æris defectionibus proxumo. Unde Valo-nicæ Legionis copiæ Frisiâ mox evocatæ, præsidiaque urbium per provinciam extenuata. Econtra foederatis amplæ spes & surgentium rerum lætiorum initia ex secundis per Zelandiam rebus, & adventu Ludovici nascebantur. Quamobrem Gallicas Germanicasque societates efferre, bello, si perseveret, firma auxilia, aut paci, si sperari posset, intercessionem daturas. Adeo fragilitatis humanæ documentum fiducia dubij exitus consilia pro certis ac profuturis acceperat. Gulielmo vero Nassovio omnia funesti ominis in Ludovici fratris exercitu videbantur. Quippe imperitum armorum militem Ludovicus ducebat, temporisque opportunitatem, quod negligenti celerrimum est, crebris itinerum stationibus morabatur. Unde Requesentio occasio nata copias cogendi, quæ per omnem oram sparsæ, versò in constantiam metu, magnâ festinatione colligebantur. Mox, quo justo exercitu pugnaret, regios vasallos in armis esse jussit, motisque Leidâ urbe, quam obsederat, castris, è minoribus Frisijs conduci copias præcepit.
units.tr: Thuanus relates that Charles the King, to lessen the infamy of the most foul crime, had sent Gaspar Scombergius into Germany to the princes of the Empire, and that the same man at Frankfurt on the Main, with Galeazzo Fulgosio, the Queen's envoy, as intermediary, had made a secret agreement with Ludovicus Nassovius in the name of his brother the Prince of Orange. It was provided by the same agreement that if war should break out with the Spaniard, King Charles would furnish to the confederates, as aid, a loan of three hundred thousand carolus, and would receive Holland and Zeeland, with a prince of the Holy Roman Empire as guarantor, and any towns that might come into the confederates' hands in the war would be ceded to the King; and otherwise he would hold Holland and Zeeland according to the pact. These matters, once reported as acts, gave confidence or fear according to the dispositions of the parties. Thus panic seized Requesens, the President of the Belgic Council, as Ludovicus had already advanced into the interior of the provinces, and the royal army was nearly in revolt through lack of money.
