Hence the troops of the Walloon Legion were soon summoned from Friesland, and the garrisons of the towns throughout the province were thinned. On the other hand, great hopes and the first beginnings of more joyful affairs arose for the confederates from the successful events in Zeeland and from the arrival of Ludovicus. Therefore they were ready to raise up the French and German alliances, and to give firm aid in war if it should continue, or intercession for peace if it could be hoped for. So confidence in an uncertain outcome had taught, as a proof of human frailty, that counsels were taken as certain and profitable. But to William of Nassau everything in his brother Ludovicus's army seemed to bear an ominous sign. For Ludovicus led a soldiery unskilled in arms, and by frequent halts on the march he delayed the opportunity of time, which is the swiftest thing for the negligent. Hence an occasion arose for Requesens to gather forces, which had been scattered along the whole coast, and, with fear turned into constancy, they were collected with great haste. Soon, that he might fight with a lawful army, he ordered the royal vassals to be under arms, and, breaking camp from Leiden, which he had besieged, he commanded troops to be brought from the Lesser Frisians.

units.la: Delectus quoque supplendis cohortibus per Germaniam habuit, Zanchiumque Avilanum, virum militiæ egregium, regio exercitui præfecit. Dein Trajectum majoribus præsidijs firmavit, quam urbem Mosa amnis modico alveo stringit, & in cujus ulteriore ripâ Ludovicus Nassovius auxilia Principum cum exercitu opperiebatur. Jam enim inviuum flumen gelu fecerat, natantemque & crepidine avulsam glaciem rapacissimi vortices agebant. Quare Requesentius, ne amnem ponte Ludovicus sterneret, soluta circa Æquinoctium glacie, naves eodem in fluflumine stantes subduci fecit, omnemque exercitum, quem subvertendo Ludovico destinabat, conduci Trajectum ad Mosam imperavit. Ludovicus vero pedestrium copiarum, quæ sex millia armatorum numerabant, ordines tuebatur, equitatumque trium millium, quem è Gallis ac Lotharingis collegerat, Christophoro Bavaro Palatino commiserat. In comitatu vero, præter Gallicæ Germanicæque nobilitatis florem, Henricum quoque fratrem circumducebat; rudimenta virtutis primis juventæ annis in illo exercitu facturum. Sic considentem haud procul Mosæ ripâ Avilanus inmisso velite tentavit, levique equitum concursu facto, ubi rudem armorum Ludovici equitem deprehendit, non obscuram victoriæ spem præconcepit. Quare equitum turmas in insidijs collocavit, Ludovicique copias elicere loricâ castrorum adnixus, præludia pugnæ non sine ostentatione, & fiduciâ prosperi exercuit. Jam enim diversis auxilijs regius exercitus increverat. Ludovici verò castra, etsi Mocam vicum tumultuario opere præmuniri curaverat, magnis intervallis discreta spectabantur. Unde factum est, ut Avilanus novem Germanorum peditum cohortes, & alam schlopetariorum per Mendozam equitum ductorem tentaverit, dieque vix orto ad septingentos ceciderit. Cujus cladis causam ut latis castrorum spatijs, ita neglectis equitum excubijs Scriptores annalium assignavere. Quare Ludovici castris ab illâ strage melius prospectum, dispositiqúe per opportuna locorum vigiles tenebrosæ noctis discrimini subvenere. Adeo magnis etiam ac præclaris belli Ducibus damnosa semper infidis rebus securitas fuit.
units.tr: He also held levies throughout Germany to fill up the cohorts, and he placed Zanchius Avilanus, a man distinguished in soldiering, in command of the royal army. Then he strengthened Maastricht with larger garrisons, a city which the river Meuse grips with a narrow channel, and on whose further bank Ludovicus Nassovius was waiting with an army for the aid of the princes. For the river, though not deep, had already been frozen by the ice, and the drifting ice, torn from the bank, was carried along by the most rapacious eddies. Therefore Requesens, lest Ludovicus should bridge the river, when the ice was loosened about the equinox, had the ships which were standing in that same river drawn up on land, and ordered the whole army, which he intended to lead against Ludovicus, to be brought to Maastricht on the Meuse. But Ludovicus was guarding the lines of his foot troops, which numbered six thousand armed men, and he had entrusted the cavalry of three thousand, which he had gathered from the French and Lorrainers, to Christopher, Count Palatine of Bavaria. In his retinue, besides the flower of the French and German nobility, he was also leading about his brother Henry, who was to receive the first lessons of valour in that army in the early years of his youth. So when Avilanus sent in light troops to test him as he was encamped not far from the bank of the Meuse, and a light skirmish of cavalry took place, he found that Ludovicus's horsemen were inexperienced in arms, and he conceived no slight hope of victory. Therefore he placed squadrons of cavalry in ambush, and, relying on the rampart of the camp, he tried to draw out the troops of Ludovicus, practising the preludes of battle not without ostentation and confidence of success. For the royal army had grown by the various reinforcements. But the camp of Ludovicus, though he had taken care to fortify the village of Mocum with a hasty work, was seen to be divided by wide intervals. Hence it came about that Avilanus attacked nine cohorts of German foot and a wing of arquebusiers through Mendoza, leader of the cavalry, and at dawn nearly seven hundred fell. The writers of the annals ascribed the cause of this disaster to the wide spaces of the camp and the neglected pickets of the cavalry. Therefore the camp of Ludovicus was better guarded after that slaughter, and the sentries posted at suitable points rescued it from the peril of the dark night. So even for great and distinguished generals, security was always ruinous in uncertain affairs.

units.la: Mox Requesentius copiás, quas Hollandiâ exciverat, subsequi ocyus, ac progredi Ruremundam jussit, Zanchiumque Avilanum ad movenda castra Ludovicum compellere præcepit. Igitur commeatuum inopiam, & ex loco discrimen præsentiens Ludovicus mutandorum stativorum consilium inijt, exercitumque cis Mosam mox trans flumen ducere, ac Rheno Mosâque amnibus circumscribere constituit. Sed viæ opportunitas, copiæ, & navigia desiderabantur. Itaque lintres traducendis copijs, Gulielmum Nassovium poposcit; fraterna fata non æquâ mente volutantem. Quippe sinistri præsagium principem animum occupaverat, dirasque rerum tristium imagines miseratio fraterni discriminis repræsentabat. Unde Aurantius, quo impulsis Ludovici rebus succurreret, copias suas in Bommeliam insulam duxit, quam in longitudinem porrectam nobilissima flumina Mosa ac Vahalis lato gurgite ambiunt. Mosæ vero dextram ripam Ludovicus, sinistram Avilanus præleǵebat, celeritateque velut conficiendi itineris uterque exercitus certabat. Quare ampla viarum spatia permensus miles lassitudinem sentiebat, pugnæque desideria & calores fatigato corpore minuebantur. Avilanus quoque Noviomagum oppidum, quod Vahali adjacet (florente olim Frisicæ gentis potentiâ regni nostri sub Radbodo terminum) novis copijs munivit, emissisque exploratoribus de Ludovico certior factus, haud procul Gravia oppido Mosæ flumini pontem imposuit, copiasque traduxit, ne Nassoviorum fratrum exercitus haud magnis terrarum spatijs discreti, suo incommodo jungerentur. Mox superato amne Mosa speculatorias equitum cohortes emisit; quo pugnan-tem tem Ludovicum detinerent, & à continuâ succedentium copiarum ve-litatione prælium inciperet. Cæterum istæ à Ludovici equite ad quadringentos cæsæ, aut in avia disparsæ, sine ullo ordine in Avilani castra rediere. Scribunt autores eâ clade tantam Hispanorum in castris consternationem fuisse, ut, si ulteriorem impressionem Ludovici equites fecissent, in fugam, aut confusionem dare totum Avilani exercitum potuerint. Sed subesse dolum, aut collocatos in insidijs Hispanos rati, signum receptui dedere. Itaque eorum umbris, qui jam an-te in Ludovici partibus occubuerant, abundè parentatum, manesque cæsorum reciproca per piamenta placati. Sic suffuso terris opaco à pu-gnâ discessum, dieque postero infida castrorum quies interrupta, ma-gno turbæ murmure, silentia noctis confudit. Tum Hispanorum acies sub lucis ortum instructa. Avilanus vero dextrum exercitus latus, quo tutius esset, juxta fluvium locavit, hastatorumque ordinibus schlopetarios pedites anteposuit. Lævum vero latus gravis levisque armaturæ equites stipabant, instarque semilunæ duo in cornua protendeban-tur. Peditatum vero Bernardinus Mendoza cum nonnullis equitum turmis sequebatur, præmisso interim lanceario, schlopetarioque equite, quem ut antecessorem, instituendæ velitationi Avilanus ordinaverat. Auxilia quoque, quæ Barlamontius Hyergius, nuper majoris Frisiæ, tum Geldriæ Præfectus, ducebat, in castra regia opportunè adducta, majorumque copiarum spes facta differendæ pugnæ dubia consilia exer-cuit. Erant qui censerent ex præscripto Medicorum crudis rebus ni-hil tentandum, & opperienda potius auxilia, quam regias res in gra-ve discrimen adducendas. Neque enim momenta rerum expendi, cæ-terum illa in pugnâ, illo in fortunæ & virtutis experimento, regis, aut partium imperia consistere. Trahi dubijs eventibus res mortalium, neque nimis fidendum præsenti fortunæ, ut plurimum suâ opinione fœlicem deferenti. Fiduciâ sui multos in præcipitia actos, neque aliâ occasione Arembergium in Frisijs se simul & exercitum perdidisse, quam quod auxiliorum certus, spretis cum Ludovico auxilijs pugnaverit. Habendam esse in bello multitudinis rationem, neque tantas fortunæ dominationes esse, quin ab humanis quoque bellorum exitus de-pendeant. Quare indulgendum moræ esse, dum ad manum auxilia sint, Ludovico metum, commilitonibus animum facturæ. Cæteri disserebant idoneum pugnæ locum, velut fato datum, neque numero dispares, virtute vero superiores regias copias esse. Trahere Ludovicum inexpertam militiæ & tyronum manum, cæterum pro Philippo veteranos & exercitatos bellis stare. Adhæc metuendum esse, si prælium protrahatur, ut Ludovicus patentibus campis nunc agens, tumultuario opere se muniat, altitudinemque aut vada fluminis ope lintrium explorans auxilia accipiat, aut in confinia se transferat fraternis copijs infessa. Itaque auspicandum potius pugnæ initium, documenta virtutis & haud dubiè fortunæ daturum. Mox Ludovicus aciem ordinavit, pe-ditumque viginti quinque cohortes, robur exercitus, dextrum per latus disposuit. Equite vero tutandis peditum ordinibus subjunxit, turmasque nonnullas, incapace universi equitatus per angustiam loco, lævum ad cornu haud procul convalle locavit, quæ clementi colle ver-sus sus Septentrionem, in ortum Moca claudebatur. Decem vero Gallorum peditum signa Ludovicus munitioni praefecit. Tum signum pugnae datum, primaque acierum velitatio coepta, in quam gloriae aut partium studijs praefervidae mentes incendebantur. Quippe alij pro Philippo rege pro retinendâ dominatione, alij pro patriae libertate, pro aris ac focis dimicabant. Itaque quaerendo pugnae compendio, Avilanus tres cohortes Hispanorum, & mox Valonum oppugnare munitionem jussit, quae modico conflictu virtute Valonum occupata, fatale rerum inclinantium praesagium fuit. Unde Ludovico res angustae, pro copiâ aut accessu novorum ordinum, tamdiu impetum adversarum partium sustinuere, donec Avilanus peditum agmen, florem exercitus, lassis vulneratisque surrogaret, Ludovicique copijs confertim immitteret. Quare per ordines Ludovici sensim confusio, & ex ea consilium fugae invaluit, à quâ etiam Ducum Tribunorumque pugnantium adhortamentis, aut equestris nobilitatis illustri fortitudine, imbellis multitudo non revocabatur. Tradunt autores Nassovianos pedites, etiam instantis periculi praemonitos, compelli prece aut jussu ad officia non potuisse, praefractosque & Ducum imperijs contumaces degenerem & inglorium sanguinem propriae perfidiae & ultricibus iris litasse. Sic ipso praelij momento stipendia poscenti turbae, justa defectionis merces, parata mors assignata. Quare Ludovicus sexcentis cum equitibus, quos in fronte exercitus collocaverat, colle descendens, in confertissimam hostium aciem se immisit, adjutusque Gallorum peditum copijs, quas sacramentum adhuc obligabat, dubiam & velut haerentem fortunam suâ diu virtute sustinuit. Post vero ubi equitatus ordines luxati, & pars edita collium peteret, pars in praerupta ac declivia ferretur, robur aciei dissolutum ingruentium lanceariorum equitum insultibus cessit.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Requesens ordered the troops he had raised in Holland to follow more quickly and advance to Roermond, and he commanded Zanchi and Avila to force Louis to move his camp. Louis, sensing both the shortage of supplies and the danger of his position, decided to change quarters. He resolved to lead his army across the Maas at once and to enclose it between the Rhine and the Maas. But the convenience of the road, the troops and the boats were lacking. He therefore asked William of Nassau for boats to ferry the troops across. William, brooding over his brother's fate, could not keep his mind calm. A foreboding of disaster had taken hold of the prince, and his pity for his brother's peril presented him with dire images of grim events. So Orange, to come to the aid of Louis's failing affairs, led his troops into the island of Bommel, which the noble rivers Maas and Waal enclose with broad streams as it stretches out in length. Louis marched along the right bank of the Maas and Avila along the left, and each army raced the other in speed, as if to finish the journey first. Consequently the soldiers, having covered a great distance, felt weary, and their eagerness for battle and their fervour waned with their tired bodies. Avila also strengthened with fresh troops the town of Nijmegen, which lies on the Waal (once, when the power of the Frisian people flourished, the boundary of our kingdom under Radboud). Having sent out scouts and been informed about Louis, he laid a bridge over the Maas near the town of Grave, not far off, and brought his troops across, so that the armies of the Nassau brothers, separated by no great distance, might not join forces to his disadvantage. Soon, having crossed the river Maas, he sent out squadrons of cavalry on reconnaissance, so that they might hold Louis back while he was fighting, and so that the battle would begin with a constant skirmishing of the troops that followed one another. However, about four hundred of these were cut down by Louis's cavalry, or scattered in the open country, and returned without any order to Avila's camp. Authors write that after this defeat there was such consternation among the Spaniards in the camp that, if Louis's horsemen had made a further attack, they could have thrown the whole army of Avila into flight or confusion. But the Spaniards, supposing that some trick lay hidden or that Spaniards had been placed in ambush, sounded the signal to withdraw. Thus the shades of those who had already fallen on Louis's side were abundantly honoured with funeral rites, and the spirits of the slain were appeased by mutual expiations. So, when the dark night had spread over the lands and the fighting ceased, the camps' uneasy quiet was broken on the next day by a great murmur of the crowd, and it disturbed the silence of the night. Then the Spanish battle line was drawn up at sunrise. Avila placed the right flank of his army beside the river, to make it safer, and he put the arquebusiers in front of the ranks of the spearmen. The left flank was flanked by heavy and light armed cavalry, and two wings extended in the shape of a half-moon. Bernardino Mendoza followed with the infantry and some squadrons of cavalry, having sent ahead meanwhile lancers and arquebusiers on horseback, whom Avila had ordered, as before, to begin the skirmishing. Also the auxiliaries which Barlaymont Hyergius, recently governor of Friesland and then of Gelderland, was leading, were brought opportunely into the royal camp, and the hope of larger forces created doubtful counsels about delaying the battle. Some thought that, following the prescription of physicians, nothing should be attempted while things were still raw, and that the auxiliaries should be awaited rather than the royal affairs being brought into grave danger. For the weight of events was not to be weighed in the balance; rather, in battle, that test of fortune and valour, the mastery of the king or of the parties depended. Human affairs are drawn along by doubtful outcomes, and one should not trust too much to the present fortune, which usually carries men along, happy in their own opinion. Many, driven headlong by self-confidence, had perished; and Arenberg in Friesland had lost both himself and his army for no other reason than that, certain of his auxiliaries, he had fought with the auxiliaries scorned. In war, account must be taken of numbers, and fortune's mastery is not so great that the outcomes of wars do not also depend on human measures. Therefore, delay should be indulged while the auxiliaries were at hand, to instil fear in Louis and courage in the fellow soldiers. Others argued that the place suitable for battle had been given, as if by fate, and that the royal troops were not unequal in number, but superior in valour. Louis was leading an untried band of soldiers and recruits, whereas the veterans and men trained in wars stood on Philip's side. Besides, it was to be feared that if the battle were prolonged, Louis, now active on open plains, would fortify himself with hasty earthworks, and, by exploring the depth or fords of the river with the help of boats, would receive auxiliaries, or would move into the borders, hostile to his brother's forces. Therefore the beginning of the battle should rather be launched, which would give proof of valour and, undoubtedly, of fortune. Soon Louis drew up his battle line and placed twenty-five cohorts of infantry, the strength of the army, on the right flank. He attached cavalry to protect the ranks of the infantry, and he posted some squadrons, since the whole cavalry could not be deployed through the narrow ground, on the left wing, not far from a valley which was closed off on the north by a gentle hill, and on the east by the town of Mook. He placed ten standards of French infantry in charge of the fortification. Then the signal for battle was given, and the first skirmishing of the lines began, in which minds burning with the zeal of glory or of party became inflamed. Indeed, some fought for King Philip, to retain his rule, others for the freedom of the fatherland, for altars and hearths. So, in order to shorten the battle, Avila ordered three cohorts of Spaniards, and soon afterwards the Walloons, to attack the fortification; it was taken by the Walloons' valour after a brief clash, and this was an omen of fatal disaster for the side that was giving way. Hence Louis's forces, hard pressed, held out so long against the attack of the opposing side, as far as their numbers or the arrival of new ranks allowed, until Avila replaced the column of infantry, the flower of the army, for the weary and wounded, and hurled it in close order against Louis's troops. So confusion gradually spread through Louis's ranks, and from this the idea of flight took hold; the unwarlike crowd was not called back from it even by the exhortations of the commanders and tribunes who were fighting, or by the outstanding bravery of the cavalry nobility. Authors relate that the Nassau infantry, though warned of the imminent danger, could not be compelled by prayer or command to do their duty; and, stubborn and refusing the orders of their leaders, they sacrificed their degenerate and inglorious blood to their own treachery and to the avenging furies. Thus, at the very moment of battle, a fitting reward for the defection, a ready death, was assigned to the crowd that demanded its pay. Therefore Louis, with six hundred cavalrymen whom he had placed at the front of the army, came down from the hill and threw himself into the most densely packed line of the enemy; supported by the French infantry, whom the oath still bound to him, he for a long time sustained with his own valour a fortune that was doubtful and seemed to hang in the balance. But afterwards, when the ranks of the cavalry were broken, and part of them made for the raised hills, part were carried over steep and sloping ground, the strength of the line, dissolved, yielded to the onslaught of the attacking lancers.

units.la: Itaq; in fugam versi Ludovici equites Hispanis victoriam reliquere. Alij tradunt, à lanceario Avilani equite Ludovici quoque pedites ita obruti fuisse, ut respirandi tempus defuerit, armorumque suorum incapaces loco cesserint. Itaque multi fugâ in avia & sylvestria sparsi, à subsequentibus Hispanis caesi, aut saevitiâ victorum flammis dati, communi velut rogo, tanquam sepulchrali igne arsere. Ludovicus ipse clarissimus belli Dux, quem fortuna & militum fides, non virtus deseruit, cum fratre Henrico, & Christophoro Bavaro Palatino ignoto mortis genere occubuit. Creditum fuit, quod inter cadavera coesorum reperti non sint, aut profundae paludum uligini immersos, aut incendio aedium, in quas se receperant, exustos perijsse. Alij addunt, Ludovicum accepto brachij vulnere, tum fratrem ac Bavarum fortiter pugnantes & mox equis proturbatos, multitudine vulnerum concidisse. Caeterum dubios viri exitus & disceptatam scriptoribus mortem nescia premi obscuro virtus illustrabit, Ludovicumque, ut patriae & exercitui illis in campis, instar victimae, se devoventem, fama humanae vocis aut perennis annalium labor in omnem temporum memoriam feret. Nonnulli è perfidis & pugnam detrectantibus, ignobili latebrâ se occulentes, non multata & intacta vulneribus corpora pugnae subduxerunt. Gallicae vero copiae, quae Ludovici fidem secutae, praeclarè se gesserant, sociorum funera, caesis post ad Mosam Rhenum-
units.tr: So Louis's cavalry, turned to flight, left the victory to the Spaniards. Others report that Louis's infantry too were so overwhelmed by Avila's lancers that they had no time to breathe, and, unable to carry their arms, gave way. Thus many, scattered in flight through trackless and wooded country, were cut down by the Spaniards who followed, or, given to the flames by the cruelty of the victors, burned together on one common pyre, as if in a funeral fire. Louis himself, the most famous commander of the war, whom fortune and the loyalty of his soldiers, rather than his valour, had abandoned, perished with his brother Henry and Christopher of Bavaria, Count Palatine, by an unknown manner of death. It was believed that, since they were not found among the bodies of the slain, they had perished either by sinking in the deep mire of the marshes, or by being burned in the fire of the houses into which they had retreated. Others add that Louis, having received a wound in the arm, and then his brother and the Bavarian, fighting bravely and soon driven from their horses, fell from the multitude of their wounds. However, the uncertain end of the man and the death disputed by writers will be illumined by obscurity, which knows not how to be pressed down; and valour, offering itself like a victim for the fatherland and the army on those plains, will be borne down the memory of all ages by the fame of human voice or the lasting labour of the annals. Some of the treacherous men who refused to fight, hiding themselves in ignoble lurking places, escaped with their bodies unharmed and untouched by wounds. But the French forces, which had followed Louis's faith, had acquitted themselves splendidly; avenging the funerals of their allies on the enemy, who were afterwards slain by the Maas and the Rhine, they returned to France without any notable disaster. The victors gained little plunder, except that thirty standards and three siege engines added to the glory of the victors. Augustus Thou, from the commentaries of Bernardino Mendoza, the leader of the heavy cavalry in that battle, writes that Louis with his men did not fight vigorously...

units.la: numque hostibus ultæ, nullâ insigni clade acceptâ in Galliam redierę. Prædæ parum victoribus obvenit, nisi quod triginta vexilla & tres machinæ claritudinem victorum auxere. Augustus Thuanus ex commentarijs Bernardini Mendozæ, cataphractorum illa pugnâ ductoris, scribit, Ludovicum cum suis non strenuè tantum Ducis, sed militis officium explevisse, equoque dejectum, & palude absorptum periisse. Creditum fuit, Ludovicum consilio suo, quo simulatâ peditum suorum fugâ insequentes, & solutos Hispanorum ordines excepturus cum integris videbatur, excidisse, alterius-que, qui paludtri Mosam inter & Valalim loco ac incilibus divisò, nec dum exercitui agendam suaserat, male obscuratum, periculis & subsecutæ cladi se exposuisse. Alijs quod ad Mocam desederit, fessis ex longo itinere ac per adultum ver ferventissimo die copijs Ludovicus dedisse creditur, & quod prælij fortunam infidis exploratoribus commisisset. Reidanus optimus scriptor addit, cum ex suarum virium fiduciâ imbecillitatem hostium æstumasse, fatumque, quo Ludovici fortunam convelleret, magni Ducis & suâ opinione prævalidi consilia corrupisse. Fugnantem occubuisse idem Reidanus autor est, eumque, si fato licuisset, maximorum belli suâ ætate Imperatorum longe gloriam superaturum fuisse. Quippe militare ingenium, etsi gerendis rebus præceps crederetur, nec vacuum prudentiæ erat, mandatisque & imperijs exequendis grave obsequium exercitus singulari autoritate moderabatur. Adhæc civilem orisque facundiâ trahendis animis peritum Ducem clarissimi scriptores adumbravere, vigiliæque & laboris patientissimum parum temporis somno, minimum odio dedisse. Ita dum multi vinum inter & epulas luxu fracti de bello consultant, laude quoque abstinentiæ & præcipue in Deum pietatis commendabatur, hoc solo cum infœlicitate fati luctatus, quod continentiæ & disciplinæ severus affectator, validiore remedijs malo, in corruptissimos militum mores, unicum gloriæ & fortunæ suæ impedimentum, incideri. Quare à clade Ludovici omnem per Frisiam supplicationum dies Regij Senatus decreto institutus, amburbiaque illustri victoriæ Pontificio ritu decreta. Cæterum prima Requesentij prospera rebellione mox cohortium, tum navalium pugnarum Hispanorumque per minores Frisios cladibus versatilis fortuna pensavit. Quippe foris victorem regium exercitum & sui fidentem intestina vitia corruperant, malisque indies invalescentibus regiæ fœlicitatis & potentiæ cursum remorabantur. Adeo ut, quantum publici luctus Ludovici & exercitus funera mœstissimo fœderi darent, tantum fere indignabundi mœroris è militarium cohortium seditione Requesentio nascereretur. Itaque à Ludovici clade per secreta patrum mœstum silentium erat, Hispanorum in castris & per præsidia urbium murmura & tumultus legionum audiebantur. Aurantium vero, ut ante futuræ adversitatis triste præsagium, ita præteritæ cladis atrocissimum vulnus tum iniquietabat.
units.tr: Having avenged themselves on the enemy and suffered no notable defeat, they returned to France. The victors gained little plunder, except that thirty standards and three siege engines added to their glory. Augustus Thuanus, drawing on the notes of Bernardino Mendoza, who led the cuirassiers in that battle, writes that Louis discharged the duty of a vigorous leader and a soldier alike, but was unhorsed and perished, swallowed up by the marsh. It was believed that Louis lost the day through his own plan, by which he meant to pursue the feigned flight of his foot soldiers and catch the scattered Spanish ranks with his fresh troops; and through the advice of another man, who, when the ground between the Meuse and the Waal was divided by marsh and ditches, had urged that the army should not yet be led on, but had poorly concealed his purpose and so exposed himself to danger and to the disaster that followed. Others hold that Louis gave his troops, worn out by a long march and by a scorching day in early spring, leave to halt at Mook, and that he entrusted the fortune of the battle to unreliable scouts. Reidanus, an excellent writer, adds that, relying on his own strength, Louis underestimated the weakness of the enemy, and that fate, which was to overthrow his fortune, corrupted the plans of the great commander, who was in his own opinion very strong. The same Reidanus states that Louis fell fighting, and that, had fate allowed, he would have far surpassed in glory the greatest commanders of the war in his time. For his military talent, though thought rash in conducting affairs, was not without prudence, and he kept the army's heavy obedience to orders and commands under firm and singular authority. Moreover, the most distinguished writers portray him as a civil man, skilled in winning minds by his speech and manners, and most patient of vigils and labour, who gave little time to sleep and little to hatred. Thus, while many, broken by luxury, debated the war over wine and feasts, he was commended for his abstinence and above all for his piety towards God. He struggled only against the unhappiness of fate in this one respect: being a strict pursuer of self-restraint and discipline, he sought to meet with stronger remedies the evil of the most corrupt soldiers' morals, which was the single obstacle to his glory and fortune. Therefore, after Louis's defeat, a royal Senate decree established a day of thanksgiving throughout Friesland, and a splendid victory was celebrated in the Papist manner in the city. Yet the fortune of war, shifting, balanced the early successes of the rebellion at Requesens, then the defeats of the Spanish in the naval battles and among the Lesser Frisians. For the royal army, victorious abroad and confident in itself, had been corrupted by internal vices, and these, growing stronger day by day, checked the progress of royal success and power. So it came about that the public grief at the death of Louis and his army was matched by an indignant sorrow arising from the mutiny of the cohorts at Requesens. Thus, after the defeat of Louis, a sad silence reigned among the senators in private, while the murmurs and tumults of the legions were heard in the Spanish camp and in the garrisons of the cities. Orange, as a sad presage of adversity to come, was now troubled also by the most bitter wound of the past defeat.

units.la: Sic scilicet infestam diu patriæ per civilia bella fortunam irasci potuisse, ut publicis cladibus fraternas & propinquorum neces subjungeret. Nec carissima pignora fato tantum ablata, caterum oculis subducta, incertum quo exitu, vitam finiisse. Iacere aut voragine paludum hauslos fratres, aut concremata. matis nullo solenni & hostili manu corporibus, sacrum ferali urnâ destitutum per deserta & squallentia spargi. Id fatum suæ domus esse, ut iratum regem, cum fide & officijs non posset, placare continuis furoribus debeat? Sic desæviri etiam in victos potuisse, ut non duorum fratrum cæde, non internecione aut fugâ exercitus, placatos victores crudelius consilium & intercepta defunctorum reliquiæ satiarent? Ita non alia sibi ab Hispano solatia relicta, quam quæ eripi nequiverint. Transcriptas haud dubiè cælo fraternas mentes novissimum spiritum infælici patriæ mancipasse, sed quæ aliquando vindicum illorum memoriam cultura sit. Quare grande ad novos luctus remedium superesse, actum scilicet fratribus præclarè ævum tam laudato exitu signari. Ita moriendo immortalitatem adeptos.
units.tr: Surely the fortune that had long been hostile to the fatherland through civil wars could be so angry as to add the deaths of brothers and kinsmen to public disasters. Nor were his dearest pledges taken from him by fate alone, but withdrawn from his sight, and he ended his life in an uncertain manner. His brothers lie swallowed by the abyss of the marshes, or, with no solemn rites and no enemy's hand to bury them, their bodies, burnt to ashes, are scattered through the wastes and the wilderness, the funeral urn left empty. Is this the fate of his house: that, unable to placate a king angered by his loyalty and services, he must placate him by continual madness? Could the Spaniard rage so cruelly even against the conquered, that neither the slaughter of two brothers nor the destruction or flight of an army should satisfy the victors, and that their cruel design should also feed on the remains of the dead that had been seized? Thus no other consolation was left to him from the Spaniard than what they had been unable to snatch away. Surely the brothers' minds, transferred to heaven, gave up their last breath for an unhappy fatherland, but the memory of those avengers will be cherished for some time. Therefore there remains a great remedy for new grief: it is clear that the brothers' life was gloriously spent, and that its end was made famous by such praise. So by dying they obtained immortality.

units.la: Tradunt nostrates concurrentium in aere acierum spectacula tum incidisse, cœlumque, sanguineis radijs velut rubescens, circa hæc fere tempora insolito fulgure obscurum noctis illustrasse. Quæ sive cruentæ ad Mocam cladis, seu ardescentium bellorum signa fuere, incertum. Unum observo Cornelium Gemmam sagacissimum cœlestium & arcanorum naturæ indagatorem cum ex oppositione Saturni ac Jovis circa Pleiadum sydus, tum ex inerrantium stellarum concursu; mense Aprili funesta atque exitiosa prædixisse, tempusque calamitatibus publicis, aut mutationibus rerum definitum Ludovici Nassovij clade, & mox Caroli ix. Gallorum Regis morte fœdatum.
units.tr: Our countrymen report that spectacles of armies clashing in the air appeared at that time, and that the sky, reddening as if with bloody rays, lit up the darkness of the night with an unusual flash around these very times. Whether these were signs of the bloody defeat at Mook or of wars about to blaze up, it is uncertain. I note only that Cornelius Gemma, the most shrewd investigator of heavenly and hidden things of nature, predicted from the opposition of Saturn and Jupiter near the Pleiades and from the conjunction of the fixed stars, in the month of April, funereal and deadly things, and a time defined by public calamities or upheavals, which was marked by the defeat of Louis of Nassau, and soon after by the death of Charles IX, King of the French.

units.la: Scribit Cambdenus in Annalibus Anglicis Theodorum Bezam ingeniosissimo carmine Novam Stellam Carolo ix. tanquam Herodi infanticidæ applicasse, monitoq; ut ad insoliti syderis & haud dubiè imminentia extrema ei portendentis occasum expavesceret, haud longo ab eo tempore per lentos & quidem acerbissimos cruciatus profluviaque, quem ad horrorem & simul satietatem effuderat, sanguinis, fatalem regno & simul vitæ diem obvenisse. Gasparus interim Roblesius res per Frisiæ provinciam curabat, aggerique marino intentus pelliciendis in partes regias minoribus Frisijs occupabatur. Quippe isthuc loci, superato, quod majores inter minoresque Frisios brevissimum est, freto, multitudo proscriptorum exulumque confluebat liberandæque patriæ consilia fabricabantur. Itaque portus & littora majoris Frisiæ à proscriptis exulibusque classe pulsata discrimen Roblesio dabant, securitatemque Præfecti, velut in pace regnantis, diurnis in continentem excursionibus obturbabant.
units.tr: Camden writes in his English Annals that Theodore Beza, in a most ingenious poem, compared the new star to Herod the infanticide, and warned Charles IX to dread the setting of that unusual star, which undoubtedly portended his final end; and that, not long after, the fatal day for his kingdom and at once for his life came upon him through slow and truly bitter torments and the flux of blood which he poured out in horror and surfeit. Meanwhile Gaspar Robles was managing affairs in the province of Friesland, and, intent on the sea-wall, was busy winning over the Lesser Frisians to the royal side. For there, across the strait which is very narrow between the Greater and the Lesser Frisians, a crowd of the proscribed and exiles was gathering and devising plans for freeing the fatfatherland. Thus the harbours and shores of Greater Friesland, struck by fleets of the proscribed and exiles, put Robles in danger, and by daily sallies into the mainland they disturbed the security of the governor, who reigned as if in peace.

units.la: Quare Roblesius, ut sedem bello in minoribus Frisijs recuperaret, ad Risvicium Medenblicanæ urbis, quæ Frisiæ majoris littori objacet, arcisque Satrapam litteras subornari fecit, quibus Risvicium, ut ad regem rediret, speciosis blandicijs hortabatur.
units.tr: Therefore Robles, in order to recover the seat of war in the Lesser Frisians, caused letters to be composed to Risvicius, governor of the city of Medemblik, which lies opposite the shore of Greater Friesland, and of its citadel, urging Risvicius with specious flatteries to return to the king.

units.la: Intellexisse se Risvicium nuper regi fidum, post in societatem fœderis pertractum, pœnitentiam defectioni tædio bellorum non semel obtendisse. Itaque sacramentum regium non dedignanter professurum, modo veniam anteactis impetrare queat. Et quoniam regiæ mentis non aliud consilium sit, quam ut urbes ac oppida citra dispendium humani sanguinis recuperet, ita velle, ut Risvicius pro se & conjuge veniæ certus Medenblicanam arcem regi tradat, extrema alias perseverantibus in rebellione decernenti. Isti quippe fini magnos & formidabiles terrâ marique rerum apparatus Philippum agitare, quo
units.tr: He had heard that Risvicius, lately faithful to the king, had afterwards been drawn into the league of the rebels, and had more than once alleged repentance of his defection, out of weariness of war. Therefore he would not disdainfully take the royal oath, provided he could obtain pardon for his past conduct. And since the king's mind had no other purpose than to recover cities and towns without the loss of human blood, he wished that Risvicius, assured of pardon for himself and his wife, should surrender the citadel of Medemblik to the king, while the king decreed extreme punishments for those who persisted in rebellion. For to that end Philip was preparing great and formidable forces by land and sea, to subdue Holland, Zeeland, and especially the Lesser Frisians.

units.la: Prodigia. clo. Io. LXXIV. Hollandiam Zelandiamque & minores præsertim Frisios domet. Redeuntibus vero ad obsequia Medenblicanis & ipsi Risvicio parciturum regem fore, ab ingenio clementem, & sui populi miserum. Ne quid dubii sit, se ac sua obligare, quin spondere filium suae simul & regiae fidei obsidem, cujus illustre documentum desiderio carissimi pignoris factururus sit. Adhæc sciret Risvicius non diuturnam fœderis fortunam fore, si potentia tot regnorum in unum coalesceat, gerendoque bello Philippus rex præficiatur, de cujus adventu certus esse queat. Adversa rebellantibus fata fore, & jam pridem haud procul Mosa ac Trajecto urbe deletas partes venturum exitium portendisse. Itaque petendum defectioni veniam aut expectandum bellum esse.
units.tr: Prodigies. 1574. Once the Medemblik men returned to obedience, the king would spare Risvicius himself, being by nature merciful and compassionate to his people. To remove any doubt, he would bind himself and his own, and would offer his son as a hostage for his loyalty and that of the king, and would give a remarkable proof of this by the loss of his dearest pledge. Moreover, Risvicius should know that the fortune of the alliance would not last long, if the power of so many kingdoms coalesced into one, and King Philip was set over the conduct of the war, whose arrival he could be sure of. Adverse fates awaited the rebels, and the destruction of the parties long since foretold that the ruin would come, as the king was soon to arrive not far from the Meuse and the city of Utrecht. Therefore they must seek pardon for their defection, or wait for war.

units.la: Hæc Leovardiæ scripta ac ad Risvicium missa nullius efficaciæ fuere. Similes quoque litteras Ericus Brunsuigius ad Enchusam Hornamque civitates dedit. Is namque conscripto Philippi regis nomine per Saxoniam exercitu, conterrendis, qui trans Flevum agebant, minoribus Frisijs duo equitum millia, decem peditum signa, haud procul Groningâ ac Lavica amne per Drentiæ fines circumferebat, validissimisque cum copijs castra ad Beilam metatus minori Frisiæ & istarum urbium præsidijs minabatur.
units.tr: These letters, written at Leeuwarden and sent to Risvicius, had no effect at all. Eric of Brunswick likewise sent similar letters to the cities of Enkhuizen and Hoorn. For, under the name of King Philip, he was carrying around with a Saxon army, to terrify those who were on the other side of the Vlie, two thousand horsemen and ten companies of foot in the Lesser Frisian lands, not far from Groningen and the river Lauwers, through the territory of Drenthe; and, having pitched his camp at Beilen with very large forces, he threatened the Lesser Frisians and the garrisons of those cities.

units.la: Interim misereri se divulsa à Rege gentù fidem faciebat, neque aliâ sollicitudine attineri, quam ut cessante bello cædum ac rapinarum tandem finis fit. Adhuc scilicet pœnitentiæ locum esse, miteque regis optimi ingenium clementiam polliceri. Esse quidem ad manum Philippo arma, in quorum apparatu esset, cæterum servati civis gloriam, quam ex oppresso decus mavelle. Severo ministrum Regis & Romani Imperij Principem daturum operam, quo Hornenses ac Enebusani, si ad regem redeant, urbesque Philippo permittant, publica pacis beneficium sentiant. Contumacibus vero & præfractis extrema parari. Nec ijs tantum, cæterum uxoribus liberisque ultimum discrimen imminere, quorum miserari naturæ affectus ac instinctus æternæ legis præciperet. Itaque velle, ut de ijs, quæ ad deditionem suarum urbium spectent, statuant eorum decretumque Senatus perferendum præconi curent.
units.tr: Meanwhile he made it plain that he pitied the peoples cut off from the King, and that his only concern was that, with the war ceasing, the slaughter and plunder should at last come to an end. There was still room for repentance, he said, and the gentle nature of the best of kings promised clemency. Philip indeed had arms at hand and the means to use them, but he preferred the glory of saving a citizen to the honour of crushing the oppressed. He would have a minister of the King, a prince of the Roman Empire, take pains that the people of Horn and Enkhuizen, if they returned to the King and allowed their cities to be handed over to Philip, would feel the benefit of public peace. For the obstinate and headstrong, however, the worst was being prepared. The danger threatened not only them but their wives and children as well, whom the natural affections and the instinct of eternal law required him to pity. He therefore wished them to decide on the matters concerning the surrender of their cities, and to have the Senate's decree carried to the herald and proclaimed.

units.la: Quæ ab Erico in castris Beilæ signata perlataque in minores Frisios contumaci silentio & non modica indignatione excepta. Ab aliijs vero in ludibrium contumeliamque Erici, velut in potestate fortunam & res provinciæ habentis, imperiosa autoritas conversa. Quare Ericus, nullâ urbium deditione sperată, æstiva per Drentiam in mensem Julium traxit, destinatâque in transmarinam provinciam expeditione abstinuit. Itaq; damna passim agris data, Drentiæq; finibus se non claudens exercitus ac in Stellingverfios se effundens omnem insolentiam patravit. Unde metus majori Frisiæ datus, quæ palam in partibus tum Philippi, clam fœderi addictior in Ludovici Nassovij clade Reip. vulnera dissimulabat. Quamobrem privato & domestico luctu pleræque domus occupabantur mœstaque civitates; quæ jam ante fœderi se adscripserant, publicis ovationibus secreta vulnera miscebant. Immodicæ namque per provinciam exactiones tum fiebant, præterque aggerum & belli impendia gravi annonâ miseri provinciales divexabantur.
units.tr: This letter, sealed by Eric in the camp at Beilen and carried into the Lesser Frisia, was received with stubborn silence and no small indignation. Others turned his imperious authority into mockery and insult, as if he held fortune and the affairs of the province in his hands. So Eric, with no surrender of cities to be hoped for, dragged out the summer in Drenthe into July, and gave up the expedition he had planned into the overseas province. Meanwhile damage was done to fields everywhere, and his army, not confining itself within the borders of Drenthe, spread out into Stellingwerf and committed every kind of insolence. This gave fear to Greater Frisia, which, openly on Philip's side at that time but secretly more inclined to the covenant, concealed the wounds of the state after the defeat of Louis of Nassau. For this reason most homes were taken up with private and domestic grief, and the towns were sad; those which had already joined the covenant mixed their secret wounds with public rejoicings. Excessive exactions were then being made throughout the province, and besides the costs of the dikes and of war, the wretched provincials were worn down by a heavy price for grain.

units.la: Notat Nicolaus consul Staurius in commentarijs suis, laftam fecalis centum florenis justi ponderis tum vænisse, populumque velut con-fluenfluentibus adversis obrutum extremâ rerum angustiâ tum egisse. Quippe mare veteres alveos emensum, haud vano naturæ miraculo, ipsâ æstate, Sole Tropicum Cancri ingresso, rariore æstu intumuit novique aggeris molem horrendâ eluvione disjecit. Unde segetes passim arvis vi fluctuum erutæ difficilem ultro annonam fecere. Notat scriptor Nobilissimus Sixtus Hemmingha in Genituræ suæ descriptione maxumam Frisiæ partem marinis aquis obtectam tum fuisse istamque calamitatem; quo incertitudinem Astrologicæ artis demonstraret, non influentijs aut conjunctionibus syderum, cæterum avaritiâ & socordiâ Præfectorum aggeris evenisse. Itaque discordi ultro nobilitate ac populo agrario validæ adversum eosdem Præfectos criminationes ortæ, velut destinata muniendo littori subsidia apud nonnullos cupidine opum & fœdissimo peculatu interciperentur. Quare censebant anniversarijs inundationibus non aliud remedium, quam rescriptum regis decerni posse, quo autoritate regnantis tot capitum dissensionibus & publicæ necessitati subveniretur.
units.tr: Nicolaus Staurius, the consul, notes in his commentaries that a last of inferior grain then sold for a hundred florins of full weight, and that the people, overwhelmed by converging disasters, were then living in the utmost distress. For the sea, having passed beyond its old channels, swelled in the summer itself, when the sun had entered the tropic of Cancer, with an unusually high tide, not by an empty wonder of nature, and with a dreadful deluge broke up the mass of the new dike. Thus the crops, torn from the fields by the force of the waves, made the grain scarce. The distinguished writer Sixtus Hemmingha notes, in his description of his own nativity, that at that time most of Friesland was covered by sea water and that this calamity came about, to show the uncertainty of the astrological art, not from the influences or conjunctions of the stars but from the greed and sloth of the dike prefects. So discord arose between the nobility and the farming people, and strong accusations were made against these same prefects: the means destined for fortifying the shore were, it was said, intercepted by some through greed for wealth and the most foul embezzlement. Therefore they thought that against the annual floods no other remedy could be decreed than a royal rescript, by whose authority the dissensions of so many heads and the public need might be relieved.

units.la: Quæ cum Philippum per equitum peditumque delectus passim gravaret ne obtinebat quidem Bruxellis Nitzenius, ut pensio honorarij æris quæ ad Martini festum præstanda erat, Frisijs condonaretur, aut ut Frisij militis regij stipendio applicarent. Quamvis proferret Legatus geminatas unâ æstate Friscarum terrarum inundationes mareque lunio mense iratum ipso quoque Bartholomæi die novas aquarum eruptiones arvis pascuisque superfudisse. Neque ajebat Legatus, alia Frisiorum rogas ex solâ liberalitate præbentium mens fuit, quam ut pecunia ista regis populique usibus inserviret, & ut bellorum, quæ multis casibus subjacerent, impendia, constituto velut sacro ærario, in extremis provinciæ periculis prospiceretur. Quæ quidem eo magis metuebantur, quod Roblesius Translavicanorum aggeribus lustrandis intentus inter cætera evulgasset, Ottonem Scouwenburgium cum equitum turmis in Frisiam contendere, istamque expeditionem firmandis apud contumacem populum indictionibus decerni. Quapropter re adhuc integrâ hærente etiam tunc apud Belgicæ Senatum Nitzenio Bruxellas amandatus Hector Ayta Iure-consultus & in Philippi Curia Senator, qui ijsdem mandatis insisteret, & ut Otto Scouwenburgius Frisiorum agris intentus & minax curis equestribus turmis minuendis, quæ supra modum increverant, Frisiorum damnis in alia locorum revocaretur. Scribit Ayta suum quoque ante adventum quosdam magnates Frisijs æquiores, & imprimis Viglium patruum id à Requesentio impetrasse, jussoque Scouwenburgio, etsi indignabundo, alio copias transferre, Frisiam isto tempore intactam direptionibus mansisse, litteras quoque à Roblesio & Senatu per Frisiam regio obtinendis Scouwenburgicis scriptas curante Viglio diu occultatas fuisse, Requesentijque decretum de mittendo in Frisiam Scouwenburgio intercessione patrui, velut legationi nepotis aliquid dantis, bono Frisicæ gentis rescissum. Quæ res Roblesium, valde offendit & quod consilia sua minus dextre, non speratis in Frisios aulæ favoribus, prosperarentur. Quare & Ulpium Aylva virum nobilem quod nupero comitio, vi. Kal. Iul. habito, amore patriæ libertatis &, ut post excusatum reperio, calore vini impulsus indictio-nibus nibus contradixisset, in arce regia & quidem teterrimo carcere, quem muliebrem vocabant vinculis dari jussit, rejectisque propinquorum supplicationibus, tanquam majestatis reo, extrema intentavit. Adversum quae ut manifestam vim spirantia etsi Ulpius publica voce in comitio obtestatus esset, ita maxima nobilitatis pars recte factum pronuntiavit, oblataque sponsione teterrima primo & illuvie foeda mox mitiore custodia liberavit. In intercessorum numero, ut illorum memoriae hoc detur D. Iacobus Leovardiensis Abbas Clarecampius, Goffo Abinga, Justus Herema, Renicus Camminga, Sibrandus Camminga, R. Andringa, Wattnia, Epius Douma, E. Herema, Scelto Tiarda, Siboldus Aylva, Petrus Camminga, Wibrandus Roorda, Edsardns Douma, Bauco Rommarda, Worpius Tiarda Iure-consultus, Tiepco Goslingha, & Dion Hania fuere.
units.tr: While these things weighed heavily on Philip through levies of horse and foot everywhere, Nitzenius at Brussels could not even obtain that the payment of the honorary money, due at Martinmas, be remitted to the Frisians, or that the Frisians apply it to the pay of the royal soldiers. The envoy argued that the Frisian lands had been flooded twice in one summer, and that the sea, enraged in June, had on St Bartholomew's day itself poured fresh eruptions of water over fields and pastures. Nor, the envoy said, had the Frisians, who gave their aid from sheer generosity, any other intention than that this money should serve the king's and the people's uses, and that the expenses of wars, which are subject to many chances, should be provided for in the extreme perils of the province, the money being set aside as a kind of sacred treasury. These things were all the more feared because Roblesius, intent on inspecting the dikes of the Translavian region, had among other things made known that Otto Scouwenburg was hastening into Friesland with squadrons of horse, and that this expedition was to be secured by levies on the stubborn people. Therefore, while the matter was still unsettled, Hector Ayta, a jurist and senator in Philip's court, was also sent by Nitzenius to Brussels, to the Council of Belgium, to press the same instructions: that Otto Scouwenburg, who was intent on the Frisian lands and threatening, should be recalled to other places, and that the cavalry squadrons, which had grown beyond measure, should be reduced, to the relief of the Frisian losses. Ayta writes that before his arrival some magnates more favourable to the Frisians, and above all his uncle Viglius, had obtained this from Requesens, and that when Scouwenburg was ordered to move his forces elsewhere, though he was indignant, Friesland remained free of plunder at that time. He also writes that the letters, written by Roblesius and the Senate to obtain royal orders through Friesland for Scouwenburg, were kept hidden for a long time through Viglius's care, and that Requesens's decree on sending Scouwenburg into Friesland was rescinded at his uncle's intercession, as if granting something to his nephew's embassy, for the good of the Frisian people. This matter greatly offended Roblesius, and because his plans were going less skilfully, the court's favours towards the Frisians not being hoped for. For this reason, too, when Ulpius Aylva, a noble man, at the recent assembly held on 26 June, moved by love of the country's liberty and, as I find after his excuse, by the heat of wine, had opposed the levies, Roblesius ordered him to be put in chains in the royal citadel, indeed in that most loathsome prison which they called the women's prison. Rejecting the entreaties of his kinsmen, he threatened him with the extreme penalty as a man accused of treason. Although Ulpius had called the public to witness in the assembly against these measures, which breathed manifest violence, the greater part of the nobility declared that he had acted rightly, and, when bail had been offered, first freed him from the most loathsome custody and then from the squalid, though milder, prison. Among the intercessors, so that their memory may be preserved, let these be named: Lord James, abbot of Klaarkamp near Leeuwarden, Goffo Abinga, Justus Herema, Renicus Camminga, Sibrandus Camminga, R. Andringa, Wattnia, Epius Douma, E. Herema, Scelto Tiarda, Siboldus Aylva, Petrus Camminga, Wibrandus Roorda, Edsardus Douma, Bauco Rommarda, Worpius Tiarda, jurist, Tiepco Goslingha, and Dion Hania.

units.la: Mox Philippus Rex, quo, invalidis Praefectorum suorum artibus, provincialium mentes pacis imagine demulceret, de rescribendo Veniae Edicto cogitavit, idemque Edictum Madriti scriptum consignatumque promulgari per omnem provinciam jussit. Quare & Requesentius quo mitiora Philippi consilia evulgaret, litteras in Frisiam expedivit, populumque dubium & quantum regiae clementiae daturus feret incertum ac animi haerentem speciosa securitatis fideique ostentatione pellicere conatus est.
units.tr: Then King Philip, so that by the feeble arts of his prefects he might soothe the minds of the provincials with an image of peace, thought of reissuing the Edict of Pardon, and ordered the same edict, written and sealed at Madrid, to be published throughout the whole province. Therefore Requesens, too, in order to spread Philip's milder plans, dispatched letters into Friesland, and tried to entice the people, who were doubtful and uncertain how much of royal clemency they would receive, and whose minds were wavering, by a show of specious security and good faith.

units.la: Itaque recitando diplomati & procurandis solemnibus pegma in foro sumptuoso paratu Leovardiae exstructum, quod diversis gradibus acclive modica altitudine exsurgebat. Circum aureum peripetasma Philippi insigne dependebat, Burgundicaeque & Austriorum imagines in horrorem populi aut reverentiam Principis speciosa & textili opere repraesentabantur. Pavimentum vero concolore panno constratum, sellaeque sericis pulvinis contectae regio ornatu visebantur. Solium quoque, quod Principi erectum erat, aureo velo obductum, reverentiamque ac majestatem absentis Philippi referebat. Pone Praefectus provinciae Roblesius spectabatur ramum olivae, velut pacis insigne, dextera tenens, circa quem Praeses Senatusque regius augusto consessu conspiciebantur. Tum Petrus Emskerckius Graphiarius Curiae silentio manu facto, circumstante populi, qui ex omni provinciae ora confluxerat, coronā diploma Philippi recitavit, regemque hoc modo differentem introduxit.
units.tr: So, for the reading of the diploma and the carrying out of the solemnities, a platform was built in the forum at Leeuwarden with sumptuous furnishings, rising by several steps at a gentle slope to a modest height. Around it hung a golden canopy bearing Philip's emblem, and images of the Burgundians and Austrians were displayed in fine woven work, to strike the people with dread or the prince with reverence. The floor was covered with cloth of one colour, and chairs with silk cushions were visible, arranged in royal style. The throne, too, raised for the prince and covered with a golden veil, represented the reverence and majesty of the absent Philip. Behind it stood the province's prefect Roblesius, holding in his right hand a branch of olive as a sign of peace, around which the president and the royal Senate were seen seated in august assembly. Then Peter Emskerck, the clerk of the court, having called for silence, and with the crowd that had flocked from every shore of the province standing round him, read Philip's diploma aloud, and in this way introduced the king as if he were speaking.

units.la: MALA quibuscum in provincijs Belgicae mea luctor, adeo publica sunt, ut celare neminem queam. Sexagesimus sextus annus foedissimus turbis initium dedit, fomenta vero subditi dedere, quos Dei, religionis Romanae, & veteris sacramenti contemptus nefariae adversum me conjurationis consilium suscipere fecit. Sic pelliciendae in partes multitudini faedus ictum, mox arma in me sumpta divinis ac humanis non pepercere. Ego vero miseratione rerum in deterius ruentium malis remedia praescripsi, ne in florentissimarum ditionum mearum & ipsorum quoque autorum perniciem tam cruda consilia verterentur. Caeterum ubi leni remedio nihil profeci exulceratis sensim animis, quo Deo, religioni, & dignitati meae satisfacerem, arma capere sistendis motibus & rebellibus frenandis coactus sum. Consilijs meis ac armis successus cessus non defuere. Itaque compressis vitiisque partibus, etsi nocentibus largiri clementiam potuissem, ita ratio mei principatus & tuendi juris ardor ad auxilia legum me pertraxit. Moderata tamen severitate usus sum, voluique ut paucos ad flagitiosos poena, ad multitudinem metus perveniret. Post vero ubi ordinandis provincijs me dedi, quas componi mea intererat, eorum arma sensi, quorum obsequia speraveram. Repressa ea uno impetu & velut turbine, extinctisque aut fugatis partium reliquijs, quo pacem meis terris redderem, Veniam dedi, quâ carere tantum eos volui, quos immanius crimen meae clementiae eximebat. Sic anno LXXII. sacramenta exuentes cuncta armis replevere, occupatisque per vim aut secreta consilia urbibus breve imperium pessimis moribus factisque polluerunt. Et quoniam per vim erepta non nisi per armorum subsidia recuperabantur, sparsas per omnem oram legiones recollegi, delectus habui. Inde tot peditum agmina, tot equitum turmae ereptis locis circumfusae, ut spes me habeat, propediem ne partium quidem reliquias fore. Sed misereri potius, quam desevire animus est, postquam imbecillum Reipubl. corpus & tot sectionibus depletum asperis remedijs curare non persevero. Ut id faciam tristis rerum per provincias meas facies & spectacula me movent. Illic urbes habitatoribus vacuae, agri cultoribus deserti, funerata commercia, attrita provinciarum opes cernuntur. Frequentiam populi ulteriore severitate converti in solitudinem nolo. Quin revocare exules, restituere proscriptos, bonos & manendi fidos profugis sociare meum potius consilium est, quo beneficia à me subditi accipiant; ego obsequia mihi conciliem meis majoribus praestita. Idem Sanatibus quod Forensibus apud me eveniet, cui regium & ab ingenio est iram simul cum injuriâ evincere. Magna humanae imbecillitatis apud me ratio est. Illum scilicet alieni consilij vehemens persuasio aut sui inopia, alium metus periculi, aut socordia circumvenit. Innocentibus nec meliora edoctis fati infelicitas proderit, omnes vos benigni nominis error aut temeritas excusabit. Itaque de consilio Ludovici Requesentij Proregis & Senatus, populo meo omne anteactum & enorme condono, statusque oppida, societates, & collegia in gratiam recipio. Idcirco mando Proregi, & per provincias Senatui, ne in praeteriti temporis res inquirant, quarum memoriam silentio aut oblivione obduxi. Neque volo ut ex anteacto crimine cujuspiam famae quid decedat, praeterquam eorum, quos indignos beneficio regio & meâ clementiâ justae damnationi reservo. Hoc vero jubeo ut à communione Romanae Ecclesiae separati paenitudinem agant sui erroris; absolvanturque pro ritu in Ecclesiâ recepto. Civitatibus vero, quae spretâ fide in partibus fuere, praecipio, ut intra bimestre se dedant meisque praesidijs permittant. Si secus fecerint exleges habebo in quas conferri ubertas mea clementia non debeat. Ceteris vero cujuscunque ordinis, sexus, aut aetatis sint; veniam anteactorum hoc ipso facio, omnibusque & singulis restitutionem eorum decerno, quae meae legis transgressione, durante civili bello, amisere. Daturus sum interim operam, ut quoniam ad tutelam populi fato votatus sum, jus atque aequum administrem, terrisque & ditionibus meis pacem at concordiam procurem. Populi salus suprema apud me lex erit.
units.tr: The troubles with which I struggle in the provinces of the Low Countries are so public that no one can hide them. The sixty-sixth year gave the disorders their foul beginning, but it was my subjects who supplied the fuel, those whom contempt for God, for the Roman religion and for the old sacrament led to take up a wicked plot against me. In this way a covenant was struck to draw the multitude to their side, and soon they took up arms against me, sparing neither divine nor human law. Yet I, moved by pity as affairs were sliding toward worse, prescribed remedies, so that such reckless designs would not turn to the ruin of my most flourishing dominions and of the authors themselves. But when a gentle remedy achieved nothing, and minds were gradually inflamed, I was compelled to take up arms to halt the disturbances and restrain the rebels, so that I might satisfy God, religion and my own dignity. My plans and arms did not lack success and failure alike. So, once the guilty parties were crushed and brought low, I could have been generous with clemency toward the wrongdoers, but the principle of my rule and my zeal for upholding justice drew me to the aid of the laws. Yet I used a moderate severity, and I wished that punishment should reach only a few criminals and fear should reach the multitude. But afterwards, when I devoted myself to settling the provinces, which it was my concern to put in order, I found arms raised by those whose obedience I had hoped for. Those arms I repressed in one onslaught, like a whirlwind, and with the remnants of the factions extinguished or put to flight, in order to restore peace to my lands, I granted a pardon from which I wished only those excluded whose crime was too monstrous for my clemency. So in the seventy-second year, casting off their oaths, they filled everything with arms, and, having seized towns by force or by secret plots, they polluted them with a brief rule of the worst morals and deeds. And since what had been snatched by force could be recovered only by the support of arms, I gathered together the legions scattered over the whole coast and held levies. Hence so many columns of infantry and so many squadrons of cavalry have surrounded the places they seized that I hope the remnants of the factions will soon not even exist. But my spirit is inclined to pity rather than to rage, since I do not persist in treating the feeble body of the commonwealth, drained by so many divisions, with harsh remedies. The sad face and spectacle of affairs in my provinces move me to do this. There one sees cities emptied of inhabitants, fields deserted by farmers, commerce buried, the resources of the provinces worn away. I do not wish the crowded population to be turned into a wilderness by further severity. Rather, it is my purpose to recall exiles, restore the proscribed, and join the good and loyal to those who fled, so that my subjects may receive benefits from me, and I may win back the obedience paid to my ancestors. The same will happen to the Senators as to the men of the courts with me, for it is in the nature of royal majesty to overcome anger together with injury. Human frailty weighs heavily with me. One man has been ensnared by the vehement persuasion of another's counsel or by his own lack of resources, another by fear of danger or by carelessness. The misfortune of fate will not harm the innocent who have not been taught better; the error or rashness of a benign name will excuse you all. Therefore, on the advice of Luis de Requesens, the Governor, and of the Council, I pardon my people for all past and monstrous offences, and I receive back into favour the towns, associations and guilds. I accordingly order the Governor, and the Councils through the provinces, not to inquire into the affairs of past time, whose memory I have covered with silence or oblivion. Nor do I wish anyone's reputation to suffer from past crime, except those whom I reserve for just condemnation as unworthy of royal benefit and of my clemency. This, however, I command: that those separated from communion with the Roman Church shall repent of their error, and be absolved according to the rite received in the Church. As for the cities which, having rejected their faith, have been on the side of the rebels, I direct that within two months they surrender themselves and entrust themselves to my garrisons. If they do otherwise, I shall have them as outlaws, to whom my clemency ought not to extend its bounty. But to all others, of whatever rank, sex or age they may be, by this very act I grant pardon for past offences, and I decree to each and all the restoration of whatever they lost through transgression of my law during the civil war. Meanwhile I shall take care, since by fate I am vowed to the protection of the people, to administer justice and equity, and to procure peace and concord for my lands and dominions. The welfare of the people will be the supreme law with me.

units.la: His additum, ut profugi & nuper foederis consortes in sua regressuri intra biduum apud Magistratus proxumorum oppidorum aut Senatum provinciae nomina sua, errores vero in religione apud Episcopum aut Delegatos Pontificis Romani profitentur & formulâ in ipclo. Io. so Veniae Edicto expresså. Bonorum vero & praesertim immobilium possessioni recuperandae agere apud Requesentium jussit, proxumumq; trimestre redituris in provincias praefinivit. Quae Madriti in tabulas redacta ac bullâ Gregorij xiii. Pontificis Romani confirmata, fidem tamen in animis hominum non invenere.
units.tr: To this was added that the fugitives and those lately joined to the covenant, on returning to their homes, should within two days declare their names before the magistrates of the nearest towns or the Council of the province, and confess their errors in religion before the bishop or the delegates of the Roman Pontiff, in the form set out in the edict of pardon, Io. so. He ordered them to bring suit before Requesens for the recovery of their goods, especially immovable property, and he set a period of three months for those who would return to the provinces. These matters were drawn up in records at Madrid and confirmed by the bull of Pope Gregory XIII, yet they found no trust in men's minds.

units.la: Creditum fuit populum foederatum per exempla tot annorum euntem & regiae fidei diffisum, spem stabilis clementiae ob exclusos à Veniâ concives sociosque posuisse, suumque discrimen ex alieno periculo æstumasse.
units.tr: It was believed that the people of the covenant, instructed by the examples of so many years and distrustful of royal good faith, placed their hope of stable clemency in the fellow citizens and allies excluded from the pardon, and judged their own danger by the danger of others.

units.la: Jam enim Philippus è primariâ nobilitate, ac agrariorum civiumque ordine praeclaris viris beneficium edicti ademerat, Doconisque Martnae, Oenonis & Vibij Grovensteiniorum, Suffridi Romkenij, Titi Hettinghae, Cypriani Anskenij Oosterzaei, Herconis Gulielmij Leovardiensis, & Ioachimi Fermerij Ecclesiastae Franequerani nomina, velut perduellium, recitabantur. Ita patria ipsumque mare gentibus commercijsque patens, errantibus foederatis infidum mansit. Annotatum in Notis Tarquinij Vallesij V. Consularis repetiio, eum quoque Veniae exemptum fuisse, Tzonerumque Vibenium Oldermannum Snecenfium, qui Philippi inaugurationi Bruxellis interfuerat, istud praemium adacti ad sacramentum Principis & collati in Philippum honoris tulisse. Tradunt autores Fredericum Perenottum publicando Veniae Edicto Ultrajectum à Requesentio missum cum Philippo Marnixio Aldegondio tentandae pacis secretum consilium tum injisse, negotiumque ad Ordines & Aurantium Principem perlatum successu caruisse. Volebant namque Ordines, ut externi militis missionem rex institueret, jusque Ordinibus faceret conventus ex arbitrio & pro necessitate rerum agendi. Quae ut iniqua Regi aut ejus Delegato videbantur, ita cum indignatione rejecta ineundae pacis actionem protraxere.
units.tr: For Philip had already taken away the benefit of the edict from distinguished men of the leading nobility and of the class of landowners and citizens. The names of Doco Martena, Oeno and Vibius of Grovestins, Suffridus Romkenius, Titus Hettinga, Cyprianus Anskenius of Oosterzee, Hercon Gulielmus of Leeuwarden, and Joachim Fermerius, minister of Franeker, were read out as if they were traitors. Thus the homeland, and the sea itself open to nations and commerce, remained hostile to the wandering confederates. It is noted in the notes of Tarquinius Vallesius, in the repetition of the consulship of the fifth year, that Tzoneras Vibenius, alderman of Sneek, who had been present at Philip's inauguration at Brussels, was also excluded from the pardon, and that he had received that reward as the price of his oath to the Prince and of the honour conferred on Philip. Authors relate that Frederick Perenot, when the Edict of Pardon was being published, was sent by Requesens to Utrecht with Philip Marnix of Aldegonde, and that then they entered upon a secret plan to attempt peace, but the business, when carried to the States and to Prince William of Orange, came to nothing. For the States wished the king to order the dismissal of foreign soldiers and to grant the Estates the right to hold assemblies as they judged and as the needs of affairs required. But since these demands seemed unjust to the King or to his delegate, they rejected them with indignation and so delayed the negotiation for a settlement.

units.la: Creditum fuit Requesentium Mocanae victoriae interventu animum ac consilium mutasse, quasi indignum majestate regnantis esset adblandiente belli fortunâ inter arma victricia & recentes triumphos in curas sanciendae cum populo suo pacis descendere. Philippum quoque Regem tanto continuandi per provincias suas belli desiderio flagrasse ut, rejectis rerum suarum & potissimum per Africam & mediterraneum mare curis, Tunetanum tum regnum, invadente Selymo Turcarum Imperatore, & cum eo paternae laudis aequandae opinionem amiserit. Addit Reidanus Francifcum quoque Valdesium, qui obsidione Leidam tenebat, ineundae pacis consilia tum retardasse, quo egenas & per luxum turbidas Hispanorum legiones urbis opulentae & quod praeconceperat, mox per vim expugnandae direptione ac spolijs sedaret. Huic rei validae classis & per Hispaniam armorum apparatus fama robur addebant, anxisque ultro foederatorum mentibus, velut innovante vetera sollicitudine, metum sinistri injiciebant.
units.tr: It was believed that Requesens changed his mind and plan after the victory at Mookerheyde, as if it were unworthy of the majesty of a reigning prince, while fortune of war smiled on him, to descend among victorious arms and recent triumphs to cares of establishing peace with his people. King Philip too was said to have been so inflamed with the desire of continuing the war through his provinces that, neglecting the affairs of his realm, especially those in Africa and on the Mediterranean, he lost the reputation of equalling his father's glory while Selim, the Emperor of the Turks, invaded the kingdom of Tunis. Reidanus adds that Francisco Valdez too, who held the siege of Leiden, then delayed the plans for making peace, so that he might sate the needy and riotous Spanish legions with the plunder and spoils of a wealthy city, which he had planned to take by force soon after. To this design the rumour of a strong fleet and of the preparation of arms in Spain lent weight, and by threatening the anxious minds of the confederates, as if old anxieties were renewed, they put fear into them.

units.la: Quem ut Requesentius provincialibus eximeret Ordinum Frisiae, ut & caeterarum provinciarum legatos, quae in partibus Philippi tum erant, Bruxellas evocavit. Ibi multa de Edicto Veniae praefatus regium & paternum Philippi animum suspectis apud quosdam clementiae praeconijs commendavit. Ita abrogatas decima vigesimaque exactiones & à Senatu capitalium re-rum, quem Albanus instituerat, in ordinarios confessus translata judicia promerendis provincialium animis, fuisse. Regia vero clementia non aliud beneficium reponi posse, quam si vicies centena aeris millia annuum tributum, necessarium bello subsidium, habeat, oblataque jam ante per Ordines liberalitatis sponsio adimpleatur. Semper quippe à publico subventum necessitati & aerario Principis fuisse, quem, pacis & Veniae largum, contumacia populi continuandum ad bellum & sumptuosos armorum apparatus cogeret. Itaque in conventum omnium Belgicae Ordinum differri negotium non posse, deficientibus militum stipendijs & exercitu regio aeris ac alimoniae indigo in turbas & seditiones, usitata egentibus vitia, propendente. Seditiosas vero legiones cogi per stipendia in ordinem & restitui disciplinam posse, sine qua bellum, ut sine animâ corpus, regi non queat.
units.tr: In order to free the Frisian States and the envoys of the other provinces, who were then in Philip's party, from this fear, Requesens summoned them to Brussels. There, after speaking at length about the Edict of Pardon, he commended the royal and paternal spirit of Philip with praises of clemency, which were suspect to some. Thus the taxes of a tenth and a twentieth had been abrogated, and the trials of capital crimes, which Alva had entrusted to a Council, had been transferred to the ordinary courts, in order to win the hearts of the provincials. But royal clemency could bestow no further benefit unless it had the annual tax of two million florins, a necessary subsidy for the war, and the promise of generosity already offered earlier by the States were fulfilled. For the public purse had always been called upon to meet the needs of the Prince's treasury, which, generous in peace and pardon, would be forced by the obstinacy of the people to continue the war and to costly preparation of arms. Therefore the business could not be deferred to a general assembly of all the States of the Low Countries, since with the soldiers' pay running out and the royal army lacking money and food, the troops were inclined to riots and mutinies, the usual vices of the needy. Mutinous legions could be brought back to order by payment and discipline restored, without which a war, like a body without a soul, cannot be governed.

units.la: Econtra Legati fidem erga Philippum regem obtestari, queri de patriae fortunâ & diuturnis civilium bellorum miserijs, quibus in praecipitium sanctissima carissimaque pignora traherentur.
units.tr: On the other hand, the envoys appealed to their loyalty to King Philip and complained of the country's fortunes and of the long miseries of civil war, by which their most sacred and dearest pledges were being dragged towards ruin.

units.la: Quippe avita religionis grande deliquium spectari, quam stabiliri sue sanguine legati mavelint, quam animum sacris majorum & regijs obsequijs vacantem novis opinionibus attaminare. Hoc vero asserenda tranquillitati rerum maxime requiri, ut indigenae regundis pro Philippo provincijs praesint, periti casuum, & in bello non unâ expeditione fidem ac virtutem professi. Sic equestres turmas à Mariâ Caesaris sorore ex ipsis provincialibus conscriptas praecipuum regij exercitus robur & fortunae instrumentum fuisse. Pugnasse pro sacris, pro incolumitate patriae & salute suorum pignorum, non abreptas in alias curas, quam ut sua adversum externa regum gentiumque arma tuerentur. Peregrinos vero non pro dominijs rerum, pro uxoribus, aut liberis certare, saterum are conductos venales manus pessimis facinoribus explendae avaritiae admovere. Vastare, rapere pro sacramento esse. Inde fieri ut opum saturi non petitis saepe missionibus suas in terras remigrent, dignitatesque facile partas facilius deserant. Sic ex mercenarijs fugitivos fieri, veterique licentiâ, quâ per nefas pecuniam corrasere, exuere sacramenta. Itaque Belgicae Ordines, principesque Aurei Velleris sub discessum Philippi regis è Belgicâ, de injurijs peregrinorum non incassum conquesto missionem Hispanicae legionis erasse, ac ut Gallici belli reliquiae assertâ pace provinciarum finibus exterminarentur. Perniciosam eam semper, & gravem sarcinam fuisse, publica provinciarum tributa privatos in usus damnato peculatu vertentem. Quare redeundum esse antiquam ad frugalitatem, erogandique aeris publici, ut olim Italico bello, potestatem indigenis faciendam. Adhaec enormem insolentiam militari lege à tribunis coercendam, quos adesse ad exercitum oportebat, ne quid dispendij privatae res & publica libertas trahant, cujus rationem provinciarum Praefecti prisci semper temporibus habuissent. Sic patrium jus, Praefecturam tenente Mariâ Hungariae Reginâ Caroli Caesaris germanâ, rite assertum mansisse, esseque è repub. modernos dominantium mores optimae & principis faemina imperio assimilari. Leni rectore, & quem elementia ac majestas, non arma & copiae muniant, ducendum populum, qui maxime velit regem ipsum intra Pyrenaeos suos ac mare Oceanum velut consepto clausum, in curas Belgicae suae caterarumque ditionum defendere. Sic prae-
units.tr: Indeed, they said, it was a great offence against ancestral religion, which the envoys preferred to see upheld with their blood, that a mind devoted to the sacred rites of our forefathers and to royal obedience should be tainted with new opinions. Moreover, to secure tranquillity, it was especially necessary that natives should govern the provinces on Philip's behalf, men skilled in local affairs who had proved their loyalty and courage in war on more than one campaign. Thus the cavalry squadrons raised from the provincials themselves by Maria, Caesar's sister, had been the chief strength of the royal army and an instrument of its success. They had fought for sacred things, for the safety of their country and the welfare of their dear ones, their only care being to defend their own against the arms of foreign kings and peoples. Foreigners, on the other hand, did not fight for the ownership of property, wives or children; hired and sold for pay, they turned their hands to the worst crimes to satisfy their greed. To ravage and plunder was, for them, a matter of routine.
