Hence it happened that, sated with wealth, they often returned to their own lands without asking for discharge, and easily abandoned the offices they had easily gained. Thus mercenaries became deserters, and, with the old licence by which they had wickedly scraped together money, they cast off their oaths. Therefore the Belgian Estates and the knights of the Golden Fleece, when King Philip left the Netherlands, complaining not without cause of the injuries done by foreigners, had ordered the discharge of the Spanish legion, and that the remnants of the French war be expelled from the borders of the provinces once peace was secured. That force had always been a pernicious and heavy burden, turning the public taxes of the provinces to private use through a condemned embezzlement. Hence they must return to the old frugality, and the power of spending public money must be given back to the natives, as once in the Italian war. Besides, the enormous insolence must be curbed by military law through tribunes, who ought to be present with the army, lest private affairs and public liberty suffer loss; a principle the former prefects of the provinces had always observed. Thus the native law had been properly maintained while Maria, queen of Hungary and Charles Caesar's sister, held the governorship; and it was for the good of the commonwealth that the present manners of rulers should be made like the rule of that excellent princess. The people, who most wish the king himself to be shut up within his Pyrenees and the Ocean sea as within a fence, should be led by a gentle ruler, one protected by clemency and majesty rather than by arms and troops, to defend their interests in Belgium and the other dominions. Thus

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXIV. praesentiâ haud dubiè ac majestate regnantis, ut olim Carolo Caesare, obsequia offensis animis reditura, reviviscuramque concordiam florentissimis nuper terris proscriptam. Sin vero regni Hispaniae negotia absentiam regis non ferant, Senatum Belgicae gentis in Hispaniâ habendum esse, quo de statu ditionum suarum Rex cognoscat, animusque regius fide veri instruatur.
units.tr: 1574. Then, through the king's presence, undoubtedly and through his majesty, as once under Charles Caesar, the offended spirits would return to obedience, and concord, lately banished from the most flourishing lands, would revive. But if the affairs of the kingdom of Spain did not allow the king's absence, a senate of the Belgian people should be held in Spain, through which the king might learn the condition of his dominions, and his royal mind be furnished with the truth.

units.la: Quorum omnium ut vanam spem Requesentius faciebat, ita de arduis scripturum se ocyus ad Philippum regem pollicebatur. Quare legati non æquis animis in Frisiam caeterasque provincias regressi Ordinum Brabantiæ & alienis patrocinijs tuendi patrij juris consilia commendavere. Sic infidæ sub Requesentio res fluebant, dolosisque cinenibus contecta incendia supponebantur. Erant quippe qui recordarentur Requesentium Granatense per regnum Proregis personâ & dignitate ante quadriennium functum, fraudulentis artibus credulam Mauritaniæ gentem circumvenisse, fideque & mandato foedisimè abusum, simplicem populum specie amicitiæ, & quidem per supplicia & sanguinem, suorum, pessimo servitio implicasse.
units.tr: Just as Requesens made all these promises an empty hope, so he promised to write about these grave matters to King Philip as quickly as possible. Therefore the envoys returned to Friesland and the other provinces not in peace of mind, and commended to the Estates of Brabant and to foreign patrons their plans for defending their native rights. Thus affairs under Requesens were drifting towards faithlessness, and fires were being laid beneath deceitful ashes. For there were those who recalled that Requesens, who a little more than four years before had held the office and dignity of viceroy in Granada, had deceived the credulous Moorish people by fraudulent arts, and had grossly abused his trust and commission, entangling the simple people, under the guise of friendship, in the worst slavery, indeed through executions and bloodshed.

units.la: Econtra firmandis in melius provincialium animis hoc repertum credebatur, quod Albani statuam populi oculis, velut rem invidiæ plenam, submovisset, credereturque, amoto infami monumento, praedecessoris imperium & hoc fallacis gloriæ spectaculum tacitâ superbiæ insimulatione damnasse. Thuanus tradit, Regi quoque Philippo erectæ statuæ consilium displicuisse missoque in Provincias Requesentio speciale mandatum dirruendæ invisæ moli dedisse. Itaque Trophæum, quod Albani clarissimi suâ ætate Imperatoris gloriæ erectum erat, dehonestamento, velut confundente superbiam adversâ fortunâ, tanto postmodum Duci cessisse. Ego existumo Philippum Regem non tam odio Albani, cui privato etiam post depositum imperium multa deferebat, quam sedandis laesi & jam eluctantis populi armis id donasse, quo diruto superbæ vanitatis & regiæ fortunæ æmulo opere, magis odia gentis in se & Albanum, quam dignitatem revocati Proregis minueret.
units.tr: On the other hand, it was believed that a measure had been devised to strengthen the minds of the provincials for the better: Alva had removed from the people's sight his statue, as something full of hatred, and it was believed that, the infamous monument being removed, he was condemning his predecessor's rule, and this spectacle of false glory, with a silent imputation of pride. Thuanus relates that the plan of an erected statue had also displeased King Philip, and that, sending Requesens into the provinces with a special mandate, he ordered the hated structure to be torn down. Thus the trophy which had been erected to the glory of the emperor, in Alva's most illustrious time, was dishonoured, as if adverse fortune were overthrowing pride, and afterwards yielded to so great a Duke. I think King Philip granted this demolition of the work of vain pride and rival to royal fortune not so much from hatred of Alva, to whom he granted many favours even as a private man after laying down his command, but to calm the arms of an injured and now struggling people; so that by tearing down the monument he would lessen the people's hatred towards himself and Alva rather than diminish the dignity of the recalled viceroy.

units.la: Notat F. Nicolaus V. Consularis Fredericum Hornium, Jacobi Comitis Hornani nothum, regio nomine Stavoranæ arcis triginta, & amplius annorum Satrapam & Praetorem Hemelolpherdium vitâ tum excessisse, Martinumque Bajartum cohortis Valonicæ Tribunum ci à Praefecto Senatuque regio suffectum. Unde odia magis in Roblesium aucta, quod amotâ & velut spretâ gentis nobilitate, praeclaram dignitatem etiam recenti apud Requesentium querimoniâ, in cohortis Tribunum hominem peregrinum contulisset. His asperata in foederatos per Frisiam edicta, damnatoque cum proscriptis exulibusque commercio fama novarum exactionum fomenta largiebatur. Jam enim Requesentius inopiam aerarij, & simul adversitatem fortunæ non dissimulabat, quæ terrâ marique lacertos moventem in diversa sollicitudinum trahebat. Itaque inefficaci Veniæ edicto litteras in Hispaniam dedit, quibus Philippum Regem instruendam ad classem hortabatur.
units.tr: F. Nicolaus V. Consularis notes that Frederick Horn, the bastard son of Count Jacob of Horn, who for more than thirty years had been governor and praetor of the Stavoren castle on the king's behalf, and Hemelolpherd then died, and that Martin Bajart was appointed tribune of the Walloon cohort by the prefect and the royal Senate. Hatred was therefore increased still more against Roblesius, because, the nobility of the nation being removed and as it were scorned, he had conferred the honourable office of cohort tribune on a foreign man, even after the recent complaint to Requesens. These measures, together with edicts against the confederates in Friesland and the banning of trade with the proscribed exiles, exasperated matters, and the rumour of new exactions supplied fuel. For already Requesens did not conceal the poverty of the treasury and the adversity of fortune, which drew in different directions a man who was moving his forces by land and sea. Therefore, by an ineffective edict of pardon, he sent letters to Spain urging King Philip to fit out a fleet.

units.la: Frustra scilicet bellum geri adversus istum populum, qui maris ac portuum beneficio potens non nisi compedito eodem mari, aut compresis fluminum ostijs vinc vinci queat. Itaque elementum terris circumfusum validissimâ prius classe cI). I). domandum. Esse quidem tot flumina Scaldim, Mosam, Rhenum, Flevum LXXIV. latissimis alveis in Oceanum se effundentia, sed quorum usus intuto foederatis mari esse non posset. Ubi illud domitum aut depurgatum fuerit, tum demum sensuros angustiam foederatos sola in continente sine mutuis auxilijs pugnaturos. Nunc discretam amnibus portubusque gentem mutuâ ope invalescere & facili trajectu naves copiasque ad incursum externae potentiae conjungere. Ibi praesto esse ubi periculum fit, invictos haud dubiè, nisi confertim regiâ mole & multitudine classium obruantur. Hoc ut fiat, navalia in promptu, aut si portubus Belgicae regiae naves prohibeantur, tutas in confinio stationes esse. Patere Amasum, amplissimum Germaniae flumen, lato sinu utrosque Frisios lambentem. Adhaec Embdam urbem commercijs validam, ut Philippo regi infidam ita fomenta & suffugia foederi praebentem. Satis causae esse gentium jure locum occupare Edzardi imperio parentem & Philippo inimicum. Neque enim violari Germaniae jura propendentis in partes, & restitui post repetenti Edzardo sua posse, si apud Caesarem agat Imperio fines asserturum.
units.tr: Clearly it was vain to wage war against that people, who, powerful through seas and harbours, could not be conquered unless that very sea were chained, or the mouths of the rivers were closed. So the element surrounding the land must first be subdued by a very strong fleet. Indeed there are so many rivers (the Scheldt, the Meuse, the Rhine, the Vlie) pouring into the ocean through broad channels, but their use cannot be safe for the confederates at sea. When that was subdued or cleared, then at last they would feel the narrowness of their position and fight on the mainland alone, without mutual aid. Now a people divided by rivers and harbours grows strong through mutual help, and by easy crossing joins ships and forces to meet a foreign power's attack. There they are at hand wherever danger arises, undoubtedly unconquerable, unless they are crushed by the royal mass and multitude of fleets. To bring this about, shipyards should be ready, or, if the royal ships are barred from the harbours of Belgium, safe stations should be set up on the border. The Ems, the most ample river of Germany, spreading in a broad bay, touches both Frieslands. Besides, Emden, a city strong in commerce, faithless to King Philip, offers help and refuge to the confederacy. There was sufficient reason to occupy the place by the law of nations, since Edzard, who obeys the Empire, is hostile to Philip. Nor would the rights of Germany be violated by taking sides, and Edzard could afterwards have his own restored if he pleaded before the Emperor, who would assert the boundaries of the Empire. 1574.

units.la: Quare Rex Philippus naves adornari per omnem maritimam Hispaniam fecit, aliasque exoticarum gentium commercia, per idem regnum exercentes detineri complerique milite jussit. Caeterum stupendâ classe fatalibus iris consumptâ magnarum rerum praeconcepti conatus inriti fuere. Igitur, navali expeditione infructuosâ, arma per continentem acrius mota Philippi regis animum aperuere. Mox tributa bello per Senatum regium specie militarium stipendiorum flagitata, quae jam ante, intactâ principis armis libertate, ipso populi comitio, assensu Ordinum, imperata ex aequo poscentibus decernebantur. Sic, quod populi longo saeculorum ambitu post extinctos gentis nostrae reges durante libertate fuerat, in Principis regisve dominationem transmigrabat, fundamentaque si fato licuisset surrecturae tyrannidi non obscuris indicijs substernebantur. Quâ in re mihi mortalium rerum ludibria contemplanti notare libet, summae potentiae raro modum fuisse, libidinemque ac superbiam dominantium vergentem ut plurimum & inclinantem potentiam antecessisse. Itaque nullâ comitiorum lege, quibus majores pace ac bello de rebus arduis consultabant, menstruae exactiones per vim repetitae, tributumque duorum stuferorum & dimidij singulos in Florenos aureos à Senatu regis ordinatum fovendis etiam malis suis infoelicem populum adigebat. Provinciales quoque idem tributum, vacante id temporis quaestorio munere, Gulielmo Brouckio apparitori Senatus decimum intra & quartum diem pendere jusi, regressique in provinciam à publicato Veniae Edicto profiteri nomina sub poenâ carceris & animadversionis coacti. Ita conculcato Ordinum jure & collecto per edictum aere Roblesius minores in Frisios expeditionem paravit, navesque xiv. onerarias adornari Snecae fecit, quarum alveos ultra communem modum excavatos armato milite compleverat. Summa vero navium levi cespite constrata, quem, deficiente sensim caeduâ, bituminosis terris effossum agrarij magnâ copiâ in fiet, confinem oram modicis navigijs emittebant. Quarum rerum famâ in minores Frisios perlata (quos regij per Hispaniam apparatus fama ad incIↄ. Iↄ. instruendam classem compulerat) instructæ ocyus naves in altum missæ, assecutæque Roblesij onerarias quæ incerto cursu per æstuaria jactabantur, in præcipitem fugam datas, Stauricum ad littus elisas adegere. Clasiarius milesque regius clam se subducens vitæ servatus est. Traditum annalibus civem quendam Snecensem, qui nuper in partibus Scouwenburgicis fuerat, noctu clam superato vallo urbe emissum, Enchusanos istius rei monuisse. Alij credebant minores Frisios, Aurantij principis litteris instructos, omnem majoris Frisiæ oram speculatorijs tum navigijs prælegisse, dispositisque per portus & marinum aggerem, qua majorem Frisiam respicit, excubijs in Roblesij secreta inquisivisse. Sic foris adverso fato res Roblesij intra provinciam magna provincialium invidia foedissimas ob exactiones agitabantur. Quippe Roblesius exercendæ potestatis immodicus, quo etiam vigentibus populi odijs obsequentem sibi fortunam, & subsidia bello pararet, novis inauditisque vectigalibus provinciæ tum minabatur, regiumque & Requesentij mandatum continuis exactionibus obtendebat. Quare Leovardiæ Comitium Ordinum provinciæ indixit, ædemque Jacobæorum habendo conventui designavit. Ibi Achlenius Præses Senatus verba fecit Ordinesque hunc in modum adlocutus est.
units.tr: Therefore King Philip had ships fitted out throughout all maritime Spain, ordered the commerce of foreign peoples carried on in that kingdom to be detained, and the ships to be filled with soldiers. But the stupendous fleet was consumed by fatal storms, and the great enterprises conceived in advance came to nothing. Thus, the naval expedition proving fruitless, arms set in motion more fiercely on the mainland revealed the king's intention. Soon taxes for the war were demanded by the royal Senate under the pretext of military pay; before, while the prince's arms had not yet touched liberty, such taxes had been decreed by the assembly of the people itself with the consent of the Estates, imposed on those who asked for them equitably. Thus what had remained with the people, through a long course of centuries after the kings of our nation were extinguished, while liberty endured, was passing into the domination of a prince or king, and the foundations of a tyranny, which fate would have allowed to rise, were being laid with no obscure signs. In this matter, as I contemplate the jests of mortal affairs, I like to note that the limit of supreme power has rarely been observed, and that the lust and pride of rulers have usually gone before, leaning and inclining power towards excess. Thus, with no law of assemblies by which the greatest men had deliberated on grave matters of peace and war, monthly exactions were extracted by force, and a tax of two and a half stuivers on each gold florin, ordained by the royal Senate, forced the unhappy people to pay even for their own afflictions. The provincials too were ordered to pay the same tax within fourteen days, the quaestorship then being vacant, to Willem Brouckhuis, an attendant of the Senate; and on returning to the province after the pardon edict was published, they were compelled, under penalty of imprisonment and punishment, to register their names. Thus, trampling on the right of the Estates and raising money by edict, Roblesius prepared an expedition against the Lesser Frisians, and had fourteen transport ships fitted out at Sneek, whose hulls he had hollowed out beyond the usual measure and filled with armed soldiers. The ships were covered with light turf, which, as the cutting gradually failed, was dug in large quantities from bituminous land for the farmers, and they sent these along the nearby coast with modest vessels. When the report of these things reached the Lesser Frisians (whom the rumour of royal preparations throughout Spain had already driven to equip a fleet), ships were quickly fitted out and sent into the open sea, and they overtook Roblesius' transports, which were being tossed about on an uncertain course through the estuaries, forced them into headlong flight, and drove them ashore on the Stavoren coast. The naval officer and royal soldier, slipping away secretly, was saved alive. It is recorded in the annals that a certain citizen of Sneek, who had recently been on the Schouwen side, having secretly crossed the rampart at night and been let out of the town, warned the men of Enkhuizen of this matter. Others believed that the Lesser Frisians, furnished with letters from Prince William of Orange, scouted the whole coast of Greater Friesland with reconnoitring ships, posted watches at the harbours and along the sea dyke facing Greater Friesland, and so inquired into Roblesius' secret plans. Thus abroad, with fate turned against him, Roblesius' affairs within the province were thrown into turmoil, amid great hatred of the provincials because of the most foul exactions. For Roblesius, immoderate in exercising power, who, while the people's hatred was running high, sought to secure a fortune obedient to himself and subsidies for the war, threatened the province with new and unheard-of taxes, and used the royal and Requesens' mandate as a pretext for continual exactions. Therefore he summoned a meeting of the Estates of the province at Leeuwarden, and designated the church of St James for the assembly. There Achlenius, president of the Senate, spoke and addressed the Estates in this manner.

units.la: NOn modico gaudio, Ordines, Roblesij Præfecti animum vestra præsentia & hic cætus perfundit. Præterquam enim, quod occasionem nactus sit diluendi calumnias, quibus maledicentium invidia impetitur, ita obtestari fidem suam mea voce voluit, nihil se unquam ab inchoato per provinciam Regis imperio egisse, quin publicè conduceret. Hoc vero præcipuè curasse, ne quid damni per externam vim provincia pateretur, caeterum, turbatissimâ etiam temporum ætate, quæ convellendis rebus videbatur, quies ei aut securitas esset. Recenti factorum memoria non opus est exemplis. Nec Vectigalium novorum, ob quæ vos convocari fecit, alia apud illum ratio, aliud secretum est, quam ut assignatis, collato à vobis ære, militi stipendijs, & restitutâ belli disciplinâ pacem publicam habeatis, armorumq; tutelæ vos, liberi vestri, atque conjuges subsistis. Isti rei litteræ Præfecti ac Senatus omnem in provinciam misæ testimonium dabunt, novamque Vectigalium legem, non à Præfecti ingenio, caeterum Requesentij mandato, aut rescripto regis procedere. Qui etsi patrijs legibus & incolumitati vestræ, Ordines, nihil detractum velit, tamen quoniam affectas erarij opes diuturna arma & sumptuosius bellum fecerunt, stipendia cohortium aliunde petenda sunt. Nam florenis aureis, quod genus tributi majores vestri ex usu reperere, plus oneris imponere, res soli & impendia aggerum non ferunt, quos Roblesius adversus tempestuosum mare & certis vicibus in terras vestras se effundens, majore curâ dubium an industriâ præmunivit. Pensioni quoque centum & viginti octo millium aureorum, (quam honorarium vos Regi, Rex creditoribus assignavit) ut decedere quid nequit, ita alendis sustentandisque copijs certum & diuturnum subsidium requiritur. Neque enim mensium, aut unius annifuror nos exercet, caeterum nostrâ infœlicitate cum tempestate luctamur multos in annos exiturâ. Quamobrem diuturnis malis quærenda remedia procurandaque cohortibus stipendia sunt, disciplinæ vincula, & vestræ quoque incolumitati servitura. Sin vero invisa collationum Vectigaliumque vocabula vos deterterrent, alia quaerite vestris moribus congrua & cogendis pecuniis idonea. Quod si feceritis, Ordines, satisfactum Praefecto erit, quem alias ad promulgandam novarum Vectigalium legem vestrae contumaciae crimen & ultima rerum necessitas incitabunt.
units.tr: Not without great joy, you Estates, does the presence of you and of this assembly fill the mind of the Governor Robles. For apart from the fact that he has had the chance to refute the slanders by which the envy of ill-wishers assails him, he wished to vouch for his good faith through my voice: that he has never done anything in the province in the name of the king's rule, begun as it was, which did not serve the public good; and that he has taken especial care that the province should suffer no harm from foreign force, and that, even in a most troubled age, which seemed bent on overturning everything, there should be peace and safety for you. There is no need of examples from recent memory. Nor has he any other reason or purpose in the new taxes, for which he had you called together, than that, with the money contributed by you assigned to the soldiers' pay, and with military discipline restored, you may have public peace, and your children and wives may rest under the protection of arms. The letters of the Governor and of the Council sent into the whole province will bear witness to this, and show that the new tax law proceeds not from the Governor's own disposition but from the command of Requesens, or from the king's rescript. Although he wishes nothing to be taken from your native laws and your security, Estates, nevertheless, since the long wars and the more costly fighting have exhausted the treasury's resources, the pay of the cohorts must be sought elsewhere. For the florins of gold, the kind of tax which your ancestors devised for your advantage, cannot bear a heavier burden; the nature of the soil and the expense of the dykes do not allow it, which Robles has fortified against the stormy sea, and against the land which at certain times pours itself over your fields, with more care than, I fear, skill. Moreover, the pension of one hundred and twenty-eight thousand gold pieces (which the king has assigned to the creditors, as the honorarium you gave the king) cannot be deferred, and therefore a certain and lasting support is required to feed and sustain the troops. For we are not struggling with the fury of a month or of a single year, but with our misfortune, which will last with the storm for many years. Therefore remedies must be sought for long-lasting ills, and pay must be provided for the cohorts, which will serve the bonds of discipline and also your own safety. But if the hated names of contributions and taxes deter you, seek other means suited to your customs and effective for raising money. If you do this, Estates, the Governor will be satisfied; otherwise the charge of your obstinacy, and the final necessity of affairs, will urge him to promulgate the new tax law.

units.la: Quâ Achlenij oratione audità Ordinum mentes novitate rei, quam jam ante solo rumore acceperant, perculsæ ferò in convulsam robusto Principis imperio libertatem tum respexere. Itaque Ordines ex Oo- ltergois Scipionem Meckamam, è Westergois Martinum Nitzenium delegavere, qui copiam diplomatis regij ac mandatorum à Graphiario Senatus poscerent. Ordinumque voluntatem Roblesio exponerent. Is vero, remisso ad Ordines eodem Graphiario, recitari tantum diploma jussit, copiamque edicti & simul mandatorum delegatis recusavit. Hoc etiam volebat, ut posterò sine ullâ dilatione quid statueretur, Ordinesque novam Vectigalium legem acciperent damnarentve, eâque de re SCtum perscriberent. Quare sequenti die ad Roblesium, qui in arce regiâ Senatum habebat, Bocatius vicarius Ripensis & Adrianus Cronenburgius misi copiam iterum diplomatis poposcere, sine quâ Ordines, præterquam spectata Regis mente, rescribere se non posse constantibus formatisque in confidentiam verbis reporebant. Igitur Roblesius, perrogatis Senatus suffragijs, Graphiarium in conventum Ordinum ablegavit, copiamque Edicti se in posterum exhibiturum fidem fecit. Hac tamen cautione interposità, ne quid morae deliberationi Ordinum interveniret, novæque Vectigalium legis publicatio socordiâ aut contatione Ordinum cessaret. His addebat de erogandis pecunijs & creando quaestore se non multum laborare, quin tacere Ordinibus distribuendi aeris potestatem, cujus quoque jam ante accepti rationes offerret. Igitur se suaque pignori obtulit, Ordinumque benevolentiam post emercari speciosis blandiciis conatus est. Caeterum Ordines ad Achlenij postulata hunc in modum responderunt.
units.tr: When this speech of Achlenius had been heard, the minds of the Estates, struck by the novelty of the matter, which they had already learned of by mere rumour, then looked back upon their liberty, shaken by the strong rule of the prince. And so the Estates chose Scipio Meckama from Oostergo and Martin Nitzenius from Westergo, who were to demand a copy of the royal diploma and of the commands from the secretary of the Council, and to set out the will of the Estates before Robles. He, however, sent the same secretary back to the Estates and ordered only that the diploma be read aloud; he refused to give a copy of the edict and of the commands to the delegates. He also wished that, without any delay afterwards, a decision be made, and that the Estates either accept or reject the new tax law, and write down a decree on that matter. Therefore on the following day Bocatius, vicar of Ripen, and Adrian Cronenburg were sent to Robles, who held the Council in the royal citadel, and again asked for a copy of the diploma, without which, they declared in firm and carefully chosen words, the Estates could not give an answer, apart from knowing the king's mind with confidence. Then Robles, having asked the votes of the Council, sent the secretary to the assembly of the Estates, and made it clear that he would provide a copy of the edict in future. Yet with this caution attached, that no delay should stand in the way of the deliberation of the Estates, and that the publication of the new tax law should not be held up by their sloth or wrangling. To these matters he added that he was not much concerned about the spending of money and the appointment of a treasurer, and that he would not hesitate to leave to the Estates the power of distributing the money, whose accounts, received earlier, he would also offer. So he offered himself and his affairs as a pledge, and tried to win the goodwill of the Estates afterwards by specious flatteries. The Estates, however, answered Achlenius's demands in this manner.

units.la: Convocati sumus, Praefecte, tuo consilio & Igramum Achlenium Praesidem verba facientem in comitio audivimus, quibus nova Vectigalia aut tributa pensitandis militum stipendijs postulabat. Nos vero etsi Saxonicæ conventiones, quas cum eo tanquam provinciæ Gubernatorc, injimus, præstare immunes ulteriorum onerum queant, Ita Florentium Iscilsteinium Hispaniæ Princeps Carolus non aliâ lege regundæ provinciæ præfecit, quam ut Saxonum imperijs suum assimilaret. Sacramentum quoque solemnepatrijs legibus adjuratum & majorum immunitatum spem clementia novi Principis tum fecit. Nec ore tenus haec dicta factaque, caeterum confirmata monumentis ad nos posteros pervenere. Neque infra majestatem Caroli Caesaris fuit fidem anteactis conventionibus pacisci. Hoc vero assignato Caesari patrimonio & annuo censu impetravimus, ne quod tributum extra conditum penderemus; sed ut omnium servitutum exactionumque immunes nos ac posteri seram in propaginem quiete ac publicâ pace frueremur. Religione jurisjurandi Caesar Carolus & Philippus Rex se obstrinxere, cum imperium deferri non nisi adacto ad sacramentum Principi voluimus. Rescriptis proregum Albani & Requesentij idem obtinuimus accepimusque per Legatos regiæ fidei & nostræ liberati nihil defore. Itaque ordinario Principis censui centum & viginti octo millia aurecorum adjecimus. jecimus, quo de affectu in Philippum Regem testaremur & ut æs erario provinciæ inlatum, adversus ingruentia casuum, regis & nostris usibus inserviret.
units.tr: We have been summoned, Governor, by your counsel, and we have heard President Igramus Achlenius speaking in the assembly, by which he demanded new taxes or tributes to meet the soldiers' pay. We indeed, although the Saxon agreements, which we entered into with him as Governor of the province, can secure us against further burdens, since Charles, Prince of Spain, appointed Florentius Iscilstein to rule the province on no other condition than that he should make its government like that of the Saxons. He also made the solemn oath, sworn according to the native laws, and by the clemency of the new prince, gave us hope of our former immunities. Nor were these things said and done merely in words, but they were confirmed by documents which have come down to us, the descendants. Nor was it beneath the majesty of Charles Caesar to make a bargain for the old agreements with good faith. Indeed, by the estate assigned to the Emperor and the yearly tax, we obtained that we should pay no tax beyond what was agreed, but that we and our late descendants, free from all servitudes and exactions, should enjoy rest and public peace. Emperor Charles and King Philip bound themselves by the religion of an oath, when we wished the rule to be conferred on the prince only after he had taken the oath. By rescripts of the viceroys Alba and Requesens we obtained the same thing, and we have learned through envoys that we shall be free from loss, both by the royal faith and by our own. And so we added one hundred and twenty-eight thousand gold pieces to the prince's ordinary tax, to show our affection towards King Philip, and so that the money brought into the provincial treasury might serve the king's and our needs against the threatening chances of events.

units.la: Reliqua quæ bello inviti aut non rogati contulimus, magna etiam fuerunt, sed quorum rationes opportuno tempore exacturi sumus. Et quoniam ex honorarij sponsione pensiones adhuc 53900. & ducenti Carolæi post annum Regi præstandæ sunt, ita parati sumus perspectâ pecuniæ inopiâ paratum æs in stipendia mili-tum conferre, modo in solutum cedat ordinarijque regis proventus gerendo etiam bello decernantur. Adhæc volumus, ut quatuordecim millia & sexcenti carolæi Gromngensibus jure mutui concessi octyus repetantur rescindanturque præterea contractus & actiones, quibus publicum æs privatis Philippi creditoribus assignatum est. Nostra tributa nostræ inopiæ destinabuntur. Tantum abest ut alios in usus converti velimus, quod nostris rebus continuâ exactione detractum est & cujus hoc ipso civilis discordiæ tempore egentissimi sumus. Quâ excusatione si nostris officijs satisfactum non censeat Præfectus, parati sumus ad arbitrium omnium provinciæ Ordinum forum experiri, quod declinare alias speciali indulto provinciales possemus. Ita enim CAROLUM inter Principem & majores nostros conventum erat, UT BINOS PER ARBITROS A POPULO FRISICO, BINOS A CAROLO NOMINATOS OMNIS LIS DIRIMIRETUR. Neq; stabit per nos quicquid controversum est ut totidem arbitris definiatur, modo apud Philippum regem paterni exempli imitatio & nostri juris memoria valeat. Servatâ cultâque per Principem fide & illæsis legibus nostris novo Vectigalium onere ad sustentandas copias non egebimus. Eâ vero spretâ aut violatâ, si tributa contra patrios ritus imperentur, sacrorum communione indignum se Princeps faciet, per quem Vectigalium diploma nobis insciis perscriptum est. Neque enim legati ad Philippum regem aut Requesentium provinciarum Præsidem à nobis aut ad nos missi. Tantum abest ut sacri ordinis aut Nobilitatis assensus intervenerit quem de patrio jure haberi æquum erat. Quin tanto fædius est nonnullos à comitio exclusos aut perorante Achlenio exire cœtu jussos publici consilij participes non fuisse, non laturos interim provinciæ libertatem novis dominantium edictis subverti, donec de ijs ad universos Ordines relationes instituantur. Secus obtestantur Ordines, Deo coram ac Rege, vim atque injuriam sibi inferri pronis in principem & non minus patriæ suæ amantibus.
units.tr: The remaining sums, which we contributed for the war, unwillingly or unasked, were also great, but we shall demand their accounts at a suitable time. And since from the pledge of the honorarium the pensions of 53,900 and two hundred Carolus-florins are still to be paid to the king after the year, we are therefore prepared, given the evident poverty of money, to contribute ready money for the soldiers' pay, provided that it is applied to what is owed and the king's ordinary revenues are set aside for carrying on the war as well. Moreover, we wish that the fourteen thousand and six hundred Carolus-florins lent by way of loan to the people of Groningen be demanded back in full, and that further contracts and actions, by which public money was assigned to the private creditors of Philip, be rescinded. Our taxes will be set aside for our own need. Far from wishing them to be turned to other uses, we say that they have been drawn from our resources by constant exaction, and that at this very time of civil discord we are in the greatest want. If the Governor does not think this excuse satisfies our duties, we are ready to submit to the judgment of all the Estates of the province, a court which otherwise we provincials could avoid by a special indulgence. For thus it was agreed between Charles, the prince, and our ancestors: that every dispute should be settled by two arbiters chosen by the Frisian people and two nominated by Charles. Nor shall it be our fault if any dispute is not settled by the same number of arbiters, provided that, with King Philip, the imitation of the paternal example and the memory of our right hold good. If the faith is kept and cherished by the prince and our laws are kept unharmed, we shall not need a new burden of taxes to support the troops. But if that is despised or violated, and taxes are imposed against our ancestral customs, the prince will make himself unworthy of fellowship in the sacred rites, through whom the diploma of taxes was drawn up without our knowledge. For neither were envoys sent by us to King Philip or to the President of the Requesens provinces, nor were any sent to us. So far from the assent of the sacred order or of the nobility having intervened, which it was right to have on the matter of ancestral right, it is all the more shameful that some were shut out of the assembly, or ordered to leave the gathering while Achlenius was speaking, and so were not taking part in public counsel. We shall not in the meantime allow the liberty of the province to be overturned by the new edicts of rulers, until reports on these matters are made to all the Estates. Otherwise the Estates call on God and the King to witness that violence and injury are being done to them, although they are devoted to the prince and no less loving of their country.

units.la: Hæc à Scipione Meckama & Livio Jelgersma præture Octopagico, pro Ooftergois, Martino Nitzenio pro Minnertsgais, Tiemarumanis, Firdgumanis ac municipio Harlingano, Boccatio vicario Ripensi pro Menaldumanis, Sixto Tiallengio presbytero Tiumano pro Franequeranis, Dione Hania pro Baerderanis, Bonnone Lyclama & Haringo Wabbæo pro Winbritferijs, Rodmero Regnero pro Hennardijs, Tincone Andringa & Tiedgero Ruardo pro Silvestribus signata.
units.tr: These things were signed by Scipio Meckama and Livius Jelgersma, praetors of the Octopagium, for the Oostergoers; by Martinus Nitzenius for the Minnertsgoers, the Tiemarumanes, the Firdgumanes and the town of Harlingen; by Boccatius, vicar of Ripa, for the Menaldumanes; by Sixtus Tiallengius, presbyter of Tiuma, for the Franekerers; by Dio Hania for the Baerderanes; by Bonno Lyclama and Haringus Wabbaeus for the Winbritferes; by Rodmerus Regnerus for the Hennardi; and by Tincon Andringa and Tiedgerus Ruardus for the Silvestrians.

units.la: Ad quæ iterum ACHLENIUS.
units.tr: To which Achlenius replied again.

units.la: ACcepimus responsum vestrum, Ordines, nostræ petitioni absonum & plenum obtestationis. Libertati vestræ vim inferri jam diu conquesti estis & quidem hodie apud nos, quos jam aliæ curæ, alia negotia exercent. Quippe violatæ libertatis querela apud Requesentium instituenda est & ut rite fiat nostrâ intercessione juvabimus. Nunc stipendia armatis petuntur, quos exautorari instans periculum & præsentes turbæ non sinunt.
units.tr: We have received your reply, Estates, which is out of tune with our request and full of protestations. You have long complained that your liberty is being violated, and you have done so today before us, who are already occupied with other cares and other business. A complaint of violated liberty must indeed be brought before the Requesens, and we shall help to have it done properly by our intercession. For now, pay is demanded for the armed men, whom the pressing danger and the present disturbances do not allow to be discharged.

units.la: Ad ea Ordines.
units.tr: To this the Estates replied.

units.la: {a}HOdiè delegati nostri nobis retulere, vestra consilia non minuendæ libertati sed poscendis ex necessitate tributis esse. Illam vero tueri ut honestum ac gloriâ dignum apud præclaros semper viros fuit, ita tandem peculiaribus in Regem studijs & necessitate temporum commoti binos sesterctios singulos in florenos aureos offerimus. Caterum hac lege ut quicquid æris ex pensionibus quas PHILIPPO regi præstare tenemur & proventurum est, in eosdem quoque usus & stipendia colortium vertatur, abstineaturque in posterum ulterioribus exactionibus libertati nostræ adversis. Quare nec conducendis copijs currus, navigia, commeatum præstari volumus, caterum cessare istiusmodi onera, monentq; prætores agrarios sub pœnâ coercitionis, ne quid tale quocunque etiam nomine aut casu præcipiant. Hoc vero si approbare grave vobis videatur, obtestamur non alia subsidia in nostrâ potestate esse, nosque ad jus patrium, ad immunitates majorum, ad patitiones Principum fugere. Nunc dimitti postulamus.
units.tr: Today our delegates have reported to us that your counsels are aimed not at diminishing liberty but at demanding taxes out of necessity. To defend that liberty has always been held an honourable thing and worthy of glory among distinguished men; so, moved by our particular devotion to the King and by the necessity of the times, we offer two sesterces for each gold florin. However, on this condition: that whatever money comes from the payments we are bound to make to King Philip shall also be turned to the same uses and to the pay of the soldiers, and that for the future you refrain from further exactions hostile to our liberty. Therefore we do not wish carts, ships or provisions to be supplied for hiring troops; rather, such burdens must cease, and we warn the agrarian praetors, under penalty of punishment, not to order anything of this kind under any name or pretext. But if it seems grievous to you to approve this, we beg you to note that we have no other aid in our power, and that we must flee to our ancestral law, to the immunities of our forefathers and to the privileges of the Princes. Now we ask to be dismissed.

units.la: Sic pro Oostergois Edzardus Douma, Suffridus Jensma, pro Westergois Bocatius Vicarius Ripensis, Dion Hania, pro Sylvestribus Pierius Renckius & Feico Tatmannus signavere.
units.tr: Thus for the Oostergoers Edzardus Douma and Suffridus Jensma; for the Westergoers Bocatius, vicar of Ripa, and Dio Hania; for the Silvestrians Pierius Renckius and Feico Tatmannus signed.

units.la: Quare ROBLESIUS parsimoniâ ac contumaciâ ORDINUM excandescens hæc rescribi fecit.
units.tr: Therefore Roblesius, enraged by the stinginess and obstinacy of the Estates, had the following written in reply.

units.la: DEcreti vestri hesterno die participem me fecistis. Et quoniam depre-hendo meis postulatis vestra responsa non convenire iniquasque condi-tiones secus quam speraveram, assignandis tributis præscribi, ita mea consilia & optumam in bonum publicum sollicitudinem confundi cerno. Militum & legionis meæ egentiæ subveniri à vobis in tempus volebam, caterum quoniam excusatione vestræ imbecillitatis & impotentiæ usi estis nec largiri nec concedere mihi exsolvendæ legioni quid posse, ita dimissos vos facio sinoque in vestra redire. Hac tamen cautione, ut mandatorum vestrorum copiam mihi servem cernamque quibus autoribus impedimentum publicis commodis injectum sit.
units.tr: Yesterday you made me a party to your decree. Since I perceive that your answers do not agree with my demands, and that you are fixing the taxes on conditions unfair and other than I had hoped, I see that my counsels and my best care for the public good are thrown into confusion. I wished help to be given to me in time for the needs of my soldiers and my legion; but since you have used the excuse of your own weakness and impotence, and have granted nothing nor been able to concede anything to pay the legion, I now dismiss you and allow you to return to your homes. Yet on this condition: that I be given a copy of your mandates, and that I may see by whose authority the obstacle has been placed in the way of the public good.

units.la: Tum dimissis agrarijs oppidorum Legati (exceptis Leovardiensibus ac Doccomiensibus) Roblesij postulatis hoc modo responderunt.
units.tr: Then, with the agrarian deputies of the towns dismissed (except those of Leeuwarden and Dokkum), the deputies replied to Roblesius's demands in this way.

units.la: NOn ita pridem, Præfecte, ex ore Achlenij Præsidis percepimus novis Vestigalibus te incumbere, quo stipendia colortibus tuis ex publico procures. Consilijs tuis jam ante sanciendæ eidem Vestigalium legi innixis non ita nuper oppidani acquievimus, censuimusque id optumum compescendæ militari insolentiæ remedium esse. Res in tabulas tum redacta mentem regis & nostrum simul consensum exponet. Nunc vero, quoniam mutatis actis aliud quæritur quod res nostras arctius premat, ita dip'oma posterius approbare nostra libertas & antiquæ immunitates non ferunt. Stipendijs vero sucturrendum esse nec ipsi ignoramus, caterum censemus tolerabili tributo onerandos provinciales esse. Nos reverentiâ Regiæ Majestatis omne officium tibi deferimus speramusque responsum hoc nostrum apud Regem & te Præfectum valiturum fore, neque nos ipsos majora onera aut damna quam par est ex tuo imperio passuros.
units.tr: Not long ago, Prefect, we heard from the mouth of President Achlenius that you were pressing for new taxes, so that you might obtain pay for your soldiers from the public funds. Earlier, the townsfolk, relying on your counsels and on a tax law to be sanctioned, had acquiesced; and we judged that this would be the best remedy for the soldiers' insolence. The matter, once committed to record, would set out the King's mind and our consent at the same time. But now, since by altering the acts another thing is sought which presses our affairs more tightly, our liberty and ancient immunities do not allow us to approve the later document. Indeed, we do not ignore that the pay must be raised; yet we think the provincials should be burdened with a bearable tax. Out of reverence for His Royal Majesty we offer you every courtesy, and we hope that this our reply will carry weight with the King and with you, Prefect, and that we ourselves shall not suffer greater burdens or losses than is fitting under your command.

units.la: Hæc pro Snecanis Douwo Roorda, pro Bolsverdijs Theodorus Joannis, pro Staurijs Simon Folpertius, pro Elostanis Serapius Andreæ cIↄ. Iↄ. Inthiema, pro Worcumijs Titus Hajonius, pro Harlingijs Cornelius LXXIV. Coninxius, pro Slotanis Simon Potterus, pro Hindelopijs Joannes Timannus confirmavere.
units.tr: These were confirmed for the Snecanes by Douwo Roorda; for the Bolsward men by Theodorus Joannis; for the Stavoreners by Simon Folpertius; for the Elahusers by Serapius Andreae Inthiema; for the Workumers by Titus Hajonius; for the Harlingers by Cornelius Coninxius; for the Sloten men by Simon Potterus; and for the Hindeloopers by Joannes Timannus.

units.la: Mox Hennardij per legatos Rodmerum Regnerium Præbendarium, & Epæum Stapertium Wommelios novis Vectigalibus assensum præbuere, ne deficientibus Stipendijs eorum agri insolentiæ militum exponerentur. Roblesius quoque Douwonem Roordam Snecensium legatum ad se vocavit, eique novorum Vectigalium diploma exhibuit, quo cæteris oppidorum legatis communicaret, potestate corrigendi immutandique, quæ ex usu aut contra publicos mores viderentur eidem Legato permissa. Itaque tum diploma correctum mitigatumq; obtestatione coram Legato Roorda & Graphiario facta, Roblesius recepit totumque negotium in acta relatum, arbitrio Requesentij permisit. Quare de vulgando per Frisiam diplomate SCtum perscriptum delectique viii. viri, Antistes Fosverdicus, Scelto Liauckama, Hero Ockingha, Douwo Roorda, Livius de Bejem, Ruardus Vibius, Sufridus Æsgema, Meinius Lyclesius Jureconsulti, qui curandis Vectigalibus publicanos crearent, totumque negotium ex formulâ diplomatis regij expedirent. Cæterum Antistes Fosverdicus & Livius Bejemus rei velut invisæ administrationem detrectavere haud inani opinione, onerosi & damnati muneris primam mercedem odium populi fore. Quare Roblesius viii. viros ad se vocavit, cosque per Præsidem Achlenium hoc modo allocutus est.
units.tr: Soon afterwards the Hennardi, through their deputies Rodmerus Regnerus, prebendary, and Epaeus Stapertius of Wommels, gave their assent to the new taxes, lest with the pay failing their fields be exposed to the insolence of the soldiers. Roblesius also summoned to himself Douwo Roorda, deputy of the Snecanes, and showed him the document of the new taxes, so that he might share it with the other deputies of the towns; the power to correct and alter whatever seemed useful or contrary to public custom was granted to this same deputy. Accordingly, with the document corrected and softened by an entreaty made before the deputy Roorda and the secretary, Roblesius accepted it, had the whole business entered in the records, and left the decision to the Requesens. Therefore a decree was drawn up for publishing the document throughout Friesland, and eight men were chosen, namely the Antistes Fosverdicus, Scelto Liauckama, Hero Ockingha, Douwo Roorda, Livius de Bejem, Ruardus Vibius, Suffridus Æsgema and Meinius Lyclesius, jurists, who were to appoint tax-farmers to collect the taxes and to carry out the whole business according to the form of the royal document. But the Antistes Fosverdicus and Livius Bejemus shrank from the administration of a thing that was, as it were, hateful, not without good reason: they feared that the first reward of an onerous and condemned office would be the hatred of the people. Therefore Roblesius summoned the eight men and addressed them through President Achlenius in this way.

units.la: DE nova Vectigalium lege apud Ordines egi & jam res exitum sortita est. Convenimus equidem, ut nec libertas vestra quid servitij nec auctoritas & commodum regis quid ignominiæ aut detrimenti ferant. Restat tantum ut decretum exequar, ad quod vestrâ ope & ministerio uti volui. Non ut odijs quibus hoc negotium vacat, provincialium ac concivium vos implicarem, cæterum ut à dignitate vestrâ novæ legis rogationem ordirer. Cujus is præcipuè fructus erit, ut agris ac possessionibus vestris bene sit & ne miles defectu æris sacramenti oblitus defectiones moliatur. Id rebellium, id hostium nostrorum consilium est, nihil aliud quærentium, quam ut in provinciam irruant pervastatisque agris ac municipijs sacra & profana conturbent. Si vero sint, quibus grave instituendorum Vectigalium munus videatur, ea profiteri secretum suæ mentis volo daboque operam ut ad Requesentium PHILIPPI Proregem eorum nomina perferantur.
units.tr: I have discussed the new tax law with the Estates, and the matter has now reached its outcome. We are agreed, indeed, that neither your liberty should bring any servitude nor the authority and advantage of the King any dishonour or loss. It remains only that I carry out the decree, for which I wished to use your help and service. Not so that I may involve you in the hatreds with which this business is burdened, in the eyes of the provincials and your fellow citizens, but so that I may begin the proposal of the new law with your dignity. Its chief fruit will be that your fields and possessions may prosper, and that the soldier, lacking money for his pay, may not forget his oath and plot revolts. This is the counsel of the rebels and of our enemies, who seek nothing else than to rush into the province and, having laid waste the fields and towns, to throw sacred and profane things into confusion. But if there are any to whom the office of establishing the taxes seems burdensome, I want them to declare the secret of their mind; and I will take care that their names are carried to the Requesens, Philip's Proregent.

units.la: Ad quæ Antistes Fosverdicus.
units.tr: To this the Antistes Fosverdicus replied.

units.la: NON comparui, Præfecte, in nupero concilio meâ sponte & rebar comitium te populi pro more gentis indixisse vocatosque esse ad deliberandam quorum interesset. Cæterum quoniam nostri ordinis & nobilitatis præcipuos excludere ab illo conventu voluisti, censeo præter receptum morem à te factum esse. Itaque me eximo molesto oneri & curâ promovendæ legis tuæ me abdico maloque privatim rebus meis quam publicè cum invidiâ tuis exactionibus vacare.
units.tr: I did not appear, Prefect, at the recent council of my own accord; and I supposed that you had summoned an assembly of the people according to the custom of the nation, and that those concerned had been called to deliberate. But since you wished to exclude the principal men of our order and nobility from that gathering, I think you have acted contrary to accepted custom. Therefore I excuse myself from this troublesome burden, I renounce the care of promoting your law, and I prefer to attend to my private affairs rather than to be occupied in public, with unpopularity, with your exactions.

units.la: Idem Beiemus vir alti animi & haud dubiè patratæ in propinquum cædis conscientiâ tactus coram Præfecto & Achlenio præside effatus est. Quare Præfectus cæteros vi. viros blandis verborum illicijs aggressus est eosque collegas alios adscisacere expediendæ Vectigalium legi præcepit. Igitur in Antistitis Fosverdici locum Hector Dekema ex Oostergois, è Westergois Abbas Floridi Campi Beiemo surrogati infidisque erga Roblesium animis ira & miseratio proscriptæ libertatis provinciam frequentavere. Tum novorum Vectigalium lex promulgata, non dissimulato Philippi regis nomine, cujus Edictum tale erat.
units.tr: Bejemus, the same man, a man of lofty spirit and moved by a conscience of a murder undoubtedly committed against a kinsman, spoke before the Prefect and President Achlenius. Therefore the Prefect, approaching the other six men with smooth enticements of words, ordered them to co-opt other colleagues for carrying out the tax law. Accordingly, in place of the Antistes Fosverdicus, Hector Dekema from the Oostergoers was substituted, and from the Westergoers the Abbot of Floridus Campus was substituted for Bejemus; and, with anger and pity for lost liberty stirring their hostile minds against Roblesius, they frequented the province. Then the new tax law was promulgated, the name of King Philip not being concealed, and his edict was as follows.

units.la: Iam ante potestatem feci GASPARO ROBLESIO Præfecto per Frisiam meo Ordines ejusdem provinciæ convocandi agendique cum ijs quo stipendia meæ cohortes haberent quas in præsidijs locavi. Id vero quia Præfecto inconsultum videbatur propter animorum dissensiones & quod sumptuoso opere meæ provinciæ littus clauserit, secreta cum iv. Deputatis Ordinum colloquia instituit fecit. Et quamvis communem assensum meis votis impetrare non potuerit, tamen sollicitudine ac solertia sua effectum dedit, ut trium Deputatorum suffragationibus fultus Ordinum ac primariæ Nobilitatis animos sibi conciliaverit. Soli vero Leovardij in partibus adversis fuere, quos ut blandis honestisque rationibus moveret mandatum à me accepit. Tantum vero abfuit, ut eosdem Leovardios sana ad consilia perducere quiverit ut illorum contumaciâ plurium in me odia auxerit. Et quoniam certus sum grandius tributum à florenis aureis peti non posse, ita censeo nova Vectigalium lege inopiam provinciæ sublevandam. Quamobrem de consilio LUDOVICI REQUESENTI Proregis & Senatus mei potestatem Frisijs facio Vectigalia portoriaque instituendi è formula mei diplomatis voloque ut panni, frumenta, legumina, cibaria meæ legi subsint. Ordinibus vero provinciæ aut eorum Delegatis erogandæ pecuniæ jus relinquo, hac tamen conditione, ut destinatis à me usibus collatum æs serviat. Si vero ex illo ære quid residui sit quam quod stipendijs & commeatui debetur, id in erarium inferri volo, si forte aut gravius bellum aut imquior fortuna mihi aut meo populo incumbat. Volo quoque ut Quæstores accepti expensique rationes reddant tabulæque assignandi æris à Præfecto aut Senatu meo scribantur. Sin autem vectigalium census stipendijs militum cæterisque rebus par non sit, viii. viris copiam facio augendi ea minuendique. Interim Præsidi, Senatui & publicarum per Hollandiam rationum magistris mando; ut diploma hoc sartum tectum curent, beneficiumque Frisicæ genti ex mea clementia indultum, firmum atque inviolabile habeant.
units.tr: Already earlier I gave power to Gaspar Roblesius, my Prefect in Friesland, to summon the Estates of the same province and to deal with them concerning the pay my cohorts, which I have stationed in garrisons, should receive. But because this seemed to the Prefect ill-advised on account of the dissensions among men, and because the shore of my province has been closed off by a costly work, he held private conferences with four deputies of the Estates. And although he could not obtain common assent to my wishes, nevertheless by his own care and skill he brought it about that, supported by the votes of three deputies, he won over the minds of the Estates and of the principal nobility. Only the men of Leeuwarden stood on the opposing side; and to move them by kind and honourable arguments he received a mandate from me. But so far was he from being able to lead those same Leeuwardeners to sound counsels, that by their obstinacy he increased the hatred of many against me. And since I am certain that a heavier tax cannot be demanded beyond the gold florins, I judge that the poverty of the province is to be relieved by the new tax law. Therefore, with the counsel of Ludovicus Requesens, my Proregent, and of my Senate, I grant to the Frisians the power of establishing taxes and tolls from the form of my document, and I want cloth, grain, pulses and food to be subject to my law. To the Estates of the province, or their delegates, I leave the right of disbursing money, on this condition: that the money collected serve the uses I have determined. But if anything is left of that money beyond what is owed for pay and provisions, I want it carried into the treasury, in case perhaps a more serious war or a less favourable fortune falls upon me or upon my people. I also want the Quaestors to render account of receipts and expenditures, and the records of money assigned to be written up by the Prefect or my Senate. But if the revenue from the taxes should not be equal to the soldiers' pay and the other needs, I grant to the eight men the power to increase or reduce them. Meanwhile I instruct the President, the Senate and the masters of the public accounts throughout Holland to see that this document is kept whole and secure, and to hold the favour granted by my clemency to the Frisian people as firm and inviolable.

units.la: Hæc Bruxellis signata ac Non. Octobr. per provinciam publicata.
units.tr: This was sealed at Brussels and published throughout the province on the Nones of October.

units.la: Tum quæstoribus leges scriptæ, ac à Thoma Groningense Antistite Floridi Campi, Sceltone Liauckama, Hectore Dekama, Douwone Roorda, Herone Qckingha, Suffrido Æsgama, Meinio Lyclesio, & Ruardo Vibio Jureconsultis signatæ.
units.tr: Then the laws for the quaestors were drawn up and signed by Thomas, bishop of Floridus Campus (Franeker), Scelto Liauckama, Hector Dekama, Douwo Roorda, Hero Ockingha, Suffridus Aesgama, Meinius Lyclesius and Ruardus Vibius, jurisconsults.

units.la: Reperio in commentarijs scriptoris Staurij rogationem novæ legis magnis acerbisque contentionibus exagitatam fuisse, ipsosque Leovardios & Sylvestres Roblesij & nobilitatis consilijs adversos solemnibusq; obtestationibus nequicquam usos, inrita libertati patrocinia commodasse.
units.tr: I find in the commentaries of the writer Staurius that a proposal for a new law was attacked with great and bitter disputes, and that the Leovardians and the Sylvestres, together with Roblesius and the counsels of the nobility, opposed it. They made solemn appeals, but in vain, and they offered their defence of liberty to no effect.

units.la: Dein Roblesius Translavicanos mille aureorum tributum singulas in septimanas popposcit abnuentesque onera & immunitatem obtendentes Hispano equite & insolentibus præsidijs pressit. Mox primatum ædibus miles immissus, iuani læsi juris querimoniâ, quod à Carolo Cæsare cIↄ. Iↄ. fare se accepisse solenni conventione Translavicanus populus obtendeLXXIV. bat. Itaq; legati eâ ex gente Bruxellas missi, vanâ enormis imperij incusatione, quod oppresso per arma foedere, vires, & maturitarem acceperat. Quamobrem Philippus primas quoque civilium armorum causas Religionis Edicta renovari, publicarique per Frisiam jussit, quae à Carolo Caesare Augusto sancita, paterni imperij & actorum haeres primis jam ante principatus sui annis inconsultâ ac juvenili pietate vulgaverat. Unde omnis concordiae pacisque spes provincialibus excussa, non ineptè reputantibus, civilibus armis ut ante materiem, ita nova fomenta, crescentibus furoribus, submini strari.
units.tr: Then Roblesius demanded from the Translavian people a tribute of a thousand gold pieces every week. When they refused, pleading their burdens and their immunity, he oppressed them with Spanish horsemen and insolent garrisons. Soon soldiers were quartered in the houses of the leading men. The Translavian people complained that their right had been violated, and claimed that Charles Caesar had granted them this by a solemn agreement in the year 1550. Accordingly, envoys from that people were sent to Brussels, where they accused the empire of enormous wrongs: it had broken the covenant by force of arms, and had taken away their strength and their maturity. Therefore Philip also ordered that the edicts on religion, the first causes of the civil wars, be renewed and published throughout Friesland. Charles Caesar Augustus had sanctioned these edicts, and as heir of his father's empire and acts, he had already, in the first years of his reign, published them out of an ill-advised and youthful piety. Hence all hope of harmony and peace was shaken from the provincials. Those who reasoned sensibly saw that, just as before, the civil arms were given new fuel, and that the fury grew.

units.la: Idoneè scilicet proclamata per Philippum Veniae Edicta & obtrusam provincialibus speciosa ostentatione clementiam, ut Philippi regis animus ad antiquae severitatis legem rediret, provincialiumque conscientijs, dulcedine, futurae pacis haud pridem delinitis, amplas, etsi lubricas concordiae spes renovatio pristinae servitutis excuteret? Hanc Ferdinandi Albani, hanc Ludovici Requesentij, hanc Roblesij, & Senatus fidem esse, ut solemnim actorum, & publicae vocis ratio non constet? Male profecto credulas mentes principum verba oraculis numinum adaequasse, postquam jurisjurandi religionem summae potentiae opinio sustulisset. Nunc certè dolosa Philippi consilia detegi, & non alio fine Edicta Veniae regio paratu in theatris recitata, quam ut persuasionibus populares animi occuparentur, velumque proclamata pacis consilia belli & prioris saevitiae inumbraret. Iterum Romanorum Pontificum, iterum Inquisitorum regna & furores exsurgere, quo, per spatia temporum intermissi, statis intervallis majore aestu recrudescerent.
units.tr: Did Philip, then, properly proclaim the edicts of Venia, and did he force upon the provincials a showy display of clemency, so that the mind of King Philip might return to the law of its former severity, and so that the consciences of the provincials, lately soothed by the sweetness of a future peace, might be shaken by the renewal of their old servitude, which destroyed their broad though slippery hopes of harmony? Is this the faith of Ferdinand of Alba, of Luis de Requesens, of Roblesius and of the Senate, that the reason of a solemn act and of a public voice does not stand? Surely it was a mistake for credulous minds to equate the words of princes with the oracles of the gods, once the opinion of supreme power had removed the sanctity of an oath. Now, at last, the deceitful plans of Philip are being uncovered: the edicts of Venia were recited in the theatres with royal pomp for no other purpose than to win over the popular minds by persuasion, and to veil the proclaimed counsels of peace with war and the former cruelty. Again the kingdoms and fury of the Roman pontiffs and of the Inquisitors rise up, which, having been intermitted for spans of time, break out again at fixed intervals with greater heat.

units.la: Sic exasperato per Edicta & exactiones regis imperio domi & intra provinciam secreta in Praefectum odia, foris incrementa foederis observabantur. Quippe littoralem Frisiae oram foederatae rursum classes infestabant, auxiliaque subinde è minoribus Frisijs nactae, non solis agrorum populationibus, sed direptionibus urbium vicorumque se exercebant. Itaque Gualterus Hegemannus foederatae cohortis Tribunus cum navibus Texaliâ solvens mox Hindelopam advectus maritimum oppidum Frisiae contra minoris littora situm, suam & fratris cohortem in continentem exposuit, congressusque cum praesidiario milite, quem defensioni invalidum inexspectata irruptio faciebat, oppidum suam in potestatem redegit. Creditum fuit illunis noctis beneficio & quod nullo sydere coelum niteseceret multâ nube obductum, eum loci potitum, opportunamque opacitatem grande momentum audaci consilio & prospero successui attulisse. Igitur civium opes & ornamenta domorum in praedam versa, oppidumque quorundam civium & militum caede occupatum infoelicibus flammis exustum est. Mox foederati praedâ foelices & loco diffisi conscensis navigijs Enchusam petiere, quae jam ante, accepto victoriae nuntio, arma & commeatum, in spem muniendae retinendaeque urbis, subministraverat. Alij addunt adventantium Valonicarum copiarum famâ conterritum compulsumque Hegemannum oppidum deseruisse, suamque fortunam latissimis freti aestuarijs, quam urbi non munitae hostili in solo concredere maluisse. Neque imprudens viri consilium fuit. Quippe Motioius, ioius, qui Stauriæ castellum regio nomine tenebat, postero militem Hindelopam duxit, positoque ibidem validiore præsidio oppidum novo opere sistendis irruptionibus præmunivit. Roblesius quoque prohibendis provinciâ fœderatis, qui actuarijs navigijs illam oram tum legebant, per marinum littus locaque accessui opportuna disponi excubias vigiliasque præcepit, reprimendæque per agros & municipia insolentiæ armatorum numerum cuique præturæ assignavit. Cæterum promiscuo provincialium metu quem continuæ fœderatorum incursiones dabant, villæ deserebantur coloniæque agrorum, non intermissis tributis exhausti & inopes, quo se suaque pignora periculis subducerent, in munita passim oppida suffugia faciebant. Unde desertis per agros habitationibus solitudo orta; cautumque Edicto ut tuendis villis profugorum ære armati alerentur privatarumque possessionum præsidiorumq; tutelâ quies ac securitas provinciæ redderetur. Mox Edicta proscriptionum repetita latâq; lex fuit: Ne quis profugis aut incerto lare per provinciam errantibus, officium subsidiumve quacunque etiam de causâ sub pœnâ perduellionis præstaret, eorumque ædes ac villæ qui exulem proscriptumve receptassent aluissentve, publicò igne tanquam flammis expiandæ cremarentur. Annotatum reperio Bolsuerdiâ & Elosto oppidis septuaginta sex familias tum in exilium pulsas fati sui & Senatus regij inclementiam singulari constantiâ pertulisse.
units.tr: Thus, with royal rule embittered by edicts and exactions, hatred against the governor grew at home and within the province in secret, and abroad the confederates' incursions increased. Indeed, the confederate fleets were again attacking the coast of Friesland, and, obtaining auxiliaries from the lesser Frisians from time to time, they busied themselves not only with plundering the fields but also with sacking towns and villages. So Gualterus Hegemannus, tribune of the confederate cohort, set sail from Texel with his ships, was soon carried to Hindeloopen, a maritime town of Friesland situated opposite the coast of the lesser Frisians, and landed his own and his brother's cohort on the mainland. He engaged the garrison, which was too weak to defend itself against the unexpected attack, and brought the town under his power. It was believed that he gained possession of the place by the advantage of a moonless night, since the sky, covered by thick cloud, shone with no star, and that this convenient darkness brought great help to his bold plan and prosperous success. Therefore the wealth of the citizens and the adornments of their houses were turned into booty, and the town, taken with the slaughter of some citizens and soldiers, was burned in unhappy flames. Soon the confederates, enriched by their plunder and distrustful of their position, went aboard their ships and made for Enkhuizen, which had already, on receiving news of the victory, supplied arms and provisions in the hope of fortifying and holding the town. Others add that Hegemannus, frightened and driven on by the rumour of the approaching Walloon troops, abandoned the town, and preferred to trust his fortune to the broad estuaries rather than to an unfortified town on hostile ground. Nor was the man's plan unwise. For Motius, who held the castle of Stavoren in the king's name, led soldiers to Hindeloopen the next day, and, after placing a stronger garrison there, fortified the town with new works to check further incursions. Roblesius also ordered watches and guards to be posted along the sea coast and at places suitable for access, to prevent the confederates, who were then sailing along that shore in small boats, from entering the province. He also assigned a number of armed men to each district to restrain the insolence of the soldiers through the fields and towns. Meanwhile, because of the common fear which the continual incursions of the confederates caused among the provincials, farmhouses and farming settlements were abandoned. Exhausted and destitute, with their taxes unrelaxed, the people fled to fortified towns wherever they could, to withdraw themselves and their pledges from danger. Hence, with dwellings deserted in the fields, a desolation arose. It was therefore provided by edict that, to protect the farms, the fugitives should be maintained at the cost of armed men, and that quiet and security should be restored to the province by the protection of private estates and garrisons. Soon the edicts of proscription were repeated and a law was passed: no one was to give any duty or aid, for whatever reason, to fugitives or to those wandering without a fixed home, under penalty of treason; and the houses and farms of those who had harboured or fed an exile or a proscribed person were to be burned publicly with fire, as if by flames to expiate the crime. I find it recorded that seventy-six families, then driven into exile from the towns of Bolsward and Workum, endured their fate and the harshness of the royal Senate with remarkable constancy.

units.la: Valerium quoque Cammingha Deputati officio fungentem Fecconem Rhalam jurisperitum Bruxellas ablegasse, quo de redintegrandis provinciæ privilegijs apud Requesentium ageret, & ut indictionum vigor rescripto ejusdem Proregis aboleretur. Pecunia quoque regia & dominiorum, ut vocant, canon stipendijs militum cederent, quo illorum rapacitati ex egentiâ æris & simul spontaneâ pravitate nascenti gubernatoris Regij prudentiâ occurreretur. Quippe indictionum per Frisiam vis fraudibus contrectantium solvebatur, subsidiumque bello quæsitum, aversis ab illo onere animis evanescebat. Itaque Roblesius præsentiâ Petri Frittema legum doctoris & senatoris regij subjutus, ad alia consiliorum provolutus est, regijq;, quod jam colligebatur, honorarij pecuniam assignari sub usuris mercatoribus petijt quo præsenti mercatorum ære accepto militum seditionibus malisq; moribus subveniretur.
units.tr: Also, Valerius Cammingha, who was performing the duties of deputy, sent Feccho Rhala, a jurist, to Brussels, to plead with Requesens about restoring the privileges of the province and to have the force of the levies abolished by a rescript of the same governor. Also, the royal money and the revenues of the domains, as they are called, were to go to pay the soldiers, so that the governor's prudence could meet their rapacity, which arose from the shortage of money and at the same time from their own voluntary wickedness. For the force of the levies throughout Friesland was being weakened by fraud on the part of those who handled them, and the aid sought for the war was fading as minds turned away from that burden. So Roblesius, supported by the presence of Peter Frittema, doctor of laws and royal senator, turned to other plans, and asked that the money of the king's honorary gift, which was already being collected, be assigned to merchants on loan at interest, so that with the money of the merchants received at once, the mutinies and bad habits of the soldiers might be remedied.

units.la: Quod cum Deputatis Ordinum grave videretur de præstando ære mutuo nobilitatem & primores quoq; sollicitavit impulsisq; Philippi per provinciam rebus quoquo modo subsidium poposcit. Hoc etiam addebat nobilitatem reliquosq; provinciales ex indictionum ære, quæ melius novo vere processurae forent, solutionem habituros quo servata regem inter populumq; fide pacis ac concordiæ spes illucesceret. Cæterum Delegati in quibus Ruardus Roorda, Valerius Cammingha & Hero Ockingha tum erant. (Meinius enim Lyclesius Nyholtpadius per invaletudinem aberat) consilia Roblesij reiecere acriq; responso quod provinciali pecuniæ usuras præstari indignarentur regis dominia & Biltanos imprimis agros gravandos proposuere. Quod si fieri non posset hoc volebant, ut pensitandis cohortium stipendijs partem Ooftergoi partem Weftergoi cum oppidanis, partem Sylvestres erogarent, exiguique Sylvestrium reditus ærarij regij ope, aut Biltanorum agrorum canone juvarencIↄ. Iↄ. LXXIV. rentur. Quæ omnia salvo provinciæ jure & cum obtestatione dicta nullum ista tempore robur habuere indignantibus Deputatis inter suorum fugas & exilia vitæ quoq; præsidia exactionibus subverti.
units.tr: Since this seemed a grave matter to the deputies of the Estates, he also pressed the nobility and the leading men to lend the money, and, with Philip's affairs in the province in whatever state, he asked for aid in any way. He added that the nobility and the other provincials would have the payment from the revenue of the levies, which would be better put into effect in the coming spring, so that, with faith kept between king and people, the hope of peace and harmony might dawn. But the delegates, among whom were Ruardus Roorda, Valerius Cammingha and Hero Ockingha at that time (for Meinius Lyclesius of Nijhuisterpade was absent through illness), rejected Roblesius's proposals, and in a sharp reply they declared that the royal domains, and especially the lands of the Bildts, should be burdened, since they were indignant that interest should be paid on provincial money. If this could not be done, they wished that part of the pay of the cohorts should be defrayed by Oostergo, part by Westergo together with the townsmen, and part by the Sylvestres; and that the small revenues of the Sylvestres should be helped by the royal treasury or by the rent of the Bildt lands. But all these things, spoken with a protest and saving the rights of the province, had no force at that time, since the deputies were indignant that, amid the flights and exiles of their own people, even the means of life were being overturned by exactions.

units.la: Unde civiles animi magis magisque à Philippo alieni, miseratione propinquorum, affinium queque sua ingenia exasperavere. Sic regij judicis rigor subvertendo fœderi decretus, ejus incremento cessit, odiumque superbè agentibus consiliorum immanitas paravit. Creditum fuit innocentis turbæ & jam in matrum amplexibus hærentis lamenta & ejulatus, tum profugientium triste spectaculum duros ac immites animos movisse civiumque ac opificum collegia à dominantium nexu ac affectu in Regem dissociasse. Quare Roblesij litteræ, quibus ad detertionem fœderis minores Frisios hortabatur, irritæ fuere, suspectâ apud eosdem Philippi regis clementiâ, quam Roblesius, emolliendis populi istius ingenijs, dolosis artibus substernebat.
units.tr: Hence the civic minds, more and more estranged from Philip, were embittered by pity for their relatives and kin, and by their own dispositions. Thus the harshness of the royal judge, intended to subvert the covenant, served instead to strengthen it, and the arrogant proceedings of the magistrate's cruelty prepared hatred. It was believed that the laments and wailing of the innocent crowd, clinging to their mothers' embraces, and the sad spectacle of the fugitives moved hard and savage hearts, and drew the guilds of citizens and craftsmen away from their bond and affection for the king and the rulers. Therefore the letters of Roblesius, by which he urged the lesser Frisians to break the covenant, came to nothing, since the mercy of King Philip, which Roblesius tried to soften the people's minds with by crafty arts, was already suspected by them.

units.la: Ideo scilicet Regem tam augusti nominis & formidabilis potentiæ, proregis Requesentij & Barlamontij litteris pacem Frisiis ac affectum Principis obtulisse, quo scirent Frisij Philippo supra fastigium regni incolumitatem suorum subditorum esse. Malle quippe Philippum ut populus per arma & turbas temporum contumax suæ quieti commodisque consulat, quam ut inquies & nullibi securus præterquam sub armis fædâ in rebellione & invertendi ordinis proposito perseveret. De fide vero regiâ nihil periculi fore, quin certa & extra dolum futura sit, modo Frisij ad reverentiam veteris imperij redeant amoveantque siniストras suspiciones fovendis discordijs pronas.
units.tr: Thus the King, of such august name and formidable power, offered peace and goodwill to the Frisians through the letters of the viceroy Requesens and Barlaimont, so that the Frisians might know that, for Philip, the safety of his subjects stood above the summit of his kingdom. For Philip would rather that the people, stubborn through arms and the turmoil of the times, look after their own quiet and advantage, than that they persist restless, nowhere safe except under arms, in a shameful rebellion and with the aim of overturning the order of things. As for the royal faith, there would be no danger, since it would be certain and free of deceit, provided only that the Frisians return to reverence for the old government and put aside the sinister suspicions that foster discord.

units.la: Hæc Leovardiæ, vergente anno, manu Roblesij scripta, ac Enchusam per tabellionem perlata, infensis animis accepta. Itaque tabellio exploratorem acturus carceri datus, subjectusque quæstionibus hostile Roblesij consilium & doli plenum aperuit. Traditum annalibus igneas nubes mense Novembri à Septentrione versus Meridiem motas, tum apparuisse cœlumque ab Horizonte verticale in punctum ardere visum, funestis flammis colluxisse. Sequentis anni initium magnâ tempestate fœdum ut marino aggeri littorique damna ita gravem ultro annonam accidit. Quippe per Dongrios qua depressius solum & planities littorum, horrea pleraque & villæ marinis aquis convulsæ subsecutaque frugum cluvio egestatem agrarij populi prægravavit. Mox puriore cœlo & Euri flatu remittens tempestas magnum aëri frigus affudit palustriaque locorum, ingenio soli humentia, aut marinâ uligine fæculenta, acerbissimo gelu constipavit. Unde utrinque incursionum hostilium metus, etsi lentiore tum bello, quod fœderatorum supplicatione Philippum ad regem ac Requesentium missâ, futuri conventus fama diu speratam pacem datura provincijs videretur. Eo namque libello, ut officium obsequiumque regi fœderati offerebant, ita innuebant servando tuendoque populo Philippum se obligasse eamque summi imperij conditionem esse, ut parentibus inserviat. Econtra Albani dominatu jura, immunitates violatas quæ ne pessum irent armorum defensione usos, postquam inritis querimonijs munimentum innocentiæ non valuissent. Et quoniam publici regijque commodi maxuma apud se ratio esset, ita orare Philippum æquâ mente cadentium rerum misemisereatur restituatque pacem terris & cum eâ commercia, potentiam haud dubiè regiæ dignitati allatura. Conciliandæ vero provincijs concordiæ & florenti fortunæ unicum remedium missionem Hispanæ peregrinæque gentis superesse & ut imperia Philippi non alienigenarum consilijs, sed procerum Ordinumque Belgicæ regantur. Id fundamentum futuræ paci substernendum. Alias continuum bellum, æternas tempestates, perpetuas lites atque discordias fore, non ante desituras, quam rerum omnium ruinam exacuens se indies civilis furor fecerit.
units.tr: These letters, written by the hand of Requesens at Leeuwarden as the year drew to a close, were carried to Enkhuizen by a notary and received with hostile minds. The notary, being taken as a spy, was thrown into prison, and under torture he revealed the hostile and deceitful plan of Requesens. It is recorded in the annals that in November fiery clouds moved from the north towards the south, and that then the sky, from the horizon to the zenith, was seen to burn into a point and to shine with deadly flames. The beginning of the following year was foul with a great storm, which brought damage to the sea dike and shore and, in turn, a grave shortage of grain. For through the Dongeradeel, where the land is lower and the shore flat, most barns and farmhouses were overturned by the sea waters, and the resulting failure of crops weighed heavily on the poverty of the country folk. Soon the storm, relenting with clearer skies and the breath of the east wind, poured a great cold over the air, and the marshy places, damp by nature of the soil or foul with sea moisture, it bound with the bitterest frost.
