Hence there was fear of hostile incursions from both sides, although the war was then slower, since by the petition of the confederates sent to the King and to the Requesens, the rumour of a future conference seemed to promise the provinces the peace they had long hoped for. For in that little book, as they offered duty and obedience to the king as confederates, so they hinted that Philip had bound himself to preserve and protect the people, and that the condition of supreme power was that it should serve its subjects. On the other hand, the Spanish rule had violated their rights and privileges, and they had resorted to the defence of arms so that they should not perish, after their complaints had been in vain and had not availed as a bulwark of their innocence. And since the greatest regard among them was for the public and royal advantage, they begged Philip to take pity, with an even mind, on the falling state of affairs, and to restore peace to the lands and with it commerce, which would undoubtedly bring power worthy of the royal dignity. But to secure concord among the provinces and a flourishing fortune, there remained only one remedy: the withdrawal of the Spanish and foreign nation, and that the government of Philip be conducted not by the counsels of foreigners but by the nobles and estates of Belgium. This foundation, they said, must be laid for the future peace. Otherwise there would be continual war, eternal storms, perpetual strife and discord, which would not cease until civil fury, daily growing, had hastened the ruin of all things.

units.la: Ita turbidi temporis fastidium desideria pacis fœderatis injecerat eorumque votis externorum Principum mentes sistendæ provinciarum inquietudini incendebantur. Jam enim missæ Maximiliano à Cæsare ad Philippum quoq; legationes erant credebanturque reciprocæ, Cæsaris ac Philippi affinitates, publicum in Bonum exituræ. Quippe Mathematici velut perspectis syderum influentijs, Belgicæ salutarem annum prænuntiaverant mitiusque cœlum etsi fallacibus conjecturis fiduciâ artis pollicebantur. His exangue regis ærarium accedebat legionumque seditio impunitate criminum & graviore egentiâ succrescens.
units.tr: Thus the weariness of a troubled time had instilled in the confederates a longing for peace, and the minds of foreign princes were kindled by their wishes to check the unrest of the provinces. For already embassies had been sent by the Emperor Maximilian to Philip, and it was believed that reciprocal alliances between the Emperor and Philip would turn out for the public good. Indeed, the mathematicians, as if they had surveyed the influences of the stars, had foretold a healthful year for Belgium, and with confidence in their art, though by uncertain conjectures, they promised a milder sky. To these troubles was added the king's empty treasury and the mutiny of the legions, growing from impunity for their crimes and from more grievous want.

units.la: Traditum commentarijs est Frisios exules, qui Bremæ, Hamburgi, Vesaliæ, Duisburgi ac Embdæ agebant, perceptâ harum rerum famâ, datis ad Aurantium litteris, certam pacem & cum eâ libertatem conscientijs orasse. Sic tentatâ re, Elbertus Leoninus, vir pacis artibus excultus, ad Aurantium Principem cum fiduciarijs ablegatus curâq; Aurantij fœderarorum Ordinum conventus Dordraci indictus. Ibi A URANTIUS solertis ingenij, & reconditæ prudentiæ Princeps, ponderato tantæ molis negotio, hæc proponi fecit.
units.tr: It is recorded in the commentaries that the Frisian exiles, who were staying at Bremen, Hamburg, Wesel, Duisburg and Emden, having received news of these matters, sent letters to William of Orange and begged for a sure peace and with it liberty of conscience. So, the matter having been tested, Elbert Leoninus, a man trained in the arts of peace, was sent with powers to Prince William of Orange, and by the care of William a meeting of the confederated estates was called at Dordrecht. There William of Orange, a prince of skilful intellect and deep prudence, having weighed the great burden of this business, caused the following to be proposed.

units.la: AD tractandum pacem destinatos à PHILIPPO rege, aut REQUESENTIO Legatos fidem mihi Elbertus Leoninus fecit ac jam locum Bredæ instituendis colloquijs ordinatum. Id porro, Fœderati ORDINES, agendum restat, ut similiter è vobis Legati edantur, expendendis evolvendisque rebus quæ in disceptationem tam arduam venturæ sunt. Pacem vero quod pro summo mortalium bono omnium ætatum gentes habuere si cum bello conferamus, expetendam promovendamque magnopere censeo, modo divini numinis cultui, libertati vestræ patrisque legibus nihil imponat. Hoc vero imprimis necessum est, ut quoniam de pace consultaturi estis, subsidia bello decernatis, ne imparatos vos & inermes quamlibet ad pacem vestra imbecillitas aut socordia compellat. Præcipuè vero de concordiâ Fœderati Populi, de stipendijs exercituum, de apparatu classium, munitionibus urbium, & commeatuum curâ cogitate, tanto magis à privatis utilitatibus alieni, quanto cariora vobis reip. commoda erunt.
units.tr: Elbert Leoninus has assured me that the envoys appointed by King Philip, or by Requesens, to treat of peace, and a place at Breda ordained for holding the conferences. It remains, confederated estates, that in the same way envoys be chosen from among you, to weigh and unfold the matters that are to come into so arduous a dispute. Peace indeed, which the nations of all ages have held to be the highest good of mortals when we compare it with war, I judge to be greatly to be sought and promoted, provided it impose nothing on the worship of the divine majesty, on your liberty, or on the laws of your fathers. Above all it is necessary that, since you are to deliberate on peace, you decide on supplies for war, lest your weakness or your negligence compel you, unprepared and unarmed, into whatever peace. Especially think on the concord of the confederated people, on the pay of the armies, on the equipment of fleets, on the fortifications of cities and the provisioning of supplies, and be all the more free from private interests as the public welfare of the commonwealth will be dearer to you.

units.la: Hæc AURANTIUS.
units.tr: So far Orange.

units.la: Mox Guntherus Suartzenburgius nomine MAXIMILIANI Cæsaris cum imperatorio comitatu Dordracum missus multaque de subortis PHILIPPUM inter populumque dissidijs & miserijs civilium bellorum præfatus sollicitudinem optimi Cæsaris, non fucatâ oratione nec alienis à vero sermonibus commendavit. Itaque asserebat, non Belgicæ tantum & vicinis ditionibus, si bellum prorogetur, instans exitium, cæterum Germaniæ periculum imminere. Causam quippe dissensionum ut initio levem, ita tractu temporis fomenta & vires accepisse. Paratum esse Caesarem robustis malis mederi. Ita legationes nec infructuosas ad PHILIPPUM regem in Hispaniam actas. Neque alium in finem se a Caesare in provincias Belgicae missum, quam ut luxata concordia stabili pace coalesceret. Sic obsequium Caesari, sic officium AURANTIO Principi, & Belgicae nobilitati praestare constituisse, quibuscum affinitate, aut jure amicitia jungeretur. Itaque non molestias itinerum, non hyberni caeli inclementiam suis conatibus obstitisse, quorum fructum abunde habituros esset, si proinde auribus accipiantur. Quamobrem rogare Principis foederataeque Nobilitatis legatos, ut, de Caesaris affectu certi, aequa paci auscultent. Ad quam si perveniri tam subito non posset, petere, ut Legatos mandatis instructos ad Caesarem mittant, liberum commeatum per ditiones Imperij habituros.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Gunther of Schwarzenburg, sent to Dordrecht in the name of Emperor Maximilian with an imperial retinue, spoke of the disputes that had arisen between Philip and the people and of the miseries of civil war. He commended the concern of the good Emperor in a speech that was neither feigned nor at odds with the truth. He claimed that the impending ruin threatened not only Belgica and the neighbouring lands if the war were prolonged, but Germany as well. The cause of the dissensions, he said, was slight at first, but with the passing of time it has gained fuel and strength. The Emperor is ready to remedy these grave evils. Embassies have been sent to King Philip in Spain, and not without result. The Emperor sent him into the Belgian provinces for no other purpose than that, with discord loosened, the country might be joined together in a stable peace. Thus he resolved to show obedience to the Emperor, duty to Prince Orange, and service to the Belgian nobility, with whom he was bound by kinship or the bond of friendship. Therefore neither the hardships of travel nor the harshness of the winter weather have hindered his efforts, and he will reap their fruit in abundance if the envoys listen to him accordingly. He therefore asks the envoys of the Prince and of the confederate nobility to be assured of the Emperor's goodwill and to listen to fair peace terms. If peace cannot be reached so quickly, he asks them to send envoys furnished with instructions to the Emperor, who will have free passage through the lands of the Empire.

units.la: Econtra Ordines Foederati Caesari & Legato grates agere, quod Caesar pronum in provincias animum imperatoriâ apud PHILIPPUM Regem intercessione praeferret, Legatus vero taedium longinqui itineris, & tempestuosae hyemis afferendae paci pertulisset.
units.tr: On the other side, the confederate estates thanked the Emperor and his envoy: the Emperor, by his imperial intercession with King Philip, had shown a favourable disposition towards the provinces, and the envoy had endured the tedium of a long journey and a stormy winter to bring peace.

units.la: Interim reponebant causam bello se non dedisse, caeterum ALBANI ac Hispanorum faeda & crudeli dominatione compulsos arma sumpsisse, non subvertendo regi, caeterum, ut ejus imperio ac rebus suae vero incolumitati consulerent. Igitur majora nunquam concupivisse quam ut bellum omnis insolentiae ac miseriae ferax pace mutaretur, ad quam perveniri non posse praeterquam dimisso regis exercitu & peregrino Philippi milite censerent. Rex vero si ejus animi sit, tum demum sperare se felicem rebus exitum Caesarique & omnibus bonis optabilem. Interim rogare Suartsenburgium Legatum, ut Bredae ad conditum se sistat suaque praesentia ac consilio negotium juvet.
units.tr: Meanwhile they replied that they had not given cause for war. Rather, driven to arms by the foul and cruel domination of Alba and the Spaniards, they had taken them up not to overthrow the king but to secure his rule and their own safety. Therefore they had never desired more than that the war, fertile of every insolence and misery, be exchanged for peace. This peace, they judged, could not be reached unless the king's army and Philip's foreign soldiers were dismissed. If the king were of such a mind, then at last they hoped for a happy outcome, desirable to the Emperor and all good men. Meanwhile they asked Envoy Schwarzenburg to present himself at Breda for the conference and to help the business by his presence and counsel.

units.la: Thuanus scribit, Requesentium quoque praedecessorem Albanum foedae saepe dominationis familiari apud suos sermone redarguentem, in consilium pacis tum propendisse, quo leniorem imperij gerendi viam ingressus dissociatas a Philippo per arma & saevitiem provincias beneficio pacis pacaret.
units.tr: Thuanus writes that Alba, the predecessor of Requesens, often condemned his own foul domination in familiar conversation with his people. He then inclined towards a plan for peace, by which he would enter upon a gentler way of governing the empire and pacify, by kindness, the provinces that Philip had alienated through arms and cruelty.

units.la: Mox nominati per Requesentium foederatosque Legati datique a parte regis obsides securitatem facialium qui jam Bredae convenerant & simul spem foelicissimi successus auxere. Tum Philippi regis rescriptum, quod libello foederatorum destinaverat in consessu recitatum spem paterni affectus & miserationem bellis prae se ferens, quod foederatorum animos sua imbecillitate, more mortalium, falsis saepe bonis indulgentes, annuntiatum pacis desiderium compleret. Caeterum externus miles grande pacis negotio impedimentum afferebat repetebantque; foederati.
units.tr: Soon the men named by Requesens and by the confederates, and the hostages given on the king's part to guarantee the safety of the negotiators, who had already gathered at Breda, increased the hope of a most fortunate outcome. Then Philip's written reply, which he had addressed to the confederates' pamphlet, was read in the assembly. It showed a hope of paternal affection and compassion, and it fulfilled the announced desire for peace, since it indulged the minds of the confederates, as mortals often do, with false goods of their own weakness. However, the confederates kept repeating that the foreign soldiery was a great hindrance to the business of peace.

units.la: Amovendum in Hispaniam exercitum esse, quo, demptu metu, sanciendam ad pacem feliciore progressu iretur.
units.tr: The army must be removed to Spain, so that, with fear taken away, they might proceed to sanction peace with better progress.

units.la: Econtra regis Legati differebant.
units.tr: On the contrary, the king's envoys objected.

units.la: Hispaniae Belgicaeque gentes unius capitis imperio subjectas, nec exterminandam provinciys nationem esse, cujus virtute & fide CAROLI PHILIP-
units.tr: The peoples of Spain and Belgica are subject to the rule of one head, and the nation whose valour and loyalty had made the affairs of the kings Charles and Philip

units.la: LIPPIQUE regum res per Belgicam floruissent. Sed nec Fœderatos cum inquilino milite & solis indigenis pugnare, caeterum ex alienigenis conscribi supplerique legiones & externis armis intestinum bellum inmitti. Interim missurum facile exercitum Regem, si eo uti non velit, procurata pace & non exigentibus periculis. Hac de causa (id enim Fœderati adjunxerant) nec conventum Ordinum haberi, praeterquam cessante bello, posse, cui finem imponere aut pacem surrogare jus ac arbitrium solius regis quaeret. Ei jus solennium convocationum & indicendorum conventuum esse coitionibus Ordinum tum semper uso cum visum fuisset. Esse Philippo Proregem & Praefectos, Praesides & Senatum, quorum consiliis, aeque ac Ordinum, regere provincias queat intraque metam coercere exorbitantis imperii lubrica. Interim reducendae in provincias paci, stabilimentum patrii juris, veniam anteactorum, abolitiones proscriptionum, restitutionem bonorum & dimissiones captivorum regem offerre, daturum porro operam ut aequis conditionibus agat. Hoc vero velle, ut Fœderatæ provincias, oppida, castella, classes, commeatum, arma, eaque omnia regi reponant, quae bello aut per vim acquisivere.
units.tr: flourish throughout Belgica must not be driven out of the provinces. Nor could the confederates fight with an inland garrison and natives alone; instead, legions were levied and filled out from foreigners, and civil war was let loose with foreign arms. Meanwhile the king would readily send an army, if he did not wish to use it, once peace was secured and the dangers no longer pressed. For this reason (for the confederates had added this), a meeting of the estates could not be held except while the war had ceased; the right and judgement of the king alone sought to end the war or substitute peace. It belongs to him to summon the solemn assemblies and to call the estates together, as had always been done whenever the estates met as seemed fit. Philip has a viceroy, prefects, presidents and a senate, by whose counsel, as well as that of the estates, he can govern the provinces and keep the slippery excesses of power within bounds. Meanwhile, for restoring peace to the provinces, the king offered confirmation of ancestral law, pardon for past acts, abolition of proscriptions, restoration of goods, and release of prisoners; he would further take care to treat on fair terms. But he wished that the confederate provinces, towns, castles, fleets, supplies, arms, and all those things they had acquired by war or force, be given back to the king.

units.la: Tum de restituendis bonis Ecclesiasticis & Romanâ religione quaedam addita, quam solam haberi per provincias ut ante aetate majorum, Philippus rex volebat.
units.tr: Then some things were added about restoring ecclesiastical goods and the Roman religion, which King Philip wished to be the only one held throughout the provinces, as it had been in the time of their ancestors.

units.la: Eam namque cum ipso principatus, cum sacramenta populi accepisse aequumque esse ut quibus auspicijs imperium acceperit, iisdem retineat. Interim permittere aliam à Pontificiâ religionem profiteri volentibus, ut divenditis bonis rebusque suis, certum intra diem provincijs excedant abstineantque interea exercitijs fidei & malis exemplis.
units.tr: For he had received that religion together with the principate itself and with the sacraments of the people, and it was fair that he keep it under the same auspices by which he had received the empire. Meanwhile he permitted those who wished to profess a religion other than the Papist one to sell their goods and property and to leave the provinces within a fixed day, abstaining in the meantime from the exercises of faith and from bad examples.

units.la: Quae dissertatio acerbitatis plena & non obscurè praefractum offensumque Philippi regis animum ostendens, Fœderatorum Ordinum & Aurantij Principis Legatos perculit.
units.tr: This speech, full of bitterness and plainly showing the king's stubborn and offended spirit, dismayed the envoys of the confederate estates and of Prince Orange.

units.la: Itaque regerebant.
units.tr: And so they replied.

units.la: Pacem se provincijs petijsse, sed hoc consilio, ut impedimenta primum concordiae auferrentur exteraque confluges tot annorum flagitijs & partis per scelera opibus se pascens in Hispaniam aut longinqua amoveretur. Naturale quippe patriae desiderium cunctis gentibus inesse & haud dubiè beneficij loco habituros veteranos, si facultas locupletibus redeundi in sua detur. Provincias certè illorum insolentiae diu pertaesas nihilque magis optare quam ut in lustra sua feroces belluae remigrent. Idem Ordines Principesque Aurei Velleris Anno CIↄ. Iↄ. LIX. à Gallico bello ursisse & ut limitaneis hostis, arcibus ac castellis rursus peregrini, sed indigenae praeficerentur. Esse quidem Hispanos Philippi subditos, caeterum ab hac gente moribus legibusque discretos, cujus exitio tot per annos egissent. Sic tot urbium excidijs illorum furores placatos, quorum recentia exempla & simul vulnera essent. Itaque Belgas Frisiosque, tot enormia perpessos sero in felicia majorum tempora respicere, quibus sinistri metus oraculi vocem olim extorsisset, SOCIATARUM BELGICAE HISPANIAE QUE GENTIUM ALIQUANDO POENITENTIAM FORE, HISPANAEQUE FOEMINAE CUM PRINCIPE BELGICI SANGUINIS CONNUBIUM INCOMMODA NEPOTIBUS PARITURUM. Non esse dubitandum de praesagij fide & promiscua hodie in Hispanos odia, satidicæ voci certitudinem adstruere. Quare utrobivis civitatibus præsidijsque per vim eijci aut ut excedant æreٖ corrumpi, quos detinere perversæ mentis & alienandæ à Rege genti esset. Affectu imperia Principum stare, si per vim aut arma teneantur, metum dare aut pati. Adhæc majora Belgici Frisicique populi quam Hispanorum in Regem merita esse vel solum Galliæ bellum ostendisse. Id namque provinciarum viribus & immodico are tractum, quo Hispanorum per Insubriam & Neapolitanum per regnum dominationibus, defecturæ alias potentiæ prospiceretur. Sic Belgicæ Frisicæque gentis nobilissimos fortissimosque Gallico bello PHILIPPI expeditionem sccutos spretoque patrio jure suis sedibus excitos victricia arma longinquis terris intulisse. Sic in Italiam cum CAROLO Cæsare irruisse, sic trajecisse in Africam, commeritos id temporis ut clarissimis per Hispaniam dignitatibus admoverentur. Cæterum moderatè fortunâ usos, æmulatione mox Hispanorum submotos, ne vestigia Belgicæ externæque dominationis trans Pyrenæos aut mare in ultimo Occidente figerentur. Hic vero regnare, vastare, perdere, proprium Hispanæ genti esse, cujus tantus quoque furor sit ut non nisi externis atque auxiliaribus armis reprimatur. Sic Gallos, Anglos, Germanos, quod exterarum nationum Belgæ ac Frisij egerent, in provincias evocatos, verum cessante bello aut belli metu missionem habituros. Regis vero istud consilium non esse. Quippe Frisios belli immunes, præsidijs copijsque peregrinorum levamenta sædissimisque oppressionibus jamdudum remedia orasse & ut belli exsortes jure & æquo regerentur. Cæterum eosdem inanes querimonias, ut ferè potentiæ per arma stanti obtulisse ipsosque fœderatos optimam sæpe turbis medicinam conventum Ordinum sollicitasse. Contra dilationes salubribus consilijs quari restringiqƺe propalam jus atque auctoritatem Ordinum, quorum cura ad pacis bellique res seorsim vero ad stabiliendam provinciarum incolumitatem se extenderet. Ita flagrante Galliæ & Hispaniæ bello, primâ Philippici principatus ætate, consilia gerendis rebus Ordines interposuisse, quo tributa & stipendia bene cederent Ordinumque subsidia in bellum collata destinatis usibus applicarentur. Adhæc rescripta Principis sæpe immutata, nonnunquam abrogata, asserendæ autoritati Ordinum quorum ope CAROLO PHILIPPOQUE regibus & eorum majoribus res prosperè cessissent. Nunc vero, etiam durante pacis actione, jus Ordinum violari, non alio aulæ arcano quam ut provincias quas nunquam stipendiarias habuisset; tributarias faciat Philippus regioque more, verso in servitia populo dominetur. Primis Belgicæ motibus id ex FRANCISCI AVILANI per Galliam Legati litteris deprehensum. Non aliud scilicet efficacius remedium subjugandæ Belgicæ ac Frisiorum ditionibus dari, quam ut post præcisas procerum cervices & conculcatam Ordinum autoritatem, attriti exactionibus provinciales per inopiam gerendo bello invalidi, serendæ vero servituti pares essent. His imperij præceptis usum Albanum, eadem superbæ dominationis subsidia successoribus legasse. Neque enim ferre PHILIPPI Proreges posse, ut potentiæ suæ quoddam frænum sit & ut Ordinum intercessione illorum ambitio, regis imperium legem accipiat. Inde rebellionis & novarum religionum etiamnum tacitè insimulari gloriosis armis implicatos, quibus Philippo provincias asserant, reliquias Albani exercitus & simul furoris suis sedibus reddant. Conjuges quoque ac liberi & quicquid sacrum aut familiare miliare esset, adversum injurias externarum gentium defenderetur. Itaque non Ecclesiae bonis violentos possessores intulisse, non occupasse aliena. Quin omnia inspectore ac arbitro numine egisse, professos fidem conscientiis suis & sacris traditionibus congruam, quo divini cultus puris mentibus constaret, PHILIPPUSQUE rex aequis obsequijs apud reverentem Principis sui populum haberetur. Quare duris pacis conditionibus auscultare non posse, evolventes anteacti temporis perfidiam & sacramentum Principis lubricis nonsemel pactionibus adulteratum. Manere adhuc sensus & punctiones priorum vulnerum ac EGMONDANI HORNIIQUE funera, tum sanguinem truncatae nobilitatis & fidissimi populi oculis obversari horrendasque imagines reminiscentibus antiqua offerre. Iterum exilia, iterum proscriptiones instare, si, quod PHILIPPUS velit, serviendum iterum conscientijs sit offuscandumque illud lumen, quod non nisi a coelo acceptum edoctae sanctius mentes acceperint. Certe vel sola cogitatione ac conceptu humano non comprehendi tam horrenda consilia posse, quibus tot millium animae aeternam in servitutem eant innocentemque multitudinem bonis exutam in longinqua iterum exilia nova Philippi saevities ableget. Nec enim pretia venaum rerum profugentibus fore adimique honesta vitae solatia & simul subsidia, si agendum procul patria inter ignotos vultus aevum sit & ut plurimum infelicibus iniquos. Quin satius esse Hispanorum legiones suis terris reddere quam solitudinem cultissimis terris decrementum commercij dare. Quae si transferantur, multum patrimonio & aerario regis, ut ante decessurum, cum in alias oras ultra flumina & ipsum mare ingresso provincias ALBANO tot familiae grassanti saevitiae se subduxere. Idem fore, si pacem hac lege foederati ineant, quae novas discordias ac turbas detrimento PHILIPPI allatura sit. Interim rogare, ut Legati regis responsum hoc, è secreto mentium proveniens, ex aequo interpretentur censeantque optumo in Regem & patriam affectu perscriptum. adhaec precari sanctum aeternumq; numen ut PHILIPPO regi ac Legatis meliora consilia inspiret.
units.tr: They said they had sought peace for the provinces, but with this aim: first, that the obstacles to harmony should be removed, and that the foreigner, feeding on the wealth gained by so many years of crimes and party-spoils, should be moved away to Spain or some distant land. For there is a natural longing for the homeland in all peoples, and the veterans would undoubtedly regard it as a kindness if the wealthy were given the chance to return to their own countries. The provinces, weary for a long time of that man's arrogance, wished for nothing more than that these fierce beasts should go back to their dens. The same Orders and the Knights of the Golden Fleece had, in the year 1559, resisted the French war, and had demanded that the frontier posts, citadels and castles be entrusted again to natives rather than to foreigners. The Spaniards, indeed, were subjects of Philip, but they were separated from this nation by their manners and laws, and for many years the nation had been working its destruction. Thus the fury of those men had been appeased by the destruction of so many cities, and these were recent examples and at the same time wounds. Therefore the Belgians and Frisians, who had suffered so many outrages, looked back late to the happier times of their ancestors, when the voice of an ominous prophecy had once wrung from them THE UNITED PROVINCES OF BELGIUM AND THE PEOPLES OF SPAIN WOULD ONE DAY REPENT, AND A MARRIAGE OF A SPANISH WOMAN WITH A PRINCE OF BELGIAN BLOOD WOULD BRING HARM TO THEIR DESCENDANTS. There was no need to doubt the reliability of the prediction, since the present general hatred of the Spaniards confirmed the certainty of that saying. Therefore the cities and garrisons must be expelled by force from both places, or else corrupted with money to leave; those whom it was the aim of a perverse mind to keep, and to alienate from the King, would be the nation's concern. The authority of princes rests on affection; if it is held by force or arms, it must either give fear or suffer it. Moreover, the war with France alone had shown that the merits of the Belgian and Frisian peoples towards the King were greater than those of the Spaniards. For that war was waged with the strength of the provinces and at immoderate expense, so that the rule of the Spaniards in Insubria and of the kingdom of Naples might be secured, lest a power otherwise bound to fail should be provided for. Thus the most noble and brave men of the Belgian and Frisian nation followed Philip's expedition in the French war and, their ancestral right being disregarded, were driven from their homes and carried victorious arms into distant lands. So they invaded Italy with Charles the Emperor, and so they crossed into Africa, deserving at that time to be raised to the most distinguished offices throughout Spain. But they used their fortune with moderation, and were soon removed by the rivalry of the Spaniards, lest the footprints of Belgian and foreign domination should be fixed beyond the Pyrenees, or across the sea in the furthest West. But to rule, to devastate and to destroy is the peculiar character of the Spanish nation, whose fury is so great that it can be restrained only by foreign and auxiliary arms. So, they said, the French, English and Germans, called into the provinces because the Belgians and Frisians were doing what foreign nations do, would receive their discharge once the war ceased or the fear of war passed. But this, they said, was not the King's intention. For the Frisians, who were free from the war, had long since begged for relief from the foreign garrisons and troops, and for a remedy against the most foul oppressions, and that they be governed by law and justice as those exempt from war. But those same men, they said, had offered empty complaints, as is almost always the case with power that stands by arms; and the allied provinces themselves had often urged the assembly of the Orders as the best remedy for disturbances. Against these delays, they complained, the rights and authority of the Orders were openly restricted by beneficial measures, whose care extended to the affairs of peace and war, and separately to the securing of the safety of the provinces. Thus, while the war between France and Spain was blazing, in the first age of Philip's rule, the Orders had interposed their counsels in managing affairs, so that the taxes and subsidies might turn out well, and the aids collected by the Orders for war might be applied to their intended uses. Besides, the King's rescripts were often altered and sometimes annulled, to the detriment of the authority of the Orders, with whose help affairs had gone prosperously for the kings Charles and Philip and their ancestors. But now, even while the process of peace is under way, the rights of the Orders are being violated, for no other secret of the court than that Philip should make the provinces, which he had never held as tributaries, tributary, and rule over the people in the royal manner, turning them into slavery. This had been detected at the first stirrings of the Belgians, from the letters of Francis Avilanus, envoy through France. Surely no other more effective remedy for subduing the dominions of the Belgians and Frisians could be devised than that, after the necks of the nobles had been cut off and the authority of the Orders trampled down, the provincials, worn out by exactions and too weak to wage war through want, should be equal to bearing slavery. Alva, they said, had made use of these precepts of rule, and had bequeathed the same means of haughty domination to his successors. For Philip's viceroys could not endure that there should be some bridle on their power, or that the ambition of the Orders, by their intercession, should receive law from the King's command. Hence, although they were engaged in glorious arms for the defence of the provinces for Philip, the remnants of Alva's army, and at the same time his fury, were still tacitly charged with rebellion and with new religions, and were restored to their own seats. Their wives and children too, and whatever was sacred or domestic, were defended against the injuries of foreign nations. Thus they had not brought violent possessors into the goods of the Church, nor occupied what belonged to others. Rather, they had acted in everything with God as overseer and judge, professing a faith in harmony with their consciences and with holy traditions, so that the worship of God might stand with pure minds, and KING PHILIP might be held by his people, who revered their Prince, to deserve equal obedience. Therefore they could not listen to harsh conditions of peace, unrolling the perfidy of past time and the oath of the Prince, many times adulterated by slippery agreements. The feelings and stings of the earlier wounds and the deaths of EGMONT AND HORN still remained, and the blood of the beheaded nobility and of a most faithful people still rose before their eyes, and offered horrible images to those who remembered the old times. Again exiles, again proscriptions threatened, if, as PHILIP wishes, consciences were again to be enslaved and that light obscured, which the minds taught by heaven had received more holily. Certainly such horrible designs could not be grasped even by thought alone or by human conception, by which the souls of so many thousands would pass into eternal servitude, and the innocent multitude, stripped of its goods, would be driven by Philip's new savagery into distant exiles. For the prices of goods would not be favourable to those fleeing, nor would the honourable comforts of life and at the same time the aids be taken away, if life were to be spent far from the homeland, among unknown faces and, for the most part, among the unfriendly. Indeed, it would be better to return the Spanish legions to their own lands than to give the most cultivated lands the loss of trade through solitude. If these were moved, the King's patrimony and treasury would suffer much, as it had before, when so many families escaped from the raging cruelty of Alva, who entered other shores beyond the rivers and the very sea, into other provinces. The same would happen if they entered a peace bound by this condition, which would bring new discords and disturbances to the detriment of Philip. Meanwhile they asked that the envoys of the King interpret this reply fairly, as proceeding from the secret of minds, and judge it to have been written out of the best affection towards the King and the homeland. Moreover, they prayed the holy and eternal Deity to inspire King Philip and the envoys with better counsels.

units.la: HÆC FOEDERATI.
units.tr: THE CONFEDERATES' RESPONSE

units.la: Ita acribus acerbisque rescriptis in negotio sanciendae pacis certabatur.
units.tr: Thus the two sides contended over the making of peace with sharp and bitter replies.

units.la: Unde Swartsenburgius ne infructuosa omnino legatione fungeretur, prolixa oratione semestres armis inducias postulavit inritusque voti ad Caesarem recessit. Creditum fuit, affinitate Aurantio Principi, cujus sororem matrimonio tenebat, junctum & religionis libertatem acrius urgentem Requesentio suspicionem injecisse, velut in partem foederis, alienior à Philippi severitate ac rigore legatorum regiorum propenderet. Quippe Requesentius unam religionem exilia foederati populi volebat iniquisque pacis conditionibus bellum involvens, magnas fortunae & gloriae spes tum concipiebat.
units.tr: Hence Swartsenburg, so that his embassy would not be wholly fruitless, asked the Emperor for a six-month truce in a lengthy speech, and withdrew from him with his request refused. It was believed that his kinship with the Prince of Orange, whose sister he had married, and his stronger insistence on freedom of religion, cast suspicion on him in Requesens's eyes, as if he leaned too far toward the side of the confederates and away from the severity and rigour of the royal ambassadors. Requesens, indeed, wanted one religion alone and would drive the people of the confederacy into exile; by harsh terms of peace he was then conceiving great hopes of fortune and glory from the war.

units.la: Itaque ruptâ pace provinciales moesti & spe dejecti visebantur exulesque qui trans Visurgim, Albim, Rhenium atque Amasum flumina secesserant, praereptam concordiae spem & solatia exilij lugebant.
units.tr: And so, with the peace broken, the provincials were seen to be sorrowful and cast down in hope, and the exiles who had withdrawn beyond the rivers Weser, Elbe, Rhine and Ems mourned the lost hope of harmony and the comfort of exile.

units.la: Nunc scilicet pejora aliis tempora instare, postquam immitium fatorum leges pacem morarentur. Sic patriae perpetuum bellum, sibi exilium parari & ut ingravescentes annos ac ultimam senectutem solâ morte claudant. Neque enim
units.tr: Now, no doubt, times worse than others are at hand, since the laws of cruel fates delay peace. Thus war without end is prepared for the fatherland, and exile for ourselves, and so they will close their advancing years and final old age with death alone. For indeed

units.la: jam fata reditum in patriam polliceri divulsis procerum conventibus & quia pacem non dedere acribus bellum daturis. Ita infructuosas preces caelo fusas, nuncupata paci vota, quo post exactos exilij terminos patriam & relicta pignora reviserent. Sed istud beneficij vitae ac fortunae suae fata invidisse, quae mutare humanae potestatis non esset. Eventus rerum & remedia malorum à caelo speranda, venturis fortasse temporum aetatibus, quibus reditum in patriam & familiares locos non pax aut induciae, sed arma & bellum daturum sit.
units.tr: the fates no longer promise a return to the fatherland, now that the assemblies of the nobles are broken up, and because they have not given peace to those who will give fierce war. Thus prayers poured out to heaven have been fruitless, and vows offered for peace, so that after the term of exile was completed they might revisit their fatherland and the pledges they had left behind. But the fates have grudged this benefit to their life and fortune, which it was not in human power to change. The outcome of events and the remedies for evils are to be hoped for from heaven, perhaps in the ages of times to come, when it will be not peace or truces but arms and war that give a return to the fatherland and to familiar places.

units.la: Multi credidere isti pacis actioni magis in specie quam sapiendis discordijs legatos regios praesedisse animisque infidis etsi publicae quietis desideria simulantibus, meliora finibus initia ostentasse. Caeterum mihi rem accuratius expendenti visum fuit, partim consilijs fatales tum adhuc moras obstitisse foedamque ministrorum regiorum saevitiem tot annis & tanta caede alitam diuturnius bellum, placandis caesorum manibus, velut piamentum exerciti furoris postulasse. Itaque dirempto conventu obsides dimissi animique in curas bellorum iterum retracti nutrimenta ulteriori discordiae quaesivere. Unde delectus utrinque per provincias habiti decretaque cohortibus supplementa, quo extenuatus diuturno bello exercitus aut spe pacis solutus, novae multitudinis & simul accessione revivescentium furorum firmaretur.
units.tr: Many believed that the royal ambassadors presided over that act of peace more in appearance than with a wish to heal the dissensions, and that, though they pretended to desire public quiet with faithless minds, they showed better beginnings than their aims warranted. But when I weighed the matter more carefully, it seemed to me that, partly, fated delays still stood in the way of the plans, and that the foul cruelty of the royal ministers, fed through so many years and so much slaughter, demanded a longer war, as a kind of expiation for the spilt blood of the slain and a satisfaction for the army's fury. And so, the meeting being broken up, the hostages were dismissed, and the minds, drawn back again to the cares of war, sought nourishment for further discord. Hence levies were held on both sides throughout the provinces, and reinforcements were decreed for the cohorts, so that the army, worn down by the long war or loosened by hope of peace, might be strengthened by a new multitude and at the same time by the addition of furies coming back to life.

units.la: Caeterum REQUESENTIUS quo se a suspicionibus violatae pacis apud Frisios purgaret, litteras ad Praesules & Nobilitatem dedit, quibus omnem gestarum rerum seriem hoc modo exponebat.
units.tr: Meanwhile Requesens, so as to clear himself among the Frisians of the suspicion of breaking the peace, gave a letter to the prelates and the nobility, in which he set out the whole sequence of events in this manner.

units.la: Postremo Ordinum Belgicae, quem Bruxellis mense Iunio habui, conventu de sanciendâ regem inter & Hollandiae Zelandiaeque proceres Aurantiumque pace actum. Quam ipse quoque propositam habui, ut majores miserias, atque bellorum incommoda ab his provincijs averterem & ut Catholica religio ac regis autoritas conservaretur. Ego vero pacem petenti bus regem Hcc ipso singulare clementiæ exemplum edidisse respondi, quod oblatâ omnium criminum veniâ pacem obtulisset. Imploravi quoque salubria adversariorum consilia, quo fructum initi conventus Bredani utraque pars sentiret. Caterum acres libelli ad Regem & me missi, acerbitatem & licentiam partium exposuere. Et quamvis rex Philippus in condonandis criminibus perseveraret, ac ut omnium memoria tolleretur, salvâ tamen religione Catholica & regis sui, cui obsequium deberent autoritate, ita congregari fecit Episcopos & provinciarum Præfectos Senatus Belgici primores quo de modo faciundæ pacis deliberaretur. Locus conventui Bredæ indictus est, & quidem mense Iulr. Lujus anni vocatis isthuc rebellium procuratoribus atque legatis, quo de voluntate regis in causâ veniæ cognoscerent. Quam etsi ampliati debuissent, ac ad principem suum redire, à quo defecerant, ita deprehendi nihil bonâ fide ab illis actum gestumve esse. Præterquam enim quod debitam regi suo venerationem seponerent, ita rex & ego voluinus compendio ad pacem viri omissisque levioribus finem præsentibus calamitatibus facere. Illi vero dum hæc aguntur dimitti ad Aurantium Dordracum petiere habitisque cum illo colloquiis velut ferociores & à pace alieni licentiam atque exercitia damnatæ religioni suæ postulavere. Quæ etsi concedi non posse scirent, quod unâ religione contineri in officio Belgicæ populum Rex velit, ita ab adversarijs nostris in Hollandiam recessum, quo cum suis conferrent. Itaq; in tertium Maj. diem rex extra-tratracta, quo die cum Regis Legati & juxta illorum etsi numero pauciores convenissent, antequam de obsidibus dandis aliquid decretum foret submoveri externas nationes à parte Regis Belgicâ voluerunt ac ut Ordinum Belgicae conventum Rex indiceret. Quod cum contra omne jus & æquitatem proponeretur, cum etiam in Germaniæ imperio Principum populique jus valeat, imitandum necessumque sit ut una Religio, unus Rex, cui fidele obsequium debent, habeatur, ita multa differebantur quæ impediendo magis pacis negotio, quam maturando erant. Hoc vero pro Philippo cavebatur. Ut si veniam daturus foret, sola Catholica religio coleretur, novæque affectatores cum liberis rebusque suis Belgicæ finibus excederent. Econtra adversarij volebant, ut æquitate Philippi spectatâ libertas conscientiis daretur, quam deserere nec in animo haberent, neque patriâ suâ exulare, pro quâ mortem obire paratissimi forent. Itaque restabiliri temeratas à Philippo leges, asseri privilegia petebant, quæ sacrosancta & immutabilia committi eorum arbitrijs non possent, qui ijstius juris incapaces essent. Quamvis rex negaturus non foret bonum in Belgicâ suâ Ordinem restitui, ac conventum indicere Ordinum Belgicæ, modo fundamenta solidæ paci substrata sint. Quæ cum hoc ipso convellerentur, quod religionis suæ exercitia vellent, ita mandata mea excedere nolui, dato regi ad deliberandum tempore, dum, quid fieri vellet, ediceret. De armistitio quoque tum propositi, quo miser populus à calamitate bellorum sublevaretur, & ut terrâ marique armorum vis cessaret. Quam cum mari cessare adversarij nollent, vellentque ut Aurantius arbitrium maris retineret, sex dies toti negotio decidendo petiere, eâ intentione, ut cum parari pax non posset tractu temporis illo brevissimo abrumperetur. Hoc enim ajebant regem illo conventu malâ fide egisse, quâ ne deciperentur, malle se suis viribus uti & fictæ pacì bellum anteponere. Quæ quamvis ex invero dicta sint, ita obtestur Deum & generis humani conscientias regis integritatem & meam, inritumque colloquium, non culpâ regis aut meâ sed illorum contumacia infructuosa fuisse, qui enormia flagitare ausi hæretici ac rebelles ministrorum & suorum pravis consiliis acquievere.
units.tr: Finally, at the assembly of the Belgic Estates, which I held at Brussels in June, a peace was discussed between the king and the nobles of Holland and Zeeland, and the Prince of Orange, to be made binding. I too had put it forward, so that I might turn away greater miseries and the disadvantages of war from these provinces, and so that the Catholic religion and the king's authority might be preserved. Indeed, I answered those who asked for peace that the king himself had given a singular example of clemency, in that, by offering a pardon for all crimes, he had offered peace. I also implored the wholesome counsels of the adversaries, so that both sides might feel the fruit of the assembly begun at Breda. But bitter pamphlets sent to the king and to me laid bare the harshness and the lawlessness of the parties. And although King Philip persisted in remitting the crimes, and that they might be removed from memory, yet, with the Catholic religion and the authority of his king, to whom they owed obedience, kept safe, he had the bishops and the governors of the provinces and the chief men of the Belgic Senate gathered, to deliberate on the manner of making peace. A place for the meeting at Breda was appointed, namely for July of this year, when the agents and envoys of the rebels were summoned there, that they might learn the king's will in the matter of pardon. Although these men ought to have been enlarged and to return to their prince, from whom they had revolted, I found that nothing had been done or carried out by them in good faith. For apart from setting aside the reverence owed to their king, the king and I had wished to make an end, by a short route to peace and by setting aside lesser matters, to the present calamities. But while these things were being done, they asked to be sent to Orange at Dordrecht, and after conferences with him, like men too fierce and alien to peace, they demanded license and the exercise of their condemned religion. Although they knew these could not be conceded, since the king wishes the Belgic people to be kept in duty by one religion alone, they withdrew to Holland from our adversaries, to confer with their own people. So on the third day of May the king ... [gap]... when the royal envoys and those of the others, though fewer in number, had met, before anything was decreed about giving hostages, the adversaries wished that foreign nations be removed from the Belgic side of the king, and that the king should summon the assembly of the Belgic Estates. Since this was proposed against all law and fairness, and since in the empire of Germany the right of princes and people also prevails, and since it must be imitated, and one religion, one king, to whom they owe faithful obedience, must be held, so many matters were deferred which hindered the business of peace more than they hastened it. But this was guarded for Philip: that, if he were to grant pardon, the Catholic religion alone should be practised, and the new seekers, with their children and goods, should leave the borders of Belgium. On the other hand, the adversaries wanted, with Philip's fairness in view, that liberty of conscience be given, which they had no intention of abandoning, nor of going into exile from their country, for which they were most ready to die. And so they asked that the laws violated by Philip be restored and their privileges be asserted, which, being sacrosanct and unchangeable, could not be entrusted to the judgement of those who were incapable of that right. Although the king would not refuse that the order of Belgium be restored, and that an assembly of the Belgic Estates be summoned, provided the foundations of a solid peace are laid. Since these were being overturned by the very thing that they wanted, the exercise of their religion, I was unwilling to go beyond my instructions, time being given to the king for deliberation, until he should declare what he wished to be done. Concerning an armistice also, it was then proposed, so that the wretched people might be relieved from the calamity of wars, and that the force of arms might cease by land and sea. But when the adversaries were unwilling that it cease at sea, and wished that Orange keep control of the sea, they asked for six days to settle the whole matter, with the intention that, since peace could not be made, it would be broken off in that very brief stretch of time. For they said the king had acted in that assembly in bad faith, and, lest they be deceived by it, they preferred to use their own strength and to set war before feigned peace. Although these things were said with untruth, I call God and the consciences of the human race to witness the integrity of the king and of myself, and that the fruitless conference, failing through no fault of the king or of mine but through the obstinacy of those men, who, heretics and rebels, dared to demand outrageous things and yielded to the wicked counsels of their own ministers.

units.la: Hæc Antverpiæ IV. Non. Sept. scripta, ac ad Senatum Philippi in Frisiam missa, inritam conventus Bredani deliberationem aperuere.
units.tr: These things, written at Antwerp on the 4th day before the Nones of September and sent to the Senate of Philip in Friesland, revealed the failure of the deliberation at Breda.

units.la: Perscriptum commentarijs F. Nicolai reperio protractum in mediam aestatem illud colloquium fuisse, populumque Friscum, durante conventu paci inhiantem, inritâ actione profundissimo mœrori servijsse. Principem quoque Aurantium, missionem externi Hispanique militis urgentem pertinacius, secessioni procerum grande momentum attulisse. Alij in Requesentium potentiâ Regis sui subnixum ac gloriæ quam è bello sperabat avidum, omnem tardatæ concordiæ culpam rejecere.
units.tr: I find, in the commentaries of Friar Nicolas, that the conference was dragged into the middle of summer, and that the Frisian people, while the assembly lasted and longed for peace, were held in the deepest grief by the failed action. The Prince of Orange also, pressing more stubbornly for the dismissal of the foreign and Spanish soldiery, lent great weight to the secession of the nobles. Others, on the other hand, laid the whole blame for the delayed harmony on Requesens, who relied on the power of his king and was eager for the glory he hoped to gain from war.

units.la: Reidanus notat de libertate Religionis & Inducijs quinquennalibus deliberatum tandem isto conventu fuisse, quo, ijsdem durantibus, omne in causâ Religionis controversum arbitrio generalium Ordinum determinaretur. Foederatos quoq; & Aurantium Principem ijsdem postulatis approbandis pronos fuisse Elbertumque Leoninum, relatione ad Philippi Senatum institutâ, diversitatem animorum in ipso consessu deprehendisse. Quippe Arschotano, Barlamontio & Assonvilio pacem suadentibus, Requesentium Proregem, Rodam, & Rasingemum se oppositisse bellumque interverso pacis & concordiæ negotio, pessimo con-hitur. consilio redintegrasse. Igitur Requesentius, quo ruptâ induciarum actione, Foederatorum res arctaret, distributis per continentem & omnem provinciam copijs, de maritimo ut jam antè bello cogitavit, gentemque commercio & ex hoc opibus viribusque validam instructissimâ classe atterere. Quod consilium pro optimo clarissimi Scriptores meminere, improbato Ferdinandi Albani etiam tantæ famæ Ducis belli gerendi modo, quod neglectâ domandi maris & fluminum curâ, omnem vim ac gloriam oppriniendis mediterraneis vertillet.
units.tr: Reidanus notes that freedom of religion and a five-year truce were at last debated at that assembly, by which, while these lasted, every controverted point in the matter of religion would be settled by the judgement of the general Estates. He adds that the confederates and Prince Orange were also inclined to approve the same demands, and that Elbert Leoninus, in a report made to the Senate of Philip, found a difference of minds in the very gathering. Indeed, while Arschot, Barlaymont and Assonville urged peace, the viceroy Requesens, with Roda and Rasingem, opposed them, and, turning the business of peace and harmony upside down, renewed the war by the worst counsel. Therefore Requesens, so as to tighten the confederates' position by breaking off the truce negotiations, spread his forces through the mainland and every province, and thought of a naval war as he had before, intending to wear down a people made strong by commerce and by the resources and power derived from it, with a fully equipped fleet. The most famous writers have recorded this plan as the best, though they disapproved of the manner of waging war by the Duke of Alba, a man of such great reputation, who, neglecting the control of the sea and the rivers, turned all his force and glory to crushing the inland districts.

units.la: Unde Requesentius, quo sociam classem suæ adjungeret, Joannem Boischotum fisci regij advocatum in Angliam amandavit, navaliumque rerum subsidia reginam Elisabetham pro Philippo poposcit. Cæterum prudens fœmina, & velut sexus sui ingenio, pacì studens, amicitiam Philippi ex damno aut injuriâ Belgicarum provinciarum non volebat populum que vicinum & fato suo intœlicem, promissis Philippo auxilijs gravari. Itaque cavit; Ne quis præsidiarias bellicasve naves per regnum & Angliæ portus instrueret & ne classiarius Anglorum miles sacramentis externis se innecteret. Vetuit quoque; Ne rebellibus & exulibus Anglis, per Philippi ditiones agentibus, Prorex Requesentius debellandis mari foederatis gauderet juratisque regni sui hostibus. Specie Hispanici foederis, littora & portus sui regni aperiret. Itaque eidem Legato contendenti ut exules Belgas Frisiosque rebellionis in Regem reos regni finibus exterminaret, modestè reposuit regiique Legati importunitatem singulari lenitate & prudentiâ repressit.
units.tr: Hence Requesens, wanting to join a allied fleet to his own, sent John Boischot, advocate of the royal treasury, to England, and asked Queen Elizabeth on Philip's behalf for naval supplies. But the prudent woman, almost by the nature of her sex, was intent on peace. She did not want friendship with Philip to be bought by harm or injury to the Belgian provinces, nor to burden with promised aid to Philip a neighbouring people unlucky in its fate. So she took care that no one should fit out garrison or warships through the kingdom and the English ports, and that no English naval soldier should bind himself by foreign oaths. She also forbade the viceroy Requesens to take pleasure in subduing at sea the confederates and the sworn enemies of her kingdom, the English rebels and exiles living in Philip's dominions. On the pretext of the Spanish alliance, he was to open the shores and ports of her realm. So when the same envoy insisted that she expel from her kingdom the Belgian and Frisian exiles, guilty of rebellion against the King, she replied with moderation and checked the royal envoy's importunity with singular gentleness and prudence.

units.la: Neque enim protegere fe perduellem populum, ajebat, caterum ex statu afflictae patriae extorrem in regnum admittere, cui latendi locum omni humano & gentium jure deberet. Non violanda esse hospitij jura justiusque & sanctius esse, ferre fato infelicem quam sensum exuere alieni vulneris & jam in oculos incurrentis. Belgas certè ac socias gentes diu temperamentum immoderatae dominationi oraffe & ut finem intestinis armis ac simul miseriis clementia PHILIPPI aut consentientium Ordinum pax imponeret. Iam MAXIMILIANUM Cæsarem missis in Hispaniam Legatis nullo eventu petyisse, planè velut PHILIPPI animus ad æquiora obduratus plus licentiæ & severitati Proregum, quam supplicationibus sui populi daret. Quemsi patriis terris infelicitas temporum exigat, non esse iniquum alia syderum, alia sedium profugo quari aut externa auxilia allevandis extremis sollicitari. Ita factum esse, ut omni intercessione Principum apud Regem præclusâ, de societate Gallicâ cogitet, regno Angliæ & simul Philippi rebus magnum discrimen allaturâ. Monuisse se ejus rei REQUESENTIUM, nihil aliud regerentem quam pumiendum esse populum malâ religione imbutum. Interim exuli Belgæ & jam antè per regnum suum recepto, facessere molestiam non posse didicisseque experiundo PHILIPPUM, incertarum sedium populum, gentium jure ac simul desperatione occupanda ad sua, & sæpè aliena impelli. Ab eo scilicet fuisse, ut sub GULIELMO LUMAEO Comite Marcano proscripta Nobilitas, à quadriennio excedere portubus regni sui jussa, Briellam occuparet, omnique gentium subsidio ac simul solatio excidens, sedem virtuti suæ & simul secunda auspicia reparandæ libertati pararet. Neque alios fructus hoc ipso tempore similium mandatorum fore, facturam interim, ut Legatum PHILIPPUM ad Regem mittat ocyus edoceatque, se nec prisci unquam societatibus, nec commodo aut pacì duorum regnorum defuisse.
units.tr: Indeed, she said, it is not right to shelter a rebellious people. Rather, she should admit into her realm, as exiles from their afflicted homeland, people whom every human and international right obliges her to give a place of refuge. The laws of hospitality must not be violated, and it is more just and more sacred to bear with an unlucky people than to strip oneself of feeling for another's wound, already before one's eyes. The Belgians and the allied peoples have long begged that a moderation be put on unrestrained domination, and that the clemency of Philip or a peace agreed upon by the Estates might set an end to civil arms and at the same time to miseries. Now they have sent envoys to Spain and sought Maximilian Caesar, but to no result, just as Philip's mind, hardened against gentler courses, grants more licence and severity to the viceroys than to the supplications of his people. And if the unhappiness of the times drives them from their native lands, it is not unjust for exiles to seek other stars and other seats, or to solicit foreign aid to relieve their extremities. So it has come about that, with every intercession of princes with the King shut off, she is thinking of a French alliance, which will bring great danger to the realm of England and at the same time to Philip's affairs. I warned her of this, and Requesens replied with nothing but that the people, steeped in a bad religion, must be punished. Meanwhile, the Belgian exile, already received earlier through her kingdom, cannot be made to leave, and she has learned by experience that Philip drives a people of uncertain seats, by the law of nations and by despair, to seize for their own, and often for others' goods. Indeed, it was from him that the proscribed nobility, under William Lumey Count of Marck, ordered four years ago to leave the ports of his realm, occupied Brielle, and, cut off from all help and at the same time from comfort, prepared a seat for its virtue and at the same time favourable omens for recovering liberty. Nor will similar orders bring other fruits at this time. Meanwhile she will cause her envoy to Philip to be sent to the King, to inform him more quickly that she has never been wanting to former alliances, nor to the advantage or peace of the two kingdoms.

units.la: Cæterum Boischoto Burgundicum ad fœdus provocante (etsi id innovare Philippus recusaret) evenit, ut Elisabetha edictum interponeret caveretque, Ne præsidiariæ fœderatorum naves Angliæ portubus excederent & ne Belgicæ fœderataeque classi portus atque littora paterent. Cambdenus scribit Elisabetham, quod Anglorum proscriptos Belgicis Philippi ditionibus, intercedente Wilsono Reginæ Legato, Requesentius exterminasset, id Philippi quoque postulato tum dedisse, quo gratiam sibi à Philippo præstitam, cujus inimicitiam declinabat, suis quoque in Hispanum officijs pensaret. Adeo verum est, plus ex alienâ potentiâ metum, quam ex justiore causâ affectum apud reginam tum valuisse. Itaque Edicto ad classis suæ & maritimorum locorum Præfectos dato, præter Aurantium Principem, Culenburgium, Bergensem & Marcanum Comites, præcipuos quosque ex fœderatâ nobilitate prohiberi regni sui ingressu jussit plusque Philippo Regi ex defunctæ sororis Mariæ matrimonio & mutatis per Angliam rebus inimico, quam favori Belgici, in quod tacitè inclinabat, Fœderis per infidos aulæ mores concessit. Quæ consideranti mihi, multa observare tum licet, Principum procerumque ingenia, ut apud mortales assolet, in stabiliendâ deprimendâque Belgicæ & nostræ gentis libertate à fortunæ secundis aut adversis tum pependisse. Igitur quantum animi Requesentius regiæque res spiritus ac virium trahebant, tanto impensius regijs partibus favebatur nostrumque in arma studium, velut à Bredano conventu spe pacis frigeratum ac regiæ magnitudini, tanquam oneri, recollecto Requesentij impetu succumbens, tacita odia & velut aversationes vicinorum Principum traxisse. Cæterum evanescente lubricæ pacis appetitu, ubi animi fœderatis è periculis redire, omne quod ex magnitudine regiâ in metum, aut ex pace in otium cesserat contemni aut acui cœptum deprehensumque fuit generosam gentem, etiam tepefacto ante sanguine, difficillimis temporibus & illo Principum à nostro fœdere divortio, ad intermissa armorum & gloriæ desideria, cum incremento virtutis processisse.
units.tr: But when Boischot invoked the Burgundian alliance (though Philip refused to renew it), it came about that Elizabeth issued an edict and ordered that the confederates' garrison ships should not leave English ports, and that the Belgian and confederate fleet should not have access to her ports and shores. Camden writes that Elizabeth, because Requesens had expelled the English exiles from Philip's Belgian dominions at the intercession of Wilson, the Queen's envoy, granted this to Philip's demand too, so as to repay with her own services against the Spaniard the favour Philip had shown her, whose enmity she was avoiding. So true it is that fear of another's power, rather than affection for a juster cause, then prevailed with the queen. Therefore, by an edict given to the prefects of her fleet and of the maritime places, she ordered that, besides Prince William of Orange and the Counts of Culemborg, Bergen and Marck, all the chief nobles of the confederate nobility be forbidden entry into her realm. She yielded more to King Philip, an enemy through the marriage of her late sister Mary and through the changed state of affairs in England, than to favour for the Belgian cause, towards which she tacitly inclined, and she yielded to the confederacy only through the faithless manners of the court. In considering these matters, many things may be observed, as is customary among mortals: in establishing or suppressing the liberty of the Belgian and of our nation, the natures of princes and nobles depended then on fortune, whether prosperous or adverse. Therefore, the more Requesens' spirit and the royal affairs gathered strength and forces, the more eagerly the royal party was favoured. Our zeal for arms, as if cooled by hope of peace from the Breda conference, and yielding to the renewed onslaught of Requesens as to a burden on royal greatness, drew hidden hatreds and, as it were, aversions from neighbouring princes. But when the appetite for a slippery peace faded, and the spirits of the confederates returned from their dangers, it was found that everything that had passed from royal greatness into fear, or from peace into idleness, began to be despised or to be sharpened. It was found, too, that the generous people, even though its blood had previously cooled, in the most difficult times and with that divorce of the princes from our confederacy, advanced with growing courage to the renewed desire for arms and glory.

units.la: Itaque onerariæ Anglorum naves Hispaniam versus cursum facientes, à fœderatorum classe direptæ, honestâ apud indignantem regnam excusatione, arterendis Hispani & sociorum rebus id fieri, quod gentium jus omni temporum ætate permisisset. Reidanus addit, Aurantium Principem offensum Elisabethæ animum, serijs litteris pupugisse monuisseque ne avaritiæ negotiantium, patrocinando suorum vitam ac fortunas discrimini exponeret nexumque gentium ex verâ religione natum, proferendo vili commercio dissolveret. Mox per Frisiam quoque terrâ marique bellum ferbuit, adeo intutis æstuarijs ut vicinarum gentium commercia partium classibus præpedirentur. Quippe Doco Martna, vir militiæ impiger & juxta pacis artibus illustris, maris imperium adeptus, præsidiarijs navibus omne fretum tenebat, quod majores minoresque Frisios tum insulares nationes latissimis undis interluebat. Igitur expugnatâ Amasso in flumine vectoriâ navi, quam in formam præsidiariæ redegerat, Lambertum Calvum virum fortem & promptæ audaciæ Austrino sinui præfecit, quo Amstelodamensium, clo. Io. um cum Translavicanis Embdanisque commercia & simul commeatum LXXV. regijs castris subverteret. Is vero omne obvium depraedatus tantum sui nominis terrorem per omnem oram sparsit, ut peiratas triremesque regias Friscis aestuarijs submoveret divexandisque maritimis Geesterlandis, Lemmarijs ac Cuneranis incumberet. Unde mapalia & villae littori contiguae vacuae cultoribus, quos bonis exutos in alia terrarum fortuna turbidi temporis agebat. Amasi vero fluminis ostium Petrus Adrianus Bolsuerdiensis nomine foederatorum tenebat. Qui licentiam suorum aegre ferens reique alienae praeterquam hostilis abstinens, cum liberius insolentiusque praedandi genus detrectaret, a classiario milite confossus ac Amaso flumini immersus est. Fratrem quoque, quem disciplinae & fraternus amor eadem ad consilia traxerant, idem exitus abstulit. Caeterum Embdae in sicarios statutum tristeq; licentiosi temporis flagitium justo supplicio expiatum. Ita depurgandi maris turandorumque portuum cura in peiraticam saepe vertebatur classiariusque miles, nulla sacramenti religione aut reverentia imperantis, tribunorum caede nefarias manus & simul imperia Praefectorum foedabat.
units.tr: Thus English merchant ships sailing towards Spain were plundered by the confederate fleet, with an honest excuse to the indignant queen: this was done to harm Spain and its allies' affairs, which the law of nations had allowed in every age. Reidanus adds that Prince William, offended, stung Elizabeth's mind with severe letters, and warned her not to expose the lives and fortunes of her own people to danger by defending the greed of merchants, nor to dissolve the bond of nations, born of true religion, by offering it up to base commerce. Soon war also flared up on land and sea through Friesland, so much so that in the unsafe estuaries the trade of neighbouring peoples was hindered by the fleets of both sides. Indeed Doco Martena, a man keen in war and equally distinguished in the arts of peace, having gained command of the sea, held every strait with garrison ships, which washed the greater and lesser Frisians and the island nations with its broadest waves. So, after capturing in the river Amasso a transport ship which he had turned into a garrison ship, he set Lambert Calvus, a brave man of ready daring, over the Austrian gulf, to overthrow the trade of the Amsterdammers, and at the same time the commerce with the Translavians and the Emdeners, and the supplies of the royal camp. He plundered everything in his path and spread such terror of his name along the whole coast that he drove the royal pirates and triremes away from the Frisian estuaries and set about harassing the maritime Geesterlanders, Lemmers and Cuneraners. Hence huts and villages next to the shore were left empty of cultivators, whom turbulent times drove, stripped of their goods, to other fortunes. At the mouth of the river Amasso, Peter Adrian of Bolsward held command in the name of the confederates. He bore his men's licence with difficulty, and kept his hands off other people's property except that of the enemy. When he refused a freer and more insolent kind of plundering, he was stabbed by a naval soldier and sunk in the river Amasso. The same end carried off his brother too, whom discipline and fraternal love had drawn to the same counsels. But at Emden sentence was passed against the assassins, and the sad crime of a licentious age was atoned for by just punishment. Thus the care of clearing the sea and guarding the harbours was often turned into piracy, and the naval soldier, with no religious respect for his oath or reverence for his commander, defiled his impious hands with the slaughter of tribunes and at the same time with the authority of the prefects.

units.la: Itaque fortuna foederis sensim mari increscente, Senatus regius velut vires adversarum partium compressurus, infoelicibus ultro exulum fatis graviorum casum adjecit statuitque Edicto; Ut bona proscriptorum venirent. Itaque tum exhauriendis civium nobiliumque familiarum patrimonijs novum & per Frisiam inauditum illa aetate malum vendendis sub hasta exulum proscriptorumque bonis repertum est, delegato Baldevino Loo Thesaurario Regio, qui e praescripto feralium tabularum auctiones bonorum exerceret. Cui actui cum Basilica in regia dies ad xv. Kal. Jun. dictus esset, exules Frisij hanc protestationis formulam Leovardiam misere.
units.tr: So, as the fortunes of the confederacy gradually grew at sea, the royal Senate, as if about to crush the forces of the opposing side, added a graver calamity to the unhappy fates of the exiles, and by edict ordered that the goods of the proscribed be sold. Thus, with the patrimonies of citizens and noble families to be drained, a new evil, unheard of in Friesland in that age, was devised: the goods of exiles and proscribed persons were sold at auction. Baldwin Loo, royal treasurer, was appointed to conduct the sales of goods according to the prescribed fatal lists. When a day for this proceeding had been set in the royal basilica for the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, the Frisian exiles sent this form of protest to Leeuwarden.

units.la: BONA nostra FERDINANDUS ALBANUS jam ante fisco addixit, postquam nos patrijs sedibus ejectos nostra infelicitas & simul saevities dominantium alio terrarum sparsit. Quae confiscatio ut legibus nostris repugnat, ita PHILIPPI regis sacramento contraria est. Quippe e sanguinario & tristi judicum collegio, quod idem ALBANUS instituerat, jam ante decreta, ut per speciem judicij nostra innocentia damnaretur. Evocati contra jus patrium, contra ritus majorum ad suspectum tribunal, nec defensione usi fuimus, nec ut eam instituueremus lex fori ferebat, intuto commeatu quem arma ac vis obsepserant. Quare ad patrios ritus, ad judicem lege nobis datum provocavimus, ut si rei cujusdam criminis essemus, nostrae leges nos damnarent, si inanis accusatio esset, nostra innocentia nos absolveret. Hoc vero fore AREMBERGIUS, qui provinciam Philippi regis nomine tum regebat, fidem fecit addiditque, nec reminisci PHILIPPUM anteactarum rerum velle, nec in corpora aut fortunas provincialium desaevire. Ita quippe Romani Imperij & CAROLI Caesaris rescriptis decretum erat, quorum communione aut beneficio nos Germaniae gentem & Imperij sociam privare nostrum jus & immunitates non ferunt. Tamen ALBANI jussu in nostrum sanguinem, in nostra viscera saevitum, quae damnationibus superbi ac cruenti Ducis nostra libertas exemerat. Nobis vero in exilium actis & peregrinum caelum tolerantibus bona ac res adimuntur, ne quid solatij aut subsidij nostræ inopiæ & miseriæ ex hæreditate majorum peregrinis in terris obveniret. Ita patimur coacti, quod nec divinæ nec humanæ leges probant & à quibus manifesta omnis æqui dissensio est. Quare jus hastæ & institutæ auctiones, ut violentæ sunt, ita damnosæ nobis aut posteris nostris de jure esse nequeunt, nisi irruere in res ac fortunas licentia temporis sinat ac gentium moribus omnia cedant occupantibus. Nec enim Regis hæc imperio aut voluntate fiunt, qui Hispaniâ suâ clausus, nostræ miseriæ aut juris rationem, imo famam ignorat. KEQUESENTII vero solius hoc mandatum est, dolosâ circumventione & quidem inscio rege quæsitum, cujus absentiâ soli exulum durioribus imperiis reservamur. Reliquarum provinciarum profugi nec ea patiuntur, nec ut ferant instituta pacis apud Bredanos actio id sinit. Eâ quippe Rex indulsit, ut si extent ad dominos suos bona redeant. Tantum abest ut malæ fidei emptor aut possessor quid juris acquirat, præsertim cum pretia venalium rerum exinde nasci-tura pravis usibus & subvertendæ patriæ cessura sint. Igitur nostro & hæredum nomine cavemus, ne quid damni istiusmodi auctiones nostris bonis ac for-tunis creent, quas quocunque etiam tempore repetere justâ vendicatione in animum induximus. Nobis denatis posteri idem agent, si præcipiti mortalita-tis lege his terris subtractos acerba fata in patriam non reducant. Quare nec retractuum jura apud nos posteriosve valebunt, lege ac exceptione asturos ma-lam fidem istis contractibus subsuisse. Monemus interim propinquos & conci-ves, ne assensum aut operam isti rei locent, cuius iniquitas manifestam sanctissimi numinis ultionem sensura sit. Pravorum consiliorum mali exitus erunt.
units.tr: Our goods Ferdinand of Alba has already handed over to the treasury, after our misfortune and the cruelty of our rulers scattered us to lands elsewhere. This confiscation conflicts with our laws, and it is equally contrary to the oath of King Philip. For from the bloody and gloomy college of judges, which this same Alba set up, decrees had already been issued that our innocence should be condemned under the appearance of a trial. Summoned, against the law of our fathers and the customs of our ancestors, before a suspect tribunal, we were neither allowed a defence, nor was the court's law such that we could set one up, since our safe passage was blocked by arms and force. We therefore appealed, according to our ancestral customs, to a judge given to us by law: if we were guilty of some crime, our own laws would condemn us; if the accusation were empty, our innocence would acquit us. Arenberg, who then governed the province in King Philip's name, gave assurance that this would happen, and added that Philip did not wish to recall past events or to rage against the persons or fortunes of the provincials. Indeed, it had been decreed by the rescripts of the Roman Empire and of Charles Caesar, and the Frisian nation, a member of the Empire and its ally, cannot be deprived by their fellowship or favour of our rights and immunities. Yet by Alba's order cruelty was wreaked upon our blood and our vitals, which our liberty had removed from the condemnations of the proud and bloody Duke. Moreover, we have been driven into exile and endure a foreign sky, and our goods and property are taken from us, so that no solace or aid for our poverty and misery might come from our ancestors' inheritance in foreign lands. Thus we suffer, compelled to what neither divine nor human laws approve, and from which all sense of justice clearly dissents. Therefore the right of auction and the sales arranged by it, being violent, are likewise harmful to us and to our posterity and cannot be valid by right, unless the licence of the times allows them to fall upon goods and fortunes, and all things yield to those who seize them by the custom of nations. For these things are not done by the king's command or will, for he, shut up in his Spain, is ignorant of our misery, of the justice of our case, and indeed of our reputation. This mandate belongs to Requesens alone, sought by deceitful circumvention and indeed without the king's knowledge, and it is by his absence alone that we exiles are kept under harsher commands. The fugitives of the other provinces suffer none of these things, nor does the Breda peace settlement allow it, for by that the king granted that, where they still exist, goods should return to their owners. So far is it from the case that a buyer or possessor in bad faith acquires any right, especially since the prices of the goods sold will arise from this to be spent on wicked uses and to the ruin of the country. Therefore we give warning, in our own name and in that of our heirs, that these auctions bring no harm to our goods and fortunes, which we have resolved to reclaim at whatever time by just vindication. If we die, our posterity will do the same, unless the law of hasty mortality returns to the homeland those removed from these lands by bitter fate. Therefore no rights of redemption will avail among us or our descendants, since they will know that bad faith was sewn into these contracts by law and by exception. Meanwhile we warn our kinsmen and fellow citizens not to lend their assent or effort to this affair, whose iniquity will feel the manifest vengeance of the most holy divinity. The outcomes of wicked counsels will be evil.

units.la: Hæc EXULES.
units.tr: These are the words of the exiles.

units.la: Tum novorum vectigalium lege, quam jam ante Roblesius Senatusque regius rogaverant, exsolvendis militum stipendijs invalida, Gasparus Roblesius ad Kal. Jul. conventum Ordinum provinciæ indixit sustentandisque copijs firma & majora subsidia flagitavit. Incertos quippe Vectigalium reditus querebatur & haud dubié fraudem novæ legi fieri, ad quam sanciendam, non malus iniquusque animus, sed inopia ærarij regij & ultima illum necessitas compulssent. Ne scilicet miles æris egens per commissam sibi provinciam stipendia è rapto faceret seditiousumque & disciplinæ oblitum quodlibet in facinus angustia rerum præcipitaret. Nunc vero Bredanæ pacis inrita spe & recrudescente bello majoribus certioribusque tributis opus esse neque aliud remedium quam ut stipendijs cohortium cæterisque necessarijs populi tributum ad-æquetur. Itaque Ordines, quos direptionis metus & militaris insolentiæ occupabat, in diversa consilia ivere, censentibus tandem pleris-que, abrogata Vectigalium lege haud dubié in servitutem eruptură, solis locupletum opibus bellum trahendum esse.
units.tr: Then, by the law of new taxes which Roblesius and the royal Council had earlier proposed, but which was insufficient to pay the soldiers' wages, Gaspar Roblesius, on 1 July, called a meeting of the Estates of the province and demanded firmer and larger subsidies to maintain the troops. He complained that the revenue from the taxes was uncertain and that the new law was undoubtedly being defrauded; it had been enacted not from a wicked or unjust spirit, but compelled by the poverty of the royal treasury and by utter necessity. Namely, so that the soldier, short of money, would not make his pay out of plunder in the province entrusted to him, and, becoming seditious and forgetful of discipline, rush into any crime from sheer straitened circumstances. Now, however, with hope of the Breda peace void and war breaking out again, greater and more certain tributes were needed, and there was no other remedy than that the tax on the people be made equal to the pay of the cohorts and the other necessities. Thus the Estates, whom fear of plunder and military insolence occupied, went in different directions, most of them at last holding that, once the tax law was repealed, the country would undoubtedly be dragged into slavery, and that the war must be carried on from the wealth of the rich alone.

units.la: Unde census familiarum per provinciam initûs cautumque decreto ut in Kal Majas proxumas quovis lunari mense octo millia æris ducen-tique & quadraginta Carolæi alendis copijs penderentur. Mox septem sestertiorum tributum singulis familijs impositum, cæterum hac conditione, ut ratio privatæ egestatis aut opulentiæ haberetur, Senatusque Regius agendo censui ex æquitate præesset. Quare ditium cœ-nobiorum antistites singulis mensibus florenos aureos duos, nobiles clo. Io. LXXV. yero caeterique, quibus aut ampla patrimonia aut modicae opes erant; unum pendere jussi supplendae illorum inopiae quos conferendi in publicum aeris incapaces fortuna fecisset. Quaestura quoque munus Heroni Burmaniae viro nobili demandatum erogandaeque singulis septiduis pecuniae potestas facta. Scriptor Stauriius notat in binielire tantum id subsidij cohortibus regijs petitum fuisse aut dum huiusmodi exercitus primo tempore Philippus Rex decrevisset. Diploma quoque regium, quo Gasparo Roblesio Praefecturae dignitatem Philippus confirmabat, idem in Basilica regia recitatum tradit eundemque Roblesium tamdiu vicario regis per Frisiam imperio praefuisse, donec anno clo. Io. LXXVII. a Legionarijs suis custodiae apud Groningamos datus Bruxellas abduceretur. His obiter Buranas, & Veteraquinatium clades nostri Scriptores adiecere.
