units.tr: Hence a census of families was begun throughout the province, and it was decreed that on the first of May next, and every lunar month thereafter, eight thousand two hundred and forty Carolus guilders were to be paid to feed the troops. Soon a tax of seven sesterces was imposed on each family, but on this condition: that the circumstances of private poverty or wealth be taken into account, and that the Royal Council preside over the assessment with fairness. Therefore the heads of the wealthy monasteries were ordered to pay two gold florins each month, while the nobles, and others who had either ample patrimonies or modest means, were each to pay one, to supply the want of those whom fortune had made unable to contribute money to the public. The office of paymaster was also entrusted to Heron of Burmania, a nobleman, and he was given power to pay out money every seven days. The writer Stauriius notes that this aid was sought for the royal cohorts for two years only, or while King Philip had decreed such an army at its first institution. He also reports that the royal diploma by which Philip confirmed the dignity of prefect to Gaspar Roblesius was read in the royal Basilica, and that the same Roblesius governed Frisia as the king's vicar for so long, until in 1577 he was handed over by his own legionaries as a prisoner at Groningen and led away to Brussels. Our writers, in passing, have added the defeats at Burum and at Veteraquinatium.

units.la: Annotatum invenio circa haec tempora quosdam e majoribus Frisijs haud lato in utrumque littus trajectu in minorem Frisiam delatos suspectosque maleficij vinculis datos, mox proditionis & incendij damnatos, innocentem animam & sceleris puram execrandae immanorum judicum severitati libasse. Quare in ipsa morte voces infantium auditas eosdemque laceris ac semiustis corporibus exeuntes spiritus, haud dubia aeterni ipe, Deo liberatori propitiasse. In ijs Petrus Joannis Coudumanus, Rombertus Simonius, Nicolaus Roelefius Doccomiens, & Isbrandus Joannis Echtenius fuere. Mox Geesterlandia, de consilio Sonnoi minoris Frisiae Praefecti a centum & quinquaginta foedera is pervagata, quos Enchusae praesidium agentes & in actuaria navigia impositos ascendere Geesterlandicum littus praeceperat. Qui in interiora, mox Balckium Geesterlandiae vicum pergentes, dum praedae quam opulentia loci dabat intenti agunt, a praesidio regio quod Lemmariá exierat, circumventi sunt. Quare ut praedae & simul vitae concluderent, ferro aperiendam viam rati cum regijs congressi sunt, quos numero superiores & in terra sua pugnantes praecipitem in fugam egere. Duodecim Valones illo conflictu caesi. Plurimi foedis vulneribus quae tergo fugientes exceperant saucij occultis locorum se claudere. Regnerus Idzius, cum praeturae Geesterlandicae actuario in inimores Frisios abductus.
units.tr: I find it noted that about this time some of the leading Frisians, after crossing a not very wide strait into Lesser Frisia, were seized and held in chains on suspicion of crime, and soon condemned for treason and arson; and that their innocent souls, pure of crime, were offered up to the execrable severity of savage judges. Hence voices of infants were heard at their deaths, and their spirits, leaving their torn and half-burned bodies, undoubtedly went to eternal God, their deliverer, in propitiation. Among them were Pieter Jansz Coudumanus, Rombert Simonius, Nicolaas Roelefius of Doccum, and Isbrand Jansz Echtenius. Soon Geesterland was overrun, on the counsel of Sonnoy, prefect of Lesser Frisia, by 150 confederates, whom he had ordered, while holding the garrison at Enkhuizen and placed on transport ships, to land on the Geesterland shore. Pressing inland, and soon making for Balk, a village of Geesterland, they were intent on plunder, which the wealth of the place offered, when they were surrounded by the royal garrison that had set out from Lemmer. Thinking that they must open a way with iron to escape both the plunder and their lives, they engaged the royalists; but the royalists, superior in number and fighting on their own soil, drove them into headlong flight. Twelve Walloons were slain in that clash. Many of the wounded, who had received foul wounds in the back while fleeing, hid themselves in hidden places. Reinier Idzes, together with the secretary of the Geesterland praetorship, was carried off by the enemy Frisians.

units.la: Quamobrem Roblesius celocium classem repente instructam aestuarijs immisit provectusque Texaliam, quam Gualtherus Hegemannus cum copijs & imperio tenebat, in altum regredi coactus est. Iam enim munitiones validas insulae praeduxerat extimamque oram dispositis excubijs tutabatur. Ideo Roblesius Flevolandiam versus cursum rexit expositque in terram milite qua latissimum Flevi ostium spectat insulae potitus est. Quippe in arenosa ac edita pavidi incolae se receperant, quae magno mari objacentia ut securitatem genti adversum maris aestus & tempestates ita suffugium tum periculis dabant. Nonnullos tardius fugientes, quos aut domesticarum rerum cura aut aetas morabatur ferrum hausit. Tum faces villis ac tugurijs subditae, horribilique incendio 450. domus conflagravere. Praeda classi impositae, non inhibentibus foederatorum praesidiarijs navibus, quae stationem vicino in alveo praeterlabentis Flevi tuendis insularibus tenebant. Post Roblesius, retro-aɑ̈ actâ ad Wiringiam classe, cui insulæ idem discrimen parabatur, nullo ibidem rerum successu in Frisios se recepit sensimque intumescentibus æstuariis & sæviente hyberno sydere classem in portus subduxit. Ita velut reciproco fortunæ æstu res fluebant subvertendisque per Frisiam fœderatis nova consilia fabricabantur.
units.tr: Therefore Roblesius suddenly sent a fleet of small boats, quickly fitted out, into the estuaries, and, having sailed to Texel, which Walter Hegemann held with troops and command, he was forced to withdraw back to open sea. For Hegemann had already set up strong fortifications on the island and was guarding the outer shore with sentries posted. So Roblesius steered towards Flevoland, landed his soldiers where the broadest mouth of the Vlie faces the island, and took possession of it. For the timid inhabitants had retreated to the sandy and raised ground, which, lying opposite the great sea, offered the people safety against the surges and storms of the sea, and so then offered a refuge from dangers. Some who fled too slowly, whom care of household things or age delayed, were struck down by the sword. Then torches were put to huts and cottages, and in a horrible fire 450 houses burned down. The plunder was loaded onto the fleet, the confederate garrison ships not hindering, although they held a station in the nearby channel of the flowing Vlie to guard the islanders. Afterwards Roblesius, having led the fleet back to Wieringen, for which island the same danger was being prepared, withdrew into Frisia with no success there; and, as the estuaries gradually swelled and the winter star raged, he drew the fleet into harbour. Thus affairs flowed as if by the reciprocal tide of fortune, and new plans were devised to overthrow the confederates throughout Frisia.

units.la: Quare per exules, qui Embdæ in Transfamasanis subsistebant, Aurantium ad Principem legatio decreta delectusque obeundæ legationi, Carolus Roorda, vir eximius, qui de arcanis dolosisve Roblesij artibus & simul patriæ statu Principem doceret. Is vero Rotterodami ad Mosæ flumen tum agebat variisque fortunæ casibus principem animum substernens pacis bellique consilia moderabatur. Quo loci postquam legatus Roorda vergente Septembri advenit, salutato pro more AURANTIO, fiduciarias litteras exhibuit. Iis perscriptum erat;
units.tr: Therefore, through the exiles who were staying at Emden in East Frisia, it was decided to send an embassy to the Prince of Orange, and Carolus Roorda, an outstanding man, was chosen for the embassy to inform the Prince of Roblesius's secret and deceitful schemes and at the same time of the state of the country. The Prince was then at Rotterdam on the Maas, and, steadying his mind against the various turns of fortune, was directing his plans for peace and war. When the envoy Roorda arrived there toward the end of September, he greeted Orange in the usual way and presented a letter of credence. It was written as follows.

units.la: Novam stabilendi per Frisiam imperij rationem Roblesium iniisse. Sic Vectigalium lege primum rogatâ, octo in quemque mensem caroleorum millia militaribus stipendiis assignata, non alio consilio quam ut tabescens per Frisiam bellum velut enerve, certo ordine & firmâ ærarij lege traheretur. Adhæc exulum bona fisco applicari & habendis bonorum auctionibus dies dictos, ut perscriptam diu tabulis sævitiem aucti furoris documenta ostenderent. Nec in exules tantum maritos, cæterum in conjuges profugorum desæviri, quas aut ingravescens ætas aut imbecillitas sexus, aut patientia durioris imperij huc usque exilio eximiset. Scilicet earum quoque bonis inhiare Præfectum, nihil aliud agentem, quam ut exactionem exactione cumulet attenuatisque populi opibus pro arbitrio imperet. Sic aut ordinarijs tributis nova adjici aut peti aliunde. Quippe famâ ferri Requesentium, suo an provinciarum Belgicarum ære consilia Roblesij fulcire tantamque rerum molem alienis nervis duci. Ita Roblesium modo classem adornare, modo reficere minoribusque Frisiis continuos per exploratores incumbere, ut eorum ope eandem in provinciam irruat, regiæ dominationi fato suo & laudatis armis subductam. Quamobrem necessum esse agitantem se per confinia Roblesium suâ in provinciâ bello petere, quo transmarinæ expeditiones per intestina & domestica arma cessent. Nec arduum id consilium aut grave molientibus fore, si loca quæ aut mare aut flumina præcingunt, fœderati occupent, auxilijs Sonnoi è minori Frisiâ adjuti. Posseinterim Sonnoio, dum navatæ operæ sumptus recipiat, maioris Frisiæ Præfecturam deferri ac tamdiu unus imperio utrumque populum regi, quamdiu in tuto res provincialium fortuna locaverit. Compositâ ordinatâque provinciâ majoribus Frisijs ærarium & necessaria bello non defore. Loca vero situ munita & facilia occupatu esse, sed quorum rationem in secreto Aurantij legatus redditurus esset. Sic Roblesii exactionibus, sic malis consilijs occurri & minoribus Frisiis pacem ac commercia reddi posse. Quippe confluxuram haud dubie multitudinem consilia bello aut arma ferentem, quorum terrâ marique ex loci commoditate magnus usus esse queat. Cætera Legati prudentiæ & fidei committere, daturi operam ut secretorum suorum conscium AURANTIUM aut participem SONNOIUM faciat.
units.tr: They have undertaken a new method of establishing their rule through Friesland, Roblesius having begun it. First, by a law on taxes being proposed, eight thousand Carolus guilders a month were assigned to the military pay, with no other purpose than that the war in Friesland, weakening like a sinew, should be dragged along in a fixed order and by a firm financial law. Besides this, the goods of the exiles were to be applied to the fisc, and days were appointed for auctioning their property, so that the increased fury might show the evidence of a cruelty long recorded in the registers. Nor were the cruelties directed only at exiled husbands, but also at the wives of the fugitives, whom either advancing age, or the weakness of their sex, or patience under a harsher rule had hitherto spared from exile. Clearly the Prefect was greedy for their goods too, doing nothing else than piling exaction upon exaction and ordering the people's wealth, now weakened, as he pleased. Thus either new burdens are added to the ordinary taxes or they are sought from elsewhere. Indeed, the rumour is that Requesens, with his own money or that of the Belgic provinces, is supporting Roblesius's plans, and that so great a load of affairs is being driven by foreign sinews. So Roblesius is now preparing a fleet, now repairing it, and is pressing continually upon the lesser Frisians through spies, so that with their help he may rush into this province, which by its fate and by its praised arms has been withdrawn from royal dominion. Therefore it is necessary that Roblesius, who is stirring about on the borders, be attacked by war in his own province, so that overseas expeditions may cease through internal and domestic arms. Nor will this plan be difficult or burdensome for those undertaking it, if the Union occupies the places that the sea or the rivers surround, aided by the forces of Sonnoy from Lesser Friesland. Meanwhile, while Sonnoy takes up the expense of the work undertaken, the prefecture of Greater Friesland should be conferred on him, and one man should rule both peoples as long as the affairs of the province stand secure by fortune. Once the province is settled and ordered, Greater Friesland will not lack money and what is needed for war. The places, however, are fortified by their position and easy to seize, but the plan for them the envoy of Orange will give in secret. Thus the exactions of Roblesius and his evil schemes may be met, and peace and commerce restored to the lesser Frisians. Undoubtedly a multitude bearing arms for the plan will flock together, and their service on land and sea may be of great use owing to the convenience of the place. The rest I entrust to the envoy's prudence and good faith, and he will take care to make Orange privy to these secrets, and Sonnoy a participant.

units.la: Hæc iv. Non. Aug. signata.
units.tr: Signed on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

units.la: Traditum actis est prolixis sermonibus usum legatum non parva istius consilii desideria Aurantio Principi instillasse.
units.tr: It is recorded in the acts that the envoy, with lengthy speeches, instilled considerable desires for this plan into the Prince of Orange.

units.la: Aurantius vero, etsi sublevandis Frisiorum rebus solertem animum praeferret, ita sparsa distributaque per omnem provinciam arma querebatur. Itaque & sex peditum cohortes in auxilia e minoribus Frisiis accitas, quos praestandis ulterioribus auxiliis imbecilles metus hostium & ingruentis brumae periculum faceret. Quod ad subsidia aeris attineret, magna impendia instruendis classibus & praesidiariis navibus eosdem Frisios conferre, quarum tres solvendae Zirizaeorum obsidioni & subvectando obsessis commeatui suo aere adornarent. Quamobrem hoc ipso tempore nec militem nec pecuniam concedere socijs poterit. Se interim mandare Sonnoio ut cum legato caeterisve ad quos hac pertinent, consilia communicet agatque quod e rep. fit.
units.tr: Orange, however, though he displayed a shrewd mind for relieving the Frisians' affairs, complained that arms were scattered and distributed throughout the whole province. "And so," he said, "six cohorts of infantry have been summoned as auxiliaries from the lesser Frisians, whom the feeble fears of the enemy and the danger of the coming winter would make it hard for them to supply further aid. As for money, the same Frisians must contribute great expenses for equipping fleets and guard ships, three of which are to be fitted out at their own cost, to break the siege of Zierikzee and to convey supplies to the besieged. Therefore at this very time he will be able to grant neither soldiers nor money to the allies. Meanwhile he commands Sonnoy to share plans with the envoy and with others concerned with this, and to do what is for the public good."

units.la: Hoc in acta relatum ac Rotterodami manu Aurantij perscriptum.
units.tr: This was recorded in the acts and written at Rotterdam in Orange's own hand.

units.la: Tum ut cnrae sibi esse res Trans-Rhenanas ac Frisiorum testaretur Aurantius, Bartholdum Entenium Menthedanum virum nobilem & manu strenuum, gerendis in Frisia foederatorum rebus cogendisque ocyus copijs praefecit. Hoc modo Legatus a Principe dimissus, ac in minores Frisios regressus Sonnoio Praefecto legationis suae secretum & mentem Principis exposuit. Caeterum Sonnoius, alio ab Aurantij responso, debiles copias & expositam incursionibus provinciam suam praefervidis Legati studijs regerebat. Sic Hyergium nuper, sic Roblesium praefecturae suae fines ingressos. Itaque perpetua arma aut continuos metus sibi incumbere, tanto graviores futuros, si fessae, lacus, aestuaria glacie aeternantur; quam ingruens bruma & in proximo occasurum Vergiliarum sydus promittant. Interim opportuno tempore auxilia missurum daturumque operam ut rescripto Aurantij & secretis consilijs innixae societati satisfiat.
units.tr: Then, so that Orange might attest that the affairs beyond the Rhine and of the Frisians were a concern to him, he placed Bartholomeus Entenius of Menthe, a nobleman vigorous in action, in charge of conducting the Union's affairs in Friesland and of gathering the forces more quickly. Thus dismissed by the Prince, the envoy returned to the lesser Frisians and laid before Sonnoy, the prefect of his embassy, the secret matters and the mind of the Prince. But Sonnoy, reporting a reply from Orange other than the one hoped for, answered the envoy's over-ardent zeal by describing his weak forces and his province, exposed to incursions: thus Hyergium had lately, and thus Roblesius, entered the borders of his prefecture. Therefore constant arms or continual fears pressed upon him, all the more serious if the fields, lakes and estuaries were to be locked in ice forever, as the coming winter and the setting of the Pleiades nearby seemed to promise. Meanwhile he would send help at a suitable time and see to it that the alliance, resting on Orange's written reply and secret plans, was satisfied.

units.la: Mox decretum in comitio quod prid. Kal. Iul. indictum erat, ut e familiarum censu Philippi per Frisiam praesidia alerentur singulisq; ccto & viginti diebus octena aureorum millia & ducenti continuatione tributi corrogarentur. Hac tamen conditione ut modus colligendi aeris, prout cuique commodum foret, praescriberetur, & ut indictiones a Kal. Sept. proximis cessarent. Ita Edzardus Douma, Haringus Oenema, Annas Tarquinius & Auco Edonius pro Oostergois ac Sylvestribus signavere. Eadem fere a Westergois decreta, sub hac tamen cautione, ut licentiam militarem vis atque autoritas Praefecti centurionum; coerceret damnumq; ulterius numeratis militi stipendijs averteretur. Quae etsi oppidanis probarentur, tamen volebant, ut ipsi ex indictionum tributo, stipendia & servitia, ut vocant, praesidijs civitatum praestita reciperent eoq; facto tollendis indictionibus delegarentur. Cuae partium consensu interveniente regis nomine Emskerckius, pro Ordinibus Hector Dekama, Hero Ockingha, Suffridus Aesgema, Scelto Liauckama, Douwo Roorda, Ruardus Vibius signavere. Non alia solemniate quam si aeternae conventionis speciem ista pactio praeberet videreturque rex Philippus pacem atque securitatem genti, gens Frisica regio militi stipendia amovendis a provincia hostibus spopondisse. Itaq; tria aureorum millia Roblesio dono data, quod cum animi quadam moderatione & regij imperij temperamento provinciam rexisset. xisset. Quare petebant Frisij ut bene gesti muneris & laudati regiminis vestigijs insisteret, mediamque regundi viam ingressus regi & simul populo egregia in posterum officia continuaret. Hæc ab Edzardo Douma, Haringio Oenema, Erasmo Douma, Ruardo Roorda, Meinio Lyclesio Nyholtpadio & Hesselo Hania. iv. Non. Iul. signata. Tum Edzardo Douma provinciæ nomine Bruxellas missó in mandatis datum.
units.tr: Soon a decree was passed in the assembly, which had been called before 1 July, that the garrisons of Philip in Friesland should be maintained from the census of families, and that eight thousand two hundred gold pieces should be collected every one hundred and twenty days by continuous taxation. On this condition, however, that the method of collecting the money should be prescribed as suited each district, and that the levies should cease from the next 1 September. Thus Edzard Douma, Haring Oenema, Annas Tarquinius and Auco Edonius signed for the Oostergo and the Sylvestrian districts. Nearly the same decrees were passed by the Westergo, under this caution: that the military licence of the prefect of the centurions be restrained by the power and authority of the civil government, and that further damage be averted by paying the soldiers their wages in full. Although these terms were approved by the townsfolk, they wanted the following: that they themselves, out of the tax on levies, should receive the pay and the services, as they call them, furnished to the garrisons of the cities, and that by doing so they should be released from the levies. When the parties agreed, with the king's name intervening, Emskerck signed for the king, and Hector Dekama, Hero Ockinga, Suffridus Aesgema, Scelto Liauckama, Douwo Roorda and Ruardus Vibius for the Estates. It had no other formality than that this agreement might appear to be an eternal convention, and that King Philip seemed to have promised peace and security to the people, and the Frisian people pay to the royal soldiers, the enemies being removed from the province. And so three thousand gold pieces were given as a gift to Roblesius, because he had governed the province with a certain moderation and with a tempering of royal rule. Therefore the Frisians asked that he follow the footsteps of his well-performed office and his praised government, and, having entered the middle course of ruling, continue excellent services in future both to the king and at the same time to the people. These were signed by Edzard Douma, Haring Oenema, Erasmus Douma, Ruard Roorda, Meinard Lycklama Nyeholt and Hessel Hania, on 4 July. Then instructions were given to Edzard Douma, sent to Brussels in the name of the province.

units.la: I. Ut Præsidi Senatuiq; regio fiscales actiones ab anno LXVI. natas judicandi potestatem impetraret.
units.tr: I. That he seek from the President and the royal Senate the power of judging fiscal actions arising from the year 1566.

units.la: I I. Ut pleniorem veniæ interpretationem peteret, ac ut ante publicationem edicti parentibus exilium passis aut morte sublatis, eorum liberi ac hæredes eodem beneficio fruerentur.
units.tr: II. That he seek a fuller interpretation of the pardon, and that, before the publication of the edict, the children and heirs of parents who suffered exile or were put to death should enjoy the same benefit.

units.la: I I I. Ut Senatoris regij Edzardi Sickingha qui custodia attinebatur, liberationem sollicitaret ac ut vir de rege ac provincia optime meritus invisi carceris incommodo solveretur. Quare Requesentius litteris iv. Non. Sept. Antverpiâ datis Joanni Carolo fisci regij advocato mandavit, ut libellum ab Edzardo Douma secretiori Senatui oblatum examinaret fiscaliumque actionum indicem Bruxellas remitteret. Hoc vero obtinuisse Legatum reperio, ut civiles in fiscalia bona actiones judicio Curiæ subessent, eâq; de re relationem in comitio Ordinum Frisiæ institutam nobilitati, Episcopo, Præsidi Clarecampio, tum Præsidi Senatuique regio placuisse. Requesentium quoque captandis Frisiorum favoribus tum intentum magnam æris ex hac provinciæ summam collegisse, quo inritâ pace armorum vi Philippi fortunam exploraret.
units.tr: III. That he press for the release of Edzard Sickinga, royal senator, who was held in custody, and that a man who had deserved very well of the king and the province be freed from the discomfort of a hated prison. Hence Requesens, by letter dated 4 September at Antwerp, commissioned Johan Carolus, royal advocate of the fisc, to examine the petition offered to the more secret Senate by Edzard Douma, and to send back to Brussels the index of fiscal actions. I find that the envoy obtained this: that civil actions concerning fiscal goods should be subject to the judgment of the court; and that this matter, brought forward by report in the assembly of the Frisian Estates, pleased the nobility, the bishop, President Clarecamp, and then the royal President and Senate. Requesens too, while intent on catching the favour of the Frisians, collected a great sum of money from this province, so that, with the peace nullified by force of arms, he might test Philip's fortune.

units.la: Sic acriore bello, quod totis viribus à Bredano conventu Requesentius gerebat, angustæ Aurantio res erant sociæque & trans Rhenum sitæ gentes etsi cupidine fœderis ardescerent, necessarijs auxilijs frustrabantur.
units.tr: Thus, while Requesens pursued the fiercer war with all his strength from the Breda assembly, Orange's affairs were in a narrow way. The allied peoples beyond the Rhine, though they burned with desire for an alliance, kept failing to provide the aid that was needed.

units.la: Quamobrem Aurantius, spectatâ belli incumbentis mole, ad alia consiliorum conversus, de sollicitandis per Europam principum sociatibus consultavit animumque tot curis infractum & in ardua asperaque sævientis fortunæ adsurgentem, sollicitudine quærendæ foris potentiæ exercuit. Quod consilium, etsi ultima rerum necessitas commendaret, quæ hac tempestate, velut deliquio syderum, imperium Regi ac libertatem populi librabat, ita perrogatis procerum suffragijs decretum. Ut externæ societates, salvo Regis & provinciarum jure, habendis tantum in bello subsidijs peterentur. Itaque nec regij nominis memoriam abolleri, nec inverti sacramenta provincialium volebant, aut ut exteri Principes prætextu protegendæ libertatis exercitum, aut copias in fines inducerent. Sic constitutis rebus in Germaniam, Gallias, aut Augliam omnium spes convertebantur. Erant qui antiquæ originis, & nuperæ societatis memoriâ, quâ Carolus Cæsar utramque nationem colligasset, Germaniæ siderent adeundumque legatione Cæsarem & Imperij Principes non invalidis rationibus contenderent.
units.tr: Therefore Orange, weighing the great burden of the war that pressed upon them, turned his counsels elsewhere. He resolved to seek alliances with princes across Europe, and in his anxiety to find power abroad he exercised his spirit, which had been broken by so many cares, and rose up against the harsh and savage turns of fortune. The plan, though the utmost need of affairs recommended it, since at this time the empire of the King and the liberty of the people were hanging in the balance, as if the stars were failing, was nevertheless adopted only after the votes of the nobles had been asked and given. External alliances were to be sought only for furnishing subsidies for the war, saving the rights of the King and of the provinces. For they did not wish the memory of the royal name to be abolished, nor the oaths of the provincials to be overturned, nor foreign princes to lead armies or troops into their borders under the pretext of protecting liberty. With matters so arranged, all hopes turned toward Germany, France, or England. Some were attached to Germany, mindful of the ancient origin and recent alliance by which Charles Caesar had bound the two nations together, and they argued with no weak reasons that an embassy should go to the Emperor and the princes of the Empire.

units.la: Quippe recordabantur arma in Imperio pro Religione & libertate haud pridem acriter mota, ne Hispaniæ dominationem & servitutem conscientijs acciperet. Manere adhuc sensum istius vulneris & fore haud dubiè generosa Imperij pectora, quæ novos furores ex antiquâ ambitione nasci & quidem apud eas gentes indignentur, quas veterum colocIↄ. Iↄ. coloniarum & fœderum jura tum affinitates & clientelæ Germaniæ commendent. Suspectam semper etiam Caroli Cæsaris inauguratione, Romano Imperio Hispaniæ potentiam fuisse, & metuere Germaniam posse ne post Belgicam serviat. Cæteri differebant varietatem religionum, æmulationes Principum, tum præcipuè Cæsaris & Hispani affinitatem novis societatibus obfuturam. Adhæc non agi cum Germaniâ præterquam Comitijs Imperij posse, quibus habendis finiendisque ne certum quidem tempus decerni queat.
units.tr: For they remembered that arms had recently been stirred up fiercely in the Empire for religion and liberty, lest Spain should win dominion and servitude over consciences. The sense of that wound still remained, and the noble hearts of the Empire, they said, would surely be indignant that new outrages were arising from old ambition, and that among those peoples which the ancient colonies and treaties, as well as the ties of kinship and clientage, commended to Germany. Also, it was always suspected that by the inauguration of Charles Caesar, Spain's power had become Roman imperial power, and Germany might fear that after the Netherlands it would be enslaved. Others objected that the variety of religions, the rivalries of the princes, and above all the kinship of Caesar and the Spaniard would hinder any new alliances. Moreover, it was said that nothing could be transacted with Germany except at the Imperial Diets, and that no fixed time could even be appointed for holding and concluding them.

units.la: Gallicam vero societatem inquietudo regni & funestæ dissensiones dissuadebant. Erant quoque qui crederent Henricum III. Caroli IX. fratris (quem in medio flore ætatis mors abstulerat) successorem, novæ & vacillanti potentiæ diffisum, alienum bellum suum non facturum infirmasq; regni vires, etiam suâ discordiâ fatiscentis, Hispanico & simul civili bello non implicaturum. Alij addebant, vetera Gallorum in Burgundiones odia pactionibus fœderum nocitura, nec committendas Gallicæ fidei provincias, quas cum Insubriâ aut Neapolitano regno permutare fluxa aulæ fides queat. Neque enim ponendam esse in lubrico provinciarum incolumitatem, nec quærenda auxilia imbecillibus suspecta & exitu dubia. Cæterum secretis fœderatorum in Galliam legationibus diffidentia minuebatur & quod Charlotta Borbonia regij Francicique sanguinis fœmina in Aurantij Principis domum pactione matrimonij transisset.
units.tr: As for an alliance with France, the unrest of the kingdom and its deadly dissensions discouraged it. There were also those who believed that Henry III, successor of his brother Charles IX, whom death had carried off in the prime of life, distrusted a new and unsteady power, would not make another's war his own, and would not entangle the weakened forces of a kingdom already falling apart through its own discord in a Spanish and at the same time civil war. Others added that the old hatreds of the French against the Burgundians would harm the treaties of alliance, and that the provinces of French faith should not be entrusted, since a shifting court's loyalty might exchange them for Insubria or the kingdom of Naples. For the safety of the provinces should not be placed on a slippery footing, nor should aid be sought from those weak, suspect, and doubtful in outcome. Yet distrust was lessened by the secret embassies of the allies to France, and by the fact that Charlotte de Bourbon, a woman of royal and French blood, had passed into the house of the Prince of Orange by a matrimonial agreement.

units.la: Itaque dubijs procerum animis sola Anglia se ingerebat, quam à Mariæ sororis morte, ut ante memoravi, Elisabetha Henrici VIII. filia moderabatur. Quæ Princeps fœmina multis molestijs & diuturnâ captivitate ad regnum evecta, magnam spem fœderatæ societati professione reformati cultus faciebat. Neque deerant qui Belgico sanguine ac in Philippâ Bavarâ Eduardi III. conjuge Hollandicæ domus propagine ortam, daturam aliquid pervetustæ propinquitati crederent rerumq; peritiâ legem sui sexus egressam, nec alienæ facundiæ aut prudentiæ egentem libertati afflictarum vicinarumque gentium patrocinaturam. Esse ei magna societati Belgicæ commoda, amplos portus & stationes errantibus, tum validas promovendis provinciarum commercijs classes, quarum ope circumfluo mari imperitet. Itaque fœderatos, procurată Anglicâ societate, commeatus, commercia, militem habituros, fœcundo populi regno & per lene imperitantis fœminæ ingenium longâ pace opulento. Sed Legatio in exitum anni protracta arctiusque fœdus fœderatos inter & Aurantium Principem tum ictum, ut concordiæ robur, ita ordinem bello, leges reip. dedit.
units.tr: Thus, with the minds of the nobles divided, England alone offered itself, a kingdom which, since the death of Mary, her sister, as I mentioned before, was governed by Elizabeth, daughter of Henry VIII. This princess, raised to the throne after many troubles and a long captivity, gave great hope to the allied confederacy by her profession of the reformed worship. Nor were there lacking those who believed that she, being of Flemish blood and descended from the Dutch house through Philippa of Bavaria, wife of Edward III, would grant something to ancient kinship, and that, having passed beyond the usual laws of her sex through her experience of affairs, she would defend with no lack of eloquence or prudence the liberty of the afflicted and neighboring peoples. They said that a great alliance with the Netherlands would bring advantages to her, with ample harbors and anchorages for wandering ships, and strong fleets for advancing trade, by means of which she might rule the surrounding sea. Therefore the confederates, once the English alliance was secured, would have supplies, commerce, and soldiers, in a kingdom made fertile by its people and made wealthy by long peace under the gentle temper of a ruling woman. But the embassy was protracted to the end of the year, and the closer treaty then struck between the confederates and Prince Orange gave concord its strength, and to the war its order, and to the commonwealth its laws.

units.la: Gulielmus Cambdenus in Annalibus Elisabethæ scribit, Aurantio Principi Gallicam tum maxime societatem placuisse eumque pacti secretioris, cum Carolo IX. & Gaspato Colinio Galliæ Admiralio nuper initi observantem, Elisabethæ societatem velut in arduo positam, tacitè & quasi ex indignatione per negata auxilia respuisse. Itaque Legatum ab Elisabethâ ad Aurantium, quo Gallicum fœdus dissuaderet, missum illoque rejecto, alium in Hispaniam ad Philippum amandasse. Eum disseruisse.
units.tr: William Camden, in his Annals of Elizabeth, writes that the French alliance then pleased the Prince of Orange most of all, and that he, observing a more secret pact recently made with Charles IX and Gaspard de Coligny, Admiral of France, had quietly and as if in indignation rejected the alliance with Elizabeth, which seemed to be in a difficult position, by refusing aid. Therefore Elizabeth sent an envoy to Orange to dissuade him from the French treaty, and when he was rejected, she sent another to Spain to Philip. He argued as follows.

units.la: Interesse utriusque Hispaniæ & simul Angliæ regni, ne fœderati Belgæ gæ Gallicam ad societatem aspirent & ne illius interventu à nexu regis cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXV. sui nota gens separetur. Ineundam potius Philippo pacem esse, quam videre subditos suos alienis dominis fidem & simul firmamenta potentiæ paciscientes. Itaque Philippum regem serium sanciendæ Pacis consilium legato approbasse Robertumque Corbettum ad Requesentium Proregem misisse, qui salubre pacis cum fœderatis & Aurantio negotium expediret. Cæterum à Joanne Villerio Ecclesiaste homine Gallo ac Anglicæ societati infenso, persuasum Principem etiam rationem reginæ consilij neglexisse animumque à cupidine Gallici fœderis difficulter revocasse. Quo arcanis de causis & ut mihi videtur, fovendis Galliæ Angliæque æmulationibus prolato, delegati in Angliam, qui Elisabethæ reginæ tanquam Principi Hollandici sanguinis, jus aut protectionem fœderatarum provinciarum deferrent statuique lubrico & per bellum exhausto patrocinium ac subsidia orarent. Cæterum multa prudenti & supra sexum reginæ expendebantur quamque arduum & difficile futurum esset regnum, ultro casui & mutationibus obnoxium, externis turbis implicare. Esse Philippum utut aulæ artibus simulet & induciæ obvelent, occulte & clam inimicum Angliæque regno ex suo in Romanam Sedem servitio infensum. Adhæc Gallum æmulum & haud dubie ex prolatis & veluti spretis Alençonij amoribus iniquum & quod matrimonium unà cum regno Gallici regijque sanguinis Principi muliebri facilitate non approbaverit. Esse etiam qui credant Protestantium in Gallia bellum Anglicis nervis ac consilijs foveri nuperque Mongomerium sublevandis Rupellanis classe instructum, suo an Protestantium sacramento egisse. Suspiciosa esse mortalium & præsertim regum ingenia, quibus nulla res minus ad custodiam regni necessaria videatur, quam externa societas diversis moribus imbuta. Quod ad Bavariæ Principum ac majorum jus attineret, id obscurum & longè repetendum esse nec confundendas Principum successiones & clientelas, ne quid talium in incerto sit & ne indistinctis dominationibus confusio gentium fiat. Dubitari posse, an transferri rerum dominia sine consensu superiorum queant & interesse haud dubie Cæsaris jus feudi non convelli. Præterea hæsitare se electione an successione principatus per provincias stet & num Philippi majoribus populum Belgicum muta hæreditas an suffragatio & consensus Ordinum obliget. Denique bellum ærario grave, suspectum sociis futurum. Itaque gratijs ex splendidâ honestissimaque legatione actis respondit Elisabetha: Facturam se bonæ Principis officium, cui curæ esse debeat ne fides extra gloriam sit & ne conscientiam recte factorum unicam in illo & quidem lubrico rerum fastigio suarum actionum moderatricem, inclinante in partes ingenio inquinet. Quare provinciarum regimen & cum eo onus imperio connexum, suscipere è re suâ non esse, daturam interim operam, ut opportunâ apud Philippum intercessione pacem procuret provincijs & juxta vicinis regnis salutarem.
units.tr: It was in the interest of both Spain and the kingdom of England that the Dutch confederates should not aspire to a French alliance, and that through its intervention the people should not be separated from the bond of their own king, whose name is known. It was better for Philip to make peace than to see his subjects pledging faith and the foundations of power to foreign lords. Therefore King Philip seriously approved the plan of establishing peace, sent Robert Corbett to Requesens, the Viceroy, to carry out a wholesome negotiation for peace with the confederates and with Orange. However, the Prince, persuaded by John Villiers, a French clergyman hostile to the English alliance, had neglected the counsel of the queen, and had found it difficult to call his mind back from desire for the French treaty. For reasons that were hidden, and, as it seems to me, to foster the rivalries of France and England, deputies were sent to England, who were to offer to Queen Elizabeth, as a princess of Dutch blood, the right or protection of the confederated provinces, and to beg for patronage and support for a state that was unstable and exhausted by war. But the prudent queen, who was above her sex, weighed many things: how difficult and dangerous it would be to entangle a kingdom, already subject to chance and change, in foreign disturbances. Philip, however much he feigned by court arts and veiled his designs with truces, was secretly and covertly hostile to England, because of his servitude to the Roman See. Besides, the Frenchman was a rival, and, no doubt, unfair, as shown by the postponed and seemingly disdained love of Alençon, and because he had not approved the marriage, which the Frenchman's ease, along with the kingdom, offered to a prince of French and royal blood. There were also those who believed that the war of the Protestants in France was being fostered by English sinews and counsels, and that Montgomery had recently sailed with a fleet to relieve the people of Rochelle, acting on his own or the Protestants' cause. The minds of mortals, and especially of kings, are suspicious, and nothing seems less necessary for the safekeeping of a kingdom than an alliance with a foreign people imbued with different customs. As for the right of the princes and ancestors of Bavaria, that matter was obscure and had to be traced from far back, and the successions and clienteles of princes should not be confused, lest something of this kind remain uncertain, and lest by indistinct dominions there be a confusion of peoples. It could be doubted whether ownership of property could be transferred without the consent of superiors, and no doubt it concerned the Emperor that the feudal right not be overthrown. Besides, she hesitated whether the principality rested on election or on succession through the provinces, and whether the inheritance of Philip's ancestors bound the Belgian people as a mere inheritance, or the vote and consent of the Estates. Finally, the war was burdensome to the treasury and would be suspect to its allies. Therefore, having thanked the envoys for their splendid and most honorable embassy, Elizabeth replied: she would do the duty of a good prince, who ought to take care that her faith should not be outside her glory, and that her conscience of right deeds, the sole guide of her actions in so slippery a height of affairs, should not be stained by a disposition inclined to one side. Therefore it was not in her interest to take on the government of the provinces, and the burden of empire linked with it; meanwhile she would make an effort to procure peace for the provinces, through a timely intercession with Philip, and one wholesome also for the neighboring kingdoms.

units.la: Thuanus existimat Elisabetham per legatum Fredericum Perenottum Cardinalis Granvellani fratrem, à Requesentio in Angliam missum ac in aulâ subsistentem, territam aliquid illius præsentiæ tum dedisse, quod legationi fœderatæ iniquior amplissimas & ex usu regni post expetitas petitas conditiones coacta simulatione renuisset. Addit Thuanus monitum tamen ab Elisabetha Perenottum, ut ad reddendam provincijs maturè pacem Regem & Requesentium hortaretur, ne aut desperatione sui instar morientium ferarum lacessita gens efferaretur & ne ipsa securitati suæ prona regni sui viribus ruentem Belgicam fulciat. Se quidem scripto olim Angliam inter ac Burgundiam fœderi violando occasionem non daturam, modo Philippus caveat ut Burgundiæ principatum majorum imperio adaptet & ne externarum gentium majore in provincias confluxu pax & quies vicini populi tollatur. Sunt qui credant auxiliorum spem ab Elisabethâ fœderatorum Legatis clam factam fuisse fundamentumque Anglicæ & post initæ societati illâ legatione substratum. Unde Henrico Galliæ Regi & Reginæ præcipuè matri æmulatio nata, commendato postmodum per legatum Principi Aurantio filio Alençonio, quo ambitiosum illius animum & velut regno ac fratri gravem à civilium bellorum quæ tum per Galliam flagrabant consilio ad externa & minus domesticis nocitura amoverent. Thuanus notat reginam matrem à Claudio Mondulceto, Henrici Regis talium ut credebatur conscij per Belgicam Legato, jam antè tentatam inclinantemque & ineundæ cum fœderatis conventioni pronam, speciosa auxilia obtulisse.
units.tr: Thuanus thinks that Elizabeth, frightened by the presence of Frederick Perrenot, brother of Cardinal Granvelle, whom Requesens had sent to England and who was residing at court, was compelled to feign and so refused the legates of the confederated provinces the most generous terms, which were afterwards sought in the interest of her realm. Thuanus adds that Elizabeth nevertheless urged Perrenot to persuade the King and Requesens to restore peace to the provinces promptly, lest the people, provoked by despair like dying wild beasts, grow fierce, and lest, leaning on the strength of their own realm for their security, they prop up a falling Belgium. She herself, as she had once written, would not give occasion for violating the treaty between England and Burgundy, provided Philip took care to adapt the principality of Burgundy to the greater empire and did not, by a larger influx of foreign peoples into the provinces, destroy the peace and quiet of the neighbouring people. Some believe that Elizabeth secretly promised aid to the legates of the confederates, and that this became the foundation of the English alliance later concluded through that embassy. Hence rivalry arose in Henry, King of France, and especially in his mother the Queen. It was afterwards recommended through a legate to the Prince of Orange, a son of Alençon, that they should turn his ambitious spirit, which was burdensome to the kingdom and to his brother, away from the plans of the civil wars then raging through France, towards foreign undertakings that would do less harm at home. Thuanus notes that the queen mother had earlier been tested by Claude Mondoucet, the legate of King Henry in Belgium, who was believed to be privy to such matters; she was inclined and ready to enter an agreement with the confederates, and she offered specious aid.

units.la: Repèrio in libris Edictorum fauxisse Philippum regem, ut annus à Kal. Jan. initium sumeret signandisque tabulis publicis, non mobilium festorum, cæterùm mensium dierumque ratio per Frisiam haberetur. Mandasse quoque ut idem Edictum, velut certitudinem temporum posterùm daturum, regijs typis ederetur rerumque judicatarum codicillorum obligationumque actis utilissimæ legis sanctio atque memoria inseretur.
units.tr: I find in the books of edicts that King Philip ordained that the year should begin on the Kalends of January, and that public documents should be dated not by moveable feasts but by the reckoning of months and days, as is customary in Friesland. He also commanded that this same edict be printed with the royal types, as a guarantee of the dates for later times, and that the sanction and memorial of this most useful law be inserted in the acts of judgments, codicils and obligations.

units.la: Mox Roblesius quo civitatum oppidorumque quæ præsidijs Philippi stipendia assignaverant, solutionibus prospiceret, Delegatos Ordinum convocari facit expositasq; à se pecunias præstari imperavit. Quæ res cum in potestate illorum non foret tributum aut subsidium agrarijs sine solenni comitiorum decreto præscribere, Roblesius Ordinum conventum ad VIII. Novemb. Leovardiæ haberi jussit vocatisque in Basilicam Ordinibus Achlenium Præsidem perorare hunc in modum voluit.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Roblesius, so that he might provide for the payment of the stipends that the cities and towns had assigned to Philip's garrisons, had the delegates of the Estates summoned and ordered that the money he had set forth be made good. Since it was not within the power of the Estates to impose a tax or subsidy on the landowners without a solemn decree of the assembly, Roblesius ordered the meeting of the Estates to be held at Leeuwarden on 8 November, and when the Estates had been summoned into the church, he wished the president Achlenius to speak to them in this manner.

units.la: STipendia militi regio, quem Roblesius per civitates atq; oppida distribuit, à Magistratibus urbicis pensitata nostis, sed hac cautione ut eos indemnes præstaremus ipsique pecunias bonâ fide cohortibus collocatas ex aerario reciperent. Et quia Præfecto, quod debetur, persolutum non est, paratus est hac æris inopia triremem Harlingæ in anchoris stantem in solutum accipere, postquam res vestræ impulsæ difficillime juvantur. Ut hoc faciatis secedere in secretum vestrum & deliberare sinam.
units.tr: You know that the stipends for the royal soldiers, whom Roblesius has distributed among the cities and towns, have been paid by the civic magistrates, but on this condition: that we should keep them harmless, and that they should recover from the treasury the money they had fairly paid out to the cohorts. Since what is owed to the commander has not been paid, he is ready, in this lack of money, to accept in settlement a galley lying at anchor at Harlingen, since your affairs are being assisted with great difficulty after being thrown into disorder. To enable you to do this, I will allow you to withdraw into your own private session and deliberate.

units.la: Quo facto Ordinum mandatarij in ædem Jacobæorum regressi expensisque quæ oportebat Roblesio triremem permisere. Cujus facti cum hominem suo ingenio an ex conditione temporum fidei dubium poeniteret, mandante Eemskerckio Graphiario pecuniam sibi dari petijt Ordinesque dum decrevissent, manere in loco comitij jussit. Oppidanorum quoque Legatos quo agrarijs pecuniam extorqueret, in conventu agrarioagrariorum verba ut facerent mandavit, præstandaeque solutioni cum dies diceretur præsentem determinavit. Cui fini tribunorum ærarij excutiendum æs mandavit ac ut illi redditis accepti expensiq; rationibus, residuum æris in provinciæ usus & redimendis obligationibus erogarent. Quare & Valerio Cammingha, Heroni Burmania, Livio Beiemo, Ruardo Roorda, Edzardo & Erasmo Douma, Gysberto Aernsma, tanquam rationum publicarum magistris dignitas continuata, quo rationes obscuræ, sicuti in administratione pecuniæ publicæ sæpe fieri assolet, illorum autoritate in apertum producerentur. Cæterum agrarij multa Regi & provinciæ subsidia collocata regerebant debereque oppidanos in communi provincialium sorte sua quoque onera redimendis impendijs sustinere. Quippe eos decem tantum aureorum millia liberandis apud Regem nominibus ex centum & viginti octo millibus contulisse obligatis econtra ad graviora agrarijs qui provinciam semper præ cæteris juvissent. Itaque agrarij dilationem petebant, revocatoque solutionis decreto dubij & rerum ancipites contumaciam induerunt ipsique Roblesio etsi succensenti solutionis loco triremem assignavere. Ita sursum ac deorsum res per Frisiam fluebant, donec, ut omnia malorum, secreta odia & æmulationes sequentia temporum aperirent.
units.tr: When this was done, the deputies of the Estates returned to the church of the Jacobites, and, with the expenses that were necessary paid to Roblesius, they granted him the galley. Although this act made him regret, whether through his own disposition or because of the circumstances of the times, that he had been trusted, he asked, at the instruction of Eemskerck the secretary, that money be given to him; and while the Estates were deciding, he ordered them to remain in the place of the assembly. He also commanded the legates of the townspeople to speak in the assembly of the landowners, so that they might extort money from the landowners, and when the day was named for payment, he fixed it as the present day. For this purpose he ordered the tribunes to examine the treasury's money, so that, once accounts of receipts and expenses had been returned to them, they might spend the remaining money on the needs of the province and on redeeming the debts. For this reason the dignity of public accountants was continued for Valerius Cammingha, Hero Burmania, Livius Beiemus, Ruardus Roorda, Edzardus and Erasmus Douma, and Gysbert Aernsma, so that the obscure accounts, as is often the custom in the management of public money, might be brought to light by their authority. The landowners, however, kept saying that many subsidies had been applied to the King and the province, and that the townspeople ought, as part of the common lot of the provincials, to bear their own burdens too in redeeming the expenses. Indeed, they had contributed only ten thousand gold pieces out of one hundred and twenty-eight thousand to free the obligations owed to the King, whereas the landowners, who had always helped the province more than the rest, were bound to heavier burdens. Therefore the landowners asked for a delay; the decree of payment was revoked, and they became doubtful and, with their affairs in the balance, took on a stubborn stance; and they even assigned to Roblesius, though he was angry, a galley in place of payment. So affairs in Friesland flowed up and down, until, as with all evils, the hidden hatreds and rivalries of the following times came to light.

units.la: Anna Oldenburgica, quæ Ennoni diu superstes vixerat, Edzardi mater, fato tum functa. Constat exules Frisios ut eâ in humanis agente multum solatij, ita terris ereptâ plurimum mœroris hausisse sumptisque lugubribus comitatos funus desideria defunctæ interno luctu, & supremis officijs velasse. Mox, x. Kal. Febr. Austro flante gravis tempestas cœlo missa edita quæque & cœli ventorumque inclementijs expositia convulsit. Itaque arborum terris erutæ radices molæque terendo per Frisiam frumento structæ, passim Leovardiæ & apud Dongrios violentiâ Austri disjectæ. Scribit in Notis suis M. Heymannus D. Viti fanum, quod longior ætas ut omnia mortalium jam attriverat, magna sui parte tum corruisse. Solum mare terminis suis etiam atrocissimâ procellâ coërcitum mansit, sive quod silente Lunâ minore æstu intumesceret, sive quod fluminum ostia in Corum quo maxime infestantur aut Cæciam se protendentia, Austri flatu plana littorum repulso in interiora Oceano denudent. Annotatum invenio cujusdam Senatoris morte secretis studijs de successore certatum hoc tempore fuisse Carolumque Nicolaium Everardi Cæsarei per Frisiam nuper Præsidis filium, commendatione Antonij Lopesij Lavalij & per eum Roblesij Præfecti usum apud Ludovicum Requesentium & Hyeronimum Rodam de obtinendo munere egisse. Eundem quoque Carolum censentibus dignitatem illam Nobili Frisio deberi, vehementer obstitisse avoque & patre Præside gloriatum, suæ nobilitatis & ex claritudine litterarum evectæ ad summum honoris fastigium familiæ, non obscuram opinionem prætulisse. Igitur Carolus Nicolaus procurante vel maxime Hyeronimo Roda viro immodicæ autoritatis (quem, ignobili apud Hispanos familiâ ortum, gravem Belgicæ administrandis rebus Philippus rex Bruxellas amandaverat) in Senatum cooptatus, validiore exterorum potentiâ, æmulæ Nobilitatis invidiem evicit obitasque diu etiam sub Carolo Cæsare majoribus dignitates illustri in seipso cio. Io. ipso familiae asseruit. Quo tempore Senatus per Frisiam Regius sanlxxvi. xit, ut erogati per privatos in militem aeris rationes supputarentur tabu- laeque ad Georgium Westendorpium Senatorem Regium maturandis solutionibus perferrentur. Creditum fuit, leniendis continuarum exa- ctionum molestijs, vano ostentui & in speciem id factum, quo lento & facili tributo privatas opes, publica dominantium avarities aut ege- stas emungeret.
units.tr: Anna of Oldenburg, who had long survived Enno, the mother of Edzard, died at this time. It is agreed that the exiled Frisians, while she was living among men she had been a great comfort, and once she was taken from the earth they drank deep of sorrow; with mournful rites they accompanied the funeral and covered the dead woman's wishes with inward grief and her last offices. Soon afterwards, on 22 January, a violent storm sent from heaven, driven by the south wind, raged, and things exposed to the inclemency of sky and winds were shaken. Hence the roots of trees torn from the earth, and millstones used for grinding grain in Friesland, were scattered everywhere, at Leeuwarden and near Dongerdeel, by the violence of the south wind. Heymann, in his Notes, writes that the church of St Vitus, which length of time had already worn away as it does everything mortal, then collapsed in great part. The sea alone kept within its bounds even in that most savage tempest, whether because, with the moon silent, it swelled with a smaller tide, or because the mouths of the rivers, where the Cor and the Caecia are especially assailed, were driven back by the blowing south wind and laid bare the flat shores to the open sea. I find a note that, at the death of a certain senator, there was a contest at this time over his successor, and that Charles Nicolaus, son of Everard, recently Caesar's president in Friesland, using the recommendation of Antonius Lopes Laval, and through him that of Roblesius the commander, pleaded with Louis Requesens and Hieronymus Roda for the office. The same Charles, though it was thought that this dignity was owed to a Frisian nobleman, strongly resisted, boasting of his grandfather and father the president, and of the nobility of his family, raised to the highest rank of honour by the distinction of its learning, and he put forward no obscure claim. Therefore Charles Nicolaus, through the especially strong influence of Hieronymus Roda, a man of immoderate authority (whom King Philip had sent to Brussels to manage Belgian affairs, though he was born of an obscure Spanish family), was co-opted into the Senate; with the greater power of foreigners he overcame the envy of his rival nobility, and for a long time, even under Charles the Emperor, he maintained the higher dignities for his own family. At that time the royal Senate in Friesland decided that the accounts of the money spent by private persons on the soldiery should be reckoned up, and that the ledgers should be taken to Georgius Westendorp, royal senator, to hasten the payments. It was believed that this was done, to ease the burdens of the continual exactions, as an empty show and in appearance only, so that by a slow and easy tax the rulers' public greed might drain private resources.

units.la: Mox Requesentius omni freto ac sinu maris defectione nautici popu- li foederatis classibus pervio edixit: Ne Frisij extra provinciam sine re- scripto Praefecti aut Senatus, stipendia mari apud foederatos facerent. Cavit quoque ut foris (etiam in ditionibus regijs) aes merentes, quocunque modo capti aut vinculis dati, primum fustigatione & confiscatio- ne bonorum, post custodiae redditi in triennium ad triremes damna- rentur. Caeteros vero non captos aut vinculis elapsos, velut exleges perpetuum exilium maneret. Caeterum eludente severa Edicta tempo- rum fato, quae firmandis militum sacramentis & corrigendae militari insolentiae reperta credebantur, incremento saepe malorum cessere de- prehensumque fuit plus ex inopia aeris licentiam quam ex reverentia re- gis praescriptos mores valuisse. Qua ex re aegritudinem animi & mox infirmitatem virium traxisse Requesentius creditus fuit, aucto insuper ex indignatione malo, quod convocato Ordinum restituendis collapsis rebus Bruxellis Concilio, pro gratia contumax odium & reparandae libertatis acerrimas sollicitudines ex petitis tributis repperisset. Quippe Ordines, ut Anno MDCIV. lxxiv. inter caetera regij imperia le- vamenta, etiam hoc volebant, ut tributa certis legitimisque usibus destinarentur restitutoque patrio jure & belli disciplina, seditiosae legio- nes ex praescripto veteris disciplinae corrigerentur. Quorum omnium ut nihil in potestate Requesentij erat robustiore malo quam ut medi- cinam admitteret, ita aspirantem ad magna animum erosit, quod le- niorem regnandi ab Albano modum professus, ne ostentando quidem optima ducendis Ordinum ingenijs par haberetur. Itaque ulciscendae contumaciae Ordinum & ut rebatur, injuriae avidus praecipuo libertatis defensori id reposuit, ut veneno sustulisse crederetur caeterisque quos convocaverat Ordinum, ex metu silentium & simul exemplum crudi servitij imponeret. Quare impulso aerario missis in Hispaniam litteris, naves, arma, commeatum poposcit, quo foederatos externa patroci- nia & suffugia ubivis terrarum angustis rebus quaerentes, ac quod me- tuebat adeptos, confertā belli mole obruerat. Judicabat quippe spira- menta temporum partibus profutura & opprimendam potentiam len- to gradu & per intervalla crescentem. Adhaec bellum in continente prosperè non geri praeterquam subacto mari posse. Sic praepediendos transcursus hostium, sic intercipienda auxilia esse. Neque alio sine Zirizaeam urbem circumvenisse, quam ut eâ hybernis, velut in invidiem naturae clausâ, vicino & mox Germanico mari dominaretur.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Requesens proclaimed that, across every strait and bay of the sea that was open to the fleets of the confederates, the seafaring people should not: the Frisians should not serve for pay at sea with the confederates outside the province without a written order of the president or the Senate. He also provided that those who served as soldiers abroad (even in the royal dominions), if they were captured in any way or handed over to chains, should first be flogged and have their goods confiscated, and afterwards, when returned to custody, be condemned for three years to the galleys. The others, however, who had not been captured or had escaped from chains, were to remain in perpetual exile as outlaws. But the severe edicts, which were thought to have been devised for confirming the soldiers' oaths and correcting military insolence, were mocked by the fate of the times, and often they ended in an increase of evils; and it was found that licence owed more to lack of money than to reverence for the king, so that the prescribed customs were powerless. From this Requesens was believed to have contracted a sickness of spirit and soon a weakness of strength, and an additional evil was added by indignation, because, when he had summoned the Council at Brussels for the purpose of restoring the fallen affairs, and the Estates had asked for relief from the royal commands, he found them stubborn rather than grateful, and found in the tributes they demanded the bitterest anxieties about recovering their liberty. For in the year 1574 the Estates, among other things, wished this too: that taxes be devoted to certain lawful uses, and that, with the ancient right of the country and the discipline of war restored, the mutinous legions be corrected according to the rule of the old discipline. Since none of these things was within Requesens's power, and a more severe evil than this could not be cured except by admitting the remedy, it wore down his spirit, which aspired to great things, the more so because, having professed a milder manner of ruling than Alba's, he was not held equal even to showing the best means of guiding the minds of the Estates. Therefore, eager to avenge the stubbornness of the Estates and what he thought was an injury, he laid up for the chief defender of liberty a plan: he was believed to have removed him by poison, and to impose silence on the rest of the Estates whom he had summoned, through fear and at the same time as an example of cruel servitude. Hence, with the treasury exhausted, he sent letters to Spain and demanded ships, arms and supplies, so that he might overwhelm the confederates, who in their straitened circumstances were seeking foreign patronage and refuge anywhere on earth, and whom he feared had already gained such aid, with a heavy weight of war. For he judged that breathing-spaces of time would benefit the rebels, and that the power, which was growing by slow steps and at intervals, must be crushed. Besides, he thought that war on the continent could not be conducted successfully unless the sea were subdued. Thus the crossings of the enemy must be hindered, and their aid intercepted. Nor, for any other reason, had he surrounded the city of Zierikzee, except that he might, by holding it in winter as if shut away from the favour of nature, dominate the neighbouring sea and the German sea soon to follow.

units.la: Haec ad PHILIPPUM.
units.tr: These things to Philip.

units.la: Itaque magnorum votorum plenam mentem ferens occupandae Embdae consilium cepit; facta Gasparo Roblesio Frisiae majoris Praefecto potestate, qui dolo aut vi commissum negotium exequeretur. Reputabat quippe multum interesse, urbem in finibus Imperij sitam, com-modo portu & latissimis ostijs Amasum flumen in mare laxantem Philippo asseri, à quâ victoriâ maris imperium inchoaturus sit. Ibi suf-fugium classibus, ibi stationem fore. Quare Roblesius magnus doli artifex praesidiarios arcis aere aut donis clam aggressus est corruptoq; ut creditum fuit, aut suis in Philippum Regem studijs pellectos in partem consilij traxit. Caeterum à Joanne fratre Edzardi, tum à populo Embdano foederis Belgici amante detectum, malis Roblesij artibus ludicros rerum exitus rependit. Ita lacertos per omnia inferioris Germaniae spatia moventem Requesentium fatale magnis consilijs impedimentum cita mors occupavit. Quippe Bruxellis acuto & pestilenti morbo correptus, inrita medicantium curâ non designato successore exspiravit.
units.tr: So, bearing a mind full of great hopes, he resolved to seize Emden. He gave Gaspar Robles, prefect of Greater Friesland, the power to carry out the business by trickery or force. He reasoned that it made a great difference whether the city, which lay within the borders of the empire and had a convenient harbour and wide mouths through which the river Ems flowed into the sea, came into Philip's hands; from that victory he would begin to establish rule over the sea. There the fleets would find refuge and a base. Robles, a great master of deceit, therefore approached the garrison of the citadel secretly, with money or gifts, and either corrupted them, as was believed, or drew them into his plan through their own zeal for King Philip. But John, brother of Edzard, and the people of Emden, who loved the Belgic league, uncovered the plot, and the outcome of Robles's wicked devices was turned into a farce. Thus, while Requesens was stirring his forces through the whole of Lower Germany, a sudden death, a serious obstacle to his great designs, seized him. He was struck down at Brussels by a sharp and pestilential illness, and despite the physicians' fruitless care, he died without having named a successor.

units.la: Scribunt autores eunti in Belgicam Requesentio id potestatis à Philippo datum, caeterum praecipitis mali importunitate, compedito vocis officio & alienatâ mente Philippi mandatum & ultimae voluntatis arcanum non explevisse. Unde regias provincias domesticus moeror publicusque simul luctus frequentavit, cum essent qui crederent Requesentium longioribus vitae spatijs servatum compresso foedere & debellatis partibus praeconceptam Philippo imperij imaginem daturum suisse. Quod omnino absimile à vero illis temporibus non fuit, cum in annales relatum sit, post dimissos ex Anglia Legatos nudam auxiliorum pollicitationem ferentes, foederatis gerendo fere bello invalidis, Principem Aurantium & prudentiores de committendâ classibus gente transferendisque more majorum alium in orbem colonijs cogitasse. Dein uxoribus liberisque in classem impositis submergendae patriae consilium caepisse, quo perforatis aggeribus diductisque ac laxatis aquarum catarractis lustrum furoris ulteriorique saevitiae materies immanissimis hostibus adimeretur. Quorum potentiam fatalibus decretis & coelestium rerum lege compressam fuisse mihi haud dubium est, Requesentiumque, quo fessae res interregno respirarent, non destinato moderatore & arbitro repentinâ morte sublatum. Itaq; rex Philippus, audità ex litteris Concilij status, Requesentij morte percussus, publicam fatorum inclementiam privato vulnere non dissimulabat. Unde per Philippi aulam, obturbato rege, moestum silentium notabatur, quod in omnem Hispaniam cum famâ Requesentij mortis proserpens acerbitatem funeris indicavit. Quippe innuebant Ducem Philippo regi fidum, nec gerendis rebus imperitum in ipso potentiae fastigio ac cursu rerum extingui, praeconceptamque opprimendarum partium spem tanti capitis jacturâ & interitu confundi. Quare Philippus, ne in confusionem Belgicae res ultro turbidae irent, omne quod Requesentius usurpaverat imperium in Concilium status Belgici rejecit, litterasque hujusmodi in provincias expedivit.
units.tr: Writers relate that Philip had given Requesens, when he set out for the Netherlands, such authority; but because of the sudden severity of his illness, his power of speech was impaired and his mind was disordered, so that he did not carry out the king's command or the secret of his final wishes. Hence domestic grief and public mourning together filled the royal provinces, since there were those who believed that if Requesens had been spared a longer span of life, he would, after the covenant was suppressed and the parties subdued, have given Philip the empire he had imagined beforehand. This was by no means far from the truth in those times, since it is recorded in the annals that, after the envoys sent from England had departed, bringing only a bare promise of aid, and the confederates were nearly exhausted by waging war, Prince Orange and the more prudent men considered handing the fleets over to the enemy's people, and transplanting the nation, after the manner of their ancestors, to colonies in another part of the world. Then, having loaded their wives and children onto the fleet, they began to plan to submerge their homeland: the dikes would be breached, the sluices of the waters opened and loosened, so that the enemy, most savage as they were, might be deprived of the material for a further season of frenzy and greater cruelty. I have no doubt that their power was checked by fated decrees and by the law of heavenly things, and that Requesens was taken away by a sudden death, without having appointed a governor and arbiter, so that the weary affairs might draw breath during an interregnum. Thus King Philip, having heard from letters of the council of state, was struck by the death of Requesens and did not hide the public harshness of the fates under a private wound. Hence in Philip's court, the king being thrown into confusion, a sad silence was noted, which spread through all of Spain together with the report of Requesens's death and showed the bitterness of the funeral. For people were implying that a leader loyal to King Philip, and not inexperienced in conducting affairs, was being snuffed out at the very height of his power and course of events, and that the hope he had conceived beforehand of crushing the parties was being confounded by the loss and ruin of so great a head. Therefore Philip, lest the affairs of Belgium, already disturbed of their own accord, should fall into greater confusion, transferred all the authority that Requesens had assumed to the council of state of the Belgian provinces, and sent letters of this kind into the provinces.

units.la: Reptum fato REQUESENTIUM provinciarum Belgicae ac Burgundiae Praesidem accepi. Neque patum indolui eâ temporum aetate extinctum, quâ civilibus armis finem & terris meis pacem fore omnia & mea consilia promittebant. Et quoniam fides procerum Concilij status onei integra & incorrupta semper fuit, ita non dubito, quin qua divino nomi-ni, mi, Romanæ religioni, meo & provinciarum bono posthac inservient, ultro facturi sint. Quare Principatus mei per provincias vim, quam resolvi non volo, illis demando, dum regiæ stirpis Principem ad vos mısero, qui meo nomine regundis provincijs præsit. Itaque jubeo ut omne obsequium Concilio status, velut mihi, præstetis, faciatisque quæ stabiliendæ Romanæ religioni, quieti & paci publicæ expedire censebitis. Quod si feceritis bene mecum actum erit, apud quem magna fidei vestræ & obsequij ratio est.
units.tr: I have received word that Requesens, president of the provinces of the Netherlands and Burgundy, has been snatched away by fate. I am not a little grieved that he has been taken from us at a time when all my plans and hopes promised an end to civil arms and peace for my lands. And since the loyalty of the nobles of the council of state has always been whole and uncorrupted, I do not doubt that they will of their own accord serve hereafter the divine name, the Roman religion, my own good and the good of the provinces. Therefore I entrust to them the power of my principality over the provinces, which I do not wish to relinquish, until I send to you a prince of royal blood who shall preside over the provinces in my name. Thus I order you to render all obedience to the council of state, as to myself, and to do whatever you judge expedient for establishing the Roman religion, public quiet and peace. If you do so, it will go well with me, to whom your faith and obedience are of great account.

units.la: Sic turbidum impurumque Belgicæ corpus, quod tot Proregum moderamini à Philippi regis è Belgicâ excessu parverat, pluribus rectoribus commissum. Unde lentius mox languidiusque bellum, cum essent qui exitialium furorum pertæsi, validâ ac stante peregrini militis ac dominantis licentiâ, ultimum exitium infoelici patriæ præformidarent. Neque alio Elisabethæ Anglorum reginæ consilia spectabant, quam, ut salutari providentiæ lege morte Requesentij unius dominatu finito, plurium lenitate molliora tempora pacem aut armistitium largirentur. Igitur gratulari clam inspera tæ foelicitati, quæ occasionem & forte materiem sopiendo bello dedisset. Eadem ratione Requesentij exitum foederati interpretabantur, illius occasu benignum sydus Belgicis terris illuxisse. Quippe amoto capite & principe rerum regius miles in seditionem provolutus parca stipendia spontaneis flagitijs & ultrò nascituræ insolentiæ obtendebat. Unde odia Ordinum in Hispanum militem nata, cujus primo, velut funesti ominis, in provincias ingressu ruptam civilem concordiam & specie præsidij destinatum bellum recordabantur. Sic magnam rerum conversionem, ut solstitia syderum, Requesentij exitus trahebat.
units.tr: Thus the troubled and corrupted body of Belgium, which since King Philip's departure from the Netherlands had been governed by so many governors, was entrusted to several rulers. Hence the war soon became slower and more languid; there were men weary of deadly frenzies, while the strong and standing licence of the foreign soldiery, which dominated, made them dread the final ruin of their unhappy country. Nor did the counsels of Elizabeth, queen of the English, aim at anything else than this: that, with the death of Requesens ending the rule of one man, the times might become milder through the gentleness of many, and grant peace or an armistice by the salutary law of providence. Hence they secretly congratulated themselves on the good fortune that had offered an occasion and a fitting material for quieting the war. In the same way the confederates interpreted the end of Requesens: with his fall a kindly star had risen over the Belgian lands. For with the head and leader removed, the royal soldiery broke into mutiny, and they pleaded meagre pay, with voluntary crimes and an insolence sure to arise of its own accord. Hence arose the hatreds of the estates against the Spanish soldier, whose first entry into the provinces, like an ill omen, they recalled as having broken civil concord and turned a war intended as protection into a war in fact. So great a change in affairs did the end of Requesens bring, like the solstices of the stars.

units.la: Mox Bartoldus Entenius Menthedanus, potestate jam ante ab Aurantio Principe acceptâ, habendis Albim intra & Visurgim delectibus incubuit militemque foederatorum & sacramento autoratum classi imposuit. Locum vero habendæ recensioni Scellingiam insulam designavit, quæ ab occasu Flevi fluminis ostio, ab ortu sinu Amelandico clausa, meridiem ac septentrionem versus Germanico mari aut latissimis æstuarijs alluebatur. Quarum rerum famâ in Frisios qui Scellingiæ insulæ objecti sunt perlatâ, Gasparus Roblesius inter otia & securitatem agens, actuarias naves una cum triremibus instrui fecit, completasque classiario & juxta suæ legionis milite mari immissas versus Scellingiam duxit. Cæterum comperto validam Entenio manum, tum in proxumo auxilia coepto destitit classemque triremium Harlinganum in portum subduxit. Jam enim Sonnoius minori Frisiæ Præfectus & Gualterus Hegemannus, (qui trium insularum Texaliæ, Wiringiæ & Flevolandiæ potiebatur) Entenio auxilia destinaverant omnemque illam oram, Germanico mari objacentem mutua ope tuebantur.
units.tr: Soon Bartholdus Entenius of Menthe, already earlier given authority by Prince Orange, set himself to holding levies between the Yssel and the Weser, and enrolled the soldiers of the confederates, sworn in, on the fleet. He designated the island of Schelling as the place for holding the muster. It is enclosed on the west by the mouth of the river Vlie, on the east by the Ameland inlet, and is washed to the south and north by the German sea or by very wide estuaries. When word of these affairs was carried to the Frisians who were opposite the island of Schelling, Gaspar Robles, who was spending his time in leisure and security, had transport ships fitted out together with triremes; he loaded them with marines and soldiers of his own legion, sent them out to sea, and led them towards Schelling. But on learning that Entenius had a strong force, and that help was being prepared nearby, he gave up and drew the fleet of triremes into the harbour at Harlingen. For Didericus Sonnoy, prefect of Lesser Friesland, and Walter Hegemann, who held the three islands of Texel, Wieringen and Flevoland, had already assigned help to Entenius, and they were defending that whole coast facing the German sea with mutual aid.

units.la: Itaque factum est, ut Entenius nullo obturbante copias per insulam lustraret collectamque Bremæ & minores per Frisios viginti octo navium classem Friscis æstuarijs immitteret. Sic florente foederatis velis mari magna majorem per Frisiam trepidatio fuit, auctis sensim populi Præfectique pavoribus, quod adpulisse classis haud procul Oostmahomà Dongrico in littore non fictis rumoribus diceretur. Ibi Entenius loci non ignarus, quem ad confluentes Eæ, tum Collumanos LavicaLavicanofque sinus gerendis rebus opportunum delegerat, militem exposuit modicumque editæ continentis spatium tumultuario opere circumduxit. Unde Roblesius sparsas per præsidia cohortes raptim colle- git plebemque agrariam habendis cohortium supplementis veteramo mi- liti immiscuit. Mox festino itinere Doccomium dein Oostmahornam duxit longaque velitatione ab ortu Solis in medium diei facta, locum natura & ex arte ab Entenio munitum inrito conatu & suorum clade oppugnavit. Quinquaginta aut sexaginta è Roblesianis illo conflictu cecidisse annotatum invenio multosque saucios percurandis vulneribus Doccomium abductos.
units.tr: So it came about that Entenius, with no one disturbing him, surveyed the island and, gathering a fleet of twenty-eight ships from Bremen and the smaller places, sent it into the Frisian estuaries. Thus, while the confederates' sails flourished on the sea, there was great alarm throughout Friesland, as the fears of the people and of the prefect grew by degrees, because it was said, and not from invented rumours, that the fleet had landed not far from Oostmahorn on the Dongerdeel shore. There Entenius, who knew the place, having chosen it as suitable for carrying out operations near the confluence of the Ee and then the Lauwers and Collumer bays, put his soldiers ashore and with hasty work drew a rampart around a modest stretch of raised land. Hence Robles quickly gathered the cohorts scattered among the garrisons and mixed the rural people into the old soldiery to make up the numbers of the cohorts. Soon, by a rapid march, he led them to Dokkum and then to Oostmahorn, and after a long skirmish from sunrise until midday he attacked the position, which had been fortified by nature and by art by Entenius, with a fruitless attempt and the defeat of his own men. I find it recorded that fifty or sixty of Robles's men fell in that clash, and many wounded were carried off to Dokkum to have their wounds treated.

units.la: Quare Roblesius suorum cæde & repulsa exardescens equitum peditumque dein rusticæ plebis auxilia, quæ ad mille & C C. collegerat, in castra evocavit retentatâque machinis munitione, post insultu repetito, majore cladis & fugæ infamiâ rejectus est. Igitur alio consilio rem orsus Entenium objecto novo opere clausit firmatifq; castris commeatum intercepit. Entenius vero, etsi discrimen expenderet, ita solutionem obsidij aliunde sperabat, Didericumque Sonnoium aut auxilia missurum aut ex condicto copijs adjutum in provinciæ fines qua minores Frisios spectant retrahendo ab obsidione Roblesio irrupturum. Jam enim Roblesius per omnem littoralem tractum præsidia militum extenuaverat Slotanæque ac Lemmeranæ munitiones solis civium excubijs asservabantur. Cæterum Sonnoium alijs rebus Aurantius tum destinabat.
