Itaque Entenius datis ad socios litteris de commeatu ac stipendijs monuit, quo sacramenti pretium miles acciperet corporumq; robur, præ inediâ aut parciore victu languescens, necessariâ & utili alimoniâ obeundis munijs refocillaretur. De se vero fidem faciebat Entenius non facturum hostibus loci copiam, quamdiu spiritus & vita superesset, quin malle fortem animam honestâ & imitandâ posteris morte ponere, quam excedere munitione si æs militum & annona suppetant. Cæterum inania Entenij ad socios adhortamenta & consilia fuere. Itaque desertâ cum suis (quos mille & ducentos fuisse Stauri-us scriptor Heymannus septingentos notat) munitione, suæ & commilitonum incolumitati prospicere coactus est, quos in diversa per defectum æris & annonæ sparsos annales tradidere. Adeo præconcepta magnarum rerum consilia sperati sæpe exitus destituunt.
units.tr: Therefore Robles, inflamed by the slaughter of his men and by the repulse, called to the camp the cavalry and infantry and then the auxiliaries from the country folk, whom he had gathered to about eleven hundred; he tried the fortification with siege engines, but after a renewed assault he was driven back, with greater disgrace from the defeat and the flight. Then, beginning the affair with another plan, he shut in Entenius with a new work placed in front of him, strengthened his camp, and cut off his supplies. Entenius, however, although he weighed the danger, hoped in this way for the lifting of the siege from elsewhere: either Didericus Sonnoy would send help, or, aided by a joint force, he would break in on Robles by drawing him away from the siege into the borders of the province where the Lesser Frisians lie. For Robles had already weakened the garrisons of soldiers along the whole coastal stretch, and the fortresses of Slootdorp and Lemmer were guarded only by the watches of the citizens. But Orange at that time had other business for Sonnoy. So Entenius, by letters sent to his allies, warned them about supplies and pay, so that the soldier might receive the price of his oath, and so that the strength of their bodies, wasting away from want of food or a meagre diet, might be restored by necessary and useful nourishment for their duties. For his own part Entenius gave assurance that, as long as breath and life remained, he would not give the enemy the chance of the place, and that he would rather lay down his brave life by an honourable death worth imitating by posterity than leave the fortification, if the soldiers' pay and provisions were lacking. But Entenius's exhortations and counsels to his allies were in vain. So, having abandoned the fortification with his men (whom the writer Heymann Stauri, noting, says were twelve hundred, though he records seven hundred), he was compelled to look to his own safety and that of his fellow soldiers, who, scattered in different directions through lack of money and food, the annals record. So often do the plans of great undertakings, conceived beforehand, fail the hoped-for outcome.

units.la: Mox Roblesius dissipatis partibus & fugato Entenio, ad pacis otia & studia conversus marino aggere, quo Westergoos adversum injurias Oceani clauserat, finem imposuit suæque industriæ æternum famæ monumentum decerni passus est. Quippe suo consilio legem isti elemento impositam intra se gloriabatur quod naturâ sui & lapsante in depressa humido sive lunari aut diurno æstu concitatum, per tot sæculorum ætates damna & clades Frisicis terris invexerat. Sic populum plurimum discordem & sua ad commoda tardum asperis jussibus flexisse, ut viritim ad erigendam validissimi aggeris molem tanquam restinguendum ad incendium concurreret. Defossa tantis terrarum spatijs prædia & colonorum ac vectigalium dispendia ac querimonias placasse, monstratâ rei necessitate & ultimæ continentis ac naturæ velut finem tam necessario opere muniendum. Hoc solo perpetuæ gentis securitati & suæ {CIↄ. Io.} suæ famæ consultum, quâ Caroli Philippique Præfectorum gloriam veris & sempiternis laudibus superasset. Victurâ haud dubiè, quamdiu natura rerum aut mari limes sit. Quamobrem aggere marino ad finem perducto, è Senatu regio Adrianus Vastartius & Ioannes Carolus Harlingam profecti, monumentum in ipso littore erexere, quod effigie TERMINI maritimis mediterraneisque Westergois limitem daret, omnemque in posterum reficiendi curandique aggeris litem amoveret.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Roblesius, with the parties scattered and Entenius put to flight, turned to the leisure and pursuits of peace. He brought to an end the sea embankment with which he had closed off the West Frisians against the injuries of the Ocean, and allowed a lasting monument to his industry to be decreed. He boasted that by his own counsel he had imposed a law on that element, which by its nature, and by the sinking of the depressed, moist land, and by the tides stirred up by the moon or the sun, had for so many ages brought losses and disasters upon the Frisian lands. So he had bent a people very discordant and slow to act for their own advantage, by harsh orders, so that each man, one by one, ran together to raise the mass of a very strong dike, as if to put out a fire. He had calmed the sinking of estates over such wide stretches of land, and the losses and complaints of the farmers and tax-payers, by showing the necessity of the thing, and by fortifying, as it were, the very end of the continent and of nature with so necessary a work. By this alone he had provided for the perpetual safety of the people and for his own fame, surpassing by true and everlasting praises the glory of Charles and of the prefects Philip. It will undoubtedly endure as long as the order of nature, or the sea, remains a boundary. Therefore, when the sea embankment had been brought to completion, Adrianus Vastartius and Ioannes Carolus set out from the royal Senate to Harlingen, and raised a monument on the very shore, which in the form of a TERMINUS would mark the boundary between the maritime and inland West Frisians, and would remove every future dispute over repairing and maintaining the dike.

units.la: Scribit M. Heymannus duodena ex coctili latere millia fundamento substrata columnamque supra aggeris marini superficiem in viginti pedum altitudinem exsurgere:
units.tr: M. Heymannus writes that twelve thousand bricks were laid as a foundation, and that a column rose above the surface of the sea embankment to a height of twenty feet:

units.tr: CASPARI A ROBLES EQVITI DOMINO DE BILLI &c.

units.tr: THIS WAS THE INSCRIPTION OF THE BOUNDARY.

units.tr: Toward the West.

units.la: CASPARI A ROBLES EQUITI, DOMINO DE BILLI, &c. FRISIAE, GRONINGAE EJUSQUE TERRITORII AC ADJACENTIUM GUBERNATORI, QUOD HANC PROVINCIAM, PRAETER ARMA, CONSILIIS ET MUNIMENTIS JUVERIT, AC INTER CAETERA, AGGERE IPSIS KAL. NOV. M.D.LXX. FUNDITUS EVERSO, AMPLISS. D. VIGLII ZVICHEMI, PATRIS PATRIAE, AUXILIARIBUS OPERIS ET ADHIBITIS IGRAMO AB ACHELEN PR. ADRIANO VASTAERT, PETRO FRITTEMA ET IOANNE CAROLO SENATORIBUS, CONCILIORUM SOCIIS, NOVUM MARIS PROPUGNACULUM, SUMMO LABORE, VIGILIA, ET CELEBRITATE, DECRETIS QUOQUE, ET DE SUO PERSOLUTIS DILIGENTIA PRAEMIIS, TRIBUS PLUS MINUS MENSIBUS A FUNDAMENTIS EREXERIT ET AD SUMMAM MANUM PERDUXERIT ATQUE HUNC LAPIDEM SUBLATIS CONTROVERSIARUM LITIBUS TERMINUM ESSE VOLUIT, GRATUS PROVINCIALIUM ORDO OB REM PRUDENTER BENE ET FIDELITER GESTAM, DE SE AC DE REP. OPTUME MERITO.
units.tr: TO CASPAR A ROBLES, KNIGHT, LORD OF BILLI, ETC., GOVERNOR OF FRIESLAND, GRONINGEN AND ITS TERRITORY AND ADJOINING AREAS: BECAUSE HE HELPED THIS PROVINCE, BESIDES WITH ARMS, BY COUNSEL AND FORTIFICATIONS, AND AMONG OTHER THINGS, WHEN THE DYKE ITSELF WAS UTTERLY BROKEN ON THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER 1570; WITH THE AID OF THE WORK OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN VIGLIUS ZUICHEMUS, FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND, AND WITH THE HELP OF IGRAM AB ACHELEN, PRAETOR, AND OF ADRIAN VASTAERT, PETER FRITTEMA AND JOHN CHARLES, SENATORS AND FELLOW MEMBERS OF THE COUNCILS; HE RAISED A NEW BULWARK AGAINST THE SEA, WITH THE GREATEST LABOUR, VIGILANCE AND SPEED, BY DECREES ALSO, AND WITH REWARDS PAID DILIGENTLY FROM HIS OWN MEANS; WITHIN ABOUT THREE MONTHS HE BUILT IT FROM THE FOUNDATIONS AND BROUGHT IT TO COMPLETION, AND HE WISHED THIS STONE TO BE THE BOUNDARY, THE DISPUTES BEING SETTLED. THE GRATEFUL ORDER OF THE PROVINCIALS, FOR A MATTER PRUDENTLY, WELL AND FAITHFULLY CARRIED OUT, AND DESERVING VERY WELL OF THEMSELVES AND OF THE COMMONWEALTH.

units.tr: IN THE YEAR 1575 THE DYKE WAS DIVIDED INTO TWO PARTS, OF WHICH THE SOUTHERN PART FELL TO THE MARITIME DISTRICT. THE DEPUTIES WERE THOMAS HIDDIUS, SIXTUS NICOLAUS, PRAETOR HECTOR DEKAMA, HERO OCKINGA, ULPIUS HIDDAMA, VITUS CAMMINGA, DOTHIA BONGA, GERARD ABBAEUS AND LOLLIUS OCKINGA.

units.tr: In the year 1576, on 19 July, M. Adrianus Vastartius and Dominus Ioannes Carolus, first fiscal procurator of the column stone, laid it down, with Ioannes Guilielmus presiding and acting as clerk.

units.la: ANNO M. D. LXXIV. AGGER FIERI COEPIT PRAEF. AGG. RUARDO ROORDA ET MEDITERR. DEPUT. FRED. OFFENHUS ET SIRIACO SIRIACI, DELECT. VERO AD BOREAL. ACGERIS PART. ERIG. TITO A CAMMINGHA VICE-PRAEF, HESSELO AB HANIA, EDONE GERBRANDA ET HANSONE ROORDA.
units.tr: In the year 1574 the building of the dyke began, Ruardus Roorda being prefect of the dyke, with Fredericus Offenhus and Siriacus Siriaci as deputies for the inland parts, and deputies chosen for the northern parts of the dykes: Titus a Camminga, vice-prefect, Hesselus ab Hania, Edo Gerbranda and Hanso Roorda.

units.la: Reperio in actis publicis aggerum à Bildâ Maccumanas ad catarractas longitudinem 632 f. pert. & 6. ped. curiosè supputantibus annotatam maritimisque Westergois 4744. pert. & 1½. ped. & in ijs Lidlumanis coenobitis, mediterraneis 1581. pert. & 4½. ped. obvenisse. His quoque sustinendo aggeri 24895. maritimis 8163. florenos aureos colligi ideoque fieri ut maritimis florenus aureus 6. ped. 10. dig. mediterraneis 9. dig. praestet.
units.tr: I find in the public records, annotated by careful calculators, that the dykes from Bilda to Maccumanas at the sluices measure about 632 rods and 6 feet in length; the maritime Westergo has 4744 rods and 1½ feet, and in it the Lidlum monks' inland section has 1581 rods and 4½ feet. For sustaining this dyke, 24,895 gold florins are collected from the maritime districts and 8163 from the inland ones; hence it comes about that the maritime gold florin is worth 6 feet 10 inches, and the inland one 9 inches.

units.la: Quo sumptuoso aggerum opere, ut Westergoorum praecipuè res lacerabantur, ita omnem provinciam continuæ exactiones exhauserant. Quare amovendis importunis in posterum tributorum flagitationibus Philippum ad Regem supplicatio decreta, quâ Ordines Frisiæ servitutis suæ & insolentiæ peregrinorum pertæsi lenius ex sacramento Philippi imperium & Concilium status orabant. Neque inania legationi auguria & vanæ spes captabantur, amoto pridem terris Requesentio & plurium regimine etiam Philippi rescripto, per provincias instituto. Unde ocyus è Frisicâ Nobilitate Valerius Cammingha, qui ab eâ legatione non diu superstes fuit & Hero Ockingha cum fiduciarijs litteris mandatisque Bruxellas missi, quibus querimoniæ oppressi juris, & violatarum conventionum continebantur.
units.tr: As this costly work on the dykes mainly wore down the Westergoers, so continual exactions had drained the whole province. Therefore, to remove the troublesome demands for taxes in future, a petition to the King was decided upon through Philip, by which the Estates of Friesland, weary of their servitude and the insolence of foreigners, begged that the rule and the Council of State be milder, in accordance with Philip's oath. Nor did they seek empty omens or vain hopes for the embassy, since Requesens had long since been removed from the land, and the government of several men had also been ended by a rescript of Philip, established throughout the provinces. Hence, more quickly, from the Frisian nobility Valerius Cammingha, who did not long survive that embassy, and Hero Ockingha were sent to Brussels with letters of trust and instructions, containing complaints of oppressed right and violated agreements.

units.la: Non eâ quippe conditione cum Hispaniæ Principe depactos, ut tabulæ pactionum subverterentur modumque ac limitem transgressa potestas patientiâ populi ad licentiam dominantium abuteretur. Assignatum Cæsari CAROLO patrimonium, adjecta ordinarijs largitionibus honoraria, ne præceps & ultro perperdendis rebus se ingerens confusio, negatis rerum subsidijs consilia Principis perverteret. Vbi vero modum res excessere etiam obtestationibus usos, suo tamen in Principem affectu novâ liberalitate accisum & tenue erarium subuvisse. Sic ante annum semestri spatio triginta tria carolæorum millia corrogasse, non eâ mente, ut nova tributorum genera à facilitate gentis nascerentur, sed ut expleta semel dominantium cupiditas satiaretur. Post singulis lunaribus mensibus octo millia aeris importunè poscentibus concessa menstruaque pensiones, non integro anno, in centum & quindecim carolæorum millia excurrisse. Adhac commeatum, currus, navigia, plebi populoque passim per agros extorta, quo in ultimam egestatem aut onera provinciales detruderentur paucorumque potentia & opes cum multorum paupertate aut servitio increscerent. Ferendis gravioribus tandem incapaces factos. Quippe angusto limite clausam provinciam & non semel inundationes suarum terrarum perpessam, incolarum fugam aut promptissimam egestatem minari. His miseriis partium arma & civiles discordias accedere. Quippe regi rebelles in provinciam irruere depraedari obvia. Nec quari his omnibus remedia, sed fomenta. Adeo certè ut conferendis in regium militem stipendijs privatae opes non respondeant. Itaque rogare, ut regis patrimonium, isti rei CAROLO Caesari decretum applicari stipendijs militum curent gravatumve nexibus aere alieno liberent. Posse scilicet creditoribus regijs alia pignorum dari. His addebant ROBLESIUM ipsum actione crediti de septem millibus & sexcentis carolaeis conveniendum, exhausto aerario & attritis privatorum fortunis, quas miles aut praedo sustulisset. Quare decreto Concilij status dimittendum militem aut cohibendas tributorum imperij grassationes esse, ne quid damni posthac per provinciam faciant abstineantque alienis.
units.tr: Certainly they had not agreed with the Prince of Spain on the condition that the tables of agreements should be overturned, and that power, passing its measure and limit, should abuse the people's patience for the licence of the rulers. The patrimony assigned to the Emperor Charles, with honorary additions to the ordinary largesses, was given so that a headlong confusion, pressing in on its own accord to destroy things, should not, by denying the means of support, pervert the Prince's counsels. When matters had exceeded their measure, and they had also used entreaties, yet out of their affection for the Prince they relieved the thin treasury by a new liberality. Thus within the space of half a year before, they had raised thirty-three thousand carolus, not so that new kinds of taxes would arise from the people's good nature, but so that the rulers' greed, once satisfied, might be sated. Afterwards, eight thousand coins each lunar month were granted to their importunate demands, and the monthly pensions, in less than a whole year, ran up to one hundred and fifteen thousand carolus. Besides this, provisions, wagons and ships were extorted everywhere from the common people across the fields, by which the provincials were thrust either into utmost destitution or into burdens, and the power and wealth of the few grew with the poverty or servitude of the many. At last they were made unable to bear heavier burdens. Indeed, the province, shut in by a narrow boundary and having more than once suffered the inundation of its lands, threatened the flight of its inhabitants or their most ready destitution. To these miseries were added the arms of the parties and civil discords, for rebels against the king rushed into the province and plundered whatever they met. Nor were remedies sought for all these things, but fomentations. So certainly that private resources do not match the payment of the royal soldiers. Therefore they asked that they might see to it that the king's patrimony, decreed to Emperor Charles for this purpose, be applied to the soldiers' pay, or else that they be freed from the burden of debt. The royal creditors could, of course, be given other pledges. To these points they added that Robles himself should be sued by an action for debt of seven thousand six hundred carolus, since the treasury was exhausted and private fortunes worn down by what the soldier or plunderer had carried off. Therefore, by decree of the Council of State, the soldiers must either be dismissed or the plundering of the imperial tributes restrained, so that they do no further damage through the province and keep their hands off others' property.

units.la: Hæc Legati.
units.tr: The Legates' Statement.

units.la: Quæ à Consilio status pronis animis accepta, hoc rescriptum nomine PHILIPPI impetravere.
units.tr: These demands, received with favourable minds by the Council of State, obtained this rescript in the name of Philip.

units.la: Nihil tarius sanctiusque sibi fore, quam pacem Frisicis terris sopito bello reddere. Caeterum quoniam motus adhuc & arma vigerent, dimitti exercitum non posse. Sopiendus vero turbis regem PHILIPPUM IOANNEM AUSTRIACUM fratrem suum destinare, facturum haud dubie quae è re provinciarum viderentur. Daturum quoque operam ut patrimonium regis à populo Frisico olim Caesari concessum, à nexu creditorum liberetur censusque Principis & vectigalium agrorum reditus veris usibus serviant. Qui etsi solis Frisijs & eorum commodis applicati non sint, tamen haud dubie majora ordinarijs rerum proventibus impendia PHILIPPUM Regem sustinuisse. Quem inter & populum Friscum, si quid litis controversive subortum esset, quod aut jus patrium, aut privatorum damna spectaret, id pro occasione compositurum daturumque, litteras ad Præfectum & Tribunos cohortium, coercendae insolentiae & ne publica gentis quies obturbetur.
units.tr: Nothing, he said, would be more pleasing and more sacred to him than to restore peace to the Frisian lands once the war was lulled. However, since movements and arms were still active, the army could not be dismissed. To calm the disturbances, the king would send his brother, John of Austria, who would undoubtedly do whatever seemed right for the interests of the provinces. He would also take care that the king's patrimony, once granted to the Emperor by the Frisian people, be freed from the bond of creditors, and that the Prince's census and the revenues of the lands and taxes serve true uses. Although these are not applied solely to the Frisians and their advantages, King Philip had undoubtedly sustained expenses greater than the ordinary revenues of affairs. If any dispute or controversy should arise between him and the Frisian people, concerning either their ancestral right or the losses of private persons, he would settle and grant it as an opportunity presented itself; and he sent letters to the prefect and tribunes of the cohorts, to curb insolence and so that the public peace of the people not be disturbed.

units.la: Hæc Concilium Status.
units.tr: These are the acts of the Council of State.

units.la: Igitur à Concilio Status litteræ ocyus in Frisiam ad Senatum regium datæ, quibus Senatus regius, Philippi Regis nomine, patrium populi jus & immunitates, sartas tectas curare asperrimo rescripto jubebatur. Unde & à Senatu regio Edicta in omnem provinciæ oram missa, popularium legum & juris antiqui fidelem observantiam agrariis Prætoribus inculcabant, ac ut Frisij scripto majorum aut Saxonico jure, quod Carolus Philippusque confirmassent, ita petentibus Legatis regerentur. Cæterum Requesentio Gubernatore vitâ functo, velut soluto disciplinæ censore, regius miles per provincias lasciviens omne in flagitium effundebatur spretisque Præfectorum Tribunorumque imperijs ac simul precibus residua stipendiorum, mercedem exercitæ virtutis poscebat. Sed ærarium tenue, divisa procerum consilia, tum expilatæ attritæque populi opes subitaneis sedandarum legionum remedijs destituebantur. Itaque sectiones passim opulentissimarum florentissimarumque urbium institutæ foedæque populi strages tum matronarum ac virginum stupra habebantur.
units.tr: Accordingly, letters were sent with all speed from the Council of State to the royal Senate in Friesland. By a very harsh rescript, the royal Senate was ordered, in the name of King Philip, to see that the ancestral right and immunities of the people remained intact. From the royal Senate, edicts were sent to every shore of the province, urging the agrarian praetors to observe faithfully the popular laws and ancient right, and directing that the Frisians, as their envoys requested, be answered according to the written law of their ancestors or the Saxon law which Charles and Philip had confirmed. Meanwhile, Requesens the governor had died, and the royal soldiers, as though the censor of discipline had been removed, ran riot through the provinces and poured out every kind of outrage. Scorning the commands of the prefects and tribunes and their entreaties, they demanded the arrears of their pay as the reward of their courage. But the treasury was meagre, the counsels of the nobles were divided, and the wealth of the people had been plundered and worn down, so there was no ready remedy for quelling the legions. Thus sackings of the richest and most flourishing cities were set up everywhere, with foul slaughter of the people, and the rape of matrons and virgins followed.

units.la: Haud dissimulante Concilio status, non servitijs ministerijsque regijs, cæterum vastandis perdendisque rebus Hispanicas legiones & earum licentiam ali. Igitur Edicto Concilij statuş, quod jure atque auctoritate Principis tum valebat, regis & provinciarum hostes judicatæ mandatumque Præfectis cæterarum legionum, ut mobiles animos & in pejora more mortalium pronos militari disciplinâ coërceant abstineantque societate Hispanicarum seditiosarumque legionum avertendis provinciarum incommodis de communi consilio corrigendâ. Quare augendis populi procerumque in Hispanos odijs adhibita fomenta, obnitentibus econtra Hispanicarum legionum Præfectis fidem suæ gentis apud Philippum regem contrarijs persuasionibus tueri. Unde æmulatio procerum, etiam in ipso Concilio ac Senatu discordiam, vim discordia traxit. Quippe Concilio status militari manu obsepto & custodiæ dato pro animorum captu, ut solet rebus turbidis, varie & acerbè adversum externæ dominationis intolerabilem licentiam differebatur & quod Hieronimum Rodam obscuræ originis & gentis Hispanæ in Concilium status adscitum, ad usurpandam regiam autoritatem & vim principatus præceps & cruda ambitio compulisset. Sic emuniendis hinc inde partibus quæsita concilia miseras provincias diversis factionibus laceravere.
units.tr: The Council of State did not hide the fact that the Spanish legions were maintained not for the service and ministry of the king, but for laying waste and destroying things, and for their licence. Therefore, by an edict of the Council of State, which at that time had the force of law and the authority of the Prince, they were judged enemies of the king and of the provinces. The prefects of the other legions were ordered to restrain, by military discipline, minds that were restless and, as men are, inclined to worse things, and to keep clear of association with the Spanish and seditious legions, so that the troubles of the provinces might be averted by common counsel. Hence hatred of the Spaniards was fanned among the people and nobles, while the prefects of the Spanish legions, resisting, defended the loyalty of their nation to King Philip with contrary persuasions. From this came rivalry among the nobles, even within the Council and the Senate itself, and discord brought its force. For the Council of State was hemmed in by a military force and placed under guard, and, as usual in troubled times, the matter was debated variously and bitterly according to the feelings of men, against the intolerable licence of foreign domination. It was also said that Jerónimo de Roda, of obscure origin and Spanish nation, had been admitted into the Council of State, and that a headlong and crude ambition had driven him to usurp royal authority and the power of princely rule. Thus the councils formed to fortify one side or the other tore the wretched provinces apart with rival factions.

units.la: Itaque missus in Hispaniam Legatus, qui Edicti rationem excusaret ostenderetque Hispanicas legiones seditionibus involutas paci & quieti publicæ obstare. Datæ quoque Maximilianum ad Cæsarem à Concilio status litteræ, quibus de miserijs decennalium bellorum & nefariâ Hispanorum per Belgicam dominatione querebantur.
units.tr: Therefore a legate was sent to Spain to excuse the edict and to show that the Spanish legions, entangled in seditions, stood in the way of public peace and quiet. Letters were also given by the Council of State to Maximilian, to be sent to the Emperor, in which they complained of the miseries of the decades-long wars and of the impious domination of the Spaniards throughout Belgium.

units.la: Litteræ à Concilio status ad Cæsarem datæ.
units.tr: Letters sent by the Council of State to the Emperor.

units.la: Polluta sacra ac profana ab ALBANI in provincias ingressu, & cum patientiâ populi (etiam ad aspera & immodesta per reverentiam PHILIPPI regis conniventis,) furorem istius gentis increvisse. Vastatos agros, florentissimas urbium occupatas ac direptas, necatam aut oppressam nobilitatem, provinciales non unâ strage deletos, tum violatas stupris matronas virginesque obtestabantur. Nihil intactum Hispanicis furoribus fuisse. Itaque naturæ sanctissimâ lege & gentium usu fultos adversum eam confugem arma induisse, ultimum exitium & peiora adhuc scelera provinciis minitantem. Nec privatâ adhuc potestate usos, caeterum, durante post mortem REQUESENTII interregno, regundis provinciis à PHILIPPO rege suffectos, hostium loco habendos publico decreto censuisse. Neque aliâ de causâ quosdam dignitate & Concilio Status movisse, quam quod fomenta Hispanicæ insolentiæ contulissent vimque decreti de reprimendis Hispanis præservidis studijs impugnassent. Sic remoras pacis & omnium fœderum fuisse. Inde suspecta H Y- ERONIMI RODAE & aliorum consilia usurpatamque superbè potentiam aversatos. Spectasse sigillum regium privatâ RODAE autoritate æri incisum & mandatis suffixum. Adhæc sollicitatas ab eo in exitium provinciarum Germaniæ legiones & in societatem consiliorum pertractas, quo eum ambitiosa dominandi cupido armis innixa ad fastigium summæ potentiæ aut imaginem regni eveheret. Adultis viribus ac magnitudine rerum fœdius adhuc regnaturum fuisse. Itaque stitisse adolescentis imperij cursum & ex officio & jurisjurandi religione cavisse; Ne quid detrimenti. Sic delectus à Concilio Status per provincias decretos, sic implorata provinciarum auxilia, ut inculpatæ tutelæ locus esset & ut exacto diuturni Hispanicique furoris circuitu, certior ad sanciendam pacem etiam inter media arma regressus esset. Igitur magnum æternumque numen, tum Cæsarem Principesque obtestari, non à Romanâ Catholicâ religione, non à P H I L I P P O rege desciscere, cæterum arma sumpsisse frænandis Hispanorum furoribus valida. De regis vero ingenio in clementiam propenso se non dubitare, cæterum assentatorum aulæ præfectorumque per Belgicam falsis persuasionibus seduci, regiæ mentis integritatem non vanis indicijs ostenderet. Neque enim aliorsum tot litteras affectum pacis præferentes ad Concilium Status missas, quam in I O A N N E A V S T R I A C O optimæ spei Principe fratre suo se daturum pollicereatur. Illius quoque adventum in provincias illorum consilijs trahi, qui secretis aulæ præfecti, & P H I-L I P P O familiares suo commodo an malitiâ ingenij pacem traherent, tantis studijs etiam optimo Cæsarum & Romano Imperio desideratam. P H I L I P-P I vero Regis præsentiâ jam diu ad eam perveniri potuisse, neque tam immodestè agente in provincijs arbitro rerum grassaturos Hispanos, quorum comminationibus peiora obnuntiarentur. Igitur desperatione rerum manum clavo admovisse, ne præcipiti ruinâ Belgicæ & simul Germaniæ res traherentur. Illam quippe ex hoc etiam bello incommodum sentire, imminutis portorijs telonijsque ac omni commercio inter utrasque nationes impedito. Majora damna, nisi Hispanicæ gentis furores sistantur utrisque imminere. Neque enim ante quieturos Hispanos, quam post subactam oppressamque Belgicam Germaniæ etiam Imperium suis regnis adjecerint. Itaque Cæsarem patrocinium rogare ac ut sub pœnâ banni Romani Imperij, Germanicarum legionum Præfectis mandet, ne seditiosis Hispanorum legionibus se socient, cæterum ea agant; quæ sacramenti militaris religio & in provincias regemque fides exacturæ sint. Caveret quoque, ne adversum provinciarum Ordines arma ferant, fœderum jure, Germaniæ sociatos & singulari affectu in Cæsarem propensos.
units.tr: Since the Duke of Alba's entry into the provinces, sacred and profane things had been polluted, and the fury of that nation had grown, while the people were patient even under harsh and immoderate treatment, out of reverence for King Philip, who connived at it. They protested that the fields had been laid waste, flourishing cities occupied and plundered, the nobility killed or crushed, the provincials destroyed in more than one slaughter, and matrons and virgins violated by rape. Nothing had been left untouched by Spanish fury. Therefore, supported by the most sacred law of nature and the custom of nations, they had taken up arms against it, since it threatened the provinces with utter ruin and still worse crimes. They had not yet used any private power. Rather, during the interregnum that followed Requesens' death, those set over the provinces by King Philip to govern them had been declared enemies by public decree. Nor had they removed certain men from their dignity and from the Council of State for any other reason than that they had furnished the fuel of Spanish insolence and opposed the force of the decree on restraining the Spaniards' overheated zeal. Thus they had been obstacles to peace and to all treaties. Hence they had rejected the suspicious counsels of Jerónimo de Roda and others, and his arrogantly usurped power. They had seen the royal seal, cut in bronze at Roda's private authority, attached to mandates. Besides, he had solicited the legions in Germany for the ruin of the provinces and drawn them into his plans, so that his ambitious lust for domination, relying on arms, might raise him to the summit of supreme power, or to the mere image of a kingdom. Once his strength had matured and his position grown, he would have reigned even more foully. Therefore they had halted the course of the young man's rule, and by their duty and the sanctity of their oath had taken care that the state suffer no harm. Thus levies were decreed through the provinces by the Council of State, and the aid of the provinces was implored, so that the guardianship they exercised might be blameless, and so that, once the long circuit of Spanish and furious rule had run its course, there might be a surer return to establishing peace even in the midst of arms. Therefore they call upon the great and eternal Divinity, and upon the Emperor and the princes, to witness that they have not fallen away from the Roman Catholic religion or from King Philip, but had taken up arms, strong enough to curb the furies of the Spaniards. As for the king's nature, which inclines to clemency, they did not doubt it; but he was being led astray by the false persuasions of the flatterers of the court and of the prefects throughout Belgium, and his integrity of mind should be shown by something more than empty signs. For the many letters sent to the Council of State, expressing the desire for peace, pointed to nothing else than that he would give them, as a prince of the best hope, his brother John of Austria. His arrival in the provinces was also being held up by the schemes of those prefects of the court who were secretly intimate with Philip, and who, whether from self-interest or from the malice of their disposition, were dragging out a peace so eagerly desired by the best of emperors and by the Roman Empire. Peace could have been reached long ago with King Philip present; nor would the Spaniards rage so immoderately, with the king as arbiter of affairs in the provinces, whose threats were announcing still worse things. Therefore, in despair of the situation, they had put their hand to the helm, lest the affairs of Belgium and at the same time of Germany be dragged into headlong ruin. For Germany too felt the inconvenience of this war, with tolls and customs duties reduced and all commerce between the two nations hindered. Greater losses threatened both unless the furies of the Spanish nation were halted. For the Spaniards would not rest until, after subduing and crushing Belgium, they had added the Empire of Germany to their kingdoms. Therefore they ask the Emperor for his protection, and that, under penalty of the ban of the Roman Empire, he order the prefects of the German legions not to join themselves to the seditious Spanish legions, but to do what the sanctity of the military oath and their loyalty to the provinces and the king would require. He should also take care that they do not bear arms against the Estates of the provinces, who are allied to Germany by the law of treaties and inclined toward the Emperor with singular affection.

units.la: HÆC CONCILIUM STATUS.
units.tr: The Council of State's Resolution

units.la: Cæterum morbo & post morte Maximiliani Cæsaris, quæ mox subsecuta, omne imperatoriæ ad pacem intercesionis subsidium interruptum est. Creditum fuit Maximilianum Cæsarem sive Mariæ conjugis, è quâ multam prolem sustulerat, sive reverentiâ Philippi, cujus affinitatem ex sorore traxerat, illectum, secreta animi dissimulasse asserendæque conscientiarum libertati pronum, domesticam & conjugalem concordiam nexumque regiæ propinquitatis salubribus consilijs prætulisse.
units.tr: But because of the illness and then the death of Emperor Maximilian, which followed soon after, all the imperial help toward peace was cut off. It was believed that Maximilian, whether won over by his wife Maria, by whom he had had many children, or out of deference to Philip, whose kinship he had gained through Philip's sister, had concealed his true feelings. Inclined as he was to uphold freedom of conscience, he had preferred domestic and marital harmony and the bond of royal kinship to wholesome counsels.

units.la: Notat in Apologetico Aurantius Princeps, eum ab Antonio Perrennotto Cardinale Granvellano veneno tentatum, ac haud dubiè religionis suspectum penetralibus pectoris sensa animi post occultasse. Addunt alij à Concilio Status litteras quoque ad Gregorium xiii Pon-tificem datas, nefarias Hispanorum per Belgicam actiones detexisse, suisque in Catholicam Religionem studijs eidem Gregorio Pontifici commendatis, intercessionem apud Philippum Romanæ Sedi orasse.
units.tr: Prince William of Orange notes in his Apologia that Cardinal Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle tried to poison him, and that William, doubtless suspected of heresy, afterwards hid his feelings deep in his heart. Others add that the Council of State also wrote a letter to Pope Gregory XIII, in which it exposed the wicked actions of the Spaniards throughout the Netherlands. Having commended its own zeal for the Catholic religion to the same Pope Gregory, it asked him to intercede with Philip on behalf of the Roman See.

units.la: Mox Rudolpho ii. Cæsaris Maximiliani primogenito suffragijs Principum Electorum Ratisbonæ in Comitijs ad Imperium evecto, quicquid Belgicæ paci morte optumi Cæsarum decesserat, successione filij repositum censebatur, prælagientibus prudentioribus traducem illum & pacis amantissimum Maximiliani spiritum, haud dubiè natalitiâ propagine in Imperatoriam sobolem transfusum. Ubi vero Rudolphi Cæsaris litteræ jam Imperium capessentis in Belgicam perlatæ, majorem certioremque fiduciam procerum mentes mox concepere. Iis namque re-scribebat Rudolphus tarditatem responsi Sacratissimi patris morte ftetisse seq; funesto illius ex his terris excessu, sepositis velut rerum & Imperij curis, solam ultimæ pietati sollicitudinem aluisse. Signandum fuisse acerbo luctu patrium funus, desiderato capite & carissimo pignore Imperatoriæ domui subducto. Restituta vero mente aut saltem allevatâ, nihil sanctius cariusque habuisse, quam ut, imitatus patrem coelo transcriptum, eadem restaurandæ per infœlicem Belgicam pacis consilia suscuperet. Itaque legatos propediem ad Imperij Principes, dein in provincias missurum, quo æquis conditionibus diuturnum & funestum bellum stabili pace finiatur. Hoc tantum optare, ne quid novi interea Belgæ moliantur documentumque ostendant patientiæ, dum imperatoriæ legationis & simul consilij fructum ferant. Cæterum increscente Legionum insolentiâ & Concilio Status majoris mali metuente, ineundi Fœderis negotium maturatum, ne omni tandem exercitu seditione velut tabe infecto, Belgicæ imperium patribus Ordini-busve provinciarum subtractum, externis legionibus traderetur. Quip-pe Edictum, quod frænandis per provinciam grassatoribus & reprimendis seditiosis Requesentius perscripserat, militari insolentiæ fomenta commodabat contumaciâ humani ingenij, velut jussa respuentis & ne Requesentius populi gratiam cum odio & per sanguinem militum mercaretur. Eo namque Edicto, ut plebi agrariæ se armandæ adversum omnem vim & insolentiam potestatem fecerat, ita impunitatem quoque factis Edicto adjunxerat, si forte legitima defensio ex injuriæ magnitudine & desiderio conservandarum rerum nata militari cæde vindices insolentiæ dexteras imbuissel.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Rudolf II, the eldest son of Emperor Maximilian, was raised to the Empire at the Diet of Regensburg by the votes of the Electoral Princes. Whatever peace for the Netherlands had been lost with the death of that best of emperors was thought to be restored by the succession of his son. Wiser men foresaw that Rudolf was the image of his father and a great lover of peace, and that this spirit had doubtless passed into the imperial line by natural inheritance. When letters from Rudolf, now taking up the Empire, reached the Netherlands, the minds of the nobles soon conceived a greater and more certain confidence. Rudolf wrote to them that the delay in replying had been caused by the death of his most holy father; that after his fatal departure from this earth he had set aside, as it were, the cares of affairs and of the Empire, and had nourished only a concern for his last duty of piety. His father's funeral had to be marked with bitter mourning, since the head and dearest pledge had been taken from the imperial house. But once his mind had been restored, or at least eased, he had held nothing more sacred or dearer than to imitate his father, now translated to heaven, and to take up the same plans for restoring peace in the unhappy Netherlands. Accordingly, he would soon send envoys first to the princes of the Empire and then to the provinces, so that a long and deadly war might be ended by a lasting peace on fair terms. He only asked that in the meantime the Netherlanders attempt nothing new, and show a proof of patience, so that the imperial embassy might bear fruit along with the counsel of the Council of State. Meanwhile, as the insolence of the legions grew and the Council of State feared a greater evil, the business of forming a union was hastened, lest at last the whole army, infected as if by a plague of mutiny, should take control of the Netherlands away from the fathers and the orders of the provinces and hand it to foreign legions. The edict which Requesens had drafted for restraining the marauders throughout the province and checking the seditious, gave fuel to the military insolence, fed by the obstinacy of human nature, which spurns commands, and by Requesens' wish to win the people's favour with hatred and at the cost of soldiers' blood. By that edict he had given the rural population power to arm itself against all violence and insolence, and he had also added impunity for these acts: if, perhaps, lawful self-defence, born of the magnitude of the injury and the desire to preserve their property, had stained the avengers' hands with the slaughter of soldiers.

units.la: Traduxit autores, flectendis tumultuantium consilijs, ad ultimum & quæsitum olim sedandis castrorum præsidiorum; seditionibus remedium, ipsos Duces processisse, quo ad concionem & tribunal imperatoris vo-catos majestas in perantis aut horror monstratæ foeditatis & exprobati furoris coërceret. Adhæc pericula seditionum & in quæ malorum ertu-ptura forent inter miserationem, indignationemque Ducum repetebantur, tam invalidâ eorum authoritate, ut, quod reducendis ad obsequia animis dictum credebatur, incremento furoris apud oblitas sacra-menmenti legiones cederet. Itaque nec Hispanici nominis aut sanguinis obtestatio, non in regem fides, non commemoratio pristinæ virtutis quid valebat & quod soli terrarum gentiumque domitores præclara facinora fœdis criminibus polluisse in tanto rerum discrimine redarguerentur. Interesse regis sui quam maximè ut ad sanas mentes, ad memoriam sacramenti redeant, quod violari non nisi perduellibus posset & quod in tanto gloriæ & secundarum rerum cursu speratos belli exitus & laudatissimum finem moraretur. Non defore Philippum regem officijs suis, cæterum daturum operam ut ex sacramentis stipendia ex virtute gloriam habeant. Quæ singula etsi ex vero dicerentur, à contumacibus & imperia detrectantibus rejecta imminentia mala & præteritis graviora urbibus ac provincijs minabantur. Igitur avertendis incommodis ad Principem Aurantium litteræ à Concilio Status datæ, quæ æquissimas fœderi conditiones, nec dolosis artibus involutam pacem offerebant. Aurantius vero, ne quid fœderatos Ordines celaret, eos istius rei certiores fecit deque mittendis ocyus ad se & deïn Gandavum Legatis commonuit. Suspectam quippe eo in negotio cunctationem esse, ad quod optimi mortalium duce naturâ traherentur. Posse fœderatos, proclivi in concordiam Concilio Status & exercitu regio seditionibus involuto, honesta & utilia Fœderi pacisci. Neque enim dubitare se, quin ista procerum congregatio divino nomini gloriam, securitatem provincijs datura sit. Hoc vero monere, ut pacis negotio intenti de bello cogitent. Instabili scilicet potentiæ semper socordiam nocuisse. Sic Bredano conventu securos & fiduciâ sui subnixos magnis periculis subfuisse. Corrigenda supina consilia esse nec fidendum hosti, qui pacis umbrâ bellum velet. Hortari insuper Fœderatos, ut Frisios cæterosque vicinos durioribus adhuc Præfectorum imperijs parentes ad subvertenda externæ dominationis subsidia instigent novisque societatibus avidum libertatis populum sibi devinciant.
units.tr: The writers report that, to bend the minds of the rioters, the commanders themselves came forward as a remedy, a thing long sought for quelling the mutinies of the garrisons. They were summoned to the assembly and the tribunal of the Emperor, so that the majesty of the sovereign might restrain them, either by the reproach of their shown foulness and the outrage of their exposed fury. Moreover, the dangers of the mutinies, and the evils that would burst forth from them, were repeated amid the pity and indignation of the commanders, but their authority was so weak that what was said to bring the minds back to obedience turned instead to an increase of fury among legions that had forgotten their oath. Thus neither an appeal to the Spanish name and blood, nor loyalty to the king, nor the recollection of their former valour, had any effect. In so great a crisis, they were rebuked for having polluted their famous deeds with foul crimes, though they were the conquerors of the lands and peoples of the world. It was in the interest of their king that they return to sound minds and remember their oath, which could be violated only by traitors, and that in such a course of glory and success they should not delay the hoped-for outcome of the war and its most praised end. Philip the king would not be wanting in his duties, but would take care that they should have their pay from their oath and their glory from their courage. Although each of these points was spoken in truth, the obstinate, who refused commands, rejected them, and threatened cities and provinces with evils impending and worse than those already past. Therefore, to avert these troubles, a letter was sent to Prince William of Orange by the Council of State, offering the fairest terms of union and a peace not entangled in deceitful tricks. William, however, so that he might conceal nothing from the united provinces, informed them of this matter and advised that envoys be sent to him quickly and then on to Ghent. Hesitation in this business was suspicious, since nature herself, the best guide of mortals, drew them towards it. The united provinces could make honourable and useful terms of union, since the Council of State was inclined to concord and the royal army was entangled in mutiny. He did not doubt that this assembly of the nobles would bring glory to the divine name and security to the provinces. But he warned them to think of war while they were busy with the business of peace, for carelessness had always harmed an unstable power. Thus at the Breda assembly they had been secure and relying on their own confidence, and had been exposed to great dangers. Lazy counsels must be corrected, and no trust placed in an enemy who wishes war under the shadow of peace. He further urged the united provinces to incite the Frisians and their other neighbours, who were still obeying the harsher commands of the governors, to overthrow the supports of foreign domination, and to bind to themselves by new alliances a people eager for liberty.

units.la: Itaque Fœderatorum Legati ad xiv. Kal. Novemb. diem Gandavum perrexere, exceptique magnâ comitate à cæterarum provinciarum Legatis è primoribus hunc in modum differentem audivere.
units.tr: Accordingly the envoys of the united provinces went to Ghent on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of November, and were received with great courtesy by the envoys of the other provinces, chiefly the nobles. They heard the speaker, who addressed them in this manner.

units.la: Miseriis nostris, LEGATI, ut sæpe modum, ita finem popo-scimus. Cæterum remedia quæ nostris malis debebantur, aulæ moribus protracta aut per improborum artes intercepta manserunt. Longiores moras ferre nostra imbecillitas non potest, postquam ut in impuro morbidoque corpore mala ex malis increvere. Partium armis tot annis attritos ipsa etiam præsidia seditiosæ legiones consumunt. Sic sacramenta, quæ tutelæ & incolumitati nostræ Hispanus miles dixerat, nostro exitio usurpat. Vastatis Trajecto & Antverpiâ civitatibus Scaldim atque Mosam flumina nostro sanguine infecit. Itaque adversum conflugem istam arma decrevimus, delectibus provincias munivimus. Unum tantum restat ut in Fœdus coëamus. Inde Bredano conventu de exturbandis peregrinis copijs & convocandis provinciarum Ordinibus eorumve Legatis consultavimus, quo Philippo regi ditiones suas, nobis religionem & patriam, utrique quietam daremus. Cæterum conventus iste inquietudine & contumacia illorum tum diremptus, qui nullâ cadentis patriæ miseratione pati & ferre extrema, quam insurgere adversum vim & injuriam
units.tr: Our miseries, envoys, as we have often asked for a limit, so we now ask for an end. But the remedies which our evils required have been dragged out by the customs of the court, or intercepted by the arts of the wicked. Our weakness cannot bear longer delays, since evils have grown upon evils, as in an impure and sickly body. Worn down for so many years by the arms of factions, we are now consumed even by the garrisons, the seditious legions. Thus the oaths which the Spanish soldier swore for our protection and safety, he now turns to our destruction. With the cities of Utrecht and Antwerp laid waste, the rivers Scheldt and Meuse have been stained with our blood. Therefore we have resolved to take up arms against this rabble, and have fortified the provinces with levies. Only one thing remains: that we unite in a Union. For this reason we consulted at the Breda assembly about driving out the foreign troops and summoning the orders of the provinces, or their envoys, so that we might give King Philip his dominions, and ourselves our religion and country, and each of them peace. But that assembly was broken up by the restlessness and obstinacy of those who, without any pity for their falling homeland, preferred to endure and bear extreme evils rather than rise against violence and injustice

units.la: juriam dominantium malebant. Nunc vero quoniam seditiosis Hispanorum legionibus bellum indiximus & convocandos provinciarum Ordines censemus, hoc agamus Legati, ut reperito Bredani conventus negotio mutuâ concordiâ jungamur. Solum illud adversum omne insolens munimentum. Nos mandata nostra, quae P H I L I P P I Regis nomine gerimus, nos officia nostra pollicemur, daturi omnem operam ut ex civili bello domesticam pacem seramus. Rogamus interim magnum illud & coeleste numen, ut nostro conventui & institutae actioni praesit.
units.tr: of their rulers. Now, since we have declared war on the seditious legions of the Spaniards, and think that the orders of the provinces should be summoned, let us, envoys, see to it that, having found the business of the Breda assembly, we are joined by mutual concord. This alone is a strong defence against every insolent force. We pledge our mandates, which we bear in the name of King Philip, and our duties, and we will take every care to sow domestic peace out of this civil war. Meanwhile we pray to that great and heavenly power to preside over our assembly and over the course we have undertaken.

units.la: Ad ea Foederatorum LEGATI.
units.tr: The Dutch envoys' reply.

units.la: Infœlicis belli diu pertæsi pacem jam ante ex Bredano colloquio praeconceperamus. Cæterum nec illud beneficium divinitus aut fato accipere, nec nostris consultationibus impetrare potuimus, etsi æquissima quaeque nostris in pacem desideriis obtenderemus. Nunc vero jussi sumus ex formulâ mandatorum nostrorum ijsdem postulatis & conditionibus insistere nostraque consilia sanciendae omnino paci adaequare. Itaque nec elabi occasionem nostris votis sinemus, ne videamur ore tenus pacis studia professi animos habere à communis concordiae curâ alienos.
units.tr: We had long been weary of the unhappy war, and had already conceived hopes of peace from the earlier conference at Breda. Yet we could obtain that blessing neither from God nor from fate, nor by our own deliberations, although we put forward every most equitable demand in the cause of peace. Now, however, we have been ordered, according to the form of our instructions, to hold to the same demands and conditions and to shape our plans to the sanctioning of peace. Therefore we will not let the opportunity slip away from our wishes, lest we seem to have professed a zeal for peace in words only while harbouring minds estranged from the concern for common concord.

units.la: Tum fiduciarijs litteris tabulisque mandatorum recitatis, armistitium decretum.
units.tr: Then the letters of credence and the tables of instructions were read out, and an armistice was decreed.

units.la: Inter Legatos vero Ordinum Generalium Joannes Lindanus Antistes D. Gertrudis apud Lovanienses, Giftenius Antistes D. Petri Gandavi, Matthæus Abbas D. Gislenij, Episcopus Attrebas, Joannes Mollius, Franciscus Halevinus, Carolus Gaverus Equestris Ordinis, Elbertus Leoninus Jureconsultus & LL. Professor, Petrus Beverius Consiliarius Flandriae, Quintinus Pratius Scabinus Bergensis, & Joannes Pennantius à Secretis fuere.
units.tr: Among the envoys of the General Estates were Joannes Lindanus, provost of St Gertrude at Louvain; Giftenius, provost of St Peter at Ghent; Matthaeus, abbot of Saint-Ghislain and bishop of Arras; Joannes Mollius; Franciscus Halevinus; Carolus Gaverus of the equestrian order; Elbertus Leoninus, jurist and professor of law; Petrus Beverius, councillor of Flanders; Quintinus Pratius, alderman of Bergen; and Joannes Pennantius, secretary.

units.la: Principis vero, & Foederatorum nomine, Philippus Marnixius SanctAldegondius, Arnoldus Dorpius, Gulielmus Zulenius Armigeri; Adrianus Mylius, & Cornelius Coninxius Principis Consiliarij, Paulus Busius Advocatus Hollandiae, Petrus Rijckius Praetor Vlissinganus, Antonius Sikelius Consiliarius Zelandiae, & Andreas Junius Consul Middelburgensis erant.
units.tr: On behalf of the Prince and the Confederates were Philippus Marnixius of Sint-Aldegonde, Arnoldus Dorpius, and Gulielmus Zulenius, esquires; Adrianus Mylius and Cornelius Coninxius, councillors of the Prince; Paulus Busius, advocate of Holland; Petrus Rijckius, praetor of Vlissingen; Antonius Sikelius, councillor of Zeeland; and Andreas Junius, consul of Middelburg.

units.la: Qui paucorum dierum conventu acto, ne quid mora damni aut ulterioris incommodi daret rebus per provincias lubricis & soluta legionum disciplinâ, v r. Eid Nov. foedus icere, praecipitatis haud dubie magnarum rerum deliberationibus, quod direptam & exustam ab Hispano praesidio Antverpiam non inueri rumores nuntiarent. Mihi verisimile est progressio jam Luxemburgum Joanne Austriaco & Philippi fratre notho, Legatos negotium maturasse, ne forte novus Princeps pro Philippo imperium adeptus suaeque gloriae & fortunae nimium indulgens acta Ordinum & simul consilia ineundi Foederis subverteret.
units.tr: After a conference of a few days, lest any delay bring further loss or harm to affairs, which were unstable across the provinces and with the discipline of the legions relaxed, they concluded the covenant on the 5th of November, no doubt having hurried their deliberations on great matters, since reports were coming in that Antwerp had been plundered and burnt by the Spanish garrison. It seems to me likely that the envoys hastened the business because John of Austria had already advanced to Luxembourg, together with Philip's bastard brother, and they feared that the new prince, having obtained power in Philip's place and indulging too much in his own glory and fortune, might overturn the acts of the Estates and at the same time the plans for forming the covenant.

units.la: Notant Scriptores, eo ipso Hispanici furoris per Antverpiam die (quem in priduanum Nonarum Novemb. diem incidisse Staurius Scriptor refert.) Joannem Austriacum Luxemburgum advenisse funestisque auspicijs damnatâ luce provinciarum fines ingressum, infœlicis imperij triste praesagium edidisse. Ego existumo, quod regio comitatu, dissimusimulato nomine celerrimo itinere processerit, eum clandestinis quæ ferebat consilijs & brevissimæ dominationi non incertum omen attulisse. Quare prodigioso coëuntium procerum assensu leges Fœderi scriptæ. Iis cautum fuit.
units.tr: Writers note that on the very day of the Spanish fury at Antwerp (which the writer Staurius reports fell on the day before the Nones of November), John of Austria came to Luxembourg, and entering the provinces on an ill-omened and doomed day, gave a sad omen of his unhappy rule. I think that, having travelled with royal retinue and with his name concealed, he went by the swiftest route, and that his secret plans and his very brief dominion were not without a portent. Therefore, with the remarkable assent of the assembled nobles, the articles of the covenant were drawn up. These provided as follows.

units.la: Ut omnium offensionum injuriarumque, quæ ex turbis Belgicis ortæ forent, oblivio esset. Fœdus utrinque sartum tectum maneret exterminandisque omni provinciâ Hispanis caterisque nationibus mutuo auxilia & tributa præstarentur. Ordinum generalium post ejectos provincijs peregrinos conventus haberetur, quo de publicis privatisque rebus, negotio Religionis, restitutione locorum, arcium ac commeatuum disponant. Commercia per provincias tuta atque libera forent & ne vis aut injuria cuiquam è professione Catholicæ Romanæ Religionis sub pænâ violatæ pacis publicæ fieret. Edicta Religionis ab Albano publicata tamdiu cessarent donec Ordines Generales de ijs statuerent. Aurantius Princeps maris, tum Hollandiæ Zelandiæque ac sociarum ditionum Præfecturam teneret nihilque innovaret, præterquam assensu Magistratuum & priusquam de Consilio Ordinum aliter decernentur. Cetera per Hollandiam Zelandiamque urbes Aurantij adhuc imperio exemptæ tam diu sui juris essent dum ex pacto Fœderi se sociaßent. Captivi utrinque & in ijs Comes Bossuvius nullo lytro, cæterum persolutis impensis dimitterentur. Edicta mandataque per Aurantium Principem, eius Senatum aut Magistratum ederentur approbarenturque, salvâ tamen magni Senatus authoritate, quem Rex daturus esset. Aurantius quoque, Nobilitas, privati in possessionem suorum bonorum mitterentur rescinderenturque acta confiscationum ex causa religionis aut armorum nata. Idem beneficij Electoris Palatini ad Rhenum canjugi Brederodij viduæ quoad urbem Vianam aliaque bona esset. Burano Comiti urbs, Castellum, agri deducto præsidio redderentur. Trophæa, statuæ, inscriptiones ab Albano erectæ, raderentur aut solo æquarentur. Vectigalia, portoria, decimæ, census, reditus non soluti, intercepti aut à D. Joannis festo proxumo infiscum illati, dominis aut cessionarijs cederent omnesque & singuli æstimatione damni dati singulas per provincias facta, bonis suis liberè fruerentur. Donationes mortis causâ aut inter vivos præteritis aut exclusis suis hæredibus ex causa Religionis & turbarum factæ, nullæ & inritæ forent. Signati æris idem per provincias valor, stabiliendo fœderi & mutuis commercijs esset. De duarum expeditionum impendijs & ære alieno per Aurantium conflato Ordines Generales decernerent. Provinciæ quæ in partibus adversis ab hoc fœdere tamdiu excluderentur, dum ei se junxissent. Fœderis tabulæ utrinque intra mensem proxumum subscriptione ac juramento firmarentur.
units.tr: That there should be oblivion of all offences and injuries arising from the Belgian troubles. That the covenant should remain whole and intact on both sides, and that mutual aid and tributes should be furnished for the expulsion of the Spaniards and other foreign nations from every province. That after the foreigners were driven out of the provinces, a meeting of the General Estates should be held, at which they might settle public and private affairs, the matter of religion, the restoration of places, fortresses and supplies. That trade throughout the provinces should be safe and free, and that no violence or injury should be done to anyone of the profession of the Roman Catholic religion, under penalty of breaking the public peace. That the edicts on religion published by Alba should cease for as long as the General Estates had not decided about them. That William, Prince of Orange, should hold the command of the sea, and of Holland, Zeeland and the allied territories, and should make no innovation except with the assent of the magistrates, and before the General Estates had decided otherwise. That the other towns of Holland and Zeeland, still exempt from the rule of Orange, should remain under their own right as long as they had not joined the covenant by its terms. That prisoners on both sides, and among them Count Bossu, should be released without ransom, the expenses however being paid. That edicts and mandates issued by Prince William, his Senate or magistrates, should be published and approved, saving however the authority of the great Senate which the King would appoint. That Orange also, and the nobility and private persons, should be restored to possession of their goods, and that the acts of confiscation arising from cause of religion or arms should be annulled. The same benefit should extend to the wife of Brederode, widow, at the Rhine, with respect to the town of Vianen and her other goods. To Count Buren the town, the castle and the fields should be restored, the garrison being withdrawn. Trophies, statues and inscriptions erected by Alba should be razed or levelled with the ground. Taxes, customs, tithes, rents and revenues not paid, intercepted, or carried into the treasury since the next feast of St John, should pass to the owners or assignees, and each and every person should enjoy their goods freely, with compensation for damage done in each province. Gifts made in view of death, or between the living, to the disadvantage or exclusion of lawful heirs on account of religion and the troubles, should be null and void. The value of the coinage should be the same throughout the provinces, to stabilise the covenant and mutual commerce. The General Estates should decide on the expenses of the two expeditions and on the debt contracted by Orange. Provinces which were on the opposing side should be excluded from this covenant until they had joined it. The articles of the covenant should be confirmed on both sides within the next month by signature and oath.

units.la: Quæ cæteras per provincias olim Burgundicæ domui parentes, decreta aut approbata, solos Frisios & Trans-Rhenum (Germaniæ ac Belgicæ limitem) sitas rationes non obligavere. Offerente velut fato, ut jure ac situ discretas gentes conditio adhuc temporum eximeret populusque per factiones & intestina arma, Principis imperio etsi deferentium vitio obstrictus, neglectis ulterioribus, quas jam ante Carolo Cæsare reprobaverat, cum Belgica gente pactionibus antiquæ libertati excusso per arma servitio redderetur. Etsi credam quoque fuisse, quos reverentia aut metus Philippi ab ineundâ societate deterruerit, frequentibus in consessu Ordinum Pontificijs, qui innovari statum provinciæ, damno cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXVI. damno ac infamiâ regiæ domus indignabantur. Quippe plurimùs per oppida ac agros regius miles, valida Senatus autoritas, foris multitudo Exulum novandis rebus obstabant. Econtra minæ ac terrores, tum Senatus Edictis Philippi nomen præfixum instabile Roblesij imperium & lubricam populi fidem tuebantur. Quæ quoniam nec ipse Roblesius ignorabat, ita senescentem & mox occasuram dominationem violentis consilijs emuniebat.
units.tr: The decrees or approvals which formerly bound the other provinces, once subject to the house of Burgundy, did not bind only the Frisians and the lands beyond the Rhine (the boundary of Germany and Belgium). It was as though fate offered that the present condition of the times should free peoples separated by law and situation, and that a people bound to the rule of the Prince through factions and internal arms, though through the fault of those who offered it, should, with later matters neglected, which Charles Caesar had already rejected, be restored by agreements with the Belgian nation to ancient liberty, the slavery having been shaken off by arms. Yet I believe there were also some whom reverence for or fear of Philip deterred from entering the alliance, since in the assembly of the Estates there were many papists, who were indignant that the state of the province should be altered to the loss and infamy of the royal house in the year 1576. Indeed, the royal soldiery throughout the towns and fields, the strong authority of the Senate, and abroad the multitude of exiles stood in the way of renewing affairs. On the other hand, threats and terrors, and the name of Philip prefixed to the Senate's edicts, defended the unstable rule of Requesens and the wavering loyalty of the people. Since Requesens himself was not unaware of this, he fortified his ageing and soon-to-fall dominion with violent measures.

units.la: Reperio in epistolâ incerti autoris III. Eid. Novemb. ad Martinum Nitzenium datâ, magna tum per Frisiam partium studia viguisse Deputatosque provinciæ, partim pro Roblesio & Senatu stantes, partim sacramento fœderis clam tractos discordibus consilijs egisse. Unde divisa & fluctuans Nobilitas, populus dubius atque discors erat, donec vertente ut omnia solet regiam dominationem fortunâ Gaspari Roblesij asperitas fatalibus rerum mutationibus obtenderetur. Quippe populum gravissimis Edictis aggressus, militem nova sacramenta popolcit, quo animos à Concilio Status alienaret præsidijsque civitatum ad stabiliendam potentiam uteretur.
units.tr: I find in a letter of an unknown author, dated the 11th of November to Martin Nitzenius, that at that time the parties in Friesland were strong, and that the deputies of the province, some standing for Requesens and the Senate, others secretly drawn to the covenant by oath, acted with conflicting plans. Hence the nobility was divided and wavering, and the people uncertain and discordant, until, as fortune usually turns against royal rule, the harshness of Gaspar Requesens was exposed to fatal changes in affairs. Indeed, he attacked the people with the most severe edicts and bound the soldiers by new oaths, so as to estrange their minds from the Council of State and to use the garrisons of the cities to secure his power.

units.la: Jam enim Gandavensi fœdere icto, & peregrinâ gente excedere finibus jussa, suæ Legioni & simul imperio metuebat, ac ut florentissimarum ditionum intra Amasum & Flevum flumina Præfecturam adeptus tantâ fœlicitate fortunæ & possessione rerum exturbaretur. Iraj; relictâ Leovardiâ ordinatisque per Frisiam rebus in Translavicanos ac mox Groningam profectus est quo civitatem validam & multo opere ac castello regio munitam suis partibus adjiceret. Jam enim imminere isti urbi Concilium Status dicebatur, misso in Translavicanos Francisco Martinio Stella viro erudito & sagaci, qui querimonijs Translavicani populi mederetur animosque mobiles ac Roblesiani dominatus pertæsos, sacramentis Ordinum & societati Fœderis innecteret. Roblesius vero, etsi durioribus per Frisiam ac Translavicanos rebus decreto Concilij Status abstinere jussus esset, ita progressum fœderis omni conatu remorabatur. Quare Franciscum Martinium Stellam Legatum vinculis dedit asservatumque à Legionarijs suis, quo secretum Legationis extorqueret quæstioni subjecit. Cæterum Martinius, etsi violari jus atque autoritatem Concilij Status quereretur, ita tormenta interritus pertulit orisque facundiâ & tam tristis spectaculi miseratione militum animos inflexit.
units.tr: For already, once the Ghent covenant had been struck, and foreign nation ordered to leave the borders, he feared for his legion and at the same time for his rule, and so that he, having obtained the command within the Ems and the Vlie rivers over the most flourishing territories, might not be thrown out of such great good fortune and possession of affairs. Hastily leaving Leeuwarden and having set affairs in order throughout Friesland, he set out for the Translauwers, and soon for Groningen, in order to add to his party the strong city, fortified with much work and a royal castle. For it was said that the Council of State was about to threaten that city, having sent to the Translauwers Francisco Martinius Stella, a learned and shrewd man, who was to remedy the complaints of the Translauwer people and bind their restless spirits, weary of Requesens's rule, by the oaths of the Estates and the fellowship of the covenant. Requesens, however, although he had been ordered by the decree of the Council of State to refrain from harsher measures in Friesland and among the Translauwers, hindered the progress of the covenant with every effort. Therefore he threw Francisco Martinius Stella, the envoy, into chains, and, having him guarded by his own legionaries, put him to torture to extract the secret of his mission. Martinius, however, although he complained that the right and authority of the Council of State were being violated, bore the torments undaunted, and by the eloquence of his speech and the pity of so sad a spectacle he moved the minds of the soldiers.

units.la: Non enim jure privati ingressum se provinciam ajebat, caterum mandata Concilij Status perferentem regiæ mentis & voluntatis executorem esse. Sic Concilio Status summam rerum à Philippo commissam, donec interregni tempus effl ueret provinciarumque moderamen regij sanguinis Principi obvenisset. Esse potestatis Ordinum aut Concilij lubricis temporibus & illo legionum furore urbes dubias & cum rep. nutantes regiæ fidei afferere. Fore alias, ut exercitam alibi terrarum ab Hispanis insolentiam Translavicani quoque sentiant, imperium Philippi durante bello & tot annis amplexi. Præcavendum esse ut provinciæ securitas, urbi Groningæ quies, populo concordia, militi stipendium sit, sine quo nec leges bellum, nec commeatum aut annonam exercitus habeat. Ita spectarent Hispanicas & Germaniæ legiones provinciis & regi graves, nullo duce, nullis tribunorum imperijs regi, caterum perfidas & viles animas solis scelerum nutrimentis pascere_. Impurum legionum corpus separandum ab integro fuisse, quod cIↄ. Iɔ. mandatis Ordinum, aut Concilij status se permittens, stipendia subsidia vita LXXVI. & militiæ præmia, ex se ipse decus atque gloriam habiturum esset.
units.tr: He said that he had entered the province not by private right but as the executor of the king's will and command, carrying out the orders of the Council of State. Philip had entrusted the supreme direction of affairs to the Council of State until the interregnum should pass and the government of the provinces should fall to a prince of royal blood. In such slippery times, and with that fury of the legions, it was for the authority of the Estates or of the Council to bring doubtful cities, which were wavering in their loyalty, back to royal allegiance. Otherwise the Translavians too would feel elsewhere the insolence the Spaniards practised, having embraced Philip's rule during the war and for so many years. Care must be taken that the province was secure, the city of Groningen quiet, the people in harmony, and the soldier paid, since without pay neither laws nor war, nor supplies and provisions, could be had by an army. Thus the Spanish and German legions would be seen as burdensome to the provinces and to the king, ruled by no leader and no tribunes' commands, but as faithless and base souls feeding only on the nourishment of crimes. The foul body of the legions should have been separated from the sound one, which, submitting itself to the orders of the Estates or of the Council of State, would have its pay, subsidies and life, and the rewards of military service, and would of itself have honour and glory.

units.la: Quæ omnia Stellam Legatum advocato obligandis vulneribus, quæ à Roblesij manu acceperat distortique corporis lacerationibus Medico, Græcâ voce aperuisse autores tradunt ipsumque medicum ægri misertum, specie artis, uni centurionum Losio militique ad custodiam legati destinato, tanquam obsignandum fide arcanum commisisse. Creditum fuit spe stipendiorum & residui aeris per Legatum Martinium facta, plurimos mox militum in partem Ordinum inclinasse alienosque à Roblesio, quod nec opes, nec aerarium assignandis stipendijs haberet, efficacissimo devinciendis mentibus remedio victos, liberandi Martinij consilium coepisse. Septuaginta in partibus fuisse autores tradunt. Quare Roblesius defectionem clam metuens, jurare in verba sua militem præcepit decimumque Kal. Decemb. diem isti negotio destinavit. Itaque omni præsidio in fanum Martino sacrum, si forte loci religione commoveret, convocato, pro concione sic locutus est.
units.tr: Authors report that when Stella the legate had summoned a doctor to bind the wounds he had received from Robles' hand and to treat the lacerations of his twisted body, he revealed the secret to the doctor in Greek speech. The doctor, pitying the sick man, under the pretext of his art, entrusted the secret, as if to be sealed in good faith, to one centurion, Losius, and to a soldier assigned to guard the legate. It was believed that, through hope of pay and of the remaining money promised by the legate Martinius, many soldiers soon inclined to the side of the Estates and turned away from Robles, who had neither wealth nor a treasury to assign pay. Overcome by this most effective remedy for binding minds, they began to plan the liberation of Martinius. Authors report that the Seventy were among the conspirators. Therefore Robles, secretly fearing defection, ordered the soldiers to swear to his words, and appointed the tenth day before the Kalends of December for the business. So, having gathered all the guard in the temple sacred to Martin, in case the sanctity of the place might move them, he spoke to them in an address as follows.

units.la: NON adsum, Commilitones, multa verba apud vos facturus. Caeterum non levibus periculis compulsus ad concionem vos voco, postquam experior Ordines provinciarum omne imperium ad se trahere, ac res novas moliri, connivente Concilio Status, quod REQUESENTIO Proregi à Philippo rege suffectum, rerum ordinem distorquet. Vos vero scitote, Commilitones, eosdem Ordines speciosis promissis me hortatos, ut sacramentum mutarem defisceremque cum Legione. A quo consilio cum abssim longius, non celo vos arcanum, censeoque è re Philippi regis & simul vestra esse, ut infidis temporibus novum mihi sacramentum dicatis, dum ex Hispania percepero, quid PHILIPPUS Rex fieri velit. Neque enim momenta rerum, sine vobis geri possunt necessumque omnino est, ut vos regi fidos frequentesque sub signis habeam, ac ab Ordinum societate ac imperio alienos. Quod si meo æquius sanctiusque nonnullis vestrum videbitur, Commilitones, ijs suadeo hortorque ut secessionem faciant, signisque se subducant.
units.tr: I am not here, comrades, to make many words with you. But I have been driven by no slight dangers to call you to this assembly, since I find that the Estates are drawing all authority to themselves and attempting new things, while the Council of State, which was set over affairs by King Philip in place of the Governor Requesens, connives at it and distorts the order of affairs. But know this, comrades: the same Estates have urged me with specious promises to change my oath and to desert with the legion. I am far from that plan, and I do not hide from you my secret: I judge it to be for the interest of King Philip and at the same time for yours, that in these faithless times you swear a new oath to me, until I learn from Spain what King Philip wishes to be done. For the turning of affairs cannot be carried on without you, and it is absolutely necessary that I keep you, faithful to the king and in large numbers, under the standards, and estranged from the fellowship and authority of the Estates. But if to some of you my course seems fairer and holier, comrades, I advise and urge them to withdraw and to leave the standards.

units.la: Itaque tum stante concione prorupit, qui fandi veniâ à Roblesio impetratâ, exclamaret PRO SALUTE ET INCOLUMITATE ORDINUM VIVERE SE AUT MORI CONSTITUISSE.
units.tr: So, while the assembly was still standing, someone burst forth who, having obtained from Robles permission to speak, cried out: "WE HAVE RESOLVED TO LIVE OR DIE FOR THE SAFETY AND WELFARE OF THE ESTATES."

units.la: Thuanus refert Galterum quendam nomine subscribere formulae jurisjurandi jussum, calamum in ignem adstante Roblesio conjecisse suosque commilitones dubios & inclinantes praeclaro constantiae & libertatis exemplo ad detrectandam servilis juramenti pactionem incitasse. Qui etsi missione accepta urbe ejiceretur, nihilominus subsecutae mutationi pondus attulit militemque ultro turbidum & ancipitem suo exemplo instigavit.
units.tr: Thuanus relates that a certain man named Galterus, ordered to sign the formula of the oath, threw his pen into the fire while Robles stood by. By this splendid example of constancy and liberty he incited his doubting and wavering comrades to refuse the servile oath. Although he was dismissed with his discharge and expelled from the city, he nevertheless contributed weight to the change that followed, and by his example spurred on a soldiery already turbulent and wavering.

units.la: Ex eo namque factum est, ut Losius cohortis tribunus novam sacramenti dictionem abnueret ipsoque Roblesio coram, novennale ad sacramentum Philippo regi praestitum egregio virtutis documento provocaret. Igitur Tribuno cohortis & mox manipularibus novam militiae religionem aspernantibus Losianorum defectio secuta. Unde Roblesius sius multâ jam ante comminatione adversum detrectantes usus, tres cohortes Lopesij, Monceavij, & Campij, qui jam in verba ejus juraverant, per insidias disposuit delendaeque Losianae cohorti mandatum dedit. Quare multitudine minutarum glandium compleri machinas fecit, ac ut dato signo disploderentur, imperavit. Caeterum Losius perceptis insidijs alia via cohortem ad forum duxit, ubi stare praesidio destituta nocturnis vigilijs cohors consueverat. Quae contractis mox in principia Ordinibus cum salutare Roblesium è fenestrâ Alberdanae domus prospectantem juberetur, haud leni murmure formatisque in contumaciam vultibus latentem iracundiam exprimebat. Quare laxare bombardas jussa defectum pulveris & menstrui aeris obtendit percussoque per Antonium Sardam vigilium Praefectum gregario, justo & decreto furori indulsit.
units.tr: For from this it came about that Losius, tribune of the cohort, refused the new formula of the oath, and in Robles' presence appealed to the oath of nine years he had sworn to King Philip, as a splendid proof of virtue. Therefore, when the tribune of the cohort and soon the manipulars scorned the new military oath, the defection of the Losians followed. Whereupon Robles, who had already used threats against the refusers, secretly arranged three cohorts, those of Lopez, Monceaux and Campo, who had already sworn to his words, and gave them the commission to destroy the Losian cohort. He therefore had the machines filled with a multitude of small bullets and ordered them to be discharged when the signal was given. But Losius, having perceived the ambush, led his cohort by another route to the forum, where the cohort, deprived of its guard, had customarily stood its night watches. Then, the Estates having been gathered at headquarters, the soldiers were ordered to salute Robles, who was looking out from a window of the Alberda house; they showed their feelings with no light murmur, and with faces set in defiance they betrayed a hidden anger. Therefore, pretending a lack of powder and of money for the pay, he ordered the guns to be loosened; and when Antonio Sarda, prefect of the watch, was struck down by a common soldier, he gave way to a just and decreed fury.

units.la: Tum Roblesius glandibus petitus, mox ab irruentibus in Alberdanam domum cum Ruysbroeckio genero captus custodiaeque datus est. Unde Villerij cohors excubias agens, stationes deseruit nulloque ordine & catervatim in forum progressa Losianis se sociavit. Lopesius vero faciendae caedi & opprimendae Losianae cohorti à Roblesio destinatus secreto domus se abdidit cohortemque dimisit, quae concepto vexillo, quod tumultuanti militari turbae proprium, in manifestam quoque furoris publici professionem eruperat. Tum reliquae copiae adversâ Praefecti sui fortunâ partibus Ordinum se adjunxere, nihil proficientibus Roblesij promissis, quibus stipendia & omne residuum aequa spernentibus addicebat. Sunt qui tradant à gregario milite ferreas compedes Roblesio injectas eumque, solidae & gravi catenae alligatum inter centumelias & ludibria suorum primos carceris dies flagrantibus adhuc in illum odijs egisse.
