Ita eorum quos supplicio destinaverat lubidini atque insolentiae paruit versoque rerum ludo, quem omne inconstans & lubricum fortunae exercet, durius aequo imperium foedo servitio & suorum spectaculo mutavit. Ferunt auditam in publico vocem, VIVAT PRINCEPS, VIVANT ORDINES, qua mutatio haud dubie militarium animorum & surgentium rerum speciosa auspicia designabantur. Tribuni cohortium vinculis dati.
units.tr: Then Robles, targeted by the bullets, was soon seized by those who rushed into the Alberda house, together with his son-in-law Ruysbroeck, and was given into custody. Thereupon Villeri's cohort, which was on guard, deserted its posts and, without order and in bands, marched into the forum and joined the Losians. Lopez, however, who had been appointed by Robles to carry out the slaughter and crush the Losian cohort, hid himself secretly in a house and dismissed his cohort. That cohort, having raised a banner proper to a tumultuous military mob, burst out also into an open declaration of public madness. Then the remaining forces, the fortune of their prefect having been reversed, joined the side of the Estates, Robles' promises achieving nothing, by which he offered pay and all the remaining money to men who scorned fairness. Some report that a common soldier put iron fetters on Robles, and that, bound with solid and heavy chains, amid the insults and jeers of his own men, he spent the first days of his imprisonment while hatreds still blazed against him. Thus he obeyed the lust and insolence of those whom he had marked for punishment, and the game of fortune, which everything inconstant and slippery in fortune practises, turned: he changed a command harsher than was just into foul servitude and a spectacle for his own men. It is said that a voice was heard in public crying, "LONG LIVE THE PRINCE, LONG LIVE THE ESTATES", by which change, undoubtedly, the favourable omens of the military minds and of the rising affairs were foreshadowed. The tribunes of the cohorts were given over to chains.

units.la: Dein F. Martinium Stellam custodiâ liberatum armati coronâ cinxere expositisque quae vellent, in verba Ordinum juravere. Novis quoque centurionibus extemplo creatis cum Francisco Martinio Stella varijs de rebus consultatum cautumque Edicto, Ne quis de nocte in publico esset. Ita composito motu urbis imperatum silentium & quiescere milites jussi, quos in concordiam foederis cum populo & Senatu turbidi temporis discrimen adigebat. Tum Stella cum delectis militum Bruxellas contendit, quo de singulis ad Concilium Status referret novumque Praefectum Groningae urbi & Translavicano populo alienatis à Roblesio animis rogaret. Pacatâ urbe in conscios flagitij quaesitum. Itaque Christophorus Vasquius qui Zutphaniae cum imperio praerat, aliique cucullâ monachum mentiti & ab ijsdem ordinis hominibus detecti, cum Ferdinando Lopesio & Antonio Sarda vigilum Praefecto caeterisque, quos intempestiva severitas seditiosis cohortibus objecerat, milimilitaribus ludibrijs expositi. Eadem Georgij Westendorpij Senatoris cIↄ. Iↄ. per Frisiam Regij centurionumque quorundam fortuna fuit. Quippe LXXVI. Dammonenses praesidiarij comprehenso Starckio Delphzilani abducto Groningam Barnicurtio cohortium Tribunis, eadem lege usi, plane velut animorum militarium aestus per exempla ebulliens, omnes Valonicae legionies per Frisiam & vicina copias stato tempore pervaderet. Itaque & arcium praefecti, (quas Leovardiae, Harlingae & Stauriae Principes olim firmandae dominationi extruxerant) in partes Ordinum inclinavere, credentibus universis Philippi regis imperio ex sacramentis Ordinum non decedere.
units.tr: Then they freed Francis Martinius Stella from custody, surrounded him with armed men in a ring, and, having stated what they wanted, swore the oath to the Estates. Immediately, with the newly created centurions, they consulted with Francis Martinius Stella on various matters, and by edict provided that no one should be in public at night. Thus, by a calmed movement, silence was ordered in the city and the soldiers were bidden to be quiet, whom the peril of a turbulent time drove into concord with the people and Senate in the covenant. Then Stella hastened to Brussels with picked soldiers, to report on each matter to the Council of State and to ask for a new prefect for Groningen and the Translavian people, whose minds were now alienated from Robles. When the city was pacified, an inquiry was made into the accomplices of the crime. Therefore Christopher Vasquez, who commanded at Zutphen, and others who had pretended to be monks in hoods and were detected by men of that order, were exposed to military mockery, together with Ferdinand Lopez, Antonio Sarda, prefect of the watch, and the others whom untimely severity had assigned to the seditious cohorts. The same fate befell Georg Westendorp, senator and royal commissioner through Friesland, and certain centurions. Indeed, the garrison of Dam, having seized Starckius of Delfzijl, led Barnicurt to Groningen before the tribunes of the cohorts, using the same law; it was as if the heat of the soldiers' minds, boiling over by example, would at the appointed time spread through all the Walloon legions and the neighbouring troops in Friesland. And so the prefects of the citadels, which the princes had built at Leeuwarden, Harlingen and Stavoren to strengthen their rule, also inclined to the side of the Estates, all believing that by the Estates' oaths they would not depart from the command of King Philip.

units.la: Sic urbs Groninga, quae a quadraginta annis Carolum Caesarem protectorem suae libertati acceperat, post ab Albano & externarum gentium praesidijs presta & diu immodeste habita, Philippi regis nomine imperijs Ordinum Belgicae asserta. Unde in patrum consessu laeta omnia atque auspicata habebantur, gratulantibus sibi invicem provinciarum delegatis, fortunam surgentis reip. adversum inclementia fata & violentas dominationes emergentem lacertos quoque trans Rhenum & per confinia Imperij movisse. Quare grates cohortibus actae & stipendia decreta, quo egenae legiones & per omnem provinciam turbidae patrum officijs sanarentur. Subventum quoque annonae per Frisiam salutari lege, qua damnatis lege coemptionibus pretijs simul & penuriae frugum occurrebatur.
units.tr: Thus the city of Groningen, which for forty years had accepted Charles Caesar as protector of its liberty, was afterwards treated harshly and for a long time immoderately by Alva and by foreign garrisons. It was then reclaimed under the authority of the Orders of the Netherlands in the name of King Philip. Hence in the assembly of the Fathers everything was regarded as joyful and auspicious. The delegates of the provinces congratulated one another that the fortune of the rising commonwealth, emerging against harsh fates and violent domination, had also set its arms in motion across the Rhine and along the borders of the Empire. Therefore thanks were given to the cohorts and pay was decreed, so that the needy legions, and those unrest throughout the province, might be soothed by the good offices of the Fathers. Relief for the grain supply was also provided throughout Friesland by a salutary law, by which the purchase contracts were condemned, and both prices and the scarcity of grain were checked at once.

units.la: Mox mense Novembri comitium Leovardiae habitum, quo de pactis foederis apud Gandavum icti acribus controversijs disceptabatur. Erant qui censerent plausibili Concilij Status aut Ordinum imperio, quod & Philippus Rex approbaret, insurgendum esse adversum externam gentem seditionibus involutam communique concordia allevandam patriam tot enormia perpessam. Coïre vero aut jungi civiles animos non nisi recepto foedere posse, quod regium Philippi nomen & simul imaginem aeternae pacis praeferret. Satis cruoris humani & sanguinis fusum neque alia discordium intentione bellum gestum esse, quam ut pace clauderetur. Alij judicabant valido foedere regiae potentiae multum detrahi, nec eodem loco stare posse populi concordiam & vim dominantis. Parendum esse sine exceptione unius imperio & serendum ingenium Principis etiam distortum. Ejus jussu missam in Frisios Roblesij Legionem sacramentum adhuc regis profiteri, non ante exterminandam finibus, quam decreto Philippi militaris jurisjurandi religione soluta arma simul & vetus sacramentum posuisset. Id solum regio imperio praesidium restare, quo amoto obscurum jus Principis ex licentia populi futurum sit. Itaque publicatio tabularum Gandavensis foederis tum prolata, donec mutato sensim rerum statu, ingruentibus regiae parti adversis, animi quoque provincialium cum fortuna Philippi verterentur.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, in November, an assembly was held at Leeuwarden, where the terms of the covenant agreed at Ghent were disputed with fierce controversy. Some judged that by the popular authority of the Council of State or of the Orders, which King Philip himself would approve, they should rise against a foreign nation entangled in seditions, and that the country, having suffered so many outrages, should be relieved by common harmony. But they said that civil minds could not be united or joined except by accepting the covenant, which bore the royal name of Philip and at the same time the image of lasting peace. Enough human blood and gore had been shed, and the war had been waged with no other purpose of the discords than that it should be closed by peace. Others judged that by a strong covenant much would be taken away from royal power, and that the concord of the people and the power of the ruler could not stand in the same place. Obedience, they said, must be rendered without exception to the rule of one man, and the disposition of the prince must be endured even when twisted. At his command the legion of Robles had been sent into Friesland, still professing allegiance to the king, and would not be driven from the territory until, by a decree of Philip, it had laid down its arms together with the old oath, released from the bond of its military oath. This alone was the king's remaining protection, and once it was removed the uncertain right of the prince would depend on the license of the people. Therefore the publication of the tablets of the Ghent covenant was then postponed, until, as the state of affairs gradually changed and adversity pressed upon the royal party, the minds of the provincials too turned with the fortune of Philip.

units.la: Mox Roblesij quoq; conjunx Leovardiae in arce regia militum manipulis circumdata attinerib; publica custodia jussa, tori societate fortunae quoque maritalis consors fuit. Creditum fuit eam secretorum manriti, quibus extrema per provinciam stabiliendae adversum Ordines dominationi parare dicebatur, conscium muliebri fragilitate aut fastu incaucautius, an insolentius praeconcepta mariti consilia vulgasse. Tum Roblesio custodiae a suis dato per Frisiam quoque & praesidia urbium cohortium murmura & criminationes auditae quod interceptis diu stipendijs novum & grave sacramentum Roblesius & Tribuni cohortium proposuissent.
units.tr: Soon afterwards the wife of Robles also, at Leeuwarden, in the royal citadel surrounded by companies of soldiers, was ordered into public custody with the outbuildings, and shared the fortune of her husband as a partner in his marriage bed. It was believed that she, being privy to the secrets which were said to be prepared for the final establishment of domination over the Orders throughout the province, had been too careless either from feminine frailty or from pride, or too insolently, in disclosing her husband's plans conceived beforehand. Then, when Robles was given into custody by his own men, murmurs and accusations were also heard throughout Friesland and in the garrisons of the cities among the cohorts, because Robles and the tribunes of the cohorts had, after the pay had long been withheld, proposed a new and burdensome oath.

units.la: Unde Feuterius, qui cum cohorte legionis Valonicae praesidium Franequerae agebat, odijs quoque suorum expositus increscente sensim militum murmure ac inquietudine, donec de illo quoque coercendo a Roblesij captivitate cogitarent. Quare propriae Kalend. Decemb. septimâ vespertinâ exequi consilium decrevere, delecto e suis Petro Argio homine tenulento & ex hoc audaci, qui disploso sub noctem schlopetto telleram facinori daret. Ad cujus rei sonum cum Feuterius centurio Botnianâ arce quam occupaverat & velut invito domino possessurus in delitijs habebat, descenderet, ab occursantibus militibus comprehensus est. Ita evenit, ut cum disciplinam insolentissimo militi intentaret pateretur custodiam. Quare Regem & sacramentum obtestatus multa aucupandae militum suorum gratiae tentavit, aerique menstruo exsolvendo fidem depactus est.
units.tr: Hence Feuterius, who commanded the garrison at Franeker with a cohort of the Walloon legion, was also exposed to the hatred of his own men, as the murmuring and restlessness of the soldiers grew gradually. Finally they considered arresting him too, as they had Robles. Therefore they resolved to carry out the plan on the first of December, about the seventh hour of the evening. They chose from among their own number Peter Argius, a slender man and bold with it, who was to fire a pistol toward nightfall and give the signal for the deed. At the sound of it, when Feuterius, the centurion, came down from the castle of Botnia, which he had occupied and kept as his delight, as if about to possess it against its owner's will, he was seized by the soldiers who ran to meet him. So it happened that, while he was threatening discipline to the most insolent soldiers, he himself suffered custody. Therefore, calling on the king and the oath, he tried many means to win the favour of his soldiers, and he bound himself by promise to pay the monthly wages.

units.la: Caeterum miles, etsi regij sacramenti retinens esset, interversa diu stipendia criminabatur; animamque ac sanguinem suum fraude & peculatu extenuatum nutricatui centurionis cessisse. Ita fieri namque ut ipsi egestate atterantur videantque per sudores & vulnera paratam mercedem luxu praefectorum subverti. Itaque illos tanquam in pace otium & ignaviam sectantes militiae curas negligere modoque hortorum cultui, modo per commessationes & nocturnis amoribus fractos, sibi affluentiam opum, militi labores, vigilias, frigora & inediam relinquere. Inde Roblesio Tribuno Legionis suae manus injectas esseque ex usu idem illis accidere, qui ad exemplum Tribuni culpatos nares & effrenem licentiam ex strangulatis militum stipendijs formassent. Non posse se solos diuturnicem patientiam ferendae inopiae profiteri, Hispanorum & externarum gentium legionibus per omnem provinciam concitatis & per tot urbium spolia opulentis.
units.tr: Meanwhile the soldiers, although they still held to the royal oath, complained that their pay had been diverted for a long time. They said that their life and blood, worn down by fraud and embezzlement, had gone to nourish the centurion. For thus it came about that they themselves were worn away by poverty, and saw the wages won through their sweat and wounds overturned by the luxury of their commanders. So, they said, those officers, pursuing leisure and idleness as if in peacetime, neglected the cares of soldiering, and were broken now by the cultivation of gardens, now by drinking parties and nightly love affairs; they left to the soldiers the abundance of wealth for the officers, and labours, watches, cold and hunger for themselves. Hence, they said, the hands of the tribune of their legion had been laid upon them, and it was fitting that the same should happen to those who, after the example of the tribune, had grown fat with blame and unbridled license from the strangled pay of the soldiers. They could not alone profess that they would endure long-lasting patience in poverty, with the legions of Spaniards and foreign nations stirred up throughout the province and made rich by the plunder of so many cities.

units.la: Ita Feuterius in arcem Siardaeam validissimam, stipante militum praesidio ductus atrioque spatiocissimo habendis excubijs destinato, instar facinorosi habitus, alieno magis quam suo arbitrio, quadrimestrem custodiam traxit. Dein gregario milite in centurionem adoptato, quem Electum vocitabant & quem forma ac venustas, tum quam maxime militare ingenium commendabat, ulterioribus turbis parcitum intactoque direptionibus oppido, citra immodestiam sub imperio Electi & ex suo corpore creati centurionis egere. Caeterum Feuterio Martio mense, ut post memorabo, reliquis cum centurionibus in Geldriam abducto, novi iterum motus orti, quod Ordinum generalium decreto alium ab Electo centurionem constitutum praeceps fama afferret. Unde murmurare primum, mox ubi potu incaluere temulenti & Ordinum imperijs graves, de deferendis signis agitavere. Igitur a novo centurione, quem Ordines cohorti praefecerant, lasta cerevisiae in aream Siardeae arcis deportata, (quo is a cohorte turbida, sed per hilaritatem evicta fidem acciperet, simulque praestaret) in diversa milites dilapsi sacramentum renuerunt effractaque Doniaea porta, per agros sparsi, circa marinum aggerem extrema littorum oberravere. Post transfretatis æstuarijs, quæ lato Frisiam & objectas insulas interluunt, inermes & profugi excep- tis paucis, quos sacramentum Electo præstitum adhuc obstringebat, incerta sedium quæsivere regijsque copijs & simul sacramentis ascripti sub Joanne Austriaco ad Rimenantum cæsi deletique sunt. Is exitus tumultuantis & imperio abutentis apud Franequeranos præsidij fuit. Reliquis in locis, ut Leovardiæ & Doccomij eadem vitia, ijdem mores dubijs & inclinantibus præsidijs valuissent, nisi Ordinum Frisiæ sollicitudo desiderata stipendia è publicis tributis collato ære egeno & turbido militi procurasset.
units.tr: Thus Feuterius was led into the very strong citadel of Sneek, escorted by a guard of soldiers, and was held in a very spacious courtyard set aside for keeping watch. Treated as a criminal, more by the will of others than by his own, he endured four months of custody. Then, when a common soldier had been adopted as centurion, whom they called the Chosen One, and whom his looks and charm, and above all his military temper, recommended, the town was spared further disorder and left untouched by plunder. Under the command of the Chosen One, a centurion chosen from their own body, they lived without excess. But when Feuterius was led away to Gelderland in March, as I shall relate later, new disturbances arose, because a rumour rashly spread that by decree of the General Orders another centurion had been appointed in place of the Chosen One. Then they first began to murmur, and soon, when the drunken men were heated with drink and burdened by the commands of the Orders, they debated abandoning their standards. Therefore a barrel of beer was carried into the courtyard of the castle of Sneek by the new centurion, whom the Orders had set over the cohort, so that the turbulent cohort, won over by good cheer, might accept his authority and at the same time give its pledge. Instead the soldiers slipped away in different directions and refused the oath. Breaking through the Dongeradeel gate, scattered over the fields, they wandered near the sea dike to the outermost reaches of the shore. Afterwards they crossed the estuaries which wash broadly through Friesland and the islands lying before it. Unarmed and fugitive, except for a few who were still bound by the oath sworn to the Chosen One, they sought uncertain dwelling places. Then they were enrolled with the royal forces and at the same time under the oath to John of Austria, and were cut down and destroyed at Rinnemant. This was the end of the garrison at Franeker, which had been stirring up trouble and abusing its command. In the other places, as at Leeuwarden and Dokkum, the same faults and the same habits would have prevailed among the wavering and hesitant garrisons, had not the care of the Orders of Friesland procured the wanted pay from public taxes, the money being collected to relieve the needy and restless soldiers.

units.la: Famâ ferunt omnem militarium per Frisios & Translavicanos seditionum causam, à suspectis Roblesij moribus originem traxisse, quod non habita militum æquâ ratione, plus severo imperio quam studijs suorum tribuerit. Alij Scriptores addunt stipendijs militaribus gravem & fraudis suspectum in odia incurrisse, indignantibus cohortium turbulentissimis, in unâ Roblesij domo superbiam Præfecti & avaritiam uxoris, lacessendis seditionibus concurrere. Id vero unum Roblesij laudibus quidam dedêre, quod illâ rerum tempestate medium se partibus gesserit regisque gratiæ & simul provincialium commodis studens, alienum animum & ab imminuendo regis jure & simul direptionibus civitatum habuerit. Sed multa talium imperitis nostrarum rerum Scriptoribus memorata, dissimulatis aut ignoratis rationibus, an Roblesium dominationis palam avidum & insolentem, reverens populi animus ab extremis consilijs, an impotentia virium deteruerit.
units.tr: Report has it that the whole cause of the mutinies among the soldiers in Friesland and across the Lauwers arose from the suspected conduct of Robles, because, without an even-handed regard for the soldiers, he gave more to harsh command than to the goodwill of his own men. Other writers add that, as the military pay was withheld, he fell into grave hatred and suspicion of fraud, and that in the single house of Robles the arrogance of the commander and the avarice of his wife, by provoking the most turbulent cohorts, combined to stir up sedition. Some, indeed, have praised Robles for this alone: that in that stormy time he held the middle course between the parties, seeking both the king's favour and the advantage of the provincials, and that he had no mind either to diminish the royal right or to plunder the cities. But many such things have been recorded by writers unskilled in our affairs, with their reasons either ignored or passed over, and whether Robles, openly greedy and insolent in domination, was turned aside from extreme measures by the respectful spirit of the people, or by the weakness of his forces, is not clear.

units.la: Siquidem speciosum populo Concilij Status imperium, gratam novi fœderis sanctionem reputabat animosque provincialium tanto magis ab imperij sui ratione averses, quanto acriora desideria reparandæ libertati obtenderentur. Sic invito populo etsi provinciæ bono sumptuosum aggerem erectum, introducta Vectigalia & collationes, dein tributa pro magnitudine opum imperasse, haud dubiè alienandis mentibus, quas apud bonos libertatis amor, apud inquietos licentiæ cupido occuparet. Inhærere adhuc recentum ingenijs severi imperij memoriam neq; laturos provinciales, ut asperis decretis quod gravius accedat acreque imperium inclinante dominatione inter exile præsidium intendatur. Adhæc militem stipendio placandum, quod non ex ærario, ut alias apud gentes, sed quasi per stipes domatim & quidem cum difficultate apud populum peteretur, tot sæculorum libertati suetum & pro jure majorum stantem. Itaque multa extquendis extremis subsidia deesse, quæ ne tum quidem parari queant, si solitudo populi, si locorum Vastitas fiat. Florentibus provincijs haberi tributa præsidia imperij posse. Sin vero agros ac oppida furor militum populetur, plerdendis rebus præceps, non renasci bello & regiæ magnitudini servitura. Disciplina omnia stare, nisi rectore coërceantur ultro fluitura facilè dilabi. Denique diu provinciæ adversa obvenisse ac præter civilium armorum tempestatem mare insolitos per æstus quotannis recrudescens privatas opes exhausisse. Posse gentem bello & injurijs cœli ac maris lacessitam, adhuc ultro mobilem ad graviora compelli si irritetur, ituram per vestigia majorum, qui acriora principum imperia rejecta servitute depulissent. Extare non obscura antiquæ virtutis monumenta populumque tot acta Cæsarum & imagines veteris gloriæ ostentantem deprimi non nisi per spatia temporum posse, & si oblivione juris, ac prinprincipis dominatum ferendo & odia præsentium & veterum memoriam excusserit. Itaque libertatis umbrâ velandum servitium, quod frustra intentes, nisi aut major vis in proximo aut depressius obsequium sit. Posterius sperari moto populo non posse & eam rationem æraríj non esse, ut evocandis in provinciam pluribus legionibus respondeat. Vbivis omnia angusta esse & cum stipendia non procedant nasci insolentiam. •Ita fieri, direptis provincialium rebus autoritas Ducum minuatur licentia militum increscat. Cui etsi aliquid dari merito posset, ob immanitatem criminis & fædissimæ in regem rebellionis tamen expendenda temporum momenta esse, ne quid crudis rebus fiat & ne consilia eventu dubia pro certis habeantur. Fortunæ humana volutantis ancebs regnum esse, quæ res etiam prudenter & bono regis excogitatas intervertere queat. Præesse vicinis provinciis Aurantium, catum Principem, subministraturum arma & consilia, si viderit Frisiorum nationem adhuc regis nomen & sacramenta præferentem, ac à Gandavensi fœdere secretum durius habere præfectoque regundis provinciis Belgici Status Concilio, Albanæ feritatis exempla recrudescere. Exspectandas potius rerum occasiones esse, quas Austriaci jam imperio destinati successio promitteret, haud dubie facturi, ut præstractum & imperia respuentem populum mole armorum & quidem cum indulgentia militaris licentiæ domet.
units.tr: For the rule of the Council of State seemed pleasing to the people, and the new covenant seemed a welcome sanction; and the minds of the provincials were turned all the more away from the method of his rule, the sharper the longings for restoring liberty were held out. Thus, although the mound had been raised at great expense for the good of the province, against the will of the people, and tolls and levies had been introduced, and then taxes were imposed according to the size of their wealth, this undoubtedly alienated the minds which love of liberty held among the good, and desire for license seized among the restless. The memory of harsh rule still clings to the dispositions of the recent past, and the provincials will not bear that, when the decrees are harsh, something graver should follow, and that, as domination leans toward severity, a fierce authority should be enforced by a slender garrison. Besides, the soldier must be appeased with pay, which could not be obtained from the treasury, as among other nations, but was sought from house to house, and that with difficulty, from a people accustomed for so many centuries to liberty and standing firm for the right of their ancestors. Hence many resources were lacking for the extraordinary needs, which could not be procured even then, if the people were made desolate and the lands laid waste. While the provinces flourish, garrisons can be maintained by taxes for the protection of the realm; but if the rage of the soldiers lays waste the fields and towns, the people, ruined by the loss of their goods, would not be restored by war and would become servants of royal greatness. All things stand by discipline; unless they are restrained by a ruler, they would of their own accord, once loosed, easily slip away. Finally, for a long time adversity had befallen the provinces, and beyond the storm of civil arms the sea, recrudescing each year with unusual tides, had drained private wealth. The nation, provoked by war and by the injuries of sky and sea, could still be driven, while it is mobile of its own accord, to heavier measures if it were goaded, and would proceed along the footsteps of its ancestors, who had cast off the harsher rule of princes and driven out servitude. Clear monuments of ancient virtue remained, and a people displaying the deeds of so many Caesars and the images of its old glory could not be pressed down except over long spans of time, and if it had shaken off, through forgetfulness of its right, the mastery of the prince, it would have cast off both the hatred of the present and the memory of the past. Therefore servitude must be veiled in the shadow of liberty, which they would attempt in vain unless either greater force lay close at hand or obedience were more thoroughly subdued. It could not be hoped that the second course would succeed once the people had been stirred up, nor was the state of the treasury such that it could meet the cost of bringing more legions into the province. Everywhere things were narrow, and when pay does not come in, insolence springs up. Thus it would happen that, with the property of the provincials plundered, the authority of the commanders would be diminished and the license of the soldiers would grow. Although something might rightly be granted to them, yet because of the monstrousness of the crime and the most foul rebellion against the king, the moments of the times had to be weighed, lest something be done in haste and plans doubtful in outcome be held as certain. Human fortune is a kingdom of tumbling chance, which can overturn even plans devised prudently and well by the king. Orange, a shrewd prince, was in command of the neighbouring provinces and would supply arms and counsel if he saw the nation of the Frisians still bearing the king's name and oaths and set apart from the covenant of Ghent. Harder measures would be taken and the cruelty of Alva would break out again, once the Council of the Belgic States had been appointed to govern the provinces. Rather, the occasions of events should be awaited, which the succession of the Austrian, already destined for rule, promised; without doubt he would bring the stubborn people, who rejected command, under control by the weight of arms, and indeed with indulgence toward the license of the soldiers.

units.la: A quo tamen consilio Roblesium parum abfuisse, etiam ij credidere qui Romanis sacris impensius dediti & regio dominatui æquiores in suis etsi rudibus commentarijs optuma libertatis studia odio Præfecti non dissimulavere. Unde ilud acerbius omnem per Frisiam in Roblesium natum exulesque trans Amasum, Visurgim ac Rhenum agentes sui in patriam reditus non obscuras spes versavere. Sic per provincias consternatio, mæror, ira, gaudium, pro animorum statu visebantur.
units.tr: Yet even those who were more devoted to the Roman rites and more compliant with royal rule did not think Roblesius was far from this plan; and in their own rough commentaries they did not hide, out of hatred for the Governor, their best feelings for liberty. Hence there arose a more bitter hatred of Roblesius throughout Friesland, and the exiles who were living beyond the Ems, the Weser and the Rhine nursed not obscure hopes of returning home. Thus throughout the provinces one could see dismay, grief, anger and joy, according to the state of men's minds.

units.la: Finis Libri Tertij.
units.tr: End of the Third Book.

units.la: P. WINSEMI Historiarum LIBER QUARTUS.
units.tr: P. Winsemius, Histories, Book Four

units.la: CTo apud Gandavum foedere ut omnia prosperè cessura avido libertatis populo videbantur, ita repentino Austriaci in provincias adventu multorum spes refrigere. Quippe lene Concilij Status imperium dominationi Principis cessurum arbitrabantur rerumque regimen magnis mutationibus subjacere. Ita Ordinum procerumque mentes suspicio sinistri occupaverat, quae ultra imminentium praesagae Hyeronimi Rodae ad Philippum Regem interceptis litteris firmabantur. Iis namque, ut nuperis legionum seditionibus fomentum subministrabatur, ita credebatur rex Philippus etsi revocandas in Hispaniam copias & suam in provincias profectionem simularet, militum suorum furoribus cladibusque populi crudelem animum pavisse. Vulgatis adhoc in commune rumoribus Joannem Austriacum Hispanicarum legionum Praefectos ad continuandam in regem officia sollicitasse actisque patratas ob caedes & enormem insolentiam gratijs, Philippi nomine omnem benevolentiam & navati furoris mercedem obtulisse. Quo ipso etsi sanctio & vis nuperi foederis convelleretur, quod vel maxime liberandis ab externo milite provincijs institutum erat, ita tamdiu Ordines ad eventus rerum, velut suspensi & fluctuantes egere, donec Austriaci litteris dissimulatae suspiciones proderentur. Alij credebant cum ipso Caroli Caesaris filio & Philippi fratre, tanquam Principe regij sanguinis, revicturam pacem fore concordiamque ex immoderatis priorum Praefectorum & nullas propinquitates regiae domus trahentium dominationibus luxatam aeterna pace coaliturum. Itaque vicinorum Principum legationibus aditus non renuente Elisabetha, quin prima imperij in Austriaco etsi suspecto initia aulica simulatione approbaret. Cambdenus scribit Ioanni Austriaco clam auxilia obtulisse, aemulatione Henrici III. Regis & quo Ordinum animos a sollicitanda Gallorum societate averteret. Neque alia ratione, mutuum aes xx. m. librarum Anglicae monetae Ordinibus assignasse, quam ut patria religione culta & stante populi in Philippum sacramento, Gallicae res retardarentur Austriacoque pacem offerente, numeratis seditioso militi ex subsidiario Anglico aere stipendijs, cum Philippo in gratiam a diuturna dissensione redirent. Adeo Gallica odia Hispanicis apud cIↄ. Iↄ. pud Elisabetham praevalebant, hoc maxime praecaventem, ne vicini LXXVI. & aemuli regis vires connivendo ad externa subjuvaret Gallorumque potentia ex foedere Belgico, regni vero sui imbecillitas incresceret. Igitur Austriacus Luxemburgi agens, ubi modum coeptandi per Provincias imperij animo volutabat, Bruxellas ad Ordines generales litteras in hunc modum dedit.
units.tr: When the Ghent Pacification was made, it seemed to the people, eager for liberty, that everything would turn out well. Yet the sudden arrival of the Austrian in the provinces cooled the hopes of many. They believed that the gentle rule of the Council of State would give way to the lordship of the Prince, and that the government of affairs would be subject to great changes. So suspicion of something sinister had taken hold of the minds of the Estates and nobles. This suspicion, beyond the forebodings of what was coming, was strengthened by letters of Jerónimo de Roda intercepted on their way to King Philip. For just as those letters fed the recent mutinies of the legions, so it was believed that King Philip, though he pretended to recall his troops to Spain and to make his own journey to the provinces, had nursed a cruel spirit in the fury and slaughter of his soldiers. Moreover, rumours had spread publicly that John of Austria had tried to win over the Spanish colonels to continue their service to the king, and that, for the murders committed and the enormous insolence, he had offered rewards in Philip's name, with all goodwill and the wages of the frenzy they had shown. Although this act threatened to overturn the authority and force of the recent covenant, which had been established chiefly to free the provinces from foreign soldiers, the Estates remained for so long hanging on the outcome of events, as if suspended and wavering, until the suspicions, hidden in letters, came to light. Others believed that with the son of Emperor Charles himself, a brother of Philip and a prince of royal blood, peace would return, and that concord, shattered by the immoderate rule of the earlier commanders, who had no kinship with the royal house, would be joined again in lasting peace. Accordingly, Elizabeth did not refuse to admit the embassies of neighbouring princes, and with courtly pretence she did not disapprove of the first beginnings of the Austrian's rule, though it was suspect. Camden writes that she secretly offered John of Austria help, out of rivalry with King Henry III and to turn the minds of the Estates away from seeking an alliance with the French. And for no other reason did she assign a loan of twenty thousand pounds of English money to the Estates, than that, with the fatherland's religion kept and the people's oath to Philip standing, French affairs would be held back, and Austria, offering peace, would be reconciled with Philip after long dissension, once the mutinous soldiers had been paid from the English subsidy. So greatly did hatred of the French prevail over hatred of the Spanish with Elizabeth, who was especially on guard against this: that by her connivance the forces of the neighbouring and rival king should not be strengthened to help foreign powers, and that the power of the French should not grow through the Belgian covenant, while the weakness of her own kingdom increased. Therefore the Austrian, acting at Luxembourg, having turned over in his mind the way to begin among the provinces of the empire, sent a letter in this form to the General Estates at Brussels.

units.la: Fratre meo Philippo rege, Ordines, ex Hispania in Belgicam missus sum, ut illius nomine vobis cum Imperio praeesem. Et quoniam fato tot annis discordes & involuti bello egistis, de mandato Regis componere dissensiones terrisque vestris pacem redonare paratus sum. Quare de reducenda stabiliendaque concordia remedijs cogitabo ocyus daboque operam ut, quicquid seditiosae legiones haud pridem deliquere, meâ severitate & militari disciplinâ corrigatur. In vobis interea erit meminisse sacramenti vestri regiqueac Romanae religioni debitum cultum & obsequium praestare. De caeteris quae in mandatis habeo, exponam coram latius. Itaque obsides à vobis dari peto, quo publicae pacis fideique certus sim periculique securus in provincias pergam meo moderamini commissas.
units.tr: I have been sent from Spain to the Netherlands by my brother, King Philip, to preside over you with the Empire in his name. And since you have for so many years been divided and entangled in war by fate, I am ready, on the king's command, to settle your disputes and restore peace to your lands. Therefore I will consider the remedies for bringing back and establishing concord as quickly as possible, and I will take care that whatever the mutinous legions have lately committed be corrected by my severity and military discipline. Meanwhile it will be your part to remember your oath and to render the due worship and obedience to the king and to the Roman religion. I will set out more fully the other matters I have in my instructions. Therefore I ask that hostages be given to me, so that I may be sure of public peace and fidelity, and may go with safety into the provinces committed to my government.

units.la: Quibus litteris in consessu recitatis altior metus Ordinum animos pervasit, indignantibus adhoc plerisque, Ioannem Austriacum mandato & autoritate Principis subnixum largasque certae pacis spes venditantem, exordia imperij desiderato obside capessere. Ita scilicet foecundam insidiarum mentem, ita mali testem conscientiam detegi juvenileque Austriaci pectus internis angoribus & secreto tortore velut indice occulti facinoris non vacare. Itaque curiosè Austriaci in consilia & actiones quaesitum, magis suspectâ indies fide quod Belgicam ingressus, longè à pacis curâ, bis mille Germanos ab Henrico III. Galliae rege, cessante civili bello exautoratos, suis stipendijs ac sacramentis adscripsisset. His accedebat, quod omne dominationis suae praesidium ab exercitu peteret, insigni errore recturi Principis, cujus imperium temperatae potius securaeque majestatis & suorum gratiae eguisset. Erant qui existumarent Austriacum quod primos vitae annos & facilem hauriendis moribus adolescentiam per Hispaniam egisset, aliquid quoque contagij ex illo coelo traxisse, quod ingenijs Belgicae & Frisiorum, Germaniae gentis, adversum, procerum & civile dissidium opprimendae libertati futurum crederetur. Sic subdolâ & indecorâ Principi arte, Mauros subegisse foedoque documento violatâ fide, quod per arma non poterat, dolo executum. Dissimulaturum quoque, erudito ad fraudes ingenio, naturae vitia fore, dum, quod potiundis ex arbitrio rebus conduceret blandimonijs & fictâ humanitate pellectum populum circumvenisset. Tum vero de opprimendo foedere, de puniend a in regem rebellione cogitaturum, facturumque ut, quod mali Principes assolent, vacuum lege imperium per servitia & sanguinem populi tueatur. His praeceptis à Roda in Hispaniam ituro, his mandatis instructum, qui hoc maxime suasisset, ut quodlibet profuturum consilium cautâ simulatione tegeret omnemque regnandi prudentiam gentis suae aut Italiae moribus assimilaret.
units.tr: When this letter was read out in the assembly, a deeper fear seized the minds of the Estates, and most of them were indignant that John of Austria, relying on the king's command and authority and holding out large hopes of certain peace, should begin his rule by demanding hostages. Clearly, they thought, a fertile mind for plots and a conscience that was witness to wickedness had been revealed, and the young Austrian's breast was not free of inner torment and of a secret torturer, like an informer of some hidden crime. So his plans and actions were examined with care, and his good faith grew more suspect each day, since, on entering the Netherlands, far from any care for peace, he had enlisted two thousand Germans, discharged by Henry III, King of France, when the civil war ceased, into his own pay and oath. To this was added that he sought every defence of his rule from the army, a notable mistake for a prince who would have needed the favour of a moderate and secure majesty and of his own people rather than of soldiers. Some thought that Austria, who had spent the first years of his life and his easily formed youth in Spain, had drawn some contagion from that climate, which was thought likely to be hostile to the Belgian and Frisian temperaments, the German race, and to the nobles and civic discord, and to crush liberty. Thus, they said, he had subdued the Moors by a crafty and undignified art, and by a shameful example of broken faith had accomplished by trickery what he could not by arms. He would also, with a mind trained in deceit, dissemble the vices of his nature, so long as he might deceive a people won over by flattery and feigned courtesy, which would serve to gain control of affairs at his pleasure. Then indeed he would plan to crush the covenant and to punish the rebellion against the king, and would make sure that, as bad princes are wont to do, he held an empire free of law by means of the service and blood of the people. He was to set out for Spain with these precepts from Roda and was instructed with these commands, by one who had especially advised that whatever counsel would be useful should be concealed by cautious pretence, and that he should model all his princely wisdom on the customs of his people or of Italy.

units.la: Reidanus tradit Austriacum, gerendo Philippi per provincias imperio, rio contrarijs mandatis inligatum publicoque restituere jus populi & cIↄ. Iↄ. amotis externis legionibus, quietem provincijs jussum, clandestinum rompendo foederi & reparandæ regiæ autoritati accepisse. Quare Aurantius lubrico foederi & ingenio Austriaci diffisus de communiendis Hollandiæ Zelandiæque provincijs cogitavit Ordinesque Generales de Joanne Austriaco his litteris commonuit.
units.tr: Reidanus relates that Austria, while carrying out Philip's rule through the provinces, was bound by contrary commands, and that he received, under the secret pretext of breaking the covenant and restoring royal authority, the order to restore the public rights of the people and, with the foreign troops removed, to give quiet to the provinces. Therefore Orange, distrusting the slippery covenant and the character of the Austrian, considered how to fortify the provinces of Holland and Zeeland, and warned the General Estates about John of Austria in the following letter.

units.la: FIdem facio apud vos, Ordines, ad alia me nunquam consilia, aut alias spes turbidis temporibus erexisse, quam ut provincia, more antiquo, Ordinum imperijs, salvo jure Principis, regerentur. Caeterum quoniam privata ambitio, jam ante modum saepe egressa, dominationem Principis accidit, ita factum est, ut potentiam suam princeps post auxerit, vestram depresserit. Ego vero etsi speraveram vos more majorum subortis malis usitata remedia, vobis jus, pacem, cujus speciem Gandavensi conventione edidistis, provincijs asserturos, ita metuo Austriacum & Hispanos, sua in vos odia falsis blanditijs tegentes, vestrâ integritate abusuros fore. Quippe ut consilijs vestris ac progressui rerum obessent, utile censuerunt, ut clam & celerrime in provincias Austriacus mitteretur vosque fucatis Austriaci persuasionibus & reverentiâ novi regnantis seductos in omnem socordiam neglectæ gerendarum rerum occasiones praecipitarent. Is vero ut in speciem vestro consessu, ita eorum praecipuè consilijs res geret, quos in conscientiam sui secreti adhibuit. Sic reputate Margaretam Austriacam Ducissam Parmensem ab Armenteri judicijs tanquam oraculis pependisse. Neque alia Austriacum hoc ipso tempore versare, quam ut imperium vestrâ servitute evat. Vos vero cogitate, Ordines, non ut privatos arduis negotijs ac regundæ tantæ moli præesse, caeterum in publico rerum fastigio locatos populi vestri res gerere, qui in sinum vestrum fortunas, libertatem, sanguinem atque spiritum depositerit. Quare potissima tuendæ libertatis apud vos ratio esse debet, quo rationem rerum aliquando reddituri, nihil servitutis (à quâ nisi praeveniamus parum absumus) inglorij & socordes vestris posteris relinquatis. Vt eam vobis imponant, Ordines, mille artibus, mille dolis vos aggredientur, tanto majus decus ac gloriam habituros, si vestra pectora, vestræ mentes illorum insidijs ac blandimonijs non patuerint. Itaque censeo cum Ioanne Austriaco non ante pacisecendum, quam terris vestris, ac finibus peregrinus miles excesserit. Quare nec poni arma, nec exercitum, qui vestris sacramentis militat dimitti volo, caeterum ius vestrum & libertatem, quam cum ipso spiritu à majoribus accepistis, vestrâ virtute retineri. Hoc etiam addo, nec longis ambagibus, nec prolixis aut crebris conventibus involvendum negotium, caeterum resignanda esse vestrarum mentium secreta detegendamque eorum iniquitatem, quâ tot annis ab oppressoribus vestrarum legum exagitamini. Enormi imperio & insolentissimis moribus remedium, patrocinium vestro juri brevi voce postulabitis. Id vero si Austriacus recusset, obtestatione utendum censeo suadeoque ut fidem faciatis non rebellione in regem, caeterum innocentiâ fretos, jura atque immunitates vestro sanguine tutaturos. Apertius quam tectius agentibus breve responsum dabitur, quod maxume Ordines, vestro bono cedet, ne morâ illius vires invalescant, vestrae atterantur. Sic reputate Philippum regem Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LIX. Gandavi à vobis liberius exceptum spem mittendi exercitus & Hispanica nicæ legionis ocyus fecisse, tracturum haud dubiè decretum, nisi vestrâ magna- nimitate & constantiâ compulsus, suæ voluntatis secretum exponere etiam in procinctu itineris coactus fuisset. Simile cogitate hoc ipso tempore faciendum esse & quidem adversus eum, quem vestri diffidentia, instabile concordiæ vinculum occupavit. Itaque muniendæ potentiæ & securitati suæ militem & exercitum petet, qui ne sacramento vestro agat, suo adstringet. Tum militaris præsidii potitus vobis securis & in commune consulentibus legem præscribet, si non æquo, saltem armis submixam. obluctantes severitate & rigore imperij, cæteros metu compescet. Inde secretorum machinator, quia fidei vestræ nec suæ integritati credere vult aut potest, obsides postulat, quos æquius esset vos petere, quorum fida semper in Regem obsequia oppressionibus Hispanorum patuere. Sic Trajectum ad Mosam, sic florentissimam urbium Antverpiam ne vestigia quidem veteris fortunæ retinentem spectate arciumque & vestræ incolumitatis præsidia vestro exitio usurpata. Quarum fundamenta ut per socordiam vestram increvere, ita satius fuisset aut nunquam extitisse aut solo æquatas vestram securitatem stabilisse. Nunc occupatis per vos castellis ejectisque præsidiis Rex intumescet sibique injuriam, vim suæ genti factam interpretabitur, ulturus haud dubiè ubi occasio feret. Quippe nostrâ imbecillitate mortales injuriæ quam beneficio facilius repenimus, præsertim vero Principes, qui dissimulandis magis, quam ponendis injurijs erudiuntur. Neque credite, ORDINES, condonaturum ea Regem, cujus imperium tam sublime, tam præfractum est, ut nec supplices ferat. Inde reputate causas publici furoris, inde exordia motuum cæpisse. Hac de causâ in EGMONDANI HORNIJQUE cervices, in sanguinem populi & nobilitatis sævitum. Idem nobis periculum, idem regiæ potentiæ fulmen impendet, cujus ea ægritudo est, ut cum imperare ex arbitrio velit, non possit. Hæc sola regiæ mentis summa imperia versantis summa imbecillitas est, quam si supplere per vim & arma nequeat, dolo supplebit. Fallacibus blandimentis adorietur incautos. Sic de revocandis in Hispaniam legionibus decernet, neque absimili fide, quam quâ olim, cum illorum missioni abscendente in Hispaniam PHILIPPO trimestre præfiniretur. Cogitate cum offenso rege, cum valido hoste rem vobis esse spectandamque aut rerum omnium ruinam, aut sumenda arma. Sin vero auscultandum conditionibus sit, censeo è re vestra esse, ut Hispani Belgicâ excedant restitutoque provinciis omni jure, vos potestatem deligendi Senatum agendique quotannis conventus habeatis, componendis ordinandisque provinciarum rebus à majoribus institutos. Hoc etiam pacificendum suadeo, ut castella ac arces solo æquentur justque habendorum delectuum disponendorumq, per provincias præsidiorum, non AUSTRIACI sed vestræ potestatis ac arbitrij sit. Ijs impetratis prospectum incolumitati vestræ erit. Sin vero secus fiat vosque assentatio aut reverentia AUSTRIACI seduxerit, novas discordias & pejus bellum feretis, quod eorum oculis animisque observatur, apud quos nec regis, nec Austriaci fides integra esse potest. De me testor, consilium hoc meo pectori vestræ & simul publicæ salutis desiderium extorsisse, cui non verebor omnia mea & hunc ipsum sanguinem ita poscentibus rebus consecrare.
units.tr: I say the same to you, gentlemen of the States: in these troubled times I have never raised any other plans or hopes than that the province should be governed, as in the old way, by the authority of the Orders, with the rights of the Prince preserved. But since private ambition, which has often gone beyond due measure already, has grown into the domination of the Prince, it has come about that the Prince has since increased his own power and depressed yours. Indeed, although I had hoped that, as your ancestors did, you would apply the usual remedies to the evils that have arisen, and would secure for the provinces the right and the peace whose outline you set forth in the Ghent agreement, I fear that Austria and the Spaniards, hiding their hatred of you under false flattery, will abuse your integrity. For they have judged it useful to obstruct your plans and the progress of affairs that Austria should be sent secretly and with all speed into the provinces, so that you, led astray by Austria's feigned persuasions and by reverence for the new ruler, might be plunged into complete complacency and lose the opportunities for managing affairs. He, indeed, will conduct affairs in your assembly in appearance only, but in reality chiefly by the counsels of those whom he has admitted into the confidence of his secret plans. Consider how Margaret of Austria, Duchess of Parma, hung upon the judgments of Armenteros as if they were oracles. And at this very time Austria has no other aim than to overturn liberty by your servitude. But you, gentlemen, should reflect that you are not placed at the summit of public affairs as private men, to preside over arduous business and the governance of so great a mass, but to manage the affairs of your people, who have deposited their fortunes, liberty, blood and spirit into your bosom. Therefore the chief consideration in defending liberty among you ought to be this: that you may one day render an account of your stewardship, and leave to your posterity nothing inglorious or spineless and nothing of servitude, from which we are scarcely removed unless we forestall it. To impose it upon you, gentlemen, they will assail you with a thousand arts and a thousand tricks, and they will think they have gained so much the greater honour and glory if your hearts and minds have not been open to their snares and flatteries. Therefore I advise that we should make no peace with John of Austria until the foreign soldier has left your lands and borders. Hence I wish that neither arms be laid down nor the army that serves under your oaths be dismissed, but that your right and liberty, which you received from your ancestors together with life itself, be kept by your valour. I add this too: the business is not to be entangled in long circumlocutions or in lengthy or frequent assemblies, but your secret thoughts must be unveiled and their iniquity, by which you have been harassed for so many years by your oppressors, must be brought to light. You will demand in a short voice a remedy for their outrageous rule and most insolent conduct, and protection for your law. If Austria refuses this, I advise that you use a solemn protest and urge you to make it plain that you will defend your rights and immunities with your blood, relying not on rebellion against the king but on your innocence. A brief answer will be given to those who act more openly than covertly, and this will most of all, gentlemen, turn to your good, so that by his delay his forces do not grow strong and yours be worn down. Consider that King Philip, when he was received by you at Ghent in the year 1559 more freely, made haste to send the army and the Spanish legion, and would doubtless have drawn out the decree, had he not been compelled, by your great magnanimity and steadfastness, to set forth the secret of his will even while preparing for the march. Think that something similar must be done at this very time, and indeed against him whom your distrust has placed in the unstable bond of concord. Therefore, to fortify his power and his own security, he will seek soldiers and an army, which he will bind to himself so that they do not act under your oath. Then, having gained the military garrison, he will dictate terms to you who are anxious for the common good and unsuspecting; if not with fairness, at least with arms lowered; he will restrain those who resist by the severity and rigour of his rule, and the rest by fear. Then, as a schemer of secrets, since he does not wish or cannot trust your loyalty nor his own integrity, he will demand hostages, which it would be fairer for you to demand, since your faithful obedience to the King has always been exposed to the oppressions of the Spaniards. Thus look at Maastricht on the Maas, and at the most flourishing city of Antwerp, which does not even keep the traces of its former fortune, and the citadels and garrisons for your safety, seized to your ruin. As their foundations have grown through your complacency, so it would have been better either that they had never arisen or that, levelled to the ground, they had secured your safety. Now, with the castles seized by you and the garrisons expelled, the King will swell with anger and will interpret it as an injury and a violence done to his nation, and he will doubtless take vengeance when opportunity offers. For by our weakness mortals repay injuries more easily than benefits, and especially princes, who are trained rather to dissemble injuries than to put them away. Nor believe, gentlemen, that the King, whose rule is so lofty and so stubborn that he does not even bear suppliants, will pardon these things. From this reflect on the causes of the public fury, and from this the beginnings of the disturbances arose. For this cause cruelty was wreaked upon the necks of Egmont and Horn, and upon the blood of the people and the nobility. The same danger, the same thunderbolt of royal power, hangs over us, whose sickness is such that, though he wishes to rule at his own pleasure, he cannot. This alone is the great weakness of a mind that manages the highest powers, and if he cannot supply it by force and arms, he will supply it by guile. He will assail the unwary with deceptive flatteries. Thus he will decree the recall of the legions to Spain, and not with a fidelity much unlike that by which, when their dismissal was once fixed at three months for King Philip's departure to Spain... Consider that you have to deal with an offended king and a powerful enemy, and that you must either look upon the ruin of all things or take up arms. But if the conditions must be listened to, I advise that it is in your interest that the Spaniards leave the Netherlands, that all right be restored to the provinces, and that you have the power of choosing the Senate and of holding assemblies every year, to settle and order the affairs of the provinces as your ancestors established them. I also advise that this be agreed upon: that the castles and citadels be levelled to the ground, and that the right of holding levies and of stationing garrisons through the provinces be at the discretion and power of yourselves, not of Austria. When these things have been obtained, provision will be made for your safety. But if it turns out otherwise, and flattery or reverence for Austria has led you astray, you will bear new discords and a worse war, which is watched by those eyes and minds before whom neither the faith of the King nor of Austria can be whole. I call this to witness: this counsel has been wrung from my breast by my desire for your welfare and for the public safety at once, and I shall not hesitate to devote all that I have, and this very blood, to such demanding times.

units.la: HÆC AURANTIUS.
units.tr: Thus Orange.

units.la: Unde consilium de admittendo Austriaco longius prolatum amplexandique, quod Gandavi ictum erat, fœderis, & simul exterminandarum darum provincijs legionum, sollicita desideria increvere. Auftriacus vero, etsi missionem regij exercitus palam non detrectaret, ita urgebat, ut classis per provincias adornaretur regiaeque legiones trans mare in Hispaniam aut destinata locorum amandarentur. Quod ad Gaedavenfis foederis negotium attineret, non aliud regerebat, quam paratum se esse, regio nomine assensum foederi dare, modo certum sit id ipsum Foedus, nec Romanae Catholicae Religioni, nec regio juri aut autoritati quid derogare. Itaque testimonia eidem Foederi à divinarum humanarumque rerum peritis, ac Concilio Status scripta, quibus judicabant posse Austriacum, salvo Philippi regis jure & intemeratâ Romanâ Catholicâ Religione in communionem Foederis ac Belgicae societatis condescendere. Id scilicet unicum sanandis malis & conciliandae paci remedium superfuisse, quam tot annis, velut diro sydere circumactam, revolutio foelicissimi temporis Belgicis terris hoc ipso Foedere promitteret. Caeterum Austriacus doli prudens & sui consilij haud ignarus, dilationem missionibus legionum quaerebat regisque exercitum classi committendum rebatur. Non posse quippe tot provincias, tot regiones intempestivo anni tempore tuto transiri, angustis dierum spatijs & hyberno coelo tempestatibus tristi. Trajicienda esse flumina, superandos montes, quorum juga aut angustiae praealtâ nive tegerentur. Esse Sebaudiam sterilem & attritos Allobroges, nec equis aut jumentis pabulo nec alimoniam copijs submínistraturos. Adhaec Italiae aditus commeantibus praeclusos infectumque pestilentiâ aërem, nec tutas itinerum stationes, nec sanas fruges aut salubrem victum polliceri. Haec Legionum, haec tribunorum murmura esse. Creditum fuit, Joannem Austriacum commisso classibus exercitu, ambitiosae menti, ut ante Tunetanum, ita tum Angliae regnum destinasse Gregoriumque XIII. Pontificem, Elisabetha Reginâ, velut rerum incapace & haereseos à Pio V. ante sexennium damnata, Joanni Austriaco titulum ac jus regni secretis tabulis assignasse.
units.tr: Hence the anxious desires grew: to put off longer the admission of the Austrian and the embracing of the covenant that had been struck at Ghent, and at the same time to drive the royal legions out of the provinces. Yet Austria, though he did not openly refuse the dismissal of the royal army, pressed so hard that a fleet was to be fitted out in the provinces and the royal legions were to be sent across the sea to Spain or to places appointed for them. As for the business of the Ghent covenant, he answered only that he was ready to give his assent to the covenant in the king's name, provided it was certain that the covenant itself did not detract anything from the Roman Catholic religion, the king's right, or his authority. Accordingly, testimonies to this covenant were written by men learned in divine and human affairs, and by the Council of State, by which they judged that the Austrian could, without prejudice to Philip's right and the inviolate Roman Catholic religion, enter into communion with the covenant and the Belgic association. This, they said, was the one remedy left for healing the evils and securing peace, which the revolution of a most happy time was promising to the Belgic lands through this very covenant, after so many years of being harried as if under a dire star. But Austria, shrewd in his deceit and not ignorant of his own purpose, sought delay in sending the legions and thought the king's army should be entrusted to the fleet. For, he said, so many provinces and regions could not safely be crossed at an unseasonable time of year, with the days short and the winter sky harsh with storms. The rivers must be crossed and the mountains surmounted, whose ridges or passes were covered with deep snow. Savoy was barren, and the Allobroges were worn out, and they would supply neither fodder for horses or beasts nor provisions for the troops. Moreover, the approaches to Italy were closed to travellers, and the air was infected with pestilence, so they could promise neither safe halting-places along the way nor wholesome food or healthy provisions. These, he said, were the murmurings of the legions and the tribunes. It was believed that John of Austria, once the army was committed to the fleets, had aimed, as he had before at Tunis, at the kingdom of England; and that Pope Gregory XIII, with Queen Elizabeth regarded as unfit to rule and as a heretic condemned six years earlier by Pius V, had secretly assigned to John of Austria the title and right to the kingdom.

units.la: Caeterum Ordines sumptuosam classem, nec tam cito instruendam, defectum navium & classiarium militem ab illâ expeditione alienum, speciosis rationibus criminabantur. Adhaec stipendijs nauticae pubis impar aerarium esse, poscentibus residuum aeris legionibus, nec sine eo exautorandis. Ita acerbis altercationibus subdolae res trahebantur, donec sequens annus novo Ordinum Foederi & instituendis cum Austriaco conloquijs destinaretur.
units.tr: Meanwhile the States, on specious grounds, blamed the costly fleet, which could not be fitted out so quickly, the lack of ships, and the shortage of seamen unsuited to that expedition. Besides, they said the treasury could not pay the sailors, and the legions were demanding the remaining money, nor could they be discharged without it. So these deceitful matters were dragged out with bitter disputes, until the following year was set aside for a new covenant with the States and for conferences with the Austrian.

units.la: Tum Joachimum Hopperum Madriti in Hispaniâ mors abstulit, quem Philippus claritudine famae ac virtutis secretis regni ac Belgicarum rerum admoverat. Viri vitam suâ & majorum laude clari ut alij scripsere, ita ulterioribus supersedeo. Hoc tantum subjungam, ituro in Belgicam Austriaco scribendis mandatis praefuisse suadentemque salubria, & nutriendis per provincias discordijs aliena, longiore morbo ac tabidâ febre extenuatum praeclaro exitu naturae legem implevisse. Cujus morte quantum moeroris luctusque regius animus hauserit magna in defuncti familiam & superstites liberos Philippi beneficia patefecere. Quippe sumptuoso ex Hispaniâ in Belgicam itineri duodena millia decrevit annuâque mille carolaeorum pensione haeredes donavit. Funus regiâ cIↄ. Iↄ regiâ quoque impensa ei factum illustrisque exequiæ solennibus laudationibus decoratæ, viri famam per ingenij opera conscientijs posterorum destinatam justis elogijs adumbravere.
units.tr: Then death carried off Joachim Hopper at Madrid in Spain, whom Philip had brought close to the secret affairs of the kingdom and of the Belgic lands because of the brightness of his reputation and his virtue. Others have written of the man's life, which was famous for his own and his ancestors' renown, so I will pass over the rest. I will add only this: that when the Austrian was about to go into the Low Countries, he had charge of writing his instructions, and, by counselling wholesome measures and not encouraging the discords that were spreading through the provinces, he, weakened by a long illness and a wasting fever, fulfilled the law of nature with an honourable end. How greatly the king's spirit was touched with grief and sorrow at his death was shown by the great favours Philip bestowed on the dead man's family and his surviving children. Indeed, he granted twelve thousand ducats for the costly journey from Spain to the Low Countries, and gave his heirs an annual pension of a thousand carolus. The funeral was also held at the king's expense, and his distinguished obsequies were adorned with solemn eulogies; and those who had devoted their works to his fame to posterity's judgement set him forth in fitting tributes.

units.la: Igitur Concilium Status Gaspe ro Roblesio Groningæ, & illius conjuge apud Leovardios custodiæ datâ, ne militare & simul provinciæ imperium rectore vacaret, Georgium Lalainium magnæ spei Principem regundis intra Flevum Amasunqque Frisijs destinavere, aucto in eum Concilij Status Belgici favore, quod octo cohortium signis ejecto urbe & simul castello Germanorum Hispanorumque præsidio, Valencenas, munitissimam Hannoniæ urbem, in fidem Ordinum, eximiâ imperij autoritate citra sanguinem redegisset. Quare & à Concilio Status litteræ in Frisiam mense Decembri datæ, quibus Lalainio commissam per Frisios gubernationem addito Philippi nomine indicabatur. Placuisse scilicet fato conversionem rerum per provinciam instituì & legum quietisque publicæ perturbatores vinculis datos possessione ejici usurpati dominatus. Violenta raro diuturna esse luendamque fuisse exercitam dominantium asperitatem inter squallores carcerum, quo æquitas fati cuncta attemperantis spectaretur. Nunc vero ne durante interregno res secius fluitarent, Georgium Lalainium Gasparo Roblesio, sed ad tempus, suffectum, dum Lalainius, amoto prædecessore, experimenta rerum & florentis juventæ in moderandâ gente edidisset. Velle igitur Frisij in spem meliorum temporum ei morem gerant ut sedantque ordinandæ provinciæ potestatem ei à consessu patrum aut Concilij Status ex decreto Philippi permissam.
units.tr: Therefore the Council of State gave Gaspar de Robles into custody at Groningen, and his wife at Leeuwarden, so that the province would not be without a ruler for either military or civil command. They appointed George de Lalaing, a prince of great promise, to govern between the Ems and the Flevo lake and in Friesland. The favour of the Belgic Council of State grew toward him, because he had, with the standards of eight cohorts, expelled the German and Spanish garrison from the city and castle and had, by his remarkable authority, brought Valenciennes, the most strongly fortified city of Hainault, into the allegiance of the States without bloodshed. Hence letters were sent from the Council of State to Friesland in December, by which it was made known that the government of the Frisians had been committed to Lalaing, with Philip's name added. It had pleased fate, they said, that the change of affairs should be brought about throughout the province, and that the disturbers of the laws and public peace, who had seized power, should be thrown out of possession and bound in chains. Violent rule is seldom lasting, and the harshness of the rulers had to be paid for amid the squalor of prisons, so that the justice of fate, which tempers all things, might be seen. But now, lest affairs should drift in a worse direction during the interregnum, George de Lalaing was substituted for Gaspar de Robles, but only for a time, until Lalaing, with his predecessor removed, should have shown his proof in governing the people and in his flourishing youth. The Frisians, therefore, wishing to hope for better times, were to comply with him and to accept his power of settling and ordering the province, which had been granted to him by the assembly of the fathers or the Council of State by decree of Philip.

units.la: Unde Lalainius salutatis Ordinibus Bruxellis, dein Brabantiâ excessit Middelburgique Zelandorum apud Aurantium Principem, cujus gratiâ pollebat, subsistens, peragrata Hollandiâ conscensoque apud minores Frisios navigio, Groningam provectus est. Cæterum vergente in occasum die, qui hyberno tempore brevissimus est, contumaciâ militum, quorum animi nuperâ ex inquietudine necdum desederant, urbe prohibitus, in Cænobium Selverdicum secessit. Ibi cum Pompeio Ufkenio, Jacobo Hildebrandio, Ruardo Alberda, Henrico Oienbruggio, Francisco Pipenpoio, & Lanceloto Parasitio, qui in ejus comitatu erant, audiendis Groningensium ac Omlandiæ Legatis præsedit exhibitisqae mandatorum suorum tabulis provincialium & simul militaris præsidij animos sibi conciliavit. Unde mœsta pridem civitas & turbidæ cohortes, excussâ insignium illuvie & contumaciâ vultuum publicam in lætitiam effusæ, magno indicio utrumque corpus, justo moderatore destitutum, velut inops consilij nullo ordine & incerto motu fluitare.
units.tr: So Lalaing, having greeted the States at Brussels, left Brabant and stayed at Middelburg in Zeeland with the Prince of Orange, whose favour he enjoyed. Then, having crossed Holland and boarded a ship at the Lesser Frisians, he was carried to Groningen. But as the day was drawing to its close, the shortest day of the winter, he was refused entry to the city because of the stubbornness of the soldiers, whose spirits had not yet settled after the recent unrest, and he withdrew to the monastery of Selwerd. There, with Pompeius Ufkens, Jacob Hildebrand, Ruard Alberda, Henry Oienbrugge, Francis Pipenpoy and Lancelot Parasitius, who were in his retinue, he presided over the hearing of the envoys of Groningen and Ommelanden, showed the provincials the records of his commission, and at the same time won over the minds of the military garrison. Hence the city, long sorrowful, and the turbulent cohorts, shaking off the squalor of their badges and their stubborn expressions, poured out into public rejoicing, a clear sign that both bodies, deprived of a just governor, were drifting like men without counsel, in no order and with unsteady motion.

units.la: Sic deducente præsidio inter erecta cohortium signa & acclamationes civium Lalainius Groningam ingressus, adeo cœcâ adhuc futuri mente, ut præsenti juvenilium annorum fortunæ & simul specioso rerum paratui intentus, nesciret eandem urbem defectioni suæ & simul extremis parari. Mox pronis populi procerumque augurijs dignitatem orsus, quod eum præter animi dotes, claritudo natalium, tum flos vividæ ætatis crescentiumque annorum non obscurae spes commendarent. His accedebat toleratum sub Albano exilium grande fidei pignus & literarum terarum ornamentis illustre pectus imbutum. Adhæc decoram faciem, vegetum corpus, flavescentem cæsariem, externam pulchritudinem, vulgus intuebatur, credulum ut solet, externis naturæ donis bonam Principis mentem inniti.
units.tr: So, with the garrison leading the way between the raised standards of the cohorts and the acclamations of the citizens, Lalaing entered Groningen, still so blind in mind to what was to come that, intent on the present fortune of his youthful years and the showy preparations of affairs, he did not know that the same city was being readied both for his own defection and for his downfall. Soon he began his dignity with the favourable omens of the people and the great men, since his nobility of birth, besides his gifts of mind, and the flower of his lively age and the not obscure hopes of his growing years commended him. To these was added his long exile under Alva, a great pledge of faith, and a breast steeped in the adornments of letters and bright with them. Besides, the crowd looked at his handsome face, his vigorous body, his golden hair and his outward beauty, credulous as crowds usually are, believing that a prince's good mind rests on the outward gifts of nature.

units.la: Cæterum, ut in rebus mortalium prosperi sæpe comes adversitas est, ita primam Præfecturæ in Lalainio infantiam exigentium stipendia cohortium non tam dubia fides, quam criminationes & querimoniæ obturbavere. Ita scilicet cum Martinio Stella Ordinum Legato convenium ajebant, ut quicquid æris competeret, transcriptis in partes Ordinum exsolveretur. Hac spe Præfectum suum & post urbem imperio Ordinum asseruisse, id certè commeritos, ut si non præmia præclaro & laudato patribus facinori, saltem stipendia militiæ mercedem ex condicto obtineant. Quare Lalainius sanandis cohortium querimonijs & ne istæ in licentiam aut defectionem erumperent, Gulielmum Doetecomium, & Joannem Mathenesium legatos in majores Frisios amandavit, litterisque fiduciarijs suâ manu prid. Eid. Jan. signatis conventum Delegatorum Frisiæ ad diem xvii. Januar. Leovardiæ indixit.
units.tr: But, as adversity is often the companion of prosperity among mortal affairs, so the first infancy of Lalaing's government was disturbed by complaints and accusations, and by no small doubt about the pay of the cohorts. It was said that he had agreed with Martin Stella, the envoy of the States, that whatever money was due would be paid out of the transcribed sums to the States' side. On this hope they had secured their commander, and after the city, the authority of the States, for they had deserved it, and if not rewards for a glorious and praised deed toward the fathers, at least their military pay as agreed should be obtained. Therefore Lalaing, to remedy the cohorts' complaints and so that they would not break out into licence or rebellion, sent William Doetecum and John Mathenesse as envoys to the Greater Frisians, and by letters of trust signed with his own hand on the day before the Ides of January he summoned a meeting of the Frisian delegates at Leeuwarden for 17 January.

units.la: Senatus vero Regius, ut Roblesio clam addictior, ita manifestâ ergâ Lalainium æmulatione ducebatur, quod interiore Aurantij amicitiâ florens, societate ac sacramento fœderum imbutus crederetur. Quare actis Senatus nomen Lalainij adhuc exclusum publicisque ac regijs edictis autoritas Senatus præfigebatur. Unde Lalainius sive calore ætatis & juventæ annis, sive ne recentis imperij vis & autoritas solveretur, Præfecti titulum à Senatu regio decerni jussit eundemque in acta Concilij Status jurare per Legatos adegit. Quippe Gulielmo Doetecomio & Joanni Mathenessio Delegatis, ut dixi, Leovardiam missis, inter alia mandaverat Lalainius, ut dignitatem sibi à Concilio Status factam apud reluctantem Senatum asserunt patrumq; acta lubricis temporibus per modum libelli exequerentur.
units.tr: The Royal Senate, however, was secretly more favourable to Robles, and it was thought to be openly jealous of Lalaing, because he flourished in the close friendship of Orange and was believed to be bound by the society and oath of the covenants. So, in the Senate's records, Lalaing's name was still excluded, and the Senate's authority was prefixed to public and royal edicts. Hence Lalaing, whether from the heat of his age and youth, or so that the force and authority of his new government would not be dissolved, ordered that the title of governor be decreed by the royal Senate, and he compelled the Senate to swear to the acts of the Council of State through envoys. For he had instructed, among other things, the envoys William Doetecum and John Mathenesse, whom I have said were sent to Leeuwarden, that they should press the Senate, which resisted, to recognise the dignity conferred on him by the Council of State, and to carry out the fathers' acts in the slippery times by way of a petition.

units.la: Isto perscriptum erat:
units.tr: This was written down:

units.la: CONCILIUM STATUS Belgici GEORGIO LALAINIO Præfecturam Frisiæ, Groningæ, Omlandiæ, & Drentiæ collocasse. Et quoniam intellexisset Senatum regium postulatis Ordinum Frisiæ rescriptum indulsisse, ab hesterna actione & suis mandatis alienum, ita petere ut Senatus de plano respondeat, an LALAINIUM pro Præfecto haberi & an parere decreto CONCILII STATUS velit actaque eâ de re ocyus perscribat. Fore alias, ut Lalainius ex contumaciâ regij Senatus causam querelæ nactus, apud CONCILIUM STATUS de læsâ ORDINUM & simul regiâ autoritate expostulet.
units.tr: The Council of State of the Belgian provinces has placed George Lalaing in charge of the prefecture of Friesland, Groningen, Ommelanden and Drenthe. Since it had learned that the royal Senate had granted the Frisian Estates a rescript at odds with yesterday's proceedings and its own mandates, it asks that the Senate state plainly whether Lalaing is to be recognised as prefect, whether it will obey the decree of the Council of State, and that it write out its acts on the matter as quickly as possible. Otherwise, Lalaing, having found in the Senate's obstinacy a ground for complaint, will lodge a protest before the Council of State over an injury to the Estates and at the same time to royal authority.

units.la: Ad quæ SENATUS.
units.tr: To which the Senate replied:

units.la: QVONIAM è CONCILIO STATUS ex litteris XV. Decemb. ad nos datis intelleximus GEORGIUM LALAINIUM in Frisiam missum, quo in res statumque provinciæ inquireret eumque ita ordinaret, ut commodo PHILIPPI regis & paci publicæ conduceret, addito insuper summi imperij mandato, donec aliter statuatur. Ita declaramus vobis Legatis, quod heri ore tenus sacIↄ. Iↄ. Eum est, nos eundem Lalainium pro Praefecto Frisiae agnoscere, daturi operam LXXVII. ut mandatorum tabulis, quas exhibiturus post erit, pareamus atque regiae majestatis aut Concilii Status, durante ejus imperio vim atque effectum sortiantur.
units.tr: Since we have learned from the letter of the Council of State dated 15 December that George Lalaing has been sent into Friesland to inquire into the affairs and condition of the province, and to put them in order so as to serve the advantage of King Philip and the public peace, with the added mandate of supreme authority until a different decision is made, we therefore declare to you, the deputies, what we stated orally yesterday: that we acknowledge this same Lalaing as prefect of Friesland, and we will take care to obey the written mandates, which he will present later, so that they may take effect and have force while his authority lasts, under the authority of His Royal Majesty or of the Council of State.

units.la: Haec XVI. Ianuar. perscripta ac Emskerckij Graphiarij Regij manu Leovardiae signata.
units.tr: These things were written down on 16 January, at Leeuwarden, and sealed by the hand of Emskerck, royal registrar.

units.la: Mox postero Conventus habitus verbaque in hunc modum à Praeside Senatus, nomine Legatorum ad Deputatos Ordinum facta.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, on the following day, a meeting was held, and the President of the Senate spoke in the following manner on behalf of the deputies to the Estates.

units.la: ASSERTA Ordinum partibus Groningâ, post Gasparum Roblesium à Legionariis suis custodiae datum, Concilium Status Belgii, regundis pro Philippo rege provinciis admotum, de mittendo in provinciam hanc Georgio Lalainio decrevit. Quippe turbidae res successorem Roblesio flagitabant, ne quid gravius regi aut vobis accideret.
