Is verò celerrimo itinere confecto quod molestissimum media ei hyeme fuit, postquam Groningam appulit, id maxime adnixus est, ut inquietas cohortes sedaret easdemque in verba sua adigeret. Caeterum Ordinum etiam partes professae sacramentum Praefecto detrectavere. Itaque nec jusjurandum dicere, nec interesse recensioni, praeterquam penitatis stipendijs voluere. Et quoniam Lalainius nec quieti publicae, nec commodis vestris consulere, praeterquam pacatis cohortium animis potest; (quos componi Concilium Status & Ordines provinciarum ex usu publico censent) ita visum ei fuit, hunc conventum indicere, quo de illius potestate & mandatis vobis constet & ut subsidia ordinandis rebus quaerantur. Vestrum erit, Deputati optamo in provinciam Lalainij affectu non abuti, cui non aliud propositum est, quam ut divino cultui & Romanae Catholicae religioni, tum vestrae patriae bene sit, ac ut legibus immunitatibusque majorum vestrorum prospiciatur. Hoc tantum necessum est, ut initis necdum supputatisque colortium rationibus, modicum aeris, pro mole tributi vestri praestetis, quo miles pretium sacramento & navatae fidei praemium accipiat. Ejus namque ope ut libertatem accepistis, ita suffugistis servitutem quae vobis ultima, liberis atque vestris posteris parabatur. Itaque, Deputati, si stipendia ocyus cohortibus decernatis, dabit operam Lalainius, ut res vestrae cum illius affectu increscant vestraeque spei abunde satisfactum testaturi sitis. Hoc etiam monendum nomine Concilij Status, Ordinum Generalium, & Praefecti duximus, ut Legatos Bruxellas mittatis, qui Foederi inter Ordines Provinciarum & Aurantium ito se jungant, consulantque in commune, exterminandis Belgica Hispanis, continua in patriam vestram edia & simul exitia professis.
units.tr: Since the cause of the Groningen Estates has been upheld, after Gaspar Robles was handed over to his own legionaries for custody, the Council of State of Belgium, having taken up the governance of the provinces on behalf of King Philip, has decided to send George Lalaing into this province. Indeed, the troubled state of affairs demanded a successor to Robles, so that nothing more serious might befall the king or yourselves. He, having completed a very swift journey, which was most troublesome in the middle of winter, after he reached Groningen, strove above all to calm the restless cohorts and bind them to his own oath. Yet the Estates, professing their own cause, refused the oath to the prefect; so they neither wished to swear the oath nor to take part in the muster, except on terms of paid wages. And since Lalaing can attend to neither public tranquillity nor your interests, except by pacifying the minds of the cohorts (which the Council of State and the Estates of the provinces judge should be settled for the public good), it seemed good to him to call this meeting, so that your powers and mandates may be established and that funds may be found for putting affairs in order. It will be for you, deputies, not to abuse the excellent disposition towards the province of Lalaing, whose only aim is that it may go well with the worship of God and the Roman Catholic religion, and with your fatherland, and that the laws and immunities of your forefathers may be looked after. This only is necessary: that, before the accounts of the cohorts are drawn up and reckoned, you pay a modest sum of money, in proportion to the weight of your taxation, by which the soldier may receive the price of his oath and the reward of his faithful service. For just as you received your liberty through his help, so by his help you escaped a servitude which was being prepared for you as the last of all, for your children and your descendants. Therefore, deputies, if you swiftly decree wages for the cohorts, Lalaing will take care that your affairs grow along with his goodwill, and that you may bear witness that your hope has been amply satisfied. We have also thought it right to advise this in the name of the Council of State, the General Estates and the prefect: that you send deputies to Brussels, who may join themselves to the Treaty between the Estates of the provinces and Orange, and take counsel in common, for the expulsion of the Spaniards from Belgium, who are continually profession fires and slaughter against your fatherland.

units.la: Creditum fuit Senatum per Frisiam regium, quod nec promovendo sanciendoque foederi legatos Gandavum misisset, nec tabulas vulgasset, ab eo ipso consilio abhorruisse obscuratumque tempori, velut magnae rerum mutationis providum, Ordinum & Lalainij imperijs paruisse.
units.tr: It was believed that the royal Senate, through Friesland, had shrunk from that very policy, because it had neither sent envoys to Ghent to advance and ratify the treaty nor published the documents; and that, veiled by the times and foreseeing a great upheaval in affairs, it had submitted to the commands of the Estates and of Lalaing.

units.la: Itaque Ordinum per Frisiam Delegati, quo legatorum Lalainij postulatis satisfieret, cum Senatu quoque regio negotium communicavere, praetentandis haud dubie animis & ut ipsorum consilia, resumendae clam libertati prona, exquisitis Senatus arbitrijs firmarentur. Non posse quippe novo Rectori Lalainio se provinciæ imperium approbare innuebant, nisi de speciali superiorum mandato constitisset & nisi Senatus regius censeret tantis rerum exordijs vim mandati subesse. Adhæc adscribi, quod legati petierant, Ordinum generalium Fœderi se non posse inconsulto Senatu, tanquam legitimo magistratu & ad cujus exemplum affirmari sua responsa & simul rescripta deberent.
units.tr: Therefore the deputies of the Estates of Friesland, in order that the demands of Lalaing's envoys might be met, also shared the matter with the royal Senate, no doubt to sound out minds and so that their own plans, inclined to secretly resuming liberty, might be strengthened by the Senate's considered judgment. They hinted that they could not approve the authority of the new ruler Lalaing over the province, unless it were established by a special mandate of his superiors, and unless the royal Senate judged that the force of a mandate lay behind such beginnings of affairs. Moreover, they said that what the envoys had requested could not be added to the Treaty of the General Estates without the Senate being consulted, as a lawful magistracy, and that their answers and rescripts ought to be confirmed by its example.

units.la: Quæ haud dubiè gravando Senatui, velut recusaturo reperta, ita specie honoris erudita humanitate deferebantur.
units.tr: These demands, no doubt devised so as to burden the Senate, as if it would refuse, were put forward with a veneer of honour and polished courtesy.

units.la: Quare Senatus regius rescripsit.
units.tr: Wherefore the royal Senate replied as follows.

units.la: Opinari se actiones GEORGII LALAINII publicæ autoritatis & Concilij Status decreto inniti, de cujus fide si dubitare Delegatos Ordinum Frisiæ contingat, posse, quo talium certi sint, mandati rationem apud eos indagare, apud quos expedire judicarent. Se interim stare mandato Regis aut Concilij Status, dum Rex partes regendi Concilio assignaverit, daturos operam, ut cum illius imperio sua parendi ratio congruat.
units.tr: We are of the opinion that the actions of George Lalaing rest upon public authority and the decree of the Council of State. If the deputies of the Estates of Friesland should happen to doubt its good faith, they may, in order to be certain about such matters, inquire into the grounds of the mandate among those whom they judge fit to ask. For our part, we will abide by the mandate of the King or of the Council of State, and while the King assigns the powers of government to the Council, we will take care that our own obedience accords with its authority.

units.la: Hæc eodem xvi. Jan. die perscripta, & ab Emskerckio actis inserta. Qua oratione ab Achlenio Præside habitâ Deputati Ordinum cum obtestatione patrij juris, ut id sartum tectumque esset, hoc modo responderunt.
units.tr: These things were written down on the same day, 16 January, and entered in the acts by Emskerck. After this speech was delivered by the President Achlenius, the deputies of the Estates, calling on the rights of their country to be kept whole and intact, replied in this manner.

units.la: Vamvis fidem fecerit rex PHILIPPUS se assignato ei annuo censu novis nos oneribus non gravaturum, ita liberalitate nostra erga impulsas PHILIPPI res ut illius necessitatibus non semel subvenimus. Anno septuagesimo etiam stupendâ maris inundatione damna passi (postquam homines, jumenta, fruges, villæ, horrea in alium acta) tamen de subsidijs cogitavimus, per quæ ærarium regis fervente bello sublevaretur. Sic bona universitatis, sic agros, sic prædia pignori dedimus, postquam instituta Vectigalia & tributum familijs impositum nostræ liberalitati & egentiæ regis non sufficerent. Dein collato menstruo ære angustiam rerum præjuvimus, ita tandem attenuatis facultatibus nostris, ut nos ulterioribus exactionibus ferendis invalidos nostra in regem studia fecerint. Tamen reverentiâ regis & affectu in LALAINIUM ducti, ut pax provinciæ, quies atque prosperitas sit, centum millia carolorum in subsidium præstabimus, cæterum hac cautione, ut patrimonium censusque regius pignori nobis sit & ut collecti in militem æris erogatio ex Delegatorum nostrorum consilio fiat oppidaque ac arces à præsidijs cohortium leventur. Hoc etiam cavemus, ne quæ exactiones in posterum fiant, & ut agri ac possessiones nostræ ab incursionibus ac præsidijs militum immunes sint. Quod ad Fœdus Gandavi ictum attinet, id testamur nos approbare, daturos operam ut hoc ipso cæteris provincijs sociati Legatos Bruxellas ocyus mittamus, qui tractandis ulterioribus pacis negotijs & curandis rebus præsint. Hat tamen conditione, ut LALAINIUS Præsectus suum per Frisios imperium nostris legibus ac immunitatibus adæquet adhibeatque in consilium Delegatos Ordinum è nostrâ gente quovis tempore deligendos.
units.tr: Although King Philip has given assurance that he will not burden us with new taxes beyond the annual sum assigned to him, we have often come to the aid of Philip's affairs out of our generosity, as the needs of his position required. In the seventieth year, when we suffered damages from a stupendous flood of the sea (when men, beasts, crops, farmsteads and granaries were carried away), we still considered subsidies by which the royal treasury might be relieved while the war was raging. Thus we pledged the goods of the community, thus the fields, thus the estates, after the established duties and the tax imposed on households proved insufficient for our generosity and the king's need. Then, by contributing money monthly, we helped relieve the straitened circumstances, until at last our resources were so worn down that our own loyalty towards the king made us unable to bear further exactions. Nevertheless, moved by reverence for the king and by goodwill towards Lalaing, so that the province may have peace, quiet and prosperity, we will provide one hundred thousand carolus guilders as a subsidy; but on this condition: that the royal patrimony and revenues be pledged to us, that the disbursement of the money collected for the soldiery be made by the advice of our deputies, and that the towns and citadels be relieved of the garrisons of the cohorts. We also provide against this, that no exactions be made in future, and that our fields and possessions be free from the incursions and quartering of soldiers. As for the Treaty concluded at Ghent, we testify that we approve it, and we will take care that, being thereby joined to the other provinces, we send envoys to Brussels forthwith, who may preside over the further conduct of the peace negotiations and the management of affairs. Yet on this condition: that Lalaing, the prefect, shall make his rule over the Frisians conform to our laws and immunities, and shall take into his council deputies of our own people, to be chosen at any time.

units.la: Hæc xiii. Kal. Febr. in acta relata, ac pro Oostergois à Paulo Cosferio Antistite Fosverdico, Decone Martna, Edzardo Douma, Jorritio Bocatio Wiarda, pro Westergois à Thomâ Groningensi Præ-sule cIↄ. Iↄ. sule Floridi Campi, Julio Botnia, Herone Ockingha, Livio Beiemo, LXXVII. pro Sylvestribus Erasmo Douma, Frederico Roorda, Foppio Douma & Annaeo Tarquinio signata. His additum fuit, ut, quoniam undecim oppidorum Delegati, nec conditionibus aequis auscultare, nec succurrere publicae necessitati vellent; se quintam praedicti aeris partem exsolvendam oppidanis relinquere, daturos operam ut LXXX. millia publicis usibus praestentur. Ita Paulus Costerius, Hero Ockingha, & Erasmus Douma signavere.
units.tr: These things were entered in the acts on 20 January and, on behalf of the Oostergo, were signed by Paulus Costerius, the bishop of Fosverdum, the deacon Martna, Edzardus Douma, and Jorritius Bocatius Wiarda; on behalf of the Westergo, by Thomas, the Groningen president of Floridus Campus, Julius Botnia, Hero Ockingha, and Livius Beiemus; and on behalf of the Sylvestrian district by Erasmus Douma, Frederick Roorda, Foppius Douma and Annaeus Tarquinius. To this was added that, since the deputies of eleven towns would neither listen to fair conditions nor be willing to help the public necessity, they would leave to the townsmen the fifth part of the aforesaid money to be paid, and would take care that eighty thousand be furnished for public uses. Thus Paulus Costerius, Hero Ockingha and Erasmus Douma signed.

units.la: Sic dimisi Legati & ad Lalainium profecti. Mox Delegati Ordinum e Frisia Bruxellas cum magna festinatione missi, quo stante adhuc Concilij Status imperio, expedita remedia malis moribus aut collapsis rebus peterentur. Quippe Austriacus, etsi in speciem pacis venisset, a restituendo provinciarum jure alienus credebatur, nondum Principis potestatem libertati iniquam prolatis jurisjurandi solemnibus induisse. Postulata Legatorum haec fuere.
units.tr: So the delegates were dismissed and set off for Lalaing. Soon afterwards, delegates of the Orders were sent in great haste from Friesland to Brussels, so that while the authority of the Council of State still stood, remedies might be sought for the bad conduct of the times and the collapsed state of affairs. For the Austrian, although he had come in the appearance of peace, was believed to be unwilling to restore the rights of the provinces, since he had not yet taken the solemn oaths that would bind him to the Prince's power hostile to liberty. The delegates' demands were these.

units.la: Ut Lalainio provinciam redituro e dignioribus gentis adjungerentur, quorum consiliis uteretur. Episcopus dignitate cederet caenobiaque & sacri reditus ad eos redirent a quibus processissent. Idem Episcopus census Ecclesiasticici rationes, mobilium vero bonorum & repertae per Caenobia suppellectilis inventarium exhiberet. De multis, quas in praejudicium regii juris privatis ac Menenitis extorsisset; similiter responderet. Officiarij contra consuetudinem juris patrii per Hispanos & eorum Praefectos constituti muneribus privarentur novisque de arbitrio Praefecti & SENATUS ORDINUM surrogarentur. Tribuni aerariorum Roblesianis temporibus creati, reddendis rationibus citarentur. Idem Thesaurarius regius de bonis fisco acquisitis coram Ordinibus Frisiae praestaret, quo tognoscant, quantum regio aerario allevandis provincialium tributis accesserit. Magistratibus per oppida constitutis imperium abrogaretur populusque civicus, delectu e suo corpore facto, suo bono novos crearet. His deductis per provinciam fossis aliisque aggerum & florenorum aureorum impendijs, addita nitioris imperij legem & simul levamenta onerum poscebant.
units.tr: That some of the more distinguished men of the nation be joined to Lalaing when he returns to the province, so that he might use their counsel. The bishop should give up his dignity, and the monasteries and sacred revenues should return to those from whom they had been taken. The same bishop should present an account of the ecclesiastical revenues, and an inventory of the movable goods and furnishings found in the monasteries. He should likewise answer for the many things he had extorted to the prejudice of royal right, and of private persons and the Menists. Officials appointed by the Spaniards and their prefects, contrary to the custom of the native law, should be deprived of their offices, and new ones put in their place at the discretion of the prefect and the Council of the Orders. The treasurers of the taxes appointed in Roblesian times should be summoned to render their accounts. The royal treasurer should present, before the Orders of Friesland, an account of the goods acquired for the fisc, so that they might learn how much had been added to the royal treasury from the provincial taxes. The magistrates set up in the towns should have their authority revoked, and the civic people, having chosen from their own body, should create new magistrates for their own good. With these things done, along with the ditches dug through the province and the other outlays on dikes and gold florins, they demanded that a milder law of government be added and that the burdens be relieved.

units.la: Caeterum an Legatorum postulatis rescriptum Bruxellis sit, in indigestis illorum temporum actis non reperio. Dolendum certe est, ea gentis nostrae & eruditorum, qui tum claruere, socordia nostrae libertatis initia certioribus actis non inserta, nisi praeclara forte ingenia dubijs incertisque temporum inquies & sine justo otio vita, tum magni Regis ac rediturae per arma servitutis timor a scribendi officio retraxit. Igitur ingravescentibus in Austriacum suspicionibus & ne corpus Gandavensi foedere colligatum paucorum facilitate aut discordia divelleretur, valida apud quosdam Austraci gratia & quod Imperatorium regiumque sanguinem suis natalibus praeferret, novum inter se Foedus Ordines concivere, celerato negotio, quod defectus habere ac exercitum parare omen instantis belli, Joannes Austriacus, nec vanis rumoribus, diceretur. Eo cautum erat.
units.tr: Whether a reply was sent from Brussels to the delegates' demands, I cannot find in the disordered records of those times. It is certainly regrettable that the carelessness of our nation and of the learned men who then flourished failed to enter the beginnings of our liberty in more reliable records. Perhaps only outstanding talents, drawn back from the duty of writing by the doubtful and uncertain unrest of the times, a life without proper leisure, and the fear of the great King and of a servitude that would return by arms. Therefore, as suspicions of the Austrian grew, and lest the body bound together by the Treaty of Ghent be torn apart by the ease or discord of a few, and because the Austrian enjoyed strong favour with some and put his imperial and royal blood before his birth, the Orders quickly brought about a new covenant among themselves. The business was hastened, since it was said that the defects and the army being raised were an omen of the war at hand, which John of Austria was preparing, and not mere empty rumours. Provision was made against this.

units.la: Ut idipsum Foedus perpetuum stabile atque firmum esset Romanaque Catholica Religio, Gaudavensis conventio, statuta, jura, immunitates ac consuetudines provinciarum integrae inviolataeque manerent, Hispanisque & earum op-prespressionibus communia arma, vires atque subsidia opponerentur. Desciscentes quoque ab eo ipso Fœdere amissio juris, status, famæ atque dignitatum sequeretur beneficiumque restitutionis in integrum tanquam hosti publico, exlegi & famoso nullum esset.
units.tr: That this same covenant should be perpetual, stable and firm; that the Roman Catholic religion, the Treaty of Ghent, the statutes, rights, immunities and customs of the provinces should remain whole and inviolate; and that common arms, forces and aid should be set against the Spaniards and their oppressions. Those who deserted from this very covenant would also suffer the loss of right, status, reputation and dignities, and the benefit of restoration to its former state would not be available to them, as to a public enemy, an outlaw and an infamous man.

units.la: Cujus tabulæ à Concilio Status, Ordinibus generalibus, manu Cornelij Wellemanni perscriptæ ac Senatui per Frisiam regio transmissæ, in acta relatæ vim atque efficaciam accepere. Itaque ab Antistitum ordine, tum ipso quoque Præfecto ac Senatu regio signata, subscriptionibus Magistratuum, Officialium & Collegiorum, mox invaluere, non dissimulantibus Pontificijs, novorum fœderum sanctionibus externæ dominationis potentiam subverti.
units.tr: The instruments of this covenant, drawn up by Cornelius Wellemann at the instruction of the General Orders and the Council of State, and sent to the royal Senate in Friesland, were entered in the acts and received their force and efficacy. Accordingly they were signed by the order of bishops, then by the prefect himself and the royal Senate, and with the subscriptions of magistrates, officials and colleges they soon gained strength. The Papists did not conceal that by the sanctions of these new covenants the power of foreign domination was being overthrown.

units.la: Igitur Lalainius, necdum sedatâ cohortium inquietudine, Mathenesium, Oyenbruggiumque Legatos cum fiduciarijs litteris in Frisiam remisit; quibus ducenta & triginta carolæorum millia, pacandis præsidijs, poscebantur.
units.tr: Therefore Lalaing, the unrest of the cohorts not yet calmed, sent back to Friesland the legates of Mathenesse and Oyenbrugge with letters of trust. By these, two hundred and thirty thousand carolus were demanded for pacifying the garrisons.

units.la: Quippe rationes æris jam initas proponebat metuendumque esse, ut Groningense præsidium mobile & turbidum in majorem Frisiam se effundat cæterisque copijs, quas dubia fides contineret, sociatum, non abstineat alieno. Adhuc vero discretas locis cohortes & ciendis seditionibus minus validas, placari stipendijs posse, modo intra præfinitum solutioni tempus præstentur, ne ex mora major militum egestas & ex ea insolentia nascatur. Decernendum esse patribus (Ordines designo) ocyus & seponendas veteres controversias ac de jure partium disceptationes pendendumque tributum collato potius ære parandum. Abrumpendam semel consiliorum tarditatem & exuenda vitia gentis, nisi festinantius consulat in sua damna ituræ.
units.tr: For he now set out the accounts of the money already reckoned, and he feared that the Groningen garrison, restless and turbulent, would pour into Greater Friesland and, joined with the other troops whom doubtful loyalty held, would not keep its hands off what belonged to others. But the cohorts, still scattered over different places and less strong for stirring up sedition, could be quieted with pay, provided it was handed over within the fixed time of payment, lest from delay a greater want of soldiers and the insolence born of it should arise. The fathers (I mean the Orders) must decide quickly, and set aside old controversies and disputes over the rights of the parties, and the tax to be paid should rather be raised from money collected. The slowness of their counsels must be broken once and for all, and the vices of the nation laid aside, unless they consult more quickly, since they were about to go to their own ruin.

units.la: Potestas quoque Mathenesio, Oyenbruggioque Legatis facta Edictis Ordinum contumaces coërcendi corrigendique, ne ad exemplum præfracti & turbidi militis formatæ provincialium mentes reverentiam imperij & parendi disciplinam exuerent.
units.tr: The legates Mathenesse and Oyenbrugge were also given power to restrain and correct those who were disobedient to the edicts of the Orders, lest, following the example of a stubborn and turbulent soldier, the minds of the provincials, once formed that way, should cast off reverence for authority and the discipline of obedience.

units.la: Cæterum Delegati Ordinum etiam LXXX. millium grave tributum criminabantur relationibusque de ea ad populum, ex more, factis ulterioribus subsidijs se destitui. Adhæc actis per Frisiam præsidijs stipendia non convenire, pendenda ab ijs quorum tutelæ inservijssent. Sparsas per Omlandiam & finitima copias agrosque incursionibus prædonum expositos justis sæpè præsidijs destitutos fuisse. Oppidanos quoque & Biltanum populum ijsdem tributi aut præstandi subsidij legibus subesse æquumque haberi ut miles sacramentum regium professus regio censu alatur. Qui etsi peregrinis creditoribus pignori datus, ita cedere publico potius quam privato usui debebat. Sic è vestigalibus Biltanorum agrorum X L. millia restare & pendendam insuper Biltanis pensionem, stipendijs potius ac bono regis applicandam, quam instituendum novum per provinciam tributi genus, cui ferendo impar populus sit. His de creditis Roblesio pecunijs addebant dandumque operam, ut rationes stipendiorum certæ sint & ut cohortes, nullis imperijs obnoxiæ militari more recenseantur. Id disciplinæ vinculum fore, quod si non satis validum retinendis in fide cohortibus sit, facturos ut majora subsidia ijsdem pacandis decernantur. Respirandum interim semel inopi populo esse & tot malis exhausto, cujus bono id quoque patiscencifcendum fit, ut Valonum Germanorumque præfidiarÿ nomina profiteantur ac-ceptisque stipendÿs oppidis arcibusque excedant. Neque velle, ut sine Ordinum Frisiæ assensu ulli in posterum delectus fiant aut ut præsidia in provinciam ducantur & ut ejus firma cautio sit. Obtestari interim ac rogare Lalainium, ut quicquid Frisios inter Groningenses & Omlandos, ex inæqualitate tributi controversum sit, componat otyus detque effectum, ut ulterioribus minis miles abstineat, justis stipendÿs & certo ære placandus.
units.tr: Moreover, the delegates of the Orders also complained of the heavy tax of eighty thousand, and, as is customary, in their reports to the people they stated that they were being deprived of further aid. Besides, the garrisons placed throughout Friesland did not match their pay, which ought to be paid by those whose protection they served. The troops scattered through Omland and the neighbouring areas, and the fields exposed to the raids of plunderers, had often been left without proper garrisons. The townsmen and the people of Bildt were also subject to the same laws of taxation or of furnishing aid, and it was held fair that a soldier who had taken the royal oath should be maintained from the royal revenue. Though the revenues had been given as security to foreign creditors, they ought to be applied to public rather than private use. Thus forty thousand remained from the revenues of the Bildt lands, and the rent still owed to the Bildt people should be applied to the pay and the king's good, rather than introducing a new kind of tax throughout the province, which the people could not bear. To these sums borrowed from Roblesius they added that care be taken that the accounts of pay be certain, and that the cohorts, subject to no commands, be enrolled in the military manner. This would be the bond of discipline; but if it were not strong enough to keep the cohorts in loyalty, they would see to it that greater aid was decreed to pacify them. Meanwhile, the needy people, exhausted by so many evils, must at last be allowed to draw breath, and for their good it must also be enforced that the Walloon and German garrisons declare their names and, having received their pay, withdraw from the towns and citadels. They did not wish any levies to be made in future without the consent of the Orders of Friesland, nor garrisons to be led into the province, and they wanted a firm guarantee of this. Meanwhile they begged and asked Lalaing to settle quickly whatever dispute there was between the Frisians, the Groningers and the Omlanders over unequal taxation, and to see to it that the soldier refrain from further threats, to be placated by just pay and sure money.

units.la: Hæc Gerardus Jacobi Præsul Clarecampensis, Doco Martna, Hero Ockinga, Bocatius Ilstij, Renicus Cammingha, D. Fogelsangus, Barthius Idzaerda, F. Tatmannus rescripserunt.
units.tr: These things were replied by Gerard Jacobi, bishop of Klarenkamp, Doco Martna, Hero Ockinga, Bocatius of Ilst, Renicus Cammingha, D. Fogelsang, Barthius Idzaerda and F. Tatmann.

units.la: Cæterum Lalainius, inter angustias fortunæ, decreti retinens postulatis institit totumque negotium se Mathenessio Oyenbruggioque Legatis permisisse v. Kal. Mart. rescripsit, factuum interim ut æqualibus tributorum portionibus provinciæ habeantur. Quod ad reprimendas co-hortium criminationes attineret, eas compescere non posse, præterquam adacto ad sacramentum milite, & qui autorari non nisi exsoluto ære queat. Hoc solo præveniri malis impendentibus & sanari sedi-tiones posse, in quas si tacita inquietudo & secretum murmur erum-pat, id non sibi cæterum intestinis discordijs & contumaciæ Delegatorum Frisiæ imputandum. Quamobrem Deputati spectatâ periculi mole & ne, ultro lubricæ res, novis dissidijs convellerentur, omne paratum æs, quod aut ærarijs provinciæ asservaretur, aut à vectigalibus Biltæ agris petendum restaret, assignandum Legatis censuerunt, cum hac ob-testatione Deo coram, Concilio Status & Ordinibus generalibus ulti-mam necessitatem hoc decretum patriæ amantibus extorsisse. Ita x. Kal. Mart. à Delegatis Ordinum Frisiæ rescriptum, ac Pauli Cofterij Antistitis Fofverdici, Scipionis Meckamæ, Oedzij Arnoldij, pro Oftergois, Everardi Ludolphi, Livij Beiemi, & Dirici Fogelsangij, pro Westergois, Auconis Edonij, Feiconis Tatmanni & Joannis Agricolæ pro Sylvestribus subscriptionibus signatum actisque publicis inser-tum. Quo rescripto, ut Legatis Lalainij non satis siebat, ita Delegati Ordinum pertinacia legatorum & angustia rerum inritati de mittendis denuo ad Ordines provinciarum Legatis consultavere. Mox regij præsidij, quod arci apud Leovardios impositum erat, recensio habita, urgentibus Mathenessio Oyenbruggioque Legatis , lustratis copijs & nomina professis ab Herone Burmania ærarij tribuno stipendi-um præstandum. Is vero acti conventus & diuturnæ disceptationis eventus fuit, ut agrorum oppidorumque delegati publicæ pacis ac secu-ritatis studio inter se convenirent exsolvendisque militum externorum stipendijs ducenta & quinquaginta aureorum millia Legatis addicerent. Notat vir consularis F. Nicolaus Stauriam urbem isti tributo mille, & quingentos carolæos dependisse civesque oppidanos insolentiâ præsidiorum & fœdis exactionibus aut attritos, cum ultimo malo tanquam va-lidiore expostulasse.
units.tr: Lalaing, however, amid the straits of his fortune, held to the decree while keeping the demands, and wrote on 1 March that he had left the whole business to the legates Mathenesse and Oyenbrugge, meanwhile arranging that the province be assessed in equal portions of taxes. As for checking the complaints against the cohorts, he said he could not restrain them except by binding the soldier with an oath, and that he could not be enrolled unless the money was paid. By this alone, he said, could impending evils be averted and seditions healed; if silent unrest and secret murmuring broke out into them, that was to be imputed not to him but to the internal discord and obstinacy of the Frisian delegates. Wherefore the deputies, mindful of the weight of the danger, and lest the already slippery affairs be shaken by new dissensions, decided to assign to the legates all the ready money that was either kept in the provincial treasuries or still had to be sought from the revenues of the Bildt lands. They added this solemn protestation, before God, the Council of State and the General Orders: that the final necessity had extorted this decree from those who love their country. So on 20 February a reply was made by the delegates of the Frisian Orders, and it was signed by Paulus Costerius, bishop of Fosverdum, Scipio Meckama, Oedzius Arnoldi for Oostergo, Everard Ludolph, Livius Beiemus and Dirk Fogelsang for Westergo, and Aucon Edo, Feico Tatmann and John Agricola for the Sylvestrine lands, and it was entered in the public acts. As this reply did not satisfy Lalaing's legates, so the delegates of the Orders, irritated by the obstinacy of the legates and the straitened state of affairs, took counsel about sending legates again to the Orders of the provinces. Soon afterwards a muster was held of the royal garrison placed in the citadel at Leeuwarden, with the legates Mathenesse and Oyenbrugge pressing for it; the troops were reviewed, their names declared, and pay was to be made by Heron Burmania, treasurer of the revenue. The outcome of this assembly and long debate was that the delegates of the lands and towns, out of zeal for public peace and security, came to an agreement among themselves and assigned to the legates two hundred and fifty thousand gold florins for paying the wages of the foreign soldiers. The consular man F. Nicolaus notes that the city of Stavoren paid fifteen hundred carolus of this tax, and that the townsmen, worn down by the insolence of the garrisons and foul exactions, complained of it as a greater evil.

units.la: Sic fluentibus per Frisiam rebus Translavicanæ quoque provinciæ sta-tum Lalainius ordinavit Delphzylanæque munitioni , quam Starckius tribunus cum imperio & cohorte tenuerat , aliud præsidium imposuit. Ære quoque Groningæ urbi , Omlandiæ & Drenthiæ provincialibus extorextorto stipendia copijs assignavit easdemque Groningâ urbe excedere cla. Iv. jussas in majores Frisios, dein Brabantiam expedire conatus est. Cl. lxxxvii. Franckena Idibus Martijs factum tradit. Post decreto Ordinum generalium arcem Groningam, cujus molem Gasparus Roblefius munien- dæ dominationi struxerat, æquari solo fecit. Itaque vacuâ præsidio civitate & castello diruto læti cives & in immodesta effusi prima gaudia in lafciviem proterviamque vertêre. Scribunt autores temulentos & socordes collucentibus passim per civitatem ignibus, Martinianæ turri incendium dedisse ipsosque exules, sive tantæ & recenter partæ fœlicitatis incapaces, sive tædiorum exilij oblitos, non votis, non gratijs numini actis, cæterum immodestis moribus & profano ritu lætiora temporum egisse. Adeo mortales adversa toleramus, prosperis corrumpimur.
units.tr: With affairs thus flowing in Friesland, Lalainius also set up the government of the Trans-Vlie province and placed another garrison in the fort at Delfzijl, which the tribune Starckius had held with his command and a cohort. He also raised money by extortion from the provincial estates of Groningen, Ommelanden and Drenthe, assigned it to his troops, and ordered them to leave the city of Groningen [Cl. Iv.] and go to the Greater Frisians; after that he tried to lead them into Brabant. Franckena reports that this happened on the Ides of March [Cl. lxxxvii]. Afterwards, by decree of the General Estates, he had the citadel of Groningen, whose bulwark Gaspar Robles had built to secure his rule, levelled to the ground. So the city was emptied of its garrison and the castle was torn down, and the citizens, glad and unrestrained, turned their first joys into wantonness and insolence. Authors write that, drunk and careless, with bonfires blazing here and there through the city, they set fire to the Martin tower. They themselves, exiles, either unequal to such and so recently gained good fortune or forgetful of the miseries of exile, gave no thanks and offered no prayers to God; instead, with licentious manners and profane rites, they spent the times in greater rejoicing. So much do we endure adversity, and so much are we corrupted by prosperity.

units.la: Mox Lalainius, compositis Groningæ & per Omlandiam rebus, Kal. Mart. magno procerum comitatu Leovardiam contendit provinciamque majoris Frisiæ suo imperio destinatam magno multitudinis applausu ingressus est. Quippe occultata jam ante servilibus temporibus desideria libertatis tum erumpebant quantoque magis ex iniquitate priorum temporum repressa, tanto patentius laxiusque nullâ dissimulatione aut metu aperiebantur. Ferunt pulcherrimas virgines civium filias, multo cultu obvias Lalainio processisse cohortesque civicas erectis signis & urbem ingredienti, velut præsidio stantes, præfervidis in Præsectum officijs certasse. Tormenta quoque continuis fragoribus laxata M. Heymannus annotavit sexumq ue imbellem totâ urbe discurrentem publicam festivitatem suis ludicris auxisse. Quæ ultro speciosa perosam anteacta servitia multitudinem eo vehementius commovebant, quod captivorum agmen secum Lalainius traheret Roblefiumque modo provinciæ rectorem & ut insimulabant, dominationis immodicum, cum Joanne filio & Ruysbroeckio filiæ marito, velut ludibria & spectacula fortunæ ostentaret. Itaque eorum adversis à populo illusum, qui secundis rebus malè usi & potentiæ suæ modum & fallacem fortunæ memoriam exuerant. Cohortium quoque tribuni, in quibus Lopesius, Lussius, Villerius, Starckius, Campius & Montioius erant, unà cum Roblefio Leovardiam duƈti, custodiæque in arce regiâ (ubi Roblefij conjunx asservabatur) dati, exercitæ insolentiæ pœnas dedere. Tradit Heymannus Roblefium declinandæ contumeliæ, & inrisui civium secretiore viâ ac tormentariam per turrim arcem ingressum, magno fortunæ ludicro, ut ante imperij sui munimentum, ita tum carceris & custodiæ lustrasse.
units.tr: Soon Lalainius, having settled affairs in Groningen and throughout the Ommelanden, set out on 1 March with a large retinue of nobles for Leeuwarden and entered the province of Greater Friesland, assigned to his rule, to great applause from the crowd. Indeed, the desire for liberty, which had been hidden during the servile times, now burst forth, and the more it had been repressed by the injustice of the earlier times, the more openly and freely it showed itself, without any pretence or fear. They report that the most beautiful maidens, daughters of citizens, went out to meet Lalainius in fine attire, and that the civic companies, with their standards raised, stood as a guard for him as he entered the city and vied with one another in their fervent services to the Governor. Heymannus noted that the cannon too, fired in continuous salvos, and the unarmed crowd of both sexes running about the whole city, added to the public festivity with their sport. These things, welcome in themselves, stirred the multitude, weary of past servitude, all the more vehemently, because Lalainius was dragging with him a train of captives: Robles, lately the governor of the province and, as they accused him, of immoderate tyranny, together with John, his son, and Ruysbroeck, the husband of his daughter, he displayed as playthings and spectacles of fortune. So they were mocked by the people in their misfortunes, since they had used prosperity badly and had cast off both the measure of their power and the deceptive memory of fortune. The tribunes of the cohorts too, among whom were Lopez, Lussius, Villerius, Starckius, Campius and Montigny, were led to Leeuwarden together with Robles and placed in custody in the royal castle (where Robles's wife was kept), and they paid the penalty of their insolence. Heymannus relates that Robles, to avoid the insult and the derision of the citizens, entered the castle by a more secret route and through the tower of the artillery, and that, as a great jest of fortune, he surveyed the place of his imprisonment and custody just as he had once surveyed the fortifications of his rule.

units.la: Itaque novo Ordinum generalium Fœdere scripto & per omnem provinciam promulgato Joannes Austriacus eorum, quæ evenerant, haud ignarus, acerbioribus in fœderatos odijs exarsit, dissimulato vix ingenio, quod suspeƈtis artibus negotium pacis trahebat. Quippe Fœderis formulâ ad eum missa, nova inritamenta vigenti discordiæ ex decretis procerum voluntatibus nata, commeante adhoc per internuntios sermonum acerbitate, quâ gliscentibus ultro odijs turbamenta paci substernebantur. Non ferentibus cordatioribus inter sana & moderata patrum consilia ab Austriaco muniementa urbium & præsidia legicum ad custodiam corporis peti, nexumque infœlicis concordiæ & tancIↄ. Iↄ. tantarum rerum ac sperataé pacis exordia fidei armorum committi.
units.tr: Therefore, when a new written treaty of the General Estates had been published throughout the whole province, John of Austria, not ignorant of what had happened, flared up with ever more bitter hatred against the confederates, his temper scarcely disguised, since he was dragging out the business of peace with suspect arts. For when the form of the treaty was sent to him, new incitements to the existing discord arose from the wishes of the nobles' decrees, and bitter words passed back and forth through intermediaries, by which, as hatreds grew of their own accord, obstacles were laid in the way of peace. The more judicious men, among the sound and moderate counsels of the fathers, did not bear it when Austria sought the fortifications of the cities and the garrisons of the legions for the protection of his person, and that the bond of unhappy concord and the beginnings of such great affairs and of the hoped-for peace should be entrusted to the faith of arms.

units.la: Unde infidis partium animis diu disceptatum, donec Rudolphi Caesaris legatione, cujus à morte Maximiliani patris spem fecerat, commeantibus modo ad Ordines, modo ad Austriacum Legatis Marchae in Faminis sanciendae paci conventus ac dies diceretur. In Legatis Imperij Gerardus Groisbecius Leodiensium Episcopus, Philippus Baro Winenbergius aulae Caesareae praefectus, Andreas Gail Consiliarius, Wernerus Gemnichius Satrapa Juliacensis & Joannes Lovermannus fuere. Ordinum vero partes, Matthias Gislenius Episcopus Attrebas, Bucho Ayta Frisius Archidiaconus Iprensis, Fredericus Perennotus, Baro Ronsaeus, Joannes Ommerius Morbequij Dominus, Franciscus Halevinius Equestris ordinis & Adolphus Meetkerckius tuebantur.
units.tr: Hence the minds of the factions, faithless to one another, disputed for a long time, until, through the embassy of the Emperor Rudolph, from whose death, that of his father Maximilian, he had given hope, while envoys went back and forth now to the Estates, now to Austria, a meeting and a day were appointed in Marche in Famenne for sanctioning the peace. On the side of the Empire were Gerard Groesbeeck, bishop of Liège, Philip Baron Winneburg, prefect of the imperial court, Andreas Gail, counsellor, Werner Gemmingen, governor of Jülich, and John Lauwerman. On the side of the Estates were Matthias Gillis, bishop of Arras, Bucho Aytta, a Frisian, archdeacon of Ypres, Frederick Perrenot, Baron Ronsau, John Ommeren, lord of Morbeke, Francis Halewijn of the equestrian order, and Adolf Meetkerke.

units.la: Hoc vero maxime illo conventu & cum vehementiâ repetebat Austriacus, ut peregrinae Legiones non terrestri, caeterum maritimo itinere Belgicâ excederent classemque & simul latum mare ingressae expeditâ profectione in Hispaniae continentem aut Celtiberiae portum exponerentur. Ordinum vero Caesarisq; legatis, ut omnes Austriaci actiones, ita haec maxime secretis rerum momentis decerni videbatur.
units.tr: Austria, however, most of all at that meeting and with great vehemence, demanded that the foreign legions should leave Belgium not by the land route but by sea, and that, once they had entered the fleet and the open sea, they should be set down by a swift voyage on the mainland of Spain or on a port of Celtiberia. Yet it seemed that this matter, like all of Austria's actions, was to be decided by the Estates and the legates of the Emperor and the Empire in the most secret deliberations.

units.la: Quippe reputabant populum olim colonias transferentem sic aliena occupasse latoque & diffuso mari commissum, commoda littora & commodas sedes quaesiisse. Ambitiosis & nova regna somniantibus etiam hanc aetatem temporum non vacare & esse quos aliarum gentium quies aut securitas sollicitet. Sic Angliae regnum Belgico littori oppositum ab Elisabethâ reginâ nullo metu & in pace teneri, tanto magis periculis obnoxium quanto Belgicae vicinius & ex se quietius foret. Posse instructam veterano milite & tot legionibus classem in Britannicum littus adigi aut in latos portus subduci bellumque & discrimen Elisabethae facessere, nulla arma, nullas gentium irruptiones metuenti.
units.tr: For they reasoned that the people, who once sent out colonies, had thus seized the lands of others, and that, having entrusted themselves to the wide and far-spreading sea, they had sought out convenient shores and convenient seats. Nor, they said, was this age free of men ambitious and dreaming of new kingdoms; there were those whom the peace and security of other nations troubled. Thus the kingdom of England, lying opposite the Belgian shore, was held by Queen Elizabeth without any fear and in peace, and was all the more exposed to dangers the nearer it was to Belgium and the more quiet in itself. A fleet furnished with veteran soldiers and so many legions could be driven onto the British shore or drawn into its broad harbours, and bring war and peril upon Elizabeth, who feared no arms and no invasions of foreign peoples.

units.la: Cujus rei suspicionem non falsus & ex Peresio Philippo Regi à Secretis auditus rumor quam maximè praegravabat, quod Austriacus Tunetani regni spe amissâ, de deturbandâ Angliae possessione Elisabethâ cogitaret primisque juventae amoribus Mariam Scotorum reginam & cum ejus velut dote Britannicarum insularum imperium immodesta ambitione deperiret. Neque enim frustra Romani Pontificis decretum, Guisiorum per Galliam & Lotharingos auxilia orasse, ac ut Philippus frater, morte Mariae uxoris Angliae regno exutus, ad redintegrandum cum Elisabetha odium & ex eo bellum in spem recuperandi regni incitaretur. Inde missum è Belgica in Hispaniam Escovedum, hominem vafrum & secretorum participem, qui portum in Cantabria instruendae classi Philippum peteret Angliaeq; invadendae consilium Philippo Regi commendaret. Autores tradunt, Austriacum praeoccupandae Manniae Hybernici maris insulae omnem apparatum destinasse profugorumque Anglorum, tum per Nortvalliam, Cumbriam Ceftriamque Pontificiorum auxilijs adjutum, occupandi Anglorum regni firmam spem aluisse. Quare amoris pacis aut foederum impedimentis Legati definiere:
units.tr: Suspicion of this matter was greatly strengthened by a rumour, not false, heard from Perez by Philip the King's secretary, namely that Austria, having lost hope of the kingdom of Tunis, was thinking of driving Elizabeth from possession of England, and that with immoderate ambition he was pining, in the first passions of his youth, for Mary, queen of the Scots, and with her, as it were, as a dowry, for the empire of the British islands. Nor was it in vain that the Roman Pontiff's decree and the Guises' appeal for aid through France and Lorraine were made, and that Philip, his brother, stripped of the kingdom of England by the death of his wife Mary, was to be stirred to renew hatred against Elizabeth and from that, war, in hope of recovering the kingdom. From Belgium Escovedo, a shrewd man and a sharer in secrets, was therefore sent into Spain, to ask Philip for a port in Cantabria to equip a fleet and to commend to King Philip the plan of invading England. Authors relate that Austria had prepared every equipment for seizing the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, and, aided by the forces of the English exiles, and then of the Papists in Northumberland, Cumberland and Cheshire, he nourished the firm hope of seizing the kingdom of England. Therefore the envoys defined the conditions for love of peace and the removal of obstacles to the treaties:

units.la: Ut omnes injuriae & offensiones cessarent foederique jam ante Gandavi illo robur esset. Peregrinus miles (quo Hispani, Itali, Germani, Burgundiones nes censebantur) acceptis stipendijs, nullo commeatu, Belgicæ provincijs intrà cIↄ. Iↄ. vigesimum diem excederet sontesque & seditionum rei militari lege punirentur. LXXVII. Captivis utrinque venia esset Comesque Buranus, quam primum Ordinibus generalibus ab Aurantio satisfactum esset, in Belgicam remitteretur. Lapsis aut dignitate exutis per Ordines Generales aut cujusque Provinciæ Senatum jus diceretur. Privilegia, jura, immunitates integræ essent. Religio Catholica Romana per provincias haberetur. Ordines omni externo fœderi renuntiarent exautorandoque militi pecuniam cæterasque res, Germaniæ vero legionibus seorsim stipendia ex æquo præstarent. Rex Philippus peregrinas copias nullo tempore in provinciis induceret. Joannem Austiacum Gubernatorem acciperent. Præfecti provinciarum sacramentum provincijs dicerent. Pensiones ab Ordinibus generalibus privatis assignatæ efficaces forent tabulæque signarentur.
units.tr: That all injuries and offences should cease, and that the treaty already made at Ghent should be given force. That foreign soldiers (among whom Spaniards, Italians, Germans and Burgundians were counted), having received their pay, without any supplies, should leave the provinces of Belgium within twenty days, and that the guilty and those responsible for mutinies should be punished by military law. (1) That captives on both sides should be pardoned; and (2) that Count Buren should be sent back to Belgium as soon as satisfaction had been made to the General Estates by Orange. That those who had fallen or been stripped of their dignity should be judged by the General Estates or by the Senate of each province. That privileges, rights and immunities should remain entire. That the Roman Catholic religion should be maintained throughout the provinces. That the Estates should renounce every foreign alliance, and should pay the discharged soldiers their money and other dues, while for the German legions they should pay separately an equal sum. That King Philip should at no time bring foreign forces into the provinces. That they should accept John of Austria as Governor. That the prefects of the provinces should swear the oath to the provinces. That the pensions assigned by the General Estates to private persons should be made effective, and that the tablets should be sealed.

units.la: Quibus à Joanne Austriaco, Concilio Status ac Ordinibus generalibus, tum Legatis Cæsaris ac Imperij approbatis, certæ pacis augurria dubijs ante mentibus se intorsere. Quippe earum fiduciæ hoc etiam accedebat, quod perpetui Edicti vocabulum isti conventioni à Philippo Rege impositum esset publicarique per omnem provinciam jussum, nec in dies aut annos scriptum memoriæ ultimi temporis & longissimæ rerum ætati adæquaretur. Scribit Cl. Franckena Joannem Austriacum, cum Luxemburgum venisset, Prid. Eid. Febr. ficto pacto se Ordinibus obligasse idemque pactum, etsi dubiæ fidei, XIII Kal. Mart. per Frisios vulgatum populi animos magno gaudio implevisse. Alij tradunt Joannem Austriacum validis Ordinum rebus & per Germaniam, Galliam atque Angliam societatibus, quo acre odium fallacibus blanditijs velaret, externa pacis & firmandi Perpetui Edicti desideria etiam apud exteros Principes prætulisse, ita formatis ex arte simulationibus, velut bellum ex prædecessorum intempestivo dominatu natum, clausurus pace, tanquam egregio fine, etiam primâ imperij sui ætate, videretur. Itaque ab Elisabethâ & per Ordines generales pro approbando Edicto apud Aurantium intercessum, ne armis libertatem obtendens, probatam vicinis innocentiam, interruptâ provinciarum pace, suspicione alitæ dissensionis foedaret.
units.tr: When these were approved by John of Austria, the Council of State and the General Estates, and also by the legates of the Emperor and the Empire, auguries of a sure peace presented themselves to minds that had been doubtful before. To this confidence was added the fact that the name of a perpetual Edict had been imposed upon that agreement by King Philip, and it had been ordered to be published throughout the whole province, and it was not to be measured by days or years, but written to match the memory of the latest times and the longest age of affairs. Franckena writes that John of Austria, when he had come to Luxembourg on 12 February, bound himself to the Estates by a pretended pact, and that the same pact, though of doubtful good faith, filled the minds of the people with great joy when it was spread among the Frisians on 17 February. Others relate that John of Austria, relying on the strong position of the Estates and on alliances through Germany, France and England, put forward the desire for peace and for confirming the perpetual Edict even before foreign princes, so that he might veil his bitter hatred with deceitful flatteries; with pretences shaped by art, he seemed, even in the first age of his rule, as if he would end the war, born from the ill-timed dominion of his predecessors, with peace as a noble goal. Thus Elizabeth, and through the General Estates, intervened with Orange for the approval of the Edict, lest, while holding arms in the name of liberty, he should stain the innocence proven to his neighbours and nourish suspicion of discord, the peace of the provinces having been broken.

units.la: Quæ ideo tanto acrioribus studijs urgebantur, quod Auftriacus, præoccupatis Principum animis, affectum pacis præferret suaeque imbecillitatis, ex conditione temporum, æstumator, afformaturus imperium arbitrijs patrum crederetur. Sed suspectum ingenium & ex superbiâ vecors, quod melioribus artibus instrui posse sagacissimi quique desperabant, minuendæ plurimum fiduciæ erat, credentibus adhoc prudentioribus tantæ moli regundæ incapacem juventam sanioribus consilijs non cessuram. Ita scilicet affectis Principum ingenijs, ut omnia facilè ad se trahant reputentque societatem generis humani multitudine extendi, imperia per consortes arctari. Itaque tanto indecentius moderamini rerum ipsum præsuturum, si pluribus administris uteretur Principisque nomen retinendo, vim ac respectum amitteret. Quæ ut callidè ex ingenio Austriaci patribus dissererentur, ita hoc maxime secretorum conscios urebat, quod Mariæ captivæ Scotorum Reginæ, nuptias cIↄ. Io ptias tum importunius ambiret clandestinosq; in foeminam amores, et- lxxvii. iam mariti sui cædis jam ante suspectam, novandis per Angliam & vicina rebus obtenderet.
units.tr: These matters were pressed all the more eagerly because the Austrian, having first won over the minds of the princes, was thought to prefer the wish for peace and, judging his own weakness from the state of the times, was believed about to shape the empire by the counsels of the elders. But his temper was suspicious and reckless from arrogance, and the wisest men despaired of training it by better arts, so there was great reason to lessen confidence in him. The more prudent believed that a youth unfit to govern so great a burden would not give way to sounder counsels. Clearly princes of such a disposition draw everything to themselves and reckon that the society of mankind is widened by numbers and that empires are narrowed by partners. He would therefore preside over the management of affairs all the more unbecomingly if he used many ministers and, while keeping the name of prince, lost his power and authority. These arguments were skilfully set out among the elders in the Austrian's manner. What most inflamed those privy to the secrets was that he was then pressing more urgently for the marriage of Mary, captive queen of the Scots, and under the pretext of it was secretly courting a woman, while his earlier suspected role in her husband's murder was already known, to upset affairs in England and the neighbouring countries.

units.la: Quorum, etsi non fallax indicium Aurantius haberet, ita tota foederis Marchici ratio, velut obfuturα autoribus, displicebat. Quare auditis Ordinum generalium Legatis, qui innecti ijsdem pactis se & simul socios volebant, litteras ad eosdem Ordines dedit, quibus ut mentis suæ arcanum, ita vitiositatem conventionis & fallacium pactorum exponebat.
units.tr: Although Orange had no unreliable sign of these things, the whole plan of the March treaty displeased him, as if it would harm its authors. Therefore, having heard the envoys of the General States, who wished to bind him and his allies by the same pacts, he sent letters to the same States in which he disclosed, as the secret of his mind, the faultiness of the agreement and its deceitful terms.

units.la: Gratulari se quidem procuratæ per studia Ordinum paci & simul provinciis, quod jam ante superbis Hispanorum dominationibus obnoxiæ tot incommoda & furores concordiâ Fœderis vertissent. Latari assertas patriæ leges, Gandavensi Fœderi robur adscriptum, eximia fati ac temporum beneficia, nisi speciosis rerum vocabulis damnosæ & nutriendis simultatibus repertæ conditiones involverentur. Sic comitiorum jus, quod majorum fuisset, non parum arctatum, & Provinciarum Ordines novis & inauditis sacramentis inligatos. Philippum Buranum filium contra jus gentium & provinciæ illâ ætate, quæ privatum adhuc præstaret, in Hispaniam abductum, Belgicorum motuum pœnas longiore custodiâ luere. Totam scilicet conventionem ut dolosis involucris, ita inhonestis servilibusque conditionibus inniti, quarum turpitudinem delere nec vertigo temporum nec gloriosi posteri quirent. Indignaturi haud dubie, cum perfidâ Hispanorum gente, majorum sanguine & spoliis satiatâ, cum publico provinciarum hoste, in gratiam rediisse, commeatum & stipendia depactos. Spretas Elisabethae reginæ & Francisci Alenconii Andium Ducis intercessiones, quorum fuisset, ut bello auxilia, ita paci autoramentum commodare. Neque Hollandiæ aut Zelandiæ provinciis satis prospectum, neque eorum commodis, qui restitui in integrum debebant eaque recuperare quæ bello perdidissent. Paciscendum fuisse, ut castella diruerentur, servitutis publicæ & simul externæ dominationis vestigia, ac ut omnium offensionum perpetua oblivio esset. Agendum certè cautius & longiore cunctatione in eo negotio fuisse, quod exitium provinciis aut incolumitatem promitteret. Optare interim, ut quoniam Fœdus haud dubiè bono zelo & proturbandis Belgicâ peregrinis legionibus maturatum foret, ejus uberes fructus essent, neve Ordines pacem sperantes bellum ex improviso ferant. Hoc vero imprimis rogare, ut asserendo Gandavensium fœderi incumbant, certi & fidentes sua officia isti ratihabendo decerni. Quin paratum esse in societatem novissimi Fœderis condescendere, si externas legiones, ultra præstitutum commorantes, communibus armis proturbandas provinciis censeant, neque ante recipiendum Austriacum, quam juri publico, & Gandavensi Fœderi sit satisfactum.
units.tr: He indeed congratulated the States on the peace procured by their zeal and at the same time on behalf of the provinces, which had now turned so many troubles and furies, caused by the proud domination of the Spaniards, into concord through the Union. He rejoiced that the laws of the fatherland were asserted, that the Ghent Union was given its strength, and that the exceptional blessings of fate and of the times were granted, were it not that hurtful conditions, productive of enmities, were wrapped up in specious words. Thus the right of the assemblies, which had belonged to our ancestors, was considerably narrowed, and the Estates of the provinces were bound by new and unheard-of oaths. Philip of Buren, his son, was carried off to Spain contrary to the law of nations, while the province, still in that age a private person, paid the penalties of the Belgian disturbances by long imprisonment. The whole agreement, clearly, rested on deceitful wrappings and on dishonourable and servile conditions, whose disgrace neither the upheaval of the times nor glorious posterity would be able to wipe away. They would undoubtedly be indignant that, with the treacherous Spanish nation, glutted with the blood and spoils of their ancestors, and with the public enemy of the provinces, they had returned into favour, and that supplies and pay had been stipulated. The interventions of Queen Elizabeth and of Francis, Duke of Alençon, were spurned, although it was their part to lend aid to the war and also a guarantee to the peace. Provision had been made neither for the provinces of Holland and Zeeland nor for the interests of those who ought to be restored to their former state and recover what they had lost in the war. The terms ought to have been that the fortresses be razed, the traces of public slavery and of foreign domination removed, and that there be a perpetual oblivion of all offences. Certainly in that business there should have been more caution and longer hesitation, since it promised either ruin or safety to the provinces. Meanwhile they hoped that, since the Union had undoubtedly been hastened with good zeal and to drive out the foreign legions from Belgium, its fruits would be rich, and that the States, hoping for peace, would not suddenly bring on war. Above all they asked that the States stand firm for the Ghent Union, confident that their own services would be approved by ratifying it. Indeed they were ready to join the newest Union if the States judged that the foreign legions, remaining beyond the prescribed time, should be driven out of the provinces by common arms, and that the Austrian should not be received again before public law and the Ghent Union were satisfied.

units.la: Hæc Aurantius.
units.tr: Thus Orange.

units.la: Addit Æmylius Adama in libro Editorum Fœdus illud Marchicum actis per Frisiam publicis inlatum publicatumque per tribunalia conciliatarum partium spem proclivi in concordiam populo peperisse.
units.tr: Æmylius Adama adds, in his book of Editors, that this March treaty, brought into the public records of Friesland and published through the courts of the reconciled parties, gave the people a ready hope of concord.

units.la: Mox Sceltoni Tiardæ, Martino Nitzenio & Feiconi Tatmanno legatis Bruxellas ituris fiduciariæ & mandatorum litteræ procuratæ, quibus bus mutationem rerum per Frisiam velare publicis commodis & utili-tatibus provinciæ iubebantur.
units.tr: Soon after, letters of trust and instructions were drawn up for Sceltonus Tiarda, Martin Nitzen and Feico Tatman, the envoys about to go to Brussels, by which they were ordered to veil the change of affairs in Friesland under the public advantages and utilities of the province.

units.la: NIhil scilicet PHILIPPO regi, nihil patriæ legibus se detra-xisse, hoc tantum admixos, ut ad bellorum pertæsos miserto{que} carissimorum pignorum pax & quies & cum ijs levamentum tributi perveniret. De exactionibus & damnis per eandem inlatas jam ante conquestos, cum regij Præfecti & Senatus dominatione, specie retinendarum in fide cohortium, æraria provinciæ & privatorum facultates evisceratæ. Nunc ijsdem malis se remedia petere, eo inopiæ redactos, ut non nisi impetratâ onerum immunitate aut remissiore saltem tributo, stare res provinciæ queant. Interim Gandavense Fœdus per hos ipsos Legatos ampletti, caterum hac lege, ut modico tributo habeantur & ne novæ societatis ratione proventus ærarij & privatæ opes subvertantur. Hoc etiam rogare Ordines generales, ut petendi Comitij jus Deputatis Ordinum Frisiæ faciant, ne Senatus regij tergiversatione & pervicaciâ salubribus patriæ consiliis moræ & dilationes nectantur. Quippe Senatum regium communionem Gandavensis Fœderis poscentibus nuper restituisse pessimo exemplo, quo provinciales dissolutis cohortium moribus & violento Roblesij imperio subessent. Inde arces, castella & judicia peregrinis obsepta, convulsis conventionibus, quas cum Carolo Cæsare majores pepigissent. Nunc vero mutato non nihil temporum statu admovendos gerendis rebus indigetes, minuenda vectigalia, censum regium publicæ necessitati applicandum curandumq; imprimis, ut per Episcopum fœdius fere quam cæteri mortales, fluxis opibus inhiantem, doti suæ adjecta ad Antistites cænobiorum redeant ipseque per vim & silentibus legibus provinciæ obtrusus, fœdo & inaudito majoribus dominatu exuatur. Statuendum esse semel in eos asperius qui provinciæ patrimonium, munera aut dignitates pravis aut imperitis pro arbitrio locassent. Hoc modo Senatum regium præturas, satrapias, nullo delectu ijs largitum, quos dominationi suæ consortes conscientia pessimorum facinorum fecisset. Subveniendum semel justis populi Frisii querimonijs, quem aut grave dominantis imperium, aut insolens præsidium fatigasset. His de tributo quædam addita petitumque ut 5000. carolæorum à Biltanis collata in solutum proxumâ pensione cedant litteræque Ordinum generalium ad Antistites, Nobilitatem & Proprietarios agrorum, tanquam Ordines provinciæ, exclusis oppidanis, darentur.
units.tr: Nothing, of course, had been taken from King Philip or from the laws of the fatherland; they had only joined in this, so that peace and quiet, and with them some relief from taxes, might come to the men weary of wars and to their dearest pledges. They had earlier complained of the exactions and damages inflicted by the same, when under the domination of the royal Prefects and Senate, under the pretext of keeping the cohorts loyal, the treasury of the province and the private wealth had been drained. Now they sought remedies for these same evils, reduced to such want that affairs of the province could stand only if an exemption from burdens, or at least a milder tax, were obtained. Meanwhile they embraced the Ghent Union through these same envoys, but on this condition: that they be held to a modest tax and that by the terms of the new alliance the revenues of the treasury and private resources not be overturned. They also asked the General States to grant the Deputies of the Frisian Estates the right to ask for an assembly, so that the royal Senate's evasions and obstinacy might not bind delays and postponements to the healthy counsels of the fatherland. For the royal Senate had lately restored communion with the Ghent Union to those asking for it, to the worst example, by which the provincials, with the discipline of the cohorts dissolved and under the violent rule of Robles, were made subject. Hence fortresses, castles and courts were closed to foreigners, and the agreements which the greater men had made with Charles Caesar were overturned. But now, with the state of affairs somewhat changed, they should bring to bear on public business men of ability, reduce the taxes, and apply the royal revenue to public necessity; and above all take care that the Bishop, who, more greedily than other mortals, gapes after fleeting wealth, should have back what had been added to his dowry for the abbots of the monasteries, and that he himself, forced upon the province by violence and against its laws, be stripped of his domination, foul and unheard of compared with that of the ancestors. It must be decided once and for all that they should deal more harshly with those who had let out the province's property, offices or dignities to wicked or unskilled men at their pleasure. In this way the royal Senate had lavished praetorships and satrapies, with no selection, on those whom the consciousness of their worst crimes had made partners in its domination. Once and for all the just complaints of the Frisian people, whom either the heavy rule of the masters or the insolent garrison had worn down, must be answered. To these matters some additions were made regarding the tax, and it was asked that the 5000 Carolus guilders collected from the Bildts be credited in payment toward the next instalment, and that letters of the General States be given to the bishops, the nobility and the landed proprietors, as the Estates of the province, excluding the townsmen.

units.la: Hæc à Gerardo Iacobi Antistite Clarecampensi, Sixto Dekema, Livio Bejemo, Docone Martna, Erasmo Douma, Aucone Edonio Prid. Non. Mart. Leovardiæ perscripta, ac Legatis communicata. Tum in florenos aureos quatuordecim stuferi stipendijs militum decreti cautumque edicto, ut quicquid æris per vim aut minas in militem erogatum esset, ejus tabulæ minuendis eorum stipendijs ad Arnoldum Molckemannum Thesaurarium Ordinum Bruxellas mitterentur.
units.tr: These things were drawn up at Leeuwarden on the 26th of February by Gerard Jacobs, abbot of Klaarkamp, Sixtus Dekema, Livius Bejema, Doco Martna, Erasmus Douma and Aucko Edonius, and were communicated to the envoys. Then fourteen gold florins were voted, as a stuiver's worth for the soldiers' pay, and it was provided by edict that whatever money had been extracted from the soldier by force or threats should be sent to Arnold Molckemann, treasurer of the States at Brussels, with the records, so that their pay might be reduced accordingly.

units.la: Dein Lalainius Leovardiæ adhuc agens, quo dissensionibus populi Frisici, Omlandiæ & Drentinorum mederetur, ad Ordines generales, Concilium Status, tum ad Aurantium Principem, Franciscum Pipenpoium Bruxellensem ablegavit fiduciariasque litteras, ipso Æquinoctio Leovardiæ exaratas, suâ manu perscripsit.
units.tr: Then Lalaing, still staying at Leeuwarden, sent letters of trust to the General States, to the Council of State, and to the Prince of Orange, and to Frans Pipenpoy at Brussels, in order to remedy the dissensions among the Frisian people, the Ommelanden and the Drenthers. He wrote them out with his own hand, and they were drawn up at Leeuwarden on the very day of the equinox.

units.la: Ijs petebat, ut quoniam Frisij à Transflavicanis & Drentinis ob inæqua-lita-
units.tr: In these letters he asked that, since the Frisians were at odds with the Transflavians and the Drenthers because of the unequal

units.la: litateu tributi dissiderent, Ordines generales ortas lites componerent portionesque tributorum ex æquo definirent. Neque enim suæ potestatis esse imperare tributa & ea partium odia esse, ut suæ intercessioni non parerent. Velle scilicet Transflavicanos ac Drentinos, ut Frisij exsolvendæ legioni, cui Roblesius præfuerat, duas trientes pendant, regerentibus interea Frisijs, Transflavicanos, validiore diuturnioreque præsidio usos, maiore tributo teneri. Plus scilicet à se erogatum esse, quam modus præscripti æris ferret esseque iniquum decretas Transflavicanorum usibus cohortes suo ære ac stipendijs haberi. Censere quoque Frisios Gasparum Roblesium non ante cum cæteris captivis custodiâ liberandum, quam rationem accepti æris fecerit deque menstruis 15000. stipendijs docuerit. Magnis quippe nexibus eum se & Provinciam inligasse. Sic pacatis dimissisque tribus cohortibus, (quæ undecim adhuc numero sint) quinquies centena & quinquaginta millia deberi. Adhæc Germanorum stipendia, in infinitam molem excrescentia, non bonum rebus exitum promittere, nisi Concilij Status, Ordinum Generalium aut Aurantij prudentiâ publicum discrimen levetur. Diuturna cunctatione peccatum esse exautorandsque cohortibus assignandum ductorum & simul stipendia fuisse. Nunc enim totum legionum corpus inquietum, turbidum arma & consilia sociare. Clamitare deceptos Tribunos, diuisa signa, non alio consilio, quam ut locorum spatijs discretus miles peius habeatur roburque cohortium dissociebitur. Itaque licentiæ & malis moribus indulgentem militem per agros se sparsisse, agrario populo gravem & sinistri suspicionibus imbutum. Ijs vero sopiendis se totum interesse, facturum propediem, ut fervescentium animorum æstus subsidat copiaque sacramentis & simul Ordinum imperijs obediant.
units.tr: distribution of the taxes, the General States should settle the disputes that had arisen and fix the shares of the taxes on an equal footing. For it was not within his power to impose taxes, and the hatreds between the parties were such that they would not obey his intercession. The Transflavians and Drenthers, he said, wanted the Frisians to pay two-thirds toward the discharge of the legion that Robles had commanded, while the Frisians replied that the Transflavians, having used the stronger and longer-lasting garrison, were bound to a greater tax. More had been spent by them than the stated sum of money allowed, and it was unjust that cohorts assigned to the uses of the Transflavians should be maintained at the expense and pay of the others. The Frisians also held that Gaspar Robles should not be freed from custody with the other prisoners until he had rendered an account of the money received and shown what the monthly pay of 15,000 had been, for, they said, he had bound himself and the Province by great obligations. Thus, with the peace made and three cohorts dismissed (which are still eleven in number), five hundred and fifty thousand were owed. Besides, the pay of the Germans, swelling into an immense sum, did not promise a good outcome unless the public danger was relieved by the prudence of the Council of State, the General States, or the Prince of Orange. The long delay had been a mistake, and the cohorts should be assigned to their commanders to be discharged, and their pay at the same time. For now the whole body of the legions was restless, and the troops were combining their arms and plans in turmoil. The deceived tribunes were crying out that the standards had been divided for no other purpose than that the soldier, scattered over the spaces of different places, would be held in worse esteem, and the strength of the cohorts would be broken up. And so the soldier, indulging in licence and bad habits, had spread through the countryside, a burden to the rural population and steeped in sinister suspicions. He himself would take a full part in quieting these things, and would soon bring it about that the heat of the seething spirits subsides and that the troops obey their oaths and, at the same time, the orders of the States.

units.la: Qui, dimisso Bruxellas Pipenpoio, ut Senatum quoque regium Gandavensi Fœderi oblucantem severioribus remedijs constringeret, ejusdem Fœderis tabulas etiam ante per municipia promulgatas, publicari in Basilica ab eodem Senatu Leovardiæ jussit iisque actui 1 v. Eid. Mart. præfixit. Ubi tubæ signo ter dato, quod majoribus nostris vulgandis actorum solemnibus institutum erat, vocato velut ad concionem populo, recitari per Emskerckium Graphiarium jussit ipsequo haud vana imperij sui fiducia, plausibili edicto arbiter præsedit. Unde cum Lalainij autoritate ac apud populum gratia Senatus odium increvit, criminante, ut solet immodestius, turbâ eundem Senatum impedimenta paci molitum regundis adhuc provinciæ rebus tolerari.
units.tr: Having dismissed Pipenpoy to Brussels, he ordered the Ghent covenant, which had already been published throughout the towns, to be proclaimed in the church at Leeuwarden by the same Senate, wishing to bring the royal Senate, which was resisting the covenant, under stricter restraint. He fixed the act for the fifth day before the Ides of March. There, after the trumpet had sounded three times, which our ancestors had instituted as the customary signal for publishing official acts, the people were summoned as if to an assembly, and he ordered the edict to be read out by Emskerck, the clerk. Trusting in his own authority, not without reason, he presided over the proceedings as arbiter with a popular edict. Hence, as Lalaing's authority and his favour with the people grew, so did the hatred of the Senate. The mob, as is its habit, too immoderately accused that body of having plotted obstacles to peace and of being tolerated while still governing the affairs of the province.

units.la: Mox exulum multitudo, tolerato quinquennali exilio, in provinciam refluxit totidemque annorum tædia & inclementiam fortunæ novæ fœlicitatis dulcedine lenivit. Quare publicæ lætitiæ per agros & oppida dies dicti, redditique penatibus suis exules domesticum gaudium publicis ovationibus miscuerunt.
units.tr: Soon the crowd of exiles, having endured five years in exile, flowed back into the province, and the sweetness of their new good fortune soothed the weariness and harshness of so many years. Accordingly, days of public rejoicing were proclaimed throughout the fields and towns, and the exiles, restored to their homes, mingled their private joy with public celebrations.

units.la: Dein Gasparus Roblesius captivam conjugem, liberos ac tribunos cohortium secum trahens, custodiâ emissus deductusque ad Hyergium, quem regundis Geldris rex Philippus præfecerat, magnum instabilis fortunæ documentum præbuit. Scribit F. Nicolaus, homo etiam Pontificijs addictior, populum Frisicum istius spectaculi non misertum, cæterum Nobilitatem, cives & agrarios, velut justas & fatales poenas luente Roblesio, viri adversitate & illo fatorum ludo oculos animosque pavisse. Addit idem Scriptor, promiscuam multitudinem decernendas palam grates divino numini censuisse, quod malorum consiliorum artificem Roblesium & Tribunos militares, velut praeconcepti furoris ministros, ut odium generis humani, ita opprobrium ludicrae captivitatis comitaretur. Id xvii. Kalend. April. factum Nicolaus tradit Martinumq; Bayartum Gantonium Stavoranae arcis Satrapam, cum Bustamantio, qui Harlingano castello praerat & Tribuno cohortis, ut memoravi, Feuterio vinculis datum, ac Stauriā Zwollam devectum, ut consiliorum Roblesij ita popularis odij communionem tulisse. Quod ex crudeli & aspero Roblesij ingenio natum autores non dissimulavere, cum in acta relatum sit, eum praeter Ducis aut Tribuni legionis dignitatem, crebrò supplicium militare, quod jubere etiam cum temperamento debuisset, iracundiae calore suā manu executum. Ita confossò, strangulato aut glande trajecto milite avidam caedis dexteram saepe sanguine imbuisse, haud dubiè, ut illius effundendi consuetudine exercitus, animum ultro immanem graviori saevitiae efferaret.
units.tr: Then Gaspar Robles, having been released from custody, led his captive wife, his children and the tribunes of the cohorts with him, and was taken to Hergen, whom King Philip had appointed to govern Gelderland. He offered a great example of unstable fortune. Nicolaus, a man more inclined to the Papists, writes that the people of Friesland were not moved to pity by this spectacle; rather, the nobility, the citizens and the farmers, seeing Robles pay what were just and fated penalties, feasted their eyes and minds on the reverse of fortune and that game of destiny. The same writer adds that the common crowd resolved to give public thanks to the divine power, because Robles, the author of wicked counsels, and the military tribunes, as ministers of a long-premeditated fury, were accompanied by the hatred of the human race and the disgrace of a mocking captivity. Nicolaus records that this was done on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April: Martin Bayart of Ganton, governor of the citadel of Stavoren, together with Bustamante, who commanded the castle at Harlingen and was a tribune of a cohort (as I have mentioned), were put in chains by Feuterius and carried from Stavoren to Zwolle, so that they bore a share of the popular hatred just as they had shared Robles's counsels. The authors do not hide that this arose from Robles's cruel and harsh character, since it is recorded in the acts that, beyond the rank of duke or tribune of the legion, he often carried out military punishment himself, in the heat of anger, when he ought to have ordered it with moderation. Thus, by stabbing, strangling or running through soldiers with a bullet, he often stained his greedy right hand with blood; no doubt, through his habit of shedding it, he drove the army's spirit, already savage, to a more severe cruelty.

units.la: Thuanus scribit Roblesium, custodiae tempore, cum Georgio Lalainio successore collocutum, tanquam commodum in Frisiā regnandi instrumentum, fovendas provincialium dissensiones commendasse quo, procerum viribus intestina per odia luxatis, formidinem popularis potentiae & simul modum imperio, confirmandae dominationi exueret.
