Ferunt Sixtum Dekama, nobilissimae stirpis & doctrinae virum, ex ore Roblesij praesente Lalainio, in cujus comitatu tum erat, istam vocem exaudivisse eundemque saepè apud familiares acta priorum temporum repetentem, veri in hoc fidem clarissimi scriptoris Aug. Thuani eruditis commentarijs adstruxisse.
units.tr: Thuanus writes that Robles, during his custody, in conversation with his successor George Lalaing, recommended the fostering of disputes among the provincials as a useful instrument for ruling Friesland. By this means, with the strength of the nobles weakened by mutual hatreds, they would strip away both the fear of popular power and the restraint on their rule, so as to strengthen their domination. It is said that Sixtus Dekama, a man of most noble stock and learning, heard these words from Robles's own mouth in the presence of Lalaing, in whose company he then was. Dekama often repeated this among his friends, recalling events of earlier times, and by his learned commentaries he confirmed the truth of this matter, as the most illustrious writer Augustus Thuanus had done.

units.la: Adeo verum est, Philippi Praefectos regiae dominandi cupidinis aemulos, parum modestis per Frisiam consiliis interfuisse ijsdemque stabiliendi regni moribus usos, non absimilia in Trans-Rhenanis provinciis ijs, quae in Belgica Philippus decumenta rerum edidisse.
units.tr: So true is it that the prefects of Philip, rivals in their desire to rule, took part in counsels that were little restrained across Friesland, and used the same methods to establish their rule. Their deeds in the Trans-Rhenish provinces were not unlike those which Philip had carried out in the Belgic provinces.

units.la: Mox Austriacus post Foedus Marchas apud Faminas confirmatum, Lovanium in Grudios progressus, pro redimendis captivis intercessit. Gasparoque Roblesio, conjugi & liberis, tum cohortium tribunis ac Josepho Talimerio quondam regiae triremi apud Stauros praefecto, veniam rogavit. Is Campis oppido ad flumen Isalam, haud procul Austrino sinu sito, duriore custodiā asservabatur patratisque sceleribus enormi saevitiae, quā famam per Frisios adeptus erat, squallore teterrimi carceris litabat. Erant qui censerent, longi furoris piaculum populari irae immolandum placandumque illius caede illorum sanguinem, quos vir ultra hominem ferox & malarum mortium repertor, per tormenta & cruciatus sustulisset. Caeterum a Magistratu urbico veniam nactus reliquis cum captivis in Brabantiam abductus est.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, the Austrian, after the covenant had been confirmed at Marche-aux-Dames, advanced from Louvain to Gruoningen and interceded for the release of prisoners. He also asked pardon for Gaspar Robles, his wife and children, the tribunes of the cohorts, and Joseph Talimer, formerly prefect of the royal galley at Staveren. Talimer was held under harsher custody at Campen, a town on the river Ijssel, not far from the Zuiderzee, and he was, for the crimes he had committed with extraordinary cruelty, which had won him a name among the Frisians, paying the price in the squalor of a most foul prison. Some thought that the punishment for his long madness should be offered to popular anger, and that the blood of those whom this man, fiercer than human and an inventor of wicked deaths, had destroyed through torments and tortures, should be avenged by his slaughter. However, the city magistracy granted his pardon and he was led off into Brabant with the other prisoners.

units.la: Tum Austriacus de dimittendis legionibus cogitavit castellumq; Antverpiense, quod ab Albano extructum Hispani praesidio tenuerant, Philippo Croio Arschotano tutandum demandavit. Mansfeldium quoque deducendis Hispanorum, Italorum Burgundionumque copijs praefecit eaedemque desertis castellis arcibusque, excedere provinciarum finibus jusit. Traditum Annalibus est, Legiones istas (sub Ferdinando Albano ad decem millia Belgicam ingressas eximius Scriptor Everardus cIↄ. Iↄ. dus Reidanus notat) eodem fere numero provincijs excesisse ipsum{q}, LXXVII exercitum, ut lixarum calonumque, ita puerorum scortorumque impura agmina trahentem, ingluvie & lascivia diffluxisse. Unde redditam terris pacem plurimi autumabant, amoto quietis publicae perturbatore, & arcium praesidijs inquilinae genti commissis.
units.tr: Then the Austrian considered discharging the legions, and entrusted the castle of Antwerp, which Alva had built and the Spaniards had held with a garrison, to Philip de Croy, Duke of Arschot, to guard. He also placed Mansfeld in charge of leading away the troops of the Spaniards, Italians and Burgundians, and ordered them to leave the borders of the provinces, abandoning their castles and fortresses. It is handed down in the annals that these legions, which had entered Belgium under Ferdinand of Alva to the number of about ten thousand, as the distinguished writer Everard van Reyd notes, left the provinces in roughly the same number; the army itself, dragging along with it, as well as its camp-followers and sutlers, the filthy crowds of boys and prostitutes, dissolved in gluttony and debauchery. Hence most people thought that peace was restored to the land, the disturber of public quiet having been removed, and the garrisons of the citadels entrusted to a native people.

units.la: Reperio in notis Cl. Franckenae Hispanos x i. Kal. Maji. Trajecto ad Mosam praedâ onustos exijsse erectisque signis, velut gestarum rerum gloriam testaturos patrum populique servilem patientiam inrisisse. Bernardinus Mendoza equitum ductor & post Philippi in Galliam Angliamque Legatus, suis commentarijs inseruit, ab ijsdem Hispanis intra decimestre spatium triginta hominum millia caesa confectaque per Belgicam fuisse, eosdemque direptis sexaginta foederatorum vexillis, propitio velut numine usos, uberem praedam partae gloriae adjecisse. Etsi sint qui exijstument id plus infamiae ex saevitiâ quam gloriae ex virtute traxisse populumque Belgicum inermem & velut in pace securum, non ut antè per conflictus & pugnas, sed latrocinia & caedes intra ipsos urbium muros, intra aedium consepta Hispanicarum gentium furoribus mactatum. Credulâ scilicet multitudine nihil fraudis & doli suae innocentiae superesse pacisque sanctionem tot confesibus procerum & solemnibus subnixam primos concordiae fructus quietem & tranquillitatem perpessae enormia genti daturam.
units.tr: I find in the notes of the distinguished Francken that on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May the Spaniards left Maastricht on the Maas, laden with plunder, and with their standards raised, as if to bear witness to the glory of their deeds, they mocked the patient servility of the fathers and the people. Bernardino de Mendoza, leader of the horsemen and afterwards ambassador of Philip to France and England, records in his commentaries that within the space of fifteen days thirty thousand men were slaughtered and destroyed by these same Spaniards throughout Belgium, and that, having stripped sixty banners of the confederates, they added rich plunder to the glory they had won, as if they had enjoyed a favouring divine power. Yet there are some who think that this brought more infamy from their cruelty than glory from their valour, and that the Belgian people, unarmed and as if secure in peace, were slaughtered not, as before, in conflicts and battles, but in robberies and murders within the very walls of the cities and the enclosures of their houses, by the fury of the Spanish nations. Clearly, the credulous multitude, having no suspicion of fraud or guile in its own innocence, and trusting the sanction of peace supported by so many solemn pledges of the nobles, expected the first fruits of concord to be quiet and tranquillity, but suffered outrages upon the nation.

units.la: Quamobrem Lalainius, quo securitati provincialium consuleret & ad formam superiorum provinciarum, Frisiorum quoque intra Flevum & Lavicam remp. ordinaret, Leovardianae arci Joannem Mathenesium praefecit eandemque regio Ordinumque nomine asservandam ei dedit. Harlingano vero castello Petrum Sickingham, Stavorano Franciscum Pipenpoium imposuit ejectisque Valonum signis, Germanicas cohortes pro praesidio locavit.
units.tr: Therefore Lalaing, in order to secure the safety of the provincials, and to order the state of the Frisians also between the Vlie and the Lauwers, in the manner of the other provinces above, appointed John Matthenesse to the citadel of Leeuwarden and gave it to him to be kept in the name of the king and the Estates. At the castle of Harlingen he placed Peter Sickingh, and at Stavoren Francis Pipenpoy. Having removed the Walloon standards, he stationed German cohorts there as a garrison.

units.la: Notat Staurius Scriptor Georgium Lalainium amplo comitatu stipatum, I I I. Non. Maij componendis rebus Stauriam urbem ingressum, à flore juventutis urbanae civiumque ac municipalium frequentiâ exceptum, flagrantis apud populum gratiae specimen tulisse, Stauriosque, jam ante Roblesium aversatos, ejusque in urbem introitu, velut facta solitudine se abdentes, publica tum loca occupasse, congiariumque accepisse.
units.tr: The writer Staurius notes that George Lalaing, surrounded by a large retinue, entered the city of Stavoren on the third day before the Nones of May to settle affairs; he was received by the flower of the city's youth and by a large gathering of citizens and townsfolk, which showed his growing favour with the people. The Stavorenes, who had earlier shunned Robles, now, as if the solitude had been ended, withdrew from hiding at his entry into the city, occupied the public places, and accepted a largess.

units.la: Itaque omni arce castelloque regio suspectis rectoribus praesidijsque liberato, externisque legionibus in Cispadanam Italiam amotis, Joannes Austriacus capessendae dominationi iter Bruxellas intendit, cujus ardore impotentius juvenilis animus flagrabat. Comitatum ejus, ut Legati Caesaris Ordinumque Belgicae, ita tria fermè spiculatorum stipatorumque millia sequebantur, quos infidis rebus, nec ultro per conscientiam metus expers, custodiae corporis loco obsidum delegerat.
units.tr: Thus, when every citadel and royal castle had been freed from magistrates and garrisons suspected of disloyalty, and the foreign legions had been sent away into Italy this side of the Po, John of Austria set out for Brussels to seize power, a desire which burned in his youthful spirit more uncontrollably. His retinue, like that of the Emperor's ambassadors and of the Estates of Belgium, was followed by some three thousand spearmen and armed attendants, whom, since affairs were treacherous and he himself was not free of fear in his conscience, he had chosen as a hostage-guard for his person.

units.la: Sic medius legatum inter Pontificis & Leodiensium Episcopum equo vectus, ipsis Kal. Majis urbem intravit, quae jam ante Brabantiae & post Burgundiae Principum sedes, ut conventibus procerum, ita tum magnificentiae & apparatui rerum serviebat. Unde pretiosae porticus per urbem erectae arcusque passim per vicos extructi trophaea famae & gestarum ab Austriaco rerum decora ostentabant. Itaque palam devictarum urbium imagines praeterque Africanae expeditionis claritudinem, Ægaei maris prospera pictis in tabulis visebantur. Antecedebat cunus aureo panno constratus, cujus utrumque latus artificum picturis adornatum, confracta aut mutilata arma, aut publicam rerum ubertatem & foecundam luxuriem exprimebat. Domorum vero editis matronae passim pulcherrimaeque virgines sistebantur jaciendisque desuper sertis corollisque intererant. Itaque humus vario flore conspersa agendis ludicris discurrentem populum exercebat. Adhaec ubivis laetae acclamantium voces totumque per urbem suavissimi vocum concentus audiebantur. Austriacus ipse decora juventa & illiciendis animis valida spectantium ora morabatur rudimentaque imperij speciosis initijs cohonestabat.
units.tr: Thus, riding between the papal legate and the Bishop of Liège, he entered the city on the Kalends of May itself. This city had long been the seat of the Dukes of Brabant and afterwards of the Dukes of Burgundy, and it now served the assemblies of the nobles as well as the display of magnificence and splendour. Hence splendid colonnades were erected throughout the city, and arches built at intervals along the streets displayed trophies of fame and honours for the deeds done by the Austrian. Accordingly, images of conquered cities were openly displayed, and besides the fame of the African expedition, the successes of the Aegean sea were seen in painted panels. A chariot covered with cloth of gold went before him, each of its sides adorned with paintings by artists, showing broken or mutilated arms, or the public abundance and fruitful luxury. From the upper windows of the houses matrons and beautiful virgins were displayed everywhere, and took part in throwing garlands and wreaths down upon him. The ground, sprinkled with various flowers, kept the people running about at their games. Besides, everywhere joyful voices of acclaiming people were heard, and the sweetest harmonies of voices resounded throughout the city. The Austrian himself, with his youthful grace and a face strong in winning the minds of onlookers, lingered, and graced the beginnings of his rule with splendid starts.

units.la: Econtra immodica gratantium studia, velut assentationibus conspersa alij dedignabantur populum, inconsulto impetu ad dubia & ut periti censebant, falsa gaudia adlurgentem, incerto pacis autori & conciliandis partibus impari servile ministerium & poenitendum officium devovisse. Erant enim, qui illum Austriaci ingressum cum Philippi inauguratione & solemnibus conferrent sumptuosumque & ingentem paratum dignitati ac fortunae Principis assimilarent. Etsi essent, qui non ignorarent, Austriacum vigore juventae & morum gratia spectabilem, tanti apparatus non equisse, quod obscuris dubijsque natalibus ortum, procul imperatoria stirpe, despectae ab eo & parum pudicae matris Germanae foeminae temeritas & imprudentia vulgasset. Neque enim alio fine eam in Hispaniam amotam, & sub cura nutricis suae in coenobium detrusam, quam ne eius ignobilitate aut inhonestiore vita offenderetur suaeque conditionis ac originis ex matris praesentia monitus, regios spiritus gerens, ultro contemptos natales majore ludibrio & despectu foedaret.
units.tr: On the other hand, some people looked down on the immoderate eagerness of those congratulating him, which was sprinkled with flattery. They objected that the people, with rash enthusiasm, were rising to joy that was uncertain and, as experienced men judged, false. They said that a servile office, one to be regretted, had been devoted to a man who was an uncertain author of peace and unequal to reconciling the parties. Some compared Austria's entry with the inauguration and solemnities of Philip and likened the lavish and huge display to the dignity and fortune of a prince. Yet there were some who knew that Austria, remarkable for the vigour of his youth and the charm of his manners, did not deserve so great a display, since he was of obscure and doubtful birth, far from an imperial line. The rashness and imprudence of his mother, a German woman whom he had despised and who was not chaste, had made this public. Indeed, she had been sent to Spain for no other purpose than that he should not be offended by her lowly station or her less honourable life. Hence, when reminded of his condition and origin by her presence, he bore royal spirits and, to his greater ridicule and contempt, would have defiled a birth that he himself had spurned.

units.la: Antonius Delrio suis in commentarijs notat, Viglium Zuichemum Senatus Praesidem morbo languidum spectandique Austriaci desiderio lecto allevatum, quid suspecti protulisse eodemque lecto, velut fatali sede repositum novendialis morbi ferocia extinctum. Creditum fuit, Viglium Praesidem, sagacitate qua pollebat ex indole, aut moribus suspecti Principis latentis vitij rationem deprehendisse, ac si sedandae tempestati, quae regem & provincias extremis odijs dissociasset, juvenile ingenium non responderet. Itaque eum, perspectis Austriaci consilij, de remedijs recrudescentium dissensionum desperasse aegritudineque mentis correptum, eadem sensim aucta & senecta ultro gravi vitam finijsse.
units.tr: Antonius Delrio notes in his commentaries that Viglius Zuichemus, President of the Senate, weak with illness and raised from his bed by his desire to see Austria, let slip some suspicion, and that, laid on that same bed as on a fatal seat, he was carried off by the fierceness of a nine-day fever. It was believed that President Viglius, through the keenness of judgement for which he excelled, had discerned from the character and manners of the suspected prince a hidden fault, namely that the young man's mind was not equal to calming the storm that had split the king and the provinces by the most bitter hatreds. So, having clearly seen the purposes of Austria, he despaired of remedies for the renewed dissensions. Seized by a sickness of the mind, which gradually grew and was aggravated by old age, he ended his life by his own accord through grave distress.

units.la: Thuanus scribit Viglium, claritudine literarum, & civilis prudentiae summas ad dignitates, Carolo Philippoque rerum potiuntibus evectum & libertati jam ante proniorem, Ordinum gratiam, post Hispanorum in partes inclinare visum, odium sibi conflasse liberalioreque ante annum custodia detentum, coram se turbidis temporibus & ex his nascituræ rerum conversioni indoluisse. Itaque multa redarguendis sinistris rumoribus effatum integerrimâ professione, se conservandae regiae autoritati omnem curam ac sollicitudinem impendisse alienumque ab Hispanicae gentis moribus, populi & rerum omnium salutem in fide de RecIↄ. Iↄ. de Regis, tanquam unico societatis vinculo collocasse. Quae à Thuano Cl. Scriptore actis tradita, virum & patriae & simul Regi suâ opinione nihil detrahentem, à suspicione totae Hispanicae immanitatis & injuriâ scriptorum exemerè. Cadaver sepulchro, quod vir suae mortalitatis & humanae legis etiam in tantâ fortunâ memor fieri apud Gandavos sibi curaverat, honoratis exequiis inlatum. Itaque patriae patris, censente per Frisiam Senatu, nomen ei decretum affixumque publicis monumentis aeternae temporum famae servatur.
units.tr: Thuanus writes that Viglius, raised to the highest offices for his distinction in letters and his civil prudence while Charles and Philip held power, and already earlier inclined to liberty, seemed to have incurred the disfavour of the Estates when he joined the Spanish side. He had been kept in custody for more than a year, more liberally than before, and he grieved over the troubled times, and over the upheaval of affairs that would come from them. Therefore, refuting many malicious rumours with the most upright declaration, he said he had devoted all his care and anxiety to preserving the royal authority. He placed the safety of the people and of all affairs, far removed from the manners of the Spanish nation, in fidelity to the king, as the one bond of society. Thuanus, a distinguished writer, reported these things in his acts and freed from suspicion of Spanish savagery and from the wrong done by writers a man who, in his opinion, took nothing away from either his country or the king. His body was carried to the tomb with honourable funeral rites; the man, mindful of his mortality and of the human lot even in such great fortune, had arranged that it be placed at Ghent. Thus, by decree of the Senate of Friesland, he was given the title of Father of the Fatherland, and the title, attached to public monuments, is kept for the eternal fame of the times.

units.la: Annotatum invenio circa Kal. Majas, aërem continuo frigore imbribusque foedum fuisse vernique coeli clementiam, velut brumali injuriâ, confudisse.
units.tr: I find it recorded that about the Kalends of May the air was foul with constant cold and rain, and that the mildness of the spring sky was confused as if by winter's harm.

units.la: Conventum quoque Delegatorum Frisiae Leovardiae ad I I I. Non. Maji habitum, Abelumque Franckenam virum eximium, in Hollandiam pro legato missum, versipelli Austriaci ingenio & suspectis actionibus diffidisse. Tradit F. Nicolaus ingentem trium millium librarum auri signati thesaurum à puerulis victum domatim quaerentibus in Jorvertae pago tum repertum Hectorique Dekamae viro nobili & praedij domino adjudicatum. Idem addit Stauriae delubrum, à Cunero Episcopo lustrali aquâ tum respersum, non alio ut creditum fuit consilio, quam ut infesta superstitionibus tempora, auctâ templi religione, sacrilegij metu deterreret. Mox Oceanus, quod in V I I I. Kal. Jul. diem incidit, supra solitos aestus se extulit superatoque littore & excelsi aggeris mole in omnem provinciam se sparsit. Unde armentorum pecorumque greges vi fluctuum abacti humana quoque cadavera, in ipsis domorum conseptis obruta, secum traxere. Foenum quoque jam ante resectum apiscendaeque maturitati & nutriendo sub hyemem pecori arídoribus Solis expositum, ipsis aquis innatavit radicibusve cohaerens salsedine marinâ erosum, spem agricolae elusit. Cujus inundationis, ut ingens damnum, ita recens adhuc memoria est, quod aestivo tempore, ut antè trienniũm recurrens diluvium, velut hybernâ tempestate, cultis agris se infudisset.
units.tr: I also find that a meeting of the deputies of Friesland was held at Leeuwarden on the third day before the Nones of May, and that Abel Franckena, an outstanding man sent as envoy into Holland, distrusted Austria's crafty nature and suspicious actions. Brother Nicolaus reports that a huge treasure of three thousand pounds of stamped gold, found by little boys searching house by house in the district of Jorverta, was then discovered and adjudged to Hector Dekama, a nobleman and lord of the estate. He adds that the shrine at Stauria, then sprinkled with lustral water by Bishop Cuner, was believed to have been done for no other purpose than to frighten off, by a greater reverence for the church and a fear of sacrilege, times hostile to superstitions. Soon the ocean, which fell on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, rose above its usual tides, and, having overcome the shore and the mass of the high dike, spread over the whole province. Hence the flocks of cattle and herds, driven by the force of the waves, dragged with them human corpses too, buried in the very enclosures of the houses. Hay, already cut and laid out in the sun to be gathered in its ripeness and to feed the cattle through the winter, floated on the waters themselves, or, still clinging to its roots and eaten away by the sea's salt, mocked the farmer's hope. The memory of this flood is still recent, as great a loss as it was; in the summer season it poured over the cultivated fields in the manner of a winter storm, like the deluge that had recurred three years before.

units.la: Notat Heymannus marinos fluctus tam insolito aestu intumuisse, ut summitatem Biltani aggeris excederent inundatâque omni Dongriâ & maritimis agris, solo Slachtano aggere coercerentur. Cl. Franckena addit, solâ tempestate tum evenisse crebroque alias commotum mare & lunae sydere impulsum, Friscis terris ordinarias ut plurimum inundationes intulisse. Grandinem quoque mirae magnitudinis caelo decidisse totamque aestatem, velut legis oblitam, frigidissimam & pluviosissimam fuisse.
units.tr: Heymann notes that the sea waves swelled with so unusual a tide that they overtopped the summit of the Biltan dike, and, with all of Dongria and the maritime fields flooded, were checked only by the Slachtan dike. Franckena adds that this happened from the storm alone, and that the sea, often stirred at other times and driven by the moon's star, generally brought ordinary floods to the Frisian lands. Hail of marvellous size also fell from the sky, and the whole summer, as if forgetful of its law, was very cold and very rainy.

units.la: Mox Austriacus Bruxellis agens, recente adhuc publicae festivitatis memoriâ Ordinum coetu acto sacramentum dixit animumque subdolum & fallacem, quem clam sceleri & defectioni obstrinxerat, manifesto perjurio provincijs obligavit. Ordines vero provinciarum, ut componendis ex Foedere rebus, ita pacandis praecipue Germanorum cohortibus occupabantur redimendisque civitatum arciumq; praesidijs, aës & fidem detrectantibus misionem offerebant. Creditum fuit eadem legiones clam ab Austriaco corruptas servandis, velut pignori, castellis urbibusque se dedisse aequisque conditionibus praefractas, aut contumaces maces foeda, & nuperis furoribus non difformia consilia agitasse. CIↄ. Iↄ. Mox approbando Fœderi à Joanne Austriaco legati ad Aurantinum LXXVII. missi speciosa anuntiavere.
units.tr: Soon Austria, acting at Brussels, while the memory of the public festivity was still fresh, held a meeting of the Estates and took the oath. By a manifest perjury he bound the provinces to a mind that was deceitful and treacherous, one which he had secretly pledged to crime and revolt. The Estates of the provinces, meanwhile, were occupied in settling affairs under the covenant, and above all in pacifying the German cohorts. They offered discharge to those who refused pay and loyalty, and offered to buy back the garrisons of the cities and citadels. It was believed that the same legions, secretly corrupted by Austria, had given themselves over to guarding the castles and cities as if they were a pledge, and that, when their demands were refused on fair terms, they were planning, as shameful and obstinate mutineers, plans not unlike their recent frenzies. (1577.) Soon afterwards, envoys sent by John of Austria to Orange announced, in fair words, the approval of the covenant.

units.la: Admotum gerundis rebus, ORDINUM consensu, AUSTRIACUM, primordiaque imperij non infaustis ominibus ingressum. Fœderum scilicet ratihabitione, non Bruxellensium solum, quos in sumptuosos apparatus rerum desiderium novi Principis egisset, cæterum superioris Belgicæ populum traxisse. Neque aliud restare, quam ut omnes provincie sanctissime adjuratique ab Austriaco Fœderis fructum sentiant, communeque bellum communi pace sopiatur. Eo perveniri signato per AURANTIUM fœdere posse. Amotas quippe ex pacto legiones Aurantiumque in patrimonia principis domus restitutum. Non relictum esse querelæ, aut tergiversationi locum. AURANTIUS verò filium Hispaniâ attineri, suasque per Luxemburgicum agrum & Burgundiam possessiones & cum iis proventus interverti criminabatur. Regis potentiam alieno stare, nihil aliud quarentis, quam, ut impulsis procerum Belgicæ rebus pro libitu regnet. Nec per vim tantum, sed dolose hoc adniti. Deceptos Marchicâ conventione ORDINES & materiem novis dissidijs ac fœde servituti scriptam, quam excutere quocunque etiam modo in Principem animum induxisset. Isti fini se ad Frisios trans Rhenum agentes litteras dedisse, mox auxilia missurum. Neque enim rei tam sanctæ se pudere, opprobrio illorum, qui extinctam per recentia imperia antiquam liberrimæ Frisiorum gentis memoriam vellent.
units.tr: Having put his hand to the business in hand, by the consent of the Estates, Austria entered upon his rule with auspices that were not unfavourable. Clearly this was by the ratification of the covenant, which had drawn not only the people of Brussels, whom the desire for lavish display in the affairs of the new prince had driven on, but also the people of Upper Belgium. Nothing remained but that all the provinces, sworn most solemnly by Austria, should feel the fruit of the covenant, and that the common war should be quieted by common peace. This could be reached, once the covenant had been sealed through Orange. The legions were withdrawn by the pact, and Orange was restored to the estates of the princely house. No room was left for complaint or evasion. Orange, however, complained that his son was being kept in Spain, and that his possessions in the Luxembourg country and Burgundy, and their revenues with them, were being diverted. The power of the king, he said, was standing on another's ground, seeking nothing else than to reign at will over the affairs of Belgium, once the leading men had been driven out. And this was being attempted not by force alone but by deceit. The Estates had been deceived by the Marche convention, and a material for new dissensions and for a shameful servitude had been written, which he had resolved to shake off by whatever means against the prince. For this end he had sent letters to the Frisians across the Rhine, promising that aid would soon follow. For he was not ashamed of so holy a cause, to the reproach of those who wished the ancient and most free memory of the Frisian nation, extinguished by recent empires, to be kept alive.

units.la: Itaque non theatralium ludorum spectaculis, quibus Austriacus captandis populi favoribus se sistebat non comitate etiam infra Principem prudentiores movebat, aulæ morum peritos & jam ante in Requesentio edoctos externa sæpe officia subltestis consilijs obtendi. Quippe asperum Religionis Edictum per provincias publicatum memoriam priorum vulnerum refricabat & quod secretis ad Senatum per Frisiam regium mandatis corrigendos hæreticos (sic enim Reformatos indigitabat) & falsâ religione imbutos prisca poenarum asperitate præcepisset. Quæ etsi à Senatu in populum non vulgabantur contegendis arcanis, ita redarguebat Edictum novis disidijs nova nutrimenta quæri. Quare exules, quos jam ante patriâ extorres religio fecerat, inclementia rursum temporum metuebant, ac ut eadem severitate patria & bonis provoluti toleratis semel exilijs destinarentur. His accedebat, quod Aurantius sociæque provinciæ fœdus cum Austriaco ictum, ut damnosum & fallax aversarentur futuræque defectionis, & instantis belli triste præsagium, interceptis in Guasconum finibus Austriaci litteris, firmaretur.
units.tr: Therefore, the more prudent men, versed in the manners of the court and already earlier schooled in Requesens, were moved not by the spectacles of theatrical games, by which Austria presented himself to catch the favour of the people, nor even by the courtesy with which he stood below a prince. They were warned that foreign services were often put forward as a cover for hidden plans. Indeed, the harsh Edict of Religion, published throughout the provinces, reopened the memory of earlier wounds. Secret royal mandates had been sent through Friesland to the Senate, ordering that heretics (for so they named the Reformed) and those steeped in false religion be corrected with the old severity of punishments. Although the Senate did not publish these things to the people, in order to conceal the secrets, the Edict refuted itself, since it sought new nourishment for fresh dissensions. Hence the exiles, whom religion had already driven from their homeland earlier, feared the renewed harshness of the times, and feared that, prostrate and stripped of their goods, they would be condemned to the same severity in their homeland, once their exiles had been endured. To this was added that Orange and the allied provinces, to avoid the covenant struck with Austria as ruinous and deceitful, and as a sad omen of coming revolt and imminent war, were confirmed in this by letters of Austria intercepted in the territory of the Gascons.

units.la: Ijs ad Regem perscripserat.
units.tr: He had written these things to the King:

units.la: Impurum Belgicæ corpus validiore remedio curandum lenius jam diu respuisse. Quinurendum secandumque potius, ne, quod medicorum filij maxime præcaverent, partis infectæ contagione cetera consensu vitientur. Damnatum fidei crimine populum acriore bello reprimendum esse, quod non magno exercitu, ut nuper Albani & Requesentij ætate, cæterum veterano milite & modicis copijs gerendum sit. Nervo autem belli imprimis opus esse, ac ut missâ continente insulæ aut circumfusa amnibus loca regi asserantur. Adhæc serendas proclo. Io. procerum & populi discordias, quo provincialium potentiam concordia florentem LXXVII. & robustam dissensio extenuet. Sic secundis rebus praesterni viam posse.
units.tr: that the impure body of the Netherlands had long rejected a gentler cure and needed a stronger remedy. It must rather be cauterized and cut, lest, as the sons of physicians take the greatest care to prevent, the rest of the body be corrupted by contagion from the infected part. The people, condemned for the crime of faith, must be suppressed by a fiercer war, to be waged not with a great army, as in the time of Alba and Requesens, but with veteran soldiers and modest forces. The sinews of war, however, were chiefly needed, and the places that are cut off by the sea or surrounded by rivers should be secured for the king. Besides, discords should be sown between the nobles and the people, so that dissension may weaken the power of the provincials, which flourishes and is strong through concord. Io. LXXVII. In this way, he said, a path to prosperous affairs could be paved.

units.la: Quarum rerum & interceptæ scriptionis ut ignarus Austriacus non erat, ita præconcepto sceleri exitum machinabatur, gnarus omnem moram malis consilijs obesse. Igitur Spadanas ad thermas, velut conducendæ Navarræornm reginæ iturus, quæ diuturnæ invaletudini salubres istorum fontium aquas morbo remedia quærebat, præter Chimæum Principem & reliquam nobilitatem Georgium quoque Lalainium flore juventæ commendatum Frisiâ Mechliniam in comitatum evocavit.
units.tr: The Austrian was not ignorant of these matters, nor of the intercepted letter, and so he planned the outcome of his wicked design, knowing that every delay would hinder his evil counsels. Therefore he went to the baths at Spa, as though about to escort the queen of Navarre, who was seeking healing from a long illness in the wholesome waters of those springs. Besides Prince Chimay and the rest of the nobility, he summoned to his retinue from Friesland to Mechlin Georges de Lalaing, commended for the flower of his youth.

units.la: Cæterum Lalainius, sive suspecta Austriaci consilia habens, sive asserendo fœderi pronior, provinciam fidei suæ commissam ex præscripto Gandavensis conventionis ordinavit Valonumque præsidia assignato æcome dimisit. Germanorum quoque ac Frisiorum cohortes, quarum delectum de mandato Ordinum egerat, custodiæ arcium imposuit curatisque Leovardiæ, Harlingæ atque Stauriæ rebus Mechliniam profectus est. Ubi serius adventans, & mox febre correptus, ingresso jam iter Austriaco, Bruxellas se recepit deque provinciæ suæ statu Delegatos Ordinum edocuit.
units.tr: Lalaing, however, whether because he held the Austrian's plans in suspicion or because he was more inclined to uphold the Ghent agreement, arranged the province entrusted to his good faith in accordance with the terms of the Ghent Pacification, and dismissed the Walloon garrisons, each to his own camp. He also placed the German and Frisian cohorts, whose levy he had made by the mandate of the States, in charge of the citadels, and, having arranged affairs at Leeuwarden, Harlingen and Stavoren, set out for Mechlin. Arriving there late, and soon seized by fever, when the Austrian had already begun his journey, he withdrew to Brussels and informed the deputies of the States about the state of his province.

units.la: Creditum fuit Austriacum, Lalainij per Frisiam instituto & mutatione rerum offensum, clam exitium ei destinasse, aut ut veneratione ac gratiâ Philippi pellectum mobilemque, eâ Lalainij ætate, animum ijsdem defectionis consilijs imbueret. Sed Lalainius sic sive fato aut arbitrio præpeditus integram & tum adhuc vitijs intactam mentem Austriaci insidijs & decreto sceleri subduxit. Quare Austriacus discerpente conscientiam metu & ne detectis dolis discrimen sentiret, Namurcum ingressus est specieque venandi, post salutatam Navarræorum reginam, Arduennæ in saltu datâ arcem circumiens suam armis fecit.
units.tr: It was believed that the Austrian, offended by Lalaing's conduct in Friesland and by the change of affairs, had secretly destined him for death, or else hoped to win him over by the reverence and favour of Philip, and to imbue his mind, still pliable at that age, with the same plans of revolt. But Lalaing, whether hindered by fate or by his own judgment, withdrew his still unspoiled mind, not yet touched by vice, from the Austrian's snares and the crime he had decided upon. Therefore the Austrian, his conscience tearing him apart with fear, and lest the danger of his treachery be discovered, entered Namur, and under the pretext of hunting, after greeting the queen of Navarre, went around his fortress in the Ardennes forest, which he then made his own by force of arms.

units.la: Scribit Thuanus, Margaretam Henrici III. Regis sororem abstinere cum marito aulâ jussam affectæ valetudini causam simulasse, quo visendis Tungrorum aquis occasione captatâ, Austriacum, jam ante Guisiorum societati desperatis rebus innexum, mutuorum auxiliorum interioribus pactis obligaret. Quod arcanum, ex Joannis Vargæ regij per Galliam Oratoris litteris detectum, Philippo horrorem incussisse memoriæ traditum est, non sine causâ indignanti, Proregem suum & illius ministros, fœdius an laxius dubium, suis mandatis usos duorum regnorum Galliæ & Hispaniæ vires secretis societatibus inligasse.
units.tr: Thuanus writes that Margaret, sister of King Henry III, was ordered to live apart from her husband, feigning an illness as the cause, so that, seizing the occasion of visiting the waters of Tongeren, she might bind the Austrian, already joined to the Guise faction in desperate circumstances, by secret pacts of mutual aid. This secret, revealed by letters of Juan de Vargas, the royal envoy in France, is said to have struck Philip with horror, not without reason indignant that his viceroy and his ministers, whether more foully or more loosely it is doubtful, had used his orders to bind the forces of the two kingdoms of France and Spain by secret alliances.

units.la: Ego existumo Margaretam, Catharinæ Medicææ matris moribus haud absimilem, ijsdem præceptis tum instituisse, ut à matre olim, Carolo filio impubere, actum Baionæ cum Albano fœdus, inscio fratre, cum Joanne Austriaco in Arduennæ solitudine, tanquam consiliorum secessu, deprimendis per Galliam Protestantibus & per Belgicam fœderatis innovaret. Itaque materiem perfidiæ sedem, quod meditabatur, bello nactus, vim sacramenti & simul gloriam boni Principis excussit.
units.tr: I think Margaret, not unlike the character of her mother Catherine de' Medici, was then instructed by the same precepts by which her mother once, while Charles her son was still a child, concluded at Bayonne with Alba a pact, unknown to her brother, with John of Austria in the solitude of the Ardennes, as if in a retreat for counsels, to renew the plan of crushing Protestants throughout France and the confederates in the Netherlands. Thus, having found in war the seat of the perfidy he was planning, he shook off the force of the oath and at the same time the glory of a good prince.

units.la: Tradunt scriptores arcis potitum circumstante coronâ illud Imperij sui initium dixisse, eundemque diem, velut suæ dominationi natalem istiusmodi cœptis atque auspicijs inchoari.
units.tr: Writers relate that when he took the citadel, surrounded by a crowd, he said that this was the beginning of his rule, and that the same day, as if it were the birthday of his dominion, was begun under such undertakings and auspices.

units.la: Mox in provinciarum Ordines acerbius invectus, dissimulata diu cum arte odia, ac simul arrogantem animum fidentemque fortunae a- perunt. Igitur Germanicarum Legionum Tribunos, quos ad sacramentum suum promisso aere ac patratae seditionis impunitate adegerat, occupandas ad civitates & castella specie praesidij sollicitavit novoq; imperio, amissa populi gratia, insolens munimentum etsi infausto exitu quaesivit. Castello quoque Namurcensi militem & commeatum procuravit istoque consilij successu, velut levi fortunae vento inflatus militare imperium praesidium dominationi popposcit. Dein quo causam occupatae per dolum arci obtenderet, ix. Kal. Aug. litteras ad Ordines dedit, quibus Gandavensi foederi asserendo operam se navasse missisque externarum gentium legionibus concordiam aluisse speciosis exemplis ostendebat.
units.tr: Soon he attacked the States of the provinces more bitterly, and, having long hidden his hatred with skill, now revealed his arrogant mind, trusting in fortune. Therefore he urged the tribunes of the German legions, whom he had bound to his oath by promised money and the impunity of the sedition he had carried out, to seize cities and castles under the pretext of a garrison; and, having lost the people's favour, he sought with his new power an unhappy fortification, though it ended ill. He also procured soldiers and supplies for the castle of Namur, and, puffed up by this success as by a light wind of fortune, he demanded military command as a garrison for his rule. Then, to cover the seizure of the fortress by a trick, on 23 July he sent letters to the States, in which he showed, with specious examples, that he had worked to uphold the Ghent Pacification and, by sending foreign legions, had nourished concord.

units.la: Sic anteactarum rerum quas bellum aut dissensio suasisset, oblitum, inlatas regi injurias posuisse, haud alia spe, quam ut se inter & Ordines aequa societas constaret publicarumque rerum, praecipue vero consiliorum communio esset. Caeterum turbida ingenia foris & intra provincias alendis discordiis haberi, paci infesta & divellendis procerum nexibus sinistra famae serentia. Adhaec sibi & comitatui suo structas insidias parricidiumque Principi aut ejus Legato intentatum certae securitatis eguisse. Ideo in arcem Namurcorum se subtraxisse, ne publica quies ulteriore malo obturbaretur & ut rerum arbitris Philippo & sibi, quos fortuna imperio destinasset, caeteris relicta obsequia deferrentur. Eorum vero provinciarum Ordines se certiorem fecisse, amovendis sinistris populi suspicionibus, qui certus esse queat adjuratam pactis fidem intemeratam fore. Neque aliud restare, quam ut regi contumaces in ordinem redigantur parecantque ex praescripto.
units.tr: Thus, forgetting the past events which war or dissension had brought about, he set aside the injuries inflicted on the king, with no other hope than that there should be an equal alliance between himself and the States, and a common sharing of public affairs and especially of counsels. Moreover, he said, turbulent minds were kept abroad and within the provinces by fostering discords, hostile to peace and sinister in sowing rumours that tear apart the bonds of the nobles. Besides, snares had been laid for him and his retinue, and an attempt at parricide against the Prince or his Legate had been made, so he had needed a sure safety. Therefore he had withdrawn into the citadel of Namur, lest the public peace be disturbed by further evil, and so that the government of affairs be left to Philip and himself, whom fortune had destined for rule, and the rest be given obedience. He had informed the States of those provinces, to remove the sinister suspicions of the people, that whoever is sure of it may know that faith sworn by pacts will be kept inviolate. Nothing remained, he said, but that those who were rebellious against the king be brought back into order and obey according to what is prescribed.

units.la: Quae litterae etsi diluendo defectionis crimini ad Ordines mitterentur, animorum tamen civilium inquietudinem & secretum murmur non sedavere. Itaque compositae vix provincialium mentes & in novas pacis spes jam ante erectae tristia rursum atque funesta ominabantur, velut fato aut iris caelestium perpetua arma aut saltem dissidia miserrimis provincijs decernerentur. Ordines vero exautoratas copias, nudatam praesidio Rempublicam, discordes provincias revicturo haud dubie bello obtendebant ambiguique consiliorum, ut solet rebus infsperatis sua imbecillitate percellebantur. Quare Legati ad Austriacum missi, qui affectus & desideria procerum, pacem publicam & si quae subesset (id namque perscripserat) ultionem conjurationis pollicerentur. Corrigendis quippe flagitijs judicia ac leges non deesse.
units.tr: Although these letters were sent to the States to wipe away the charge of revolt, they did not calm the restlessness and the hidden murmuring of the civil minds. Therefore the minds of the provincials, scarcely settled and already raised to new hopes of peace, again foresaw sad and deadly things, as if, by fate or by the heavenly rainbow, perpetual arms or at least dissensions were decreed for the most wretched provinces. The States, indeed, pointed to the disbanded troops, the Republic stripped of its garrison, and the provinces at odds, as they would surely be revived by war, and, uncertain in their counsels, were struck down by their own weakness, as usually happens in unexpected circumstances. Therefore envoys were sent to the Austrian, who should promise the feelings and desires of the nobles, public peace, and, if anything lay beneath (for he had written that), vengeance on the conspiracy. For, they said, courts and laws would not be lacking to correct crimes.

units.la: Repeteret Austriacus Bruxellas sedem Senatus, reperturus haud dubie majora pacis quam belli praesidia & procerum pectora subortis aemulationibus perculsa.
units.tr: The Austrian should return to Brussels, the seat of the Council, where he would surely find greater protections of peace than of war, and the hearts of the nobles struck down by the rivalries that had arisen.

units.la: Caeterum detecta, quas Austriacus corruperat, Germanicarum Legionum fide, ut restaurandae concordiae spes incisa, ita Ordinum consilia se exacuere. Quare asserta foederi & mox diruta castella turbidaeque legiones oppidis arcibusque ejectae, aut praefectorum imperijs adversae improsperos Austriaci conatus retardavere.
units.tr: Meanwhile, the discovery of the fidelity of the German legions, which the Austrian had corrupted, cut off the hope of restoring concord, and so sharpened the counsels of the States. Therefore castles that had been secured for the confederacy and soon razed, and turbulent legions thrown out of towns and citadels, or opposed by the commands of the prefects, delayed the Austrian's unprosperous attempts.

units.la: Annotavit F. Nicolaus x. Kal. Sept. castellum Antverpianum Ferdinandi Albani cura extructum, a civibus solo aequatum fuisse praesidiaigioni & nostris sacris minus aequi, aut spes suas civilibus in discordijs ponentes, implicare novis bellorum furoribus infelices provincias in animum inducant.
units.tr: F. Nicolaus noted that on 23 August the citadel of Antwerp, built under the care of Ferdinand of Alba, was levelled to the ground by the citizens. Those less fair to our sacred things, or who place their hopes in civil discords, induce the unhappy provinces to take on new frenzies of war.

units.la: Itaque autoritate suâ, quâ prævalere factiosos & turbidos demiror, omnis ordinis homines suæ societati inne&tunt & quod fœdius est, in Religionem, in Principem, in patriam, in sua viscera se armant, sanguinis avidi & alienâ miseriâ se pascentes. Apud me vero inculpatæ tutelæ potissima ratio erit, neque reponam arma præterquam coactus & si sensero Romana Religioni, Regi aut meo capiti insidias aut periculum parari. Vos vero hoc faciendo impia arma tractabitis patriæque religionibus adversi animos sacrilegio imbuetis. Sin vero Principi vestro bellum decernitis, reputate quid divina, quid humana leges vetent & num causa vestris armis obtendi queat. Reputate nihil asperi, nihil iniqui Regem in vos molitum, præsertim ab eo tempore quo cum eo pacta & Fœdera inyistis, quorum sacra reveritus est. Vos quoque ut rebellionis, ita majestatis crimine vestras mentes polluetis clementiâque regis abusi derivabitis in vestra exitia potentiam tot regnis subnixam. Mei autem odio si quid turbidi infidis animis agitatis expendite, quo jure æmulationes vestræ fulciantur & an pactis unquam conventis defuerim. Ego Hispanicas & Italorum Legiones facessere jussi, ego castella & arces vobis tradidi. Singulari post patientiâ adversum obtrectatores usus dissimulavi injuriam, postquam vigente justitio corrigere immoderatiam severis legibus nequibam. Itaque rationem reddere gesti imperij non abnuo, paratus adhoc, si memoriam meorum beneficiorum, si mea apud Regem intercessionis posuistis & quod Fœderum jus sartum tectum curaverim imperium, quod accepi, deponere, modo successorem anteponendum mihi censeatis, meoque ingenio, tanquam infelici sydere nato, fatale bellum esse. Istius consilij secretum Ordinibus provinciarum jam ante expositi testorque etiamnum, si alium Regy sanguinis Principem desideretis missionem me petiturum. Itaque Italiam aut Hispaniam honestè dimissus repetam, cæterum hac lege, ne gravis vobis successor sit & ut arma sistantur. Provincialium rebus atque fortunis abstineri volo, & belli onus ac simul grave populo tributum meo discessu allevari. Igitur dimitti atque exauctorari quemcunque suspectæ fidei peto & cujus usus in pace nullus sit. Cui conditionum æquitati si assensum detis nullus bello locus erit, quod aureæ paci omnis mortalium ætas postposuit. De me testor discordijs ac armis inimicum nec de reparando bello nec revocandis legionibus cogitare. Cujus animi si non fuissem, ad dimovendum exercitum nulla vis me compulisset, aut ut castella ac arces meæ dominationis munimenta excussis veteranorum præsidijs novis rectoribus dederentur. Itaque certi estote, pacem me cupere & ut provincia vestræ patrio ritu regantur meumque imperium veterum Præfectorum, qui Caroli patris ætate egere, imperijs conforme sit. Catholicam vero Romanam Religionem imprimis haberi & coli Regem volo togoque ne admissis rumoribus, quos senescere sinetis, me aut regem ad iniqua & illicita & per hæc ad arma incitetis. Cogitate civile bellum externo fœdius hac occasione revitturum vosque sacrilegijs & spoliis templorum ruinis urbium & vastationibus agrorum superesse. Latrociniis, virginum ac matronarum stupris, vestra servitute bellum redimetis quod commercia & vestras opes exhauriet, artium & pacis decora subvertet. Adhæc gravem annonam, aut pestilentiam cœlestes iræ dabunt vestræque miseriæ non una calamitas incumbet. Taceo de insolentiâ & oppressionibus militum, quibus per vim & ex rapto stipendia parabuntur, postquam ærarij census exhausto exsolvendis copijs non erunt.
units.tr: Therefore, by his authority, by which I marvel that the factious and turbulent prevail, they bind men of every order to their own party, and, what is more shameful, arm themselves against religion, the prince, the fatherland, and their own vitals, greedy for blood and feeding on another's misery. With me, however, the chief consideration will be the blameless defence, and I will lay down arms only when compelled, and if I perceive that a plot or danger is being prepared against the Roman religion, the king, or my own head. But you, in doing this, will handle impious arms and imbue minds hostile to the religion of the fatherland with sacrilege. If, however, you decide upon war against your prince, consider what divine and human laws forbid, and whether any cause can be put forward to cover your arms. Consider that the king has planned nothing harsh or unjust against you, especially from the time when you entered pacts and covenants with him, whose sacred bonds he has respected. You too will pollute your minds with the crime of rebellion no less than of treason, and, abusing the king's clemency, you will turn power supported by so many kingdoms to your own destruction. If you weigh anything turbulent that you stir up in faithless minds from hatred of me, consider by what right your rivalries are supported, and whether I have ever failed the agreements made. I ordered the Spanish and Italian legions to depart; I handed over castles and citadels to you. Afterwards, with singular patience toward my detractors, I overlooked injury, since, while the license of the times prevailed, I could not correct excess with severe laws. Therefore I do not refuse to render an account of my rule, ready even now, if you remember my benefits and my intercession with the King, and if you consider that I have taken care that the law of the covenants be kept whole and safe, to lay down the rule I have received, provided you judge a successor to be placed before me, and that war is fatal to my nature, as if I were born under an unlucky star. The secret of this plan I have already set out to the States of the provinces, and I call God to witness that, if you desire another prince of royal blood, I will ask for my dismissal. So I will honourably depart and return to Italy or Spain, but on this condition: that the successor be not burdensome to you, and that the arms be laid down. I wish the affairs and fortunes of the provincials to be spared, and the burden of war, and at the same time the heavy tax on the people, to be lightened by my departure. Therefore I ask that whoever is of suspected loyalty, and whose service is useless in peace, be dismissed and discharged. If you give your assent to the fairness of these terms, there will be no place for war, which every age of mortals has postponed to golden peace. Of myself I bear witness that I, an enemy of discords and arms, think neither of renewing the war nor of recalling the legions. If I had not such a mind, no force would have compelled me to move the army, or to have the fortifications of my rule, the castles and citadels, stripped of the veteran garrisons and given to new commanders. Therefore be certain that I desire peace, and that your provinces be governed in their ancestral manner, and that my rule be in harmony with the commands of the old prefects who served in the time of my father Charles. Above all, I want the Catholic Roman religion to be held and worshipped by the King, and I ask that you not, by admitting rumours, which you allow to grow old, incite me or the king to unjust and unlawful acts, and through these to arms. Consider that civil war will return on this occasion, more foul than foreign war, and that you will survive by sacrilege and the plunder of temples, the ruin of cities and the devastation of fields. By robberies and the rape of virgins and matrons, you will buy war with your servitude, which will drain commerce and your resources, and subvert the glory of the arts and of peace. Besides, heavy grain prices or pestilence will be sent by heavenly wrath, and not one but many calamities will fall upon your misery. I say nothing of the insolence and oppression of the soldiers, by whom pay will be obtained by force and plunder, once the treasury's funds are exhausted and there is no money to pay the troops.

units.la: Viritim vero & æs vdisto conferri populus respuet, vili magistratuum autorita-te & imperij corrupta plebis obnoxiâ. Præterea cogitate cum Rege ac Principe vestro bellum vobis fore, quem, ut nec curandæ paci præsidia, ita nec bello nervi destituent. Quod si expenderitis, damnabitis belli concitores, qui ut religiones ac sacra vestra, ita obsequia distorquent, quo sibi securitatem vestris dissidijs parent. Quare æternum numen & conscientias generis humani testor, si ad arma redeundum sit, nec Regi nec mihi bellum imputandum, quos justam ad defensionem publica necessitas & vis ultima compellet. Sic arma bellum volentibus, etsi inviti reponemus, ne provinciarum salus nobis fato commissa vacillet, & ne regiæ autoritatis apex debitis obsequijs privetur.
units.tr: Moreover, the people will refuse to contribute money by head, since the authority of the magistrates is cheap and the common folk are under their control. Think, too, that you will have war with your King and your Prince, who, just as they will not lack the means to secure peace, will not lack the sinews for war. If you weigh this carefully, you will condemn the instigators of war, who twist your religion and your sacred worship as they twist your obedience, so that they may secure their own safety through your quarrels. Therefore I call the eternal Deity and the consciences of mankind to witness that, if we must return to arms, the war cannot be laid to the King or to me, whom public necessity and extreme force will compel to a just defence. Thus we will lay down our arms, though unwillingly, for those who wish for war, lest the safety of the provinces, entrusted to us by fate, be shaken, and lest the crown of royal authority be deprived of its due obedience.

units.la: HÆC AUSTRIACUS.
units.tr: THUS WROTE THE AUSTRIAN.

units.la: Post singulis ex provincijs Legatos Namurcum vocavit cautionemque publicæ pacis & fidei præstitit. Creditum fuit Austriacum, interversis per Lalainium Leovardiæ urbis & simul provinciæ rebus, odio Aurantij hæc perscripsisse spirantemque arma & bellum demulcendis enervandisque provincialibus quietem & concordiam suasisse. Itaque litteræ Austriaci Leovardiæ in vulgum sparsæ præsumptis suspicionibus non caruere. Unde Georgio Westendorpio Senatori regio à Joanne Mathenefsio arcis Satrapa & globo militum manus injectæ, ductoq; in arcem regiam crimen objectum, quod Martino Bajarto, capitalium nuper rerum præfecto & Groningæ custodiæ dato subjectoque quæstionibus mala & exitiosa reipublicæ consilia instilasse, nec falsâ accusatione, diceretur. Scribit autor eundem Westendorpium à Drentiæ finibus retractum septumque custodiâ militum bis deliquio animi correptum metuque aut mali consilij conscium regiam in arcem abductum.
units.tr: Afterwards he summoned envoys from each province to Namur and gave a guarantee of public peace and good faith. It was believed that the Austrian had written these things out of hatred for Orange, after the affairs of the city of Leeuwarden and of the province as a whole had been thrown into confusion by Lalaing, and that, breathing arms and war, he had urged the provincials to calm and concord, so as to soften and weaken them. Accordingly, the letter of the Austrian, scattered among the common people at Leeuwarden, did not escape suspicion. Hence hands were laid by John Mathenesse, governor of the citadel, and a band of soldiers, on Georgius Westendorp, a royal senator, and he was led into the royal citadel and charged with a crime: that he had poured bad and destructive counsels into the ear of Martin Bajart, recently the prefect of capital cases, who had been handed over to custody at Groningen and put to the question, and that this accusation was not false. The author writes that the same Westendorp was dragged back from the borders of Drenthe, shut up under guard of soldiers, twice seized by a faint, and, from fear or conscious of some evil plan, led away into the royal citadel.

units.la: Igitur ne toti Senatui vis fieret, decuriæ vigilum à Magistratu urbico conscriptæ fœcundam partium civitatem magis magisque turbavere. Mathenefsius quoque diurnis noćturnisque civium excubijs territus muniendæ arci regiæ incubuit cohortemque militum justo præsidio adjecit. Unde totam per urbem & ut turbidis rebus assolet, multa famæ largientem rumores sparsi, quibus Senatui regio & Roblefianæ factioni strui insidiæ ferebantur. His movendis populi ingenijs gravius additum, velut auctum à Mathenefsio præsidium sectioni civitatis destinaretur. Quare populus nullâ partium ratione metuens direptionis armatus forum obsepsit erectaque per urbem signa circumferens vigilias duplicavit.
units.tr: Therefore, lest force be done to the whole Senate, companies of watchmen enrolled by the city magistracy inflamed the city, which was already fertile in factions, more and more. Mathenesse too, frightened by the daily and nightly watches of the citizens, applied himself to fortifying the royal citadel and added a cohort of soldiers as a proper garrison. Hence rumours were spread throughout the whole city, as is usual in troubled times, lavishly feeding gossip, to the effect that plots were being laid against the royal Senate and the Roblesian faction. To stir the minds of the people further, it was added that the garrison increased by Mathenesse was being directed against a section of the city. Therefore the people, fearing plunder and paying no heed to party, took up arms, occupied the marketplace, carried standards about the city, and doubled the watches.

units.la: Mox multitudine factionibus imbecillâ & ex se discordi facile sedatâ, Mathenefsius militem Doccomium ac mox Oostmahornam expedivit, quam à Bartoldo Entenio jam ante justo opere circumductam Renicus Dekama Prætor Collumanus vir nobilis diuturno etsi debili præsidio tenebat. Quippe semiplenâ cohorte propugnaculum maris æstuario & Eæ flumini imminens velut in pace aut per inducias habebatur, hæsitante adhoc præsidio cujus sacramento per incerta & toties repetita procerum fœdera ac dubiam dominantium fidem militaret.
units.tr: Soon, with the multitude of factions weakened and, being mutually discordant, easily calmed, Mathenesse sent out the soldier Doccomius and soon afterwards Oostmahorn, which Renicus Dekama, the praetor of Colmer, a nobleman, held with a long but weak garrison; this place had earlier been surrounded with solid works by Bartholdus Entenius. Indeed, with a half-filled cohort, the bulwark overhanging the estuary of the sea and the river Ee was held as if in peace or under a truce, the garrison still wavering, since they served under an oath that was tied to uncertain and repeatedly renewed agreements of the nobles and to the doubtful loyalty of the rulers.

units.la: Quare postulata ocyus deditio, quod Roblefius xv. pedestribus copijs ac tribus Equitum turmis adjutus, irrupturus in provinciam consessione Majarti diceretur. Adeo difficile mortalibus desideria secundis rebus nata adversis exuere. Cui Majarti confessioni etiam hoc accedebat, quod Martinus Nitzenius, ut ante memoravi, cum Sceltone Tiarda & Feicone Tatmanno Bruxellas missus Doconem Martnam imminentium insidiarum praemonuisset esseque cavendum, ne subdola Ordines inter & Austriacum concordia omnique foedere & provincia insidijs expolita, quid detrimenti Respub. perpetua patriae amantium infamia ac exitio sentiret. Libertas quoque vigilando, consulendo, incrementum adepta in infensius servitium verteretur. Non ideo scilicet constantiam mentium Roblesio & pravorum consiliorum structoribus oppositisse, ut deterius in malum per socordiam provinciales recidant pulsiq; provincia dominantibus desides & securi peiora primis imperia patiantur. Insistendum esse capto operi & premenda majorum vestigia, qui cateras res viriliter, libertatem sanctissime habuissent.
units.tr: Therefore surrender was demanded at once, because Roblesius, aided by fifteen companies of foot and three troops of horse, was said to be about to burst into the province with Majart's consent. So hard it is for mortals to strip off desires born in prosperity when adversity comes. To this confession of Majart was also added the fact that Martin Nitzenius, as I mentioned before, when he had been sent to Brussels with Schelto Tiarda and Feico Tatman, had warned Don Juan Martnam of the impending plots, and that care must be taken lest, through a treacherous concord between the Estates and the Austrian, and with every treaty and province laid open to plots, the Commonwealth should suffer the harm that perpetual infamy and ruin bring upon lovers of their country. Liberty too, won by watchfulness, counsel and growth, would be turned into a harsher slavery. Certainly they had not set the constancy of minds against Roblesius and the architects of evil counsels so that the provincials, through sloth, might fall back into a worse evil, and that, once the province was driven out, the idle and secure might suffer harsher rule than before. The begun work must be pursued, and the footsteps of our ancestors, who had handled other matters manfully and held liberty most sacred, must be pressed.

units.la: Mox Oostmahornae munitio a praesidiarijs deserta. Itaque Vibius Goutumanus, Renici Dekamae subpraefectus, vir militiae impiger; sub Maximiliano Heninio Bossuvio stipendia faciens suppletam mox cohortem suburbio Leovardiae induxit, speculatusque occasionem superata clam fossa in arcem pervasit. Quod etsi aegre ferret Mathenesius tutandae arci a Lalainio praefecto & fidei per litteras praemonitus, ita econtra Goutumanus interpretabatur fortius praesidium & utrumque sacramenta Ordinum professum comprimendis civium turbis conducere. Unde Mathenesius ut temeritatis ita ignaviae insimulatus, quod demandatam sibi arcis custodiam armato ac dubiae fidei credidisset, & quem dimittere pro arbitrio nequiret. Posse istiusmodi consilijs dolum & simul periculum urbi subesse, quae non velit peregrinis validioribusque praesidijs suum castellum attineri. Sic increpitus Mathenesius Vibium Goutumanum excedere castello jusit. Is vero virtuti suorum fidens ad arma conclamavit, praesidiumq; a Mathenesio arci impositum ponere arma praecepit. Mathenesium ipsum, adinstar captivi, per ludibria & contumelias habitum custodiae dedit arciq; praesidium statuit. Quare cives armati diem atque noctem sub dio egere pultatiique tandem Achlenij Praesidis foribus dimitti praesidium postulavere.
units.tr: Soon the fortification at Oostmahorn was deserted by its garrison. Accordingly Vibius Goutumanus, sub-prefect under Renicus Dekama, a man vigorous in soldiering, who had served under Maximilian Henin, Lord of Boussu, brought in a cohort, now made up, into the suburb of Leeuwarden; watching for his chance, he crossed the ditch unseen and seized the citadel. Although Mathenesse, warned in writing by Lalaing, the prefect, to guard the citadel and keep faith, bore this badly, Goutumanus, on the other hand, interpreted it as a stronger garrison serving to restrain the disturbances of the citizens, since he professed to obey both the oaths of the Estates. Hence Mathenesse was accused of rashness and also of cowardice, because he had entrusted the guard of the citadel, which had been committed to him, to armed men of doubtful loyalty, whom he could not dismiss at will. Such plans, he said, carried with them the danger of treachery and at the same time peril to the city, which did not wish its fortress to be held by foreign and stronger garrisons. Thus rebuked, Mathenesse was ordered by Vibius Goutumanus to leave the castle. He, trusting in the valour of his men, shouted to arms and ordered the garrison placed in the citadel by Mathenesse to lay down their arms. He himself, like a captive, was treated with mockery and insults, handed over to custody, and a garrison was set in the citadel. Therefore the armed citizens spent day and night in the open air, and at last, knocking at the doors of the president Achlenius, they demanded that the garrison be dismissed.

units.la: Neque enim ante (inquiebant) aut arma deposituri, aut sumpturi cibum nostris corporibus alimenta sumus, toleraturi inediam dum arcem nostrae potestatis feceris. Id si recusas tuo capite & sanguine nobis securitatem parabimus.
units.tr: For we will neither lay down our arms nor take food for our bodies as nourishment before (they said) you make the citadel ours, enduring hunger. If you refuse this, we will secure our safety with your head and blood.

units.la: Quare Achlenius turbae fremitu qui furori proxumus vicebatur, haud parum obturbatur, haberi ocyus Senatum fecit promissoque civium nomine trimestri aere, seditiosam Vibij cohortem & simul inquietudinem civilium animorum sedavit. Illud additum in gratiam militum fuit, ut veteranae cohortes in stipendijs essent. Mathenesio imperium in adventum Lalainij abrogatum castellumque praesidio civium permissum Armatorum ductores sacramentum regio Senatui dixere. Quare sexaginta delecti, ductoribus Renico Cammingha viro Nobili & Aesgone Harmanno Consule, arcem occupavere, cujus diruendae desiderium illo aestu rerum, ardore libertatis concors populus capiebat. Caeterum per absentiam Lalainij, qui exspectabatur, tum prolatum subsecutae rerum mutationi superfuit.
units.tr: Therefore Achlenius, greatly disturbed by the roar of the crowd, which seemed close to fury, had the Senate convened at once, and, with a promise of three months' pay in the name of the citizens, he calmed both the mutinous cohort of Vibius and the unrest of the civic minds. This was added as a favour to the soldiers: that the veteran cohorts should remain in pay. Mathenesse's command was revoked until Lalaing should arrive, and the citadel was entrusted to the garrison of citizens; the leaders of the armed men swore an oath to the royal Senate. Accordingly sixty picked men, under the leaders Renicus Cammingha, a nobleman, and Aesgo Harmann, the consul, occupied the citadel; the people, united in that heat of affairs and burning with love of liberty, desired its demolition. However, through Lalaing's absence, for he was expected, a delay was granted to the change of affairs that followed.

units.la: {*} QuipcIↄ. Iↄ. LXXVII. Quippe Lalainius Bruxellas profectus, quo de statu provinciæ referret, omnem gerendarum rerum curam sui imperij æmulo regio Senatui commiserat munerisque bene obiti præmium gratiam patrum & legitimam Præfecti potestatem sollicitabat. Cujus cum imaginem magis quam vim tenuisset, legato cum mandatis in provinciam misso quam Præfecto similior, ita tum demum Præfecturæ suæ diploma à patribus accepit frænandisque partium moribus & ordinandæ provinciæ tabulas hujusmodi impetravit.
units.tr: {*} In 1577. For Lalaing had set out for Brussels, to report on the state of the province, and had committed the entire care of managing affairs to the Senate, his rival in power, and, seeking as reward for good service the favour of the fathers and the lawful power of prefect, he sought these things. Since he had grasped the image rather than the substance of that power, he at last received from the fathers the charter of his prefecture, sent to the province a envoy with instructions more like a prefect's deputy than a prefect himself, and obtained tablets of this kind for curbing the conduct of the factions and ordering the province.

units.la: EGregia factorum ratio, quæ GEORGIUS LALAINIUS RENNENBERGIUS patriæ suæ & præsertim Frisiæ ac adjacentibus ditionibus non semel collocavit, commovit nos, ut quoniam retinere in fide Regis ac boni ordinis ratione eadem provincias expedit, eundem LALAINIUM de consilio nostro Frisiæ ac vicinis provincijs moderandis præficiamus. Quâ in re, ut meritorum gloriam & populi illius in Lalainium inclinationem & affectum spectavimus. Itaq; GEORGIUM LALAINIUM RENNENBERGIUM Præfectum Frisiæ, Groningæ, Omlandiæ & Drentiæ declaramus facimusque ei potestatem jure Præfecti curandi, ut jus PHILIPPI Regis & quicquid isti connexum est integrum servet cæteraq; faciat aut ordinet, quæ boni Præfecti mandata exigent. Imprimis vero volumus singulis in Præfecturis Fœdus Gandavense & quod inter Ordines Belgicæ initum ac sacramento confirmatum est, inviolatum curet, ne quid Romanæ Catholicæ Religioni & obedientiæ Regis decedat. Id si faciat, pensionem, jus ac dignitatem Præfecti ante ei collatam assignamus statuimusque ut à XXIII. Novembris, quo ROBLESIUM Præfecturâ submovimus, fructum imperij sui sentiat, ac pensione, jure ac dignitate Præfecti ab eo tempore gaudeat. Quod ut ratum præstemus sigillo Brabantiæ Ordinum, & manu CORNELII WELLEMANNI Graphiarij munÿimus. Datum Bruxellis Prid. Kal. Sept. Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXVII.
units.tr: The distinguished record of deeds by which GEORGIUS LALAINIUS RENNENBERGIUS has more than once rendered service to his country, and particularly to Friesland and the adjacent territories, has moved us, since it is expedient for the same provinces to be kept in the loyalty of the King and in the order of good government, to appoint the same Lalaing, by our decision, to govern Friesland and the neighbouring provinces. In this matter we have regarded both the glory of his merits and the inclination and affection of that people towards Lalaing. Therefore we declare GEORGIUS LALAINIUS RENNENBERGIUS prefect of Friesland, Groningen, Ommelanden and Drenthe, and we grant him power, by the right of a prefect, to take care that the right of King PHILIP and whatever is connected with it be kept whole, and to do or order whatever the duties of a good prefect require. Above all we wish that in each prefecture he see to it that the Ghent Pacification and what has been agreed among the Estates of Belgium and confirmed by oath be kept inviolate, so that nothing be lost to the Roman Catholic Religion and the obedience owed the King. If he does this, we assign to him the pension, right and dignity of prefect previously conferred on him, and we decree that from 23 November, when we removed Roblesius from the prefecture, he shall enjoy the fruit of his command and possess the pension, right and dignity of prefect from that time. To make this ratified we have confirmed it with the seal of the Estates of Brabant and with the hand of CORNELIUS WELLEMANNUS, the clerk. Given at Brussels, the day before the Kalends of September, in the year 1577.

units.la: Igitur firmato tabulis Ordinum generalium Lalainij per Frisiam cæterasque trans Lavicam provincias Imperio, Lalainius ad Kal. Octob. conventum Ordinum Leovardiæ indixit. Ibi ore Præsidis Achlenij de approbando diplomate, de ratihabendo Gandavensi & provinciarum fœdere, de exsolvendis Germanicarum cohortium stipendijs egit rescriptumque Ordinum Frisiæ & assensum postulavit.
units.tr: Therefore, once the tablets of the General Estates had confirmed Lalaing's authority over Friesland and the other provinces beyond the Lauwers, Lalaing called a meeting of the Estates at Leeuwarden for the calends of October. There, through the mouth of the president Achlenius, he spoke about approving the decree, ratifying the Ghent treaty and the provinces' covenant, and paying the wages of the German cohorts. He also presented a written reply from the Estates of Friesland and asked for their assent.

units.la: Cæterum dissidentibus provincialium animis, cum exclusis oppidanis, ut ante dixi, soli agrarij jus ac titulum Ordinum præferrent, concordibus suffragijs nihil actum, volentibus agrarijs, ut oppidani renunciato civitatum & simul comitiorum jure in jus ac nomen agrariorum concederent. Id postulatum in acta II. Octob. relatum. Oppidani vero, quo novi Præfecti animum sibi devincirent jusque suum defendendo laborantibus provinciæ rebus opitularentur, responderunt.
units.tr: However, since the minds of the provincials were divided, and the townsmen had been excluded as I said before, only the landowners claimed the right and title of the Estates. With the votes not in agreement, nothing was done. The landowners wanted the townsmen to renounce the right of their cities and at the same time the right of the assemblies, and to transfer both to the rights and name of the landowners. This demand was recorded in the acts on 2 October. The townsmen, however, in order to win over the new governor and to help the province in its troubles while defending their own right, gave this reply.

units.la: Parere se ORDINUM Belgicæ decreto & LALAINIUM pro provinciæ Præfecto agnoscere, daturos operam ut illi & simul Senatui regio autoritas constet suumque obsequium sacramento regi præstito conveniat. Itaque Fœdus Gandavense & juxta Ordinum generalium ampletti, salvo tamen patrio jure, à quo si discrepet, obtestari se universos singulosque. Et quamvis vis non dubitent, quin agrarij sociaturi consilia sint, ita petere ut seorsim aut conjunctim decernant, quod ex usu provinciæ videbitur. Quod ad postulatum agrariorum & renuntiandi juris attineret, reponebant convocatos se esse à Præfecto, ut recepto ritu comitio interessent, quibus more majorum jus comparendi consulendique in publicum esset. Et quoniam litteris PHILIPPI Regis, ac ORDINUM BELGICAE constet, FRISIAE ORDINUM nomine Antistites, Nobilitatem, Proprietarios & Oppidanos habitos fuisse, ita æquum esse ex Præfecti & Senatus Regij litteris, seorsim cum suis membra provinciæ consultare. Neque enim pro loci aut situs ratione separandos esse, quos jus aut ejus communio connectat. Conserendis vero in publicum tributis etsi majores florenos aureos è solo provenientes, tanquam paratissimum subsidium, gerendis rebus applicaverint, neque alius mos nisi cum obtestatione & salvo jure observatus fuerit observarique conquirendis militum stipendijs etiamnum debeat, tamen pacis ac concordiæ causâ subventuros necessitati publicæ daturosque operam, ut quicquid exsolvendum Germanorum cohortibus erit, in promptu sit, quo ocyus provincia quies & tranquillitas dimissis militaribus copijs habeatur. Salvo tamen in futurum partium jure.
units.tr: They said that they would obey the decree of the Estates of Belgium and would recognise Lalaing as governor of the province. They would take care that his authority and that of the royal Senate be made certain, and that their obedience agree with the oath sworn to the king. Accordingly they embraced the Treaty of Ghent and the decrees of the General Estates, but with the native right saved; if anyone departed from that right, they called upon all and each to bear witness. Although they did not doubt that the landowners would join in their counsels, they asked that they decide either separately or together, as the good of the province seemed to require. As to the landowners' demand and the renunciation of right, they replied that they had been summoned by the governor so that they might take their seats in the assembly, which by the custom of their ancestors has the right to attend and to deliberate in public. And since it is clear from the letters of King Philip and of the Estates of Belgium that the bishops, nobility, landowners and townsmen were held in the name of the Estates of Friesland, it was right, according to the letters of the governor and the royal Senate, that the members of the province consult separately with their own. For those whom right or a common right binds together should not be separated on account of place or location. Indeed, although they had applied the greater florins of gold, arising from the soil, to the conduct of affairs as a most ready aid, and no other custom than with protest and saving the right had been or still ought to be observed in collecting the taxes for soldiers' wages, nevertheless, for the sake of peace and concord, they would come to the aid of public necessity and take care that whatever must be paid to the German cohorts be ready at hand, so that the province might sooner have quiet and tranquillity once the military forces were dismissed. The right of the parties is nevertheless saved for the future.

units.la: Hæc Leovardiæ in Æde Jacobæorum III. Octob. acta, & Æmylij Adamæ Jureconsulti manu pro Oppidanis signata.
units.tr: These things were done at Leeuwarden in the church of the Jacobites on 3 October, and were signed for the townsmen by the hand of Æmylius Adama, jurist.

units.la: Cujus decreti cum agrarijs copiam pridiè oppidani fecissent, Douwonem Meium actuarium cum duobus testibus ad eosdem agrarios mandarunt, cum mandato urgendi responsum declarandique præterea, oppidorum & civitatum legatos etiamnum, ut à primo conventus die, paratos esse ex formulâ convocationis cum agrarijs ad postulata Præfecti rescribere. Quos si alia exerceant ijsque agrarij inconsultis oppidanis inhæreant aut immorentur, obtestari oppidanos, id omne quicquid scriptum, factum decretumve fuerit, fraudi sibi non fore, ac cavere de damnis & expensis. Id v. Octob. actis traditum ac Matthiæ Rommartij & Æmylij Adamæ subscriptionibus roboratum.
