units.tr: When the townsmen had given the landowners a copy of this decree the day before, they sent the secretary Douwo Meius, with two witnesses, to the same landowners, with instructions to press for an answer and further to declare that the envoys of the towns and cities were still ready, from the first day of the assembly, to reply to the governor's demands together with the landowners, according to the form of the summons. If the landowners should do otherwise, and if they should cling to or linger over their demands without consulting the townsmen, the townsmen call upon them to witness that whatever has been written, done or decreed will not be held against them, and that they will take care of losses and expenses. This was handed over in the acts on 5 October and confirmed by the signatures of Matthias Rommartius and Æmylius Adama.

units.la: Ab Agrarijs quoque ad Lalainij postulata responsum.
units.tr: The landowners likewise gave their answer to Lalaing's demands.

units.la: POpulum scilicet Friscum ex patrio & conventionum jure immunem omnium, sive res sive personas spectent, onerum esse, neque teneri ad Vectigalia & tributa, præterquam ea quæ regi, administrando juri & æquo tuendoque adversum injurias populo assignata essent. Itaque regem mandasse Præfectis ut pacta conventa rata curarent. Caeterum quoniam nec præteriti aut præsentis temporis conditio id ferat, ut provinciæ securitatem stabilire Rex queat necessumque sit, ut propriâ ope, salvo tamen partium jure, populus Friscus immunitati ac juri suo hoc tempore consulat, sub câ cautione ne exemplo sit, ita ORDINES censent è Rep. esse, ut LALAINIUS in communionem regundæ provinciæ (excepto civili & criminali jure) Deputatos Ordinum adhibeat. Quo indulto decernunt ijdem Ordines statuuntque Lalainium pro Præfecto habendum, sub istâ tamen obtestatione mense Januario factâ, & dein conventione xv. Martij initâ. Rogare interim LALAINIUM, ut fidem faciat se provinciam ex patrio jure, statutis & moribus de consilio Deputatorum & ad formulam Gaudavensis fæderis recturum. A quo consilio si alienum Lalainium spectent, non stare se pactis Januario men-se. cIↄ. Iↄ. se aut Martio confectis, neque habituros eum pro Praefecto, cujus regimen ut an-te in populi damna ac oppressiones recasurum sit. Quod ad stipendia numeranda Germanorum cohortibus attineret, decernere Ordines, ut Lalainius omne jus amissum prius restituat ac redintegret eaque integra curet, de quibus Ordines, Lalainium & Deputatos suos plenius docturi sint. Hoc interea agat Lalainius, ut Episcopo & Sedi adjecta ad dominos suos redeant caveaturque, ne ante pensionibus ex aerario qui gaudeant, quam Episcopus caeteriqué occupatis caenobijs & simul Haskerano cesserint. Hoc quoque effectum det, ut vitio & contra jus patrium creati Praetores caeteriqué Officiary tam saeculares, quam Ecclesiastici partis male dignitatibus se abdicent eorumque mandatis palam rescissi novi ex constitutione Anni cIↄ. Iↄ. xxii. deligantur. Isti quippe rei xv. Mart. Lalainium fidem fecisse & expedire publice ut ea servetur. Itaque ne quid provincialium juri decedat, velle Ordines ternos & quosdem idoneos in unaquaque Praetura nominari, quo Lalainius una cum Ordinum Delegatis tam ex veteribus, si nominentur, quam novis creet, qui praetoris personam agat. Idem Praetores in designandis Secretarijs facient, sed ita ut consensu & suffragatione delegatorum singulorum, quos ex pagis edituri sunt, constituantur. Et quoniam magnum tuendae libertatis & pacis publicae praesidium ab armis peti debet, velle Ordines, ut armari populum curet ex formula, eum inter & Delegatos Ordinum scribenda. Quae si Lalainius approbari faciat testeturque rescripto se decretis Ordinum obsecuturum, res bono apud Ordines loco fore, quorum ea mens esset, non velle tributum, praeterquam subsecuta postulatorum ratihabitione, poscentibus rebus pensitare. Velle se interea pacem & concordiam & ut in bono ordine, tanquam optumo perennitatis custode, res provinciae perfistant.
units.tr: Namely, the Frisian people, by their native right and by the agreements, are free from all burdens, whether these concern goods or persons, and are not bound to pay excises and taxes, except those assigned to the king, to the administration of justice, and to the protection of the people against injuries by fair means. Therefore the king ordered the governors to see that the agreed pacts were kept. However, since neither the condition of past nor present times allows the king to establish the province's security, and since it is necessary that the Frisian people, by their own help and with the rights of the parties saved, look after their immunity and right at this time, on condition that this does not become a precedent, the Estates judge that it is in the public interest that Lalaing should, in the sharing of the regulation of the province (excepting civil and criminal jurisdiction), call in the deputies of the Estates. By this concession the same Estates decree and establish that Lalaing shall be held as governor, under the proviso, however, made in January and then concluded by the agreement of 15 March. Meanwhile they ask Lalaing to assure them that he will govern the province according to the native law, the statutes and customs, with the advice of the deputies and in accordance with the form of the Ghent treaty. If Lalaing should look on this advice as foreign to him, they declare that they will not abide by the pacts made in January or March 1577, and will no longer hold him as governor, since his rule would again lead to the damages and oppressions of the people. As to paying the wages of the German cohorts, the Estates decree that Lalaing shall first restore and renew every right lost, and keep these intact; the Estates will inform Lalaing and his deputies more fully about these matters. Meanwhile Lalaing should see to it that the bishopric and the places attached to it return to their lords, and it shall be guaranteed that no one receives pensions from the treasury before the bishop and the other occupied monasteries have also given way, together with Haskerus. He should also bring it about that the magistrates and other officials, both lay and ecclesiastical, who were wrongly created against the native law, be openly deprived of their offices, and that new ones be chosen in their place under the constitution of the year 1522. For on 15 March they had made Lalaing a promise, and it is expedient that this be kept publicly. Therefore, so that nothing be lost of the provincials' right, the Estates wish that three or more suitable men be nominated for each magistracy, so that Lalaing, together with the deputies of the Estates, may appoint from both old, if they are nominated, and new men one who shall act as praetor. The same magistrates shall do this in designating the secretaries, but in such a way that they are appointed by the consent and vote of the individual deputies whom they are to choose from the districts. And since a great safeguard for defending liberty and public peace must be sought from arms, the Estates wish that Lalaing see to the arming of the people according to a form to be drawn up between him and the deputies of the Estates. If Lalaing has this approved and testifies in a written reply that he will obey the decrees of the Estates, the matter will stand well with the Estates, whose intention this is; they do not wish to levy any tax, except after the demands have been ratified, as circumstances require. Meanwhile they wish peace and concord, and that the affairs of the province remain in good order, as the best guardian of its permanence.

units.la: Actum iii. Octob. ac jussu Ordinum a F. Thoma Groningense Abbate Floridi Campi, Epaeo Douma Hallemio, Livio Beiemo, Laurentio Buwonio pastore Ferverdico, Foppio Douma, Menenio Taconio Sceltingha, Cellio Roorsma, Aucone Edonio signatum.
units.tr: Done on 3 October, and by order of the Estates signed by Brother Thomas of Groningen, abbot of Floridus Campus; Epaeus Douma of Hallum; Livius Beiemus; Laurentius Buwonius, minister at Ferwerd; Foppius Douma; Menenius Taconius of Sceltinga; Cellius Roorsma; and Aucho Edonius.

units.la: Ad quae LALAINIUS rescripsit.
units.tr: To which LALAING replied.

units.la: Se de consuetudine veteri una cum DEPUTATIS provinciam gubernaturum neque suae potestatis esse quicquam immutare aut statuere quod privilegijs populi adversum sit. Quae si violata aut antiquata opinentur Ordines, posse per acta id docere agereque apud Concilium regij status aut Ordines generales, & quidem sua intercessione, quam reparandis rebus offerret. Neque enim se Praefecturam per provinciam alijs auspicijs sumpsisse, quam ut stabilito gentis jure & omni immunitate, sui in populum favoris & simul libertatis incrementa essent & ut ex antecessorum suorum imperio praegravati provinciales antiquis moribus & quidem ex praescripto Gandavensis foederis reddantur. Interim reputandum esse Ordinibus quantum incommodi denegata copijs stipendia allatura sint & quam periculosum sit differre remedium sopiendis legionum seditionibus salutare. Nulla quippe gentium arma unquam sine stipendijs, nulla stipendia sine tributis fuisse, quae tanto graviora fore necessum esset, quanto cunctantius in tam praecipiti malo amovendo socordia Ordinum ageretur. Aequissimum esse copias sacramento Ordinum militantes illorum are merere, qui per arma & armorum subsidia ad libertatem properarent. Quod ad restituenda caenobiorum bona attineret, id conventui ORDINUM GeneGeneralium ex conventione Gandavensi reservatum, inquam, proferri negotium non posse censerent ORDINES, decretum CONCILII LXXVII. STATUS interponi debere, aut eorum quos determinandis controversiis regiæ voluntatis mandatum præscripsset. Quæ de Prætoribus immutandis dicta essent, ea facturum se ex pacto xv. Martij inito, neque laturum ut reciprocis conventionibus fraus aut vis fiat. Armando vero populo, etsi omnium Belgicæ provinciarum Præfecti mandatum antè annum acceperint, tamen assensum præbere se non posse, amotis in Italiam Hispanorum legionibus & pace publicâ extra omne discrimen constitutâ. Non gravandam esse Frisiæ gentem illo onere aut servitio, nisi probet veteris instituti instans periculum egere & legionum insolentiæ graßatorum licentiam succedere.
units.tr: He would govern the province as before, together with the Deputies, according to the ancient custom, and it was not within his power to change or decree anything contrary to the privileges of the people. If the Estates thought these had been violated or abolished, they could show this by the records and act on it before the Council of State or the General Estates, and indeed by his intercession, which he would offer towards repairing matters. For he had not taken up the governorship of the province on any other auspices than that, with the law of the nation and all its immunities established, there should be increases of his favour towards the people and at the same time of their liberty, and that the provincials, weighed down under the rule of his predecessors, should be restored to their ancient customs, indeed in accordance with the terms of the Treaty of Ghent. Meanwhile the Estates should consider how much harm the denial of money to the troops would bring, and how dangerous it is to delay the remedy that would be salutary for quelling the mutinies of the legions. For no nation's arms had ever existed without pay, nor pay without taxes, and these would of necessity become the heavier the more sluggishly the Estates' inaction proceeded in removing so headlong an evil. It was most just that the troops serving under the Estates' oath should earn the pay of those who hasten to liberty through arms and the aid of arms. As for restoring the monastic properties, the Estates thought that this matter, I say, which was reserved by the Ghent convention to the General Assembly of the Estates, could not be brought forward, and that a decree of the Council of State should be interposed, or of those whom the royal mandate had prescribed for settling controversies. As to what had been said about changing the Praetors, he would do this in accordance with the agreement made on 15 March, and would not permit reciprocal agreements to be defrauded or violated. As for arming the people, although the governors of all the Belgic provinces had received a mandate a year earlier, he could nevertheless not give his assent, with the Spanish legions removed to Italy and public peace established beyond all danger. The people of Friesland should not be burdened with that charge or service, unless they prove that a pressing danger threatens the old institution and that the licence of the marauders is following upon the insolence of the legions.

units.la: Hæc Leovardiæ v. Octob. Lalainij manu signata.
units.tr: These things were written at Leeuwarden on 5 October and signed by Lalaing's hand.

units.la: Quo responso cum satisfactum sibi Ordines non censerent, L. Lalainius rescripsit.
units.tr: Since the Estates did not think they had been satisfied by this reply, L. Lalaing replied again.

units.la: DEPUTATOS vestros in consilium à me adhiberi jam antè petiistis, neque ab eo postulato alienus fui, quo consortes meo imperio natus oneris publici magnitudinem lubricis temporibus allevarem. Itaque fidem vobis paciscor, me non nisi de illorum consilio provinciam recturum daturumque operam ut regium jus & simul populi valeat fœdusque Gandavense vestris legibus ac immunitatibus affirmetur. Cæterum hoc peto, ut scripto documenta læsi violatique juris faciatis, quo remedia morbis publicis & licentiæ dominantium parem videamque quantum à libertate vestrâ & suo officio mei antecessores recesserint. Hoc vero expendite, quam salubre consilium exsolvendis copijs ingesserim & quam vestra interest insolenti & rapaci turbæ, seditiones ex inopiâ stipendiorum agitanti, vestris tributis subveniri, quæ inferri in ærarium illæso patrimonio possunt. Quæ si præstetis, prout præstanda aliquando erunt, dabo effectum, ut Sedi & Episcopo adjecta ad cœnobitas redeant, si forte cæteras per provincias idem ordinari publica auctoritas decreverit. Interim censeo conveniendos ea de re provinciarum Belgicæ Ordines suadeoque, ut meâ approbatione id fiat. Quod ad immutandos Prætores agrarios & officiales attinet, id meæ potestatis non esse existimo, paratus tamen, de consilio Deputatorum Frisiæ, ex formulâ Anni MDCIX. xxxix. Prætores ordinare ÿsque pro tempore abrogare imperium, quos edoctus ero criminum convictos præclaras dignitates manifestis enormibus fœdasse. De cæteris Ordines Belgicæ haud dubiè statuent, quorum arbitrij erit, malè administratæ provinciæ reos legitimis remedijs corrigere. Interim actorum xv. Mart. magna apud me ratio erit censeoque, ORDINES, non acrioribus disceptationibus aut querelis me fatigandum esse, in hoc maximè intentum, ut Prætores & Secretarios ad normam antiqui moris formem. Neque & hoc abnuo, ut defendendæ adversum vim atque insolentiam patriæ arma sumatis, aut plebem agrariam promiscuè armetis, cæterum hac lege, ne cui sine nostro mandato intententur & ut eorum ope hostes tantum & pacis publicæ perturbatores coërceantur. Itaque caveri mihi peto, neminem armis suis male usurum, nec ore aut linguâ tenus, cæterum jure-jurando firmandum. Interim ex usufore censeo, ut è gente vestrâ binos legatos ad Concilium Status aut Ordines generales mittatis, qui de singulis agant & quidem meâ commendatione ac operâ, quam vestræ incolumitati addico.
units.tr: You had already asked earlier that your Deputies be brought into my council, and I was not averse to that request, so that those who share in my office might lighten the great burden of public affairs in these slippery times. I therefore pledge my faith to you that I will govern the province only on the advice of those men, and I will take care that the royal law and at the same time the people's, and the Treaty of Ghent, be confirmed by your laws and immunities. Furthermore, this I ask: that you put in writing the records of the violated and infringed right, so that I may see the remedies for the public ills and the licence of those in power, and see how far my predecessors have departed from your liberty and their duty. Yet consider this carefully: how wholesome a counsel I have offered for paying the troops, and how much it is in your interest that the insolent and rapacious mob, stirring up sedition from lack of pay, be relieved by your taxes, which can be brought into the treasury without harm to your patrimony. If you do this, as at some time they will have to be done, I will see to it that the properties added to the See and the bishop return to the monks, if perhaps public authority should decree the same across the other provinces. Meanwhile I think the Estates of the Belgic provinces should be convened on this matter, and I advise that it be done with my approval. As for changing the agrarian Praetors and officials, I do not think this is within my power; nevertheless, I am ready, with the advice of the Deputies of Friesland, to appoint Praetors according to the formula of the year 1609 and to revoke their authority whenever, the time being, I shall have learned that they, convicted of crimes, have disgraced their distinguished offices by manifest and monstrous acts. As for the rest, the Belgic Estates will doubtless decide, and it will be for them to correct, by lawful remedies, the guilty who have governed their provinces badly. Meanwhile I will give great weight to the agreement of 15 March, and I think the Estates should not weary me with more bitter disputes or complaints, since I am intent above all on ensuring that the Praetors and Secretaries are brought back to the norm of the ancient custom. Nor do I refuse this: that you take up arms to defend the fatherland against violence and insolence, or that you arm the agrarian commons indiscriminately; but on this condition, that no one be attacked without our mandate, and that by their help only enemies and disturbers of public peace be restrained. I therefore ask that it be made certain to me that no one will misuse his arms, not merely with words or the tongue, but that this be confirmed by oath. Meanwhile I think it expedient that you send two envoys from your people to the Council of State or the General Estates, who may treat of the individual matters, and indeed with my recommendation and help, which I pledge to your safety.

units.la: Qo 2 Hæc cIↄ. Iↄ. Hæc à LALAINIO in arce Leovard. VII. Octob. scripta LXXVII ac ab eo signata.
units.tr: Q o 2. These things were written by Lalaing in the castle at Leeuwarden on 7 October 1577 and signed by him.

units.la: Ad quæ iterum ORDINES.
units.tr: To which the States replied again.

units.la: QVOD imperij tui rationem affirmare Deputatorum nostrorum arbitrijs velis, id gratum nobis fuit PRAEFECTE & quod pensitanda copijs stipendia suaseris. De interverso cænobiorum censu, quem præpositeri temporum mores Leovardiensium Sedi applicavere, non semel quæsti fuimus rogavimusque, ut per vim acquisita Episcopus restitueret factisque accepti expensique rationibus jurisdictione Ecclesiastica cederet. Prætores quoque, ab Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. xxxix. contra jus patrium constitutos, dignitatibus exueres, postquam deprehensum fuit, eos non bonis artibus quæsitam dominationem malis moribus exercuisse. Neque enim volumus, ut institutâ Senatum apud regium actione aut per formam judicij corrigas, sed ut curiosâ omnium criminum inquisitione per pagos & districtus facta, tuâ & Deputatorum nostrorum autoritate submoveantur. Novos quoque ex statuto majorum & Anni cIↄ. Iↄ. xxii. nominatos gerendis per præturam rebus substitutas, planè ita formatis consilijs tuis, ut censeas omne vitiosum in Rep. sanandum esse. Armandis vero agrarijs potestatem tibi facimus, sed ita, ne quid in hoc juri patrio & consuetudini decedat & ut ipse expendas quam lubrico adhuc loco & casibus expositio patriæ nostræ res fortuna temporum posuerit. Quæ ne magis ex inquietudine cohortium in nos desæviat, tuo & Deputatorum arbitrio definiendorum stipendiorum modum relinquimus, cæterum hac cautione adhibitâ, ut ratio quotæ habeatur & ut sinas nos corrogandi aris de jure antiquo & simul tributa imperandi potestatem retinere. Hoc etiam volumus, ut quotquot in copijs nostris aut sub signis sunt exleges & scelesti, stipendia non accipiant & ut prima stipendiorum pensione soluta Concilium Status aut Ordines generales provinciæ jus restituant, quod aut ex dominatione Principis, aut ex turbis temporum violatum erit. Nos interim dabimus operam, ut de in jus nostrum communis Concilium Status, aut Ordines generales doceamus testemurque nos, si non patrij juris vim atque efficaciam, saltem memoriam retinuisse.
units.tr: As to your account of your government, which you wish to confirm by the judgement of our Deputies, we are glad, Prefect; and also that you have advised paying the soldiers' wages out of the available funds. We have often asked and urged that the Bishop restore the church property that the troubled times of the past had transferred to the See of Leeuwarden from the monasteries, and that, once the accounts of receipts and expenditures were rendered, he give up ecclesiastical jurisdiction. We also ask you to remove from office the magistrates appointed contrary to the ancestral law from the year 1539 onward, since it has been found that they used a power not gained by good means with bad conduct. We do not want you to proceed by a formal action before the regional Senate or by a legal process; rather, after a careful inquiry into all the crimes throughout the districts and rural areas, they should be removed by your authority and that of our Deputies. Likewise, the new officials named under the ancient statute and the year 1522 to carry out the affairs of the magistracy are to be replaced, your plans being framed so that you judge that every fault in the commonwealth must be remedied. We grant you power to raise the agrarian forces, but in such a way that nothing is lost from the ancestral law and custom, and so that you yourself weigh how slippery the present position is, and how exposed to dangers our country's fortune has placed it in these times. Lest the troops rage against us more fiercely out of restlessness, we leave to you and our Deputies the fixing of the amount of the wages; yet with this caution, that an account of the quota be kept, and that you allow us to retain the right, from ancient law, to raise money by levy and also the power to impose taxes. We also want this: that whoever in our forces or under the standards are outlaws and criminals should not receive wages; and that once the first installment of wages is paid, the Council of State or the General States restore to the province the right which has been violated either by the Prince's domination or by the disturbances of the times. Meanwhile we shall take care to inform and assure the Council of State or the General States of our right, and to show that we have kept, if not the force and efficacy of the ancestral law, at least its memory.

units.la: Ita Epæus Douma, Livius Beiemus, Otto Herama, W. Groventeinius, Idzardus Reinius, Joannes Agricola rescripsere. Quæ x. Octob. à Delegatis præturarum Laurentio Bernardo Presbytero Ferverdico, Ernesto Aylva, Sibrando Burmania, Siuckio Humalda, Louiò Allema, Edone Allema, Oedzio Arnoldio, Hercone Arnoldio, Sixto Idzio, Sceltone Tiaerda, Siriaco Haersma, Syboldo Aylva, Jorsa Lolckma Pastore Schingensi, Hansone Albada, Jeltone Gellio, Joanne Cornelio Presbytero Witmarsumano, Regnero Allartio, Tito Waltesio, Hansone Roorda pro Hennardijs, Joanne Ægydio, Jelgero Feitsma pro Franequeranis, Jeronimo Winterio, Jacobo Wichero pro Scoterlandis & Haskerijs, Joanne ter Wisga, Vibio Watzonio, Piboone Witsio Abbema pro Utingeranis signata actorum fidem meruere.
units.tr: Thus Epaeus Douma, Livius Beiemus, Otto Herama, W. Groventeinius, Idzardus Reinius and Johannes Agricola replied. These documents, signed on 10 October by the delegates of the districts, Laurentius Bernardus, elder at Ferwerd, Ernestus Aylva, Sibrandus Burmania, Siuckius Humalda, Louio Allema, Edo Allema, Oedzius Arnoldus, Hercon Arnoldus, Sixtus Idzius, Sceltonus Tiaerda, Siriacus Haersma, Syboldus Aylva, Jorsa Lolckma, minister at Schingen, Hanso Albada, Jeltho Gellius, Johannes Cornelius, elder at Witmarsum, Regnerus Allartius, Titus Waltesius, Hanso Roorda for Hennardia, Johannes Aegidius, Jelgerus Feitsma for Franeker, Hieronymus Winterius, Jacobus Wichers for Stellingwerf and Hasker, Johannes ter Wisga, Vibius Watzonius, and Pibo Witsius Abbema for Utingeradeel, were accepted as trustworthy.

units.la: Mox quatuor stuferi assignandæ primæ stipendiorum militarium pensioni in florenos aureos decreti, eâ tamen cautione ut Deputati Ordinum cum Oppidanis ac Biltanis agant, pro ratione aureorum florenorum subsidia præstandi dandique operam ut tributum commune sit. Potestas quoque ijsdem Deputatis recensendi militares copias transfigendiq; cum cohortibus facta; ne quod jam antè Lalainius monuerat solutionem differendo, magnitudo menstrui æris & per eam seditionum militarium metus increuerat. Quæ etsi allevando oneri publico & simul maturandæ cohortium missioni reperta essent, ita dissensiones Ordinum peperere, decernentibus Westergois ne quod tributum ultra à florenis aureis peteretur & ut lite ex causâ tributorum natâ, aliud ærario subsidium & quidem intrà spatium tridui publica necessitas reperiret. Secus obtestabantur, se comitio excessuros, facturosque secessionem. Hæc x i i i. Octobris Joannes Cornelius pastor apud Witmarsios, S. Galama, W. Grovensteinius, Jelgerus Feitsma, Siriacus Haersma, Everardus Ludolphi, Regnerus Allartius signavere. Quod decretum ne damno sibi foret, Oostergoi & Sylvestres intercessere & ne promptissima ac à majoribus petita contribuendi ratio novitate recentis tributi dissolveretur. Sic Scelto Tiaerda, Sibrandus Burmania, Siriacus Haersma, F. Grovensteinius, Joannes Ægydius, & Hector Waltesius rescripsere.
units.tr: Soon afterwards it was decreed that four stuivers in the florin should be assigned to the first installment of the military wages, payable in gold florins, on the condition that the Deputies of the States deal with the townsmen and the Biltanis, and provide subsidies in proportion to the gold florins, and that they take care that the tax be common. The same Deputies were also given power to review the military forces and to move them about with the cohorts; this was done so that, as Lalaing had already warned, the delay in payment should not increase the size of the monthly debt, and with it the fear of mutinies among the soldiers. Although these measures were devised to lighten the public burden and at the same time to hasten the discharge of the cohorts, they produced disagreements among the States: the Westergoers decreed that no tax should be demanded beyond the gold florins, and that, since a dispute had arisen over the taxes, the public necessity should find another source of funds for the treasury within three days. Otherwise, they protested, they would leave the assembly and secede. This decree was signed on 13 October by Johannes Cornelius, minister at Witmarsum, S. Galama, W. Groventeinius, Jelgerus Feitsma, Siriacus Haersma, Everardus Ludolphi and Regnerus Allartius. Lest this decree be to their harm, the Oostergoers and the Sylvestrians interceded, and so that the most ready method of contribution, sought from their ancestors, should not be dissolved by the novelty of the recent tax. Thus Sceltonus Tiaerda, Sibrandus Burmania, Siriacus Haersma, F. Groventeinius, Johannes Aegidius and Hector Waltesius replied.

units.la: Tum curationes publicarum rationum iterum ordinatæ, quo consusis provinciæ rebus ordo aliquis ærario esset, collapsisque populi tributis subveniretur. Itaque ex decreto comitij, quod x v. Jan. Lalainius jam antè & mox mense Septembri indixerat, Sceltoni Tiaerda, Livio Beiemo, (cui Siriacum Haersma suffectum reperio) Theodoro Fogelsangio Jurec. Hectori Wibenio, Auconi Edonio & Feiconi Tatmanno dignitas continuata, dato eisdem mandato, ut quæstorum per provinciam & præcipuè Balduini Loi Thesaurarij regij rationibus præsiderent ijsque faciendis quæstores aliosque debendi recs jure atque actione publicâ convenirent. Hoc etiam mandati additum, ut pensionibus per Ordines promissis, exsolvendis interessent tribunosque ærario & simul modum tributo, cujus corrogandi potestatem accepissent, in proximum comitium constituerent. Hæc à Paulo Costerio Antistite Fosverdico, Siuckio Humalda, Sixto Dekama IC. Cornelio Hitsumano IC. Gellio Broërio, Ioanne Ægydio & post Everardo Ludolpho, Upcone Burmania, Ielgero Feitsma, Edone Allema, Ioanne Ægydio & Vibio Gualterio x i v. Octob. confirmata.
units.tr: Then the management of the public accounts was reorganised again, so that some order might be imposed on the province's confused affairs and the people might be relieved of their collapsed taxes. Accordingly, by the decree of the assembly which Lalaing had already announced on 15 January and again in September, the office was continued for Sceltonus Tiaerda, Livius Beiemus (in whose place I find Siriacus Haersma was substituted), Theodorus Fogelsangius, jurist, Hector Wibenius, Auco Edonius and Feico Tatmannus. They were given the mandate to supervise the accounts of the treasurers throughout the province, and especially those of Balduinus Loi, the royal treasurer, and to summon the treasurers and other debtors to pay what was owed by public right and legal action. It was also added to the mandate that they should be present at the payment of the installments promised by the States, and that they should set up, for the next assembly, tribunes for the treasury and at the same time a limit for the tax whose levying they had been empowered to decide. These were confirmed on 14 October by Paulus Costerius, minister at Franeker, Siuckius Humalda, Sixtus Dekama, jurist, Cornelius Hitsuma, jurist, Gellius Broërius, Johannes Aegidius, and afterwards Everardus Ludolphus, Upco Burmania, Jelgerus Feitsma, Edo Allema, Johannes Aegidius and Vibius Gualterius.

units.la: Post Lalainius submotis Præfecturæ suæ & imperij æmulis (inter quos Bossuvium & Arschotanum autores nominavere) salutatis apud Bruxellas Ordinibus in provinciam revertit factaque cum tribunis Germanicarum cohortium transactione munitiones & castella marino litori versus occasum impositia præsidijs liberavit. Ea pactione cautum fuit, ut trium mensium stipendia cohortibus darentur eædemque cohortes, residuum æris deducto alieno certis pensionibus acciperent. Scribit F. Nicolaus biennium ijsdem pensionibus scriptum fuisse Germanicaque præsidia nullâ insolentiâ aut murmure dimissa. Itaque tum Slotâ, Lemmariâ, Hindelopâ, Maccomio & Oostmahorná munitionibus præsidia excessere.
units.tr: Afterwards Lalaing was dismissed from his prefecture and from the rivals of his command (among whom they named Bossu and Arschot as the instigators). After greeting the States at Brussels, he returned to the province, and by an agreement with the tribunes of the German cohorts he freed the fortifications and castles placed along the coast towards the west from garrisons. By this agreement it was provided that the cohorts should be given three months' wages, and that these same cohorts should receive the remainder of the money, less the debt, in fixed installments. Friar Nicolaus writes that they were enrolled for two years on these payments, and that the German garrisons were dismissed without insolence or grumbling. Accordingly, at that time they left the garrisons at Slooten, Lemmer, Hindeloopen, Makkum and Oostmahorn.

units.la: Mox ab Ordinibus generalibus ad Hollandiæ Zelandiæque proceres, dein Aurantium Legatio decreta, quâ instanti haud dubie bello Hollandiam Zelandiamque subsidia, Aurantium vero regundis rebus & Austriaci subdola fide lubricis salubria consilia poscebant.
units.tr: Soon afterwards the General States decreed a legation to the nobles of Holland and Zeeland, and then one to Orange. In the coming war, which was undoubtedly imminent, they sought help for Holland and Zeeland, and for Orange sound counsel on the government of affairs, and on the treacherous good faith of the Austrian, which was unstable.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. Jam enim Austriacus per Germaniam, Galliam, Allobroges, Italiam LXXVII. & Hispaniam capias clam autorabat Belgisque provincijs, detectâ desectione, etsi suis artibus desideria pacis ostentaret, bellum minabatur.
units.tr: In the year 1577. For already the Austrian, by secret plots, was ambitiously pursuing captures through Germany, France, Burgundy, Italy and Spain; and to the Belgic provinces, now that the defection had been discovered, he threatened war, even though he displayed his desire for peace by his own arts.

units.la: Quare Ordines Philippum regem, violatae per Austriacum fidei & imminentium discriminum praemonitum, novum Belgicis Friscisq; terris Praesidem ac Austrico successorem oravere, quem à recto Principis aut Proregis officio inconsulti juvenilium consiliorum impetus & praecipue Ioannis Escovedi turbulentum ingenium abduxissent. Illo autore, etsi in Hispaniam ab Austiaco missus esset, fletisse turbatae Belgicae causam ideoque exigi, ut fraudes paci professus suis artibus pereat suoque sanguine, cui effundendo consilium locasset, crimen expiet Regem inter & provincias dissoluti nexus. Qui reparari tamen vel hoc solo possit, si fidem gentis, si libertatem Philippus expendat & quos ex Hispania in Belgicam Frisiamque missos, nutriendis simultatibus aluerit. Traditum annalibus est, magnam tempestatem in Hispania tum exortam collisisque ventorum turbine nubibus, mox horrendo fragore subsecuto, regiam Philippi fulmine & coelesti igne tactam fuisse. Arguente, ut ego existumo, velut naturae inclementiâ, resurgentem per provincias Philippi bellorum flammam, diuturnâ & tot annorum face arsuram non Belgicae tantum ditionibus, caeterum Philippi regno funestum incendium minari.
units.tr: Therefore the States begged King Philip, who had been warned of the faith violated by the Austrian and of the dangers impending, to send a new Governor to the Belgic and Frisian lands, and a successor to the Austrian, one whom the impetuous and ill-considered youthful counsels, and especially the turbulent temperament of Juan de Escobedo, had drawn away from the proper duty of a Prince or Governor-General. On his authority, although he had been sent into Spain by the Austrian, they said he had wept over the cause of the troubled Belgium; and therefore it was demanded that he, who had professed to deal in frauds, should perish by his own arts and atone with his own blood for the crime of having planned to shed it, and that the dissolved bond between the King and the provinces should be expiated. Yet this bond might be repaired by this alone, if Philip weighed the good faith of the nation and its liberty, and if he dismissed those whom he had sent from Spain into Belgium and Friesland, who had nourished enmities by fostering them. It is recorded in the annals that a great storm then arose in Spain, and that, with the whirlwind of the winds crashing the clouds together, and soon after a dreadful crash following, the royal palace of Philip was struck by lightning and heavenly fire. As I judge, this was like a sign of the harshness of nature, portending that the flame of wars rekindled through the provinces by Philip, long fed and blazing through so many years, would threaten a deadly conflagration not only in the Belgic dominions but also in Philip's kingdom.

units.la: Ad Palatinum quoque Electorem ab Ordinibus Provinciarum litterae datae militem rogavere, sed qui provinciarum stipendijs haberetur. Elector vero, innexam affinitatibus Belgicis domum trahens, de auxilijs ad Ordines rescripsit suisque in Belgicum populum affectus certos esse jussit. Se Frederici patris (is Ameliam Brederodij viduam matrimonio tenuerat) divae memoriae pronis in Belgas favoribus insistentem, non minora paternis desideria liberandis provincijs profiteri. Interesse scilicet Germaniae, impulsas provinciarum res auxilijs Principum sublevari, quorum fortuna & prosperitas subversâ Belgicâ in incerto sint. Ijsdem fatis ac simili ruinae utramque gentem subjacere. Itaque misereri se infoelicis Belgicae, ut ante firmatâ foederibus pace, voluptatem ita moerorem è ruptâ violataque sensurum. Dolere se iniqua imperia affectantes pessima consilia resumere externumque militem jure Foederis dimissum, in provincias reducendum fore. Igitur Ordines bellum minantibus optumo consilio arma decernere, omni gentium jure subnixa, quas ad propulsandam vim patriae & carissimorum pignorum cura tot aetatibus temporum compulisset. Se vero etsi exercitum non alat, daturum interim operam, ut per ditiones suas ac vicinas, non inopes virorum nec à suo sacramento alienas, intra bimestre militem colligat mittique in provincias faciat. Hoc vero imprimis desiderari, ut non tam de milite quam justo Duce cogitent, ac ut militare corpus ex se turbidum & licentiae studens, tum omnis gerendi belli ratio perito rectore coërceatur. Se Aurantium tot annorum studia & fidem erga provincias complexum Ordinibus commendare, non ut eorum prudentiae se interponat, caeterum quod eorum incolumitati consultum perspectumque hoc ipso existumet. Igitur Aurantius, Ioanne Nassovio fratre ac Charlottâ Borbonia conjuge comitantibus, Antverpiam & mox Bruxellas las inter Ordinum vota & applausum exsultantis populi magno rerum apparatu evocatus, non dissimulante Austriaco ejus in Brabantiam ingressu sui imperij ac autoritatis vim haud parum resolvi. Cæterum Ordines ex pactis foederum tutum liberumque socijs per provincias commeatum & communionem consiliorum obtendebant, modo hoc ageretur, ut Belgicæ quies esset. Non posse Aurantium, Gandavensi pace Ordinum societati innexum, ullius provinciæ finibus prohiberi, accitum decreto eorum qui censuissent illius prudentiæ nutantem Rempublicam eguisse.
units.tr: Letters were also sent by the States of the Provinces to the Elector Palatine, begging him for a soldier, but one who would be maintained at the provinces' expense. The Elector, however, drawing his house into the ties of affinity with the Belgians, replied to the States about aid and ordered that his affection for the Belgian people be held certain. He professed that his father Frederick (who had held Amalia, the widow of Brederode, in marriage), of blessed memory, had been persistently favourable to the Belgians, and that his desire to free the provinces was no less than his father's. Clearly it was in the interest of Germany that the affairs of the provinces, shaken, should be supported by the aid of princes, since their fortune and prosperity, with Belgium overthrown, would be uncertain. Both nations were subject to the same fates and a similar ruin. Therefore he pitied unhappy Belgium; as peace had been firmly established beforehand by treaties, so would the pleasure be replaced by sorrow once it was broken and violated. He grieved that those who aimed at unjust rule had resumed their worst counsels, and that the foreign soldiery, dismissed by right of treaty, would have to be brought back into the provinces. Therefore, since the States were threatened by war, it was the best counsel to decide on arms, supported by every right of nations, to which the care of their country's defence and their dearest pledges had driven them through so many ages. As for himself, although he did not maintain an army, he would take care in the meantime, so that within two months he might gather soldiers through his own and neighbouring domains, which were not lacking in men nor alienated from their oath, and cause them to be sent into the provinces. Above all, he said, it was to be desired that they think less of the soldiers than of a just commander; and that the military body, turbulent in itself and eager for licence, be restrained by a skilled leader, as well as the whole method of waging war. He commended to the States Orange, who had embraced for so many years his zeal and loyalty towards the provinces; not that he would interpose himself in their prudence, but because he judged that their own safety was thereby consulted and understood. Therefore Orange, accompanied by his brother John of Nassau and by Charlotte of Bourbon his wife, was summoned with great display, first to Antwerp and soon to Brussels, amid the prayers of the States and the applause of the rejoicing people; and although the Austrian did not conceal that his power and authority were considerably weakened by Orange's entry into Brabant. Yet the States, relying on the terms of their alliances, claimed for their allies a safe and free passage through the provinces and a shared counsel, provided only that this be done so that Belgium might have peace. Orange, bound to the society of the States by the Treaty of Ghent, could not, they said, be excluded from any province's borders; he had been summoned by the decree of those who had judged that the Commonwealth, wavering, needed his prudence.

units.la: Quare Aurantio in Concilium adscito, ne quid incrementi inter Ordines Austriacumque invalescens morâ disidium acciperet, solenni rescripto decretum. Ut nupera pacta, & conventiones integræ essent & ut ante actorum omnis memoria obliteraretur. Austriacus Castello Namurcensi & simul urbe cederet Germanicarumque copiarum præsidijs oppida ac arces liberaret. Adhæc omnem militem veteranum sive ascititium missum faceret dederetque loca contra jus Fœderum occupata. Mandaret insuper Burgundiæ & Luxemburgi Præfectis, ne quem militem intra fines admittant. Ipse Austriacus, dum successorem ei Philippus Rex destinaret, Luxemburgum se subduceret proque dimittendo ex Hispaniâ Comite Burano intercederet. Hoc si faceret, rata firmaque pax esset, Ordinumque exercitus, reservatis tantum per Germaniæ Galliæque confinia præsidijs, dimitteretur. Elisabetha Anglorum reginâ, antiqua regni Anglici & Burgundicæ domus societate, fœderi subesset. Captivis utrinque liberatis ablata restituerentur. Populus per provincias oppidanus præsidijs suetus fidem faceret, se nulla, nisi Ordinum & Austriaci decreto, præsidia admissurum daturumque operam, ut Catholicâ religione cultâ civitates regio Philippi nomine teneanrur. Eo præfixo Fœdus scriberetur, religione juris jurandi & Philippi manu signandum.
units.tr: Therefore, with Orange admitted to the Council, so that no discord between the Estates and Austria would gain strength through delay, it was decreed by solemn rescript that the recent pacts and agreements should stand whole and that all memory of past acts should be wiped out. Austria was to withdraw from the castle of Namur and at the same time from the city, and free the towns and citadels from the garrisons of German troops. He was also to dismiss all his veteran and hired soldiers and give back the places occupied in breach of the law of the Covenants. He should further order the governors of Burgundy and Luxemburg not to admit any soldier within their borders. Austria himself, while Philip the King designated a successor for him, should withdraw to Luxemburg and intercede for the dismissal of Count Buren from Spain. If he did this, the peace would be ratified and firm, and the army of the Estates would be dismissed, keeping only garrisons along the German and French borders. Queen Elizabeth of England was to be included in the treaty through the old alliance between the English kingdom and the house of Burgundy. Prisoners on both sides were to be released and things taken away were to be restored. The townspeople of the provinces, accustomed to garrisons, were to give assurance that they would admit no garrison except by decree of the Estates and Austria, and would take care that, with the Catholic religion maintained, the cities be held in the name of King Philip. With this fixed, the Covenant was to be written out and sealed with an oath on religion and with Philip's hand.

units.la: Quod decretum Joanni Austriaco per delegatos traditum juvenile ejus ingenium belli & per hoc gloriæ cupidissimum infensioribus odijs irritavit. Itaque præfracte respondit:
units.tr: When this decree was delivered to John of Austria through delegates, his youthful temper, eager for war and for glory, was provoked into fiercer hatred, and so he replied obstinately:

units.la: Non ignorare se tam iniquis postulatis Romanam Catholicam Religionem & simul autoritatem Regis convelli, cui excusso principis jure sola imperij umbra & nudum nomen relinqueretur. Regem vero istiusmodi enormia pessimè habituram. Sic Aurantium Ordinum consessui adscriptum, sic dirutas arces munitioesque laturum molestius, & quidem tantæ potentiæ regem, qui sibi à populo suo legem scribi non velit solam obsequij gloriam professuro.
units.tr: He was not unaware that by such iniquitous demands the Roman Catholic religion and at the same time the authority of the King would be overthrown, since with the rights of the prince shaken off, only the empty shadow of rule and the bare name would be left to the King. The King, indeed, would take such outrages very badly. Thus he would take it more grievously that Orange was admitted to the assembly of the Estates, and that fortresses and fortifications were razed; and indeed a king of such great power, who would not wish the law to be written for him by his own people, would profess only the glory of obedience.

units.la: Mox Austriacus Castello Namurcensi validius præsidium impositi, metuenseque obsidionis aut ut Ordinum castris circumveniretur, Marchas Faminas, dein Luxemburgum concesit.
units.tr: Soon Austria placed a stronger garrison in the castle of Namur, and, fearing a siege or being surrounded by the camp of the Estates, withdrew to Marche-en-Famenne, and then to Luxemburg.

units.la: Jam enim Aurantius conducendas copias claudendumque Namurco Austriacum in consessu Ordinum disseruerat, ancipiti ex mutatione temporum Austriaco & Namurcanâ arce necessarijs commeatibus destituta. Ibi scilicet finem bello fore, unde alias certa initia eruptura forent & facilè esse convellere potentiam novi rectoris intra principia adhuc positam. Adultis vero Austriaci viribus minus profecturos patres & fi cIↄ. Iↄ. is revocatis ex Italiâ veteranorum legionibus, è Germaniâ novis copijs LXXVII. accitis occasionum haud segnis, opprimendis rebus invaluerit. Prolatando magnas rerum occasiones negligi, quas frustra cum effluxere aut ubi consilium mutaveris captes.
units.tr: For Orange had already argued in the assembly of the Estates that troops should be hired and Austria shut in at Namur, since Austria's position was precarious because of the changing times and the citadel of Namur was cut off from necessary supplies. There, clearly, would be the end of the war, whereas elsewhere certain beginnings would break out, and it would be easy to overthrow the power of the new ruler while it was still fixed within its first foundations. But once Austria's forces had grown, the Fathers would achieve less. With the veteran legions recalled from Italy and new troops, LXXVII, summoned from Germany, he was not sluggish in seizing occasions to crush affairs. By delaying, great opportunities are neglected; you seize them when they are gone in vain, or when you have changed your plan.

units.la: Quæ etsi ex vero dicta in vanum recidebant, cum essent quos ordinis sui mansuetudo aut mitius minusque obfirmatum ad pericula ingenium exerceret & qui propositâ inritâ pace manifestius bellum eluderent. Erant quoque, qui occultata diu consilia profiteri verererentur censerentque dissimulanda in tempus secreta esse, dum fortuna potiores Regis aut patriæ partes ostendisset. Cæteros regiæ iræ & juxta potentiæ horror percellebat, abnuentes Philippi Proregem conloquiis adhuc patrum affectantem, in ipsâ Namurcorum arce, hostili exercitu & validissimis castris à cœtu procerum & simul accessu provinciarum intercludi. Adeo verum est infirmitatem animorum ex introspectis & sæpè fictis periculis natam magnis conatibus adversam esse, deprehensis in patrum consessu qui servilem reverentiam honestæ libertati posthaberent. Itaque divulsis procerum mentibus omnique spe pacis ac ulteriorum fœderum amotâ, præsagia belli se ostenderunt, cui utrinque (etsi fatorum dispositione haud dubiè duceretur) velamenta pacis speciosis rationibus obtendebantur. Quamobrem Ordines, ne quid criminis aut invidiæ exteros apud Principes suæ integritati affingeretur, hunc in modum obtestatione usi.
units.tr: Although these things were said with truth, they came to nothing, since there were some whose gentle nature or less hardened temper shrank from dangers, and who, with peace proposed to no purpose, evaded open war more plainly. There were also those who wished to profess plans long hidden, and who thought that secret aims should be concealed for the time being until fortune showed which side was stronger, whether the King's or the country's. Others were struck with dread of the royal anger and of the power close at hand, refusing to be cut off from the assembly of the nobles and from access to the provinces, while the Proregent Philip still sought conferences with the Fathers, in the very citadel of Namur, surrounded by a hostile army and very strong camps. So true it is that weakness of spirit, born of imagined and often fictitious dangers, is adverse to great undertakings, when in the assembly of the Fathers men are found who prefer servile deference to honourable liberty. Thus, with the minds of the nobles divided and every hope of peace and of further covenants removed, the omens of war showed themselves, and for both sides it was covered with specious reasons of peace (although by the disposition of fate it was undoubtedly being led on). Therefore the Estates, lest any blame or ill will be attached to their integrity among foreign princes, made this protest in the following manner.

units.la: CALAMITATIS nostræ ac omnium malorum initia ingressis ALBANO Duce provincias Hispanis accepimus. Quare eosdem fœdius insolentiusque agentes hostium loco habuimus dedimusque effectum, ut jure fœderum quæ cum AUSTRIACO inijmus, alias in terras amoti levamenta nostris miseriis adferrent. Pastionum sacra per Regem approbata dimissis Legionibus firmas pacis spes nostris animis injecerant. Itaque Austriacum intra provincias mox oppida ac urbes admissum tantâ festivitate accepimus, ac si salutis nostræ certissimum pignus cœlo missum sanandis funestis dissensionibus adventaret. Caterum, ut humana omnia, ita nostræ spes in lubrico fuere, postquam Austriacus deductis in Italiam Hispanorum cæterarumque gentium legionibus suspectis imperij arbitris usus, Germanicarum copiarum fidem secretis artibus corrupit. Quare ut Fœdus Gandavi istum nostramque cum Aurantio societatem & simul nervum nostræ potentiæ incideret, inferenda socio Principi arma suasit, quorum mandatum à Philippo rege clam in Hispaniâ acceperat. Vbi vero nos ab ipso consilio alienos sensit, suspectos fidei habuit. Ideo in nostra exitia Germanicas legiones movit, occupandarum urbium ac castellorum consilia captavit. Bergis Hannoniæ ÿsdem artibus etsi delusus incubuit, Namurcum post cæpit. Ibi natalem imperÿ suâ confessione & pessimo facinore exorsus, falsæ conjurationis crimen pessimæ defectioni obtendit. Nos vero bellum agitantem & fœderis nostri hos ipso desertorem Bruxellas Namurco revocavimus fidem publicam & cum eâ validius præsidium obtulimus. Offerentibus honesta & paci conducentia omnia infructuosa fuere, postquam animus Austriaci altioris doli capax suo secreto nostram in perniciem exercebatur. Interceptis quas in Hispaniam destinabat litteris fidei ambiguum deprehendimus. Igitur rebus nostris consulere compulsi opeppida ac castella nostræ securitati vendicavimus. Tamen in speciem pacis nos & Aurantium Principem, tum Elisabetham Anglorum reginam sollicitavit & cum pessima animo agitaret, societates ac amicitias obtrusit. Nunc detectis insidiis pollutam religionem, violatam auctoritatem Regis criminatur. Atqui nos legibus fœderum ac conventionibus submixi, religionem ex pacto professi sumus. Legato Pontificis & Cæsaris, tum Leodiensi Episcopo, noster zelus placuit, neque sivimus ullibi, ut patria religio externis sacris inquinaretur. Regis vero quantoperè reverentes fuerimus, decreti Austriaco honores testabuntur, postquam ipse imperii exordio simulare edoctus pacis desiderio arcanis odiis velavit. Igitur intra provincias, intra urbes receptum necdum missis quod ante fieri debuerat, legionibus provinciarum Præfectum etiam inconsulto Aurantio declaravimus. Adhæc externo suspectoque comitatu stipatum non aspernati omne ei obsequium officiumque detulimus. Ita, agente adhuc in præsidiis urbium Germano milite, exercitum dimisimus, munimenta imperii & vacillantis patriæ nudavimus. Quare dum nostræ integritati nihil imponi potest, odio Aurantii nos consectatur, velut ejus societate rumpendi Fœderis consilia agitemus. Atqui alienæ culpæ, si quæ subsit, reos reddere nostra innocentia nos non potest, quorum studia & desiderio stabiliendo fœderi sacrantur. Tantum abest, ut conjuratione adversus eum initâ puras & impollutas manus fœdare parricidio Principis aut præfecti voluerimus. Quærenti causam armis ficta conspiratio obtentui fuit, ut quoniam fœderis pertæsus esset, occasione falsi criminis bellum redintegraret. Ejus indices datæ in Hispaniam & interceptæ litteræ fuere, non alio consilio à nobis resignatæ, quam ut fato insidiæ detegerentur lubricamque aulæ regiæ & agentium per provincias Hispaniæ procerum fidem tam fœdè apud Regem delationes aperirent. Itaque Philippi post litteræ priscam severitatem spirantes, dissimulanda in tempus suppliciia indicavere diemque assore, quo in provinciarum Præfectos, in procerum cervices statueretur. Adhæc Austriacus subjugandis provincijs Angliæ regno expeditionem comminatus, præservidas impotentis animi cogitationes bello non paci destinavit. Igitur excusso torpore ac ruptâ patientiæ nostræ lege defensioni tandem nostræ incubuimus, ne videremur assignatum nobis à Deo munus fœdâ in patriam proditione defugisse. Nos patrys legibus, nos populi immunitatibus fidem nostram pigneravimus & ne quæ vis nostris sacris fieret, juramentum Regem ac Præfectos poposcimus. Frænandæ dominantium lubidini, ex sacro Ordine, Nobilitate & Oppidano populo coalescentes, adstricta legibus imperia Principi præscripsimus. Qui, ut externo bello implicare præterquam nostro assensu se nequit, ita majoris potentiæ spem præconcipiens, civili dignum se fecit. Quare justiore causa in Præfectum, in ministrum Principis insurgimus, suum per provincias imperium non à religione fœderum ac conventionum, cæterum vi & armis exorsum. Ita castella & arces præsidia dominationi affectavit, ut jus nostrum ac libertas in obscuro esset nesque degeneres majorum posteri (qui suos Principes ad certam imperandi legem semper adegere) fœdam servitutem nostris liberis ac nepotibus legaremus. Itaque Deum & fidem generis humani obtestamur nos insontes & innoxios causam bello non dedisse, cæterum arma cogitantem Austriacum continuis precibus ac desiderijs patem atque concordiam orâsse. Quæ quoniam infensante numine, sive fato terris nostris cessura est, ita provincialium atque concivium fidem imploramus petimusque, ut spectatâ causæ nostra æquitate, liberorum ac conjugum, tum maxumè per-
units.tr: We have learned that the beginnings of our calamity and of all our evils came with the entry of the Duke of Alva into the provinces with the Spaniards. Therefore we regarded those men, behaving more foully and insolently, as enemies, and we brought it about that, by the law of the covenants which we made with Austria, the troops removed to other lands should bring relief to our miseries. The sacred pacifications, approved by the King, with the legions dismissed, had cast firm hopes of peace into our minds. Therefore we received Austria within the provinces and afterwards into towns and cities with such festivity as if a sure pledge of our safety, sent from heaven, had arrived to heal the deadly dissensions. But, as with all human things, so our hopes were slippery, after Austria, having led the Spanish and other foreign legions into Italy, and making use of suspicious counsellors of rule, corrupted the loyalty of the German troops by secret arts. Therefore, that he might cut the Covenant of Ghent, and this our alliance with Orange, and at the same time the sinew of our power, he urged that arms be turned against our allied prince, a commission which he had secretly received from King Philip in Spain. When he perceived that we were alien to this plan, he held us suspect in faith. Therefore he moved German legions against our destruction and sought plans for seizing towns and castles. Though he was deceived, he next attacked Bergen in Hainaut by the same arts, and afterwards Namur. There, beginning his rule with a birthday celebration, he covered a wicked deed with a confession and a false charge of conspiracy, to cover a most wicked defection. But we, when he was waging war and recalled from Namur to Brussels the very deserter of our covenant, offered him public faith and with it a stronger garrison. When all the honourable offers and those conducive to peace proved fruitless, since Austria's mind, capable of deeper guile, was busy with its secret plans for our destruction, we, having intercepted the letters he was sending to Spain, discovered that his faith was doubtful. Therefore, compelled to look to our own safety, we claimed the towns and castles for our security. Yet under the guise of peace he also tried to win over us, Prince Orange and Queen Elizabeth of England, and, while harbouring the worst intentions, he thrust upon us alliances and friendships. Now, with his plots discovered, he accuses us of polluting the religion and violating the authority of the King. Yet we, bound by the laws of the covenants and agreements, have professed the religion according to the pact. The zeal of ours has pleased the Pontiff's legate and the Emperor's, and the Bishop of Liège, and we have not allowed the native religion to be defiled by foreign rites anywhere. How greatly we have reverenced the King, the honours shown to Austria will bear witness, since he, having learned at the very start of his rule to feign, veiled secret hatreds under a desire for peace. Therefore, having received him within the provinces and within the cities, though the legions which ought to have been sent away earlier had not been dismissed, we also declared him governor of the provinces, even without consulting Orange. Moreover, we did not scorn his foreign and suspect retinue, but paid him every obedience and service. So, while German soldiers still held the garrisons of the cities, we dismissed the army and stripped the defences of the realm and of our wavering country. Therefore, while nothing can be laid against our integrity, he pursues us with hatred of Orange, as if we were plotting to break the covenant by means of his alliance. Yet our innocence cannot make us guilty of another's fault, if any exists, since our efforts and desire are dedicated to establishing the covenant. So far were we from wishing to stain our pure and unpolluted hands with a conspiracy against him, by a parricide of prince or governor. A fabricated conspiracy was made a pretext for arms, so that, since he was weary of the covenant, he might renew the war on the occasion of a false charge. The informers sent into Spain and the intercepted letters were handed over by us for no other purpose than that the plots might be revealed by fate, and that the slippery faith of the court and of the Spanish nobles administering the provinces might be exposed to the King through such shameful denunciations. Therefore, after Philip's letters breathing their former severity, they declared that punishments must be deferred for the time being, and that the day was at hand when the heads of the governors of the provinces and of the nobles would be set up. Moreover, Austria, threatening an expedition to subdue the kingdom of England, destined his overheated and unrestrained thoughts for war, not peace. Therefore, having shaken off our torpor and broken the law of our patience, we at last turned to our own defence, lest we seem to have shrunk from the duty assigned to us by God through foul betrayal of our country. We have pledged our faith to the laws of the fatherland and to the liberties of the people, and, lest any violence be done to our sacred things, we demanded an oath from the King and the governors. To curb the lust of rulers, we, joined together from the sacred order, the nobility and the townspeople, prescribed to the prince rule bound by laws. He, since he cannot entangle himself in a foreign war except with our assent, and conceiving hope of greater power, has made himself worthy of civil war. Therefore we rise up in a juster cause against the governor, the minister of the prince, whose rule through the provinces began not from the religion of the covenants and agreements but from force and arms. He has aimed at seizing castles and citadels as garrisons for domination, so that our right and liberty are in obscurity, and lest we, the degenerate posterity of our ancestors, who always compelled their princes to a fixed law of ruling, should bequeath foul slavery to our children and grandchildren. Therefore we call God and the faith of mankind to witness that we, innocent and blameless, have given no cause for war, but that Austria, while planning arms, with constant prayers and entreaties sought peace and concord. Since, with the divine will hostile, or by fate, this will not be granted to our lands, we implore and beseech the faith of the provinces and of our fellow citizens, that, having regard to the fairness of our cause, and to the children and spouses, and above all to the country that is perishing, they prepare themselves for the most sacred defence.

units.la: {P p} pereuntis patriæ miserti sanctissimæ defensioni se parent. Quin rogamus Cæsarem, Philippum Regem, vicinos Reges & Imperij Principes, ut nostræ calamitatis, & innocentiæ miserentur, rebusque satisfacientibus & bello expositis suppetias ferant, postquam in Fœdus nos & Aurantium coire inevitabilis necessitatis lex & furores hostium compellunt.
units.tr: Moved with pity for the perishing fatherland, they prepare themselves for its most sacred defence. Moreover, we ask the Emperor, King Philip, the neighbouring kings and the princes of the Empire to take pity on our calamity and our innocence, and to bring aid to us, whose goods are at stake and who are exposed to war, now that the inescapable law of necessity and the rage of the enemy drive us to unite in a covenant with Orange.

units.la: Hæc ORDINES.
units.tr: THESE ARE THE WORDS OF THE STATES.

units.la: Econtra Austriacus vulgatis per omne confinium ad Imperatorem, Reges ac Principes litteris eadem fere, quæ ad Senatum Leovardiæ urbis differebat dolosisque actionibus erudita pacis simulatione patrocinabatur.
units.tr: On the other hand, the Austrian, by letters sent throughout the neighbourhood to the Emperor, the kings and the princes, set out almost the same things he had written to the Senate of the city of Leeuwarden, and with crafty actions he defended a pretence of peace.

units.la: Mox juvenili animo longioris moræ incapace litteras Luxemburgo, quo concesserat, ad Ordines scripsit, suæque & regiæ mentis interpres hoc modo exorsus est.
units.tr: Soon, with a youthful spirit that could not bear further delay, he wrote from Luxembourg, whither he had withdrawn, to the States, and, as interpreter of his own mind and the king's, began in this way.

units.la: NON semel, Ordines, fidem apud vos feci nullum aliud meo per provincias imperio stabilimentum desiderari præterquam observantiam fœderum, in quam ego & post Rex PHILIPPUS juravimus. Quare omne officium, quod fato & ex commissâ mihi provinciarum Præfecturâ vestræ incolumitati debebam, reddendæ paci adaptavi, quo subortas æmulationes, discordias aut bellum secum tracturas meis in vos studijs sanarem. Malui scilicet regio juri ac autoritati quid decedere, quam spectare populum vestrum mutuis discordijs pereuntem. Cæterum votorum meorum merces contumaciæ vestræ incrementum fuit, quâ ad turpia & dominantium fastigijs indigna regem & me adigere in animum induxistis. Itaque actioni pacis & successui rerum diffisus, v. Non. Octob. die Luxemburgum me recepi, quo certiorem omnium Philippum regem facerem & ut illo in loco velut tuta sede mandata ejus expenderem. Is vero VII. Kal. Octob. litteras Madrito ex Hispania ad me dedit voluitque ut sartum tectumque, in quod convenimus, Fœdus esset vosque Romanâ Religione ad morem majorum cultâ, ei tanquam Regi aut Principi vestro obsequium ex lege præstaretis. Cui etsi vestris moribus haud parum detractum sit, ita vult ut violatam venerationis legem majoribus officijs pensetis. Quare jus edicendi, quod divino humanoque jure Principis semper fuit, reddi sibi ex pacto fœderum postulat & ut arma quæ non interveniente ejus assensu ac autoritate sumpsistis ponatis ocyus. Adhæc sacramentis suis haberi exercitum petit, ac ut Aurantij & aliorum qui imperium Regis, qui fœdera & publicam pacem attemeravere societati, renuntietis. Et quoniam oppidis, arcibus ac castellis indudta præsidia autoratus miles, ita disponendorum per loca præsidiorum arbitrium Rex sibi depescit & ut populum turbidum ac inquietum arma tractantem vestrâ autoritate coerceatis detisque effectum ut domesticas ad operas & simul quietem redeat. Quin hoc etiam Regis nomine præcipio, ut captivos Germanicarum Legionum Tribunos quam primum dimittatis & ut omne apud vos odium, omnis insolentia cessat. Idcirco Aurantium à premendis Amstelodamensibus retrahetis, stipendia Germanorum Legionibus procurabitis, quo in tutâ vestrarum rerum possessione locati malis miseriisque vestris remedia per conventum, quem Rex ocyus decernet, Ordinum generalium habeatis. Interim consilia paci commodabitis jusque & æquum regio Philippi nomine dicetis neque sinetis in posterum, ut ullo modo regis auto-riritas vestrum obsequium minuatur. Quæ singula, ut præstari à vobis jubeo at-que edico, ita supersedere vos invisis ac superbis postulatis volo, & quæ maiestatis apici ac fastigio Regis adversabuntur. Quod si feceritis elementiam ac gratiam Philippi vobis conciliabitis, qui hoc modo exercitus sui reliquias vestris adhuc urbibus, vestræ securitati graves, confestim missurus erit. Sin vero perseveretis in proposito Religioni ac Regi contumaces & injurij indignationem ac magnitudinem regiam & cum eâ arma & bellum denuntio, quorum jus ac arbitrium regia mihi mandata fecere. Itaque moneo, ut rebus vestris ac saluti consulatis sciatisque vestram incolumitatem meis adhortamentis, exitium vestris consilijs inniti.
units.tr: I HAVE, Gentlemen of the States, more than once assured you that nothing else is needed for the stability of my rule throughout the provinces than observance of the treaties, which both I and, after me, King Philip swore to keep. Therefore I have adapted every duty that I owed, by fate and by the charge of the governorship entrusted to me, to your safety and to the restoring of peace, so that I might heal the rising rivalries, dissensions, or war that my own zeal toward you would bring in its train. I preferred, of course, to yield something of royal right and authority rather than see your people perishing through mutual discord. But the reward of my wishes has been an increase in your obstinacy, by which you have resolved to drive the king and me to base things, unworthy of the summit of rulers. Therefore, distrustful of the peace effort and of its success, on the fifth day before the Nones of October I withdrew to Luxembourg, so that I might inform the king of everything and weigh his commands from that place as from a safe seat. He, indeed, on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, sent me a letter from Madrid in Spain, and wished that the covenant, the house in which we have met, should remain whole and intact, and that you, with the Roman religion observed as of old, should render obedience by law to him as your king or prince. Although this has been not a little diminished by your customs, he wishes you to repay the violated law of reverence with greater duties. Therefore he demands that the right of issuing edicts, which has always belonged to a prince by divine and human law, be restored to him under the terms of the covenant; and that you lay down quickly the arms you have taken up without his assent and authority. Besides, he asks that the army be kept under its oaths, and that you renounce association with Orange and with others who have disturbed the king's rule, the covenants and the public peace. And since soldiers have been quartered in towns, citadels and castles, the king has sent word to me that he has the right to arrange the posting of garrisons through the places; and that you, by your authority, should restrain the turbulent and restless people who take up arms, and see to it that they return to their domestic work and at the same time to quiet. Indeed, I also direct in the king's name that you release as soon as possible the captive tribunes of the German legions, and that all hatred and all insolence cease among you. Therefore you will withdraw Orange from pressing the Amsterdammers, and you will provide pay for the German legions, so that, placed in secure possession of your affairs, you may have remedies for your evils and miseries through the assembly of the General States, which the king will decree quickly. Meanwhile you will lend your counsels to peace, and speak what is just and right in the name of King Philip, and you will not allow in future that the authority of the king be diminished in any way by your obedience. These particulars I command and direct you to perform; so I wish you to desist from hateful and arrogant demands, and from whatever is opposed to the majesty and dignity of the king. If you do so, you will win for yourselves the clemency and favour of Philip, who in this way will shortly send away the remnants of his army, still a burden to your cities and to your safety. But if you persist in your purpose, rebellious against religion and the king, and defiant, I denounce upon you the king's indignation and greatness, and with it arms and war, the right and decision of which the king has entrusted to me. Therefore I advise you to look to your affairs and your safety, and to know that your ruin rests on your own counsels, not on my exhortations.

units.la: HÆC AUSTRIACUS.
units.tr: THESE ARE THE WORDS OF THE AUSTRIAN.

units.la: Igitur lubrico rerum statu & infidâ dominantium concordiâ, Georgius Lalainius (qui prid. Eid. Sept. Leovardiam advenerat) vergente eodem mense Comitium ordinavit. Quo coacto ut erant qui mutandis rebus id indictum scirent, ita aut veteris imperij satietate aut quod fato destinatum dominationi suæ terminum crederent, conditionibus temporum acquievere. Quare dignitates Austriaci partes professis nulla comitij tempestate abrogatæ, urgente Lalainio nutantem Remp. certioris præsidij egere. Esse dubiam superiorum provinciarum fidem, incerta fœdera & Austriaci defectione bellum provincijs proxumum. Igitur consulendum coeptæ securitati esse, ne penes libertatis & fœderum inimicos regimen Reip. sit & ne Austriacus pacis ruptor ac mox Legiones reducturus, ex hac ipsâ provinciâ fomenta sui furoris & simul auxilia accipiat. Placere Ordinibus provinciarum, placere Aurantio, ita res componi ut æterna imperij per provinciam possessio non sit & ut in societatem Reip. tandem adsciscantur, qui exilia, contemptum, qui orbitates propinquorum pertulissent. Itaque prævalescente per Frisiam fœderatorum potentia, regioq; Senatu ex actionibus Austriaci suspecto, de fundando Deputatorum collegio ab agrarijs cogitatum, laxiore ad huc Ordinum populique Frisici comitio, quod multitudine consultantium & ut rebus dubijs solet, diversitate sæpè animorum obturbabatur. Quippe Pontificios, etsi senescente dominatione, ut antè linguis immodestos & obsequij insolentes, ita asperos & acres redituros ad ingenia metuebant, amissâque cohortium fide, omne veteris imperij robur turbulentis consilijs tutaturos. Quare attenuperandis odijs, sacro ex Ordine in hoc Collegium pacandæ mobili turbæ cooptati, quæ credebat Pontificijs sacris & simul partibus illo instituto prospectum & si cœnobiorum Præsules consortes imperio facti, retundendis novorum fœderum molitionibus intercederent. Ita namque immodesta libertatis studia frænum habitura interpretabantur foresque diuturniora regiæ dominationi præsidia, quam extingui cum avitâ religione, ne Belgicæ quidem Ordines etsi odio Austriaci fœderibus inligati tot actorum documentis concupiscerent. Igitur represso religionis & simul partium odio ab agrariorum Ordinibus tabulæ scriptæ, quo de assignatâ novis provinciæ rectoribus potestate arbiter rerum populus, semotâ æmulatione cognosceret: Istæ sic habebant.
units.tr: Therefore, with the slippery state of affairs and the faithless concord of the rulers, Georgius Lalainius (who had arrived at Leeuwarden the day before the Ides of September) convened an assembly at the end of that month. When it was gathered, those who knew that the change had been announced yielded to the conditions of the times, whether from weariness with the old rule or because they believed the term destined by fate for their domination had come. Hence the offices of those who professed the Austrian party were not abolished in any storm of the assembly; but, with Lalainius pressing, the wavering commonwealth needed a surer garrison. The loyalty of the upper provinces was doubtful, the covenants uncertain, and with the Austrian's defection war was close to the provinces. Therefore it had to be considered that the security begun should be guarded, lest the government of the commonwealth remain in the hands of enemies of liberty and of the covenants, and lest the Austrian, a breaker of the peace who would soon bring back the legions, receive from this very province the fuel of his rage and at the same time aid. It pleased the Estates of the provinces, it pleased Orange, that matters be arranged so that perpetual possession of rule through the province should not remain, and that those who had endured exile, contempt and the loss of kinsmen should at last be admitted into partnership in the commonwealth. Thus, while the power of the confederates prevailed through Friesland, and the royal Senate was suspected because of the Austrian's actions, the founding of a college of deputies was considered by the landed men, in an assembly of the Estates and people of Friesland which was still rather loose and, as usual in doubtful matters, was disturbed by the multitude of those deliberating and by the diversity of minds. For they feared that the Papists, although their domination was waning, would return as before, insolent in tongue and unrestrained in manners, now harsh and sharp in temper; and that, the loyalty of the cohorts having been lost, they would defend all the strength of the old rule by turbulent counsels. Therefore, to soften hatreds, men were co-opted from the sacred Order into this college, to calm the restless crowd; they believed that by this arrangement provision was made both for the Papist rites and for their party, and that the abbots of the monasteries, made partners in rule, would intervene to check the schemes of the new covenants. For they interpreted that thus the immoderate zeal for liberty would have a bridle, and that there would be longer-lasting defences of royal domination, rather than its extinction together with the ancestral religion; not even the Belgian Estates, though bound by covenants out of hatred for the Austrian, would desire this, despite so many documents of their deeds. Therefore, with hatred of religion and of parties suppressed, tables were drawn up by the landed Orders, in which the power assigned to the new rulers of the province was set out, so that the people, the judge of affairs, might know it with rivalry set aside. They read thus.

units.la: NOS ORDINES, & agrariorum per Frisiam Delegati, ipso comitio Leovardia ultimo Septembris die inchoato congregati, Notum facimus nos concorditer delegasse, Reverendos, Nobiles, Honoratos & scientiâ rerum praeclaras viros Gerardum Iacobi Praesulem Clarecampensem, Doconem Martna, Serapium Galama, Goslicum Hiddama, Erasmum Douma & Barthium Idzaerda IC. quo cum GEORGIO LAINIO RENNEBERGIO Frisiae Praefecto ocyus conveniant, deque jure patrio, privilegijs & immunitatibus laesis cognoscant, jusque populi quocunque etiam loco & apud quosvis provinciae afferant. Foedus quoque Gandavense & post ORDINES inter generales & AURANTIUM Principem ictum approbent exequanturque, omneque pro re natâ definiant statuantque, quod avertendis provinciae detrimentis & afferenda libertati conducere existumabunt. Id quoque effectum dent, ut praeter cetera publica, ngeres, vias, aquaeductus, catarractas, emissaria & similia curent habeantsque rationem singulorum officialium provinciae earumque rerum, quae ad Remp. spectabunt. Quae omnia singulaque, nullo salario praestari volumus, nisi quod ex erario provincia decernet & exclusis partium expensis, quas ipsae partes ferent. Sin vero Praefectus rei definiendae difficultate motus id recipere in se recusaverit, facimus DEPUTATIS nostris potestatem ad Concilium Status, Ordines generales aut alio se transferendi, legatosque mittendi simulque sollicitandi, ut omne controversum decidatur decisumque à ratione patrij juris non recedat. Adhaec in causis gravioribus ex unaquaque praturâ delegatum evocandi convocandique, si necessitas exigat, provincie ORDINES, jus ijs facimus, ratione tamen sumptuum habitâ & ne damno provincialium modum excedant. Itaque absentibus & morbo aut alia de causâ impeditis alios substituendi potestatem permittimus simulque determinandi quod ex usu erit. Idque tam diu valebit, dum proximo comitio aliter statuatur. Volumus quoque ut DEPUTATI circa exitum Comitiorum anniversariorum diplomata sua, ac tabulas mandatorum Ordinibus redhibeant, quo aut novos crearent constitutiveve dignitas prorogetur. Conventum quoque illius Collegij quotannis bis & in triduum haberi, octavo scilicet à Pentecostes die & xv. Octobris mensis, expediendis provincialium rebus ac postulatis sanciendisque quae è Republ. videbuntur & quae rata fore cum clausula indemnitatis cavebimus. Haec à Joanne Poppio Presbytero Wirdumano, Sceltone Tiarda, Feicone Tiallengio, Jeltone Gellio Presbytero Oosterlittano, Vibio Grovesteinio, Menenio Taconio, Idzio Reinio, Tito Waltesio & Edone Idzio xiii. Octobris signata. Reperio in actis publicis Carolo Caesare rerum potiunte sub Georgio Scenco provinciae Rectore, non absimilia his mandatis per Ordines Frisiae Delegatis suis exhibita, caeterum tanto minore cum successu, quanto magis supra libertatem vis ac dominatio Principis increverat. Qui etsi curas Ordinum in tuendo patrio jure improbare non videretur, ita de industriâ simulasse creditus tum fuit, quo populi animos principalis imperij rudes & ex factionibus pridem licentiae proxumos, connivendo ad minus placita secretis servitijs inneeteret. Sunt qui tradant Collegium istud hoc ipso tempore suasu Aurantij Principis institutum, quo Frisiorum Respubl. regiarum partium huc usque dominationibus oppressa, pressa, auctis ex hoc ipso Hollandiae Zelandiaeque rebus promovendae libertati assimilaretur. Caeterum imbecillibus rudibusque, ut omnia mortalium opera solent, initijs usa per incrementa tandem libertatis revaluit, erecto ijs auspicijs patrum Collegio, ut haerentem in ipsis patriae vitalibus regiae servitutis sarcinam dubium magis consilio an armorum cura ex intervallis temporum ejecerit.
