Stauricus Scriptor notat, Doconem Martna & Serapium Galama è Nobilitate in Delegatos Ordinum & provinciae tum constitutos, indignante Senatu regio, totam Reip. vim & autoritatem suo ordini ereptam novos in dominos transferri.
units.tr: WE THE STATES, and the Delegates of the landed men throughout Friesland, gathered at the assembly itself, begun at Leeuwarden on the last day of September, make known that we have unanimously delegated the Reverend, Noble and Honourable men, distinguished for knowledge of affairs, Gerardus Jacobi, Provost of Klarkamp, Doco Martena, Serapius Galama, Goslicus Hiddama, Erasmus Douma and Bartius Idzaerda, Doctor of Laws, who are to meet quickly with GEORGIUS LAINIUS RENNEBERGIUS, Governor of Friesland, and learn about paternal right, privileges and immunities that have been injured, and bring the right of the people to any place and to any of the provinces. They are also to approve and carry out the Covenant of Ghent, and the covenant struck afterwards between the General States and Prince Orange, and to define and decide everything as circumstances require, and to establish whatever they judge conducive to averting the province's losses and to asserting liberty. Let them also bring it about that, besides other public matters, they take care of dykes, roads, aqueducts, sluices, outlets and the like, and keep account of the individual officials of the province and of those affairs which concern the commonwealth. We wish all these things, each one, to be performed without any salary, except what the province shall decree from the treasury, and excluding the expenses of the parties, which the parties themselves will bear. But if the Governor, moved by the difficulty of settling the matter, refuses to take this upon himself, we grant our DEPUTIES the power to transfer themselves to the Council of State, the General States or elsewhere, and to send and press envoys, so that every controversy be decided, and, once decided, not depart from the rule of the paternal law. Besides, in more serious cases we grant the provincial STATES the right to summon and convene a delegate from each praetorship, if necessity requires, with regard however to expenses, and so that they do not exceed the measure to the loss of the provincials. Therefore, for those who are absent, or hindered by sickness or some other cause, we permit the power to substitute others and at the same time to determine what shall be expedient. This will hold so long as it is not otherwise decided at the next assembly. We also wish that the DEPUTIES, about the end of the annual assemblies, return their commissions and the tables of mandates to the Estates, so that either new ones be created or the dignity be prolonged. We also provide that the convention of that College be held twice a year, for three days, namely on the eighth day after Pentecost and on the fifteenth of October, for dispatching the affairs and demands of the provincials, and for sanctioning what seems to be for the good of the commonwealth; and we will guarantee that these shall be valid with a clause of indemnity. Signed on the thirteenth of October by John Poppius, Presbyter of Wirdum, Sceltonus Tiarda, Feico Tiallingius, Jeltonus Gellius, Presbyter of Oosterlittens, Vibius Grovesteinius, Menenius Taconius, Idzius Reinius, Titus Waltesius and Edo Idzius. I find in the public records, with Charles Caesar in control of affairs and George Scencus as Governor of the province, orders not unlike these, presented by the Delegates appointed by the Estates of Friesland; but with so much less success as force and the domination of the Prince had increased above liberty. Although he did not seem to disapprove the Estates' care in defending their ancestral right, he was then believed to have pretended this on purpose, so that by overlooking minor measures he might entangle in secret services the minds of a people unschooled in the principal rule and, by factions long since, close to licence. There are those who relate that this College was instituted at that very time at the persuasion of Prince Orange, so that the commonwealth of Friesland, hitherto oppressed by the rule of the royal party, might be made like the promoted liberty of Holland and Zeeland by these same affairs. But, using weak and rude beginnings, as all human works are wont to, liberty at length revived through growth, the college of fathers being erected under those auspices; so that the burden of royal servitude, clinging to the very vital parts of the fatherland, was cast out at intervals more by doubtful counsel than by care for arms. Staurikus the writer notes that Doco Martena and Serapius Galama, from the nobility, were then constituted as Delegates of the Estates and of the province, and that the whole force and authority of the commonwealth, snatched from their own order, was transferred to new masters, the royal Senate being indignant.

units.la: Lalanius quoque ne provinciae finibus revivíscente Austriacum inter & Ordines bello quid periculo incumberet, agrarios quosque per omnes praeturas edicto Senatus armari fecit rusticaeque plebi tribunos cohortium delegit. Tum munitiones quasque littori aut aestuarijs impositas, solo aequari curavit duriorisque imperij muhimenta & simul vestigia demolitus est. Igitur Slota, Lemmaria, Hindelopa, Oostmahorna multo ante opere circumductae, funditus dirutae antiquam provinciae faciem reddidere. Quare clarum per Frisios Lalainij nomen superstitiosius habitum, quod illius aetas lubricis alias consilijs per se obnoxia primâ juventâ in tam sublimem prudentiam & moderationem rerum exsurgeret. Notat Stauricus codex ipso Michaelis Archangeli die ad Rurem undam ditionis Geldricae acre Germanos inter & Valonum cohortes quae per Frisiam praesidium egerant, praelium fuisse plurimosque è Valonum gente caesos exercitae per provinciam insolentiae justas & fatales poenas luisse.
units.tr: Lalanius also, lest anything dangerous threaten the province from a war revived between the Austrian and the States, had the farmers in every district armed by decree of the Senate and appointed tribunes of the cohorts from the rural commons. He then saw to it that the fortifications placed along the shore or the estuaries were levelled to the ground, and he tore down the bulwarks and even the traces of harsher rule. Thus Slota, Lemmaria, Hindelopa and Oostmahorna, long ago enclosed by works, were razed to the ground and restored the old appearance of the province. For this reason the name of Lalanius was held in great reverence among the Frisians, because his age, otherwise prone to slippery counsels, rose in his early youth to such high prudence and moderation in affairs. The Stauricus codex notes that on the feast day of Michael the Archangel, at the river Rur in the territory of Guelders, a sharp battle was fought between the Germans and the Walloon cohorts that had been holding the garrison in Friesland, and that many of the Walloon people were slain, and that the insolence they had shown throughout the province paid just and fatal penalties.

units.la: Tum Aurantius, frigescente Austriaci gratiâ, regundae Brabantiae Praefectus. Quod consilium, ut promovendae sociarum provinciarum prosperitati repertum credebatur, ita econtra noxijs aemulationibus, ut procerum ingenia, concordiam publici Foederis & post provincias divulsit.
units.tr: Then Orange, as the favour of Austria cooled, was made governor of Brabant. This plan, though it was devised, as it was believed, to advance the prosperity of the allied provinces, on the contrary broke apart, through harmful rivalries, the concord of the public league and, afterwards, of the provinces, as the minds of the nobles were set against one another.

units.la: Erant quippe qui alienae potentiae magnitudine suam imminui opinarentur Aurantijque fortunam, more mortalibus infito, aegris oculis intuspicerent. Ideo illi in plures spargere, Pontificum sacris grande discrimen imminere, si Aurantius novâ religione imbutus majoris per provincias imperij potiatur, quod imperantium animos suâ sive lubidine, sivè imbecillitate ut plurimum in deterius vertisset. Metui posse, ne successu rerum ac consiliorum suorum elatus, omne provinciarum regimen affectet modumque, ut cupiditates mortalium ferè solent, ambitioni non ponens suae potentiae autores obscuret. Deligendum potius esse aliud rerum caput, in quod omnium provinciarum arduum onus tutò reclinet, divulso à patribus Austriaco & Repub. multorum procerum secessionibus discordi.
units.tr: Indeed there were those who thought that Orange's fortune would be diminished by the greatness of another's power, and who, as is the habit of mortals, looked askance at his success with jaundiced eyes. Therefore they spread about among many people that great danger hung over the rites of the Papists, if Orange, imbued with a new religion, should gain a greater power over the provinces, a power which, as is usually the case, had turned the minds of rulers, whether by their own lust or by weakness, for the worse. It could be feared that, elated by the success of his affairs and counsels, he would aim at total control of the provinces, and, as the desires of mortals usually do, would not set a limit to his ambition, and would obscure those who were the authors of his power. Rather, another head of affairs should be chosen, on whom the heavy burden of all the provinces could safely be laid, the Austrian being estranged from the Fathers and the Commonwealth, and many nobles divided by discordant secessions.

units.la: Igitur de vocando in Belgicam Matthiâ Austrio Maximiliani Caesaris filio Rodolphi fratre clam consultatum, quo fortunae impetus Aurantium magnis negotijs & famae innectens, medio in cursu rerum secreta aemulatione sisteretur. Quippe Matthiam Philippi Regis ex sorore nepotem, ut Pontificiae religionis acre studium, ita imperatorij sanguinis continua claritudo commendabat, confidentibus ad hoc plurimis eum gerendis rebus fato delectum, sanandis regem inter populumque discordijs intercessorem destinari. Certè apud Philippum acIↄ. Iↄ. LXXVII. vunculum sororis connubio innexum multum valiturum omnium judicia augurabantur gratumque haud dubiè Philippo regi fore, propinquum Principem à suae Pontificiaeque factionis administris, jam antè mediantibus internuntijs sollicitatum, regundis provincijs se offerre. Itaque praeterito Alençonio Andium Duce, in quem nonnulli inclinabant, Malstedius pro legato in Germaniam missus, qui Matthiae Austrio provinciarum regimen deferret capessendumque ad imperium secretis illicijs sollicitaret. Caeterum Matthiae animus magnis in principio cogitationibus fluctuabat. Quippe reputabat molestum fore, primam juventam rerum adhuc rudem tantae tempestati admoveri, cui sedandae propinqui Regis Praesides & Legatos adhuc impares magnae molis negotium fecisset. Econtra omne discrimen, omne onus, speciosò honore leniebat & quod lubricae adhuc aetatis annos ingressus regiae fortunae insereretur. Igitur dominandi cupidine & simul gloriae pelleCtus, quam è pacatâ Belgicâ juvenili cogitatione sperabat, sui spem Legato fecit adscitoque comitatu noctis obscuro Viennâ egressus celerrimo itinere in provincias advenit. Quae res etsi à fratre Caesare ac Joanne Austriaco aegrius accepta, altam tamen indolem famae ac magnarum rerum, ut Principum mentes solent, avidam à proposito non revocavit. Igitur datis ad Rudolphum fratrem litteris sui consilij & facti rationem exposuit. Ideo scilicet moderandis provincijs se summisisse, ut earum discordijs mederetur & ne turbidis temporibus Austriam domum possessione imperij externâ dominatio exueret.
units.tr: Therefore there was secret consultation about summoning Matthias the Austrian, son of the Emperor Maximilian and brother of Rudolf, into Belgium, so that by binding Orange to great undertakings and to fame, the course of his fortune might be halted in mid-career by a hidden rivalry. Indeed Matthias, nephew of King Philip through his sister, was recommended both by his fervent zeal for the Papist religion and by the continuous distinction of his imperial blood. Many who trusted in fate believed that he had been chosen for managing affairs, and that he would be appointed as mediator to heal the discords between the king and the people. Certainly they predicted that at Philip's court the bond of his sister's marriage would carry great weight, and that it would surely be pleasing to King Philip if the kinsman prince, already solicited earlier by his servants of the Spanish and Papist faction through intermediaries, offered himself to govern the provinces. So Malstedius was sent to Germany as envoy, passing over the Duke of Alençon, Duke of Anjou, towards whom some were inclined, to offer Matthias the Austrian the government of the provinces and to urge him by secret enticements to take up the power. But Matthias's mind at first wavered with great doubts. For he reflected that it would be troublesome to bring a youth still inexperienced in affairs to so great a tempest, which the king's kinsman, the governors and envoys, not yet equal to the great task, had failed to calm. On the other hand, a fine honour softened all danger and every burden, and the fact that the royal fortune was entrusted to him, now that he had entered the years of a still slippery age. Therefore, driven by the desire to rule and at the same time by the glory which he hoped for from a pacified Belgium in his youthful thinking, he gave hope of himself to the envoy, and, taking a small retinue in the dark of night, left Vienna and came to the provinces by a very swift journey. Although his brother the Emperor and John of Austria took this badly, the deep disposition of a man avid for fame and great affairs, as princes' minds usually are, did not call him back from his purpose. Therefore, by letters sent to his brother Rudolf, he set out the reasons for his plan and his action: namely, that he had undertaken the governance of the provinces in order to remedy their discords, and so that in troubled times the house of Austria should not be stripped of its dominion by the possession of a foreign rule.

units.la: Cujus rei famâ in populum proceresque diffusâ alios consternatio, nonnullos fastidium, plerosque & in ijs consilij autores poenitentia occupavit deprehensumque fuit, inconsultos animorum impetus initijs validos tractu temporis languescere. Itaque fuere, qui prohibendum munitis locis remittendumque in Germaniam censerent, validiore sensim diffidentiâ, quod Philippi affinitatem non unâ propinquitate praeferret & quod ad Rheni Maeniq; confluentes, connivente Rudolpho Caesare, nova auxilia Joanni Austriaco scriberentur. Quare dissentientibus, ut in tantâ consultantium multitudine solet, sententijs evenit, ut nihil certi in consessu Ordinum definiretur Anglicumque Foedus, quod Legati provinciarum tum orabant & cum eo subsidia patrum discordijs vanescerent.
units.tr: When the news of this matter spread among the people and the nobles, consternation seized some, disgust others, and most, and among these the authors of the plan, regret; and it was found that rash impulses of mind, strong at the outset, gradually weaken with the passage of time. Therefore there were those who advised that he be prevented from entering the fortified places and sent back into Germany, with distrust growing gradually stronger, because his kinship with King Philip carried more weight than a single near relation, and because, with Emperor Rudolf conniving, new troops were being levied for John of Austria at the confluence of the Rhine and the Main. Hence, as usually happens in so large an assembly of advisers, opinions differed, and nothing certain was decided in the meeting of the States; and the English alliance, which the envoys of the provinces then sought, and with it the aid of the Fathers, vanished through their discords.

units.la: Quippe Elisabetham procerum Belgicae aemulatio & praeter hanc lubrica temporum offendebant, velut metuentem, ne per propensa in provincias studia Philippi odio & communi cum Belgicâ ruinae se exponeret. Dubiae scilicet fidei copias omnem per oram colligi. Ita Guisium per Lotharingiam, Alençonium Galliae regis fratrem in Veromanduis militem autorare. Adhaec Italiam & Hispaniam delectibus compleri reversuraque haud dubiè in Belgicam Legiones jam antè dimissas. Hoc modo copias & auxilia Austriaco fore, qui peritiam belli, qui militarem gloriam, qui animum magnis rebus devotum regio exercitui adjecturus esset. Econtra Ordinum res scissas, tarda consilia, laesum Aurantium peritissimum belli & gerendarum rerum Ducem, haud dubiè Hollandiâ & suis insulis se clausurum. Matthiae vero Austrio, ut annos tantae moli impares, ita rude militiae ingenium esse. Praeter haec, opes sublevandis rebus invalidas, patripatrimonio Maximiliani Cæsaris Augustâ fæcunditate multam in sobolem devoluto. Metui quoque posse ut Philippus Rex ultionis ac vindictæ avidus, Matthiam nepotem secretis artibus corrumpat, virili Mariæ Imperatricis Philippi sororis in filios imperio & Austriâ domo Hispaniæ viribus subnixâ. Atqui Ordinum societatem & infirmas res optimum exercitus ductorem, senilem prudentiam, amplum ærärium flagitare. Itaque Elisabethæ consilium eò spectabat, ut si auxilia & æs bello conferendum esset, ratio fœderis haberetur Ordinesque Aurantium, propinquioribus societatibus innexum, Matthiæ Austrio subjungerent.
units.tr: Indeed Elizabeth was offended both by the rivalry of the nobles of Belgium and by the slippery state of affairs besides, as if she feared that by inclining her favour towards the provinces she would expose herself to the hatred of Philip and to a ruin shared with Belgium. Forces of doubtful loyalty, it seems, were being gathered from every shore: Guise through Lorraine, and Alençon, brother of the King of France, was urged to serve as a soldier among the Veromandui. Besides, Italy and Spain were being filled with levies, and the legions previously dismissed were without doubt going to return into Belgium. In this way forces and aid would come to the Austrian, who would bring to the royal army his skill in war, his military glory, and a spirit devoted to great undertakings. On the other hand, the affairs of the States were torn asunder, their counsels slow, and Orange, a most skilled commander in war and conductor of affairs, had been wounded, and would doubtless shut himself up in Holland and its islands. But Matthias the Austrian, they said, was unequal to the years of so great a task, and his mind was untrained in military matters. Besides, his resources were too weak to support the affairs, since the patrimony of Maximilian the Emperor had devolved upon a large progeny by its abundant fertility. It could also be feared that King Philip, avid for revenge and punishment, might corrupt his nephew Matthias by secret arts, since the empire of the sons of Maria, the Empress and sister of Philip, rested on the strength of the House of Austria and of Spain. Yet the alliance of the States and their weak affairs demanded the best leader of an army, the prudence of an old man, and a large treasury. Therefore Elizabeth's plan looked to this: that if aid and money had to be contributed to the war, account should be taken of the treaty, and that the States should join Orange, who was bound by closer alliances, to Matthias the Austrian.

units.la: Ab aliis vero pro eodem Matthia speciosa disserebantur. Provincias scilicet suis discordijs ac longo bello lassas rectoris eguisse. Posse sperari uberem juventæ in Matthiâ Austrio fructum & crescens ingenium per annorum spatia experiendo solertiam adepturum. Sed Principum mentes justis ætatibus non alligari, maturitatem tum nactas, ubi ad imperium quod ijs fato deberetur poscentibus motalium rebus pervenerint. Ne quid periculi lubricæ ætati subsit, habiturum Matthiam arbitros consortes rerum & provincijs fidos. Neq; enim eam Reip. conditionem esse, ut ab unius nutu pendeat, cæterum fore, qui præcipitem juventam, qui ejus consilia moderaturi sint. Id quoque fœlicitatis animo concipi posse, ut per eum pacem provinciæ habeant ac ut ejus intercessione propinqui regis ira sanetur. Posse Regem Matthiæ Austrio majorem filiam & cum eâ provincias in dotem locare, quo sunestum bellum ut fere solet, matrimonio Principum sopiatur. Hæc & similia à curiosis & fati providis speciosis rationibus disserebantur.
units.tr: Others, however, argued in favour of the same Matthias with plausible reasons: namely, that the provinces, weary of their discords and of the long war, had lacked a ruler. It could be hoped that abundant fruit would come from the youth of Matthias the Austrian, and that his growing talent would gain skill by experience over the course of years. But the minds of princes are not bound by the measure of their age; they attain maturity when they arrive at that rule which is owed to them by fate, when the mortal affairs demand it. To guard against any danger lurking in his slippery youth, Matthias would have advisers, partners in affairs, and men faithful to the provinces. For, they said, the commonwealth was not in such a condition that it hung on the nod of one man; on the contrary, there would be men to moderate his headlong youth and to guide his counsels. They could also conceive, with a cheerful mind, that through him the province might have peace, and that the anger of the king of Spain might be calmed by his intercession. The King could give his elder daughter to Matthias the Austrian as wife, and with her the provinces as dowry, so that the baleful war, as usually happens, might be quieted by a marriage of princes. These and similar things were argued by the curious and the far-sighted in fate, with plausible reasons.

units.la: Igitur Matthias Austrius xi. Kal. Dec. Antverpiam magnâ solemnitate & paratu rerum ingressus ab Aurantio Legatisque Ordinum exceptus est, dissimulante Aurantio Matthiam inumbrandæ gloriæ suæ clam ab æmulatoribus accitum suis officijs cohonestari. Quo in viro singulare civilis prudentiæ exemplum notare mihi libet, eum secreti contemptus oblitum plus concordiæ publicæ quam privatis odijs dedisse cæterisque etiam qui acciverant deliberantibus, præficiendum rebus Matthiam retinendis dignationibus suasisse. Sunt qui tradant Matthiam etsi Arschotani & suorum partibus irretitum, societatem post Aurantij prætulisse, quod civitatum fide pollens, firmius boni imperij instrumentum, gratiam populi suis consilijs præstruxisset. Ita principum virorum æmulationibus & sæpe odijs certabatur, quos inter spem metumque dubijs temporibus defixos, sollicitudo ac cura publicæ salutis trahebat. Quippe formidinem siniistri ardescens cœlo crinitum sydus ingerebat, quod circa Eid. Novemb. exortum magno horrore omnium animos implevit. Scribit M. Heymannus Oceanum Cymbricum enavigantibus serenoire cœlo circa Non. Novemb. conspectum, caudamque ab occasu versus ortum Solis æstivum protendentem intuentium mentes secreto metu conterruisse. Quod prodigium tanto nocentius generi humano ac terrarum orbi credula mortalitas rebatur, quod supra Lunæ orbem, ut Tycho Brahe eximius illius artis restaurator tradit, procul Meteoris & trajectionum loco generatum, vim naturæ & simul perpetuitati coelestium corporum intulisse crederetur. Fuere qui asserrerent, quod caudatum accensumque ab astris sydus versus Andromedæ medam moveretur, insidiosum Belgicæ libertati Austriacum expresse-rit suoque occasu mortem ei portenderit violentâ, ut post memorabo, fati specie extincto. Quo in sensu Adrianum Antonij Alcmarianum fuisse in Mathematicis illorum temporum notis reperio. Quicquid sit ferale & proculdubio prænuntium mali prodigium, triste & ominosum intuentibus creditum rerumque mutationibus prævium, turbidis terris tanquam funestum illuxisse. Mihi verisimile est ardentissimi corporis comam defectionem Austriaci & imminentia resurgentis belli suo ortu signasse, quod in tot annorum discordias & furores exiturum, etiam hoc ipso quo hæc scribo tempore malis suis remedia firmam pacem desideravit. Sanciente velut fato aut naturâ, ut rupti fœderis ac omnium rerum defectio horribili ostento & cœlesti irâ notaretur. Thuanus ex illorum temporum Mathematicis notat, Cometem magnitudine suâ xxx. amplius gradus lustrantem porrectâque caudâ occidentem versus Sagittarium & Capricornum complexum fuisse cœloque & ut alij rebantur, orbi Veneris inlocatum, propria illis phænomenis exitia indicasse. Quæ malorum quoque ut domesticam & civilem concordiam morabantur, ita foris regum ingenia sublevandis provinciarum rebus atque discordijs accendebant.
units.tr: Therefore Matthias the Austrian entered Antwerp on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December with great solemnity and preparation, and was received by Orange and the envoys of the States, Orange dissembling that Matthias, summoned secretly by his rivals to overshadow his glory, was being honoured by his services. In this man I am pleased to note a singular example of civic prudence: he, forgetting secret contempt, gave more to public concord than to private hatreds; and, when the others who had summoned Matthias were deliberating, he advised that Matthias be kept in charge of affairs and retained in his dignities. There are those who report that Matthias, though entangled in the party of Arschot and his followers, preferred the alliance of the cities to that of Orange, because Orange, strong in the loyalty of the cities, had by his counsels built up a firmer instrument of the good commonwealth and the favour of the people. Thus the men of princely rank contended with rivalries and often with hatreds, while hope and fear, fixed in doubtful times, and anxiety and care for the public safety, drew them on. Indeed a comet with long hair, blazing in the sky, stirred up fear of disaster; it appeared about the Ides of November and filled the minds of all with great dread. M. Heymann writes that it was seen by those sailing the Cimbrian Ocean about the Nones of November, in a clear sky, and that its tail, stretching from the west towards the summer sunrise, struck secret fear into the minds of those who beheld it. Credulous mortals believed this portent to be all the more harmful to the human race and the whole world, because it was thought to have been generated above the orb of the Moon, as Tycho Brahe, the outstanding restorer of that art, reports, far from the meteors and in the region of the trajectories, and to have inflicted violence on the order of nature and at the same time on the permanence of the heavenly bodies. There were some who maintained that the comet, lit and tailed, moving from the stars towards the middle of Andromeda, had clearly indicated the Austrian as hostile to Belgian liberty, and that its setting foretold for him a violent death, as I shall relate later, by the appearance of fate. In this sense I find that Adrian Antonius of Alkmaar was among the mathematicians of those times. Whatever it was, a deadly and undoubtedly foreboding portent of evil, regarded as sad and ominous by those who looked upon it and as a herald of changes in affairs, shone forth like a funeral sign over troubled lands. It seems to me probable that the hair of that most fiery body marked the defection of the Austrian and the imminent resumption of war at its rising, a war which would end in the discords and frenzies of so many years, and which, even at the very time in which I write these things, longs for firm peace as the remedy for its own evils. As if fate or nature had decreed it, the breaking of the covenant and the defection of all affairs was to be noted by a dreadful omen and by heavenly wrath. Thuanus, among the mathematicians of those times, notes that the comet, traversing more than thirty degrees by its own magnitude, and with its tail stretched out towards the west, embraced Sagittarius and Capricorn, and, as others thought, was placed in the orb of Venus, and indicated by its own appearances ruin peculiar to these things. These portents also delayed the domestic and civil concord of the evils, just as, abroad, they stirred the minds of kings towards the relief of the provinces' affairs and their discords.

units.la: Quippe Angliæ gravis Gallia, Gallo Germania & Anglorum res habebantur, non ferente Medicæâ ambitiosâ fœminâ regis matre, Elisabetham etsi nurui destinasset, suo commodo Philippi & simul Ordinum amicitiam specie affectatæ pacis captare. Igitur à morte Caroli filij, Henrico è Poloniâ accito & regni hærede, de promovendo Alençonio cogitare, præferre favorem & auxilia, quo regiam prolem, angusto domi fratribus regno externis quoque dignitatibus insinuaret. Et erant adhuc in Belgicæ proceribus, qui Galliæ societatis affectatione incalescerent, nondumq; ut ante Gandavensis pacis sanctionem, veteris sub Carolo ix. beneficij memoriam & proniora in Gallos studia exuissent. Quod Elisabetha ne dissimulando quidem ægrius interpretabatur, Belgicæ scilicet Ordines brevissimo freti interjectu à suo regno secretos & si cœlum metientibus fides, sub eodem positu sitos, Gallici fœderis dubios & jam ante in deterius exploratos fructus neglectâ Angliæ societate repetere. Igitur legatione Ordinum sub Marchione Haureo & Adolpho Metkerckio in Angliam missâ, semotâ offensione, cum Ordinibus provinciarum subsidia ex jure innovati fœderis, c. millia librarum sterlingarum in annum depacta est, interpositâ cautione, ut civitates Belgicæ, quas nominatura foret, redimendis syngraphis obligarentur. Foederis vero tabulae huiusmodi erant.
units.tr: Indeed, France was a grave concern for England, and Germany for France, while the affairs of the English were regarded as dangerous. Elizabeth, though she had destined her daughter for the king's son, could not bear the ambitious woman Medici, the king's mother. Seeking her own advantage, she tried to win the friendship of Philip and of the States by a show of cultivated peace. Therefore, after the death of Charles, the king's son and heir, Henry was summoned from Poland, and she began to consider advancing Alençon. She offered him favour and assistance, so that the royal offspring, whose brothers were confined to a narrow kingdom at home, might win for themselves dignities abroad as well. Some of the Belgian nobles still burned with eagerness for an alliance with France. They had not yet, as before the sanction of the Pacification of Ghent, cast off their memory of the old kindness shown them under Charles IX and their readier inclination toward the French. Elizabeth took this as no small offence, and she did not even try to hide it. The Belgian States, relying on the very short stretch of water between them and her kingdom, and, if one may trust astronomers, lying under the same sky, were seeking again, neglecting the English alliance, the fruits of the French treaty, which were doubtful and had already been found to turn out worse. Therefore an embassy of the States, under Marquis Haure and Adolf Metkerke, was sent to England. The offence was set aside, and with the States of the provinces, by the right of the renewed treaty, a subsidy of 100,000 pounds sterling was agreed upon for the year. As security, the Belgian cities which she should name were to be bound by mortgage deeds to redeem them. The articles of this treaty were of the following kind.

units.la: R E G I N A equitum mille, peditum quinque millia Ordinibus in auxilia mittet, quibus tertio postquam ex Angliâ solverint, mense stipendia & expensas Ordines persolvent belloque confecto suis sumptibus in Angliam remittent. Harum copiarum dux Anglicæ gentis in Ordinum consessum admittetur. Nihil Ordines quod bellum aut pacem spectet, Reginâ aut illo inconsultis statuent. Nullum fœdus præterquam illâ consentiente cum quocunque inibunt & eodem si velit comprehendetur. Si quis Princeps contra Reginam aut regnum Angliæ quocunque prætextu aliquid hostile
units.tr: THE QUEEN shall send to the States for their assistance a thousand horse and five thousand foot. The States shall pay their wages and expenses for each month, beginning on the third month after they leave England, and when the war is ended they shall send them back to England at their own cost. The commander of these forces shall be admitted to the council of the States as a man of the English nation. The States shall decide nothing that concerns war or peace without the Queen's knowledge or consent. They shall make no treaty with anyone except with her consent, and she may include herself in any such treaty if she wishes. If any prince

units.la: moliatur, Ordines quantum poterunt resistent, eodemque numero & ijsdem legibus auxilia Reginæ mittent. Si qua Ordines inter discordia oboriatur, Reginæ arbitrio permittetur. Si classis contra hostes per Reginam adornanda sit, Ordines x l. naves justæ magnitudinis cum nautis & singulis necessarijs instruent, quæ Angliæ Amirali parebunt, Reginæ sumptibus merebunt. Ordines rebelles Anglos intra Belgicam non admittent. Si pacem cum Hispano fecerint, curabunt ut hi articuli simul aut seorsim pro Reginæ arbitrio confirmentur.
units.tr: plots anything hostile against the Queen or the kingdom of England on any pretext, the States shall resist as far as they are able, and they shall send assistance to the Queen in the same number and on the same terms. If any discord arises among the States, it shall be left to the Queen's arbitration. If a fleet is to be fitted out by the Queen against enemies, the States shall equip forty ships of proper size with sailors and all necessary supplies. These shall obey the English Admiral and shall serve at the Queen's expense. The States shall not admit rebellious Englishmen within Belgium. If they make peace with the Spaniard, they shall take care that these articles are confirmed, either all together or separately, as the Queen decides.

units.la: Igitur ito fœdere, quo suspicionem fotæ per Belgicam rebellionis apud Philippum amoveret, properè Legatum in Hispaniam misit eun- demque hunc in modum differere jussit.
units.tr: Therefore, by this treaty, which was meant to remove Philip's suspicion of the rebellion that was seething throughout Belgium, she quickly sent an envoy to Spain and ordered him to speak in this manner.

units.la: NE calumniis aut traductionibus apud te locus esset, PHILIPPE Rex, Legatum ad te mitto & ne serendis inter nos inimicitijs pravitas assentantium interveniat. Equidem nec ejus animi unquam fui ut voluptatem ex vicino bello caperem, cum non semel etiam cum obtestatione meæ integritatis suaserim, ut impendentibus malis provideres. Quæ etsi in ipso ortu extingui debuissent, ita neglecto eorum remedio saltem cavi, ne defectio populi à te fieret & ut mansura cum subditis concordia tuum imperium staret. Isti fini ad ORDINES & simul AURANTIUM literas dedi ac ne obsequio se exuerent serio commonui. Itaq; & provincias mihi oblatas renui, ne in hoc quidem cupidini obsecutus ut meæ tutelæ permitterentur. Pecuniâ saltem aut ære in mutuum dato nonnunquam præjuvi, ne peregrino Principi tuus populus se manciparet & ne sancita inter te & illum fœdera turbarentur. Quæ ipsa quoque detrectanti Aurantio ut approbaret, non suasi tantum, sed velut imperavi, quo formidabilis & vicinos quoque in cladem tractura tempestas, mea intercessione postulato componeretur. Hæc vero si me Reginâ pacis & juxta de te bene merendi cupientissimâ indigna censes, singula quæ à me facta sunt Principum Regumque judicijs & simul tuo expendendum relinquo petoque etiamnum, ut bello finem des populoque jus ac simul obsequium tibi principatum recuperes. Quem ut quietum & fœlicem habeas, hoc imprimis necessum est, ut amoto Belgicæ finibus Austriaco cujus odio tenentur, alium regundis ditionibus tuis præficias. Is namque ut populo tuo, ita meo quoque regno infestus est, fabricatis cum Scotorum Reginâ clandestinis consilijs, quo me securam & in rerum mearum tutâ possessione collocatam præter expectationem insidijs aut armis subverteret. Quæ cum ab eo parari per omnem oram non ignorem & copias Gallorum ad manum esse opem genti tuæ tuli, quo & meo & simul tuo periculo occurrerem. Id namque pactione cavi, ut in fide tuâ perseveraret religionique & tibi se obstringeret. Quod si improbare te sentiero teque populum tuum mancupio habere, dabo porro operam ne & vicinæ gentis miseriæ & meæ securitati desim. Ea vero si fidem mutet pactorum ac conventionum oblita, arma mea pro auxilijs sentiet meque meis erga te officijs & simul conciliandæ dissensioni non defuisse.
units.tr: So that there may be no room for calumny or misrepresentation before you, King Philip, I send an envoy to you, lest the wickedness of flatterers intervene to sow enmity between us. Indeed, I have never been so minded as to take pleasure from a war on our border. More than once, and even with an appeal to my own integrity, I have advised you to provide against the evils that threaten. Although these should have been extinguished at their very beginning, I have at least taken care, though I neglected their remedy, that the people should not revolt from you, and that your rule might stand with a lasting harmony with your subjects. To that end I sent letters to the States and at the same time to Orange, and I earnestly warned them not to cast off their obedience. Therefore I also refused the provinces offered to me, not even yielding to desire in this, that they should be placed under my protection. At times I have helped them with money or with loans of bronze, lest your people hand themselves over to a foreign prince and the treaties concluded between you and him be disturbed. Even when Orange refused to approve these things, I not only advised him but, as it were, commanded him to do so, so that a storm which would have been dangerous and which would also have drawn in the neighbouring states might be settled by my intercession, as requested. But if you think that these things are unworthy of me, a Queen most eager for peace and equally desirous of deserving well of you, I leave every single thing that I have done to be weighed by the judgment of princes and kings, and at the same time by yours. And I still ask that you bring the war to an end, and that you recover for your people their right and at the same time their obedience to you as prince. In order that you may have that government quiet and prosperous, it is above all necessary that, the Austrian being removed from the borders of Belgium, whom they hate, you set over the governing of your domains someone else. For he is hostile to my kingdom no less than to your people, having contrived with the Queen of Scots secret plans, by which he would overthrow me, placed in secure possession of my affairs, by ambush or arms, beyond expectation. Since I am not unaware that he is preparing these things along the whole coast, and since the troops of the French are at hand, I have brought help to your nation, so that I might meet the danger both to myself and to you. For I have secured this by agreement, that he should persevere in faith to you and bind himself to you in religion. But if you perceive that he is disapproved, and that you hold your people as in bondage, I shall further take care not to fail either the miseries of the neighbouring nation or my own safety. And if he should change his faith, forgetting the pacts and agreements, he will feel my arms in place of help, and he will know that I was not wanting in my duties to you, nor in the effort to reconcile the dissension.

units.la: Creditum fuit, illam reginæ excusationem Philippum regem æquo animo tulisse Austriacæque pravitatis & juxta ambitionis conscium, non inrito metui inanem fiduciam & affectum amicissimi Principis reposuisse. Reidanus scribit syngraphas, ab Ordinibus provinciarum Elisabethæ cIↄ. Iↄ. datas, hac formulâ scriptas, Quod pro servitio Regis Catholici & pro con-servatione provinciarum in ejus obedientiâ Regina mutuo dederit, haud dubie, ne Philippum ultro æmulum & veteris discordiæ memoriam alentem, locato illius subditis ære, exercendis majoribus odijs, inritaret. Austriacus quoque, quo sinistris Elisabethæ cogitationibus subveniret, legatum in Angliam amandavit increpitisque Ordinum actionibus, velut paci adversis, redintegrandi belli consilium exposuit.
units.tr: It was believed that King Philip bore that excuse of the Queen with an even mind. Being aware of Austrian wickedness and equally of its ambition, he did not, not without reason, fear an empty confidence and placed his trust in the affection of a most friendly prince. Reidanus writes that the mortgage deeds, given to Elizabeth by the States of the provinces in the year 1585 and 1586, were written in this form: That the Queen has lent money for the service of the Catholic King and for the preservation of the provinces in his obedience. Undoubtedly this was done so that Philip, who was not a man to become a rival of his own accord and was nursing the memory of the old discord, would not be provoked, by her lending money to his subjects, to exercise greater hatreds. The Austrian also, in order to meet Elizabeth's sinister designs, sent an envoy to England, and, denouncing the actions of the States as hostile to peace, he set out his plan of renewing the war.

units.la: Mox Lalainius per civitates & oppida immutandis Magistratibus se dedit primariæque Frisiorum intra Flevum & Lavicam Leovardiæ urbi, Adium Lambertium, Jarichum Wopconium, Gellium Sibæum & Meinardum Wigerium, iltius anni Consules nominavit. Dein Carolum Roordam, virum pacis artibus excultum, Franequeram cum mandatis & ampla potestate misit exuendoque imperio Magistratui Julium Bontiam virum antiquæ Nobilitatis collegam ei adjunxit. Quare praeconis voce populus in templum convenire jussus, quo mandata Præfecti ac Legatorum consilia in publico acciperet. Cæterum Magistratus futuri perspicax cœptis obstitit congregatusque in Curiâ accersi legatos imperavit tabulasque mandatorum popposcit. Itaque fiduciariæ litteræ à Legatis in Senatu exhibitæ, quibus Magistratus dignitate ac imperio urbis se abdicare Decreto Lalainij jubebatur.
units.tr: Soon Lalaing gave himself to changing the magistrates through the cities and towns. Among the chief men of the Frisians, between the Flie and the Lauwers, he nominated for the city of Leeuwarden, as consuls of that year, Adius Lambertius, Jarichus Wopconius, Gellius Sibaeus and Meinardus Wigerius. Then he sent Carolus Roorda, a man trained in the arts of peace, to Franeker with instructions and full authority, and, stripping the magistracy of its power, he joined to him as colleague Julius Bontius, a man of ancient nobility. Therefore the people were ordered by the voice of a herald to assemble in the temple, to receive publicly the instructions of the prefect and the counsel of the envoys. But the magistrate, shrewd about what was to come, opposed the undertaking, and, gathered in the council hall, he ordered the envoys to be summoned and demanded to see the written instructions. Accordingly, letters of trust were produced by the envoys in the Senate, by which the magistrates were bidden, by Lalaing's decree, to give up the dignity and authority of the city.

units.la: Cæterum Magistratus rei novæ & insperatæ indignatione majorem contumaciam alens, Legatis se oppositit causæque suæ vota civium & pactiones fœderum, tum rescripta Lalainij obtendit. Ea quippe nupero comitio, quod Septembri mense Leovardiæ fuisset, agrarijs, post oppidorum delegatis à Præfecto indulta semelque placita pro æternis habenda. Tum cautum fuisse, ne quid per provinciam in civitate aut præturâ novaretur possessuroque UTI POSSIDERENT, modo paci publicæ vis non fieret fœdusque Gandavense sacrum & inviolabile Magistratibus oppidorum Prætoribusque præstaretur. Atqui civitates, atqui agrarium populum ex præscripto foederum rexisse. Tantum abesse ut imputare suæ integritati quid posset, cui testimonium adstruere conscientia & vox populi quiret. Itaque Carolus Roorda speciatâ Senatus oppidani pertinacia Leovardiam regressus, Joannem Mathenesium Leovardianæ arcis Satrapam cum quibusdam schlopetarijs in comitatum adscivit provectusque Franequeram templi fores obsideri armato fecit. Mox civium quosque, repetito per præconem edicto, in fanum evocavit militemque & stipatorem suæ & aliorum securitati destinatum stare præsidio jusit. Igitur Magistratus confluente sensim populo, tanquam aliud acturus cum Mathenesio in secretum fani secessit hominique ignavo & gerendis momentis rerum imperito magnâ acerbitate se objecit. Quippe leges civitatis, jura populi, receptas consuetudines, Lalainij rescripta violari criminabatur legatosque violentis & inefficiosis consilijs subnixos novas res damnatis moribus ordiri. Ideò ex suis ad Lalainium misisse, intra triduum reversuros perlaturosque ad Senatum quæ præstari vellet. Ea propter rogare ut legati negotium in tempus differant, dum de voluntate Præfecti cognoscant, qui haud dubie Principis fidem suis decretis interpositurus sit. Secus obtestari dignitatem Senatus, leges populi atque vota, vim suis sacris ininferri. Mox Legati gnari discordijs civilibus facto non consulto opus esse, globo armatorum stipati in sacellum irruere diductisque per vim foribus nuncupandi novi Senatus potestatem civibus fecere. Annotatum invenio eosdem Lalainij legatos arma & carceres praefracto Senatui comminatos eundemque gravi voce & stipatorum turba conterritum stantibus periculis se subduxisse.
units.tr: But the magistrate, feeding a greater obstinacy from indignation at this new and unexpected thing, set himself against the envoys, and he put forward in defence of his cause the wishes of the citizens, the agreements of the treaties, and also the rescripts of Lalaing. For at the recent assembly, which had been held at Leeuwarden in September, it had been granted to the representatives of the agrarian people, after the delegates of the towns had been chosen by the prefect, and it was to be held as settled for ever. Then it had been provided that nothing should be changed through the province in a city or in a praetorship, and that the possessor should keep the right to possess as they possessed, provided that no violence was done to the public peace, and that the Ghent treaty, sacred and inviolable, was guaranteed to the magistrates of the towns and the praetors. Yet the cities, and the agrarian people, had been governed in accordance with the terms of the treaties. So far was it from being imputed to his integrity what he could do, when conscience and the voice of the people could bear witness to it. Therefore Carolus Roorda, having returned to Leeuwarden with the obstinacy of the Senate of the town especially noted, took with him Johannes Mathenesius, the commander of the Leeuwarden citadel, with some men armed with harquebuses into the district. Then, advancing to Franeker, he had the doors of the temple besieged by armed men. Soon he called together the citizens, by a repeated edict proclaimed by the herald, into the shrine, and he ordered the soldiers and the guards, appointed for his own and others' safety, to stand guard. Therefore the magistrate, as the people gradually gathered, withdrew with Mathenesius into the secret part of the shrine, as if he were about to do something else, and he rebuked that cowardly man, unskilled in handling critical moments, with great bitterness. For he accused him of violating the laws of the city, the rights of the people, the customs received, and the rescripts of Lalaing, and of initiating new affairs with corrupt ways, the envoys relying on violent and ineffective plans. Therefore he had sent men of his own to Lalaing, who would return within three days and bring to the Senate what he wished to be done. For that reason he asked that the envoy's business be put off until they learned the will of the prefect, who would undoubtedly confirm the prince's faith by his decrees. Otherwise, he protested, the dignity of the Senate, the laws and wishes of the people, and their sacred things would be violated by force. Soon the envoys, aware of the civil discord and judging that action, not deliberation, was needed, crowded into the little shrine with a troop of armed men, forced the doors open by violence, and gave the citizens the power of nominating a new Senate. I find it recorded that the same envoys of Lalaing threatened the Senate, which was disobedient, with arms and prisons, and that the magistrate, terrified by their heavy voices and the crowd of their attendants, withdrew himself from the dangers that surrounded him.

units.la: Igitur Magistratu, velut civitatis interregno, Carolus Roorda vir facundus pro concione verba fecit:
units.tr: Then, with the magistracy as it were in an interregnum of the state, Carolus Roorda, an eloquent man, addressed the assembly:

units.la: VT in urbem vestram pergeremus, CIVES, mandatum Praefecti nos compulit. Qui lubrico rerum statu muniendam Remp. ratus, suo imperio, nostris officijs uti voluit. Igitur postquam fiduciam Senatus suspicione excussit, e Rep. censuit veterem Magistratum regimine civitatis exuendum & ut vos ipsi novos urbi rectores patriae fidos vestris arbitrijs ac suffragijs designaretis. Isti fini convocari vos huc in locum fecimus, CIVES, quem colendo numini a majoribus dedicatum, curandae rerum saluti & stabiliendae Reip. hoc ipso tempore delegimus. In vobis erit, ex praescripto Praefecti triginta duos regundae civitati nuncupare, quo ejusdem Praefecti & nostro arbitratu e numero designatorum Magistratus constituatur civitatemque partium facundam publica posthac autoritas contineat. Igitur potestatem vobis facimus, nullo religionis Pontificiae respectu, optimum quemque e tota multitudine deligendi & cui ex virtute dignitas deferri queat. Nos operam dabimus, ut hoc incendio rerum, quod doloso cineri diu contectum exardescit, Reip. securitati & simul vestris desideriis satisfaciamus.
units.tr: We were compelled to march into your city, citizens, by the order of the Governor. Believing that the Republic must be fortified in the slippery state of affairs, he wished to use his own authority and our services. Therefore, after he had shaken off the Senate's trust with suspicion, he judged from the standpoint of the Republic that the old magistracy must be stripped of the government of the state, and that you yourselves should designate new rulers of the city, faithful to the fatherland, by your own judgments and votes. For this end we have brought you together here, citizens, to this place, which was dedicated by our ancestors to the worship of the divine power, and which we have chosen at this very time for the care of the safety of affairs and the stabilising of the Republic. It will be up to you, according to the prescription of the Governor, to nominate thirty-two men to govern the state, so that by his judgment and ours a magistracy may be constituted from the number of those designated, and that public authority may hereafter hold the city, eloquent in its factions, together. Therefore we give you the power, with no regard for Papist religion, of choosing from the whole multitude the best person, and anyone to whom dignity can be granted on account of virtue. We shall take care that, by this fire of affairs, which has long smouldered covered over with deceitful ashes and now flares up, we satisfy both the security of the Republic and at the same time your desires.

units.la: Qua Oratione finita pro cujusque captu, ut in turba fieri solet, dissentientium animorum haud obscura signa miseraeque civitatis secretum & triste dissidium visebatur. Itaque fuere, qui secessione a reliquo coetu facta tacito murmure se proderent taedioque mutati temporis secreta vulnera contumaci vultu & domestico luctu placarent. Scriptum in commentarijs illorum temporum invenio, secedentem in sine actus turbam ab armatis stipatoribus in templum retractum etiam invitam & renitentem istis solemnibus & nuncupando Magistratui interfuisse. Presbyteros econtra majore rei institutae invidia correptos abscedere jussos, ne importunitate indignantium capitum progressus rerum & imperatum silentium obturbaretur. Quamobrem circumstante populo, etsi opinionibus discordi, novi Consules dicti eorumque nomina actorum fidei inserta ac multitudini praelecta, privatae fraudis & famosas suspiciones adversarum partium oppressere. Tum Mathenessius, nuncupatione Senatus facta, Leovardiam recessit.
units.tr: When this speech was finished, according to each man's understanding, as usually happens in a crowd, the clear signs of minds in disagreement and the secret and sorry discord of a wretched city were visible. And so there were some who, having withdrawn from the rest of the gathering, betrayed themselves by silent muttering, and, weary of the changed times, soothed their hidden wounds with a stubborn expression and domestic grief. I find it written in the records of those times that the crowd, withdrawing at the end of the proceedings, was dragged back into the temple by armed attendants, even unwilling and resisting, and was present at these solemnities and at the nomination of the magistrate. The elders, on the other hand, seized with greater hatred of the institution, were ordered to withdraw, lest the progress of affairs be disturbed by the importunity of indignant heads and the enforced silence be broken. Therefore, with the people standing round, although divided in opinions, the new consuls were named, their names were inserted into the record of the acts and read aloud to the multitude, and they suppressed the private fraud and infamous suspicions of the opposing party. Then Mathenessius, after the nomination of the Senate had been made, withdrew to Leeuwarden.

units.la: Igitur ab Oldermanno & Magistratu priore quorundam nobilium civiumque nomine ad Lalainium Praefectum & simul Senatum Regium litterae missae, quibus majestati regnantis & Gandavensi Foederi vim illatam acerbis narrationibus repetebant. Non eguisse scilicet negotium tantae molestiae & armati apparatus, ac ut Legatis Praefecti miles & spiculator ad custodiam corporis decerneretur. Sibi rationem gesti imperij constare, quod posituri ultra fuissent, modo ex lege & recepto ritu licuisset. Itaque Deum testem actorum & suae innocentiae advocare rogareque Senatum regium, ut apud Lalainium intercedat consulatsulatque populo civico, ex hac ipsa rerum mutatione manifesta exitia formidanti.
units.tr: Therefore letters were sent, in the name of the Alderman and the former magistracy, and of certain nobles and citizens, to Lalaing the Governor and at the same time to the Royal Senate, in which they repeated with bitter narratives the violence done to the majesty of the reigning king and to the Ghent Union. The matter, they said, and the armed preparation of such great trouble had no need of it, and that a soldier and a lictor should be assigned to the Governor's envoys for the guard of their persons. The reasoning of their conduct of office, they said, was consistent, since they would have proceeded further, had it been permitted by law and accepted custom. Therefore they asked God to be called as witness of their acts and of their innocence, and asked the Royal Senate to intercede with Lalaing on behalf of the consuls and the civic people, who feared manifest destruction from this very change of affairs.

units.la: Mox composito quarundam civitatum statu, Renicus Camminga & Barthius Idzaerda ad Ordines generales missi, qui instituendis ulterioribus rerum conversionibus autoramentum rescriptumque impetrarent. Quippe, mutatis per oppida magistratibus, praetores adhuc agrarios Hispanicae dominationis mancupia praesse dicundo juri & administrandis rebus indignabantur arciumque ac castellorum validas moles arctandae libertati structas magno sumptui & premendis provincialibus superesse. Adhaec attenuatum Roblesij exactionibus aerarium & privatas opes querebantur leniusque tributum censumve regium e vectigalibus Biltae agris provenientem in subsidium orabant. Hoc etiam volebant, ut quod ex pacto foederum communi provinciarum aerario inferendum esset, suo arbitratu conquiteretur sibique corrogandi, quovis modo per provinciam aeris libera potestas foret.
units.tr: Soon, with the condition of some cities settled, Renicus Camminga and Barthius Idzaerda were sent to the General Estates, to obtain authority and a written reply for arranging further changes in affairs. Indeed, with the magistrates changed through the towns, the praetors still in the fields, mere chattels of Spanish rule, were indignant that they should preside over justice and administer affairs; and they complained that the strong masses of fortresses and castles, built to constrict liberty, were a great expense and a burden to the provincials. Besides, they complained that the treasury, weakened by the exactions of Roblesius, and private resources were exhausted, and they begged for a gentler tribute or royal census, to be relief from the revenues arising from the lands of Bilt. They also wished that what was to be paid into the common treasury of the provinces under the compact of the union should be collected at their discretion, and that there should be free power for them to raise money in any way throughout the province.

units.la: In Cunerum vero Episcopum eorum mandata atrocissime invehebantur, quod aequatis solo coenobiorum structuris eorum reditus, foeda avaritia suae doti adjecisset dirutisque sacris aedibus sepulchra majorum agro pascuo & nutriendo pecori applicasset. Neque enim ferendum esse, ajebant, ut ossa ac cineres solo eruti per plana agrorum spargantur Soliique expositia, quae tegi natura voluisset, feris alijsque animantibus in pabulum cedant. Sacrilegio saltem violandisque defunctorum monumentis parcendum fuisse & quidem isti homini, cui professio pietatis & divini cultus incumbat. Caeterum eundem Episcopum ambitione & simul avaritia correptum suae cupiditatis modum jam diu transmigrasse. Ita prolatata jurisdictione & aere presbyteris extorto avidum imperij & simul pecuniae animum ostendisse, haud vano indicio, eum simulata in speciem religione, proferendae dominationi & venalibus sacris interesse. Igitur petebant, ut Ordines provinciarum legem eidem Episcopo praescriberent insolentemque ac in enormia effusum severitate novorum mandatorum coercerent. Et quoniam Haskerani coenobij proventus, (cujus quaesturam Heymanno Senatus regius contulisset) contra jus ac fas idem Senatus vindicaret, addici provinciae eosdem reditus urgebant & ut Heymannus quaestorio munere de mandato Ordinum se abdicaret.
units.tr: Against Cuneraus the bishop, their instructions attacked most savagely, because, having levelled the buildings of the monasteries, he had added their revenues with foul greed to his own endowment, and, having destroyed the sacred buildings, had applied the tombs of their ancestors to pasture land and the feeding of cattle. For they said it was not to be endured that bones and ashes, dug up from the soil, should be scattered over the flat fields and exposed to the sun, and that what nature had willed to be covered should become fodder for wild beasts and other animals. At least, they said, sacrilege and the violation of the monuments of the dead ought to have been spared, and especially by that man, to whom the profession of piety and divine worship belongs. Moreover, they said, the same bishop, seized by ambition and at the same time by avarice, had long since passed beyond the measure of his desire. Thus, by extending his jurisdiction and extorting money from the presbyters, he had shown a mind greedy for dominion and at the same time for money, by no empty sign that, under a pretence of religion, he was engaged in extending his rule and in selling sacred things. Therefore they asked that the orders of the provinces should prescribe a law for the same bishop and restrain his insolence, poured out into enormities, by the severity of new mandates. And since the Royal Senate claimed for itself the revenues of the monastery of Haskerum (whose stewardship the Royal Senate had conferred on Heymannus), contrary to right and law, they urged that those revenues be assigned to the province, and that Heymannus should resign his treasurer's office by the mandate of the Estates.

units.la: Adhaec vigente per Frisiam Hispanorum dominatu plurimos dignitatibus bonisque exutos a Senatu regio criminabantur eosdemque exilia & vim fisci perpessos, veteri actione & nova lite apud Senatum Regium conveniri. Quamobrem volebant, ne ejus quod mala fide gestum acquisitumve esset, usucapio aut jus foret & ut provincialium lites per exilia & turbas temporum ortae non a Senatu regis, caeterum a Praefecto aut ejus Delegato dirimerentur. Post armandae per provinciam plebi more majorum potestatem oravere, ne Gasparus Roblesius veteris per provinciam imperij manifestus affectator, de Austriaci consilio vim aut insidias per socordiam populi moliretur. Quod etsi mense Octobri spontaneo Ordinum provinciae & Lalainij motu factum esset, ita volebant, ut SCtum ea de re scriberetur, Ordinesque defertore foederis Austriaco, summis imperijs, & fastigio rerum admoti, publicam autoritatem necessarijs consilijs interponerent.
units.tr: Besides, while the Spanish domination was in force throughout Friesland, they accused the Royal Senate of having stripped very many men of dignities and goods, and said that these, having suffered exile and the violence of the treasury, were being summoned before the Royal Senate in an old action and a new suit. Therefore they wished that what had been done or acquired in bad faith should not be subject to usucaption or any right, and that the lawsuits of the provincials, arising through exiles and the disturbances of the times, should be settled not by the Royal Senate but by the Governor or his delegate. Afterwards, they begged for the power, after the custom of their ancestors, of arming the common people throughout the province, lest Gaspar Roblesius, a manifest aspirant to the former rule in the province, might, on the counsel of Austria, attempt violence or plots through the carelessness of the people. And although this had been done in October by the spontaneous movement of the provincial Estates and of Lalaing, they wished that a decree be written concerning this matter, and that the General Estates, who had deserted the Austrian alliance and were raised to the highest authority and the summit of affairs, should interpose public authority by necessary counsels.

units.la: Igitur Ordines generales rescripsere: Daturos se litteras ocyus ad Lalainium Frisiæ Præfectum, quo in ingenia, consilia, & actiones prætorum inquirat, suspectosque violati fœderis, quod Gandavi ictum esset, possessione dignitatum ac munerum amoveat. Quod ad demoliendas arces attineret, id arbitrio Lalainij ac Leovardiæ Magistratuum permittere. De Biltanis agris & eorum proventibus provinciæ applicandis ac colligendi æris potestate decretum facturos. Petere interea, ut Frisij Vectigalium legi, per omnes provincias promulgandæ, salvâ populi sui immunitate se submittant, quo provinciarum res parabili pecuniâ, tanquam firmiore nervo trahantur. Ea vero, quæ adversus Episcopum ac Senatum regium proferebantur, dilui ab eodem Episcopo & Senatu volebant, ac ut læsorum per Frisiam in integrum restitutio (quod Gandavense Fœdus nihil certi determinaret) proximo Ordinum generalium conventui reservaretur. Interim actiones in res bonaque exulum institutas componi debere ex lege Gandavensis fœderis censebant reliquasque lites ex distractis divenditisque exulum bonis natas & earum vendicationem jure & æquo doceniri. Armandis vero provincialibus autoritatem Lalainio pro more gentis & necessitate rerum facere, ac ut ipse aut Deputati Ordinum comitium populi indicant statuantq; quod è Republica sit.
units.tr: Therefore the General Estates replied in writing: they would send letters as quickly as possible to Lalaing, Governor of Friesland, so that he might inquire into the dispositions, counsels and actions of the praetors, and remove from possession of dignities and offices those suspected of breaking the covenant that was struck at Ghent. As for demolishing the fortresses, they would leave this to the judgment of Lalaing and the magistrates of Leeuwarden. They would make a decree concerning the applying of the Bilt lands and their revenues to the province, and of the power of collecting money. Meanwhile they asked that the Frisians submit, saving their people's immunity, to the law of tribute, to be promulgated through all the provinces, so that the affairs of the provinces might be carried on by money at hand, as by a firmer sinew. But those things which were brought forward against the bishop and the Royal Senate, they wished to be refuted by the same bishop and Senate; and that the restoration to their former state of those injured throughout Friesland (since the Ghent Union determined nothing certain) be reserved for the next assembly of the General Estates. Meanwhile, they judged that actions instituted against the goods and property of exiles ought to be settled by the law of the Ghent covenant, and the remaining lawsuits arising from the sold and disposed goods of exiles, and the claim to them, should be decided by right and equity. As for arming the provincials, they gave authority to Lalaing, according to the custom of the nation and the necessity of affairs, and that he or the deputies of the Estates should summon the people's assemblies and decide what is for the good of the Republic.

units.la: Ita Renicus Cammingha, & Barthius Idzaerda Legati in Frisiam & ad Lalainium regressi, cujus animum istorum temporum fato, gravissimis curis implexum, Pontificiorum per provinciam contumacia & exitiales Translavicanorum discordiæ exercebant. Creditum fuit Pontificios quosque Austriaci armis ac potentiâ irati Regis subnixos, magna consilia tum concepisse mandatisque novorum imperantium adversos conversionem rerum & cum eâ fortunam aniteacti temporis sperasse.
units.tr: So Renicus Camminga and Barthius Idzaerda, envoys, returned into Friesland and to Lalaing; his mind, entangled by the fate of those times with the gravest cares, was troubled by the obstinacy of the Papists throughout the province and the destructive discords of the Trans-Vlieters. It was believed that the Papists, relying on the arms and power of the Austrian and of the angry king, had then formed great designs, and hoped, with the upheaval of affairs, for the fortune of past time, through the commands of the new rulers.

units.la: Unde Austriacus optimus serendæ in Ordines invidiæ artifex, hostis Ordinum rescripto judicatus, quod Fœderum pacisque publicæ ruptor Namurcanam arcem & cum eâ securitatem Reip. doloso consilio circumvenisset. Igitur imperium, scriptis in consessu Ordinum generalium eâ de re tabulis, ei abrogatum damnatque perduellionis, qui cœtui Ordinum jam ante ascripti per fœdissimas secessiones, nova sacramenta perniciosæ societati nuncupassent. Perduelles quoque ipsi decimum intra & quintum diem redire in sua ac renuntiare nefario fœderi jussit, si forte destertâ partium fide Remp. complexis scriptæ legis rigor, clementiâ judicum attemperaretur. Bona quoque eorum in commentarium redacta vetitumque edicto, ne quis militem, arma, commeatum perduellibus præstaret. Cujus decreti tabulæ v r i. Eid. Dec. Bruxellis scriptæ ac in Frisiam quo vulgarentur missæ, civilium animorum statum non parum conturbavere. Igitur à fautoribus Austriaci (referente eâ de re Hesselo Aysma provinciæ Legato) conspirationes adversus Remp. initæ, indignantibus conjuratis Joannem Austriacum regij Imperatorijque sanguinis Principem moderandis per Frisiam rebus Philippo suffectum, majestatis postulari. Quamobrem Decreti Edictum pertinaciâ partium in bimestre suppressum, donec in ipsum etiam Lalainium, velut supinum & conniventem, tum Senatum
units.tr: Hence the Austrian, a past master at stirring up hatred against the Orders, was declared an enemy of the Orders by a rescript, because by a treacherous plan he had got possession of the citadel of Namur, and with it the security of the Republic, and had broken the covenants and public peace. The authority was therefore taken from him by documents written at the assembly of the General Orders on that matter, and he was condemned for treason. The men who had earlier been enrolled in the Orders' assembly and had, through the most shameful secessions, sworn new oaths to a ruinous society were also declared traitors. He ordered them to return to their own side within fifteen days and renounce the impious covenant, in case the rigour of the written law might be softened by the judges' clemency, since they had broken faith with their party. Their goods were also listed in an inventory, and an edict forbade anyone to supply soldiers, arms or provisions to the traitors. The tablets of this decree, written at Brussels on 8 December and sent to Friesland to be published, greatly unsettled the minds of the citizens. Then, as Hessel Aysma, the province's legate, reported, conspiracies against the Republic were begun by the Austrian's supporters. The conspirators, angry, demanded that Don John, a prince of royal and imperial blood, who had been appointed to govern affairs in Friesland in Philip's place, be charged with treason. For this reason the edict of the decree was suppressed for two months by the obstinacy of the parties, until suspicion was increased against Lalaing himself, as lax and conniving, and then against the Senate. The people's anxiety and unrest grew, and in March the decree was read out in the Basilica of St Philip and in every tribunal of the province.

units.la: Anno regium aucta suspicione & inquietudine populi, Martio mense in Basilica S. Philippi & per omne provinciae Tribunal recitaretur. LXXVIII. Tum Matthias Austrius, quo praescriptum imperij acciperet, Antverpiâ per Legatos Ordinum Bruxellas evocatus sacramentum dixit, sociumque ac consortem rerum Aurantium, velut juventae moderatorem & suorum consilorum accepit. Quae omnia regio adhuc Philippi nomine istâ temporum aetate velabantur; quo reverentiam Principis juramentum Praefecti & precerum conventio non minuerat. Ea cautum fuit.
units.tr: In the year 1578 Matthias Austria, to receive the authority prescribed for him, was summoned from Antwerp to Brussels by the legates of the Orders and took the oath. He accepted as partner and associate in affairs William of Orange, as moderator of his youth and of his own counsels. All these things were still veiled in the name of King Philip in that period of the times, and the respect owed to the Prince was not diminished by the oath of the Governor and the agreement of the nobles. That was the provision made.

units.la: Ut Matthias Austrius Philippi Ordinumque nomine incolumitati omnium singularumque provinciarum jurandum faceret omnisque insuper exercitus sacramento Regis & simul Ordinum haberetur. Adhaec, ut Matthias Concilio Status adjutus, quod Ordines generales ex inquilinis & peritis rerum constituti essent) tutandis provinciarum legibus immunitatibusque suum imperium affornaret omneque decretum plurium suffragationibus scriberetur. Dispensationem munerum quae regis essent Philippo relinqueret, reliquas vero dignitates ex pacto Gandavensis Foederis Ordinum generalium arbitrio permitteret. Bellum, pacem, societatem aut foedus cum externo Rege aut gente sine assensu Ordinum non iniret. Secreta epistolarum Concilio Status communicaret. Indicendorum prolongandorumque conventuum jus Ordinibus aut eorum Delegatis permitteret, Foedusque Gandavense integrum intemeratumque praestaret. Stipatores, spiculatoresque è Belgica gente conscriberet militiaque dignitatibus, legendis copiis aut disponendis praesidiis interveniente assensu Ordinum praeesset. Provinciae praefectum sine mandato Ordinum aut assensu provincialium non daret, caeterum res bellicas de Concilio Status & Senatus belli decerneret. Pecuniae publicae, regio censu excepto, administrationem Ordinibus aut eorum Delegatis relinqueret. Ordinum foedera auxiliaque ex ijs profecta integra inviolataque curaret. Cum ijs qui in partibus Austriaci adversus patriam arma tulissent, lege agi faceret. Castella ex decreto Ordinum diruenda solo aequari mandaret. Omnium rerum veniam faceret actaque & rescripta Ordinum à defectione Austriaci publicata, firma atque rata haberet. Pro Ordinibus & recuperandis locis ab AUSTRIACO occupatis apud Caesarem & Imperij Principes intercederet, quo Burgundiae circulo comprehensa tutelâ Imperij vendicentur. Omnia ac singula sarta facerent, secus agendo Ordinum armis corrigeretur.
units.tr: That Matthias Austria, in the name of Philip and of the Orders, should swear to the safety of all and of each province, and that the whole army should be held under the oath to the King and at the same time to the Orders. Further, that Matthias, aided by the Council of State (since the General Orders were made up of residents and men experienced in affairs), should shape his authority to protect the laws and immunities of the provinces, and that every decree should be written by the votes of the majority. He should leave to Philip the distribution of offices that belonged to the King, and by the terms of the Ghent Union should allow the remaining posts to the judgment of the General Orders. He should not undertake war, peace, an alliance or a treaty with a foreign king or people without the assent of the Orders. He should communicate secret letters to the Council of State. He should grant the Orders, or their delegates, the right to call and prolong assemblies, and should keep the Union of Ghent whole and inviolate. He should enlist guards and spearmen from the Belgian people, and preside over military offices, the choice of troops and the placing of garrisons, with the assent of the Orders. He should not appoint a governor of a province without a mandate from the Orders or the assent of the provincials; otherwise, war matters should be decided by the Council of State and the Senate. He should leave the administration of public money, apart from royal revenue, to the Orders or their delegates. He should see that the covenants of the Orders, and the aid arising from them, remain whole and inviolate. He should have those who had taken up arms against the country on Austria's side dealt with by law. He should order castles to be razed to the ground by decree of the Orders. He should grant a pardon for all things, and hold the acts and rescripts published by the Orders since Austria's defection as firm and valid. On behalf of the Orders, he should intercede with the Emperor and the princes of the Empire to recover the places occupied by Austria, so that the Burgundian circle, which is included, may be claimed under the protection of the Empire. All and each of these things were to be done firmly; if they acted otherwise, they would be brought to order by the arms of the Orders.

units.la: Quae conditiones à Matthia Austrio & Aurantio Matthiae vicario jurejurando firmatae in Germaniam ad Caesarem, in Hispaniam ad Philippum regem, quo approbaret transmissae, in aulâ suis moribus obnoxiâ & male instructa parum gratiae reperere. Quippe Austriacus, factâ contra eas obtestatione, Philippi animum anteceperat, incusatis Ordinum & Matthiae conventionibus, quod sacramentis foederum, pacci & consensui regis adversarentur. Igitur, Matthia sacramentis Belgicae & provinciarum innexo, ultra dissimulare nescius undique exercitum recollegit relictoq; Luxemburgo Marchas ad Faminas, quo conduci copias praeceperat, audiendae Anglorum legationi substitit.
units.tr: These conditions, confirmed by oath by Matthias Austria and by Orange as Matthias's deputy, were sent to the Emperor in Germany and to King Philip in Spain for approval; but in a court bound to its own customs and badly informed they found little favour. Austria, having protested against them, had got ahead of Philip's mind, accusing the agreements of Orange and Matthias of opposing the oaths of the treaties, the peace and the King's consent. So Matthias, bound by the oaths of Belgium and of the provinces, and unable to dissemble any longer, gathered the army from every side. Leaving Luxembourg, he moved to Famars, where he had ordered troops to be brought together, and there he halted to hear the English embassy.

units.la: Ea petebat Elisabetha, ut rebus bellum spectantibus induciae scriberentur, dum ex Legato quem in Hispaniam amandaverat, de Philippi mente & voluntate cognovisset.
units.tr: Elizabeth asked that truces be drawn up in matters concerning war, until she had learned Philip's mind and will from the legate whom she had sent to Spain.

units.la: Non esse scilicet festinandum in tam gravi negotio, quod PHILIPPO CIↃ. IↃ. LXXVIII. Regi disterimen, aut exitium populo allaturum sit & ex quo periculi metus ad conterminas transmarinasque gentes perveniret. Sistenda potius aequis conditionibus arma, ut per spiramenta temporum divulsae mentes, in concordiam redeant bellumque recrudescens suâ & aliorum Principum intercessione honestâ pace claudatur.
units.tr: Surely it was not to be hurried in so grave a matter, which might bring danger or ruin to King Philip and his people, and from which fear of peril would spread to the neighbouring and overseas nations. Arms should rather be laid down on fair terms, so that in the breathing space of time the divided minds may return to concord, and the renewed war may be closed by an honourable peace, through the mediation of their own and other princes.

units.la: Caeterum Austriacus, sive aemulatione in Matthiam, sive Edicto Ordinum praereptum sibi Belgicae imperium indignatus, omnem inducias aut pacis rationem rejecit Angliaeque Legato praefractum & contumax responsum reposuit. Creditum fuit, memoriâ veteris in Elisabetham odii commotum, ac nuper regno insidiatum acerbas voces iniquo & necdum sedato pectore depromplisse.
units.tr: Moreover Austria, whether out of rivalry with Matthias, or indignant that the rule of Belgium had been snatched from him by the edict of the Orders, rejected every truce and every plan for peace, and gave the English legate a stubborn and defiant answer. It was believed that, moved by his old hatred of Elizabeth, and having recently plotted against her kingdom, he spoke bitter words from an unjust heart that was not yet calmed.

units.la: QUARE (inquiebat) NULLIS CONVENTIONIBUS AUT PACTIS FOEDERUM ASTRINGI ME SINAM, PARATUS, COACTO JAM EXERCITU, DE MANDATO REGIS BELLUM DARE. IGITUR NEC ANGLICA, NEC GALLORUM, NEC GERMANIAE AUXILIA, SI QUAE PROVINCIJS LOCENTUR, ME A PROPOSITO DETERREBUNT. QUIN DATURUS SUM OPERAM, UT SOCIETATE TURCICA CAESARI AC IMPERIO BELLUM CREEM, GERMANIAEQUE PAX ET QUIES MEIS ET TURCARUM ARMIS LUXETUR. TANTUM ABEST, UT, QUID SUPPETIARUM MATTHIAS AUSTRIUS SPERARE A RUDOLPHO FRATRE QUEAT, DUM EGO BELLO OCCUPOR, QUI PROPEDIEM BRUXELLENSIUM AD PORTAS EXERCITUM ADDUCTURUS SUM. ITAQUE VOLO, UT, ME ETIAM ARMATO, ORDINES ARMA PONANT MEISQUE IMPERATIS PARERANT.
units.tr: "Therefore," he said, "I will not allow myself to be bound by any agreements or treaty pacts. I am ready, with the army now assembled, to give battle by the King's command. Thus neither English, nor French, nor German auxiliaries, if any are offered to the provinces, will turn me from my purpose. Indeed I will work to bring war upon Caesar and the Empire through an alliance with the Turks, and the peace and quiet of Germany will be dissolved by my arms and those of the Turks. So far is Matthias Austria from being able to expect any help from his brother Rudolph, while I am occupied in war, that I shall soon lead my army to the gates of Brussels. Therefore I want the Orders to lay down their arms even while I am armed, and to obey my commands."
