units.la: Mox Marchis adhuc in Faminis agens & Pontificio diplomate à Gregorio ejus nominis xiii. tanquam debellandis paganis praemunitus, bellum edixit, velut certâ fatorum ordinatione, ut eodem in loco adjuratam Foederi fidem foedissimus conventionum infractor violaret. Quare ad castra metatum externa auxilia, tum Hispanorum Italorumque legiones refluxere, quas Gandavensi pactione dimissas Alexander Farnesius rudimenta belli primâ juventâ facturus in provincias reducebat. Indignantibus provinciarum Ordinibus Margaretam Alexandri matrem, nuper Belgicae Frisijsque Praefectam reverenterque habitam, Alexandrum filium opprimendis provincijs rescindendisq; antiquis conventionibus enutrijsse. Dein repetitâ Philippi regis & suâ integritate, velut animum paci etiam contractis auxilijs ac perarmato exercitu praeferret, provincias, oppida, societates ad defectionem foederis sollicitavit Ordinumque sacramenta deserentibus veniam anteactorum fecit. Caeteros Ordinum auspicijs signisque militantes hostes judicavit publicaeque pacis & securitatis sponsione factâ, instanti bello subsidia & comcIↄ. Iↄ. & commeatum poposcit. Tum supinis Ordinum rebus, velut fatali tot consulentium ignavia, exercitum Marchis ac Luxemburgensium finibus movit subsecutusque cum omni procerum comitatu apud Namurcum desedit, quo urbem violando Foederi & suae defectioni fatalem, gerendo sedem bello deliberet.
units.tr: Soon the Marquis, still at Famars and armed with a papal diploma from Gregory XIII, as though he were fortified for crushing the pagans, declared war, as if by a fixed decree of fate, so that in the very same place the most foul breaker of agreements might violate the faith sworn to the covenant. Hence foreign auxiliaries and the Spanish and Italian legions flowed back to the camp; Alexander Farnese, who was about to make his first trial of war in his early youth, was leading them back into the provinces, having been dismissed under the Ghent pact. The Orders of the provinces were indignant that Margaret, Alexander's mother, formerly held in high regard as governess of Belgium and Friesland, had reared her son Alexander to oppress the provinces and overturn the old covenants. Then, repeating King Philip's integrity and his own, as though he preferred peace, even while he had gathered auxiliaries and an army fully armed, he solicited provinces, towns and associations to abandon the covenant, and he granted pardon for past deeds to those who deserted the oaths of the Orders. He judged the others, who fought under the authority and standards of the Orders, to be enemies; and having made a pledge of public peace and security, he demanded subsidies and provisions for the impending war. Then, with the affairs of the Orders being lax, as though through the fatal idleness of so many counsellors, he moved the army from the borders of Hainaut and Luxembourg. Following it with all his nobles, he settled at Namur, where, in order to violate the city, which was fatal to the Union and to his own defection, he deliberated on making it the seat of the war.

units.la: Ordinum vero castra, haud longis ab eo intervallis discreta, non justo duce, nec consilio regebantur. Jtaq; maxime à Matthia Austrio Aurantioque cavebatur, ne exercitus imperij vacuus pugnae & discrimini committeretur unumque sub fortunae ictum provinciarum vires & rerum incolumitas recideret. Caeterum Austriacus praelium poscens castris Ordinum velitem immisit coactumque retrocedere redire in castra praecepit. Mox repetito pugnae consilio, quod ex captivis de movendis Gemblacum Ordinum castris agi comperisset, tergum foederati exercitus premere constituit delectorumque equitum turmas unā cum pedestribus copijs, iterandae velitationi praemisit. Reliquum exercitum rite instructum pergere ocyus Ordinumque aciem velitando iter facientem, haud procul ripā fluminis adsultari jussit, quod hyberno tempore tumidius difficilem transitum foederato exercitui dabat. Igitur Alexander Farnesius, quo militiae rudimenta praeclaro facinore caeptaret, Octavio Gonzaga, Gasparo Roblesio nuper Frisiae Praefecto & Baptista Taxio stipatus, adacto fortius equo, magnam in castra Ordinum impressionem fecit illustrique fortitudinis exemplo, ut commilitonibus ad virtutem, ita sibi ad promerendam gloriam fuit.
units.tr: The camps of the Orders, separated from his by no great distance, were not directed by a proper commander or by any plan. Therefore Matthias Austria and Orange took especial care that the army of the state, left without a leader, should not be committed to battle and danger, and that the strength and safety of the provinces should not fall on one stroke of fortune. Austria, however, demanding battle, sent skirmishers against the camp of the Orders and forced them to retreat and return to camp. Soon, renewing his plan of battle, because he had learned from captives that the camp of the Orders was to be moved to Gembloux, he resolved to press on the rear of the allied army. He sent forward picked squadrons of horse, together with foot soldiers, to renew the skirmishing; and he ordered the rest of the army, properly drawn up, to advance quickly and harass the line of the Orders as it marched, not far from the river bank, which in winter, swollen, made the crossing difficult for the allied army. Then Alexander Farnese, in order to begin his military career with a distinguished deed, attended by Octavio Gonzaga, Gaspar de Robles, recently governor of Friesland, and Battista Tassis, urged his horse harder and made a great charge into the camp of the Orders. By this illustrious example of courage he set a model of valour for his fellow soldiers, and at the same time won glory for himself.

units.la: Quippe mox omnis Austriaci exercitus, quem dubia adhuc praelij fides ignavum aut timidum faciebat, confertim in aciem Ordiuum se ingesit imparemque sustinendae adsultantium moli in fugam dedit. Sex millia è foederatis illo praelio desiderata.
units.tr: Indeed, soon the whole Austrian army, which the still uncertain outcome of the battle made sluggish or fearful, crowded in a mass into the line of the Orders and, unable to withstand the assault of its attackers, took to flight. Six thousand of the Confederates were lost in that battle.

units.la: Scribit in commentarijs suis M. Heymannus perlatā in Frisiam cruentae cladis fama, magnam consternationem populo obvenisse, quod viginti septem millia foederatorum coesa deletasque ad internecionem Ordinum copias, fallax & ut ipse ait, falsitate suā se prodens rumor nuntiaret. Ingens è fugientium caesorumque spolijs praeda signisque militaribus adjectae machinae per omnem oram victoriae decus auxere.
units.tr: M. Heymannus writes in his commentaries that when the news of the bloody defeat reached Friesland, great consternation came over the people, because a false rumour, which (as he himself puts it) betrayed its own falsehood, reported that twenty-seven thousand Confederates had been cut to pieces and the forces of the Orders destroyed to the last man. A huge booty taken from the fugitives and the slain, military standards, and the added machines increased the glory of the victory throughout the whole coast.

units.la: Tum sexcentorum captivorum sanguine victoris furor placatus, hoc ipso indicantis in potestate se fortunam, non vero animum habuisse. Itaque uno velut impetu obvia prosternens oppida plurima ac castella coepit foedaque saevitie ubivis victor usus magnum sui terrorem disseminatis provincijs injecit. Quippe truncata & deformitate vulnerum foeda corpora, ejus jussu minutis ictibus confossa, praeter fati sui infoelicitatem inclementiam quoque cruenti victoris pertulere. Scribunt Austriacum justis viribus & tot legionum accessione instructum, optumam accelerandae pugnae occasionem captasse foederatique exercitus Ducum aut incuria aut absentia prudenter usum secundo praelio conflixisse.
units.tr: Then the victor's fury was appeased with the blood of six hundred captives, which showed that he had fortune in his power but not his spirit. Thus, by a single rush, he overran and laid waste many towns and castles, and, using his victory savagely everywhere, he spread great terror through the provinces. Indeed, the bodies, mutilated and disfigured by wounds, were stabbed with small blows at his command, so that they suffered not only the unhappiness of their fate but also the cruelty of a bloody victor. They write that the Austrian, equipped with full strength and the addition of so many legions, seized the best opportunity to hasten the battle, and that the commanders of the Confederate army, through either carelessness or absence, did not act wisely and joined battle with him a second time.

units.la: Ita dum Ordines sui fiducia & in bello securitas occupabat, Duces primarij inter ludicra & nuptiale festum, (quod Berselius cum Marchionissa Bergensi Bruxellis celebrabat) vino & epulis delibuti procul castris agebant, foederis res in discrimen adductae, etsi dissimulantibus aut elevantibus cladem, qui tot sociarum civitatum fide, post diruta rutas arces & ejecta partium praesidia stare Remp. gloriabantur. Adeo verum est nullos facilius opprimi quam nihil timentes & eos for- tunae mores esse, ut securos aversetur. Qua clade, etsi provinciarum res haud parum affligerentur, ita singulari constantia adversitatem desævientis fortunae tolerabant.
units.tr: So while the Orders were occupied with their trust and their security in war, the chief commanders, steeped in wine and feasting amid games and a wedding celebration (which Berselius was holding in Brussels with the Marchioness of Bergen), were far from the camp. The affairs of the Confederacy were brought into danger, although those who minimised or made light of the defeat boasted that the state stood firm on the loyalty of so many allied cities, after the destruction of certain fortresses and the expulsion of the garrisons of the parties. So true it is that none are more easily crushed than those who fear nothing, and that it is the way of fortune to turn away from the careless. Although the affairs of the provinces were not a little afflicted by this disaster, they bore the adversity of the raging fortune with singular constancy.

units.la: Quare Legatio Caesaris in pacem Belgicam proni, perorante Suart- senburgio modeste accepta subsidiaque & intercessiones quas Legatus offerrebat, non omnino servilibus studijs petitae.
units.tr: Therefore the Legation of the Caesar, which had come to treat for peace in the Netherlands, was received with favour, Suartsenburgius speaking in moderate terms. The help and intercession which the Legate offered were not sought with altogether servile zeal.

units.la: Innuentibus Belgicae proceribus, se nec iniquis casibus subito prosterni, nec erigi secundis, ceterum expositos fatorum decretis bona consilia supremis necessitatibus & funestis rerum eventibus locare. Summae potestatis esse remedia ac finem suis miseriis dare, aut Caesarem Principesque flectere ad honestam misericordiam sublevandae Reip. quae sub ALBANIS & REQUESENTIIS asperrima temporum, sub AUSTRIACO insidias & mox bellum pateretur. Struì scilicet novis artibus antiqua consilia & Ioannis Norcarmij (nam is in speciem pacis ex Hispania tum mandatis PHILIPPI advenerat) legatione non scriptorum nuper foederum, ceterum Carolinae dominationis, & veteris imperij imaginem proponi. Ita servituras rursum conscientias & Edicta interminatae potestatis novis parentium exitijs ac mox bello cessura, cui occasio a Philippo Rege non obscuris indicijs quaratur. Neque enim de revocando in Hispaniam Austriaco, quod maxime datis ad regem litteris petierant, quid statuere aut admiti Philippum, ut religio Foederum servetur, ceterum arma & legiones desideriis pacis reponere. Quae quoniam inrita ac infructuosa passuris bellum forent, ita justam ad defensionem cogi, per quam sacra, legis, liberi, conjuges in tuto habeantur.
units.tr: The Netherlands nobles signified that they were neither suddenly cast down by unfavourable events nor raised up by fortunate ones; rather, they committed good counsel, exposed to the decrees of fate, to the utmost necessities and deadly turns of affairs. It lay within the power of the highest authority to find remedies and to bring an end to their miseries, or to move the Caesar and the Princes to an honourable mercy, to relieve the commonwealth which under Alba and Requesens suffered the harshest conditions of the times, under the Austrian snares and soon war. Clearly, old designs were being built up by new arts, and under the pretext of peace, the image of the old power was being set forth, not of recently written treaties, but of the domination of Charles, through the embassy of Jan Norcarmius (for he had come from Spain at that time with the commission of Philip). Thus consciences, about to be enslaved again by the new slaughter of subjects and the edicts of a threatening power, would soon yield to war, for which an opportunity is being sought by King Philip with unmistakable signs. For they had earnestly asked, in their letters to the king, that the Austrian be recalled to Spain, yet they had decided nothing about this, nor had they admitted Philip, so that the faith of the treaties might be kept; instead they set arms and legions aside for the desire of peace. Since they would suffer war to be idle and fruitless, they were compelled to a just defence, by which sacred things, laws, children and wives might be kept safe.

units.la: Mox arma trans Lavicam mota, indignantibus agrarijs, delegatos ad Comitium, quod Lalainius mense Novembri superiore anno Gro-ningae habuerat, manuum injectionem passos, inter squallores carcerum & indecentem custodiam Groningensium ludibrijs servari.
units.tr: Soon arms were moved across the Lauwers, the farmers being indignant. The delegates who had been summoned to the assembly which Lalaing had held at Groningen the previous November suffered the laying on of hands, and amid the squalor of prisons and the shameful custody of the Groningers they were kept for the amusement of their jailers.

units.la: Neque enim ferendum esse, libero populo & Reip. causa ad conventum vocato contumeliam ac vim inferri, quam publico & velut judicio sistentibus sisti oporteret. Caeterum in civitate turbida & juris sui ac simul boni moris oblita, nullum honesti respectum valuisse, ita immoderatis Groningensium actionibus, ut furoris sui infamiam, ne per praesentiam quidem Praefecti reverentiam superioris imperij compresserint. Spectasse scilicet LALAINIUM Magistratum urbis suis mandatis contumacem locumque comitio a majoribus destinatum, damnatis armis & sociali manu circumventum. Intercepisse mox AL-DEGONDIUM & SYLLAM Ordinum Belgicae Legatos, neque alio eventu quam ut auctoritatis despectu, insolentia & vis increscerent. Sic Delphzilae munitionem, etsi sub MARIA, CARROLI Caesaris sorore, provinciarum Gubernatrice, post ab ALBANO arctandae libertati extructam, solo aequatam, ipsamque Omlandiam quâ Amasio fluminis objacet, ne antiqua quidem munimenta suorum finium retinuisse. Ita Winkenium centurionem cum cohorte & imperio Delphzilae praefectum, alio revocatum, minisque Groningensium & post aere expugnantum, commissam sibi munitionem deseruisse.
units.tr: For it could not be borne that a free people, summoned to a meeting for the sake of the commonwealth, should be subjected to insult and violence, which those who appear before a public and quasi-judicial body ought to be spared. Moreover, in a turbulent city forgetful of its rights and at the same time of good custom, no regard for honour prevailed, so that by their immoderate actions the Groningers did not restrain the infamy of their madness, not even out of respect for the presence of the Governor and the authority of the higher power. Lalaing, of course, had regarded the magistrates of the city as defiant of his orders, and the place which the ancestors had designated for the assembly as condemned by arms and surrounded by a band of allies. Soon Aldegonde and Sylla, envoys of the Orders of Belgium, were seized, and this had no other outcome than that contempt for authority, insolence and violence grew. Thus the fortress of Delfzijl, although built under Mary, sister of Charles and governess of the provinces, and afterwards under Alba to restrain liberty, was levelled to the ground, and even Omlandia, where it lies on the Ems, did not keep even the ancient defences of its borders. Thus the centurion Winkenius, prefect of the garrison of Delfzijl with a cohort and command, was recalled elsewhere, and the fortress entrusted to him was abandoned under threats from the Groningers and afterwards by bronze cannon.

units.la: Igitur agrarij indicto apud Winsumum conventu Bartoldo Entenio ex agrariâ nobilitate viro manu strennuo & promptæ audaciæ, conscribendi x i i. cohortes potestatem fecere, quo vim ac ludibria suorum ulturi, præsidio cohortium domesticam & simul comitio securitatem pararent.
units.tr: Therefore the farmers, having called a meeting at Winsum, gave Bartold Entenius, a man of the farming nobility, vigorous in hand and of ready daring, the power to enlist twelve cohorts, so that they might avenge the violence and mockery done to their people, and by the protection of the cohorts secure both their homes and the safety of the assembly.

units.la: Cæterum rudi & tumultuariâ quam collegerat manu, per Gualterum Hegemannum virum militiæ impigrum profligatâ, Entenius Covardiam profugit cladeque suorum & mox perfidiâ vinculis datus, Groningam abductus est. Ubi periculo capitis expositus, quod spretis Ordinum generalium sacramentis suo militem autorasset, intercessione tandem iplorum Ordinum liberatus, reputantium virum patriæ amantem & ab ipsis belli initijs fidem fœderi professum nimium affectibus indulgendo publicam autoritatem & pacis publicæ curam neglexisse. Itaque de ponendis utrinque armis Ordinum & Matthiæ Austrij decreto intercessum jussique Groningenses simul Omlandi litis suæ compositionem arbitrio Aurantij permittere. Quæ in annum protracta ut post memorabo, partium comminationes & dissidia gliscentibus ex injuria odijs non sustulit.
units.tr: However, with the rough and tumultuous band he had gathered, routed by Walter Hegemann, a man active in war, Entenius fled to Covarda, and after the defeat of his people, and soon, by treachery, being given into chains, he was led off to Groningen. There, exposed to danger of his life because, scorning the oaths of the General Orders, he had led his soldiers away, he was at last freed by the intercession of the Orders themselves, who reflected that the man, who loved his country and from the very beginning of the war had professed loyalty to the Union, had through excessive indulgence of his passions neglected public authority and care for public peace. Thus an agreement was reached about laying down arms on both sides by the decree of the Orders and Matthias of Austria, and the Groningers were ordered at the same time to leave the settlement of their quarrel with Omlandia to the arbitration of Orange. This dispute, which was protracted for a year, as I shall relate afterwards, did not, with hatreds kindled by injury, put an end to the threats and dissensions of the parties.

units.la: Igitur post Gemblacensem cladem Senatus per Frisiam regius ut mortales assolent, cum fortunâ Austriaci animos erigens, mandatis novorum Deputatorum se objecit recitandoque edicto, quo Reip. hostis Austriacus censebatur, pertinacibus studijs se opposuit. Itaque novis turbis per Frisiam initia ex hoc ipso serebantur, discordi ad exemplum imperantium populo, qui partium quoque fortunam ex prosperis aut adversis rerum adorabat. Quare curâ Ordinum Delegatorumq; Frisiæ Lalainius Groningâ, quo componendis dissensionibus concesserat accersitus, qui præfracto Senatu decretum Ordinum generalium exequeretur immodestisq; ingenijs reverentiam novi imperij injiceret.
units.tr: Therefore after the defeat at Gembloux, the Senate of Friesland, royal as mortals usually are, raising its spirits with the fortune of the Austrian, set itself against the mandates of the new Deputies, and, by reading out an edict in which the Austrian was counted an enemy of the commonwealth, opposed them with stubborn zeal. Thus new disturbances in Friesland were set in motion from this very cause, the people being divided in imitation of their rulers, who worshipped the fortune of the parties according to whether things went well or badly for them. Therefore, by the care of the Orders and of the Delegates of Friesland, Lalaing, who had gone to Groningen summoned to settle the dissensions, was to carry out the decree of the General Orders against the obstinate Senate and impose reverence for the new authority on its unrestrained spirits.

units.la: Is Leovardiam progressus, ubi omnia turbida & partium plena per victoriam Austriaci erant, eundem Austriacum ad xvi. Martij diem proclamari pro rostris hostem Reip. fecit arduumque ordinandæ, eâ tempestate Reip. negotium singulari constantia executus est. Quorum omnium, etsi Ordines Frisiæ certiorem Matthiam Gubernatorem fecissent, ita volebat Matthias ut actis & testimonijs publicis eâ de re doceretur.
units.tr: He proceeded to Leeuwarden, where everything was turbulent and full of factions because of the victory of the Austrian. He had the same Austrian proclaimed a public enemy from the rostra on the sixteenth day of March, and carried out with singular constancy the difficult task of putting the commonwealth in order at that time. Although the Orders of Friesland had informed Matthias the Governor of all this, Matthias nevertheless wished to be instructed about it by official acts and testimonies.

units.la: Igitur Ordinum decreto Joannes Matthenessius Satrapa arcis, Julius Botnia Oldermannus Franequerensium, Meinardus Wigerius Consul Leovardiensis Bruxellas cum actis probatorijs missi, coram Matthia disseruere.
units.tr: Therefore by decree of the Orders, Johannes Matthenessius, governor of the citadel, Julius Botnia, alderman of the Franekerers, and Meinardus Wigerius, consul of Leeuwarden, were sent to Brussels with the attesting documents and pleaded before Matthias.

units.la: SENATVM regium, GUBERNATOR, custodiæ dare in animum induximus & causæ nos movent. Præterquam enim, quod illius imperium à nostrâ libertate alienum est, ita deprehendimus eundem Senatum plus Austriaci consilijs quam nostris mandatis tribuisse. Ex interceptis ad eundem AUSTRIACUM quas exhibemus litteris, nostræ integritatis documentum immotescet & alere nos in sinu, qui nostris rebus & salutipublicæ adversentur. Ita Senatus Regius, capto ROBLESIO, & ne is nefarium consilium, quod præconceperat, exequeretur, à cohortibus suis in vincula dato, de eo liberando cogitavit, & ut id obtineret, apud Austriacum intercessit. Adhæc magistratum Leovardiæ urbis in Basilicam ac suum con-sessum evocavit monuitque, ut defendendæ adversum Ordines, urbi se pararet rebusque trans Lavicam à Roblesij captivitate malè fluentibus, regiæ parti intra suæ civitatis muros prospiceret. Austriaci responso eidem Senatui eâ ex re grates actæ & quod Senatus in Philippi fide, ac curâ tuendæ regiæ dominationis perseverasset. Planè, ac si reparandæ libertati sanctissimæ nostræ sollicitudines à regis imperio discrepárent essetque in hac provinciâ, quod ex nostrâ fortunâ ac felicitate Philippi commodum moraretur. Post in Magistratuum per provinciam mutatione, quos libertati nostræ graves & molestos diuturna dominationis possessio fecerat, nostris decretis se objecit, ne diu usurpato & quasi æterno imperio, suffectis patribus, cederet. Igitur specie antiquæ electionis & quæsiti juris res per oppida disposuit, quo civitatum fidem, munimentum solidioris per provincias imperij retinendo, eadem hostium usui habendis præsidijs tueretur. Neque aliâ intentione binas è Germanis cohortes autoravit ac per munitiones provinciæ dispositit, quam ne per agros aut præturas ex decreto Ordinum & simul tuo quid novaretur & ne firmamenta imperij, neglectis ijsdem munitionibus amitteret. Id Renicum Dekama cohortis tribunum & tot annorum stipendia adversis partibus professum, acceptâ fide publicâ, coram Lalainio in consessu patrum non dissimulasse, ne prava Senatus consilia, exitio patriæ reperta, morâ aut secreto invalescerent. Postremo, ne Edicta quidem Ordinum & tua, Gubernator, per Basilicam & tribunalia publicavit, ac ne in populum vulgarentur, damno ac infamiâ publicæ auctoritatis suppresisit. Quam ut integram incorruptamque præstes, Gubernator, tuâ & simul Reip. interest, ne hæc fato post tot aspera & inclementias temporum emergens, primum fortunæ suæ obstaculum contemptum imperij sentiat. Igitur mandatum interpones nostris consilijs, quo legum & libertatis nostræ oppressores possessione & usu durioris imperij submoveamus faciamusque, quæ corrigendo rerum per provinciam ordini & Senatus Regij dominationibus expedient.
units.tr: We, the Governor, have resolved to place the royal Senate under guard, and our reasons move us. For, besides the fact that its authority is foreign to our liberty, we have found that this same Senate has given more weight to the counsels of the Austrian than to our commands. From the letters intercepted to this same Austrian, which we exhibit, the proof of our integrity will be made clear, and that they are nourishing in their bosom men who are hostile to our affairs and to the public safety. Thus the royal Senate, after Roblesius was taken, and lest he should carry out the wicked plan he had devised in advance, had him put in chains by his cohorts, and thought about freeing him, and to obtain this it interceded with the Austrian. Moreover, it summoned the magistracy of the city of Leeuwarden into the basilica and into its own assembly, and advised it to prepare the city to defend itself against the Orders, and, since affairs beyond the Lauwers were going badly after the capture of Roblesius, to provide for the royal party within the walls of its own city. The Austrian sent a reply to the same Senate giving thanks for this, and that the Senate had persisted in loyalty to Philip and in care for maintaining the royal dominion. Plainly, as if our most sacred anxieties for restoring liberty were at odds with the king's rule, and as if there were in this province something that delayed Philip's advantage, which depended on our fortune and prosperity. Afterwards, in the changing of magistrates throughout the province, those whom the long possession of domination had made burdensome and odious to our liberty, the Senate set itself against our decrees, so that it would not yield, with fathers appointed in their place, the power so long usurped and, as it were, eternal. Therefore, under the appearance of an ancient election and of a right sought for, it arranged matters in the towns, so that by keeping the fidelity of the cities, it might hold the stronger support of power throughout the provinces, and protect the same garrisons for the use of the enemies. And it appointed two German cohorts, and distributed them through the provinces' fortifications, for no other purpose than that nothing might be changed in the fields or the districts by decree of the Orders and at the same time by your decree, Governor, and that it might not lose the strongholds of power by neglecting those same fortifications. That Renicus Dekama, tribune of a cohort, who had professed for so many years of service the opposite party, having received a public pledge, did not conceal this before Lalaing in the assembly of the fathers, lest the wicked counsels of the Senate, devised for the destruction of the country, should grow strong through delay or in secret. Finally, it did not even publish the edicts of the Orders and yours, Governor, through the basilica and the tribunals, and to keep them from spreading among the people, it suppressed them to the loss and disgrace of public authority. That you may keep it whole and uncorrupted, Governor, it is in your interest and at the same time in the interest of the commonwealth that this, rising up after so many harsh and cruel times, should not, as the first obstacle to its fortune, feel the contempt of authority. Therefore, interpose your command in our counsels, by which we may remove from possession and practice of a harsher rule the oppressors of our laws and liberty, and do what the restoration of order throughout the province requires, and what the domination of the royal Senate shall bring to completion.

units.la: Mox Lalainius è Senatu regio Focconem Rommartium, Antonium Lavailium & Dimerum Senatores, cum Arnoldo Gemenio & Siccone Suffridæo duci captivos in arcem regiam jusit, aliosque Senatorij ordinis & in ijs Igramum Achlenium Præsidem, Adrianum Vastartium, Petrum Frittema & Carolum Nicolaium privatis domesticisque custodijs attineri curavit. Post Rommartium & Dimerum Senatores, publico carcere dimissos, clementiore custodiâ haberi præcepit, Juliumque Dekema & Vibrandum Ayta citari in Senatum jussit. Sed forum discriminis plenum & istiusmodi rerum conversionibus modum sæpè egressa æquitas, subterfugia judiciorum suadebant. Quippe mota plebes, novi urbis Magistratus regijs dominantibus infensi, quod Philippus Austriaci fratris malis artibus & nefariæ defectioni, præter spem Ordinum publico Edicto patrocinaretur.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Lalainius, from the royal Senate, had the senators Focco Rommartius, Antonius Lavailius and Dimerus, together with Arnoldus Gemenius and Sicco Suffridus, taken captive and sent to the royal citadel. He also saw to it that others of the senatorial order, among them Igramus Achlenius, the president, Adrianus Vastartius, Petrus Frittema and Carolus Nicolaius, were kept under private house arrest. After the senators Rommartius and Dimerus were released from the public prison, he ordered them held under milder custody, and he ordered Julius Dekema and Vibrandus Ayta summoned to the Senate. But the forum, full of danger, and a sense of fairness that often went beyond measure in such upheavals, suggested ways of evading the courts. For the common people, stirred up and hostile to the new city magistrates who sided with the royal party, were angered because Philip, by a public edict and contrary to the hopes of the Estates, was defending the wicked arts and unnatural revolt of his brother Austria.

units.la: Edictum Philippi Regis tale erat.
units.tr: The edict of King Philip was as follows.

units.la: QVANQVAM missô in provincias Belgicæ Joanne Austriaco fratre meo in id maxumè incubui, ut civiles discordias certa pace componerem ac Romanæ Religioni cultum, mihi (quos antiquis moribus & paterno ritu regere animus erat) subdito-rum rum obsequium asserrem, ita deprehendo multos ex subditis meis, suae legis ac officij oblitos, fovendis turbis se dare, quo gravius bellum meis in ditionibus exardescat. Et quoniam subditorum meorum salus, mea autoritas mihi curae est, ut jure Principis imperem, ita fratri meo Joanni Austriaco justum obsequium conferri volo. Secus facientes perduellium loco habiturus sum. Quamobrem Ordinum coetus Bruxellis, non meo assensu, sed privatis consiliis institutos, ut illicitos habeo voloque ut conventus iste solvatur ocyus, ac ut suas in provincias quisque remigrent, dum ego regia potestate legitimum confessum ordinavero. Itaque illorum acta hoc ipso rescindo statuoque, ut, quae singulis in provinciis non meo rescripto decreta sint eadem lege antiquentur. Quare Tributa ab ipsis imperata praestari nolo populumque, sacramentis Ordinum exsolvo. Quin ei jus ac potestatem facio sua defensione adversum oppressores utendi provocandique ad subsidia quae amovendis oneribus ac servitiis facient. Adhaec imperia, dignitates universis singulisque abrogo, ijs praesertim, quos a fratre meo secessio incapaces munerum ac meorum beneficiorum fecit. Quapropter volo, ne quid pensionum ex meo aut publico aerario habeant et ut publicarum rationum fides me aut fratre cognoscente probetur. Hoc quoque Edictum meas per ditiones ac tribunalia recitetur typisque vulgatum in omnem provinciam et memoriam temporum exeat.
units.tr: Although I sent my brother John of Austria into the provinces of Belgium and devoted myself most earnestly to this end, that I might settle the civil discords by a sure peace and secure for myself the obedience of my subjects in the Roman religion, which I intended to rule in the old customs and paternal manner, I nonetheless find that many of my subjects, forgetful of their law and duty, give themselves to fomenting disturbances, so that the war may blaze more fiercely in my dominions. Since the welfare of my subjects and my authority are my concern, I wish to rule by the right of a prince, and I wish my brother John of Austria to be given due obedience. Those who act otherwise I shall hold as enemies of the realm. Therefore I declare that the assemblies of the Estates at Brussels, set up without my assent and by private counsels, are illicit, and I will and command that this gathering be dissolved at once, and that each man return to his own province until I have summoned a lawful assembly by royal authority. Accordingly I hereby rescind their acts and decree that whatever has been decided in each province without my written decree shall be annulled by the same law. Hence I do not wish the taxes imposed by them to be paid, and I release the people from their oaths to the Estates. Indeed I give them the right and power to defend themselves against oppressors and to appeal for aid to those who will remove burdens and servitudes. Furthermore I revoke all offices and dignities from everyone, singly and together, especially from those whom the secession from my brother has made incapable of offices and of my favours. Therefore I wish that they have no pensions from my treasury or the public treasury, and that the reliability of the public accounts be examined by me or my brother. Let this edict also be read through my dominions and in the law courts, be published in print throughout every province, and be remembered for all time.

units.la: Quo Edicto, ut publicum provinciarum jus haud dubie convellebatur, ita maxime regis & civiles discordiae fomentum accipiebant. Quare diu infidae res & falsis affectibus contectae in deterius apertiusque odium ac bellum tum erupere, quod in id etiam temporis ardescente crinito sydere, (etsi deficiente sensum flammae pabulo) instantium motuum certissimo praesagio signabatur.
units.tr: By this edict the public law of the provinces was undoubtedly overthrown, and in this way the seeds of royal and civil discord were given a further spur. Therefore affairs that had long been treacherous and covered over with false feelings now burst forth into open hatred and war, worse than before; and at that time the comet blazing in the sky, though lacking fuel for its flame, was a most certain omen of the coming disturbances.

units.la: Igitur in Joannem Austrium publicum libertatis hostem multa atrocia jaciebantur, quod humanae societati injurius speciosis pacis illecebris praeconceptum bellum velasset. His addebatur immoderatior victoriae apud Gemblacum usus & quod infoelices ac ex pugna saucios per acerbas mortes velut lentis supplicijs necasset. Sic scilicet per Granatam, sic alibi militiam egisse neque aliud sperari posse, quam ut Caroli Principis & nepotis parricidio coopertus (id enim Historiae tradunt) animum peioribus furoribus satiet, modo annos impleat cumulandis sceleribus validos.
units.tr: Accordingly many atrocious charges were hurled against John of Austria as a public enemy of liberty: that he had veiled, with specious enticements of peace, a war planned in advance that was hostile to human society. To these was added his excessively harsh use of victory at Gembloux, and that he had put to death, by cruel deaths as though by slow tortures, the unfortunate men wounded in the battle. Thus, it was said, he had conducted his warfare in Granada and elsewhere, and nothing else could be hoped for than that, cloaked in the murder of Prince Carlos, his own nephew (for the histories hand this down), he should sate his mind with still worse furies, provided he lived long enough to heap up crimes in abundance.

units.la: Unde Lalainius ferventius Austriaco addictos, arctioribus custodijs sepsit Cunerumque Episcopum, imperijs Frisiae Ordinum contumacem & superstitionibus populum trahentem Harlinganae arci captivum induxit. Creditum fuit immodestos Episcopi mores & per sacrorum cultus luxu ac commessationibus foedatos, parum gratiae, multum odij serium apud populum ei conciliasse & quod conquirendo aeri sordidus & simul asper sacrij aerarij opes prodigentia & molliore vita disiparet. Ego existumo coenobiorum Praesules in partem Reip. tum adscitos, fundatione Sedis & Episcopali autoritate offensos, exitium ei paravisse, quo Pontificum & Albani sanctionibus quas Gandavensis conventio aboleverat, coenobitarum censui detracta ac Sedi decreta, ijsdem coenobijs intercessione Praesulum redderentur. Indignantibus adhoc quibusque, ultimas mortuorum voluntates & scripta pijs usibus aut nuncupacupata testamenta non adimpleri detractaque hæredibus patrimonia, luxu & paratu Episcopalis magnificentiæ insumi. Romanorum quoq; Pontificum & ipsius Philippi in constituendâ Sede institutum, destinato fine excidere coërcendisq; populi ingenijs & simul opinionibus repertum pessimo magistri exemplo per ludibria & contumeliam fœdari.
units.tr: Hence Lalainius, more ardently, shut up those devoted to Austria in closer custody, and brought in as a captive to the citadel of Harlingen Bishop Cuneras, who was contumacious towards the commands of the Frisian Estates and drew the people into superstitions. It was believed that the bishop's immoderate manners, and his conduct of worship defiled by luxury and carousing, had won him little favour and much bitter hatred among the people; and that, being sordid in seeking money and at the same time harsh, he squandered the wealth of the sacred treasury by extravagance and a softer way of life. I judge that the abbots of the monasteries, who had then been brought into a share of the government and were offended by the founding of the See and by the episcopal authority, had prepared his ruin, so that, by the sanctions of the Pontiffs and of Alba, which the Ghent agreement had abolished, the tithes taken from the monks and assigned to the See would be restored to those same monasteries through the intercession of the prelates. Moreover, indignation was felt by everyone that the last wishes of the dead and their writings and testaments made for pious uses were not carried out, and that inheritances were taken from heirs and consumed by the luxury and expense of episcopal magnificence. Also, the institution of the See, devised by the Roman Pontiffs and by Philip himself, had fallen from its intended purpose, had been found to restrain the minds of the people and at the same time their opinions, and was disgraced by ridicule and insult through the worst example of its teacher.

units.la: Tradunt cum Gasparo Roblesio sæpius commessantem, mox vino, cujus appetens erat, madidum, in saltationes & impudicos corporis gestus effusum cantuque & tripudij ad probra & satietatem usum ordinis sui reverentiam & simul respectum decentis vitæ posuisse. Unde contemptus & ex fastidio sensim odium, adeo alienis populi ad suspiciendam Sedis & simul Episcopi autoritatem animis, ut ex conscientiâ factorum & multitudinis voce, tanquam integerrimo judicio damnaretur. Mox Harlinganæ arcis custodiâ emissus, cœnobium in Bergumanum, quod Leovardiæ urbi in ortum milliari distat, decreto Ordinum amandatus, quo illo in loco tanquam secessu, supputandis reddendisque rationibus commodo & anteactorum memoriam & neglectam muneris sui rationem expenderet.
units.tr: They report that he often feasted and, soon drenched with the wine he craved, gave himself up to dancing and immodest bodily gestures, and that with songs, revelry and insults he cast aside both the reverence due to his order and any regard for a decent life. Hence contempt and, from disgust, gradually hatred arose, so that the minds of the people were so alienated from respecting the authority of the See and of the bishop that, from awareness of his deeds and the voice of the multitude, he was condemned as if by a most upright judgment. Soon, released from the custody of the citadel of Harlingen, he was sent by decree of the Estates to the monastery at Bergum, which lies a mile east of the city of Leeuwarden, so that in that place, as in a retreat, he might reckon up and render his accounts conveniently, and weigh up his past life and his neglected duty.

units.la: Tum, ne Gasparus Roblesius quod in ore vulgi tum erat, hostili cum exercitu in provinciam irrueret, Translavicanos tuendorum fidelium habere curam jussit Iarichumque Hottingha virum Nobilem & cohortis Tribunum explorandis curandisq; trans Lavicam rebus expedivit. Decreto quoque Frisiæ Ordinum novas cohortes conscripsit, omnemq; provinciam gliscentibus periculis, majore quam ante curâ ordinavit.
units.tr: Then, lest Gaspar Robles, as was then the common talk, should rush into the province with a hostile army, he ordered the Trans-Lavicani to take care of protecting the loyal, and he dispatched Iarichus Hottingha, a noble man and tribune of a cohort, to scout out and manage affairs across the Lauwers. By decree of the Frisian Estates he also enrolled new cohorts and arranged the whole province with greater care than before, as the dangers grew.

units.la: Mox v. Kal. April (qui dies Episcopo funestus fuit) flante Coro horrenda tempestas Frisiæ terris incubuit mareque procellâ concitum in litus se adigens Frisiam omnem, qua Flevo flumine, Pasenio & Reiderio amnibus alluitur, effusis in plana contexit. Itaque Dongria, vili per turbas aggerum curâ, undis obruta cultique circa arcturum agri eruta per eluviem semina infœlicibus colonis reddidere. Inde frugum mox egestas & ingravescens annona invalidam tributis provinciam fecit. Stauricus scriptor addit, homines alibi cum jumentis vi fluctuum abreptos, nec Dongrios solos aut littorum accolas, cæterum depressos fertilesque provinciæ agros marinis undis subfuisse.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April (a day fatal to the bishop), a dreadful storm, with the north-west wind Corus blowing, fell upon the lands of Friesland. The sea, stirred by the gale and driving itself onto the shore, covered all of Friesland that is washed by the rivers Vlie, Paesens and Reider, pouring over the plains. Thus Dongen, worn down by the labour of the common people in raising dykes, was overwhelmed by the waves, and the fields cultivated near the Arctic were stripped by the flood, and the seed was lost to the unhappy farmers. Then came a shortage of grain, and the growing scarcity made the province, already weakened, unable to pay its taxes. The writer Stauricus adds that men elsewhere, together with their beasts, were swept away by the force of the waves; and that not only the people of Dongen or the dwellers on the coast were affected, but that the sunken and fertile fields of the province lay under the sea's waves.

units.la: Tum Anna Austriaca Philippo Regi avunculo cognominem filium Ænixa, susceptore regij infantis Wenceslao Reginæ fratre, qui haud multo post tempore extinctus imperatoriam Maximiliani domum augustæ sobolis fœcundam, immaturâ morte funestavit.
units.tr: Then Anna of Austria bore a son named after King Philip her uncle; the godfather of the royal infant was Wenceslas, the queen's brother. He died not long afterwards, and by his untimely death he brought mourning to the imperial house of Maximilian, which was fruitful in illustrious offspring.

units.la: Cæterum isti Annæ Austriacæ partui, ut antè ANNO CIↄ. Iↄ. LXXIII. decretas per Frisiam supplicationes non reperio, alienatis haud dubiè à regio sanguine animis, quem sicut cætera malorum, à naturâ edi transferendis in posteros superbis dominationibus tacitâ fati incusatione interpretabantur. Ita scilicet Carolum Cæsarem titulo Gubernatoris, cessione Saxonicâ per Frisiam receptum, primis annis lenius, post adultâ potestate acrius imperium exercuisse, velut ita fato compositum esset, ut Philippum filium, etsi naturæ vitia primâ imperij & simul vitæ ætate obtegentem, exercendo deterrimo principatui relinqueret. Raro certè dominationes suas in melius Principes mutasse, ne sic quidem formatis syderum temporumque revolutionibus, ut benignius nignius polliceantur. Desperandum potius esse de bono Philippi successore, quem haud dubie ambitio regiis ingenijs connata & repressi sub patre imperij tædium vindicandis injurijs impulsurum sit. Quod in Philippo III. de cujus nativitate nunc loquor, adimpletum fuisse, paternis consilijs & actionibus non dispar ingenium turbatissimorumq; temporum tristissimæ imagines ostendere. Adeo veterem regiæ domus affectum incivilis Philippi II. dominatio perverterat.
units.tr: Yet I do not find that prayers of thanksgiving were ordered throughout Friesland for the birth of this Anna of Austria, as had been done before in 1573. The people were undoubtedly alienated in mind from the royal blood, which they interpreted, as they did other evils, as born of nature and as a silent accusation of fate, one that carries proud dominions over to posterity. Thus, they said, Charles the Emperor, received in Friesland under the title of Governor by the cession of Saxony, ruled more gently in the first years, but afterwards, once his power had matured, exercised his rule more harshly, as though it had been so ordained by fate that he should leave his son Philip, who was hiding the vices of his nature in the first years of his rule and at the same time his life, to govern a most wretched principate. Surely dominions have seldom changed their princes for the better, not even when the courses of the stars and the revolutions of the times were so arranged that they promised a kinder rule. Rather, one should despair of a good successor to Philip, whom ambition, innate in royal natures, and a weariness of the power held down under his father, would certainly drive to avenge their wrongs. That this came to pass in Philip III, of whose birth I now speak, the spirit that was not unlike his father's counsels and actions, and the most sorrowful pictures of most troubled times, show. So thoroughly had the tyranny of the uncivil Philip II perverted the old affection of the royal house.

units.la: Igitur Ordines, redintegratis fœderum actis, multa in populum stabiliendæ ex intervallis temporum libertati vulgabant, tanto laxioribus religionum edictis, quanto acrius immodestiusque Carolus Philippusque reges à triginta annis damno regiæ & simul popularis fortunæ extruserant. Iis cautum fuit.
units.tr: The Estates therefore, having renewed the acts of the covenants, from time to time published many measures for establishing the people's liberty, with edicts on religion all the milder because Charles and Philip had for thirty years pressed harder and more arrogantly, to the loss of both royal and popular fortune. They provided for the following.

units.la: Ut Gandavense reliquaque posteriora fœdera sacrosancta essent damnatoque omni cum hostibus commercio, seditiosæ concliones, verba atque dicteria turbandæ paci publicæ cessarent. MATTHIAE quoque AUSTRIO & AURANTIO Principi autoritas ac veneratio constaret populusque tuendis fœderum actis jusjurandum diceret.
units.tr: That the Ghent Pacification and the later covenants should be held sacrosanct, and that all dealings with the enemy should be condemned; that seditious sermons, words and insults that disturb the public peace should cease. Also that authority and respect should attach to Matthias, Archduke of Austria, and to the Prince of Orange, and that the people should swear an oath to defend the acts of the covenants.

units.la: Igitur regressio in Hispaniam Joanne Norcarmio Philippi ad Belgas Legato omnique pacis ac inducarum spe irritâ, de gerendo bello cogitatum, quod Gemblacensi clade affectum, fortioribus nervis trahendum, sanando cladis vulneri & pellendo finibus Austriaco Princeps Aurantius suadebat. Itaque decreto Ordinum certæ stipendiorum rationes, initæ castrorumque impendia menstruo ære sublevata. Petita quoque ex pactione fœderis Anglorum auxilia & postquam regnum delectibus exhauriri Elisabetha detrectabat, subsidijs Anglicis copiæ per Germaniam conscriptæ, quas Casimirus Elector in provincias ducturus pactione fœderis ferebatur.
units.tr: Therefore, Philip having returned to Spain and left John Norcarmius as his legate to the Belgians, and every hope of peace and truces having come to nothing, war was considered. Weakened by the defeat at Gembloux, it had to be pursued with stronger sinews. The Prince of Orange urged that the wound of that defeat be healed and the Austrians driven from the borders. Accordingly, by decree of the Estates, fixed rates of pay were settled, and the expenses of the camps were eased by monthly payments. English auxiliaries were also sought under the treaty of the covenant, and since Elizabeth, having her kingdom drained by levies, refused them, troops raised through Germany were to be paid with English subsidies. Elector Casimir was said, by the treaty, to be about to lead these into the provinces.

units.la: Reidanus tradit Elisabetham vix scripto cum Ordinibus fœdere, de mittendis in Belgicam Anglorum copijs consilium mutasse missoque ad Ordines Daniele Rogersio Legato, Galliæ regis offensas mutato consilio obtendisse. Quippe Henricum regem in magno belli apparatu versari afferebat, laturum haud dubie ægrius, Anglicæ gentis exercitum classi commissum in Belgicæ provincias trajicere. Ita forte de præjuvandis Philippi, aut faciendis sibi in Belgicâ partibus deliberaturum, à quibus etsi vacuum & intactum cupidine Belgicæ dominationis animum ipsa haberet, tamen difficulter facturam ut suspicione Gallum liberet, aliena consilia suo ut solet ingenio æstumantem. Igitur satius esse Joannem Casimirum Palatinum cum quinque equitum, sex Helvetiorum peditum millibus suo ære in Belgicam evocari, quam Anglicis auxilijs inritare Henricum regem nutriendis in se æmulationibus pronum. Quod Reginæ consilium etsi Ordines & præcipue Pontificiæ factionis percelleret, indignantes Protestantium & reformatæ religionis Principem tantis copijs instructum impulsis Belgicæ rebus offerri, ita ex necessitate temporum conventum fuit, ut quinta peditum millia, quaterna equitum Casimirus reginæ nomine in auxilia duceret, hac tamen lege, ut erogandi in copias etiam Anglici æris potestatem Ordinibus regina concederet. Cujus juris prærogativâ ac possessione, ne exui quiquidem etiam angustis rebus volebant, qui meminerant id Philippi per Italiam bello assertum, causam ac initia primis dissensionibus dedisse. Unde novae quoque Vectigalium leges in secreto Patrum scriptae, quo tributa magnitudinem potentis regni aequatura populi opibus, etsi privato onere, collato in publicum aere traherentur.
units.tr: Reidanus reports that Elizabeth, scarcely after her written agreement with the Estates on sending English troops into Belgium, changed her plan. Having sent Daniel Rogers as envoy to the Estates, she pleaded the offences of the French king as her reason. For she said that King Henry was busy with a great war preparation and would no doubt take it very badly if an English army, entrusted to the fleet, were carried over into the Belgian provinces. So perhaps she would deliberate about helping Philip, or about taking a side in Belgium. Although her own mind was free of the desire for dominion in Belgium and untouched by it, she would find it hard to free the Frenchman from suspicion, since he judges the plans of others by his own nature. It was therefore better that John Casimir the Palatine be summoned into Belgium at his own expense with five thousand horse and six thousand Swiss foot, than to provoke King Henry with English aid, being prone to nourish rivalries against himself. Although this plan of the queen displeased the Estates, and especially the Papists, who were indignant that the prince of the Protestants and of the reformed religion, equipped with such forces, would be brought into Belgian affairs, yet the necessity of the times was such that it was agreed that Casimir should lead five thousand foot and four thousand horse as auxiliaries in the queen's name. This was on the condition that the queen would grant the Estates the power to spend English money on the troops as well. Of this right and possession they did not want to be stripped even in straitened circumstances. They remembered that Philip's claim to it in the war in Italy had given the cause and the beginnings of the first dissensions. Hence new tax laws were also written in secret by the Fathers, so that taxes, which would make the people's resources equal to the power of a mighty kingdom, might be drawn into the public treasury, though by a private burden.

units.la: Quare curandis Frisiae rebus, (Ne quid detrimenti patrijs legibus illa sanctione inferretur) Hesselus Aysma vir eruditus, & magnae auctoritatis ad concessum Ordinum generalium missus, relicto domi socio legationis Renico Cammingha, quem suffragijs comitij ei subjunctum provinciae res attinebant. Iis in mandatis datum erat, Gandavense Foedus sartum tectum praestandi cavendique, ut omne Frisici, populi jus impollutum inviolatumque autoritate ejusdem foederis staret. Ipsis quoque Legatis jus considendi inter patres foret petendique novas Frisijs immunitates, quo praesidijs legionum, ac continuis inundationibus exhausta gens, per levamenta onerum, veterem ad opulentiam & fortunam rediret. Hoc etiam additum. Ut de actis rescriptisque Ordinum ad provinciam referrent. Annotatum invenio Legatum Aysma Antverpiam iturum reciproca pactione & speciali scriptura provinciae se obligasse, per reverentiam haud dubie & securitatem Reip. ne magnarum rerum negotia per incuriam Legati negligerentur, & ut certis terminis coercita potestas lubricis temporibus, grassante ubivis per malas artes Austriaco, invidiem aemulantium elevaret. Caeterum novis per Germaniam delectibus & per stipendia tot legionum tenue Ordinum aerarium lenius Frisicae gentis tributum non ferebant.
units.tr: Therefore, for managing Frisian affairs (lest anything be taken from their native laws by that sanction), Hessel Aysma, a learned man of great authority, was sent to the council of the Estates General. He left at home as his fellow legate Renicus Camminga, who had been assigned to him by the vote of the assembly to attend to provincial business. His instructions were to ensure and guard the Ghent Pacification intact, so that all the rights of the Frisian people stayed unpolluted and inviolate under the authority of that same covenant. The legates themselves were to have the right to sit among the Fathers and to seek new immunities for Friesland, so that the people, exhausted by garrisons of legions and continual floods, might by relief from burdens return to their old prosperity and fortune. This was also added: that they should report the acts and rescripts of the Estates back to the province. I find it noted that the legate Aysma, going to Antwerp, bound himself to the province by a reciprocal agreement and a special written pledge, out of reverence and for the security of the commonwealth. This was so that the business of great matters would not be neglected through the legate's carelessness, and so that a power restrained by fixed limits might lift up the envy of rivals in these slippery times, while the Austrian everywhere spread his influence by evil arts. Moreover, the thin treasury of the Estates, burdened by new levies across Germany and the pay of so many legions, could not bear the gentler tribute of the Frisian people.

units.la: Quare & Ordinum generalium litteris, xviii. April. Bruxellis datis, Frisij copias per Sylvestria & Drentiam sparsas retinere in stipendijs jussi, ne in Brabantiam & superiores provincias traductis accessione novarum cohortium languescens aerarium extenuaretur.
units.tr: Therefore, by letters of the Estates General dated Brussels, 18 April, the Frisian troops scattered through Sylvestria and Drenthe were ordered to be kept on pay. This was lest, if they were moved into Brabant and the higher provinces, the already weakened treasury be further worn down by the addition of new cohorts.

units.la: Lalainius econtra evocari in Brabantiam copias petebat, valido ad praesidia populo & gentis censu onerosis stipendijs impari. Non esse eam belli per Frisiam molem ut tot copijs egeat, quas exsolvi sacramentis, & Reip. & militantium interfit. Quippe novem annorum stipendia meritos missionem orare, quo patriam & antiquas sedes revisant, avidos quietis aut ut respiratione ad tempus data, ad priora sacramenta magis vegeti redeant. Nunc parentum amicorumque desiderijs trahi totque incommoda & simul pericula perpessus toleratis molestijs solatia quaerere. Igitur rogare Ordines ut easdem copias in Brabantiam evocent, aut inquietudinis bellicae pertaesis honestam missionem largiantur.
units.tr: Lalaing, on the other hand, asked that the troops be summoned into Brabant, since the people were strong enough for garrisons, while the burdensome pay drawn from the nation's wealth was not equal to it. The war in Friesland was not of such magnitude as to need so many troops, whom the oath must release, since it concerns both the commonwealth and the soldiers. For soldiers who had earned nine years' pay beg for discharge, so that they may revisit their country and their ancient homes, eager for rest; or, having been given a breathing space, return more vigorous to their former oaths. Now, drawn by the longing of parents and friends, they seek solace after so many hardships and dangers endured. Therefore Lalaing asked the Estates either to summon the same troops into Brabant, or to grant an honourable discharge to those weary of the unrest of war.

units.la: Haec à Lalainio xxi. April. Leovardiae scripta, ac per Franciscum Pipenpoium Lalainij Legatum Bruxellas perlata. Notat F. Nicolaus Magistratum Stauriae urbis, Fredericum Campensem Presbyterum in arce regia custodiae tum dedisse, exutumque sacerdotio, Hemelumanum in Coenobium, urbi vicinum relegasse.
units.tr: Lalaing wrote this at Leeuwarden on 21 April, and it was carried to Brussels by Francis Pipenpoy, Lalaing's legate. Father Nicolaus notes that the magistracy of the city of Stavoren then placed Frederic of Campen, a priest, in custody in the royal citadel, and, stripping him of the priesthood, banished Hemelumanus to a monastery near the city.

units.la: Litterae quoque ad Gubernatorem Matthiam à Deputatis Ordinum datae, quibus singularem Matthiae, in mutandis Magistratibus, erga Frisios affectum & reprimendis Austriaci partibus commendabant.
units.tr: Letters were also sent to Governor Matthias by the deputies of the Estates, commending his singular goodwill toward the Frisians in changing the magistrates and in curbing the party of Austria.

units.la: Tutiore scilicet impositorum loco res provinciae fore, seque daturos operam, ne ex
units.tr: Namely, that the affairs of the province would stand in a safer position for those placed in office, and that they would take care that

units.la: ex Frisiorum trans Rhenum terris Belgicæ res quid periculi sentiant, ceterum sociorum securitas ex securitate Frisicæ gentis habeatur. Quippe Lalainium Transisulanis & quæ Vidro aut Isalâ amnibus perluuntur, dittombus cum imperio præfectum, facturum haud dubiè, ut omnis Drentia, redactis in potestatem castellis atque munitionibus fœderatis gentibus societur. Hoc tantum necessarium esse ut quoniam L A L A I N I U S curandis rebus iter in Transisulaniæ confinia intendisset, copias atque auxilia & cum ijs ex ærario provinciarum stipendia haberet, magna in bello momenta & sine quibus nec retineri in bono ordine fortuna fœderis, nec prolatari queat. Domesticis quippe adhuc insidijs tenerrima Reip. initia exponi & esse conjuratos, qui scelera, qui seditiones, qui incendia & latrocinia moliantur. Id ex litteris apud Antonium Lavailium, regium nuper Senatorem repertis, abundè detectum exutisque imperio non voluntatem nocendi, sed vires deesse. Postremo spectari etiamnum intra urbium consepta, arces & castella, externi & indecentis imperij munimenta, popularibus servitijs extructa & ut adversum dominantium metus valerent. Quærenda esse alia civitatum & populi præsidia, externo opere ex arte circumducto & Vectigalium ratione habendis præsidijs & simul stipendijs institutâ. Hanc quoque ipsam approbaturos se fore, si viderint, id socijs provincijs, id patribus & populo placuisse.
units.tr: from the lands of the Frisians beyond the Rhine, the affairs of Belgium should feel any danger; the safety of the allies is to be held as the safety of the Frisian people. For Lalaing, placed in command over the districts of Overijssel and those watered by the Vecht or the IJssel, would certainly bring it about that all Drenthe, with its castles and fortifications brought under control, would be joined to the confederate peoples. This only is necessary: since Lalaing has directed his journey to the borders of Overijssel to attend to affairs, he should have troops and auxiliaries, and with them pay from the provincial treasuries, which are great factors in war and without which the fortune of the covenant can neither be kept in good order nor advanced. For among domestic plots the very tender beginnings of the commonwealth are exposed, and there are conspirators who plan crimes, seditions, arson and robberies. This has been fully revealed by letters found with Antonius Lavailius, lately a royal senator, and stripped of power he lacked not the will to do harm, but the strength. Lastly, there are still to be seen within the enclosures of cities, the citadels and castles, the fortifications of an external and unseemly rule, built by popular servitude so that they might be effective against the fears of masters. Other safeguards of cities and people are to be sought, with external works laid out by art, and with a system of taxation set up to maintain garrisons and pay at the same time. They would themselves approve this too, if they saw that it had pleased the allied provinces, the Fathers and the people.

units.la: Hæc Leovardiæ vergente Aprili scripta, ac à Docone Martena, Goslico Hiddama, & Barthio Idzaerda signata.
units.tr: This was written at Leeuwarden toward the end of April, and signed by Doco Martena, Goslick Hiddama and Bartius Idzaerda.

units.la: Mox Deputatorum Frisiæ curâ (quod jam antè à Senatu regio factum erat) conventus Ordinum Leovardiæ Kal. Maijs indictus. Ibi de constituendo novo per Frisiam Senatu consultatum, cavente per literas Matthiâ Gubernatore, ne dicundi juris officia per provinciam vacarent.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, through the care of the deputies of Friesland (as had already been done earlier by the royal Senate), an assembly of the Estates was called at Leeuwarden for 1 May. There the setting up of a new Senate for Friesland was discussed, Governor Matthias warning by letter that the offices of administering justice should not lapse throughout the province.

units.la: Quippe licentiam justitio crescere, immodestis adhuc eorum actionibus, qui veteris fortunæ recordatione, nova consilia recuperandis honoribus fabricarent. Posse hoc modo dissociatâ Regis & populi fide, facilem olim nutriendis factionibus gentem divelli ac in sueta majoribus prolabi, nisi majestate legum at reverentiâ judicij coërceatur. Sic Saxonem, fundato Cæsarum jure & instituto Senatu, inveteratas factiones, CAROLUM AUSTRIUM bella & inimicitias partium sopijsse. Nec aliam ferè hodiè temporum legem esse. Divulsos proceres, discordem populum & acerbis odijs innutritum iturum in violentias, nisi lege refrenetur. Adhæc lites fori indefinitas esse belloq; aut per vim bonis exutos, jure fœderum restitutiones in integrum & officia judicum implorare. Publicæ pacis tranquillitatisque præsidia hoc ipso consilio habenda, cavendumque, ut summum tribunal per Principem primitus erectum, integro adhuc ejus imperio non evilescat.
units.tr: For license grows out of the injustice, through the still unrestrained actions of those who, recalling their former fortune, were devising new plans to recover their honours. In this way, with the loyalty of king and people sundered, a people once easily nourished in factions might be torn apart and slide back into the customs of its elders, unless it is restrained by the majesty of the laws and the respect due to judgment. Thus Saxon, with the right of the Caesars established and a Senate instituted, put to rest long-standing factions, and Charles of Austria put an end to wars and the enmities of parties. Nor is there almost any other law for the present times. Nobles divided and a people discordant and fed with bitter hatreds will go over into violence unless it is restrained by law. Moreover, lawsuits in the courts are undecided, and those stripped of their goods by war or force seek restitution to their former state by the right of the covenants, and the help of judges. The safeguards of public peace and tranquillity are to be held by this very plan, and care must be taken that the supreme tribunal, first erected by the Prince, does not grow out of measure while its authority is still whole.

units.la: Cæterum Oostergoi instituendam hac de re ad suos relationem censuerunt, sponsione factâ octiduum intra decretum se facturos. Westergoi vero & Sylvestres, ut parati erant suffragia interponere, ita provinciæ Deputatis nuncupandi Senatus potestatem fecere, sed hac cautione, ut suo corpore bini ijsdem Deputatis jungerentur votisque concordibus, indigenis & legum peritis Senatoria dignitas committeretur. Hæc ab Hesselo Eminga, Oedzio Arnoldo pro Oostergois, OedJulio Botnia & Jelgero Feitsma pro Westergois, Gellio Hepkenio & Si-brando Idzio pro Sylvestribus signata.
units.tr: The Oostergoi, however, decided that a report on this matter should be taken back to their constituents, and promised to give their answer within eight days of the decree. The Westergoi and the Sylvestres, though ready to cast their votes, granted the provincial deputies the power to nominate members of the Senate, but on this condition: that two of the same deputies should join the Senate as members, and that by their unanimous votes the Senatorial dignity should be given to natives skilled in law. These terms were signed by Hessel Eminga and Oedzius Arnoldus for the Oostergoi, Oedjulius Botnia and Jelger Feitsma for the Westergoi, and Gellius Hepkenius and Sibrandus Idzius for the Sylvestres.

units.la: Italiaque Burgundicæ domus statutum, quod peregrinos æquali numero à Carolinis temporibus admiserat, illo decreto antiquatum, reputantibus peritioribus legem à Carolo Cæsare stabiliendæ fori innocentiæ latam depravandis judiciis & post violentis dominationibus cessisse. Ab eo scilicet fuisse, ut assentatione & in Principem servitio, sædis probrosisque rescriptis conscientiam consensus polluerit querimoniisque clientum ac ipsorum etiam ORDINUM præfractum tribunal clauderetur. Non necessum esse exempla temporum repetere & jam fato ostendi, ut antè nimiam Senatus potentiam, ita maximè infidam fuisse. Neque egere externis arbitris judicium quod citra hoc incorruptum esse queat & æquitati subnixum. Conscientiâ judicum stare fori casus & litium eventus, nec eam solam Burgundici statuti vim esse, ut inquilini fidem suspectet. Quæsisse scilicet CAROLUM, ut adulteratis provinciarum consessibus, consuetudines quoque & jura miscerentur Frisiosque communio juris, Burgundiæ moribus externæque & jam ante, sub MARIA Gubernatrice, damnatæ societati inneteret.
units.tr: The experts, however, judged that the statute of the Burgundian house, which since the time of the Carolines had admitted foreigners in equal number, was abolished by that decree. They held that the law laid down by Emperor Charles for establishing the integrity of the courts had given way to the corruption of judgments and to the violent domination that followed. Charles, they said, had so arranged matters that, through flattery and servility to the Prince, with shameful and disgraceful rescripts, the conscience of the council was defiled, and the stubborn tribunal was closed to the complaints of clients and even of the Estates themselves. It was unnecessary, they said, to recall past examples, since it had already been shown by experience that the Senate had been most untrustworthy just as it had been overbearing. Nor did a court that could not be incorrupt without outside arbiters need them, for it ought to rest on equity. The outcome of cases and lawsuits depended on the conscience of the judges, and the force of the Burgundian statute was not the only reason for the tenant's distrust. Charles, clearly, had sought, by mixing up the assemblies of the provinces, to mix their customs and laws as well, and to bind the Frisians to a common law, to Burgundian ways and to that foreign society already condemned under Governor Mary.

units.la: Igitur per Delegatos Comitij Julium Botniam, Orichium Doiemum, Feiconem Tatmannum & Hyeronimum Winterium Deputatis provinciæ justum Senatorij Ordinis numerum supplendi potestas facta, si fortè litium ferax provincia plurium judicantium egeret, aut honesta excusatio arduæ onerosæque dignitati obtenderetur. Hæc in acta v. & vi. Non. Maï à Wibrando Roorda, Sixto Sceltema, Jetsone Galama, Regnero Albertio & Govartio Petraeo relata. Mox Senatotes & in ijs Franciscus Eysingha, Gysbertus Aernsma, Joannes Versteveranus & Fecco Rhala nominati, quos aut celebratæ majorum imagines, aut eruditæ virtutis fama, præter scientiam legum & civilis prudentiæ commendabat.
units.tr: Accordingly, through the delegates of the Assembly, power was given to Julius Botnia, Orichius Doiemus, Feico Tatmannus and Hieronymus Winterius to fill up, for the deputies of the province, the full number of the Senatorial order, should the province, rich in lawsuits, need more judges, or should an honourable excuse be offered against so heavy and burdensome a dignity. This was recorded in the acts of 5 and 6 May, and reported by Wibrand Roorda, Sixtus Sceltema, Jetso Galama, Reginer Albertius and Govert Petraeus. Soon afterwards, senators were named, among them Franciscus Eysingha, Gysbert Aernsma, Johannes Versteveranus and Fecco Rhala, whom either the famous images of their ancestors or the reputation of learned virtue recommended, in addition to their knowledge of law and civil prudence.

units.la: Post Georgius Lalainius magnam ex ordinatâ Flevum inter & Lavicam provinciâ gloriam adeptus majorique imperio florentes juventæ annos præferens, Transisulaniæ quoque Præfecturam accepit, quæ potiunte rerum Carolo Cæsare uni cum Frisiorum gente Præfecto paruerat. Quare ut auctæ dignitatis gloriam belli pacisque artibus ornaret, de obsidendis Transisulaniæ urbibus cogitavit, quas in ripâ Ialæ fluminis sitas regia & Germanicæ legionis præsidia modicis cohortibus & effrəni insolentia tenebant. Cæterum arduis rerum cœptis copiæ & commeatus, tum pensitandis stipendijs æs desiderabatur. Igitur novarum collationum tabulæ ab Ordinibus provinciarum vulgatæ cautumque decreto ut eorum omnium, quæ usu consumerentur, certum vectigal esset mercesque provincijs exportatæ aut aliundè advectæ determinatis onerum legibus subessent. Quæ in Frisiam una cum Matthiæ Austrij Gubernatoris litteris v. Maï Antverpiâ datis perlatæ, civiles animos & cum ijs tranquillitatem provinciæ obturbavere. Quippe plebes annonam imminutoque commerciorum jure, decrementa veteris fortunæ & in his versam servitio libertatem criminabatur.
units.tr: Afterwards Georgius Lalainius, who had won great renown in the province of Ordinated Flevum and Lavica, and who, while holding a greater command in the flower of his youth, also received the Prefecture of Transisulania, which under Emperor Charles had obeyed a single prefect together with the Frisian people. Therefore, in order to adorn the glory of his increased dignity with the arts of war and peace, he considered besieging the towns of Transisulania, which lie on the bank of the river Ijssel and were held by royal and German garrisons, with small cohorts and unbridled insolence. But for these difficult undertakings, troops and supplies were needed, and money also to pay the soldiers. Therefore tables of new taxes were published by the Orders of the provinces, and it was decreed that a fixed levy should be imposed on all things consumed by use, and that merchandise exported from the provinces or imported from elsewhere should be subject to set laws of duty. These measures were carried into Friesland, together with letters of Governor Matthias Archduke, dated 5 May at Antwerp, and they disturbed the civil spirit and with it the peace of the province. The common people complained that the grain supply was being reduced and the right of trade curtailed, that the decline of their old prosperity was being imposed, and that liberty was being turned into servitude.

units.la: Ideone scilicet decimas vigesimasque ab ALBANO, prapediendis commerciis & redigenda ad egestatem genti repertas, obnitente populo Frisico abrogatas,
units.tr: Was it for this, then, that tithes and twentieths, devised by Alba to hinder commerce and reduce the nation to poverty, were abolished when the Frisian people resisted?

units.la: S f tere esse, reverentiam latæ legi stare populumque civilibus ante turbis & dissensionibus effrænem, ideo inter provincias fœdere honesta ad obsequia perduci. Subjungebat Legatus clam cum Gallis & Francisco Alençonio Bruxellis per Aurantium agi eosdemque Galliæ Legatos occultâ in Matthiam Austrium Aurantiumque æmulatione secretis artibus Belgicæ imperium ambire. Gallorum quoque auxilia, etsi rumoribus valida, omnino infirma, cæterum equites Germanos à Casimiro conscriptos iter ingressos in provinciarum finibus haberi. Quare aucto equestribus copijs exercitu majora quoque stipendia per provincias flagitata Frisiosque subsidia tuendo fœderi & gerendis rebus petita. Quippe septies centena æris millia lustrando exercitui menstruis equitum stipendijs poscebantur, grande bello adjumentum, si dominantium decretis liberalitas populi aut fortuna convenisset.
units.tr: ...that the reverence owed to the law made it stand, and that the people, unrestrained by earlier civil disturbances and dissensions, were therefore brought by honourable treaty among the provinces to obedience. The envoy added that, secretly, with the French and with Francis, Duke of Alençon, negotiations were being carried on at Brussels through Orange, and that these same envoys of France, out of a hidden rivalry with Matthias Archduke and Orange, were seeking by secret arts to win dominion over Belgium. The French auxiliaries, though strong in rumour, were in fact entirely weak; but German cavalry raised by Casimir was on the march and was believed to be within the borders of the provinces. Therefore the army, increased with cavalry, required greater pay from the provinces, and aid from the Frisians was sought both to protect the treaty and to carry on the war. Indeed, seven hundred thousand florins a month were being demanded to pay the cavalry, a great aid to the war, if the generosity of the people or fortune matched the decrees of the rulers.

units.la: Reidanus tradit à Gemblacensi clade Matthiæ Austrio & Aurantio Principi amplissimam potestatem novas è quibusque nationibus copias, eo quo visum foret numero conscribendi autorandiqueconcessam, cautione tamen addita, ne sexcentorum millium summam, menstruum æs sustentando fœderato exercitui definitum, gravandis provinciarum tributis excederet. Creditum fuit secretam belli rationem soli Ducum prudentiæ & fidei commissam fuisse, ne arcana reipub. in plures rerum conscios evulgata curiosis talium hostibus proderentur. Multitudine scilicet bellum geri, selectis consilia stare eumque esse optimum rei gerendæ modum, ut pauci decernant, plures exequantur.
units.tr: Reidanus reports that after the defeat at Gembloux, Matthias Archduke and Prince Orange were granted ample power to raise new troops from whatever nations and in whatever number seemed fit, and to hire them, with the proviso, however, that the sum of six hundred thousand, fixed as the monthly pay for sustaining the allied army, should not exceed the burdens of the provincial taxes. It was believed that the secret plan of the war was entrusted to the prudence and loyalty of the commanders alone, lest the secrets of the state, spread among many who shared them, be betrayed to curious enemies. Clearly, war is waged by the many, counsels rest with the chosen few, and this is the best way of conducting affairs: few decide, many carry out.

units.la: Igitur obtinendis subsidijs Matthias Gubernator atque Aurantius apud Frisios intercessere, indignantes quam maxime accisam jam ante imperio Principis libertatem novis Vectigalium oneribus & servilibus ludribrijs convelli. Neque enim aliâ conditione, ut antè deminatum Principis, ita post Fœdus amplexos, quam ut decora priscæ libertatis servarentur Friscaque gens ignara servitij antiquis moribus & præscripto suarum legum victitaret.
units.tr: Therefore, to obtain subsidies, Governor Matthias and Orange interceded with the Frisians, who were deeply indignant that their liberty, already curtailed under the Prince's rule, was now to be torn apart by new burdens of taxation and servile mockeries. For they had embraced the Union on no other condition, as they had previously lived under the Prince's rule, than that the honour of their ancient liberty be preserved and the Frisian people, ignorant of servitude, live by their ancient customs and by the prescribed rules of their own laws.

units.la: Itaque factum est, ut Ordines generales misso, aut in tempus prolato Collationum Statuto ad alia consiliorum transfirent publicamque egentiam collato ære aut subsidio mutuo elevandam decernerent. Propositum quoque de auro ac argento, quod adulta gentis quies ac luxuries in nimium verterat pignori dandis, quo opulentiâ provinciæ etsi non signato auri argentive pondere, ærarium fœderis juvaretur. Supellex quoque sacra, quam cœnobijs solutior luxu ætas induxerat, ijsdem legibus permissa, haud vanâ sancientium intentione, res superstitionibus servientes & luxu reprobatas pignori locandas esse, quo antiquâ frugalitate etiam Reip. benefaciendo, divinum numen coleretur. Cæterum Ordinum consilia (quemadmodum angustis rebus solet) ut fluxa & varia, ita ferè instructuosa fuere, tenace rerum familiarium populo & ut antè decimis vigesimisque, ita alienandis pignerandisq; bonis, haud absimili contumaciâ obluctante. Quare conquirendis corrogandisque per Frisiam pecunijs Sixtus Sceltema, Julius Botnia, Goslicus Hiddama & Henricus Jarichius à Matthia Austrio delecti, regerentibus ijsdem Delegatis privatas opes bello attritas aut fertilium terrarum inundationibus haustas egestatem & angustiam rerum florentissimæ quondam cIↄ. Iↄ. dam genti attulisse. Itaq; ultimâ æris egestate factum est ut Ordines generales Bossuvianæ legionis cohortibus olim per Frisiam Principi tributa exsolvendis stipendijs assignarent regijque censu annuum egeno militi & iniquis creditoribus pignerarētur.
units.tr: And so it happened that the General Estates, having dropped the schedule of levies, either sent aside or postponed to another time, turned to other counsels and decreed that public want should be relieved by collecting money or by mutual loan. There was also a proposal to pledge gold and silver, which the grown prosperity and luxury of the nation had turned into excess, so that the province, though not by coined weight of gold or silver, might help the treasury of the Union.
