Sacred furniture also, which a more relaxed age had introduced into the monasteries for luxury, was permitted under the same rules; the intention of those who decreed it was not vain, namely that things serving superstition and condemned as luxury should be pledged, so that by restoring the old frugality, God might be worshipped while the commonwealth was also served. But the counsels of the Estates, as is usual in straitened circumstances, were wavering and varied, and for the most part fruitless; the people clung tenaciously to their private property, and, as before with tithes and twentieths, they resisted with similar stubbornness the alienation and pledging of goods. Therefore Sixtus Sceltema, Julius Botnia, Goslicus Hiddama and Henricus Jarichius, chosen by Matthias Archduke to collect and gather money throughout Friesland, replied that the private wealth had been worn away by war, or swallowed up by floods of fertile lands, and that poverty and distress had come upon a nation once most flourishing. Thus, in the utmost scarcity of money, the General Estates assigned to the cohorts of the Bossuvian legion, which had once been granted the Prince's tribute through Friesland, to pay their wages from the annual royal revenue, and the needy soldier and unjust creditors were given pledges.

units.la: Quod Ordines Frisiæ ægrius ferre, obtestari jus provinciæ, cui ex foedere cum provincijs icto nihil detrahi deberet. Neque enim aliâ intentione se societati Belgicæ, se foederibus inligasse, quam ut majorum jura, conventiones & acta valerent censusque Principi olim decretus, ex pacto Anni cIↄ. Iↄ. xxiv. provinciæ usibus applicaretur. Eo scilicet cavisse Principem, ut onerum & belli immunes præstaret omneque, si quod ingrueret, in gratiam assignati census, suo ære ac stipendijs haberet. Igitur Legato Aysma inter cætera mandatum, ut pro provinciâ intercedat curetque, ne quid in fraudem publici juris statuatur & ne patrimonia Frisici populi externo ære graventur. Talium vero si quid statutum sit, id rescindi faciat, onerosis belli per Frisiam impendijs & residuorum stipendiorum pensionibus Valencicæ adhuc legioni exsolvendis.
units.tr: The Estates of Friesland bore this with great difficulty, and protested the right of the province, from which, under the treaty made with the provinces, nothing ought to be taken away. For they had bound themselves to the Belgian society and its treaties with no other purpose than that the rights, agreements and acts of their ancestors should remain in force, and that the revenue once granted to the Prince, by the agreement of the year 1524, should be applied to the uses of the province. By that arrangement, they said, the Prince had provided that the province should be free of burdens and war, and that whatever might threaten should be met from its own money and wages out of the assigned revenue. Therefore the envoy Aysma was ordered, among other things, to intercede on behalf of the province and see to it that nothing be decreed to the detriment of public right, and that the patrimony of the Frisian people not be burdened with foreign money. If anything of this kind had been decreed, he was to see that it was annulled, since the costly expenses of the war in Friesland and the payment of arrears of wages were still owed to the legion at Valenciennes.

units.la: Unde extenuatis provinciarum subsidijs Brabantiâque & Hannoniâ armis partium oppressâ, auxilia per Germaniam quæsitâ, misso Wormaciam Philippo Marnixio Aldegondio, quo loci Rudolphus II. Comitia imperij indixerat.
units.tr: Then, with the provincial subsidies weakened and Brabant and Hainault crushed by the arms of the Spanish party, aid was sought through Germany. Philip Marnix of Aldegonde was sent to Worms, where Rudolf II had summoned the Diet of the Empire.

units.la: Ibi coram Legatis, quos Cæsar Principesque ad conventum misérant, vir celebratæ eloquentiæ, ab Albani Requesentijq; Philippi Præsectorum, superbâ & crudeli dominatione orsus mox de adventu Austriaci & subdolâ fide questus, redintegratum ab eo bellum exposuit.
units.tr: There, before the envoys whom the Emperor and the princes had sent to the assembly, this man of celebrated eloquence began with the proud and cruel domination of the governors Alva, Requesens and Philip. Soon he complained of the coming of the Austrian and of his treacherous faith, and set out the war as renewed by him.

units.la: Ita occupato Namurco reductisque in provincias contra jus foederum legionibus, suis partibus urbes ac castella adjecisse fidemque Germanicarum legionum fœdæ defectioni implorasse. Itaque eo majestatis postulato, Ordines publicâ tabe foederum, quæ nullo jurisjurandi discrimine violarentur, Matthiam Austrium Cæsaris fratrem in provincias accivisse, quo per ejus cum Philippo rege interrimam affinitatem fructuosa intercessio & afflictis provincijs certa pax sperarētur. Igitur non legem obsequij, non modum parendi transgressos, cæterum jure suo ac rescripto Ioannis Brabantiæ Ducis, post Mariæ Principis submixos, in invidiem oppressoris & pesrimi regnantis, more majorum & Germaniæ etiam gentium, patrocinium imminutæ libertati quæsivisse. Sic honestis remedijs usos & quidem adversum eos, qui restitui interminatum Principis imperium vellent, asperrimamque servitij sortem & nascendi conditionem degeneri populo relinqui. Carolinas quippe dominationes repeti importunius & potestatem imperantis, non conventione aut pacto, sed exemplo mensurati, quo severis rursum Edictis lacessitæ gentes capessenda ad arma compellantur. Neque alio consilio ad ea ipsa Philippum regem rediisse, quam ut provincias, sicut olim colonijs, ita post societatibus Germaniæ inligatas Imperio subtrahat Belgaque ac Frisios, auxilijs ejusdem Germaniæ destitutos, lege regiâ circumscribat vitiisque alibi terarum gentibus & mancupijs adæquet. Subactis vero Belgicæ ac Transrhenanis Frisiorum provincijs Germaniam aggressurum, quo paternæ potentiæ terminos æquet cæcaque fortunæ lascivia intumescens, palam faciat & Germaniæ se Imperatorem & provincijs regem dare posse. Quippe regundis gentibus intentum Ger-
units.tr: Namur had been occupied, and the legions had been brought back into the provinces contrary to the law of the treaties. He claimed that the Austrian had added cities and castles to his own side and had implored the loyalty of the German legions to a shameful defection. On this charge of treason, he said, the Estates, through the public ruin of the treaties, which were violated with no regard for any oath, had summoned Matthias of Austria, the Emperor's brother, into the provinces. Through his kinship with King Philip, a fruitful mediation and a sure peace for the afflicted provinces might be hoped for. The Estates, therefore, had not transgressed the law of obedience or the limit of obeying, but had sought protection, by their own right and by the rescript of John, Duke of Brabant, issued after the princess Mary had been subdued, against the hated oppressor and the most wicked ruler. They did this, he said, in the manner of their ancestors and of the German peoples, to protect their diminished liberty. Thus they had used honest remedies, and indeed against those who wished the princely rule, which had been threatened, to be restored, and the harshest lot of servitude and the condition of birth to be left to a degenerate people. For the Carolingian dominations were being demanded more insistently, and the power of the ruler was measured not by agreement or pact but by precedent, by which peoples provoked again by harsh edicts were driven to take up arms. Nor, he argued, had King Philip returned to these lands with any other plan than to detach the provinces from the Empire, as he had once detached colonies, and afterwards to bind the Belgians and Frisians, deprived of the aid of Germany, under royal law, and to make them equal to the subject peoples and slaves of other lands. Having subdued the Belgian and Transrhenish provinces of the Frisians, he would attack Germany, so that he might equal the limits of his father's power. Swelling with the blind wantonness of fortune, he would openly show that he could make himself Emperor of Germany and king of the provinces. For he was intent on ruling peoples, and

units.la: Germaniæ suam libertatem diu invidisse, importunâ dominandi cupiditate, cui explendæ terrarum orbis angustus sit. Conscientiam generis humani consulit pos- se satisque ostensum, nihil Hispano tam infalens esse, quam abstinere alieno. Sic Ferdinandi Albani ætate, non Coloniæ tantum aut Monasterio civitatibus, cæterum Westphaliæ & Rheni tractui, post sub Requesentio instinctore Roblesio Frisiæ Præfecto Embdæ urbi insidiatum, quo Germanico Balthicoque mari dominaretur strangulatisque Vandalicarum urbium commerciis gerendo bello, aut ferendis in socios auxiliis debilem Germaniam pararet. Quæ serius missa tum demum Germani sensuri forent, cum eidem ruinæ utramque gentem Hispaniæ implicuisset regressumque ad socia arma & communem concordiam vires hostium & res casuræ vetarent. Sic Cyprum, sic Rhodum insulas occupatas, sic expugnatum Byzantium, sic Græciam Othomannicæ domui subjectam neque aliâ occasione, quam quod tardis sociorum auxiliis Christianorum res inclinarent publicâque ac socordi ignaviâ barbaræ gentis vigor & simul fortuna increvisset. Idem in Hispano fore, quem Turcicis Imperatoribus peritia belli facile exequet. Eum caloris, inediæ, frigoris patientem, sui imperii, alienæ servitutis incrementa quærere, non laturum, nisi fato prævediatur, ut libertas ullibi terrarum sedem figat laxioribusque gentium obsequys dominantis arbitrium arctetur. Igitur frænandis Hispanicæ gentis cupiditatibus immovanda fœdera esse, quibus Carolus Cæsar triginta ante annos utramque gentem inligasset. Tum sociam Imperii Belgicam Carolum declarasse sacramentoque cavisse, Ne peregrinus miles per Germaniam ageret quiesque ac securitas Germaniæ nationum externis armis obturbaretur. Cæterum ut jurisjurandi istius, ita memoriam quoque illorum fœderum obliteratam, postquam vicina miseriæ spectatrix Germaniâ, alieno periculo aut clade, suâ quiete ac ignaviâ conturpuit. Eo scilicet matrem illam ferocissimarum gentium olim Romanum Imperium, post Othomannorum furores sustinere ausam recidisse, ut nec suæ nec sociorum libertati consulat fœdasque per assentationes Hispanicæ genti metus aut ignaviæ ludibrium præstet. Non jam imbumatorum cadaverum struem, non campos sociorum ossibus constratos & albentes ad miserationem aut virtutem accendere, sublevandis per auxilia socijs, quorum veteres colonias, quorum fœdera & societates prisciis temporum ætatibus adoravisset. Non ferendum scilicet esse, ut regnum in limine Germaniæ ac Romani Imperii finibus, superba Hispaniæ gens figat transque suos Pyrenæos in conceptas fluvijs montibusque terras effusa, jus ac gloriam vetustissimi populi obruat. Id quippe jam diu consilij cœpisse, postquam Mosellam, Rhenum, Mosam præcingentia Germaniam sumina arcibus ac castellis presit, affectatrix haud dubiè illius Imperij, cujus libertatem etiam Carolo Cæsare mutare cum inhonestâ & infami servitute decreverat. Quin satius esse Cæsari ac Principibus, Ioannem Austriacum & illius asseclas libertati Germanicarum Gentium infestos, banno Imperii multare Ericumque Brunsuigium cæterosque Legionum Præfectos in sua revocare, ne publica utriusque Germaniæ libertas per ipsas Germaniæ gentes debelletur. Hoc Archiducem Matthiam Belgicæ Gubernatorem, hoc Ordines provinciarum orare, agnituros Germaniæ beneficium, si ab externâ colluvie, perdundis subvertendisque terrarum imperijs natâ, si ab onere belli & imminentibus periculis auxilijs Imperij liberentur.
units.tr: Germany had long envied its liberty, with an importunate desire to rule, for which the orb of the earth is too narrow. He consults the conscience of the human race, and it has been sufficiently shown that nothing is so unbearable to the Spaniard as to abstain from what is another's. Thus in the time of Ferdinand of Alva, the plot was laid not only against the cities of Cologne and Münster, but also against the tract of Westphalia and the Rhine. Later, under Requesens, with Robles as instigator, the prefect of Friesland plotted against the city of Emden, so that he might rule the German and Baltic seas, strangle the commerce of the Vandal cities, and by waging war or by bringing aid against allies make Germany weak. The Germans would perceive this too late, when the same ruin had entangled both nations in Spain, and the strength of the enemy and the state of affairs, now about to fall, forbade a return to common arms and common concord. So Cyprus was occupied, so Rhodes; so Byzantium was taken, and Greece was subjected to the Ottoman house, by no other occasion than that the affairs of the Christians were declining through the slow aid of allies, and that through public and dull sloth the vigour of the barbarous nation, and at the same time its fortune, had increased. The same would happen in the case of the Spaniard, whom his skill in war would easily enable to imitate the Turkish emperors. Patient of heat, hunger and cold, he sought increases of his own empire and of others' servitude. He would not endure, unless fate forbade it, that liberty should fix its seat anywhere on earth, or that the will of the ruler should be constrained by looser obedience of the peoples. Therefore, to curb the desires of the Spanish nation, the treaties must be renewed by which Charles Caesar had bound both nations thirty years before. Then Charles had declared the Belgian provinces an ally of the Empire, and had provided by oath that no foreign soldier should march through Germany, and that the peace and security of Germany should not be disturbed by foreign arms. But, as the oath has been forgotten, so too has the memory of those treaties been obliterated, since Germany, a spectator of misery close at hand, has been defiled by its own quiet and sloth, by another's danger or defeat. Clearly the mother of the most fierce peoples, the Roman Empire, which once dared to withstand the frenzies of the Ottomans, has so fallen back that it cares neither for its own liberty nor for that of its allies, and through flatteries it shows fear, or becomes the mockery of its own sloth, before the Spanish nation. No longer do heaps of unburied corpses, or fields strewn and whitened with the bones of allies, kindle pity or courage, to relieve allies by aid, whose old colonies, treaties and alliances the ancient ages had honoured. It is surely not to be endured that the proud Spanish nation should fix a kingdom on the threshold of Germany and at the borders of the Roman Empire, and, poured out beyond its Pyrenees into lands bounded by rivers and mountains, overwhelm the right and glory of the most ancient people. This design has indeed been long conceived, since Spain has seized the great rivers that gird Germany, the Moselle, the Rhine and the Meuse, with its citadels and castles. Spain is undoubtedly an aspirant to that Empire, whose liberty it had decided, even under Charles Caesar, to change into a dishonourable and infamous servitude. Indeed it would be better for the Caesar and the princes to put John of Austria and his followers, hostile to the liberty of the German peoples, under the ban of the Empire, and to recall Eric of Brunswick and the other prefects of the legions into their own service, lest the public liberty of both Germanies be destroyed by the German peoples themselves. This they urge on Archduke Matthias, governor of Belgium, and on the Estates of the provinces. They will acknowledge Germany's kindness if they are freed from the foreign crowd born to destroy and subvert the empires of the lands, and if they are relieved, by the aid of the Empire, of the burden of war and of imminent dangers.

units.la: Legati quoque ab Austriaco ad eundem conventum Wormatiam missi, tardandis rerum processibus & ne Germaniæ patrocinio Belgicæ gentes datum.
units.tr: Envoys were also sent from Austria to the same assembly at Worms, to delay the progress of affairs and to prevent the protection of Germany from being given to the Belgian peoples.

units.la: gentes levarentur. Cæterum Legato grates à consessu procerum adæ responsumque Imperij nomine, daturos operam Cæsarem Principesque, ut provinciæ aut bello auxilia aut intercessione certam pacem accipiant ratioq; priscorum fœderum & antiquæ societatis quam maxumè habeatur.
units.tr: ...the peoples be relieved. But thanks were given to the envoy by the assembly of nobles, and an answer was given in the name of the Empire: Caesar and the princes would take care that the provinces receive either aid in war or a sure peace through mediation, and that the principle of the old treaties and the ancient alliance be held in the highest regard.

units.la: Mox Lalainius, Vollenhoæ adhuc agens, tributa gerendis per Transifulaniam rebus popposcit assensuque eorum impetrato, qui in fœdus condescenderant, Campos oppidum circumvenire copijs constituit. Comprimendis quoque per Leovardiam urbem & simul provinciam seditionibus, quas Pontificij fœderi publico & Collationibus infesti nullâ furoris sui dissimulatione minabantur, Edictum Vollenhoâ de mandato Ordinum generalium in Frisiam misit, Gandavensemque conventionem Pontificijs suspectam ratam esse jussit. Militarem quoque disciplinam, quam inopia stipendiorum non parum dissolverat, restitui eodem Edicto fecit asperisque poenarum decretis insolentiam militum coercuit. Quippe templorum sacrarumque ædium plurimæ direptiones tum fiebant pravaque multitudo, velut subsidia vitæ flagitaret, planos per agros nullo tribunorum Centurionumve metu sparsa sacrilegijs pascebatur.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Lalaing, still staying at Vollenhove, demanded taxes for carrying on operations through Overijssel. When he had obtained the assent of those who had come to terms with the treaty, he resolved to surround the town of Kampen with troops. In order to check the seditions in the city of Leeuwarden and at the same time in the province, which the Papists, hostile to the public treaty and the Collations, threatened without any concealment of their fury, he sent from Vollenhove an edict into Friesland, by order of the General Estates, and commanded that the Ghent Pacification, which the Papists suspected, be ratified. By the same edict he also had military discipline restored, which the lack of pay had loosened no little, and with harsh decrees of punishment he curbed the insolence of the soldiers. For at that time very many plunderings of temples and sacred buildings were taking place, and a wicked crowd, as if demanding the means of life, was feeding on sacrileges scattered over the open fields, with no fear of tribunes or centurions.

units.la: Quare compresso milite attenuatisque urbium præsidijs, cohortes quadam pedestri itinere Lemmariam expedivit navibusque impositas exponi in ripam Isalæ amnis jusit. Aurantium quoque, quem Gallicæ societatis secretum Bruxellis tum attinebat auxilia petijt novisque quas ante conscripserat cohortibus supplementa procuravit.
units.tr: Therefore, with the soldiers checked and the garrisons of the cities weakened, he sent a number of cohorts on foot to Lemmer, and ordered that they be placed on ships and landed on the bank of the river Yssel. He also sought the help of Orange, who was then detained at Brussels by the secret alliance with France, and he arranged reinforcements for the new cohorts he had raised before.

units.la: Oppido vero Camporum Polvilerius Germanicæ legionis præfectus, binis cum cohortibus præerat, dubiâ diu sacramenti fide, Ordinum an Austriaci teneret, cujus societatem capto Namurco, velut egregio defectionis successu induerat. Igitur Lalainius, necdum acceptis auxilijs dolo rem aggressus delectis per cohortes, qui flumine qua vadosum esset, superato & contrucidatis vigilibus in urbem irruerent foroque urbis occupato, secutura per auxilia præsidium disturbarent. Cæterum detecto consilio, postquam auspicandæ obsidioni delectorum sanguine litatum, castra multo mox opere præmunita, quæ Gualterus Hegemannus vir manu strennuus, per minores majoresque Frisios etiam Scouwenburgicis temporibus stipendia meritus, haud procul colle modico opportuna loco tutabatur.
units.tr: But in the town of Kampen, Polvilerius, prefect of the German legion, was in command with two cohorts, his loyalty to the oath long doubtful, whether he held for the Estates or for the Austrian, whose alliance he had adopted after the capture of Namur, as if it were a fine success of his defection. Lalaing, not yet having received the reinforcements, attempted the matter by stratagem: he chose men from the cohorts who, where the river was shallow, should cross it, slay and cut down the sentries, rush into the town, occupy the forum, and disrupt the garrison that would follow with reinforcements. But the plan was discovered, and after the siege had been begun with the blood of the chosen men, a camp was soon fortified with much labour. Walter Hegemann, a man strenuous with his hand, who had earned his pay among the lesser and greater Frisians even in the times of Schouwenburg, guarded it opportunely, not far from a modest hill.

units.la: Lalainius quoque in castra adventans, Joannem Mulartium cohortis ductorem tuendo, qui amni imponitur, ponti destinavit trajectoque post flumine & munitione Hegemanni lustratâ, adduci in castra omnem commeatum præcepit. Hegemannus vero locum militari vallo clausum, Jaricho Hottinghæ viro nobili demandavit ipseque cum copijs Bruneppense in cœnobium progressus, Hagium suburbium longâ velitatione suum fecit. Mox ope rusticæ plebis, quàm è vicino Mastenbroeckano agro collegerat, idem suburbium terreo opere circumduxit, non angustâ adhuc obsessæ urbis fortunâ, quæ excurrentis præsidij virtute magnitudinem periculi elevabat. Cæterum accitis ex Hollandiâ quinque cohortium auxilijs, (in quibus Sonnoi, Wingardij, Duvenvordij, Teilingij & Renoi fuere) obsessis periculum, animus Lalainio increvit munijsque castrorum cautius prospectum, quæ imbecillibus antè copijs laxius obita majore curâ exercebantur. Triremis quoque è minoribus Frisijs missa premendo do Isalæ fluminis ostio, ne obsessi in sinum Austrinum se effunderent prædatoriisque navigijs auxilia & commeatum compararent.
units.tr: Lalainius also came to the camp. He assigned John Mulartius, a cohort leader, to guard the bridge that is laid across the river. After crossing the river and inspecting Hegemann's fortifications, he ordered all supplies to be brought into the camp. Hegemann entrusted the place, enclosed by a military rampart, to Jaricho Hottingha, a nobleman, and himself advanced with his forces to the cloister at Bruneppe. By a long skirmish he made the suburb of Hagium his own. Soon, with the help of country folk he had gathered from the nearby Mastenbroeck fields, he surrounded that suburb with an earthwork. The fortunes of the besieged city were not yet desperate, since the bravery of the sallying garrison lessened the magnitude of the danger. But when auxiliaries of five cohorts had been summoned from Holland (among them those of Sonnoy, Wingardius, Duvenvoorde, Teilingen and Renoy), the courage of the besiegers grew, and Lalainius looked to the defences of the camp more carefully. Previously, with weak forces, these had been held somewhat loosely, but now they were guarded with greater care. A trireme was also sent from Lesser Friesland to hold the mouth of the river Isala, so that the besieged could not pour out into the southern bay and procure auxiliaries and supplies by pirate vessels.

units.la: Sic ordinatis rebus relictoque in castris cum imperio Diderico Sonnoio minoris Frisiæ Præfecto Lalainius in Frisiam revertit mutandis minorum urbium magistratibus, quo fœderati populi & simul Reip. securitas omnem per provinciam novis rectoribus firmaretur. Undé Austriaci partes professis abrogatum imperium, quod à Justi Scouwenburgij fugâ per exilia & proscriptiones clarorum virorum suarum partium defensoribus Senatus regius indulserat.
units.tr: With affairs thus arranged, and with Diderick Sonnoy, prefect of Lesser Friesland, left in command of the camp, Lalainius returned to Friesland to change the magistrates of the smaller towns, so that the confederated people, and at the same time the security of the Commonwealth, might be strengthened throughout the province by new rulers. Hence the authority of the Austrian party, which the royal Senate had granted to the defenders of that faction through exiles and proscriptions of distinguished men after the flight of Justus Scouwenburg, was abolished.

units.la: Annotavit F. Nicolaus, Staurienfium Magistratum ix. Kalend. Jun. imperio cessisse, potestatemque nuncupandi Senatus & solennium votorum civibus factam, non leve auspicium reviciturae libertati attulisse. Igitur factum est, ut quos ante regij Senatus favor regundis oppidis, agrisque præfecerat, eos suffragatio populi moderamini rerum tum destinaret omnisque provincia, quà Flevo & Lavicâ amnibus clauditur, majorum more ut antè Principum tempora, consensu parentium regeretur. Mox Lalainius formato provinciæ statu in castra regressus, quæ circa id temporis obsessorum eruptionibus & continuo velite, nullâ externæ necessitatis formidine, infestabantur. Unde pecus suburbano adhuc rure ab obsessis pastum, donec Hollandicis copijs propius ad urbem suggresiis omne suffugium excurrenti præsidio adimeretur. Quare rebus sensim angustioribus solæ in auxilijs obsessorum spes locabantur, quorum fidem clandestinos per nuntios Ioannes Austriacus faciebat. Cujus litteræ ab exploratoribus post interceptæ, ut ad solatium obsesis, ita ad virtutem ultrò fortibus non profuere missæque ad Lalainium Zutphaniam, (ubi Joannes Nassovius Geldriæ Præfectus comitium populi partiendis castrorum impendijs habebat) maturandum obsidium suasere. Igitur decreta Geldris quarta sumtuum pars, triens Frisijs ac Transisulanis cederet, Lalainius lustratis castris Zuollas profectus, quo civitatem fœderi pronam ad arbitrium formaret, missas Ultrajecto machinas admoveri jussit murisque parte ad xxxiii. pass. latitudinem subrutâ, terrorem obsessis injecit.
units.tr: F. Nicolaus notes that the magistracy of Stavoren yielded its authority on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, and that the power of electing a Senate and of taking solemn votes was granted to the citizens. This was no slight omen of returning liberty. Therefore it came about that those whom the favour of the royal Senate had earlier placed in charge of governing towns and lands were now designated by the people's vote to direct affairs. The whole province, bounded by the rivers Flevo and Lavica, was governed by the consent of its citizens, as in the custom of former times before the age of princes. Soon Lalainius, having settled the state of the province, returned to the camp, which at that time was harassed by sorties of the besieged and by constant skirmishing, though there was no fear of any outside need. Hence the cattle of the besieged were still grazing in the countryside around the suburb, until the Holland forces advanced nearer to the city and took away from the sallying garrison every means of retreat. As affairs gradually grew tighter, hope rested solely on help from outside the besieged, whose secret messages John Austria arranged through couriers. His letters were intercepted by scouts afterwards and did not profit the besieged for comfort, nor did they spur on the brave to courage. They were sent to Lalainius at Zutphen, where John Nassau, prefect of Gelderland, was holding the assembly of the people for dividing the expenses of the camp, and they urged him to hasten the siege. Therefore it was decreed that a quarter of the costs should fall to Gelderland and a third to Friesland and Overijssel. Lalainius, having inspected the camp, set out for Zwolle, to bring the city, inclined to the union, into shape at his pleasure. He ordered the machines sent from Utrecht to be brought up, and, with a section of the wall about thirty-three paces wide undermined, he struck terror into the besieged.

units.la: Quare à Magistratu, & militari præsidio, ad Lalainium Zuollis adhuc agentem ac Transisulaniæ optumates, qui cum eo agebant litteræ datæ, quibus obsessi tutum caduceatoribus commeatum paciscendæ deditionì & cum eà æquas conditiones pro arbitrio moderati victoris orabant. Igitur conventum Ut complicatis signis armatum præsidium urbe excederet, deducturque Benthemicos in agros, intra semestre adversum Ordines non militaret. Stipendia quoque aut residuum æs, si quod peti posset, nullo tempore exigeret dimissisque utrinque captivis urbs partibus Ordinum & fœderi adscriberetur. Magistratus urbis Georgio Lalainio Frisiæ Præfecto sacramentum præstaret præsidiumque illius arbitrio acciperet. Sic Germanorum præsidium, quod sex per annos eâ in civitate insolenter ac superbè egerat, urbe excessit Lalainiusque Jarichum Hottingham, Uternum & Mularitum cohortium tribunos urbi præsidio esse jussit.
units.tr: Therefore letters were given from the magistracy and the military garrison to Lalainius, who was still at Zwolle, and to the nobles of Overijssel who were dealing with him. In them the besieged asked for safe conduct for heralds so that terms of surrender might be arranged, and they begged that equal conditions be set, moderated at the victor's discretion. So an agreement was reached: the armed garrison was to leave the city with colours furled and be led to the fields of Bentheim, and for six months was not to bear arms against the States. Nor was it ever to demand its wages or any remaining money, if any could be claimed. Prisoners were to be released on both sides, and the city was to be counted among the party of the States and the union. The city magistrates were to take the oath to George Lalaing, prefect of Friesland, and receive the garrison at his discretion. Thus the German garrison, which for six years had behaved insolently and arrogantly in that city, left it. Lalainius ordered Jaricho Hottingha, Uternus and Mularitus, tribunes of the cohorts, to be the garrison of the city.

units.la: Reperio in archivis provinciæ, à Dongrijs qui in ortum Paseni rivi agunt, continuas ob inundationes struendo reficiendoque marino aggeri adlum. cIↄ. Iↄ. geri tabulas tum scriptas curanteque Wigero Gabinio, aggerum istius LXXVIII. anni præfecto, à Georgio Lalainio Leovardiæ v i i i. Jun. approbatas, vim ac sanctionem legis eam apud gentem retinuisse. Ab eodem quoque Gabinio libellum supplicem Lalainio exhibitum, quo de sumptuosis aggerum impendijs quærebatur populoq; Dongrico ad inopiam & egestatem redacto aut per diluvia maris extorri publici operis utilitatem & simul progressum retardari. Igitur petebat, ut eorum agri, quos derelictos colentium fuga fecisset, more recepto per tribunalia publicati per apparitorem decreto Senatus venderentur onusque sustinendi aggeris marini privato ære aut si aliter visum proventibus ærarij levaretur. Neque enim suæ potestatis esse tantæ moli erigendæ privatas facultates impendere cogereque ad officia populum suarum possessionum desertorem. Quamobrem consummando operi legis vigorem, autoritatem Præfecti, commune subsidium requiri, ac ut Dongricæ gentis lites tamdiu in suspenso sint, donec perducto ad finem opere, ad officium fori redire parta Dongricis terris securitas permittat. Unde Lalainius eidem Gabinio plenam potestatem agendarum rerum fecit rescriptumque eâ de re Leovard. xiii. Jun. indulsit. Controversias quoque aggerum, Igramo Achlenio nuper Præsidi Senatus, Arnoldo Doccomiensi, Cellario Wertensi, Francisco Cantero & Joanni Sippio, ut arbitris commissas, aliud in tempus proferri jussit, dum publicæ securitati, laborantium industria ac cura Præfectorum aggeris prospexisset. Mox Lalainius Camporum urbe fœderi assertâ, Aurantium ejus rei certiorem per litteras fecit fortunæque benignitate & prospero rerum cursu utendum ratus, obsidendæ Daventriæ consilium eidem Aurantio aperuit.
units.tr: I find in the archives of the province, from the people of Dongeradeel who dwell on the east side of the Paseno stream, a set of records, written for the continual repair and rebuilding of the sea dyke because of constant floods, and drawn up and managed by Wiger Gabinius, prefect of the dykes for that year of 1578. These were approved by George Lalaing at Leeuwarden on 8 June, and they kept the force and sanction of law among that people. From the same Gabinius there was also a supplicating petition presented to Lalaing. In it he complained of the costly expenses of the dykes, and that the Dongeradeel people had been reduced to poverty and want, or driven away by the floods of the sea, so that the usefulness of the public work and its progress were held back. He therefore asked that those lands which the flight of their cultivators had left deserted be sold, as is the accepted practice, by a decree of the Senate published at the tribunals by an officer. He also asked that the burden of maintaining the sea dyke be lightened by private money, or, if it seemed otherwise, by the revenues of the treasury. For it was not within his power to compel private resources to be spent on so great a structure, nor to force the people to duties on the possessions they had deserted. Therefore, to complete the work, the force of the law, the authority of the Prefect, and common help were required. He also asked that the lawsuits of the Dongeradeel people be suspended for as long as the work was carried to its end, after which the security won for the Dongeradeel lands would allow them to return to the duties of the courts. Hence Lalainius gave Gabinius full power to manage the affairs and issued a rescript on this matter at Leeuwarden on 13 June. He also ordered the disputes over the dykes, which had been entrusted as arbiters to Igram Achlen, recently president of the Senate, Arnold Doccomius, Cellarius of Wert, Francis Cantero and John Sippius, to be postponed to another time, until he had provided for public security through the diligence and care of the dyke prefects at work. Soon afterwards Lalainius, with the city of Kampen secured for the union, informed Orange of this by letter. Thinking that the favour of fortune and the prosperous course of affairs should be used, he disclosed to Orange his plan for besieging Deventer.

units.la: Notant nostrates, adjectis Reip. Ordinum Campis magnam Frisiæ per oppida Fœderati populi festivitatem fuisse reformatosque privatis adhuc sacris publicum fati beneficium professos, servidis votis continuæ fœlicitatis progressum divinum numen orasse. Quare increscente reformati populi per provincias zelo & simul multitudine jus publicorum exercitiorum Ordines & Matthiam Archiducem modeste petitum, ac ut rem divinam in posterum facturis, angustis privatarum ædium conseptis, templa ac fana assignarentur. Libellus supplex istiusmodi erat.
units.tr: Our people note that, with the towns of Kampen added to the Commonwealth of the Estates, there was great rejoicing among the confederated people in the towns of Friesland. Those who had been reformed, though still meeting in private for worship, professed the public benefit that fate had brought them, and with fervent vows they begged the divine power to continue this progress of happiness. Hence, as the zeal and at the same time the number of the reformed people grew through the provinces, they modestly petitioned the Estates and Archduke Matthias for the right of public exercises, and asked that, for those who were to perform divine worship in future, temples and chapels be assigned in place of the cramped enclosures of private houses. The supplicating petition was of this kind.

units.la: Libellus supplex, ad Matthiam & Ordines.
units.tr: A humble petition to Matthias and the Estates.

units.la: Quinquaginta ante annos, Serenissime Archidux, P.C. majores nostri sanctionibus Pontificum, & illorum temporum caligini se exemere. Quibus corrigendis, etsi Albano & Requesentio regnantibus ad asperrima & detestanda remedia provocatum, ita fato quodam cum illorum crudelitate nostra pietas inorevit. Octodecim & ultra hominum millibus Albani furoribus & nostris sacris litatum. Ceteros miseratio numinis & sua fœlicitas sævitiæ subduxit fecitque, ut peregrinis in terris genuinum colendi numinis ritum profiteremur. Ita desertâ patriâ externis gentibus nostra sacra, ac religiones detteximus & quidem tanto majore zelo, quanto gravius in nos fortuna & asperitas temporum desæviebat. Sic dum relicta domi pignora bellum, vastationes, supplicia affligebant, nos exilia toleravimus. Inde artium decora & simul commercia alio terrarum translata, adnitentibus Hispanis, ut sout solitudine florentissimis provincijs inductâ, majore licentiâ grassarentur. Ne- que aliud Austriaci institutum fuit, quam ut violatæ polluteque religionis prætextu, eundem seviendi modum exequeretur nosque Deum & patriam semper reveritos, falsis accusationibus attaminaret. Cujus consilia etsi tardante fato non processerint, hoc tamen effecere, ut nobis iniquos procerum affectus fecerint teterrimâque defectione subsecutâ, Remp. divulserint. Quare metuendum est, ne invalescente diffidentia malo pejora nascantur & ne nostra societas, nostrum Fœdus Gandavi & alibi iđtum, in discordiam ac secessionem vertatur. Eâ vero per AUSTRIACUM procuratâ hostium res secundæ, nobis vero adversæ erunt. Itaque necessum est, ut positis in medium odijs, promiscuas religiones toleremus, quas terrenis potestatibus & serviendi conditionibus natura rerum exemit. Quippe civile in Fœdus coïre, pacem colere etiam dissociati religionibus possumus, modo nostræ fidei is fructus sit ut patriæ serviat. Cujus amore tracti nostris afflictionibus diu remedia oravimus, illorum consilijs præpedita, qui aut labi nos in omnem insolentiam desperatione rerum volebant rescindendisque Fœderum sacris unâ religione societatem Belgici Frisicique populi stare. Hoc vero moliendo, ut consensum generis humani, ita exempla veterum sæculorum confundunt, quæ priscis sub Imperatoribus conscientijs libertatem illæsa pace publica indulsissent. Non dicendum de priscis temporum ætatibus, postquam tanta recentium ubertas, ut nostram quoque ad memoriam pervenerint. Sic Gallijs, sic Germaniæ post diuturna & intestina bella pax illuxit, tamdiu extorris & proscripta quamdiu dominantibus consilium defuit ea ferendi quæ divinitus darentur. Ita reputa, Serenissime ARCHIDUX, CAROLO V. Cæsare, obturbatum imperium non aliâ tranquillitate quam tolerata religionis desedisse. Volente velut fato, ut tanti Cæsaris majestas suâ opinione fastigium fortunæ & subactarum gentium assecutâ, hoc solo caducæ sortis moneretur, neque imperandum esse mentibus, quæ divino imperio regerentur. Sic FERDINANDUM avum, sic MAXIMILIANUM patrem divæ memoriæ jam cælo redditum, latam & discordem sensu Germaniam rexisse, ut religiones populi per Impe-rium ferret, unâ ruituram. Quin spectâ RUDOLPHVM fratrem, sic Hungariam, sic Bohemiam ordinasse, ut quia uno voto non poterat, pluribus viveretur. Neque aliter Gallias intestinis bellis fessas & velut cum anima luctantes respirasse, quam promiscuâ per omne regnum religione indultâ populoque opinionibus discordi ad civilia obsequia retractio. Cogita sic Othomannicam domum, sic Africæ Regulos, sic Pontificem ipsum Latio imperare. Quin tanto æquius erit nos indigenas nostram fidem nostra sacra in publico profiteri. Itaque, hoc cavebitis, Serenissime ARCHIDUX, P. C. ut omnium rerum, quæ à dissidijs sacrorum religionumque obvenere certa oblivio fit, quo consilijs hostium conjuncti obstemus patriamque per discordias peritturam conterdia tueamur. Id si faciatis, dabimus operam ut majoribus quam antè officijs nos Reip. obligemus, cui inservire nostræ mentis & voti summa est. Hoc vero si non assequamur, perstabimus tamen in proposito pietatis patriamque etiam cadentem amplexi, labentem spiritum divino cultui & saluti publicæ mancipabimus.
units.tr: Fifty years ago, most serene Archduke, our forefathers freed themselves from the decrees of the Pontiffs and from the darkness of those times. Although under the reigns of Alba and Requesens they were driven to the harshest and most detestable remedies for correcting these things, our piety, by some fate, grew up together with their cruelty. Eighteen thousand and more men were sacrificed to the fury of Alba and to our rites. The mercy of God and his own good fortune withdrew the rest from savagery and made it so that we professed the genuine ritual of worshipping God in foreign lands. Thus, having abandoned our homeland, we carried our sacred rites and religion to foreign peoples, and with all the greater zeal, as fortune and the harshness of the times raged more heavily against us. So while war, devastation and punishments afflicted the pledges we had left at home, we endured exile. Hence the ornaments of the arts and at the same time commerce were carried to other lands, with the Spaniards pressing so that, with the countryside emptied by desolation, they might rage with greater licence in the most flourishing provinces. Nor was there any other policy of the Austrians than that, under the pretext of a violated and polluted religion, they should carry out the same method of raging and assail with false accusations us, who have always revered God and country. Although their plans did not go forward because fate delayed, they achieved this: they made the nobles unfriendly to us, and once that most foul defection followed, they tore the commonwealth apart. Therefore it is to be feared that, as distrust grows, worse evils may arise, and that our association, our covenant made at Ghent and elsewhere, may turn into discord and secession. If this is brought about through Austria, the enemy's affairs will prosper and ours will be adverse. Therefore it is necessary, with hatreds set aside in the open, that we tolerate mixed religions, which the nature of things exempts from earthly powers and the conditions of servitude. For indeed we can unite in a civil covenant and cultivate peace even when divided by religion, provided that the fruit of our faith is that it serves the fatherland. Drawn by love of that, we have long prayed for remedies to our afflictions, which were hindered by the counsels of those who wanted us either to slip into every insolence through despair of affairs, or to cancel the sacred rites of the covenants, and to have the alliance of the Belgic and Frisian peoples stand on one religion. In attempting this, they confound the consent of the human race and the examples of earlier centuries, which under the ancient emperors granted liberty of conscience without harm to public peace. I need not speak of earlier ages, since the abundance of recent examples is so great that they have come even into our memory. Thus peace dawned for France, and for Germany after long and internal wars, and they were exiled and proscribed for as long as their rulers lacked the wisdom to bear with what was given by God. Consider, most serene Archduke, that under Charles V the empire was thrown into confusion and settled into calm only by a tolerated religion. It was as if by fate's will that the majesty of so great an emperor, having reached the summit of fortune in his own opinion and the subjugation of peoples, was admonished by this alone of a fragile lot: that minds which are governed by divine rule must not be commanded. Thus Ferdinand, his grandfather, and Maximilian, his father of divine memory now restored to heaven, ruled a wide and divided Germany in such a way that, since they allowed the religions of the people throughout the empire, it would fall together with them. Moreover, Rudolph, his brother, has so ordered Hungary and Bohemia that, since they cannot live by one vote, they live by several. Nor did France, weary from internal wars and struggling as if with its last breath, otherwise draw breath than by granting a mixed religion throughout the whole kingdom and by calling back to civil obedience a people divided in opinion. Consider likewise that the Ottoman house, the kings of Africa, and the Pontiff himself rule in Latium. Indeed it will be all the more just for us, who are natives, to profess our faith and our rites in public. Therefore, most serene Archduke, you will ensure that there be a sure oblivion of all things which have arisen from disputes over sacred matters and religions, so that, joined in counsel, we may resist the enemy and by harmony protect a fatherland that would otherwise perish through discord. If you do this, we shall take care to bind ourselves to the commonwealth by greater services than before, to which serving is the highest aim of our mind and wish. But if we do not attain this, we shall nonetheless persist in our purpose of piety, embracing even a falling fatherland, and we shall devote our failing breath to divine worship and public safety.

units.la: Hæc Provinciarum · REFORMATI.
units.tr: The petition of the Reformed of the provinces.

units.la: Mox Bolsverdij è Frisijs nomine Nobilitatis ac municipalium ad eundem MATTHIAM hunc in modum scripsere.
units.tr: Soon afterwards the men of Bolsward, on behalf of the nobility and the municipal authorities of Friesland, wrote to the same Matthias in the following manner.

units.la: TURBIS ac miseriis nostris, quas tot per annos perpessi sumus, non aliæ causæ subfuerunt, quam quod asperrimis regis P hilippi Edictis adversati profiteri religionem vetiti simus nostris mentibus delectam. Nec eâ tantum servitute nostrâ calamitas stetit, cæterum adacti ad ceremonias ritusque nostris conscientiis adversas, nec privatis sacris tuto interesse, nec patriâ frui potuimus. Inquisitum quippe in nos asperius & nullius in Deum, in patriam criminis reos sola accusatio morti aut exilii destinavit. Nunc vero, quoniam divino numini terminum præfigere istis temporum furoribus placuit, ac Gandavensi fœdere conscientiis tranquillitatem, securitatem nostris fortunis ac possessionibus largiri, hoc unum nostris votis ac desideriis relictum est, ut religionem, quâ ut ante in patriâ ita post exilio animos imbuimus, publicè & nullo metu profiteamur. Reprimere quippe fervidos spiritus, nec nostræ potestatis est nec conscientiæ patiuntur, hoc solo etiam felices, quod divortio ab erroribus temporum facto lumen acceperint cælo infusum. Et quoniam habendis cætibus privatæ domus pares non sunt, templa ac fana à majoribus nostris divino cultui dedicata, assignari nostris exercitiis petimus, ac ut ministri nostri sacris operati censu publico alantur. Nobis quoque posteris liberalitas majorum & privatæ opes pijs usibus collatæ tandem subserviant nosque firmiore sacrorum nexu colligati, hoc quicquid ævi per turbas & inquietudines diu actum, honestâ quiete & tranquillitate mentis expleamus.
units.tr: The troubles and miseries we have suffered through so many years had no other cause than this: by the most severe edicts of King Philip we were forbidden to profess the religion our minds had chosen. Nor was our calamity confined to this servitude; moreover, compelled to ceremonies and rites contrary to our consciences, we could neither safely attend private worship nor enjoy our country. For an inquiry was pursued against us more harshly, and a mere accusation, with no proven guilt towards God or country, destined us to death or exile. Now, however, since it has pleased the divine will to set a limit to these furies of the times, and since the Ghent covenant grants tranquillity to consciences and security to our fortunes and possessions, this one thing is left to our prayers and desires: that we may profess publicly and without any fear the religion with which we imbued our minds in our homeland and, after exile, still hold. For to restrain fervent spirits is neither in our power nor do our consciences permit it; they are happy in this alone, that, by their separation from the errors of the times, they have received a light infused from heaven. And since private houses are not equal to holding assemblies, we ask that the temples and shrines dedicated to divine worship by our forebears be assigned to our exercises, and that our ministers who serve in the sacred offices be supported by public funds. May the generosity of our ancestors and private means devoted to pious uses at last serve us and our posterity too, and, bound by a firmer bond of worship, may we fill whatever time has been spent in turmoil and unrest with honourable quiet and tranquillity of mind.

units.la: Neque absimilia Harlingani.
units.tr: The people of Harlingen wrote in no very different terms.

units.la: Quippe populus, velut laxatis spatiis & alienatâ mente, ut fastidio priscorum rituum, ita desiderio novæ religionis accendebatur ægriusque ferebat:
units.tr: For the people, as if their bounds were loosened and their minds estranged, were inflamed with disgust for the old rites and with longing for a new religion, and bore it with impatience:

units.la: Mutato in melius Reip. statu serviles animas domesticis sacris aut antiquis superstitionibus alligari. Sic scilicet Cæsaris ac Philippi Edicta, sic Albani arma & sanguinolentiam, sic proscriptiones atque exilia pertulisse, quo meliora fato tempora darentur omneque adversæ fortunæ solatium à stabilienda religione & cultu numinis inciperet. Non negligendum esse id boni per servilem patientiam aut turpem socordiam, quod occasionem horrendæ tempestati dedisset & quo solo æquitas causæ & fœlicium armorum etiamnum stet. Ejus obtentu, intercessiones Cæsarum ac Regum orasse foreque fœdissimum, ut in spem libertatis per auxilia Principum erectæ gentes fastiditis diutius superstitionibus serviant veraque religio à summo rerum mentibus infusa & lacertos fato latius motura privatis parietibus ac conseptis ædium circumscribatur.
units.tr: Now that the state has changed for the better, souls that were enslaved should not be bound to domestic rites or ancient superstitions. Clearly the edicts of Caesar and Philip, the arms and bloodshed of Alba, the proscriptions and exiles were endured so that better times might be given by fate, and every solace of adverse fortune might begin with the establishment of religion and the worship of the divine will. That benefit should not be neglected, which through servile patience or shameful sloth gave occasion to a dreadful storm, and on which alone the justice of our cause and the success of our arms still rest. Under the pretext of this, they say, the intercessions of Caesars and kings were sought, and it would be most shameful that nations, raised to hope of liberty through the aid of princes, should serve longer under despised superstitions, and that true religion, infused into minds by the highest ruler and destined by fate to extend its arms more widely, should be confined within private walls and the enclosures of houses.

units.la: Leovardij quoque & in ijs reformatæ religionis primarij antistites annuas ministris suis pensiones ex bonis Ecclesiasticis Lalainium oravere aut ut Præsule Bergumano morte extincto sexcenti carolæi qui ei decernebantur, reformatis ministris assignarentur. Quæ à Joanne Aysma, Tiallengo Wikelio, Popkone Roorda, Petro Arentio, Joanne Arentio, Francisco Joannis signata approbataque post à Lalainio, Burgalæ in castris agente, tum ipsis Ordinum Deputatis incrementa reformatæ religioni attulere.
units.tr: At Leeuwarden too, the leading ministers of the reformed religion there asked Lalaing for annual pensions for their ministers out of church revenues, or else, when the Provost of Bergum died, that the six hundred carolus guilders decreed to him be assigned to the reformed ministers. These requests, signed and approved by Johannes Aysma, Tiallengo Wikelius, Popko Roorda, Petrus Arentius, Johannes Arentius and Franciscus Joannis, were afterwards approved by Lalaing, then acting at the camp at Burgala, and by the Deputies of the Estates themselves, and they brought increase to the reformed religion.

units.la: Mox novo Senatui introducendo dies dictus missique Ordinum Frisiæ nomine ad Igramum Achlenium nuper Præsidem Senatus, qui claves Basilicæ poscerent sigillaque publica obsignandis actis impetrarent. Sed Achlenius, sive ægritudine adversæ Fortunæ, sive recuperandæ dignitatis spem alens mandatis Ordinum se oppositit Antistiteque Clarecampensi Gerardo Jacobi provinciæ tum Deputato nequicquam urgente munimenta Senatus & veteris imperij non nisi de voluntate Matthiæ Gubernatoris se traditurum asseruit. Quare Hesselo Aysma Legato Antverpiæ agenti impositum, apud Matthiam Archiducem eâ de re agendi curandique, ne cœptæ res & bono Fœderis institutæ tergiversatione ac contumaciâ exautorati Senatus præpediantur. Unde rescripto Gubernatoris decretum, Ut claves, sigilla, judiciales libri & quicquid in secreto Curiæ asservaretur, Ordinibus aut eorum Delegatis cederet augurandique Senatus solemnitas priduano Eid. Jul. die inciperet. Ita Franciscus Eysingha, Joannes Versterveranus, Gysbertus Aernsma, Fecco Rhala legum periti in possessionem Senatorij munieris missi.
units.tr: Soon afterwards a day was set for introducing a new Senate, and envoys were sent on behalf of the Estates of Friesland to Igram Achlenius, lately President of the Senate, to demand the keys of the Basilica and to obtain the public seals for sealing the acts. But Achlenius, whether from sickness caused by adverse fortune or nursing hope of recovering his dignity, opposed the orders of the Estates; and though Gerard Jacobi, Provost of Klaarkamp and then Deputy of the province, urged him in vain, he declared that he would hand over the strongholds of the Senate and of the old government only with the consent of Governor Matthias. Hence Hessel Aysma, then a legate at Antwerp, was charged to deal with Archduke Matthias about this matter and to see to it that the affairs begun and instituted for the good of the Union should not be hindered by the evasion and obstinacy of the Senate that had been removed from office. Whereupon, by rescript of the Governor, it was decreed that the keys, seals, judicial books and whatever was kept secret in the court should yield to the Estates or their delegates, and that the solemn taking of office by the new Senate should begin on the day before the Ides of July. Thus Franciscus Eysingha, Joannes Versterveranus, Gysbertus Aernsma and Fecco Rhala, learned in the law, were sent into possession of the senatorial office.

units.la: M. Heymannus scribit à Deputatis provinciæ, Gerardo Jacobi Præsule Clarecampensi, Docone Martna, Serapio Galama, Goslico Hiddama, Barthio Idzaerda & Erasmo Douma, de mandato Lalainij, in Basilicam regiam ductos, comitante urbis magistratu, quem Lalainius in castris ad Campos agens celebrandis honorandisque illius Ordinis auspicijs delegerat. Idem addit sub conditione & ne juris dicundi ac fori munia vacarent, in possessionem dignitatis missos, dum de prioris Senatus crimine aut innocentiâ Matthias Gubernator & provinciarum Ordines cognovissent.
units.tr: M. Heymannus writes that the deputies of the province, Gerardus Jacobi, provost of Klaarkamp, Docho Martna, Serapio Galama, Goslicus Hiddama, Bartius Idzaerda and Erasmus Douma, were led into the royal basilica on Lalaing's orders, accompanied by the city magistrates, whom Lalaing had chosen while he was in camp at Campen to celebrate and honour the installation of that order. He adds that they were admitted to possession of their office on the condition that they would not take up the duties of judging and of the court until Governor Matthias and the Estates of the provinces had examined whether the former Senate was guilty of the charges or innocent.

units.la: Quare postero die in loco judicij idem Senatus & pro tribunali desedit Joannemque Versteverannum virum oris facundi verba facere jussit.
units.tr: Therefore on the following day the same Senate took its seat in the place of judgment, on the bench, and ordered Joannes Versteverannus, a man of fluent speech, to address them.

units.la: Quippe non privatâ ambitione, non affectuum lubidine, non odio prædecessorum arduum molestumque judicandi munus in se recepisse, caeterum procerum suffragijs compulsos lubricum tribunal & præcipitia fori ingressos dicundo juri sacramentum fecisse. Placuisse scilicet patribus & post Archiduci justitium exui & intermissa amoto Senatu judicia repeti. Igitur conscientiæ rationem habituros daturosque operam, ut cultâ jurejurandi religione, officia judicum præstent.
units.tr: He said that they had not undertaken the difficult and burdensome duty of judging out of private ambition, the lust of their feelings or hatred of their predecessors; rather, compelled by the votes of the nobles, they had entered the slippery tribunal and the precipitous court and had taken the oath to administer justice. It had evidently pleased the fathers, after the archduke's suspension of justice, to strip off the old Senate and to resume the interrupted trials. They would therefore take account of their conscience and take care that, with the due observance of the sanctity of the oath, they discharged the duties of judges.

units.la: Tum judicium de more prolatum bimestribusque fermè ferijs ardente Seirio lites sterère.
units.tr: Then judgment was pronounced as usual, and during the almost two-month holidays they let lawsuits lie while the summer heat raged.

units.la: Post Gubernatoris Matthiæ rescripto plures eligendi potestate Delegatis Ordinum factâ, Hesselus Aysma, Douwo Burmania, Barthius Idzaerda Jurisperiti in Senatorium ordinem cooptati eorumque nomina Matthiam ad Gubernatorem transmissa, actis publicis inserta. Mox tolerandis per provincias religionibus à Matthia Austrio & concilio Status leges scriptæ, ne modestia supplicantis populi veterem ad contumaciam & dissoluta morum istâ Reipub. infantiâ rediret.
units.tr: After Governor Matthias's rescript, the power of choosing several more was granted to the deputies of the Estates, and Hesselus Aysma, Duwo Burmania and Bartius Idzaerda, jurists, were co-opted into the senatorial order. Their names were sent by Matthias to the Governor and inserted in the public records. Soon afterwards, Matthias of Austria and the Council of State enacted written laws on tolerating religions throughout the provinces, lest the people, humbly petitioning, should return to their old obstinacy and dissolute manners in this infancy of the republic.

units.la: Ijs rescriptum fuit.
units.tr: These were the terms given to them.

units.la: Ut omnium injuriarum quæ è diversitate religionis post Pacificationem Gandavensem natæ essent, oblivio foret. Religio libera inturbataque esset. Romana Catholica, ut per Hallandiam & Zelandiam, ita reliquas provincias admitte-
units.tr: That there should be an amnesty for all injuries arising from the difference of religion since the Pacification of Ghent. Religion should be free and undisturbed. The Roman Catholic religion should be admitted in the other provinces as it is in Holland and Zeeland.

units.la: mitteretur. In Reformatâ idem valeret istiqué profitendæ si 1000. familiæ se dedissent, locus assignaretur. In privata domesticaque religionis exercitia nemo inquireret, singulis libertas & pax esset. Alienos cœtus turbandis conventibus nemo frequentaret. Religiosi bonis suis, exceptis per Hollandiam & Zelandiam, quos Pacificatio Gandavensis excluserat, liberè fruerentur, dum aliter per Ordines generales statueretur. Famosos libellos nemo conficeret aut vulgaret. Conciones moderatæ essent. Miles teserarn religioni non usurparet. In causis matrimonialibus jus Pontificium valeret. Locis publicis ac sacris ægri ac scholares utriusque religionis promiscuè reciperentur. Dies festos è præscripto Catholicæ Romanæ religionis colerent, Esu carnium abstinerent. Utriusque religionis publicorum munerum ac dignitatum capaces essent. Indici legitimo quisque se sisteret. Accusationes licitæ forent, nemo temerè litigaret. Leges ac statuta ab utrisque modò patriæ amantibus perscriberentur. Ii jus dicerent, politiam & oppida curarent. Nemo jus dicentibus curantibusque publica molestiam crearet. Edictis, mandatis & rescriptis Matthiae Gubernatoris & Concilii Status, universi singulique parerent. Iuri patrio hæc statuta non derogarent. Quæ ferè, à Matthia Austrio & Concilio Status Antwerpiæ xii. Iul. in acta relata & per Frisiam mense sequenti publicata.
units.tr: In the Reformed religion the same should hold, and if a thousand families should declare themselves for it, a place would be assigned to them. No one should inquire into private and domestic exercises of religion; each person should have liberty and peace. No one should frequent the meetings of others so as to disturb their gatherings. Ecclesiastics should enjoy their goods freely, except in Holland and Zeeland, from which the Pacification of Ghent had excluded them, until the matter was otherwise settled by the General Estates. No one should compose or publish defamatory pamphlets. Sermons should be moderate. A soldier should not usurp the pulpit for his religion. In matrimonial causes the Papal law should hold. In public and sacred places, the sick and scholars of either religion should be received indiscriminately. They should keep feast days as prescribed by the Roman Catholic religion and abstain from eating meat. People of either religion should be eligible for public offices and dignities. Each should appear before the lawful judge. Accusations should be permitted, but no one should litigate rashly. Laws and statutes should be drawn up by men of either religion who love their country alone. Those men should administer justice and look after the government and the towns. No one should cause trouble to those who administer justice and govern public affairs. Everyone, both collectively and individually, should obey the edicts, mandates and rescripts of Matthias the Governor and of the Council of State. These statutes should not derogate from the law of the fatherland. These were nearly the terms recorded by Matthias of Austria and the Council of State at Antwerp on 12 July, and published in Friesland the following month.

units.la: Notat M. Heymannus publicato Leovardiæ Religionis Edicto à reformatæ religionis ministro xxii. August. in Jacobæorum fano habitam concionem fuisse populumque ab Anno cIↄ. Iↄ. lxvi. ad intermissa sacra haud pridem ab exilio redeuntem audiendis sermonibus sua desideria innovasse. Idem addit, ex pacto Magistratum inter & Jacobæos inito, ita conventum fuisse recenteque Edicti reverentiâ & simul memoriâ, stabilem in religione concordiam etsi, ut memorabo, non diuturnam moderatis partibus ostentasse,
units.tr: M. Heymannus notes that when the Edict on Religion was published at Leeuwarden, a sermon was preached on 22 August by a minister of the Reformed religion in the church of the Jacobites, and that from the year 1566 the people, returning from exile to hear sermons after the sacred services had lately been interrupted, had renewed their desires. He adds that by agreement between the magistrates and the Jacobites it was so arranged, and that, with reverence for the recent Edict and at the same time with memory of it, they showed a stable concord in religion, though, as I shall relate, not a lasting one among the moderate parties.

units.la: Sunt qui tradant, recrudescente post defectionem Austriaci bello, religionis dissidium civili tum maxumæ concordiæ obfuisse indignantibus Pontificijs, ex Statuto Ordinum & Matthiæ Gubernatoris Reformatam profitentibus fana ac sacella assignari populumque jure & si fato licuisset, sub unius Principis imperio connexum communione publicorum locorum modestis sacrorum exercitijs interesse. Itaque factum esse, ut Magistratuum ex Pontificiâ factione contumaciâ inritata plebes templa ac fana occuparet ejectoque sacerdotum cœtu & sublatis Pontificum sacris, negato ex pervicaciâ beneficio per vim frueretur. Inde asperatis religionibus inimicitias concivium natas animosque ante fœdus Gandavense concordes & Hispanorum dominationibus infestos extrema consilia ac sæpe arma induisse. Tum tota ac circos excubijs obseptos adversasque partes civitatibus ac oppidis expulsas, meliore illorum causâ quorum validior fuisset. Sic ex civili discordiâ incerta & lubrica Magistratum imperia profluxisse, adeò invalidâ autoritate ut moderata suadentium non proficeret. Deinde validis populi rebus & amotis partium Ducibus, ne tum quidem hoc fati beneficium civilem concordiam isti temporum ætati obvenisse, criminantibus adhuc Pontificijs, Philippi prospera publicam servitutem, res fœderis securdas opprel-
units.tr: Some write that when the war with Austria broke out again, the division of religion was harmful to the civil concord, which had then been greatest; the Papists were indignant that, by the decree of the Estates and of Governor Matthias, churches and chapels were assigned to those who professed the Reformed religion, and that the people, bound together under one prince's rule, would, if fate had allowed, have shared in the common use of public places for their moderate religious exercises. So it came about that the common people, their anger roused by the contumacy of the magistrates of the Papist faction, occupied the temples and churches; and, with the company of priests ejected and the rites of the Papists abolished, they enjoyed by force a privilege that had been refused them through obstinacy. Hence, with religions embittered, enmities arose among citizens, and the minds that had been united before the Ghent covenant and hostile to Spanish domination adopted extreme counsels and often arms. Then the whole city and its districts were blockaded by guards, and the opposing parties were expelled from cities and towns, though the cause of those who were stronger was the better. Thus from civil discord arose uncertain and slippery governments of the magistrates, with authority so weak that the advice of moderate men achieved nothing. Then, when the popular affairs had grown strong and the party leaders had been removed, even at that time this blessing of fate did not bring civil concord to that age, the Papists still accusing that the prosperity of Philip meant public servitude and that the affairs of the covenant were being threatened with oppression of the Roman religion.

units.la: Notat M. Heymannus ... oppressionem Romanæ religioni comminari. Itaque frænandis seditionibus urbes passim præsidijs emunitas, magis ex civilium furorum quam hostilis potentiæ metu, cujus incrementa non tam ex magnitudine Philippi quam intestinâ dissensione profluxisse clarissimi Scriptores annotavere. Adeò difficile erat, etiam asperrimis temporibus & affectâ tam graviter libertate, publica odia publicis utilitatibus postponere populumque opinionibus divisum & fovendis pertinacem salubritate legum coërcere. Eædem quoque decreto Ordinum reliquas in provincias missæ, pro temperie civilium animorum murmura aut assensum inquieti populi invenere, etiam tum criminantis provinciarum Ordines levissimæ societatum externarum famæ auscultantes subdolis Principum artibus fortunam publici fœderis exponere. Quippe alij Germaniæ & Anglorum auxilia, alij Galliarum societatem in Alençonio regis fratre, immodestius affectabant patrociniaque religionibus & privatis simul affectibus ervidissima per studia quærebantur.
units.tr: M. Heymannus notes ... Therefore, to curb the seditions, cities were everywhere fortified with garrisons, more from fear of civil frenzies than of hostile power, whose growth, as the most distinguished writers have remarked, arose not so much from the greatness of Philip as from internal dissension. So difficult was it, even in the harshest times and with liberty so gravely injured, to put public hatreds after public advantages, and to restrain a people divided in opinions and stubborn in their partisanship by the salutary force of laws. The same measures, sent by decree of the Estates into the remaining provinces, found murmurs or assent among an unquiet people according to the temper of civil minds; and the provincial Estates too, accusing one another, listened to the very slight rumours of foreign alliances and, by the devious arts of princes, exposed the fortune of the public covenant. For some sought the aid of Germany and England, others, more immoderately, sought an alliance with France through the king's brother, Alençon, and in pursuing these, patronage was sought most ardently through studies serving both religion and private passions.

units.la: Indignante Elisabethâ Anglicâ fluctuantes provincias & suo regno innexas propioribus Galliarum fœderibus implicari.
units.tr: Elizabeth of England, indignant that the wavering provinces, bound to her realm, should be entangled in the nearer treaties with France.

units.la: Quare non dissimulatâ æmulatione ad Henricum III. Galliæ regem litteras dedit, quibus obtestabatur, sua in populum Belgicum inclinatione non imaginem imperij, non suspectas pactiones involvi, caterum eo spectare, ut divulsæ à Philippo provinciæ ad Principem suum redeant ipsaq; regnum suum procuratâ vicina gentis quiete firmet. Igitur ferre non posse dubys temporibus Angliæ incommodo provincias Galliarum societatibus arctius obstringi, quarum secretum stabiliendæ per Belgicam dominationi inservire posset, fato suo & adultis hostium viribus, manifestâ cum imbecillitate luctantem. Caterum HENRICUS Rex fraterna non sua consilia captæ actioni obtendebat, quæ non prensandis imperij occasionibus, sed conciliandæ Regem inter & subditos paci instituretur. Rediturum quippe ad saniora PHILIPPUM, si senserit, populum externis auxilijs sublevari esseque qui non ferant, gentem extingui olim Burgundicæ domui & vicinis suis fidam.
units.tr: Therefore, without disguising their rivalry, they wrote to Henry III, king of France, letters in which they entreated him that their inclination towards the Belgian people did not involve the image of empire or suspicious pacts, but aimed rather at this: that the provinces, torn away from Philip, should return to their own prince, and that he himself, by securing the neighbouring people's quiet, would strengthen his own kingdom. Therefore they could not bear that, in these doubtful times to England's disadvantage, the provinces should be bound more tightly by French alliances, whose secret purpose might serve to establish French domination over Belgium, struggling with its own weakness in the face of its fate and the mature forces of its enemies. But King Henry, for his part, put forward brotherly counsels rather than his own as the pretext for the action undertaken, which was intended not to seize opportunities for empire but to bring peace between the king and his subjects. For Philip would return to saner counsels, he said, if he saw the people sustained by foreign aid; and there were some who would not bear that a nation long faithful to the house of Burgundy and to its neighbours should be extinguished.

units.la: Legati quoque Elisabethæ ad Ordines missi, offensum reginæ animum obnuntiavere, velut ferentis indignius reciproca Belgicæ & Anglorum fœdera medio in cursu rerum Gallicis artibus interverti. Igitur de remittendo in Germaniam Casimiro, de renuntiando fœdere multa acerbè afferebantur, excusantibus Ordinum Delegatis ultimâ necessitate ad implorandam Gallorum societatem compulsos, lubrica provinciarum fatalibus legibus permisisse. Quippè Alençonium mobilis juventæ & ut principes ferè solent, gloriæ avidum, quæ è bello speretur. Potuisse eum repudiatâ aut retardatâ societate in partes Austriaci transfire, hoc tantum quarentem, ut ostendat regiam indolem otij ac torporis impatientem tractandis armis destinari. Igitur non Angliæ, non Galliæ, non Germaniæ, non ullarum gentium rationem habitam, modo hoc ageretur ut in angustum redactis auxilium adesset. Ruinæ proximus alieni fulcimenti eguisse.
units.tr: The envoys of Elizabeth, too, sent to the Estates, announced the queen's offended mind, as if she bore it more indignantly that the reciprocal covenants of the Belgians and the English were, in the middle of their course, being overturned by French devices. Therefore many bitter things were said about sending Casimir back to Germany and about renouncing the alliance, while the deputies of the Estates excused themselves, saying that they had been driven by the last necessity to implore the French alliance, and that the wavering provinces had yielded to fatal laws. For Alençon was of a restless youth and, as princes generally are, eager for the glory that might be hoped for from war. He could, if the alliance had been rejected or delayed, have passed over to the side of Austria, seeking only this, that he might show a royal nature impatient of leisure and torpor and destined for the handling of arms. Therefore no account had been taken of England, France, Germany or any other nation; the only aim was that help should be present for a people reduced to straits. Those close to ruin had needed another's support.

units.la: Creditum fuit rerum peritis Ordines, ut ante Elisabethæ societatem amplexos, ita Alençonij respuere noluisse, parandis majoribus auxilijs & ne Belgicæ imperium, per æmulationes concertantium Principum, in unius arbitrium & simul dominatum concederet.
units.tr: Men experienced in affairs believed that the Estates, as they had earlier embraced the alliance with Elizabeth, were unwilling to reject Alençon, so that they could raise larger aid and so that the rule of the Belgian provinces would not pass, through the rivalries of contending princes, into the power and dominion of one man.

units.la: Ita pacatis ægrè Elisabethæ Legatis cum Alençonio conventum.
units.tr: So, with the Elizabethan envoys having with difficulty pacified the Estates, an agreement was reached with Alençon.

units.la: Vt decem peditum Gallicæ gentis, equitum duo millia suo ære & stipendijs haberet eaque Ordinibus provinciarum in trimestre pro auxilijs forent. Pace quoque cum AUSTRIACO aut ipso rege intrà mensem Augustum proxumum factâ, tria peditum millia, quingentos equites securitati provinciarum aleret præstitorumque auxiliorum ratione Defensor Belgicæ libertatis diceretur. Fœdus cum ELISABETHA, NAVARRAEO, CASIMIRO aliisque procuraret belloque socijs Ordinum inferendo abstinaret. Conventio hæc rata, & perpetua foret ORDINESQUE nisi bellum in causâ Religionis sit, reciprocis auxiliorum pactis ALENÇONIO se obligarent. Belli potior administratio ALENÇONIO, si ad exercitum esset, permitteretur, eo alibi agente, Ordinum Duci cederet. Civile Reipub. regimen penes ORDINES aut eorum Præfectos pro more esset. ORDINES & ALENÇONIUS nulla fœdera præterquam utriusque assensu inirent. Novum Principem aut Protectorem eligituri ORDINES ALENÇONIUM cæteris anteferrent eaque de re finito bello intra trimestre conventum agerent. Tria quoque oppida Quesnacum, Landrechios & Bavesium pignori & reficiendis saucijs ALENÇONIO assignarent. Reliqua oppida trans Mosam sita, & per Alençonium expugnata, si exempta Fœderi fuissent, Alençonio & hæredibus, Fœderi comprehensa Ordinibus cederent, dedititia utriusque obvenirent. Pignori vero data liberatâ apud Alençonium fide & restituto ære ad Ordines redirent. ALENÇONIUS JOANNEM AUSTRIACUM hostem declararet daretque operam, ne Gallicis auxilijs quoquo modo AUSTRIACUS juvaretur. Pacem cum Hispano & cum ijs, qui istarum partium forent, præterquam communicatis consilijs, ORDINES & ALENÇONIUS non sancirent eaque honesta & utilis foret. Oppida ALENÇONIO assignata suis legibus & militari ab ALENÇONIO disciplinâ haberentur, ne Gallici præsidij insolentiâ per querimonias provincialium novum fœdus ac speciosa conventio infirmaretur.
units.tr: That he should maintain ten thousand French foot and two thousand horse at his own cost and pay, and that these should be lent to the Estates of the provinces for three months as aid. Also, once peace was made with the Austrian, or with the king himself, before next August, he should keep three thousand foot and five hundred horse for the security of the provinces, and be called Defender of Belgian liberty in return for the aid given. He should arrange an alliance with Elizabeth, Navarre, Casimir and others, and refrain from making war on the allies of the Estates. This agreement was to be ratified and perpetual, and the Estates should bind themselves to Alençon by reciprocal pacts of aid, unless the war was over religion. The chief direction of the war should be given to Alençon, if he was with the army, and when he was elsewhere it should pass to the Duke of the Estates. The civil government of the Republic should rest with the Estates or their magistrates, as was customary. The Estates and Alençon should make no alliances except with the consent of both. The Estates, when they were to choose a new prince or protector, should prefer Alençon to all others, and about this they would hold a conference within three months after the war ended. Also they should assign to Alençon three towns, Quesnoy, Landrecies and Bavay, as a pledge and for the repair of the wounded. The other towns beyond the Meuse, taken by Alençon, if they were excluded from the treaty, should go to Alençon and his heirs; if included, they should go to the Estates, and surrendered places should belong to both. Those given as pledge should return to the Estates when Alençon's faith was discharged and the money repaid. Alençon should declare John of Austria an enemy and take care that the Austrian was in no way aided by French troops. The Estates and Alençon should not make peace with the Spaniard or with those of his party except after consultation together, and such peace should be honourable and useful. The towns assigned to Alençon should be governed by their own laws and by military discipline from Alençon, so that the insolence of the French garrison should not, by the complaints of the provincials, weaken the new treaty and the specious agreement.

units.la: Hæc XIII. Aug. signata ac in Frisios post missa Societati Germaniæ æquiores, non læto rumore mobilem populum affecere.
units.tr: This was signed on 13 August, and afterwards sent to the Frisians, and to the Society of Germany, which was more fair-minded; it did not please the fickle people with joyful report.

units.la: Indignantem nec falso se alienis arbitrijs (quippe per superioris Belgicæ Ordines ea res acta dicebatur) in novos dominos & suis moribus sæpè contrarios transferri exutumque prisci sociétatibus nova per fœdera, nova servitia & clientelas Principum accipere. Sollicitata Germaniæ & Anglorum auxilia minimâque Trans-rhenanarum gentium ratione habitâ, superaddi quæsitis socijs Principem, Germanicæ Anglicæque; societatis æmulatorem & Pontificiâ religione superstitiosus imbutum. Neque placuisse Legato provinciæ novarum rerum molitiones antiquis semper Burgundiæ societatibus velari Galliæque Legatos prensando fœderi, mutuas Galliæ Belgicæque gentium cognationes, communia instituta tacitis in Trans-rhenanos odijs allegasse. Sic scilicet, ut antè prævaricatione MAXIMILIANI atque CAROLI Cæsarum, (qui incrementa Burgundicæ domus damno Romani imperij quæsissent) à Germaniæ antiquissimâ societate separatos, ita nunc ab eadem longius divelli Frisiosque specie fœderum & conventionum externis imperijs subesse,
units.tr: The people were indignant, and not without reason, that they were handed over, against their own wishes, to new masters, by other men's decisions (for it was said that the matter had been settled by the Estates of Upper Belgium), and that, stripped of their old alliances, they received new covenants, new servitudes and the clientage of princes. The aid of Germany and England was sought, and with little regard for the peoples across the Rhine, a prince was to be added to the allies, a rival of the German and English alliance, and imbued with Papist superstition.
