Nor did it please the Legate of the province that the new undertakings should be veiled under the ancient alliances of Burgundy, and the envoys of France, by seeking the treaty, alleged the mutual kinship of the French and Belgian peoples and their common institutions, with hidden hatred of those across the Rhine. Thus, just as earlier, through the betrayal of the Emperors Maximilian and Charles (who had sought the growth of the house of Burgundy at the expense of the Roman Empire), they had been separated from the most ancient alliance with Germany, so now they were to be torn further away from it, and the Frisians, under the pretext of treaties and agreements, were subject to foreign rule.

units.la: Scribit F. Nicolaus, Staurios solenni sacramento societatem Austriaci tum ejurasse signatisque eâ de re actis, communnem concordiam machinationibus partium opposuisse. Igitur quantum ægritudinis ex Austriaci defectione & Gallico Alenconij fœdere habebatur, tantum econtra gaudij percrebescens pacis falsa credulis mentibus adferebat, quam Legati Cæsaris, Galliarum & Angliæ allaturi provincijs credebantur. Ferebatur quippe Austriacus ejus ineundæ mandatum ex Hispania accepisse Gemblacensisque victoriæ gloriâ, velut egregio fine, belli initia & mox incerta clausurus. Cæterum Ordines certam pacem, nec dolis involutam Legatos poscebant, ac ut solidâ conventione æterno silentio memoria priorum rerum obsignaretur. Acta quoque & decreta Ordinum, MATTHIAE Gubernatoris, & CONCILII STATUS rata essent, AUSTRIACUSQUE Belgicæ finibus excessurus, otyus oppida, castella, commeatum fœderatis provinciis restitueret. MATTHIAE quoque AUSTRIO imperium prorogaretur Ordinumque jus & simul Gaudavense Fœdus integrum foret. Religionis negotium proxumo Ordinum conventu definiretur bonaque per Burgundiam ex Gandavensi conventione dominis suis redderentur. Captivis utrinque dimissis, BURANUS ex Hispania in Belgicam remitteretur, MATTHIAQUE AUSTRIO imperio cedente, provinciarum Præfectus à PHILIPPO rege assensu ORDINUM crearetur. Fœdere quoque, si quod cum AUSTRIACO iniretur, ANGLIAE REGINA, DUX ANDIUM, NAVARRAEUS, ac CASIMIRVS comprehenderentur.
units.tr: Father Nicolaus writes that the Staurios had then renounced their alliance with the Austrian by solemn oath, and, with records drawn up on this matter, opposed common concord to the plots of the parties. Hence, as much sorrow as there was from the Austrian's defection and Alençon's French treaty, so much joy, growing on the other side, brought to credulous minds the false hope of peace, which the envoys of the Emperor, of France and of England were thought about to bring to the provinces. For it was reported that the Austrian had received from Spain a mandate to make this agreement, intending to end the beginning of the war, and soon its uncertain course, with the glory of the victory at Gembloux as a fine conclusion. The Estates, however, demanded from the envoys a certain peace, not entangled in deceits, and that by a firm agreement the memory of past events should be sealed with eternal silence. The acts and decrees of the Estates, of Governor Matthias and of the Council of State, should also be ratified, and the Austrian, on leaving the borders of Belgium, should restore idle towns, castles and supplies to the allied provinces. The rule of Matthias should also be extended to Don John, and the rights of the Estates and at the same time the Treaty of Ghent should remain intact. The question of religion should be settled at the next assembly of the Estates, and the goods of Burgundy should be restored to their owners according to the Ghent agreement. Prisoners should be released on both sides, Bourgogne should be sent back from Spain to Belgium, and when Matthias gave up power to the Austrian, the governor of the provinces should be appointed by King Philip with the consent of the Estates. Also, if any treaty were made with the Austrian, the Queen of England, the Duke of Anjou, Navarre and Casimir should be included in it.

units.la: Econtra Austriacus suspectis dilationibus conventionem trahebat speciosumque pacis desiderium apud Legatos obtendens bellum meditabatur. Quare inritis fœcialium studijs & infructuosâ Rudolphi Cæsaris, tum Galliæ Angliæque regum intercessione, arma partium strepere, quæ circa Isalam flumen perdomandis Austriaci per Trans-Isulaniam præsidijs Georgius Lalainius circumferebat. Ordinum vero castra in finibus Brabantiæ ad Rimenantum posita conciendis colligendisque auxilijs, quæ Casimirus Elector ad duodena millia in interiora provinciarum conducebat.
units.tr: On the other side, the Austrian, suspecting delays, dragged out the agreement, and while putting forward a specious desire for peace before the envoys, he was planning war. Therefore, with the efforts of the heralds coming to nothing, and the intercession of the Emperor Rudolph, and then of the kings of France and England, proving fruitless, the arms of the parties clashed. Around the river Yssel, George Lalaing led garrisons to subdue the Austrian's forces across Overijssel. The camp of the Estates, placed in the borders of Brabant at Rimenant, was busy gathering and assembling aid, which Elector Casimir was bringing into the interior of the provinces, to about twelve thousand men.

units.la: F. Nicolaus scribit, eum haud procul Frisiorum finibus v. Jul. octo equitum millia & quadraginta peditum signa Drentinos per agros duxisse eundemque exercitum, etsi perarmatum & stipendijs gravem, procerum spei & conditioni temporum non satisfecisse.
units.tr: Father Nicolaus writes that not far from the borders of Friesland, on 5 July, he led eight thousand horse and forty companies of foot through the fields of Drenthe, and that this army, though fully armed and burdensome with pay, did not satisfy the hopes of the nobles or the condition of the times.

units.la: Austriacus quoque cum exercitu in propinquo gloriæque majoris spem alens se ad prælium parabat. Igitur Ordinum castra etsi multo operre vallata, oppugnare cum omnibus copijs constituit, quæ Italicis auxilijs auctæ triginta armatorum millibus adæquabantur. Rebus quoque gerendis Alexandrum Farnesium, Octavium Gonzagam equitatui præfecit reliquisque proceribus, quos peritissimos belli & Philippi militiam diu secutos in comitatu habebat, alia castrorum munia & Legionum regimen assignavit. Quare ordinata acie Prid. Kalend. Aug. pugnæ consilium iniit præmissisque, qui prætentarent, reliquum exercitum recto itinere confertim progredi jussit.
units.tr: The Austrian too, with his army nearby and nourishing hopes of greater glory, was preparing for battle. Therefore, although the camp of the Estates was fortified with a great rampart, he resolved to attack it with all his forces, which, increased by Italian auxiliaries, amounted to thirty thousand armed men. He put Alexander Farnese and Octavio Gonzaga in command of the cavalry, and assigned the other duties of the camp and the command of the legions to the rest of the nobles, whom he had in his company, very skilled in war and long followers of Philip's service. So, with his line drawn up, on 30 July he formed a plan of battle, and sent forward men to test the enemy, and ordered the rest of the army to advance in a straight line, in close order.

units.la: Bossuvius vero, qui partes Ordinum cum imperio tuebatur, re per exploratores cognita quo insultum sustineret, castrorum latera validioribus præteuturis munivit dispositisque excubitoribus, qui de adventu hostium subindè nuntiarent, sexcentos schlopetarios per insidias collocavit. cIↄ. Io. cavit. In primâ quoque acie constitutis demandavit ut ingruente Austriaco pedem referrent signoque fugæ aut simulati pavoris dato, eum circâ locum gradum figerent, quem schopetarijs asservandum præcesperat. Igitur impetu per Austriacum in castra Ordinum facto qui in fronte exercitus erant tamdiu ex condicto recessere donec Austriacus in fœderatorum equitum ordines & quidem levis armaturæ provectus eorum virtute sisteretur, quos Bossuvius egregio Ducis exemplo saucijs fatigatisque suffectos ad dimicandum hortabatur.
units.tr: Bossu, however, who defended the cause of the Estates with full command, learning through scouts where the attack would fall, fortified the sides of the camp with stronger outworks, placed sentries who would report the enemy's approach from time to time, and secretly posted six hundred musketeers. He also ordered the men stationed in the front line that, when the Austrian advanced, they should fall back, and, giving a signal of flight or pretended panic, should hold their ground at the place they had been told to guard for the musketeers. So, when the Austrian made his assault on the camp of the Estates, those at the front of the army, by agreement, withdrew for so long, until the Austrian, carried forward into the ranks of the allied cavalry and light-armed troops, was halted by their courage. Bossu, by the noble example of his commander, urged these men, who had been replaced after the wounded and exhausted, to fight on.

units.la: Fortiter quippe pugnando manes sociorum qui ad Gemblacum occubuerant, ulturos consulturosque suæ & simul publicæ incolumitati, quam in illorum dexteris illius diei fortuna posuisset. Respicerent patriam, conjuges, liberos & potiorem privato pignore libertatem, quam Austriacus provinciarum hostis primum dolo post armis impetisset. Itaque honestius fore generosa virtute benignitatem fati lacessere, quam aut fuga aut ignavia victos immoderati victoris lubidini ac sævitiæ servire. Sic quippe cum socijs contrà datam fidem actum mactatosque victimarum ritu fortes viros præclara [corpora poscenti patriæ & furoribus hostium immolasse. Voluisse scilicet, exemplo ad mortem & simul gloriam præire tacito voto, quo superstites imitarentur.
units.tr: For by fighting bravely they would avenge the shades of their comrades who had fallen at Gembloux, and would secure their own safety and that of the public, which the fortune of that day had placed in their right hands. They should look to their country, their wives, their children, and a liberty more precious than any private pledge, which the Austrian, enemy of the provinces, had first attacked by treachery, and then by arms. It would therefore be more honourable to challenge the kindness of fate with noble courage than, defeated by flight or cowardice, to serve the lust and cruelty of an immoderate conqueror. For thus, breaking faith with their allies, they would be butchered and sacrificed like victims, and would offer brave men, with splendid bodies, to their country demanding them and to the rage of the enemy. They wished, of course, to go before to death, and at the same time to glory, by a silent vow, which the survivors would imitate.

units.la: Quare Austriacus ab exercitu fœderato, cujus ordines luxare annitebatur, tandem repulsus, magnâque suorum clade acceptâ simulque sauciorum agmen trahens in fines Namurci se recepit, ubi Gabriel Cerbellion regio sumptu validam jam antè munitionem exstruxerat. Octo horarum prælium fuisse autores tradunt ipsosque pugnantes, velut ipso Solis æstu inflammatos, acriore pugnâ conflixisse. Sic vulnus Gemblacensi prælio Fœderi illatum clade hostium tum pensatum ipsequeAustriacus jam antè fortunâ intemperanter usus & fiduciæ velut certus, cum fatorum legibus acerbâ mentis ægritudine expostulavit.
units.tr: Therefore the Austrian, at last driven back by the allied army, whose ranks he had struggled to break, and having received great slaughter of his men, and at the same time drawing the column of the wounded, withdrew into the borders of Namur, where Gabriel Cerbellon, at royal expense, had already built a strong fortification earlier. Writers report that the battle lasted eight hours, and that the combatants themselves, as if inflamed by the very heat of the sun, fought with greater fury. Thus the wound inflicted on the alliance at Gembloux was then balanced by the slaughter of the enemy; and the Austrian, who had already used fortune intemperately and as if certain of his confidence, complained with bitter vexation of mind against the laws of fate.

units.la: Mox inritâ apud Frisios novarum Collationum ac Vectigalium lege, exactiones tributorum repetitæ decretumque à Matthia Gubernatore, Vt menstruo stipendio fœderatis copijs pendendo æs in mutuum à locupletibus sub usurâ peteretur creditisque in publicum pecunijs omne juris beneficium adversum fiscum & quoscunque creditores valeret. Hoc etiam additum, ut publicarum Collationum census pignori esset actioque in eum retardatâ solutione competeret. Cæterum ut omnia apud populum angusta è diuturno bello erant, ita invalida pignorum censebantur, non cessante Matthia Gubernatore ultimæ necessitatis legem exigendis pecunijs allegare.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, the new law on tolls and taxes, which had been annulled among the Frisians, was revived, and the collection of taxes was resumed. Governor Matthias also decreed that money for paying the allied troops each month should be borrowed from the wealthy, and that once the money had been put to public use, every legal privilege should apply against the treasury and against any creditors. It was further added that the revenue from the public tolls should stand as security, and that an action would lie against it if payment were delayed. Yet, since everything among the people was narrow after the long war, these securities were considered weak. Governor Matthias did not stop urging the law of extreme necessity to justify demanding the money.

units.la: Lustrandum scilicet exercitum esse qui nisi stipendia accipiat, nec sub signis nec sacramentis retineri queat. Ita disciplinam militiæ exuturum laxaturumque frena licentiæ, quo ostendat se animam, se sanguinem, se virtutem & pericula non partium studijs sed stipendijs obligasse. His sacramenta, his fidem stare, si deficiant, ex justo milite transfugam aut desertorem fatura. Neque posse solis Belgicarum provinciarum nervis omne belli momentum trahi necessumque esse, ut trans Rhenum populi olim jure Principis, nunc sacramento fœderis socij & fertilium terrarum cultores subsidia afflictis locent. Nisi aut mavelint Frisii sub illorum dominatum recidere, quos exleges & hostes habuissent, aut auxiliarem Imperij ac Gallia exercitum spectare, sacrilegis & provincialium spolijs fe pascentem. Ita patriam; ita dulcissima pignorum intuerentur, ac ii officii non nisi cum miseratione & cura queant, quâ cavendum sit, ne quid oppressa & sensim se erigens libertas, ne sociale jus quid patiatur.
units.tr: "Clearly the army must be reviewed, for unless it receives its pay it cannot be kept under its standards or its oaths. Thus it will strip off military discipline and loosen the reins of licence, so that it may show that it has bound its life, its blood, its courage and its dangers not to party zeal but to wages. Its oaths and its loyalty depend on these; if they fail, it will turn from a lawful soldier into a deserter or a runaway. Nor can the whole weight of the war be carried by the strength of the Belgian provinces alone. It is necessary that the peoples across the Rhine, once subject to a prince by law but now allies by the oath of the league and cultivators of fertile lands, should lend aid to the afflicted. Unless the Frisians would rather fall back under the rule of those whom they once held as outlaws and enemies, or look to the auxiliary army of the Empire and of France, feeding itself on the sacrilegious plunder of the provinces. Let them look to their country and to their dearest pledges in this way; and let them, who alone can do this duty with pity and care, take heed lest freedom, crushed yet slowly raising itself up, suffer any harm to its common right."

units.la: Igitur conquirendis exercituum stipendijs Frisij in mensem xxxii. M. Groningenses & Omlandi x x. Transisulani xiii. Drentini & Tenc teri vi. Carolaeorum M. pendere rogati, adeo efficaci Matthiae praescripto ut decreto aeri omne subsidium offerrent. Hoc vero volebant Frisij, ut Matthias Gubernator de commodissimo corrogandae pecuniae modo disponeret & aut è pensionibus Biltanorum ac Vectigalium agrorum, quae x l. M. aequarent, anticipandis divenditiue maritimis Biltae agris aut coenobiorum praedijs reditibusque publico applicatis, petendum decerneret. Cogi scilicet Biltanos posse, ut pensiones ad Martini & Petri ad Cathedram solvendas extemplo colligant, urgente publica necessitate quae legem non ferret. Neque absonum esse, distrahi maritima & Biltano littori nova alluvione adjecta aut pacisci cum coenobiorum rectoribus, ut sustentandae vitae annuum nacti, jure & possessione monasticorum bonorum cedant luxuique & malis moribus applicata publicos in usus & subsidia provinciae converti sinant.
units.tr: Therefore, to raise the pay of the armies, the Frisians were asked to pay 32,000 for a month: the people of Groningen and Ommelanden 20,000, the Transisulani 13,000, the Drenthe and Tenterden people 6,000, and 1,000 Carolus. They were so moved by Matthias's proclamation that they offered all aid in money by decree. The Frisians, however, wanted Governor Matthias to arrange the most convenient way of raising the money, and to decree that it be sought either by anticipating the pensions of the people of Bilt and the revenues from the tilled lands, which amounted to 40,000, or by selling off the seaward fields of Bilt, or the estates and incomes of the monasteries taken over for public use. It was clear that the people of Bilt could be compelled to gather their pensions at once, to be paid at the feasts of St Martin and St Peter's Chair, since public necessity, which knows no law, demanded it. Nor was it absurd to sell the seaward lands, added by new alluvion along the shore of Bilt, or to bargain with the heads of the monasteries: once they had secured an annual sum for their support, they might give up the right and possession of monastic goods, and allow what had been given to luxury and bad morals to be turned to public uses and the relief of the province.

units.la: Itaque illustri ad Rimenantum clade fractis Austriaci viribus, qui auxilia suis etiam trans Rhenum ac circa Ifalam, destinaverat, Lalainius Camporum urbe capta, castra Daventriam movit, quae tribus Germanicae legionis cohortibus tenebatur. Foeminarum quoque & scortorum non minor numerus, tanto parciore sensim annona, quanto pluribus nutriendis destinaretur. Quare praesidium instantis obsidij metuens & quo provisis populi commeatibus pro arbitrio uteretur, civitatem exarmavit & ne pronis in partes Ordinum civium animis Lalainius per interna auxilia juvaretur. Is quippe nova munitione per Gualterum Hegemannum, haud procul ingressu Velaviae extructa, auxiliares Hollandorum copias ad urbem praemiserat reliquosque pedestrium copiarum ductores Vlietium, Vedam, Oenonem Grovensteinium, Hermannum Olthovium & Cornelium Gallum propero itinere subsequi jusserat. Unde praesidiarij necdum firmatis castris impressionem in obsidentes fecere, quos patentibus adhuc campis expositos, non lorica castrorum sed arma & virtus tutabantur.
units.tr: Accordingly, after the Austrian's forces had been broken by the famous defeat at Rimenant, Lalaing, who had earlier sent auxiliaries across the Rhine and around the Yssel, captured the town of Camp and moved his camp to Deventer, which was held by three cohorts of the German legion. There was no small number of women and prostitutes there too, and the food supply was gradually growing scarcer, the more mouths there were to feed. Therefore the garrison, fearing a siege that was coming and wishing to use the supplies of the people as it pleased, disarmed the city, and to prevent Lalaing from being helped by internal allies, whose minds were inclined to the parties of the Orders. For he had sent the Hollander auxiliaries ahead to the city through Walter Hegeman, through a new fortification built not far from the entrance to Velp, and had ordered Vlict, Veda, Oenon Groenestein, Hermann Olthof and Cornelius Gallus to follow with the rest of the infantry commanders at speed. Hence the garrison, before its camp was secured, made a sortie against the besiegers; but these, exposed on the open fields, were protected not by the rampart of a camp but by their arms and courage.

units.la: Igitur praesidiarij in urbem retroacti, auxilia mox petiere, missō ad Austriacum Joanne Frederico Schonavio viro nobili & cohortis Tribuno, qui de statu urbis referret. Sonnoius vero, qui pro Lalainio rem gerebat, munitis justo opere castris, Noricam versus turrim, quae urbi propugnaculum erat, suffodi cuniculos jussit Geldricaque ac Transisulaniae auxilia conduci in castra praecepit. Quare & obsesi civium ope ac imbellis turbae, intuta maenium objecto vallo & adversis cuniculis firmavere. Sonnoius econtra, muri parte quae Noricae turri proxuma erat, machinis disjecta, ope fossorum terream molem castris praeduxit propinsque ad urbem suggressus sibi periculum creavit. Quippe eruptione per praesidiarios facta, ut fossorum plurimi trucidati ita impedimentum ducendo operi injectum, insimulato ab invidis Sonnoio quod officio providi ducis defuisset. Sed evicta invidie vir egregius cIↄ. Iↄ. & sui conscius coeptis institit, Noricæque turris summitatem tormen-torum ictibus disjecit.
units.tr: So the garrison was driven back into the city and soon sought reinforcements, sending to Austria Johann Friedrich Schonau, a nobleman and tribune of a cohort, to report on the state of the city. But Sonnoy, who was acting in Lalaing's place, fortified his camp with proper works and ordered mines to be dug toward the Noricus tower, which was the bulwark of the city, and instructed that auxiliaries from Gelderland and the Transisulani be brought into the camp. Therefore the besieged, with the help of the citizens and the unwarlike crowd, strengthened the walls by raising a rampart that could not be taken and by countermining. Sonnoy, on the other hand, having broken down with his machines the part of the wall nearest the Noricus tower, advanced his camp with an earthen mound made by the diggers and, approaching close to the city, created danger for himself. Indeed, when the garrison made a sortie, many of the diggers were slaughtered, and the work was hindered; Sonnoy was then accused by his envious rivals of having failed in the duty of a prudent commander. But the outstanding man overcame the envy, and, conscious of his purpose, pressed on with his undertaking, and with the blows of his cannon shattered the top of the Noricus tower.

units.la: Quamobrem obsessi ex periculo animos capessentes, alto silentio vix orto die prima in castra perrexere trucidatisque vigilibus, & plurium cæde edita pugnantes fortiter & post multitudine succrescentium copiarum obruti intra urbem regressi. Meilander vir fortis & egregiè dimicans isto conflictu ex obsessis confossus est. Tradunt autores tantam famuli erga Meilandrum fidem fuisse, ut conspecto cadaveri eximiâ in dominum pietate se superinjecerit percussoremque admiserit. Mox novis fœderatorum auxiliis, quæ Joannes Cornuttius, Joannes Bonga è Frisijs cæterique auxiliarium cohortium Tribuni ducebant, obsessæ civitatis res arctatæ, angusto sensim commeatu & quod inani auxiliorum & solvendæ obsidionis spe discors civitas traheretur. Quippe miles sacri nec profani abstinens sua in commoda ac luxum privatas res vertebat intestinâque dissensione & simul externa vi attritæ vires lacerabantur.
units.tr: Wherefore the besieged, taking courage from their danger, marched out to the camp in deep silence just before dawn, slaughtered the sentries, and after a great slaughter fought bravely; but at last, overwhelmed by the crowd of reinforcements that kept coming, they returned within the city. Meilander, a brave man who had fought outstandingly in that encounter, was stabbed among the besieged. Authors report that his servant showed such loyalty to Meilander that, on seeing the corpse, out of extraordinary devotion to his master he threw himself over it and let himself be struck down by the killer. Soon afterwards, with fresh reinforcements of the allies, which John Cornut, John Bonga from the Frisians and the other tribunes of the auxiliary cohorts led, the condition of the besieged city was pressed; the supply was gradually narrowed, and the city, divided by its vain hope of relief and of raising the siege, was dragged along. For the soldiers, abstaining from nothing sacred or profane, turned their private goods to their own advantage and luxury, and their strength was torn apart by internal dissension as well as by external force.

units.la: Quare Julius Dekama nuper Frisiæ Senator, Daventriæ tum agens ad Hectorem Dekama & Petrum Boymerum Colloniam Agrippinam litteras dedit, quibus de auxilijs ocyus mittendis moneri Austriacum petebat. Adhæc robusto præsidio sterilem annonam causabatur, urbemque arcto castrorum ambitu obleptam civium ac militaris præsidij discordiâ debilitari.
units.tr: Therefore Julius Dekama, lately a senator of Friesland, who was then at Deventer, wrote a letter to Hector Dekama and Peter Boymer at Cologne Agrippina, in which he asked that the emperor be urged to send auxiliaries more quickly. Besides this, he complained that the grain supply was barren with a strong garrison, and that the city, hemmed in by the narrow circle of the camps, was weakened by the discord of the citizens and the military garrison.

units.la: Cæterum Austriaci morte, etsi incertis adhuc rumoribus vulgaretur, præconcepta auxiliorum spes elanguit, firmatâ veri fide quod per castra & fœderatum exercitum ovationum militarium solennia ac velut funebres ludi illius è terris excessui decernerentur. Quippe colluentes passim castrorum ignes visebantur horrendisque machinarum fragoribus motus aër repercusso intra urbem murmure audiebatur. His accedebat, quod proserpens lues cælo missa grassari per ejus exercitum ferocius diceretur, credentibus obsessis iras syderum & contagem supernis influentijs motam promiscuâ importunitate desævire. Itaque Lalainius rudi tyronum manu, quam Schonavius jam antè ad Austriacum missus collegerat, dissipatâ confluentibusque in castra novis auxilijs oppugnare urbem constituit machinisque muralibus opportuno loco dispositis laxatisque vallum urbis & simul edita concussit.
units.tr: Moreover, although rumours of the Austrian's death were still uncertain and circulating, the hope of auxiliaries that had been formed beforehand faded, and the truth was confirmed: that throughout the camp and the allied army, the solemn rites of military celebration and, as it were, funeral games were decreed for his departure from the earth. For fires were seen blazing everywhere in the camps and the army, and the air, shaken by the dreadful crashes of the machines, was heard echoing inside the city. To this was added that a creeping plague, sent from heaven, was said to be raging more fiercely through his army; the besieged believed that the anger of the stars and the contagion, stirred by the heavenly influences, were raging with indiscriminate harshness. Therefore Lalaing, with the raw band of recruits that Schonau had earlier gathered when sent to the Austrian, and with fresh auxiliaries flowing into the camp, decided to attack the city. Placing his siege engines at a suitable spot, he shook the rampart of the city and at the same time the walls that had been raised.

units.la: Unde obsessi deficiente adhuc alimoniâ & difficili commeatu deditionem fecere, delectis è Magistratu qui ab æquo victore leges acciperent. Iis conventum fuit, Vt supinis signis, nullo damno urbi aut agris dato, præsidiarij oppido ac finitimis excederent deductiq; Boeckholtum in fines Imperij, adversum Ordines intra trimestre stipendia non facerent. Obsides quoque servandis pactis utrinque dati Lalainiusq; amoto præsidio urbem victor ingressus perdomatæ Transisulanorum provinciæ insignem gloriam tulit.
units.tr: Whereupon the besieged, with their food still failing and supplies difficult, made a surrender, choosing men from the magistracy to receive terms from the fair victor. It was agreed with them that the garrison should leave the town and the neighbourhood with their standards lowered, without any damage being done to the city or the fields, and be led to Boeckholt on the borders of the Empire, and that they should not serve against the Orders for three months. Hostages were also given on both sides to keep the agreements, and Lalaing, having removed the garrison, entered the city as victor, and bore away distinguished glory for having subdued the province of the Transisulani.

units.la: Igitur Austriacum cum adversis fortunæ luctantem & velut vitæ pertæsum pestilentia invasit. Cujus mali cum brevissimos circuitus medici monerent, de extremis suis cogitare occœpit omniqué sacrorum ritu qui moribundis ex præscripto Romanæ Sedis decernitur, celebrato, Kalend. Octob. decessit, surrogato ei à prætorianis tur, celebrato, Kalend. Octob. decessit, surrogato ei à prætorianis & mox universo exercitu Alexandro Farnesio. Scribunt Albanum, cujus militarem gloriam suo ingenio ac peritia armorum obscurare annitebatur, magnæ in aulâ regiâ gratiæ, æmulatorem ei fuisse, quo retardatis belli subsidijs & simul Philippi mandatis, cum ipsâ mole rerum juvenile & procax ingenium tabesceret.
units.tr: Then the Austrian, struggling with adverse fortune and, as it were, weary of life, was seized by a pestilence. When physicians warned that his end was very near, he began to think of his last things, and after the rites of the sacred offices which the Roman See prescribes for the dying had been celebrated, he died on the Kalends of October. He was succeeded by Alexander Farnese, chosen by the praetorians and soon afterwards by the whole army. Writers relate that Alva, who strove to obscure Farnese's military glory by his own talent and skill in arms, was a rival of his in the royal court, which had great favour; and that, with the war's supplies held back and also Philip's orders, the youthful and bold spirit wasted away together with the very weight of affairs.

units.la: Notat Cambdenus Ratelissum & Greium Anglos stipendio Austriaci militantes à profugis Anglis decretæ in Austriacum cædis insimulatos fuisse inditosque vinculis odio Anglici sanguinis & ut arguebat Austriacus, gravitate sceleris, quod Valsingamus reginæ actuarius suasisse dicebatur, ultimo supplicio affectos. Etsi traditum memoriæ sit proscriptos Anglos & regno extorres crimen aliquod Elisabethæ aut illius aulicis affinxisse, quo meritæ proscriptionis probrum & exilij tædium innocentium & gentili sanguine placarent.
units.tr: Camden notes that Ratcliffe and Gray, English men serving in the pay of Austria, were charged by English exiles with a plot to murder Don John of Austria. Because of their hatred for English blood, and because of the gravity of the crime (as Don John argued), they were put to death with the utmost penalty. Walsingham, the queen's secretary, was said to have urged this. Yet it is recorded that the proscribed Englishmen, exiled from the realm, invented some crime against Elizabeth or her courtiers, so that they might atone for the disgrace of their deserved proscription and the tedium of exile by the blood of innocent men of their own nation.

units.la: Mox Austriaci cadaver differtum odoribus regiâ funeris impensâ, Namurcum & post in Hispaniam deportatum, juxta Caroli Imperatoris Mausolæum terræ inlatum est. Itaque pro affectu animorum mœror, luctus per castra & exercitum visebantur, indignantibus Legionibus eundem Austriacum Cæsaris filium, fratrem regium, magnarum rerum spes & exordia versantem, ipso ævi flore immaturo funere occidisse. Ita scilicet illustrium votorum conatus interversos velut invidente fato, ut regium decus assequeretur formatumque primis juventæ annis animum & simul desiderium regij fastigij expleret. Creditum fuit eum Tunetani regni non obscuras spes jam ante agitasse illustrique ad Echinadas victoriâ elatum paria fraternæ fortunæ aut certè majora concupivisse. Quare de antiquæ Carthaginis celebritate regioque per Africam dominatu multa effatum, haud dissimulante Philippo socium & consortem se potentiæ non ferre. Igitur in Belgicam regundis pro Philippo provincijs missum, Guisiorum per Galliam auxilijs sollicitatisque Mariæ Scoticæ nuptijs, Angliæ regnum affectasse, non ante repressa juvenilis animi inexplebili cupiditate, quam inclementiam fati præsentiens repentinâ morte raperetur. Notat Nobilissimus scriptor Sixtus Hemmingha, positiones cœli illius fortunæ convenisse, certoque artis præsagio, ut vitæ ei cursum, ita simul terminum fatali horâ indicasse.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Don John's body, packed with perfumes at royal expense, was carried to Namur and then to Spain, and laid in the earth beside the tomb of the Emperor Charles. So the army and the camp showed grief and mourning, as their mood required, and the legions were indignant that this son of the Emperor and brother of the king, who was occupied with great undertakings and the beginnings of greater hopes, had died in the untimely flower of his age. Thus, as if fate envied him, the attempts of his illustrious vows were overturned, so that he might attain royal dignity and fulfil the spirit that had been shaped in the first years of his youth and his longing for a royal height. It was believed that he had already entertained no obscure hopes of the kingdom of Tunis, and that, elated by his famous victory at the Echinades, he had desired fortunes equal to his brother's, or even greater. Hence he spoke much of the ancient fame of Carthage and of royal dominion over Africa, and Philip did not conceal that he could not bear a partner and colleague in power. Therefore, when he was sent into the Low Countries to settle the provinces on Philip's behalf, he was said to have aimed at the kingdom of England, through the help of the Guises in France and by seeking the marriage of Mary of Scotland. His youthful spirit, insatiable in its desire, was not checked before a sudden death snatched him away, foreseeing the harshness of fate. The most noble writer Sixtus Hemmingha notes that the positions of the heavens agreed with that fortune, and that by a sure prediction of the art he indicated the course of his life and at the same time its end at a fated hour.

units.la: Finis Libri Quarti.
units.tr: End of Book Four.

units.la: P. WINSEMI Historiarum LIBER QUINTUS.
units.tr: P. Winsemius's Histories, Book Five.

units.la: ALEXANDER FARNESIUS ab excef-su IOANNIS AUSTRIACI belli imperator obvia legionum fide salutatus, meliorem fuispem per provincias vulgabat, credulis plerique eundem Farnesium primis vitae annis, gubernante Margaretâ matre, familiaritate virorum Principum Belgicaeque nobilitatis usum sui imperij rationem populi moribus afformaturum. Quippe antecessores per Italiam aut Hispaniam alio sub coelo aut sydere educatos, magis suarum gentium ingenijs quam Belgicae innutritos, domesticam indolem externâ consuetudine non emollijsse, quam Farnesius facili aetate, tanquam naturae bona, longâ ex conversatione induissel.
units.tr: Alexander Farnese, saluted as commander of the war after the death of John of Austria by the loyalty of the legions, spread among the provinces better hopes. Many believed that Farnese, in his early years under the governance of his mother Margaret, would through his familiarity with the princes and the Belgian nobility adapt his rule to the customs of the people. For his predecessors had been educated in Italy or Spain, under another sky and star, and were nourished more by the talents of their own nations than by Belgium. They had not softened their native temper by foreign habits, whereas Farnese, at a young age, had as it were taken on, as a gift of nature, a long familiarity with the country.

units.la: Caeterum de Austriaci morte, etsi divinum quiddam subesset, quod in pestilentiâ à maligno stellarum influxu ortâ deprehendi clarissimis medicorum proditum est, diversum disserebatur, cum essent, qui ae-gritudine animi extinctum opinarentur, eumque spiritu vitali indignatione adversae fortunae exhausto, cum excelsâ & regiâ indole gerendarum rerum & spem vitae posuisse. Praeterquam enim quod rupti foederis imaginem conscientia repraesentaret, ultra inquies & foeditate fusi sanguinis se exercens, ita & hoc accedebat, quod generosae menti praeconcepta secius procederent, ipsaq; in Philippi fratris aulâ gloriae & simul magnitudini suae serviturâ, virorum principum & fraternâ aemulatione evanescerent. Sunt qui tradant eum occupandae Belgicae spe quoq; animum clam pavisse, feruntq; ab Aurantio interventu legati persuasum in momenta temporum & majora virium rejecisse. Quae Philippo fratri non ignorata, frænandae immodestae cupidini longiore morâ vilescebant.
units.tr: Concerning the death of Austria, although something divine lay beneath it, which, as the most famous physicians have reported, was detected in a pestilence arising from a malignant influence of the stars, opinions differed. Some thought he had died of a sickness of the mind, and that, with his vital spirit exhausted by indignation at his adverse fortune, he had lost hope of living, since his lofty and kingly nature had been set on carrying out great affairs. For besides the image of the broken covenant, which his conscience presented to him, he was also tormented beyond measure by the foulness of the blood he had shed. And this was added: things he had planned in advance for his noble mind went less well, and in the court of his brother Philip, which was to serve his glory and at the same time his greatness, they dwindled away through the rivalry of the leading men and of his own brother. Some report that he secretly nourished in his heart the hope of seizing Belgium too, and that he was persuaded by the intervention of Orange's envoy to put this off until the moment and greater forces were at hand. Philip, his brother, was not unaware of this, and by long delay he made light of checking his unbridled ambition.

units.la: Igitur Austriaco, datis ad Principes viros litteris, ne ista quidem disimulabantur, expostulanti acrius se inter patientiam & ludibria jactatum tam odio & ignavia suorum quam vi hostium perire. Neque aliud restare, quam ut horum armis obsessus ferro viam & ad extrema aperiat, omniaque regis & sua fortunae committendo amputatâ manu, aut jugulum praebeat aut beneficio fugae servetur. Quae praeter alia, cum indignatione effusa oppressum angoribus & desperatione rerum principem animum indicavere. Adhaec repetita inter pro-vincio. Io. LXXVIII. vincias foedera, quae simulando ne quidem profecisset, hostem ex sociis per omne tribunal etiam titulo regis proclamatum, neq; reditu-rum in gratiam ijs artibus quibus occupari aut stare imperium posse caecâ cogitatione & juventae lubrico praeconceperat.
units.tr: So, when Austria sent letters to the leading men, these things were not even concealed. He complained more bitterly that he was tossed between patience and mockery, and that he was perishing as much by the hatred and cowardice of his own men as by the force of the enemy. Nothing remained, he said, but that, besieged by these men's arms, he should open a way out by the sword to the last extremity, committing all to the king's fortune and his own, and so, his hand as it were cut off, either offer his throat or be saved by the benefit of flight. These words, among others, poured out in indignation, revealed a prince whose mind was oppressed by anxieties and despair over his affairs. Besides this, the covenants between the provinces were repeatedly broken, which feigning would not even have achieved. He had been proclaimed an enemy by the allies in every court, even under the title of king. In his blind thinking and youthful rashness he had supposed that he would not be restored to favour by those arts by which empire could be seized or maintained.

units.la: Denique provinciarum opes magis invalescere, aerarium vectigalibus & collato aere sublevatum, arma & consilia hostium externis societatibus atq; auxiliis firma, & quidem eorum, qui suis regnis solam pacem ex Philippi bello sperent, & qui everso regis imperio accidi quoq; potentiam velint, incrementa non nisi cum pernicie sui habituram. Postremo arcium & castellorum dubia praesidia, infida munimenta esse, quae si exist-ant, vel tunc maxime defutura, nisi obsequio firmentur, quod principatui alienum arma & ferociam pro virtute induisset. Quae aegritudini conciliandae ex adversis apud Austriacum suborta, Alexandri Farnesij successoris gloriae atq; foelicitati cessere.
units.tr: Finally, the resources of the provinces grew stronger, the treasury was relieved by taxes and collected money, and the arms and plans of the enemy were made firm by foreign alliances and aid, and indeed of those who hope for peace in their own kingdoms only from the war of Philip, and who, if the king's rule were overthrown, would want his power to fall too. They would gain nothing from the growth of Austria's power except with ruin to themselves. Lastly, the garrisons of citadels and castles were uncertain and their defences unreliable; and if they existed, they would fail most of all at that very time unless they were strengthened by obedience, which, being foreign to government, had taken arms and ferocity in place of virtue. These things, which had arisen among the adversities in Austria's time to stir up the sickness, gave way to the glory and good fortune of his successor, Alexander Farnese.

units.la: Reidanus tradit D. Gertrudis Abbatem causaria Austriaci morte gloriatum non dubiam propinati veneni suspicionem suis familiaribus injecisse, quasi patriae & Philippi interfuisset percussore aut pharmaco tolli, qui libertatem impugnando jus insuper ac mandatum sui regis privatae ambitioni post habuisset. Itaq; Austriaci funus nec regi luctuosum nec libertati habitum, innuentibus prudentioribus, eum vitae servatum subsecutis provinciarum secessionibus perite usurum fuisse, suaeq; potentiae fundamenta ex discordia populi structurum. Mihi animus res pro libertate aut dominatione gestas justo opere enarrare procul gratia & odio, quae in partem admissa clarissimorum saepe Scriptorum judicia & simul gloriam foedavere. Externas cum provincijs societates infirmata fide ruptas, & auxilia libertati scripta venalibus sacramentis corrupta. Secessione partium bello provisum & post foederum societatem infida pace aut eius simulatione tardatam. Domi populum civili concordia ex novo foedere colligatum, & rationes gerendo bello socijs scriptas. Inde tributa nec sine disceptationibus reperta & salubre fere consilium, etiam sub prima libertate, sola aemulatione turbatum. Mox provinciarum dissensiones ex periculis & metu sanatas, dirutisq; per provincias castellis stabilitam remp. defectione rectoris concussam. Diversos praeliorum rerumq; exitus, & partium fortunam trahendis rebus variantem. Post Philippo imperium mutatis sacramentis abrogatum, libertatemq; foederatis provincijs validissima armorum tempestate assertam.
units.tr: Reidanus relates that the abbot of St Gertrude, boasting about the death of Austria, cast a suspicion of poison, which was not doubtful, upon his intimates, as though it had been to the advantage of the country and of Philip that he should be removed by an assassin or a poison, since he, by attacking liberty, had placed the right and command of his own king beneath his private ambition. So the death of Austria was regarded neither as mourning by the king nor as a blow to liberty, since the wiser men hinted that, had he been kept alive, he would have used with skill the secessions of the provinces that followed, and would have built the foundations of his power on the discord of the people. For my part, I intend to narrate with due labour the affairs done for liberty or for domination, far from favour and hatred, which, when admitted into partisanship, have often stained the judgments and the glory of the most distinguished writers. Foreign alliances with the provinces were broken once faith was weakened, and the aids written for liberty were corrupted by sacraments bought for money. The war was provided for by the secession of the parties, and the peace, faithless after the alliance of the covenants, was delayed by its pretence. At home the people were bound together in civil concord by a new covenant, and accounts were written for the allies of how the war was conducted. From this came taxes, not found without dispute, and a salutary plan, which even under the first freedom was troubled by rivalry alone. Soon the dissensions of the provinces were healed out of danger and fear, the castles were razed through the provinces, and the state, shaken by the defection of its ruler, was stabilised. There were various outcomes of battles and affairs, and the fortune of the parties varied as affairs were drawn out. After this, the rule of Philip was abolished by the changing of the oaths, and liberty was asserted for the United Provinces in a most violent storm of arms.

units.la: Igitur ab excessu Austriaci superiorum provinciarum pace discordijs virorum principum affectâ dissidia quoq; religionibus quaesita quarum libertati illi maxime adversabantur, qui suâ nec sine superstitionibus imbuti unam retineri, & quidem à majoribus receptam é re Principis arbitrabantur. Alijs placebat priorum temporum caliginem fato detectam hominum oculis submovendam cultusque divinos manifestis erroribus depravatos, cum ipsâ indecentis regni immodestiâ tollendos. Reliquis quibus moderatius & pronum paci ingenium erat, mitiora suadebantur, haud male indicantibus civili lege stare populi etiam diversa sententis concordiam posse & communi libertatis cupidine ferendas religiones, legum auxilio coituras. Caeterum turbulentis concionibus impulsa plebes, ultro partium foecunda, dissidijs rectorum trahebatur, armisque que & seditionibus infesta, reverentiam foederum, cum regiae dominationis superbia exuerat. Quae omnia Alexandro Farnesio regium per provincias imperium capessenti commodo & usui evenere, & quod externorum Ducum aemulatione exercituum quoque stipendia mora & per ignaviam consumerentur. Unde Casimiri, etsi Elisabethae sacramento ac stipendijs evocaretur, gloria atque autoritas imminutae etsi palam conquerentis Maximilianum Heninium cum imperio gerendis Ordinum rebus praefectum suae aut Reginae dignitati non cessisse.
units.tr: Therefore, after the death of Austria, when peace in the upper provinces had been impaired by the discords of the leading men, disputes also arose over religions. Those who were not free of superstition themselves, and who thought one religion, received from their ancestors, should be kept for the good of the prince, were most hostile to liberty in this matter. Others held that the darkness of earlier times, revealed by fate, should be removed from the eyes of men, and that divine worship, corrupted by manifest errors, should be abolished together with the unbecoming excess of the kingdom itself. For the rest, whose disposition was more moderate and inclined to peace, milder counsels were urged, not badly pointing out that by civil law the concord of the people can stand even with divergent opinions, and that religions, which are to be tolerated through a common desire for liberty, can come together with the aid of the laws. Meanwhile the common people, stirred by turbulent sermons, eager to take sides of their own accord, were dragged along by the discord of their rulers. Hostile to arms and seditions, they cast off reverence for the covenants together with the pride of royal dominion. All these things turned out to the advantage and use of Alexander Farnese, when he took up the royal rule through the provinces. It also served him that, by the rivalry of foreign commanders, the pay of the armies was consumed by delay and sloth. Hence the glory and authority of Casimir were diminished, although he was called in by the oath and pay of Elizabeth; and though he openly complained, Maximilian Henin, appointed to manage the affairs of the Orders with authority, did not yield to his own dignity or to that of the Queen.

units.la: Itaq; Aurantij & Ordinum quoque ipsorum odio ardens reputansq; Alençonium Gallicis auxilijs subjutum suae famae obfuturum, inertia se & militem tabescere passus est.
units.tr: And so Casimir, burning with hatred of Orange and of the Orders themselves, and reckoning that Alençon, supported by French aid, would harm his own reputation, allowed himself and his soldiers to waste away in inactivity.

units.la: Econtra Alençonium infirmata conventio & praerepta gloriae spes ure-bat, indignantem ex pacto pignori data Ordinum, non suis praesidijs attineri, seque regij sanguinis ac potentiae Principem, subjuvandae Belgicae validum aliorum Ducum nominibus inseri. Neque Elisabethae Anglicae animus idem censebatur offenso Casimiro & quod Alençonij à cujus societate jam ante provincias averterat, jus ac dignationem muliebri vehementia ac simul fragilitate tueretur. Quamvis essent qui scirent aliquid amori in foemina dandum esse, qui reginae animum ultro ex sexu imbecillum, occultis illecebris exercerent.
units.tr: On the other hand, the weakened agreement and the hope of glory snatched away troubled Alençon, who was indignant that, under the terms of the pact, he was held back by the garrisons of the Orders, which had been given in pledge, and not by his own forces; and that he, a prince of royal blood and power, a strong man for aiding Belgium, was being enrolled under the names of other commanders. Nor did Elizabeth of England seem to have the same mind, since she was offended with Casimir, and because she had earlier turned Alençon away from her alliance with the provinces. With a woman's vehemence, and at the same time her frailty, she defended her own right and dignity. Yet there were those who knew that something must be granted to love in a woman, and who by hidden allurements played upon the queen's mind, which was of its own accord weak because of her sex.

units.la: Cambdenus scribit Elisabetham hoc tempore commendato ab Astleia, quae reginae à cubiculis, Roberto Lycestrio graviter commotam fuisse, quasi infra dignitatem regiae majestatis esset, hominem suis honoribus auctum socium tori atque regni ascisccere regiumq; sanguinem, & ex potentissimis Principem, quo Andinum designabat, novae & suâ ex aulâ nobilitati postponere. Ita provincias dubia principum foedera ac auxilia, civiles & procerum discordiae extenuabant, quae nullâ ratione aut lege coercitae sua vi effrenes publicas in secessiones ex privatis dissidijs eruperant: Unde omnia in consessu Ordinum turbida atque angusta spectabantur, non dissimulantium quantae molis esset externis potentum societatibus satisfacere, & spectare socios mutuas vires & sacramenta foederum lacerantes. Adhaec validissimum exercitum & fraudatis stipendijs & Ducum per discordias tabidum, civitates atque oppida contrarijs praesidijs obnoxia, socios reges atque Principes ex jure societatum laesos, denique regias vires nullâ disciplinae remissione solutas spirante adhuc & halante animam Austriaco sub militare Farnesij imperium & fidem regis concessisse.
units.tr: Camden writes that at this time Elizabeth, having been commended by Astley, who was the queen's chamberlain, was gravely moved against Robert Lycestrius, as if it were beneath the dignity of royal majesty, that she should take as her consort in bed and in the kingdom a man raised by her own honours, and should place royal blood, and a prince of the most powerful family, whom she designated as Andinum, below a nobility newly made from her own court. Thus the uncertain covenants and aids of the princes, and the civil and noble discords, weakened the provinces; these, restrained by no reason or law, had broken out by their own violence from private quarrels into public secessions. Hence everything in the assembly of the Orders was seen as turbulent and narrow, and men did not hide how great a burden it was to satisfy foreign alliances of the powerful, and to regard allies who tore apart mutual strength and the oaths of covenants. Besides this, the most powerful army, cheated of its pay and wasting away through the discords of its commanders, the cities and towns exposed to hostile garrisons, the allied kings and princes injured in the right of alliances, and finally the royal forces, loosed from all discipline, yielded, while Austria still breathed and gasped his last, to the military command and loyalty of Farnese, under the king.

units.la: Itaque premente Ordines suprema aeris inopia, quo solo civitatum praesidia, commeatus ac stipendia parari oportebat, Matthias Austrius postrid. Kal. Octob. Antverpiâ ad Sixtum Hellemum, Julium Botnia, Goslicum Hiddama & Henricum Jarichium litteras in Frisiam dedit, conquirendis per provinciam transmittendisque Antverpiam pecunijs, quarum summam suppleri praeturarum ac urbium syngraphis invii. Oct. mensis diem postulabat. Alias scilicet metui posse ut formidabilis hostium exercitus qui in ipsis provinciarum visceribus haereret, progressum facturus sit, foederato exsangui & in defectiones ac turbas ituro, nisi nutantis disciplinae robur commeatu & stipendijs firmetur. Mirari se tam supina procerum ingenia tam obtusa, ut praesens discrimen men non spectent, aut spectando dissimulent culpabili socordiae aut securitatis vitio, quae omnem metum imminentis ruinae sustulisset. Miserari certe se humanae caliginis quam non patriae morientis cura non hostilium furorum exempla detergerent, convulsura haud dubie clarissimi foederis societatem cum isto collato aere tot gentium armis stipendia parentur. Itaq; timendum post ut provinciae, quos stipendiarios putent, hostes habeant, obviam egestatem & insolentiam militaribus omnibus auctu같 uros.
units.tr: Therefore, with the Estates pressed by the utmost shortage of money, which alone could provide garrisons, supplies and pay, Matthias Austrius wrote from Antwerp on the day after the Kalends of October to Sixtus Hellema, Julius Botnia, Goslicus Hiddama and Henricus Jarichius in Friesland. He ordered them to collect money throughout the province and send it to Antwerp, and he demanded that the sum be made up from the bonds of the bailiffs and towns by the seventh of October. Otherwise, he said, the formidable enemy army, which was lodged in the very heart of the provinces, might advance, and the exhausted confederacy, already tending toward revolt and disorder, would be unable to resist, unless the weakening discipline were strengthened by supplies and pay. He wondered that the leading men were so dull and sluggish that they did not see the present danger, or, seeing it, pretended not to, through the culpable carelessness or complacency that had removed all fear of the impending ruin. He pitied the human blindness of those whom the examples of hostile fury did not rouse to care for their dying country, since the alliance of the most famous confederacy would undoubtedly be shaken if pay were raised from that money with the arms of so many nations. Therefore, he warned, it was to be feared that the provinces, whom they considered paid soldiers, would become enemies, and that, in the face of want and insolence, they would increase the number of all the soldiers.

units.la: Quare per Frisiam, etiam regio Senatu amoto & Transisulania Lalainij armis in fidem recepta, ne partium quidem odia & reliquiae cessabant, urgentibus nonnullis restituendum Philippi Senatum, aut retinendum laudatissimum Burgundiae Principum morem esse qui senatorium ordinem stabiliendae integritati peregrinis judicibus & rectoribus provinciae miscuisset: Quorum dominationem econtra illi respuebant, qui externae opis aut consilij egere provinciam non arbitrabantur, repressaque peregrini Senatus autoritate, quod benignitas temporum indulsisset, reip. & judiciorum regimen suorum ingenijs committendum. Neque enim bonae mentis aut prudentiae vacuos provinciales esse quos non pro socijs, sed veluti servis herili imperio externae potestatis superbia habuissent. Itaque & aes alienum superiores per provincias conflatum exsoluendium Frisijs decrevisse, ac si patrimonium istius populi externis creditoribus diripiendum exponeretur, ipsaque provincia Valonum & Germanicis stipendijs obstricta liberandis suis & simul externis nominibus sufficeret. Ita Bossuvianae legioni censum vectigalem pignori assignatum, quod ne ijs quidem ultima rerum necessitas permisisset, qui jure dominij possidebant. Neque enim Ultrajectinos quorum stipendijs Bossuvius militasset, laturos fuisse, ut Philippi creditoribus suo ex censu intacto regio satisfieret, quem olim per Frisiam suo Gubernatori tutandis provincialibus majorum liberalitas concessisset. Tantum abesse ut Bossuvius Ultrajectinorum in finibus res gerens obligare Frisios potuerit, aut aliquo jure Drentinos per agros in aliena & Lalainij praefectura legionem exigendis stipendijs spargere, quae Lalainius exsolvendis cohortibus ex aerario provincialium obtinuisset.
units.tr: For this reason, through Friesland, where the royal Senate had been removed and Transisulania had been brought into submission to Lalaing by force, the hatreds and remnants of the parties did not cease. Some insisted that the Senate of Philip must be restored, or that the most praiseworthy custom of the princes of Burgundy must be kept, who had mixed the senatorial order with foreign judges and governors of the province in order to establish its integrity. Those who opposed this domination, on the other hand, did not think the province needed foreign help or counsel, and, with the authority of the foreign Senate suppressed, they wanted the government of the state and the courts entrusted to the abilities of their own people, since the kindness of the times now allowed it. For they said the provincials were not lacking in good sense or prudence, whom the arrogance of foreign power had treated not as allies but as slaves under a master's rule. And so the superiors had decreed that the debt contracted across the provinces should be paid by the Frisians, as if the patrimony of that people were to be plundered by foreign creditors, and the province itself, burdened with Walloon and German pay, would be enough to free its own people and at the same time foreign creditors. Thus the tax levy had been pledged to the Bossuvian legion, something that not even those who held the property by right of ownership had allowed in the extremity of their need. For the Ultrajectines, whose pay Bossuvius had served on, would not have agreed that the creditors of Philip be satisfied from their revenue, left untouched by the king, which the generosity of their ancestors had granted to their governor through Friesland to protect the provincials. Bossuvius, acting within the bounds of the Ultrajectines, could no more bind the Frisians than, by any right, spread a legion through the fields of the Drenthians in another's territory and under Lalaing's command, to exact pay, which Lalaing had obtained from the treasury of the provincials to pay his cohorts.

units.la: Caeterum istos fructus peregrinae dominationis atq; autoritatis fuisse, sed quae non aliunde quam vitio Frisicae gentis increvisset, cum exterorum vilissimi quoque Senatoriam ad dignitatem protrusi magno cultu & assentationibus habiti animos atq; spiritus ex servitijs populi sustulere. Quod etsi Saxonica conventione majores prohibuissent, ita cum imperio Principis introductum esse, qui judiciorum vim cum ipsa libertate occupasset. Nunc vero Gandavensi Foedere in integrum restitutos eniti debere, ne qui peregrini in remp. ac tribunalia adscisccantur, quos Groningensium, Trans-Isulanorum, atque Drentinorum cura atque consuetudo ab omnibus honoribus excluderet. Itaque factum esse, ut Drentini coram Lalainio in castris ad Daventriam & provinciae legato Carolo Roorda effati sint, se cum Groningensibus ac Trans-Isulanis in ferendis tributis ac indictionibus paria facturos, alienos a Frisiorum societate, quod peregrinis dominationibus regerentur. Quae, quamquamquam ex vero dicta, pudore legatum suffudissent, ita emendanda temporum & simul vitia gentis esse, ne peregrinos revocando in ignorata vicinis nationibus mala, supplicia ac servitutes recidat. Neq; enim gentium trans-Lavicam atque Isalam flumina sanguini neque per Drentiam, quicquam, praeterquam in Frisijs detractum esse, quasi ita decretum esset, ut Principis & exterorum saevities ex libertate populi se efferasset graviusq; servirent, quos omnium gentium, praeterquam proprijs imperijs, clarissimi majores exemissent. Tanta cum acerbitate peregrinae dominationis reducendae consilia subvertebantur.
units.tr: Moreover, those fruits were the outcome of foreign domination and authority, which had grown up not from any other source than the fault of the Frisian people, since the lowest foreigners were thrust into senatorial dignity, treated with great honour and flattery, and took away the spirit and vigour of the people's servitude. Although their ancestors had forbidden this by the Saxon agreement, it had been introduced in this way along with the rule of the prince, who had seized the power of the courts together with liberty itself. Now, however, they ought to strive to restore everything to its former state by the Treaty of Ghent, lest any foreigners be admitted into the state and the tribunals, whom the care and custom of the Groningers, the Transisulanians and the Drenthians exclude from all offices. And so it happened that the Drenthians, in the camp at Deventer before Lalaing, and to Carolus Roorda, the province's envoy, declared that they would make payments of taxes and levies equal to those of the Groningers and the Transisulanians, being alien to the Frisian alliance because they were governed by foreign domination. Although these statements were true, they had put the envoy to shame; and so the remedy for the times and at the same time for the people's faults was that, by recalling foreigners, they should not bring back into the country the evils, punishments and servitudes unknown to neighbouring nations. For the nations beyond the rivers Lauwers and Yssel had not been drained of blood, nor had anything been taken through Drenthe except from Friesland, as if it had been decreed that the cruelty of the prince and of foreigners should, out of the people's liberty, grow fierce and that they should serve more harshly, when their most famous ancestors had freed them from all nations except their own rule. With such bitterness the plans to restore foreign domination were overthrown.

units.la: Itaq; dicundi juris potestas indigenis facta, prioribusq; Hesselus Aylma Praeses, Barthius Idzaerda, Douwo Burmania Idi omnes, superadditi qui supremo per Frisiam judicio atq; tribunali praeessent. Mox constitutis judicijs ad Ordines generales e primaria nobilitate Doco Martina & Renicus Camingha Antverpiam missi. Eorum mandata erant:
units.tr: And so the power of speaking law was given to natives, and, with the former ones, Hesselus Aylma as president, Barthius Idzaerda and Douwo Burmania, all of them were added to preside over the supreme judgment and tribunal throughout Friesland. Soon, when the courts had been established, Doco Martina and Renicus Camingha, from the leading nobility, were sent to the General Estates at Antwerp. Their instructions were:

units.la: Ut de castellis regijs provincialium fidei committendis de restituenda libertate, de confirmando judiciali Senatu agerent eoque beneficio impetrato octodecim aureorum millia & quingentorum subsidia bello & socijs provincijs offerrent. Hoc quoq; eorum mandatis additum erat, ut promovendae actioni e consessu Ordinum delegatum poscerent, qui de singulis referret & ut apocham numerato aeri acciperent. Frisijs quoq; sicut socijs provincijs jus esset in Concilio Status & collegio rationum aliquem ex suis delegare, quo aequalitate juris gauderent, qui societate foederis colligabantur.
units.tr: To deal with the handing over of the royal castles to the trust of the provincials, with the restoration of liberty, and with the confirming of a judicial Senate; and, having obtained this favour, to offer to the war and to the allied provinces a subsidy of eighteen thousand five hundred gold pieces. In their instructions it was also added that they should request that a delegate be sent from the assembly of the Estates to advance the business, who would report on each matter, and that they should receive a receipt for the money paid. The Frisians, too, like the allied provinces, should have the right to send one of their own to the Council of State and the board of accounts, so that those bound together by the alliance of the confederacy might enjoy equal rights.

units.la: Denique postularent legati, ut quicquid aeris Lalainius tam tuendis provinciae finibus, quam promovendis Camporum & Daventriae obsidionibus ex aerario sumpsisset, id apud Ordines generales Frisijs insolutum cederet, idemque Lalainius nullo Ordinum generalium aut statuum Frisiae decreto munitus administratione & usu publicarum pecuniarum prohiberetur. Quibus mandatis litterae quoque ad Ordines generales & Matthiam additae, per quas de sua in socios fide atque liberalitate testabantur. Ita scilicet omnem pecuniam, quae conquiri potuerit, delegatis suis perferendam credidisse, quo prosperitas foederis, ex quo restitui in integrum populus Friscus deberet, subsidiario aere etiam in tanta rerum omnium angustia praejuvaretur.
units.tr: Finally, the envoys were to demand that whatever money Lalaing had taken from the treasury, both for defending the province's borders and for pressing the sieges of Campen and Deventer, should be left unpaid to Friesland by the General Estates, and that Lalaing, without any decree of the General Estates or of the Estates of Friesland, should be barred from the administration and use of public moneys. With these instructions, letters were also added to the General Estates and to Matthias, in which they bore witness to their own faith and generosity toward the allies. Clearly they believed that all the money that could be collected should be carried by their delegates, so that the prosperity of the alliance, from which the Frisian people ought to be restored to their former state, might be helped even in such great scarcity of everything, by the subsidiary money.

units.la: Quae vitio injuriae liberalitatis & ex studio recuperandae libertatis nata, hoc impetrare jure societatis debuisset, ut suum reciperet. Quippe trecenta millia Valonum legioni, cui Roblesius praefuisset, proxumis pensionibus decreta & nonaginta millia Germanicis cohortibus assignata publicae egestatis causas, quam ipsum mare terrarum inundationibus auxisset. Ad haec tribuno legionis Christophoro Schenckio quinque millibus subventum, multa occupandis Camporum & Daventriae civitatibus collata, sacrum aes & ex patrimonio Cuneri Episcopi ac coenobiorum corrasum a Lalainio qui cum Hauraeo aerario regis propositus est. Thuanus interceptam annonam & commeatum Casimiro a civitatibus Frisiae submi-nistratum, intacto regis aerario, quod in provinciae usus ex carolina conventione converti deberet. Igitur metui posse, ne ex sua in socios propensione damnum sentiat, publicusque creditor concessa actione provincialium res impigneret.
units.tr: These claims, born from the fault of injury and from the zeal to recover liberty, ought to have obtained by right of the alliance that the people recover what was theirs. Indeed, three hundred thousand Walloon pay for the legion commanded by Robles had been decreed for the next instalments, and ninety thousand had been assigned to the German cohorts, the causes of public poverty, which the very flooding of the seas had increased. Besides this, five thousand had been granted to the tribune of the legion, Christopher Schenck; much had been contributed for seizing the cities of Campen and Deventer; and the sacred money, scraped together from the patrimony of Bishop Cuneri and from the monasteries, had been put, by Lalaing, under Hauraeus, the royal treasurer. Thuanus, who had intercepted the grain and supplies provided to Casimir by the cities of Friesland, had left the royal treasury untouched, although by the Carolingian agreement it ought to be turned to the use of the province. Therefore, it was to be feared that, through his inclination toward the allies, the public creditor would suffer loss, and that, with the right to act granted, the provincials' property would be pledged.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXVIII Quibus malis & hoc accedebat, quod agrarij oppidaniq; vetere tum discordia exercerentur, publicisque provinciarum sociarum indictionibus Frisia gravaretur. Quæ quanquam in speciem receptæ permulcendis illorum ingenijs qui acrius servitium nostrâ ex libertate aucupabantur, ita dissensionibus quoq; provincialium remedium adhibitum, quæ à Caroli Philippiq; ævo fotæ paucos ante annos vix cum ipsâ libertatis infantiâ eruperant.
units.tr: 1578. Among these evils was also this, that the country and town people were then at odds over old quarrels, and Friesland was burdened by the public levies of the allied provinces. Although these were received in appearance to soothe the minds of those who more eagerly sought after our servitude out of our liberty, a remedy was also applied to the dissensions of the provincials, which, nurtured from the age of Charles and Philip, had barely burst forth a few years before, along with the infancy of liberty itself.

units.la: Quippe soli adhuc agrarij confessus, & suffragia usurpabant, indignantibus è contra oppidanis, jus utrique populo commune ex cupiditate dominationis subverti & separari ex privatâ æmulatione quos publica societas tot sæculorum ætatibus junxisset. Itaque conventum ut quartam reip. ac confessus partem oppidani in proximum comitium constituerent deque tributis & oneribus provinciam spectantibus pari suffragiorum jure cum agrarijs deliberarent. Hoc etiam additum ut quicquid ex commeatu Casimiri copijs concesso oppidanis competeret, id ex collationum publicarum ære præstaretur, deductis octo aureorum millibus quæ thesaurarius regius necessitati publicæ elocassèt. Hæc à Gerardo Iacobi, S. Galama, Goslico Hiddama, Barthio Idzaerda pro agrarijs, ab Adio Lamberti, Douwone Sixma, Gellio Sibæo, Abbæo Douwonio, Simone Pottero & Cornelio Jacobæo pro oppidanis signata. Reperio in litteris Barthij Idzaerdæ ad Carolum Roordam qui in comitatu Lalaimij tum erat, datis, corrogandi subsidiarij, de quo dixi, æris necessitatem isti bono occasionem tum dedisse agrariosq; à Balduino Loæo thesaurario regio super præstandâ cautione compellatos, non nisi admissis in remp. oppidanis, beneficium ærarij & crediti æris obtinuisse. Adeo quæ ex collatione tributi discordiam auctura videbantur, propter spem diffidentium concordiæ cessere.
units.tr: Indeed, the country people alone still claimed the right of voting in the assemblies and their suffrages, while the townspeople, on the contrary, indignant that a right common to both peoples was being subverted by the desire for domination and that those whom a common alliance had joined through so many centuries were being separated by private rivalry, objected. Therefore it was agreed that the townspeople should have a quarter of the state and of the assemblies at the next gathering, and that they should deliberate with the country people, with equal voting rights, about the taxes and burdens concerning the province. It was also added that whatever was due to the townspeople from the supply of Casimir's troops should be paid from the money of the public collections, after deducting eight thousand gold pieces, which the royal treasurer had allotted to the public necessity. These terms were signed by Gerardus Jacobi, S. Galama, Goslicus Hiddama and Barthius Idzaerda for the country people, and by Adius Lamberti, Douwo Sixma, Gellius Sibaeus, Abbaeus Douwonius, Simon Potter and Cornelius Jacobaeus for the townspeople. I find in the letters of Barthius Idzaerda to Carolus Roorda, who was then in Lalaing's retinue, that the need for the aforesaid subsidiary money, from the collection, had then given that good cause an opportunity, and that the country people, pressed by Balduinus Loaeus, the royal treasurer, about giving security, obtained the benefit of the treasury and of the credit money only when the townspeople had been admitted to the state. So those things which through the collection of taxes seemed about to increase discord gave way, because of the hope of the distrustful for concord.

units.la: Cæterum mihi actorum fidem introspicienti, dubium non est isti actionii Mandatum Matthiæ Gubernatoris intervenisse, Ordinesq; tam agrarios quam oppidanos ex conventione anni 1524 pro recuperandis dominijs ut vocabant regij, Matthiam Gubernatorem ultimâ rerum necessitate sollicitasse. Hoc etiam postulatum invenio ut creditoribus regijs usurae in annum cessarent, Ordinibusque ex violatæ conventionis actione in dominium censumq; Principis & simul Ecclesiasticorum prædiorum jus assignaretur. Deïn ut Germanorum cohortes turbidæ & per munitiones dispositæ à Senatu regio olim conscriptæ & publicis provinciarum sacramentis auctoratæ ab Ordinibus provinciarum Belgicæ exsolverentur Gerardoque Gramaio exautorandi potestas sicut in missione caeterarum esset conveniendiq; de stipendijs, quæ ex ærario provinciarum Belgicæ non suo peti æquissimum esset. Postremum erat, ut Matthias Gubernator tam ad Ordines Frisiæ, quam magistratus oppidorum de possidendis castellis scriberet, volentibus Ordinibus castella stabiliendo Principis dominatui erecta, Ordinum majestati repressâ principatus insolentiâ cederent.
units.tr: Looking closely at the records, I have no doubt that the mandate of Governor Matthias lay behind this action. The Estates, both the landed nobility and the townsmen, under the agreement of 1524 for recovering what were called the royal domains, had pressed Governor Matthias in their extreme need. I also find these demands: that the royal creditors' interest be suspended for a year; that, because the agreement had been violated, the domain and rents of the Prince and also the rights over ecclesiastical estates be assigned to the Estates; that the unruly German cohorts, raised long ago by the royal Council and posted in the fortresses, and bound by the public oaths of the provinces, be discharged by the Estates of the Belgic provinces, with Gerard Gramaye given power to dismiss them as he would the others, and that payment be demanded for their wages, which it was most just to demand not from the treasury of the Belgic provinces but from another source. Last, Governor Matthias was to write both to the Estates of Friesland and to the magistrates of the towns about holding the castles. The Estates, who wanted the castles built to secure the Prince's rule to be handed over, would thereby restrain the arrogance of the Prince and yield to the majesty of the Estates.

units.la: Tum lubricis superiorum provinciarum rebus, & haud procul Rheno ac Agrippinensium finibus regio milite conducto de novis quoque copijs conscribendis Ordines & Matthias Archidux cogitavere, potestate Gunthero Suartzenburgio factâ, qua tria equitum Germanorum millia suo murui ære, provinciarum sacramento autoraret. Cæterum apud legiones vagas ac oberrantes, tribunos equitum insolentes & exemplis offensos, multa difficilia proponebantur, cum & essent, qui cautionem stipendijs postularent & ut Matthiæ, Ordinum ac provinciarum fides solemnibus tabulis, etiam sub jure pignorum, interponeretur.
units.tr: Then, since the affairs of the upper provinces were unstable, and a royal army had been hired not far from the Rhine and the borders of Cologne, the Estates and Archduke Matthias also considered raising fresh troops. Power was given to Gunther Schwarzenburg to equip three thousand German horse at his own expense and to bind them by the oath of the provinces. But among the wandering and roaming legions, and among the insolent cavalry officers who were angered by past examples, many difficulties were raised. Some demanded security for their pay, and that the good faith of Matthias, the Estates and the provinces be given in formal documents, even under the law of pledges.

units.la: Quod quanquam Ordines & Matthiam vreret, qui suspiciosis legionibus implicari provincias indignabantur, ita tamen omne publicum privatumque pignori datum cautumque ut sacramentis stipendia quovis tempore, etiam sub repressaliorum, ut loquuntur, pactione, provincijs præstarentur.
units.tr: Although this galled the Estates and Matthias, who were indignant that the provinces should be entangled with suspect legions, all public and private property was nonetheless pledged and secured, so that the wages would be paid to the soldiers by the provinces at any time, even under what they call the agreement of reprisals.

units.la: Quarum nomine, ut clarorum virorum memoriæ hoc datur, in confessu Ordinum generalium I. Baro Merodius, Ph. Hornius, Richardus Merodius, Rolandus Rickius, Ioannes Ægydius, W. Hagius, H. Blomaius, Fredericus Boimerus, Iacobus Imannus, Carolus Rhinius, Provinius, I. Goulartius, L. Sommanius, T. Offegnius, A. Muffartius, I. Vlietius Biessartius, I. Warckius, Carolus Bom-kerckius, Dionysius de Capella, B. Liebartius, Florentius Hermelius, Hesselus Aysma, Hajo Manningha, & Joannes Rengerius tum fuere.
units.tr: On behalf of these provinces, as the memory of distinguished men records, the following were then present at the assembly of the General Estates: Baron Merode, Ph. Hornius, Richard Merode, Roland Rick, John Egidius, W. Hagius, H. Blomaius, Frederick Boimerus, James Imannus, Charles Rhinius, Provinius, J. Goulart, L. Sommanius, T. Offegnius, A. Muffart, J. Vlietius Biessartius, J. Warck, Charles Bomkerck, Dionysius de Capella, B. Liebart, Florentius Hermelius, Hessel Aysma, Hajo Manningha, and John Rengerus.

units.la: Qui ut affectis provinciarum ærarijs mederentur promovendas ad indictiones Magistratuum primos hortabantur, quo tributa imperij & rerum firmamenta in usum ac consuetudinem perducta tractu temporum invalescerent. Sed nutriendis simultatibus acris multitudo & licentia solutior omne molestum atque difficile aspernabatur, interque dubia actorum interpretamenta libertati indulgens, fraudum ingenio imperia Ordinum & vim indictionum eludebat. Quare colligendis pecunijs destinati metu popularium turbarum, ne rigorem quidam scriptarum legum retinebant, quæ per oppida & præturas ex indiscretâ jurisdictione & verborum ambiguitate litibus ac disceptationibus involvebantur. Itaque factum est, ut alibi usæ receptæ, alibi exolescerent, paucorumque ex contumaciâ aut socordiâ vis edictorum dedignatione parendi subverteretur.
units.tr: These men, to remedy the ailing treasuries of the provinces, urged the magistrates first to press forward with the levies, so that the taxes and the financial supports of the empire, brought into use and custom, might grow strong over time. But the crowd, fed by sharp rivalries and a loosened licence, scorned every burden and difficulty, and, indulging its freedom amid the doubtful interpretations of the acts, used its cleverness in fraud to evade the commands of the Estates and the force of the levies. So those appointed to collect the money, fearing popular disturbances, held back from the strict enforcement of the written laws, which in the towns and provinces became entangled in lawsuits and disputes because of indiscriminate jurisdiction and ambiguous words. And so it came about that some practices were received in one place and fell into disuse in another, and the force of the edicts was overturned because a few, from obstinacy or carelessness, disdained to obey them.
