Quare monere Artesios caterosque, ne Catholicae religionis studium superstitiosius retinendo amittant & cum ea dulcissimae pacis possessionem, quam solam praestare religio possit, cum civili concordia peritura. Hanc Artesios sociosque amplecti debere ac sua potius, quam externa consilia sequi & quidem eorum, quorum vires ex domestica provinciarum secessione habiturae incrementa essent. Haec cum caeteris v. Non. Mart. scripta.
units.tr: To this the General Estates replied: nothing had ever been of greater concern to them than to keep the Ghent treaty intact and inviolate. Its first and chief law was to secure the provinces undivided and to bind them to mutual aid, and, besides the restoration of the native law that had been violated, to the expulsion of the foreign people. They did not yet wish to be released from the obligation of that treaty, and they were ready to confirm the pledge given to the agreement not merely in words but in deed. But the Artesians, driven by discord over religion, whose author had been the Austrian, were the first to cast off the union, as those whom the testimony of their own conscience refuted would know. For their part, they would yield nothing to the empty favour sought from Spain, nor to the evil arts of Escovedo, and they would bring it about that the provinces, bound together by the most holy Ghent treaty, were not dissolved by the fickleness and defection of a few. Therefore, having been bound by the same convention with Holland and Zealand, they said that religion, which is the bond of civil life and effective for reconciling disputes, should not be devised as a means of sowing discord. Hence they warned the Artesians and the others not to lose, by keeping zeal for the Catholic religion too superstitiously, the possession of the sweetest peace, which religion alone can provide, and which would perish along with civil concord. The Artesians and their allies ought to embrace this, and to follow their own counsels rather than foreign ones, and indeed those of men whose strength would gain increase from the domestic secession of the provinces. These things were written, together with the rest, on 7 March.

units.la: Hoc vero per Frisiam Deputatos Ordinum urebat, quod Renneb-ergij intercessione Senatus regius velut libertati restitutus animos eferret, sacraque & conciones frequentando ad intermissa rei divinae officia cum sui invidia redijsset. Quare ijdem & rationibus provinciae praefecti per suos ad Achlenium Praesidem missos copiam decreti poposcerunt, libellumque Senatus foedis & haud dubie falsis criminationibus aspersum una cum rescripto Gubernatoris ostenderet. Caeterum Achlenius praeses, laesae dignitatis indignatione & quod augusti confessus primatum privata ac diu suspecta custodia vertisset, libellum petentibus negavit, eorumq; non interesse ut de eo cognoscerent, acribus verbis respondit. Dein interrogantibus, num collegialiter, ut vocant, ac universi confessus nomine obtulissent; idem ex vero constanter affirmavit, coactoque Senatu Emskerckium & Heymannum Curiae regiae actuarios exhibere libellum una cum rescripto urgentibus Deputatis fecit. Igitur innuebat Senatus non secreta aedium, non domesticum limen egressos, in templo ac coetu comparuisse, quam ut venia a Gubernatore provinciarum impetrata, audiendis sacris sermonibus se darent, animosque aegritudine ex injurijs temporum correptos foelicis verbi solatio allevarent.
units.tr: But what troubled the deputies of the Estates in Friesland was that the royal Senate, restored as if to liberty through the intercession of Rennenberg, was lifting up its spirits, and that by frequenting sacred services and sermons it had returned to the interrupted worship, to their own envy. Hence the same men, along with the officials in charge of the province's accounts, sent men through their agents to President Achlenius, demanding a copy of the decree and asking him to show them the Senate's petition, stained with foul and no doubt false accusations, together with the governor's rescript. However, President Achlenius, indignant at the injury to his dignity, and because he had turned the primacy of the august assembly into a private and long-suspected custody, refused the petition to those asking, and answered sharply that it was no business of theirs to learn of it. Then, when they asked whether they had presented it collegially, as they say, and in the name of the whole assembly, he affirmed truthfully and consistently that they had. The Senate being convened, he had the royal court notaries Emskerck and Heymann produce the petition along with the rescript, as the deputies pressed. Therefore he implied that the Senate had gone out not from private rooms or their domestic threshold, but had appeared in church and assembly only because, with permission obtained from the governor of the provinces, they were devoting themselves to hearing sacred sermons, and were relieving their spirits, seized by sorrow over the wrongs of the times, with the comfort of the blessed Word.

units.la: Heymannus scribit Deputatos censoria tantum & veteri, etiam sub Carolo ac Philippo usurpata potestate instructos, habendis legum rationibus praesedisse, in ijsque eo anno Doconem Martna, Epeum Douma Hallenium, Lasium Iongema,' Diricum Fogelsangium Jurisperitum, Erasmum Douma, Barthium Idzaerda jureconsultum, Gellium Sibaeum Consulem Leovardiensium, & Douwonem Sixma Consulem Franequerensium fuisse. Siriacum quoque Haersma, Oedsium, Arnoldium, Gellium Broerium & Ioannem Aysma provinciae rationes & aerarij ordinem administrasse.
units.tr: Heymannus writes that the deputies, equipped only with the censorial power, long used under Charles and Philip, presided over the conduct of legal business. In that year the members were Doco Martna, Epeus Douma Hallenius, Lasius Iongema, Dirk Fogelsang, a jurist, Erasmus Douma, Barthius Idzaerda, a jurisconsult, Gellius Sibaeus, consul of Leeuwarden, and Douwo Sixma, consul of Franeker. Siriacus Haersma, Oedsius, Arnoldus, Gellius Broerius and Johannes Aysma managed the province's accounts and the order of the treasury.

units.la: Mox a Rodolpho II. ejus nominis Caesare in provincias Belgicae Otto Henricus Suartsenburgius cum mandatis missus, praetentandis Ordinum & Aurantij animis, quos ab ineunda cum rege Philippo pace amplae foederum spes & externae societates, tum praecipue diffidentia debilis in regem fidei alienabant. Itaque Legati in diversa locorum communitis industria & sollicitudine nihil omittebatur, quod validum atque utile faciundae paci esset, cuius auspicium Philippi quoque litterae in provincias & ad civitates missae detecta sollicitatione morabantur. Sed maxime Artesijs sociisque ob institutas a caeteris provincijs defectiones grates clam actae, quamvis fama & communione secretorum non inhiberet, quin in plures etsi Philippi aemulos emanarent. Litterae hujusmodi erant.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Rudolph II sent Otto Henry Schwarzenberg into the Belgian provinces with instructions to test the minds of the States and of Aurantius. Hopes of wide alliances and foreign support, and above all a weak lack of trust in the king, were turning them away from making peace with King Philip. So the envoys, in various places, left nothing undone with industry and care that might be strong and useful for making peace. Philip's letters sent to the provinces and cities delayed the beginning of this peace, since the solicitation was detected. But the Artesians and their allies in particular gave thanks secretly for the defections made by the other provinces. Although rumour and the sharing of secrets could not prevent these letters from spreading to many, even to rivals of Philip, they were of this kind.

units.la: INTELLEXI cum gaudio quo pro confervando Artesiæ comitatu fecistis cum pulsâ hæreticorum & pravâ religione imbutâ neque à seditionis crimine immuni multitudine, Romanæ Religioni stabiliendæ animos atq; consilia impendistis. Cæterum quoniam metus adhuc ab oppressione hostium, & Aurantij præsertim principis imminet, dabo operam meis auxiliis ut ab illo vos liberem, onusque belli, quod grave vobis ferundo erit mea subsidia levent. Igitur omne, quod à Deo concessum meæ potestatis erit, polliceor regiâ fide, submovendis sinistris suspicionibus caveo, me ab Hispanorum consilio vos liberaturum. Quos quoq; alio terrarum facessere aut revocari faciam, modo videro repressum Aurantium in sua redijsse. Neque aliud interim peto, quam ut in Romana religione & eâ obedientia perseveretis, quam sacratissimo Cæsari vos & Majores præstitistis. Igitur vos ipsi & nostrum in vos affectum & vestra commoda circumspicite, hac præsertim tempestate, qua de imperio & simul regio fastigio nos dejicere Gallorum consilia moliuntur. Quæ aut si sint inter vos, qui foveant, aut qui suarum rerum incuriosi negligant, in sua damna proni atque proclives, testor extra culpam ejus esse, qui bellum coactus sustineo. Inter arma tamen quæ gero, voto pacem completor, cujus certissima spes assulsura est si in meo obsequio duretis. Interim ad cccasiones quasq; gerendarum rerum attenti estote, neque sinite negligi elapsuram è manu fortunam, cujus rationem jam antè minus vos habuisse, & ego rex non dissimulo & quotquot boni inter vos sunt, non ignorant. Qui de affectu meo regio quâ certi esse queant, experimentum abundè sensuri sunt, modo hoc agant, ut Lamotij consilio locum faciant, de quâ in posterum salute solliciti sint.
units.tr: I have learned with joy how you have resolved, for the preservation of the county of Artois, to set your minds and plans on establishing the Roman religion, after driving out the heretics and a multitude imbued with a wicked religion and not free from the crime of sedition. But since fear still hangs over you from the oppression of the enemy, and especially from the prince Aurantius, I will take care to free you from him with my auxiliary forces, and my aid will lighten the burden of war that is grievous for you to bear. Therefore I promise, under royal faith, everything that will be granted by God and lie within my power, and I pledge, to remove sinister suspicions, that I will free you from the counsel of the Spaniards. Those men too I will cause to depart to some other part of the world, or to be recalled, as soon as I see Aurantius crushed and returned to his own place. Meanwhile I ask nothing more than that you persevere in the Roman religion and in that obedience which you and your ancestors have shown to the most sacred Caesar. Therefore consider well your own interests and my affection towards you, especially in this time, when the plans of the French are aiming to cast us down from our rule and from the royal dignity at once. If there are any among you who foster such plans, or who, careless of their own affairs, neglect them, inclined and prone to their own harm, I call to witness that the fault lies not with me, who am forced to sustain war. Yet amid the arms I bear I am fulfilled with the wish for peace, whose most certain hope will dawn if you remain in my obedience. Meanwhile be attentive to the opportunities for acting, and do not allow fortune to be neglected, which is slipping from your hand. I, the king, do not conceal that you have had too little regard for this before, and all the good among you know it. Those who wish to be assured of my royal affection will feel the proof abundantly, provided they make way for the counsel of Lamotte, and are anxious about their future safety.

units.la: Litterae 111. Jan. Mantuæ Carpentanorum Philippi manu signatæ ac in Frisiam post perlatæ pro animorum statu odia aut gratiam invenere.
units.tr: This letter, dated 3 January at Mantua of the Carpetani, signed with Philip's own hand, and afterwards carried into Friesland, met with hatred or favour according to the state of men's minds.

units.la: Econtra Aurantius Gandavi adhuc huc agens & de mitigando Andino & pacunda Artesiæ Hannnoniæque defectione laborabat, non sine vanâ mentis & fiduciæ interpretatione optumæ paci propediem locum soere, & quæ omnia dissensione aut bello depravata aut amissa reparare aut restituere queat. Sed quippe confectum per Artesios ac Hannonios foedus, Andinus ob mortem fratris revocabatur, offensionem ex arte tegens, pacis negotio non serviebant ei quod de deserendis quoque provinciis cogitans vim alicujus imperij ex antiquâ conventione præferret. Itaq; affectus & velut juris antiqui argumenta speciosis litteris præferebantur, quamvis indignissime haberet Ordines Belgicæ Suartsenburgio Cæsaris legato urgente, plus Cæsari & Germaniæ quam Galliæ regno & suo principatui deferre.
units.tr: On the other hand, Aurantius, still active at Ghent, was labouring to soften Andino and to calm the defection of Artois and Hainault. He laboured under a vain interpretation of his own mind and confidence, believing that the best peace would soon find its place, and that it could repair or restore everything spoiled or lost through dissension or war. But since the alliance made by the Artesians and Hainaulters had been concluded, Andino was recalled on account of his brother's death, concealing his offence under a pretext. The matter of peace did not suit him, for he was also thinking of abandoning the provinces, and he put forward the force of some authority based on an old agreement. Hence feelings, and as it were arguments from ancient law, were advanced in fine words. Yet he was most indignant that the Belgian States, at the urging of Schwarzenberg, Caesar's envoy, preferred to defer more to Caesar and Germany than to the kingdom of France and to his own principality.

units.la: Itaque datis ad Ordines x v. Kal. Febr. per Prunicauxium legatum litteris increpando commonuit ne quam pacem, quam Suatzenburgius proponebat, cum Hispano, nisi se consulto ex formulâ antiquæ conventionis facerent Cæsariq; ejus sanciendæ potestatem factam se petente revocarent. Neque Ordinum Generalium decretis Artesij eorumque socij suffragabantur qui pertinacem sui foederis, de quo dixi, sententiam profitendo Philippi regis plus gratiæ quam antiquo sociorum foederi dabant asperumq; & breve remedium hærenti ut ajebant, in visceribus suis malo flagitabant. Quo negato, statuturos de sua Salute reregerebant, postquam alienâ destituti propriæ & ex se petitæ medicinæ usum implorare poscenti miseriæ cogerentur. Ita omnia præter Aurantij opinionem infida publicum bellum spectabant.
units.tr: Therefore, by letters sent to the States on 18 January through the envoy Prunicaux, he warned them with rebuke not to make any peace, such as Schwarzenberg proposed, with the Spaniard, unless they did so with his consent and according to the form of the ancient agreement; and he recalled them, since they were asking that power be granted to Caesar to ratify it. Nor did the decrees of the General States support Artois and its allies, who, professing their stubborn opinion about their covenant (of which I have spoken), gave more favour to King Philip than to the old alliance of the allies. They demanded a harsh and brief remedy, as they called it, for the sick man, and preferred to bear it in their own bowels. When this was refused, they replied that they would decide on their own safety, since, abandoned by others, they would be forced by their misery to seek the use of a remedy from themselves and sought for themselves. Thus, contrary to Aurantius' expectation, everything tended unfaithfully towards open war.

units.la: Quamvis actorum fide probatum sit Matthiam gubernatorem & Aurantium principem de consilio Status & Ordinum generalium æquis-sima quæque Montinio & ducibus partium aliena à religionis pace postulantibus, vergente Januario mense obtulerint. Cæterum consilia procerum confundens fortunâ & velut crudæ bellorum tempestatis avida multis in civitatibus civilia & præsidiorum arma commiscebat, dif-fidioque sacrorum templa ac fora partium conflictibus destinabat. Itaque motus Antverpiæ & Neomagi exitio domesticæ pacis ortos optumi quisque ominabantur, Hispanosque expugnatâ Carperiâ arce superbas & per Cliviam ac Iuliacensium fines sparsos, Geldriæ oppidis ac munitionibus certissimas obsidiones comminari. Sed communem provincialibus metum Rudolphi Cæsaris sollicitudo & desiderium Belgicæ pacis allevabat & quod Otto Henricus Suartsenbergius Imperij legatus modo ad Ordines, modo ad Alexandrum Farnesium regiæ militiæ imperatorem commeando animos, etiam fato aut sponte dissidentes ad studia pacis sollicitaret.
units.tr: Yet the faith of the records proves that Matthias the governor and Aurantius the prince, with the counsel of the State and the General States, offered the fairest terms, late in January, to Montigny and the leaders of the party, who sought things alien to the peace of religion. But Aurantius, mixing the councils of the nobles with chance, and as if eager for the raw storm of war, mingled civil and garrison arms in many cities, and by his dissensions assigned the sacred temples and the marketplaces to the clashes of the parties. Thus the disturbances at Antwerp and Nijmegen, arising from the ruin of domestic peace, were taken as omens of disaster by all good men. They feared that the Spaniards, having taken the citadel of Carperia, were proud, and spread through Cleves and the lands of Jülich, threatened certain sieges of the towns and fortifications of Guelders. Yet Rudolph's concern and his desire for peace in Belgium relieved the fear common to the provincials. Otto Henry Schwarzenberg, envoy of the Empire, moved to and fro, now to the States, now to Alexander Farnese, the commander of the royal army, trying to stir men's minds, even those disagreeing by fate or by will, to zeal for peace.

units.la: Hoc vero Ordines nonnihil urebat, quod Farnesius totum negotium de mandato & exemplo Philippi regis deferri arbitrio Cæsaris vellet, aliâque sub conditione etiam honestâ & ad pacem suasoriâ omnem conventum aspernaretur.
units.tr: But this somewhat irritated the States: Farnese wished the whole business to be referred to Caesar's judgement, on the command and example of King Philip, and he rejected every conference on other terms, even honourable terms persuasive to peace.

units.la: Itaque decreto Antverpiæ xv. Kal. Februarij perscripto declararunt à Farnesio se molliora & servitura paci sperasse, cæterum relatione Suartsenbergij audita, difficultates quosdam pacis actioni injectas offendisse. Tamen ejus amore & in regem fide, paratos esse Cæsari cognitionem rerum & judicium deferre, modo æqua essent, quæ Farnesius postularet & Cæsar tantæ molis tædium non defugeret. Quare legatum ad Cæsarem ocyus missurae, qui de suo in pacem affectu eum edoceat & quam optent funestam belli tempestatem optumæ & æternæ pacis novâ serenitate sedari. Neq; alibi Rudolphi optimi Cæsarum consilia spectabant imperatoriâ voce coram Belgicæ legato, mox misso ad Ordines decreto, fidem facientis nihil magis illi post susceptam Romani imperij & tanti regiminis molem curæ fuisse, quam ut Belgicæ cæterarumque ditioni miseriæ & calamitati subveniretur. Itaq; de illius remedio cum principibus Imperij multum consultasse, quibus ut & ipsi Cæsari visum esset, belli mala non nisi maturatâ pace persanari posse. Sed moræ rerum alia quædam, velut malo, ut loquebatur, fato intervenisse, quæ salutari procurandæ pacis consilio facile emendarentur. Igitur se Cæsarem neq; labori, neq; sumptui, neq; molestiæ parciturum, facturumque ocyus ut turbis per provincias quies, bello pax succedat. Eum in finem supremo Curiæ suæ Marescħallo Ottoni Henrico Suartzenburgij Comiti per unum ex purpuratis suis Danielem Printsium in mandatis dedisse, ut de Ordinum voluntate cognoscat deq; eâ ad Cæsarem referat. Et quamvis ipse de Ordinum ad pacem inclinatione interea certior factus sit, ita tamen se metuere, ne Alençonij & Casimiri cum Ordinibus res remoram paci aut armistitio facturae sint.
units.tr: Therefore, by a decree written at Antwerp on 18 January, they declared that they had hoped from Farnese for milder terms that would serve peace; but, having heard Schwarzenberg's report, they had perceived that some difficulties had been thrown into the work of peace. Nevertheless, for love of him and in fidelity to the king, they were ready to refer the knowledge of affairs and the judgement to Caesar, provided that what Farnese demanded was fair and that Caesar did not shun the weariness of so great a burden. Wherefore they would send an envoy to Caesar as quickly as possible, who would inform him of their inclination to peace, and of how they wished the deadly storm of war to be calmed by the new serenity of a best and eternal peace. Nor did the counsels of Rudolph, the best of emperors, look elsewhere. He said as much with imperial voice before the Belgian envoy, and afterwards in a decree sent to the States, making it plain that nothing had been more his care since taking up the burden of the Roman empire and so great a rule, than that the misery and calamity of Belgium and of his other lands should be relieved. So he had consulted much with the princes of the Empire about its remedy, and it seemed to them, and to Caesar himself, that the evils of war could be healed only by a speedily made peace. But other delays had intervened, as if by an evil fate, as he put it, which could easily be remedied by a salutary plan for securing peace. Therefore he would spare neither labour, nor expense, nor trouble, and would see to it quickly that quiet should succeed the tumults through the provinces and peace follow war. To that end he had given instructions, through one of his purple-clad men, Daniel Printz, to his supreme marshal of the court, Count Otto Henry of Schwarzenberg, to learn the will of the States and report it to Caesar. And although he himself had meanwhile been informed of the States' inclination towards peace, he nevertheless feared that the affairs of Alençon and Casimir might cause a hindrance to peace or to the armistice.

units.la: Igitur Matthiam Archiducem Belgicae Gubernatorem & ipsos quoq; Ordines de amovendis Alençonij & Galliarum copiarum incommodis monuisse, minuendis Philippi regis suspicionibus, quas ex Alençonij societate hausisset. Se vero totum in eo esse, ut non habita Farnesij aut Ordinum cunctatione & arma utrinque sistat & locum conventui Coloniam Agrippinam designet, legatosq; suos istiusmodi mandatis instruat, quae ditionum Belgicarum tranquillitati ac usui cedant. Sperare se Deum pacis autorem isti concilio interfore, nisi divinae benignitatis cursum praeposterae conditiones morentur. Nam id paci non conducere, quod Ordines, nisi intra trimestre actio coeptae pacis definiatur, de revocando Andino cogitent. Neque enim laturos Caesarem & Romani imperij Electores, externum principem in finibus Imperij aut ijs provinciis constitui, quas non separari a Rom. imperio Caesaris & Philippi domusque Austriacae interesset. Sed hoc necessum esse ut Ordines suae salutis & incolumitatis rationem habeant, & ne perniciosa consilia exitio patriae suae destinata in praecipitando pacis negotio tueantur. Oportere rationem temporis & ponderosae actionis haberi & aut non praefiniri diem, aut praefinitum proferri ne Matthiae Gubernatoris & Austriacae domus exitumatio injuriam ex tam odiosis conditionibus sentiat. Quin eorum potius qui evocandi in Belgicam Archiducis autores fuere, officij esse reliquos apud socios hoc effectum dare, ut & cetera sua mandata valeant, de quibus Suartsenbergius serenissimum Archiducem doctiurus sit. Itaque huic fraternam integerrimamque mentem, illi Caesaris gratiam & propensum animum deferre.
units.tr: Therefore he had warned Archduke Matthias, the Governor of Belgium, and the Orders themselves, to remove the difficulties caused by Alençon and the French troops, so as to lessen the suspicions King Philip had gathered from Alençon's alliance. For his own part, he was intent on this: without waiting for any delay from Farnese or the Orders, he would have arms laid down on both sides, designate Cologne as the place for the assembly, and instruct his envoys with such commissions as would serve the peace and welfare of the Belgian provinces. He hoped that God, the author of peace, would be present at this council, unless perverse conditions were to hinder the course of divine kindness. For it did not help the peace that the Orders were thinking of recalling Andin, unless the business of the peace that had been begun was settled within three months. The Emperor and the Electors of the Roman Empire would not tolerate a foreign prince being placed within the borders of the Empire or in those provinces which it mattered to the Emperor, Philip and the House of Austria not to be separated from the Roman Empire. But it was necessary that the Orders should have regard for their own safety and security, and not uphold harmful plans, aimed at the ruin of their country, in hastening the business of the peace. The time and the weighty business had to be taken into account, and either no day should be fixed, or a fixed day should be postponed, so that the Governor Matthias and the House of Austria would not suffer injury from such hateful conditions beyond what they expected. Indeed, it was rather the duty of those who had been the authors of summoning the Archduke into Belgium to see to it, among their remaining allies, that this was achieved, so that their other commissions might be effective, about which Suartsenberg was to inform the most serene Archduke at greater length. Thus he offered a brotherly and most upright mind to the one, and to the other the Emperor's favour and a well-disposed spirit.

units.la: Mox RUDOLPHI litterae ad Ordines subjunctae hunc in modum.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, the letter of Rudolph to the Orders was appended, in this manner:

units.la: Reverendi Illustr. Gener. & caet. Fideles & Dilecti;
units.tr: Reverend, illustrious, general, and so forth, faithful and beloved:

units.la: COGNOVIMUS ex consiliarij nostri ac supremi Curiae Marschalli Comitis SUARTSENBERGII relatione vos concordiae deditos non pacem solum, sed armistitium insuper arti temporis flagitare. Quod consilium majestati nostrae quam maxime placuit. Caeterum quoniam FARNESIUS ab illo alienior est, remque ad CAROLUM Aragonium Castrenantium deferri curavit, dabimus operam, ut eidem Aragonio regis PHILIPPI Legato ejusdem vobiscum consilij autores simus. Interim Alexandrum Farnesium Parmae principem per litteras commonemus, ne morosum isti negotio se praebeat, quod facile promoturus erit si ANDINUM Gallicis cum copijs excedere Belgica, reliquaque mandata vim ac robur habere faciatis, quae Legato ac Oratori nostro Suartsenburgio commisimus. Et quoniam nobis cura est, ut pacis actio quam primum celeretur, locum Coloniae ad Rhenum legatis nostris, PHILIPPI atque vestris praescripsimus, de die quoque deliberaturi ut eum quod ocius bono publico praesmiamus.
units.tr: We have learned from the report of our councillor and chief Marshal of the Court, Count Suartsenberg, that you, devoted to concord, seek not only peace but also an armistice in the meantime. This plan has pleased our majesty very greatly. However, since Farnese is more alienated from it and has had the matter referred to Charles of Aragon, the governor of Castrenantium, we shall take care that we ourselves become advisers of this same plan to you, through the same Aragon, legate of King Philip. In the meantime we are admonishing Alexander Farnese, Prince of Parma, by letter, not to make himself a hindrance to this business; this he will readily advance if you cause Andin to withdraw from Belgium with the French forces, and cause the remaining commissions, which we have entrusted to our legate and envoy Suartsenberg, to have force and effect. And since it is our concern that the business of the peace be hastened as soon as possible, we have prescribed the place at Cologne on the Rhine for our legates, for Philip's and for yours, and we shall also deliberate about the day, so that we may as quickly as possible prefer what is for the public good.

units.la: Litterae Praga XVI. mensis datae & Rodolphi Caesaris manu signatae.
units.tr: Letter dated Prague, the 16th of the month, and signed with the hand of the Emperor Rudolph.

units.la: Reperio in actis provinciae Melchiorem Suartsenbergium praesidium Trajecti ad Mosam cum imperio agentem, velut obsidionis sollicitum, auxilia & commeatum Ordines generales tum petisse, deque eorundem Ordinum tarditate & incuria questum, funestum provincijs & sibi ipsi fatalem civitatis casum praevidisse.
units.tr: I find in the records of the province that Melchior Suartsenberg, who was exercising command of the garrison at Maastricht on the Meuse, being anxious as though about a siege, then sought aid and provisions from the General Orders, and complained of the slowness and negligence of those Orders, foreseeing the disastrous fate of the provinces and the fatal downfall of the city for himself.

units.la: Mox Ordinum ad Rodolphum II. litteræ missæ.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, the letter of the Orders sent to Rudolph II.

units.la: NIHIL studij, laboris atq; molestiæ IMPERATOR AUGUSTE, à nobis prætermissum est, quod & conciliandæ cum PHILIPPO Catholico rege nostro & quidem æquis conditionibus, pati conduceret & semel provincias à bello liberaret. Igitur Oratorem tuum Ottonem Henricum Suartsenburgium rogavimus, ut ex præscripto mandatorum tuorum ad Farnesium iret, cumque illo de conditionibus pacis conferret. Quod cum ab eo factum esset, post mensem isti legationi insumptum, rettulit, Farnesium non aliâ conditione pacisci velle, quàm si totum negotium, quod à Catholico Rege factum erat, tuo arbitrio peruoluteretur. Quod subterfugium pacis tanto magis admirationi nobis fuit, quod ex Oratore jam antè accepissemus, Regem nostrum Catholicum non aliâ ratione negotium hoc, quam ad intercedendum, tuæ majestati detulisse & quæ ipsa non vellet, veteriore onere, aut mandato se gravari. Interim ut majestati tuæ, atque adeo terrarum orbi de nostrâ in pacem propensione & præstandâ Regi Catholico obedientiâ testaremur, modo justo & moderato imperio nos regat, fidem facimus, nos totam pacis actionem tuæ sententiæ permittere, si quod Orator tuus cavit, medium te ex litterarum tuarum formulâ 22. Dec. dat. conciliandis partibus geras. Hoc vero maximè cupere nos scias, ut antè Kal. Mart. proximas totum negotium terminetur, ne morâ elusi incerta auxilia quærere cogamur & actionem deserere cum Andino captam, cui Kal. Martiæ præfinite sunt. Quod ipsum ex Legato Archiducis Matthiæ Antonio Lalaino Morvillerio te accepisse non dubitamus. Quamobrem, Imperator Auguste, quod facturum te confidimus, etiamnum rogamus, ut reip. nostræ securitas, Status, dignitas atque splendor tibi curæ sint & ut ea restituantur, quæ dolo aut per vim amissa sunt. Quod beneficium nos tuæ majestati quoque acceptum feremus, id voto complexi, ut Deus Imperio tuo desideratam nobis pacem & felicitatem largiatur. Antverp. vii. Kal. Febr.
units.tr: Most august Emperor, we have omitted no zeal, labour or trouble that would serve to reconcile us with Philip, our Catholic king, and indeed on fair terms, and that would free the provinces from war at last. Therefore we asked your envoy Otto Henry Suartsenberg to go to Farnese according to the instructions you gave him, and to confer with him about the conditions of peace. When he had done this, after a month spent on that embassy, he reported that Farnese would not agree on any condition other than that the whole business, which had been done by the Catholic King, should be overturned at your discretion. This evasion of peace was all the more a cause of wonder to us, since we had already heard from your envoy that our Catholic King had referred this business to your majesty only for the purpose of mediation, and that he would not be burdened with an older obligation or mandate which he himself did not want. Meanwhile, so that we may bear witness to your majesty, and indeed to the whole world, of our inclination towards peace and of our readiness to render obedience to the Catholic King, we assure you that we entrust the whole business of peace to your judgment, provided that he who rules us does so with a just and moderate rule. If, as your envoy has promised, you act as mediator in reconciling the parties, according to the form of your letter dated 22 December, you know that we desire this above all: that the whole business be concluded before the Kalends of March next, lest, delayed and deceived, we be forced to seek uncertain aid and abandon the negotiation begun with Andin, which was fixed for the Kalends of March. We do not doubt that you have received this from Antonius Lalaing de Morvillers, legate of the Archduke Matthias. Therefore, most august Emperor, we ask you once more, as we trust you will do, that the safety of our commonwealth, its standing, dignity and splendour be your concern, and that those things be restored which were lost by fraud or by force. We shall also count this benefit as received by your majesty, and we embrace this wish, that God may grant to your rule the peace and happiness we desire. Antwerp, 25 January.

units.la: T. Cæs. Majest. devinctissimi,
units.tr: Your Imperial Majesty's most bound servants,

units.la: Ord. & Status Provinc. Belg.
units.tr: The Orders and States of the Belgian Provinces.

units.la: Invenio ex litteris Caroli Roordæ xv. Kal. Febr. ad Deputatos Frisiæ Daventiâ datis Andinum discessus sui causam in morbum regis fratris, qui morti proximus ferebatur, rejecisse, etsi essent qui crederent ex detecto secretiore consilio pudefactum & velut fortunæ succensentem allevando animi morbo Galliam repetijsse. Cæterum Condæi subsistens & à legatus salutatus, ne tum quidem consilij certus spectabatur, ita variâ & mutabili mente ut locum custodiæ corporis & præsidio idoneum poscens, de reditu cogitaret. Sed regijs litteris per Guadagnium Præsulem & ab ipsâ matre sollicitatus nobilissimâ juventute, quam in comitatu habebat, præcipuos in Galliam præmisit datisque Condæo supremis ad Ordines litteris eosdem valere, deque affectu principis animi certos esse jussit. Hoc etiam subjunxit, ut quoniam Ordinibus Belgicæ novam legationem sui in gratiam instituì placuisset, eam gratam sibi acceptamque fore, non sine certâ spe in finibus Provinciarum & Galliæ agenti offerri adhuc posse. Adeo generosæ & nacIↄ. Iↄ. tæ ad magnâ indolis consilium secretâ erroris confessione vincebatur.
units.tr: I find from the letter of Charles of Roord, dated 18 January, to the deputies of Friesland at Deventer, that Andin attributed the cause of his departure to the illness of the king's brother, who was reported to be near death, although there were some who believed that, his more secret plan having been detected, he had been put to shame and, as though angry at fortune, had returned to France to ease his mental distress. Yet Condé, who was staying there and was greeted as legate, was not even then seen to be certain of his plan, so changeable and inconstant was his mind, seeking a place of custody for his person and a suitable garrison, and pondering a return. But, urged by royal letters through Guadagni the bishop, and by the mother herself, and by the most noble youth whom he had in his retinue, he sent the principal men ahead into France; and having given Condé his final letters to the Orders, he bade them farewell and assured them of the prince's feelings. He added this as well: since it had pleased the Belgian Orders to institute a new embassy in his favour, it would be welcome and acceptable to him, and could still be offered, not without a sure hope, while he was active in the borders of the provinces and of France. So far was that noble and high-spirited nature, aiming at a plan of great character, overcome by a secret confession of error.

units.la: LXXIX.
units.tr: LXXIX.

units.la: Igitur Andino in Galliæ fines provecto ac suspicione defectionis Valonicæ magis validâ Aurantius præveniendis ulterioribus malis, de maturando inter provincias inferiores novo foedere cogitavit, non ignarus correptam odio aut gratiâ provincialium multitudinem facilè in partes trahi animosque diversis opinionibus & studijs imbutos velut tempestate quadam aut æstu gravandis secessionibus impelli. Quippe Hannoniam & Artesiam exemplo præisse reliquosque aut societati eorum inligatos, aut imprimis faciles, peculiari animorum morbo, vetere disciplinâ superstitiosius imbutos, in majorum sacris suam & publicam provinciarum salutem atque incolumitatem collocare. Neque Hollandiam & Zelandiam etsi societatem ex communi periculo induissent, tanto armorum oneri & regiæ potentiæ parem, quæ tanto major futura sit, si Austriaci morte & successione Farnesij peritissimi belli & legionum Ducis retecta, intestinis quoque dissidentium provinciarum defectionibus subjuvetur. Itaq; expedire Geldriam hostium armis maximè expositam & recentium malorum sensu ad huic ingemiscentem Hollandico Zelandicoq; fœdere allevari, ex quo iste nationes ea commoda quoq; accipere queant, quæ potestatis hostium facta, magna ad res prosperè gerendas momenta allatura sint. Quippe Rhenum, Mosam, Vahalim & Isalam flumina provinciarum olim sub Romano imperio munimenta, firmitati istarum terrarum cessisse, quarum adhuc ripas lato & patiente navium alveo perstringentia torrentium aquarum vis emuniret. Frisios quoque, etsi longius disitos, ubertate soli & nato ad libertatem ingenio felices societati Hollandicæ innectendos, subvectandis in vicina commeatibus, quos fertilissimis terris editos aut apertum mare aut latissima æstuaria præstarent. Denique nihil magis securitati rerum, quam sanctionem utilissimi fœderis conducere, quod discretis provinciarum opibus viribusque vinculum ac robur daturum sit.
units.tr: Therefore, with Andin advanced into the borders of France and with suspicion of Walloon defection stronger than before, Orange thought that to forestall further evils the provinces of the Low Countries should quickly form a new covenant. He was not unaware that a multitude seized by hatred or by favour for one side is easily drawn into factions, and that minds steeped in different opinions and pursuits are driven into secession, as if by a storm or a fever. Hainault and Artois had already gone first, and the rest were either bound to their alliance or, above all, easy to lead, and, being infected with a peculiar sickness of spirit and more superstitiously steeped in the old discipline, placed their own and the provinces' safety and well-being in the rites of their ancestors. Nor could Holland and Zeeland, even though they had joined in alliance from a common danger, bear so great a burden of arms alone, against a royal power that would be far greater if, with Austria dead and the succession of Farnese, the most skilled commander of war and of legions, exposed, it were also helped by the internal defections of the dissenting provinces. Therefore, he judged, Gelderland, most exposed to enemy arms and groaning under the recent evils, should be relieved by a covenant with Holland and Zeeland, from which those nations could also gain those advantages which, once the enemy's power was taken away, would bring great weight to the successful conduct of affairs. Indeed the rivers Rhine, Meuse, Waal and IJssel, once fortifications of the provinces under the Roman empire, had yielded to the firmness of these lands, whose banks the force of torrents, grappling with a broad and patient channel for ships, still defends. The Frisians too, though further away, fortunate in the fertility of their soil and in a temperament born for liberty, were to be bound to the Dutch alliance, for carrying supplies to neighbouring regions, which the fertile lands produce and which the open sea or the widest estuaries afford. Finally, nothing contributes more to the security of affairs than the sanction of a most useful covenant, which will give a bond and strength drawn from the distinct resources and forces of the provinces.

units.la: Itaque negotio fratri Joanni Nassovio, qui Geldriæ præfecturam susceperat, commisso selectisque per Frisiam, qui profutura fœderi curarent, conventum Gorcumi ad Vahalim flumen Ordinum Hollandiæ Zelandiæq; indixerat. Ibi Nassovius verba faciens inter cætera de promovendo imprimis fœdere propo suerat, ac ut Frisij ad adeundam necessarij fœderis societatem honestis rationibus sollicitarentur. Sed per istam provinciam cruda omnia & salubribus consilijs necdum excocta reperiebantur, ambiguis provincialium & simul præfecti studijs, quæ regij adhuc nominis & Romanæ religionis professione velata, plerosque ut imperitam multitudinem solent, superstitiosus & in ijs potentissimos quosque ad alia trahebant. Itaque omne debile ac infirmum non nisi lento remedio curabatur, quod ingruentis periculi moles non ferebat, indivisasque Belgicæ gentes, etiam populo Friseo suæ libertatis & simul fœderis incuriosò, hostium furoribus expeni. Quanquam actis perscriptum sit, Hollandiæ Zelandiæque legatos Aurantij & Ioannis Nassovij consilium, quod sollicitandos Frisios suaserat, approbasse decretoque cavisse; Ut Frisij in communicem præconcepti fœderis adscisccrentur.
units.tr: Accordingly, the business having been entrusted to his brother John of Nassau, who had taken up the governorship of Gelderland, and men chosen from Friesland to attend to what would serve the covenant, he had called a meeting of the Estates of Holland and Zeeland at Gorinchem on the river Waal. There Nassau, speaking among other things, had proposed above all the advancement of the covenant, and that the Frisians should be urged by honourable arguments to enter the alliance that was necessary. But in that province everything was found raw and not yet ripened into wholesome counsels, because of the uncertain pursuits of the provincials and of the governor at the same time, which, veiled by the still-existing name of the king and the profession of the Roman religion, drew most people, as an ignorant multitude usually is, and the most powerful of them superstitiously, towards other ends. Thus every weak and feeble part was treated only with a slow remedy, which the mass of the impending danger did not allow; and the Belgian peoples, undivided, were exposed to the fury of the enemy, the Frisian people also being careless of their liberty and at the same time of the covenant. Yet it is recorded in the acts that the delegates of Holland and Zeeland approved the plan of Orange and John of Nassau, which had urged the winning over of the Frisians, and by decree provided that the Frisians should be admitted into the common covenant already conceived.

units.la: Cui sanciendo conventus ad iv. Eid. Ian. Ultrajecti indictus, ubi loan. Ioannes Nassovius fraterni consilij & foederis auspex coeteris cum legatis se sistebat. Quorum prudentia & festinatione conscriptum & in acta relatum, causam initae societatis & simul formam hunc in modum expresit:
units.tr: For sanctioning this, a meeting was summoned at Utrecht for 10 January, where John of Nassau, the patron of the fraternal counsel and covenant, presented himself with the other delegates. Their prudence and haste drew up and entered in the acts the cause of the alliance thus entered into, and at the same time its form, in the following manner:

units.la: QUANDOQUIDEM deprehensum est à tempore pacificationis Gandavensis, (quae mutuae fidei Belgicae provincias ad pallendos finibus Hispanos aterosque peregrinos obligaverat) eosdem Hispanos cum Joanne Austriaco caeterisque fautoribus, nihil aliud molitos esse, & etiamnum moliri, quam ut easdem provincias tyrannicis suis dominationibus ac perpetuae servitutis subjiciant, foedus Gandavense infirment aut subvertant, earundem provinciarum certissimo exitio, missis eum in finem clam ad diversas civitates litteris, & in Geldriam armata manu irruptione facta. Ea de causa Geldriae, Com. Zutphaniae, Hollandiae Zelandiaeque Comitatuum, Ultrajecti & Frisiorum Omlandiae inter Amasum & Lavicam Ordines necessarium duxerunt, in artius & specialius foedus condescendendi, non ut anteacti foederis vim & efficaciam solverent aut resolvi curarent, caeterum ut illud robur acciperet, adversumque omnia incommoda & conatus hostium provinciae suae defensionis certae forent. Igitur ad amovendam graviorem inter provincias secessionem, salva Gandavensi conventione & Rom. imperij jure, ijdem Ordines per delegatos mandatis suorum instructos definierunt sanciveruntq;. I. Provinciae in foedus coiunto. Illud firmum, indivisumque perpetuumq; maneto. Testamenta, codicilli, donationes, cessiones, permutationes, emptiones, pacis aut matrimonij pactiones non infirmanto. Provincijs, oppidis, provincialibusque singulis immunitates, statuta, consuetudines omniaque ac singula jura integra sunto. Ea adversum oppressores, etiam quoscunque jure aut armis experiuntor. Controversias inter provinciales ex eorum causa natas, ordinaria judicia aut arbitrorum compositiones dirimunto. Socijs inter cedendi jus est. II. Provinciae adversum quosq; etiam regij nominis praetextu utentes, auxilia & subsidia mutuum conferunto. Ista ex illo apud Gandavum foedere, aut recepto Matthiâ Gubernatore, aut reducendâ Romanâ Catholicâ religione, aut ob motus ab anno CIↃ. IↃ. VIII. ortos, aut huius foederis sanctionem non cessanto. Vnius discrimini commune auxilium subvenito. III. Idem adversum exteros, inquilinosque Principes, provincias, civitates vim aut injuriam inferentes paratum esto, caeterum de eo Ordines generales pro re nata cognoscunto. IV. Defendendis quibusque provincijs oppida caeteraque loca limitanea muniunto. Sumptuum partem mediam provinciales, alteram socij ferunto. Novae munitiones impendio omnium provinciarum extruuntor. V. Impensarum subsidia tributa sunto. Ea è vino, cerevisiâ, terendo frumento, sale, aureo, argenteo sericoque panno, animalibus cornutis atque quadripedibus, agris seminato, mactato pecore, equorum bovumque venditione aut permutatione, dein ex rebus libra subjectis habento. Formulam communi suffragio concipiunto. Census regius deducto aere alieno subsidiarius esto. VI. Collationes, pro rerum exigentia tuendo foederi eiusque oneribus de communi consilio intenduntor remittuntorq;. Aliis usibus quam publicis non serviunto. VII. Limitaneae caeteraeque urbes, ubi necessitas exiget, provinciarum arbitrio, de consilio Praefecti provinciae praesidium recipiunto. Provinciae stipendia danto. Centuriones militesque, praeter sacramentum foederi dictum, urbi quoque aut pro-vinvincie pigneranto. Id in formulâ militaris Articuli scribitor. Præsidium disciplinæ pareto. Civibus agrariisque damnum aut vim non facito. Eorum onera in collationibus ferto. Provinciæ præsidiale æs pendunto. VIII. Habendis in promptu auxilijs intra mensem provinciales ab anno XVIII. in LX. describuntor. Censu capitum acto, quod provinciarum securitati serviat, primo conventu fœderati Ordines statuunto. IX. Ordines generales pacem aut indutias non faciunto, bellum non suscipiunto. Tributa nisi de consilio provinciarum ordinanto. Earum suffragijs, si præponderent, dum aliter statuatur, pro more stanto. De bello, pace aut tributo, dicidentibus Præfectis provinciarum subveniunto, qui si discrepent, alios arbitros adiscunto, litem terminanto. X. Provincia, oppidum fœdus aut societatem sine sociorum consensu cum vicino Principe aut gente non facito. XI. Externus Princeps populusve in fœdus aut societatem de suffragio provinciarum recipitor. XII. Moneta usus ac valor, ex formulâ de eo concipiendâ, par ac unus per provincias esto. XIII. In causâ Religionis Ordines Hollandiæ Zelandiaeque suo arbitratu agunto. Reliquis fœderatis provincijs ab edicto religionis (à Matthiâ Gubernatore de suorum consilio & Ordinum generalium decreto) promulgato non recedere liberum esto. Pace publicâ de singulorum privatorum jure ac fortunis cavento. Conscientiæ nullam vim ex Gandavensi fœdere faciunto. XIV. Cænobitæ ceterique Ecclesiastici bona sua; uti possiderunt, ita possidento. Reliquis, qui durante bello, desertis cænobijs in Hollandiam Zelandiamque aut ex his alias in provincias se contulere, alimenta præstantor. XV. Eadem ecclesiasticis ex æquâ causâ ordinem statumque vita mutare cupientibus, dantor. Reliquis vero à tempore scripti fœderis monasticam vitam professis & deserentibus nullum beneficium obvenito. Religionem & habitum eligere cuique liberum esto. Cænobiorum rectoribus pareto. XVI. Dissensiones inter provincias seorsim natas, reliquæ aut ij qui isti actui destinabuntur, sananto. Omnium vero provinciarum controversias intra mensem & citius ex æquo Præfecti componunto. Ab ijs vero, quæ aut Provinciæ, aut delegati earum, aut præfecti definierunt, nulla provocatio esto. XVII. Provinciæ exteris Principibus aut populis, occasionem belli non danto, exteris inquilinisque jus dicunto. Id prolatum cetera ex proprio provinciarum jure & consuetudine corrigunto. XVIII. Provincia in præjudicium alterius sine communi decreto tributum aut navale vectigal, non imponito. Æqua omnibus onera sunto. XIX. Fœderati eorum autoritate quibus ista competet Ultrajectum citati ad diem dictum, qui in citatorijs litteris nisi res silentium exigat, exprimetur, instituendis consultationibus se sistunto. In omnibus suffragiorum pluralitatem sequuntor. Absentium ratio non habetor. Qui comparuerunt, bono publico rem definiunto ac observanto. Isti absentes (nisi secus rei gravitas exigat, etsi illa moram non ferat) parento. Aliter repetitâ citatione certum ad diem evocantor, nisi compareant suffragandi jus, nisi scripto id transmissum fuerit, amittunto. Reliqui, quod ex usu erit, sanciunto. XX. Fœderati de singulis, quæ aut provinciarum commodo, bono aut detrimento cedent, ad proximos perscribunto. Isti reliquos provincijs evocanto. XXI. Fœderati dubiâ hoc fœdere comprehensa concordibus suffragijs decidunto. Ista si divisa sient, præfecti provinciarum componunto. XXII. In conditionibus fœderis si quid mutandum aut addendum fuerit, id in potestate fœderatorum esto. XXIII. Leges fœderis sartas tectas provinciales præstanto, nisi fafi faciant, eorum qui infringent, personæ & bona ubivis locorum, apud quemcunque etiam judicem detinentur. Nullâ juris exceptione aut beneficio fruuntur. Generali renuntiationi, nisi speciali præcesserit, locus non esto. xxiv. Præsecti provinciarum tam præsentes quam futuri, Magistratus & supremi officiales provinciarum, oppidorum & partium in leges fœderis & earum fidelem observantiam juranto. xxv. Idem collegia & sodalitates in oppidis vicisque faciunto. xxvi. Acta fœderis ritè concepta Præfecti & Magistratus supradicti sigillis muniunto, suâ & actuariorum manu signanto.
units.tr: Whereas it has been discovered that since the time of the Pacification of Ghent (which had bound the provinces of the Belgians in mutual faith to drive out the Spaniards and other foreigners from their borders), the same Spaniards, with John of Austria and other favourers, have planned nothing else, and are still planning, than to subject these same provinces to their tyrannical dominations and perpetual servitude, to weaken or overturn the Ghent covenant, to the most certain ruin of those same provinces, sending letters to various cities secretly for that purpose, and making an armed invasion into Gelderland: for this reason the Estates judged it necessary for Gelderland, the county of Zutphen, the counties of Holland and Zeeland, Utrecht and the Frisian Omlands between the Ems and the Lauwers, to enter into a closer and more special covenant; not so as to dissolve or to arrange the dissolution of the force and efficacy of the earlier covenant, but so that it might receive strength, and that its provinces might be sure of their defence against all the inconveniences and attempts of the enemy. Therefore, to remove a more serious secession among the provinces, saving the Ghent convention and the right of the Roman empire, the same Estates, through delegates instructed by their mandates, defined and sanctioned the following: I. The provinces joined in covenant: let that be firm, undivided and perpetual. Testaments, codicils, donations, cessions, exchanges, purchases, and agreements of peace or marriage shall not be invalidated. The privileges, statutes, customs and all and each of the rights of the provinces, towns and individual provincials shall remain whole. Let them be pursued against oppressors, even against any whoever, by law or by arms. Disputes among provincials arising from their cause shall be settled by the ordinary courts or by the decisions of arbiters. Partners have the right of intercession. II. The provinces shall confer mutual aid and subsidies against all who use even the pretext of royal name. Let them not cease for these purposes: from the former covenant at Ghent, or from the reception of Matthias as governor, or from the restoration of the Roman Catholic religion, or from the movements that arose in the year 1578, or from the sanction of this covenant. Let common aid be given to the peril of one. III. Likewise, let there be readiness against foreign and resident princes, provinces and cities that inflict force or injury; but concerning this the General Estates shall take cognisance as the occasion arises. IV. For the defence of each province, let the towns and other frontier places be fortified. Let the provincials bear half the cost, and the partners the other half. New fortifications shall be built at the expense of all the provinces. V. The subsidies for expenses shall be taxes. These shall be levied on wine, beer, ground corn, salt, gold, silver and silk cloth, horned and four-footed animals, sown fields, slaughtered livestock, and the sale or exchange of horses and oxen, and then from the other goods listed below. Let a formula be drawn up by common vote. The royal tax, after deducting debts, shall be a subsidiary one. VI. Contributions shall be levied and remitted, according to the needs of the times, for the defence of the covenant and its burdens, by common counsel. They shall not be used for any purpose other than public ones. VII. The frontier and other cities, where necessity demands, shall receive a garrison at the discretion of the provinces, on the advice of the governor of the province. The province shall pay the wages. Captains and soldiers, besides the oath stated in the covenant, shall also pledge themselves to the city or to the province. This shall be written in the form of the military article. The garrison shall obey discipline. They shall not do damage or violence to citizens or farmers. They shall bear their share of the contributions. The provinces shall pay the garrison money. VIII. In order to have aids ready at hand, the provincials shall be enrolled within a month, from the age of eighteen to sixty. When a census of heads has been taken, which may serve the security of the provinces, the United Estates shall decide at the first meeting. IX. The General Estates shall not make peace or truce, nor undertake war. They shall order taxes only with the counsel of the provinces. Their votes, if they prevail, shall stand as the custom is, until otherwise decided. In the case of war, peace or taxes, the governors of the provinces, if they disagree, shall be given assistance; and if they still differ, they shall choose other arbiters and end the dispute. X. No province, town, covenant or association shall be made with a neighbouring prince or people without the consent of the partners. XI. An external prince or people shall be received into covenant or association by the vote of the provinces. XII. The currency, its use and value, shall be one and equal throughout the provinces, according to a formula to be drawn up for that purpose. XIII. In matters of religion the Estates of Holland and Zeeland shall act at their own discretion. It shall not be free for the other united provinces to depart from the edict on religion (promulgated by Matthias the governor, with the counsel of his men and the decree of the General Estates). Let them take care of public peace and of the right and fortunes of each private person. Let them do no violence to conscience on account of the Ghent covenant. XIV. Monks and other ecclesiastics shall hold their goods as they have possessed them. Maintenance shall be given to the others who, during the war, abandoned their monasteries and betook themselves into Holland and Zeeland, or from there into other provinces. XV. The same shall be given to ecclesiastics who for the same reason wish to change their order and state of life. But to others who, from the time of the written covenant, have professed monastic life and desert it, no benefit shall accrue. Each person shall be free to choose his religion and dress. They shall obey the superiors of the monasteries. XVI. Disputes arising separately between provinces shall be healed by the rest, or by those who are appointed for that act. The disputes of all the provinces, however, the governors shall settle equitably within a month, and sooner. From those decisions which the provinces, or their delegates, or the governors have defined, there shall be no appeal. XVII. The provinces shall not give occasion of war to foreign princes or peoples; they shall administer justice to foreigners and residents. This having been extended, they shall correct the rest according to each province's own law and custom. XVIII. A province shall not impose a tax or naval toll to the prejudice of another without a common decree. The burdens shall be equal for all. XIX. The partners, summoned to Utrecht by the authority of those to whom this belongs, shall present themselves on the appointed day, which shall be stated in the summons unless the matter demands silence, to hold consultations. In all votes they shall follow the plurality. The absent shall not be taken into account. Those who have appeared shall settle and observe the matter for the public good. Those absent shall obey (unless the gravity of the matter demands otherwise, though delay is not to be borne). Otherwise, after the summons is repeated, they shall be called to a fixed day; unless they appear, they shall lose the right to vote, unless it has been sent in writing. The rest they shall sanction as is expedient. XX. The partners shall write to the nearest of them about each matter which will fall to the advantage, good or harm of the provinces. Those nearest shall summon the rest of the provinces. XXI. The partners shall decide by concordant votes the doubtful matters comprehended in this covenant. If these should be divided, the governors of the provinces shall settle them. XXII. If anything in the conditions of the covenant should need changing or adding, that shall be in the power of the partners. XXIII. The provinces shall maintain the laws of the covenant whole and intact; unless they make it fail, the persons and goods of those who infringe it are detained anywhere, before any judge whatever. They shall enjoy no exception or benefit of law. A general renunciation shall have no place, unless a special one has preceded it. XXIV. The governors of the provinces, present and future, and the magistrates and chief officials of the provinces, towns and districts, shall swear to the laws of the covenant and to their faithful observance. XXV. The same shall be done for colleges and fellowships in towns and villages. XXVI. The acts of the covenant, duly drawn up, the aforesaid governors and magistrates shall fortify with their seals and sign with their own hand and that of the clerks.

units.la: Quæ fœderis capita à Joanne Nassovio Geldriæ Præfecto, Alexandro Tellichio, Ægydio Piekio, Ioachimo Lirano, Alexandro Bentinigio pro Geldris. Pro Hollandis G. Poelgeest, Paulo Busio, Regnero Cantio, pro Zelandis Gulielmo Roelsio, Nicolao Blanciæ, Petro de Rijcke & Casparo Vosbergio. Pro Ultrajectinis ab Antonio Galama à Schora, de mandato Capituli, Jacobo Verhario, Vicedecano S. Petri, de mandato Capituli, Adriano Zuylio, Lamberto à Binchio, F. Utenengio, Reinardo Asuinio, Bartholomæo Valio, Nicolao Zuilio, A. de Leyden, Lubberto Clivio. Pro Omlandis Egberto Clantio & Eysone Iarges x. Kal. Febr. signata Ultrajecti.
units.tr: The heads of this covenant, as drawn up by John of Nassau, governor of Gelderland, with Alexander Tellichius, Egidius Piekius, Joachim Liranus and Alexander Bentinigius for Gelderland; for Holland, G. Poelgeest, Paulus Busius and Regnerus Cantius; for Zeeland, Gulielmus Roelsius, Nicolaus Blanciae, Petrus de Rijcke and Casparus Vosbergius; for Utrecht, Antonius Galama à Schora, by mandate of the Chapter, Jacobus Verharius, vice-dean of St Peter's, by mandate of the Chapter, Adrianus Zuylius, Lambertus à Binchius, F. Utenengius, Reinardus Asuinius, Bartholomaeus Valius, Nicolaus Zuilius, A. de Leyden and Lubbertus Clivius; for the Ommelanden, Egbertus Clantius and Eysso Iarges. Signed at Utrecht, 23 January.

units.la: Quod etsi 23. Novemb. proxumo apud Ultrajectinos Barthius Idsaerda & Douwo Sixma Legati Frisiorum nomine se facturos cavissent, ita gliscentes per eam provinciam civilium factionum infoelices discordiæ etiam tum morabantur. Quippe alij pro Rege & ejus dominatione, alij pro libertate, ut alibi armis, ita domi odijs & æmulationibus certabant, quas tolli non posse, nisi alterutrâ parte subversâ indicia gravissimæ acerbitatis ostendebant.
units.tr: Although Barthius Idsaerda and Douwo Sixma, legates of the Frisians, had promised at Utrecht on 23 November last that they would act in the name of their people, the unhappy discords of civil faction, which were growing throughout that province, still lingered. For some fought for the King and his rule, others for liberty; as they contended with arms elsewhere, so at home they contended with hatreds and rivalries, which, they showed, could not be removed unless one side or the other were overthrown, a sign of the gravest bitterness.

units.la: Quippe Deputati Ordinum libello supplice novo Senatui exhibito, in veterem Philippi senatum invehebantur, quod is acta & instrumenta partium, adhuc consignatum æs supprimendo sanguine & succo obviæ & redactæ ad mendicimoniam paupertatis pascerentur. Itaque otio & luxu gravem & præter hoc alienâ limina circumeuntium innocentiam & res strangulantem mandato Senatus coërcendum esse, quo libelli & disceptantium in foro acta, nullo fructu, cum nocte & putredine luctantia partium usibus & expediendis judicijs serviant. Non esse credendam ijs controversi juris materiem, qui dilationibus & minus necessarijs tempora trahendo suspecti & dignitatibus quasi exuti & fori cursum & litigantium commoda morarentur. Quare Senatus, quem præsidere judicijs Ordines fecerant, exhiberi sibi acta, libros, munimenta rescripto jusit, Ordinumque petitioni velut æquissimæ & tot innocentium querelis subnixæ morem gessit. Igitur Deputati Ordinum Wigero Mockamæ apparitori Curiæ potestatem fecere à vetere Senatu acta & processus litigantium effagitandi, addito, ut nisi pareat, de eo referat. Cæterum cum alij decorâ animi moderatione etiam in tam asperâ accusatione, officia offerendo, alij excusationibus honestis uterentur erant tamen, qui innatam, instar morientium ferarum, ingenijs ferociam acuerent injuriamq; & vim sibi fieri obtendendo nihil de prioris fortunæ conditione & moribus remitterent.
units.tr: For the Deputies of the Estates, in a new supplication presented to the Senate, attacked the old Senate of Philip, complaining that it, by suppressing the records and documents of the parties, and while the money was still held back, was feeding on the blood and sap of those who stood in its way and had been reduced to beggary. Therefore, they said, the idleness and luxury of the Senate, which was a heavy burden besides and strangled the innocence and property of those who went about its doorstep, must be checked by the order of the Senate, so that the petitions and the records of those pleading in the forum, which, with no profit, struggle at night and in decay, might serve the needs of the parties and the despatch of trials. The matter of contested law should not be entrusted to men who, by dragging things out with delays and unnecessary business, were suspect and, as it were, stripped of their dignity, and who delayed the course of the court and the convenience of litigants. Wherefore the Senate, which the Estates had made to preside over the trials, ordered by rescript that the acts, books and records be delivered to it, and it complied with the petition of the Estates as most just and supported by so many complaints of the innocent. Accordingly, the Deputies of the Estates empowered Wigerus Mockama, an usher of the Court, to demand from the old Senate the acts and proceedings of the litigants, adding that if it did not obey, he should report this. Yet while some, with dignified moderation of spirit, even under so harsh an accusation, offered their services, and others used honourable excuses, there were some who, like dying wild beasts, sharpened their native ferocity and, pleading that wrong and violence were being done to them, gave up nothing of the condition and character of their former fortune.

units.la: Annotatum est Antonium Lavailium, nuper communicati cum Ioanne ne Austriaco secretioris consilij suspectum, contumaci silentio per indignationem abrupto paucas voces, sed compresso sanguinis fervore prolocutum, Georgioque Westeudorpio affectuum immodico multa cum vehementiâ & ex impatientiâ animi sibi non constantis, excidisse. Itaq; de injuriâ suo & collegarum nomine obtestatum, quorum interim accusationibus apud Matthiam Archiducem aliquid antiquæ Senatus dignitati & Regijs mandatis adhuc dantem, non obsoleta patrocinia quærebantur.
units.tr: It was noted that Antonius Lavailius, recently suspected of association with John of Austria in the secret council, broke off his stubborn silence in indignation, and, though he restrained the heat of his blood, spoke a few words; and that Georgius Westeudorpius, with great vehemence and an excessive emotion, burst out from an impatience of spirit that was not steady. Accordingly he protested about the wrong done to himself and his colleagues, and they sought, through their accusations before Archduke Matthias, who still gave some weight to the dignity of the old Senate and its royal mandates, protection that was not out of date.

units.la: Unde factum est, ut Cunero Episcopo etiam absenti & de residuis insimulato honestam cœtingentorum carolæorum pensionem & mobilia bonorum sustentandæ vitæ assignaret, Frisiæq; Ordinibus lege adversus eundem Cunerum agentibus negotium & velut ex importunitate procedendi invidiam facesserent. Quare Frisiæ Ordines Matthiam Gubernatorem serið rogarunt, ne publicis reorum criminibus impunitatem præferret, hominemque sui Ordinis & quod fœdius morum ac modestiæ oblitum odioso beneficio sublevaret. Neque enim eam provincialis ærarij rationem esse, ut iltiusmodi largitionibus respondeat, neque id præmij in illum erogandum fuisse, quem præstandis rationibus administratæ & prostitutæ fœditer sedis imparem neglectæ disciplinæ & frugalitatis incuria fecisset. Itaque mandasse Pompeio Roordæ Episcopalium redituum aut mobilium quæstori, ne quid æris ex illo rescripto in Episcopum conferat, nisi libellum supplicem exhibuerit haud dubiè falsâ materiè instructum. Sperare se Archiducem ex Gandavensi conventione missionem Episcopo facturum, ne provinciæ in posterum oneri sit, quæ restitutionis in integrum indigeat. Quod ad priorem Senatum attineret, illi velut abitum paranti mandatum injecisse, ne nisi traditis actis judicialibus cæterisque partium rebus provinciâ excedat. In eo proposito se etiamnum perseverare ac rogare interim Archiducem, ut negotium cum Julio Bottnia legato occœptum ratum præstat.
units.tr: Hence it came about that the Archduke assigned to Bishop Cuneras, even though he was absent and accused of arrears, an honourable pension of a hundred and forty Carolus guilders and movables from his goods for the support of his life, while the Frisian Estates, proceeding by law against the same Cuneras, stirred up the business and, as it were, odium from the importunity of their prosecution. Wherefore the Frisian Estates earnestly asked Matthias the Governor not to give impunity to the public crimes of the accused, nor to relieve with a hateful benefit a man of their own order who had forgotten, to his disgrace, both morals and moderation. For that, they said, was not the principle of the provincial treasury, that it should answer to such largesses, nor was that the reward to be paid to one whom the neglect of discipline and the carelessness of thrift had made unequal to rendering accounts for an administered and shamefully abused see. Therefore, they said, he had ordered Pompeius Roorda, the quaestor of the episcopal revenues or movables, not to pay any money to the Bishop under that rescript unless he had presented a supplication, undoubtedly built on a false matter. They hoped that the Archduke, in accordance with the Ghent agreement, would dismiss the Bishop, so that the province would not in future be burdened by one who needed to be restored to his former state. As for the former Senate, they said, he had, as it were, ordered it, while preparing to depart, not to leave the province unless it had handed over the judicial acts and the other affairs of the parties. They said they were still persevering in this purpose, and meanwhile asked the Archduke to ratify the business begun with Julius Bottnia, the legate.

units.la: Ita omnia partium plena & signando Ultrajectino fœderi adversa, procul domesticæ pacis cuiâ, per provinciam fluebant. Quæ fatali discordiæ malo, velut tristi sydere, impulsa, nec sola extra fortunæ discrimen esse poterat, nec in civilem concordiam pertrahi, seligendis Philippi aut patriæ partibus, intra quas stabant aut stare videbantur noxiarum factionum consilia.
units.tr: Thus everything in the province was full of partisanship and opposed to the Utrecht covenant, and flowed far from any concern for domestic peace. Driven by the fatal evil of discord, as by a baleful star, it could neither remain alone outside the risk of fortune, nor be drawn into civil concord, the parties of Philip or of the fatherland being chosen, within which the designs of harmful factions stood, or seemed to stand.

units.la: Itaque plurimos fama solemnis sacramenti Carolo Cæsari & Philippo filio præstiti & simul recordatio afficiebat, quarum utraque retineri integra non posset, si novo & secessionem à Rege facturo fœderi Ultrajectino subscribant. Quod etsi superficie tenus inspectando non præferret, tamen id arcanum arctioris societatis interpretamentum esse, ut regis populique dissidijs fomentum subministret. Cæteris vero patriæ nomen imperio principis reverentius videbatur, quod vi & armis subnixum excusâ principalis sacramenti memoriâ cessaret. Neq; iniquum & à gentium moribus alienum esse repellere quæ nocerent aut sanguinis pretio empta triste servitium minarentur. Id liberos, id conjuges, id sacra & domestici liminis religionem implorare, ut quam longissime arceatur, nec animorum secretum subeat efferati regis veneratio. Coëundum potius, sicuti armenta solent, ad ferœ incursum esse, quo si animi suo fato non posint, dexterœ saltem & vires repelen-
units.tr: Thus very many were moved both by the report of the solemn oath sworn to Emperor Charles and to his son Philip, and by the memory of it, since neither of these could remain intact if they subscribed to the new covenant of Utrecht, which would make a secession from the King. Although on the surface, looked at superficially, it did not show this, nevertheless this was the hidden meaning of a closer alliance, that it should supply fuel for the quarrels of king and people. To others, however, the name of the fatherland seemed more reverent than the authority of the prince, which, supported by force and arms, would cease once the memory of the principal oath was set aside. Nor did they think it unjust, or alien to the customs of nations, to repel what would harm them or threaten a sad slavery bought at the price of blood. This, they said, was what wives and children, and the sacred things and religion of the household threshold, begged them to do, so that it might be kept as far away as possible, and that the reverence for a maddened king might not creep into the secret of their minds. They should rather gather, as herds usually do, against the onslaught of a wild beast; so that if they could not do so by their own spirit, at least their skill and strength might be joined to repel the enemy.

units.la: In Martio scribendum ex Chronico sol. 641. lendis hostibus jungantur. Manere posse suum cuique de divinis sensum ne conscientiae provincialium serviant, quas liberrimas, ut illarum opifex legesque humanae, ita maxime Ultrajectini foederis sanctio voluisset. Caeterum reparandae libertatis curae mutuis odijs & novarum partium affectatione turbabantur, cum essent, qui in Hannoniae Artesiaeque foedere omnem publicae salutis spem collocarent, quod & à Gandavensi conventione non abiret & Philippi jus atque majestatem tueretur.
units.tr: Each man may keep his own opinion about divine matters, so that the consciences of the provincials are not enslaved, which the Utrecht covenant, as the maker of those liberties and the sanction of human laws, would most of all have wished to be most free. Yet the care for restoring liberty was disturbed by mutual hatreds and the pursuit of new parties, since there were those who placed all their hope of public safety in the covenant of Hainault and Artois, which did not depart from the Ghent agreement and protected the right and majesty of Philip.

units.la: Itaque factum est, ut Montinius alijque defectores proclivem partibus suis Frisiam jactitarent omnemque illum tractum à Flevo, Rheni ostio, in Lavicam flumen protensum, cum Artesiâ, Hannoniâ, Insulis, Duaco & Orchijs coiturum. Quasi interjectis tantis terrarum spatijs, quae Geldri, Hollandi, Zelandi & Ultrajectini tenerent, auxilia Frisijs ab illis gentibus proficisci possent, quae sedibus, linguâ, moribus discretae polliceri sibi nequirent, non duraturi foederis fidem. Adhaec agros trans Lavicam sitos & ad Amisi fluminis ripam procurrentes Ultrajectinae societati innexos, neque ipsum mare, etsi adeundis gentibus patens, apertum credi posse, quod Hollandiae sociorumque classibus infestatum, ne commercia quidem cum Artesijs aut Hannonijs Frisiorum populo permissurum esset.
units.tr: Thus it came about that Montigny and the other defectors boasted that Friesland was inclined to their side, and that the whole tract stretching from the Flevo, the mouth of the Rhine, to the river Lauwers, would join with Artois, Hainault, the Isles, Douai and Orchies. As if, with such great stretches of land lying between, which Gelderland, Holland, Zeeland and Utrecht held, help could come to the Frisians from those peoples, who, being divided by seats, language and customs, could not promise themselves that the covenant would last. Moreover, the fields lying beyond the Lauwers and running out to the bank of the river Ems, being bound to the Utrecht alliance, could not be believed open even by the sea itself, though it was open to the approach of nations; since it was harassed by the fleets of Holland and her allies, it would not even permit trade between the Frisian people and Artois or Hainault.

units.la: Sed omnes istas difficultates factionum amor & caeca cupido amovebat. Quibus Leovardiae attemperandis 23. Februarij mensis, usurpato Lalainij etiam absentis nomine, postulantibus Renico Cammingha & Adio Lamberto Deputatis Ordinum supremus Curiae Senatu datis in omnem provinciam litteris à quo Lalainius alienior erat, comitium ad IV. Non. Martij judixit. Cui rei occasionem quoque commodabat, quod ad foederis Ultrajectini societatem Frisij ferventius tum sollicitarentur & quod rex Philippus, prout ante factum erat, perscriptis Mantuae Carpentanorum VII. Eid. Febr. ad Ordines Artesiae litteris, Gandavense foedus & inter Ordines Belgicae post ictum, dein perpetui Edicti nomine habitum regiâ ratihabitione se firmaturum polliceretur.
units.tr: But love of faction and blind desire removed all these difficulties. To bring Leeuwarden into line, on 23 February, in the name of Lalaing, though he was absent, and at the request of Renicus Camminga and Adius Lambertus, deputies of the Estates, the supreme Senate of the Court, having sent letters throughout the whole province, and by which Lalaing was rather estranged, appointed an assembly for 2 March. This was also made an occasion for it, because the Frisians were then being more eagerly solicited to join the Utrecht covenant, and because King Philip, as had already happened, having written letters from Mantua to the Estates of Artois on 9 February, promised that he would confirm, by royal ratification, the Ghent covenant and the Perpetual Edict, which was held after the agreement made between the Estates of Belgium.

units.la: Quae vana & speciosa regiae gratiae ostentatio in animum quoq; Rennebergij quam maxime se infuderat. Igitur quo moram foederi Ultrajectino per Frisiam injiceret, more priorum temporum, vocari ad Comitium Regi ac Romanae religioni addictissimos volverat, ac ut in Ordinum coetum, plenâ cum agendi decernendique potestate admitterentur, quos suis consilijs ac ingenio faventes secretâ familiaritate exploraverat.
units.tr: This empty and showy display of royal favour had sunk deeply into the mind of Rennenberg as well. So, to put a delay in the way of the Utrecht covenant across Friesland, he resolved, as in earlier times, to summon to the assembly men most devoted to the King and the Roman religion, and to admit them to the gathering of the Estates with full power to act and decide. He had sounded out through secret intimacy those whom he judged favourable to his plans and disposition.

units.la: Ipse postero die. III. Non. Mart. magno comitatu urbem ingressus, quo comitij rebus praesideret, alitas diu inter potentissimos quosque simultates aulicis artibus nutriebat. Ibi procerum conventui Ansonius quoque Galama & Florentius Thinnius Ultrajectinorum legati interfuere. Verbisque ad populum pro more factis, ad amplectendam ocyus Ultrajectini foederis sanctionem praefervidis studijs hortabantur.
units.tr: On the following day, 3 Nones of March, he entered the city with a large retinue to preside over the business of the assembly, and he kept nourishing, by courtly arts, the long-standing feuds among the most powerful men. At this gathering of the nobles, Ansonius Galama and Florentius Thinnius, envoys of the Utrechters, were also present. In the customary speeches to the people, they urged with fervent zeal that the sanction of the Utrecht covenant be embraced more quickly.

units.la: Omnem scilicet prolatationem conditioni temporum inimicam repetebant, festinandumque esse, ubi poenitentiae ex morâ metus esset. Diffindi scilicet & dissolvi provinciarum foedera & validissimos quoq; prout animus aut ingenium esset, novis rebus studere denique in ancipiti remp. ex procerum dissidijs & per arma hostium esse, quorum in‐commodis subvenire posset concordia foederis vires bello, occasionem paci factura.
units.tr: They kept demanding that every postponement hostile to the state of affairs be abandoned, and that they must hurry, since there was fear of repentance from delay. The covenants of the provinces, they said, were being torn apart and dissolved, and the most powerful men, according to their temper or talent, were pursuing new schemes. In short, the commonwealth was in peril from the quarrels of the nobles and from the enemy's arms; a concord of covenant, which could remedy these ills, would bring strength for war and an opportunity for peace.

units.la: Igitur maturanda ocyus consilia bono cessura, ne per consulentium incuriam aut ex intempestivis partium studijs animos sumat praevalentis & superbi hostis immanitas.
