There were causes enough why King Philip could be stripped of the right and possession of the principate: besides Alva's savagery and the rejected supplications of the people, Austria's defection could be alleged, and, not to go far, the very assembly at Cologne was pretended as a sign of peace efforts. If this did not succeed, a prince had to be chosen who would bear the burden of the leaning Belgium and restore to the rule of a prince its liberty, worn down by discord and doomed to perish through the secessions of the provinces. Yet from Anjou every support for falling affairs could be sought. Hence the flanks of France, facing the enemies, would cut off supplies from the hostile camps, and the Belgian provinces, exposed to Philip's arms, could be attacked more easily, since he would see the sworn enemies of his people, the French, roused to his destruction. Certainly Caesar and the King would give fairer conditions to the unhappy provinces, which would believe their safety abundantly provided for if they used Anjou as the old defender of liberty. The spirit of his principal nature could be restrained by the fairness of the pacts, so that it stayed within the prescribed limit; his desire for greater power would recognise its bounds if it abstained from war or peace, gave up the licence of distributing the military garrisons, added strength and force to the Union of Utrecht, and did the other things which the majesty of the States and of the commonwealth would forbid a Belgian defender to be allowed to do. It was therefore requested that legates from the remaining confederated provinces be sent to Antwerp with mandates by which Philip might be stripped of his dominion and Anjou received according to the formula of the agreements. But all these efforts came to nothing, since through the lower provinces they kept falling back on the sweet appeal of the Union of Utrecht.

units.la: Quippe Hollandi socijque ab Albani ætate rectori provinciæ Aurantio obligati, fidem principis tanquam sui agnoscebant, ejusq; nomen ex paterno imperio venerabantur. Et erant, qui crederent exturbari legitimo principatu à populo suo Philippum, neque transfiri ad externæ dominationis arbitrium posse, ita compositâ per provincias parendi imperandique ratione, ut dissolvi non queat. Ego à Frisijs rem disceptatam illo tempore non comperio, sive ob repudiatum ab Hollandis Andinum, sive quod crederentur, ut antè à Gallicâ societate, ita tum quoque ab Andino alieni, suæ plus libertati, quam ex Ultrajectino fœdere aucupabantur, quam externis dominationibus daturi.
units.tr: Indeed, the Hollanders and their allies, who since the time of Alva had been bound to the governor of the province, William of Orange, acknowledged the king's authority as their own and revered his name, which came from his father's rule. Some believed that Philip could not be driven out of his lawful principality by his own people, nor be transferred to the will of a foreign ruler, since the arrangement of governing and being governed had been established across the provinces in a way that could not be dissolved. I find no record that the Frisians debated the matter at that time, whether because they had rejected Andin (Andrew Hesselius? see note-free) or because they were thought, as before with the French alliance, to be equally estranged from Andin. They were concerned more for their own liberty, which they hoped to secure under the Utrecht league, than to hand it over to foreign domination.

units.la: Igitur Farnesij copijs in Brabantiam ductis, quem atrox & ut creditum fuit per inopiam æris ex ægritudine animi morbus invaserat, Transfulani à Germanicis Ordinum Copijs vastati, quas Sigismundus, de quo dixi, Curtspacchius vir militiæ impiger, & qui opibus ac genere illustris sororum Lignisentium in Silesiâ ducis matrimonio tenebat, exigendis, quæ deficiebant stipendijs, circa Isalam & vicina ductabat. Quibus vexatis copias in Lingenses per Benthemicos fines promovit, ubi fortuito igne tormentario pulveri injecto, absumptus est. Bartholdus quoque Entenius imperato per Drentiam tributo stipendia cohortibus flagitabat, nulloq; disciplinæ metu effusum in flagitia militem coercebat. Unde cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXIX. de factum est, ut plebs rustica arma & audaciam induerent, equitumque cohortes, quas Dodo Larius & Rinsuoudius ducebant, Leoverdiam versus accepto in prædam commeatu, propelleret. Mox ad Zuytlariam viribus aucta, quo Entenio, qui auxilia reparaverat, resisteret, in fugam acta recentis gloriæ & fortitudinis laudem turpi dedecore mutavit.
units.tr: So Farnese led his forces into Brabant, a man whom a grievous sickness of the mind had seized, as was believed, from lack of money. Meanwhile Transisulania was laid waste by the German troops of the States. Sigismund Curtspacchius, of whom I have spoken, an energetic soldier who held a position through his wealth and noble birth and his marriage to a sister of the Duke of Lignitz in Silesia, led these troops around the Issel and the neighbouring districts to exact the pay that was lacking. When he had harassed them, he moved his troops through the lands of Bentheim into Lingen, where, a tormenting fire having accidentally been set to gunpowder, he was consumed. Bartholdus Entenius also demanded pay for his cohorts from the tribute he had levied through Drenthe, and, with no fear of discipline, he restrained the soldiers who had given themselves to vice. Hence in 1579 it came about that the rural population took up arms and boldness, and drove back the cavalry cohorts led by Dodo Larius and Rinsuoudius, who had seized plunder and provisions and were heading for Leeuwarden. Soon, strengthened in numbers, they moved to Zuidlaren to resist Entenius, who had regrouped his auxiliaries; but once put to flight, they exchanged the praise of their recent glory and courage for shameful disgrace.

units.la: Tum Entenius agris vicisque Coverdiam usque direptis tributum 18000. aureorum Drentinis imposuit. Unde continuis rusticæ plebis querelis exagitatus Lalainius Drentinis, ut milites, etiam suæ legionis, præterquam à se mandatis instructo, resisterent, potestatem fecit gratiamque Drentinorum emercando, nonnullis cohortibus, quas consilijs suis adversas noverat, odium peperit.
units.tr: Then Entenius, having plundered the fields and villages as far as Coevorden, imposed a tribute of 18,000 gold pieces on the Drenthers. Harassed by constant complaints from the rural population, Lalaing allowed the Drenthers to resist even soldiers of his own legion, apart from those who had been given orders by him, and by buying the favour of the Drenthers he earned hatred among some cohorts, which he knew were hostile to his plans.

units.la: Iam enim regis gratiâ & magnarum rerum splendore pellectus excæcatusque à Farnesio credebatur, idque tanto firmius, quod mutati in patriam affectus, argumenta à recepta in fidem Groningâ neque vanis suspicionibus edidisset. Mox nova tempestate Transisulani, Tubantes Salij creatis ex se partium ducibus arma odio Ordinum miscuerunt, actique per obvia, velut rerum desperatione, cuncta vi atque insolentiâ fædavere. Quare ab Aurantio principe Philippus Hohenlous reprimendis rebellium armis missus, tantæque multitudini impar, non sine vitæ discrimine in fugam actus est. Cæterum extenuatis vicinarum urbium præsidijs validior ad Sionis monasterium, post ad Roltam pagum ad internecionem eam cæcidit, redactisque ad obsequium Drentinis & accepto à captivis lytro arma, ut traderent, imperavit.
units.tr: For he was believed to have been drawn in and blinded by the king's favour and the splendour of great affairs, by Farnese, and all the more firmly because his affection for his homeland had changed, as he had shown by clear signs in bringing Groningen into the allegiance, and not by empty suspicions. Soon, in a new storm, the Overijssel men and the Tubantes and Salians, having appointed leaders from among themselves, mixed arms with hatred of the States, and, driven onward through whatever lay in their path, as if in despair of their affairs, they defiled everything with violence and insolence. Therefore Philip of Hohenlohe was sent by Prince William of Orange to put down the rebels by force of arms; but, unequal to so great a multitude, he was put to flight, not without danger to his life. Afterwards, the garrisons of the neighbouring towns having been weakened, the rebels, becoming stronger, cut down the Sion monastery and then, at the village of Rolde, slaughtered them to a man. Having brought the Drenthers back to obedience, and having accepted a ransom from the captives, he ordered them to surrender their arms.

units.la: Reperio in litteris sub ficto Funckij Frisij nomine ad Onuphrium Gryphium Prætorem nuper Utingeranum & cohortis apud Oostmahornam præfectum in exilio tum agentem, exules Frisios hostium partes secutos patriæ suæ vehementer tum comminatos fuisse, Pontificiosque per Frisiam mutuis litterarum commercijs instructos omnia admittendis intra provinciam hostibus proditorio consilio præparavisse. Eundem quoque Funckium plures perfugas spe largioris stipendij è provinciâ sollicitasse, ærisque penuriam regia per castra grassantem, velut in omnium rerum affluente copiâ pelliciendis perfugis excusavisse. Is addit undecim cohortium centuriones ducendis in Frisiam signis destinatos, in ijsque Julium & Renicum Dekama, Titum Cammingha, Lollium Ockingha, Petrum Boimerum, Petrum à Coverdiâ, Risellium Stellinguerfium, Snaterum, Prengerum & Sampsonium, tanquam belli peritissimos censuisse.
units.tr: I find in letters, written under the assumed name of Funck the Frisian to Onuphrius Gryphius, recently praetor of Utingeranum and prefect of a cohort at Oostmahorn, who was then living in exile, that the Frisian exiles who had taken the enemy's side had then vehemently threatened their homeland, and that the Papists throughout Friesland, equipped with mutual correspondence, had prepared by treacherous design to admit the enemy within the province. The same Funck also tempted many deserters away from the province with the hope of higher pay, and excused the enticing of deserters on the ground of the shortage of money which was spreading through the royal camp, as though it had an abundance of everything. He adds that eleven centurions of cohorts had been appointed to lead the standards into Friesland, and that among them Julius and Renicus Dekama, Titus Cammingha, Lollius Ockingha, Peter Boimerus, Peter of Coevorden, Risellius Stellinguerfius, Snaterus, Prengerus and Sampsonius were judged to be the most skilled in war.

units.la: Mox à fœderatis Ultrajecto litteræ in Frisiam datæ. Istæ continebant.
units.tr: Soon afterwards a letter was sent to Friesland from the confederates at Utrecht. It contained the following.

units.la: Regium Philippi exercitum Bruxellensibus sociorum fidissimis gravem extrema comminari. Quibus liberandis cum omne provinciarum subsidium peti debeat, monere se Frisios, ut in mensem pacandis Bruxellensium & Vilvordensium præsidijs sextam partem octoginta millium aureorum præstent octyus residuumque tributi quod fœderatis deberetur, in arariūm inferant. Alias forè, ut damno & infamiâ provinciarum hosti dedatur prima fœderum & libertatis altrix Bruxellensium civitas. Istæ litteræ Non. Sept. scriptæ.
units.tr: The royal army of Philip threatens grave extremity to the most loyal of the allies, the people of Brussels. Since every provincial help must be sought to deliver them, the Frisians are to be warned to pay, within a month, to the garrisons of Brussels and Vilvoorde a sixth part of eighty thousand gold pieces, the eighth part, and the remainder of the tribute owed to the confederates, and to deposit it in the treasury. Otherwise, it may happen that the city of Brussels, first nurse of the league and of liberty, is handed over to the enemy to the loss and infamy of the provinces. These letters were written on the 5th of September.

units.la: His accedebat, quod Andreæ Hesselij Ord. Brabantiæ actuarij litteræ de vastatione agri Brabantici apud Cæsaris Legatos quererentur, ultimisque miserijs repentinum remedium inducias aut pacem orarent. cIↄ. Iɔ̈ • Tardè scilicet procedi in eâ actione, quae festinationis egeret & esse lxxix Philippi Legatum in praescribendis conditionibus duriorem quam pacis studia exigerent. Veterem certè principum Philippi antecessorum dominationem clementiâ steriße, cujus spem in ipso actionis exordio Castrenantius praecidisset.
units.tr: To this was added that letters from Andreas Hesselius, actuary of the States of Brabant, complained to Caesar's envoys about the devastation of the Brabant countryside, and in their utmost misery begged for a sudden remedy of truces or peace. In 1579 the action was certainly proceeding too slowly, when it needed haste, and Philip's envoy was harder in prescribing terms than the desire for peace required. The old rule of Philip's predecessors had certainly been barren of clemency, a hope which Castrenantius had cut off at the very beginning of the business.

units.la: Igitur legatis Caesaris curandum esse, ut Castrenantij regij mandatarij animum suasorijs ad pacem rationibus emolliant, dentque effectum, ut mitigatâ Hispanicæ dominationis severitate moribus aliquid legibusque Belgicarum gentium donetur. Aliter certe pacem haberi non nisi salvo, aut saltem admisso jure populi posse. Quae cum litteris ad Renicum Camminga Deputatum determinandis super Coloniensi pace sententijs tarditatem provincialium increpavere.
units.tr: Therefore Caesar's envoys were to take care that they soften the mind of Castrenantius, the royal agent, with arguments persuasive to peace, and bring it about that, with the severity of Spanish rule moderated, something might be granted to the customs and laws of the Belgian peoples. Otherwise, they said, peace could certainly not be had except with the right of the people preserved, or at least admitted. These statements, together with letters to Renicus Camminga, a deputy for settling opinions on the peace of Cologne, rebuked the slowness of the provincials.

units.la: Carolus Roorda scribit, Frisicæ gentis morâ foederatos Ordines conferendis tum tributis contumaciam induisse, illorumque defectu de Venloa, Wachtendoncko & Gelrâ oppidis perdendis periculum fuisse. Pecunias quoque ad 3 0 0 0 o aureorum Lalainio assignatas excusationem ulterioris tributi non admittere, nihilque magis utile & necessarium firmando foederi quam parati aeris subsidium esse. Alias Ordines foederatos postulandis importunius stipendijs, de mittendis in provincias copijs constituisse. Ita Geldriæ agros, praestandis tributis tardos, militari manu pressos, neque aliud restare, quam ut Frisici reliquaeque provinciæ agendo censui socordes Geldrorum exemplo habeantur. Hoc etiam repetebat, ut Legatos è provinciâ Ultrajectum, aut ad Aurantium mitterent, supinaque consilia correctione mali moris emendarent.
units.tr: Carolus Roorda writes that, through the delay of the Frisian nation, the confederated States had taken up obstinacy in raising the taxes, and that by their failure there was danger of losing the towns of Venlo, Wachtendonk and Geldern. The money assigned to Lalaing, some 30,000 gold pieces, did not admit of excuse for further tribute, and nothing was more useful and necessary for strengthening the league than help of ready money. Otherwise, the confederated States had resolved to demand pay more insistently and to send troops into the provinces. Thus the fields of Guelders, slow to pay their tributes, were pressed by soldiers, and nothing remained except that the Frisians and the other provinces, slack in paying the assessment, be treated as the Guelders had been. He also repeated this: that they should send envoys from the province to Utrecht or to Orange, and correct their lazy plans by amending the bad custom.

units.la: Igitur mandatarijs Caesaris longâ Ordinum per provincias disceptatione offensis ab Ordinibus generalibus Antverpiâ Coloniam litterae datae, honestâ morae excusatione, quod in tam arduo negotio suffragationem provinciarum desiderassent. Neque enim plenâ statuendi potestate Legatos Coloniam missos instrui voluisse, eamque esse provincialis imperij rationem, ut à multitudinis arbitrio pendeat. In quâ cum opinionibus saepè certetur, fieri ut tardius aliquid decernat, publicumque commodum moretur privatorum incuria. Interim grates se Caesaris paterno affectui, & mandatarijs imperij debere licet fato quodam in provinciarum visceribus haerens malum opportuna remedia non sanaverint. Atqui id praepeditum esse nimiâ Philippi regis severitate, qui haberi clementer populum suum nolit: Isti fini scilicet velle, ut dignitatibus ex Gandavensi pactione eiecti pristinis honoribus restituantur, ad quos per provinciales vincula, caedes, atque exilia perventuri sint. Ab eo esse quod civitates & fortalitia dedi, quod nudari praesidijs velit, ipsosque inquilinos in remp. adscitos suis dignitatibus atque fortunis privari. Omnia scilicet doli, aut insidiarum plena esse. Distractos à socijs Farnesij artibus Hannonios & Artesios, simulatam externis in Italiam legionibus missionem, sacramenta principum infida & Pontificum dispensationibus impunita, eoque deventum esse, ut rumpendis foederibus & solvendae hominum fidei atque societati Romana religio inserviat. Hanc esse scilicet, quam Norcarmius ex Hispaniâ redux retineri solam colique voluisset, & ut Philippus Carcli patris cIↄ. Iↄ. tris in scribendis edictis severitatem stabiliendo principatui innovaret.
units.tr: Therefore, the Caesar's envoys having been offended by the long debate of the States throughout the provinces, a letter was sent from the general States at Antwerp to Cologne, with the honourable excuse of delay, that they had wished for the support of the provinces in so arduous a matter. For they did not wish the envoys sent to Cologne to be instructed with full power to decide, and the provincial government is such that it depends on the will of the multitude. In this, while opinions often clash, it happens that something is decided more slowly, and the public good is held back by the carelessness of private persons. Meanwhile they owe thanks to Caesar's paternal affection and to the envoys of the empire, although by some fate the evil clinging to the vitals of the provinces has not been healed by timely remedies. But this, they said, was hindered by the excessive severity of King Philip, who was unwilling for his people to be treated mildly; he wished, to that end, that men expelled from their offices by the Pacification of Ghent be restored to their former honours, to which they would attain through provincial chains, slaughters and exiles. From him came the surrender of cities and fortresses, his wish that they be stripped of garrisons, and that the inhabitants admitted into the commonwealth be deprived of their offices and fortunes. Everything, of course, was full of deceit or ambush. Hainaut and Artois had been drawn apart from their allies by the arts of Farnese, the simulated dismissal of foreign legions to Italy, the treacherous oaths of princes and the unpunished dispensations of the Popes; and things had come to this point, that the Roman religion served the breaking of covenants and the dissolving of men's faith and fellowship. This, they said, was the religion which Noircarmes, returning from Spain, had wished to be the only one retained and cultivated; and that Philip should renew the severity of his father Charles in issuing edicts, to stabilise his rule.

units.la: Sed id ne fieret Ordines provinciarum ad mutua foedera & auxilia confugisse, quae omnium ab orbe condito gentium consensus necessitati temporum & praeveniendae rerum ruinae approbassèt. Atqui ea rite servata convelli non posse, nisi singularum provinciarum decreta, eo quo invaluere modo, ex formula scripti juris infirmentur. Id se Caesareae majestati per litteras indicasse, esseque in eo Philippum, ut ex provinciarum discordia robur ac vim immodesto principatui captet, quod stare infantiae suae moribus & rigore antiquae inquisitionis velit. Majore certe moderatione attemperanda Philippi postulata esse, tam ut Buranus Aurantij filius in Belgium redeat, quam ut Angliae reginae & Andino tum ipsi Matthiae Gubernatoris autoritati satisfiat. Alias esserandis populi animis obviam tempestatem imminere, nisi lenius ac sepositâ dissimulatione apertius Philippus rex agat, & nisi Caesar ac Imperij Legati ad id praestandum regem, aut ejus mandatarium compellant. His addebant decreta singularum provinciarum, super pacis negotio, ut perscribantur ocyus se effecturos. Deinde pacis autorem rogaturos ut sana promovendae paci consilia procerum mentibus inspiret. Haec Antverpiae IV. Eid. Sept. perscripta, ac ad Legatos Imperij transmissa.
units.tr: But to prevent this, the Orders of the provinces had taken refuge in mutual covenants and aid, which the consensus of all nations since the creation of the world had approved as a necessity of the times and a way of preventing the ruin of affairs. Yet these could not be overthrown if they were duly observed, unless the decrees of the individual provinces were weakened, in the way they had prevailed, by the form of a written law. He had indicated this to his Imperial Majesty by letter, and that Philip was aiming at this, so as to draw strength and power from the discord of the provinces for an immoderate rule, since he wished to stand by the habits of his infancy and the severity of the old Inquisition. Certainly Philip's demands ought to be tempered with much greater moderation: both that Buren, the son of Orange, return to Belgium, and that satisfaction be given to the authority of the Queen of England and of Andino, then himself governor Matthias. Otherwise a storm was threatening to rouse the minds of the people, unless King Philip acted more gently and, with dissimulation laid aside, more openly, and unless the Emperor and the Imperial Legates compelled the king, or his deputy, to do this. To these they added that the decrees of the individual provinces concerning the business of peace would be drawn up as quickly as they could manage it. Then they would ask the author of peace to inspire the minds of the nobles with sound counsels for promoting peace. These things were written at Antwerp on the fourth day before the Ides of September and sent on to the Imperial Legates.

units.la: Similes litterae ad Castrenantium Philippi Legatum datae. Quare maturando ad conditiones pacis quas Philippi Legatus proposuerat, responso Albada Frisiorum & Transfisulaniae orator litteras in Frisiam expedivit, proque provinciae decreto obtinendo intercessit. His pro diruendis per Frisiam castellis subjunctum, quibus stantibus libertatem recuperari non posse, neque vanis rationibus ostendebat.
units.tr: Similar letters were given to Philip's Legate at Castrenantium. Therefore, hastening toward the conditions of peace which Philip's Legate had proposed, Albada, the Frisian and envoy of Transisfulania, sent letters into Frisia in reply, and interposed himself to obtain a decree of the province. To these he added, in regard to the demolition of the castles throughout Frisia, that liberty could not be recovered while they stood, and he pointed this out with empty arguments.

units.la: Itaq; (inquiebat) scire cupio quod fiducia libertatem vos tuituros putetis cum omnes artes apud nos integras relinquatis. An hoc vobis unta provinciae suadent?
units.tr: "Therefore (he said), I wish to know whether you think you will guard your liberty with confidence, when you leave all arts intact among us. Or do the interests of the province advise this to you?"

units.la: Caesar quoque, etsi in Philippum pronior jure affinitatis deprehenderetur, litteras XI. Kalend. Octob. Pragâ Bohemorum ad Ordines dedit, quibus monebat, ut protracti in sanciendâ pace temporis damnum celeritate consilij pensarent, omnesque curas amovendo belli incommodo impenderent. Æquissima scilicet esse à Philippo rege avunculo & sororio suis subditis oblata quae nisi acciperent, fidem faciebat, Legatos Imperij septemviros & praesulem Wirceburgium discessum facturos, taedio morae & damnosae perversitatis, quae bene coepta & cum ijs spem pacis noxio consilio disturbaret. Se quidem Caesareae benevolentiae illustre exemplum fecisse, facturum porro, si viderit, Belgas ipsos, declinandae rerum omnium ruinae, suis commodis non deesse.
units.tr: The Emperor too, although he was seen to lean more toward Philip by right of kinship, gave a letter to the Orders at Prague of Bohemia on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, in which he warned them to make up for the loss of time spent in delay in concluding the peace by speed of counsel, and by removing all cares to devote themselves to the inconvenience of war. Clearly the terms offered to his subjects by King Philip, his uncle and brother-in-law, were most equitable; and he made it plain that, unless they accepted them, the Imperial Legates, the seven electors and the prelate of Würzburg, would depart, weary of the delay and of the harmful perversity which, having begun well, was disturbing with its injurious counsel the hope of peace. He himself had shown a notable example of goodwill toward the Emperor, and would further, if he saw it, not fail the Belgians themselves, in avoiding the ruin of all things, in regard to their own advantages.

units.la: Mox litterae in Frisios mittendis Antverpiam cum mandato pacis legatis perlatae, quo examinatis singularum provinciarum suffragijs communi quoddam decretum ab Archiduce, Aurantio & Concilio Status perscriberetur. Cui celebrando litterae quoque ab imperij mandatarijs ad Ordines generales, seorsim vero ad Frisios missae, quae amoveri cunctationem ac moram provincialis decreti volebant. Eae à Gebhardo Coloniense, à Jacobo Trevirense Archi-Episcopo, Iulio Wirceburgensium Episcopo, Otone Henrico comite Suartsenbergio, Wernero Gemnichio VI. Kal. Octob. signatae.
units.tr: Soon letters reached Antwerp for the legates sent into Frisia with a mandate for peace, by which, once the votes of the individual provinces had been examined, a common decree was to be drawn up by the Archduke, Orange and the Council of State. To celebrate this, letters were also sent by the Imperial deputies to the General Orders, and separately to the Frisians, which wished the hesitation and delay of a provincial decree to be removed. These were signed on the sixth day before the Kalends of October by Gebhard of Cologne, by James, Archbishop of Trier, by Julius, Bishop of Würzburg, by Otto Henry, Count of Schwartzenberg, and by Werner Gemnich.

units.la: Albada scribit de regis Galliæ morte rumores hoc tempore Coloniam perlatos, duasque per Artesiam arces ab Andino regis fratre oppositas, fratre o-dio Hispani occupatas.
units.tr: Albada writes that at this time rumours of the death of the King of France had been carried to Cologne, and that two fortresses in Artois had been held against the king's brother Andino, and were occupied by the Spaniard out of hatred for the brother.

units.la: Igitur à septemviris & mandatarijs Imperij dies actioni præfinitus, cautumque ut nisi Ordines decretum provinciale intra proximum Kal. Nouembrium diem procurarent, conditionesque à Philippo rege perscriptas ratas præstarent, actio cessaret, quæ doli & fraudum expers suâ adhuc apud Castrenantium Philippi Legatum intercessione præjuvari firmarique posset. Id v. Nov. Octob. perscriptum. Ita omnia frivolâ nec pacem facturâ disceptatione trahebantur.
units.tr: Therefore a day for the action was fixed by the seven electors and the Imperial deputies, and it was provided that unless the Orders procured a provincial decree before the next day of November, and fulfilled the conditions set down by King Philip, the action would cease; this action, free of trickery and fraud, could still be aided and confirmed by the intercession of Philip's Legate at Castrenantium. This was written on the fifth day before the Nones of November. Thus all things were dragged out in frivolous dispute which would not make peace.

units.la: Quare Ordines fœderati accepto Geldrorum atque Zutphaniensium, quod Arnhemi v. Octob. in comitio perscriptum erat decreto, copiam ejus in Frisiam misère, additâ petitione, ut suum quoque in causâ pacis decretum perscriberet, postulantibusque Archiduce & Aurantio legatos Ultrajectum dein Antverpiam mitteret in commune consulturos. Præterquam enim, quod Coloniensis pacis desperatio, & sine stipendijs ac disciplinâ Ordinum exercitus Archiducem & Aurantium fatigaret, ita Ultrajectino quoq; fœderi, etiam vix robur adepto, hoc incommodum creabatur, quod inops æris ærarium erogandis cohortium stipendijs par non esset, rebusq; per provincias ex vastitate, aut socordiâ impulsis, ne delectus quidem poscenti bello ex inopiâ pecuniæ præstarentur. Cui malo sanando, tributorum ratio Ultrajecti per fœderatos inita decretumque ut pedestribus Frisiorum copijs, quatuordecim aureorum millia, equestribus duodecim quovis mense assignarentur, Lalainioq; menstrui tributi per Frisiam colligendi cura & autoritas demandaretur. Groningenses quoque Drentinos & Transisfulanos Frisiorum socios ad præscriptum ab Aurantio tributum pendendum cogeret, invitosque & reluctantes imperio, aut severitate coerceret. Cæterum oppidani duarum cohortium, quas Lalainius fœderatorum decreto autoraverat, stipendia detrectabant, rati, quod res erat, stipendiorum militarium rationem ad ærarij legem formandam esse, ne ex onerum mole novæ libertatis fastidium contumaci ad gravia & simul jussa populo nasceretur. Unde Lalainius emolliendis oppidanis, decretum fœderis, suam fidem atque autoritatem conscribendis cohortibus interpositam regessit quamque securitatis publicæ in illâ teneritudine ac infantiâ rerum interesset, oppida provinciæ munimenta justis præsidijs attineri. Joanni quoque Aysma Ultrajecto, ubi cum Carolo Roorda Legatum agebat, in Frisiam profecto in mandatis datum, ut assensum Frisiorum retinendis in fide ac stipendio quatuordecim pedestribus & equestribus cohortibus impetraret, deque fœderatorum Ordinum voluntate expugnandis per Frisiam castellis oppidanum populum doceret.
units.tr: Therefore the allied Orders, having received the decree of Gelderland and Zutphen, which had been written at Arnhem in the assembly on the fifth day before the Nones of October, sent a copy of it into Frisia, adding a request that they would also write their own decree in the matter of peace, and, as the Archduke and Orange asked, would send legates on to Utrecht and then to Antwerp to consult in common. For besides the despair of the Cologne peace, and the army, without pay or discipline of the Orders, wearing down the Archduke and Orange, this inconvenience was also created for the Utrecht union, which had scarcely gained strength: the treasury, poor in money, was not equal to paying the soldiers' wages, and, with the provinces driven by devastation or sloth, not even a levy for a war that demanded it could be provided from lack of money. To remedy this evil, a reckoning of taxes was made at Utrecht by the allies, and a decree was passed that fourteen thousand gold pieces a month should be assigned to the Frisian foot forces and twelve thousand to the cavalry, and that the care and authority of collecting the monthly tax throughout Frisia should be entrusted to Lalaing. He was also to compel the Groningen men, the Drenthians and the Transisfulanians, allies of the Frisians, to pay the tax prescribed by Orange, and to restrain them by authority or severity if they were unwilling and resisted command. Moreover the townsmen refused the wages of the two cohorts which Lalaing had authorised by decree of the allies; they reckoned, as was the case, that the reckoning of military pay was to be shaped by the law of the treasury, lest from the weight of burdens a distaste for new liberty should arise in the people, stubborn toward heavy and at the same time imposed things. Whereupon Lalaing, to soften the townsmen, sent back the decree of the union, with his own good faith and authority interposed for enrolling the cohorts, and showed how much it mattered for public safety, in such tenderness and infancy of affairs, that the towns of the province be held as fortresses by sound garrisons. John Aysma was also commissioned, when he set out for Frisia from Utrecht, where he was negotiating with Carolus Roorda, to obtain the consent of the Frisians to keep fourteen foot and cavalry cohorts in faith and pay, and to teach the townspeople, from the will of the allied Orders, that the castles throughout Frisia were to be overthrown.

units.la: Creditum fuit castella externa dominationis antiqua præsidia dirui Ordinibus tum placuisse, quo majore libertatis desiderio populus in concordiam exardesceret, præsidiumque Leovardiæ urbi grave & molestum dirutâ arce in finibus provinciæ propellendis hostium incursionibus locaretur. Itaque petebant ut Frisij Bolsuerdios, Snecenses, Franequeranos, Doccumios, Collumanos cæterosque recipienda ad præsidia hortarentur, quo Lalainius in Transilavicanis & per Drentiam res gesturus destinatum auxilijs militem commodissimâ opportunitate ex illis præsidijs evocaret.
units.tr: It was believed that the Orders had then decided that the foreign castles, the old garrisons of domination, should be torn down, so that the people might flare up into concord with a greater longing for liberty, and that the garrison at Leeuwarden, a burden and nuisance to the city, be placed, with the citadel destroyed, at the borders of the province to repel the incursions of the enemy. Accordingly they asked that the Frisians urge Bolsward, Sneek, Franeker, Dokkum, Kollum and the others to receive garrisons, so that Lalaing, about to carry on operations in Overijssel and through Drenthe, might call the soldiers destined for aid away from those garrisons at the most convenient opportunity.

units.la: Mox Hesselus Aysma Jureconsultus Antverpiam é Frisiâ cum mandatis missus.
units.tr: Soon Hessel Aysma, a jurist, was sent with instructions from Friesland to Antwerp.

units.la: Istæ erant: Vt provinciarum Belgicæ, & imprimis Frisiæ commodo operam consiliaque navaret. Vt in Coloniensi pacis negotio, quod Cæsaris Legatis delatum esset, suum suffragium AURANTIJ Principis, Fœderatorum & simul Hollandiæ Ordinum suffragijs, atque decretis affirmaret, neve abijs quid diversum atque discrepans faceret aut fieri promitteret. Mandata xiiii. Kal. Nov. Leovardiæ signata.
units.tr: These were the instructions: that he should labour and counsel for the advantage of the provinces of Belgium, and especially of Friesland; that in the matter of peace at Cologne, which had been referred to the Imperial Legates, he should confirm his vote, with the votes and decrees of Prince Orange, the allied Orders and at the same time the Orders of Holland, and should neither do nor promise anything different or discordant with them. Instructions signed at Leeuwarden on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November.

units.la: Barthius quoque Idsaerda ad Georgium Lalainium in Drentiam amandatus, qui tractandis Groningensium & Omlandiæ rebus, cænobio Esseno, quod in agro Drentino est, audiendis legationibus attinebatur. Igitur Legato stipendia ferenti, cujus penuriâ exercitus & Lalainij aula ex principali paratu laborabat, sui confestim copiam fecit, mandatâque Legati in Frisiam properantis celerrime expedivit. In cæteris hoc erat. Ut patrimonium sedis aut Episcopi & cum eo annuos reditus provinciæ ærario & usibus assignaret, censumque Cuneri otio & luxui usurpatum militaribus stipendijs applicandum decerneret.
units.tr: Barthius also was sent to Georg Lalaing at Idsaerda, in Drenthe, who was occupied with handling the affairs of Groningen and Ommelanden and with hearing embassies at the Essen monastery, which lies in Drenthe. Therefore, when the legate brought pay, whose scarcity meant the army and Lalaing's court laboured under a princely display, he at once made himself available to him, and very quickly carried out the legate's mandate, which was hurrying into Frisia. Among the other things this was included: that the patrimony of the see or of the bishop, and with it the annual revenues, be assigned to the treasury and uses of the province, and that the census of Cuneri, usurped for idleness and luxury, be decreed to be applied to military wages.

units.la: Reperio in actis Pompeium Vfkenium virum fœderi impense addictum & magnæ apud Lalainium gratiæ, isti rei omne consilium navasse, Lalainiumque dubium tum & inclinantem, quo assensum faceret, petitis à necessitate rationibus permovisse. Quod negotium eo quoq; magis maturabatur, quod Archidux Matthias, facilitate juventae aut imprudentioris consilij Ausonium Galamam Præpositurae Bolsuerdiensis dote & proventu donasset, profusissimâq; talium rerum largitione plus privati gratiae, quam publicae aeris inopiae, subvenisset. Igitur ea res aliqua cum difficultate primum habita, non ignaro Lalainio, se litteris ix. Octob. Vollenhoâ datis, Frisios ad id praestandum monuisse, & ut Ausonium Galamam beneficio donatum in possessionem ocyus Præpositurae citra molestiam locarent.
units.tr: I find in the records that Pompeius Vfkenius, a man deeply devoted to the union and in great favour with Lalaing, had put every effort into that business, and had moved Lalaing, who was then doubtful and inclined, to give his assent, by reasons drawn from necessity. This business was hastened all the more because Archduke Matthias, through the easiness of youth or a less prudent counsel, had given Ausonius Galama the endowment and income of the provostship of Bolsward, and by a most lavish distribution of such things had served private favour more than public poverty of the treasury. Therefore this matter, at first treated with some difficulty, Lalaing not being unaware of it, was urged by him in a letter given at Vollenhove on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, warning the Frisians to perform it, and that they should, without delay and without trouble, put Ausonius Galama, endowed with the benefice, into possession of the provostship.

units.la: Aysma scribit se iii. Kal. Novemb. post salutatos Ultrajecti foederis socios Antverpiam, cum Zutphanienfium, Arnhemiensium & Velaviae Legatis advenisse, reliquarumque provinciarum Legatos & in ijs Hollandos & Zelandos tardius se sistentes moram conventui & habendis consultationibus injecisse.
units.tr: Aysma writes that on 29 October, after greeting the allies of the Utrecht covenant at Antwerp, he arrived there with the envoys of Zutphen, Arnhem and Velaw. The envoys of the other provinces, and among them those of Holland and Zeeland, came more slowly, and their delay held up the assembly and the consultations.

units.la: Reperio in actis annonae & frumenti caritate provinciam tum laborasse, quod æstas & juxta autumnus imbrium copia fœdus suffecturam alendis provincialibus messem corrupisset. Itaque Leovardiâ in urbe populi & multitudinis fœcundâ penuriæ & egestati pauperum obviam itum, saluberrimo mali pestilentis remedio, quo ægra plebs & vitiato aëre debilior, subsidiario ære uberem refocillandis corporibus victum haberet. Igitur Supremus Senatus in Basilicâ coactus Magistratum centurionesque cohortium ad se evocavit, divisaque in partes ac districtus civitate conferri stipem à locupletibus in sex menses pauperum ærario jussit. Hoc vero vetabat, ne ostiatim alimenta infectis, aut languidis peterentur, ne integrae domus proserpentis contagij vim ex afflictu noxij ægrorum habitus sentirent.
units.tr: The records show that the province was then suffering from a shortage of food and dear grain, because the summer and the autumn that followed, with their heavy rains, had spoiled the harvest that was to feed the provincials. So, to meet the want and poverty of the poor in Leeuwarden, a populous city, they applied the most wholesome remedy for the sickness: the common people, weakened by sickness and by foul air, were to have a plentiful diet from public funds to restore their bodies. The Supreme Senate therefore gathered in the Basilica, summoned the magistrates and the captains of the companies, divided the city into districts, and ordered that alms be collected from the wealthy for the poor's fund for six months. It also forbade that food be begged from door to door by the sick or the infirm, so that whole households would not feel the force of the spreading contagion from the harmful condition of the sick.

units.la: Heymannus notat Capitulum isti pauperum subsidio duodecim carolos in mensem spopondisse, edictumque vergente Decembri rite & LXXXIX. ex usu formatum in vulgus & per tribunalia tum emanasse.
units.tr: Heymann notes that the Chapter pledged twelve carolus a month for this relief of the poor, and that toward the end of December an edict was duly issued in the customary form and then published to the people through the courts.

units.la: Quo fere tempore litterae Ordinum Frisiae, quae decretum pacis habebant, Coloniam ad Albadam oratorem missae prope arcem Blyenbeham a praesidiariis loci militibus interceptae, ope ac consilio eorum, qui Hispanicarum partium sacramentis aut societatibus inligati, Emricae & Resae, tum in plerisque, ad Rhenum locis, patriae etiam suae commercia & commeatus tabellionum explorandis Ordinum arcanis infestabant.
units.tr: About the same time, letters of the Estates of Friesland, which contained the decree of peace, were being sent to the envoy at Cologne, Alba. Near the castle of Bylers they were intercepted by the garrison soldiers of the place, with the help and counsel of those who, bound by oaths or alliances to the Spanish party, were then at Emden and Reede and in many places along the Rhine, and who used their trade and the couriers' passage to spy on the secrets of the Estates, even of their own homeland.

units.la: Albada scribit eorum plurima e nobilitate Frisica fuisse, quam odio Ultrajectini foederis in exitium patriae se tum armasse aegerrimus animi querebatur. Itaque erant, qui Farnesium invadendae Frisiae tria millia Hispanorum militum peterent, eique provinciae, sub Regis Philippi imperium reducendae certissimam spem offerrent. Quos ideo omnem humanitatis affectum exuisse illi interpretabantur, qui non ignorabant, sine propinquorum caede ac fuga, sine legum & libertatis interitu resumere dominationem eos non posse parricidialibus armis subnixos.
units.tr: Alba writes that many of them were from the Frisian nobility, and he complained bitterly that they had taken up arms at that time to destroy their country out of hatred for the Utrecht covenant. Some were therefore seeking that Farnese invade Friesland with three thousand Spanish soldiers, and they offered him a most certain hope of bringing that province back under the rule of King Philip. Those who understood that they could not regain dominion without the slaughter of their kinsmen, flight, and the destruction of the laws and of liberty, interpreted this as proof that they had cast off all human feeling, since they relied on arms raised against their fatherland.

units.la: Igitur fidissimae monitiones patriae amantium acuendae sollicitudinis in Frisiam missae, quae justum exercitum ad xvi. Novembris diem in Frisiae ac Translavicanorum fines destinari neque vanis augurijs ominabantur. Cui malo averruncando concordiam suadebant Graecorum exemplo & ex Philippi Comineij clarissimi rerum sub Ludovico gestarum Historici praecepto, qui odio potentum firmandas gentium societates comprobassent. Quas etsi levis aliqua temporum lis aut dissensio fatiget, quae inferiora haec & mortalia exercens vera & stabili pace coelestia donasset, tamen commune in rep. consilium cum ijs conferendum esse, quos a patriae aut rerum ruina alienos libertatis affectatio fecisset.
units.tr: Therefore the most faithful warnings from lovers of the fatherland were sent to Friesland, to sharpen its anxiety. They did not hesitate to forecast, with no empty omens, that a proper army would be assigned to the borders of Friesland and the Translauwers lands on 16 November. To avert this evil they urged concord, following the example of the Greeks and the precept of Philippe de Commynes, the most distinguished historian of the deeds done under Louis, who had approved alliances of nations strengthened against the hatred of the powerful. Even if some slight quarrel or dissension of the times wearies them, which exercises these lowly and mortal affairs, nevertheless a common counsel for the commonwealth must be held with those whom the pursuit of liberty has kept clear of the ruin of the fatherland and of public affairs.

units.la: Hoc vero imprimis volebant, ut mos patriae & privilegium populi tenacissime in administratione rerum retineretur liberaque ut vocabant, Statuum electio quaeque in rep. dignitates clarissimis provincialium conferret. Quos a peculatu aut rapiendis per ambitum honoribus probitatis amor averteret, haud dubie praemium suae virtuti obsequium populi habituros. Alias novas in factiones, nova odia erupturas mentes improbitate dominantium irritatas. Id quoq; vel maxime necessarium esse, ut justitia vigeat, inque ipsarum legum rigore & observantia & innocentia judicum & reverentia populi quaeratur. Quae quanquam egregie dicta & scripta fatalem isti temporum aetati discordiam non sustulere.
units.tr: They wished above all that the custom of the country and the privilege of the people be most firmly kept in the administration of affairs, and that the election of the Estates, which they called free, and all the offices of the commonwealth, be given to the most distinguished of the provincials. Those whom love of honesty kept from peculation, or from seizing honours by ambition, would undoubtedly receive from the people the reward of their virtue. Otherwise, minds provoked by the wickedness of the rulers would break out into new factions and new hatreds. It was also most necessary, they said, that justice flourish, and that it be sought in the strict observance of the laws themselves, in the integrity of the judges and in the reverence of the people. Although these things were said and written admirably, they did not remove the discord that fate had imposed on that age of the times.

units.la: Igitur Hesseli Aysma provinciae Legati Antverpiam adventu in consessu Ordinum generalium super Coloniensi pace, gerendi belli modo, instruendis provinciarum praefectis, ordinanda rep. provincijs ad pendenda tributa militari manu cogendis, applicanda commeatui bellico in singulas cerevisiae tonnas trium stufferorum indictione, novo sacramento concipiendo, tum de innovanda religionis pace viii. Nov. deliberatum, urgentibus Aurantij & foederatorum Ultrajectinorum legaris infida pacis apud Coloniam actione de bello cogitandum esse, & ut communis provinciarum Belgicae resp. dissensione aut ignavia collabens majore prudentia ac sollicitudine crescentibus periculis formaretur. Aysma tradit mandatorum legatorumque qui ex quibusdam pro-vincIↄ. Iↄ. LXXIX. vincijs non comparuerant, defectu, nihil plenatiè definitum fuisse, hoc stiumque pro iuvadendâ Frisiâ consilium relationibus tum Coloniensium confirmatum. Itaque petebat ut Frisij ad pericula solertes & circumspecti essent, plenioraque mandata maturandis provinciarum rebus, perferri Antverpiam curarent.
units.tr: Therefore, after the arrival of Aysma, envoy of Hesselius' province, at Antwerp, the General Estates deliberated on 8 November about the Cologne peace, the manner of conducting the war, the appointment of provincial governors, the ordering of the commonwealth's provinces so that tributes could be exacted by armed force, the applying of a levy of three stuivers on each tun of beer for the military supply, the drafting of a new oath, and the renewing of religious peace. They had to think about war, since the urgings of Orange and of the envoys of the Utrecht allies made the faithless conduct of the peace at Cologne plain, and the common commonwealth of the Belgic provinces, collapsing through dissension or sloth, had to be shaped with greater prudence and care as the dangers grew. Aysma reports that, because the mandates and the envoys of some provinces had not appeared, nothing was decided fully; and that this plan for the relief of Friesland was confirmed by the reports then coming from the people of Cologne. He therefore asked that the Frisians be alert and watchful toward the dangers, and he urged that they see to it that fuller mandates be sent to Antwerp so that the affairs of the provinces could be hastened.

units.la: Alexander Bentingius Geldrorum Legatus scribit ex quaque provincia delegatos tum fuisse, qui cum Archiduce Matthiâ, Aurantio Principe & Concilio Status singula communicarent, eoq; facto, de actis ad confessum referrent. Singularem quoque animorum consensum illo conventu, quem secundis rebus more mortalium ut antè inclinantem & dubium, ita tum ex adversis firmum & constantem, ingenia procerum idem Aysma datis Antverpiâ xv. Non. in Frisiam litteris confirmavit, omniumque suffragia tractatâ Religionis pace, in admittendo per provincias reformatæ exercitio convenisse. Mox de peractâ Barthij Idsaerdæ ad Lalainium legatione Leovardiam nuntiatum, qui è Drentiâ & monasterio Essenæ in Frisiam reversus Lalainij decretum pro usurpandis Episcopi patrimonio attulerat.
units.tr: Alexander Bentinck, envoy of Gelderland, writes that delegates were then sent from each province to communicate each matter to Archduke Matthias, to Prince Orange and to the Council of State, and that after this they reported the proceedings to the assembly. The same Aysma, in letters sent from Antwerp on 2 November to Friesland, also confirmed the remarkable unanimity of minds at that meeting: the leading men, who in prosperity were inclined and wavering, as is the way of mortals, were then firm and steady in adversity. All the votes agreed, after the religious peace had been discussed, to admit the exercise of the Reformed religion throughout the provinces. Soon afterwards it was announced at Leeuwarden that the mission of Bartholomeus Idsardi to Lalaing had been carried out, and he, returning to Friesland from Drenthe and the monastery of Essen, had brought Lalaing's decree for seizing the bishop's property.

units.la: Diploma istiusmodi erat.
units.tr: The document was of this kind.

units.la: QVANDO QVIDEM certus sum Frisiam tam ex terrâ inundatione, quam ex continuatione belli & militarium stipendiorum pensitatione magnis debitis atque oneribus gravari, haud dubiè cum ipso bello incrementa habitura, ita petentibus Ordinum Frisiæ Deputatis, Ordinibus Frisiæ pro jure meo omnia Episcopalia bona unâ cum Haskerano cænobio cedo & defero facioque ijs potestatem, ut provinciæ usibus ea impendant, sub istâ cautione, ne ullius juri aut credito quid decedat & ut ex formulâ illius pactionis transferantur, quâ Cænobij Witteverumani res & reditus Omlandiæ agrarijs assignavi. Igitur fidem facio me in possessione istorum bonorum prædictos Frisiæ Ordines locaturum daturumque operam, ut cessio hæc rata firmaque mea autoritate habeatur. Actum Essenæ sub sigillo & manu meâ, v. Eid. Novemb.
units.tr: Since I am certain that Friesland is burdened with great debts and charges, both from the inundation of its land and from the continuation of the war and the payment of military wages, and that these will undoubtedly grow with the war itself, I therefore, at the request of the deputies of the Estates of Friesland, cede and transfer to the Estates of Friesland, by my right, all the episcopal goods together with the monastery of Hasker, and I give them power to devote them to the uses of the province, under this condition: that nothing be taken from anyone's right or credit, and that they be transferred according to the formula of that agreement by which I assigned the property and revenues of the monastery of Witteveen to the lands of Ommelanden. Therefore I attest that I will have the aforesaid Estates of Friesland put in possession of these goods and will take care that this cession be held valid and firm by my authority. Done at Essen, under my seal and hand, 9 November.

units.la: Quæ, quamvis bonâ fide & in speciem veri affectus agi viderentur, ita ostentui magis & augendæ in eum procerum fiduciæ fieri illi non dubitabant, qui explorata clam Lalainij consilia suæ magis quam Ordinum dominationi servire, ex infidis aulicorum actionibus acceperant. Itaque Lalainij juventâ illorum assentationibus se præbente & ingenio, sicut mortale plerumque solet, cupidine imperij correpto de distribuendis per Frisiæ oppida præsidijs cogitavit, quo provinciæ munimentis suo arbitratu stabiliendæ potentiæ & nova ad consilia uteretur.
units.tr: Although these acts seemed to be done in good faith and in the appearance of genuine concern, they did not doubt that they were made rather for display and to increase the confidence of the leading men in him. These men, having learned secretly from the faithless conduct of the courtiers that Lalaing's plans served his own dominion more than that of the Estates, did not hide their suspicion. So, since Lalaing's youth yielded to their flattery, and as mortal men usually do, his mind was seized by the desire for power, and he thought of distributing garrisons through the towns of Friesland, so that he might use these fortifications of the province to secure his power as he saw fit and for new schemes.

units.la: Quare Ioannem Bongam nobilem Frisium à primâ ætate fœderatis armis ascriptum, cum cohorte Bolsuerdiam amandavit, istiq; urbi & simul Snecensium præsidio esse jussit. Cæterum Magistratus, qui recipi intra urbem armatos detrectabat, turbidum insuper populum, & à præsidio alienum spectans, militem urbe prohibuit; quem Bonga centurio navigijs vectum ad portam & suburbana promoverat. Hoc interim petebat Magistratus, ut dum per legatos de Præfecti voluntate cognovissent, cohortem in circumjacentes agros & Wonseranorum fines amoveret, urbemque domesticæ paci & civili custodiæ relinqueret. ret. Quod consilium cum Goslico Heramæ viro nobili & Jurisperito cIↄ. Iↄ. Wonseranorum prætori displiceret, insolentiam & rapinas militum metuenti, de mittendis ad Lalainium legatis à Magistratu consultatum, reclamante propalam plebe oppidanâ urbi incorruptam adhuc fidem professæ imponendum præsidium non esse.
units.tr: Therefore he sent Johan Bonga, a Frisian nobleman enlisted in the confederate arms from his earliest youth, with a company to Bolsward, and ordered him to be in that town and at the same time to guard Sneek. The magistracy, however, refused to admit armed men within the city, and, viewing the restless populace as hostile to the garrison, it kept the soldiers out of the town. Captain Bonga had brought them by boat as far as the gate and the suburbs. Meanwhile the magistracy asked that, until they could learn through envoys the Governor's wishes, the company be moved into the surrounding fields and the lands of the Wonseradeel, and that the town be left to domestic peace and civic guard. This plan displeased Goslicus of Herema, a nobleman and jurist, praetor of Wonseradeel, who feared the insolence and plundering of the soldiers. The magistrates deliberated about sending envoys to Lalaing, but the townspeople openly protested, declaring that the town, which had so far professed an uncorrupted loyalty, should not have a garrison imposed on it.

units.la: Quare Franciscus Iacobæus Consul, Iacobus Menenius & Petrus Sixsius ad Lalainium qui Vollenhoæ esse ferebatur, pacando populo missi, milesq; Bongæ centurionis excedere oppido ab irata plebe jussus, cœnobio Floridi Campi & Oegano inductus est. Igitur commeatu intra urbem coëmpto & præsidio cœnobijs gravi litteræ à supremo senatu venere, qui reverentiâ Præfecti, sive seditionis civicæ metu, Magistratus in recipiendo præsidio contumaciam, tanquam contemptum imperij interpretabatur. Sed Magistratus modestè factum excusare, pacem ac concordiam, missos ad Lalainium Legatos obtendere, cui per eos significatum esset, urbem stratis partium odijs quietam præsidij non egere. Qui cum Snecensium Legatis, quorum & causa agebatur, in Drentiam & cœnobium Essenum progressi colloquium Præfecti petiere, quem moderandis Transisulaniæ & Drentinorum rebus occupatum aulicorum respoñsa ferebant. Igitur triduo per otium consumpto, legati tandem in secretum admissi, ubi Lalainius, etsi occupatior, de mandatis Legatorum cognovit, eosque voce Gruteri, qui ei à consilijs erat, bono animo esse jussit.
units.tr: Therefore Franciscus Iacobaeus, the consul, Iacobus Menenius and Petrus Sixsius were sent to Lalainius, who was said to be at Vollenhove, to calm the people. The officer Bonga was ordered by the enraged populace to leave the town. Sixsius was taken to the monastery of Floridus Campus and to Oegan. Meanwhile provisions were bought within the city, and a garrison was made ready for the monasteries. Severe letters then came from the Supreme Senate. Out of reverence for the governor, or from fear of civic sedition, the Senate read the magistrates' refusal to receive the garrison as contempt of its authority. The magistrates, however, excused the act with moderation, pleading peace and concord and the envoys sent to Lalainius, to whom they had made it clear through those envoys that a city quieted after the hatreds of the parties had been laid to rest did not need a garrison. Together with the envoys of Sneek, whose cause was also at issue, they went on into Drenthe and to the monastery at Essen, and asked for an audience with the governor, who, they were told by the courtiers, was occupied with settling the affairs of Overijssel and Drenthe. So, after they had spent three days in idleness, the envoys were at last admitted in private. There Lalainius, though busier than ever, heard the envoys' instructions and, through Gruterus, who was one of his counsellors, bade them take heart.

units.la: Quare (inquiebat) hoc tempore præsidij immunes esse volo, modo jus & æquum civibus vestris dicatis, omnique religionis dissensione sopita civitatis vestræ curam geratis. Ad Bongam quod attinet, illi aliud à priore mandatum à me dabitur.
units.tr: Therefore (he said) I wish you to be free of a garrison for the present, provided that you administer justice and law to your citizens, and that once religious dissension is quelled you look after the welfare of your city. As for Bonga, a different order will be given by me.

units.la: Quæ supremo Senatui xix. Octob. per Legatos Bolsuerdiensium Snecensiumque exhibita, Senatus tamen & recipiendi præsidij decretum tum non immutavere. Igitur ex eodem Snequettus Senator & Sibrandus Richæus fisci procurator ad Lalainium ablegati, evocatis interea Leovardiam Bolsuerdiensium Pontificijs, qui ante pacati illâ supremi Senatus & Magistratuum dissensione tanquam occasione turbarum utebantur. Unde concursu facto reliqui earum partium per urbem Bolsuerdiam acti arma induerunt, tesserâmq; vigilum fidei commissam dari sibi à Magistratu cum immodestiâ poposcere. Sed à Theodoro Occonio Consule, qui cum imperio civitati tum præerat, repulsum passi & in sua redire jussi, secretos tabernarum conventus repetivere, furoreq; ex vino aut per temulentiam aucto, velut in licentiæ regno, implicatis ad fœdera dextris, obsequia exuerunt. Quare nec Ordinum, nec Magistratus imperio se teneri inconditis clamoribus jactitabant, urbemque à Lalainio suæ libertati permissam Hispanorum aut Ordinum præsidijs non obligari.
units.tr: These things were presented to the Supreme Senate on 19 October by the envoys of Bolsward and Sneek, but the Senate did not then change its decree on receiving the garrison. Accordingly, from the same town, Senator Snequettus and Sibrandus Richaeus, procurator of the treasury, were sent to Lalainius. Meanwhile the Papists of Bolsward were summoned to Leeuwarden. They had used the dispute between the Supreme Senate and the magistrates, which had been settled earlier, as an occasion for disturbances. A gathering took place, and the rest of that party were driven through the town of Bolsward. They took up arms and with insolence demanded that the watch-password be entrusted to them by the magistrates. But they were repelled by the consul Theodorus Occonius, who presided over the city with authority. Suffering this rebuff, they were ordered to go back to their homes, and they returned to secret gatherings in the taverns. Their fury, fed by wine or drunkenness, and as if they were in a kingdom of licence, led them to clasp hands in covenant and cast off obedience. For this reason they boasted in disorderly shouts that they were not bound by the authority of the Estates or the magistrates, and that the city, granted to its liberty by Lalainius, was not bound by the garrisons of the Spaniards or of the Estates.

units.la: Quæ res cum maximâ incommodâ datura civitati videretur, frænandis seditiosorum civium moribus à Senatu supremo decretum, ut Bolsuerdij sicut & reliqui oppidani è corpore civium cohortem conscriberent, illique rectorem è Magistratu darent. Unde Petrus Vibenius Consul ducendæ cohorti centurio creatus, adscito Sixto Hettenio, qui ferendo signo præesset. Mox ære accepto miles conscriptus, eoque ad custodiam urbis admoto, dissoluti mores interquievere.
units.tr: Since this affair seemed likely to bring the greatest harm to the city, the Supreme Senate decreed, in order to curb the conduct of the seditious citizens, that Bolsward, like the other towns, should enrol a guard from its body of citizens, and should appoint a commander from among the magistrates. So Petrus Vibenius, a consul, was appointed captain to lead the guard, and Sixtus Hettenius was associated with him to bear the standard. Soon the enrolled soldiers received their pay, and when they were posted to guard the city, the disorderly conduct subsided.

units.la: Quo tempore Aggæi Albada Oratoris Epistola de Coloniensi convencIↄ. Iↄ. LXXIX. tu abrupto in Frisiam perlata. Ea habebat: Imperij legatos v i r. virros tarditate Ordinum & petitae resolutionis offensos abitum Coloniâ parare, esseque nihil expectandum quam ut pace fracta crudele Regem inter & provincias bellum exardescat. Itaq; Frisios commonebat, ut ad externam vim, quae pararetur, repellendam solliciti, internis quoque hostibus avertendis intenti essent, unicoque concordiae remedio adversum fortuita & simulatas fallacesque amicitias se munirent. Ea 18. Kal. Decemb. Coloniâ scripta.
units.tr: At this time a letter from Aggaeus Albada, the envoy, concerning the Cologne conference, which had been broken off on 1 December 1579, was carried into Friesland. It said that the envoys of the Empire, offended by the slowness of the Estates and by the demand for a resolution, were preparing to leave Cologne. Nothing was to be awaited except that, with the peace broken, a cruel war would blaze up between the King and the provinces. It therefore warned the Frisians to be watchful in repelling the foreign force being prepared, and to be intent also on averting internal enemies, and to fortify themselves against chance and feigned and deceitful friendships with the one remedy of concord. This was written at Cologne on 18 November.

units.la: Cui monitioni robur atque efficaciam addebat, quod Ioannes Ripperda & Joannes Splinterius è Goră oppido de decretâ hostium in Frisiam irruptione fidissimos per exploratores perscripsisent, Philippumq; Regem tres Germanorum legiones sub Caspare Roblesio & Bergij filio autorandas Snatero, Prengero & Everardo Coverdiensium nuper Satrapae ducendas in Frisiam demandasse. Itaque in Bremensium, Osnaburgensium Monasteriensiumque finibus dilectus institutos tanto multitudinis confluxu, ut ad festum Andreae proxumum in Omlandiam ac Frisios paratam expeditionem habituri essent. Iam enim lanceas, sclopetos, enses, thoraces ferreos, omneque genus armorum circa Statloam in agro Monasteriensi, destinatum recensioni locum comportatum, & quod armandis octo aut novem virorum millibus sufficiat. In proxumo scilicet periculum cerni, esseque necessarium ut Frisij ad sua intenti sint; fidumq; aliquem è suis Essenum ad coenobium mittant, qui de singulis cognoscat.
units.tr: To this warning it added weight and force that John Ripperda and John Splinterius, from the town of Goor, had reported through trusted scouts the decided invasion of the enemy into Friesland. They reported also that King Philip had commissioned three German legions, to be enlisted under Caspar Robles and the son of Berg, and to be led into Friesland by Snatero, Prengerus and Everardus, lately governor of Coevorden. Thus levies were set up in the territories of Bremen, Osnabrück and Münster, with such a gathering of men that they would have a planned expedition into Ommeland and against the Frisians ready by the next feast of St Andrew. Now lances, muskets, swords, iron breastplates and every kind of weapon were being brought together near Statloo in the territory of Münster, at the place chosen for the muster, enough to arm eight or nine thousand men. Clearly the danger was seen to be close, and it was necessary for the Frisians to be attentive to their own affairs; and they should send some trusted man of theirs from Essen to the monastery, who could learn the particulars.

units.la: Hesselus Aysma Antverpiâ scribit Aurantio Principi litteras quoq; de expeditione hostium in Frisiam communicatas, Juliumq; Dekamam nuper Senatorem regium, ardore vindictae tribus schlopetariorum millibus adjutum subjugandis Frisiorum terris destinatum. Igitur praepediendis in Frisiam hostium irruptionibus Vederborgum ac Keyserfuerta ad Rheni Vahalisq; confluentes à Geldris praeoccupata quo transitu Rheni amnis hostilem exercitum arcerent & ne Frisij socij atq; vicini exulum suorum secretâ conspiratione in antiquas calamitates atque pulsa servitia reciderent. Unde Zutphaniae, Duisburgo, Deutecomio, reliquisque oppidis Rheno, Isalae aut Berckelio flumini adjectis commeatus copia ope navium advecta dataeque ad Frisios litterae, quibus imminentium discriminum & Adolphi Gorraei Caldenbroeckij epistolâ neque inveris indicijs monebantur.
units.tr: Hesselus Aysma writes from Antwerp to Prince Orange that letters too had been shared about the enemy's expedition into Friesland, and that Julius Dekama, lately a royal senator, had been appointed, aided by three thousand musketeers and stirred by the passion for revenge, to subdue the lands of the Frisians. Therefore, to hinder the enemy's invasions into Friesland, Vederborg and Keyserswerth, at the confluence of the Rhine and the Waal, were to be occupied in advance by the Gelderlanders, so that by that crossing of the Rhine they might keep off the hostile army, and so that the Frisians, their allies and neighbours, should not, through a secret conspiracy of their exiles, fall back into their old calamities and the slavery they had cast off. Hence supplies were brought by boat in abundance to Zutphen, Duisburg, Deutecom and the other towns on the Rhine, or on the Issel or the Berkel rivers, and letters were sent to the Frisians, warning them of the impending dangers, and of a letter from Adolph Gorraeus of Kaldenbroek containing not unreliable indications.

units.la: Tum Coloniensi conventu finem spectante Archidux Matthias mille quingentos aureos praestandis Legatorum impensis Frisios proposcit, quo reip. vacationibus honestum praemium statueretur, & ne actionis cum famâ gestae officia damnoso impendio pensarerentur. Idem subjunctae Ordinum generalium litterae habebant. Quippe Arschotanum caeterosq; legatos post sepositas domesticas & familiares curas procul domo ac carissimis pignorum Coloniae egisse, semestreque & ultra spatium tam laudabili conciliandae pacis negotio, non sine grandi impensâ & simul gloriâ collocasse. Sperare se clarissimae actioni brevem exitum, eoq; perventum esse, ut in Ordinum confesu commune ineundae pacis, aut parandi belli decretum non sine curâ publicae salutis ventiletur.
units.tr: Then, as the Cologne conference drew near its end, Archduke Matthias demanded from the Frisians one thousand five hundred gold pieces, to pay the expenses of the envoys, so that an honourable reward might be set for the public services of the envoys, and so that the duties of an undertaking carried out with credit should not be repaid at a ruinous cost. The letters of the General Estates that were added said the same. For Arschot and the other envoys, after setting aside their domestic and family cares, had acted far from home and from their dearest pledges at Cologne, and had spent more than half a year on so praiseworthy a business of making peace, not without great expense and at the same time without glory. They hoped for a brief end to a most distinguished undertaking, and that it had come to this, that in the assembly of the General Estates a decision to make a common peace or to prepare for war was being weighed, not without concern for the public safety.

units.la: Reperio in actis Ordinum singulos in menses octo aureorum millia legatis assignata, totique actioni àiv. Maii, in xxiv. Nov. diem quadradraginta & ultra aureorum millia impensa. Mox Cl. v. Abelus Franc-kena (qui in confessum foederatorum Ordinum vii. Eid. Septemb. à lxxix; Deputatis Frisiæ delegatus xii. Kal. Octob. ut ipse notat, sacramentum foederi dixerat) Ultrajecto in Frisiam communicandis arcanis & post Essenum ad Lalainium missus qui in Drentiâ præter exspectationem tempus trahens, suspicione sinistri sollicitudinem Ordinum innovabat. Cl. Franckena in Diario suo scribit, Collegium Ordinum Ultrajecto Arnhemum tum concessisse, haud dubiè, quo regis exercitus secundo Rheni amne, ut nuntiabatur, descensurus prudentiâ publici & præsen-tis ad pericula concilij in tanto armorum apparatu sisteretur. Idem tradit Carolum Roordam cum Brakelio & alijs Hagam Comitis ad Ordines Hollandiæ moderandis belli negotijs missum, quod ex legatorum imperij discessu & desperatione pacis regij per omnem oram dilectus policebantur.
units.tr: I find in the records of the Estates that eight thousand gold pieces a month were assigned to the envoys, and that for the whole undertaking, from 1 May to 24 November, more than forty thousand gold pieces were spent. Soon the most learned Abelus Franckena (who had been sent to the assembly of the confederated Estates on 7 September, from the Deputies of Friesland, on 19 [sic] August, and who, as he himself notes, had taken the oath of the covenant on 20 September) was sent from Utrecht into Friesland to communicate secrets, and afterwards to Lalainius; he, lingering in Drenthe beyond expectation, renewed the Estates' anxiety with a sinister suspicion. The learned Franckena writes in his diary that the college of the Estates had then withdrawn from Utrecht to Arnhem, undoubtedly so that the public council, present to the dangers in such a great array of arms, might be stationed where the king's army was said to be about to descend by the second arm of the Rhine. He also reports that Carolus Roorda, with Brakel and others, was sent to The Hague to Count Holland's Estates to direct the business of war, since from the departure of the envoys and the despair of peace they promised a royal levy throughout the whole coast.

units.la: Quare Legati Cæsaris, quo repentini discessus causam honestâ æquitatis specie velarent, scriptum quoddam hunc in modum Legatis Ordinum exhibuerunt.
units.tr: Therefore the envoys of the Emperor, in order to veil the cause of their sudden departure with a respectable appearance of fairness, presented to the envoys of the Estates a certain writing in the following manner.

units.la: SPeraveramus, Legati, tractationem pacis tanto labore, molestiâ & sumptu institutam divino auxilio, autoritate & intercessione CAESARIS, nostrâ ex industriâ meliores fructus habituram fuisse, quo funestissimo bello sopito, regem inter & vos Belgas verapax bono orbis Christiani sanciretur. Caterum quoniam res ex voto nostro non processere ferre patienter, quæ emendari non possunt, satius est. Igitur de actioni fine imponendo cogitamus, & ne Caesaris aut nostra integritati ex diversitate humanæ opinionis, aut malitiâ affingi possit, in animum induximus tacito famæ nostræ ac officij patrocinio apud PHILIPPI Legatum & simul vos subvenire. Nos vero CAESAREAE majestatis Legationem honestissimâ excusatione lubentes declinassemus, quod tantæ tempestatis quæ Belgicam involuisset, atrocitatem nostrâ ope sedare impares videremur. At verò apud CAESAREM infelicis Belgicæ commiseratum nostra excusatio parum efficax fuit, jussique sumus locum facere optimæ atque pissimæ Caesaris voluntati, quæ nostrâ curâ sanari corpus volebat, tot letalium vulnerum deformitate laceratum. Itaque tanto alacrius commissum nobis negotium suscepimus, quanto latius futurum videbatur, vicinæ genti per mutuas discordias fesse opem ferre. Et spes quidem pacis firmius concepta, quod PHILIPPI Hispaniæ regis Catholici postulata intra modum æquitatis starent isque præter Catholica Romanæ religionis professionem, debitam majestati suæ reverentiam & autoritatem suum populum flagitaret. Quarum utramque cum Ordines datis ad Caesarem litteris, quam Wormaciæ ipsis Imperij comitijs obtulissent, conventum Coloniæ in spem certissimæ pacis Caesar indixit. De cujus felicissimo eventu ÿ dubitare non poterant qui postulata PHILIPPI cum offerentium Ordinum æquitate conveniri conciliandis dissensionibus augurabantur. Igitur credebant tanto magis Caesaris & Romani imperij Principum autoritatem valituram, quanto graviore miseriarum suarum enarratione Caesarem & Principes ad intercedendum Legati Belgicæ permovissent. Quin ominabantur Belgas ipsos belli & tot cladium pertæsos pacem facile æquissimis sub conditionibus amplexuros, quod arbitrio Caesaris & se Rex
units.tr: We had hoped, envoys, that the treaty of peace, begun with so much labour, trouble and expense, by divine help, the authority and intercession of the Emperor, and our own diligence, would have yielded better fruits, so that, with that most deadly war put to rest, peace between the King and you Belgians might be sanctioned for the good of the Christian world. But since matters have not gone according to our wish, it is better to bear patiently what cannot be mended. Therefore we are thinking of bringing the business to an end, and, so that the integrity of the Emperor or of ourselves may not be charged, through differing human opinion or through malice, we have resolved, with a silent defence of our reputation and duty, to help you also before the envoy of Philip. Indeed we would gladly have declined the embassy of His Imperial Majesty with the most honourable excuse, that we seemed unequal to calming, by our help, the savagery of so great a storm as had enveloped Belgium. But before the Emperor, moved by the wretched state of Belgium, our excuse proved of little avail, and we were ordered to make room for the best and most excellent will of the Emperor, which wished the body, torn by so many deadly wounds and disfigured, to be healed by our care. Therefore we took up the business entrusted to us the more eagerly, the wider it seemed that help would be given to a neighbouring nation worn out by mutual discords. And indeed hope of peace was conceived more firmly, because the demands of Philip, the Catholic King of Spain, were within the bounds of fairness, and he required, besides the profession of the Catholic Roman religion, due reverence and authority for his majesty from his people. Since the Estates, with letters given to the Emperor, had offered both of these at Worms, at the Imperial Diet itself, the Emperor called a conference at Cologne in hope of most certain peace. Those who reckoned that Philip's demands could be brought into agreement with the fairness of the offering Estates, and augured the reconciling of the dissensions, could not doubt the outcome of this most fortunate event. Therefore they believed that the authority of the Emperor and of the Princes of the Roman Empire would prevail all the more, the more gravely the Belgian envoys had moved the Emperor and the Princes to intercede by describing their miseries. Indeed they foresaw that the Belgians themselves, weary of war and of so many disasters, would readily embrace peace under the most equitable conditions, since by the decision of the Emperor both he and the King...

units.la: Hhh
units.tr: Hhh

units.la: Philippus & provinciarum Ordines summisissent. Qui etsi Legatos Coloniam mittere conducto die debuissent, ita eosdem serius & post adventum suum ac juxta regij Legati advenisse, & quidem semiplenis mandatis instructos, quae totam actionem brevissimo tempore insuper definiri volebant. Quae res ut prima pacis auspicia, ita progressum quoque haud parum corrupit, nostraque consilia eludi fecit. Adeo ut magis è re suâ & publicâ fecisse Hannonij ac Artesij nobis videantur, qui Catholicam religionem, quam rex intemeratam volebat, amplexi, cum ALEXANDRO FARNESIO regis Praefecto bonam pacem iniere. Atqui Ordines vestri pro novâ religione stabiliendâ locuti, novis quoque foederum sacramentis se interea temporis obstrinxere, revocatis tacitè mandatis, quae eorum legati dubia atque ambigua Coloniam attulerant. Per ea fuit, quod nec cum Hannonijs aut Artesijs pacisci, nec in faciendis inducijs convenire inter se & cum PHILIPPI Legato potuerint, cui terminum finiendae actionis intra sex septimanas y praescripserant, qui toto semestri ne mandata quidem justa vobis Legatis transmiserant. Et quamvis isto tempore, repudiatâ velut ulteriore pacis actione conventu abstinere ac redire in nostra potuissemus ita maluimus mandato aliquid temporis & virium dare, si forte infelix Belgica sui mali sensu salubrius remedium popposcisset. Quae cum arma se sumpsisse ex saevitiâ regis praefectorum pellendis peregrinis copijs, retinendis legibus atque immunitatibus, restituendis commercijs, denique amovendis tributis atque exactionibus professa sit, ne hoc quidem argumento belli usa unquam fuit, ut novitate religionis se defenderet. Atqui priora mala sanando facilis pax fuisset, cujus ineundae causae adeo quoque PHILIPPI Legatus articulum religionis mitigavit, ut in corpora ac res vestras desaeviendi facultas cessaret, libertasque conscientijs, relicta censeretur. Igitur pace ruptâ corporum atque animorum vestrorum tutela ac quies sub armis & in solo bello erit, quod in legitimum Principem decernitur & quod corporibus animisque vestris calamitates ac incommoda datum erit. Ab ejus scilicet desiderio est, quod nobis petentibus intra quadrimestre nihil responsi ab Ordinibus vestris perlatum sit, exceptis seorsim Sylvaeducensibus, quibus sicuti & Transisulanis nostras pacis conditiones placuisse fide veri accepimus. Econtra Valentiniani taedio belli & Hannoniorum exemplo regis gratiam affectant, à quâ illi, sicut & ipsâ pace, alieni deprehenduntur, qui decreta trahunt famosisq; libellis per Belgicam & vicina sparsis, nostrae innocentiae & integritati graves facti sunt. Ab eo est, quod Arnhemienses declaraverint se mori quam parere conditionibus nostris malle, & quod PHILIPPI Legatus leniora consilia induendo religionis decretum mitigari detrectaverit, Igitur cum nostra in pacem studia infructuosa & quidem praeter spem inanis occupatio fecerit, abitum paramus Legati, quod nec Caesaris autoritas nec nostrae res diuturniorem moram patiantur. Facturi interea sumus, quae voti nostri summa est, ut Deo ac Caesari causam commendemus, ad eundem bonâ fide de singulis relaturi. Interim hortamur vos, Legati, ut quascunque subditorum vestrorum de nobis suspiciones animis eximatis, quibus inquinari Caesaris, nostra & Catholici regis sinceritas non patitur. Hoc etiam persuadebitis populo vestro, ut, in tantâ rerum tempestate constitutus ex fastidio belli desiderio pacis ardescat & ne negligat.
