Conditiones pacis à nobis praescriptas suo commodo, bono terrarum orbis. Caesari aut Catholico Regi exhibere, quo in veteri fortunae prosperitate sub legitimi principis imperio securè conquiesceat. Id precamur, idvovemus, Legati, qui non cessabimus omnem porro benevolentiam atque amicitiam vestris vestris ORDINIBUS deferre, non alium laboris nostri & molestiæ fructum sperantes, quam ut sub nostris, aut Hannoniorum Artesiorumque conditionibus pacem ineatis.
units.tr: Philip and the Orders of the provinces had sent. Although they ought to have sent their Legates to Cologne on the appointed day, they arrived later than that, after our own arrival and after the royal Legate, and moreover they came furnished with only half-complete mandates, and they wanted the whole business settled in a very short time. This, as it spoiled the first auspices of peace, so also it corrupted its progress not a little and caused our counsels to be mocked. So much so that the Hainaulters and the Artois men seem to us to have acted more wisely and in their own and the public interest, for they embraced the Catholic religion, which the king wished left untouched, and made a good peace with Alexander Farnese, the king's governor. Yet your Orders, while speaking of establishing a new religion, bound themselves in the meantime by new sacraments of covenants, having tacitly revoked the mandates which their Legates had brought to Cologne in doubtful and ambiguous terms. Because of this they could agree neither with the Hainaulters nor with the Artois men, nor among themselves and with Philip's Legate, to whom they had set a limit of six weeks for finishing the business, although for a whole half-year they had not even sent you Legates proper mandates. And although at that time we could have, by rejecting further action for peace, withdrawn from the assembly and returned to our own lands, we preferred to give the matter some time and strength by mandate, in case the unhappy Netherlands, aware of its own evil, might seek a more wholesome remedy. Although it has professed that it took up arms to drive out foreign troops, to keep its laws and liberties, to restore trade, and finally to remove taxes and exactions, from the cruelty of the king's governors, it has never used this pretext of war in order to defend itself by means of a novel religion. Yet the former evils would have been easily cured by peace, and Philip's Legate so softened the article on religion, for the sake of making peace, that the power of raging against your bodies and property would cease, and liberty of conscience would be considered left to each. Therefore, with the peace broken, the protection and quiet of your bodies and souls will be under arms and in war alone, which is decreed against the lawful Prince, and calamities and inconveniences will be given to your bodies and souls. It is clearly from this desire that, although we have been waiting for more than four months, no answer has been brought to us from your Orders, except that the people of Bois-le-Duc separately, and likewise the people of Overijssel, we have learned on good authority, were pleased with our conditions of peace. On the contrary, the people of Valenciennes, weary of war and following the example of the Hainaulters, seek the king's favour, and from him, like the peace itself, they are found estranged; they have drawn up decrees and, with infamous pamphlets scattered through the Netherlands and neighbouring lands, have done grave harm to our innocence and integrity. It is from this that the people of Arnhem have declared that they would rather die than submit to our conditions, and that Philip's Legate, by adopting milder counsels, has refused to let the decree on religion be softened. Therefore, since our efforts for peace have been unfruitful and, beyond expectation, a vain occupation, we are preparing to depart as Legates, since neither the authority of Caesar nor our own affairs allow a longer delay. Meanwhile we shall do what is the chief of our wish: commend the cause to God and to Caesar, and report to him in good faith on each point. In the meantime we urge you, Legates, to remove from your subjects' minds whatever suspicions of us they have, by which the sincerity of Caesar, of ourselves, and of the Catholic King is not permitted to be stained. You will also persuade your people of this, that, placed in such a storm of affairs, they should not neglect to kindle a desire for peace out of weariness of war. The conditions of peace prescribed by us are to be presented to Caesar or to the Catholic King for their advantage and the good of the whole world, so that in the prosperity of their former fortune they may rest securely under the rule of a lawful prince. This we pray for and wish, Legates; we shall not cease to offer all further goodwill and friendship to your to your ORDERS, hoping for no other fruit of our labour and trouble than that you enter into peace under our conditions or those of the Hainaulters and Artois men.

units.la: Ad quæ breviter Ordinum Legati.
units.tr: To which the Legates of the Orders briefly replied.

units.la: Quæ hesterno die Arschotano Duci ore tenus dicta & post exhibita sunt, ad illis articulatim satisfacere brevitas temporis non sinit, facturi alias, ut dignitati vestræ & officijs nostra respondeant. Hoc verò unum favoris & benevolentiæ argumentum dari nobis cupimus, ut fructum diuturnæ actionis sentiamus, quæ cessare non debet tanto labore ad finem atq; exitum perducta. Neq; enim dubitamus, quin intra biduum decretum Ordinum habituri simus, quod acceptum & vestri officij molestiam grate agnoscet & de jure nostræ actionis testabitur. At eâ abruptâ nec securitati nostrarum provinciarum, nec religionis postulatæ prosperitum erit, prodetque illum affectum Cæsaris & vestro nomine nobis oblatum vestris consilijs non subfuisse. Quin metuimus, quod Deus avertat, ne scriptum hoc majora odia & perturbationes excitet & præcipuè in animis illorum, qui libertatem conscientiæ suis dari in tanta rerum tempestate durante bello postulavere. Quam si concedere nobis clementia Regis non voluisset, & labori tanto & impensæ parcere detectum regij legati mandatum potuisset. Ordines verò nostri quod tardius decretum transmiserint id justæ morâ condonandum indicavimus, quod impeditis itinerum commeatibus intermedia loca gasatoribus & prædonibus infestarentur. Ad procurationes autem nostras quod attinet, eas justas atq; æquas esse palam apud vos fecimus, nosque hic subsistere jussos fuisse, dum amplioribus mandatis tam ponderosa in re nos instruere Ordinibus placuisset. Interim paciscendis inducijs mandatum accepimus, quam regis Legatus non suo, sed Farnesij arbitrio reliquit. Et certè si tam de vestra voluntate, quam de mandato regij Legati constitisset, non sex septimanarum sed totidem dierum consultatione tota actio eguisset. Postremum petimus, ut perspectis actis mense Julio perscriptis & postremis Ordinum litteris in quatriduum discessus, vestri consilium proferatis. Quod beneficium si obtinere non possumus, grates agimus vobis Legati, quod huc usque vestra dignitas atque occupatio actioni pacis vacaverit. Et id cognoscere quidem ac amore & officijs demereri in animum quocunq; etiam tempore induximus. De Reliquo testamur nos Deo æquitatis judici totum negotium committere.
units.tr: The matters which were stated orally to the Duke of Aarschot yesterday, and afterwards presented in writing, the shortness of time does not allow us to answer point by point; we shall do so at another time, so that our replies may match your dignity and duties. We wish only this one token of favour and goodwill to be given to us, that we may perceive the fruit of this long negotiation, which ought not to cease, having been brought to its end and conclusion after so great a labour. For we do not doubt that within two days we shall have the decree of the Orders, which will gratefully acknowledge the trouble of your office and will bear witness to the justice of our action. But if it is broken off, there will be neither security for our provinces nor prosperity for the religion we have demanded, and it will show that that affection of Caesar and of yourselves offered to us was not present in your counsels. Indeed we fear, which God forbid, that this writing may stir up greater hatreds and disturbances, especially in the minds of those who demanded liberty of conscience to be granted to their souls in such a storm of affairs while war continues. If the clemency of the King had not been willing to concede this to us, the royal Legate's mandate could have been disclosed, to spare such great labour and expense. As for our Orders, who sent their decree more slowly, we have declared that this delay is to be pardoned for a just cause, since the passage of supplies was hindered and the intervening places were troubled by plunderers and robbers. As for our procurations, we have made it plain to you that they are just and fair, and that we were ordered to remain here until the Orders were pleased to furnish us with fuller mandates in so weighty a matter. Meanwhile we have received a mandate to agree a truce, which the royal Legate has left not to his own judgment but to Farnese's. And certainly, if it had been settled both by your will and by the royal Legate's mandate, the whole business would have needed not six weeks but as many days of deliberation. Lastly we ask that, having examined the proceedings written down in July and the Orders' final letters, you put forward your counsel for a four-day adjournment. If we cannot obtain this favour, we thank you, Legates, that your dignity and occupation have so far been free for the business of peace. And we have resolved, at whatever time, to recognise this and to deserve it by affection and services. For the rest we declare that we commit the whole matter to God, the judge of equity.

units.la: Ita conventus Legatorum Cæsaris, Regis & Belgicæ Coloniæ solutus, soloqae Suartsenburgio excepto, quem Cæsar hærere Coloniæ in spem procurandæ adhuc pacis jusserat, Septem-viri cum Wirceburgio Prasule & Iuliacensibus in sua reversi. Carolus quoq; Aragonius Philippi Legatus Bonnam concessit, negatoque reditu Ordinibus Regis gratiam, sua decreta commendavit. Mox articuli Ordinum prid. Kal. Decemb. Coloniam Antverpiâ perlati. Istorum summa erat:
units.tr: Thus the assembly of the Legates of Caesar, of the King, and of the Netherlands at Cologne was dissolved; only Schwarzenberg, whom Caesar had ordered to remain at Cologne in hope of still procuring peace, was excepted. The Seven returned home with the Bishop of Würzburg and the people of Jülich. Charles of Aragon, Philip's Legate, also withdrew to Bonn, and, refusing a return to the Orders, commended the King's favour and his own decrees. Soon afterwards the articles of the Orders were brought from Antwerp to Cologne on the day before the Kalends of December. The substance of these was:

units.la: I. Ut Conventio Gandavensis, Bruxellensis Vnio & Fœdus Edicti perpetui nomine insignitum & à rege approbatum ratum efficaxque esset. II. Omnium tam quæ ante conventiones supradictas ex causa turbarum patrata, quam post facta in demoliendis castellis, caterisque actionibus, venia ac oblivio foret. Castella quoque diruta restaurare aut nova extruere rex & posteri prohiberentur. III. Illi jura omnium singulorum que per præfectos tam præsentes quam
units.tr: I. That the Convention of Ghent, the Union of Brussels, and the Edict of Perpetual Edict, as it is named, approved by the King, be ratified and made effective. II. That pardon and oblivion be granted for all the things done on account of the disturbances, both before the aforesaid conventions and after, in the demolition of castles and other actions; and that the King and his successors be forbidden to restore the castles demolished or to build new ones. III. That the rights of all and each, as much present as

units.la: H h h 2 quam futuros confirmari facerent. IV. Peregrinum militem tam ex causâ turbarum in provincias transductum, quam ante praesidio habitum intra quindecim dies proximos ex oppidis & praesidys rex conduci fateret, è finibus provinciarum intra dies viginti. Eum revocare non nisi bello externo aut de consensu Ordinum, regi fas foret. Tormenta omnemque commeatum oppidis atque munitionibus restitueret, praefectosq; Burgundiæ & Luxenburgi pro non admittendo peregrino milite jurare cogeret. Ordines commercia pacemque publicam restituerent, V. Artesij sociyque circa excessum peregrini militis, omnia oppida, fortalitia in aliys provinciis occupata cum omni commeatu bellico restituerent. Idem Ordines facerent. Militem in sua quique revocarent, dum persolutis stipendijs provinciis excedat. VI. Artesij sociyque societati atque pati firmandæ cautionem praestabunt, se peregrino militi per ditiones suas transitum non permissuros. Idem Ordines Luxenburgensibus, Burgundis & Artesijs facerent, modo ne illarum partium fuerint, secus exautorari dimittiq; curarent. Oppida, castella, peregrini praesidiarij Ordinibus tradent, eaque Ordines nec nisi in limitaneis & ex recepto usu, praesidio non gravarent. VII. Tributa & indictiones ex hoc bello natas, redimendo ære alieno & restituendis commerciis Ordinum arbitratui relinqueret. VIII. Omni dissensioni amovendæ Ecclesiasticæ personæ & AURANTIUS Princeps in bona tam immobilia quam mobilia eorumque usum restituerentur. Hypotheca aut alienatio, si quæ à pace Gandavensi facta scriptave sit, nulla foret. IX. Provincialibus utrinque dignitates & beneficia Ecclesiastica, abolitâ tamen in perpetuum novorum Episcoporum ordinatione, redderentur. Similiter praefecturæ provinciarum, officia politica & dignitates restituerentur, exceptis iis, qui æquâ compositione contenti erunt. Iis quoque qui laesi forent, compensatio per arbitros ex æquitate, qui post quatuor menses à promulgatâ pace isti rei delegabuntur, amovendis novis turbis praestaretur. Dignitatibus restituti sacramentum ex formulâ sequentis articuli dicerent, quod si secus factum esset, irritum nullumque haberent. X. Nulli in Concilium Status, Secretiorum, Rationumve, reliquaque Collegia, quæ provincijs communia forent, admitterentur, praeterquam Ordinibus Generalibus accepti. Idem in praefectis provinciarum, oppidorum, arcium, cohortium ductoribus, militaribusque officiarys valeret. Qui ad generales & eminentes dignitates admovebuntur, inquilini, obeundisque dignitatibus ex jure privilegiorum idonei forent. Regi, Ordinibus, huic conventioni juramentum praestarent. Concilia quoque aut facta contra Statum publicum concepta aut patrata, singulis provinciarum Ordinibus communicarent. XI. Captivi utrinq; nullo lytro dimitterentur. XII. BURANUS comes intra trimestre patriæ ac libertati redderetur. XIII. Acta MATTHIAE Gubernatoris Ordinumque, tam ante tempus posteriorum motuum & provinciarum defectiones, quam post perscripta, valida rataque forent. Idem in decretis, quae regy juris fuissent, hac vice valeret. XIV. Magistratuum per oppida & alibi creatio, in futurum recepto ritu & secundum jus ac privilegium cujusque loci fieret. XV. Regi autoritas quam primum ex divinis atque humanis legibus, tum jure privilegiorum, statutorum, consuetudinum, ex formulâ pacificationis Gandavensis Vnionis & Editi perpetui restitueretur. XVI. Gubernator provinciis à Rege, qui regy sanguinis, legitime natus, Ordinibus acceptus foret, constitueretur. Is cum aequitate & justitiâ regeret, juxta privilegia, jura, idoneos mores, statuta & hanc ipsam pacificationem, cui juramento se obligaret. Et
units.tr: H h h 2 future, be confirmed through the governors. IV. The King should acknowledge that foreign soldiers, brought into the provinces on account of the disturbances as well as previously kept in garrison, be led out of the towns and garrisons within fifteen days, and out of the borders of the provinces within twenty days. He would have the right to recall them only in an external war or with the consent of the Orders. He should restore artillery and all supplies to the towns and fortifications, and compel the governors of Burgundy and Luxembourg to swear that they will not admit foreign soldiers. The Orders shall restore commerce and public peace. V. The Artois men and their allies shall restore, with regard to the departure of the foreign soldiers, all towns and fortresses occupied in the other provinces together with all military supplies. The Orders shall do the same. They shall each recall their soldiers to their own places, provided that they depart from the provinces once their pay has been settled. VI. The Artois men and their allies shall give a guarantee for the strengthening of the alliance and the peace that they will not permit passage of foreign soldiers through their lands. The Orders shall do the same for the men of Luxembourg, Burgundy and Artois, provided they are not of those parts; otherwise they shall take care that they are discharged and dismissed. The towns, castles and foreign garrisons shall be handed over to the Orders, and the Orders shall not burden them with a garrison except on the frontiers and by accepted custom. VII. The taxes and levies arising from this war the King shall leave to the judgment of the Orders, for redeeming debts and restoring trade. VIII. To remove all dissension, ecclesiastical persons and the Prince of Orange shall be restored to their goods, both immovable and movable, and to their use of them. Any mortgage or alienation made or drawn up since the Peace of Ghent shall be null. IX. Ecclesiastical dignities and benefices shall be restored to the provincials on both sides, although the ordination of new bishops shall be abolished for ever. Likewise the governorships of the provinces, political offices and dignities shall be restored, except for those who are content with a fair settlement. Those who have been harmed shall also receive compensation through arbiters, chosen equitably, who shall be appointed for this matter four months after the peace is proclaimed, so that new disturbances may be removed. Those restored to their dignities shall take an oath according to the formula of the following article; if they did otherwise, the oath would be void and of no effect. X. No one shall be admitted to the Council of State, of the Secret Affairs, or of Accounts, nor to the other Colleges which are common to the provinces, except those accepted by the General Orders. The same shall apply to the governors of provinces, towns and citadels, the leaders of cohorts and military officers. Those who are raised to general and eminent dignities shall be natives, and suitable by right of privilege to hold the dignities. They shall swear an oath to the King, to the Orders, and to this convention. They shall also communicate to the individual Orders of the provinces any councils framed or carried out against the public state. XI. Prisoners on both sides shall be released without any ransom. XII. Count Buren shall be restored to his country and liberty within three months. XIII. The acts of Matthias, the Governor, and of the Orders, both before the time of the later troubles and the revolts of the provinces, and those written down afterwards, shall be valid and ratified. The same shall hold for the decrees which had been the King's right, for this occasion. XIV. The creation of magistrates in towns and elsewhere shall take place in future according to the accepted custom and according to the law and privilege of each place. XV. The King's authority shall be restored as soon as possible, under divine and human laws, and under the right of privileges, statutes and customs, according to the formula of the Pacification of Ghent, the Union, and the Perpetual Edict. XVI. A Governor shall be appointed for the provinces by the King, who shall be of royal blood, legitimately born, and acceptable to the Orders. He shall govern with equity and justice, according to privileges, rights, honourable customs, statutes, and this very pacification, to which he shall bind himself by oath. And since Archduke Matthias has duly administered the provinces, the King shall give effect to his continuing in office, or else he shall receive a new mandate of government.

units.la: Et quoniam Matthias Archidux rité provinciis administrasset, Rex effectum daret, ut in dignitate continuaretur, aut novum gubernationis mandatum acciperet. XVII. Urbes, castella, munitiones, tormenta, commeatus bellicus, arma, naves, quæ Hollandorum Zelandorumque forent, dispositioni pacificationis Gandavensis relinquerentur. In ceteris vero provinciis, quæ Ordinum generalium essent, conservarentur, administrarenturque à Præfectis, tribunis cæterisque quibus id à Matthiâ & Ordinibus commissum esset, cautione addita, ut Regi, Ordinibusque sacramentum dicerent. Rex quoque missione peregrino militi factâ, oppidorum, arcium munitionum, præfectos ex inquilinis idoneos Ordinibusque probatos constitueret, quique defendendis oppidis, castellisve fidem pignerarent, dum aliter de concilio Ordinum statueretur. Patrimonium interim Regis Præfectis committeretur. XVIII. Redit. uum regiorum ex hac conventione in subsidium belli ab Ordinibus impensorum, nullæ rationes essent, regi in posterum cederent. XIX. ORDINES omnibus fœderibus excepto Anglico & ANDINO renunciarent. XX. Hac conventione Angliæ REGINA & ANDINUS comprehenderentur. XXI. Ad religionem quod attinet. Quandoquidem provinciæ ex commerciis & diuturnâ regis absentiâ, mutationem in religione accepissent, tollendis dissidiis intestinis, rex tam Reformatam & Augustanæ confessionis, quam Romanam Religionem haberi in iis locis permitteret, in quibus publicè exercerentur. Econtra ORDINES effectum darent, ut à pace vulgatâ Romana Catholica religio sub æquâ & perpetuâ formulâ restitueretur, exercituque utrinque dimisso, pax haberetur. ORDINES quoque conventum primâ occasione instituerent eoque durante, præsentibus regiis mandatariis, operam navarent, ut reformatæ quibusdam in locis aut saltem provinciis locus esset, salvo Ordinum Hollandiæ sociorumque expacificatione Gandavensi jure, apud quos pro Romanâ in ditionibus suis tolerandâ ageretur. XXII. De confirmatione, ac observantia hujus conventionis à definitis articulis decernerent.
units.tr: And since Matthias the Archduke had administered the provinces properly, the King would bring it about that he remain in office, or else receive a new commission to govern. XVII. The cities, towns, fortifications, artillery, military supplies, arms and ships that belonged to Holland and Zeeland would be left to the arrangement of the Pacification of Ghent. In the other provinces, which belonged to the General Estates, they would be preserved and administered by the prefects, tribunes and others to whom Matthias and the Estates had entrusted them, with the added guarantee that they would swear an oath to the King and the Estates. The King, too, having dismissed the foreign soldiers, would appoint as prefects of the towns, citadels and fortifications men from the native inhabitants who were suitable and approved by the Estates, and who would pledge their faith to defend the towns and fortresses until a different decision was reached by the council of the Estates. Meanwhile the royal patrimony would be entrusted to the prefects. XVIII. The royal revenues, from which the Estates had met the expenses of the war under this agreement, were to be returned to the King in future, with no accounts being demanded. XIX. The Estates were to renounce all leagues except the English one and the one with Andinus. XX. By this agreement the Queen of England and Andinus would be included. XXI. As for religion: since the provinces, through trade and the King's long absence, had undergone a change in religion, in order to end internal strife the King would permit both the Reformed and the Augsburg Confession, as well as the Roman religion, to be held in those places where they were publicly practised. On the other side, the Estates would bring it about that, after the general peace, the Roman Catholic religion be restored under an equal and lasting arrangement, and that, with the army disbanded on both sides, peace be kept. The Estates would also, at the first opportunity, convene an assembly, and while it lasted, with the royal agents present, they would take pains that the Reformed religion be allowed in certain places or at least in certain provinces, the Pacification of Ghent right of Holland and its allies being preserved, and in whose territories the question of tolerating the Roman religion would be taken up. XXII. They would decide on the confirmation and observance of this agreement from the articles agreed upon.

units.la: Hæc VIII. Kal. Dec. Antverpiæ in consessu Ordinum generalium perscripta, isque omne mandatum Legatorum affornatum est, ad promovendam tamen pacem non suffecit.
units.tr: These terms, written out at Antwerp on the eighth day before the Kalends of December in the assembly of the General Estates, were sent to the Estates together with the full mandate of the delegates; yet they were not sufficient to promote peace.

units.la: Sunt qui tradant, durante Coloniensi conventu, Legatum Cæsaris Ottonem Henricum Suartsenburgium nomine Philippi Regis cum Aurantio Principe seorsum de ineundâ pace egisse, eidemq; peramplas conditiones præter damni ex bello dati reparationem restitutionemque bonorum, filium quoque Buræ Comitem è custodiâ relaxandum, & cum religionis libertate quietissimum securitate secretum explendæ vitæ obulisse. Aurantium quoque regiæ gratiæ sive diffisum, sive contemptorem oblatâ Philippi beneficia fastidio privati commodi respuisse, deque suo erga populum affectu testatum, omne officium tuendæ libertati & integritati conscientiæ confecrasse. Quæ ab animo supra metum & fortunam posito profecta interritam tantâ rerum desperatione mentem ulterioribus curis & simul periculis reservavere. Mihi actorum fidem expendenti visum semper fuit, actionem istam tanto apparatu rerum & post principes viros honestandæ fabulæ in scænam introductos, fictâ personarum repræsentatione institutam, Philippumque Regem simulatis apud propinquum Cæsarem in pacem studijs, quo tardatis Ordinum
units.tr: Some relate that, while the Cologne conference was in progress, the imperial envoy Otto Henry Schwarzenberg, on behalf of King Philip, negotiated a peace privately with the Prince of Orange, and offered him very generous conditions: besides compensation for the damage caused by the war and the restoration of his property, the release of Count Buren's son from custody, and a most peaceful and secure retirement for the rest of his life with freedom of religion. They say Orange, whether he distrusted the royal favour or despised it, rejected the benefits Philip offered, scorning private advantage, and, bearing witness to his own affection for the people, devoted all his efforts to defending liberty and the integrity of his conscience. These acts, springing from a mind raised above fear and fortune, preserved an undaunted spirit, in such despair of affairs, for later cares and dangers. Weighing the evidence of the deeds, I have always thought that this action was staged with such display, with princely men brought onto the stage to lend honour to the drama, and with a feigned representation of the characters, and that King Philip had, under the pretence of seeking peace with his kinsman the Emperor, prepared commands contrary to the will of the Estates, by which he might delay the affairs of the Estates

units.la: Aurantius opima conditiones seorsum oblatas repudiat. cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXIX. dinum rebus incrementa potentiæ faceret, alienæ ab Ordinum voluntate mandata præconcepisse. Ipsos quoque Ordines in societatem Anglicam, aut Andini desixos minus fervida paci desideria professos, ordinante providentiâ, ut scænicâ partium simulatione, veros ad actus & in tragœdiam exituros occulto miraculo uteretur.
units.tr: Orange rejects the rich terms offered to him separately. 1579. ...the affairs of the Estates, to increase the power of Philip's party. Likewise, the Estates themselves, who professed a less eager desire for peace, were either bound to the English alliance or fixed on Andinus; by an ordering of Providence, this hidden wonder used the play-acting of the parts, so that they would come forth to real deeds and into tragedy.

units.la: Quare à Cæsaris & Philippi Legatorum discessu, Mandatarij quoque Ordinum Antverpiam revocati, delegatis Bernardo Merodio Rumenio & Aggæo Albada Frisiorum Oratore, qui cum Suartsenburgio Cæsaris Legato pacis actionem ex voluntate Cæsaris continuarent. Cujus desperatione id tum factum est, ut ex Ordinum Legatis à societate Belgici fœderis deficerent, regiæque potentiæ & imminentis belli metu patriæ libertati & veteri sacramento lubricum & fragilem Philippi gratiam anteponerent. In quibus Philippus Crojus Dux Arschotanus princeps legationis, Joannes Lindanus D. Gertrudis, Fredericus Hyperius Marolius Abbas, Buccho Ayta Præpositus D. Bavonis & Caspar Schætus Grobendonckius fuere. Quæ defectio Antverpiam perlata, ut Ordinum conventum non parum conturbavit, ita econtra hostium partibus & armatæ in patriam Frisicæ nobilitati animos addidit. Itaque Farnesij jussu delectus ad Rhenum & per confinia instituti, novæque copiæ, quæ exulum confluxu celerius cogebantur, sub Legionis Frisicæ nomine in cohortes distributæ. Quare & centuriones ex eadem gente & profugâ nobilitate cohortibus dati, in eosque Julius Dekama, Renicus Dekama, Titus Cammingha, & Lollius Ockingha delecti.
units.tr: Therefore, after the departure of the Emperor's and Philip's envoys, the deputies of the Estates were also recalled to Antwerp, and delegates were sent, Bernard Merode of Rumen and Aggaeus Albada, envoy of the Frisians, to continue the negotiation for peace with Schwarzenberg, the Emperor's envoy, according to the Emperor's will. Because of this despair, some of the Estates' envoys then defected from the society of the Belgian league, and, out of fear of royal power and of the impending war, preferred the slippery and fragile favour of Philip to the liberty of the fatherland and their old oath. Among them were Philip Croy, Duke of Arschot, leader of the embassy, John Lindanus, Dean of St Gertrude's, Frederick Hyperius, Abbot of Marolles, Buccho Ayta, Provost of St Bavo's, and Caspar Schaets of Grobbendonk. This defection, when it reached Antwerp, disturbed the assembly of the Estates no little, but on the contrary it strengthened the hopes of the enemy's side and of the Frisian nobility that had taken up arms against the fatherland. Thus, by Farnese's command, levies were made along the Rhine and in the border lands, and new troops, which were gathered more quickly through the flocking of exiles, were distributed into cohorts under the name of the Frisian Legion. Accordingly, captains from the same people and from the exiled nobility were given to the cohorts, and Julius Dekema, Renicus Dekema, Titus Cammingha and Lollius Ockinga were chosen for this.

units.la: Albada scribit Georgium Liauckema ferendo vexillo Dekameæ cohorti ascriptum, Everardumque Ensium hominem obscurum & famâ ignotum nobilitati Frisicæ & militaribus dignitatibus insertum. Idem addit tria vexilla colore albo, fimbriis ex rubro & flavo contextis Coloniæ conspecta, unumquemque quatuor ensibus & liliatis capulis interstinctum Dekameæ gentis haud dubie insignia protulisse. Reliqua duo Burgundicâ cruce insignita conspectui nullâ simulatione data pelliciendæ ad proferenda nomina reliquorum exulum multitudini quæ Philippi dominationem ex reverentiâ Burgundici tanquam laudati imperij venerabatur.
units.tr: Albada writes that George Liauckema, enrolled to bear the standard for the Dekema cohort, and Everard Ensius, a man of obscure origin and unknown reputation, were admitted into the Frisian nobility and to military rank. The same writer adds that three standards, of white colour with fringes woven of red and yellow, were seen at Cologne, each marked with four swords and lily-tipped hilts, which undoubtedly displayed the insignia of the Dekema family. The other two, marked with the Burgundian cross, were displayed openly, with no pretence, to win over the multitude of exiles to proclaim their names, who out of reverence for Burgundy venerated Philip's rule as that of a praised empire.

units.la: Annotatum invenio solemni exulum epulo Coloniæ habito, vini scyphos firmandis partium sacramentis per mensam circumlatos, unumque ex centurionibus mero gravem & temulentum trucidandis quinquaginta Frisiorum nobilibus parem se furiosâ insaniâ jactitasse. Itaque retundendis perfugarum consilijs multa adversum eos in consessu Ordinum differebantur, cum essent, qui revocandos edicto in patriam censerent, & ut adversum contumaces edictumque respuentes lege ageretur. Alij existumabant, eorum propinquos & affines honestâ custodia & incutiendo terrori coërcendos, quo conceptæ perfugarum immanitati & efferis ingenijs propinquorum captivitas mederetur. Igitur & in domesticos publicæ libertatis hostes virili exemplo aliquid statuendum suadebant, muniendaque imprimis adversus irruptiones oppida, quo externa vis tam perfugæ quam interni hostis auxilio innixa poenarum metu languesceret. Itaque & dum de domanijs ut vocant regiis reip. & bellorum usui applicandis inter alia quoque deliberatum suadente prudendentum juris consilio ut defendendæ provinciæ olim Saxoni & Carolo Austrio assignata premente necessitate ijsdem usibus impenderentur.
units.tr: I find it noted that at a solemn banquet of the exiles held at Cologne, cups of wine were passed round the table to confirm the oaths of the parties, and that one of the captains, heavy and drunk with neat wine, boasted in a furious madness that he would slaughter fifty Frisian nobles in the same way. Therefore, in order to blunt the plans of the deserters, many measures against them were debated in the assembly of the Estates: some were for recalling them to the fatherland by edict, and for proceeding by law against the stubborn and those who scorned the edict. Others thought that their relatives and kinsmen should be restrained by honourable custody and by inspiring terror, so that the captivity of the relatives might remedy the monstrous conduct and savage dispositions of the deserters. Accordingly, they urged that something be decided with manly resolve also against the domestic enemies of the public liberty, and that towns be fortified above all against incursions, so that the external force, supported by the help of the deserters as well as of the internal enemy, might be weakened by the fear of punishment. Thus, while the so-called royal domains were being deliberated upon, among other matters, for application to the needs of the commonwealth and of the wars, on the advice of prudent men of law, it was urged that those lands, once assigned to Saxony and to Charles of Austria for the defence of the province, should, under pressing necessity, be spent on the same uses.

units.la: Cæterum iste armorum apparatus & decretæ in Frisiam expeditionis festinatio fortunâ aut fato abrupta, illo tempore disparuit. Sunt qui tradant, ex Valonum Hispanorumque qui ex Hannoniâ ac Artesiâ facturi justum exercitum credebantur, tardioribus auxilijs injectum impedimentum fuisse, & quod Ericus Brunsuigius equestribus, quos per Saxoniam collegerat, copijs, trans Rhenum ducendis maturum consilium non adhibuissēt. Quamvis essent, qui scirent nobilissimum Germaniæ amnem hybernis aquis intumescentem, ut difficilem sternendo ponti, ita trajiciendo militi esse, inviumque aut imbrium fluxu auctum, sicut magna flumina solent, tam ripæ, quam alicujus molis impatientem, torrentium aquarum vi solertiam humanæ artis respuere. Alij censebant, occupatis à Gallo per Hannoniam Artesiamque oppidis regias Philippi vires sistendis Gallorum irruptionibus admovendas tum fuisse, factumque esse, ut Farnesius, etsi Frisiorum exulum conatibus faveret, consilium mutare tutandis Hannoniensium ditionibus coactus sit. Alij addunt famâ Egmondanæ defectionis expeditionem quoque non parum inpeditam etsi in tantâ opinionum varietate fato evenisse videatur, ut tam crudelibus cœptis atque consilijs arcanum obstaculum injiceretur.
units.tr: But this display of arms and the haste of the expedition decided upon against Friesland were broken off by fortune or fate and vanished at that time. Some relate that the slower aid from the Walloons and Spaniards, who were thought likely to form a proper army out of Hainault and Artois, was an obstacle, and that Eric of Brunswick had not adopted a timely plan for leading the cavalry troops he had gathered through Saxony across the Rhine. Yet there were some who knew that the noblest river of Germany, swollen by winter waters, is as difficult to bridge as it is to cross with soldiers, and that, swollen by the flow of rains as great rivers usually are, it resists the cleverness of human art with the force of its torrents, not enduring either banks or any structure. Others thought that the royal forces of Philip should then have been brought to stop the incursions of the French, since the towns in Hainault and Artois had been occupied by the French, and that it happened that Farnese, although he favoured the attempts of the Frisian exiles, was forced to change his plan in order to protect the domains of Hainault. Others add that the expedition was also no little hindered by the report of Egmont's defection; although, amid such a variety of opinions, it may seem to have come about by fate, so that a hidden obstacle was thrown in the way of such cruel undertakings and plans.

units.la: Hesselus Aysma litteris prid. Non. Decemb. Antverpiâ scriptis tradit, Ordines generales de reparando pacis & belli ordine ac disciplinâ serio tum egisse, interque assiduas consulentium preces cœlo fusas virilem constantiam circumstrepentibus periculis induisse. Itaque movebat Frisios, ut pudori ac infamiæ illorum, qui parvâ militum manu Frisiam regi se asserturos jactitaverant, secundis rebus ritè usi animos ex adversis acuerent, Principisque Aurantij, quo cum clam egerant, monitu Tornacensis ac Flandricarum civitatum exemplo, interriti patriæ quietem ac fortunam suis in dexteris quærerent. Quare censfus per Frisiam gerendis rebus confestim actus, æreque eximia provincialium liberalitate collato, socio Ordinum ærario & simul domestico provisum.
units.tr: Hesselus Aysma, in a letter written at Antwerp on the day before the Nones of December, relates that the General Estates were then seriously dealing with the restoration of the order and discipline of peace and war, and that, amid the constant prayers poured out to heaven by those consulting, they put on manly constancy while dangers clamoured around them. Thus he urged the Frisians to use their successes properly, so that they might sharpen their spirits from adversity, for the shame and infamy of those who had boasted that they would make Friesland subject to the king with a small band of soldiers; and, with the advice of Prince Orange, with whom they had secretly dealt, and following the example of Tournai and the Flemish cities, to seek the quiet and fortune of the fatherland, undaunted, in their own hands. Accordingly, a census was at once carried out throughout Friesland to conduct affairs, and, with outstanding bronze contributed by the generous provincials, provision was made both for the common treasury of the Estates and for the domestic one.

units.la: Reperio in actis octo stufferos é florenis aureis decreto Ordinum tum collectos Abelumq; Franckenam nomine fœderati Ultrajectinorum collegij cum Scipione Meckama viro nobili ad Lalainium Essenum in Drentiam missum, præter parati æris copiam, commeatum quoque bellicum instruendis copijs attulisse. Quippe metuebatur ne Sigismundus, de quo dixi, Curtspacchius equitum ductor, captivitatis Ultrajectinæ vulnus atque memoriam adhuc alens, à partibus Ordinum deficeret, equitemque sacramenti dubium & æris inopem vastandis Frisiorum terris conduceret. Ipsi quoque arcium castellorumque per Frisiam Satrapæ, quod Coloniæ profuga nobilitas sparsis in publicum rumoribus circumferebat, à Lalainio æré & commeatu destituto & fidei tum ambiguo ad defectionem sollicitarentur, rebusq; per provinciam lubricis externæ armorum tempestati domesticam perfidiam adjicerent. Igitur Bolsuerdiæ omnia turbida atque inquieta erant, auctâ finisti suspicione, quod adventare copiæ neque invero rumore è Noviolandis dicerentur, urbisque præsidium, à quo aliena esset, cum invidiâ civium daturæ. Unde Pontificij duplicari excubias, portas occludi, convenire armatos petierè,
units.tr: I find in the records that eight stuivers' worth of gold florins were collected by decree of the Estates at that time, and that Abel Franckena, on behalf of the confederated college of Utrecht, was sent with Scipio Meckama, a nobleman, to Lalaing at Essen in Drenthe. Besides a supply of ready money, he also brought military provisions for equipping the troops. For it was feared that Sigismund, of whom I have spoken, Curtspacchius, leader of the horsemen, still nursing the wound and memory of his captivity at Utrecht, would break from the Estates' side and hire a cavalry, doubtful in its oath and short of money, to lay waste the lands of the Frisians. It was also feared that the governors of the castles and fortresses throughout Friesland, as the exiled nobility from Cologne spread about in public rumours, were being urged to defection by Lalaing, who lacked money and provisions and whose loyalty was then doubtful, and that they would add domestic treachery to the external storm of war that was unsettling the province. Therefore everything at Bolsward was turbulent and restless, suspicion of the neighbouring towns having increased, because troops were said to be approaching, and in truth by rumour from Noviolandis, and because the citizens, resenting it, would admit a garrison that would be foreign to them. Hence the Papists demanded that the guards be doubled, the gates be shut, and the armed men assemble.

units.la: prohibendo præsidio, quod Lalainius qui Groningam ut Cl. Franckena notat, iv. Kal. Jan. intraverat recipi arcano, ut credebatur, consilio jusse-rat. Sed Vlietio Snecanam ad portam stativa habenti obviam legati Hes-selus Leo Aysma & Sixtus Hettenius missi, qui de voluntate Lalainij & mandato centurionis cognoscerent. Illud habebat ut Bolsuerdij centuriam militum, mediam Snecenses pro præsidio acciperent, Vlietiusque infidæ ex factionibus partium concordiæ armatorum ope subveniret. Quod etsi Magistratus metu plebis nollet, ita res in nobilitatis oppidanæ & con-cilij jurati arbitrium rejecta, urgente Vlietio, ut Noviolandis gravi responsum maturaret. Quare Gosllicus, Douwo, & Geroldus Heramæ u-na cum Concilio jurato in curiam evocati decretumque ut exquirendo Præfecti consilio Geroldus Herama & Suffridus Petraeus Groningam irent, populoque civico tuendæ urbi prompto militare præsidium deprecarentur. Unde Lalainius auditis Legatis animi dubius & ex futuri erroris instinctu fluctuans, mandatum Vlietio datum revocavit, Bolsuerdiosque dato obside, præsidij immunes esse jussit. Hoc verò volebat, ut exigente necessitate, pro admittendo præsidio caverent & ne clan-destinas cum hostibus societates Pontificia multitudo moliretur. Quod malè à Bolsuerdijs & præsertim Pontificijs interpretatum causam altercationis & civilis dissidij dedit. Itaque coacto in Curiam Magistratu, decretum ut ex potentioribus & quibus amplæ facultates essent, sedecim in Senatum citarentur, ijsque Lalainij sententia nullâ gratiæ aut odij simulatione prælegeretur. Quo facto plebs quoque signo campanæ dato, audiendo Legationis secreto, in templum evocata, delectique ex totâ multitudine Quatuor-viri, qui cum Senatu sedandæ civilium animorum inquietudini remedium invenirent. Sed religionis acre dis-sidium, sicut plerisque in locis rerum quieti adversum erat, omniaque concordiæ destinata opinionum impetu subvertebantur. Quippe Senatus motâ plebe & ex Pontificiorum immodestiâ tacitè præsidium compescendis turbis implorabat, dandoque obsidi aut præstandæ cautioni quam ante facilior sua obsequia præfecti imperio afformabat. Pontificij contra, affectuum vehementes postulari obsides, præscribi cautionem à præ-secto indignabantur, in cujus potestate non esset, civili præsidio ultro ex licentiâ temporum insolenti, militares & egenas stipendiorum cohortes adjicere. Spectare scilicet se quibus moribus militiæ sacramenta habeantur & quam Noviolandos premat rusticæ plebi gravis & peti-ta ab armato securitas. Igitur decretum, ut rejecta cautione Legati ad Lalainium remitterentur, æquisq; cum eo conditionibus transigerent.
units.tr: By refusing the garrison, which Lalaing, who had entered Groningen (as Cl. Franckena notes, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January), had ordered to be received by a secret plan, as was believed. But the envoys Hesselus Leo Aysma and Sixtus Hettenius were sent to meet Vlietius, who was encamped at the Sneek gate, to learn Lalaing's intention and the centurion's mandate. The arrangement was that Bolsward should take a company of soldiers, and the people of Sneek half of them, as a garrison, and that Vlietius should come to help with armed force against the faithless concord of the factions. Although the magistrates, from fear of the common people, were unwilling, the matter was thrown back on the judgment of the town nobility and the sworn council, Vlietius pressing that Noviolandis should hasten a serious reply. Accordingly Gosllicus, Douwo, and Geroldus Herama were summoned to the court together with the sworn council, and a decree was passed that Geroldus Herama and Suffridus Petraeus should go to Groningen to seek the prefect's counsel and to beg for a military garrison to defend the town, the people being ready for its defence. Hence Lalaing, having heard the envoys, uncertain in mind and wavering from a premonition of future error, revoked the order given to Vlietius and commanded that Bolsward, upon giving a hostage, be exempt from a garrison. But he wished this: that, should necessity demand, they would make provision for admitting a garrison, and that the Papist multitude would not contrive secret alliances with the enemy. This, badly interpreted by the Bolsward people, and especially by the Papists, gave cause for quarrel and civil dissension. So the magistracy, assembled in the court, decreed that sixteen of the more powerful men, those of ample means, be summoned to the Senate, and that Lalaing's opinion be read out to them without any pretence of favour or hatred. Upon this, the common people too were called into the church by the sounding of the bell, to hear the envoys' report in private, and four men were chosen from the whole multitude who, together with the Senate, should find a remedy for calming the civil unrest. But a bitter religious discord, as in most places was hostile to public tranquillity, overturned every plan for concord with the onslaught of opinions. For the Senate, the commons having been stirred up and the Papists being unruly, was secretly imploring a garrison to check the disturbances, and in giving a hostage or providing the security it had earlier been more ready to promise, it was shaping its compliance to the prefect's command. The Papists, on the other hand, vehement in feeling, were indignant that hostages were demanded and security prescribed by the prefect, in whose power it was not to add soldiers and cohorts of needy mercenaries to the civil garrison of their own accord, in the insolent licence of the times. Clearly they were looking to what customs the military oaths were held by, and how heavily Noviolandis weighed on the country people, and the security demanded from an armed man. Therefore it was decreed that, the security being rejected, the envoys should be sent back to Lalaing and should settle terms with him on fair conditions.

units.la: Istæ erant; Ut claves portarum non centurio aut præsidium, sed Ma-gistratus asservaret. Urbis custodia non penes solum præsidiarium militem, sed & civem foret. Præsidium commeatum & as ex seipso haberet, civi etiam ex causâ religionis sub pœnâ ruptæ pacis molestiam non crearet. Pacem concor-diamque cum eo coleret.
units.tr: These were the conditions: that the keys of the gates should be kept not by the captain or the garrison but by the magistrates; that the guard of the city should belong not to the garrison soldiers alone but also to the citizens; that the garrison should have its own supplies and pay; and that it should not cause trouble to a citizen even on account of religion, under penalty of breaking the peace; and that it should cultivate peace and concord with the city.

units.la: Quibus perscriptis Joannes Romckenius cum Petro Sixtino ad Lalai-nium amandati communicatoque cum Deputatis, quorum conventus Leo-vardiæ tum habebatur, legationis suæ arcano immutare libellos, ac re-dire Bolsuerdiam jussi. Ijs namque obtulerant. Ut Lalainio centurionem civium praesidio praeficiendi potestas esset, quâ instrui Lalainium dubijs temporibus illi nolebant, qui futurorum sagaces prima provinciae rectoris facta atque consilia ex posterioribus interpretabantur. Posse scilicet Praefectum, qui dominantium mos suâ licentiâ & oblato civium beneficio male usum peregrinum civicae cohorti praeficere, & qui Hispanicarum partium clandestinâ professione urbi atque provinciae vim, aut saltem periculum creet. Neque enim nimis fidendum mobili ex aetate ingenio, quam etsi inter praeclarae indolis exempla cum incremento famae Lalainius transegisset, ita metui posse, ne optimos juventae mores virilibus annis corrumpat permissusque fortunae, cujus magnam in dominantes & expugnandae virtuti imperium sit, naturam exuat veteris gloriae & suae legis oblitam. Prospectum satis esse foederatorum Ordinum curâ Frisicarum civitatum tranquillitati, qui amovendae militum insolentiae civilia quadringentorum armatorum praesidia Frisiorum oppidis indulsissent. Sic Leovardiae, sic Franequerae securitatem suam itare, nec aliud superesse, quam ut Bolsuerdiorum armati & sacramentum provinciae dicant & ex more recenseantur. Itaque Douwo Sixma è Collegio Deputatorum Bolsuerdiam profectus civicam cohortem recensuit, dicendoque sacramento ex praescriptâ formulâ obligavit.
units.tr: When these terms had been drawn up, John Romckenius, together with Peter Sixtinus, was sent to Lalaing. After conferring with the deputies, whose assembly was then being held at Leeuwarden, they were ordered to alter the little papers of their embassy's secret instructions and return to Bolsward. For they had proposed that Lalaing should have the power to set a captain over the civic garrison, a power which they were unwilling to give Lalaing in uncertain times, since they were men shrewd about the future who judged the first acts and plans of the province's governor by their later results. Of course the governor could set over the civic cohort a foreigner who, abusing the custom of rulers by his licence and the favour offered by the citizens, would, by secretly professing the Spanish cause, create violence, or at least danger, for the city and the province. For one should not trust too much to the fickle nature of youth. Although Lalaing had passed through his youth among examples of a brilliant disposition and with growing fame, it could still be feared that in manly years it would corrupt the best morals of youth, and, given free rein to fortune, whose power over rulers and over the conquest of virtue is great, it would cast off its nature, forgetting its old glory and its own law. The General States had taken enough care for the tranquillity of the Frisian cities, since, to remove the insolence of soldiers, they had granted civic garrisons of four hundred armed men to the Frisian towns. Thus Leeuwarden and thus Franeker had secured their safety, and nothing remained but that the armed men of Bolsward take the oath to the province and be mustered in the customary way. Therefore Douwo Sixma, who had set out for Bolsward from the college of deputies, mustered the civic cohort and bound them by the oath in the prescribed form.

units.la: Eâ continebatur; Ut delecti custodiae urbis Regi & simul populo oppidano pro more sacramentum dicerent, Regemque ut hereditarium principem & Dominum, tum Ordines generales & foederatos ut superiores agnoscerent. Matthiam Archiducem pro regio per Belgicam Gubernatore, Aurantium Principem Archiducis vicario, Lalainium pro Frisijs praefecto, Magistratum urbis pro legitimo haberent, decretisque eorum è formulâ Gandavensis Ultrajectinique foederis parerent. Disciplinae militaribus per Belgicam legibus subessent. Inconsulto Magistratu oppidano nihil agerent.
units.tr: The oath contained this: that the chosen men of the city guard should take the customary oath to the King and at the same time to the town's people, and should acknowledge the King as hereditary prince and lord, then the General States and the confederated States as superiors. They should hold Archduke Matthias as governor of Belgium in the King's place, the Prince of Orange as the Archduke's vicar, Lalaing as governor for the Frisians, and the city magistracy as lawful, and should obey their decrees according to the form of the Ghent and Utrecht union. They should be subject to the military laws of Belgium. They should do nothing without the consent of the town magistracy.

units.la: Tum viritim aes promissum censorque militaris Franequeram & deïn Leovardiam recessit. Itaque Vlietij cohors Pingumi & per vicinos agros collocata modoque in Ilstanos, modo Worcumios se spargens Bolsuerdiâ urbe prohibita est.
units.tr: Then the promised money was paid out man by man, and the military commissioner withdrew to Franeker and from there to Leeuwarden. So Vlietius's cohort was quartered at Pingjum and in the neighbouring fields, and, now scattering among the men of Ilst and now among those of Workum, was barred from the city of Bolsward.

units.la: Reperio in archivis edictum Religionis paci observandae per Frisios tum vulgatum, cautumque esse ne cui ex causâ divini cultus vis atque injuriâ fieret. Eorum quoque qui foris in provinciam advenirent, ratio haberetur, exulumque & patriae desertorum bona annuique reditus pignori essent. Mox Ordinum generalium litterae pro obtinendâ Matthiae Gubernatoris annuâ pensione in Frisios missae, quos, sicut & foederatos, eidem in tempore praestandae provinciarum conventio obligaverat. Quibus Matthiae quoque Gubernatoris seorsim additae & oneratam alieno aere domum, & tarda, etiam in publicis, consilia querebantur. Pericula scilicet ob ocultos versari, à quibus si patriam, si familiam, si uxores atque liberos redimi Frisij velint, maturè subveniendum aerario, ex quo ipsae fortunae suae levamentum & simul resp. sensura sit.
units.tr: I find in the archives that an edict for observing the peace of religion was then published among the Frisians, and it was provided that no one should suffer violence or injury on account of divine worship. Account was also to be taken of those who came into the province from abroad, and the goods and annual revenues of exiles and of those who had deserted their fatherland were to be held as security. Soon after came letters of the General States sent to the Frisians to secure the annual pension of Governor Matthias, which the convention of the provinces had obliged them, like the confederates, to pay on time. To these letters were added separate ones from Governor Matthias himself, who complained that the house was burdened with debt and that counsels, even in public affairs, were slow. Dangers, of course, lay hidden from secret enemies, and if the Frisians wished to redeem their fatherland, their families, their wives and children from these dangers, the treasury must be aided promptly. From this their own fortunes would be relieved, and at the same time the commonwealth would feel the benefit.

units.la: Invenio in archivorum actis Brabantiam, nam ita series habet, solvendis 1767 5. cum quadrante aureis, Geldriam 6548. Flandriam 23568. Artesiam 3926. octodecim stufferis, Hannoniam totidem, Valencenas cIↄ. Iↄ. 6 5 4. decem sestertijs, Lillam, Duacum & Orchias 2 9 4 5. quatuor sestertijs, Tornacum 2 6 1. duodecim sestertijs, Tornesios 4 9 0. octodecim sestertijs, Machlinienses 5 3 5. Hollandiam, 8 0 8 7. Zelandiam 6 1 2 ●Ultrajectum 1 0 0 0 5. Frisiam 3 0 1 5. Trans-Isulaniam 1 4 0 0 6. Omlandiam 8 0 4. Dentiam 7 0 3. Groningam 1 6 0 0 8. aureis adimplendae Archiducis pensioni se obligasse. Tum de mittendis Coloniam ad Arschotanum caeterosque pacis sanciendae Legatos, mille & quingentis aureis repetitum, & ut Francisco Martino Stellae Roblesianis temporibus Frisiae liberatori carcerem & tormenta passo ducentos Carolaeos ex aerario Pauli Gellij leniendis infirmi corporis lacerationibus & in praemium clarissimi facinoris assignarent.
units.tr: I find in the archive records that Brabant (for so the list runs) bound itself to pay in gold toward the Archduke's pension: 1767 and a quarter; Gelderland 6548; Flanders 23568; Artois 3926 and eighteen stuivers; Hainault as much; Valenciennes 1500, 1000, 654; Lille, Douai and Orchies 2945 and four stuivers; Tournai 261 and twelve stuivers; Tournesis 490 and eighteen stuivers; Mechlin 535; Holland 8087; Zeeland 612; Utrecht 10005; Friesland 3015; Transisulania 14006; Omlanden 804; Drenthe 703; Groningen 16008. Then, concerning the sending of envoys to Cologne to Arschot and the others to sanction the peace, a payment of fifteen hundred gold was demanded back. And they assigned two hundred carolus from the treasury of Paul Gellius, both to ease the lacerations of the weak body of Francis Martin Stella, who had suffered imprisonment and torture in the time of Robles and was the liberator of Friesland, and as a reward for his most famous deed.

units.la: Igitur sole Capricorni signum ingresso, quod bruma glaciem transducendis in Frisiam copijs promitteret, exulans nobilitas de suscipiendâ in patriam hostili expeditione cogitavit, novumque delectum circa Rhenum & per Colonienfium agros habitum maturandis rebus in Geldriae finibus conduxit. Sed aeris mutatione primum anni frigus subortis imbribus solutum consilio obstitit, mollitâque paludum uligine, quae gelu induruerat, impedita itinera fecit. Unde mittendi in Frisiam auxilij Ordinibus generalibus & simul foederatis Ultrajectinis opportunitas data, hostiumque damno ac morae enata tempestas, Frisiorum securitati cessit.
units.tr: So when the sun had entered the sign of Capricorn, and the winter promised that the troops could be led into Friesland over the ice, the exiled nobility began to consider undertaking a hostile expedition into their homeland. They gathered a fresh levy near the Rhine and through the fields of Cologne, and they hastened to bring their plans to completion within the borders of Gelderland. But first, a change in the air, with the cold of the new year dissolved by showers, thwarted the plan; and the softening of the marsh moisture, which had hardened under frost, made the roads impassable. Thus the States-General were given an opportunity to send auxiliary troops to Friesland, and the storm that arose, to the loss and delay of the enemy, yielded to the safety of the Frisians.

units.la: Aysma scribit xii. Kal. Ian. decretum Antverpiae pro mittendis in Frisiam auxiliarijs copijs scriptum, foederatorumque Legatis qui Ultrajecto advenerant approbatum, metum imminentis periculi amovisse. Itaque Doco Martna ex Hollandiâ celerrimo itinere in Frisiam & mox Drentiam profectus, Lalainium de singulis docuit, auxilijque removendis hostium copijs certum esse jussit.
units.tr: Aysma writes that on 19 December a decree was drawn up at Antwerp concerning the sending of auxiliary troops into Friesland, and that, once approved by the envoys of the allies who had arrived at Utrecht, it removed the fear of impending danger. Accordingly, Doco Martna hurried from Holland into Friesland and soon afterwards into Drenthe, informed Lalaing of each matter, and ordered that the enemy's forces be removed with certainty as an aid.

units.la: Reliquae, quae per Transf-Isulaniae, Drentiae ac Tubantum fines nullo stipendio aut disciplinâ oberrabant, mitioribus consilijs pacatae, delegatis Scipione Meckama viro nobili & Abelo Franckena doctrinae egregio, qui cum Curtspacchio socijsque de stipendiorum residuis paticiserentur. Caeterum equorum pabulo per omne confinium attrito, cum nec alimenta immodesto & perdendis frugibus jam ante intento, militi suppeterent, Curtspacchius in superiora militem duxit, isq; nullo aere è Frisiâ accepto Curtspacchij, quae mox secuta est, morte in Germaniam recessit. Cl. Franckena notat id exeunte Decembri factum seq; cum collega legationis inritum Leovardiam redijsse. Ita, totum annum aut domestica dissensio, aut ex dubiâ pace, aut provinciarum defectione, aut insolentia militum ictum Ultrajecti foedus extraxit.
units.tr: The remaining troops, which wandered without pay or discipline through the territories of Transisselania, Drenthe and the Tubantes, were calmed by milder counsels, with Scipio Meckama, a nobleman, and Abel Franckena, a man distinguished in learning, appointed as delegates to negotiate with Curtspacchius and his associates concerning the arrears of pay. However, since the fodder for the horses had been used up throughout the whole neighbourhood, and the soldiers had no provisions, the soldiers already being bent on wasteful plundering of the crops, Curtspacchius led the soldiers further inland; and they withdrew into Germany without receiving any money from Friesland, soon after Curtspacchius' death. The learned Franckena notes that this happened at the end of December, and that he and his colleague returned to Leeuwarden with the embassy having achieved nothing. Thus the whole year was spent in domestic dissension, or an uncertain peace, or the defection of the provinces, or the insolence of the soldiers, which delayed the Treaty of Utrecht.

units.la: Finis Libri Quinti.
units.tr: End of Book Five.

units.la: P. WINSEMI Historiarum LIBER SEXTUS.
units.tr: The Sixth Book of P. Winsemius's Histories

units.la: Oloniensi pace aut ruptâ aut saltem exitu suspecta, quod Alexander Farnesius per provincias regias & earum confinia, magno armorum apparatu occuparetur, Gulielmum Aurantium suæ quoque curæ exagitavere, quæ eo magis augebantur, quod Philippi gratiæ & per Hannoniam Artesiamque conceptæ pacis blandimentum florem Belgicæ nobilitatis à provinciarum fœderibus & continuandâ indies fide alienaret. Cui & hoc accedebat, quod bellum, velut soluto imperij metu laxiore disciplinâ à partibus Ordinum fluitaret, exque inopiâ militaris stipendij languidum acriore exercitus licentiâ intenderetur. Itaque agris passim vastatis urbium quoque direptiones formidabantur, & ne militum præsidia egestate æris sacramenti oblita, oppida & castella dedendo, dissolutos mores inopiâ velarent.
units.tr: The Ghent peace had either been broken or at least its outcome was in doubt, since Alexander Farnese was busy throughout the royal provinces and their borders with a large military force. William of Orange was also troubled by these developments, and his concern grew all the more because Philip's courtesies, and the peace offered through Hainault and Artois, were designed to draw the flower of Belgian nobility away from the provincial alliances and from the loyalty that was daily being kept. In addition, the war, with the fear of imperial authority removed, was drifting into looser discipline on the side of the States. Because the soldiers were unpaid, the army's licence grew fiercer and its operations more sluggish. Accordingly, the countryside was laid waste on every side, and the sacking of towns was also feared. The garrisons, forgetting their oath for want of pay, might surrender their towns and fortresses and cover their lax morals with their poverty.

units.la: Erant quoque qui dubiam Præfectorum nobilitatisque fidem tractu-ram, in declivia populum metuerent & ut mobilis multitudo ex suorum Ducum ingenio, ostentatione pacis & aulicis potentum artibus, facili ad talia servitio, circumveniretur. Quare pro recensendo fœderato exercitu pro formandis castris & commeatu procurando, pro muniendis oppidis, pro adornandâ præsidiariâ classe & instruendo ærarij omniumque rerum ordine postulata ab Aurantio in Frisiam missa, haud ignaro, quam per istam provinciam exulum suorum armis & conspirationibus obnoxiam, suum quoque virus specie pacis invertendis rebus Farnesij vafrities sparsisset. Neque cæteras, etsi aliud simuletur, periculi immunes esse. Quippe hostem verè proxumo exercitum foras educturum, quem nec brumæ tempus, etsi tempestatibus aut frigore asperum, intra præsidia & modestiam contineat. Depasci agros & omnem commeatum, quo absumpto frumento civitates annonâ destitutæ sustinendis obsidionibus impares fiant, victuque extenuato præsidiorum robur elanguescat. Adhæc auxilia ex intestinis Galliæ motibus dubia esse, quæ per Germaniam & ad Rhenum ab hostibus parentur, irruptura haud dubiè in provincias, nisi equestribus copijs Ordinum infirmitas præjuvetur.
units.tr: There were also those who feared that the loyalty of the commanders and nobles was doubtful, that the people would slide into decline, and that the fickle crowd, given to following its own leaders, would be won over by the display of peace and the courtly arts of the powerful, and so easily enslaved to such things. Hence Orange sent to Friesland the demands he had made: the review of the allied army, the forming of camps, the provisioning of supplies, the fortifying of towns, the equipping of a garrison fleet, and the ordering of the treasury and of all affairs. He was not unaware that Farnese's cunning, under the appearance of peace, had scattered its own poison through that province, which was exposed to the arms and conspiracies of his exiles, in order to overturn affairs. Nor were the other provinces free from danger, however they might pretend otherwise. The enemy would certainly lead his army out of its quarters close at hand, and neither the winter season, harsh with storms and frost, would keep it within the garrisons and good order. It would graze the fields and consume every supply; once the grain was used up, the cities, deprived of provisions, would be unequal to sustaining sieges, and with food reduced the strength of the garrisons would grow feeble. Besides, the aid from the internal disturbances in France was uncertain; and the help that the enemy was preparing through Germany and along the Rhine would undoubtedly break into the provinces, unless the weakness of the States were supported by cavalry forces.

units.la: CIɔ. Iɔ. LXXXX. Agendum esse cum Suartsenburgio & Hohenloo Rom. Imperij Comitibus ut turmas equitum colligant, ijq; ad quatuor mille pedestribus duodecim copiarum millibus junçti exercitum constituant, removendis hostibus parem. Et celerrimi quidem temporis rationem in instituendis delectibus habendam provectâ & adultâ hyeme, quæ conducendis copijs opportuna esse queat. Se monere Ordines, ut maturè deliberent, qui paratus sit animum atque auxilia offerre, cum innocentiæ suæ obtestatione, si fortunæ ex socordiâ adversitas provincias affligat. De Andino jam antè monuerat, eï Belgicæ principatum deferendum, Regis filio & fratri & qui Elisabetham Angliæ reginam principali matrimonio destinaret. Cui rei Hesselus Aysma Frisiorum legatus, datis Antverpiâ ix. Kal. Ian. litteris fidem fecerat, Condæumque in Galliæ finibus copias conducentem tacitâ infœlicis matrimonij suspicione, Casimiri quoque auxilia inuandis per Galliam Protestantibus implorasse. Cæterum Aurantij consilium æmulatio, ut tum ferè aut incuria neglexerat.
units.tr: In 1590: it was to be arranged with Schwarzenburg and Hohenlohe, counts of the Holy Roman Empire, that they should gather troops of horse, and that these, joined with about four thousand foot to twelve thousand of the forces, should form an army equal to driving off the enemy. Moreover, the most rapid possible timing should be observed in raising levies, although the winter was far advanced and mature, which might still be suitable for bringing up the troops. He advised the States to deliberate promptly, and to offer the mind and aid of a man who was ready, calling upon the innocence of his own conduct, if adversity through the sloth of fortune should afflict the provinces. He had already warned earlier about Anjou: the leadership of the Netherlands was to be handed to him, the brother and son of the king, who was destined for a principal marriage with Elizabeth, queen of England. Hessel Aysma, envoy of the Frisians, had given assurance of this matter in letters written at Antwerp on the ninth day before the Kalends of January. He also reported that Condé was gathering troops on the borders of France, and, with a silent suspicion of an unhappy marriage, had sought from Casimir auxiliaries to help the Protestants in France. Yet Orange's plan had been neglected, as was then almost always the case, either through carelessness or through rivalry.

units.la: Itaq; repetitâ Id. Ian. consultatione, de instituendo status publici Concilio proposuit & ut illius confessus imperium gerendis cum autoritate rebus intenderetur. Ejus scilicet defectu res tam pacis quam belli transversim actas postquam earum opportunitatem singularum provinciarum incuriâ aut ignaviâ subvertisset. Ita privata curando publica in discrimen adducta, mandatorumque defectu aut per longas relationes civitatum obsidia & expugnationes protractas. Intra defensionis suæ terminos quamque provinciarum, velut nullâ fœderis imagine, stetisse, quod integrum & florens facere res secundæ potuissent, si unius Senatus aut summi Concilij autoritas privatorum socordiæ aut ignaviæ subvenisset. Eâ solâ extenuari provinciarum urbiumque præsidiâ, exercitum educi in hostem potuisse, quem impunè per agros & obvia grassantem privatæ securitatis cupiditas aut dulcedo spectasset. Ac contra & ponenda in hostico afligendis agris castra fuisse, & edendum generosæ virtutis exemplum, quod externas principum gentiumque societates conciliare Ordinibus & incutere hosti metum potuisseт, contusione fœderatarum rerum superbo. Et illi quoque sua impedimenta ad victoriam obstare. Quippe præter æris & commeatuum inopiam seditiosas legiones imperia Ducum aspernari, spretâque disciplinæ lege rapto & cum invidiâ gentium sustineri. Quæ mala ne clarissimi & bene cæpti fœderis fortunam turbent, supremum Concilium deligendum, quod & rem Nummariam & tributa à provincijs decreta exequi & cum imperio exercitui rebusque provinciarum præsit. Satis scilicet condonatum regis dominationi, qui cum pacem non nisi inhonestam largiri Belgicæ velit, omnè in bello præsidium esse. Cui gerendo cum provinciæ pares non habeantur, sollicitandos exteros & inter eos Andinum, qui jure principis provincias regat & qui Galliarum auxilijs subjutus infestare agros possit Hannoniæ & Artesiæ ascriptos. Sed & ipsum quoque Andinum sacramento innectendum, ut æquo imperio populum habeat, & ut assertis provinciarum legibus atque immunitatibus pacem religioni procuret.
units.tr: Therefore, after the consultation was renewed on the Ides of January, he proposed the establishment of a council of the state, so that its authority might be directed with power to carry on affairs. This was plainly because, without such a council, affairs of both peace and war had been managed at cross purposes, and through the carelessness or sloth of individual provinces their proper opportunities had been destroyed. Thus, while private matters were attended to, public affairs were brought into peril; and sieges and assaults on towns were dragged out through the lack of orders and long reports. Each province had stood within the limits of its own defence, as though there were no image of a federation at all; yet, if the authority of a single senate or a supreme council had come to the aid of private sloth and idleness, prosperous affairs could have made the whole intact and flourishing. By that alone, the garrisons of provinces and cities could have been strengthened, and an army could have been led out against the enemy, who was ravaging the fields and whatever lay in his way with impunity, while the desire for private security or its sweetness looked on. On the contrary, camps should have been pitched in the enemy's country to harass his fields, and an example of noble courage should have been given, which could have won over foreign alliances of princes and peoples for the States and struck fear into the enemy, while the proud joined forces were crushed. Their own hindrances also stood in the way of victory. For, apart from the lack of money and supplies, the mutinous legions scorned the commands of their leaders; and, the rule of discipline being disregarded, they sustained themselves by plunder and under the hatred of the nations. So that these evils might not disturb the fortune of a most famous and well-begun alliance, a supreme council was to be chosen, which would both carry out the financial business and the taxes decreed by the provinces, and would have command over the army and the affairs of the provinces. It was plainly granted enough to the king's dominion, since, although he wished to bestow on the Netherlands no peace except a dishonourable one, the whole defence lay in war. Since the provinces were not thought equal to conducting that war, foreigners were to be solicited, and among them Anjou, who should rule the provinces by right of a prince and who, aided by French forces, could harass the lands enrolled in Hainault and Artois. Anjou himself was also to be bound by oath, so that he might govern the people with an even-handed rule, and that, by upholding the laws and immunities of the provinces, he might secure peace for religion.

units.la: Quæ conditiones si Philippo regi offerantur, fore, præter provincias ejus gratiam amplexas, quæ in eum studijs certent & quidem in spem reregiæ largitionis & magnarum dignitatum, quarum cupido & in patriam fidei obstet & permulcere plures posset alieno exemplo corruptos. Adhæc Philippum Regem potentiâ gravem aut nimium fore, neque sperari aliud posse, quam ut Portugallici regni accessione & civitatum Belgicæ præsidijs Andino validior, vestigia veteris imperij legat. Sive vitio ingenij (quod ex se ferox & immane præclari annalium scriptores tradxere) sive vindictæ cupidine, quæ placari iram sanguine arderet, certè metuendam esse illius dominationem, qui & ignoti orbis exemplis per Italiam & infoelicem Belgicam immanissimum furorem adjecisset. Eum fore, qui nec pactis gentium, nec legibus foederum stare velit aut debeat, ita formato regnandi artificio ut ex Pontificum disciplinâ ad perfidiam instruatur principis severi ingenium in rebelles subditos animadversurum. Quibus fidem servare ne naturæ lege is quidem debeat, quem omnibus licentia regni exsolverit. Id Cunæri Episcopi, id aliorum scriptis evulgatum & esse tam Romanæ Sedi, quam Inquisitioni per Hispaniam præfectos, qui exuere regem ferociam animi nolint, & clementiâ mollire ingenium consuetudine sæviendi exercitum. Simulatione ac dolo potentum imperia stare, neque alijs artibus Joannem Austriacum egisse, certa dominationi auspicia & fundamenta orsum, si tectius simulavisset.
units.tr: If these conditions were offered to King Philip, it would happen that, apart from the provinces embracing his favour and vying with one another in zeal toward him, hopes of royal bounty and great dignities would follow; and the desire for these would stand in the way of loyalty to the fatherland and could win over many who had been corrupted by another's example. Besides, King Philip would be either too heavy or too powerful in dominion, and nothing else could be hoped for than that, strengthened by the addition of the kingdom of Portugal and by the garrisons of the Belgian cities, he would become stronger than Anjou and would tread the traces of the old empire. Whether through a fault of temperament (which the famous writers of the annals have said was fierce and savage by nature) or through a desire for vengeance, which burned to appease its anger with blood, certainly his dominion was to be feared, since he had added, by the examples of an unknown world, the most monstrous frenzy throughout Italy and unhappy Belgium. He would be a man who would neither stand by nor be bound to the pacts of nations or the laws of treaties; his method of ruling was so shaped that, instructed in perfidy by the discipline of the Pontiffs, he would punish rebellious subjects with the temper of a severe prince. He ought not, by the law of nature, to keep faith with those whom the licence of his kingdom had released from all obligations. Bishop Cunerus and others had made this public in their writings, and it was true of those set over Spain by the Roman See as well as by the Inquisition, who did not wish the king to lay aside his fierceness of spirit, and who by the habit of cruelty kept his army from softening its disposition by mercy. The rule of the powerful stands by pretence and deceit, and John of Austria had acted by no other arts; certain auspices and foundations of dominion had been laid, had he simulated more discreetly.

units.la: Econtra Andinum minus ex viribus aut externâ societate suspectum, foelicius provincias administraturum, facturumque haud dubiè ut fraterni regni in tolerandâ utraque religione moribus suum principatum afformet. Ita scilicet ditiones ejus, ita aulam, ita comitatum instrui, ut ex ea odia non sint, & ne sanguine polluantur cogendis hominum coetibus & colendo numini reperta. Ad ingenium quod attineret, illud lene & rectoris patiens in ipsis Galliæ suæ furoribus neque cæde aut intestino bello se pavisse, quod ex religione, ut fere solet, in fratris Henrici regno natum firmâ & solidâ pace egregius arbiter clausisset. Sed dubiam, si talis forte sit, indolem pactis ac legibus coercendam, ne exorbitare juvenile ingenium posset, mobiles spiritus ex solo Hispani odio & suorum caritate repressurum. Ita fore ut Hispani nec arma, nec commeatum è Galliâ habituri sint, & ut fratre Andino in principem Belgicæ evecto rex Henricus Philippum hostem proclamet, quasi Gallicæ Belgarum societati infensum. Hannoniam quoque & Artesiam ad fœdus Ordinum ex Gallico metu rediturac, neque timeri posse, ut Valonum partes Andinus eligat, qui Ordinum profiteretur. Sic Andinum Gandavense fœdus, Hispanorum invidiæ ictum, quod nec Elisabetha Anglica renuat, facile approbaturum, & quæ ipsa quoque; malit Andinum à cujus amoribus aliena non sit, insulæ suæ vicinum, quam Philippum regem esse, occupatâ Portugalliâ tantis terrarum spatijs & omni Oceano imperitantem.
units.tr: On the contrary, Anjou, being less suspect because of his forces or foreign alliances, would govern the provinces more happily, and would undoubtedly bring it about that his principality took the form of his brother's kingdom, in tolerating both religions by its customs. Thus, it was said, his dominions, his court, and his retinue would be so arranged that hatred would not arise from them, and so that they would not be polluted with blood by compelling people into assemblies and by the worship of the deity that had been discovered. As to his character, it was mild and submissive to a ruler; even amid the furies of France itself he had not fed on slaughter or civil war, and he had, as an excellent arbiter, closed with a firm and solid peace the disorders that, as usually happens, had arisen from religion in the kingdom of his brother Henry.
