But if his disposition, whatever it might be, was doubtful, it would have to be restrained by pacts and laws, lest his youthful temper should be able to run beyond bounds; and, by hatred of the Spaniard alone and by love for his own people, he would curb his restless spirits. So it would happen that the Spaniards would have neither arms nor supplies from France; and, with Anjou raised to be prince of the Netherlands, King Henry would proclaim Philip an enemy, as though he were hostile to the French alliance with the Belgians. Hainault and Artois would also return to the alliance of the States out of fear of France; nor could it be feared that Anjou would choose the Walloon party, since he professed himself a champion of the States. Thus the Ghent alliance, struck by the Spaniards' hatred, would readily be approved by Anjou, and, as Elizabeth of England would not refuse it either, he would prefer Anjou, to whose loves she was not indifferent, as a neighbour to her island, rather than King Philip, who, having seized Portugal, ruled over such wide lands and the whole ocean.

units.la: Quæ speciosè ab Aurantio proposita Ordinum animos diu sollicitos & suspensos in tantâ consultantium varietate habuerunt.
units.tr: These things, speciously put forward by Orange, kept the minds of the States, long anxious and unsettled amid such a variety of counsels, in suspense.

units.la: Aysma scribit pacis actionem Coloniæ hoc tempore finitam, etsi petente Cæsare, ut per mandatarios Ordinum & Suartsenburgium Imperij Oratorem, etiam absente Philippi Legato, prolongaretur. Ordinum quoque mandatarios, velut ad hoc non instructos, id Cæsari re-cucusasse, evulgatà publicæ vocis fide, Regem firmandis viribus actionem trahere, quo coacta omni manu validior tripartito aut quadripartito exercitu impulsis provinciarum rebus certum exitium adferret. Cæterum infida regiæ potentiæ documenta fortuna tum confundebat. Quippe vocatis à Philippo ad arma socijs aut externis gentibus cœlum quoque & sydera obstitere, quæ malignis aspectibus & influentijs efferata venenato ac pestilenti habitu singulos per exercitus cœleste virus effundebant. Itaque aëre impuro etiam intacta pesti corpora suis quoque malis afficiebantur, unico ferocissimæ luis & latentis vitij remedio, ut, quod olim retinendis in fide militaribus copijs arte Ducum repertum erat, longis terrarum spatijs discreti exercitus ad sistendam vitandamque intemperie mconverterent. Unde languidæ & semiægræ gentes, velut alibi salubre cœlum tracturæ, per diversa locorum sparsæ diffluentes fugâ exercitus odio Philippi extenuavere. Tum Billianæ aut Roblesij copiæ in Frisiam destinatæ, quæ mille ducentos milites numerabant, armorum & pecuniæ inopes, suo quoq; fato consumptæ, indignante Farnesio belli apparatum tantâ famâ & de perfugarum exulumque consilio susceptum, nullo aut lento successu evanescere.
units.tr: Aysma writes that the negotiation for peace at Cologne was ended at this time, although the Emperor asked that it be extended, through the States' deputies and Suartsenburg, the Imperial envoy, even in the absence of Philip's legate. He writes that the States' deputies, as if not instructed for this, refused the Emperor's request, and it was publicly reported that the King was dragging out the negotiation to strengthen his forces, so that, with a larger army gathered, he might bring certain ruin upon the affairs of the provinces with a three- or four-fold army. Meanwhile fortune then confounded the proofs of royal power's faithlessness. For when Philip called allies or foreign peoples to arms, heaven too and the stars opposed him. Made fierce by malign aspects and influences, they poured a heavenly poison, venomous and pestilential in character, upon individual armies. Thus, in the impure air, even bodies untouched by plague were afflicted by their own ills. The only remedy for this fierce and hidden disease was the one that the skill of commanders had once devised for keeping soldiers loyal: the divided armies were dispersed over long stretches of land, to avoid and escape the intemperate air. Whence weakened and half-sick peoples, as if about to draw healthy air elsewhere, scattered through various places and dissolved; the flight of the army, out of hatred for Philip, wore down his cause. Then the troops of Billian or Robles, destined for Friesland, numbering 1,200 soldiers, lacking arms and money, were consumed by their own fate too. Farnese was indignant, and the preparation for war, undertaken with such fame and on the counsel of refugees and exiles, faded away with little or no success.

units.la: Sunt qui tradant, unum è primarijs faciendæ in Frisiam expeditionis autoribus ægritudine animi Coloniæ extinctum, quod Farnesij spem & simul suam elusis magnarum rerum desiderijs non implevisset.
units.tr: Some relate that one of the chief promoters of the expedition into Friesland died at Cologne from mental distress, because his hopes of Farnese, and at the same time his own desires for great achievements, had been mocked and not fulfilled.

units.la: Albada in litteris prid. Kal. Jan. Coloniâ datis scribit copias faciendæ in Frisiam expeditioni ab exulibus conscriptas dissipatas aut evocatas ad Farnesium tum fuisse, eundemque Hispanos pedites aut Italorum equitatum ne exulum copijs se jungerent vetuisse. Julium quoq; Dekamam ex catharri fluxione repentinâ morte magna suorum sociorum consternatione sublatum, diemque ab eo lustrandis copijs dictum esserendo funeri obvenisse.
units.tr: Albada, in a letter dated Cologne, 31 December, writes that the troops raised by the exiles for the expedition into Friesland were then either dispersed or called away to Farnese, and that Farnese had forbidden the Spanish infantry or the Italian cavalry to join the exiles' forces. He also writes that Julius Dekama was carried off by sudden death from a catarrhal flux, to the great consternation of his comrades, and that the day he had set for reviewing the troops fell on his funeral.

units.la: Mox edicto de re Nummariâ Antverpiæ scripto, & per Hollandiam Zelandiamq; inconsultis socijs evulgato lenis inter Ordines foederatos & Hollandiæ dissensio orta, petentibus foederatis ut Antverpiæ per Geldros, Hollandos, Zelandos sine speciali mandato decreta nummaria lex rescinderetur, suoq; consessui & provinciarum arbitrijs relinqueretur scribendæ legis usurpatio. Quod quanquam Hollandi datis ad foederatos 8. Jan. litteris nullo foederis præjudicio aut despectu factum excusarent, ita Frisiorum arbitrijs tam emendatio legis quam per provinciam publicatio quoque permissa, tacitâ tamen violati foederis increpatione, quod æris ac monetæ rationem suæ dispositioni reservaverat. Ita primam quoque Ultrajectini foederis infantiam ex æmulatione usurpatæ autoritatis dissensio invasit, quæ Coloniensi pace, velut omnium rerum communi vinculo, abruptâ per universas provincias & ipsam præfertim Frisiam occultis fomentis nutriebatur.
units.tr: Soon afterwards an edict on monetary affairs, written at Antwerp and published throughout Holland and Zeeland without consulting the allies, caused a mild dissension between the United Orders and Holland. The allies asked that the monetary decree made at Antwerp by Gelderland, Holland and Zeeland without special mandate be rescinded, and that the right to write the law be left to their own assembly and to the judgment of the provinces. Holland, by letters to the allies dated 8 January, excused the matter as done without prejudice to or contempt of the covenant. Friesland likewise permitted the amendment of the law and its publication throughout the province by its own judgment, yet with a silent reproach for violating the covenant, which had reserved the regulation of money and coinage to its own disposition. Thus dissension, born of rivalry over usurped authority, invaded even the first infancy of the Union of Utrecht. With the Peace of Cologne broken, the common bond of all affairs, this dissension was nourished by secret encouragement throughout all the provinces, and especially in Friesland.

units.la: Quippe Lalainium, ut ante memoravi, Groningæ agentem, munitione loci ac valentis præsidij superbum Bolsuerdij offenderant, quod autoratâ civicâ Vlietij & Bongæ cohortes, etsi Ordinum ac suo sacramento innexas urbis custodiâ prohibuissent. Itaq; Legatos eorum Non. Jan. Groningam, sollicitandis præsidiorum immunitatibus progressos, diu accessu & colloquio arcuit, ægrèque & cum difficultate in secretum admissos & praesidium militare deprecaturos vix audiri fecit. violatam praefecti authoritatem prolixè criminatus civicam cohortem extemplo dimitti, Vlietijque milites recipi iure potestatis & imperij jussit, obsidesque sex testandae in se fidei ocyus imperavit.
units.tr: Indeed Lalaing, as I mentioned before, while acting at Groningen, had offended Bolsward, proud of the strength of its position and garrison, because the civic cohorts of Vliet and Bonga, though bound by oath to the Orders and to him, had forbidden access to the city's guard. So on 5 January he refused for a long time to admit their envoys, who had come to Groningen to seek immunities for the garrisons. Admitting them in secret only with difficulty and reluctance, he barely let them be heard when they begged for a military garrison. Lavishly accusing them of violating the prefect's authority, he ordered at once that the civic cohort be dismissed and the soldiers of Vliet received by right of his power and command, and he quickly demanded six hostages as a guarantee of their fidelity to him.

units.la: Quo decreto Bolsuerdiam per Legatos perlato coactus in Curia Senatus de mittendo ad Deputatos Ordinum Legato deliberavit, signoq; majoris campanae dato, concilium juratum cum populi delectis in Curiam evocari fecit. Ibi habita consultatione, Theodorum Occonium Consulem Leovardiam cum mandato misit, introspiciendis Ordinum voluntatibus, quae à Lalainij consilijs clam averse civicam cohortem praesidio & in fide retineri tutandae urbi demandabant. Econtra Pontificij ut nuper ejus consilijs adversi, ita tum per diversa temporum consentientes, Lalainio parendum sine exceptione vociferabantur, malitiâ animi & haud dubiè fovendis intra urbem discordijs, quae sicut in talibus fieri assolet, cumulatâ suspicionum mole, Ordines inter & Lalainium neq; obscuris apud populum indicijs augebantur. Itaque Theodoro Occonio Consuli responderunt: se apud Lalainium pro retinendâ in armis centuriâ civicâ intercessuros, omnemque interim molestiam ex eo nascituram in se recipere. Hoc tantum suadere, ut Bolsuerdij concordes agant & ut Leovardiensium Franekerensiumque exemplo infidis temporibus urbem cive suo tueantur. Eam scilicet foederatorum Ordinum mentem esse, cui à Lalainio quid derogari non permitteret publica & inviolabilis conscriptorum patrum authoritas.
units.tr: When this decree was carried to Bolsward by the envoys, the Senate, compelled, deliberated in the Curia about sending a legate to the deputies of the Orders. Giving the signal of the great bell, it had the sworn council, with chosen men of the people, summoned into the Curia. There, after deliberation, they sent Theodore Occonius, consul, to Leeuwarden with a mandate, to find out the wishes of the Orders, which secretly turned away from Lalaing's counsels and entrusted the defence of the city to the civic guard, kept under arms and in loyalty. On the other hand, the Papists, as they had recently opposed his counsels, now agreed with him in various ways and shouted that Lalaing must be obeyed without exception. With malice of mind, and without doubt fostering discord within the city, they increased, as is customary in such matters, the heap of suspicions; and between the Orders and Lalaing, signs not obscure among the people were growing. So they answered the consul, Theodore Occonius, that they would intercede with Lalaing for keeping the civic company under arms, and in the meantime would take upon themselves whatever trouble might arise from it. They only urged that the men of Bolsward act in harmony and, following the example of Leeuwarden and Franeker, guard their city with its own citizens in faithless times. That, certainly, was the mind of the allied Orders, and nothing of it could be taken away by Lalaing, since the public and inviolable authority of the conscript fathers did not permit it.

units.la: Quod responsi, ut grave Pontificijs erat, ita majoribus odijs mobiles animos accendebat.
units.tr: This answer, as it was grievous to the Papists, so it inflamed their restless minds with greater hatreds.

units.la: Igitur (inquiebant) nobis satis perspectum est, malle vos Deputatis, quam praefecto obtemperare, cujus ne nomini quidem apud vos locus est. Nos verò Deo coram, Rege, Magistratu, jurato plebis Concilio de innocentiâ nostrâ testamur, neque nobis damnosum fore, quod adversus Praefectum in retinendâ civicâ cohorte apud vos statutum est.
units.tr: Therefore (they said), it is sufficiently clear to us that you prefer to obey the deputies rather than the prefect, whose very name has no place among you. But we testify, before God, the King, the magistracy and the sworn council of the people, to our innocence, and it will not be harmful to us that a decision has been made among you against the prefect concerning the retention of the civic cohort.

units.la: Creditum fuit Pontificios tam Bolsuerdiae, quam reliquas per Frisiam civitates secreto Lalainij instinctu corruptos pro admittendo ejus praesidio tantâ cum vehementiâ certasse, quo militari custodiâ praevalente, & cessantibus civium excubijs nihil invium pessima meditanti inermis multitudo opponeret. Unde Magistratus latentis consilij non ignarus Pontificijs in sua redire & excedere Curiâ jussit, auditoque abeuntium murmure & contumaci gestu notato litteras & cum ijs Tetardum Siccamam actuarium ad Deputatos Frisiae ablegavit.
units.tr: It was believed that the Papists, bribed secretly at Lalaing's instigation both at Bolsward and in the other cities throughout Friesland, contended so vehemently for admitting his garrison that, with the military guard prevailing and the citizens' watches ceasing, the unarmed multitude would have nothing to oppose to a man intent on the worst. Whence the magistrates, not ignorant of the hidden design, ordered the Papists to return to their own places and leave the Curia. Having heard the murmuring of those departing and noted their defiant gesture, they sent letters, and with them Tetard Siccama, their clerk, to the deputies of Friesland.

units.la: Idem Siccama notarum autor tradit, se in secretum & simul colloquium Deputatorum Frisiae admissum multa elevandis Bolsuerdienium actionibus suspecta de Lalainio inaudivisse, quasi jam animi & foederum dubius Ordinum partes hostium aut defectorum societate subdolo consilio vertisset. Quas suspiciones hoc imprimis confirmabat, quod in aulâ, in familiâ, in Comitatu, Pontificiorum acerrimos aleret, clerique reverentiâ & domesticâ consuetudine permotus, Romanis sacris aut superstitionibus juvenilem animum crescentibus annis erudijset. Hoc modo scilicet secreta actionum & arcana pectoris Romanorum titu clo. Io. lxxx. ritu expiandis juventæ erroribus professum, non dissimulato quoque futuræ defectionis consilio, quod ex perniciosâ aulicorum familiaritate & confessarij instinctu jam tum induisse, illâ ætatis fragilitate credebatur. Itaque factum est, ut oppida corruptis aut inclinantibus præsidijs firmanda censeret, Bolsuerdijsque sua signa & præsidia respuentibus ex impedito concepti facinoris arcano extrema irarum comminaretur.
units.tr: The same Siccama, author of these notes, relates that when he was admitted in secret and at the same time to a conference with the deputies of Friesland, he heard many things about Lalaing, suspicious and tending to disparage the actions of the Bolsward men: as if Lalaing, now doubtful in mind and of the covenants, had with a crafty plan turned the side of the Orders toward the enemy or toward deserters. These suspicions were especially confirmed by the fact that in the court, in his household and in his retinue, he kept the most fierce Papists, and that, moved by reverence for the clergy and by domestic custom, he had brought up his youthful mind, as the years grew, in Roman rites and superstitions. In this way, of course, he laid bare the secrets of his actions and the hidden thoughts of his heart, professing to expiate the errors of youth by the Roman rite (1580), and not concealing a plan of future defection, which he was believed to have already adopted at that fragile age, from the pernicious familiarity of courtiers and at his confessor's urging. So it came about that he judged the towns to be fortified with garrisons that were corrupted or inclined to him, and threatened Bolsward, which rejected his standards and garrisons, with the utmost vengeance of his anger, from the concealed purpose of a crime conceived and thwarted.

units.la: Quorum causam ut purgaret, Hesselus Aysma vir & peritiâ juris & eloquentiæ famâ celebratus, qui Antverpiâ tum in Frisiam concesserat, Groningam ad Lalainium missus, quem spreti præsidij injuria & læsæ auctoritatis ultio odio fœderis efferaverat. Igitur in Bolsuerdios fidei & sacramenti ruptores coram Legato invectus, tectioris, in quam naturâ falcilè exardescebat, iracundiæ indicium fecit violatæque autoritatis crimen à Bolsuerdijs commissum severitate quadam veteris imperij corrigendum evulgavit. Cæterum à Legato, qui ad Archiducem Matthiam, ad Aurantium, denique ad judicia exterorum Principum provocabat, admonitus, juvenilem sensim immodestiam repressit, civiumque præsidium à Magistratu ritè & ex statuto Ordinum conscriptum clam agnoscere coactus est. Unde animus & cum eo iracundiæ fervor subsedit, nolente conscientiâ ut vocis fiduciam & constantiam animi fœdissimæ defectionis affectator retineret.
units.tr: To clear their cause, Hessel Aysma, a man celebrated both for his skill in law and his reputation for eloquence, who had then withdrawn from Antwerp into Friesland, was sent to Lalaing at Groningen. Lalaing had been inflamed with hatred of the covenant by the injury of the scorned garrison and the desire for vengeance for his wounded authority. So Aysma, inveighing against the men of Bolsward as breakers of faith and oath in the legate's presence, showed some indication of anger, which in his nature flared up easily, though he kept it somewhat covered, and announced that the crime of violated authority committed by the Bolsward men must be corrected with a certain severity of the old rule. But being admonished by the legate, who appealed to Archduke Matthias, to Orange, and finally to the judgments of foreign princes, he gradually repressed his youthful intemperance and was compelled to acknowledge secretly that the civic garrison had been rightly and according to the Orders' statute enrolled by the magistracy. Whence his spirit, and with it the heat of his anger, subsided, since his conscience was unwilling that he, an aspirant to the most foul defection, should keep up the boldness of his voice and the firmness of his spirit.

units.la: Quare Ordinum Delegati, cæterique spectatæ autoritatis proceres prævisco ejus consilio & ne castella peregrinis commissa suo arbitrio premendis civitatibus abuteretur, libellum ei supplicem obtulere, proq; stodiâ arcium inquilinis demandanda hunc in modum disseruere.
units.tr: Therefore the deputies of the Estates and the other nobles of recognised authority, foreseeing his plan and fearing that he would use the castles entrusted to him to oppress the cities at his own pleasure, presented him a humble petition. In it they set out, in this manner, their demands concerning the guarding of the fortresses, which were to be committed to the local residents.

units.la: NE in ista mala recideremus, PRAEFECTE, quæ ante perscriptum Gandavi fœdus perpessi fumus, necessarium imprimis & utile reip. duximus, ut Præfectum & Officiarios eligeremus nobis acceptos & de quorum fide constaret. Igitur tuæ integritatis fiduciâ odio partium, quæ tui invidiâ tam intra provinciam quam foris in te exarserant, te de Præfectum legimus, sed ea cautione, ut excepta juris dicundi potestate, tuo imperio, nobis arbitris utereris, sciresque te rectorem isti populo datum, qui & rerum conscius esse velit & regendi arcanum ad plures pervenire. Et quanquam fidei tuæ fiduciâ nostra se spes huc usque aluerit, ita deprehendimus insciis Ordinibus & inconsultis tria per provinciam castella per externæ gentis Satrapas teneri, infringique conventionem, quam post dimissas Hispanorum Italorumque legiones cum IOANNE AUSTRIACO pepigimus. Itaque de consilio MATTHIAE Gubernatoris defuncto Petro Sickingha Harlinganæ arcis rectore, nuncupatis in successorem Docone Martna, Henrico Oyenbruggio, Martino Nitzemio & Gerardo Sickemensi, Doconem Martnam de communi Ordinum consensu regundæ arci præfecimus, jussimusque ut Oyenbruggio arcem cum præsidio tenenti missionem nostra voluntate faceret. At is, etsi contra provinciæ leges, contra pactorum fidem castello non decessit & tuâ indulgentiâ satrapæ dignitatem retinuit exterorum solertiâ & intercessione, qui clam fœderi hostes & integritate tuâ malè usi, Archiducis rescripta malis artibus & facilitate aulicâ pro asservandis castellis impetravere. Præter hæc recrudescente bello & sub ejus apparatum recensendis copijs Remicum Cammingham cum Censoria potestate præfecimus, voluimusque ut, te etiam consensentiente, lustrandae legioni praesset. Quod decretum quoniam infirmari cum invidiâ tanti viri & ipsorum quoq; Ordinum nec potest nec debet, ita intelleximus Pompeio Vskenio homini Translavicano, à Matthia Gubernatore, sinistris & contra bonam fidem repertis rationibus circumvento dignitatem Censoris collatam. Qui procedendi mos, ut ab Hispanicâ & veteri dominatione, ita ab injuriâ & contemptu Ordinum alienus non est. Quem ut corrigas, omniaque quae collapsa sunt restitui in integrum cures, unicè petimus, ac ut ex Matthiae Gubernatoris Ordinumq; generalium decreto tria castella Ordinibus Frisiae tradas, quo solo aequentur. Quod si intempestivum videatur, Doconem Martnam, sponsione fidei & cautione 20000. praestitâ, Harlingana arci pro rectore imponas, monereque censorio, Pompeio Vskenio abrogato Kenicum Camminghan lustrandis copijs admoveas. Hoc etiam postulamus, ne quid in publicâ provinciae administratione inconsultis Ordinibus aut eorum Deputatis facias, peregrinorumque sua commoda quaerentium, assentationi aut consilio aurem praebeas. Sin vero contra feceris exterosque honoribus, à quibus aequissimè arcentur, admoveris, dabimus operam, ut eâ, quâ valemus, autoritate, libertati, quâ supra caeteras gentes efferimur & legibus nostris prospiciamus, convocatisque provinciae Ordinibus statui faciamus, quod bono regis & reip. cessurum sit. Hoc vero ipsum, si contra jus foederis apud Ultrajectum inuti tuâ aut aliorum ope tardius fiat aut subvertatur, testamur, nos nec tributis nec indictionibus locum facturos, neque laturos, ut provinciales nostri patriae fidi pravorum interventu collatis dignitatibus arceantur. In quarum possessione ut eos Archidux M A T T H I A S locet & ut emendet, quae contra jus & aequum invalucre, rogamus P R A E F E C T E morbis nostris jure Praefecti remedia praescribas & affectui & rationi temporum convenientia.
units.tr: PREFECT, so that we do not fall back into those evils which we suffered before the treaty of Ghent was drawn up, we judged it above all necessary and useful to the commonwealth to choose a Prefect and officials acceptable to us and whose loyalty was assured. Therefore, trusting in your integrity, and in opposition to the factions which had flared up against you through envy both within the province and abroad, we chose you as Prefect. But we did so on this condition: that, apart from the power of administering justice, you should exercise your command with us as arbiters. You should know that you were given as ruler to that people, one who would wish to be privy to affairs and to whom the secret of government would come to be shared by many. And although our hope has hitherto been nourished by confidence in your loyalty, we have found that, without the knowledge and consultation of the Estates, three castles in the province are held by satraps of a foreign nation, and that the agreement we made with John of Austria after the Spanish and Italian legions were dismissed is being infringed. Therefore, on the advice of Governor Matthias, after the death of Peter Sickingha, commander of the fortress of Harlingen, we nominated as successor Docco Martna, Henry Oyenbrugg, Martin Nitzemius and Gerard Sickemensis. By the common consent of the Estates we appointed Docco Martna to govern the fortress, and we ordered that Oyenbrugg, who held the fortress with its garrison, should surrender it at our will. But he, although against the laws of the province and the faith of the agreements, did not withdraw from the castle. With your indulgence he retained the rank of satrap, through the cleverness and intercession of foreigners who were secretly enemies of the treaty and who, misusing your integrity, obtained from the Archduke, by bad arts and courtly facility, rescripts for keeping the castles. Besides these things, with war breaking out again and the troops to be reviewed in its preparation, we appointed Remicus Cammingha with censorial power, and we wished that, with your consent too, he should preside over the muster of the legion. Since this decree cannot and ought not to be weakened, with ill will toward so great a man and toward the Estates themselves, we have learned that the office of Censor was conferred on Pompeius Vskenius, a man from across the Vecht, by Governor Matthias, who was won over by sinister devices and contrary to good faith. This manner of proceeding is not foreign to the old Spanish domination, nor to the injury and contempt of the Estates. We ask only that you correct him, and see to it that everything that has collapsed is restored to its former state, and that, by the decree of Governor Matthias and the general Estates, you hand over the three castles to the Estates of Friesland, by which alone they may be placed on equal footing. But if this seems untimely, then appoint Docco Martna as governor of the fortress of Harlingen, he having given a pledge of faith and security of 20,000; and, with Pompeius Vskenius removed, advise the censor to bring Remicus Cammingha to the review of the troops. We also demand this: that you do nothing in public administration without the knowledge of the Estates or their deputies, and that you not lend an ear to flattery or to the counsel of foreigners seeking their own advantage. But if you act contrary to this and bring foreigners to honours from which they are most justly excluded, we shall take care that, with the authority we have, we provide for our liberty, by which we are exalted above other nations, and for our laws. Having convened the Estates of the province, we shall bring about a decision that will be for the good of the king and the commonwealth. Moreover, we testify that if this itself, against the right of the treaty of Utrecht, is done more slowly or overturned through your aid or that of others, we shall make no room for taxes or levies, nor shall we allow our provincials, faithful to their country, to be shut out from their offices through the intervention of the wicked. We ask that Archduke Matthias place them in possession of these offices and correct what has been brought in against right and justice. And you, Prefect, as Prefect, prescribe remedies for our ills, suited both to feeling and to the circumstances of the time.

units.la: Ita Gerardus Iacobi Antistes Clarecampensis, Iarichus Bottnia Satrapa Coverdiae & per Drentiam, Iarichus Bottnia F. Thomas Groningensis Abbas Floridi Campi, Ioannes Bisteñius Prior in Thabor, Erasmus Douma, Serapius Galama, Barthius Idsaerda, Iulius Bottnia, Lasius Iongama, Renicus Cammingha, Sixtus Bottnia, GeroldusHerama, Taco Cammingha, G. Herama, Vitus Cammingha, Justus Heringha, Wibo Holdingha, Epius Douma Junior, Sibrandus Cammingha, Justus Ockingha, Kempo Donia, Foppius Grovensteinius, Siricius Donia, Sixtus Scheltema, Franciscus Ubeli Praebendarius Goutumanus signavere.
units.tr: So signed Gerard Jacobi, head of Klarenkamp; Iarichus Bottnia, satrap of Coevorden and throughout Drenthe; Iarichus Bottnia, brother; Thomas, abbot of Floridus Campus of Groningen; John Bisteñius, prior of Thabor; Erasmus Douma; Serapius Galama; Barthius Idsaerda; Iulius Bottnia; Lasius Iongama; Renicus Cammingha; Sixtus Bottnia; Gerold Herama; Taco Cammingha; G. Herama; Vitus Cammingha; Justus Heringha; Wibo Holdingha; Epius Douma Junior; Sibrandus Cammingha; Justus Ockingha; Kempo Donia; Foppius Grovensteinius; Siricius Donia; Sixtus Scheltema; and Franciscus Ubeli, prebendary of Gouda.

units.la: Cui libello an à Lalainio rescriptum sit, in illorum temporum actis non invenio. Mihi verisimile est eum, auctis in se procerum suspicionibus, nihil rescripsisse, ne clandestini, quod agitabat, consilij turpitudinem, adhibito malis auxilio, recentis perfidiae famâ aggravaret.
units.tr: I do not find in the records of those times whether Lalaing sent any written reply to this petition. It seems likely to me that, with the suspicions of the nobles against him increased, he sent no reply, lest by calling in outside help he should make the shamefulness of his secret design worse, adding to it the fame of a fresh treachery.

units.la: Reperio in archivis foederatarum provinciarum Ordines, xix foederis articulo in litteris expresso, è Frisiâ Legatos gravi de causâ, & silentio obsignandâ Ultrajectum cum justis mandatis evocasse, quo in re ponderosâ &, ut ajebant, foederi damnum aut commodum allaturâ decerni posset, quod è Rep. foret. Litterae iii. Eid. Jan. scriptae.
units.tr: In the archives of the United Provinces I find that the Estates, under the nineteenth article of the treaty, which is expressly stated in their letters, summoned from Friesland envoys with full instructions to Utrecht, to a matter for which secrecy was to be sealed, on account of a serious cause. In this weighty matter, which, as they said, would bring either loss or advantage to the treaty, a decision could be taken which was for the good of the commonwealth. The letters were written on the third Ides of January.

units.la: Cl. Franckena tradit, se accepto 2500 militari stipendio Groningam circa hoc tempus profectum, Hesseliq; Aysmae Frisiorum Legati acerrimam cum Lalainio contentionem inclinante Januario accidisse. Itaque foederato militi per Drentiam sparso & extorquendis quae defiderabantur tributis importuno, odium rusticae plebis conflavit, ac si parcissimus aeris exactor militarem immodestiam & solutos mores amore disciplinae reprobaret. Econtra Drentinos afflictis agris & refamiliari attritos ad ultionem militaris injuriae instigavit, potestate ijs clam facta ut vim vi arcerent, captisque armis & resumpta veteri ferocia fines suos & simul fortunas virilibus factis tuerentur. Unde populus ultro inquies & ex damnis ferox ad arma provocavit, equitumque copias, quas Dodo Larius & Rinsuoudius ducebant, agris suis atque finibus abscedere coegit. Ita & militum insolentiam & rebellionem Drentini populi egregius talium artifex dissimulando & odia partium nutriebat, & fortunam Ultrajectini foederis morabatur, a quo ij magis alieni fiebant, qui recenti & aspero militaris injuriae sensu ex immodestis militum moribus Ordinum imperia tanquam minus civilia interpretabantur. Cl. Franckena in Diario notat, illum Drentinorum cum foederato equite conflictum v. Kal. Febr. factum, Lalainiumque Esseno secessu, de deserendis Ordinum partibus agitantem secretis colloquijs Drentinam nobilitatem corrupisse. Itaque illo, ut creditum fuit, consilij instinctore, de incundo cum Transisulanis seorsim foedere agitavit, haud dubie ut Ultrajectino soluta Hannoniae & Artesiae exemplo ad regis Philippi gratiam & simul sacramentum rediret. Jam enim eo inclinare palam Lalainius credebatur, cum aulicorum, ut dixi, suasu, tum secreto litterarum commercio, quod ei ex Hannonia etiam in Frisijs aut per confinia agenti cum propinquis aut familiaribus intercedebat. Quae singula firmioribus suspicionum indicijs prodebantur, quod Oyenbruggio & Grutero ex intimae admissionis & regiarum partium aulicis uteretur, repudiatoque indigenarum consilio sui imperij arcana exterorum vilissimis vulgaret. His accedebat quod quadrimestri apud Essenum monasterium secreto, recepta in fidem Groningae in eandem urbem cum honesto comitatu & medico ac suspecto Pontificijs praesidio admissus, Pontificios & in ijs partium vehementissimos favore & benevolentia prosequeretur, comminicatisque rerum arcanis spe honorum, neque vanis auspicijs lactaret. Quare obsides Groninganos, quo per eos suffragijs polleret, & ut in Senatum deprimendis foederatis cooptaret, Campis revocavit, liberosque & pactione fidei solutos creandis magistratibus delegit. Quae res subsecutae in Groningae urbe calamitati causam ac initium dedit. Ubi namque obsides Pontificij a Campensi custodia tanquam exilio reduces, jus suffragij & petendorum honorum adepti, immutato civitatis statu, foederatae res retro ex potentia adversarum partium cessere. Quae eo quoque magis firmabantur, quod Lalainius Pontificiae factionis principem se efferret, ac a suae fortunae autoribus alienior, regem Philippum adorare cum invidia erectae libertatis videretur. Itaque munitissimae urbis tum constituti ex suo arbitrio Magistratus fiducia, diu dubium & simulandis partibus facilem animum exercuit, non sine manifesto indicio in illo conscientiae certamine futuri facinoris faeditatem cum anteactorum fide atque gloria conferri.
units.tr: Franckena writes that, having received a military pay of 2,500, he set out for Groningen at about this time, and that the very sharp dispute between Hessel Aysma, envoy of the Frisians, and Lalaing took place as January drew to a close. And so the soldiers of the treaty, scattered through Drenthe and troublesome in extracting the taxes that were demanded, kindled the hatred of the rustic commons, as if the most sparing collector of money, out of love for discipline, were rejecting the military licence and the loose morals of the soldiers. On the other side, he stirred the Drenthers, worn down by ruined fields and impoverishment, to revenge for the military injury. He had secretly given them leave to repel force with force, and, taking up arms and recovering their old ferocity, they defended their borders and at the same time their property with manly deeds. Hence the people, restless of their own accord and fierce from their losses, took up arms and forced the cavalry forces, which Dodo Larius and Rinsuoudius led, to withdraw from their fields and borders. Thus the skilled manipulator of such things, by dissembling, both fostered the insolence and rebellion of the soldiers and the hatred between the parties among the people of Drenthe, and delayed the fortune of the Utrecht treaty, from which those became more estranged who, with a fresh and bitter sense of military injury, interpreted the orders of the Estates as less than civil because of the unrestrained conduct of the soldiers. Franckena notes in his Diary that this clash between the Drenthers and the federal cavalry took place on 27 January, and that Lalaing, while in retreat at Essen and pondering in secret conversations the abandonment of the Estates' cause, had corrupted the Drenthe nobility. Therefore, with him, as was believed, the instigator of this plan, he deliberated on making a separate treaty with the men of Overijssel. Undoubtedly he aimed at having Utrecht released from the treaty, following the example of Hainaut and Artois, and returning both to the favour of King Philip and to his oath. For Lalaing was already openly thought to be leaning that way, both by the persuasion of the courtiers, as I have said, and by a secret correspondence of letters which passed between him and his relatives or intimates from Hainaut, even while he was acting in Friesland or along the borders. These particulars were revealed as stronger indications of suspicion: that he used as his counsellors Oyenbrugg and Gruter, courtiers of the royal party and of his most intimate admission, and that, rejecting the counsel of the natives, he made the secrets of his government common to the vilest foreigners. To this was added the fact that, after a four-month stay in secret at the monastery of Essen, he was received back into the good graces of Groningen, entering that city with an honourable retinue, a doctor, and a garrison suspected by the Papists. There he courted the Papists, and especially the most zealous of their party, with favour and kindness; and, by sharing the secrets of affairs, he fed them with hopes of honours and with no empty promises. Therefore he recalled the Groningen hostages from Kampen, so that through them he might have influence in the votes, and so that they might be co-opted into the Senate to depress the members of the federation. He also chose as magistrates, freed from the bond of their pledge, those who were free to be elected. These events which followed gave the cause and beginning of the disaster in the city of Groningen. For when the Papist hostages were brought back from their custody at Kampen, as if from exile, and had gained the right to vote and to seek office, the state of the city was changed, and the federal affairs gave way from their power to the strength of the opposing party. This was made all the stronger because Lalaing presented himself as leader of the Papist faction, and, being more estranged from the authors of his own fortune, seemed to adore King Philip with resentment against the freedom that had been raised up. And so the Magistrate, which was then constituted at his own discretion in that most fortified city, exercised for a long time, in doubt and with a heart easily turned to feigned parties, a confidence which showed, in that struggle of conscience, a clear sign that the foulness of the future crime was being weighed against the faith and glory of past deeds.

units.la: Sic in binio velut constituto & cum fato suo luctanti Cornelia Lalainia soror supervenit, quae imperiosi ac ferocis animi foemina, Baroni Montjoio denupta, lubricum & praecipitio tum proximum muliebri bribus artibus & sororijs blanditijs tentavit. Cui rei conducebant & cIↄ. Iↄ. Philippi gratia per Farnesium oblata, & magna aeris summa expugnando LXXX, inopis Praefecti ingenio valida & dignitatum incrementa redeunti ad Regem promissa. Quippe Marchionatus titulum, si animum in melius mutet, Lalainiae domui a Philippo rege destinatum, cujus potentiae & majestati reputaret plus tribuendum, quam illorum foederi, qui temerata majorum religione novis sacrorum opinionibus se attaminassent: Excelsius & suae familiae, suae virtuti, suae famae convenientius esse, potentissimi regis ministrum se ferre, quam imperio vilissimae plebis obsequi, quae dominationis immodica & cum res gerit, sui ac affectuum impotens principum virorum laudes atque gloriam invidia aut despectu obscuraret. In cujus servitio si perseveret, avitum familiae decus, denique honestas laudabilis patrimonij opes amissurum. Adhaec propinquorum gratiam & ne dissimulet, carissimae matris perditurum, quae unice velit filium suum & regis sacramento quo imbutus esset, & religione in qua ab infantia & primo spiritu egisset, persistere, aegritudinem animi & infirmitatem senectae auctura, si suae stirpis & officij oblitum aliena sacra & foedera videat majorum ritibus vertentem. Neque avunculum, cujus beneficio Rennebergicae domus patrimonium accepisset, ex aequo id laturum, cujus votorum summa sit, ut nepotem habeat prementem vestigia majorum, qui clarissimas imagines & titulos illustribus factis atque exemplis ornassent. Satis libertati, satis patriae retributum, ci majus in praesens officium collocare non queat, quam si factionum civilium taedio ad Deum & Principem suum redeat, illorum exemplo, qui partium fessi violatae fidei crimen seriore resipiscentia expiavissent. Spectaret Hannonios suos & eorum socios, affines & propinquos sana consilia, praevisio regiae magnitudinis fulmine, professos aeternae bellorum tempestati pacem antehabuisse, cujus solam foelicitatem dare non civilium partium fessae vires, sed in regiae gratiae amplexum provoluta meditatio posset. Cui praefecturae suae ditiones asserere neque arduum neque difficile foret, Groningâ munitissimâ urbium in potestatem redactâ, & castellis per Frisiam regio adhuc praesidio obseptis.
units.tr: Thus, while he was still hesitating and wrestling with his own fate, his sister Cornelia Lalaing came upon him. She was a woman of imperious and fierce spirit, married to Baron Montigny, and she tried with womanly wiles and sisterly flattery to tip him over the edge, which was now close at hand. Helping her were the 1500 florins offered in King Philip's name through Farnese, a large sum of money for winning him over (80, as an unskilled prefect's mind is strong for it), and promises of promotion when he returned to the King. She pointed out that the title of Marquis, which King Philip had destined for the house of Lalaing, would be given to him if he changed his mind. He should consider that more was owed to the power and majesty of so great a king than to the league of men who had defiled the religion of their ancestors with new opinions of worship. It was more fitting for his family, his courage and his reputation to show himself a minister of the most powerful king than to obey the rule of the vilest mob, whose immoderate domination, and whose temper, unrestrained by reason or passion, would cloud the praises and glory of great men with envy or contempt when they did their work. If he persisted in its service, he would lose the ancestral honour of his family and finally the respectable wealth of his inherited estate. Besides this, he would lose the favour of his kinsfolk and, let him not pretend otherwise, of his dearest mother, who wished above all that her son should persist in the oath of allegiance to the King, in which he had been brought up, and in the religion in which he had lived from infancy and his first breath. Her distress of mind and the infirmity of her old age would be increased if she saw him forgetful of his duty and his station, turning to foreign rites and alliances, abandoning the customs of his ancestors. Nor would his uncle, through whose kindness the house of Rennenberg had received its estate, bear it calmly; his greatest wish was that his nephew should tread in the footsteps of ancestors who had adorned their families with famous images, titles and illustrious deeds. He had given enough to liberty and to country; he could place no greater service in the present than to return, weary of civil factions, to God and his Prince, following the example of those who, tired of parties, had atoned by late repentance for the crime of broken faith. Let him look to his Hainaulters and their allies, kinsmen and neighbours, who had sound counsel: they had foreseen the thunderbolt of royal majesty, and had professed that peace was to be preferred to the eternal storm of wars. Only a mind bowed in embrace of the royal favour, not the exhausted strength of a civil party, could give them happiness. It would be neither hard nor difficult for him to assert the rule of his prefecture, now that Groningen, the most strongly fortified city, had been brought under his power, and the castles across Friesland were still held by royal garrisons.

units.la: Addunt alij, de ipso populo in factiones scisso quaedam addidisse, quasi delectâ Philippi gratiâ regias partes, etsi infirmas & nutantes erigere cum oppressione languidi foederis & fatiscentis Ordinum concordiae quiret. Tandem fraternum animum etsi altius permanendi in fide consilium se aliquando aperiret, fluctuantem & mutationis adhuc incertum promissis fallacibus Mariae Brineae Comitissimae Meganae nuptijs expugnavit, commendatâ dote & eximiâ foeminae formâ, in quam Lalainius à primo etiam juventae flore diuturnis amoribus exarserat. Quippe Barlaemontio, in cujus matrimonio vixerat, defuncto vidua, tractura aetatem & singularis formae indulgentiam inter solitudinem vitae & orbitatem conjugalis lecti non videbatur, caeterum illius affectum amplexura, cujus vernantes annos amoris igne praeoccuperaverat. Placituras foeminae praeclaras in fratre suo naturae dotes, qui praeter vultus & oris venustatem & virentem juventam excultum artibus ingenium & tot provinciarum nobilem recturam ostentaret. Itaque victus CIↄ. Iↄ. Corneliæ illecebris, inanibus nuptiarum promissis gloriam, decus, fidem LXXX. denique patriam posthabuit.
units.tr: Others add that he had made some proposals concerning the people themselves, which had been split into factions, as though, having chosen the royal cause, he could raise its weak and wavering fortunes, even at the cost of weakening the feeble league and the fading concord of the States. At last, when he revealed to his brother's mind, though it had long been fixed on remaining loyal, that he meant to change sides, the promises of Mary Brinas, Countess of Megen, and her marriage overcame him while he still wavered and was uncertain of change. Her dowry and her exceptional beauty commended the match. From the early bloom of youth Lalaing had burned with lasting love for her. Now that Barlaymont, in whose marriage she had lived, was dead and she was a widow, she would not, it seemed, spend her life, and the indulgence of her singular beauty, amid the loneliness of life and the bereavement of the marriage bed. Rather she would embrace the affection of the man whose love had kindled in her youth. She would be pleased by the outstanding gifts of nature in her brother: besides the comeliness of his face and mouth and his youthful vigour, he showed a mind cultivated in the arts and fit to rule so many noble provinces. So, overcome by the enticements of Cornelia, he preferred the empty promises of marriage to glory, honour, faith, and finally his country.

units.la: Reidanus scribit, illi cum Farnesio etiam ad Trajectum Mosæ castra tenenti, secretum aliquod intercessisse, velut provincias suo imperio commissas redditurus regi occultâ conventione crederetur. Sed impotentiâ virium & infœlicis consilij præpeditum solam Groningam regijs partibus asseruisse, nutritâque inter oppidanos & Omlandiæ agrarios veteri simultate, fatali illorum temporum & Translavicani populi discordiâ suam dominationem emunijsse. Idem addit, defectionis suspicionem in Lalainio natam, minus tamen apud peritos rerum fidei invenisse; quod sepositâ simulatione Philippum regem apertius læsisse ex ordine factorum notaretur. Ita scilicet Daventriæ & Camporum oppidis regia præsidia ejecisse, indultaque per Frisiam & vicina religionis pace, & Ultrajectino fœdere cum invidiâ procerum asserto, regis Senatum, suffecto Ordinum, amovisse. Quare creditum fuit, cum crudis & intempestivis quorundam actionibus offensum odium fœderis induisse, oblutante interea animo, qui veteris sub Albano exilij & cum eo sacramenti memoriam non absconderat.
units.tr: Reidanus writes that some secret arrangement passed between him and Farnese, who was still holding camp at Maastricht on the Meuse, so that it was believed he would hand over the provinces entrusted to his command to the King by a hidden agreement. But, hindered by the weakness of his forces and an unfortunate plan, he secured Groningen alone for the royal side. Nursed by the old rivalry between the townsmen and the Ommelands farmers, and by the discord of the Translavicani people, which was fatal to those times, he fortified his own rule. The same writer adds that suspicion of defection had arisen concerning Lalaing, but found little credence among those experienced in affairs. Yet from the sequence of events it was noted that, laying aside pretence, he had injured King Philip more openly. Thus, it seems, he drove the royal garrisons out of the towns of Deventer and Kampen, and by the peace granted throughout Friesland and the neighbouring areas, and by the Union of Utrecht, which was asserted to the envy of the nobles, he removed the King's council and substituted one chosen by the States. Therefore it was believed that his hatred of the league was roused by the rash and ill-timed acts of certain men, while in the meantime his mind, which had not hidden the memory of his old exile under Alba and of the oath he had sworn with him, was wavering.

units.la: Ego existumo Romanâ Religione, quam cum animâ & materno lacte hauserat, solidius imbutum, ut multum regio nomini, ita reverentiæ dedisse, primisque recturæ annis optimè usum posteriora temporum defectionis consilio fœdasse. Igitur oppidis castellisque pendentia à suo nutu atque imperio præsidia destinasse, eaque spe per delectas Leovardiæ, Franequeræ & apud Bolsuerdios armatorum civium centurias delusum, consilijs suis adversa duris & trahi nescijs procerum ingenijs ac suspicionibus imputavisse. Ita odium cessante utrinque fiduciâ natum, postquam nec ille Ordinum sollicitudinem & curam, ut reip. utilem, nec hi immodesta Lalainij concepta pro legitimis aut profuturis interpretarentur. Adeo verum est bonam quoq; indolem, sive vitio temporis, quod vertendis rebus pronum est, sive fortunæ aut magnarum rerum inlicio depravari, animique mores semel in declivium actos, majore quam coeperunt, præcipitio impelli.
units.tr: I think that, having been more solidly imbued with the Roman religion, which he had drunk in with his soul and his mother's milk, he had given much reverence to the royal name, and, having used it very well in the first years of his office, afterwards tarnished it by the plan of defection. Therefore he had designed garrisons dependent on his nod and command for the towns and castles, and he was deceived in this hope by the companies of armed citizens chosen at Leeuwarden, Franeker and Bolsward. He blamed the hard and implacable minds and suspicions of the nobles, which were unfavourable to his plans. Thus distrust, arising on both sides, grew into hatred, since neither did the one interpret the States' anxiety and care for the commonwealth as legitimate or useful, nor did the others interpret Lalaing's immoderate designs as lawful or beneficial. So true is it that even a good disposition is corrupted, whether by the vice of the times, which is prone to overturning affairs, or by fortune, or by the allurement of great undertakings, and that once the habits of the mind have been driven downhill, they are hurried into a fall greater than they began with.

units.la: Unde Lalainius defectorum exemplo in prava mox consilia provolutus, de opprimendo per Frisiam fœdere agitavit ac ut conscientiam tormenta pectori ferentem festinato scelere exoneraret. Quare octo peditumcohortes è Translavicanis in Frisiam, velut in sui adventum præmissas, ocyus expedivit, tutandis pro Philippo castellis, quorum Satrapas etiam durante Colonien si conventu corruptos Pontificij exules jactitaverant. Ita Lalainij consilium, quod altius animo desederat, tunc detectum, quasi nolente fato ut tardè & cum violatione fidei decretum per festinationem foedissimi facinoris iuvalesceret.
units.tr: Hence Lalaing, following the example of the defectors, was soon swept into wicked plans; he considered crushing the league in Friesland, and wanted to discharge the torments of conscience from his breast by a hasty crime. Therefore he quickly dispatched eight companies of foot from the Translavicani into Friesland, as if sent ahead of his own arrival, to guard the castles for Philip. The Papist exiles had boasted that the governors of these castles had even been corrupted at the Cologne convention during the lasting truce. Thus Lalaing's plan, which had settled deep in his mind, was then revealed, as if fate was unwilling that it should grow strong, decided late and with a breach of faith, through the haste of a most foul crime.

units.la: Quare oppidanorum Deputati, quorum sollicitudo ex periculis increverat, de redigendo in potestatem Leovardiensi castello deliberare, petito agrarios auxilio, qui veteri æmulatione obligari oppidanos ad reciproca officia exigebant. Ista erant, oppidani ut beneficium diruendæ arci ab agrarijs præstitum agnituros se caverent, agrariosque ingruente bello laribus profugos intrà urbem reciperent, commeatu atque annonâ sublevarent. Quod à Gellio Sibæo & Douwone Sixma oppidanorum norum Deputatis signatum, Leovardiensium quoque Magistratum, ve- clo. Io. lut fructum diruta arcis & auxilij sensurum obligavit. Quare ab Adio Lxxx. Lambertio Consule & centurione civico, post à Ioanne Aysma Consule, Henrico Iarichio è Concilio jurato & Laurentio Venone actuario firmatum, destruendo regio operi intentos cives accinxit. Igitur, illi in toetus coïre, capita & consilia miscere, hortari se invicem & admonere libertatis, cujus recuperandæ occasionem defectio Præfecti & æterni servitij metus fecisset. A quo si vindicare se in animum inducant, fortem audaciam resumerent, ostenderentq; traduces majorum spiritus in gloriosis adhuc posteris superesse. Neque enim cum Philippi exercitu, cum multarum gentium confluge sibi rem esse, aut ut in acie & conflictu evocati extra fines cadant, cæterum in ipsâ civitate, intra infoelices muros hostem esse, qui depelli familiari limine debeat, rituque ignobilium ferarum suis latebris excedere. Nam istarum molium atq; operum fundamenta in spem subjectionis & popularis servitij jacta, quæ illi imponi sibi passi essent, qui intestinis factionibus fessi & mutuo sanguine fracti & enervtes moderati primum principis leniore imperio fascinabantur. At per illum diu paterne & sanctè habitum, post de augenda dominatione & opprimendis legibus cogitantem & arces extructas, & præsidia civitatibus imposita, ne qui essent, qui modum principali imperio ponerent. Ita Saxonum, ita Austriacorum monumenta spectari, quæ in speciem tuendæ provinciæ erecta, opprimendæ libertati per adolescentiam principalis potentiæ invaluissent. Per ea fuisse, ut legum, in quas Principes peieraverant, vigore sublato, vix memoria quidem antiqui juris retineretur, quod etiam reminiscentibus silentio victum, invidiæ potentis metum removebat.
units.tr: Therefore the deputies of the townsmen, whose anxiety had grown with the dangers, deliberated about bringing the castle of Leeuwarden under their power. They sought the help of the country people, who, bound to the townsmen by old rivalry, demanded reciprocal services. These were the terms: the townsmen would undertake to acknowledge the benefit given by the country people in the demolition of the citadel; and in the coming war they would take in the country people who fled from their homes within the city, and would relieve them with provisions and corn. This was sealed by Gellius Sibaeus and Douwe Sixma, deputies of the townsmen, and it also bound the magistrates of Leeuwarden, who would enjoy the fruit of the demolished citadel and of the help given. Accordingly, having been confirmed by Adio Lambertus, consul and civic captain, and afterwards by Johannes Aysma, consul, Henricus Iarichius of the sworn council, and Laurentius Venon, the actuary, they armed the citizens who were intent on destroying the royal work. Then they came together from all sides, mixed their heads and counsels, and urged and reminded one another of liberty, whose recovery the prefect's defection and the fear of perpetual servitude had made an opportunity. If they resolved to defend it from him, they would resume a brave boldness, and show that the spirit of their forefathers still survived in their glorious descendants. For they had to deal not with Philip's army or the gathering of many nations, nor with men who fall outside the borders when called into battle and combat, but with an enemy within the city itself, inside their unhappy walls, who must be driven from the threshold of home, and forced out of his lair like an ignoble beast. For the foundations of those mounds and works had been laid in hope of subjection and popular servitude, which they had allowed to be imposed on themselves; wearied by internal factions and broken and weakened by mutual bloodshed, they were first bewitched by the milder rule of a prince. But that prince, long regarded as paternal and holy, afterwards turned his thoughts to enlarging his dominion and overturning the laws, and to building citadels and imposing garrisons on the cities, so that there should be none to set limits to royal power. Thus the monuments of the Saxons and of the Austrians were to be seen, which had been raised under the pretext of defending the province, but had grown into the suppression of liberty by the rising of princely power. By these means the force of laws, in which princes had sworn, had been abolished, and scarcely any memory of the ancient right was retained; and even this, with those who remembered it kept silent through fear, removed the fear of a powerful envy.

units.la: Per ea Cæsaris & Philippi inquisitiones & edicta, per ea novos Episcopatus invito populo introductos, Senatumque Principis majestate regni suffultum, ne aures quidem & judicia querimonijs populi præbuisse. Ex istâ scilicet officinâ omne violentum emanasse, in qua per cruciatus & supplicia in liberam gentem exercita insontium cruor adhuc piacula reposceret. Itaque repurgandum illud clarissimi & prolibertate fusi sanguinis lustrum, non ut igne ac thure adoleat superstitio; aut aspergine depuret, sed ut manus posterorum sentiat, qui vindicias majorum manibus & servili temporum patientiæ deberent. Ita inferias fortium, aut innocentiam umbris fore, si munimenta effræxis imperij aboleantur tanto planius aditum ad libertatem factura, quanto minus vestigiá quidem invitæ molis retineant. Itaque viritim ad auxilia coëundum, ut quam quisque erga conjuges, liberos, denique; patriam affectus sit, tam facilem se præbeat gloriosissimo facinori, quod præsens ævum in libertate moriturum, denique in eâ nascitura posteritas cum gratitudine & veneratione agnitura sit. Ut vero id ocyus fiat, instans discrimen præmonere, ne Lalainius aliquando præsens & militaribus copijs ad arbitrium usus, destruendæ arcis ut ante consilium disturbet. Neque enim id privato motu, aut impetu se aggredi, sed Belgicæ procerum decreto, quod Gubernator Matthias & Aurantius confirmavissent. Eâ ex causâ Frisios liberalitate quadam in communé provinciarum ærarium octodecim aureorum millia & quingentos
units.tr: Through these, the inquisitions and edicts of Caesar and Philip, through the new bishoprics imposed against the people's will, and through a Senate propped up by the majesty of royal power, the complaints of the people were not even given a hearing or a court. Clearly all the violence came out of that workshop, where the blood of innocents, spilled through torture and punishment inflicted on a free nation, still demanded expiation. That most famous cleansing of blood shed for freedom must therefore be purged, not so that superstition may honour it with fire and incense or cleanse it with a sprinkling, but so that the hands of posterity may feel it, since they owe the vindication of their ancestors to the hands of the dead and to the slavish patience of their times. The offerings of brave men, and their innocence, would then be for the shades, if the bulwarks of the tyrant's power were abolished, which would make the way to liberty so much easier as they retained fewer traces of that hateful structure. Therefore let men come together individually to give aid, so that whatever affection each has for wife, children, and finally country, he may show himself as ready for this glorious deed, which the present age will die in freedom and which the posterity born in freedom will acknowledge with gratitude and veneration. That it may happen all the sooner, the imminent danger must be forewarned, lest Lalaing, present with military forces and using them at his pleasure, disrupt the plan to destroy the citadel as he did before. For this is not undertaken from private impulse or passion, but by the decree of the Belgian nobles, which Governor Matthias and Orange had confirmed. For this reason the Frisians, with a certain generosity, had paid eighteen thousand five hundred gold pieces from the common provincial treasury, so that by the benefit of the money contributed they might obtain the consent of public authority for pulling down the castles.

units.la: erogasse, ut ex beneficio collati aeris diruendis castellis assensum publi- cæ autoritatis impetrarent. Cæterum eam à Lalainio occultâ suorum conspiratione elusam, sed quæ non ferat diutius consilium trahi, vindicando Ordinum contemptui & reparandæ libertati salubre. Itaque Lalainij, quas castello destinaverat, copijs proprius ad oppidum & in suburbana suggressis, qua ea amnis è Sylvestribus ortus modico & patiente navium alveo Fletam perlabitur, præmissi in arcem, qui primores præsidij tentarent, dubijsque temporum, ad. exemplum provinciæ rectoris, lubricam quoque militum fidem ære aut gratiâ mercarentur. Cæterum nonnullorum animos, ut Lalainij odium, ita libertatis amor anteceperat. Ita egregiâ simulandi & ne quid enuntiaretur, silentij arte quidam ex præsidiarijs evicti, ne suspectis quidem internuntijs qui miscendis sermonibus, aut pro veteri consuetudine è civitate in castellum commeabant.
units.tr: Otherwise, Lalaing had frustrated this by a secret conspiracy of his own men, but a plan that cannot bear to be delayed for long must be pursued, since it is salutary for avenging the contempt of the States and restoring liberty. Therefore Lalaing's troops, whom he had destined for the castle, advanced closer to the town and its suburbs, where the river, rising from the Sylvestrian lands, flows through Fleta with a modest channel suitable for boats. Men were sent ahead into the citadel to test the leaders of the garrison, and, given the uncertainty of the times, to buy with money or favour the wavering loyalty of the soldiers, following the example of the governor of the province. But the minds of some had already been won over, both by hatred of Lalaing and by love of liberty. Thus some of the garrison, with admirable skill in dissembling and in the art of silence so that nothing would be disclosed, were persuaded, and they did not even trust the go-betweens who, as was their old custom, went from the city to the castle to mix in conversation.

units.la: Quare præparatis rebus Ioannes Bonga, Oeno Grovensteinius & Ioannes Feruovius arcem à tergo circumvenire cum copijs jussi, dispositis Andringanam per domum arci vicinam civium quoque excubitoribus, qui auxilia castello præcluderent.
units.tr: Therefore, with matters prepared, Johannes Bonga, Oeno Grovensteinius and Johannes Feruovius were ordered to surround the citadel from the rear with their forces, while the citizens' sentries were posted at Andringa's house, which is near the citadel, to cut off all help from reaching the castle.

units.la: Heymannus tradit fuisse ex præsidiarijs ,' qui arce deserta inermes centuriæ civicæ sacramentum dicerent, primique ut commilitonibus ad defectionem, ita armatis civibus ad virtutem essent. Igitur illi, sub lucis ortum ad portam progressi, relicta in castello arma tradi sibi petiere, ac ut eorum inopes recepto more in arcem admitterent. Cæterum ejus accessu prohibiti vim intentavere, janitorque glande petitus & fugâ in castellum actus præsidiarij ut arma induerent imperavit. Itaq; signo dato armati convenere, inconditoque clamore, velut obsidium soluturi, regiam arcem, atq; proxumam urbis partem implevere.
units.tr: Heymannus relates that there were some of the garrison who, having abandoned the citadel, were unarmed in a company of the civic guard and took the oath, and were the first, as they had been to their fellow soldiers in defection, so now to the armed citizens in valour. So at sunrise these men went up to the gate and asked that their weapons, left in the castle, be handed over to them, and that, as was customary, they be admitted to the citadel in their unarmed state. But when they were prevented from entering, they threatened violence, and the gatekeeper was struck by a sling-stone and driven in flight into the castle, and the garrison was ordered to arm. Therefore, at a signal given, they assembled armed, and with a disorderly shout, as if about to lift the siege, they filled the royal citadel and the nearest part of the town.

units.la: Cl. Franckena notat Foxium Selsmam cohortis præfectum, colloquio in ponte castelli cum præsidiarijs instituto admitti in arcem postulasse, veriqueq familiaritate salutatis commilitonibus vinum atque officia obtuliße. Henricum quoque Cleinsorgium promptæ audaciæ militem clam à civibus mercede conductum sclopetum janitori intentasse, eundemque ictu evitato, intra arcem receptum, præsidiarios somno graves capienda ad arma instigasse. Idem addit tesseram quoque occupandæ arci datam, ac ut Lambertus cognomento Crassipes ex præsidiarijs, alba fascia, velut facie detersâ, opportunitatem tempori indicaret. Cæterum plenilunium isti maxime consilio adversum, quo fiebat, ut ea quæ obscuro noctis tegi potuissent, interventu syderis & clarissimi lu- minis innotescerent. Præsidiarij quoque quæ per urbis partem arci proxumam fierent, tanquam ex edito colle, beneficio collucentis astri specularentur, quod pernox uti plenilunijs solet, nobilissimum facinus & in posteritatis memoriâ valiturum ab insidijs incipi, velut inglorio & vili consilio dedignabatur. Itaque clariore lunâ & sub lucis ortum discussâ opacitate, quasi palam ad virtutem surgens dies hortaretur, clasficum per urbem datum, pulsatæque civium fores magno sonitu strepuere. Unde milites qui vigilijs noctem extraxerant, secretis domorum, ut & cives exciti sparso in vulgus rumore, præsidiarios novis copijs auctos populandam ad urbem regiâ arce descendere. Quare cives sumptis armis, quæ non nisi capta arce se posituros affirmabant, recta ad arcem ordinatum agmen duxere, in quo sacerdotum turba, tum præsidiariorum arcis liberi atque conjuges captivarum ritu trahebantur. Quæ per principia & primos manipulorum ordines pro munimentis castelli dispositæ tristi spectaculo maritos affecere, quos miseratione inspERATI casus & captivarum conjugum perculsos ad exerendam vim impelli impotentia amoris prohibebat.
units.tr: Franckena notes that Foxius Selsma, prefect of a cohort, asked to be admitted into the citadel when a parley was held with the garrison on the castle bridge, and that, greeting his fellow soldiers with the familiarity of a true comrade, he offered them wine and services. He also notes that Henricus Cleinsorgius, a soldier of ready audacity, was secretly hired by the citizens for money and aimed a musket at the gatekeeper, and that, having avoided the shot, he was received within the citadel and urged the garrison, heavy with sleep, to take up arms at once. The same writer adds that a password was also given for seizing the citadel, and that Lambertus, surnamed Crassipes, of the garrison, with a white band, as if to wipe his face, signalled the opportunity. But the full moon was especially unfavourable to that plan, for it meant that what might have been hidden in the darkness of night became known through the presence of the star and its very bright light. The garrison too, as if from a high hill, could watch by the help of the shining star what was happening in the part of the town nearest the citadel, for the night is wont to be bright in full moons. They disdained that the most noble deed, which would be remembered by posterity, should begin from an ambush, as if it were an inglorious and base plan. Therefore, with the moon brighter and the darkness dispersed at sunrise, as if the day were rising openly to urge them to valour, a trumpet call was sounded through the town, and the doors of the citizens' houses were struck with a loud noise. Whereupon the soldiers, who had spent the night on watch, and the citizens, roused by a rumour spread among the people, that the garrison had been reinforced with new troops and was about to descend from the royal citadel to plunder the town, came forth from the secret parts of the houses. Therefore the citizens, taking up arms which, they declared, they would lay down only after the citadel was taken, led an orderly column straight to the citadel. In it were a crowd of priests, and the children and wives of the garrison were dragged along as captives. These, placed along the headquarters and the front ranks of the companies as a shield for the castle, moved the husbands to sorrow at the sight; moved by pity at the calamity and stricken at the sight of their captive wives, they were driven to use force, but the helplessness of their love held them back.

units.la: Igitur majore conjugalis fidei quam sacramenti apud milites imperio machinis & sclopetis parcitum, ne in innocentes liberos & imbellem conjugum sexum, suum in sanguinem pro tuendâ arce fortis ferocia desæviret. Quare vi omisså in crepidine fossæ, quæ arcem latitudine c c. pedum præcingebat, civium agmen collocatum, quod ab eâ urbis parte, ubi regis viridarium frugiferâ arborum & egregiâ atmocenitate consitum cultumque visebatur, evitando periculo, leni opere communitum. Arbores quoque admotis securibus dolabrisque passim per urbem cæsæ, truncique eminentissimam in struem congesti, altitudinem fossæ opplevere. Tum humo quoque truncis ingestâ, cadu-ceator in arcem missus, quæ à tergo militaribus, à fronte civium copijs & muliebri agmine cincta, auctam ex interceptis auxilijs formidinem præsidio incusserat. Quare Joannes Scagenus vir ex Hollandicâ nobilitate, præfecturam regiæ arcis à morte Mateneffij adeptus, de eâ tradendâ agitavit eamque, salvum & incolume præsidium, sibi pensionem ducentorum aureorum quotannis depactus, dedi civibus fecit.
units.tr: Therefore, through greater loyalty to their marriage than to the oath among the soldiers, they spared the machines and muskets, lest the bold ferocity of brave men rage in its own blood to defend the citadel against innocent children and the unwarlike sex of the wives. Therefore, having laid aside force, the column of citizens was posted on the edge of the ditch, which surrounded the citadel at a width of two hundred feet, and it was fortified with light work, avoiding danger from that part of the town where the king's garden, planted with fruit trees and set in an admirable amenity, could be seen and tended. Trees, too, were felled everywhere through the town with axes and hatchets, and their trunks were heaped into a great pile and filled the depth of the ditch. Then, with earth also heaped on the trunks, a herald was sent into the citadel, which was surrounded at the rear by soldiers and at the front by the civic forces and a crowd of women, and which had been struck with fear, increased by intercepted reinforcements. Therefore Johannes Scagenus, a man of the Holland nobility who had obtained the command of the royal citadel after the death of Mateneff, bargained over its surrender, and had it given up to the citizens, having secured for the garrison a safe and unharmed withdrawal and for himself a pension of two hundred gold pieces a year.

units.la: Creditum fuit Scagenum à Lamberto Crassipede, qui pro dedendo castello apud milites concionatus ferebatur, imprimis persuasum Ordinum partibus eam permisisse, & quod auxiliorum Lalaiñij exspes aut incertus animum ultro imbellem subortis pavoribus despondisset.
units.tr: It was believed that Scagenus had been persuaded, above all, by Lambertus Crassipes, who was reported to have preached to the soldiers in favour of surrendering the castle, to yield it to the party of the States; and that, having lost hope or being uncertain of Lalaing's help, he had of his own accord despaired, his spirit made timid by sudden fears.

units.la: Mox valli propugnaculum, qua urbem spectat, à populo civico disjectum, fossâque framento pulvere ac cæno oppletâ, apparitores civesque armati præsidio arcis delecti.
units.tr: Soon the bastion of the rampart, which faces the town, was broken down by the civic populace, and the ditch was filled with rubble, dust and mud; the officers and armed citizens were then assigned to guard the citadel.

units.la: Viginti sex sclopetarios fuisse Cl. Franckena notat, idque memorabile civicæ virtutis & libertatis facinus in Kalendas Februarias incidisse. Idem subjungit explicatâ ad fossæ marginem captivâ sacerdotum fœminarumque turbâ, unam masculi animi & ex primis viraginem maritum in vallo arcis stantem sacramenti regij & officij altâ voce monuisse, pectusque marito convulnerandum muliebri temeritate, aut singulari in regem fide obtulisse. Eandem quoque à cive quodam ictum comminante ægrè ad modestiam perductam, perseverantemque & occasionem turbis aut cædi intemperantiâ linguæ datuam extra contubernium captivi agminis abductam. Ita arx octoginta ante annos civium sumptu Willibrordi Scouwenbergij Alberti Saxoniæ Ducis Præfecti tempore extructa, ab ijsdem excusso veteris servitij onere, diruta atque solo æquata. Mox civibus destruendo castello occupatis Bongæ, Grovensteinij & Feruovij cohortes in urbem evocatæ, Franciscanique cum Canonicis & omni Clero inter tympanorum tibiarumque sonos & simul contumelias ac ludibria militaris lasciviæ urbe eductí. Sunt qui tradant præter centuriam è cive conscriptam, quatuor quoque civium cohortes obsesso castello erectas, earumque ductores
units.tr: Franckena notes that there were twenty-six musketeers, and that this memorable deed of civic courage and liberty fell on the first of February. He adds that, when the crowd of captive priests and women had been set out at the edge of the ditch, one woman of a manly spirit and foremost among the viragos called out in a loud voice to her husband, who was standing on the rampart of the citadel, to remember his royal oath and duty; and that with a woman's rashness, or singular loyalty to the king, she offered her breast to be pierced by her husband. He also says that she was, with difficulty, brought to moderation by a citizen who threatened to strike her, but that, persisting and giving occasion for a riot or slaughter through the intemperance of her tongue, she was led away outside the tent of the captive column. Thus the citadel, built eighty years earlier at the expense of the citizens, in the time of Willibrord Scouwenberg, prefect of Duke Albert of Saxony, was by the same citizens, having shaken off the burden of the old servitude, demolished and levelled with the ground. Soon, while the citizens were busy destroying the castle, the cohorts of Bonga, Grovensteinius and Feruovius were called back into the town, and the Franciscans with the canons and all the clergy were led out of the city amid the sound of drums and pipes, and at the same time amid the insults and mockery of military wantonness. Some relate that, besides the company enrolled from the citizens, four cohorts of citizens were also raised for the siege of the castle, and their commanders...

units.la: Ar-
units.tr: Ar-

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. lxxx. Ebbæum Douwonium cum Gellio Paulino, Adriano Leonartio, Cornelio Cornelij & Pibone Douwonio vexilliferis egregia civicæ sortitudinis exempla ciendis militum studijs edidisse. Eosdem quoque caedendis arboribus & opplendæ fossæ sacerdotum captivarumque mulierum ministerio usus, tormentaque grandiora Saxoniæ Ducum, tum Caroli Philippique insignibus notata per imbellem puerorum turbam in urbem abducta. Ita machinas moveri loco difficiles impotens virium ætas tractabat, non sine fati, sicuti creditum fuit & commentarijs perscriptum, miraculo, ut easdem adulterata libertate peregrini militis ope majorum ævo in castellum invectas inter ludum jocumque inops armorum civilis posteritas amoveret.
units.tr: 1580. Ebbaeus Douwonius, together with Gellius Paulinus, Adrianus Leonartius, Cornelius Cornelii and Pibo Douwonius, the standard-bearers, gave outstanding examples of civic courage in rousing the zeal of the soldiers. The same men also used the labour of priests and captive women to fell trees and fill in the ditch, and the larger cannon of the Dukes of Saxony, marked with the arms of Charles and Philip, were dragged into the town by a feeble crowd of boys. So the unfit age of the defenceless citizens managed the engines that were hard to move there, not without what was believed and recorded as a miracle of fate, since those same engines, which in an earlier age a foreign soldier had carried into the castle by his help and with liberty corrupted, were now removed amid play and jokes by a posterity of citizens without arms.

units.la: Arce capta & omni opere urbem versus diruto Harlingam quoque cohortes, quas Feruovius & Bonga ducebant, oppugnando castello praemissæ, quod ad occasum solis æstivum olim Groningensium & Saxonum ætate extructum, oppido nullo aut rudi mænium ambitu præcincto æstuario maris dominabatur. Iter navigijs quidem nocturno tempore institutum, quod sublustre navigantibus & Luna faciebat & officijs nautarum opportunum, quæ beneficio claræ noctis & ut lucem antevenirent, militum quoque ministerijs celerabantur.
units.tr: With the castle taken and all its works razed on the side facing the town, the cohorts led by Feruovius and Bonga were also sent ahead to attack Harlingen castle. It had been built in the time of the Groningers and Saxons, facing the midsummer sunset, and, with no town or only a rude circuit of walls around it, it commanded the estuary of the sea. The approach was made by boat at night, which the faint moonlight made visible to the sailors and suited to their work. Thanks to the clear night, and so as to get ahead of the daylight, it was also speeded along by the soldiers' service.

units.la: Igitur naves Harlingam provectæ, alto silentio intra urbem admissæ, credulo janitore mercibus aut frumento onustas vicinis ex agris appulisse. Sunt qui tradant eum secreti conscium à Delegatis Ordinum Douwone Sixma & Econe Isbrandio, qui in comitatu Grovensteinij & Vedæ, quæ sequebantur, cohortium erant, clam in partes pertractum omnem sinistri suspicionem dissimulavisse, etsi fulgore noctis & militarium armorum facilè proderentur, quæ corrupti janitoris credulitas velaverat.
units.tr: Accordingly the ships were carried to Harlingen and admitted into the town in deep silence, and the credulous gatekeeper supposed they had come from the nearby fields laden with goods or grain. Some relate that he, being privy to the secret, was secretly won over to their side by the deputies of the Estates, Douwo Sixma and Ecco Isbrandius, who were with Grovensteyn and Veda, whose cohorts followed, and that he dissembled all suspicion of wrongdoing. Yet the brightness of the night and the glint of soldiers' arms would easily have betrayed them, had not the gatekeeper's bribed credulity veiled them.

units.la: Tum miles per vicinas arci civium domos clam distributus, missusque sub lucis ortum in castellum caduceator, qui deditionem peteret, aut ut in colloquium pacificendis conditionibus veniretur.
units.tr: Then the soldiers were quietly distributed through the houses of citizens near the castle, and at sunrise a herald was sent to the castle to demand its surrender, or else to be admitted to a parley to settle terms.

units.la: Formula hæc erat. Quoniam Præsidiarij arcem Harlinganam contra expressa decreta MATTHIAE Archiducis Austriæ Belgicæ Gubernatoris, AURANTII Principis & DEPUTATORUM foederataram provinciarum præsidio tenerent: Ita DEPUTATOS ORDINUM Frisiæ tam agrarios, quam oppidanos arcem eandem dedi ORDINIBUS suis postulare, ac ut cum eadem de voluntate MATTHIAE Archiducis, AURANTII & ORDINUM generalium agatur, horario interim spatio ad deliberandum dato.
