Intra quod si non decernant, pro contumacibus habituros. Sin vero præsidiarij introspiciendis ORDINUM Frisiæ actis & rationibus delegare è suis parati sint commeatum sejs hoc ipso facere, idque sub sigilli publici fide. IV. Non. Febr.
units.tr: The formula was this. Since the garrison holds the castle of Harlingen against the express decrees of Matthias, Archduke of Austria and Governor of the Belgian provinces, of William, Prince of Orange, and of the Deputies of the United Provinces, the Deputies of the Estates of Friesland, both rural and urban, demand that the same castle be surrendered to their Estates, and that this be negotiated with the will of Matthias the Archduke, Orange and the General Estates, an hour's space being given meanwhile for deliberation. If within that time they do not decide, they will be held as contumacious. But if the garrison is ready to send some of its own to inspect the acts and accounts of the Estates of Friesland, they will thereby grant a safe-conduct, and this under the faith of the public seal. February 2.

units.la: Quo ipso, etsi præsidiarij, velut inæperato casu, percellentur, ita evoluto horæ spatio responderunt:
units.tr: Although the garrison were struck as by an unexpected blow, after an hour had passed they replied in this way:

units.la: • Optimo jure & ex formulâ sacramenti (quam MATTHIAS Gubernator, AURANTIUS princeps & Generales ORDINES approbassent) LALAINIO Comiti Rennebergio & HENRICO OYENBRUGGIO Satrapæ præstita, arcem se præsidio tenere. Neque enim enim eo sacramento per MATTHIAM Archiducem AURANTIUM aut Generales ORDINES se exsolutos esse, in quo perstare etiamnum in animum inducerent. Nisi forte ex actis de voluntate MATTHIAE, AURANTIJ, ORDINUM, LALAINIJ, aut OYENBRUGGIJ secus doceantur. Quod si fiat facturos quod aequum esset. Se vero, si vim parari sentiant, suis officijs atque partibus non defore quin daturos operam ut factorum suorum ratio à sacramenti sui lege ac religione non discrepet. IV. Non. Febr. in arce horâ ante meridiem decimâ.
units.tr: • Under the best right, and according to the formula of the oath (which Matthias the Governor, William the Prince and the General Estates had approved) sworn to Lalaing, Count of Rennenberg, and to Henry Oyenbrugge, Satrap, we hold the castle with a garrison. For we are not released from that oath by Matthias the Archduke, William, or the General Estates, and we intend to persist in it still, unless perhaps the acts show otherwise concerning the will of Matthias, William, the Estates, Lalaing or Oyenbrugge. If that is done, we shall do what is just. But if we perceive force being prepared, we shall not fail in our duties and parts to take care that the account of our deeds does not depart from the law and religion of our oath. February 2, in the castle, at ten o'clock before noon.

units.la: Ita praesidium veteris sacramenti retinens, virtutis quoque opinionem de se induerat, aucta ex loco fiduciâ, quem latiore vallo & fossâ emunitum, tum commeatu bellico instructum aperti quoque maris vicinum aestuarium commendabat. Quare ne mari, quod arci in occidentem est, auxilia à Lalainio aut aliunde, advenirent, praesidiariâ Ordinum navis in portu cum armatis stare jussa, quae hostilium velorum cursus moraretur, ostiumque latissimi portus defenderet. Itaque omnia obsidionem diuturnam & periculi plenam spectare videbantur validâ inprimis & inexpugnabili arce, quae promontorij in modum ad mare excurrens, ne aditum quidem nisi pontis beneficio venientibus ex urbe concedebat. Adhaec in eâ castelli parte, qua ortum solis & urbem spectabat, valli derupta ac summitates conspiciebantur, quae machinis ac tormentis aeneis longâ serie instructa difficilis loci accessu obsidentes copias prohibebant.
units.tr: Thus holding the garrison of the old oath, it had also gained a reputation for courage, its confidence raised by the place itself. It was strengthened by a wide rampart and ditch, furnished with military supplies, and it commanded the nearby estuary of the open sea. Therefore, lest help should come by sea to the west of the castle from Lalaing or elsewhere, a naval vessel of the Estates' garrison was ordered to lie in the harbour with armed men, to hold back the course of enemy sails and guard the mouth of the very wide harbour. So everything seemed to point to a long and dangerous siege, especially since the castle was strong and impregnable. Jutting out into the sea like a promontory, it allowed no access to those coming from the town except by the bridge. Moreover, on the side of the castle facing the rising sun and the town, broken ramparts and summits could be seen, which, equipped with a long line of engines and bronze cannon, kept the besieging forces away by the difficulty of access to the place.

units.la: Cl. Franckena notat eas quoque in urbem displosas incendium dedisse, quod etiam civili militumque ope per initia emergentis flammae repressum tamen dubijs & de eventu desperantibus terrorem incusserat. Alius quidam scriptor, etsi rerum ignarus, tradit tres è civibus machinarum globis verberatos inriti laboris atque consilij conjecturam aggravasse & quod praesidij vigor primo obsidij impetu fractus, velut resumptâ virtute, sedato sanguine revalesceret. Itaque apud Ordinum Legatos & inter cives triste silentium erat, dispositis tantum circa proxumam urbis partem, qua arcem spectat, excubitoribus, qui securitati urbis & obsidentium haberentur. Unde praesidiarijs, ut humanum ingenium apprehendendis suspicionibus facile & pronum est, opinio hostilis consilij nata ac si de opplendis terra civium aedibus arci vicinis & tumultuario opere specie excubiarum erigendo obsidentes praefecti agitarent. Cui rei imprimis non vanum indicium faciebat, quod captiva Graphaei uxor qui pro Oyenbruggio, Groningae apud Lalainium tum agente, arcem cum imperio tenebat, ab obsidentibus asservaretur, filiumque infantem innocenti & quae extra odium sit aetate materna captivitatis communio gravaret. Itaque litteris ex arce per tympanotribam ad legatos Ordinum exaratis de vi atque injuria conquesti petiere, ut milites habendis excubijs delectos à fronte arcis amoverent, uxoriq; captivae & Satrapae filio venia daretur. Alias statuturos se egregium fidei & fortitudinis exemplum usurosque viribus suis quas ad tutelam commissae sibi arcis Deus daturus foret. Obtestari interim Deum, Matthiam Gubernatorem, Aurantium Principem, Ordines generales & imprimis optimorum civium fidem, insontes & extra culpam se fore si quid incommodi miserae civitati ex illo clo. Io. illo consilio obveniat. Quibus litteris ab ORDINUM LEGA-LXXX. TIS responsum:
units.tr: Franckena notes that these engines, when they were fired into the town, also set a fire going, which, though checked in its first stages by the efforts of the citizens and soldiers, nonetheless struck terror into those who were doubtful and despaired of the outcome. Another writer, though ignorant of the facts, relates that three citizens struck by the engines' balls increased the conjecture of a vain and fruitless effort and plan, and that the garrison's strength, broken at the first assault of the siege, revived as if its courage had been regained and its blood had settled. So among the deputies of the Estates and among the citizens there was a grim silence, with sentries posted only around the nearest part of the town, which faces the castle, to guard the town's safety against the besiegers. Hence the garrison, since the human mind readily and naturally seizes upon suspicion, conceived the opinion that the besieging commanders were plotting a hostile plan: under the pretext of sentries, they would fill the citizens' houses near the castle with rubble and erect a hasty work. Especially did this give no empty sign, that the captive wife of Graphaeus, who held the castle with command for Oyenbrugge, then acting at Groningen with Lalaing, was kept in custody by the besiegers, and that her infant son, an innocent of an age beyond hatred, was burdened with his mother's captivity. Therefore, by a letter written from the castle and carried by a drummer to the Deputies of the Estates, they complained of violence and injury, and asked that the soldiers chosen for guarding be removed from the front of the castle, and that pardon be granted to the captive wife and to the Satrap's son. Otherwise, they said, they would set an outstanding example of faith and courage and would use the strength which God would give for the defence of the castle committed to them. Meanwhile they called God, Matthias the Governor, William the Prince, the General Estates, and above all the good faith of the best citizens, to witness that they would be innocent and free of blame if any harm should befall the wretched city from that plan. To this letter the Deputies of the Estates replied:

units.la: Munimentis actorum se stare & esse in ijs, quod praesidiarios inofficiosi aut temerata in Matthiam Gubernatorem reliquosque fidei redarguat. Quorum copiam si vellent, mitterent ex suis aut obsides darent, qui introspicerent. Non dubitare quin eo facto Ordinum arbitrijs se permissuri sint exemplo Scageni & Adriani Potteri Leovardianae arcis rectorum, qui militares animos atq; gloriam honestae paci atque transactioni interposuissent. Atque eam ipsam Matthiam Gubernatorem, Aurantium Principem & Ordines generales ratihabituros se cavere, non alia consilij sui intentione, quam ut singula rite & decenter fiant. Sin vero nec legatos expedire perseverent, missuros se in arcem captiam decreti fide publicorum testium roboratam, ut intelligant summae procerum autoritati suum consilium inniti. Quod ad amovendas militum excubias, ad captivam cum filiolo matrem Graphaei conjugem attineret, eam non hostili animo in custodiam pertractam, caeterum ut miseratione captivorum pignorum mariti pietas accenderetur, facilius-que loci deditio ex legitimi amoris imperio procederet.
units.tr: They stood by the record of the acts, and asserted that in them the garrison was refuted as disobedient or as having violated its faith to Matthias the Governor and the rest. If they wished for copies, they should send some of their own or give hostages, who would inspect them. They did not doubt that by doing so they would submit themselves to the judgment of the Estates, after the example of Scagenius and Adrianus Potter, governors of the castle at Leeuwarden, who had placed the soldiers' spirits and glory at the service of an honourable peace and agreement. And they would see that Matthias the Governor, William the Prince and the General Estates would ratify the same, their only intention being that each matter be done rightly and properly. But if they persisted in refusing to send deputies, they would send into the captured castle a decree confirmed by the good faith of public witnesses, so that they might understand that their plan rests on the supreme authority of the nobles. As for removing the sentries, and the captive mother, wife of Graphaeus, with her little son, she had not been taken into custody with hostile intent; rather, the husband's loyalty should be kindled by pity for captive pledges, and the surrender of the place would more easily follow from the rule of lawful love.

units.la: Caeterum praesidiarij cum fide dicta aut scripta pro dolosis interpretabantur.
units.tr: Meanwhile the garrison interpreted the words spoken or written as treacherous.

units.la: Quorsum enim (inquiebant) inter amicos, ac unius rectoris & sacramenti consortes excubias ordinari, innocentissimos suorum in vincula duci, quam ut ab hostili actione negotium inciperent, cujus animum praeferrent? Communicanda fuisse, si quae essent, Gubernatoris aut Ordinum acta neque mox ad vim & auxilia cohortium provocandum absente Oyenbruggio satrapa, quem publica auctoritas regundae arci praefecisset. Se in Lalainy verba adstante Pompeio Vfkenio juraisse, homine quod scirent Aurantij partibus addictissimo. Sed in faciem pacis venire bellum cogitantes.
units.tr: Why, they said, should sentries be posted among friends and partners in one command and one oath, and the most innocent of their own be led into chains, unless they were beginning an action of hostility, whose intent they were displaying? If there were any acts of the Governor or of the Estates, they should have been shared with us, and not straightaway, without Satrap Oyenbrugge, whom public authority had set over the government of the castle, a call to force and to the help of the cohorts. They had sworn to Lalaing's words with Pompeius Vfkenius standing by, a man who, as they knew, was most devoted to Orange's party. But they were planning war under the face of peace.

units.la: Unde omnium animis paucorum calore ac impulsu sustinendam ad vim excitatis, grandiores machinae in urbem laxatae, donec vespera-scente die priora repetendo sententiam, veluti mansuram, scripto hunc in modum enuntiarent.
units.tr: With the minds of everyone roused to take up arms by the heat and urging of a few men, larger engines were let loose against the city. As the day drew towards evening, they repeated their earlier resolution and announced it in writing, in this form, as though it would stand.

units.la: PETIIMVS, Legati Ordinum & militares praefecti, ut Matthiae Gubernatoris, Aurantij Principis, Ordinum generalium, Lalainij aut Satrapae decretum, si quod esset, exhiberetis. Quorum sacramento quia nostra nos fides obligavit & etiamnum obligat, ita sine eorum mandato dedere castellum in animum non induximus. Quare ex commilitonibus aut socijs nostris legare ad colloquium aut visenda acta non necessarium censemus, cum totum negotium a mandato supremae autoritatis pendeat. Id a Lalainio aut Satrapa Oyenbruggio si habeamus morem geremus vestro & Ordinum desiderio, arcemque nobis commissam vestrae potestatis faciemus. Sed diem sermonibus aut scribendis actis terere, nobis otium aut integrum non est. Quin ejus sententiae sumus ut de repellenda & simul inferenda vi cogitemus & ut ferro ac incendio nostra virtus se defendat. Igitur non feremus noctem quietam in urbe eos agere, qui ejus beneficio abusi, cum sola mandati exhibitione ad pacem potuissent rem, ad arma deduxere.
units.tr: We ask you, Legates of the States and military commanders, to show us the decree of Matthias the Governor, of Prince William, of the General States, of Lalaing, or of the Satrap, if there is one. Since our own faith has bound us by oath to them, and still binds us, we have not brought ourselves to surrender the castle without their mandate. For this reason we do not think it necessary to send any of our fellow soldiers or associates to a conference or to inspect the records, since the whole matter depends on the mandate of the supreme authority. If we have it from Lalaing or the Satrap Oyenbruggio, we will comply with your wish and that of the States, and place the citadel committed to us under your power. But we have no leisure to waste the day in talk or in writing up documents. Indeed, we are of the opinion that we should consider repelling force and at the same time inflicting it, and that our courage should defend itself with sword and fire. Therefore we will not suffer those who abused his kindness, and who could have settled the matter peacefully by merely producing the mandate, but instead brought it to arms, to spend a quiet night in the city.

units.la: Quae ubi Groningam perlata, animum Lalainij multum famae ex conscienscientiâ largientem subiere, Ballæus à secretis & epistolis è Translavica- nis in Frisios missus qui consilia Ordinum exploraret, tantaque rerum mutationi clam se interponeret. Itaq; Leovardiam progressus, ubi omnia ex recenti arcis destructione adhuc servebant murorum ruderâ & disjecta veteris imperij munimenta cum indignatione speculatus praefecti fidem Senatui Ordinum in fereto commendavit, dirutaque arcis pulcherrimum facinus & Lalainio placiturum insigni elogio extulit. Quod quanquam falsâ laude aspersum & ab animo secus sentiente profectum prudentiores scirent, ita suspectioris & falsae vocis fiduciâ non movebantur, gnari hominem aulae moribus & ultro peregrinâ ac versatili levitate mobilem venalis linguae officia corrupto pectori obtrudere. Igitur recidentibus in vanum assentationibus & quod secreta literarum perferre à Lalainio crederetur, custodiae datus amandatusque in arcem est, quam miseranda facie deformem & vestigia civici furoris adhuc repraesentantem, velut reciproco fati solatio, captivus & gemens intuebatur. Ibi inquisitionibus judicum, post evulgandis, quae abstruserat arcanis tormentorum & mortis metu ad confessionem mandati adactus, chartas aperit, quas solo Lalainij sigillo & nomine signatas caeterum occasionibus rerum & temporum serviturás optumus, ut censebatur, doli artifex circumferebat. Quae commoda potiundae arcis occasio fuit. Quippe praescribere, quae Ordines vellent, jussus pro faciendâ celerandâque deditione Lalainij literas figuravit ementitusque mandatum Praefecti, quod retinendis in officio arcium rectoribus clam acceperat, fidem constanter datam terrore mortis aut cruciatuum evinci passus est.
units.tr: When this was carried to Groningen, Lalaing, who was conscious of much blame he could not avoid, was alarmed. Ballaeus, secretary and clerk of letters, was sent from Overijssel to the Frisians to spy out the plans of the States and to insert himself secretly into the change of affairs. So he went on to Leeuwarden, where everything was still boiling from the recent destruction of the citadel: the rubble of the walls and the scattered fortifications of the old government. Observing these with indignation, he commended the loyalty of the prefect to the Senate of the States in a festal speech, and praised the razing of the citadel as a splendid deed that would please Lalaing, with the highest commendation. Although the more prudent knew that this praise was false and came from a mind thinking otherwise, they were not moved by the confidence of such a suspicious and false voice. They knew that the man, by the habits of the court and by a foreign and fickle lightness, was ready to thrust the services of a venal tongue upon a corrupt heart. So, since his flatteries came to nothing, and since he was believed to carry secret letters from Lalaing, he was placed under guard and sent to the citadel. Looking upon it, disfigured in its pitiful appearance and still showing the traces of civic fury, he gazed at it as a captive and groaning, as if it were a kind of reciprocal consolation of fate. There, under the interrogations of the judges, and afterwards, when the fear of torture and death drove him from the secrets he had concealed, he was forced to confess the mandate and opened the papers. These bore only Lalaing's seal and name, and were carried about, as was thought, by the best artisan of deceit, ready to serve the opportunities of the moment and the times. This was the opportunity to seize the citadel. He was ordered to write whatever the States wished, to hasten and effect the surrender. So he forged letters of Lalaing, and, pretending to have the mandate of the prefect, which he had secretly received for keeping the commanders of the citadels in their duty, he allowed the pledge given with steady faith to be overcome by fear of death or of torments.

units.la: LITTERAE ad praesidiarios datae hae erant.
units.tr: LETTERS sent to the garrison were as follows.

units.la: QVANDO QVIDEM non sine animi dolore intelligo motus per Frisiam ex causa diruendarum arcium ortos (quas in manus suas tradi aut solo aequari ex decreto Matthiae Gubernatoris Senatus Ordinum petierat) ita negotium à sedecim mensium spatio prolatum exequi paratus sum. Itaque arces aut castella Ordinum potestatis facio, mandoque ut meae voluntatis per has certiores facti, arcem, quam defenditis, dedatis oc-yus. Vos quoque deserta arce (cujus commeatum in commentarium Ordines referent) conduci ex illorum arbitrio vos sinatis dum praesens de stipendijs exsolvendis cum Senatu egero. In fidem harum manum meam & sigillum subjunxi. Groningae iv. Non. Febr.
units.tr: Although I understand, not without grief of mind, the disturbances arising in Friesland over the demolition of the citadels (which the Senate of the States had asked, by decree of Matthias the Governor, to be handed over to them or levelled with the ground), I am prepared to carry out the matter, which has been deferred over a space of sixteen months. Therefore I make the citadels or castles subject to the power of the States, and I order you, being informed of my will by these letters, to surrender the citadel you are defending. Also, having abandoned the citadel (whose provisions the States will report in their records), you are to allow yourselves to be led away at their discretion, while I am present and treat with the Senate about paying your wages. In witness of these things I have subscribed my hand and added my seal. Groningen, 2 February.

units.la: His à Balleio ad Graphaeum additae, quae habebant Barthio Idzaerdae cum praesidiarijs transfigendi potestatem à Praefecto factam, cujus id severum & pertinax mandatum esset & arcem derent. Igitur à praesidiarijs Barthius Idsaerda, fide datâ & oblato obside in arcem ad colloquium evocatus eoque sive periculi metu, sive ex conscientiâ doli repudiato ad aequissima conditionum & in ijs exsolvendis stipendijs praesidio se obligavit. Itaque tum mitigatis animis ad colloquium deventum, missique in arcem Regnerus Nicolaus Consul civitatis & Eco Isbrandius Ordinum actuarius, qui cum praesidiarijs pacisceretur. Quae dum fiunt litterae quoq; à Lalainio & Oyenbruggio Groningâ venere, quibus præsidiarij fortes strenuosq; se gerere in tolerando obsidio monebantur. Ita scilicet fidem sibi Præfecto & Satrapæ datam, ita militare sacramentum servaturos, habiturosque ex se decus atque gloriam ubi in provinciam advenerint, stipendiâ & donativa egregiæ virtutis præmia. Adhæc auxilia brevi ad fore, quæ si terrâ intercludantur, mare apertum polliceri, per quod arx adiri navigijs & cum necessario commeatu posset.
units.tr: To these letters Ballaeus added others, which gave Barthius of Idzaerda the power, granted by the prefect, to dispatch the garrison, although the prefect's order was stern and firm, and to abandon the citadel. So Barthius, having given his word and offered a hostage, was summoned from Idzaerda by the garrison to a conference in the citadel. Whether from fear of danger or from awareness of the deceit, he rejected the very fair conditions and bound the garrison to them, including the payment of their wages. So, with minds now calmed, they came to a conference, and Regnerus Nicolaus, consul of the city, and Eco Isbrandius, clerk of the States, were sent into the citadel to negotiate with the garrison. While this was going on, letters from Lalaing and Oyenbruggio also arrived from Groningen, urging the garrison to behave bravely and steadfastly in enduring the siege. They were to keep faith with the prefect and the Satrap, keep their military oath, and win honour and glory for themselves once they had arrived in the province, with pay and gifts as rewards of distinguished courage. Moreover, help would soon be at hand, and if they were cut off by land, an open sea was promised, by which the citadel could be approached with ships and with the necessary supplies.

units.la: Quamobrem Legati Ordinum resignatis quas interceperant litteris, festinandum rati, præsidiarios dedendæ arcis monuere, ac ut excusså vani & non apparentis auxilij spe honestas certasque pacis conditiones, obversantibus periculis anteponerent. Cæterum præsidiarij, nocte ad deliberandum petitâ, in posterum consilium extraxere, quod ut in talibus solet, dubium & sui incertum inter præsentium tædia & discrimina ac futuri spem fluctuabat. Quam ipsam quoque visæ ex arce quasi ex speculâ naves obfirmavere, quæ ex alto venientes subvectare auxilia fervidius sperantibus credebantur. Sed deprehenso onerarias esse, mutatoque velorum flexu à littore recedere, languor aliquis & mox desperatio præsidiarios invasit. Itaque stipendia & omne æris residuum depaēti, arcem dedidere ex quâ cum armis & impedimentis effusi omnem infamiæ metum ardore futuræ hilaritatis excusserant.
units.tr: Therefore the legates of the States, having handed over the letters they had intercepted, thought haste necessary. They warned the garrison to surrender the citadel, and to put honourable and sure terms of peace before the dangers threatening them, having cast off the hope of an empty and non-existent relief. The garrison, however, asked for a night to deliberate, and the next day they dragged out their council, which, as usual in such matters, wavered doubtfully and uncertain of itself, between the weariness and dangers of the present and the hope of the future. Ships seen from the citadel, as if from a lookout, strengthened this hope: they were coming from the deep, and were believed to be bringing help to men who hoped eagerly for it. But when they were recognised as merely transport ships, and, their sails turning, withdrew from the shore, a certain languor and soon despair seized the garrison. So, having lost hope of pay and of all the money left, they surrendered the citadel. Pouring out of it with their arms and baggage, they had shaken off all fear of disgrace with the eagerness of their coming cheer.

units.la: Quippe cunctantibus, mediam Anglicæ cerevisiæ lastam liberalitas Consulis addixerat, qui multitudinem tenui victu diu habitam, illo liquore permulcendam celerendæ deditioni persuaserat. Unde versâ in securitatem militarium animorum formidine, per tabernas arci proxumas distributi præsidiarij genialem diem egere. Id Non. Febr. annales tradunt validissimisque castellis in potestatem redigendis vix quintiduum insumptum.
units.tr: For while they hesitated, the generosity of the consul had secured a measure of English beer, which he had persuaded them, who had long been kept on slender fare, to soothe with that liquor, so as to hasten the surrender. Thus the fear in the soldiers' minds turned into carelessness, and the garrison, distributed through the taverns next to the citadel, spent a festive day. The annals record this as the Nones of February, and that scarcely five days were spent in bringing the strongest castles under power.

units.la: Mox ex Groningensium mercatoribus, qui cum præsidiario milite sermones miscuerant, una cum buccinatore vinculis dati, quos Lalainius deditionis auxius firmando ad constantiam præsidio summisisse, neque fallacibus conjecturis credebatur. Henrico Crabbio civi Harlingano glande plumbeâ per temeritatem icto, funus mox factum. Alij ex actis addunt præsidiarios præter stipendiorum solutionem operariorum quoque mercedem depactos & ut captiva Graphæi uxor cum filio patri ac marito traderentur. Ista pro legatis Ordinum à Dominico Richæo qui Franequerano Magistratui ab epistolis tum erat & ab Everardo Keilero, Egberto Huisinghio vexillifero, Thoma Livio, Conrado Meicro & Graphæo signata. Sic validissimo castello nullo sanguine redempto, civium ope, qui præsidio militum successerant, propugnacula valli disjecta ipsaque arx eodem cum urbe mænium ambitu sepTA, validissimis operibus nudata.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, some Groningen merchants who had mixed in conversation with the soldiers were bound in chains together with a trumpeter, whom Lalaing had sent in, anxious to secure the surrender and to strengthen the garrison in its resolve. It was not believed that this was a mere guess. Henry Crabbe, a citizen of Harlingen, struck by a leaden bullet through recklessness, was soon given a funeral. Other accounts add that the garrison, besides the payment of their wages, also stipulated the wages of the labourers, and that the captive wife of Graphaeus should be handed over with her son to her father and husband. These terms were signed on behalf of the legates of the States by Dominicus Richaeus, who was then secretary of letters to the magistracy of Franeker, and by Everardus Keilerus, Egbertus Huisinghius the standard-bearer, Thomas Livius, Conradus Meicrus, and Graphaeus. So the most powerful castle was taken without any bloodshed, by the help of the citizens, who had succeeded the soldiers in the garrison. The defensive works of the rampart were pulled down, and the citadel itself, enclosed within the same circuit of walls as the city, was stripped of its very strong defences.

units.la: Nicolaus vir apud Staurios consularis suis in notis tradit, Graphæo arcis rectori & vicario Oyenbruggij Satrapæ mille quingentos aureos ex causâ deditionis assignatos, stipendiaque præsidiario militi præsenti aere exsoluta. Tum Oenonis Grovensteinij & Cornelij Modæ cohortes navibus impositæ eaque cum præsidiarià, quæ legatos vehebat superato mari aut interiore æstuario Stauriam appulere. Quæ vetus oppidum olim regni sede, post commercio & opibus florens arce tum premebatur, tur, quæ ad ortum solis hybernum in maris littore primum sub Alberto Banero, post à Georgio Schenckio Tautenburgio, Carolo v. Cæsa-re, libertatem & simul luxuriam divitis populi arctaverat. Ibi legatis in terram egressis obvij cives armato agmine processerunt, salutatosq; humaniter & velut servitium cervicibus depulsuros in urbem duxere.
units.tr: Nicolaus, a consular man at Stavoren, records in his notes that one thousand five hundred gold coins were assigned to Graphaeus, the commander of the citadel and deputy of Satrap Oyenbruggio, as the price of the surrender, and that the garrison soldiers present were paid their wages in cash. Then the cohorts of Oeno Groveneveld and Cornelius Moda, loaded on ships, together with the garrison that carried the legates, crossed the sea or the inner estuary and landed at Stavoren. This old town, once the seat of a kingdom and afterwards flourishing with trade and wealth, was then oppressed by its citadel. The citadel lies towards the winter sunrise on the shore of the sea, and was first tightened under Albert Bane and afterwards under Georgius Schenck of Tautenburg, under Charles V, Caesar, which had restrained the liberty and at the same time the luxury of a rich people. When the legates had landed, citizens came to meet them with an armed band, and, greeting them courteously, led them into the city as if they were about to cast off servitude from their necks.

units.la: Sanoiius quoque Baudimontij Graphiarij Ordinum litteris in auxilium advocatus isthuc loci copias quoque trium cohortium adduxerat. Unde qui deditionem poscerent, in castellum missi, quod Franciscus Pipenpoius Bruxellensis illius orae praetor Satrapae titulo modico cum praesidio tenebat. Is non ignarus quibus artibus Harlinganum praesidium solertia legatorum circumvenisset, postulata Ordinum non sine contemptu rejecit, loci & suarum virium imprimis fiducia, quae hominem gloriae avidum, etsi partes libertatis ante professum, retinendae apud Lalainium gratiae corruperat. Caeterum auxiliorum spe excusa & quod Oyenbruggius cum Lubberto Gallo Lalainij fidissimo defecisse diceretur, animum mutavit, totumque negotium Aurantij decreto permisit.
units.tr: Sonoy, too, was called in to help by the letters of Baudemont, the Clerk of the States, and brought up three companies of troops to that place. Those who demanded surrender were sent to the fort, which Franciscus Pipenpoy of Brussels, governor of that coast, held with a garrison under the modest title of Satrap. Knowing well by what tricks the envoys had gained the garrison of Harlingen through their skill, he rejected the demands of the States with some contempt, relying above all on the strength of his position and his own forces. This had corrupted a man greedy for glory, who had earlier professed the cause of liberty, and who wished to keep the favour of Lalaing. But when the hope of reinforcements failed, and it was reported that Oyenbrugge had deserted to Lubbert Gallus, Lalaing's most faithful man, he changed his mind and left the whole business to the decision of Orange.

units.la: Quo faciebat, quod praeter signorum ductores in fugam abreptos, militum quoque fides & sacramentum nutaret, rectoremque exercitus suâ virtute, quamdiu integer fuisset ad res magnas evectum nunc documenta instabilis animi edentem acerbiore odio consectaretur. Igitur retentatus à Legatis Pipenpojus, qui praesidiario militi stipendia ipsi Satrapae retinendae praeturae dignitatem & cum eâ annuam 400. aureorum pensionem & aerario provinciae offerebant, inducias fieri passus est, otijque dulcedine & honorati muneris possessione delinitus vim suorum inhibuit. Sunt qui tradant tria carolaeorum millia eidem Pipenpoio oblata, eumque modeste recusantem & à cupidine suspecti aeris alienum ultro sua officia ad arbitrium Aurantij retulisse. Quare durante armistitio Doco Martna & Eco Isbrandius ad Aurantium amandati, qui comitio Hagiensi soluto, Ultrajectino foederatorum Ordinum conventui intererat. Ibi de Lalainij perfidia, de rerum per Frisiam statu sermone facto, Stauriae castellum foederato milite obsideri retulerunt, praesidiariosque si de voluntate principis constet, dedendae arci pronos se ut pridem inducijs, ita foederi permissuros. Itaque castellis foelici rerum successu Leovardiae & Harlingae dirutis nihil aliud restare, quam ut Stauriae arx urbi & marino littori imminens eadem destructione habeatur, Lalainiusque fide rupta superbae molis praesidio, & simul fati solatio orbetur. Unde Aurantius pro dedendâ arce ad Satrapam & praesidiarios scripsit, Ordinesque emuniendae urbi intentos esse voluit.
units.tr: This was made easier because, apart from the standard-bearers who had fled in panic, the loyalty and oath of the soldiers themselves were wavering. Orange had raised the commander of the army to high office by his own valour, but now that he showed signs of an unstable mind, he pursued him with bitter hatred. So Pipenpoy, whom the envoys were trying to win over, was offered pay for the garrison by the Satrap himself, together with the rank of governor and an annual pension of 400 gold pieces from the provincial treasury. He allowed a truce, and softened by the sweetness of leisure and the possession of an honourable post, he restrained his men. Some report that three thousand Carolus guilders were offered to the same Pipenpoy, and that he, though refusing modestly, and moved by his greed for borrowed money, put his services entirely at the disposal of Orange. Therefore, while the armistice held, Doco Martna and Eco Isbrandius were sent to Orange. He was at Hague, where the assembly had been dissolved, and was present at the meeting of the allied States at Utrecht. There they spoke about the treachery of Lalaing and the state of affairs throughout Friesland, and reported that the fort of Stavoren was being besieged by the troops of the allied States. They added that, if it was certain that this was the will of the Prince, the garrison would be as ready to surrender the fortress as they had been before to agree to a truce, and would allow it to join the alliance. Since Leeuwarden and Harlingen had been razed with happy success, nothing remained but that the fort of Stavoren, which overhangs the town and the sea coast, should be treated in the same way, so that Lalaing, having broken faith, would be bereft both of the protection of his proud fortress and of the comfort of his fate. Therefore Orange wrote to the Satrap and the garrison about surrendering the fort, and wished the States to be intent on fortifying the town.

units.la: LITTERAE hujusmodi erant.
units.tr: The letter was of this kind.

units.la: CONVENTIONIS inter vos & Consules Secretariumque urbis Stauriae capita deditionem castelli spectantia mihi exhibita sunt. Quae quoniam MATTHIAE ARCHIDUCIS litteris ac ORDINUM Belgicae, in quae MATTHIAS juravit, deretis congrua sunt, ita censeo ys locum dandum esse. Salus enim publica, tum Frisiae gentis tranquilitas ut id fiat exigunt vosque castellum ORDINUM Deputatis aut populo civico dedatis ocyus. Quo illud eocIↄ. Io. rum arbitrio permissum de voluntate Matthiae & Ordinum generalium solo et- LXXXX. quetur bono patriae, cujus usui cedet. Litterae Prid. Idem Mart. Ultra- jecto datae.
units.tr: The agreement between you and the consuls and the secretary of the town of Stavoren, concerning the surrender of the fort, has been shown to me. Since it agrees with the letters of the Archduke Matthias and with the States of Belgium, to which Matthias swore, I judge that it should be granted to them in this way. For the public safety and the peace of the people of Friesland demand that this be done, and that you hand over the fort to the deputies of the States or to the civic people, as quickly as possible. This has been left to their judgment, with the will of Matthias and the General States, and will turn to the good of the fatherland, whose use it will serve. Letter dated at Utrecht, the day before the Ides of March.

units.la: Caeterum Pipenpojus, etsi aliud simulavisset, ne tum quidem tradendae arcis consilium maturavit, suspecta sensim apud militem cunctatione, qui vinculorum terrore impulsum, dedandam ad arcem adigebat. Itaque militum magis imperio, quam suo ingenio obsecutus, arce cum praesidio excessit, Gulielmumq; Petraeum civem Stavoranum ante decem & sex menses regundo castello delectum successorem accepit. Tum armati cives arci praesidio dati, quintoque ab occupato castello die, tormenta atq; commeatum in urbem abduxere. Arx ipsa a fundamentis qua urbi imminet diruta solo veteris imperij vestigio in ruderibus murorum relicto. Id xviii. Febr. die factum in ephemeride sua Cl. Franckena annotavit.
units.tr: However, Pipenpoy, although he had pretended otherwise, did not hasten to hand over the fort even then, since his hesitation gradually aroused suspicion among the soldiers, who, driven by fear of chains, forced him to surrender the fort. So, yielding more to the command of his men than to his own judgment, he left the fort with its garrison, and received as his successor Willem Petreus, a citizen of Stavoren, who had been chosen to govern the castle eighteen months before. Then armed citizens were posted to guard the fort, and on the fifth day after its capture they carried the artillery and supplies into the town. The fort itself was razed to its foundations on the side facing the town, leaving only traces of the old power in the ruins of its walls. Clarus Franckena noted in his diary that this was done on 18 February.

units.la: Germanus quidam scriptor tradit per Renicum Cammingham, Scipionem Meckamam, Barthium Idsaerdam, Janconem Osingham aliosq; e nobilitate eam arcem destrui jussam, ne Lalainius defectionis infamia jam gravatus ullius arcis munimentis, tanquam furoris sui praesidio se tueretur. Mox de circumducendo urbi vallo agitatum, ac ut intuta moenium otio & per ignaviam collapsa prohibendis hostium irruptionibus firmarentur. Caeterum levissima securitatis imago arcium potitos fascinabat, omnemque periculi metum dirutae moles amoverant. Quippe in orientem provinciae Doccomium quoque oppidum, quod ea flumen dividit, suspecta praesidia deseruerant, quae Collumi etiam, sicut in oppidis, a Lalainio posita, sui magis pavore quam terrore foederati militis aufugerant. Sic discriminis formido ex debellatis arcibus ac sociorum praesidijs orta disciplinam aut fidem non retinebat, priorque fiducia in sollicitudinem conversa suo neque rectoris imperio coercebatur. Quos adversae fortunae impetus tanto aegrius ac impatientius tulisse La- lainius creditus fuit, quanto jactantius & insolentius secundam habuisset, facto in se experimento, nunquam satis fidam potentiam esse, ubi nimia sit. Neque enim aut castella, aut corrupta ad nutum praesidia, munimenta veteris per Frisiam imperij superesse, caeterum omne militum robur aut imbelle & palans oberrate, aut sacramenta Ordinum induisse, quorum favore, tanquam firmissimo dominationis suae & gloriae fulcimento, primos & laudabiles praefecturae annos egisset. Nunc dilabi omnia atque effluere stabiliendis rebus reperta; neque aliud solatium isti fatorum inclementiae reponi posse, quam si Frisia ejectus
units.tr: A certain German writer reports that this fort was ordered to be destroyed by Renicus Cammingham, Scipio Meckama, Bartius Idsaerda, Jancon Osingha and other nobles, so that Lalaing, already burdened by the infamy of his defection, might not protect himself by the defences of any fort, as if by a bulwark of his own madness. Soon afterwards there was talk of drawing a rampart around the town, so that the unguarded walls, collapsing from neglect and idleness, might be strengthened to repel enemy attacks. But the very slight appearance of safety from the forts bewitched those who had gained control of them, and the destruction of the fortifications had removed all fear of danger. Indeed, in the east of the province, they had abandoned the suspect garrisons of Dokkum, the town which that river divides, and the garrisons posted by Lalaing at Coevorden had fled from fear of their own men rather than from terror of the allied soldiers, as had happened in the other towns. Thus the dread of danger arising from the conquered forts and the garrisons of allies did not preserve discipline or faith, and their former confidence, turned into anxiety, was not restrained by the authority of any commander. Lalaing was believed to have borne the attacks of adverse fortune all the more bitterly and impatiently, the more boastfully and insolently he had enjoyed success, having learned by experience that power is never safe enough when it is excessive. For neither forts nor garrisons bought to obey his nod, nor the old fortifications of the empire throughout Friesland, remained to him; instead, the whole strength of his soldiers either wandered about unwarlike and scattered, or had gone over to the oaths of the States, under whose favour, as under the firmest support of his rule and glory, he had spent the first and praiseworthy years of his command. Now everything was collapsing and slipping away, and nothing had been found that could steady affairs; nor could any consolation be offered to this harshness of fate, except that he, driven out of Friesland,

units.la: Groningâ ac Transflavicanis se muniat, Drentiaeque populum ultro mobilem & vindicias cladibus spirantem, tum vicinos Transf-Ifulanos à societate Ordinum Frisiae pollicendo meliora deterreat. Pro se scilicet speciosum Philippi regis nomen valiturum, qui tanti imperij ac tot regnorum arbiter gratiam ad se redeuntibus, arma perseverantibus in rebellione daturus foret, quibus ne Ordinum quidem exanguis & brevi casura libertas par esse queat. Sui quoque reverentiam necdum TransfIfulanos aut Vidri fluminis accolas exuisse, qui contra experiundo didicissent, speciosos & revera inanes libertatis titulos turpi servitio velari. Intendi namque onera & vectigalia quibus excutiendis qui arma sumpsissent eos victimarum more in suis quoq; campis ac paludibus mactatos ultionem poscere. Esse liberos, esse attines propinquæ cadis & effræn is injuriæ pertæsos, qui sua potius quam Ordinum signa secuturi sint.
units.tr: should fortify himself in Groningen and the Transflavian lands, and should frighten the people of Drenthe, who were eager to move and breathing vengeance for their defeats, and the neighbouring Transisulanians away from the alliance of the States of Friesland by promising them better things. For his own name, the famous name of King Philip, would surely have weight, since he, the arbiter of so great an empire and of so many kingdoms, would give favour to those who returned to him and arms to those who persisted in rebellion. Neither the drained liberty of the States nor the short-lived hope of those things could be equal to this. Nor had the Transisulanians or the dwellers by the river Vidrus yet cast off their reverence for him; they had learned by experience that the splendid but empty titles of liberty were hidden under shameful servitude. For burdens and taxes were imposed, and those who had taken up arms to throw them off were slaughtered like victims even in their own fields and marshes, and they cried out for vengeance. They were free, they were men weary of the close pressure of their neighbours and of unbridled injustice, and they would follow their own standards rather than those of the States.

units.la: Itaque missis in omnem Drentiam exploratoribus, Stenvicanos quoque & per Trans-Isulaniam Magistratus tentavit, tantumque sive minarum terrore, sive inlicio profecit, ut sperata ex ijs locis supplendis aut conscribendis copijs auxilia Frisiorum genti interceperit. Quare Joanni Petræo Sannio centurioni creato & palam delectum Stenvicæ pa- ranti, ut talibus parceret jussum est, obtendente Senatu, Præfecti indignationem ex æquatis solo arcibus efferatam omne auxilium cogendis armatis inhibuisse. Adeo veneratio aut metus Præfecti, etiam à via recti descisentis credulum & ad subita consilij inopem populum obsederat.
units.tr: So, having sent scouts throughout the whole of Drenthe, he also tried the Steenwijk people and the magistrates throughout Transisulania. And he achieved so much, whether by the terror of threats or by enticement, that the auxiliaries he had hoped to raise or enlist from those places were cut off from the Frisian nation. Therefore Joannes Petreus Sannius, who had been appointed captain, and who was openly recruiting at Steenwijk, was ordered to desist from such activity, since the Senate pleaded that the indignation of the Governor, roused by the levelling of the forts, had prevented all help from being raised for arming the men. Such was the reverence or fear of the Governor, which had even seized a people who had turned aside from the path of right, and were credulous and unable to make sudden decisions.

units.la: Igitur Sannius centurio, etsi connivente Magistratu, clam & in secreto, militem autoravit, eundemque ut scribit, omni & necessario armorum genere instructum Blessam Stellinguerfiæ pagum dixit, quem Ordinum Frisiæ cura tutandis istius oræ finibus objecto vallo munierat. Eo commeatus quoque & annonâ largior navi subvecta, quam haud procul Tungro flumine, ubi in Tincanum lacum se effundit, cum tempestate conflictatam rudibus in notis istorum temporum reperio. Quippe Auster turbidus fuso desuper imbre validior & prorae objectus onerariam immissis fluctibus & aquâ pluviâ deprimebat ultroque ex pondere gravem assultu hyberni fluminis & simul procellosi aeris infestabat. Nam minore imbrium copiâ, aër frigori ac naturæ suæ redditus quicquid humore fluxum erat, in nivem coëgerat, quæ densâ & visui obstans oculis regentium navem caliginem offuderat. Sunt qui tradant sex pedum altitudinem multis in locis superavisse, eaque molliore cœlo sensim solutâ, flumina & stagna manifestis aquarum incrementis intumuisse. Igitur suspicionibus adversus Lalainium seipsum prodentem indies auctis, captâ Stauriâ urbe & commeatu Blessæ ac vicinis locis subministrato, Didericus Sonoius vir fortis & militiæ impiger Suarteflusam cum copijs de Ordinum Frisiæ consilio missus; quem locum accipiendis è Trans-Isulaniâ; Drentiâque auxilijs opportunum tum arcendis Frisiâ hostibus commodum solertia Ordinum delegerat. Vidrus nam- que lato alvei flexu isthuc loci delatus in omnem oram facilem trajectum promittebat, foreque ut aquæ beneficio, quam è Drentiæ palu- dibus ac bituminosis agris haurit, per ripas stato anni tempore effusus, firmamentum aliquod erectis in ripâ munitionibus præstaret.
units.tr: Therefore Captain Sannius, although the magistrates connived, secretly and privately enlisted soldiers, and, as he writes, having equipped them with every necessary kind of arms, he led them to Blessum, a village in the Stellingwerf district, which the care of the States of Friesland had protected with a rampart to guard the borders of that coast. Supplies and a larger quantity of grain were also conveyed there by ship. I find in the scanty records of those times that this ship, not far from the river Tongre, where it empties into the Lake of Tjeukemeer, was battered by a storm. For the stormy south wind, stronger from the heavy rain poured down from above, struck the bow of the cargo ship, and by sending in waves and rainwater it weighed her down, while by its own force it assailed her, heavy as she was, with the violence of a wintry river and a tempestuous air at once. For, since there was less rain, the air, returned to its cold and natural state, had turned all the moisture that was flowing into snow, which, dense and blocking the sight, had poured a mist into the eyes of those who steered the ship. Some report that in many places the snow had risen to a height of six feet, and that when the sky grew milder it gradually melted, and rivers and pools swelled with clear increases of water. Therefore, suspicions of Lalaing, who was daily betraying himself more openly, having increased, after the capture of the town of Stavoren and the supplies had been brought to Blessum and the neighbouring places, Didericus Sonoy, a brave man and vigorous in war, was sent with troops to Zwartsluis by the decision of the States of Friesland. He had been chosen by the foresight of the States as a place convenient for receiving auxiliaries from Transisulania and Drenthe, and suitable for keeping out the enemies of Friesland. For the Vidrus, bent in a wide curve of its channel at that spot, promised an easy crossing along the whole shore, and it was expected that, when it overflowed its banks at the set time of year, its waters, drawn from the marshes of Drenthe and the bituminous fields, would provide some defence in the raised fortifications on the bank.

units.la: Quare Sonoius impositio in naves milite Suartesluscam transmisit, opereque tumultuario industriâ militum erecto commeatum quoque Vidro amne subvehi fecit. Cujus facti, ut per Frisiæ Ordines ratio redderetur, vetante lege, gentium fines transmigrari, missus pro Legato in Trans-Isulaniam Pompeius Roorda, Caroli de quo sæpe diximus, germanus tribunatum sacri ærarij tum gerens, qui apud istius gentis primores facti consilium excusaret. Itaque Suollam progressus, ubi conventus nobilitatis & Trans-Isulaniæ oppidanorum celeberrimus tum habebatur, multa proposuit, ac ut copias Ordinum suorum decreto Suar- tesiuteslusam missas benignè interpretarentur. Neque enim juris violandi, aut contumeliæ inferendæ studio id fecisse, cæterum necessitate, quæ legi non pareret, adactos locum præsidio & novo opere munijsse, qui Frisiorum terras intranti hosti aperiret. Cogitasse de securitate suæ gentis & ut liberis atque uxoribus anxia periculi pietas subveniret, eâ præsertim temporum ætate, quæ suspectum rectoris animum & simul imperium fecisset. Eum namque occultæ Alexandri Farnesij societati haud dubie inligatum omne hostile, omne immodestum, atque violentum agitare, metuique posse, ut auxilijs, quorum spe foveri dicatur, subjutus in Frisiam ducat, cujus invidiâ ex præoccupatis arcibus flagraret. Itaque petebat, ut aliquid juri socio, aliquid contiguis finibus, aliquid æquitati darent, quæ non prohibeat, gentes eodem fœdere connexas cautam & simul honestam sollicitudinem communibus & jam instantibus periculis interponere: Ad ea Trans-Isulani se provinciâ suspectis præsidijs oppressa de muniendis limitaneis locis cogitare non potuisse. Nunc vero amotis militaribus copijs consilium tuendorum finium coepisse, delectis è plebe rusticâ quinque millibus armatorum, qui versus Tubantum agros Trans-Isulaniam defendant. De reliquis ex suis delegasse, qui provinciæ limites munitionibus ac fortalitijs firment, operisque necessarij rationem ac situm inspiciant. Arcem quoque Gelmudanam velut præsidij ac roboris incapacem solo æquent. Quamobrem petere, ut Sonoi miles Suarteslusà excedat, ne dissensione inter agrarium populum militemque ortâ ad pugnas atque sanguinem veniatur. De cæteris paratam sore plebem rusticam mutuâ fœderis fide atque concordiâ, cum Sonoi præsidiarijs agere, ne hostis aut socius hostium moribus agens in provinciam irruat suæ necdum calamitatis oblitam. Cæterum Roorda Suarteslusæ præsidiarios nullis loci incolis graves, suo ære ac victu haberi, neque alio mandato instructos regerebat, quam ut communem hostem finibus arceant, Frisiamque Vidro flumini, & ejus ostijs, qua in mare vergit, objectam tutam ab incursionibus præstent. Quod quanquam cavere Trans-Isulani debuissent, ex quorum socordia atque ignaviâ periculum foret, ita ex hoc ipso præsidium Suarteslusæ retinendum esse. Se interim Legatum Frisiorum daturum operam, ut de singulis ad suos scribat, deque eorum voluntate Trans-Isulanos edoceat. Sed intercessione foederatorum Ordinum dissensio composita, cautumque ut Suarteslusa, nullo Trans-Isulanæ gentis aut provinciæ præjudicio, præsidium ex periculi metu retineret, excessurum regionis finibus, ubi Frisiorum agris atque securitati provisum foret. Sic eruptura in discordiam ut videbatur, æmulatio interquievit.
units.tr: Therefore Sonoy embarked troops in ships and sent them across to Sneek, and by the soldiers' diligence he had a hastily built work raised there and also had supplies brought up the river Vidro. Lest an account of this deed be demanded from the Frisian Estates, since the law forbade crossing into another people's territory, Pompeius Roorda, the brother of Carolus, of whom we have often spoken, who was then serving as treasurer of the sacred treasury, was sent as envoy to Trans-Isulania to excuse the decision before the leading men of that people. Advancing to Suolla, where a very crowded assembly of the nobility and the townsmen of Trans-Isulania was then being held, he set out many points, and asked them to interpret kindly the troops that the Estates had sent to Sneek by decree. For they had done this not from a desire to violate rights or to inflict insult, but driven by necessity, which does not obey the law, they had fortified the place with a garrison and new works, to open the way for the enemy entering the lands of the Frisians. They had thought about the safety of their own people, and about how a loving concern, anxious for children and wives in danger, might come to their aid, especially in an age such as this, which had made the ruler's mind and the empire suspect. For Alexander Farnese, without doubt bound to a secret alliance, was stirring up everything hostile, everything unrestrained and violent, and it was to be feared that, supported by the aid on which he is said to rely, he would lead his forces into Friesland, and from the odium of the fortresses seized in advance, would set the country aflame. Therefore he asked that they grant something to the right of an ally, something to neighbouring territories, and something to fairness, which does not forbid peoples bound by the same covenant to interpose a cautious and at the same time honourable concern against common and now imminent dangers. In reply, the Trans-Isulanians said that, with their province oppressed by suspect garrisons, they could not have thought about fortifying the border places. But now, with the military forces removed, they had begun to devise a plan for defending their frontiers: five thousand armed men had been chosen from the rustic common people, who would defend Trans-Isulania toward the lands of the Tubantes. From their own people they had also appointed others who would strengthen the province's boundaries with fortifications and forts, and would inspect the plan and site of the necessary work. They would also level the citadel of Gelmuda to the ground, as it was incapable of serving as a defence or a strength. For this reason they asked that Sonoy's soldiers withdraw from Sneek, lest, with a quarrel arising between the country people and the soldiers, the matter come to fighting and bloodshed. As for the rest, the rustic people would be ready, by mutual good faith and concord under the covenant, to deal with Sonoy's garrison, so that no enemy, or an ally acting with the habits of an enemy, should burst into the province, which had not yet forgotten its own calamity. But Roorda replied that the garrison at Sneek was no burden to the inhabitants of the place, was maintained at its own expense and provisions, and had no other instruction than to keep the common enemy from the borders, and to keep Friesland, lying opposite the Vidro river and its mouths where it runs into the sea, safe from incursions. Although the Trans-Isulanians ought to have guarded against this, through whose carelessness and sloth the danger lay, the garrison at Sneek must for that very reason be kept. Meanwhile he, as envoy of the Frisians, would take care to write to his people about each point and to inform the Trans-Isulanians of their wishes. But by the intervention of the allied Estates the dispute was settled, and it was provided that Sneek should, without any prejudice to the Trans-Isulanian people or province, keep its garrison out of fear of danger, and that the troops would leave the limits of the region once provision had been made for the security of the Frisian lands. Thus the rivalry, which seemed about to break out into discord, subsided.

units.la: Tum Joannes Michaëlius minores in Frisios ablegatus. Illi mandatum erat: Ut quoniam Sonoius in Frisios advenisset, Suarteslusæ muniendæ subsidia commodarent, locumque Frisiæ utrique commodum necessario opere circumducerent. Et quoniam Frisico in solo sita non sit, nec fossores ære conduci nec transmitti è Frisiâ possint, omni opere gelu impedito, missum Coverdiam Sonoium vallandæ arci excusaret fide datâ se Suarteslusa ut muniatur, opportuno tempore aduros. Erinas quoque cohortes ut contectis navibus Frisij minores
units.tr: Then John Michael was sent as a minor envoy to the Frisians. He had this commission: that since Sonoy had come into Frisia, they should lend assistance for fortifying Sneek, and should carry round, with the necessary work, a place convenient to both sides. And since the soil of Friesland is not suited to it, and diggers can neither be hired for money nor brought over from Friesland, with all work hindered by frost, he was sent to Coevorden to excuse Sonoy for fortifying the citadel, having pledged his word that they would come at a suitable time to fortify Sneek. The Erinas cohorts also, as the ships were covered, the Frisians being minor ...

units.la: Intercessione foederatorum Ordinum æmulatio inter Frisios & Trans-Isulanos componitur. ad Suartesłusam expedirent peteret, ac ut fossores minorem per Frisiam cIↄ. Iↄ. conductos commeatu ac mercede instruerent. De se testaretur fidem ex lxxx. jure foederis redimendo aeri interposituros, scripturosque foederatos ad Ordines, ut ex communi aerario, quoniam publicae securitati conducat, habeatur. Tum de interceptis litteris lubricam Lalainij fidem prodentibus quaedam addita.
units.tr: Through the mediation of the allied Orders the rivalry between the Frisians and the Trans-Isulanians is settled. He was to bear witness on his own behalf to his good faith, and that they would pay the money for redeeming the covenant out of the 80 [...]; and that they would write to the Orders of the allies that it should be counted as coming from the common treasury, since it serves public safety. Then something was added about the intercepted letters, which betrayed the unreliable faith of Lalaing.

units.la: Igitur Stauriā urbe ac arce in deditionem receptā, Suartesłusā & Sylvestri tractu per praesidia firmatis evenit, ut res secundae & ex arbitrio fluentes insolentiam darent, amotoque arcium metu sui impotens libertas modestiam per adversa exercitam odio Pontificiae factionis licentiā morum mutaret. Quippe imagines & picturae sacrarum aedium ornamenta loco mota, eaque aut solo illisa, aut per vim exfurore auctam, confracta inter eluviem & sordes jacuere. Quae tempestas, tanquam ab aliquo sydere statis vicibus excitata omnem per Frisiam civilia militumque ingenia stupendo aestu commovit. Itaque nullo consilij aut facti nedum ex rumore aut famā conscio singuli destinata fato exequebantur, quod amovendis, ut creditum tum fuit, superstitionibus inquietam multitudinem accenderat. Tradunt autores praeter monasticarum sodalitatum fana, Franciscanorum Dominicanorumque nomine celebrata, velatarum quoque virginum aedes direptas, amissoque cultu veterem nec sine luxu magnificentiam perdidisse. Itaque sacra supellex, vasa aurea & argentea, tum infulae ac sacerdotales vestes in spolium abductae omneque rei divinae Pontificio ritu administrandae inserviens avaritie aut nocendi impetu amotum. Ipsi sacerdotes & monasticam vitam professi. Leovardiā urbe ante Solis occasum non sine contemptu & ludibrio exacti fati sui infoelicitatem explevere, quo laudati majoribus sacrorum ritus luxu & libidine profanati fugā sacri ordinis & destructione sacrarum aedium expiarentur. Unde Leovardiensium exemplo apud Franequerenses, Snecanos, Doccomienses & Harlinganos templa ac fana depurgata, submotoque imaginum ac statuarum ornatu, reformatis, ut vocabant, concionibus praeparata.
units.tr: So when the city and citadel of Staveren had been taken by surrender, and Sneek and the Sylvester district had been secured with garrisons, it came about that prosperous successes and affairs going according to their own will bred insolence. With the fear of the citadels removed, liberty, which had been practised with moderation in adversity, changed its manners into licence out of hatred of the Papist faction. For images and paintings, the ornaments of sacred buildings, were moved from their places, and these were either dashed against the ground or, with violence fed by fury, broken and lay trampled in filth and dirt. This storm, as if stirred at fixed intervals by some star, shook all of Friesland, both civilians and soldiers, with a remarkable ferment. Thus, with no one aware of any plan or deed, still less from rumour or report, individuals carried out what fate had determined, since, as was then believed, the removal of superstitions had inflamed an unquiet multitude. Authors relate that, besides the shrines of the monastic brotherhoods celebrated under the names of the Franciscans and Dominicans, the houses of veiled virgins were also plundered, and that, having lost their worship, they lost their ancient magnificence, which was not without luxury. Thus the sacred furnishings, the gold and silver vessels, and the mitres and priestly vestments were carried off as spoil, and everything that served the performance of divine worship according to the Papist rite was removed by greed or by a rage to do harm. The priests themselves, and those who had professed the monastic life, at Leeuwarden before sunset, not without contempt and mockery, fulfilled the unhappiness of their appointed fate, so that the rites of the sacred order, praised by their ancestors but profaned by luxury and lust, might be atoned for by the flight of the sacred order and the destruction of the sacred buildings. Whence, following the example of the people of Leeuwarden, the churches and shrines were cleansed among the people of Franeker, Sneek, Dokkum and Harlingen, the adornment of images and statues was removed, and the way was prepared for what they called reformed sermons.

units.la: Tetardus Siccama tradit, post sacram aedem Burchuerti direptam, D. Mariae in Bolsuerdiā urbe sacellum à militibus quoque expilatum, ipsamque D. Virginis statuam tantae famae & tot miraculis, ut scriptores tradidere, celebratam, igne exustam. Aureos quoq; argenteosque calices per opificum collegia sacris subductos, omneq; ex ruinis templorum reliquum majori Choro per pontificios inlatum. Caeterum noctis obscuro perruptā fenestrā per milites in sacellum admissos omne residuum praedae applicatum, librisque ritualibus discerptis aut perustis militaris insolentiae reliquias, curante Magistratu, servatas. Quae in commentarium, sicuti debebant perlarae, pauperis aevi laudatam innocentiam suspicione avaritiae aut pejorum criminum foedavere. Sed mihi istorum temporum motus, sicut caetera, ex fide narranti plurima silentio involuta fuisse dubium non est, multosque illius furoris ministerio functos posteris aetatibus opinionem virtutis ex oblivione anteactorum retinuisse.
units.tr: Tetardus Siccama relates that, after the sacred building of Burchuert was plundered, the chapel of St Mary in the town of Bolsward was also pillaged by soldiers, and the statue of the Blessed Virgin herself, celebrated for great fame and many miracles, as the writers have handed down, was burned with fire. Golden and silver chalices were also taken from the sacred places by the guilds of craftsmen, and whatever remained of the temples' ruins was carried off by the Papists to the greater choir. Moreover, after a window was broken open in the dark of night and the soldiers admitted into the chapel, the whole remainder of the booty was seized, and the ritual books were torn up or burned, while the remnants of military insolence were preserved under the care of the magistracy. These things, as they should be recorded in the commentary, have stained with the suspicion of greed or of worse crimes the innocence of that poor age, which has been praised. But I do not doubt that many things about the movements of those times, as about other matters, were passed over in silence by me, who narrate in good faith, and that many who served as instruments of that frenzy have kept, for later ages, a reputation for virtue, forgotten of their past deeds.

units.la: F. Nicolaus scribit 22. Febr. majori apud Staurios templo omnem cultum militari violentiā detractum, altariaque cum statuis mutilata, cIↄ. Iↄ. aut disjecta miserrimam loci faciem ostendisse. Igitur direptis cœnobijs LXXX. ac fanis multi Præsulum Leovardiam captivi inter militarem quoque custodiam abducti, reddendis, ut creditum fuit, administrationis suæ rationibus, quas discerptis tabulis, cum egregijs haud dubiè disciplinarum atque scriptorum monumentis tempestatis atrocissimæ injuria confuderat. Sic quod explendæ paucorum avaritiæ aut lubidini repertum erat, damno posteritatis & sequentium sæculorum cessit, quæ ex anteriorum temporum factorumque ignoratione rerum caligine involuta, ne virtutes quidem & vitia prioris ævi suis annalibus perscripsere. Siccama addit, redigendis in commentarium Floridi Campi mobilibus, post Thomam Groningensem loci antistitem Leovardiæ vinculis datum, Petrum Vibenium Consulem & civicæ cohortis præfectum cum Justo Ockingha viro nobili delegatum, addito Siccama notarum autore & Magistratus actuario, qui in acta suâ manu referret. Mox cœnobiorum sacrarumq; ædium bona veno posita, pecuniaque ex divenditis fisci jure ærario provinciæ inlata. Itaque captivitate Præsulum terrore per omnia monasteria & conventus quoq; virginum aucto, cœnobitæ & moniales de deserendis possessoribus suis agitavere, ac ut annuas pensiones à sacris & secessu ad aliud vitæ genus transituræ æquitate Ordinum impetrarent. Ex quorum ideo consessu Poppius Grovesteinius & Hobbius Baerdius Legisperitus delegati, qui stipendia pro statu & dignitate personarum conferrent, honestaque & utili transactione cessionum acta à cœnobiorum rectoribus mercarentur. Unde Baiomense monasterium, quod velatarum virginum ordo tenuerat, Henrico Termoelio Præsule & Gulielmo Gulielmi vicario autoribus, tum Gerardæ Corneliæ, Titiæ Obbiæ, Tiempkiæ Vassoniæ reliquarumque monialium assensu, cum agris, possessionibus, reditibus & mobilibus specie cessionis & sub jurisjurandi religione provinciæ transcriptum impetrato tantum in singulos stipendio, quod ad alimenta & honestis vitæ subsidijs obtinebatur. Idem à Neoclosterijs cæterisque inclinanre Februario factum reperio, Annamque Herenniam loci rectricem, institutâ supplicatione, modico victui annui æris subsidium ex decreto virginum otase. Igitur testimonia passim fidei & moribus per alienæ probitatis conscios scripta piam Ordinum liberalitatem auxere, ultro censentium beneficium ex beneficio miserabili turbæ deferendum. Quod in illo perturbatissimo temporum statu unicum otijs & simul delitijs assueto sexui solatium fuit, & ne mollioris vitæ quietem manuum opere, parando victui mutaret. Quippe creditum fuit magnificentissimis & ex luxuriâ ad invidiem provectis ædificijs ac structuris extrusos importuno mœrori succubuisse, interque nemora & culti ruris amœnitatem sacra & otia professos veteris contubernij solitudinem sine ægritudine consternatæ mentis non hausisse. Præter hoc, aureamargenteamque supellectilem, quam divino cultui protervior ætas adornaverat, sacris ministerijs detractam, pieque & cum aliquâ veluti consecratione templis dedicata auferri, aut cessantibus exercitijs exolescere.
units.tr: Frater Nicolaus writes that on 22 February, in the greater temple at Stauria, all worship was stripped away by military violence, and the altars with their statues were mutilated, and [...] or thrown down, showing the most wretched face of the place. Therefore, after 80 monasteries and shrines had been plundered, many prelates were brought captive to Leeuwarden, led away under military guard, to render, as was believed, accounts of their administration, which they had confused by tearing up the records, along with distinguished monuments of learning and writings, through the injury of the most savage storm. Thus what had been found to satisfy the greed or lust of a few turned to the loss of posterity and of succeeding centuries, which, wrapped in the darkness of ignorance of earlier times and deeds, have not written even the virtues and vices of the former age into their annals. Siccama adds that, to be entered into the commentary, the movable goods of Floridus Campus, after Thomas of Groningen, the head of the place at Leeuwarden, was put in chains, were handed over; Petrus Vibenius, consul and prefect of the civic cohort, was deputed with Justus Ockinga, a nobleman, Siccama being added as author of the notes and as clerk of the magistracy, who was to record the proceedings in his own hand. Soon the goods of the monasteries and sacred buildings were put up for sale, and the money from the sales was brought into the provincial treasury by right of the exchequer. Thus, with the captivity of the prelates increasing terror throughout all the monasteries and also the convents of virgins, the monks and nuns discussed abandoning their possessions, and sought from the equity of the Orders annual pensions to pass from their sacred life and retirement to another way of living. Hence Poppius Grovesteinius and Hobbius Baerdius, a learned jurist, were deputed from this assembly to provide stipends according to the rank and dignity of the persons, and to obtain, by an honourable and useful settlement, deeds of cession from the heads of the monasteries. Thus the monastery of Bayum, which the order of veiled virgins had held, was transferred to the province by a deed of cession, with the authority of Henricus Termoelius, prelate, and William of Gulielmus, vicar, and with the consent of Gerarda Cornelia, Titia Obbia, Tiempkia Vassonia and the other nuns, together with lands, possessions, revenues and movable goods, under the sanction of an oath, with only a stipend granted to each, sufficient for food and honourable support in life. I find the same was done by the nuns of Neuklooster and the other houses in February, and that Anna Herennia, the superior of the place, after a supplication was instituted, obtained by decree of the virgins a modest annual sum of money for sustenance. Thus testimonies of faith and character, written everywhere by those who knew the probity of others, increased the pious liberality of the Orders, which willingly voted that a benefit should be extended to a wretched crowd. In that most troubled state of the times this was the only comfort for a sex accustomed to leisure and at the same time to delights, and so that they would not exchange the quiet of a softer life for manual labour to earn their living. For it was believed that they had succumbed to unbearable sorrow, thrust out of the most magnificent buildings, raised to envy by luxury and construction, and that, amid the groves and pleasantness of the cultivated countryside, they, who had professed sacred retirement, did not drink in the loneliness of their former companionship without a troubled spirit. Besides this, the golden and silver furniture, which a more wanton age had adorned for divine worship, was taken away from the sacred ministries, and things piously dedicated to the temples with a certain consecration were carried off, or, with the exercises ceasing, fell into disuse.

units.la: Quæ res Lalainium ultro fœderi ex receptâ Philippi gratiâ inimicum majore odio efferavit. Quare, quod antè per Drentiam Transf-Isulaniamque ab eo factum erat. Frisiæ quoque & præsertim Sylvestr bus exploratores immisit, quo ad arma sumenda adversum foederatos instiga- ret & ut pacem à Farnesio nomine regis oblatam, missâ inani libertate acciperent. Unde foederato militi, quem Joannes Sannius Stellinguerfiæ prætor & cohortis centurio, vir bonis artibus imbutus ex Scoterlandiæ finibus in Donieverstallenses ducebat, primi Sylvestres se objecere, facto ab Oelanis initio, qui Sannij cohortem per glaciem, etsi infidam laboriosum & pedestre iter facientem sumptis quæ furor suppeditaverat, armis loco & præsidio prohibuerunt. Tum ut malum pestilentiæ instar, latius serperet, signo campanæ dato, suspensisque è turre Oelanâ ignibus vicini quoque ad auxilia vocati, quot eodem consilio imbutos exploratorum astus corruperat. Itaque tantus repente agrarij populi concursus factus est, ut de suorum vitâ atque incolumitate centurio desperaret, experimento priorum temporum edoctus rusticam Frisiorum plebem militaris insolentiæ & præsidij impatientem pro amovendis armatis tanquam retinendâ libertate certasse. Cæterum noctis beneficio quæ hybernâ opacitate minus sublustris visum interceperat, militem Legemarios reduxit, sanoque occupato curare corpora & somnum capere jussit. Ubi vero lux orta, quæ tardius isto anni tempore, cælum occupabat, Donieverstallenses, nequicquam, ut se componerent, moniti arma resumpsere, postremoque in ordines militum invecti commeatum & impedimenta in prædam verterunt.
units.tr: This event, together with Lalainius being received into Philip's favour, drove him to an even greater hatred of the covenant. Therefore, just as he had already done through Drenthe and Overijssel, he also sent spies into Friesland, and especially among the Sylvestrians, to incite them to take up arms against the confederates and to accept the peace offered in the king's name by Farnese, dropping the empty talk of liberty. Hence, when Johannes Sannius, governor of Stellingwerf and captain of a cohort, a man trained in good arts, was leading a confederate soldier from the borders of Schoterland toward the men of Donieverstal, the Sylvestrians were the first to block his way. The Oelanians started the trouble. They kept Sannius's cohort from a place of shelter and defence, and although the ice was treacherous and the march was slow and on foot, they took up whatever arms their rage supplied. Then, so that the evil might spread more widely like a plague, a bell was rung and fires were lit on the tower at Oelan, and the neighbours were summoned to help, all of them already corrupted by the cunning of the spies, who had won them over to the same plan. So sudden a crowd of country people gathered that the captain despaired of the lives and safety of his men. Taught by experience of earlier times, he judged that the rustic Frisian commons, impatient of soldiers and of garrisons, were fighting to drive out the armed men as if to defend their liberty. Meanwhile, under cover of night, which in winter's gloom had let little light into the scene, he led the soldiers back to Legemeer and ordered them to occupy a safe place, to tend their bodies and to take rest. When daylight came, which at that season of the year rose more slowly over the sky, the men of Donieverstal, though warned in vain to compose themselves, took up arms again. At last they charged into the ranks of the soldiers and turned their supplies and baggage into plunder.

units.la: Scribit Sannius sclopetos quoque cum nitrati pulveris & glandium copiâ militi ereptos, conjugisque ægrae & in mariti comitatu tum agentis viscéribus vim inlatam. Quæ omnia miles nocere vetitus singulari patientiâ sufferebat, haud ignarus ex disciplinæ lege magis imperio ducis aut rectoris, quam ingenio parendum. Mandato scilicet ut pugnet, non consilio opus esse utendumque armis, non ut privato & ad tutelam corporis, sed ex hostium cæde atque damno salus ac victoria sperantur.
units.tr: Sannius writes that they also seized the muskets, along with a quantity of gunpowder and bullets, from the soldiers, and that violence was done to his sick wife and to the bodies of those who were then in her husband's company. The soldier, forbidden to resist, bore all this with remarkable patience, well aware that by the law of discipline he must obey the command of his leader or ruler rather than his own judgement. Obviously, he was ordered to fight, not to deliberate, and arms must be used not for private protection of the body but because safety and victory are hoped for from the slaughter and loss of the enemy.

units.la: Creditum fuit Titi Waltæ opera atque instinctu rusticam manum coactam, perceptaque militum quorundam, qui pecuniam immodestius familijs extorserant, insolentiâ propriam isti genti virtutem atque ferociam induisse. Cujus rei fama Leovardiam perlata Ordinum animos non parum conturbavit. Itaque primum de cohorte cum ignominiâ exautorandâ in consessu dissertatum, cum essent qui militari licentiæ frænos injici severiore exemplo vellent, provocandumque ad veteris disciplinæ rigorem, quæ in decimum quemque conterrendæ multitudini atrocibus pænis animaduertissét. Alij censebant incertis rumoribus & ut senescerent, dandum tempus esse tractandoque clementiâ potius illorum animos, qui ambiguis temporum inritati sacramenta mutare, facto ad hostem transfugio, incommodo reip. possent. Quippe Lalainium manifesti, etsi adhuc simularet defectoris personam jam induisse, retentaturum haud dubiè signa, si viderit cohortium fidem inclinare, easque Ordinum odio effrænes & solutas, nullo rectore aut domino vastandis agris venales manus admovere. Perspecta scilicet militum obsequia & modestiam fuisse, parcitumque rusticorum sanguini, qui scire debuissent, flagrante bello provinciâ, aliquid privati incommodi ex publicâ calamitate ferendum esse. Sannius subjungit, se sedandis militum animis
units.tr: It was believed that through the work and instigation of Titus Walta the country folk had been gathered together, and that some soldiers, who had extorted money too immoderately from households, had by their insolence given that people their own courage and fierceness. When word of this matter reached Leeuwarden, it greatly troubled the minds of the States. So first the cohort was debated in council, to be dismissed with disgrace. Some wanted to curb soldierly licence with a severer example and appealed to the rigour of the old discipline, which had punished every tenth man with terrifying savage penalties to frighten the crowd. Others argued that, since the rumours were uncertain, time should be allowed for them to grow old, and that the minds of those men should be handled with clemency rather than harshness, since they had been provoked by the uncertainties of the times to break their oaths, and by deserting to the enemy might do harm to the commonwealth. Indeed, Lalainius was plainly the author of the defection, and although he still pretended to have assumed the role of a deserter, he would undoubtedly try to win back the standards if he saw the loyalty of the cohorts wavering. He would then employ men who, unrestrained and unbridled by hatred of the States and without any leader or master, were for sale and would be used to lay waste the fields.
