It was clearly known that the soldiers had been obedient and moderate, and that the blood of the rustics had been spared; they ought to have known that, while the province was ablaze with war, some private loss must be borne as a result of public calamity. Sannius adds that he had, to calm the soldiers' spirits, first interposed his authority and command, and afterwards entreaties, so that they would not stain their brave right hands with the blood of the provincials and allies.

units.la: Ordines ille tumultu tum male habet.
units.tr: The States were then badly disturbed by the tumult.

units.la: cIↄ.Iↄ. mis, quos ardor pugnæ repellendam ad vim inflammabat, primo auto- lxxx. ritatem ac imperium, post preces interposuisse, ne fortes dexteras provincialium ac sociorum sanguine macularent. Charlesium quoque cohorti præfectum præsidium Lemmariæ agentem, auxilia compescendæ rusticæ plebi obtulisse, seque ijs posthabitis in Scoterlandos, post Stellinguerfios celerrimo itinere, declinandis malis, pronum conflictui militem ductitasse. Qui in illo Sylvestrium tractu populares motus, ut ante Joanni Roordæ Alexandri Farnesij, de quo dixi, in Frisiam legato, ita tum Lalainio imputabantur, ac si trahendis ingenijs egregius artifex specie pacis regiæ, discordias & secessiones serendo firmamentum suæ defectioni debilitate fœderis captaret.
units.tr: Charlesius, the prefect of the cohort, who was in command of the garrison at Lemmer, had also offered his help to restrain the country folk. Giving up that task, he hurried by the quickest route into Schoterland, and after Stellingwerf, he was keeping the soldiers eager for battle, so as to avert the evils. In that district of the Sylvestrians the popular disturbances were charged, just as before to Johannes Roorda, the envoy of Alexander Farnese, of whom I have spoken, when he went into Friesland, so now to Lalainius, as if he were an outstanding craftsman in stirring up minds, sowing discord and secession under the appearance of a royal peace, and seeking to make his defection secure by the weakening of the covenant.

units.la: Quamobrem, ne rudi Sylvestrium plebe corruptâ, procerum quoq; in Groningâ urbe & per Omlandiam animos venenaret, Abelus Franckena vir eximius & singulare patriæ suæ ornamentum Groningam ex Frisijs pro legato missus, qui propiore fœdere Frisiorum gentem cum Groninganis, Omlandis atque Drentinis connecteret. Bartoldo quoq; Entenio viro nobili & militiæ impigro legionem, jam ante Lalainio commissam, nomine Frisiorum regendam daret, totumque militare per Omlandiam & vicina imperium homini bellis à primâ ætate innutrito, pro tempore deferret. Cæterum Entenius Coverdiæ agens, quo concitatos in arma per Lalainium Drentinos compesceret, de legati adventu non cognovit, cujus mandata ad portam urbis tabellionì in ingressu ab excubitoribus extorta, in manus Lalainij pervenerant. Quare detecto legationis secreto, Lalainius Legatum, quem arcano odio consectabatur, maledictis apud suos & imprimis Ioannem Wisseringium hominem turbulentum & suæ factionis principem traduxit, ejusque consilio in aulam evocatum violato gentium jure custodiæ dedit. Cæterum Legatus tertio post die per fenestram præceps datus carcere excessit, inscio & non cogitante Lalainio, quæ redimendum Balleium, quem in arce Leovardianâ Ordines Frisiæ asservabant, legati captivitate sommiaverat. Ubi verò de ejus fugâ cognitum ædium locorumque secreta perquiri per urbem jussit, inque spiculatores custodiæ Legati destinatos à Senatu oppidano animadverti. Is verò perspecto Lalainij consilio ad criminationes dissimulavit, legatumque in urbe primariâ domo occultatum bono animo esse jussit. Franckena in Ephemeride notat carceris sui diem in xvi. Kal. Martias incidisse seq; xiv. Kal. liberatum & periculo exemptum legationis suæ secretum bono exitu, etsi infælici auspicio, obivisse.
units.tr: Therefore, lest he corrupt the simple Sylvestrian commons and poison the minds of the leading men in the city of Groningen and throughout Omlandia, Abel Franckena, an outstanding man and a singular ornament of his country, was sent from Friesland to Groningen as envoy, to bind the Frisian people more closely with the Groningers, Omlanders and men of Drenthe. He was also to give to Bartold Entenius, a noble man and vigorous soldier, the legion already entrusted earlier to Lalainius, to be governed in the name of the Frisians, and to hand over to him, as the occasion required, the whole military command in Omlandia and the neighbouring districts, since he had been trained in war from his earliest age. But Entenius was then at Coeverden, where he was restraining the Drenthers, whom Lalainius had roused to arms, and he did not learn of the envoy's arrival. The envoy's instructions had been seized from a notary by the guards at the city gate as he entered, and had come into Lalainius's hands. So, when the secret of the mission was discovered, Lalainius slandered the envoy, whom he pursued with secret hatred, among his own men, and especially Johannes Wisseringius, a turbulent man and the leader of his faction. On Wisseringius's advice, he summoned the envoy to the court and, in violation of the law of nations, placed him under guard. But on the third day after, the envoy was thrown headlong from a window, escaped from prison, and Lalainius neither knew nor suspected it. He had planned to ransom Balleius, whom the States of Friesland kept in the citadel at Leeuwarden, in exchange for the envoy's captivity. When he learned of the flight, he ordered the secret places of the houses and sites to be searched throughout the city, and the guards assigned to the envoy were punished by the town council. Yet the council, seeing through Lalainius's plan, dissembled his accusations and ordered the envoy, who was hidden in a leading house in the city, to be of good cheer. Franckena notes in his diary that his imprisonment fell on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, and that on the fourteenth day before the Kalends he was freed and, by a good outcome, though under an unlucky omen, escaped the danger and kept the secret of his mission.

units.la: Ferunt Lalainium, percepto Legati effugio, affectum impotentem, & per animum furori proximum, velut à ratione alienum, severius quiddam si potiretur legato comminatum, interque fascinatæ mentis illusiones & futuri sceleris ludibria, de licitando Legati capite & immittendo percussore cogitasse. Quod quanquam immanissimi sceleris infamiam non effugeret, ita legatus fato & ministrorum curâ vitæ & simul patriæ servatus est. Quare Lalainius ut è crudeli voto omnia fluerent meliusque procederent, optimum potentiæ fomentum civiles per urbem discordias prosevit sparsis in vulgus Pontificium rumoribus, fœderatarum provinciarum Ordines urbi & quæsito majorum juri atque imimmunitati iniquos, propensioribus in Omlandiæ populum studijs inclinare. Quæ ideo tanto facilius Pontificij persuaderi sibi patriebantur, quod Omlandi per Clantium & Iargæum Legatos Ultrajectinum fœdus inijssent, crederenturque ex initæ societatis clientelâ gratiam Ordinum ex odio civitatis obtinuisse. Neque enim Omlandos vinculorum & nuperi carceris oblitos sensum atque memoriam recentis injuriæ posuisse, cæterum esse qui illius violentiæ ac contumeliæ placamenta ab imminuto urbis jure sperent. Quod si perdant, se grande rerum detrimentum æmulos Omlandos solatium & vindictam injuriæ habituros, cujus ulciscendæ calorem in ipso vultu, in omni actione, in externis animi spirarent. Ab ijs esse, quod de erigendis per agros munitionibus cogitent, urbemque quæ sola inter Lavicam Amasiamque flumina fossâ & vallo claudi debeat jure veteris per Omlandiam imperij privare. Quæ speciosè dicta à Lalainio cives apud pontificios pronis auribus accipiebantur. Itaq; cætus & conventus nocturni passim per urbem faciendis conspirationibus instituti, ad quas ære alieno nexi & mollitie vitæ aut turpitudine infames, velut regem reducturi, magno numero confluebant. Quippe quindecim cohortium auxilia Novesium advenisse Benthemius nuntiaverat, Farnesiumq; magno armorum apparatui intentum de recuperando per Frisiam imperio & subvertendo Fœdere cogitare. Quod cum ex fide veri diceretur, ita conjuratos ad celerandâ consilia impellebat, quæ mutandis per urbem rebus parari non vanis & incertis prodigijs observabantur.
units.tr: They say that when Lalainius learned of the envoy's escape, he was seized by an uncontrollable passion, and his mind, nearly beside itself with rage and removed from reason, threatened some harsher measure should he gain the envoy in his power. Amid the delusions of a bewitched mind and the mockeries of a crime yet to come, he thought of putting a price on the envoy's head and sending in an assassin. Although this would not have escaped the infamy of a most monstrous crime, the envoy was saved by fate and by the care of his servants, both for his own life and for his country. Therefore, so that everything might flow from his cruel wish and proceed better, Lalainius fostered the greatest source of his power: civil discord throughout the city. He spread among the people rumours, put about by the Papists, that the States of the confederated provinces were hostile to the city and to the claimed right and immunity of its ancestors, and were inclining with greater favour toward the people of Omlandia. These rumours were the more easily believed by the Papists because the Omlanders had entered into the Union of Utrecht through their envoys Clantius and Jargaeus, and it was thought that by the clientship of that association they had won the favour of the States at the expense of the city's hatred. For the Omlanders, they said, had not forgotten the chains and the recent imprisonment, nor had they put aside the feeling and memory of the fresh injury; rather, there were some who hoped for compensation for that violence and insult from a diminished right of the city. And if they lost it, the Omlanders, their rivals, would have a great loss of their own fortune as consolation and revenge for the injury, the heat of which they breathed in their very face and in every action, and in their outward bearing. From them, it was said, came the plan of raising fortifications through the fields, and of depriving the city, which alone among the rivers Lauwers and Ems ought to be closed by a ditch and rampart, of its ancient right of rule over Omlandia. These fair-sounding words of Lalainius were received with open ears by the citizens who were inclined to the Papists. Therefore, nocturnal gatherings and meetings were held in various places throughout the city for conspiracies, and men bound by debt, or infamous for their softness or disgrace, flocked together in great numbers as if they were about to restore the king. Indeed, Benthemius had reported that the auxiliary troops of fifteen cohorts had arrived at Nijmegen, and that Farnese, intent on a great array of arms, was planning to recover power in Friesland and to overthrow the covenant. When this was said to be true, it urged the conspirators to hasten their plans, which, as the city's affairs were to be changed, were observed by empty and uncertain portents.

units.la: Tradunt incerti autoris rudes notæ, inconditos clamores de nocte auditos, equorumque hinnitibus etiam altissimo rerum silentio verberatum aerem metum futuræ tempestatis fœderato per Groningam populo incussisse. Cui ut obviam iretur, Pompejus Ufkenius cum Joanne Cornputio viro nobili Lalainium adijt, eumque purgandis suspicionibus ut Ultrajectum eat familiari & secreto sermone hortatus est. Premi scilicet vestigia veteris gloriæ posse, si mentem errore aliquo seductam suspicione infœlicis consilij exoneret, provolutusque ad Aurantij principis secretum egregia monituro obtemperet. Patère adhuc innocentiæ locum, si præcipitia labantis ingenij obfirmet retractusque à malis cogitationibus in amplexum & simul consilium optimi principis se effundat. Ab eo remedium si quis sit erroris & amissi imperij ac simul gloriæ beneficium peti posse, neque recusaturos Præfecturam Frisios si viderint lubricâ ætate sororis consilio aut assentatione aulicorum seductum sanitatis auxilio non respuere. Quod ad disjectas arces attineret, id æquiter & benignè, tanquam ab Ordinum Belgicæ decreto profectum, interpretaretur, habiturus firmius provincialis recturæ præsidium, si spretis arcium ac castellorum munimentis, infidâ imperij tutelâ, benevolentiæ procerum se insinuet, redeatque in gratiam cum ijs quibus dignitatem, titulos & splendorem fortunæ ac clarissimi nominis deberet. Moderandam esse juvenilis animi cupiditatem, quæ nisi in præsentium possessione conquiescat, inexplebilem & futuri incertam esse. Mitteret regiæ gratiæ inanem umbram interque majoris fortunæ lubricam spem constitutus satietate adepti honoris se nutriat, quam ex virtute haberet. Majora certè à Philippo sperari non posse. Quippe commissas imperio suo provincias fœcunditate soli & fertilibus agris fœlices esse, quos præter clarissimarum urbium ornamenta divitis populi fortunæ commendaret. Adhæc amplissimorum portuum commoditate, quam maris æstuaria aut lati sinus præstarent, regiones munitas infestis gentibus accessum negare, vel maxumè ad securitatem sui per Frisiam imperij, ex quo, si in fide perseveret, opes ac gloriam, suæ domui decora atque ornamenta habituras esset. Quin reputaret eam ipsam regiâ dominatione, atque insolentiâ externæ gentis attritam in tutâ quietis ac rerum possesione tandem collocandam esse, quod præstare suâ virtute posset & si in actos in exilio suos & propinquorum annos, fugiendæ Albani sævitiæ, memoriâ non excusserit. Proponeret illius temporis tristissimam imaginem, cum viduæ & mœstissimæ matri fugæ comes, primæ pubertatis lanuginem Albani gladio atque furoribus subduceret, tædiaq; & molestiam sui & materni exilij in spem redituræ libertatis honestissimarum artium meditatione & simul solatio levaret. Uteretur primæ ætatis egregiâ institutione dimissisque Oyenbruggio, Grutero, Conteravio & Balleio aulæ suæ dehonestamentis, generosam & natam ad alta indolem optumæ matris & eorum præceptis instrueret, qui ne suspicionem quidem defectionis, etsi in aperta productam sui odio invalescere ex fiducia antiquæ virtutis paterentur. Id si fecerit animum recti conscium, & sine domestico tortore habiturum, qui alias internos cruciatus haud dubiè sensurus sit, si manifestus clarissimi fœderis desertor omnem vanæ salutis spem in auxilio jurati & perfidi hostis posuerit. Cæterum Lalainius optuma suadentibus omnia inconstantis animi signa edebat, modoque rubore suffuso vultu, modo repentinis palloribus occupato, angorem pectoris evulgabat.
units.tr: Reports from unnamed authors tell that rough notices, disorderly shouting heard at night, and the neighing of horses, which broke the air even in the deepest silence of things, struck fear of a coming storm into the people bound together in covenant at Groningen. To meet this, Pompeius Ufkenius went with Johannes Cornputius, a nobleman, to Lalaing, and urged him, to clear away the suspicions, to go to Utrecht as a friend and talk with him in private. The footprints of his former glory, he said, could still be pressed, if he freed his mind, led astray by some error, from the suspicion of an unhappy plan. Let him throw himself at the feet of Prince Orange in secret and obey the counsel of that excellent man. There was still room for his innocence, if he steadied the headlong course of his unstable mind and, withdrawn from evil thoughts, embraced the wise counsel of the best of princes and gave himself over to it. From him, if a man sought a remedy for his error, and a restoration of his lost authority and of his glory at the same time, the Frisians would not refuse him the governorship, if they saw that, led astray in his slippery youth by his sister's advice or by the flattery of courtiers, he did not reject the help of recovered sanity. As for the dismantled citadels, he should take this in good part and kindly, as coming from the decree of the States of Belgium. He would have a firmer protection for ruling the province if, having rejected the fortifications of citadels and castles and the untrustworthy guardianship of empire, he ingratiated himself with the goodwill of the nobles and made peace again with those to whom he owed his rank, his titles, and the splendour of his fortune and his most distinguished name. The eagerness of a youthful spirit must be restrained; unless it rests in the possession of present things, it is insatiable and uncertain of the future. Let him accept the empty shadow of royal favour, and, placed between the slippery hope of greater fortune, let him nourish himself on the satisfaction of the honour he has obtained, which he holds from his own virtue. Certainly greater things could not be hoped for from Philip. The provinces committed to his rule were fortunate in the fertility of the soil and their rich fields, which, apart from the ornaments of their most famous cities, recommended a wealthy people. Besides, the regions, protected by the convenience of the very large harbours which the estuaries of the sea and the wide bays afforded, denied access to hostile peoples; and this was most of all a safeguard for his rule through Friesland, from which, if he persevered in loyalty, he would have wealth and glory, and ornaments and honours for his house. Indeed, let him reflect that the very province, worn down by royal domination and the arrogance of a foreign people, would at last be settled in the secure possession of peace and affairs, which he could bring about by his own virtue, if he had not shaken off from his memory the years he and his relatives had spent in exile, and his flight from the savagery of the Alba. Let him set before himself the most sorrowful picture of that time, when, the companion of his flight, his widowed and most grieving mother, he withdrew the first down of his youth from the sword and fury of Alba, and eased the weariness and burden of himself and of his mother's exile with the hope of returning freedom and with the study of the most honourable arts, and at the same time with consolation. Let him make use of the excellent education of his early age, and, having dismissed Oyenbrugge, Gruter, Conteravius and Balleius, the disgraces of his court, let him instruct his noble nature, born for lofty things, through his excellent mother and through those who would not suffer even the suspicion of defection, though it was brought into the open and grew strong with hatred of him, trusting in the ancient virtue of the house. If he does this, he will have a mind conscious of what is right, and will have no domestic torturer, which he will certainly otherwise feel as inner torments, if, a manifest deserter of the most illustrious covenant, he places all his hope of vain safety in the help of a sworn and treacherous enemy. But Lalaing, while they were advising the best course, showed every sign of an inconstant mind, and his face, now flushed with shame, now seized by sudden paleness, revealed the anguish of his breast.

units.la: Tradunt autores, præter ruborem ingenuæ adhuc mentis & necdum excussi pudoris testem, lachrymas quoque Lalainio ex Ufkenij sermonibus fluxisse, perculsumque desperatione rerum, quod & fide apud Ordines & simul Farnesium in præstandis promissis excidisset, perturbato animo ex colloquio Ufkenij egisse. Quod etsi silentio premeret, ne quid de icta cum Farnesio societate incautè expromeret, ita velum aliquod præsumptis suspicionibus obductum. Infractam scilicet religionis pacem & præter contumeliam sibi rectori provinciæ inlatam rebelles Frisios arma induisse, æquatisque solo castellis specie libertatis moderata & justa imperia per enormem licentiam detractasse. Sic ad mores suos & ingenitam quoque majoribus ferociam redijsse, qui dominantium suorum cauta & aspera ingenia, primis quoque temporum ætatibus non pertulissent. Ita vitia gentis nomine virtutis ad posteros transmissa, qui everso principis imperio, ne rectores quidam libertatis ferrent, aut ut intra terminos staret coercita legibus atque præsidijs inquieti & simul ingrati populi insolentia. Hæc scilicet præmia sui in patriam, in fœderatum populum affectus esse, ut injuriam atque contemptum pro beneficio accipiat, cui vicem exsolvere grave mortalium ingenijs foret.
units.tr: The authors relate that, besides a blush, a witness of a mind still noble and of a shame not yet shaken off, tears also flowed from Lalaing at Ufkenius' words, and that he, struck down by despair of his affairs, because he had failed both in his faith toward the States and at the same time in carrying out the promises made by Farnese, went away from the conversation with Ufkenius in a troubled state of mind. Although he kept silence about this, lest he carelessly reveal anything of the alliance made with Farnese, it was nonetheless veiled as with some covering of conjectures. The rebellious Frisians, they said, had broken the peace of religion and, besides the insult offered to themselves as governors of the province, had taken up arms, and with the castles razed to the ground, under the pretence of liberty they had withdrawn the moderate and just commands through an enormous licence. Thus they had returned to their own manners and to the fierceness innate in their ancestors, who could not even in the earliest ages of their history endure the cautious and harsh characters of their rulers. So the vices of the nation, under the name of virtue, were handed down to posterity, who, with the rule of the prince overthrown, would not bear even certain governors of liberty, or so that it might stay within its limits, restrained by laws and garrisons against the restlessness and at the same time the ingratitude of the people. These, of course, were the rewards of his feelings toward his country and toward the allied people: he received injury and contempt in return for a kindness, when to repay a favour is a burden even to the minds of mortals.

units.la: Pacatos Mechlinienses, Valentinos fœderi adjectos, receptos in fidem Groninganos totàque Transisulaniâ, qua Isala & Vidro amnibus perluitur, victricibus armis perdomata se laudabile per Frisiam imperium exexercuisse. Cæterum trophæorum loco, quæ in memoriam gestarum fœlicissimè rerum erigi debuissent, fanum invidiæ extructum, ac si seminatis per provincias discordijs, religione sacramenti ruptâ fœdissimi proditoris personam induisset. A quâ cum absit longius se Pompeio Vfkenio potestatem facere, Ultrajectum ad Ordines eundi, deque suâ in provincias fide atque integritate testandi. Cæterum Vfkenius Ultrajectum progressus, excusationem Lalainij in criminationem convertit incusatâ fœderati consessus socordiâ atque securitate quod perniciosa Lalainij consilia adolescere amotis suspicionibus ac simul remedijs sivissent. Eo namque rem deductam, ut defectio metuenda sit & ut fœderatæ provinciæ Frisiorum & Translavicani agri tractu ac societate exuantur. Vigilandum consulendumq; patribus esse, ne tempore malis Lalainij consilijs dato, majus discrimen oriatur cui prospici ante maturitatem conceptæ defectionis possit. Commeare scilicet ex hostili agro & Farnesij aulâ secretorum sermonum internuntios, qui dignitates, qui gloriam, qui regis gratiam & auxilia polliceantur, haud dubiè adfutura ocyus si moram & tarditatem Ordinum anteceperint. Momenta temporum prudentibus curanda & ne effluat amovendis periculis nata & se offerens occasio. Itaq; expediendas celerius in Frisiam copias, erigendas aut reparandas munitiones, ne Lalainius detectâ defectione ex amico & socio hostis nudatas justis præsidijs & inermes provincias auxiliorum ope debellet. Quæ ab Vfkenio proposita Frisiorum & Omlandiæ Legatis, qui in isto consessu erant, magno assensu commendabantur, non ignaris Surquetum Lalainij scribam missum ad eum fasciculum litterarum & cum eo regis gratiam per imprudentiam & temeritatem linguæ evulgasse. Quæ etsi Aurantio Principi ex fide verissimi rumoris indicarentur, ita omnem de Lalainio suspicionem anteactorum memoria & renovatio clarissimæ laudis amoverat. Itaq; Aurantius etiam in tam apto communis sinisteriorisq; famæ testimonio diu incertus quid ageret mutato, quæ ad Amsterodamenses decreverat, itineris consilio Campos per Velaviam profectus est, præmisso Groningam Pompeio Vfkenio, qui Lalainium sui ad colloquium in urbe Camporum sollicitaret.
units.tr: The Mechlinians had been pacified, the Valencians had been added to the covenant, the Groningers had been received into the faith, and, with victorious arms, he had subdued the whole of Overijssel, through which the rivers Ijssel and Vecht flow, and so he had exercised a praiseworthy rule through Friesland. But instead of trophies, which ought to have been raised in memory of his most fortunate deeds, he had built a shrine of hatred, as if, with discords sown through the provinces and the bond of the oath broken, he had assumed the character of the most foul traitor. Since he was far from this, he would not allow Pompeius Ufkenius any power over himself: he would go to the States at Utrecht and bear witness to his loyalty and integrity toward the provinces. But Ufkenius, having gone on to Utrecht, turned Lalaing's excuse into an accusation, blaming the negligence and complacency of the assembly of the covenant, because they had allowed Lalaing's pernicious plans to grow up, with suspicions removed and the remedies likewise. For the matter had come to such a point that defection was to be feared, and that the confederate provinces of the Frisians and the land beyond the Vecht would be stripped of their union and alliance. Care must be taken and the Fathers must be consulted, lest, with time given to Lalaing's plans, a greater danger should arise, against which provision could be made before the defection, now conceived, reached maturity. Surely messengers of secret talks were coming and going from enemy territory and from the court of Farnese, promising dignities, glory, the king's favour and help, which would undoubtedly come the sooner if they got ahead of the delay and slowness of the States. The moments of time must be cared for by the prudent, and the opportunity born to remove dangers and offering itself must not slip away. Therefore the troops should be sent into Friesland more quickly, and the fortifications erected or repaired, lest Lalaing, once the defection was discovered, should, from a friend and ally become an enemy, and strike the provinces, stripped of proper garrisons and unarmed, with the help of auxiliaries. These proposals of Ufkenius were heartily commended by the envoys of Friesland and Ommelanden, who were in that assembly, not unaware that Surquetus, Lalaing's secretary, sent to him, had revealed a bundle of letters and, with it, the royal favour, through the carelessness and rashness of his tongue. Although these things were reported to Prince Orange as the very true account of a rumour, the memory and renewal of past deeds had nonetheless removed all suspicion of Lalaing, given his most distinguished reputation. Therefore Orange, still uncertain even in so suitable a testimony of common and rather sinister report, changed his plan of what he had decided for the Amsterdammers, and, setting out for the Campen district through Velavia, he sent Pompeius Ufkenius ahead to Groningen, to summon Lalaing to a meeting with himself in the city of Campen.

units.la: Thuanus ex commentarijs istorum temporum refert, Aurantium sanandæ in Lalainio imbecillitati omnem solertiam tum navasse & ut homine m manu strenuum, vigore juventæ laudatum in veteris officij continuatione revocando à deterioribus obfirmaret. Quare ducendo mobili ingenio, quod omne imperium sicuti mortalia solent, vitio contumaciæ detrectaturum metuebat, leviore remedio usus est, congressusq; & amicitiam dissimulando obfutura benigno per Vfkenium alloquio obtulit. Creditum fuit Aurantium Principem de componendâ Frisios inter & Lalainium æmulatione ac dissidio tum cogitasse & ut impulsos motæ mentis in Lalainio spiritus beneficio oblatæ pacis sedaret. De cujus eventu cum Frisij desperarent, malo, ulterius, quam ut medicinam admitteret, provecto, ita tacitè indignabantur, manifesti defectoris aperta & indies se prudentia consilia dissimulari, principemq; Aurantium more procerum aulicas ad artes & infidum percurandis secessionibus alienationis remedium illa temporum perturbatione confugere. cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXXX. fugere. Erant namque qui infidæ & mox exspiraturæ societati apertum bellum anteferrent & ut Lalainius inter non obscura defectionis indicia deprehensus, spem aut gratiam fœderatæ societatis ex hostili ingenio amitteret. Quod ipsum quoque etsi jam ante regiæ gratiæ inlicio circumventum esset, ita Lalainius simulare doctus colloquij cum Aurantio desiderium præferebat, seque interno pectoris gaudio attactum & humanitatem Aurantij Principis, & optumam consulendi de rep. occasionem aguoscere. Itaq; vultu in hilaritatem formato, etsi aliud sentiret, omne erga Aurantium studium erudità tamdiu simulatione professus est, donec Ellethæ Dongiæ suspectæ fœminæ captivitate prævisa in illo desectio se aperiret. Ea namq; in matrimonio Hermanni Pellenij (is Roblesij Armisabrum egerat) agens ac Delphzilam transiens ubi Bartoldus Entenius tum forte erat, ab eodem in custodiam data, secreta litterarum à Roblesio signata & omne arcanum muliebri fragilitate evulgaverat & quod Entenius vir acer & immitis ingenij terrore quæstionis mollitiem incauti sexus evicisset. Itaq; præter Roblesianas chartas syngraphan quoq; pro acceptis à Farnesio litteris manu Cornelij Kempij hominis Frisij & procuratoris exaratam exhibuit, additâ Farnesij epistolâ, quam instigandis ad arma & rebellionem Drentinis perscribi, deferriqué per fœminam, velut suspicioni minus obnoxiam, Groningam ad urbem imperaverat.
units.tr: Thuanus, from the memoirs of those times, relates that Orange then applied all his skill to heal the weakness in Lalaing, and to strengthen him, a man vigorous in his hand and praised for the vigour of youth, by recalling him to the continuation of his former duty from worse courses. Therefore, since he feared that a man of changeable nature, who, as mortals usually do with all authority, would refuse to submit out of a vice of obstinacy, he used a milder remedy, and, dissembling the meeting and the friendship, he offered him, through Ufkenius, a kindly address. It was believed that Prince Orange then had in mind to settle the rivalry and dissension between the Frisians and Lalaing, and to calm the impulses of his disturbed spirit by the benefit of an offered peace. When the Frisians despaired of its outcome, and the illness had advanced to the point where it would not admit a remedy, they silently resented that the open plans of a manifest deserter were, day by day, being concealed by prudence, and that Prince Orange, after the manner of nobles, had recourse to courtly arts and to deceitful means of healing secessions and alienation in that disturbance of the times. For there were some who preferred open war to an unfaithful alliance that was soon to expire, and who wanted Lalaing, caught among plain signs of defection, to lose the hope or favour of the allied covenant because of his hostile nature. Although he had already been ensnared by the lure of royal favour, Lalaing, trained to dissemble, professed a desire for a conference with Orange, and he showed that he was touched with an inner joy of heart and acknowledged the kindness of Prince Orange and the best opportunity of consulting for the commonwealth. So, forming his face into cheerfulness, though he thought otherwise, he professed all his goodwill toward Orange with learned dissimulation for so long, until, with the capture of Elletha Dongia, a woman under suspicion, the defection in him revealed itself. For she, while serving in the household of Hermann Pellenius (who had acted as Roblesius' agent at Harlingen), passing through Delfzijl, where Barthold Entenius happened to be at the time, was placed by him in custody; and she had revealed the sealed private letters of Roblesius and every secret through the frailty of her sex, and because Entenius, a keen man of harsh temper, had overcome the softness of the incautious sex by the terror of questioning. So, besides the Roblesian papers, she also produced a bond drawn up in the hand of Cornelius Kempius, a Frisian man and agent, as a receipt for letters received from Farnese, with Farnese's letter added, which had been written to stir the Drenthers to arms and rebellion, and she had ordered it carried through the woman, as less open to suspicion, to Groningen.

units.la: Unde, quæ nox aliqua & quorundam conjuratorum conscientia occuluerat, fato detecta, quod adolescere concepti sceleris immanitatem exitio innocentis turbæ non sinebat. Igitur Lalainius detectis, quæ profundo mentis & per artem diu abstruserat, vecors & consilij rursum inops, suâ conscientiâ & Aurantij metu augebatur, quem cum præsidiaria cohorte, destinatoque ad custodiam corporis spiculatore. Campis per Drentiam in Translavicanos iter admoliri famæ plurimum largiens sollicitudo acceperat. Quare ruptâ omni morâ decretum facinus intra se exequi constituit, dimisso sine solatio ac fructu Ufkenio, qui soluto colloquio aulâ & mox urbe excesit.
units.tr: Thus what a night and the conscience of some conspirators had hidden was revealed by fate, since the enormity of the planned crime could not allow the innocent crowd to be destroyed. Lalainius, his designs now exposed, which he had long concealed in his deep mind and by craft, became frantic and again without counsel; he was tormented by his own conscience and by fear of Aurantius, whom he had been anxious, out of regard for his reputation, to march with a guard cohort and a lancer chosen for the protection of his person across the fields through Drenthe toward the Translavians. Therefore, breaking off all delay, he resolved to carry out the deed by his own hand, having dismissed Ufkenius without comfort or result; Ufkenius, the conference ended, left the court and soon after the city.

units.la: Annotatum invenio Upconem quendam Douwonium hominem Frisium, & pertinacius regiâ factione imbutum, in Lalainij aulâ; sumpto districtoque clam gladio de trucidando Ufkenio cogitasse, eumque consilij patrandæ fœdissimæ cædis incusatum indulgentiâ conniventis judicij absolutum. Eundem quoque in via Ufkenio vim post intentantem & conjurationis in patriam manifeste reum, ad honores ac Lalainij spe provectum, trecentos Frisios exules occupandæ urbi & patrandæ cædi obtulisse.
units.tr: I find it noted that a certain Upco Douwonius, a Frisian man and more stubbornly steeped in the royal faction, in Lalainius's court, drew a sword in secret and plotted to slay Ufkenius; and when he was accused of planning this most foul murder, he was acquitted through the indulgence of a complaisant judgment. The same man, too, after threatening Ufkenius on the road, and being manifestly guilty of conspiracy against the country, was promoted to honours on the hope of Lalainius, and offered three hundred Frisian exiles to seize the city and carry out the slaughter.

units.la: Cl. Franckena in Diario notat, se prævisa quoque futuri tempestate vigesimo nono Februarij anni intercalaris die Groningâ Dammonam concessisse, ne semel vinculis datus & terrore mortis perculsus in deterius majusque vitæ discrimen ex infidi temporis conditione recideret. Cæteros econtra fœderis, etiam in Senatu, socios, sua socordia ac suus stupor adeo dementaverat, ut & urbis suæ & salutis curam ex vetere in Lalainium fiduciâ exuerent. Quod cum à sagacibus rerum palam deprehenderetur, famâ suspiciones aggravante, Iacobus Hildebrandius Consul, fœderatarum partium in civitate Princeps, Hovetmanni dignitate functus, ad Lalainium se contulit, cujus interrimâ familiaritate tate ac consuetudine floruerat. Qui in secretum admissus, multaq; de cIↄ. Iↄ. sinistris populi primatumque rumoribus praefatus, ecquid periculi subʟ xxx. esset interrogavit, Lalainiumque rubore, velut consilij conscio, suffu- sum confidenti porro sermone aggressus est.
units.tr: Cl. Franckena notes in his Diary that, foreseeing the coming storm, he withdrew from Groningen to Dammona on the twenty-ninth day of February in the intercalary year, lest, once given over to chains and struck down by terror of death, he should fall back, under the uncertain condition of the times, into a worse and greater peril of life. The rest of the allies of the league, even in the Senate, had so stupefied themselves through their own carelessness and sloth that they cast off care for both the city and their own safety, trusting in Lalainius as before. When this was openly perceived by the shrewd men of affairs, and rumours increased the suspicions, Jacobus Hildebrandius, the Consul, the leader of the confederate party in the city, who had held the office of Hovetman, went to Lalainius, with whom he had flourished in the closest intimacy and friendship. Admitted into secret, and having spoken at length of the sinister rumours about the people and the chief men, he asked whether there was any danger, and, seeing Lalainius flushed as if conscious of the plan, he went on to address him in a more confident discourse.

units.la: Neque enim abs re esse, quod Pontificij clandestinos in coetus co- eant, arma per domos & in secessu moliantur, suspecto talium appara- tu, qui haud dubie in exitium urbis & miserorum recasurus sit. Inde scilicet esse, quod in aula & per viciniam attineri armati, duplicatus spiculatorum numerus perhibeatur, nihil ministerij aut officij reperturus si extra conceptum criminis, aut foedissimae caedis praefecti inno- centia sit. Caveret manus adhuc puras & flagitij insontes sanguine eo- rum imbueret, quorum auxilio ad provinciarum regimen, post ad glo- riam profecisset, ituram in egregiae laudatasque domus dehonestamenta si foederatam multitudinem inter timores ac anxietates fiduciae adhuc plenam ferro aut fuga subverterit.
units.tr: For it was not beside the point, he said, that the Papists gathered in secret meetings and prepared arms in private houses and in seclusion; such preparation, being suspect, would undoubtedly end in the destruction of the city and of the wretched people. Hence, clearly, it was that armed men were kept in the court and in the neighbourhood, and that the number of lancers was reported to be doubled; these would find no office or duty at all, unless the commander of the foul slaughter were innocent of the conceived crime. He should take care not to stain hands still pure with blood, and not to imbue with the blood of the innocent those by whose help he had advanced to the government of the provinces and afterwards to glory; he would go to the disgrace of a distinguished and praised house if he overthrew by sword or flight a confederate multitude still full of trust amid fears and anxieties.

units.la: Caeterum Lalainius prolixa innocentiae obtestatione usus facessere su- spiciones, Hildebrandiumq; Consulem, (quem blandissimo patris no- mine indigetabat) reliquosque foederatos bono animo esse jussit, & ut fragiles levesque conjecturas in fidei metus & aegri pectoris argumenta certissimis fidei suae documentis postponeret. Se isti semel datae obli- gatum bonis artibus & factis aetatem & simul imperium egisse, facturum ut perseveret, deprehendantq; foederati plus invidiae & obtrectationibus, quibuscum luctaretur, quam veritati & eventui tributum. Sua omnia fraudis ac doli expertia esse, neque metuendas ab eo insidias, cujus fide ac fortuna securitas foederis tot annorum decursu stetisset. Quapropter excuteret Hildebrandius infoelicis curae sarcinam & amotis veteris fiduciae impedimentis, praeteriti temporis merita, non futuri metum introspiceret. Nimis certe credulos mortales naturam rerum finxisse. Quae verba manantibus per vultum lachrymis Lalainius exprimebat, sive miseratione periturí, sive ut magnitudinem futuri sceleris bonae mentis & attacti pectoris indicio velaret. Addita etiam dexterae fides, quam multoties foederi datam foedissimo perjurio tum obligabat. Itaque Hildebrandius, velut reciproca pietatis lucta, in pares lachrymarum fletus effusus coenam cum eo sumpsit, eamque inter blandicias infidi oris actam nulla sinistri suspicione clausit. Sunt qui addant, musicos quoque vocum concentus ferali in coena auditos, interque vinolentiam & tripudia partem noctis actam, ne locum quidem apud aperti cordis hominem anteactis suspicionibus reliquisse. Quare salutato tandem Lalainio ad suos conversus Hildebrandius periculi secu- ros esse jussit, ordinarijsque vigilum stationibus quos duplicari opor- tuerat, custodiam urbis & suorum reliquit. Mox Cornelio Kempio, manus injectae, vinculisque dato tormenta eliciendis arcanis decreta. Caeterum Lalainius, qui ad foedus Gandavense signandum, tanquam novum sacramentum suos clam adegerat, cum vehementia intercessit, quaestionibusque habendis supersedere Senatum jussit. Is vero ad Ultrajectinam & Aurantij societatem provocabat, seque a Lalainio adam- plectendas foederis partes vi adactum, stare sacramento ac animadver- tere in flagitiosos statuisse. Ea scilicet severitate disciplinam reip. stare, lapsuram ocyus, si inter domesticam proditorum turbam constituta auroritas rigore poenarum non fulciatur. Improbi quoq; & ex moribus licentiosi temporis malis ingenijs insolentius usi majestate legum, & supplicorum metu non coërceantur, quem omnis aetas conterren-dis, aut emendandis pravorum animis ac delictis, nullâ criminum indul-gentiâ, injecisset. Quae à Lalainio aegrè audita, quod patrocinia reorum invidiâ Senatus suscepisset, infoelicem animum maturando sceleri egere. Itaque Hagenio Campos in magnâ festinatione ablegato, circa primam vigiliam convenire conjuratos jussit, ijsque ut arma induerent monitis, aulicorum quoque domesticorumque turbam inter mistis spiculatoribus armavit. Ipse vigilijs & continuâ inquietudine noctem extinxit, quam illunem & exequendo sceleri commodam cogendis conjuratis sacraverat.
units.tr: Lalainius, however, using a long protestation of innocence, banished suspicions, and bade Hildebrandius the Consul (whom he called by the most flattering name of father) and the other confederates be of good cheer, and to put aside such fragile and light conjectures, which were signs of fearful faith and a sick heart, in favour of the most certain proofs of his own loyalty. He said that he had once given his word to that party, and had spent his life and his rule bound to good arts and deeds, and that he would make sure to persevere; and they would find that more envy and detraction, with which he was struggling, were attributed than truth and outcome. All his acts were free of fraud and guile, and there was no treachery to fear from one whose faith and fortune had kept the security of the league standing through so many years. Therefore Hildebrandius should cast off the burden of unhappy care, and, with the hindrances of old trust removed, look into the merits of past time rather than the fear of the future. Nature had surely made mortals far too credulous. These words Lalainius uttered with tears running down his face, whether out of pity for the one about to perish, or so as to veil the magnitude of the future crime with a sign of a good mind and a touched heart. He also added the pledge of his right hand, which he then bound with a most foul perjury, as he had so often bound it to the league. Thus Hildebrandius, as in a mutual contest of piety, poured forth tears in equal measure, and took supper with him; and the supper, passed amid the flatteries of a faithless mouth, he closed with no suspicion of harm. There are those who add that musical concerts of voices were heard at the feast, and that part of the night was spent in drunkenness and revelry, so that the man of open heart left no room at all for earlier suspicions. Therefore, having finally taken leave of Lalainius, Hildebrandius turned to his own people and ordered them to be safe from danger; and the ordinary watch posts of the guards, which ought to have been doubled, he left to the custody of the city and of his men. Soon afterwards Cornelius Kempius was seized, put in chains, and given over to torture, to extract secrets. Meanwhile Lalainius, who had secretly driven his men to swear to the Treaty of Ghent as if it were a new sacrament, vehemently interceded, and ordered the Senate to refrain from holding examinations. The Senate, however, appealed to the Utrecht union and the alliance of Aurantius, and declared that it had been forced by Lalainius to embrace the parts of the league, that it stood by its oath and had resolved to punish the criminals. Such severity, it said, was what kept the discipline of the commonwealth, which would fall the more quickly if authority established among a domestic crowd of traitors were not supported by the rigour of punishments. Wicked men, too, who, in the evil morals of a licentious age, used their talents more insolently, and were not restrained by the majesty of the laws or by fear of punishment, which every age had instilled to frighten or correct the minds and crimes of the depraved, with no indulgence toward crimes. These things, which Lalainius heard with ill grace, because the Senate had taken up the defence of the accused out of hatred, drove his unhappy mind to hasten the crime. Therefore, sending Hagenius hurriedly to the fields, he ordered the conspirators to assemble about the first watch of the night, and armed them with the warning to put on their arms; he also armed the throng of courtiers and household men, mingling them with the lancers. He himself spent the night in vigils and constant restlessness, a night which, moonless and suited to carrying out the crime, he had consecrated for gathering the conspirators.

units.la: Scribunt militem quoque clam intra urbem admissum, perque pontificiorum domos & secreta in insidijs collocatum, oppressos somno foederatos, & occasionem incipiendae caedis indicasse. Ita quintâ tandem matutinâ conjurati convenere, emissiqué quadraginta à Lalainio equites, qui albâ fascià sinistro brachio dignoscendis conjuratis affixâ, per urbem vicosque discurrerent. Pontificij quoque ab exilio nuper in urbem intercedente Lalainio revocati solito ferociores animos acuerunt, coactique in coetus, dein in plateas more bacchantium effusi, incondito & nocturno clamore totam civitatem complevere. Forum quoque ipsum Everardus Simonius civicae cohortis ductor, Petrus vero Oldendorpius reliqua urbis loca destinatis eâ nocte vigilibus observerat. Quo urbis motu Consul Hildebrandius ad nocturni clamoris auditum, & furentium insaniam domo se effudit, auxilijsque suorum, quos in comitatu habuerat, nequicquam imploratis, velut manum conserturus, à Lalainij famulo glande plumbeâ ictus occubuit. Ita fidissimus patriae civis à familiari suo proditus, miseram urbem suo primus sanguine respersit. Cujus caede factum est, ut reliquis in fugam abreptis, conjurati per urbem ex arbitrio rem gererent, in quam è suburbijs faex quoque nautica, vallo fossaque superatis, ad diripiendas foederatorum aedes dulcedine praedae confluebat. Itaque tum eorum fores magnis ictibus pultatae, quos aut altus sopor, aut pavoris magnitudo secretis domorum abstruserat. Lalainius ipse equo in forum provectus, strictumque gladium nefariâ manu tenens, ordinem & imperata sceleribus dabat, ministrosque conjurationis conturbandas ad domos hortabatur.
units.tr: They write that soldiers too were secretly admitted within the city, and placed in ambush through the houses of the Papists and in hidden places, and that they reported the confederates overcome with sleep and an opportunity to begin the slaughter. Thus at last, at the fifth morning hour, the conspirators assembled, and Lalainius sent out forty horsemen who, with a white band fixed to the left arm to distinguish the conspirators, ran about through the city and its lanes. The Papists, too, recently recalled into the city from exile through the intercession of Lalainius, sharpened their usual fierce spirits, and, gathered into crowds and then poured out into the squares in the manner of frenzied revellers, filled the whole city with confused and nocturnal shouting. Everardus Simonius, leader of the civic cohort, observed the forum itself, and Petrus Oldendorpius the remaining places of the city, with watchmen posted there for that night. At this uproar in the city, Consul Hildebrandius, on hearing the nocturnal clamour and the madness of the raging men, rushed out of his house; and when the help of his own people, whom he had with him in his retinue, had been implored in vain, as if about to join hands in combat, he was struck by a leaden ball from the servant of Lalainius and fell. Thus the most faithful citizen of the country, betrayed by his own familiar, was the first to sprinkle the wretched city with his blood. By his slaughter it came about that, the rest having been swept away in flight, the conspirators acted at their pleasure through the city; into which, from the suburbs, the dregs of the seafaring folk too, having overcome the rampart and ditch, flocked to plunder the houses of the confederates, drawn by the sweetness of booty. Then their doors were battered with great blows, the doors of those whom either deep sleep or the magnitude of their fear had hidden in the secret recesses of their houses. Lalainius himself, carried on horseback into the forum, holding a drawn sword in his wicked hand, gave orders and commands for the crimes, and urged the ministers of the conspiracy to disturb the houses.

units.la: Quippe triginta schlopetarijs stipatus, quos aulae secreto detinuerat, animum sumpserat, auxiliaq; altâ voce gerendis rebus implorans velut ipso natali praefecturae die, dominum rectoremq; populi se professus est. Tum tribus campestribus tormentis ritè instructis, quaternâ tubâ signum dari jussit, tympanorumque consonantium clangore turbidam & ad pericula pavidam civitatem excitari.
units.tr: Indeed, surrounded by thirty musketeers whom he had kept secretly in the court, he took courage and, crying aloud for help in carrying out the affairs, as on the very birthday of his governorship, declared himself the lord and ruler of the people. Then, with three field guns properly arranged, he ordered a signal to be given by a four-fold trumpet call, and the city, troubled and fearful of dangers, to be roused by the clangour of sounding drums.

units.la: Quare plurimae tunc familiae non sine ludibrio in captivitatem abductae, faeminaeque imbelles, muliebri cultu à furentibus detracto, maritorum & juxta suae calamitati ingemuere. Theodorus Schafferus, Hildebrandio in consulatu collegâ graviter vulneratus, cum Regnero Alberda, Gulielmo Ubbena, Alberto Horenkenio, Everardo Huningio caeterisque que militaribus excubijs traditus, consularis & summae in urbe potestatis dignitatem protervia militum & facinorosorum civium deludi conspexit. Ferunt vulgus ipsum & ex plebe infimos ad quingentorum sexcentorumque capitum numerum confluxisse, ipsumque Lalainium auspicium nefario facinori facturum, velut praesentanea morte palluisse. Volente scilicet providentia ut reprobae mentis index facies mortiferi coloris foeditate inquinaretur, ruboremque sanguinis & genarum suffecto luridlo & deformi pallore venturae tabis indicio amitteret. Adeo instantis & ultimi periculi momentum omnem fiduciam anxia sollicitudine mutaverat. Tradunt factionum studia & earum acerbitatem tantam in urbe Groningâ fuisse, & praeter propinquorum animos partium discordijs corruptos, fratrum quoq; affectus, & naturae amicitias foedissimis odijs divulserit.
units.tr: Consequently many families were then led off into captivity, not without mockery, and unwarlike women, their women's clothing torn off by the madmen, lamented the fate of their husbands and their own misfortune alike. Theodorus Schafferus, his colleague in the consulship Hildebrand having been severely wounded, was handed over with Regnerus Alberda, Gulielmus Ubbena, Albertus Horenkenius, Everardus Huningius and the others to the military guard. He saw the dignity of the consulship and of the highest power in the city mocked by the insolence of the soldiers and criminal citizens. They say that the crowd itself, and the lowest of the common people, gathered to a number of five or six hundred heads, and that Lalainius himself, about to begin his wicked deed, turned pale as if at the prospect of immediate death. Providence willed, of course, that the face, the index of a reprobate mind, should be stained with the ugliness of a deadly colour, and that the flush of blood from his cheeks should be lost, replaced by a livid and hideous pallor, the sign of coming decay. So far had the weight of imminent and final danger turned all his confidence into anxious care. They report that the zeal of the factions and their bitterness were so great in the city of Groningen that, besides corrupting the minds of relatives with party quarrels, they tore apart even the affection of brothers and the bonds of natural friendship with the foulest hatreds.

units.la: Tum Lalainius patrato scelere, à quo ordiri se imperium vecors & amens exclamaverat, in forum tabernâ vinariâ descendens, Thomam Ballenium, Pompeium Everardum, Joannem Wiferingium, Joannem Thomaeum, Theodorum Robertium, Everardum Simonium urbis Syndicum, Joannem Goudanum, Hermannum Winbruggium, Jacobum Vinckeburgium & Nigellium Stellinguerfium cohortium ductores & conjuratorum primos factâ coronâ convocavit, verbisque pro concione factis sacramentum exegit. Itaque manus à circumstantibus passim in altum erectae, dictoque obediens turba, ulteriori furoris ministerio se obligavit. Unde biduum abducendis in carceres familijs denuo exactum, non sine ejulatu ac lamentis eorum, quos aut sexus aut aetatis infirmitas ad perferendum crudele spectaculum non obduraverat. Mox convocatis sodalitatum opificumque collegijs, novum juratum concilium priore abrogato creari fecit Theodorumque Robertium & Christophorum Diestanum Consules designavit. Igitur ex fugâ civium quos timor in fossam amnemque Hunesum praecipites agebat, foeda passim per urbem & tristis solitudo, quae ministrorum reformatorum primorumque civitatis sub ignoto quoque habitu subsequentium discessu augebatur. Erant namque qui mutatis tantâ urbis tempestate rebus omnem spem salutis in exilio ponerent, quod modo huic, modo isti parti ex infido temporum statu obveniens fati, velut in orbem euntis, solatio praesentem miseriam allevabat. Dein redacta in potestatem urbe, paceque velut per solitudinem ex fugâ foederatorum clarissimorumque civium partâ, regiae gratiae initiq; cum Farnesio foederis edictum pro rostris publicavit, populumque recentis mali terrore consternatum illius in acta jurare jussit. Litteris quoque confestim exaratis agrariam nobilitatem opprimendis foederatis sollicitavit, & ut illustriores familiae regis gratiam amplexae similiter per agros saevitiae experimento suis partibus ac simul in rempe conjurationibus se innecterent.
units.tr: Then Lalainius, the crime committed, the crime with which he had cried out, mad and frantic, that his rule would begin, came down from the wine-shop into the forum. Forming a ring, he summoned Thomas Ballenius, Pompeius Everardus, Johannes Wiferingius, Johannes Thomaeus, Theodorus Robertus, Everardus Simonius, the city syndic, Johannes Goudanus, Hermannus Winbruggius, Jacobus Vinckeburgius and Nigellius Stellinguerfius, the leaders of the cohorts and the chief conspirators. After making a speech to them, he exacted an oath. So hands were raised high on all sides by the bystanders, and the crowd, obedient to his word, bound itself to further service of his frenzy. Whereupon two more days were spent dragging families off to prison, not without wailing and lamentation from those whom sex or the frailty of age had not hardened to endure the cruel spectacle. Soon, having summoned the guilds of the craftsmen and tradesmen, he had a new sworn council created in place of the old one, which was abolished, and appointed Theodorus Robertus and Christophorus Diestanus as consuls. Hence, as citizens fled, driven headlong by fear into the ditch and the river Hunse, a foul and sad desolation spread through the city, increased by the departure of the reformed ministers and the chief men of the city, who were also leaving in disguise. For there were those who, with affairs so overturned by such a storm in the city, placed all hope of safety in exile. Exile, as fortune turned now to this party, now to that, from the faithless state of the times, went round like a wheel, and by its consolation eased their present misery. Then, the city having been brought under his power, and peace, as it were, won through the desolation caused by the flight of the confederates and the most distinguished citizens, he published on the rostra an edict of royal favour and of the alliance he had made with Farnese. He ordered the people, stunned by the terror of the recent calamity, to swear to his acts. Immediately letters were also written, urging the country nobility to crush the confederates, so that the more illustrious families, embracing the king's favour, might likewise, by a trial of cruelty in the countryside, bind themselves to his party and at the same time to the conspiracies against the commonwealth.

units.la: Caeterum nobilium animis immanitas sceleris & aversatio se infudederat. Cui expiando, ne quod placamentum teterrimo facinori deforet, propiore foederis sacramento se obligavere, armaque & pecuniam in mutua auxilia depacti cum recentissimi furoris infamiâ veteris in ur-bem odij memoriam refricavere. Quibus & hoc accedebat, quod Bartoldum Entenium clarissimorum per Omlandiam familiarem propinquitates & studia trahentem Lalainius hostem decreto Senatus oppida‑ ni proclamasset, omnisque suburbanus ager vastationi expositus nec‑ dum remissi furoris insaniam redargueret. Quare metuebant, ne La‑ lainius à Farnesio auxilijs instructus, in omnem Amasum inter Lavicam‑que flumina agrum se effunderet, insolensque civitas & ex peracto sce‑lere immanior domos atque arces & cum ijs omne sacrum ac familia‑re diriperet. Itaque legati Franckenæ litteris auxilia è Frisijs Dam‑monam evocata, quos prævisa Lalainij defectio, perferente eam fa‑mâ, minus ut solet perculerat. Econtra plurimis nationibus, quas Lalainij nomen atque gloria pervaserat, defectionis pessimæ nuntium stuporem incusserat, quod Aurantio quoque à Diderico Sonnoïo com‑municatum, in principe animo fidem veri non inveniebat. Igitur ve‑lut illusione mentis aut insomnio attactus, spem & fiduciam falsi ru‑moris retinuit, donec Joannis Cornputti & Lubberti Ulgeri centu‑ rionis, qui discrimen clam evaserat, sermone tanquam certissimo te‑ stimonio vinceretur. Quare tunc primum vacillare inanis fiducia coe‑ pit, verso econtra in diffidentiam principis ingenio, quod omne secre‑ tioris consilij cum Pontificijs commercium ex illà Lalainij defectione ac levitate respuebat.
units.tr: Moreover, horror at the enormity of the crime and aversion had filled the minds of the nobles. To make atonement for it, lest any expiation be lacking for that most foul deed, they bound themselves by a closer oath of alliance; and by agreeing on mutual aid in arms and money, they revived the memory of the old hatred against the city together with the infamy of the recent frenzy. To this was added that Lalainius, by decree of the town senate, had proclaimed Bartoldus Entenius an enemy, although Entenius drew his kinship and sympathies from the most distinguished families through the Ommelanden, and that all the suburban land had been exposed to devastation, which still proved the madness of a fury not yet abated. Therefore they feared that Lalainius, supplied with aid from Farnese, would spread over the whole land of the Ems between the Lauwers and the Vechte rivers, and that the insolent city, made more savage by the crime just committed, would plunder houses and strongholds and with them everything sacred and household. Therefore the envoys of Franeker, by letter, summoned auxiliaries from Friesland to Dammona, whom the anticipated defection of Lalainius had, as the report carried it, struck less than usual. On the other hand, to many nations that had been pervaded by the name and glory of Lalainius, the news of his most wicked defection had brought stupor. It had also been communicated to Orange by Dirk Sonoy, but in the prince's mind it found no belief in its truth. So, as if seized by a delusion of the mind or by a dream, he kept his hope and confidence in the false rumour, until he was convinced, as by the most certain testimony, by the account of Johannes Cornputtus and the centurion Lubbertus Ulgerus, who had secretly escaped the danger. Then for the first time the vain confidence began to waver, and the prince's nature turned to distrust, which, because of that defection and levity of Lalainius, rejected every secret council and every dealing with the Papists.

units.la: Albada scribit, se in litteris iv. Kal. Mart. ad Frisios perscriptis, ab eâ ut caverent monuisse, ac ut prædictionem istam ex arcano men‑tis praesagio profectam, tanquam futurae defectionis fatidicum oraculum interpretarentur. Quod ipsum etsi Regnero Alberdæ Groningensium Consuli ab eodem quoque communicatum fuisset, ita simulationibus La‑lainij nimium tribuisse, quas supra ætatem & juventæ calores exercere doctus credulis & ad sua securis obtrusisset. Itaq; famâ Lalainiæ defe‑ctionis Coloniam perlatâ, ubi Albada Frisiorum Legatus ex pacis adhuc negotio hærebat, ovationes & gaudiâ hostium visebantur, quos motum & juxta fortunæ lascivies luxu & commessationibus solutos ex unius de‑ sectione faciebat. Scribunt à temulentis turpissimas proditiones fœde‑ ratis quoque afflictas, Lalainiumque avertendis, quæ struebantur, infi‑ dijs sui securitatem inimicorum captivitate parasse. Igitur poscendis pro Lalainio auxilijs, Farnesium eorum importunitate sollicitatum, quem sola aëris, ut tradunt, inopia maturandis delectibus morabatur. Alba‑da notat copias quaedam circa Karpenam arcem & per Cliviam tum ob‑ errasse, nulloque rectore, aut stipendio effraenes, regis Philippi sacra‑ mentum & signorum fidem defectu pecuniæ abnuisse. Quorum quoq; inruptionibus ne Frisia reliquaeque trans Rhenum provinciæ infestaren‑ tur Aurantius Campis adhuc agens, de erigendis per Frisiæ confinia munitionibus cogitavit, & ut Coverdiam Vidro fluvio & paludum ulti‑gine inaccessam, rudi & imperfecto opere nuper cirdumductam, ma‑jore curâ emuniret. Burtangam quoque haud procul Reiderio ad A‑ masum agro & Lingensium finibus palustri loco sitam in formam justæ munitionis efformaret, impositoq; fœderatorum Ordinum præsidio tue‑ retur. Cujus negotij Diderico Sonnoïo viro nobili & strenuo ad emis‑sarium Vidri fluminis, ut ante dixi, præsidium tenenti potestatem fe‑cit, eaque de re Campis diploma præscripsit. Hohenloum quoque vi‑rum militiæ impigrum retinendo in fide mobili populo in Trans-Isulaniam misit, & ut omnem Drentiæ, qui Frisijs obtenditur, tractum una cum Traiect. Isulaniæ oppidis Lalainio addictis Ordinum fœderi assereret.
units.tr: Albada writes that in letters written to the Frisians on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, he had warned them to beware of him, and to interpret that prediction, which came from a secret foreboding of the mind, as the prophetic oracle of a coming defection. Although he had communicated the same thing to Regnerus Alberda, consul of the Groningers, Albada confesses that he had himself put too much trust in Lalainius's pretences, which, as he had learned, were practised beyond his years by the heat of youth, and had been thrust upon the credulous and the careless for his own ends. So when the report of Lalainius's defection was carried to Cologne, where Albada, envoy of the Frisians, was still engaged in the business of peace, the exultation and joy of the enemy could be seen. The defection of one man made them bold, and they were loosened, moreover, by the wantonness of fortune into luxury and carousing. They write that the most shameful betrayals were also inflicted on the confederates by drunkards, and that Lalainius, to ward off the plots being hatched against him, had secured his own safety by the capture of his enemies through treachery. Therefore, with them demanding aid for Lalainius, Farnese was pressed by their importunity; only a shortage of money, as they report, delayed him from hastening the levies. Albada notes that certain troops were then roaming about the fortress of Karpen and through Cleves, unrestrained, without a commander or pay, and that for lack of money they refused the oath to King Philip and the loyalty of their standards. To prevent Friesland and the other provinces beyond the Rhine from being harassed by their raids, Orange, still at Kampen, thought of erecting fortifications along the Frisian borders. He also decided to fortify more carefully Coeverden, which is inaccessible because of the river Vecht and the swamp-mist, and which had recently been surrounded by a rough and unfinished work. He would also shape Burtanga, situated in a marshy place not far from Reiderland, on the Ems and at the borders of Lingen, into the form of a proper fortress, and protect it with a garrison of the confederated Estates. For this business he gave power to Dirk Sonoy, a noble and vigorous man who held the garrison at the outlet of the river Vecht, as I said before, and about this he prescribed a commission at Kampen. He also sent Hohenlo, a man vigorous in war, across the Ijssel to keep the fickle people in allegiance, and to secure for the league of the Estates the whole district of Drenthe, which lies before Friesland, together with the towns of Trajectum on the Isala that had been won over to Lalainius.

units.la: Econtra Lalainius clementiæ & simul Philippi virium documenta ostentabat, interque minas & blandimenta suspensum illius oræ populum militaribus potissimum præsidijs coërcebat. Quare Sonoius ne ultra Lalainius lacertos moveret, & ut Isala amne Rheni fluminis commeatu ac commercio prohiberet, Camporum oppido Michaëlis Samplonij cohortem induxit, potissimamque Traiectinæ partem, adinuante Hohenloo, in officio retinuit. Itaque Daventriæ & apud Suollanos Frisiorum exemplo templa statuis ac ornamentis nudata, ope potissimum & consilio illorum, qui Lalainij ac conjuratorum detestandum facinus & maculatam perjurio fidem execrabantur. Itaque per illam & vicinas regiones Lalainij & Groningensium litteræ odio sœdi facinoris per fœderatorum exploratores interceptæ, quos observandis tabellionibus per omnia viarum spatia periculosissimi temporis sollicitudo præmiserat. Computtus quoque Drentino ex agro ubi stativa cum cohorte agebat, datis Groningam ad Lalainium litteris pro captivo Senatu & fœderatis civibus intercessit, pariaque nisi illæsi redderentur comminatus pronum ad sævitiem defectoris ingenium conterruit. Cujus odio post sacerdotum fugam, cœnobitæ quoque reliquis per Frisiam monasterijs etsi specie liberæ cessionis excedere jussi, omniaque sacrarum ædium bona in tabulas redacta. Quare inter Oostergoos Wolsendij Carmelitæ, Clarecampij & Doccomienses, è Westergois pensionibus annuis ad alimenta in vitam impetratis cœnobia deseruere, quæ magna religiosorum multitudine per censum & opulentiam referta mæstâ solitudine squallebant.
units.tr: On the other hand, Lalainius displayed proofs of clemency and at the same time of Philip's strength, and between threats and flattery he kept in check, chiefly with military garrisons, the people of that shore, who hung in suspense. Therefore Sonoy, to prevent Lalainius from moving his forces further, and to stop traffic and trade on the Isala, an arm of the Rhine, brought a cohort of Michael Samplonius into the town of Kampen, and with Hohenlo's help kept the greater part of the Utrecht region in its duty. Thus at Deventer and among the people of Zwolle, following the example of the Frisians, churches were stripped of statues and ornaments, chiefly by the help and counsel of those who execrated the detestable deed of Lalainius and the conspirators, and their faith stained with perjury. Thus through that region and the neighbouring ones, letters of Lalainius and of the Groningers were intercepted by the confederates' scouts, out of hatred for the foul deed. The anxiety of that most dangerous time had sent these scouts ahead to watch the couriers along every stretch of the roads. Cornputtus too, from the district of Drenthe where he was encamped with his cohort, interceded by letter sent to Lalainius at Groningen on behalf of the captive Senate and the confederate citizens. Threatening reprisals in kind unless they were returned unharmed, he frightened the defector's nature, which was prone to cruelty. After the flight of the priests, hatred of him led to the monks too of the remaining monasteries throughout Friesland being ordered to leave, though under the pretence of a free surrender, and all the goods of the sacred buildings were recorded in ledgers. Hence, among the Ostergo, the Carmelites of Wolsen, the houses of Clarecamp and Dokkum, and in the Westergo, the monasteries were abandoned, having obtained annual pensions for life for their maintenance. These houses, once crowded with a great multitude of religious and rich through their wealth, now lay squalid in sad solitude.

units.la: F. Nicolaus notat Stauriensi sano à militibus direpto, vastatisque altaribus, Cornelium Wedam centurionem cum præsidio urbe excessisse, Martioq; mense pleraq; per Frisiam fana & monasticorum collegia, velut publico tempestatis consensu, spoliata. Magnum quoq; religiosorum numerum in custodiam conditum, redimendis, ut creditum fuit, captivis quos Lalainius satiato necdum furore Groningæ in vinculis asservabat.
units.tr: Friar Nicolaus notes that after the Stavoren shrine was plundered by soldiers and its altars destroyed, Cornelius Wedda, a centurion, left the town with his garrison. In March most of the shrines and monastic houses throughout Friesland were likewise despoiled, as though by a common agreement of the storm. A large number of monks were also thrown into custody, to be ransomed (so it was believed) against the captives whom Lalaing, his fury not yet sated, was still holding in chains at Groningen.

units.la: Reperio in actis Carmelitarum apud Ilstanos cœnobio eandem vim inlatam, ejusque dotem ab Hobbone Bardio ex professione consulum commentario perscriptam. Ita sacer census gerendo in regios bello & stipendijs militum destinatus, quæstoresque ærarij illâ rerum angustiâ reddendis rationibus & ad præstandum æs decreto Ordinum adacti. In quibus cum esset qui pecuniam ærarij exsolvendis Germanorum quæ Philippo & Senatui militaverant cohortibus & provinciæ debitis assignandam criminaretur homo Pontificius & ex regiâ factione, Delegati è collegio Deputatorum Barthius Idsaerda & Gellius Sibæus, qui pecuniæ administratione eum prohiberent, invitoque & forte reluctanti paratum æs extorquerent. Quare vigilum urbis præfecto, duobus schlopetarijs & ferrario fabro stipati in ejus ædem irruere malleoque seræ admoto, effringi cistam jussere, in quâ publicas pecunias asservari famâ perceperant. Cæterum de vi obtestatus ad Deum, Justitiam, Regem suum & terrarum orbis fidem provocavit, cavitque ne ista actio oneri sibi aut damno esset, & ut obtestatio ad innocentiæ probationem valeret.
units.tr: I find in the records of the Carmelites at Ilst that the same violence was done to that house, and its endowment is described by Hobbo Bardius from the consuls' declaration in their commentary. Thus the sacred revenue, destined for the king's war and the pay of soldiers, was used up, and the treasurers, pressed by that shortage of resources, were forced by decree of the Orders to render accounts and to pay out money. Among them was a man, a Papist of the royal faction, who was accused of assigning the treasury's money to the payments owed to the German cohorts that had served Philip and the Senate, and to the province. The deputies from the college of Deputies, Barthius Idsaerda and Gellius Sibaeus, were to prevent him from managing the money and to extract ready cash from him, though he was unwilling and perhaps resisting. Hence, accompanied by the prefect of the city watch, two musketeers and a smith with an iron tool, they burst into his house, applied a hammer to the lock, and ordered the chest broken open, since they had heard that public money was kept in it. But he, calling God, Justice, his king and the faith of the whole world to witness against the violence, protested. He took care that this action would not be a burden or loss to him, and that his protest would serve as proof of his innocence.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. lxxx. Mox reclusò ærarij secreto, pecuniâ omnis Paulo Gellio successori tradita, ipseq; tanquam decreto Ordinum contumax omni æris possessione ac tribunatu ærarij submotus est. Id iii. Non. Mart. factum. Quibus & hoc accedebat, quod collatis pridie accepti expensique rationibus tre-decim carolæorum millia, quadringenti & nonaginta Septem in ærario de-siderarentur, tabulæq; ea de re scriptæ malè administrati æris hominem importunum convincerent. Tum omnium rerum venalium, quæ provincià exportabantur, indictiones ab agrarijs in comitio scriptæ, quod alieni æris magnitudo & apparatus belli exhauserant. Itaque equorum pecorumque pretia æstumata, vigesimaque quinta æris portio in ærarium inferri jussa divitem armenti provinciam ditavit. Tum butyri, casei adipis, tergorum, bovis sevi, laridi, mellis, salitarum carnium pisciumque, lanæ, cespitum, lignorum, calcis, leguminum, frumenti, fœni, similiumque rerum pondera ac mensuræ tributo subjectæ, omneque vicinarum gentium victui atque commercio inserviens onere ac portorio gravatum. Tabulæ ab Epæo Douma Hallemio & Suffrido Fockenio pro Ooftergoïs, Foppio Grovensteinio, Joanne Hottingha, Justo Ockingha, Horatio Hettenio Douma, Dyonisio Adama pro Westergois, Regnero Idsio, Feicone Tatmanno & Gellio Hepkenio pro Sylvestribus signatæ.
units.tr: In 1580. Soon afterwards the treasury's secret chest was opened, and all the money was handed over to Paulus Gellius, his successor. He himself, as though contumacious against the decree of the Orders, was removed from all possession of the money and from the office of treasurer. This was done on 3 March. Moreover, when the accounts of receipts and expenditure were compared the day before, 13,497 Carolus guilders were found to be missing from the treasury, and the written records on this matter convicted the troublesome man of maladministration of money. Then the land-tax officials posted in the assembly the levies on all saleable goods exported from the province, since the size of the public debt and the costs of war had drained the treasury. Thus the prices of horses and cattle were assessed, and a twenty-fifth part of their value was ordered to be paid into the treasury, which enriched the province, rich in livestock. Then the weights and measures of butter, cheese, fat, hides, tallow, lard, honey, salted meats and fish, wool, turf, wood, lime, pulses, grain, hay and similar goods were subjected to tax, and everything serving the food and trade of the neighbouring peoples was burdened with duty and toll. The tables were signed by Epaeus Douma, Hallemius and Suffridus Fockenius for the Oostergoes; by Foppius Grovensteinius, Joannes Hottinga, Justus Ockinga, Horatius Hettenius Douma and Dionysius Adama for the Westergoes; and by Regnerus Idsius, Feico Tatmannus and Gellius Hepkenius for the Sylvestrians.

units.la: Refert F. Nicolaus, Martio mense comitium Frisicæ gentis indictum, eoque decretum ut in bimestre quadraginta octo aureorum millia in tributum præstarentur. Frisij quoq; in provinciali aut Status concilio socio jure ternos haberent, Omlandiaque cum Groningâ urbe Ultrajectino fœderi aut generalium Ordinum societati restituta unius provinciæ nomine censeretur. In dignitatibus etiam primi Ordinis obtinendis terni à provincialibus nuncuparentur, unusque à Deputatis Ordinum jure repræsentationis Electus, diploma à Gubernatore Generali & provinciali Concilio acciperet.
units.tr: Friar Nicolaus reports that in March an assembly of the Frisian people was called, and it was decreed that forty-eight thousand gold pieces be paid in tax within two months. The Frisians too were to have three representatives each in the provincial or States council, by equal right. Ommeland, together with the city of Groningen, was to be restored to the Union of Utrecht or the fellowship of the general Orders and would be counted under the name of one province. In obtaining offices of the first order too, three candidates would be nominated by the provincials, and one would be elected by the Deputies of the Orders by right of representation, and would receive his commission from the Governor General and the provincial council.

units.la: Invenio in actis, Ordines generales Antverpiæ congregatos, centesimam bonorum aut quintam annuorum redituum partem, in subsidia Frisios tum reliquasque Belgicæ provincias inter cætera tum poposcisse, Frisiosque à repetendis perferendisque istiusmodi oneribus alienos mollioribus ut haberentur tributis decrevisse. Itaque Legatis Antverpiam ituris mandatum est duriora tributa & ingenio gentis adversa removeri Frisiâ curarent, populique fortunæ & tenuioribus rebus terrarum suarum inundationes & dissipatas præsidijs opes obtenderent. Secus, invalidâ excusatione, vicinarum provinciarum moribus ac decretis se afformarent. Quod ad applicanda reip. ærario Ecclesiastica bona, aut emendandos eorum usus (nam id Ordines generales petierant) attineret, fidem facerent, quoniam jure Ultrajectini fœderis cuique provinciæ in causâ religionis disponere liberum foret, se statuisse stabiliendæ paci ac concordiæ Romana Pontificia per Frisiam religio aboleretur. Quippe sacerdotum plurimos conjurationis in patriam & hostilis consilij conscios provinciâ fugisse, religionisque pacem & Ultrajectinum fœdus aversatos beneficijs suis ultro renunciasse, aut in prava consilia serendis per Frisiam discordijs deflexisse. Itaque decrevisse se, ut Missæ exercitio sacerdotes prohibeantur, & ut omnis antiqua beneficij collatio ces-sset, set, exemptoque patronatus & privato possessorum jure, à provinciali cIↄ. Iↄ. Senatu & Deputatis Ordinum rescindatur. Postremum de bonis fisco adjudicatis (nam & hoc subjunxerant) aut post acquirendis Senatusconsf. perscripsisse, ut ea publico Frisiæ ærario inferenda censuerint, Deputatorumque consilio ac autoritate muniendis agris ac civitatibus admonenda, dum commune provincialis fisci ærarium applicandis in certos usus fiscalibus bonis ac actionibus erectum sit.
units.tr: I find in the records that the general Orders, assembled at Antwerp, demanded, among other things, a hundredth of goods or a fifth of annual income as subsidies from the Frisians and the other Belgic provinces. They decided that the Frisians, who were exempt from repeating and bearing such burdens, should be treated with milder taxes. So the envoys about to go to Antwerp were instructed to see to it that the harsher taxes, which were contrary to the nature of the people, were removed from Friesland, and to put forward as their excuse the poverty of the people, the flooding of their lands, and resources scattered by garrisons. Otherwise, with a weak excuse, they would conform themselves to the customs and decrees of the neighbouring provinces.
