As for applying church property to the public treasury, or changing its uses (for the general Orders had asked for this), they should assure them that, since by the law of the Union of Utrecht each province was free to make arrangements in matters of religion, they had decided, in order to establish peace and concord, that the Roman Pontifical religion would be abolished throughout Friesland. For very many priests, conscious of conspiracy against the fatherland and of hostile plans, had fled the province, and, shunning the peace of religion and the Union of Utrecht, had of their own accord renounced their benefices or had turned to wicked schemes by sowing discord throughout Friesland. Therefore they had decided that the priests be forbidden to celebrate Mass, and that every ancient collation of benefices cease; and that, with the right of patronage and the private rights of possessors removed, it be rescinded by the provincial Senate and the Deputies of the Orders. Finally, concerning goods adjudged to the fisc (for they had added this too), or acquired afterwards, they had set down by senatus-consult that they judged these should be paid into the public treasury of Friesland, and, with the advice and authority of the Deputies, be applied to fortifying lands and cities, until the common treasury of the provincial fisc was established to apply fiscal goods and actions to fixed uses.

units.la: Mox Ordinum fœderatorum decreto ne dubijs temporum ex licentiâ militum, disciplina & autoritas imperij labasceret, leges innovando formandoque militari sacramento scriptæ, Frisiorumq; præsidijs à Renico Cammingha Censore copiarum solemni ritu prælectæ. Istæ erant:
units.tr: Then, by decree of the confederated Orders, lest in these uncertain times discipline and the authority of government should falter through the licence of the soldiers, laws were renewed and written out, and the military oath was framed. These were read out with solemn ceremony to the Frisian garrisons by Renicus Cammingha, the Censor of the troops. They were as follows:

units.la: Vt fœderatus miles Geldriæ, Zutphaniæ, Hollandiæ, Zelandiæ, Vltrajectli, Frisiæ & Omlandiæ Ordinibus fidem præstaret, eorumque tribunis, centurionibus aut vicarijs pareret. Damna quoque & incommoda à fœderatis provincijs earum socijs averteret, hostique removendo, terrâ, mari, in acie ac locorum oppugnatione, denique in stationibus expeditionibusque faciendis, officia atque vitam impenderet. Matthiæ Archiduci, Aurantio principi ejus Vicario, Ordinibus generalibus fœderatis & Frisiæ sacramentum diceret, consiliaque aut facta saluti publicæ adversa aut noxia, si quæ innotescerent, apud ductores cohortium profiteretur. Arma in promptu noctu & interdiu quibuscunque in locis haberet ijsque tam in Hispanos eorumque socios, quam grassatores pacis publicæ & Ordinum hostes uteretur. Ijs addictos, aut subducere se imperio Archiducis, Aurantij, Ordinum fœderatorum & Frisiæ in spem regiæ pacis agitantes ad centuriones vicariosque deferret. Conventus & conspirationes inconsultis Tribunis ac centurionibus non iniret; cæterum binos aut ternos perferendis ad Ordines, Præfectum, Deputatos aut eorum legatos querelis deligeret, Provinciâ inopiâ æris laborante, modico stipendio aut victu haberetur, residuumq; æs quaternis mensibus acciperet. Signum pugnæ, non nisi de mandato Centurionis ederet, id si daretur, in armis foret, à signis non nisi ex causâ sonticâ abesset. Expeditionis, excubiarum, aut pugnæ tempore pecuniam non flagitaret, id faciens, laqueo necaretur. Mandata Superiorum detrectans respuensq; vitam amitteret. Iustitiæ impedimentum nemo faceret, cæterum isti administrandæ juramento se obligaret. Recensioni quovis tempore se permitteret istâ durante, Sclopetum glande non instrueret, laxaretur. Id si faceret, pœnâ mortis aut arbitrariâ corrigeretur. Censori copiarum omnem honorem atq; officium deferret, verba facienti dicto audiens esset, pecuniam sub pœnâ mortis non poscueret. Ad signa temulentus non veniret, pugnâ, convicio, maledictis aut blasphemijs sub arbitrariæ correctionis pœnâ abstineret. Glande plumbeâ non nisi in hostem, aut tempore excubiarum & de mandato Præfecti cohortis sub pœnâ extremi supplicij uteretur. Excubias ad mandatum Superioris faceret, eæ nullo tempore intermissæ unius aut duarum horarum essent. Procul somno miles vigilijs vacaret. Præsidij loco excessurus nulli damnum aut injuriam crearet, id si faceret, libram Flandricam penderet.
units.tr: That the confederate soldier shall pledge faith to the Orders of Gelderland, Zutphen, Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, Friesland and Ommeland, and obey their tribunes, centurions or deputies. He shall also avert damage and inconvenience from the confederate provinces and their allies, and in removing the enemy, by land and sea, in battle and in the assault on places, and finally in keeping guard and making expeditions, he shall spend his duties and his life. He shall swear the oath to the Archduke Matthias, to the Prince of Orange his vicar, to the confederate general Orders and to Friesland, and whatever counsels or deeds, if any become known, are adverse or harmful to the public safety, he shall declare before the leaders of the cohorts. He shall keep arms ready night and day in whatever places, and use them against the Spaniards and their allies, as well as against the disturbers of public peace and the enemies of the Orders. Those who are devoted to them, or who plan to withdraw from the authority of the Archduke, the Prince of Orange, the confederate Orders and Friesland in hope of a royal peace, he shall report to the centurions and vicars. He shall not enter into assemblies or conspiracies without the consent of the tribunes and centurions; but he shall choose two or three men to carry complaints to the Orders, the Prefect, the Deputies or their envoys. While the province labours under a shortage of money, he shall be content with modest pay or food, and he shall receive the remaining money in four months. He shall give the signal for battle only on the order of the centurion; if it is given, he shall be under arms, and he shall not be absent from the standards except for a guilty cause. At the time of an expedition, of guard duty or of battle he shall not demand money; whoever does so shall be hanged by a noose. Whoever refuses and rejects the commands of his superiors shall lose his life. No one shall hinder justice; rather he shall bind himself by oath to administer it. He shall submit to inspection at any time while it lasts; he shall not load his musket with ball, on pain of dismissal. If he did so, he would be punished by death or at the discretion of the court. He shall show all honour and duty to the Censor of the troops, be obedient when he speaks, and not demand money, on pain of death. He shall not come to the standards drunk; he shall abstain from fighting, abuse, insults or blasphemy, under penalty of discretionary correction. He shall use lead shot only against the enemy, or during guard duty and by order of the prefect of the cohort, on pain of the extreme penalty. He shall keep watch at the command of his superior, and these watches shall never be interrupted and shall last one or two hours. The soldier shall keep far from sleep during his watches. One who is about to leave a garrison post shall cause no damage or injury to anyone; if he does, he shall pay a Flemish pound.

units.la: Quæ singula 1 v. Eid Mart. Franekeræ, dein alijs in locis juramento firmata, labantem fato aut ex moribus temporum disciplinam emendavere.
units.tr: These individual items, confirmed by oath at Franeker on the Ides of March (1 v. Eid. Mart.) and then in other places, improved a discipline that was failing, whether from fate or from the customs of the times.

units.la: Sic tributo pensitandis bimestribus stipendijs per provinciam decreto & militari populo parendi legibus adstricto, signa è Frisijs in Transl LavicIↄ.Iↄ. LXXX. Lavicanos missa, quae in spem ultionis & obsidij Ioannes Computtus vir militiae & consilij impiger ex Weddano castello omnique vicinâ munitione Groningam ad urbem conduxerat. Quod consilium eo magis festinabatur, quod Lalainius, in scisså & factionibus debili civitate ageret, invidiaeq; civium ex caede & tantâ mutatione rerum exposiitus raris munitionibus circumductâ urbe, tanquam imbelli, se tueretur. Cui facto etsi velum aliquod adhuc obtenderet, facili talium artium juventâ, ita erant nihilominus, qui pristinum amorem ejus odio mutarent, scelerisq; infamiam diritate atrocissimi criminis exsecrarentur.
units.tr: Thus, with the province having decreed that the pay for every two months be raised by tax, and with the soldiers bound by law to obey, the standards were sent from Friesland to the Lavicani in Transisalania (1580). Johannes Computtus, a man vigorous in war and counsel, had brought these from the castle of Wedde and every neighbouring fortification to the city of Groningen, in hope of revenge and a siege. The plan was pressed all the more urgently because Lalaing, who was acting in a city divided and weakened by factions, and who was exposed to the citizens' hatred for the slaughter and so great a change of affairs, and who had the city surrounded by only a few fortifications, defended himself as if he were unwarlike. Although he still threw some veil over this deed, and such arts easily gained him a hearing, there were nonetheless those who turned his former affection into hatred and who cursed the infamy of his crime with the harshest of charges, that of the most atrocious wrong.

units.la: Legi epistolam Georgij Gruteri consiliarij aulici ad Theodorum Lonckium foederati apud Ultrajectinos collegij in Frisiam tum Legatum, manu scriptam, quâ foeditatem patrati facinoris elevabat, ac si Lalainij, aulicorum & Groningani populi securitas in ultimo discrimine constituta extremi & praecipitis remedij esse, Quippe dolosis inimicorum consilijs circumventum afferebat & potissimum illorum, qui seditiosis turbidisq; ingenijs diu usi, vitae, famaeq; fortunis Lalainij paratum exitium destinavissent. Igitur festinato ad praeveniendos insidiantium astus, opus fuisse, ne dissimulato periculo paucissimarum horarum spatio tracta praeclari facinoris tarditas perniciem daret, quod propediem publica patrocinia & terrarum orbis conscientiam pro teste laudis habiturum esset. Quare petebat Gruterus, ut Lonckius Burchiusq; apud Frisios Legati id factum, tanquam ex necessitate petitum, benignè interpretarentur, crederentque non malum & iniquum foederi animum, caeterum subitaneae rerum mutationi tuendae salutis justam sollicitudinem velut causam subfuisse. Notarum ad epistolam autor scribit, illam fascinando potissimum Aurantio & quibusque probissimis exaratam, quo persuasione necessariae defectionis & suae credulitatis vitio decepti, veterie in Lalainium fiduciâ socordiam & ignaviam induerent. Caeterum fraudi & fucandis mentibus destinata foederatorum procerum cura atque sollicitudo perverterat.
units.tr: I have read a handwritten letter from Georgius Gruterus, a councillor of the court, to Theodorus Lonckius, who was then envoy to Friesland of the confederated council at Utrecht. In it Gruterus tried to play down the foulness of the deed committed, claiming that the safety of Lalaing, of the court officials and of the people of Groningen had been brought into the gravest danger and required an extreme and headlong remedy. For he asserted that they had been caught in the crafty schemes of enemies, and above all of those who, having long used seditious and turbulent minds, had planned the ready destruction of Lalaing's life, reputation and fortunes. Therefore they had to hurry to forestall the tricks of the plotters, lest, by hesitating for even a few hours in dealing with a danger they knew of, the delay in so splendid a deed should bring ruin; soon the deed would have public protection and the conscience of the whole world as its witness to its glory. Hence Gruterus asked that Lonckius and Burchius, the envoys among the Frisians, interpret the deed favourably, as if it had been done of necessity, and believe that it sprang not from a wicked and unjust intention toward the confederacy, but from a just concern for their own safety, which lay behind the sudden change of affairs. The author of the marginal notes to the letter writes that it was composed chiefly to lull Orange and all the most upright men, so that, deceived by the persuasion of a necessary defection and by the fault of their own credulity, they might cast off their old trust in Lalaing and grow careless and slothful. Yet the care and anxiety of the confederate leaders, aimed at deceit and at clouding men's minds, had perverted this purpose.

units.la: Sonnoius namque muniendae Coverdiae ac Burtangae mandatum exequi jussus, binas peditum cohortes, quas Cornputtus & Wingardius ducebant, Coverdiam festino itinere expedierat, quo praesidijs cohortium munitionis erigendiq; novi operis consilium foelicius procederent. Ubi seditione militum duorum supplicio sedatâ, qui immodestius stipendia flagitantes caedes & direptiones signorum comminabantur, Adriani Antonij Alcmariani arte septemplicis valli fundamenta erexit, operisque utilissimi propositum admoliri annixus est. Sed vallo jacto perducendi ad finem operis consilium abrupit, tergiversantibus Frisijs castellum premendis Drentinis olim extructum, novo sumptui atque servitio emuniri. Non ideo scilicet arces per Frisiam regiae externaeque dominationis munimenta civilibus se armis destruxisse ut quiete Frisiorum terris reddita severioris imperij novum exemplum in vicinâ gente spectaret, castellaque domi diruta foris extrueret. Ea certe infida regni documenta diu fuisse, regnaturumque adhuc foelicius Philippum, fiamotâ arcium fiduciâ, stabilis imperij praesidium favore populi firmet, superbasque moles & dissociandis dominantium parentiumque ingenijs extructas, cum vestigijs veteris invidiae aboleat. Simile patribus cogitangitandum esse, ne reprobato regis imperio spem libertatis vicinis gentibus præcludant, suaeque servitutis pertæsi, alienæ autores habeantur. Cæterum utilissimo operi, ut ex provinciarum dissensionibus ita ærarij angustiâ impedimentum potissimum nascebatur, indignante Sonoio tantæ molis exordium in illo castrensi & tuendorum finium apparatu morâ aut æmulatione exolescere. Recludendas potius provinciarum opes, removendamque inutilem patrimoniam esse, muniendæ ocyus Coverdiæ, quæ securitatem omni trans Rhenum provinciæ, metuiū ac desperationem obsessæ urbi allatura sit. Nam & ita auxilia sperantibus intercludi, & penuriam commeatus atque annonæ Groninganis orituram si Coverdiam ex arte munitam justis foederati præsidijs impleverint. Cæterum viri tuendæ patriæ studio flagrantis hortamentis monitionibusque parum retributum, æmulatione potissimum illarum nationum, quarum incolumitati perficiendi operis desiderium destinabatur. Adeo ad propria commoda socors quoque & supina securitas illis temporibus erat. Quare Burtangæ quoque multo opere vallandæ ardor intepuit, frigescente rusticæ plebis & fossorum officio, quod Entenius Weddano ex agro pecus abegisset, populationibusque ipsi Drentiæ, infestus sociatatem illius populi hostilibus moribus infirmaret. Itaque Sonoium etsi pro restituendo pecore apud Hohenloiim intercedentem, laborantium multitudo destituit, operisque neglecti & mox deserti incuriâ omne Frisiorum ad firmandam Burtangam salubre consilium disparuit. Quippe non subsidij, aut æris pollicitatio, non instantis periculi timor continuando labori eos incitebat, quorum animos à publici boni curâ socij foederatiq; militis insolentia & rapinarum dulcedo avverterat. Igitur hosti colligendis circa Rhenum auxilijs occupato planum in Drentiam & Transflavicanos iter patefactum est, quod alias ex foeculentâ paludum altissimarum uligine imperium, parantibus irruptionem monstrabatur.
units.tr: For Sonoius, ordered to carry out the fortification of Coevorden and Bourtange, had quickly sent ahead to Coevorden the two infantry cohorts led by Computtus and Wingardius, so that the strengthening of the garrisons and the plan for building a new work might proceed more favourably. When a mutiny of soldiers was quelled by the execution of two men, who, demanding their pay too insolently, threatened slaughter and plunder of the standards, he laid the foundations of a sevenfold rampart by the skill of Adrian Antonius of Alkmaar, and strove to begin the project of a most useful work. But once the rampart was thrown up, he broke off the plan to bring the work to completion, because the Frisians were dragging their feet about strengthening, at new expense and labour, the castle of Drenthe built long before. Certainly the Frisians had not destroyed their citadels by civil arms in order that, once their lands were restored to quiet, the neighbouring people should see a new example of harsher rule and build new castles abroad after tearing down those at home. Those had certainly long been unreliable tokens of the kingdom, and Philip, who would reign more happily still, would strengthen the defence of a stable empire by the favour of the people once confidence in the citadels was removed, and would wipe out, together with traces of old hatred, the proud structures raised to separate rulers and subjects. The fathers must think in the same way, lest, by rejecting the king's rule, they cut off the hope of liberty from neighbouring peoples and be thought the authors of someone else's slavery, since they were weary of their own. Yet while the lack of money, which arose chiefly from the disagreements of the provinces, was an obstacle to this most useful work, Sonoius was indignant that the beginning of so great a construction, in that military preparation for guarding the borders, was fading away through delay or rivalry. He argued that the wealth of the provinces should rather be unlocked and useless patrimony removed, and that Coevorden should be fortified as quickly as possible, since it would bring security to the whole province beyond the Rhine and fear and despair to the besieged city. For thus help would be cut off from those hoping for it, and a shortage of supplies and grain would arise for the Groningers if they filled Coevorden, fortified by art, with the proper garrisons of the confederacy. Yet the ardour of the man, burning with zeal for defending the fatherland, received little in return from his exhortations and warnings, chiefly because of rivalry with those nations whose safety was intended to be the goal of finishing the work. So far did sluggishness and lazy complacency, aimed at private advantage, prevail in those times. Hence the zeal for fortifying Bourtange also cooled, as the peasant folk and the diggers' duty grew cold, because Entenius had driven off cattle from the fields of Wedde and, by raids on Drenthe itself, had weakened the alliance of that people with hostile habits. So although Sonoius pleaded with Hohenlohe for the return of the cattle, the crowd of labourers deserted him, and by the carelessness of a work neglected and soon abandoned, all the healthy plan of the Frisians for strengthening Bourtange vanished. For neither the promise of subsidy or money nor the fear of imminent danger spurred on those men to continue the labour, whose minds the insolence of the allied and confederate soldiers and the sweetness of plunder had turned away from care for the public good. Thus, with the enemy occupied in gathering auxiliaries along the Rhine, a clear route into Drenthe and the lands beyond the Vlie was opened, which otherwise the empire would have shown, from the foul damp of the deepest marshes, to those preparing an invasion.

units.la: Clarissimus fidissimusque illius temporis scriptor tradit internissi operis damnum & simul dedecus avaritiæ præcipuè Sonoij imputatum, quod strangulatâ laborantium mercede, pecuniam erigendis munitionibus decretam privatos in usus foedissimo peculatu convertisset. Quare omissa istarum munitionum curâ, parum quoque ad Groningæ obsidionem profectum, quam rudi castrorum forma & auxiliorum defectu infructuosam fore sagaces futurorum ominabantur. Quippe in castris triginta tantum pedestres, equitum binæ cohortes numerabantur, quas vagas, & planos per agros, rarâ virtutis ad urbem ostentatione se spargentes, licentia militaris imprudentisq; ac temulenti Ducis debile imperium faciebat. Econtra ab oppidanis defectus quoq; per urbem instituti, quæ eâ parte, qua Hunesum amnem excipit, & genuino molari colle exsurgit, permunita, pascendi per suburbana pecoris curam non intermittebat.
units.tr: The most famous and most trustworthy writer of that time relates that the loss of the work broken off, and at the same time the disgrace, was charged chiefly to the avarice of Sonoius, because, by strangling the wages of the labourers, he had diverted the money decreed for building the fortifications into private uses by the most shameful embezzlement. Therefore, with the care of these fortifications neglected, the expedition against the siege of Groningen also achieved little, and shrewd men foresaw that it would be fruitless because of the crude form of the camp and the lack of auxiliaries. For in the camp only thirty foot soldiers and two cohorts of horse were counted, and the weak authority of a leader who was careless and drunk made them wander and scatter over the open fields, displaying themselves rarely before the city, under the licence of the soldiery. On the other hand, the townsmen also set up defences throughout the city, which was strongly fortified on the side where it receives the river Hunze and rises on its natural mound, and did not stop caring for the grazing of cattle in the suburbs.

units.la: Entenius verò, Reiderio amni, qui ad Alæ Hunesiique confluentes omne aquæ declivium ad æstuaria longo tractu defert, terra atq; obice oppilato, reliquos minores pontibus constravit, quo urbem frequentiâ populi amplam, intercepto commeatu, annonæ penuriâ gravaret. Quod tantillis cum copijs facere arduum ac difficile expendentibus periculum videbatur, auctâ insuper potiundæ urbis desperatione, quod præter tormentorum machinarumque defectum, pecuniæ quoque & stipendio diorum inopia insolens exercitus laboraret. Itaq; Winsumano comitio, campanarum per Omlandiam æs fundendis tormentis decretum, & ut omne cœnobiorum, templorumque aurum atque argentum monetæ forma signaretur. Unde sacræ opes, & per eas in luxum profusior divini cultus, templis ac monasterijs detractus, indulgentiâ quoque & decreto ipsorum Præsulum, quos vetus in urbem odium profanandis, ut credebatur, sacris quoque suis accenderat. Quare & de eorum antistitum, qui civitates partes delegerant bonis fisco addicendis eodem comitio deliberatum, & ut Entenio premendæ arctius civitati majora auxilia decernerentur.
units.tr: Entenius, however, blocked the river Reider, which, at the confluence of the Aa and Hunze, carries all the downhill water a long way to the estuaries, with earth and an obstacle, and built bridges over the smaller streams, so that he might burden the city, crowded with people, with a shortage of grain by cutting off supplies. Since he weighed the danger, this seemed arduous and difficult with such slender forces, and the despair of taking the city was increased, because, apart from a lack of artillery and engines, the insolent army also laboured under a lack of money and of daily pay. Therefore, at the assembly at Winsum, it was decreed that bells be melted down across the Ommelanden to cast cannon, and that all the gold and silver of the monasteries and churches be stamped into coin. From this, sacred wealth was taken from the temples and monasteries, and divine worship, more lavish through them, became more extravagant, with the permission and decree of the prelates themselves, whose old hatred of the city had, as was believed, also inflamed them to profane their sacred things. Therefore, at the same assembly it was also deliberated that the goods of those bishops who had sided with the cities be handed over to the treasury, and that greater auxiliaries be decreed to press the city more tightly on Entenius's behalf.

units.la: Cæterum Entenius gloriæ suæ, ultra quam par erat, indulgens, alienæ æmulator, magnosque & supra fortunam spiritus gerens, omne auxilium respuebat, ratus civitatem, etsi inexpiabili erga se odio affectam, suo arbitrio se permissurum. Quod ne fieret, & ne Philippus omni inter Amasum, Vidrum & Lavicam orâ submoveretur, Farnesius liberandis Groningensibus auxilia conduci ad Rhenum fecit, quæ jam antè per Cliviam tumultuarie & sparsim collecta, populationibus ac omni insolentiâ illum agri tractum divexaverant. Cæterum copiæ in procinctu expeditionis stantes, & Rhenum trajecturæ à Philippo Hohensaxio, Iselsteinio alijsque fœderati exercitus ductoribus cæsæ ac dissipatæ, omneque auxilium solvendæ Groningensium obsidioni & opprimendis Frisijs destinatum, Rheni ripâ supra Novesium & in Coloniensium fines submotum.
units.tr: Entenius, however, indulging his own glory beyond what was right, a rival of others' glory, and carrying lofty spirits beyond his fortune, rejected all help, thinking that the city, although affected by an inexpiable hatred toward him, would surrender itself to his judgment. To prevent this, and so that Philip might not be pushed back along the whole shore from Amasum, the Vidrum and Lavicum, Farnese had auxiliaries hired on the Rhine to free the Groningers; these, collected earlier in a disorderly and scattered way through Cleves, had harassed that tract of country with raids and every kind of insolence. But the forces standing ready for the expedition and about to cross the Rhine were cut to pieces and scattered by Philip of Hohensax, Isselstein and the other commanders of the confederate army, and all the help intended to loosen the siege of the Groningers and crush the Frisians was driven back to the bank of the Rhine above Neuss and into the territory of Cologne.

units.la: Unde Lalainium pænitentia festinatæ defectionis invasit, quod æquo tardioribus, velut cunctantis & hærentis Farnesij, auxilijs infestam manum cœlestis ira, aut fortunæ adversitas injecisset. Cæterum, à Cornelia sorore obfirmatus, animum recepit, primamque pectoris ægritudinem ex adversis rebus patam spe secundarum, & mollioris fati excussit. Adeo, more mortalium, juvenili mente ad instantis ævi fœlicitatem arrectâ, futura præsentibus Lalainio potiora videbantur. Quippe virilis ingenij fæmina, commendandis Philippi partibus indefessa, præter dignitates & honores à Farnesio supplementa novæ cladis policebatur, foreque propediem ut regiæ gratiæ & deserti fœderis amplos fructus accipiat. Necdum scilicet fortunam res obsessas civitatis, & juxta fratris sui in extremo posuisse, esseque inter confusa hostium castra quod auxilium periculo promittere queat, tanto certius & validius adfuturum, quanto majoris curæ & apparatus egeret. In Farnesij certè verba & fidem se jurare, quæ non latura sit fratrem suum, & optumam civitatem in hostium manus ac lubidinem recidere. Quæ muliebri arte ac confidentiâ ex prompta Buchonis quoque Aytæ Præpositi Gandensis secretioribus litteris confirmabantur. Itaque mittendi auxilij commeatus, pecuniæ fide datâ, fama quoque nuperæ ad Rhenum cladis extenuata, quo Lalainius pœnitudine defectionis excors novi auxilij fiducià allevaretur.
units.tr: Lalaing was then seized with remorse for his hasty defection, because Farnesius was slow and hesitant in sending aid, as though heavenly anger or some adverse turn of fortune had laid a hostile hand on the help. But his sister Cornelia steadied him and restored his courage. She drove out his first sickness of heart, which came from adversity, by hope of better fortune and an easier lot. So it is with mortals: with a youthful mind fixed on the happiness of the coming age, the future seemed better to Lalaing than the present. This woman of manly talent, untiring in advancing Philip's cause, promised him, besides dignities and honours, reinforcements from Farnesius for a new disaster, and assured him that he would soon receive ample rewards for the royal favour and for his desertion of the confederacy. She did not yet, of course, believe that the besieged city was reduced to its last hope, nor that the relief which could be promised amid the confused camps of the enemy would come the more surely and strongly the more it needed care and preparation. She swore that she trusted Farnesius's words and good faith, which would not leave her brother and the best city to fall back into enemy hands and lust. Her womanly skill and confidence were confirmed by secret letters from Buchon Aytta, provost of Ghent, who was quick to act. And so the provisions for sending aid were ordered, money was promised on trust, and the report of the recent disaster on the Rhine was made light of, so that Lalaing, out of remorse for his defection, might be lifted up by hope of new help.

units.la: Itaque Lalainio intra muros Groningæ obsesso, Legatio Hagam ad fœderatos Ordines instituta, delegatiq; Doco Martna, Hesselus Aysma Iᵒᵘ. Carolus Roorda & Jacobus Iacobæus Bolsuerdiensium Consul, qui eadem fungerentur.
units.tr: So, with Lalaing shut within the walls of besieged Groningen, an embassy was sent to the confederate Estates at The Hague. Docko Martna, Hesselus Aysma, Iᵒᵘ. Carolus Roorda and Jacobus Iacobaeus, consul of Bolsward, were chosen to perform this office together.

units.la: Eorum MANDATA erant.
units.tr: Their instructions were these.

units.la: Vt in eligendo ANDINO reliquarum provinciarum suffragijs se affor marent, ca- verentq; universi, ne quid mali, Galliæ exemplo, ex ANDINI, aut suorum confilijs obveniret. Concilium provinciale sub cautione antè expressâ constituifacerent, in tributo & censu ærarij agendo tum vectigalibus nauticis ac portorijs commune consilium sequerentur. Centesimam bonorum aut quintam redituum ob rationes jam antè dictas excusarent, binos sestertios in cu usq; cerevisiæ tonnas parando commeatui bellico imponi sinerent. Decretum de domanijs, ut vocant, regijs, & cænobiorum bonis bello applicandis factâ relatione perferrent. Divino nomini, patriæ saluti, præservandis ab hostium incursu agris sua officia, suam legationem impenderent. Curarent quoque, ut quod publicæ causæ ex Ecclesiasticis bonis impensum esset, ratum haberetur. AURANTIUS desertam à LALAINIO Præfecturam suscipéret, vicariæ administrandæ GULIELMUM LUDOVICUM NASSOVIUM, aut alium sui sanguinis sufficeret. Hæc xiv. Kal. April. signata.
units.tr: That in choosing Andinus they should join their votes with those of the other provinces, and all should take care that no harm, as in the case of France, come from the plans of Andinus or his men. They were to set up a provincial council under the caution stated above, and in managing the taxes and the treasury, as well as the naval duties and tolls, they were to follow the common counsel. They were to excuse the hundredth part of goods or the fifth of revenues for the reasons stated before, and to allow two stivers on each cask of beer to be imposed for procuring war supplies. They were to bring back a report and carry through the decree concerning the so-called royal domains and the goods of the monasteries to be devoted to the war. They were to give their services and their embassy to the divine name, to the safety of the fatherland, and to protecting the fields from enemy incursions. They should also see that whatever had been spent for the public cause from ecclesiastical goods be ratified. Orange was to take over the prefecture deserted by Lalaing, and to supply William Louis of Nassau, or another of his blood, to administer it as vicar. Signed on the fourteenth day before the kalends of April.

units.la: Mox fœdus inter agrarios oppidanosque percussum, dissidentesque & velut divisi antè provinciales certo reip. corpore conclusi.
units.tr: Soon afterwards a league was struck between the country people and the townsmen, and the provincials, who had been divided and at odds before, were brought together into a fixed body of the commonwealth.

units.la: FORMULA FOEDERIS erat.
units.tr: The formula of the covenant was this.

units.la: Mutua inter provinciales societas & communio reip. esto. Oppidani agrarios cum uxoribus atque liberis, quovis tempore, salvo tamen civitatis jure recipiunto. Tormenta, pulverem, cæteraque belli subsidia ex armamentario de consilio Deputatorum oppidani agrarijs subministranto. Tuendis provinciæ privilegijs mutuas operas præstanto, eorum violatoribus communi consilio occurrunto. Fœdus hoc nemo, nec nisi perduellis, aut pacis publicæ ruptor infringito; id facientem lege coercento.
units.tr: Let there be a mutual fellowship and communion of the commonwealth among the provincials. The townsmen shall receive the country people with their wives and children at any time, saving however the right of the city. The townsmen shall supply cannon, powder and other war supplies from the arsenal to the country people, by the advice of the Deputies. They shall render mutual services in defending the privileges of the province, and by common counsel they shall oppose those who violate them. Let no one, except a traitor or a breaker of the public peace, infringe this covenant; let the one who does so be restrained by law.

units.la: Quod fœdus pro agrarijs à Serapio Galama, Geroldo Intenio, I. Sannio, S. Fockenio, F. Tatmanno, Horatio Hetteni, Scipione Meckama, Iancone Osingha & Aucone Edonio signatum, soli Harlingani in spem muniendæ publico sumptu urbis tum confirmavere. A reliquis vero oppidanis post annum & alterum, ut memorabo, approbatum, spem etsi lubricam, communi concordiæ injecit.
units.tr: This covenant was signed for the country people by Serapius Galama, Geroldus Intenius, I. Sannius, S. Fockenius, F. Tatmannus, Horatius Hetteni, Scipio Meckama, Iancho Osingha and Aucho Edonius. Harlingen alone then confirmed it, in the hope of fortifying the city at public expense. The other townsmen approved it only after a year and more, as I shall relate. This hope, though slippery, brought a common concord.

units.la: Itaque ito fœdere, disjectisque cœnobijs (quæ ante sæcula rudi temporum ætate zelo pietatis extructa incrementa opum, fœdissimi luxus fecerant) immensi proventus & in invidiem nobilium familiarum ultra modum auctí, scholarum templorumque ministerijs admoti, consensu ipsorum Antistitum, quibus modica sustentandæ vitæ subsidia valitura ad frugalitatem decernebantur.
units.tr: Thus, with the covenant made and the monasteries broken up (which, founded in a rude age by zeal for piety, had grown in wealth and produced the most shameful luxury), their immense revenues, increased beyond measure and becoming an envy to noble families, were turned to the support of schools and churches, with the consent of the superintendents themselves, for whom modest allowances sufficient to sustain life were decreed, to encourage frugality.

units.la: Cæteris hostium partes secutis omne pensionis annuæ beneficium interceptum, eorumque ætas, quieti & otio destinata, facili transfugio inter arma aut eorum metum consennuit. Quare templis ac fanis, aurea atque argentea vasa, tum infularum, vestiumque sacerdotalium pretiosissimi habitus subducti, omneque antiquæ pietatis donarium sacris ministerijs decretum, alijs usibus applicatum. Quippe post præsulum fugam monasterijs Floridi Campi, Thaboritano, & Lidlumensi mense Februario cœnobitæ decesserant, amotisque locorum rectoribus, sacrorum quoque exercitia solitudo aut metus internisserat. Quo tempo-
units.tr: When the rest had taken the side of the enemy, every benefit of the annual pension was cut off, and their age, meant for quiet and leisure, grew old amid arms or fear of them, through an easy desertion. Therefore golden and silver vessels were carried away from the temples and shrines, and also the mitres and the most precious priestly vestments, and every gift of ancient piety, set aside for sacred ministries, was applied to other uses. For after the flight of the prelates, in February the monks had left the monasteries of Floridus Campus, Thabor and Lidlum, and with their superiors removed, solitude or fear had also interrupted the sacred exercises. At which time—

units.la: regē
units.tr: regē

units.la: re una cum Clarecampensium Docomiensiumque monasticis sodalitatibus, Sioneæ quoque virgines alimenta ad vitam depactæ cœnobio profugerant, quod ab illo sexu diu frequentatum, triste tum silentium pro conditione temporis admiserat. Tunc ditium quoque pagorum fama omni auro atque argento privata, ornatusque sacrarum passim ædium tanquam superstitioni obnoxius, provincialium oculis subductus est.
units.tr: —together with the monastic brotherhoods of Clarecamp and Docomium, the virgins of Sioneae also, who were bound to live on fixed allowances, had fled to a convent, which, long frequented by that sex, had then fallen into a sad silence, as the times required. Then also the reputation of the wealthier villages, stripped of all gold and silver, and the ornaments of sacred buildings everywhere, as liable to superstition, were withdrawn from the eyes of the provincials.

units.la: Reperio in actis celebri apud Dronripios fano, quod suis opibus, & municipalium liberalitate inclaruerat, præter sex argenteos reliquamque argenteam supellectilem, undecim libras æquantem, tres quoq; e rubro holoserico sacerdotes togas sacris surreptas redactasque in inventarium, incerto aut obscuro autore, disparuisse. Postremum Anna Herennia cum suarum monialium turbâ novo quoque propè Snecam cœnobio cessit, singulæque cum cæteris eodem fato in diversa terrarum sparsæ, aut connubijs, aut civili vitæ transcriptæ, annuarum pensionum usu, ac tori dulcedine fugæ tædia & primam ægritudinem lenivere.
units.tr: I find in the records that at the famous temple of the Dronrip people, which had grown renowned through its wealth and the generosity of the townsfolk, six silver pieces and the rest of the silver furnishings, weighing eleven pounds, had vanished, as well as three priestly togas of red silk, which had been taken from the sacred things and entered in the inventory; the author of the theft is uncertain or unknown. Lastly, Anna Herennia, with a crowd of her nuns, also gave way to a new convent near Sneek. Each of them, scattered with the others by the same fate to different parts of the world, either by marriage or by return to civil life, eased the weariness of flight and the first sickness by the use of the annual pensions and the sweetness of the bed.

units.la: Quippe omne signatum paratumque æs fugientium Præsulum avaritiæ abscónderat, qui nocturnis itineribus, expilatis ac desertis cœnobijs Groningam profecti, conducendis in patriam militibus raptum ex ærario censum suggerebant.
units.tr: For the greed of the fleeing prelates had hidden away all the coined and ready money. They travelled by night, having plundered and abandoned the monasteries, went off to Groningen, and proposed that the tax taken from the treasury be used to hire soldiers to bring back to the country.

units.la: Itaque ditium cœnobiorum gazâ direptâ, regia excisa, ut vocant, in Basilicâ 26. April. in tres annos & medium publicanis locata, cæterum eâ cautione, ut sublevando ærario, biennale locarium specie anticipationis intra quatriduum penderent, reliquumque locarij ad Kal. Majas anni octuagesimi primi præstarent. Cui oneri, ut veteri immunitate & ex beneficio Cæsaris nobilitas eximeretur, libellum supplicem Deputatis Ordinum hunc in modum exhibuit.
units.tr: Thus, with the treasure of the wealthy monasteries plundered, the so-called royal excise was let to tax farmers in the Basilica on 26 April for three and a half years. But on the condition that, to relieve the treasury, they should pay two years' rent in advance, under the guise of an anticipation, within four days, and should pay the rest of the rent by the kalends of May in the eighty-first year. To be exempted from this burden, the nobility, by its old immunity and the favour of the Emperor, presented a supplicating petition to the Deputies of the Estates in the following words.

units.la: Nobilitatis Frisicæ bona, DEPUTATI, Anno 1515. translatâ à SAXONE in Austrium provinciâ CAROLUS post Cæsar divæ memoria onerum immunia esse jussit. Quod beneficium ijs potissimum Carolinâ liberalitate indultum, qui Saxoniæ Duci fidem professi, fidelitate obsequij, aut pretio, omnia rerum servitia redemerunt. Igitur decretum, ut illi eorumq; colonı in perpetuum ab omni onere liberi forent, vimque & fructum beneficij ex merito, aut pro munere servatæ fidei sentirent. Cæterum nobilitas in ejus possessionem, aut umbram vix admissa, obliteratum quorundam morte, aut decursu temporis beneficium non retinuit, cum per vim regiæ, aut suorum dominationis oppressojure & abolitâ immunitate, excisæ & omnium onerum sarcinam ferre coacta est. Nunc vero ex Gandavensi fœdere in integrum restituta, quod postliminij jure beneficia reddebat, vestram opem implorat, ac ut veteris beneficij legem ex eodem fœdere renovetis. Quin scitote humanæ societatis lubricum non alio, aut saltem firmiore fulcro sustineri, quam si boni præmia & mercedem fidelis obsequij ferant, mali & defectores pœnis aut supplicijs corrigantur. Qui ipsi ut contumaciam parendi plerumque ex amissi juris aut beneficij sensu induunt, ita econtra affectus animorum conciliat, & æquitatis ratio introspecta & antiqui juris confirmatio. Cujus usu ut nos redonetis, DEPUTATI, ad vetustatis reverentiam, & vestram gratiam provocamus, quæ non malum experimentum sua sinceritatis ac judicij factura scit, si nostram & majorum eminentiam, illaesi ceteris provincialibus agnoverit. Id si fecerit, familiam & posteros nostros immunitate onerum & imprimis Excise donaverit, arctiore vinculo nostra gratitudo & agnitio beneficij provincie nos obligabit, quibus animus erit cum profes-sione obsequij, vitam atque fortunas nostras nascenti reip. impendere.
units.tr: The goods of the Frisian nobility, Deputies: in the year 1515, when the province was transferred from Saxony to Austria, Charles, afterwards Emperor of blessed memory, ordered that they be free from all burdens. This benefit was granted by Charles's liberality chiefly to those who had professed loyalty to the Duke of Saxony and had bought back all services by fidelity and obedience or by payment. It was therefore decreed that they and their tenants should be free from every burden forever, and that they should feel the force and fruit of the benefit in proportion to their merit, or as a reward for faith kept. But the nobility, scarcely admitted to its possession or even its shadow, did not keep the benefit, which was blotted out by the death of some or the passage of time; oppressed by the power of the king or of their own lords, and with the immunity abolished, they were forced to bear the weight of all burdens, the excise included. Now, however, it has been restored in full by the Ghent covenant, which by the right of postliminy gives back benefits, and they implore your help and ask that you renew the law of the old benefit from the same covenant. Indeed, know that the slipperiness of human society is supported by no other, or at least no firmer, prop than when the good receive rewards and the wages of faithful service, and the bad and deserters are corrected by penalties and punishments. As they themselves put on contumacy in obeying mostly from a sense of a lost right or benefit, so, on the other hand, a regard for equity and the confirmation of ancient right win over men's affections. That you may restore us to the use of it, Deputies, we appeal to your reverence for antiquity and to your favour, which knows how to make no bad trial of its sincerity and judgment, if it acknowledges the eminence of us and our ancestors unharmed in comparison with the other provincials. If it does so, and grants immunity from burdens, and especially from the excise, to our family and our posterity, our gratitude and our acknowledgment of the benefit will bind us to the province with a closer tie, and we, with a profession of obedience, will be willing to devote our lives and fortunes to the newborn commonwealth.

units.la: Hæc Wilconis Holdingha, Heronis Burmania, Sibrandi Burmania, Renici Camminga, Iulij Botnia, Upconis Burmania, Renici Camminga, Kemponis Donia, Hesseli Emingha & Sibrandi Camminga manu signata.
units.tr: Signed by the hand of Wilco Holdingha, Heronis Burmania, Sibrandus Burmania, Renicus Camminga, Iulius Botnia, Upco Burmania, Renicus Camminga, Kempo Donia, Hesselus Emingha and Sibrandus Camminga.

units.la: Quæ res quod à meri imperij aut majestatis dispositione petenda esset, à Deputatis ad Archiducem Matthiam aut in proximum si velint comitium rejecta.
units.tr: This matter, since it ought to be sought from the disposition of the sovereign power or majesty, was referred to the deputies to Archduke Matthias or, if they wish, to the next assembly.

units.la: Quo fere tempore omnem per Belgicam occulto tremore tellus concussa, stupentibus plerisque subterraneos illos motus, rarâ temporum ætate his in provincijs observatos, novo rerum prodigio invalescere. Quippe montanis locis, quæ natura beneficio internæ cavitatis extulisset, eos obvenire edocti, tanto magis in admirationem illius tremoris rapiebantur, quod sereno tranquilloque cælo fieret, proculque tempestatibus & vi ventorum solidam terræ molem & vicinis aquis interfusam impellente spiritu concuteret.
units.tr: About that time the earth was shaken throughout Belgium by a secret tremor. Most people were astonished, since such underground movements had been observed in these provinces only rarely in living memory, and they grew into a new portent. Those who had learned that such quakes came upon mountainous places, which nature had raised by the benefit of internal hollows, were all the more stirred to wonder that the tremor happened under a clear and calm sky, when no storms or force of winds were at hand, and yet it shook the solid mass of the earth, which lies wedged among neighbouring waters.

units.la: Tradunt scriptores lapides passim ex ædificijs dilapsos, omneque æs campanum, vibratis quasi turribus, agitatum sonitus edidisse. Mare quoque ipsum etsi placidissimum & strato æquore blandiens, manifestâ succussione actum, fluoreque suo, vacui expers, profundiore causâ impulsum, superficiem movisse. Quod sive vaporum exitum parantium, & velut enitentium vi evenit, quæ compactas quoque nubes in ipso aëre diffindit ac movet, sive maris aut aquarum æstu maritima, aut fluminibus proxuma agitante, mihi persuasum est, motum illum ab imo in superiora provectum, suo quoque sine ac prædictione non caruisse. Decernente velut naturâ rerum, ut pace Belgica Regem inter & Ordines apud Coloniam tum abruptâ, illo insoliti tremoris præludio funestos bellorum motus aperiret. Id 8. Eid. April. horâ post meridiem sextâ factum autores tradunt.
units.tr: Writers relate that stones fell here and there from buildings, and that all the bronze of the church bells, as if the towers were struck, sounded when set in motion. The sea itself, though most calm, its surface smooth and flattering, was moved by a plain shaking, and stirred its surface from below, without any flow of its own, being driven by a deeper cause. Whether this came about from the exit of vapours preparing to escape, as if struggling forth with force, which also splits and stirs the compacted clouds in the air itself, or whether the tide of the sea or the waters, or the nearby rivers, were the agents, I am persuaded that this motion, carried upward from the depths, did not lack its own purpose and foretelling. It was as if nature, deciding the course of things, through this prelude of unusual tremor, were to reveal the deadly movements of war, since the peace of Belgium between the King and the Estates had then been broken off at Cologne. The authors report that this happened on the eighth day before the Ides of April, at the sixth hour after noon.

units.la: Invenio in actis istorum temporum Ordines fœderatos Ultrajecti tum confidentes, jam ante mense Februario de Coloniensis pacis fœlici eventu desperasse, omnemque salutis suæ & juxta publicæ spem in sanctissimi optimumque fœderis tutelâ, tanquam certissimo fortunæ præsidio posuisse. Itaque decrevisse ut ambiguis animorum inclinationibus præter Præfectos, Magistratus, collegia, sodalitates provinciarum & civitatum populus quoque universus ad jusjurandum fœderis adigeretur, nullam pacis cum Philippo rege conventionem, præterquam servato Ultrajectino fœdere, adiret. Magistratus quoq; suspicione aliquâ regiæ partis attaminati, etiam ante diem loco ac dignitate moverentur, velut poscente reip. discrimine, ne vanâ pace regiâ, suspectis aut incertæ in patriam fidei rectoribus administratio rerum demandaretur. Cui pacis tractationi continuandæ, etsi Cæsar in speciem se interponeret, ira erant, qui non ignorarent, Cæsarem avunculi & simul sororij regis, plus propinquitati & amicitiæ, quam Belgarum causæ, durante apud Coloniam conventu, dedisse. Igitur sumptis clam de removendo Philippo deliberationibus in Andinum eorum consilia reflectabantur, qui Cæsaris, cIↄ. Iↄ. Philippique propinquitatibus & Electorum principum in Romanam religionem propensioribus studijs diffisi, Gallicæ & Andinæ societatis lxxxx. ligionem propensioribus studijs diffisi, Gallicæ & Andinæ societatis commendatione concilia patrum inquietabant. A qua amplectendâ, etsi suspecta regnantium indoles, & funestissimi eâ ætate Galliarum motus deterrerent, ita necessitati obtemperandum censebant, qui æquissimi Belgicæ imbecillitatis æstumatores omne ad auxilia externi principis suffugium præclusum provincijs opinabantur. Quæ etsi in secreto patrum disceptarentur, ita Philippo & Cæsari non ignorabantur, adeo parum contectis eo tempore magnarum rerum arcanis, ut aut aliorum imprudentiâ aut aliorum levitate aut malitiâ evulgarentur.
units.tr: I find in the records of those times that the confederated Estates at Utrecht, who were then confident, had already in February despaired of a fortunate outcome at Cologne, and had placed all their hope of safety and of the public good in the protection of the most holy and best covenant, as the surest support of their fortunes. Accordingly they decided that, besides the prefects, magistrates, guilds and fraternities of the provinces and cities, the whole populace should also be bound by oath to the covenant, and that no agreement for peace with King Philip should be entered into, except with the Utrecht covenant preserved. Magistrates also who were tainted by some suspicion of the royal party were to be removed from office and rank even before the day, as if the danger to the commonwealth demanded it, so that the administration of affairs would not be entrusted to rulers who were suspect, or whose loyalty to the fatherland was uncertain, through a vain royal peace. Although Caesar interposed himself in appearance in this continuing negotiation, there were some who knew well that, while the assembly at Cologne lasted, Caesar had given more weight to the kinship and friendship of his uncle and at the same time brother-in-law, the king, than to the cause of the Belgians. Therefore, after secret deliberations about removing Philip, their counsels turned toward Antwerp, those who, distrusting Caesar, Philip's kinsmen, and the princes of the Electors more inclined to the Roman religion, troubled the councils of the fathers with recommendations of the French and Andine alliance. Although the suspect disposition of the rulers, and the most deadly movements of France in that age, deterred them from embracing it, they judged that they must yield to necessity. These men, the most fair assessors of Belgian weakness, believed that every refuge for the provinces in the aid of a foreign prince was closed. Although these matters were debated in the secret of the fathers, they were not unknown to Philip and Caesar, the secrets of great affairs being then so little concealed that they were divulged either through the imprudence of some, the levity of others, or malice.

units.la: Quare Cæsar litteras xii. Maï Pragâ Bohemorum ad Ordines generales hunc in modum dedit:
units.tr: Therefore Caesar, on the twelfth day of May, gave from Prague of Bohemia a letter to the General Estates in this manner:

units.la: CVM Andino societatem vos agitare intelligo, Ordines, & repetere ea velle, quæ dissuaseram. Ac quanquam spes me adhuc cæperat, fore, ut cum Philippo rege, cum principe vestro in gratiam rediretis meâ & Romani Imperij intercessione, ita deprehendo externa fœdera domesticâ pace apud vos potiora esse. Quod cum ita sit, ab obsequio regis à majorum religione alienos vos esse indicium facitis, præter fidem mihi Cæsari & Romano Imperio factam, quâ in religione Romanâ & regio obsequio perseverare vos constituisse, non semel professi estis. Qui animus si vobis etiamnum esset, pro bello pacem haberetis, neque esset, quod vos à principe vestro, principem à vobis divelleret. Quod malum ut sanari aut tolli possit, hortor ut ab Andini societate abstineatis, & ut fide in Philippum regem & simul receptam religionem proni legatos ad me Caesarem mittatis ocyus. Nam id facturos vos soluto ad Coloniam conventu vestris ex litteris arbitrabar, quod cum cæteris neglectum, ut redintegretis moneo. Quo facto daturus sum operam, ut me Caesarem juvandis rebus vestris, & conciliandæ regem inter & vos paci pronum, atque facilem habitum sitis.
units.tr: Since I understand, Estates, that you are being urged toward an alliance with Antwerp, and that you wish to revive those things which I had dissuaded, and although hope had begun to arise in me that through my intervention and that of the Roman Empire you would be restored to favour with King Philip and with your prince, I find that foreign treaties are preferred by you before domestic peace. Since this is so, you show by your conduct that you are estranged from obedience to the king and from the religion of your ancestors, besides the faith pledged to me, Caesar, and to the Roman Empire, by which you have more than once professed that you had resolved to persevere in the Roman religion and in royal obedience. If that disposition still remained in you, you would hold peace rather than war, and there would be no reason for anyone to tear you away from your prince, or your prince from you. So that this evil may be healed or removed, I urge you to abstain from the alliance with Antwerp, and, with faith in King Philip and the religion once received, to send envoys to me, Caesar, with all speed. For I was of the opinion, from your letters, that you would do this when the assembly at Cologne was dissolved, and since this has been neglected along with the rest, I advise you to renew it. Once this is done, I shall take care to assist your affairs, and to bring about peace between the king and you, so that you may find him inclined and easy to deal with.

units.la: Ad quas ORDI- NES:
units.tr: To which the States:

units.la: LITTERARVM nostrarum argumentum quibus abrupto Coloniensi conventu legatos à tractandâ pace revocavimus, Invictissime Imperator, memoriâ adhuc tenemus. Interea de mittendis ad te Legatis cogitavimus, qua tuorum & Philippi mandatariorum immodestis criminationibus nostra innocentia se purgaret. Caeterum minuendis obtrectationibus atque odijs legatio intermissa. Nunc verò cum nova cum Andino Galliarum regis fratre pepigisse fœdera arguamur, professione integritatis nostræ nos excusamus, testamurque procul novorum fœderum consilio, anteactæ tantum cum Andino societatis contractum atque memoriam innovasse: Non ut tuæ majestati, aut Romano Imperio ista conventionis confirmatio aliquid derogaret, cæterum ut sub auxilijs potentissimi principis nostra vita atque fortuna protegeretur. Quod ideo consilium maturare coacti sumus, postquam non sollicitati ad intercessionem Reges & Principes, non gemitus aut lachrymæ populi nostri, non imminentis ruinæ miseratio immitem Philippi animum flexit, ut sibi honestam, & nobis vero exspectatam pacem novo clementiæ exemplo largiretur. Quare omni spe pacis & regiæ gratiæ amotâ, ritè & more majorum fecisse videbimur, si in conservandarum provincialium curas hac implacabili regis irâ descendamus, subtractoque immitissimo Regi obsequio immodestæ dominationis triste servitium declinemus. Quod quanquam æquissimis conditionibus oblatis (& quas sedandis discordiis nostra sollicitudo offerrebat cessantibus armis melius pacis atque otii res tractatura) tuæ majestati & Romani Imperii Electoribus, tum cogitare & velle professi simus, ita molliendo eferati regis ingenio tantum non profecimus, ut in suspenso arma essent, quæ regii ministri majore crudelitate an insolentia miseris provincialibus intentavere. Quarum quoq; utramq; cum Carolus Arrogonius Philippi Legatus suis quoque in litteris spiret, gentium exemplo, protegendis jure divino & humano corporibus, uxoribus atque liberis nostris pro libertate majorum & nostrâ arma capere parati sumus, provocareque ad auxilia externorum Principum, ne civitates nostras, atq; earum merces bellis vis convellat, nosque in imbellis turbæ amplexibus pati exilia, patriamque inermem prædæ & furoribus exponere cogamur. Et quoniam omne tuum ac juxta Rom. Imperii auxilium nobis præclusum est, quod contra hostium nostrorum exercitus, commeatu atque annonâ subjuvit, ita testamur, nuperum Coloniæ super pace Conventum damno nobis fuisse, omnesque felicium armorum grogressus internis secessionibus atque discordiis subversos. Unde fit ut tuo in pacem affectui & voluntati, CAESAR, morem gerere nostra impotentia non posset, eosque nos perducere, ut semel infida pace læsi, ejus repetendæ consilium induamus. Interim gratis agimus paternæ tuæ in nos ac pacem propensioni, daturi operam Invictissime IMPERATOR, ut religiosa apud nos tuæ benevolentiæ recordatio fit, testemurque nihil carius sanctiusque nobis fore, quam tuæ & Rom. Imperii prosperitati nostra officia reposuisse.
units.tr: Most unconquered Emperor, we still remember the subject of our letters, by which we recalled our envoys from the peace negotiations when the Cologne conference was broken off. Meanwhile we considered sending envoys to you, so that our innocence might clear itself of the unrestrained accusations of your agents and those of Philip. The sending of the embassy was, however, suspended in order to lessen the slander and hatred. Now we are accused of having concluded new treaties with Andin, brother of the King of France. We excuse ourselves by professing our integrity, and we testify that we had no thought of new treaties at all, but have only renewed the contract and the memory of the former alliance with Andin. This confirmation of the agreement was not meant to derogate anything from your majesty or the Roman Empire, but so that our life and fortune might be protected under the aid of a most powerful prince. We were compelled to hasten this plan because neither the kings and princes, whom we invited to intercede, nor the groans and tears of our people, nor pity for our impending ruin, softened Philip's merciless heart, so that he might grant an honourable peace to himself and the peace we long for to us, by a new example of clemency. Therefore, with all hope of peace and royal favour set aside, we will seem to have acted rightly and in the manner of our ancestors if, in caring for the preservation of the provinces, we take up arms under this implacable wrath of the king, and, withdrawing obedience from the most savage king, avoid the sad servitude of an unbridled domination. Although we professed to your majesty and to the electors of the Roman Empire that we were willing and ready to consider the most equitable conditions offered (conditions by which our care would, once the discords were calmed and the arms laid down, handle the affairs of peace and quiet better), we achieved so little by softening the fierce king's temper that the arms which the royal ministers threatened against the wretched provincials, with greater cruelty or insolence, remained poised. Since Charles Arrogonius, Philip's envoy, breathes both of these threats in his own letters, we are ready, following the example of other nations, to take up arms for the liberty of our ancestors and our own, to protect our bodies, wives and children by divine and human law, and to appeal for the aid of foreign princes. Otherwise we shall be forced to let force tear our cities and their trade apart in war, to endure exile among an unarmed crowd, and to expose our defenceless fatherland to plunder and fury. And since all aid from you and from the Roman Empire is closed to us, aid which had supported our enemies' armies with supplies and provisions, we testify that the recent conference at Cologne on peace was a loss to us, and that all the progress of our successful arms was overturned by internal secessions and discords. Hence our weakness cannot comply with your inclination and will toward peace, CAESAR, and has brought us to the point where, once wounded by a faithless peace, we adopt a plan of seeking it again. Meanwhile we gladly acknowledge your fatherly goodwill toward us and your inclination toward peace, and we intend, most unconquered EMPEROR, that the religious memory of your benevolence be kept among us. We testify that nothing is dearer and holier to us than to have devoted our services to the prosperity of you and the Roman Empire.

units.la: Igitur velut fide procerum animis atque ingenijs proscriptâ, ipsoq; pacis nomine apud edoctos fallaciam ingrato, ad armorum curas properatum, quæ Farnesius etsi levi ad Rhenum clade affectus, liberandis Groningensibus superiorem per Belgicam conquirebat. Quorum ut obsessos certiores faceret, tabelliones passim annuntiandis auxilijs magno ære conducti, quos per omnes viarum aufractus dispositi speculatores intercipiendis arcanis observabant. Unde factum est, ut secretioribus à Farnesio litteris instructi rarius ad urbem commearent, quam Entenius Philippi Hohenloi & Iselsteinij legionibus validior, majoribus castris obsepserat.
units.tr: Thus, with good faith banished from the minds and characters of the leaders, and with the very name of peace used as a deceitful trick on the unwary, they hastened to the cares of war. Farnese, though afflicted by a slight defeat on the Rhine, was seeking through Belgium to relieve the Groningers, who were besieged by a superior force. To let the besieged know this, messengers were hired at great expense and sent out everywhere to announce the coming aid, but scouts posted along every winding of the roads intercepted them and seized their secrets. As a result, those who carried more confidential letters from Farnese came to the city less often than Entenius, stronger with the legions of Philip, Hohenlo and Iselstein, had hemmed it in with larger camps.

units.la: Quippe Aurantius talium prudens urbi amplæ & natura loci, ac justis præsidijs validæ admonendas plures copias decreverat, ratus, quod res erat, Entenium etsi animi ingentem, peculiari sibi temeritate viribus suis sibi rerum temporisque impendio castrense imperium exercere. Itaq; præmisså Hohenloi, Iselsteiniaque legione, Gulielmum quoque Ludovicum Nassovium ex fratre nepotem prima stipendia tum saucientem, in castra cum legione expedivit, Entenioque etsi invito & reluctanti, socium atque consortem consilij ac juxta imperij adhibuit. Caeterum omnem castrensem profectum Entenij potissimum immodestia retardabat, fiebatque ut alienæ gloriæ contemptor, suam amitteret. Unde discors sæpè agendi consilium nascebatur; quod in castris & per stationes observata, Ducum reverentiam & militaris disciplinæ autoritatem minuebat. Itaque miles munijs castrorum neglectis, aut spretis suo ingenio cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXX. genio magis, quam imperio rectoris obsequebatur, excursionibusque ac praedae intentus ne sociorum quidem rebus abstinebat. Quare fœderatae naves provisis quoque commeatibus onustae in Reiderio amne, & per aestuaria Lavicae ab Entenianis interceptae, vicinisque é Frisiorum agris, quos idem flumen exili alveo lambit, pecus abactum. Quod praedandi & licentiae exemplum etsi ab Entenio complures alienaret, ita illi hoc quam maxime odia conciliabat, quod cives ex mutatione rerum in castra, deserta urbe profugos asperrime tractaret, hominesque foederi pronos injurijs afficiendo, castrorum commercio prohiberet. Unde à Docone Martna viro nobili, post ab Abelo Franckena homine moris antiqui & celebratae doctrinae Frisiorum per Omlandiam & in castris legato vehementer increpitus, ne ferocis quidem ingenij violentiam repressit, animumq; spectatâ exulum fortuna emolliri passus est.
units.tr: Indeed Orange, wise in such matters, had decided to send more troops to the large city, which was strong both by its position and by its adequate garrisons. He thought, as was the case, that Entenius, though high-spirited, was squandering his own resources and time through his peculiar rashness in exercising military command by himself. So, after sending ahead the legion of Hohenlo and Iselstein, he dispatched into the camp, with a legion, William Louis of Nassau, the nephew of his brother, who was then still earning his first military pay. He forced Entenius, though unwilling and resisting, to accept him as partner and associate in counsel and in command. But the whole advance of Entenius's camp was held back above all by his unrestraint, so that, though a scorner of others' glory, he lost his own. Hence discordant plans of action often arose, which, as observed in the camps and at the posts, diminished the reverence due to the leaders and the authority of military discipline. Thus the soldiers neglected or scorned the duties of the camp and obeyed their own inclinations rather than the commander's orders. Intent on sorties and plunder, they did not even refrain from the goods of their allies. Hence allied ships, laden with provisions, were intercepted by the Entenians on the river Reider and through the estuaries of the Lauwers, and cattle were driven off from the fields of the Frisians, which the same river laps in a shallow channel. Although this example of plunder and licence alienated many from Entenius, it especially won him hatred, because he treated very harshly the citizens who had fled into the camp from the city after the change of fortune, and by injuring men inclined to the league he barred them from trade with the camp. Hence Docon Martna, a nobleman, and afterwards Abel Franckena, a man of old-fashioned character and celebrated learning and the Frisians' envoy through Omlandia and in the camp, rebuked him vehemently. He did not restrain even the violence of his fierce temper, but allowed his spirit to be softened by the sight of the exiles' fortune.

units.la: Cl. Franckena in litteris VII. Kal. Mai. ad Deputatos Frisiae missis, scribit se Entenium, ut Ultrajectini foederis ministrum se esse recordaretur, acerbè & instanter commonuisse, ac ut lenitate exulum animos ducendo, præfractos & superbos spiritus, evincendis Groningensibus, mollioribus & ad victoriam profuturis officijs mutaret. Cujus etsi spem faceret Entenius, ita econtra fidem exulibus datam foedissimâ injuriâ violavit, eorumque mercimonia, etsi stipendijs duarum cohortium sustinendis se obligavissent, diripi præcepit. Diploma quoque ijsdem mercatoribus concessum revocari fecit, pecoraque habendis castrorum commeatibus coëmpta, & in pascuum persolutis indictionibus missa abigi jussit. Unde Groningenses majores fortunâ animos induerunt, ne in crudelissimi victoris & jurati hostis arbitrium permissa clementiae civitas recideret.
units.tr: The learned Franckena, in a letter of 25 April sent to the deputies of Friesland, writes that he had sharply and repeatedly reminded Entenius that he was a minister of the Union of Utrecht. He urged him, by treating the exiles with gentleness, to change his stubborn and proud spirit into milder services that would help to conquer the Groningers and would benefit the victory. Although Entenius held out hope of this, he did the very opposite. He violated the faith given to the exiles with the foulest injury, and ordered their merchandise to be plundered, though they had bound themselves to support the pay of two cohorts. He also had the charter granted to the same merchants revoked, and ordered the cattle bought for the camp's supplies, and sent to pasture after the levies had been paid, to be driven off. Hence the Groningers took courage from their greater fortune, lest the city, which had been granted mercy, fall back under the will of a most cruel victor and sworn enemy.

units.la: Franckena quoque jure Legati, ut eidem Entenio castrense imperium abrogaretur obnixè apud Frisios intercessit, datisque Dammonâ litteris Gulielmum Ludovicum cum imperio & duodecim cohortium auxilijs gerendis rebus popposcit. Itaq; palam nullâ veri simulatione, professus est, inter collegij foederati errores nullum vel perniciosiorem, vel crassiorem (verba litterarum sunt) fuisse, quam quod Entenium peculiari Omlandorum ingenio civitati infensissimum Transflavicanæ militiæ & obsidio æmulæ urbis præfecissent. Quare tormenta & machinas Leovardiâ in auxilium petenti, ne morem gererent, Frisios suos commonuit, & ut, lubricâ sociati fide, extirpatis domesticis factionibus, Deum pacis autorem profutura ad concordiam consilia orarent. Quippe Ufkenium & Sterckenburgium Omlandiæ legatos non communicatis, sicuti oportebat, mandatis Ultrajectum è castris profectos criminabatur, haud vano indicio validiores secretioresque gentium amicitias sustinendis foederibus requiri. Igitur amovendis sociorum querelis, stipendia quoque Frisios castrensibus copijs popposcit, & ne debilem ultro legionum disciplinam tardatâ menstrui aeris solutione dissolverent.
units.tr: Franckena, also by right of his office as envoy, earnestly interceded with the Frisians that Entenius's command of the camp be taken away from him. In letters sent to Dammona, he demanded that William Louis be given command and twelve cohorts of auxiliaries to conduct the affairs. He declared openly, without any pretence of truth, that among the errors of the allied council none was more pernicious or more gross (these are the words of the letter) than that they had placed Entenius, most hostile to the city by the particular temper of the Omlanders, in charge of the militia across the Lauwers and the siege of the rival city. Therefore, when Entenius asked for artillery and machines from Leeuwarden to help him, Franckena warned his Frisians not to comply. He urged them, since the faith of the alliance was slippery, to root out domestic factions and to pray to God, the author of peace, for counsels that would further concord. He accused Ufkens and Sterckenburg, the envoys of Omlandia, of leaving the camp for Utrecht without their mandates having been shared, as they should have been. He judged, by no empty sign, that more powerful and secret friendships among nations were needed to sustain the alliances. Therefore, to remove the complaints of the allies, he also demanded that the Frisians pay the camp forces, lest, by delaying the monthly payment of money, they dissolve the legions' discipline, which was already weakened.

units.la: Unde Frisij, quo Entenianorum licentiae & populationibus mederentur, qui terrâ, prædones, mari quoque peiraticam in socios exercebant, præsidiariam navem milite ac commeatu instruxere, eamque propè Ooftmahornam in æstuario, ubi eam amnem accipit, stare jussam redimendo aperti maris commercio habuere. Mox Joannes Jodocius cius vir fortis, & qui navale sub Philippo stipendium meruerat, navi bellicæ cum imperio præfectus, Jeldertusque Wigerius magnæ famæ prædo, qui sacramentum Entenij suis rapinis ac flagitijs obtendebat, Eæ fluminis ac Frisici maris æstuario submotus est. Adeo Entenij consilia & facta hostibus ad virtutem, socijs ad metum & invidiem erant. Itaq; urgebat Aurantius, ut munitiones in castris ad Groningam erectæ justis præsidijs firmarentur, & ut auxilia è Flandriâ ac Brabantiâ illarum gentium menstruo stipendio oppugnandæ Groningæ haberentur. Deïn ut Ordinum exercitus trans Rhenum, & per confinia agens supremo militiæ rectori pareret, Philippum Hohenloïm manu promptum & animi ingentem gerendis cum imperio rebus destinavit, Bernardoque Merodio Rumænio vicariam belli administrandi potestatem decrevit. Tum provincijs Rheno amni contiguis legatos ut ederent ordinavit, qui Ducum militarium consilia, & lubrici moderaminis impetus prudentiæ solertiâ castigarent. Denique ne obsessæ Groningensium civitati auxilia subvenirent, expediri in Trans-Isulaniam, Drentiamque peritissimos locorum voluit, qui eorum situm specularentur, quantisque paludibus à Weddâ in Geelmudam aut Vidri emissarium Drentinus ager subjaceret. Itaque munitionibus extruendis commoditas delecta, repetitumque firmandæ Coverdiæ & Burtangæ consilium, quod Sonoi, ut memoravi, culpâ, aut, ut ille vaticinabatur, fato quodam, ex solâ conferendi æris parsimoniâ, aut provinciarum æmulatione neglectum Trans-Rhenanas gentes gravioribus casibus reservabat. Quare non Drentiæ, etsi in Ultrajectinum fœdus transcriptæ, non sociæ nationis finibus, aut securitati prospectum, quam Frisiæ & Translavicanis quoque agris patentes Drentiæ campi, & immunitæ paludes adimebant.
units.tr: Hence the Frisians, to check the licence and depredations of the Entenians, who practised robbery on land and piracy at sea against their allies, equipped a guard ship with soldiers and provisions. They ordered it to stand near Ooftmahorn, where the estuary receives the river, and by keeping it there they kept open the sea trade. Soon afterwards Joannes Jodocius, a brave man who had served at sea under Philip, was placed in command of the warship. Jeldertus Wigerius, a plunderer of great fame who used Entenius's commission as cover for his thefts and crimes, was removed from the estuary of the river and the Frisian sea. So far were the plans and deeds of Entenius a spur to the enemies' courage, and a cause of fear and resentment to the allies. Therefore Orange urged that the fortifications erected in the camp near Groningen be strengthened with proper garrisons, and that auxiliaries from Flanders and Brabant be kept on monthly pay for besieging Groningen. Then, so that the army of the States across the Rhine, acting along the frontiers, would obey the supreme commander of the war, he appointed Philip of Hohenlo, a man ready of hand and great of spirit, to carry out affairs with command. He gave Bernard Merode of Rumen the deputy power of conducting the war. Then he ordained that envoys be sent to the provinces bordering the Rhine, to correct the plans of the military leaders and the impulsiveness of unsteady management with the skill of prudence. Finally, so that no aid would reach the besieged city of the Groningers, he wished the most skilled men of the locality to be sent into Overijssel and Drenthe to survey their terrain, and to determine through what marshes the Drenthe land lies open from the Wedde to Geelmuiden, or to the outflow of the Vidri. Thus a convenient place was chosen for building fortifications, and the plan of strengthening Coevorden and Borculo was taken up again. That plan had been neglected, through Sonoy's fault, as I have mentioned, or, as he prophesied, by some fate, from mere thrift in spending money or rivalry among the provinces, and it kept the Trans-Rhenish peoples for harsher misfortunes. Hence no provision had been made for the security of Drenthe, though it had been brought into the Union of Utrecht, nor for the borders of an allied nation. The open plains and unwalled marshes of Drenthe, which reach into Friesland and the lands across the Lauwers, offered them no protection.

units.la: Cl. Franckena in Ephemeride notat acta Drentini fœderis Leovardiam ad collegium tum transmissa, quæ cum plurimis, procerum malitiâ, aut incuriâ interversa, ne posterorum quidem usibus infœlicitas temporum reliquit. Igitur Groningensium rebus in arcto constitutis Georgius Lalainius sui metuens, transituræ auxilia Farnesium poposcit, ultimamque perituræ mox civitatis angustiam nullâ periculi dissimulatione, professus est. Præter annonæ namque sensim deficientis, penuriam, nitrati pulveris defectu laborare se obsessum asserebat, deditionem necessario factum nisi per auxilia levetur. Quæ si destituant, tristem certe suscepti consilij fructum se habiturum, si inter magnarum rerum auspicia inimicorum & jam hostium gratiæ se permiserit. Ad hæc regem omni Amasium inter Rhenumque flumini (Flevo illi in Frisijs nomen) regione cessurum, nisi agrarijs passim in fœdus Ordinum receptis, urbem tueatur solam suarum partium fidissimos intrà intuta mœnium claudentem. Neque enim aliud regiæ dominationis munimentum superesse, omni Frisiâ, cum Omlandiæ, Drentiæque populo novis societatibus inligatâ, & quæ latura non sit, in illo fertilissimo terrarum tractu urbem relinqui sedem bello, & hostilibus armis fracturam. Quin sciret Farnesius auxilia illarum gentium jam castris inducta, famaque ferri præter commeatus è fœcundissimâ frumenti regione subvectos, tormentis quoque è Frisia petendis consilia capi. Denique mare ipsum classibus impeditum, adeo intuto omni ad urbem aditu, ut ferro aperiendus sit.
units.tr: Cl. Franckena notes in his Ephemeris that the acts of the Drenthe covenant, which had then been sent to the college at Leeuwarden, were lost, most of them through the malice or carelessness of the nobles, and the misfortune of the times left not even a copy for the use of posterity. Therefore, with the affairs of the Groningers in a tight spot, Georgius Lalainius, fearing for himself, asked Farnese for the auxiliaries that were to be sent, and, concealing no danger, declared the city's final distress, which would soon be its ruin. Apart from the gradual failure of the grain supply, he claimed to be short of gunpowder and saltpetre, and said that unless he were relieved by auxiliaries, surrender would inevitably follow. If these failed him, he would certainly reap a sad reward for the plan he had undertaken, if amid the omens of great affairs he entrusted himself to the favour of enemies who were already foes. Besides this, he warned that the king would lose the whole region between the Ems and the Rhine (called Flevo in Frisian), unless the rural districts were received throughout the covenant of the Estates and the city alone, with its most faithful supporters of his party, were protected within its unharmed walls. For no other bulwark of royal rule remained: all Friesland, and the people of Ommelanden and Drenthe, were bound in new alliances, and in that most fertile tract of land the city would be left as a seat for war, to be broken by hostile arms. Moreover, Farnese should know that auxiliaries from those peoples were already brought into camp, and that it was rumoured plans were being made to fetch artillery from Friesland too, as well as provisions carried from the most fertile grain region. Finally, the sea itself was blocked by fleets, so that access to the city was so unguarded that it had to be opened by the sword.

units.la: Quæ quoniam Entenium in cujus manus pervenerant, non fallebant, ita continuis velitationibus tamdiu obsessos attrivit, donec temeritatis fortitudini triste præmium fortissimo viro pervicax fortuna decerneret, & solvendi obsidij diem importunitas fati præfiniret. Qui Roldæ in Drentinis, vergente Maio, ab Hohenloo & Nassovio liberaliore convivio exceptus jactantiusque, velut hostem super mensâ debellaturus, se gerens, oppugnandæ acrius urbis, & ostentandæ virtutis consilium cæpit, æmulorumque Ducum gloriam suâ obscurare adnixus est. Cui propposito dies inter comessationem & vinolentiam actus incitamentum addebat.
