Quare temulentus, & mero gravis equum conscendit, provectusque in castra tribunos, & signorum ductores hunc in modum allocutus est.
units.tr: Since Entenius, into whose hands these letters had come, did not disregard them, he wore down the besieged with constant skirmishes for so long, until stubborn fortune decreed a sad reward for his rashness to a very brave man, and an untimely fate fixed the day of his release from the siege. At Roden in Drenthe, as May drew on, he was entertained by Hohenlo and Nassau at a rather lavish banquet, and, behaving with too much boasting, as if he were going to defeat an enemy over the table, he resolved to press the attack on the city more fiercely and to show his courage, and he strove to dim the glory of his rival commanders. The day, spent in revelry and drinking, added fuel to this plan. So, drunk and heavy with wine, he mounted his horse and rode into the camp, where he addressed the tribunes and the standard-bearers in this manner.

units.la: Diu est, Commilitones, ex quo invalidam urbem, & sociorum nostrorum cæde ac perfidiâ imbutam, castris de mandato Ordinum clausi. Eam oppugnare, quia longioris moræ pertæsus sum, in animum induxi, facinusque admoliri, quod præsentis ævi laudem mereatur, in futuri memoriâ perennet. Sed vestræ ignaviæ & imperitiæ debetur, quicquid ad gloriam omissum est, quarum utramque si vultis, meo exemplo emendate. Quippe fidem vestram, vestras manus nunc imploro, ac ut me Duce fortes strenuique sitis, habituri mecum tam commune periculum, quam gloriæ fructum.
units.tr: It is a long time, comrades, since I was posted by the Estates' order with the camp before this weak city, which is steeped in the slaughter and treachery of our allies. Being weary of so long a delay, I have resolved to attack it and to undertake a deed that deserves praise in the present age and will live on in the memory of the future. But whatever has been left undone for glory is owed to your idleness and inexperience. If you wish, correct both by my example. I now implore your loyalty and your hands, so that under my leadership you may be brave and vigorous, and share with me as great a danger as the fruit of glory.

units.la: Sic pro concione locutus labri butyracei operculum, clypei loco, numu sumpsit, signoque dato, ut se sequerentur, ad Schutendiepam & suburbana properavit, quæ præfluente flumine, tum vallo, fossisque emunita, egregiâ obsessorum virtute defendebantur. Ubi cæsis vulneratisque centurionibus ac plurimis quoque militum saucijs, etsi infoeliciter rem gerens, suos animavit, inferiorisq; propugnaculi & reductuum oppugnationem repeti jussit. Quo capto, cum Scutendiepæ quoq; immineret, quam solâ scalarum ope superari posse sagacissimi centurionum ominabantur, speculandæ per jaculatoriam fenestram dimicationi defixior, glande verberatur, capitisq; saucij lætali vulnere sternitur. Unde mœror orba ductore suo castra, & triste juxta silentium occupavit; magnumque obsidionis perficiendæ commodum morte Entenij interruptum est. Seditione namque militarium copiarum stipendia flagitantium omnis disciplina ordoque belli laxatus, conturbatis adhoc animis, quos prostrati Ducis spectaculum, & miseratio à continuando pugnæ officio revocabat. Adeò verum est in bello, multitudinem ab unius ductu atque imperio pendere, amissoque rectore desolatos exercitus, & eorum virtutem, tanquam intercepto vitali spiritu, flaccescere. Quippe Entenius etsi in iram fervoremque animi, tum comessationes atque luxum pronior, & ex hoc profusus æris foret, ita militarem gratiam popularitatis laude emercabatur, & quod, cætera incivilis, vitæ suæ ac imperij rationem moribus militum adaptaret. Hoc verò imprimis eum commendabat, quod in expeditione, in pugnâ, denique in omni belli negotio fidissimum Ducem se præberet, animique impavidus, nullo sui discrimine, tam militis, quam Ducis laudabili officio fungeretur. Itaque frigora, sitim, ardores, inediam, tum soli & itinerum incommoda juxta militem perferebat, corpusque à primâ ætate tolerandis asperis obduratum quibuslibet molestijs objectabat. Quare animo, qui excelsus & verae nobilitatis affectator erat, supra fortunam positus, vinci se non posse deprehensus fuit, spiritumque externi regisque servitij acerrimum hostem periclitanti patriae impendisse. Caetera viri vituperio, aut laudi scripta, studio a me omissa, sub benigna naturae rerum excusatione, quae in illo, sicut in omni mortalium turba, foeda vitia egregijs virtutibus miscuisset. Cujus mors nobilitatem Omlandicam haud parum conturbavit, ne laeta quidem Eusumiorum gente, etsi patratae in patrem caedis suspicione, infensissimum domui suae hostem abstulisset. Cadaver Middelstumum in Hunesgonijs, ubi natus erat, deportatum; tumuloque majorum conditum. Econtra intra urbem, audita jurati hostis morte, omnia laetiora agitabantur, simulante prudentius Lalainio, temerarij castrorum Ducis interitu Ordinum rebus nihil decessisse. Igitur metuebat; ne illius excessu, peritioribus militiae rectoribus obsidionis negotium demandaretur, civesque ante ab Entenij saevitia ac immanitate alieni, mitiorum Ducum veniae suo incommodo se permitterent. Jam enim duobus castellis amissis, quae urbi praduxerant, fiducia civilium animorum & auxilij minuebatur, & quod extenuato victu, omnique commeatu imminuto pristina sensim pugnantium virtus elanguesceret.
units.tr: Having spoken thus to the assembly, he took the lid of a buttered-dish in place of a shield, and, giving the signal for them to follow him, hurried to the Schuttendiep and the suburbs next to it, which, with the river flowing past them and defended by a rampart and ditches, were held by the excellent courage of the defenders. There, after the centurions and many of the soldiers had been killed or wounded, he encouraged his men, though he was acting unluckily, and ordered the attack on the lower outwork and the redoubts to be renewed. When these were taken, and the Schuttendiep too was about to fall, which the most shrewd centurions predicted could be taken only with ladders, he stood too intently gazing through a loophole at the fighting, and was struck by a musket-ball, and fell with a mortal wound to the head. Then sorrow and a dreadful silence seized the camp, bereft of its leader, and the great advantage of completing the siege was lost with Entenius's death. For through the mutiny of the soldiers, who demanded their pay, all discipline and order in the war were relaxed, and minds were thrown into confusion, held back from continuing the fight by pity and by the sight of their fallen commander. So true it is in war that a multitude depends on the leadership and command of one man, and that when the commander is lost, the armies are left leaderless and their valour wilts, as if the vital breath had been cut off. Indeed, Entenius, though he was prone to anger and passion, and even more to revelry and luxury, and for that reason was lavish with money, bought the favour of the soldiers with the reputation of popularity, and, otherwise unrestrained, shaped his way of life and command to suit the habits of the soldiers. What especially commended him was that on campaign, in battle, and in every part of war he showed himself a most loyal commander, and with a fearless spirit, regardless of his own danger, performed the praiseworthy duty of soldier and general alike. So he endured cold, thirst, heat, hunger, and the hardships of sun and marches alongside the common soldier, and, hardened from early youth to bear hardships, he exposed his body to any trouble. Hence, lofty in spirit and a seeker of true nobility, he was held to be beyond fortune, and unable to be conquered, and he devoted his spirit, most bitter enemy of foreign and royal servitude, to his imperilled fatherland. As for the rest, what is written in reproach or praise of the man I have deliberately omitted, let it be excused by the kindly nature of things, which in him, as in all mankind, had mingled foul vices with outstanding virtues. His death greatly disturbed the Ommelandic nobility, not even the joyful Eusumian people, though suspected of having committed the murder of his father, had removed the most hostile enemy of their house. His body was carried to Middelstum in Hunsingo, where he had been born, and buried in the tomb of his ancestors. On the other side, inside the city, when the news of the enemy's oath-breaking death was heard, everything was in higher spirits, though Lalainius, with greater prudence, pretended that the Estates' affairs had lost nothing by the death of the reckless commander of the camp. Still, he feared that after his departure the business of the siege would be entrusted to more skilled military leaders, and that the citizens, who had previously been alienated by Entenius's cruelty and savagery, would submit to the pardon of milder commanders to their own disadvantage. For now, with two forts lost which had protected the city, confidence in the spirits of the citizens was diminishing, and, as supplies were reduced and all provisions cut off, the former courage of the fighters was gradually growing feeble.

units.la: Caeterum certiore auxilij fama res allevatae, quod Farnesius, etsi aeris angustia premeretur, obsessae civitati haud procul Rheno & Novesio urbe reparabat. Quippe omni provinciarum exule ad sacramentum adacto, quem nulla stipendij dulcedine aut cura, sola fati sui infoelicitas, & ulciscendae injuriae cupido in patriam armaverat, Epirotarum quoque equitum (quos Thomas Epirota vir secundis praelijs clarus inter caeteros ducebat) auxiliares cohortes adjunxit, omnesque copias Trajecto ad Novesium Rheno pergere in adversam ripam jussit. Ubi Rora flumine superato, impetratoque a Juliacensium Duce Joanne Gulielmo per suas ditiones commeatu, Lippam quoque fluvium haud procul Dorsta oppido traductae, festinante Martino Schenckio Niddachio homine Geldro, ut Juliae Cliviaeque campos emensus, Geldriae & Transf-Isulaniae hostiles agros properandis auxilijs peragraret. Eam vero provinciam Gasparo Roblesio Farnesius demandaverat, quo veteris imperij & per tumultum militarem amissi vestigia adhuc cerneret, Frisiorumque gentem rebellionis in se & regem ream, ardore vindictae, & prioris injuriae solatio, armata manu debellaret: Caeterum absens, & in Farnesij comitatu per superiorem Belgicam tum agens, ne expeditionis quidem in Frisios suscepta consilium executus est, etsi sollicitatis exulum auxilijs, quos recuperandae dominationi & veteri fortunae, faciendam ad conspirationem, & sumenda in patriam arma instigaverat, signa vero Renicus Dekama, Jarichius Liauckema, Titus Camminga, & Lollius Ockingha Frisiorum exulantium nobilissimi ducebant, praeter caeteros cohortium centuriones, quos e Frisia mutatis rebus praescriptos, aut dignitatibus exutos, sacramento arctius regio fortuna temporum obligaverat. In quorum numero Vibius Goutumanus, Arnoldus Gemenius, & Everardus Ensius Coverdiae & Drentinorum Satrapa, fuere, quos nulla retinendae dignitatis spes externis clientelis obtruserat. Reliqui Germaniae, aut aliarum liarum gentium natalibus adscripti novam exornandis majorum imagini-bus materiem, inassueti otio & gloriam & juxta opes ex bello quærebant.
units.tr: Meanwhile, news of the approaching help cheered the besieged, since Farnese, though pressed by a shortage of money, was preparing to relieve the beleaguered city not far from the Rhine and the town of Neuss. For, when every exile from the provinces had been bound by oath, whom no sweetness of pay or care, but only the unhappiness of his own fate and a desire to avenge the injury, had armed against his country, he also added auxiliary cohorts of Epirote horsemen, whom Thomas the Epirote, a man distinguished among the others for his successes in battle, led, and he ordered all the forces to march from Utrecht to Neuss across the Rhine to the opposite bank. There, after crossing the Roer, and having obtained passage through his lands from John William, Duke of Jülich, they were led across the Lippe, not far from the town of Dorsten, by Martin Schenck of Nideggen, a Gelderland man, who, hastening through the fields of Jülich and Cleves, was to range through the hostile lands of Gelderland and Overijssel to bring on the auxiliaries. Farnese had entrusted that province to Gaspar Robles, so that he might see traces of the old rule, which had been lost through the military mutiny, and with burning desire for revenge, and the consolation of the earlier injury, might crush by armed force the Frisian people, who were guilty of rebellion against himself and the king. Yet he, being absent and at that time busy in the upper Netherlands in Farnese's train, did not carry out the plan of the expedition undertaken against the Frisians, although by the aid of exiles whom he had urged to conspiracy and to taking up arms against their country, in hope of recovering their rule and former fortune. The standards were carried by Renicus Dekama, Jarichius Liauckema, Titus Camminga, and Lollius Ockinga, the most noble of the exiled Frisians, together with the other centurions of the cohorts, whom the changed fortunes of the times had marked out from Friesland or stripped of their offices, and whom the royal cause had bound more tightly by oath. Among their number were Vibius Gotumanus, Arnoldus Gemenius, and Everardus Ensius, Satrap of Coevorden and Drenthe, whom no hope of keeping their office had driven to foreign service. The rest, born in Germany or among other peoples, sought glory and wealth from the war, unaccustomed to idleness, to furnish new material for the portraits of their ancestors.

units.la: Cl. Franckena optimus autor notat exercitum istum ad Mollum pagum Rheno assitum, constrato navali ponte fluvio, trajecisse, victoriaque velut occulto animorum præsagio, certa in præsentia pro futuris habuisse. Quo nuntio in castra ad Groningam perlato, Gulielmus Ludovicus Nassovius, defuncto Entenio cum imperio rem gerens, 13. Maii literas ad Deputatos Frisiæ dedit, æneaque ad quinarium numerum tormenta iternendo vallo & oppidanorum munitionibus Harlinganos poposcit. Cæterum proprij discriminis pavor in externa difficillimè respiciebat, suarum rerum, velut incertis, qui inter domesticos hostes, & teterrimarum conjurationum arcana fluctuare infantiam minus robusti fœderis non ignorabant.
units.tr: The excellent author Franckena notes that this army crossed the Rhine at the village of Molle, which lies beside the river, by means of a pontoon bridge built across the water. They held the coming victory as already certain, as though by a hidden presentiment of their minds. When this news reached the camp at Groningen, William Louis of Nassau, who was directing affairs since Entenius had died, wrote a letter to the Deputies of Friesland on 13 May. He asked the people of Harlingen for bronze guns, about five in number, to be carried round for the rampart and the townspeople's fortifications.

units.la: Unde Harlinga post subministratas Gulielmo Ludovico grandiores machinas rudi mænium ambitu cincta, majore ac validiore opere circumducta, effosso, diductoque introrsum portu, qui tutum navale venienti ex Oceano classi præstaret. Igitur ad aquarum quoque impetus sistendos, quas aut mare vento motum, aut æstu portui ingerit, aut rivulorum urbem influentium declivia deducunt, claustra magni operis fabricata, quæ laxandis, aut recipiendis aquis reperta onerarijs navigijs permeabiles alveos faciebant. Tum lata quoque profundaq; fossa vallo, & propugnaculis præducta, tantaque molis opera, ære publico, trimestri spatio absoluta. Quod consilium ab Aurantio potissimum principe profectum Traslavicanæ gentis non inglorius scriptor prodit, quo novæ urbis fortunam, florente commercio juvaret, portumque subministrandis Hollandiæ sociarumque gentium auxilijs habilem reparandis in Hispanum exercitibus aperiret. Qui ut regundæ post Lalainium provinciæ ex decreto solennis comitij præficeretur, missus Ordinum Frisiæ nomine ad eum Doco Martna vir primariæ nobilitatis & elegantis ingenij, qui supremum Præfecti imperium ei deferret, offerendæque dignitatis ac simul molestiæ vicem repeteret. Itaq; præter mandata Doconi Martnæ commissa, litteræ quoq; à foederatarum provinciarum Legatis & Senatu per Frisiam Ordinum exaratæ, permovendo optumi principis ingenio, quod in illâ tempestate rerum constitutum graviorem curarum sarcinam respuebat. Econtra omnem Principis excusationem continua provincialium vota ac desideria diluebant, ac si in illo capite ac rectore omnium rerum salus atque incolumitas versaretur.
units.tr: Harlingen, after William Louis had been supplied with heavier siege engines, was enclosed by a rough circuit of walls, and then surrounded by a larger and stronger work. The harbour was dug out and opened inwards, so that it would give a safe anchorage to the fleet coming in from the ocean. Then, to check the rush of waters, whether the sea stirred by the wind drove them into the harbour with the tide, or the slopes of the streams flowing into the town carried them down, sluices of great construction were built. These were devised to let the waters out or take them in, and they made channels passable for cargo ships. Next, a wide and deep ditch was drawn along the rampart and bastions, and so great a work was finished in three months at public expense. An author of no little renown from the Trasławian (Traslavian) nation records that this plan came chiefly from the Prince of Orange, so that the new town might benefit from its growing trade, and that the harbour might be opened, fit for supplying the armies of Holland and the allied nations against the Spaniard. Afterwards, when the province had to be governed following the Lalaing affair by decree of a solemn assembly, Doco Martna, a man of the first nobility and of refined talent, was sent in the name of the Orders of Friesland to him, to offer him the supreme command of the Governor and, at the same time, to take back the burden and the trouble of the office. So, besides the instructions committed to Doco Martna, letters were also drawn up by the Envoys of the united provinces and by the Senate, through the Orders of Friesland, to move the excellent prince's nature, which in that storm of affairs shrank from so heavy a load of cares. On the other hand, the continual prayers and wishes of the provincials set aside every excuse of the Prince, as though the safety and well-being of all things rested in that head and ruler.

units.la: LITTERAE DEPUTATORUM hujusmodi erant.
units.tr: THE LETTER OF THE DEPUTIES WAS OF THIS KIND.

units.la: POSTREMVM & solenne gentis nostræ comitium, PRINCEPS, concordibus suffragijs Præfecturam tibi provinciæ destinavit. Eam ut cum imperio & absolutâ Præfecti potestate acciperes, spes nos aluit, eosq; imprimis, qui patriæ fideles, optumaque in eam studia diu professi hoc calamitosissimorum temporum statu de te solo clarissimam opinionem concepere. Prudentia tua & multarum rerum usus, ijsius de te judicij fidem firmavit, postquam mentem boni consilij plenam ac à DEO tibi infusam isti moli regundæ parem ostendisses. Denique continuæ paternæque in populum & remp. sollicitudinis tuæ plurimum dedimus; PRINCEPS, deprehensò sublimem animum cu-tis ris infractum, & in agendo indefessum, omne officium provincialium saluti impen-dere. Quare nostra in te fides, tua virtus & clarissimae animi dotes, hoc ad consilium nos traxere; Itaque missis Hagam, dein Campos ad te Legatis administrandae gubernandaeque provinciae dignitatem, ac simul molestiam tibi obtrusimus, eâ spe aliti, ut ratione nostri status habitâ politiae & bello praesses, tuisque capite & moderatore rerum orbos potentiâ & autoritate tuâ regundos susciperes. Sed fluxas spes nullo huc usque aut parvo solatio redemimus, in tam tristem maestitiam ac sollicitudinem projecti, ut perire proximi sine tuo imperio videamur. Rerum nostrarum statum, etsi nos ignores, Legatus tibi aperiet, bis mandatis à nobis instructus, ut rectiuram provinciae tibi offerat. Quare rogamus, Frisij, ut imponi in humeros tuos id oneris, ac molestiae patiaris, ac ut ipse regundae Frisiae spe facta, fessis rebus succuras, Legatumq; aut Vicarium tui per provinciam imperij, quam ocyssime constituas. Id si feceris, PRINCEPS; fortunas, vitam atque sanguinem in adjumentum offerimus, daturi omnem operam, ut illius regimen nostro, quantum fieri possit, consilio juvetur. Hoc etiam petimus, ut Senatum juri dicundo praefectum justo numero ac autoritate instruas, quo malis per provinciam indies exorientibus tua prudentia medeatur. Reliqua, quae votis complexi sumus, Legatus MARTNA exponet, quorum ea summa est, ut te diu felicem florentemque nostris rebus habeamus.
units.tr: At last, PRINCE, our nation's solemn assembly, by unanimous vote, has appointed you to the governorship of the province. We were encouraged to hope that you would accept it with full command and absolute authority as Governor, especially those who had long professed loyalty to the fatherland and the best zeal for it, and who in this most calamitous state of affairs have formed the clearest opinion of you alone. Your prudence and your long experience of many affairs confirmed the trust of that judgment, since you had shown a mind full of good counsel, poured into you by God, equal to the task of governing such a mass. Lastly, we have greatly relied on your continual and fatherly care for the people and the commonwealth. We have observed, PRINCE, that your lofty spirit is unbroken by adversity, tireless in action, and that you devote every duty to the safety of the provincials. Therefore our trust in you, your virtue and your most distinguished gifts of mind have drawn us to this plan. Accordingly, having sent Envoys to The Hague and then to Kampen to you, we have thrust upon you the dignity of administering and governing the province, and also its burden, nourished by the hope that, with regard to the state of our affairs, you would take up the presidency in war and policy, and that, bereft of a head and director of affairs, we would be governed by your power and authority. But so far we have bought these fleeting hopes with no or only slight comfort; we have been cast into such sad grief and anxiety that we seem about to perish unless you hold command. The Envoy, whom we have instructed with these commands, will explain to you the state of our affairs, though you do not know it, so that he may offer you the rule of the province. We therefore ask, Frisians, that you allow this burden and trouble to be laid on your shoulders, and that, since the hope of governing Friesland has been given, you hasten to help our distressed affairs, and that you appoint, as quickly as possible, a Deputy or Vicar of your power through the province. If you do this, PRINCE, we offer our fortunes, lives and blood as aid, and we shall take every pains that its government may, as far as possible, be assisted by our counsel. We also ask that you equip the Senate, which is set over the administration of justice, with a fitting number and authority, so that your prudence may remedy the evils which arise daily through the province. The rest, which we have embraced in our prayers, the Envoy MARTNA will set out; the sum of which is that we may keep you long happy and flourishing for our affairs.

units.la: Hae Litterae x v. Kalend. Jun. signatae.
units.tr: These letters were sealed on the 18th of May.

units.la: Quo die Senatus quoq; juri dicundo delectus Francisculm Baudimontium Graphiarium suum hominem Flandrum mandatis instruxit, legationisque ad eundem principem obeundae potestatem fecit. Mandata erant, ut salutato principe, litteras foederatorum Ordinum, Senatus & Deputatorum Frisiae suae fidei commissas exhiberet, nuperisq; mandatis, quae ad foederatos Ordines Daventriam pertulerat, repetitis de miserrimo provinciae statu, & subortis turbis principem doceret. Rectoris quoque potentiâ, famâ, prudentiâ atque exemplorum usu conspicui necessitatem monstraret, exorataque voluntate principis Doconis Martnae & Hesfeli Aysmae, qui Antverpiae agebat, in communicandis consilijs ope uteretur. Hesfelo Aysmae Praesidi, Douwoni Burmaniae, Barthio Idsardae nuncupatis jam ante Senatoribus diplomata impetraret; Ea ex antiquâ formulâ cum absolutâ potestate Sibrando Richaeo Senatori & fisci Advocato, Wilconi Holdingha, Foppio Grovensteinio & Tiallengo Wikelio procuraret; Eysingaeque Versteverano, ac Rhalae Senatorum procurationes immutari, redigiq; in priorem formam faceret. Sibi quoque de absoluto diplomate obtinendo prospiceret, omneque officium saluti & commodo publico impenderet. Hoc x v. Kalend. Jun. à Tetardo Herennio in acta relata.
units.tr: On the same day the Senate also chose Franciscus Baudimontius, its clerk, a Fleming, and instructed him with commands and gave him authority to go as envoy to the same prince. His instructions were: after greeting the prince, he should show the letters of the united Orders, of the Senate and of the Deputies of Friesland entrusted to his good faith, and, repeating the recent commands which he had carried to the united Orders at Deventer, he should tell the prince of the most wretched state of the province and of the disturbances that had arisen. He should also show the necessity of a ruler conspicuous for power, reputation, prudence and experience, and, having won the prince's consent, he should seek the help of Doco Martna and of Hesfelus Aysma, who was then at Antwerp, in sharing counsels. He should obtain diplomas for Hesfelus Aysma, the President, and for Douwo Burmania, Barth Idsardus, already named Senators; he should procure, in the old form with full power, the same for Sibrandus Richaeus, Senator and advocate of the fisc, for Wilco Holdingha, Foppius Grovensteinius and Tiallingus Wikelius; and he should make the commissions of Eysinga of Versteveen and of the Senators of Rhala altered and restored to their former form. He should also provide for obtaining for himself a full diploma, and devote every duty to safety and the public good. This was recorded in the acts by Tetardus Herennius on 18 May.

units.la: Eo halante animam rep. inter tantos proditorum & civilis licentiae metus potentium collegiorum aemulatio, & caeca gloriae ambitio cruda ingenia propellebat. Itaq; vulgus ipsum, potentum exemplo, qui publicas provinciarum indictiones irrogaverant, mobile & seditionibus proximum erat, Magistratuumque imperia velut in licentiae regno, aspernabatur. Ferunt seditiosis vocibus in publico auditis, manus quoque Magistratibus intentatas, conjuratosque è regiâ factione, octasione eminentis inter proceres discordiae usos, turbulenta consilia atque facta agicIↄ. Iↄ. LXXX. agitavisse. Quippe Senatui, qui regio suffectus erat, nec decens numerus, nec prisca autoritas erat, quà imminutà antiquæ quoque severitatis majestas, & tristissimus rigor remiserat. Itaque terni cum fisci actore jus dicebant, quod Octo-viris sub Saxone, sub Carolo Cæsare & Philippo filio pluribus Senatoribus commissum, æmulatione politici ordinis, & paucitate præsidentium judicijs eviluerat. Unde plebi quoque minor metus quam ingratum publicarum indictionum vocabulum, tum fato & incuriâ dubijs angustisq; rebus repetitum, & in eâ seditiosissimos quosq; efferaverat. Quem affectum asperiore medicinâ percurare illi quam maximè aversabantur, qui popularium morborum periti non ignorabant, gravissimum quemque tumorem ex præcepto medicorum principis beneficio quietis sanandum. Etsi essent, qui ferrum mox remedio poscerent, & ut asperâ paucorum correctione, multitudo metum sentiret. Cæterum pluribus indulgentiæ, magis quam severitatis vitium placebat, & ut plebis ob gravitatem tributi motæ sanguini honestâ clementiâ parceretur. Quippe communi mortalium vitio, jussui & imperio contumacem ad bonam frugem & ingenia redituraм, quæ diuturnitas & mora temporis ingerendo pœnitentiam ab omni ævo sedavisset. Ita variantibus procerum sententijs omne parcendæ, excusandæ aut corrigendæ plebis decretum intermissum, donec Baudimontius inter cætera Antverpiam profectus de eo ad Aurantium referret.
units.tr: While the commonwealth was breathing its last amid such great fears of traitors and of civil license, rivalry between powerful bodies and a blind ambition for glory drove on rash minds. So the common people themselves, following the example of the powerful who had imposed the public levies on the provinces, were restless and prone to sedition, and they scorned the commands of the magistrates as if in a kingdom of license. It is reported that, with seditious words heard in public, and with hands raised against the magistrates, conspirators from the royal faction, taking advantage of the discord that had arisen among the leading men, were planning turbulent counsels and deeds in (1580). For the Senate, which had been placed over the province by the king, had neither a fitting number nor its old authority; with these diminished, the majesty of its ancient severity and its stern rigour had also slackened. So three men with the fisc's advocate were administering justice, which the Octumvirs under Saxo, under Charles Caesar and his son Philip had committed to more Senators; through rivalry within the political order and the small number of presiding judges, it had lost its dignity. Hence the common people had a smaller fear, and the unwelcome word "public levies", renewed in those doubtful and straitened times through fate and carelessness, had made all the most seditious fierce. Those who knew well the diseases of the people were most unwilling to cure this condition with harsher medicine, since, by the precept of physicians, every most serious swelling should be healed by the Prince's kindness of quiet. Although there were some who soon called for the iron as the remedy, so that the multitude might feel fear through the harsh correction of a few, most people preferred the fault of indulgence to that of severity, and that the blood of the commons, stirred by the weight of the tax, should be spared with honourable clemency. For by the common vice of mortals, the man who is stubborn against command and authority would return to good conduct and better disposition, as long duration and the passing of time had always calmed repentance. So, with the opinions of the leading men varying, the decision to pardon, excuse or correct the common people was suspended, until Baudimontius, having set out for Antwerp among other business, should report about it to Orange.

units.la: Invenio in actis Bethleæmas virgines libello supplice Matthiæ Gubernatori v. Non. Maï exhibito, liberam bonorum cœnobij administrationem, deducto, quod præstandum provinciæ foret, locarto ad vitam orasse, & ut monasterium, cautione de non recipiendis sine consensu Ordinum Frisiæ novis monialibus præstitâ, habitandum ætate provectis aut ævi maturis permitteretur. Matthiam quoque Gubernatorem postulatum velut æquissimum Ordinibus Frisiæ commendasse, litterisq; iv. Non. Maï in Frisiam expeditis, relicto tamen ijsdem secus disponendi arbitrio, humanissimo officio intercessisse.
units.tr: I find in the records that the Bethlehemite virgins, by a suppliant petition presented to Governor Matthias on 3 May, asked for the free administration of the monastery's goods for their lifetime, with a deduction of what was owed to the province, and that the monastery be allowed to be inhabited by women advanced in years or mature in age, with a pledge given not to admit new nuns without the consent of the Estates of Friesland. Governor Matthias, too, at their request, commended them to the Estates of Friesland as most fair, and by letters dispatched to Friesland on 4 May, while leaving the Estates free to decide otherwise, interceded with a most kindly office.

units.la: Igitur Baudimontius acceptis mandatis festino itinere Antverpiam progressus, litteras Aurantio Principi exhibuit, legationisque suæ seriem scripto complexus, hunc in modum disseruit.
units.tr: Therefore Baudimontius, having received his instructions, hurried to Antwerp, presented his letters to Prince Orange, and, having set out the course of his embassy in writing, spoke as follows.

units.la: SENATUS provincialis, PRINCEPS, ut te salutarem in mandatis mihi dedit, ac ut exponerem quanto in discrimine periculosissimis temporibus resp. constitueretur. Præterquam enim humanis ac barbaris hostium imperijs amovendis, tum excutiendæ æternæ servituti, præ nobis destinabatur, tributorum onera pati & ferre cogatur, ita multa quoque pro mutationibus temporum immutanda sunt, quæ emendationi labentium in deterius rerum inserviant. Imprimis vero emuniendæ resp. adversum eos est, qui viperarum more patriæ suæ infesti & ejus exitio nati Hispanicæ dominationis reducendæ consilia capiunt, omneq; populi & libertatis commodo serviturum occultis artibus subvertunt. A quibus certè est quod civilis discordiæ semina per provinciam spargantur, & quod omne tributum quieti nostræ & securitati decretum contumaciâ rebellis populi, & quod sædius, in ipsâ etiam rep. è potentioribus respuant. Unde simultates natæ, & diu perniciosis fomentis alitæ, in hoc, quod vides, discrimen, provinciam duxere. Cui avertendo deligendum ocyus rectorem Senatus natus censuit, cuius solertiâ malorum impetus retundantur, boni pacem atque securitatem habeant. In te vero, PRINCEPS, cum omnium vota, ana- que spes conspirent intercessionem fœderatorum procerum & Senatus mei mandatum expleo, rogoque ut Frisiæ imperium capessere in animum inducas, tuiq; absentiam, ita postentibus fatis & provinciarum rebus, vicario, aut Legato suffecto leves quam occyssimè. Vt scilicet is cum Senatu meo, quem jam antè cum Præfecto provinciæ moderamini rerum dispositio temporum admoverat, simulque cum Deputatis Ordinum consilia communicet, statuatque cum ijs quod ex usu & rep. futurum sit. Et quoniam moram ferre non potest periculi quo cum luctamur, magnitudo, ita peto Princeps, ut sepositâ cunctatione, quod visum fuerit, decernas, neque in provinciam ad Senatum faciendis relationibus remittas. Hoc vero ante omne necessum est, ut judicantium in Senatu numerum augeas, amplissimiq; Senatus consessum in integrum, & absolutæ potestati restituas. Quare nomine ejusdem Senatus peto, ut Heßeli Aysma, Præsidis, Sibrandi Richaei Fisci actoris, Douwonis Burmania, Barthÿ Idsaerda, Wilconis Holdingha, Foppÿ Grovensteinÿ, & Tiallingi Wikelÿ procurationes ex formula antiquâ conscribi cures, eorumque porrò innovari atque ampliari, qui cum laude ac famâ supremo tribunali & dignitatibus suis judice populo præfuere. Quas quoniam sustinere ex salarÿ tenuitate honestè alendis familijs non possunt, auctâ rerum omnium caritate & monetæ valore corrupto, ita peto, ut ijsdem pensionibus quo reliquum per Hollandiam & Geldriam Senatum haberi sinas. Tum ut mandes Deputatis Ordinum, ut intra terminos mandati sui se continendo pacem cum Senatu colant, dicundiquè juris (quod coram Deo & terrarum orbe conscientiâ teste, ritè administratum profitetur) officio se non immisceant. Denique de exulum bonis fisco applicandis decretum facias, expediasque in Frisiam Legatos, qui in seditiosos quosque & Magistratuum imperio contumaces inquirant, eosdemque ex lege ac tuâ autoritate puniri faciant.
units.tr: The provincial Senate, Prince, has instructed me to greet you and to explain in what danger the commonwealth stands in these most perilous times. For, besides the removal of the human and barbarous rule of enemies, which is set before us, we are also compelled to bear and endure the burdens of taxes, and many things must be changed in response to the changes of the times, to serve the correction of affairs that are sliding for the worse. Above all, the commonwealth must be fortified against those who, hostile to their country like vipers and born for its ruin, plan to restore Spanish domination and by hidden arts overturn everything for the advantage of the people and of liberty. From these men certainly come the seeds of civil discord scattered through the province, and every tax decreed for our quiet and security is spurned by the obstinacy of a rebellious people and, what is more shameful, even in the commonwealth itself by the more powerful. Hence quarrels arose, and, nourished for long by pernicious fomentations, have led the province into this peril that you see. To avert this, the Senate has resolved that a ruler be chosen as quickly as possible, by whose skill the assaults of evils may be beaten back and good men may have peace and security. In you, Prince, since the wishes and hopes of all agree, I fulfil the intercession of the confederate nobles and the mandate of my Senate, and I ask you to resolve to take up the government of Friesland, and, since fates and the affairs of the provinces are so pressing, to appoint a deputy or lieutenant in your absence as lightly and as quickly as possible. So that he, with my Senate, which the arrangement of the times had already assigned to govern together with the governor of the province, and at the same time with the deputies of the Estates, may confer on policy and decide with them what will be for the advantage and good of the commonwealth. And since the magnitude of the danger with which we are struggling cannot bear delay, I therefore ask, Prince, that, setting hesitation aside, you decree what seems best, and not send matters back to the province for reports to the Senate. Above all, this is necessary: that you increase the number of judges in the Senate and restore the full assembly of the most august Senate to its absolute power. Therefore, in the name of the same Senate, I ask that you see to it that the commissions of Hessel Aysma, President, Sibrand Richaei, procurator of the fisc, Douwo Burmania, Barthy Idsaerda, Wilco Holdingha, Foppy Grovenstein and Tialling Wikely be drawn up after the ancient form, and that those who presided over the people with praise and good repute in the supreme tribunal and in their dignities as judges be further renewed and enlarged. Since they cannot honourably support their families on the meagreness of their salaries, with the dearness of all things increased and the value of money corrupted, I ask that they be allowed, by the same pensions, to receive what the Senate has in the rest of Holland and Gelderland. Then that you order the deputies of the Estates to keep within the bounds of their mandate, to cultivate peace with the Senate, and not to meddle with the office of declaring the law, which they profess, with God and the world as witness of conscience, to administer rightly. Finally, that you make a decree for applying the goods of exiles to the fisc, and dispatch commissioners to Friesland who may inquire into all seditious men and those disobedient to the authority of the magistrates, and have them punished according to law and by your authority.

units.la: Hæc BAUDIMONTIUS.
units.tr: Thus far Baudimontius.

units.la: Quâ in re miserëri humanæ fragilitatis lubet, eos vix in Senatum, repente adhuc comitio, lectos, & jam ante severis crudelibusque antecessorum imperijs adversos, illâ infirmitate rerum de premendis damnatæ abolitæque dominationis vestigijs cogitavisse. Eosdem quoque Aurantium Principem, etsi necdum provinciæ inligatum, ad explenda immodesta desideria, & simul mandata sollicitasse, quæ præfectis provinciarum subtracta, Ordinum juri atque supremæ majestati gentium libertas reliquerat. Adeo fluxæ & fallacis potentiæ affectatio patriæ quoque amantium ingenia, fortunæ subjecerat. Igitur illa lubidini atque cupiditatibus permissa, nec asperi temporis, nec tolerati plerisque exilij memoriam retinuerant, & quod in illo tristioris concilij secreto Carolo ac Philippo regnantibus oppressæ, leges & mœstissimæ libertatis silentia jacuissent. Ipsa etiam resp. inter regni adhuc minas & metum, continuis tempestatibus obnoxia, illam refricandæ antiquæ litis importunitatem non pateretur, quam à quadraginta annis nostræ gentis infamiâ, & externæ potestatis commodo fotam, seponere hoc temporum lubrico, sollicitudo publici discriminis debuisset.
units.tr: In this matter it is fitting to pity human frailty: that these men, scarcely chosen to the Senate on a sudden while the assembly was still new, and already hostile to the harsh and cruel rule of their predecessors, should in that weakness of affairs have thought of reviving the traces of a condemned and abolished domination. The same men also pressed Prince Orange, though not yet bound to the province, to fulfil their immoderate desires, and at the same time their commands, which the liberty of the nations had withdrawn from the governors of the provinces and left to the right of the Estates and the supreme majesty. So far did the pursuit of a fleeting and deceitful power subject even the minds of those who loved their country to fortune. Therefore, men given over to lust and desire retained the memory neither of the harsh times nor of the exile that most of them had endured, and forgot that under the reigns of Charles and Philip, in the secret of that gloomy council, the laws had been crushed and the most sorrowful silence of liberty had lain prostrate. The commonwealth itself, still exposed to continual storms amid the threats and fear of the kingdom, would not allow the troublesome reopening of that old quarrel, which, nursed for forty years on the infamy of our nation and the advantage of foreign power, anxiety for the public danger ought to have set aside in this slippery time.

units.la: Iam enim fœderatarum provinciarum Legatos, Ultrajecto Davente- riam periculâ evocaverant, adeò late diffuso hostilium incursionum & advencIↄ. Iↄ. adventantis auxilij metu, ut omnem provinciam, & circumjacentia locorum impleret. Quippe fama, ut solet, suspectis etsi certis, rumoribus pondus atque incrementum addiderat, ferebaturque Farnesius totam belli molem conquisitis etiam per agrum Luxemburgicum Germanorum copijs trans-rhenanæ genti, & solvendo Groningensium obsidio destinare.
units.tr: For already they had summoned the envoys of the confederated provinces from Utrecht to Deventer, in peril, so widely had the fear of hostile incursions and of approaching help spread that it filled the whole province and the surrounding regions. For rumour, as usual, had added weight and growth to suspicions which, though sure, were only rumours, and it was reported that Farnese, having gathered the whole mass of war, even by drawing German troops through the Luxembourg country, intended to hand it over to the trans-Rhenish nation and to lift the siege of Groningen.

units.la: Quare Concilij Status decreto in inferiores provincias missus Elbertus Leoninus vir doctrinâ atque prudentiâ pollens, qui res Groninganas & Frisiorum curaret, Philippoque Hohenloo cæterisque provinciarum Legatis à consilio esset. Igitur in Frisios ituro ducenti Carolæi ex ærario Frisiæ assignati, qui homo pacis artibus ætatem agens castrensium & molestarum vacationum impensas, & simul tædia illâ Ordinum remuneratione ac beneficio allevaret. Adeo Groningam in urbem omnium spes atque metus fortuna defixerat, quæ auxilij Rhenum traducti certo ar-ctatos antè spiritus, velut recepto aëre, laxaverat.
units.tr: Therefore Elbert Leoninus, a man strong in learning and prudence, was sent to the lower provinces by decree of the Council of State, to take care of the affairs of Groningen and of the Frisians, and was to be an adviser to Philip Hohenlohe and the other envoys of the provinces. Accordingly, for him going into Friesland, two hundred Carolus guilders were assigned from the treasury of Friesland, so that he, a man who spent his life in the arts of peace, might relieve the expenses of military and troublesome duties and at the same time the tedium, by that reward and favour of the Estates. So completely had fortune fixed the hopes and fears of all upon the city of Groningen, which, by the sure arrival of help brought across the Rhine, had loosened breaths previously constricted, as if fresh air had been admitted.

units.la: Reperio in incerti autoris Ephemeride ad Ordines Frisiæ scripta, exercitum illum à præsidiariâ fœderatorum Ordinum navi, quæ in flumine stabat, facilè & initio Rheni trajectu prohiberi potuisse, nisi eam tempestatis cœlo editæ ferocia & aquarum ex imbrium copià torrentium vis statione & loco depulisset. Cui & hoc accedebat, quod lapi-dosum ripæ marginem velocior Rhenus perstringeret, anchoraque saxis minus inhærens; rapidissimi fluminis declivio ac impetu vinceretur.
units.tr: I find in the journal of an unknown author, written to the Estates of Friesland, that that army could easily have been prevented at its first crossing of the Rhine by the guard ship of the confederated Estates, which lay in the river, unless the fierceness of the storm raised by the sky and the force of the waters, torrents swollen by the abundance of rain, had driven it from its station and place. To this was added that the swifter Rhine was grazing the stony margin of the bank, and the anchor, holding less firmly among the rocks, was overcome by the slope and rush of the very rapid river.

units.la: Itaque hostem depressiore præsidiario, vectorio aliisque navigijs Bonnam solventem, Bergensium animis, quam ut ripâ arcerent, languidioribus, haud procul Coloniâ Nelam pagum appulisse, ope imprimis Solmensium Comitis, qui in ripam expositos commeatu atq; omni necessario præjuverat. Ibi aulæ Clivicæ & nobilitatis jussu (quarum utramque ære ac largitionibus corruptam, ne ipsi quidem venales & corrupti etiam in foro Dusseldorpiensi dissimulabant) bellica quoque Ordinum navis cum reliquis Rheno discedere jussa, quæ in adversum flumen enitentes suorum arte ac mandato non alieno imperio regebantur. Itaq; hostes abductis in prædam Bergensium equis in præturâ Holeradensi stativa habuere, donec refocillati ex itinerum molestijs, & ante fame ac somno marcidi, spoliatis atque direptis pagis, fœminisq; in captivitatem abductis post cu-rata ritè corpora Mullum pervenirent. Quatuordecim signa peditum, sex equitum fuisse idem autor notat, ac in ijs Equestrem Italorum alam, tum ducentos ex Epiro ac Illyrico equites lancearios robur equitatus confecisse. Reliquos equos operi rustico subductos, ac regi rudes fuisse, ipsosque sessores sessos, atque exsangues levi equitum, ac ducentorum sclopetariorum manu concidi, fugarique potuisse. Quod Aggæi Albadæ oratoris Frisij prudens consilium suppremendum non duxi, suadentis hostem tumul-tuariè & sine ordine coactum in Iuliacensium aut medijs saltem Cliviæ agris tentandum debellandumque fuisse. Cæterum rustica plebe so-ciorum clade perculsâ, vires, arma, auxilia deërant, amotis procul fœderatorum Ordinum copijs, quas in interiora provinciarum formido, andicam cura periculi protuserat. Ita Clivicæ Ducis aut aulicorum, clandestino cum hoste pacto ac auxilio omnia clam habita, ne conscio quidem populo aut castellorum satrapis, ad quos sola & dubia militarium copiarum fama, pervaserat. Idem autor scribit Martinum Schenckium copiapiarum ductorem Coloniæ in monasterio quodam epulo exceptum, ac CIↃ. IↃ. LXXX à Bergensibus, ut agris suis parceret, sollicitatum præfractè ac superbè respondisse, nuperæque cladis & dissipatarum haud procul Novesio cohortium incommoda, Bergensium insolentiæ tanquam causæ regij decrementi imputavisse. Vel eâ scilicet sola vastationem ac cædem commeritos & ut amissâ socij regis gratiâ ac veniâ militum suorum furoribus in vindictam atrocis injuriæ exponantur. Cæterum se, etsi alio mandato instructum, clementius acturum parciturumq; illorum fortunis atq; sanguini, quorum incauta & temeraria vis tuendo agro obtenta, regem Philippum solido infortunio multasset. Alias sui arbitrij esse an Bergensium agros stativis castrorum, an transducendis copijs reservare velit, & an violatam principum gentiumq; mutuam societatem rariore exemplo expiare. Aulici quoq; Bergensium legatis abactos equos iniata damna querentibus immodestè responderunt, militemque eorum feritate ac licentiâ incitatum & sola prædæ dulcedine contentum, extremis abstinuisse. Nihil scilicet esse, de quo queri possint, qui scirent omnem injuriam talione aut vindictâ pensandam. Itaque Dux Gulielmus animi fato inops, calore iracundiæ multa ab aulicis effundi inaudiens, de distringendo in suorum Bergensium legatos gladio agitavit, impeditusque à circumstantibus rerum cognitionem sicut infausti principatus regimen corruptæ aulæ judicio permisit.
units.tr: And so the enemy, having landed at Nelam, a village not far from Cologne, with a lower guard ship, a transport and other vessels sailing from Bonn, the men of Bergen being too slack in spirit to keep them from the bank, and chiefly with the help of the Count of Solms, who had supplied the men put ashore with provisions and every necessity. There, by order of the Cleves court and the nobility (both of which, corrupted by money and bribes, not even the venal and corrupt men themselves concealed in the marketplace of Düsseldorf), the warship of the Estates was also ordered to withdraw from the Rhine with the rest; these ships, straining against the current, were steered by the skill and orders of their own men, not by a foreign command. So the enemy, with the horses taken as plunder from the men of Bergen, made camp in the jurisdiction of Holeradensis, until, refreshed after the hardships of the marches, and before that exhausted by hunger and sleep, they reached Mullum after the bodies had been properly tended, the villages having been stripped and plundered and women led off into captivity. The same writer notes that there were fourteen companies of foot and six of horse, and among them an Italian cavalry wing; then two hundred lancers from Epirus and Illyria formed the strength of the cavalry. The remaining horses, taken from rustic labour and unbroken to riding, and the riders themselves, who sat on them exhausted and bloodless, could have been cut down and put to flight by a light band of horsemen and two hundred musketeers. I did not think fit to suppress the prudent advice of Aggaeus Albada, the Frisian envoy, who urged that the enemy, gathered in a tumultuous and disorderly fashion, should have been attacked and defeated in the lands of Jülich, or at least in the midst of Cleves. But with the rustic populace struck down by the defeat of the allies, forces, arms and aid were lacking, the troops of the confederate Estates having been withdrawn far off, which fear of the inner provinces and anxiety for danger had driven away. Thus everything was kept hidden by the Duke of Cleves or his courtiers through a clandestine pact and aid with the enemy, the people not even knowing of it, nor the governors of the castles, to whom only a doubtful rumour of the military forces had spread. The same author writes that Martin Schenck, leader of the troops, was entertained at a banquet in a certain monastery at Cologne, and that when the men of Bergen asked him to spare their fields for a sum of 1580, he answered them stubbornly and haughtily, and blamed the insolence of the men of Bergen as the cause of the king's loss, for the setback of the recent defeat and of the cohorts scattered not far from Neuss. Clearly, by that alone they had deserved devastation and slaughter, and, having lost the favour and pardon of the king's ally, they were to be exposed to the fury of his soldiers as vengeance for an atrocious injury. Otherwise, though he had been given different orders, he himself would act more mildly and spare the fortunes and blood of those whose incautious and rash violence, employed in defending their land, had fined King Philip with a solid misfortune. It was otherwise his own choice whether he wished to spare the fields of Bergen by quartering the camp there or by moving his troops through, and whether he should expiate the violated mutual alliance of princes and nations by a rarer example. The courtiers, too, answered the envoys of Bergen immodestly, when they complained of the horses driven off and the damage done, saying that their soldier, roused by ferocity and licence and content with the mere sweetness of plunder, had abstained from extremes. Clearly there was nothing for them to complain of, since they knew every injury must be repaid by retaliation or vengeance. So Duke William, lacking firmness of mind, hearing many things poured out by the courtiers in heat of anger, debated drawing the sword against the envoys of his own men of Bergen; but, hindered by those standing around, he left the knowledge of affairs, and the government of his unhappy principality, to the judgment of a corrupt court.

units.la: Tradit idem scriptor Colonienses Præsulem promovendo Schenckiani exercitus Trajectui Walravio Soæstio, Schenckianæ cohortis optione operam atque auxilia in oppido Meursæ depactum, eundemque Walravium ab ipso præsule liberalissime exceptum bonam spem concipiendæ expeditionis concepisse. Igitur præsidiarium navigium, removendis Rheno, quæ transierant, copijs invalidum, interceptas Farnesij Litteras & captivum ex agro Dusseldorpiensi vehens secundo flumine descendit, Schenckijque exercitus binoctio Mullumi acto, decimo mensis Junij die Buranum vicum emensus, Horstianam inter atque Raesfeldiam arces desedit. Ubi curatis in diem corporibus Elam, Halteram atque Dulmam processit intensissimis cœli ardoribus, quod sole Cancrum ingresso in mediterraneis & per myriceta omnem humorem squallentium rivulorum aut putentis stagni depaverat. Unde sitis fame, quâ identidem vexabatur, acrior, arentibus militum faucibus nata, quas jam ante in Rheni tractu vino prolutas, ne limosæ quidem paludis illuvies irrigabat. Cæterum à Dulmensibus cibo & potu, in spem pretij ac parati æris, quo destituebantur, refecti, animos excusso languore sumpserunt, obviâ insuper novi auxilij famâ, quod supra Coloniam & ad Rhenum cogi Nigellius Gorcumanus perfugâ etsi vanissimo rumore nuntiaverat. Cui urbi in partes hostium propensæ à bellicâ ordinum navi, quæ objectum flumen occupaverat, terror injectus, aucto magis Coloniensium pavore, quod Cloierus Amstelodamensium præfectus binas naves præsidiarias cum instructissimâ triremi Rheno flumini induxisset. Is vero Dusseldorpium Cliviæ ad Rhenum oppidum cum classe progressus Satrapa Horstio, ac ipso navium inspectore conscio, Joannem Gulielmum Ducem offendit, hominiq; ultro mente capto iracundiam & mox furorem excitavit.
units.tr: The same writer reports that when the Bishop of Cologne was advancing, Walravius Soestius, an officer of Schenck's cohort, arranged aid and assistance at the town of Meurs in Utrecht. Walravius was received most generously by the bishop himself and conceived good hope for the expedition. So the garrison ship, its forces weakened because the troops who had crossed the Rhine had been withdrawn, sailed down the river with the current, carrying intercepted letters of Farnese and a prisoner taken from the Düsseldorf region. Schenck's army, after two nights at Mullum, covered the distance to the village of Buren on 10 June and settled between the castles of Horst and Raesfeld. There, having rested the men for a day, they advanced to Elten, Halteren and Dülmen under intense heat, for the sun, having entered Cancer, had dried up every drop of moisture from the inland streams and from the stagnant pools among the myrtle bushes. Thirst, by which they were repeatedly tormented, grew more severe, because the soldiers' throats were parched, and the wine with which they had been washed earlier in the Rhine region could not be replaced even by the filth of a muddy marsh. But the men of Dülmen gave them food and drink in hope of payment in ready money, which they lacked, and so they were restored, shook off their weariness, and took heart. They were further encouraged by the report of a new reinforcement, which Nigellius of Gorcum, a deserter, had announced, though with very empty rumour, being gathered above Cologne along the Rhine. Terror was struck into that city, which leaned to the enemy's side, by a warship of the States that had occupied the river opposite. The Cologners' fear grew greater because Cloierus, prefect of the Amsterdammers, had brought two garrison ships and a very well equipped trireme onto the Rhine. He advanced with his fleet to Düsseldorf, a town of Cleves on the Rhine, and there found Duke John William. The governor Horst and the inspector of the ships were aware of the situation. The Duke was already of unsound mind, and the sight of the man roused first anger and soon fury.

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXXX. Quare Dux vocato ad se navium inspectori strictum gladium intenjtavit, ægrique Horstij Marschalli interventu admisso acerrimum vulnus inflixit. Tum fervore & rabie aucta repellendis Ordinum navigijs Rhenì per ripam, qua Dusseldorpio obtenditur, disponi tormenta fecit, omneque alienatæ mentis & pro Hispano stantis indicium prodidit. Cæterum naves ferendis tormentorum ictibus validas ferramenta & densissimæ trabium compages fecerant, inridente Cloiero imbellem vesani Principis & aulicorum iram, potiundo Rheni fluminis imperio evanescere. Itaque adverso defluentis Rheni alveo naves milite & commeatu instructas Bonnam provexit, omniq; ad Rhenum oræ & speratis Schenckij auxilijs metum ac impedimentum injecit.
units.tr: 1590. Therefore the Duke summoned the inspector of the ships to him, threatened him with a drawn sword, and, when the sick Marshal Horst intervened, let him in and inflicted a most fierce wound. Then, his heat and rage increased, he ordered artillery to be set along the bank facing Düsseldorf to repel the ships of the States, and showed every sign of a disordered mind and of one standing for the Spaniard. But the ships, strengthened against the blows of artillery with iron plates and very dense timber frames, and Cloierus mocking the powerless anger of the mad prince and his courtiers, which would vanish once the empire of the river was seized. So, with the current of the Rhine against them, he brought the ships, equipped with soldiers and supplies, up to Bonn, and struck fear into the whole shore of the Rhine and hindered Schenck's hoped-for aid.

units.la: Erant qui suaderent in illo hostium apparatu Rheni alveum intra ripas ardore solis & imbrium caritate contractum triremium ope, tardioribus præsidiarijs navigijs, occupandum, quo remigum ministerijs, silente vento & depressiore fluminis alveo, quamlibet in ripam adigerentur. Easdem quoque triremes quingentorum sexcentorumve militum numero armandas impediendis copiarum transvectionibus, quas Farnesius extenuato superiore exercitu Trans-Rhenanis provincijs decernebat. Itaque Fronsbergium, Polvilerium, reliquosque Germanicarum legionum tribunos, ob stipendia immodeste flagitata in Lutsenburgensium fines amotos in auxilia sollicitavit, residuumque stipendiorum æs Lutetiæ Parisiorum brevi exsolvendum promisit. Tum Hispanicæ quoque factioni per provinciam addictos secretioribus litteris instruxit, plurimosque habendo per Cliviam commeatui Sanctis & Embricæ promissâ proditionis mercede corrupit. Quare & Frisios ex eadem factione in Sylvestribus & ad Cuneram congregari fecit, omnemque in liberandâ ocyus Groningâ fortunæ ac victoriæ spem collocavit. Unde exercitum stativa apud Dulmenses habentem, instigantibus proditoribus & in ijs Splinterio quodam pergere ocyus Schenckius iussit, audito populum ciendis per Frisiam seditionibus promptum sola auxilia, exequendis rebus, opperiri.
units.tr: There were those who advised seizing the channel of the Rhine, which the heat of the sun and the lack of rain had contracted within its banks, with triremes, while slower garrison ships held the rest. Then, with the wind still and the river lower, the oarsmen could drive the ships to the bank, however much resistance there was. These triremes were also to be armed with five or six hundred soldiers to hinder the transport of troops which Farnese, having weakened his army in the upper provinces, was sending into the Trans-Rhenish provinces. So Fronsberg, Polviller and the other tribunes of the German legions, who had been removed into the territory of Luxembourg because they had demanded their pay immoderately, were summoned to aid, and he promised that the remaining pay would soon be paid in Paris. Then he instructed by secret letters those throughout the province who were devoted to the Spanish faction, and corrupted very many in Cleves by promising the reward of treason, while supplies were given to Xanten and Emmerich. For this reason he also had the Frisians of the same faction gathered in the woods and at Cuneram, and placed all his hope of fortune and victory in the quick liberation of Groningen. Therefore, at the urging of the traitors, among whom was a certain Splinter, Schenck ordered the army, which was quartered at Dülmen, to move quickly, having heard that the people of Friesland were ready for sedition and waited only for aid to carry out the plan.

units.la: Scribit autor, Dekamam quendam in aulâ Alexandri Farnesij Robleslio familiarem, assignato honorario ære, certam intestinarum turbarum spem per Frisiam fecisse, eaq; animatum Schenckium, movendis Groningâ fœderatorum castris, sacramentum dixisse. Frisiorum quoque fertiles agros spem messi tum facientes, adhæc divitis populi fortunas prædæ à Farnesio datas, militemque ejus dulcedine pellectum, rapiendis provincialium opibus expeditionis consilium maturasse.
units.tr: The author writes that a certain Dekama, a familiar of Robles in the court of Alexander Farnese, promised, for an assigned sum of money, certain civil strife throughout Friesland. Encouraged by this, Schenck ordered the camps of the confederates to be moved from Groningen and swore the oath. The fertile fields of the Frisians, which then promised a harvest, the wealth of a rich people given to plunder by Farnese, and his soldiery drawn by the sweetness of it, hastened the plan of the expedition to seize the provincials' wealth.

units.la: Itaq; Philippus Hohenloüs, qui in castris ad Groningam tum erat, literas iv. Jun. in Frisiam dedit, atq; firmandis præsidio Leovardiâ, Snecâ & Harlingâ oppidis commonuit. Se scilicet cum copijs recta in hostem iturum, ut fluminum transitu illum prohibeat, Frisiamque & omnem trans Rhenum provinciam ab ejusdem irruptione liberet. Sed eventus rerum dubios esse, se victoriam quidem à Deo sperare, sed in cujus potestate sit adversa bene speranti obtrudere. Quod si eveniat Frisiam conspirationibus suorum obnoxiam fore, quibus amovendis commoda civitatum præsidia esse queant opportune distributa.
units.tr: Therefore Philip Hohenlo, who was then in camp at Groningen, wrote to Friesland on 4 June and warned that the garrisons of the towns of Leeuwarden, Sneek and Harlingen should be strengthened. He himself, he said, would march straight against the enemy with his forces, to prevent their crossing of the rivers and to free Friesland and the whole province beyond the Rhine from their invasion. But the outcome of affairs was uncertain. He hoped for victory from God, yet it lay in God's power to bring adversity upon one who hoped well. If it should happen that Friesland was exposed to conspiracies among its own people, well-placed garrisons in the cities could be useful for removing them.

units.la: Quæ prolixius reliquis silentibus mihi narrata, & quod illâ memorabili expeditione armam in Frisiam ope exulum ducta, multis annis duraverint. Quod ipsum quoq; incommodum, quamvis fato eventurum crederetur, castigandæ procerum in extruendis Burtangæ & Coverdiæ munitionibus discordiæ potissimum obvenit, volente, sicuti solet, providentiâ inermem populum & nullius inofficiosi conscium ex dominantium incuriâ affligi. Creditum fuit, Martinum Schenckium occupandæ cum suis Brevortæ, aut Lingæ tacitum àFarnesio mandatum accepisse, aut ut, istius consilij successu frustratus, opperiendis reliquis, quæ parabantur, auxilijs commissa apertis campis castra prædu&o multuario opere muniret. Cæterum mutato animo, rapto Dulmam exercitu, iter Benthemicos per agros pronuntiari jussit, instigatus tum vel maximè Suollensium precibus, quos excusâ fœderis Ultrajectini religione, admittendis intra muros hostibus domesticæ factiones armaverant.
units.tr: These matters I have been told at greater length, while others remain silent, and that in that memorable expedition arms were led into Friesland with the help of exiles, lasted for many years. This misfortune too, though it was believed to come by fate, arose chiefly from the discord of the nobles over building fortifications at Borculo and Coevorden. Providence, as usual, allowed an unarmed people, conscious of no wrong, to be afflicted through the carelessness of its rulers. It was believed that Martin Schenck had received a secret order from Farnese to occupy Breda or Linge with his men. Or else, frustrated in that plan, he was to wait for the remaining aid being prepared, and meanwhile fortify his camp in the open fields with a hastily made work built by many hands. But he changed his mind, seized Dülmen with the army, and ordered the march through the lands of Bentheim to be announced. He was urged especially by the entreaties of the people of Zwolle, who, disregarding the religion of the Union of Utrecht, had armed domestic factions to admit the enemy within the walls.

units.la: Quare Hohenloïs, quo hostem anteveniret, mandato à Frisijs & fœderato simul consessu, qui Daventriæ habebatur, accepto copias atq; auxilia contraxit, quæ sex cohortium numero è castris ad Groningam petita, cum alijs ex Iselsteinij legione Joannes Cuningamus vir militaris ducebat. Gulielmus verò Ludovicus, cum Diderico Sonoïo, qui Cuningamo suffectus erat, rem ad Groningam gerere jussus, festinante écontra Schenckio ut obsessorum angustiæ & afflictis per Transf-Isulaniam suorum rebus subveniret. Quippe Suollâ in potestatem à fœderato præsidio redactâ, tum rusticorum, qui Schenckio favebant, villis atque agris populatis Gelmuda quoque arx à Transf-Isulanis diruta, atque solo æquata erat, quam premendo Vidri fluminis ubi in mare labitur, ostio Carolus olim Cæsar extruxerat. Igitur ordinatis ritè per Transf-Isulaniam rebus, motis Ulsenâ castris Hohenloïs exercitum Coverdiam duxit, refectisque ex fatigatione militum corporibus opperiri hostem, ac decertare prælio constituit. Cæterum novo mandato conferre signa prohibitus (ne infirmo peditatu & rarioribus hastatorum ordinibus in discrimen venire) spreto, quod præliaturis auspiciorum loco esse solet, imperio Coverdiâ in hostem duxit, quem intercepto commeatu, morâ consumendum peritissimi rerum ac locorum suaserant. Adeò præclaris sæpè Ducibus ad momenta temporum introspicienda consilij maturitas defuit. Itaque ferventissimo die, quem Sol Cancri Tropicum percurrens, ut plurimum facit, citò agmine copias irè jussit, quarum robur ex intemperato æstu, præter viæ longitudinem, armorum pondera & profusissimi corporum sudores dissolverant. Hostem verò itinerum spatia jam ante permensum, quies permulserat, quæ objectu umbræ gratior, fractas cœlesti ardore vires utili alimoniâ reparaveras. Quare Schenckius ritè curatis suorum corporibus medio Hardenbergio myriceto signa explicuit, initoque pugnæ consilio aciem ordinavit.
units.tr: Therefore Hohenlo, to get ahead of the enemy, gathered troops and auxiliaries on the mandate of the Frisians and of the confederate assembly held at Deventer. Six cohorts' worth were sought from the camp at Groningen, and with others from the Iselstein regiment John Cuningham, a soldier, led them. William Louis, ordered to take charge of affairs at Groningen with Diederik Sonoy, who had succeeded Cuningham, hastened against Schenck so that he might relieve the distress of the besieged and the afflicted condition of his men in Transisalania. Zwolle had been taken into the power of the confederate garrison; then the farmhouses and fields of the country people who favoured Schenck were plundered, and the castle of Gelmuda, which Charles, once emperor, had built to press upon the mouth of the Vidri where it flows into the sea, was demolished by the Transisalanians and levelled with the ground. Having duly arranged affairs in Transisalania, Hohenlo moved his camp from Ulsen and led the army to Coevorden. After the soldiers' bodies had recovered from exhaustion, he decided to await the enemy and fight a battle. But he was forbidden by a new order to join the standards, lest the infantry, weak and with thinner ranks of spearmen, be exposed to danger. He scorned this order, which usually serves commanders about to fight in place of the auspices, and led his forces from Coevorden against the enemy, whom the most experienced men in affairs and places had advised to wear down by delay, by cutting off supplies. So often the wisdom to foresee the turning points of events is lacking in famous commanders. Therefore on a scorching day, such as the sun usually brings when it passes the tropic of Cancer, he ordered the forces to march quickly. Besides the length of the road, the weight of their arms and the profuse sweat of their bodies had dissolved their strength in the intemperate heat. The enemy, having already measured out the distances, had been refreshed by rest, which, more welcome for the shade it offered, had restored with nourishment the strength broken by the heavenly heat. Hence Schenck, having duly tended his men's bodies, unfurled his standards in the middle of the myrtle thicket at Hardenberg, and, having settled the plan of battle, drew up his line.

units.la: Hohenloïs quoque etsi itineris lassitudine fractus & aquarum penuriâ, quæ multos extinxerat, ne quiete quidem in tam intensis caloribus militi datâ, exercitum ad pugnam disposuit, in quo dextrum aciei cornu Joannes Cuningamus cum Nassoviani & Wingardio & mediâ Cornuputti cohorte, lævum Iselsteinius & Zerulca tenebant. Ipsam verò ante aciem, Onstæ, Rinsuoudij & Asinghæ Entenij, equestres turbas ri-
units.tr: Hohenlo too, though broken by the weariness of the journey and by the lack of water, which had killed many, and though not even rest had been given the soldier in such intense heat, arranged his army for battle. In it John Cuningham, with the troops of Nassau and Wingarden and the middle cohort of Cornuputt, held the right wing of the line, and Iselstein and Zerulca the left. In front of the line itself, the Onstes, Rinsuoudij and Asinghe Entenius, the troops of horse ri-

units.la: Hohenloïs contra man- datum Orca dinum in præliū descendit. te instructas collocavit, quarum adversum latus ipse septem majoribus tormentis reliquoque equitatu munierat. Sed aperta loci planities exercitus latera nudaverat, quae melius ipsa Hardenberga aut proximi campi firmandis ordinibus & ad refugium munijssent. Quippe pagum praeter hortorum villarumque sepimenta amnis quoque Vechta praefluebat, qui ex Benthemiorum finibus modico fonte procedens majore alveo, sterilium camporum spatia latioribus ripis dirimebat. Sed fato destinata ne Ducis quidem errore aut prudentia vitabantur, etsi essent, qui crederent, vel maxime ex fiducia peccatum quae Hohenloo victoriae velut certo, omnem periculi metum atque sollicitudinem ademerat. Adeo verum est, nullos facilius opprimi, quam nihil timentes, adversamque isti virtuti, ut plurimum, fortunam esse, quae vi suâ nixa & occasionum seguis aut negligens securitate fati aut inconsulto impetu regeretur.
units.tr: Contrary to orders, Hohenlo went down into battle. He posted the drawn-up ranks, whose flank he himself had protected with seven heavier guns and the rest of the cavalry. But the open plain had left the army's flanks exposed. Hardenberg itself or the nearby field would have better protected them, both for strengthening the ranks and as a place of refuge. Besides the gardens and farm enclosures of the village, the river Vechte flowed past it. Rising from a small spring in the territory of Bentheim, it had gathered into a larger channel and divided the wide stretches of barren fields with broader banks. But what fate had determined was not avoided even by the Duke's error or prudence, although some believed the fault lay chiefly in overconfidence. This had removed from Hohenlo all fear and anxiety of danger, as though victory were certain. So true is it that none are more easily overcome than those who fear nothing, and that fortune, which rests on its own strength, is usually hostile to such courage. It is governed by opportunities, either by careless complacency or by rash impulse.

units.la: Quare ne coeli quidem & castrorum positu observato solem, pulverem Hohenlous sibi adversum, hosti secundum fecerat, qui declivi sensim astro umbras corporum ardoris refrigerio trahens aestum ac obtutum clarissimi syderis Hohenloo reliquerat: Tandem medio diei effluxo signa cecinere, postquam preces utrinque propitiando numini fusae alacritatem aut metum pugnaturis addiderant. Igitur displosis tormentis Frisiorum equitum turmae in Epirotas lancearios invectae, qui ad sustinendos primos & saepe ferociores impetus invalidi, dissipati aut caesi felicia pugnae initia Hohenloo ostentabant. Quippe Schenckianos in fugam abreptos Germani ocyus atque alacrius insequebantur, ne pedite quidem ita compositò, ut pugnae locum, quem ceperat, ex sociorum clade retineret. Unde victoriae spes Hohenloo illucescebat, nisi prima fronte blandiens fortuna secundis adversa reservasset. Ubi namque equestres Frisiorum turmae repetendis viribus ac insultibus parum recessere, hostibus fugam ratis animus increvit, quos velut semi-victos & sociae cladis spectaculo truces in medios Hohenloi pedites vindictae cupido atque gloriae impellebat. In quibus praecipui Epirotae, redintegrata acie, cum ferentariis fuere, qui impetu Frisici equitatus repulso, dissipatos ante lancearios reparandis viribus incitabant. Tum Hohenloi eques pedem ad tormenta retraxit, quae confertim rumpendis Schenkianorum ordinibus, laxata nullo pulvere aut globo tenebantur. Unde pedestres Hohenloi copiae, retroactis sensim equestribus, & quod hastati excipiendis Epirotarum equitum insultibus deessent, in planitiem digressae, quae aperta & nullo opere vallata, qua qua versum fugae proximos impressionibus hostium exponebat. Quare, edito aliquandiu virtutis exemplo, fugae consilium cepere, quae ut solet, inclinante acie ne fortissimos quosque in stratione aut officio retinebat. Sic pedestri exercitu dispersò equestrium quoque turmarum ordines dissoluti, quos peditum exemplo conterritos, nec pugnantium tribunorum virtus, nec imperium Ducis coercebat. Itaque multi in amnem praecipites acti, eo vadoso in avia ac deserta se recepere, quae humanis ante vestigijs intacta, palantium multitudini ac fugae serviebant. Quippe faeculentam paludum uliginem continuae siccitates & ardentius coelum induraverant, ut ferendo peditì habilis, ne equinae quidem ungulae iter atque vestigium respueret. Unde de multi omnia ad laevam relicta Coverdiam celerrimo cursu profugere, quam Hohenlous, adversae fortunae metu, recipiendis profugis asylum ordinaverat. Ita bituminosae uliginis duritiei multis saluti, plurimis quoque exitio fuit, quos hostium equites per plana myrticeta & palustres campos assecuti, sedato nondum pugnae calore, vulneribus ac caede sternebant.
units.tr: Therefore Hohenlo, who had not observed the position of the sky and the camp, made the sun and the dust work against himself and for the enemy. As the sun sank gradually, it cast the shadows of bodies, which gave relief from the heat, and left Hohenlo the glare and blaze of that most brilliant star. At last, when midday had passed, the signals sounded. Prayers had been poured out on both sides to propitiate the divine power, and these gave eagerness or fear to those about to fight. So, after the cannon were fired, squadrons of Frisian horsemen charged the Epirot lancers. These, too weak to withstand the first and often fiercer assaults, were scattered or cut down, and their defeat gave Hohenlo the first signs of a happy battle. The Germans pursued the Schenck men, who had been driven into flight, the more quickly and eagerly, since the infantry was not so arranged as to hold the ground it had taken once its allies had been defeated. Hence Hohenlo's hope of victory began to dawn, had not Fortune, flattering at the outset, kept adversity in store for what followed. For when the Frisian cavalry squadrons had withdrawn only a little to recover their strength and renew their charges, the enemy's spirit rose, taking the flight as their cue. Seeing their allies defeated, they were half-victorious and fierce, and a desire for vengeance and glory drove them into the midst of Hohenlo's infantry. Among them the Epirots were foremost; the line having been re-formed, they fought alongside the light-armed troops. Repulsing the Frisian cavalry charge, they urged on the lancers who had been scattered earlier, so that they might regather their strength. Then Hohenlo's horse drew back toward the artillery, which, having been loosed, were held without powder or shot, since the ranks of Schenck's men were being broken by them in close order. Thus Hohenlo's foot soldiers, as the cavalry gradually retreated, and because the pikemen were lacking to meet the Epirot horsemen's attacks, went off onto the plain. It was open and unfortified, and it exposed to the enemy's onslaughts those nearest the line of flight. So, after showing courage for some time, they resolved to flee. As usually happens, once the line began to give way, this kept even the bravest from holding their post or doing their duty. Thus, with the infantry scattered, the ranks of the cavalry also broke up. Terrified by the infantry's example, neither the courage of the fighting officers nor the Duke's command could restrain them. Many were driven headlong into the river, and by crossing at the shallow ford they withdrew into pathless and deserted country, which had been untouched by human footprints before and served the scattering crowd in its flight. Indeed, continual droughts and a fiercely burning sky had hardened the foul mud of the marshes so that it was passable for foot soldiers, and even a horse's hoof would not refuse to leave a track on it. Hence many, abandoning everything on the left, fled at full speed to Coevorden, where Hohenlo, fearing reverse, had ordered a refuge for fugitives to be prepared. Thus the hardness of the bituminous mud was a salvation for many, but for very many it was a destruction. The enemy cavalry overtook them across the flat myrtle thickets and marshy fields and, while the heat of the battle had not yet cooled, cut them down with wounds and slaughter.

units.la: Wingardius cohortis ductor, qui in dextro cornu fuerat, fortiter pugnans & a suis destertus occubuit, multique ex vulnere, aut in ipsa fuga effervesacto sanguine ex siti debiles in potestatem hostium venere. Pompeius quoque Ufkenius pensili, quod ad spectandum praelium ferebatur, curru excussus ac ab hostibus interemptus est. Vir meliore vitae exitu dignissimus, quae promovendo foederi inter curas & inquietudines acta patriae amantem superfuso militari tribunitioque sanguine superbi cruentique victoris arbitrio objecit. Itaque tantus pavor ex fuga multitudinem invasit, ut ne Coverdiae quidem subsisteret, ligneoq; ac trabali viae objice objecto, aut Cornputti praesidio stantis prece aut imperio retineretur. Quare palustres, qui Coverdiam Burtangamque interjacent, campos pervagata monasteriense in agrum se effudit, incerto & haesitante Cornputto, an Coverdiam praesidij debilem & non munitam, incursionibus victorum servaret. Caeterum sollicitatis nequicquam profugorum auxiliis, quos speciose ad virtutem & gloriam hortamento perflectere conabatur, metu tandem evictus, cum paucissimus suorum dubio & per avia itinere in Frisios properavit, tristissimaeq; cladis obnuntiatione patrum animos perculit. Qui Hohenloi litteris Oldenzela, in quem locum cum reliquis fusi exercitus se partim receperat, postero a clade die Leovardiam expeditis parum firmati egregiam futuri temporis & mollioris fortunae spem concepere.
