So, once the sacred bond of their former obedience was cast off, the centurions were seized by their own soldiers, and not even then, with decency intact, did the men keep respect for their officers after shamefully abandoning the fortification. Among these were Asinga, John and James Entens, Nicolaus Burmania, Vogelius Auricanus and Vliegerus Nikerckius, whom fortune led away from Delfzijl to Groningen, along with the captured money, reserving them for death, flight, or the other chances of war. For, once they were sent to prison, the law and discipline of war had left no room for cruelty, although it was believed that Lalaing, irritated by the insults of his soldiers and of Heftenius, and fierce on his own account over the defection, had prepared revenge by spilling the blood of the captives as a fresh mockery. Vogelius Auricanus, one of the centurions, died in custody; the rest, freed from their chains by ransom or by cunning, returned to their standards.

units.la: Mox Hohenloiis Zuythormi in Transiavicanis castra metatus, vulgatā novorum auxiliorum famā, ad Ordines Frisiae scripsit, eosq; conducenda navigia atque commeatum postulavit. Tum Joanni Stupero viro forti, & qui foederata jam ante stipendia ad Daventriam sub Lalainio fecerat, autorandis novis copijs pecuniam Frisios petijt, ac ut aucto in dies exercitui annonam & stipendia excitandae militum alacritati praestarent. Sed omnia per provinciam angusta continuae hostium populationes effecerant, & quod alendae tantae armatorum multitudini ne foecunditas quidem fertilissimae regionis sufficeret.
units.tr: Soon Hohenlo pitched camp at Zuidhorn, in the camps beyond the Lauwers, and, upon hearing the rumour of new auxiliaries, wrote to the Estates of Friesland, asking them to provide ships and provisions. Then he asked the Frisians for money to enlist new troops, sending it to Johan Stuper, a brave man who had already served under Lalaing at Deventer; and he asked that they supply provisions and pay that would stir the soldiers' zeal for an army growing day by day. But the continual raids of the enemy had made everything in the province scarce, and the fertility of even the most fertile region would not suffice to feed so great a multitude of armed men.

units.la: Jam enim ex Ioannis Norritij movendis Delphzilā Lalainij castris, decem Anglorum pedestres copiae & equitum turma in Frisiam advenerant, praeter Michaelem Caulerium, qui sex pedestria Valonum signa cum equitum quoque cohorte adduxerat. Anglos vir e Scotica nobilitate pro Norritio Morganus, Valones Pettinius pro Caulerio ducebat. In prioribus centuriones Cottonus, Episcopius, Fitsuillamius, Chastertonius & Daylius erant, Pettinium Grenus Norius, Casparus Cressonierus alijque sequebantur. His Germanorum equestres copiae accedebant, quae relictis ad laevam Suollā, Hasselto & Steenuicā Transf-Isulaniae oppidis, Vidro, qua angustior est, superato Drentinis agris se infuderant peragratoque Sylvestrium tractu Oostergoam, intraverant.
units.tr: For already, from the removal of John Norreys's forces from Lalaing's camp at Delfzijl, ten companies of English foot and a troop of horse had arrived in Friesland, along with Michael Caulier, who had brought six Walloon foot companies and a squadron of horse. The English were led by Morgan, a man of Scottish nobility, for Norreys; the Walloons by Pettinius, for Caulier. Among the English captains were Cotton, Bishop, Fitzwilliam, Chesterton and Daley; Grenus Norius, Casparus Cressonierus and others followed Pettinius. To these were added German cavalry, which, leaving Sneek, Hasselt and Steenwijk, towns of Overijssel, on the left, crossed the Vecht where it is narrowest, poured into the fields of Drenthe, and, passing through the woodland district, entered Oostergo.

units.la: In eā Hohenloūs castra haud procul Doccomio Rinsumagesti celebri apud Dantumanos vico posuerat, quae Anglicis Valonicisque auxiliis validiolidiora recta Collumum duxit, quem locum Schenckius Doccomio refugus levi operum figurâ vallaverat. Is comperto Hohenloüm Dantumanos per agros iter cum exercitu facere, conductis qui obstantia locorum amolirentur, Collumo cum copijs acceptâ levi clade decessit, copiasque pavore debiles in interiora Omlandiæ retraxit. Quare Ho-henloüs Schenckium insecutus, rapto celeriter agmine post superatum Lavicam amnem, qui Visfletam ponte stratus perlabitur, Grypskerckam, mox Northornam duxit, Abrahamumq; Lindenanium virum Danicæ gentis & clarorum natalium binis cum hostium vexillis Leovardiam ablegavit. Mox Martinum Nitzenium virum nobilem, quem in comitatu habebat, communicandis secretis Leovardiam quoque expedivit, datisque ad Bernardum Merodium, Aurantij per Frisiam vicarium litte-ris omnem foedioris calumniæ accusationem discussit. Quippe ferebatur Hohenloüs commeatum Frisiæ per agros mercatoribus Groningensium concessisse, hostiumq; commercia, velut pretio corruptus, beneficio salvi conductus præjuvisse. Quæ cum falso præducarentur quod classiarium castrensemque militem detinendis bonis ac mercibus hostium habuisset, ita Merodio tacitè credulitatis vitium objecit, & quod sinistris ac se indignis rumoribus senescendi tempus ademisset.
units.tr: Hohenlo had pitched camp in this area, not far from Dokkum, at Rinsumageest, a well-known village among the Dantumani. Advancing with the English and Walloon auxiliaries, now stronger, he led the army straight to Collum, a place which Schenck, retreating from Dokkum, had fortified with a light system of earthworks. When Schenck learned that Hohenlo was marching with his army across the fields of the Dantumani, having hired men to clear the obstacles of the terrain, he left Collum with his forces after a slight defeat, and drew his troops, weakened by panic, back into the interior of Ommeland. Therefore Hohenlo pursued Schenck, moving his column swiftly; after crossing the river Lauwers, which flows past Visvliet over a bridge, he led it to Grijpskerk and then to Noorderhorn. He sent Abraham Lindenaer, a man of Danish stock and distinguished birth, to Leeuwarden with two enemy standards. Then he also dispatched Martin Nitzen, a noble man whom he kept in his retinue, to Leeuwarden to communicate confidential matters, and, giving letters to Bernard Merode, the deputy of Orange in Friesland, he cleared himself of the whole accusation of a most shameful calumny. For it was rumoured that Hohenlo had granted the Frisian trade through the fields to merchants of Groningen, and, as if bought with money, had favoured enemy commerce by the benefit of a safe-conduct. Since these charges were falsely spread, on the ground that he had kept the naval and camp soldiers detaining the goods and merchandise of the enemy, he tacitly charged Merode with the fault of credulity, and with having robbed him, by such sinister and unworthy rumours, of the time to grow old.

units.la: Igitur Northornæ adhuc commoratus exercitu siti languido adulta enim æstas erat, sexaginta quinque tonnas cerevisiæ in castra importatas militibus distribuit, coctoresque aut eorum negotia gerentes exigendo pretio Leovardiam remisit. Tum de emuniendâ Oostmahornâ Ordinum Deputatos acriter commonefecit, ac ut locum Eæ flumini ac æstuario Frisici maris adjectum firmioribus operibus vallarent. Dein Norritio ac Michaëli Caulerio legionum tribunis, lancearioque quem in castris habebat equiti lanceas Leovardiâ mitti postulavit, ac ut præter Bongæ, Fervouij, Grovensteinij, Hettinghæ, Bottniæ, Vrielsmæ & Idsij cohortes ex Leovardiensium Snecensiumque tum Bolsuerdianâ ac Franekeranâ juventute signa pro auxilijs expedirent. Pulverem quoq; tormentarium, tum ducentorum fossorum manum complanandis viarum obstaculis poposcit & ut naves vectando, ut plurimum cespiti delectæ Lavicæ ad ostium perferendis castrorum sarcinis mitterentur. Imprimis vero Frisiorum Delegatis stipendiorum curam demandavit, & ut peditum quæ Opslachum præsidio tenuerant, tum equitum, quas Holsteinius & Drutenitzius ductarent, turbidis cohortibus de menstruo ære datâ fide prospicerent. Gerardum quoque Entenium, qui egenum in Amaso militem privato ære subjuverat, indemnem præstarent, sibiq; stipendium Northornam quam ocyssime transmitterent.
units.tr: Thus, while still staying at Northorn with his army, which was suffering from thirst (for it was high summer), he distributed sixty-five tuns of beer brought into the camp to the soldiers, and sent the brewers, or their agents, back to Leeuwarden at a fixed price. Then he strongly reminded the Deputies of the Estates to fortify Oostmahorn, and to protect with stronger works the place added to the Ee river and the estuary of the Frisian sea. Next he asked that lancers be sent from Leeuwarden to the tribunes of the legions, Norritius and Michael Caulerius, and to the lancer he kept in camp; and that, besides the cohorts of Bongum, Fervouw, Grovenstein, Hettinga, Bottnia, Vriesland and Idsega, standards be sent out for auxiliaries from the young men of Leeuwarden, Sneek and then Bolsward and Franeker. He also asked for gunpowder, and a band of two hundred diggers to level the obstacles on the roads; and that boats be sent to carry the camp's baggage to the mouth of the Lauwers, a place chosen mostly for its turf. Above all, he entrusted to the Frisian Delegates the care of the pay, and ordered them to provide, out of the monthly money and with good faith given, for the disturbed cohorts: the infantry who had held Opsloot as a garrison, and the cavalry led by Holstein and Drutenitz. He also asked them to indemnify Gerard Entenius, who had supported the needy soldier at Ames from his own money, and to send his own pay to Northorn as quickly as possible.

units.la: Igitur Entenio ad foederatos Ordines à Frisijs remisso, mille Caro-lei ad Hohenloüm Northornam perlati, quo loci, velut grande aliquod acturus, omnes copias atque auxilia contraxerat. Quæ ipsa, ne è Belgica superiore continuis copiarum transvectionibus Lalainius in Frisiam & Omlandiam evocaret, Rheni flumen, qua Clivicis ripis advolvitur, foederatâ classe occupatum, & ne adverso flumine negotiantium fraudibus subvectæ merces hostile commercium sublevarent. Cæterum Principum curâ, quorum ditiones atque ripæ Rheno prætexebantur, classis instructa foederatam descendere jussit, usumque amplissimi flu-minis,
units.tr: So Entenius was sent back by the Frisians to the allied Estates, and a thousand Carolus-gulden were brought to Hohenlo at Northorn, where he had gathered all his forces and auxiliaries, as if about to undertake something great. He also occupied the River Rhine, where it rolls past the Cleves banks, with the allied fleet, so that Lalaing could not summon troops continually from Upper Belgium into Friesland and Omland by constant transport of soldiers, and so that goods carried up the river by the frauds of traders could not relieve the enemy's commerce. Moreover, by the care of the princes whose lands and banks were stretched along the Rhine, the fleet was equipped and ordered to go down to the allied forces; and he opened the very wide river to Farnese and the enemy, by his own right or by the right of nations.

units.la: {y} Hohenloi curæ & consilia. cIↄ. Iↄ. minis, suo an gentium jure Farnesio hostibusque aperuit.
units.tr: Hohenlo's cares and counsels. 1587.

units.la: LXXX.
units.tr: LXXX.

units.la: Quare Philippo rege Iuliacensi ac Clivicâ societate eorum officijs innexo quos principi rectores ejus innocentia aut fati infoelicitas admoverat, de revocando in Belgicam Andino clam & fervidissimè actum commendantibus principem, qui suarum virium haud ignari externae & juxta paratissimae opis egere obnoxiam aemulationibus societatem, & ut ante in secessiones desituram, non dissimulabant. Itaq; vetera in Andini gratiam ab ejus fautoribus repetebantur, proclivi caeteros inter proceres Aurantio cui Germaniae suae infidis societatibus traductae; ut creditum fuit, apud Coloniam pacis offensâ, Galliarum auxilia velut certiora anteponebantur. Quippe Andinum prima in protestantes odia, emollito ingenio posuisse, esseque in illo quod conciliandis Elisabethae amoribus & Anglorum regno se ostendat. Adhaec Andinum vigore aevi & anterioribus rerum successibus laudatum foelicem militiam egisse, acturum haud dubiè majora, nisi in medio cursu rerum ab aemulâ potissimum matre revocatum & odio in provincias accensum, aulae inconstantia alienasset. Sed obruendam aut saltem obtegendam priorum memoriam, ita compositis principum sicuti reliquorum mortalium ingenijs, ut offensae gratiam parent. Sperari posse ut infestam sibi Galliam Hispania sentiat, & ut ex fratris regij innovatâ cum provincijs societate foelicius cum Elisabetha principale matrimonium procedat, regni sui opulentiam & auxilia impulsae libertati subministrante. Econtra erant, qui accidi potentiam Andini durioribus conditionibus volebant, & divisam in nonnullis provincijs popularis imperij rationem unius juventae ac ingenio non committi. Quippe tenacissimos libertatis antiqui juris opinio faciebat, quod olim etiam ex sanguine regio principes regendi legibus alligasset. Non eam scilicet desperationem rerum esse, ut pro libertate pugnantes eam externo principi transcribant, & quâ illi assertâ ne bello quidem locus aut discordijs dominantium esse possit. Ita pacari Philippum, arma tot cruoribus respersa poni posse, si parere citrà exceptionem, aut servire libertas velit, resque naturâ sui diversissimas mirabili societate ac commercio conjungere. Atqui attemperari regnare volentium cupiditates & illorum modestiam non posse, quibus effraenis potius, quam nulla libertas arrideat. Quapropter habendam gentium & animorum rationem esse, neque committendam illorum magnitudini ac arbitrio libertatem, qui regnare didicissent.
units.tr: Therefore, since Philip, king of Jülich, and the Cleves alliance were bound by the services which the rulers of that prince, through his innocence or the unhappiness of his fate, had brought to bear upon them, they secretly and most fervently urged, as to the recall of Anjou into Belgium, that the prince, who was not unaware of his own strength yet needed an alliance that was exposed to rivalries and was ready for outside help, would (as they did not conceal) cease from secessions earlier. And so old favours were sought again for Anjou's sake by his supporters, and it was easy to set Aurantius aside among the other nobles, whose Germany had been drawn into treacherous alliances; as was believed, after the breach of peace at Cologne, the help of the French was put ahead as more certain. For Anjou was said to have laid aside his first hatred of the Protestants, his temper softened, and to show in himself the means of winning the loves of Elizabeth and the kingdom of the English. Besides, Anjou, praised for the vigour of his age and his earlier successes, had carried on a fortunate war and would doubtless have done greater things, had he not, in the middle of his course, been recalled by his rival mother and, kindled with hatred against the provinces, estranged himself through the fickleness of the court. But the memory of the earlier events had to be buried, or at least covered over, since the minds of princes, like those of other mortals, are so composed that they prepare grace from offence. It could be hoped that Spain would feel France to be hostile to her, and that, through the renewed alliance of the king's brother with the provinces, the principal marriage with Elizabeth would proceed more fortunately, the wealth of his kingdom and its auxiliaries supplying the freedom that had been stirred up. On the other side there were some who wanted Anjou's power to be cut down by harsher conditions, and who held that the popular form of government, divided in some provinces, should not be entrusted to the talent and the temper of one young man. For the opinion of the ancient law made the most stubborn defenders of liberty, since it had once bound princes, even of royal blood, by the laws. Surely, they said, things were not so desperate that men fighting for liberty should hand it over to a foreign prince, and in a state where liberty had been asserted there could be no room for war or for the quarrels of those in power. Thus Philip might be pacified, and arms steeped in so much blood laid down, if liberty were willing to obey without exception or to be a slave; and things most different in nature could be joined by a wondrous partnership and commerce. But the desires of those who wish to rule cannot be curbed, nor their moderation trusted, for to them unbridled power rather than no liberty at all is pleasing. Therefore, they said, regard must be had to the characters of peoples and of minds, and liberty must not be committed to the greatness and the will of men who have learned to rule.

units.la: Itaque Frisij degustatis, quae nunquam antea agnovissent, principum imperijs Andino adversabantur, non sine metu ut sicut olim domesticis factionibus, ita nunc ex bello fessi ac exsangues in immoderati principis dominatum speciosis pactionum blandimentis reciderent. Quare volebant, ut non Saxonico, non Caroli Caesaris, aut Philippi filij jure aut exemplo Andinus reciperetur, caeterum ut ad veterem libertatis statum & Caesarum diplomata Andini omniumq; praefectorum potestas formaretur. Igitur Sigismundi & Frederici iii. tabulae in comitio repetitae, respectantibus in majorum tempora & simul foelicitatem qui praesentis aevi miserias & triste ad tutelam Andini perfugium licentiae principalis imperij & nato ex hac bello imputabant.
units.tr: And so the Frisians, having tasted what they had never known before, opposed Anjou with the rule of princes, not without fear that, as once by domestic factions, so now, worn out and bled white by war, they would fall back under the dominion of an immoderate prince by the specious flatteries of pacts. Hence they wanted Anjou to be received not by the Saxon right or example, nor by the right or example of Charles the Emperor or of Philip's son, but that the power of Anjou and of all the governors be shaped according to the ancient state of liberty and the charters of the Emperors. Therefore the documents of Sigismund and Frederick III were read again in the assembly, looking back to the times of their ancestors and at the same time to the happiness of the past; while they laid the miseries of the present age, and the sad refuge of Anjou's guardianship, to the licence of princely rule, and to the war born from it.

units.la: Caeterum omne libertatis retinendae studium in aegrâ & cum fato suo luxante rep. invalidæ leges aut soluti mores subvertebant, & quod ea continuis tempestatibus obnoxia, ne autoritate quidem Ducum, aut arte gubernantium regeretur. Quippe tardis, aut cessantibus provinciarum tributis stipendia non procedebant, militemque ultrò per infantiam belli morum rudem rapiendis alienis extimulabant. Quare per agros distributus ordinario athletarum victu se non explebat, caeterum lautitie cibi aut condimento, quod oppida subministrabant, natam ex egestate famem propulsabat. Unde civitates passim à licentioso milite alienæ, qui praesidio destinatus insolentiæ aut direptionis metu inopem aeris populum exercebat. Quæ ut militarem turbam domesticæ paci gravem, ita bello inutilem faciebant. Robur namque corporum, luxu atque commessationibus fractum æstum, inediam frigora, aut labores non sufferebat, dejectumque de statu suo minimâ cœli inclementiâ, aut periculo offendebatur. Igitur in oppugnatione civitatum ac castellorum in transnandis amnibus, aut fossis, aut ad collata signa languorem, aut contumaciam induebat luxuque & mollitie vitæ enervatus, pavorem & spreta obsequia non solutis stipendijs obtendebat. Sed animus vino otioque marcidus & ex hoc ad disciplinam corruptus fracti & velut unguentati corporis ministerio non utebatur, quod in acie aut insultu inter querelas ac murmura fraudati aeris vulneribus caedibusque exponebatur. Ita populus Ordinum imperijs iniquior ex licentia militum fiebat, eademq; agri annonæ & opum fertiles nullo inhibente & connivientiâ quoq; ipsorum Ducum atterebantur. Quare tributis & simul praestando foederis subsidio invalidis, sociale aerarium contabescebat animiq; etsi aperta dissidia dissimulando, secretis odijs dissociabantur. Quippe bello pressos sociæ foelicitatis occulta invidies urebat, & quod foecundissimo in otio velut securâ pace constituti in omnium rerum affluentiâ commercio & opibus invalescerent. Sibi pauperiem ex bello, sibi squallentes situ aut vastitate agros relinqui, ac ut inter conjugum atque liberorum lamenta & angores, si non serviles saltem tristes animas possideant. Sic regiæ lubidini ac dominationi vix exemptos in deterius malum insolentissimi & egeni militis arbitrium recidisse, fierique ut ad sua quoque signa & sacramenta professos ipsi provinciales exhorreant. Quippe tributa stipendijs paria non esse, & belli onera supra fortunam communis aerarij exsurgere. Atqui ut contrahi exercitum, ita rationes assignati aeris non posse, ne dum parsimoniæ aut fraudi apud socios locus est, inofficiosis partibus tota societas quemadmodum in humano corpore ex consensu pereat. Igitur autó externis gentium legionibus exercitu & in insolentiam ex egestate aeris provoluto, ne fraenis quidem militaris licentia coërcebatur, ad quam in spem spolij, sicut turbatis rebus assolet, corruptissimotum quoque ducum neglecta severitas dissimulabat.
units.tr: Moreover, every zeal for keeping liberty was being undermined in a sick republic, lame and struggling with its own fate, by weak laws and loose morals; and since it was exposed to constant storms, it was governed neither by the authority of the leaders nor by the skill of those who ruled. For when the provinces' taxes were slow or failed, the pay did not go forward, and the soldier, in this infancy of the war still unused to discipline, was driven by his own greed to seize other men's goods. Thus, scattered through the countryside, he did not satisfy himself with the ordinary fare of athletes, but made up for the hunger born of want with the delicacies of food and seasoning that the towns supplied. Hence the towns everywhere were troubled by the licentious soldiery, who, sent as a garrison, harassed the people, poor in money, with fear of insolence and plunder. These things made the soldiery burdensome to domestic peace and useless in war. For the strength of their bodies, broken by luxury and drinking bouts, could not endure heat, cold or labour; and, knocked out of their condition by the slightest harshness of the sky or by danger, they gave way. So in the storming of cities and castles, in swimming rivers or ditches, or in the face of standards that were raised, they put on sluggishness or defiance; and, enervated by the luxury and softness of life, they alleged fear and scorned obedience while their pay was unpaid. But a mind made sluggish with wine and idleness, and corrupted by this towards discipline, did not use the service of a broken and, as it were, perfumed body; for, cheated of their money, they were exposed in battle or in attack, amid complaints and mutterings, to wounds and slaughter. So the people became more hostile to the orders of the States because of the licence of the soldiers; and the same fields, fertile in harvests and wealth, were worn down with nobody restraining it, and even with the connivance of their own leaders. Hence, weakened by taxes and at the same time unable to furnish the subsidy of the alliance, the common treasury was wasting away, and their minds, though they hid open quarrels, were estranged by secret hatreds. For envy of a partner's happiness burned those who were pressed by war, since they were settled in the most fruitful leisure, as if in a secure peace, and grew strong in commerce and wealth amid the abundance of all things. For themselves, they said, poverty from the war was left, and fields squalid with neglect or wasted, so that, amid the laments and anguish of wives and children, they might possess souls that were, if not slavish, at least sad. Thus those barely freed from royal lust and domination had fallen back into a worse evil, the will of the most insolent and needy soldier; and it came about that even the provincials who had professed allegiance to their standards and oaths shuddered at them. For taxes, they said, were not equal to the pay, and the burdens of war rose above the fortune of the common treasury. But just as the army could be reduced, so the accounts of assigned money could not be, and there was no room for thrift or fraud among allies; with dutiful parts, the whole alliance, as in a human body, would perish by common consent. And so, with the army made up of foreign legions and fallen into insolence through the want of money, the licence of the soldiers was not restrained even by bridles; and into this hope of plunder, as is usual in disturbed times, the neglected severity of even the most corrupt leaders connived.

units.la: Per Matthiam namque Gubernatorem & Aurantium principem in secretius concilium abstrusos belli lex & disciplina flaccescebat, quod ultro pacis moribus adversum foedissimis apud Transf-Rhenanos exercitus exemplis Philippus Hohenlous administrabat. Qui etsi animi ingens & ad pericula intrepidus virilem factis audaciam praeferret, ita praeclaras virtutes solutior vita obscurabat, velut ita compositum esset, ut bellicæ licæ indolis gloriam probrosa juventus & fœdata libidinibus ætas attaminaret. Quippe corpori in speciem pulchro animus. suberat, voluptatibus immersus & cui inter armorum etiam aspera, Veneris ardor aut vinolentia imperabat. Quæ ideo mala, non tam ætatis, etsi adtalia lubricæ, quam ingenij vitio prodebantur, quod impurum & exinde socors, ac futuri improvidum bona consilia interventu libidinis negligebat. Itaque dies agendis sæpè rebus dicti, ortà per temulentiam lubidine, impuris fœminarum amoribus terebantur, in quos gregarius etiam quisque aut lixa exemplo corruptus nullâ honestatis curâ proruebat. Quare grave scortorum agmen castra ut plurimum sequebatur, quæ omni turpitudine, velut pestilenti lue infecta, ægre sacramenti fidem & cum eâ modestiam retinebant. Igitur infidâ provinciarum societate & diffluente sine boni rectoris imperio, exercitus provinciarum regimen Andino decretum, ac ut jure principis, etsi legibus inligati Belgicam ac Trans-Rhenana teneret.
units.tr: Through Matthias the Governor and Prince Orange, who were absorbed in a more secret council, the law and discipline of war were growing slack; and in the regions beyond the Rhine, Philip Hohenlohe commanded armies whose conduct, quite contrary to peaceful manners, was most disgraceful. Although he showed a great spirit, fearless in dangers, and a manly boldness in his deeds, a rather loose life clouded such outstanding virtues, as if it had been so arranged that a shameful youth and an age defiled by lusts should tarnish the glory of his warlike nature. For the mind lay beneath a body beautiful to look upon, immersed in pleasures, and the ardour of Venus or drunkenness ruled it even amid the hardships of arms. These faults were revealed not so much by his age, though that too was slippery, as by a defect of character, for an impure and therefore sluggish and improvident mind neglected good counsel once lust intervened. And so the days appointed for transacting business were often wasted in drunken revelry and impure love affairs with women; into these, following his example, every common soldier and camp-follower rushed headlong, with no regard for decency. Hence a grievous crowd of prostitutes usually followed the camp, and these, tainted with every kind of filth as if with a plague, scarcely kept faith with their oath or any modesty with it. So, with the allied provinces unfaithful and the whole thing falling apart without the rule of a good commander, the government of the army in the provinces was assigned to Andino, who held Brabant and the lands beyond the Rhine with the authority of a prince, though bound by laws.

units.la: Sunt qui tradant Ordines Belgicæ non tam in Andinum fiduciâ quam necessitate impulsos, eum regundis provincijs delegisse, & ut fraterni ac potentis regni vires Philippi armis objiceret. Quæ etsi in secuto patrum clam agerentur, ita peritius tamen dissimulabantur, parum cautis talium scriptoribus, qui arcana & silentij fide obtecta suis commentarijs evulgavere. Mihi gentis nostræ acta rimanti non est dubium, eam ut ante ab Andini societate, ita tum quam maxumè alienam fuisse, velut tacitâ futuri inspiratione, mobile principis ingenium & matris foederi infensissimæ imperio obnoxium diversa à patrum voluntate ac salute Reip. facturum. Cæterum omne sinistri præsagium immutabilis quoque apud Frisios rerum necessitas eluebat, quos bellorum moli turbante trans-Rhenum res fortunâ & juxta seditionibus militum expositos stipendiorum egentia faciebat.
units.tr: Some writers relate that the Orders of Belgium were driven to choose Andino to govern the provinces not so much from trust in him as from necessity, and so as to set the forces of Philip, a brother and powerful king, against him. Although these things were being done in secret among the Fathers, they were dissembled the more skilfully, since writers of such matters, too careless of the faith of silence, published in their commentaries things that had been concealed. To me, searching through the acts of our nation, there is no doubt that it was then, as before, very far from the society of Andino, as if by a silent inspiration of the future, and that the changeable temper of the prince, subject to the rule of his most hostile mother to the covenant, would act in a way different from the wishes and welfare of the fathers and the commonwealth. Moreover, an unchangeable necessity of affairs was revealing every ill omen among the Frisians too, whom the turbulent state of affairs beyond the Rhine, and in addition the mutinies of soldiers, and the lack of pay exposed to ruin.

units.la: Igitur Anglicis & Valonum auxilijs in Bergumanos, mox ad Hohenloïum conductis Abelus Franckenâ Antverpiam ad Aurantium, mox Antverpiâ Gandavum amandatus, sollicitandis Anglorum Valonumque stipendijs qui Norritio & Caulerio legionum ductoribus Flandrico ære in Frisiorum finibus militabant. Cui rei etsi spem Aurantius datis in Frisiam diversissimis litteris & relatione Legati faceret, ita Flandri tenuitatem ærarij tardioribus solutionibus obtendebant, & quod obsesso ab hostibus Buchaino Hannoniæ oppido omne subsidium liberandis vicinis & tutandis suorum agris impendissent. Fervere scilicet bello omnem oram & nihilominus socio affectu Frisiorum rebus prospexisse, missis in Trans-Rhenanos auxilijs, quorum ipsi vergente in Flandriam bello, egentissimi forent. Darent Frisij in tempus suis legionibus stipendia, dum circa fines suos tempestas interquievisset, quâ sedatâ, alio terrarum amotâ defuturi sociæ fideî & justis officijs non essent.
units.tr: Therefore, with English and Walloon aid against the men of Bergen, and soon after Abel Francken, hired by Hohenlohe, was sent from Antwerp to Orange, and then from Antwerp to Ghent, to stir up the pay of the English and Walloons who, under the captains of the legions Norris and Caulery, were serving in the territory of the Frisians at Flemish expense. Although Orange gave hope of this matter by letters sent to Friesland, quite varied in tone, and by the report of his envoy, the Flemings excused their slow payments by the poverty of their treasury, and by the fact that they had spent all their help on relieving Bouchain, a town of Hainault besieged by the enemy, and on defending their neighbours and their own fields. Clearly the whole shore was aflame with war, and yet, with a friendly feeling towards the Frisians, they had provided for their affairs by sending aid beyond the Rhine, though they themselves, with the war bearing down on Flanders, were in the greatest need. Let the Frisians pay their own legions in time, while the storm around their borders had subsided; once it was calmed and had moved to another part of the world, they would not be lacking to their faithful ally and to just duties.

units.la: Aurantius quoque sublevando Buchainio & isti terrarum tractui, qui Flandros ac Tornacenses interjacet, commeatum atque pecuniam Frisios popposcit, ac ut ipsi bello præssi sociorum angustiam ex suâ æstumarent. Opus scilicet esse, ne tributis mora aut cunctatio interveniat, & ne miles spontaneæ lasciviæ flagitia raritate stipendij obvelet. Se daturum operam, ut Flandri auxilijs in Frisiam missis, menstruum amplius æs procurent, & ne seditione aliquâ belli ordo per Frisios & Omlandiam turbetur.
units.tr: Orange also demanded from the Frisians, to relieve Bouchain and that district lying between the Flemings and the men of Tournai, provisions and money, and asked them to estimate the straits of their allies from their own, since they were pressed by war. Clearly there was need that no delay or hesitation should intervene in the taxes, and that the soldier should not cover the shameful deeds of voluntary wantonness with a scarcity of pay. He would take care that, with aid sent into Friesland, the Flemings should procure a larger monthly sum, and that no sedition should disturb the order of the war through Friesland and Ommelanden.

units.la: Eadem Ordinum generalium litteris. v i. Aug. perscripta ac Norritio retinendis in officio cohortibus communicata. Igitur stativis Northornæ per Hohenloum actis quina peditum signa Slochtero quoque evocata, quæ cum Jargæo, Scageno, cæterisque copiarum præfectis Cornelius Veda vir nobilis conducebat. Quæ medio itineris per lancearium Epirotarum equitem & pedestres copias, quas Lalainius Groningâ emiserat, disjectæ aut cæsæ, improsperum prælio, quod Hohenloüs parabat, omen attulere. Cornelius Veda, qui à dirutâ arce Staurïæ præsidium egerat, cohortis ductor, fortiter pugnans occubuit. Quare Hohenlous vindicandæ cladi equitum Anglorum turmas modico cum peditatu Slochterum ocyssimè expedivit, signaq; militaria fugientibus hostibus detracta, suorum virtute recepit.
units.tr: The same was written in the letters of the General States on the sixth of August and communicated to Norris to keep the cohorts in their duty. Therefore, with the winter quarters at Northorn arranged by Hohenlohe, five companies of foot were also summoned to Slochteren, which, with Jargaeus, Scagen and the other commanders of the troops, Cornelius Veda, a noble man, was leading. In the middle of the march, these were scattered or cut down by the lancers of the Epirote cavalry and the foot troops whom Lalaing had sent out from Groningen, and this proved an unlucky omen for the battle that Hohenlohe was preparing. Cornelius Veda, who had held the garrison of the ruined citadel of Stauria, a leader of a cohort, fell fighting bravely. Therefore Hohenlohe, to avenge the defeat, hastened to Slochteren with the troops of English cavalry and a modest force of foot, and the enemy fleeing, the military standards were taken from them, and he recovered them by the valour of his men.

units.la: Mox lustratum Northornæ omnem exercitum subsequi jussit, compertoque hostem Slochtero & è Nyennortijs Groningâ movisse, ritè ordinatum agmen ducere ad urbem constituit. Quare Michaeli Caulerio cum sex Valonum signis, primam aciem in qua, Bongæ, Cornputti, Eschedæ & Regneri Idsij cohortes erant, mediam Norritio cum Anglorum copijs & Gulielmi Ludovici decem cohortium legione ducendam commisit, quam Ifelsteinius cum Belgarum legione, Donavij & Zedenitschæ signis sequebatur. Equites verò in utroque cornu locati, quorum dextrum Germanorum turmæ, lævum cum Gorio & Pieckijs Frisij tenebant. Pedestre verò agmen sarcinæ atque impedimenta claudebant, præmissis Norritij, Caulerij & Limburgij equestribus copijs, quæ munitum tribus campestribus tormentis agmen antecederent. Ita dispposito exercitu iter Groningam Hohenlous pronuntiat. Cæterum ponte, qui Horendiepæ imponitur, à Lalainij milite abrupto, adversaque ripæ margine tumultuario castelli opere firmato, parum substitit summissis interim, qui altitudinem fluminis tentarent nandique peritiâ aut vadosi amnis beneficio hostile castellum oppugnarent. Unde hostes metu acti locum deseruere, latioreque fugâ Harenum palantes provecti in castra se recepere, quæ Lalainius illo in pago, velut tuta stationum sede posuerat. Sed comperto Hohenloum post fusas ad Deum preces, calore pugnæ inardescere, ac jam proxumis signis conspici Harenocastra movit, exercitumque ne petendo quidem commeatui ac impeditis tempore dato, Groningæ ad muros & suburbana revocavit.
units.tr: Soon afterwards he ordered the whole army, reviewed at Northorn, to follow, and having learned that the enemy had moved from Slochteren and from Nieuwe Nordijk towards Groningen, he decided to lead the column in proper order to the city. So he entrusted to Michael Caulery, with six Walloon standards, the first line, in which were the cohorts of Bonga, Cornputt, Eschede and Regner Idsia, and the middle to Norris with the English forces and the legion of William Louis of ten cohorts, which Ifelstein followed with the legion of the Belgians and the standards of Donau and Zedenitz. The cavalry were posted on each wing; on the right the squadrons of Germans, on the left the Frisians with Gorio and the Pieckens held the ground. The foot column was closed by the baggage and impedimenta, the cavalry of Norris, Caulery and Limburg being sent ahead, which were to precede the column, fortified with three field guns. With the army so arranged, Hohenlohe announced the march to Groningen. But the bridge that is placed over the Horn was broken by Lalaing's soldiers, and the opposite bank was hastily fortified with a makeshift work; he halted there briefly, meanwhile sending men to test the depth of the river and to attack the hostile fort, by their skill in swimming or with the help of a shallow stream. Then the enemy, driven by fear, abandoned the place, and fleeing more widely, wandering, they withdrew into the camp that Lalaing had set up in that district as a safe seat for his posts. But when it was learned that Hohenlohe, after pouring out prayers to God, was growing hot with the fury of battle, and was already seen with the nearest standards, he moved towards Harenkastra, and, not even giving his army time to seek provisions, which were hindered, he recalled it to the walls and suburbs of Groningen.

units.la: Hohenlous vesperascente jam die, Harenum pagum ingressus noctem ibi egit, soleque orto signum dari jussit. Tum exercitus, cito agmine suburbanis agris immissus, metum obsidij civitati Groningæ incussit, quæ repetitâ nuperæ molestiâ ad novi famam ex penuriâ annonæ inhorrescebat. Quippe frumenta prioris anni frequens in urbe præsidium attriverat, noviq; spes, etsi adultâ messe, vastatione circumjacentis agri accidebatur. Quare castrorum spatia Ordinum Frisiæ suasu ac imperio per Hohenloûm ordinata, levibusque castellis pro opportunitate loci circumscripta obsidio fidem fecere. Cæterum legionum tribunis in concilium advocatis, qui præcludi commeatu urbi posse diffidecIↄ. Iↄ. sidebant, castra mota omnisque obsidij apparatus temeritate ac imprudentiâ Hohenloï evanuit.
units.tr: Hohenlohe, as the day was already growing towards evening, entered the village of Haren and spent the night there, and at sunrise he ordered the signal to be given. Then the army, quickly advancing into the suburban fields, struck fear of a siege into the city of Groningen, which, recalling the recent annoyance, bristled at the new rumour from the scarcity of food. For the grain of the previous year had been used up by the large garrison in the city, and the hope of a new harvest, though the crop was ripe, was being taken away by the devastation of the surrounding countryside. Therefore the camp's bounds, arranged by Hohenlohe at the advice and command of the Orders of Friesland, and enclosed by light forts as the position allowed, made the siege credible. But when the tribunes of the legions were called into council, who were doubtful that the city could be cut off from supplies, the camp was moved, and all the apparatus of the siege vanished through Hohenlohe's rashness and lack of foresight.

units.la: Cl. Franckena in notis istorum temporum tradit, nullâ necessitate compulsâ continuandæ obsidionis consilium mutasse, corruptumque ut suspicabantur, aut meritis impotem, amplas potiundæ civitatis spes fœdissimo metu aut crimine præcidisse. Creditum fuit, Mularti, qui Lingam præsidio tenebat, acerbissimis litteris, quibus Groningense obsidium eludebatur, irritatum, Groningâ exercitum reduxisse, quo versis in Linganos castris privatam inimici injuriam publico detrimento vindicaret. Adeò consilij inconstantem vinum sæpè aut ira faciebat, in quam ultrò fervore sanguinis & ætatis pronior vini quoque immoderato usu exardescebat.
units.tr: Clarus Francken, in his notes on those times, relates that, with no necessity compelling him, Hohenlohe changed his plan of continuing the siege, and, either corrupted, as they suspected, or unequal to his merits, he cut off by a most shameful fear or crime the ample hopes of taking the city. It was believed that Mularts, who held Lingen with a garrison, provoked by bitter letters by which the siege of Groningen was mocked, led the army back from Groningen, so that, turning his camp against the Lingeners, he might avenge a private injury of an enemy with public loss. So inconstant in counsel did wine or anger often make him, a man who, prone to such fervour of blood and youth, also flared up in the immoderate use of wine.

units.la: Id certè compertum est, Hohenloum Aurantium apud principem Frisiæ tum præfectum, prolixâ excusatione usum omnemque desertæ urbis culpam in Ordinum socordiam & defectum æris necessarijque commeatus rejecisse. Sed ea falsa ac inania fuisse, istorum temporum fidissimus Scriptor in fragmentis historicis Cl. Franckena annotavit.
units.tr: This at least is certain: Hohenlohe, at that time prefect under Orange for the prince of Friesland, used a lengthy excuse and laid all the blame for the abandoned city on the negligence of the Orders and the lack of money and of necessary supplies. But that these were false and empty pleas, the most faithful writer of those times has noted in Francken's historical fragments.

units.la: Quippe præter æs in stipendia erogandum commeatus quoque abundè castris decretos præclarus autor tradit, Hohenloumque ut coeptam obsidionem & bonum exitum haud dubiè habituram continuaret, monitum severa Ordinum imperia pro ludicris aut non profuturis habuisse. Itaque retractas Groningâ copias partitus cum Gulielmi Nassovij & Iselsteinij legionibus Sutlaræ stativa habuit, Anglisque cum Valonum legione apud Nortlaram relictis, tum Bonga ac Idsio ad emissarium Adoardicum missis robur exercitus extenuavit. Corrumpente velut illius consilium fortunâ quo mali moris & exempli Ducem repetità cladium atrocitate emendaret. Ita bellum sine Ordine ac disciplinâ per Frisios & Omlandiam fluebat, revocandoque è Gallijs in provincias Andino fundamenta substernebantur.
units.tr: Indeed, the distinguished author relates that besides money to be paid out as wages, provisions were also decreed to the camp in abundance. He adds that Hohenlo, though urged to continue the siege he had begun, which would undoubtedly have a good outcome, held the severe orders of the States to be trifling or useless. So, withdrawing the troops from Groningen and dividing them, he took up quarters at Sutlaren with the regiments of William of Nassau and Iselstein. He left the English with the Walloon regiment at Nortlara, and then, sending men to Bonga and Idsio and to the Adoardicum outlet, he weakened the strength of the army. It was as if fortune were thwarting his plan, so that by the repeated atrocity of defeats the commander might correct this bad custom and example. Thus the war drifted on without order or discipline through Friesland and the Ommelands, while the foundations were being laid for recalling Andino from France into the provinces.

units.la: Finis Libri Sexti.
units.tr: End of the Sixth Book.

units.la: P. WINSEMI Historiarum
units.tr: P. Winsemius, Histories

units.la: LIBER SEPTIMUS.
units.tr: Book Seven.

units.la: VNEST a prælij apud Hardenbergam fortunâ, novissimi, quod Ultrajecti ictum erat, Belgicæ ac Frisiorum res collapsæ cernebantur. Quippe LALAINIUS more mortalium, quos secundæ res inflant, prosperis elatus in patentes quaquaversum campos se effundebat, utendumque victoriâ ratus, quo fortunæ beneficia agnosceret, dissipatis aut disjunctis foederatorum copijs, suo arbitrio moderandi belli rationes gerebat. Itaq; Lavicam amnem, qui medius provinciam dirimit, transgressus in Oostergoam se effudit, vastatisque circa Collumum & vicina agris captivum illius oræ populum Groningam abduxit. Econtra foederatorum copiæ in præsidia partim, partim in Drentiam reductæ, quam Hohenlous, velut fati adversitatem in illâ regione, in quâ cladem acceperat, ulturus, modico cum exercitu peragrabat. Joanni verò Bongæ & Regnero Idzio copiarum Frificarum ductoribus emissarium Adoardicum tutandum demandaverat, quo Reiderij amnis commoditate castrensem commeatum subvectaret. Quod etsi Lalainij magnâ tum vi oppugnarent, virtute præsidiariorum semel rejecti ita postero die copijs auti, retentatâque oppuguatione loci compotes facti sunt, Joanne Bonga glande plumbeâ icto, quem à primis nascentis belli exordijs libertatis patriæ amor melioribus partibus obligaverat. Reliquum præsidij, quod excessit, Opslachum se recepit, quem locum situ & naturâ munitum, militares viri Taco Hettingha vir nobilis, Ielsmanus & Stamlerus tutabantur.
units.tr: After the outcome of the battle near Hardenberg, which had been fought most recently, near Utrecht, the affairs of the Belgians and the Frisians were seen to be collapsing. Lalaing, as men are wont to be when success puffs them up, was carried away by his good fortune and spread himself over the open plains on every side. Thinking he ought to make use of victory to show his gratitude for fortune's favours, and with the allied forces scattered or divided, he conducted the conduct of the war by his own judgement. Accordingly he crossed the river Lauwers, which divides the province in the middle, poured into Oostergo, and after laying waste the fields around Kollum, led the people of that district captive to Groningen. On the other side, the allied troops were partly withdrawn into garrisons and partly into Drenthe, which Hohenlohe was traversing with a small army, intending to avenge the reverse of fortune in that region, where he had suffered his defeat. To John Bonga and Regnerus Idzinga, leaders of the Frisian troops, he had entrusted the defence of the fort at Oostwoudum, so that by the convenience of the river Reiderij they might bring supplies for the camp. Although the Lalaing forces attacked it with great force, the garrison, by its courage, first drove them back; then, reinforced with troops the next day, they renewed the assault and became masters of the place, though John Bonga was struck by a leaden ball, a man whom the love of his country's liberty had bound to the better cause from the first beginnings of the new war. The rest of the garrison that survived withdrew to Opslaag, a place fortified by its position, which was held by the soldiers Taco Hettinga, a noble man, and Ielsmanus and Stamler.

units.la: Tradunt autores emissarium Adoardicum defectu imprimis tormentarij pulveris deditum fuisse, etsi credendum sit amotâ auxiliorum spe, & Hohenloo per superiora Drentiæ signa circumducente, animos obsessorum elanguisse. Is namque ut illo in tractu res foelicius securiusque gereret, & ne periculum ab insequente hoste pateretur, pontem quo ad Werdenbrassium amnis sternitur, dejici jusserat, omnesque copias circa Coverdiam & ripam Vidri fluminis conduci. Ubi Gulielmus Ludovicus Nassovius, quo cum vires Hohenloüs conjunxerat, metandorum castrorum opportunitatem speculatus, glande verberatus est, castrisq; lectica elatus ad instituendam periculosi vulneris curationem Zuollam devectus est. Hohenlous præcone misso deditionem Covar-
units.tr: Authors relate that the fort at Oostwoudum surrendered chiefly for lack of gunpowder, though it must be believed that with hope of help cut off, and with Hohenlohe leading his standards about the upper parts of Drenthe, the spirits of the besieged had grown weak. For he had ordered the bridge by which the river is crossed toward Weerdinge to be broken down, so that he might carry on affairs in that district more fortunately and safely, and might not suffer danger from the pursuing enemy; and he had ordered all his forces to be brought together around Coevorden and the bank of the river Vecht. There William Louis of Nassau, whom Hohenlohe had joined to his own forces, seeing the opportunity of measuring out the camp, was struck by a sling-bullet, and was carried from the camp on a litter to Zwolle, to have treatment for the dangerous wound begun. Hohenlohe sent a herald and demanded the surrender

units.la: cIↄ. Iↄ. Coverdianæ arcis aut castelli postulavit; concessoque in posterum deliberandi spatio deditionem impetravit. Eâ conventum fuit, ne præsidium hostile intra trimestre adversus fœderatos militaret, accinctumq; sine impedimentis castello excederet, moreq; belli Benthemicos in fines deduceretur. Tum præsidium ex Donavij, Rashornij Renoï (qui Groningæ apud Lalainium captivus asservabatur) Coverdianæ arci impositum, indignante nequicquam Lalainio prospera sua, repentinâ adversitate obtundi. Quare collectis copijs & omni necessario apparatu instructus signa Opslachum movit, tormentisque muralibus valli hiatu facto præsidij fugâ an perfidiâ munitionem suam fecit. Opslachum solo Lalainij jussu æquatum, cujus sacramento magna præsidij pars prioris oblita, tanquam fœlicitati victoris se permisit. Hohenloum verò, velut novis cladibus reservaretur, in alia locorum continua fati infœlicitas trahebat. Quippe exercitum partitus ex hoc solo imbecillum & debilem, Lingæ Oppido & Weddano castello admovit, Gulielmumq; Ludovicum Nassovium cum Michaële Caulerio Slochterum cum copijs amandavit. Quod speculatus Lalainius, festino quoque itinere Slochterum duxit, legionesq; Gulielmo Nassovio & Michaëli Caulerio commissas ex improviso adortus est. Cæterum Nassovius ordines colligens sensim copias retrocedere jussit, Winschotumque ac Heiligerlæum Cœnobium (Adolphi Nassovij & Arenbergij clade famosum) salvas & incolumes reduxit, quo loci Hohenlous equite cum Germano inops consilij commorabatur. Qui cum omnem Lalainij & hostilis exercitus impetum sustinere non posset, animi insuper territus, fugæ se dedit, milesque Hohenloï sine signis ac ullo ductorum imperio per Drentiam fugiens circa Zutphaniam in finibus Geldricis & haud procul ripâ amnis Isalæ consedit. Unde magnus Ordines terror tum invasit, metuentes exercitum fœderatum tot cladium continuatione fractum & dissipatum, recolligi non posse.
units.tr: of the citadel or castle of Coevorden; and when time for deliberation had been granted for the future, he obtained the surrender. It was agreed that the hostile garrison should not serve against the confederates for three months, and that it should leave the castle with its arms but without baggage, and be conducted, by the custom of war, to the borders of Bentheim. Then a garrison from Donauw, Rasshorn and Renoy (who was being held captive by Lalaing at Groningen) was placed in the citadel of Coevorden; and Lalaing, indignant that his prosperous fortunes were so suddenly beaten down by reverse, gathered his troops, equipped himself with every necessary provision, and moved his standards toward Opslaag. With his wall guns he made a breach in the rampart, and the garrison, either by flight or by treachery, gave up its defence. Opslaag was levelled to the ground at Lalaing's sole command; a large part of the garrison, forgetful of its earlier oath, surrendered itself to the good fortune of the victor. Hohenlohe, as though he were kept for new disasters, was dragged by unbroken misfortune into other places. For, having divided his army, and leaving the weak and feeble part of it here, he moved against Lingen, the town, and the castle of Wedde, and sent William Louis of Nassau with Michael Cauler to Slochteren with troops. Lalaing, observing this, also hurried to Slochteren by a rapid march, and attacked unexpectedly the legions entrusted to William of Nassau and Michael Cauler. However, Nassau, gathering the companies, ordered the troops to fall back gradually, and brought them back safe and sound to Winschoten and the monastery of Heiligerlee (notorious for the defeat of Adolf of Nassau and Arenberg). There Hohenlohe, without plans, was staying with his German cavalry. When he could not withstand the full attack of Lalaing and the enemy army, and was moreover terrified in spirit, he gave himself to flight; and Hohenlohe's soldiers, fleeing through Drenthe without standards and without any command from their leaders, settled near Zutphen in the territory of Gelderland, not far from the bank of the river Ijssel. Thereupon a great terror seized the States, who feared that the army of the confederates, broken and scattered by so many successive defeats, could not be gathered again.

units.la: Cæterum Gulielmi Nassovij litteris consternatis Ordinum animis, quos pavor majoris infortunij ex continuâ infœlicitate occupaverat, robur quoddam additum, monentis novum militem supplendis autorandisque cohortibus habendum, modo provisum militaribus stipendijs foret, quæ fortissimis gentium ac libertatis amantibus inevitabilis necessitas extorsisset. Exercituum verò cladibus animorum firmitatem & constantiam opponendam esse, quæ nec prosperis erigi & insolescere nec adversis deprimi aut cedere deberet. Itaque Frisios ad minores litteras datæ auxilia imploravere, ac ut maritimas civitates Stauriam, ac Hindelopam, aperiendo navigantibus mari socio præsidio firmarent. Qui acceptis è majore Frisiâ litteris binas extemplo cohortes Neomago ad Vahalim evocatas Stauriæ atque Hindelopæ imposuere, quo cum præsidiarijs, qui Harlingæ agebant, adversus hostium excursiones marinum littus tuerentur.
units.tr: Yet by the letters of William of Nassau, a certain strength was added to the spirits of the States, which fear of a greater disaster, arising from continuous misfortune, had seized; he advised that new soldiers should be raised to fill up and reconstitute the companies, provided only that they were supplied with military pay, which the inevitable necessity had wrung from the bravest of peoples and lovers of liberty. The firmness and constancy of spirit, he said, must be set against the defeats of armies, which ought neither to be lifted up and grow insolent by prosperity, nor be depressed or give way by adversity. Accordingly they implored help from the Frisians by letters of lesser importance, and that they should strengthen the maritime cities of Stavoren and Hindeloopen, opening the sea as a friendly route for shipping. These, having received letters from greater Friesland, at once placed two cohorts, called from Nijmegen to the Waal, in Stavoren and Hindeloopen, so that together with the garrison that was at Harlingen they might guard the seacoast against hostile raids.

units.la: Cæterum occidentali provinciæ tractu præsidijs munito ab oriente nova Frisiæ tempestas incubuit, ductoribus hostilium copiarum Everardo Ensio & Paulo Blancevortio prætore Hardenbergico, qui Oostergoæ fines continuis populationibus infestabant. Quare fœderatus miles excursionum pertæsus, loco præsidij quod Doccomi & Colluumi mi habebatur, relicto, Adoardicum coenobium petijt, praesidiariosq; vino ac somno graves caecidit. Trecentos ex caesis annales memorant, Paulumque Blancevortium gravi è vulnere saucium Doccomium captivum abductum. Ingens praeda parta, ipsumque coenobium magnâ sui parte injecto igne exustum. Quam adversitatem ut vindicaret Lalainius castellum ad Coverdiam castra posuit, nullaque loci firmitate & debili praesidio invalidum, suum fecit. Quippe jam aquae, novo diversio deductae fossas depleverant, obsessisque & campestria hostium tormenta verberandis muris admota expugnationis periculum minabantur. Sic castello Coverdiano in potestatem redacto, Oldenzelam tentavit, in Salijs aut Tubantibus pervetustum & celebre oppidum, quod duarum cohortium praesidio Suetenius vir nobilis tenebat. Qui propterea, quo sustinendo obsidio par esset, è vicinis equitum peditumq; auxilia evocavit, quae aut stipendiorum egentiâ, aut periculi metu retardabantur. Itaque Lalainius ut auxilia & commeatum urbi praecluderet, castra propius admovit, incensisq; suburbijs & igne portis injecto oppugnationem acerrimam instituit. Sed virtute ac fortitudine praesidij repulsus, trecentis militum & in ijs centurione Prumstio amissis à continuanda obsidione destitit, revocatusq; à civibus, qui libertatem regio imperio postponebant praesidioque valentiores habebantur, Oldenzelâ potitus est.
units.tr: Yet while the western part of the province was secured by garrisons, a new storm of Frisian troubles fell on it from the east, under the leaders of the hostile forces, Everard Ens and Paul Blankevoort, the praetor of Hardenberg, who harassed the borders of Oostergo with continual raids. Therefore the confederate soldiers, weary of the incursions, left the garrison which was held at Dokkum and Kollum, and made for the monastery of Oudwoude, and cut down the garrison heavy with wine and sleep. The annals record that three hundred were slain, and Paul Blankevoort, wounded by a grievous wound, was led away captive to Dokkum. Great booty was taken, and the monastery itself was largely burned by fire set to it. To avenge this disaster, Lalaing pitched his camp at the castle of Coevorden, and, since the place was weak in its strength and feeble in its garrison, he made it his own. For already the waters, drawn off by a new diversion, had emptied the ditches, and the enemy's field guns, brought up to batter the walls, threatened the danger of an assault upon the besieged. Thus, the castle of Coevorden having been brought under his power, he tried Oldenzaal, a very ancient and famous town among the Salians or Tubantes, which Suetenius, a noble man, held with a garrison of two cohorts. He therefore, to sustain a siege of equal strength, called in auxiliary horse and foot from the neighbourhood, who were delayed either by lack of pay or by fear of danger. Accordingly Lalaing, in order to cut off help and supplies from the town, moved his camp nearer, and, setting the suburbs on fire and laying fire to the gates, began a most fierce assault. But he was repulsed by the courage and bravery of the garrison, and, having lost three hundred soldiers, among them the centurion Prumstius, he desisted from continuing the siege; and being recalled by the citizens, who preferred liberty to royal rule and were held stronger than the garrison, he took possession of Oldenzaal.

units.la: Mox ab illâ motis castris regressus famae & magnarum rerum occasionem quaerens, Zuollam Transl-Isulaniae oppidum coronâ militum cinxit, exististumans fore, ut quod Oldenzelae factum erat, plus favore ac gratiâ civium quam exercitus magnitudine proficeret. Quare in antiqui affectus memoriam & populum regis reverentem continuo resipiciebat, recordatus se Transl-Isulaniae haud ita pridem victorem documenta veteris gratiae non amissurum. Caeterum modestiore populo civico & metu militaris praesidij compresso, etiam bis mille militum auxilio adjutus, castra Lalainius movit, non sine manifestâ indignatione, quod nuper in summo per Transf-Isulaniam fastigio collocatus accessu istorum locorum prohiberetur partumque jam ante foederato bello nomen foedissimo sui contemptu commutaret. Quâ re cognitâ Hohenlous Lochemo, Dotechemo, ac Duisburgio praesidia imposuit, Lalainiumque multa animo, sed nullo successu, agitantem morâ comminuere conatus est. Ipse Linga ac Weddano castello regijs praesidijs relicto, per incerta ac avia locorum nullo insequente in Frisios recessit. Metuebat namque Schenckius, qui divisas cum Lalainio copias in Translavicanis tenebat, ne miles adulto autumno, quo tempore uligines paludum laxantur, minus expedito itinere laboraret, armorumque pondere & lassitudine tardior discrimen inveniret.
units.tr: Soon after, having moved his camp from there and returned, seeking a chance of fame and great deeds, he surrounded Zwolle, a town of Overijssel, with a ring of soldiers, thinking that what had been done at Oldenzaal would succeed more by the favour and goodwill of the citizens than by the size of the army. Therefore he kept returning to the memory of his former affection and to a people reverent of the king, recalling that he, the recent victor in Overijssel, would not lose the proofs of his old favour. But the civic population was rather restrained and the garrison had been kept down by fear, and Lalaing, aided even by a force of two thousand soldiers, moved the camp, not without manifest indignation, because, placed lately at the height of power throughout Overijssel, he was now kept from access to those places, and was changing, by his own most shameful contempt, the name he had already won in the confederate war. Hohenlohe, learning this, placed garrisons at Lochem, Doetinchem and Duisburg, and tried to wear down Lalaing, who was busy with many plans in his mind but with no success, by delay. He himself, leaving the royal garrisons at Lingen and the castle of Wedde, withdrew into Friesland by uncertain and out-of-the-way roads, with no one pursuing him. For Schenck, who held the troops divided from Lalaing's in the Trans-Ijssel region, feared that the soldiers, in the late autumn, when the moisture of the marshes loosens, would labour on a less passable road and, slower through the weight and weariness of their arms, would meet danger.

units.la: Lalainius quoque etsi, desertâ Zuollâ castra Dotechemo admovisset, ab obsessis & Anglorum equitum turmis, quae Doesburgi agebant, infestatus obsidionem finivit, copijsque per paludes Ommam & Meppelium versus transductis Steenvicam obsessurus contendit. Quod oppidum Transl-Isulaniae ditionis Aam ad flumen, quod modico alveo muros praeterlabitur, situm premendis majoribus Frisijs commodum ei videbatur, quo ex illo, tanquam belli sede, ereptam sibi provinciam continuis excursionibus vexaret. Oppidum vero Otdinum nomine Hermanorum cIↄ. Iↄ. mannus Olthovius cohorte cum suâ præsidio tenebat. Cui ne auxilia LXXX. deessent sustinendis hostium castris oppugnationibusque valida, Joannes Cornputtius vir militiæ egregius magnâ cum festinatione ad oppidum missus, succedentibus insuper celerrimo itinere Platio & Stupero centurionibus, quorum cohortibus præter spem Lalainij debilius præsidium duplicabatur. Igitur præsidiarij, numero auctí in prima Lalainij castra, quæ medio diei 18. Octob. Onningam ad portam advenerant, excursionem fecere, repressique à lanceario equite intra oppidum recepti. Joannes Mommius apud Lalainium legioni Frisicæ, quam vocabant, præfectus glande verberatus illo in conflictu occubuit suffecto ei in tribunatu legionis Joanne Baptista Taxio, quæ è veteranis collecta decem & quatuor cohortibus tum censebatur.
units.tr: Lalaing too, though after abandoning Zwolle he had moved his camp up to Dotechem, was harassed by the garrison and by squadrons of English cavalry operating out of Doesburg. He therefore ended the siege and, leading his troops across the marshes towards Ommen and Meppel, set out to besiege Steenwijk. That town, in the district of Overijssel, lies on the river Aa, which flows past its walls in a narrow channel. It seemed to him a convenient place from which, as a base of war, he could press the greater Frisians and harass with constant raids the province he had seized. The town of Otdinum, in the territory of the Hermans, was held by Hermannus Olthovius with his cohort as garrison. To ensure that this garrison, strong enough to withstand the enemy's camps and assaults, did not lack reinforcements, Johannes Cornputtius, a man distinguished in war, was sent to the town in great haste. Then the centurions Platius and Stuperus followed by a very rapid march, and their cohorts, beyond Lalaing's expectation, doubled a garrison that had been too weak. Accordingly the garrison, now increased in numbers, made a sortie from the first camp of Lalaing, which had reached the Onninga gate at midday on 18 October. They were driven back by a lancer horseman and received inside the town. Johannes Mommius, prefect of the Frisian legion, as they called it, at Lalaing's camp was struck by a sling-shot and fell in that engagement. Johannes Baptista Taxius succeeded him as tribune of the legion, which, collected from veterans, was then counted at fourteen cohorts.

units.la: Mox è Geldricis copijs, quas pro Philippo rege autorari Lalainius per Geldriam fecerat, novem & quinque signa addita, adductiqué præterea in castra mille & ducenti equites, quos partim lanceis partim Sclopetis instructos cingere coronâ oppidum munitionesque præducere jussit. Quas cum eruptione factâ portis obsessi interdiu complanarent, obsidentes beneficio noctis reficerent, factum est, ut de petendis auxilijs Steenvicani & ex præsidiarijs cogitarent, Cornputtioque abnuente & invito Ordines ad Fœderatos tabellarij mitterentur. Ita defixis ad Steenvicam castris, Arnoldus Gemenius nuper Prætor Stellinguerfius, G. Snaterus cum modicâ militum equitumque manu quam ducebant, Cuneram progressi, quem locum in orâ maris Austrini situm tumultuario levique opere circumductum binæ ex fœderatis cohortes præsidio tenebant. Eas Escheda & Rudolphus cognomento Longus moderabantur. Qui de hostium adventu nihil suspicati, quos illunis nox & offuscatus nebulosò aëre syderum splendor contexerat, cum somno ac quieti se dedissent à Lalainianis facile oppressi ac dissipati sunt. Escheda expugnatis per hostem tentorijs vigilum vivus in hostium potestatem venit, Rudolpho Longo cum cohorte beneficio schapharum, quæ in portu stabant, in Hollandiam subducto. Reliqui ex Eschedanis suis in dormitorijs nulla miseratione confossi, Cuneræque pagus, quem olim justo titulo Comites tenuerant, nullo resistente direptus est.
units.tr: Soon fourteen companies were added from the Gelderland forces which Lalaing had enlisted through Gelderland in the name of King Philip. Besides, twelve hundred horsemen were brought into the camp, some armed with lances and some with carbines, and he ordered them to encircle the town and to advance the siege works. While the besieged, by sallying out through the gates, levelled these works by day, and the besiegers repaired them under cover of night, the people of Steenwijk and the garrison began to consider seeking help. Cornputtius, however, refused and opposed it, but messengers were nevertheless sent to the States and to the Confederates. While the enemy remained encamped before Steenwijk, Arnoldus Gemenius, lately mayor of Stellingwerf, and G. Snaterus, with a small body of foot and horse which they commanded, advanced to Kuinre. This place, situated on the shore of the Zuiderzee, had been enclosed with a rough and hasty earthwork, and two cohorts of the Confederates held it as a garrison. Escheda and Rudolphus, called Longus, commanded them. Suspecting nothing of the enemy's approach, since the moonless night and the dim starlight through the hazy air had concealed them, these men gave themselves up to sleep and rest, and were easily overpowered and scattered by Lalaing's men. Escheda, after the enemy had overrun the sentries' tents, came alive into the enemy's hands, while Rudolphus Longus with his cohort escaped to Holland by boats which were lying in the harbour. The rest of Escheda's men were cut down without mercy in their dormitories, and the village of Kuinre, which the counts had once held by lawful title, was plundered without resistance.

units.la: Cl. Franckena tradit utrumq; centurionem incolumem servatum, plurimosque præsidiariorum, quos ad internecionem deletos alij tradunt, fugâ Lemmariam pervenisse, quæ Pierij Anskenij Prætoris Lemmariensis & cohortis præfecti præsidio habebatur. Quæ dum in maritimo tractu fiunt Steenvicani arctius quam fuerant obsesi, periculi ex magnitudine virtutem acuebant, incendijsque suburbanis ac crebris oppugnationibus tentati hostium castra diversis eruptionibus infestabant. Quare spolia, captivi, armenta sæpe in oppidum perducta, quod Lalainius misso præcone quamvis inrito consilio, dedi crebrius postulaverat. Itaque Lalainius spem præter & expectationem trahi obsidionem videns admoveri muris tormenta jussit, globisq; ferventibus ignitisque immissis incendium dedit. Quod ipsum flante acri subsolano vires sumens magnam domorum moeniumque partem una cum commeatu absumpsit hostibusque qui oppidum cineribus involutum opinabantur, animum auxit. Unde Lalainius erectis signis velut oppidum, mororum parte
units.tr: Franckena reports that both centurions were saved unhurt, and that most of the garrison, whom others say were utterly destroyed, reached Lemmer by flight. Lemmer was held by the garrison of Pierius Anskenius, mayor of Lemmer and prefect of a cohort. While these things were happening on the maritime coast, the people of Steenwijk were besieged more tightly than before. The greatness of the danger sharpened their courage, and, though attacked by fires in the suburbs and by frequent assaults, they harassed the enemy camps with repeated sorties. Hence spoils, prisoners and herds were often brought into the town, which Lalaing had repeatedly demanded to be handed over, sending a herald with a useless proposal. Lalaing, seeing that the siege was dragging on beyond his hope and expectation, ordered the artillery to be brought up to the walls. He hurled red-hot balls and fire into the town, and the blaze, fed by a strong south-east wind, consumed a large part of the houses and walls together with the provisions. This encouraged the enemy, who supposed the town had been wrapped in ashes. Then Lalaing raised his standards, as if he would attack the town, now stripped of part of its walls, and drew up his ranks. Sending heralds again to offer pardon of life, he demanded the surrender of the town once more.

units.la: Præsidium Cunera à Lalainio opprimitur.
units.tr: The garrison of Kuinre is overwhelmed by Lalaing.

units.la: Steenvicani egregiè suarum rerum satagunt. parte nudatum, oppugnaturus, Ordines instruxit, missisque denuo caduceatoribus qui veniam vitæ offerrent, deditionem oppidi repetijt. Cæterum Platius centurio vir magni animi & belli vetus, qui Onnianæ portæ custodiam sibi sumpserat, elato ac generoso animo Lalainij postulata rejecit, missosque caduceatores, velut alias discrimen passuros, ocyus se recipere in castra jussit. Quod responsum velut præfractum & insolens etsi plurimis & urbico quoque Magistratui displiceret, tamen prævaluit, obsessosque in fide nutantes & ex periculo ancipites in officio continuit. Platius cum suis porta erumpens globo in caput acto haud multo post exspiravit, egregiumque fortitudinis exemplum imitandum commilitonibus reliquit. Igitur Lalainius, negata deditione, tormentis oppidum concussit, datisque crebro incendijs, etsi remedium igni adhiberetur, terrorem obsessis incussit, spemque auxiliorum imminuit. Jam enim rumor percrebuerat, copias è Frisijs missas in itinere cæsas aut dissipatas esse, nihilque restare, quam ut obsessi inter cædes & incendia, famem ac frigora, quæ præcipitante autumno ingravescebant, vitam atque animas sustinerent. Sed senescens rumor sollicitudinem allevavit, comperto duas tantum cohortes, quas Frisij tuendo Sylvestrium tractui ijs in locis collocaverant, ad Ouram profligatas. Istas Joannes Feruovius & ex Danica nobilitate tum per Sylvestria ductabant, quo hostium in Frisiam irruptionibus occurreretur & ne tributa à Frisijs hostilibus copijs præstarentur. Quod speculatus Lalainius, Arnoldum Gemenium Snaterum & Oyenbruggium tribus cum cohortibus castris emiserat, Frisorumque copias, quibus Julius Bottnia & Doco Martena præerant, paucis cum equitibus in Sylvestribus agentes invadi præceperat. Cæterum Julium Bottniam & Doconem Martnam cohortium ductores periculo fortuna exemerat. Quare Feruovius, qui præsidio loci relictus cum imperio ibi erat, hostium adventu intellecto, suam ac Malsemij cohortem derepente instruxit, manumque egregio facinore, etsi infœliciter cum hoste conserut. Quippe fortiter pugnans & fœditate vulnerum à suis vix agnitus Georgio cum fratre occubuit, Frederico Feruovio fratre altero, qui signum ferebat cum paucissimis militum servato. Ea clades ad Ouram in Sylvestribus prid. Kalend. Novemb. facta.
units.tr: The Steenwijkers took great care of their own affairs. But Platius, a centurion of great courage and a veteran of war, who had taken on the guard of the Onninga gate, with a high and noble spirit rejected Lalaing's demands. He ordered the heralds sent back to the camp to retire at once, as if they would soon face danger. This reply, though it seemed to many, and even to the civil magistracy, too defiant and arrogant, nevertheless prevailed. It kept the besieged, who were wavering in their loyalty and divided between danger and fear, in their duty. Platius, sallying out with his men through the gate, was struck on the head by a ball and died not long after, leaving his fellow soldiers an outstanding example of courage to imitate. Therefore Lalaing, the surrender having been refused, battered the town with artillery and, by setting fires repeatedly, struck terror into the besieged, even though they applied remedies against the fire, and diminished their hope of help. For a rumour had now spread widely that the forces sent from Friesland had been cut to pieces or scattered on the march, and that nothing remained except for the besieged to sustain life and breath amid slaughter and fire, hunger and cold, which grew worse as autumn drew to a close. But this rumour, as it grew older, eased their anxiety, once it was learned that only two cohorts, which the Frisians had posted in the Sylvestrian district to guard that tract, had been routed at Oure. These were led at that time through the Sylvestrian region by Johannes Feruovius, of the Danish nobility, to meet the enemy's raids into Friesland and to keep the Frisians from paying tribute to the hostile forces. Lalaing, having learned of this, had sent out Arnoldus Gemenius, Snaterus and Oyenbrugge from the camp with three cohorts, and had ordered them to attack the Frisian troops, under Julius Bottnia and Docco Martena, who were operating with a few horsemen in the Sylvestrian district. But fortune had rescued Julius Bottnia and Docco Martena, the cohort commanders, from danger. Feruovius, who had been left in the place with command, when he learned of the enemy's approach, suddenly drew up his own cohort and that of Malsemius, and engaged the enemy with a brave deed, though unsuccessfully. Fighting bravely, he was scarcely recognized by his own men because of the foulness of his wounds, and fell together with his brother Georgius. His other brother, Fredericus Feruovius, who carried the standard, survived with a very few soldiers. This disaster happened at Oure in the Sylvestrian district on 31 October.

units.la: Mox Slota in ijsdem Sylvestribus oppidum quod rivus Austrino è ma-ri proveniens interluit, vastissimique circum lacus ambiunt à Docone Martna & Stenone Malsemio desertum à Lalainianis occupatum, eodem Martna à suis prope Balckios deserto, ac in castra hostium perducto. Tum Geesterlandiam peragrantes Stauriam quoque antiquissimam Frisiæ urbem in littore ejusdem maris Austrini sitam suam Lalainiani fecere, nullâ aut certe quam parvâ difficultate, quod præsidium militare excessisset, civesque illâ rerum temporumque mutatione ambigui & ancipites partium magis fortunam, quam jus sequerentur. His accedebat, quod castellum, sicuti & reliqua per Frisiam jam ante dirutum, defensioni invalidum foret, ejusque tutela, aut perditio à statu civitatis dependeret. Quare Lalainius, quo Castella, quæ odio sui, gubernante provincias Matthia Austrio Ordines everterant, ocyssime redintegraret, velut spem in illis ac fiduciam recuperandi per Frisiam impecIↄ. Iↄ. rij conciperet Stauriense extemplo reparari, emunirique fecit, Maccoʟxxx. miumque septentrionem versus eodem in maris littore terreo opere, valoque conclusit. Ita maritimis vicis oppidisque in potestatem redactis Harlingam usque dein Franekeram, Bolsuerdiamq;, post totam fere per Westergoam populationes egit, Frisiæque partem, quæ Slachtano marinoque aggere coërcetur, tributariam fecit. Quâ ut excedere Lalainius coegeretur Frisij catarráctas, atque emissaria, quæ pro ratione æstuum lunarium aquas emittunt ac recipiunt, aperiri curarunt, quo maris influxu facto aquarum quoque per campos stagnantium pellendis hostibus augmenta haberentur. Sed aversa à littore ventorum vis tum serenius sicciusque cœlum, quod etiam vergente autumno post vergiliarum occasum imbres negabat, omne consilium subvertit, Frisiofque nuperæ ad Ouram cladis infœlicitate perculsos hostium populationibus permisit.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Slota, a town in the same Sylvestrian district, washed by a stream that rises from the southern sea and surrounded by very extensive lakes, was abandoned by Docco Martena and Stenon Malsemius and occupied by Lalaing's men. Martena, too, was deserted by his own men near Balckios and was brought into the enemy camp. Then, ranging through Geesterland, Lalaing's men also took Stavoren, the most ancient city of Friesland, situated on the shore of the same southern sea, with little or no difficulty, since the garrison had withdrawn, and the citizens, in such a change of affairs and times, were uncertain and wavering, following the fortune of the parties more than justice. Added to this was the fact that the castle, like the others throughout Friesland which had been dismantled earlier, was too weak for defence, and its safety or destruction depended on the state of the city. Therefore Lalaing, so that the castles which the States had overthrown out of hatred for Matthias of Austria, when he governed the provinces, might be restored at once, and so that he might recover hope and confidence of recovering Friesland, had Stavoren repaired and fortified at once. He enclosed it with an earthen rampart and a palisade on the shore to the north. Thus, with the coastal villages and towns brought under his power, he then laid waste Harlingen, afterwards Franeker and Bolsward, and nearly all of Westergo, and made the part of Friesland that is held in check by the Slachter and sea dike pay tribute. To force Lalaing to withdraw from there, the Frisians took care to have the sluices and outlets opened, which let out and take in water according to the tides of the moon, so that by letting in the sea's inflow, there would be an increase of waters also spreading over the fields, to drive out the enemy. But the force of the winds, blowing away from the shore, brought a clearer and drier sky, which, even as autumn declined, denied rains after the setting of the Pleiades. This overturned the whole plan, and left the Frisians, struck down by the misfortune of the recent defeat at Oure, exposed to the enemy's plundering.

units.la: Igitur Lalainius velut fortunæ pro arbitrio imperaret, superbus & simul secundarum rerum & ex voto fluentium vecòrs subactam majoris Frisiæ provinciam ratus, animum quoque minores in Frisios intendit, quo ultroq; littore, quod medio & interfluo mari obtenditur, suæ potestatis facto utrique Frisiorum regioni & latissimis æstuarijs dominaretur.
units.tr: Lalainius, as if fortune were obeying his will, was proud of his success and of events flowing as he wished. Thinking the province of Greater Friesland already subdued, he turned his attention to the Lesser Frisians.
