By taking the opposite shore, which lies across the middle sea and the intervening water, he meant to control both regions of the Frisians and their broadest estuaries.

units.la: Quare litteras Enchusanum ad Magistratum misit, fiduciæ plenus populum quoque transmarinum victoriarum ac prosperorum famâ suis partibus accessurum.
units.tr: So he sent a letter to the magistrates, full of confidence that the people across the sea would also join his side, drawn by the reports of his victories and successes.

units.la: NON dubito, quin rerum mearum prosperitas qua maritimam majorù Frisiæ regionem regi PHILIPPO, meaque verò Præfecturæ asserui, ad vos perlata sit. Et quoniam intelligo esse ex vobis, qui turbatissimorum temporum pertæsi, Fœdus Gandavense à rege confirmatum amplecti velint, nostramque societatem & commercia mutua expetant hasscribendas duxi, ut deliberatione inter vos & cum Statibus oppidisq; minoris Frisiæ habitâ, animi vestri apud me secretum exprometis. Quare si ad Gandavense fœdus redire vobis mens atq; animus est, legatos quanto ocyus mittite, cum mandatis. Sin vero id vobis grave videatur, etsi commeatum illis daturus sim, operam date, ut litterarum saltem responsa ad me perveniant. Datæ in castris regijs ad Steenvicam VIII. Eid. Dec. cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXX.
units.tr: I do not doubt that news of the good fortune of my affairs, by which I have secured the maritime region of Greater Friesland for King Philip and for my own command, has reached you. And since I understand that some of you, weary of these most troubled times, wish to embrace the league of Ghent confirmed by the king, and seek our alliance and mutual commerce, I have thought it right to write to you, so that, after you have deliberated among yourselves and with the States and towns of Lesser Friesland, you may reveal to me the secret of your minds. Therefore, if your intention and inclination are to return to the league of Ghent, send envoys with instructions as quickly as you can. But if this seems hard to you, then although I would grant them safe conduct, take care at least that your answer in writing reaches me. Given in the royal camp at Steenvijk, 8 days before the Ides of December, 1580.

units.la: Cl. Franckena notat coeptâ obsidione, quod in xv. Kal. Nov. diem incidit, agente in Frisijs Lalainio, obsessos annonæ prospexisse munitoque divisis operis oppido, puteos quoque tardandis impediendisque hostium cuniculis novâ quadam arte repertos. Auxilia quoq; Novembri mense dimissis ex oppido per noctem Campos tabellarijs socios Ordines petita, nullumque hostile tam in castris regijs quam apud obsessos intermissum. Itaque eruptiones obsessorum cottidianæ & hostes fatigabant & obsessi oppugnationibus obsidentium exercebantur, ægrè ferente Lalainio acre obsidium & ultrique parti grave per initia asperæ hyemis proferri. Quare ut finem consilio Lalainius faceret, muralia tormenta adduci Groningâ jusserat avertendisque Ordinum auxilijs quæ jam parabantur, firmioribus operibus castra circumduci. Iam eniim Ordinum ac Aurantij litteræ solutionem obsidio pollicebantur, quod fœderatæ reip. interesset limitaneum tot provincijs oppidum in defestoctoris Lalainij potestatem arbitriumque non recidere. Ea res Caroli Roordæ & Abeli Franckenæ datis ad Cornputtium litteris confirmabatur. Cæterum Cornputtius vir futuri providus rescriptis ad Ordines Principemque qui Delphis agebat, litteris compositiis cuncta quam festinantius agi petebat, totumque solvendæ obsidionis negotium motioni magis quam casui committendum. Igitur decreto Ordinum maturandæq; solutioni castrorum Stuperus cum cohorte Suarteslusam, Hegemannus legionis tribunus sex cum signis in D. Joannis Campos haud procul Vollenhoâ missus quo destinata liberandis Steenvicanis auxiliarijs in locis contraherentur. Quo cognito obsidentes castris egressi in cœnobium D. Joanni sacrum, quod campos vocant, celerrimo itinere irrupere, adortiq; Hegemanni legionem, etsi fortiter resistentem, non sine cæde in fugam egerunt. Capti ex centurionibus Joannes Vianensis, Joannes Wichmannus & Gedeon Pomeranus, vexillo ejusdem cohortis, haud citrà ostentationem, equinæ caudæ alligato ac in castra ad Steenvicam perducto. Creditum fuit, quod cœnobium plano apertoque loco situm nec fossâ aut vallo emunitum foret, facile occupatu fuisse, fœderatisque non tam animos aut virtutem quam infirmitatem patentis cœnobij obfuisse. Quâ clade intellectâ languentes obsessi de mittendis ocyus auxilijs Ordines sociosq; monuere, animatique responso, quod militiæ stipendia ac virtuti juxta præmia policebatur, egregiâ fortitudine sua pericula & hostium impetus sustinuerunt. Igitur tum apud Ordines de solvendâ Steenvicæ obsidione serio agitatum, contractæque maturanda ad auxilia ex omni regione copiæ, quo laborantibus Steenvicanis subveniretur. Iam enim Norritius Anglus vir militiæ impiger cum x i. cohortium pedestri legione, ac turmâ equitum circa Zuollas advenerat, ejusque copijs Stuperi, Appelij, Clerhagij, Couwenbergique cohortes conjunctæ solutionem obsidio minabantur. Illas præterea Michaël Caulerius vi. cum signis, Caulerium Iselsteinius alijque cum v. peditum sequebantur. Reliquæ equestres copiæ quas Caulerius idem, Pieckius & Simon Limburgus ducebant, eidem consilio destinatæ ablegato in minores insuper Frisios Duvenvordio Hollandici maris præfecto, qui celoces aliquot tam solvendæ Steenvicanæ obsidioni, quam recuperandis majorem per Frisiam oppidis munitionibusque adornaret. Vigboldo quoque Eusemio Niennortio viro nobili & strennuo legionem pedestrem vi. sub signis conscribendi potestas ab Ordinibus facta, quo omni ex orâ collecto autoratoque milite Lalainius animi insolens campo & castris pelleretur. Econtra Lalainium diuturnius apud Steenvicam obsidium urebat & quod Nyennortius collectas autoratasque in agro Translavicano copias Winsumi collocasset, objectisque quo defenderentur propugnaculis tributariam Omlandiam fecisset. Quare etiam inter famem & frigora reliquasq; hyemis naturæque inclementias castra adhuc tenens continuare obsidionem constituit, citiusque vitâ quam obsesso oppido se abiturum fidem apud Tribunos legionum fecit. Igitur ut instantia mala averteret, utque miles æris egens & inops in castris duraret, legionum primores ac legatos convocavit, editoque & modicis collibus adsurgente loco consistens hunc in modum disseruit.
units.tr: Franckena notes that the siege was begun on the 15th day before the Kalends of November, while Lalainius was in command in Friesland. The besieged, he says, had foreseen the shortage of food, and they fortified the town by dividing the work, and they also devised a new kind of method for digging wells, to delay and hinder the enemy's mines. In November, letters were sent out of the town by night, through the fields, to the allied States, asking for help, and there was no break in hostilities, either in the royal camp or among the besieged. So the daily sorties of the besieged wore out the enemy, while the besieged were harassed by the attacks of the besiegers. Lalainius was displeased that the siege was sharp and a burden to both sides, and that it was being prolonged into the beginning of a harsh winter. So, to bring the matter to an end, he had ordered the siege artillery brought from Groningen, and the camp to be surrounded with stronger works, to head off the help of the States that was already being prepared. For already letters from the States and from Orange promised that the siege would be lifted, since it was in the interest of the confederated commonwealth not to let a town on the border of so many provinces fall back into the power and control of Lalainius. This was confirmed by letters written by Carel van Roorda and Abel Franckena to Cornputtius. Cornputtius, a man far-sighted about the future, wrote to the States and to the Prince, who was then at Delft, asking that everything be done as speedily as possible, and that the whole business of lifting the siege be entrusted to a planned movement rather than to chance. So, by decree of the States and to hasten the lifting of the camp, Stuperus with a cohort went to Suarteslusa, and Hegemannus, tribune of a legion, with six standards, was sent to the fields of St John, not far from Vollenhove, so that the troops destined to relieve the Steenwijk auxiliaries might be gathered in those places. When this was known, the besiegers left their camp and rushed by the swiftest route into the monastery sacred to St John, which they call the Fields, and attacked Hegemannus's legion; although it resisted bravely, it was put to flight with considerable slaughter. Among the centurions taken were John of Vianen, John Wichmann and Gedeon the Pomeranian, and the standard-bearer of the same cohort, who was tied by the tail to a horse, with some show, and led into the camp at Steenwijk. It was believed that the monastery, being situated in a flat, open place and not fortified with ditch or rampart, was easily taken, and that it was not so much the spirit or courage of the confederates as the weakness of the exposed monastery that caused the disadvantage. When this disaster was understood, the besieged, growing weak, warned the States and allies to send help more quickly; and, encouraged by the answer that pay and rewards for their service were promised in proportion to their valour, they bore the dangers and attacks of the enemy with outstanding courage. So then, at that time, the question of lifting the siege of Steenwijk was seriously discussed among the States, and troops were being gathered from every region, to be brought up quickly so that the Steenwijk men in distress might be relieved. For already Norris, an Englishman, a man vigorous in war, had arrived near Zwolle with eleven companies of foot in a legion, and a troop of horse, and with his forces were joined the cohorts of Stuperus, Appel, Clerhagius and Couwenberg, and they threatened to lift the siege. Michael Caulerius followed them with six companies, and Iselstein and others with five companies of foot followed Caulerius. The remaining cavalry forces, which Caulerius himself, Pieck and Simon of Limburg commanded, were destined for the same purpose. Duvenvoorde, prefect of the Holland sea, was also sent to the Lesser Frisians, so that he might equip some light vessels both for lifting the Steenwijk siege and for recovering the towns and fortifications in Greater Friesland. The States also gave Vigbold Eusemius of Nienoort, a noble and energetic man, the power to raise a foot legion of six companies under standards, so that, with soldiers gathered and hired from every shore, Lalainius, insolent in spirit, might be driven from the field and camp. On the other hand, the prolonged siege of Steenwijk was wearing Lalainius down, and because Nienoort had gathered and hired forces in the Translavian country and had stationed them at Winsum, and had put up defensive fortifications to protect them, he had made the Ommelanden tributary. Therefore, although still holding the camp amid hunger, cold, and the other harshness of winter and nature, he decided to continue the siege, and he assured the tribunes of the legions that he would leave only with his life rather than abandon the town under siege. So, to avert the threatening evils, and so that the soldier, short of pay and in want, might endure in the camp, he called together the leading men and legates of the legions. Standing on a raised place, rising in gentle hills, he spoke in this way.

units.la: IAM diu cognovi, Commilitones, ut secundis rebus animos, ita mollioribus corpora corrumpi. Diutinam hanc obsidionem vexantibus inedia & frigore tolerastis, magno & fœlici indicio ipsum cœlum, etsi triste & asperam, ipsa sydera, etsi pruinis aut nivibus infesta virtute vestra susserri. Præter stipendia quoque angusta, quæ petentibus hoc tempore præstari non possunt, difficilem commeatum habuistis. Omnia quæ movere animos possent ad deteriora, nisi sacramenti dulcedo atque memoria seditione ac tumultu cariora esset. Et quoniam vobis ista superare atque evincere patientia placuit, date operam porro, ut ego voti compos fiam & ne in blandissima victoria spe aut certissimâ constitutus consilio meo excidam, vestraq; virtus in fine rerum minuatur. Nam obsessos ad extrema redactos ipsi non ignoratis, auxiliaque, quæ pellendis castris nostris parantur, imbecilla neque nostræ magnitudini paria esse. Equitatu certè longè nos prævalere in aperto est, qui cum concretis stratisque glacie paludibus non impediatur, promptus ad officium erit. Itaq; peto, ut sacramenti, quod regi Philippo præstitistis, memores in fide ac disciplinâ breve ad tempus persistatis, credatisque omnes molestias, pericula, vulnera, mortes lenimentum à victoriâ, gloriam à vestrâ fortitudine habituras.
units.tr: I have long known, fellow soldiers, that as success corrupts the spirits, so softness corrupts the bodies. You have endured this long siege, plagued by hunger and cold, and the sky itself, though gloomy and harsh, and the very stars, though hostile with frost and snow, have been overcome by your courage, a great and happy sign. Besides, you have had narrow pay, and scarce supplies, which at this time cannot be given to those who ask. All these things could move your minds to worse, were it not that the sweetness and memory of your oath are dearer than any mutiny or uproar. And since you have decided to overcome and conquer these things by patience, take care from now on that I may attain my wish, and that I may not fall from my most certain plan through hope of a most flattering victory, and that your courage may not diminish at the end of the affair. For you yourselves know that the besieged have been reduced to extremity, and that the help being prepared to drive us from our camp is feeble and not equal to our strength. Surely it is plain that we far surpass them in cavalry, which, since it is not hindered by the marshes, frozen and hardened with ice, will be ready for its duty. So I ask that, mindful of the oath you swore to King Philip, you persevere in loyalty and discipline for a short time, and that you believe all troubles, dangers, wounds and deaths will bring comfort from victory and glory from your courage.

units.la: Quâ oratione aversa, quæ in proxumo erat, seditio contorpuit, milesque repetitâ sacramenti dictione poscenti Lalainio se obligavit. Mox Ioannes Norritus justis copijs instructus Suarteslusam contendit, compertoq; Ottonem Santium nuper Satrapam Herdervicenum regiæ parti ascriptum in Giethornis præsidium habere delectam sclopetariorum manum celerrimo istuc itinere expedivit, occupatoq; loco Santium captivum cæso filio abduxit. Reliqui hostium à Norritio in fugam acti ipseq; pagus immisso rectis igne spectantibus hostibus conflagravit. Cl. Franckena in Ephemeride suâ tradit Hattumanam arcem quæ præsidio fœderis tenebatur à Præsecto proditam, paucisque post diebus eandem à Campensibus Daventriensibusque receptam lætiora obsessis Steenvicanis evulgavisse. Pulverem quoque tormentarium cujus penuriâ obsessi laborabant, culeis inditum quadragiuta peditum ope obsessam in urbem importatum majores animos propugnantibus fœderatis addidisse. Addunt alij in isto Norritij Angli cum hostibus ad Suarteslusam conflictu peritissimos belli ac Lalainij veteranos cecidisse, Arnoldumq; Gemenium sub Philippo & per Frisiam in Stellinguersijs prætorem castra regia tum secutum finem vitæ implevisse. Præter cæsos multos quoque Vidro amni immersos & extinctos annales tradunt. Unde clarum Norritij Angli apud fœderatos nomen, quod cum bellicæ artis peritia conjunctum egregijs fortunæ quoque successibus augebatur. Quibus uendum ratus, ut res prosperæ audaciam pariunt, solvendæ obsidioni Steenvicanæ animum atque consilia intendit & ut Lalainium vincendæ urbis certum & sacramento pertinaciam obsidij alentem, movenda ad hyberna compelleret. Igitur pecuniâ & commeatu sublevatis obsessis, auxiliijsq; minorum Frisiorum, quibuscum Sonoïus vir bello acer Blocz-zylam advenerat, ipse instructus manu decertare cum Lalainio statuit, suæque virtutis ac secundarum rerum fiducia totius exercitus salutem aperto discrimini unique fortunæ ictui committere. Cæterum à Frisijs monitus ut majora auxilia, ut pecuniam & stipendia, pugnaturis robur, bur, atque alacritatem additura, expectaret, neu fortunæ ex se insta- bili tenerrimas sociorum res crederet, cæpto desitit, consiliumq; im- prudens & nullâ futuri providentiâ ex temeritate natum mutare coactus est. Iam enim Lalainius, quo Norritium, erumpentesq; à fronte obsessos exciperet, magnam regij exercitus partem in insidijs collocaverat, quarum commoditatem, ut de hyeme solet, spissius cœlum & exsurgens nebula præjuvabat. Quâ fato seu forte retegendis, quæ Lalainius agitabat, arcanis discusså litteras ad obsessos dedit, deditionemque si gratiam vellent, hortatus est.
units.tr: When this speech was over, the sedition that had been close at hand grew quiet, and the soldiers, repeating the words of the oath, pledged themselves to Lalainius as he demanded. Soon afterwards John Norris, equipped with suitable forces, hurried to Suarteslusa, and learning that Otto Sant, lately governor of Herdervich, attached to the royal party, had a picked band of musketeers as a garrison at Giethoorn, he sent them there by the swiftest route; he seized the place and carried off Sant captive, after his son had been killed. The rest of the enemy were put to flight by Norris, and the village itself was set on fire, with flames directed straight at it while the enemy looked on. Franckena, in his diary, reports that the Hattem citadel, which was held as a garrison for the league, was betrayed by its prefect, and that a few days later the same place was retaken by the men of Kampen and Deventer; this brought cheerful news to the besieged at Steenwijk. Also, gunpowder, of which the besieged were short, was loaded into sacks and brought into the besieged town by forty foot soldiers, and this gave greater courage to the confederate defenders. Other writers add that in this clash of Norris the Englishman with the enemy at Suarteslusa, some of the most skilled in war and veterans of Lalainius fell, and that Arnold Gemen, who as praetor of Stellingwerf in Friesland had then followed the royal camp under Philip, met his end. Besides the many who were slain, the annalists record that some were drowned and killed in the river Vidro.

units.la: Satius scilicet esse obsessos regis sui veniam atque fidem amplecti, quam sum- mâ rerum desperatione spem collocare in auxilijs, quæ ne Aurantius quidem & totum fœdus præstiturum sit. Scire se quo loco Ordinum res sint, qui neque vellint, ut salvâ unius oppidi fortunâ totius exercitus flos atque robur incertis belli eventui & uni ictui subjaceat. Huic rei fidem se interponere ex notitiâ arcanorum, quæ patrum secretis eliminarentur.
units.tr: It would surely be better for the besieged to accept their king's pardon and good faith than, in utter despair, to place their hope in aid that not even Orange and the whole alliance could supply. He knew how matters stood with the States, who did not wish the flower and strength of a whole army to depend on the uncertain outcome of war and a single blow, for the sake of one town's fortune. He pledged his good faith on this, from his knowledge of secrets that would be revealed by the confidences of the fathers.

units.la: Cæterum centurionibus cohortiumq; præfectis alia mens erat. Itaque respondebant perstare se in Ordinum Aurantijq; societate velle & per- mittere Rennebergio, ut quod ē re suâ sit agat, experiaturq; quid aut aliena virtus discrimine irritata aut sua posset. Mox Norritius Anglorum cum legione auxiliaribusque copijs, quæ sub signis Gulielmi Ludovici Nassovij erant, Glethorno duxit, Steenvicanumque saltum, qui urbi adjacet, ingressus captis cæsisq; pluribus incendium excitavit. Quo velut signo dato, perlucente flammis sylvâ obsessi de faciendâ eruptione deliberarunt, fusisque in foro precibus & peractâ re divinâ partem præsidij portâ emisere, quæ ad munitionem lapideæ viæ adjectam recto itinere ducebat. Quâ occupatâ, datis in fugam præsidiarijs, captaque fœminâ, quæ utero gerens, ut Franckena tradit, & fugæ impar erat, majorem munitionem oppugnavere, quam ipse Rennebergius justò præsidio tutabatur. Ubi fortiter virtute præsidiariorum, qui intra munitionem erant, excepti in diversa se sparsere, tantâ noctis, quæ illunis erat, opacitate, ut commilitonem ab hoste vix distingueret. Unde confusio enata, nescientibus in quos armorum vis converteretur & quod Rennebergius munitione, quam defenderat, egressus justum agmen per emissarium Aæ fluminis ductaret. Igitur obsessi factâ ad parvam munitionem carragine, quam à suis teneri opinabantur, simile in discrimen errore noctis inciderunt, diversisque conflictibus extenuati carris impedimentisque exustis in oppidum se recepere. Berenbroeckius Hagiusque re præclare gestâ vi hostium in oppidum quoque compulsi, cujus portam, prementibus obsessorum terga hostibus, regij facile occupavissent, nisi occultæ viæ beneficio, quam Cornputtius fieri curaverat & in quam obsessi se receperant, rejecti fuissent. Olthovius centurio portam, quæ sylvestrem Frisiæ tractum respicit, claudi fecit, justâque custodiâ sepsit. Traditum annalibus magnum utrinque militum numerum illâ nocte cecidisse multosque captivos ut in oppidum, ita Rennebergij castra perductos utriusque partis damna & incommoda pensasse. Tum Norritius in arbustum modico aggere cinctum, juxta Tuccam pagum copias haud procul emissario duxit, per quod Aa fluviolus tenui cIↄ. Iↄ. tenui alveo se emittit. Quo cognito Rennebergius cum potissimâ exercitus parte magno impetu Norritium adortus est, quem in magnâ annonæ commeatusque penuriâ equestre insuper auxilium destituebat. Iam enim deletas ad internecionem Norritij pedestres copias suspicione credebatur, qui in maxumo rerum discrimine constitutus aliena consilia, suam temeritatem & juxta fortunam incusabat. Cui incommodo & hoc accedebat, quod densissimæ nebulæ obortus omnem conspectum impediret, quæ ab oppidanis auxilia mitti aut transferri in tuta exercitum cœli opacitate prohibebat. Cæterum post repulsum Rennebergium & signum receptui dare jussum à cive quodam locorum gnaro, qui oppido exploraturus regia excesserat, Bloczilam perductus periculum evasit, quo loci Sonnoius vir belli egregius præsidium tutandæ oræ maritimæ agebat. Ubi datis litteris Steenvicanos suo de discrimine totoque rerum statu certiores fecit, subnixusque majorum Frisiorum auxilijs, quæ ventura credebantur, certam solvendi obsidij spem annuntiavit. Mox Bloczilâ copias movens in cœnobium D. Joanni sacrum concessit, obsessusque à Rennebergio, qui magnâ celeritate illum circumvenerat, Frisiorum auxilijs liberatus est.
units.tr: The centurions and cohort commanders, however, had a different mind. They replied that they wished to stand firm in the alliance of the States and Orange, and they allowed Rennenberg to do what suited his own interest and to test what either foreign valour, roused by danger, or their own could achieve. Soon afterwards Norris led the English legion and the auxiliary troops, who served under William Louis of Nassau, from Glethorn. He entered the Steenwijk wood, which lies beside the town, and after taking and cutting down several men he raised a fire. As if at a signal given by this, the besieged, with the forest lit up by the flames, deliberated on making a sally. After prayers in the marketplace and a religious service, they sent out part of the garrison through a gate that led in a straight line to the stone road-embankment next to the fortification. Once that was seized, they routed the garrison troops and captured a woman who, as Franckena reports, was pregnant and unable to flee. They then attacked a larger fortification, which Rennenberg himself guarded with a proper garrison. There they were bravely met by the garrison troops inside the fortification and scattered in different directions, so thick was the darkness of that moonless night that a man could scarcely tell a comrade from an enemy. From this came confusion, as no one knew at whom the force of their weapons should be turned; and Rennenberg, having left the fortification he had defended, led his full column through the outlet of the River Aa. The besieged then made a barricade at a small fortification, which they believed was held by their own men, but through the same night's error they fell into a similar danger. Weakened by separate skirmishes, with their carts and baggage burned, they withdrew into the town. Berenbroeck and Hagius, having performed their task well, were also driven back by the enemy's force into the town; the royalists could easily have seized its gate, as the besieged pressed their backs against the enemy, had they not been repulsed by the help of a secret path, which Cornputt had arranged to be made and into which the besieged had withdrawn. Captain Olthof had the gate that faces the wooded district of Friesland closed and put under strict guard. The records state that a great number of soldiers fell on both sides that night and that many were taken prisoner. Both sides' losses and hardships were balanced, as the prisoners were led into the town and into Rennenberg's camp alike. Then Norris led his troops into an orchard enclosed by a modest embankment, near the village of Tuck, not far from the outlet through which the little River Aa empties its shallow bed. Rennenberg learned of this, and with the main part of his army attacked Norris with great force. Norris was already short of food and supplies, and the lack of cavalry support added to his distress. Indeed, it was believed that Norris's infantry had been wiped out, and he, placed in the greatest danger, blamed others' plans and his own rashness, and likewise his luck. To this misfortune was added a very dense mist that blocked all view, and the darkness of the sky prevented the townspeople from sending help or moving the army to safety. Afterwards, when Rennenberg had been repulsed and the order to sound the retreat had been given, Norris was led by a local citizen who knew the country, and who had left the town to scout the royal positions, to Blokzijl, where the excellent warrior Sonnoy commanded the garrison guarding the coast, and so he escaped danger. There Sonnoy, having sent letters informing the people of Steenwijk of his peril and the whole state of affairs, relied on the help of the greater Frisians, which was believed to be coming, and announced a sure hope of raising the siege. Soon Norris moved his troops from Blokzijl and withdrew to the monastery sacred to St John. Besieged there by Rennenberg, who had surrounded him with great speed, he was freed by the aid of the Frisians.

units.la: Quippe Wigboldus Nienortius cum Menningeo, qui Bernardi Merodij Frisiæ præsidis copias titulo optionis ducebat, victoriâ Windeschotanâ (ubi hostium coitiones xviii. Kal. Feb. notante Franckena dissipaverat) animatus cum auxilijs (cIↄ. Iↄ. numerabant) Scutam post Oldemarctum progressus de Norritij sociorumq; consilio Bloczilam pervenerat, evulgatâ in castris Rennebergij famâ Frisiorum Translavicanorumq; justa auxilia solvendo obsidio adesse. Quare Rennebergius magnâ in festinatione P. Joannis cœnobium reliquit exustoque Grethorno in castra ad Steenvicum magno animi mœrore militem & quidem seditiosum reduxit.
units.tr: For Wigbold Nienorts, together with Menninge, who led the troops of Bernard Merode, the governor of Friesland, under the title of deputy, had been encouraged by the victory at Windesheim (where, as Franckena notes, he had scattered the enemy's gatherings on 17 January). With auxiliaries, who numbered 1500, he advanced past Oldemarkt to Scoten, and on the advice of Norris and his allies had reached Blokzijl. Meanwhile the rumour had spread through Rennenberg's camp that the Frisians and Translavicani were coming with real help to raise the siege. So Rennenberg, in great haste, left the monastery of St John, burned Glethorn, and withdrew to his camp at Steenwijk with the deep distress of soldiers who were, indeed, mutinous.

units.la: Quippe non pensitato stipendio totus exercitus & consilia miscere, mox fidem & sacramenta exuere coeperat, additâ comminatione se ipsi Duci, nisi prospiceret, manum injecturos. Quamobrem Rennebergius Schenkij Ojenbruggijque consilio usus centum aureos unicuique cohorti assignavit, passusq; domus suæ & rerum direptionem militarium furorum incommoda in singulorum capita pendere xxi. sestertios coactus est. Additâ insuper fide, nisi promisso staret, castra se moturum, copiasque cœli inclementiâ & hybernâ asperitate ferocientes molliore vitâ & dulcedine otij placaturum. Ita cæpta seditio interquievit Rennebergiusq; deserto Steenvicano saltu & Tuccâ pago urbi vicino sparsas hinc inde copias peculiari castrensium motuum remedio ad Aam flumen contraxit, tormentaque ad pontem flumini impositum perduci imperavit.
units.tr: For the whole army, since its pay had not been reckoned, had begun to stir up plans, and soon they began to cast off their loyalty and oaths, adding the threat that they would lay hands on the Duke himself unless he made provision. Therefore Rennenberg, acting on the advice of Schenk and Ojenbrugge, assigned a hundred gold coins to each cohort, and, since the hardships of soldiers' frenzy had to be paid by each individual, he was compelled to allow his house to be plundered and his goods looted, and to pay twenty-one sesterces per head. He added a pledge that, unless he kept his promise, he would move the camp, and he would appease the troops, made fierce by the harshness of the sky and the hardness of winter, with an easier life and the sweetness of leisure. So the mutiny that had begun was quieted. Rennenberg, having abandoned the wood at Steenwijk and the village of Tuck, which is near the town, gathered his troops, scattered here and there, to the River Aa by the particular remedy for military disorders, and ordered the artillery to be brought to the bridge laid over the river.

units.la: Quæ dum in Frisiorum finibus geruntur Belgicæ Ordines de revocando Francisco Vallesio Andium Duce Galliarum regis fratre cogitavere, quod Matthias Austrius sive imperij & tantæ molis regundæ pertæsus, sive propinqui regis aut fratris Cæsaris consilio in Germaniam revocandus successorem moderamini provinciarum desideraret. Iam enim auxilia subsidiaque bello potentiam & fortunam tanti Principis secutura infirmioribus rebus expetebantur ac ut ostendentia se jam tum popularis imperij aut libertatis vitia & vix adversis inhibita unius eminentis autoritas ac fastigium comprimeret. Neque enim à subjuvandis Belgis alienam GalGalliam esse, odio Hispani & aversis à se invicem istarum gentium ingenijs, quæ interventu sui Principis Belgarum societati innexa arma quoque Hispano per Belgicam furenti intentatura haberentur. Posse Lutzenburgum, Hannoniam, Artesiam conterminas Galliæ regiones si non arma potentissimi Principis, saltem metum sentire & qui laturus non sit in fratris sui regno, militem, commeatum, pecuniam, arma conquiri augendæ Hispanorum dominationi, aut subvertendæ Belgarum libertati destinata. In quam cum rarò Principum exemplo inclinaverit, quorum cupiditatibus gravis ut plurimum & suspecta libertas sit, ita Galliæ regno funestis, ut ferè solet, incendijs flagranti moderata consilia collocasse. Quod ad Angliæ regnum attineret, male Elisabetham vicinum Belgicæ rectorem Vallesium, quam Philippum habere, adjectâ jam Hispaniæ Lusitaniâ vastissimis terris & mari Oceano imperitantem. Præstructas quoque inter Alençonium & Elisabetham connubio occasiones, observatumque; reginæ pectus à Vallesij Principis amoribus alienum non esse. Quæ ut in secreto patrum disserebantur, ita eo res perducta est, ut repetitâ societatis auspicandæ actione tabulæ quoque firmandis pactis, non Alençonij tantum, sed regi & foederatorum sociorumque (inter quos Frisicam gentem fuisse reperio) sigillis consignarentur.
units.tr: While these things were happening in the territory of the Frisians, the Belgian States considered recalling Francis of Valois, Duke of Anjou and brother of the French king, because Matthias of Austria, either weary of ruling so great an empire and so vast a burden, or on the counsel of the king his cousin or of the emperor his brother, was to be recalled to Germany and wanted a successor to govern the provinces. For aid and subsidies were being sought by the weaker party, to follow the fortunes and power of so great a prince in war, and so that the authority and eminence of one outstanding man might restrain the faults of popular rule and of liberty, which were already showing themselves and were scarcely held back by adversity. For France was not alien to helping the Belgians, given the hatred of the Spanish and the opposing dispositions of those peoples towards one another; and through the intervention of its prince, these arms, bound to the Belgian alliance, would also be aimed at the Spanish, who were raging through Belgium. Luxemburg, Hainault and Artois, the regions of France bordering on it, could feel, if not the arms of a most powerful prince, at least his fear; and soldiers, supplies, money and weapons would be gathered in his brother's kingdom, which would not be sent there, destined to increase Spanish domination or to overthrow Belgian liberty. Yet France had rarely inclined to this course, as the example of princes shows, whose desires usually make liberty burdensome and suspect; and so, as is usual, moderate counsels were placed in the blaze of fires that were fatal to the kingdom of France. As for the kingdom of England, Elizabeth was the nearer ruler of Belgium, and Valois was held to be a worse one than Philip, who already ruled Portugal, now added to Spain, and vast lands and the Ocean Sea. The opportunities for a marriage between Alençon and Elizabeth had also been arranged in advance, and it was observed that the queen's heart was not alien to the love of the prince of Valois. While these things were discussed in the secret councils of the fathers, the matter was carried so far that, by renewing the act to begin the alliance, the documents too for confirming the agreements were sealed, not only with the seal of Alençon, but also with those of the king and the allied confederates (among whom I find the Frisian people).

units.la: Reperio in actis provinciæ Aurantium principem, quò belli ordinem ac disciplinam terrâ marique stabiliret, postulata quædam mense Ianuario exhibuisse, perlataque; in Frisios ne remedia quidem depravatis militiæ rebus attulisse. Joannem quoque Verckenium Frisiæ cohortis ductorem in Omlandiam ac Translavicanos cum cohorte missum; non damna tantum & incommoda hostibus, sed socijs quoque intulisse, eundem quoque Wigboldi Eusemij curâ vinculis datum; ipsumque Eusemium datis in Frisiam litteris socij juris violati rationem allegasse. Similes litteras à R. Ackema præsidium Winsumi agente perscriptas fuisse reperio. Cujus Verckenij causam etiam hoc prægravabat, quod Decembri mense perfuga ac proditor quidam cum Rennebergio in castris ad Steenvicam positis consilium communicasset, deprehensusque à Verckenio sexcentis aureis immunitatem redemisset. Adeo illo tempore, velut rudi adhuc militiâ, licentia invalescebat. Quæ per Frisiam atq; adeo ipsam Westergoam vires sumens Wonseranam quam maxime præturam afflixit. Quippe Dodo Larius equitum turmæ, tunc cohortis peditum ductor inordinatis fœdisque exactionibus illius oræ populum exhauriebat, hostisque magis ingenio quam socij usus in omnem insolentiam effundebatur. Unde supellex non tantum & villarum rusticarum instrumenta ac utensilia, sed pecora quoque abacta, aut alendis flagitiosorum ventribus mactata, ne tuto quidem integroque hospitali ac templorum jure, quod omnia patrantibus fœdâ immanitate ac sacrilegio violabatur. Quare à rusticâ gente criminationes & querelæ Novem-virale ad Collegium per Ianconem Ofingam virum nobilem istius loci Prætorem perlatæ, dissimulante enormem militum proterviam illorum patientiâ, qui in fide ac sacramento retineri ægrè militem nisi leni factorum indulgentiâ opinabantur. Quæ correctionum animadversionumque militarium tarditas ne majus incommodum daret Translavicano-
units.tr: I find in the records of the province that the prince of Orange, in order to establish the order and discipline of war by land and sea, had in January presented certain demands, and that, being sent to the Frisians, they had not even brought remedies for the corrupted state of military affairs. John Verckenius, the commander of the Frisian cohort, had been sent with a cohort into Omland and the Translavicani, and had inflicted losses and hardships not only on the enemy but also on allies. The same man had been put in chains by the care of Wigbold Eusemius; and Eusemius himself, by letters sent to Friesland, pleaded the reason of his violated right as an ally. I find that similar letters were written by R. Ackema, who commanded the garrison of Winsum. A further grievance against Verckenius was that in December a certain deserter and traitor had communicated a plan with Rennenberg in the camp placed at Steenwijk, and, when caught by Verckenius, had bought his immunity for six hundred gold coins. So lawlessness grew strong at that time, as if the troops were still raw in their soldiering. Gathering strength through Friesland and indeed through Westergo itself, it struck hardest at the district of Wonseradeel. For Dodo Larius, a leader of a troop of horse, then commander of a cohort of foot, drained the people of that shore by disorderly and foul exactions, and the enemy's temper, rather than an ally's, was poured out into every kind of insolence. Hence not only household goods and the implements and utensils of country farms, but also cattle were driven off, or slaughtered to feed the shameless bellies of the wicked; and not even the safe and intact right of hospitality and of temples was spared, all of which was violated by the perpetrators with foul savagery and sacrilege. Therefore complaints and accusations from the rural people were brought to the Board of Nine by Jancko Ofinga, a nobleman of that place and its governor, while the forbearance of those who thought that soldiers could scarcely be kept in faith and oath except by gentle indulgence of their misdeeds ignored the outrageous insolence of those troops. The slowness of such military corrections and punishments, lest it cause a greater inconvenience to the Translavicani, [the legates of the Translavicani sent letters also to the Board of Nine of Friesland].

units.la: PRÆSIDIVM quod Doccomij posuistis, FRISIJ, nobis ac genti nostrae molestum & grave est. Præter damna data municipibus nostris in captivitatem abductis de remedio & emendatione præstandâ jam ante monuimus. Cæterum vestrâ morâ ac cunctatione abusus quasi miles insolentiam auxit, etsi non ignarus sociale jus ac sacra foederum auspicatò & cum religione inita istâ militari protervia auferri. Quin pauci dies sunt, quibus instiusmodi furoribus frœna laxata sunt, abductis in fines vestros Grypskerckyis, quos domui suae ac familiae reddi, praeterquam pensitato 100. dalerorum lytro vestri milites noluerunt. Quae cum pacem publicam, cum jus foederum turbent, cum sanctissimæ societatis fundamenta convellant, hortamur denuò ut malis subnascentibus medicinam adferatis, ne tandem vestra dissimulatione aucta omne remedium respuant. Imprimis ut ablatarum rerum pretia numerando liberos homines & nostro imperio subjectos, sine ullo lytro rebus suis restituatis, moneatisque cohortium præfectos & simul militarem turbam, ne fines vestros excedendo trans Lavicam tanquam ditionis vestrae terminum aliquid pravum aut hostile moliantur. Ne nos aut aliò querelas deferre, aut invenire duriora malis remedia cogamur.
units.tr: The garrison that you have placed at Doccum, Frisians, is burdensome and grievous to us and to our people. Apart from the losses inflicted on our townsfolk, some of whom have been carried off into captivity, we have already warned you about the remedy and redress that must be given. But your delay and hesitation have been exploited, and the soldiers' insolence has grown, although you are not unaware that this military wantonness is at odds with the law of alliances and with the sacred bonds of the covenant, which were entered into under good auspices and with religious solemnity. Indeed, only a few days ago such frenzies were let loose, and the Grypskerck men were taken into your territory. Your soldiers refused to return them to their homes and families unless a ransom of one hundred daler was paid. Since these acts disturb the public peace and the law of covenants, and undermine the foundations of a most sacred fellowship, we urge you once more to apply a remedy to these growing evils, lest, through your continued neglect, they grow and reject every cure. Above all, restore the seized goods to their owners, and return free men who are subject to our rule without any ransom, once the price of the goods has been paid. Also warn the commanders of the cohorts, and the soldiery with them, not to cross the Lauwers, as if it were the boundary of your domain, and plot anything wicked or hostile there. Otherwise we shall be forced either to bring our complaints elsewhere or to seek harsher remedies for these evils.

units.la: Quæ Snecæ, quo Delegati Omlandiæ confugerant, perscripta, meliores in curas Frisiæ proceres traxere. Tum valori monetæ, auro atque argento signato per provincias prospectum, vinoque ac cerevisiæ exoticæ indictiones impositæ augendis ærarij opibus, quæ terrâ marique strepentibus armis lacerabantur. Unde fiebat ut Ordinum provincialium legati subsidia ex ærarijs fœderatarum nationum urgerent, gravissimisque in rebus, sicuti fieri mos est, consensum ac judicium cujusliber provinciæ flagitarent. Jam enim postulata quædam in Frisios transmissa, quæ de impensis legationum in Gallia factis, de Matthiæ Gubernatori in Germaniam abituro præstando residuo, de Elisabethæ Anglorum reginæ credito exsolvendo, de Aurantij annuâ pensione augendâ, de pactis cum Alençonio supplendis confirmandisque habebant. Quibus ut satisfieret provinciæ nomine Delphos Batavorum Julius Bottnia Oldermannus Franekerensium cum Orichio Dojemo Ordinum Frisiæ Syndico missi: Ijs in mandatis datum ut actorum defectum postulatis obtenderent, fidemq; facerent Gallicæ ad Alençonium legationis impendia Andreæ Hesselio Graphiario Brabantiæ ad cIↄ. c. xviii. carolæos exsoluta. Quod ad Matthiam Auftrium missionem Belgio petentem attineret, velle Ordines Frisiæ ut idem, quod vicinæ provinciæ præstent, habitâ interim ratione ærarij Frisici, quod atrocium bellorum & per ipsa provinciæ viscera grassantium crudelis tempestas minueret. Ad augendam provincialis Senatus, qui cis ac trans Mosam institutus erat, numerum, Leoni Beiemo fato functo Doconem Martnam suffecisse, missuros eundem quanto ocyus cum litteris publicis, quæ subveniendis belli necessitatibus & ordinandis provinciarum tributis expedirentur. Elisabetham Anglicam quod attineret censebant, inquirendum per Legatos esse, an Frisij præstandæ solutioni tenerentur, eoque posito assensum vicinis provincijs, aut æquiora volentibus habituros. Idem in causa Aurantij velle, exsolvique debita, ac æris magnitudinem præstanstandam, quam Aurantius liberandis defendendisque provincijs impendisset. De Alençonio respondebant grave & molestum fore ulteriorem isti actioni assensum præbere, quod à vicinis provincijs in deliberationem missa esset, quorum judicijs arbitrijsque staturi Frisij essent. Invenio in actis publicis Matthiam Archiducem missis ad Ordines Egberto Leonino, Antonio Lalainio, Joanne Asselerio legatis speciosis & ad movendos provincialium affectus validis rationibus usum apud eosdem de præstando ære & liberandis nominibus egisse, suaeque familiae ac gentis Austriae, tum aulae suae incommoda ignominiamq; obtendentem, solutionem residui aeris postulasse. Frisios quoque præstandae solutioni octo millia aureorum assignasse, duobus millibus Anglorum Reginae in usuris adjudicatis. Omnia quoque prioris belli impendia magno provincialium incommodo petita attritis impulsisque privatorum rebus & facultatibus, quas tributi ex bello onus & per agros exactio vastatioque diripiebat.
units.tr: These matters, written down by Snek, whither the deputies of Ommelanden had fled, drew the leading men of Friesland to more pressing concerns. Then provision was made for the value of the coinage, gold and silver being struck throughout the provinces, and excise duties were imposed on wine and foreign beer to increase the resources of the treasury, which was being torn apart by arms on land and sea. As a result, the deputies of the provincial Estates pressed for subsidies from the treasuries of the allied nations and demanded the agreement and judgement of each province on the most serious matters, as is customary. For certain demands had already been sent to the Frisians concerning the expenses of the embassies made in France, the balance to be paid to Governor Matthias on his departure for Germany, the debt owed to Elizabeth, Queen of the English, the increase of William of Orange's annual pension, and the completion and confirmation of the agreements with Alençon. To satisfy these, Julius Bottnia, alderman of Franeker, was sent to Delft in the name of the province, together with Orichius Dojema, syndic of the Estates of Friesland. Their instructions were to plead the lack of records concerning the demands and to assure them that the expenses of the French embassy to Alençon had been paid, in Carolus gulden, by Andreas Hesselius, Graphiarius of Brabant, in the year 1118. As for the mission of Matthias to Austria, which was seeking money from Belgium, the Estates of Friesland wished to do what the neighbouring provinces did, while taking into account in the meantime the state of the Frisian treasury, which the cruel storm of atrocious wars raging through the very heart of the province was diminishing. To increase the number of the provincial Senate, which had been set up on both sides of the Meuse, they reported that Doco Martna had been appointed in place of Leo Beiemo, deceased, and that he would be sent as quickly as possible with public letters to be dispatched for relieving the needs of war and arranging the provincial taxes. As for Elizabeth of England, they thought the legates should inquire whether the Frisians were bound to make the payment; once that was settled, they would have the assent of the neighbouring provinces, or of those who wished for fairer terms. The same position was taken regarding William of Orange: the debts should be paid and the amount of money he had spent in freeing and defending the provinces should be settled. As for Alençon, they replied that it would be grievous and burdensome to give further assent to that business, since it had been referred to the neighbouring provinces for deliberation, and the Frisians would abide by their judgements and decisions. I find in the public records that Archduke Matthias, when he sent to the Estates the envoys Egbert Leoninus, Antonius Lalainius and Johannes Asselerius, pleaded with them, using specious arguments and forceful reasons to move the feelings of the provincials, about paying the money and freeing the names. Pointing to the disgrace and damage to his own family, the house of Austria, and to his court, he demanded payment of the outstanding money. The Frisians also assigned eight thousand gold pieces for the payment, with two thousand going to the Queen of England as interest. They also demanded all the expenses of the earlier war, to the great hurt of the provincials, by wearing down and driving on the private property and resources of individuals, which the burden of war taxes and the exactions and devastation of the fields were plundering.

units.la: Unde Bernardi Merodij regiaeque Curiae edicto paci tranquillitatiq; publicae prospectum, cautumque ut Focconi Oenonio caeterisque partium regiarum suspectis bona salva intactaque essent, omniq; in posterum violentiae parceretur, ne foederis vires & bellorum nervi, privatorum rapinis succiderentur. Rerum quoque venalium, quae usu consumuntur, indictiones per provincias scriptae, cautumque Aurantij, qui imperium maris gerebat, litteris, ut ad x. Febr. diem omnes naves imprimis onerariae portubus attinerentur, dum provinciarum Ordinumq; cura omni commercio prospexisset.
units.tr: Hence, by an edict of Bernard Merode and the royal Court, provision was made for peace and public tranquillity, and it was ordered that the goods of Focco Oenonius and the other suspects of the royal party should remain safe and untouched, and that violence should be spared in future, lest the strength of the alliance and the sinews of the wars be cut away by the plunder of private persons. Excise duties on saleable goods, which are used up in consumption, were also proclaimed throughout the provinces, and by a letter of William of Orange, who held command of the sea, it was ordered that all ships, especially the transport vessels, should be kept in port until 10 February, while the care of the provinces and Estates provided for all commerce.

units.la: Mox Sonoius Bloczilae curandis Steenvicanorum rebus agens, communicato cum provinciarum legatis & Joanne Norritio foederati exercitus ductore consilio, Vollenhoam maritimum & arce validissimâ firmatum oppidum tentavit, ductisque quatuor marinum per aggerem signis suum fecit, præsidio regio equitum peditumq; exire jussho.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Sonoy, who was dealing with the affairs of Steenwijk on behalf of Bloemendal, having communicated his plan with the legates of the provinces and with John Norris, leader of the allied army, attempted Vollenhove, a town on the coast and strongly fortified by a citadel. Having led four naval standards through the dyke, he made it his own, ordering the royal garrison of horse and foot to leave.

units.la: Traditum commentarijs Belgicis reperio Antonium del Vailium nuper Philippi 11. nomine per Frisiam Senatorem efferi & crudelis animi virum eo in oppido captum, Campos-que ad Delegatos foederis missum. Famâ additum eundem del Vailium multitudinis ad captivitatem sanguinarij hominis frequentissimo occursu in magnum vitae discrimen incidisse, parumque abfuisse; quin ponte, quo longissimo Ilala annis aeternitur, dejectus effusum per Frisiam innocentium sanguinem lustralibus aquis expiaret. Memorant annales durante Steenvicanâ obsidione 4. Febr. tres perdices intra obsessam urbem captas prodigio ascriptum fuisse, interpretante Cornuttio, viro erudito & antiquitatis peritissimo evoluto trium septimanarum spatio annonam divinâ ope obsessorum fami atque extremae inediae subventuram. Quae res in omen quoque pertracta Norritium solvendae obsidionis momenta atque consilia agitantem majoribus desiderijs accendit. Quare modico equitum peditumq; numero castris emisso, Rennebergij Schenckijq; equites in Deveris pago Drentiae commorantes nocte & ex improviso adortus est, trecentosque ex ijs, ut Franckena notat, praeter reliquos in fugam datos delevit. Quo in conflictu Rombertum Friesma regium nuper per Stellinguerfios praetorem, qui castrorum Rennebergij mensorem tum agebat, accepto vulnere Groningam perlatum expirasse in annalibus Cl. Franckena memorat, eundemque Friesmam quod in æstuario apud Harlingam navi vectus Batenburgicos fratres anno 1568. detexisset, per scelus ad præturam evectum dignum proditioni suæ factisque exitum sortitum. De quorum proditione, etsi suppresso tum quod ignorabatur nomine, primo Historiæ libro perscripsi. A quâ victoriâ Norritius, justo agmine, (in quo præter suam Nassovicam, Merodæam, Nienortiam, Cauleriam, Iselsteiniam legiones, cum Hegemanni & Stuperi signis & sex equitum turmis ducebat) instructus Steeuvicano saltui in ortum ad montem Hindigerum castra posuit, qui modico terreo opere ac tramite exaggeratus, versus septentrionem, qua planior erat, factâ carragine defendebatur. Vexilla quoque signaque quo obsessis in conspectum daret, in edito montis proximorumq; collium posuit, quos inter hostiumque castra planities ad bis mille pass. interjacebat, quæ nullo arboreto consita, paludibus pascuisque, qua oppidum spectat, distincta, commodissimum gerendis rebus & pugnæ locum designabat.
units.tr: I find in the Belgian commentaries that Antonio del Vaille, lately a senator in Friesland in the name of Philip II, was a man of cruel spirit. He was captured in that town and sent to Campen to the deputies of the alliance. Report added that this del Vaille, by the very frequent gathering of a multitude against this bloodthirsty man's captivity, had fallen into great danger of his life, and was barely spared from being thrown from the bridge, where he would expiate the innocent blood he had shed across Friesland with purifying waters, the bridge across which the Ijssel is said to flow for ever. The annals record that during the siege of Steenwijk, on 4 February, three partridges were caught inside the besieged city, and this was taken as an omen; Cornutius, a learned man very skilled in antiquity, interpreted it to mean that within a space of three weeks, by divine aid, food would relieve the besieged from hunger and extreme want. This matter, pressed into service as an omen, inflamed Norris, who was planning the moments and strategy for lifting the siege, with greater desires. Accordingly, having sent out a small number of horse and foot from the camp, he attacked by night and without warning the horsemen of Rennenberg and Schenck, who were quartered in the village of Deventer in Drenthe. As Franckenus notes, he destroyed three hundred of them, apart from the rest who were put to flight. In this encounter, Romberto Friesma, lately royal praetor of Stellingwerf, who at that time was acting as surveyor of Rennenberg's camp, was wounded and taken to Groningen, where he died; so Clarissimus Franckenus records in his annals. The same Friesma, who had betrayed the Batenburg brothers by sailing in a ship in the estuary at Harlingen in 1568, was raised by treachery to the praetorship, and met an end worthy of his betrayal. I have written about their betrayal in the first book of this History, though at that time the name was suppressed because it was not yet known. From this victory Norris, marching in good order (leading, besides his own Nassau, Merode, Nieuwenaar, Cauler and Isselstein legions, the standards of Hegeman and Stuper and six troops of horse), pitched camp to the east of the Steenwijk wood at Hindiger hill, which was defended by a small earthwork and a path, raised up and fortified with a palisade towards the north, where it was flatter. He also placed banners and standards on the high ground of the hill and of the nearby hills, so that they would be seen by the besieged. Between these hills and the enemy camp lay a plain about two thousand paces across, bare of trees, divided by marshes and pastures on the side facing the town, which marked it as the most suitable place for conducting operations and fighting.

units.la: Quare Rennebergius ingenio loci usus, neque insidiarum metuens, quod apertius cœlum camporum planities ostenderet, decem peditum cohortes, equitumque pauciores turmas justâ acie instruxit, displosisque machinis, ante lucis ortum Norritij in castra inveêtus est. Qui omnis, etiam ultimi, discriminis contemptor suos quoque desiderio pugnæ accensos castris eduxit, juxtaque Tuccam pagum extimumque lapideæ viæ marginem cum hoste congressus est. Ubi retro citroque habitis velitationibus cum obsessi quoque portâ egressi levi ponticulo per Aam amnem jacto damnum hosti facerent, sole meridiem permenso justum prælium subortum est, adnitentibus regijs, ut carrorum compage, quam castris præduxerat, luxatâ solutâq; castra Norritij excinderet. Cæterum regij male excepti amissis quam plurimis ac saucijs signum receptui dedere Henrico Snatero, qui ab Albani ætate regias partes propugnaverat, fortiter pugnante desiderato. Obsessi, quos portâ egressos memoravi, castra, qua ortum diei spectabant hostium occupavere, excitatoque igne & confossis ægris, ac imbelli trium fœminarum sexu interempto, victores Steenvicam rediere, quæ in ultimo discrimine constituta defeêtu alimoniæ prægravabatur.
units.tr: Therefore Rennenberg, making use of the nature of the place, and fearing no ambush because the open plain showed the sky more clearly, drew up ten cohorts of foot and a smaller number of troops of horse in battle order. Having fired his engines, he was carried against Norris's camp before dawn. Norris, a scorner of every danger, even the greatest, led out his men, who were also burning with desire for battle, and engaged the enemy near the village of Tuk and the outermost edge of the stone road. There were skirmishes back and forth, and when the besieged also came out of the gate and, throwing a light bridge across the River Aa, did damage to the enemy, a full battle broke out as the sun passed the meridian. The royal troops strove to break up and dissolve the line of wagons which Norris had drawn in front of his camp, in order to tear down Norris's camp. But the royalists were badly handled, losing very many men both killed and wounded, and gave the signal for retreat, Henry Snatert, who had defended the royal cause since the time of Alba, being missed as he fought bravely. The besieged, who I mentioned had come out of the gate, seized the enemy camp on the side facing the rising sun, and after lighting a fire and slaughtering the sick, and killing the defenceless sex of three women, they returned as victors to Steenwijk, which, placed in the greatest danger, was pressed hard by a shortage of food.

units.la: Neque Rennebergius etsi æris inops, in tantâ cœli & omnium rerum exacerbatione animum despondebat, quin erigendis novis castellis, reficiendisque castrorum munitionibus incumberet, militemque penuriâ cibi languidum, virtutis constantiæq; commoneret. Idem à Norritio factum, qui asperrimum gelu, quasi frigidissimorum siderum concursu alto defluens, omnique malo sæviorem famem suis in castris tolerabat. Cæterum clementius cœlum 17. Feb. hyemis asperitati subveniens, mox pluvia tempestas flante Favonio subsecuta uberiori annonæ spem fecit, viasque glacie interclasas subvehendis castrorum commeatibus aperuit. Quare Norritius castra propius ad urbem posuit, locumque mil-le pass. à castris distantem juxta Aæ veteris ripam extruendæ novæ munitioni designavit. Unde noêtu & interdiu militum operæ desideratis fossoribus provectæ, donec terreo vallo præduêto nova munitio & duobus tormentis instructa oppugnationibus hostium sufficeret. Quam et-si si tentaret oppugnaretque Rennebergius, tamen experiundo discebat cIↄ. IÞ. virtute magis militaris præsidij, quam objectis operum molibus erectam LXXX I. munitionem defendi.
units.tr: Rennenberg, though short of money, did not lose heart amid such a storm of weather and such general hardship. He set about raising new forts and repairing the fortifications of his camp, and he urged his soldiers, weakened by lack of food, to keep their courage and steadfastness. Norris did the same. Though the sky was harsh with bitter frost, as if the coldest stars had gathered together, he endured hunger, the worst of all evils, in his own camp. On 17 February, however, the sky grew milder and relieved the harshness of winter. Soon a rainy spell followed, with the west wind blowing, which raised hopes of a fuller harvest and opened roads, broken up by ice, for carrying supplies to the camp. Norris therefore moved his camp nearer the town and marked out a site a thousand paces from the camp, beside the bank of the old Ae, for building a new fortification. From there the soldiers' work went on by night and by day, with diggers called in to make up for the shortage, until a new fort, equipped with two guns, was finished and could withstand the enemy's attacks. Rennenberg tried to attack and assault it, but by experience he learned that a fortification built in 1581 was defended more by the courage of its garrison than by the piles of earthworks thrown up against it.

units.la: Annotatum invenio quosdam ex obsessis vitæ ac animæ prodigos oppido egressos, spretis hostium castellis excubijsque novam in munitionem perrexisse, subjutosque à quibusdam Norritianis panem ac caseum obsessæ urbi importasse. Norritium quoq; provisio magnæ munitionis commeatu, minorem fieri propius oppidum curasse, extructamq; è regione munitionis hostium carraginem Rennebergij subvertisse. Unde gravissimo conflictui nata occasio, ita commissis implicatisq; equitum peditumque ordinibus, ut hostis à commilitone non distingueretur, videreturq; justo prælio, fortunam castrorum determinaturo, commissa velitatio reservari. Sed obsessis erumpentibus tergaq; hostium & imprimis equitum ferientibus, quos agendis rebus minus idoneos densissimi imbres & soluta fossarum glacies faciebat, Rennebergij pedites ordines suos deseruere, flagitatisque stipendijs turbulenti & palantes, multis utrinque desideratis, in castra reversi sunt. Tum Norritius, quo faventi fortunæ manum præberet, notatâ in Rennebergij castris seditione aut saltem contumaciâ dedignationeque parendi, quosdam annonâ commeatuque onustos ad oppidum misit, subjutosque ab obsessis, qui erumpebant, repetere officium jussit. Quod etsi impedire Rennebergius conaretur, tamen tempori & præsentibus rebus obsequi coactus est, ne mobiles militum animos & vile sanguinis vitæque pretium criminatos majora ad incommoda regijs castris inferenda irritaret.
units.tr: I find it recorded that some of the besieged, reckless of their lives, left the town on foot, ignored the enemy's forts and sentries, and made for the new fort. Some of Norris's men helped them and carried bread and cheese into the besieged town. Norris also took care, now that he had provided a large store of supplies for the fort, to make his position closer to the town smaller, and he destroyed a redoubt of Rennenberg's that had been built opposite the fort. This gave an opportunity for a very serious fight. The ranks of horse and foot became so tangled and mixed together that an enemy could not be told from a comrade, and what had begun as a skirmish seemed likely to become a proper battle that would decide the fate of the camps. But the besieged sallied out and struck the enemy in the rear, especially the cavalry, whom the very thick rain and the melting ice in the ditches made unfit for action. Rennenberg's foot soldiers then deserted their ranks. Loud and wandering, demanding their pay, they returned to camp with many killed on both sides. Norris, eager to lend a hand to fortune's favour, noticed that there was mutiny in Rennenberg's camp, or at least defiance and a refusal to obey. He sent some men loaded with grain and supplies to the town, and he ordered them to bring back the men who had sallied out of the besieged town to do their duty. Rennenberg tried to prevent this, but he was forced to yield to the moment and to the present situation, lest he provoke, by fresh outrages, the already restless spirits of his soldiers, who were ready to make light of their blood and their lives, and so bring greater harm upon the royal camps.

units.la: Cl. Franckena in Ephemeride VIII. Kal. Mart. id factum tradit, Steenvicanosque impressione in castra Rennebergij Aam ad flumen facta cum numero plures superioresque evasissent, primos hostium ductores præfectosque cohortium cecidisse. Hostium quoque peditatum fugæ datum nec contineri per equitem in officio, nec reduci capessenda ad arma potuisse, totumque conflictum imbrium interventu diremptum. Quare Rennebergius provisis urbi commeatibus & suorum contumaciarum exspes, de movendis castris agitavit, nulloq; signo dato & conquisitis tormentis castella munitionesq; suas deseruit, ne observato quidem ab obsessis hostili consilio, quod nocturnâ opacitate & nebuloso insuper spissoque coelo tegebatur. Cæterum die postero omni castrensi officio silente, desideratisq; excubitoribus Rennebergij castra à Norritianis lustrata, quæ equorum militumque qui recenter occubuerant, cadaveribus oppleta, tristissimâ facie visebantur. Intra ipsas verò munitiones castellaque Rennebergij armorum quæ projecerant, copia & castrensis quoque supellex reperta prædæ illorum cessit, qui liberatam virtute urbem lætabantur. Mox Rennebergius, etsi motis jam castris quo dedecentis fugæ suspicionem velaret, aciem editiore loco explicavit, potestatemque pugnæ Norritio fecit. Qui foelici suarum rerum successu contentus, simulque varietatem fortunæ, quæ in res bellicas dominatur, expendens oppidum fame exhaustum ubere annonâ ac commeatu instruxit, Ordinesque fœderatos Campis ad Ifalam agentes solutæ Steenvicanorum obsidionis certiores fecit. Rennebergius consilij inops palans & errabundus copias quaquaversum duxit, donec in Sal-
units.tr: Franckena, in his Ephemeris, reports that this happened on 22 February: the men of Steenwijk made an attack on Rennenberg's camp by the river Ae, and having got through in greater numbers and with the upper hand, they cut down the first enemy leaders and the commanders of the cohorts. The enemy infantry was also put to flight. The cavalry could neither be kept in order nor brought back to take up arms, and the whole fight was broken off by the intervention of the rain. Rennenberg therefore, having provided supplies for the town and having no hope of his men's obedience, thought about moving his camp. Without giving any signal, and after gathering up his guns, he abandoned his forts and fortifications, without the besieged even noticing the enemy's plan, which was hidden by the darkness of night and by a misty, thick sky. The next day, with all military activity silent and his sentries missing, the Norrisians searched Rennenberg's camp. It was full of the corpses of horses and men who had recently died, and it looked very grim. Inside the fortifications and forts of Rennenberg, a quantity of the arms that his men had thrown away, along with the camp equipment, was found and became the spoil of those who rejoiced that the town had been freed by their courage. Soon Rennenberg, though his camp had already been moved, drew up his battle line on higher ground, so as to hide any suspicion of a shameful flight, and offered Norris a chance to fight. Norris, content with the happy outcome of his affairs, and at the same time weighing the changeable nature of fortune, which rules over war, stocked the starving town with plenty of grain and supplies. He also informed the allied companies, who were operating in the fields near the Ijssel, that the siege of Steenwijk had been lifted. Rennenberg, without a plan and wandering about, led his forces in every direction, until he turned aside into Salland and left Norris free to arrange the garrisons and occupy the fortifications as he thought fit.

units.la: landiam deflecteret, Norritiumque arbitrio suo in ordinandis præsidijs occupandisque munitionibus relinqueret. Qui Cunerâ olim Comitatus titulo insigni fœderi adjectâ, reliquas cohortes Friscas Merodij imperio parentes Lemmariam atque Slotam duxit, quo omnis ora maritimo, quæ Austrino maris sinui, aut latissimis æstuarijs obtenditur, Rennebergij regioque præsidio liberaretur. Lemmaria ac Slota tormentis machinisque verberatæ fœderatis se permisere, deserto insuper à regijs Maccomio, qui Rennebergio ægritudine angoreque animi ex adversis correpto vanis discriminum pavoribus percellebantur. Quare & Stauria quoque olim regni Frisici sede & nobili orientis commercio clara urbs, quam Renicus Dekama vir nobilis cum cohorte regiâ tenebat, à Friscis copijs tentata, metuentibus Ordinibus ne regis auxilia illo in loco, tanquam limitaneo, contraherentur, & ne Rennebergius animum ab adversitate resumpturus sedem bello divexandis Frisijs deligeret.
units.tr: Norris, after adding the famous title of Count to Cuneraa, which had once belonged to the confederacy, led the remaining Frisian cohorts, who obeyed Meroy's command, to Lemmer and Slooten. The aim was to free the whole coast, which faces the southern bay of the sea or the widest estuaries, from Rennenberg's and the royal garrison. Lemmer and Slooten, battered by guns and siege engines, surrendered to the allies. Makkum was also abandoned by the royalists, and its men, seized by sickness and by anguish of mind after the reverses, were struck down by vain fears of danger. Stavoren too, once the seat of the Frisian kingdom and a town famous for its trade with the East, which Reinier Dekama, a nobleman, held with a royal cohort, was attacked by the Frisian forces. The States feared that the king's auxiliaries would be gathered in that place, as on a frontier, and that Rennenberg, to recover his spirits after his setbacks, would choose that seat from which to harass Friesland with war.

units.la: Igitur Sonoius Bloczilæ hærens cohortem è minoribus Frisijs transmissam Stauriam amandavit, quod oppidum præsidij vacuum solâ arce ac castello regio defendebatur. Mox pluribus copijs auctus portuque actuarijs navigijs occupato, rusticam plebem erigendo terreo operi adesse jusit, objectoque ex opposito arcis vallo, machinâq; ligneâ, quæ summitatem mœnium superabat, fabricatâ obsidionem promovit, adductisque Harlinga ac è minoribus Frisijs tormentis, post cuniculos ultra fossam ac ad ima mœnium perductos arcem deditione accepit. Creditum fuit obnitente & invito Dekama arcis Præfecto Friscisque præsidiarijs id obtigisse, qui à Germanis, qui sub cohorte militabant, vinculis dati catarractas ad nigras, ut vocant, Vidrumque flumen perducti sunt. Renicus Dekama fratre cum captivo Enchusam missus, custodiæque traditus est. Addunt commentarij vexillum majus præsidiarijs ereptum Enchusæ majore in templo à Sonnoio appensum expugnatæ arcis Stauricæ illustre monumentum dedisse.
units.tr: Accordingly, Sonoy, who was staying at Blokzijl, sent a cohort of the lesser Frisians across to Stavoren. The town was without a garrison, and only the citadel and the royal castle were defended. Soon, strengthened by more troops and having seized the harbour and the transport ships, he ordered the country folk to help him build an earthwork. He pushed on the siege, setting up opposite the citadel a rampart and a wooden tower that rose above the top of the walls. Then, bringing up guns from Harlingen and from the lesser Frisians, and after running mines beneath the ditch to the foot of the walls, he received the citadel by surrender. It was believed that this happened against the wishes of Dekama, the commander of the citadel, and of the Frisian garrison. They were seized by the Germans who served in the cohort and were led in chains to the so-called Black Sluices and the river Vliet. Reinier Dekama was sent to Enkhuizen with his brother as a prisoner and handed over to custody. The chronicles add that the greater standard, taken from the garrison, was hung by Sonoy in the great church at Enkhuizen, as a famous memorial of the capture of the citadel of Stavoren.

units.la: Franckena notat mensis Martij initio capta Slotâ cohortem quoque Friscam Leovardiæ collocatam, Ordinumque Comitio, quod ibi habebatur, decretum, ut trium per Frisiam arcium castellorumque regiorum reditus emuniendis in posterum oppidis destinarentur. Sixtum quoque Sceltemam virum nobilem & Novemviri dignitate functum cohorti Iulij Botniæ præfectum, qui Oldermanni titulo regundo Franekerensium oppido accitus, militare ingenium pacis artibus exercebat.
units.tr: Franckena notes that at the beginning of March Sloten was taken, and that a Frisian cohort stationed at Leeuwarden was also ordered, by a decree of the States gathered there, that the revenues of three royal citadels and forts across Friesland should be assigned to fortifying towns in future. He also notes that Sixtus Schelte, a nobleman who had held the office of Nine Men, was summoned to Franeker to be made commander of Julius Botnia's cohort, with the title of Alderman to govern the town of Franeker. He used the arts of peace to practise his military talents.

units.la: Quæ dum fiunt Wigboldus Eusemius Nienortius prospere res in Transl Lavicanis gerebat, liberatoque obsidione Winsumo Marrensium pago, secundaq; velitatione cum Rennebergicis habitâ (in quâ Oyenbruggius glande ictus occubuerat) majore belli apparatu occupabatur. Quare auxilia petenti quatuor signa peditum ipso verno Æquinoctio, ut Franckena notat, ei decreta, duæque cohortes à majoribus Frisijs post additæ consilia Nienortij subjuvere.
units.tr: While these things were happening, Wigbold Eusemius Nienort was doing well in the Lauwers district. He had freed the Marrum district of Winsum from siege, and after a successful skirmish with the Rennenbergians (in which Oyenburg fell, struck by a bullet), he was occupied with a much greater military preparation. Accordingly, as Franckena notes, four companies of infantry were granted to him, on the very day of the spring equinox, at his request for help, and two cohorts from the greater Frisians were later added, and these helped Nienort's plans.

units.la: Quare Rennebergius cum apertâ vi parum proficeret, clam multorum qui regijs in partibus per Frisiam adhuc erant, animos tentavit, eisque potestatem colligendi pro Philippo militis fecit. Inter Cæteros Petrum quoque Everardum Dureuoutium, qui Rinsmageestæ apud Dantumanos agebat, illo autoramento instructum reperio, eundemque vinculis culis datum ac Leovardiam in arcem regiam pertractum, velut proditionis reum, mox intercessione popularium liberatum relapsumque in graviora tragico exitu sontem vitam finivisse.
units.tr: Since Rennenberg was making little progress by open force, he secretly tested the minds of many who were still in the royal party across Friesland, and he gave them the power to raise soldiers in Philip's name. Among others, I find that Pieter Everard Dureuoutius, who was acting at Rinsma-geest among the Dantumans, was equipped with that commission. He was thrown into chains and taken to the royal citadel at Leeuwarden as a man accused of treason. Soon, freed by the intercession of his fellow countrymen, he relapsed into worse offences and ended his life in a tragic way, a guilty man.

units.la: Principem quoq; Aurantium missis id temporis Leovardiam Laurentio Jacobæo & Joanne Maertio legatis eundem Magistratum ad colligenda exigendaque mercium reique nauticæ onera ac tributa 23. Iulij anni 1580. Antverpiæ sancita sollicitasse, ipsumque Magistratum tenerrimâ adhuc libertate, & ne frequentia mercantium in solitudinem verteretur damno civitatis honestis rationibus facti invidiam abnuisse. Godscalcum quoque Hiddamam cum Jacobo Jacobæo Consule Bolsuerdiano Legati personam agentem, & à Principe Aurantio mandatis instructum multa de centurionum tribunorumque militarium peculatu & imprimis Iselsteinij proposuisse, & ut militari licentiæ exactionibusq; fraeno impositο & emunitâ Harlingâ maritimo oppido, Bernardum inter Merodium, qui autoritatis vilipendium apud Aurantium criminatus erat, vicarium Provinciæ Rectorem Ordinumque Delegatos & Senatum Juridicum ut Franckena vocat, pax ac concordia firmaretur.
units.tr: Also, at that time, the Prince of Orange sent envoys to Leeuwarden, Laurens Jacobsz and Joan Maertsz, to press the same Magistracy to collect and exact the duties, the charges on goods and shipping, which had been sanctioned at Antwerp on 23 July 1580. The Magistracy itself, still very tender in its freedom, and fearing that the town would be turned into a desert by the loss of merchants, refused the odium of such a measure, for honourable reasons, to the detriment of the city. Godschalk Hiddama, acting as envoy together with Jacob Jacobsz, the Bolsward consul, and instructed with mandates by the Prince of Orange, also put forward much about the embezzlement of the captains and military tribunes, and especially about Iselstein. He proposed that military licence and exactions should be bridled, that the maritime town of Harlingen should be protected, and that peace and concord should be confirmed between Bernard, the deputy governor of the province, whom Meroy had accused before Orange of holding his authority in contempt, the Delegates of the States, and what Franckena calls the Judicial Senate.

units.la: Igitur decretum in Comitio Oostergoorum Sylvestrium & Oppidanorum.
units.tr: Thereupon the following decree was issued at the assembly of the Oostergoers, for the Sylvestrians and the townsmen:

units.la: Vt in florenum aureum avertendis rapinis grassationibusque militum quatuordecim sestertij penderentur, tribunique ærariorum Boudewinus Loeus, Paulus Gellius, Gellius Sibæus, Popko Roorda, Siboldus Ayfma & Otto Svalue juriperitus ad præstandas in publico rationes coram nobilitate populoque, Frisico adigerentur. Liberando quoque Doconi Martnæ, qui in Sylvestri ad Ouram tractu captus erat tria millia aureorum assignarentur, sub cautione tamen, ut repeterentur. Quod ad Merodium Vicarium provinciæ gubernatorem attineret, decernebant Ordines ut si in provincia foret, pro more, confessus Novem-viralis caput atque præses haberetur, deq; ijs, quæ ad bellum pacemque denique ad conservationem juris publici spectarent, cum Novem-viris consultaret. Hac tamen cautione interposita, ut per illius absentiam consultandi deliberandique Ordinibus eorumque Delegatis jus foret. Quod ad Senatum juridicum spectaret, nam & hoc criminabatur Merodius, quod regundæ provinciæ se immiscere illum facturum & lege recepta, curaturosque, Ordines ne quid detrimenti. Hæc in Comitio 8. Kalend. Mart. perscripta.
units.tr: That, to prevent the plundering and raids of the soldiers, fourteen stivers be paid for each gold florin; and that the paymasters, Boudewinus Loeus, Paulus Gellius, Gellius Sibaeus, Popko Roorda, Siboldus Ayfma, and Otto Svalue, a jurist, be compelled to render account in public before the nobility and the Frisian people. Also, for the release of Doco Martna, who had been captured in the Sylvestrian district near the Oura, three thousand gold pieces were to be assigned, under the condition, however, that they be repaid. As for Merodius, the vice-governor of the province, the Estates decreed that, if he was in the province, he should, as is customary, be regarded as the head and president of the Nine-men council, and should consult them about matters concerning war and peace and, finally, the maintenance of public law. Yet this proviso was added: that during his absence the Estates and their delegates should have the right to consult and deliberate. As for the Judicial Senate, for Merodius was also accused of this, that he would meddle in regulating the province, and, once the law was received, would take care that the Estates suffered no harm. These things were drawn up at the assembly on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.

units.la: Quæ partim ex æmulatione, quæ surgenti reip. quoque innascebatur, partim ex studio tuendæ libertatis aut dominationis profecta tenerrimas res fatigavere.
units.tr: These measures, partly arising from the rivalry that was also being born within the rising commonwealth, and partly from zeal for defending liberty or for dominion, wore down its most delicate affairs.

units.la: Mox Transl-Isulani per Olthovium & Cornputtium cohortium ductores, qui Steenvicam oppidum egregiâ virtute ac laude defenderant, auxilia, bellicumq; commeatum majores Frisios poposcere exemplo Nienortij qui isto tempore apud Husingium (pagus Omlandiæ est) cum hoste congressus pulveris pyrij inopiâ, ut Franckena notat, evitandæ cladi retrocesserat. Idem autor tradit Nienortios omnium indigos omnia petijsse, effusosque in omnem militarem luxum & intemperantiam saevioris belli brumaeque aspera geniali hilaritate emollijsse.
