Unde saevior armorum tempestas cis ac trans Lavicam exorta, adhitente Renneberigio, ut ægritudinem animi ex desertâ Steenvicâ contractam fiduciâ Gro-
units.tr: Soon the Trans-Isulanians, through the commanders of the cohorts, Olthovius and Cornputtius, who had defended the town of Steenwijk with outstanding courage and renown, and the greater Frisians, demanded help and military supplies, after the example of Nienortius. At that time Nienortius, having met the enemy at Husingen (a village of Omlandia), had withdrawn, as Franckena notes, to avoid defeat because of a shortage of gunpowder. The same author reports that the Nienortians, lacking everything, asked for everything, and, given over to every kind of military luxury and excess, softened the harsher storm of war and the harsh winter with pleasant merriment. Hence a fiercer storm of arms arose on both sides of the Lauwers, with Rennenberg encouraging it, so that he might lessen the distress of mind caused by the abandonment of Steenwijk by the confidence of

units.la: cIↄ. Io. Groninganæ urbis, sparsis per omnem agrum copijs minueret. Quod LXXXI. incommodum ut Frisijs majoribus, ipsisque etiam Transla-vicanis grave erat, ita maxime eos premebat, qui Groningam potentissimam urbem ac libertatis sedem crudis Philippi imperijs, & imprimis defectori Rennebergio serviliter parere indignabantur.
units.tr: of the city of Groningen, by scattering his forces over the whole countryside. This misfortune in the year 1581 was as grievous to the greater Frisians, and even to the Trans-Lauwersians themselves, as it was especially burdensome to those who indignantly endured that Groningen, the most powerful city and seat of liberty, should obey, like slaves, the harsh commands of Philip and especially of the deserter Rennenberg.

units.la: Igitur tecto nomine, sub specie sollicitandæ societatis scriptum quoddam, Londini Anglorum, ut præferebatur, impressum ad Groninganos transmissum, quo jus antiquum, avitæque libertatis gloria cum novæ servitutis fœdâ professione conferebatur:
units.tr: Therefore, under a disguised name, and under the pretext of stirring up a league, a certain writing, printed at London in England, as it was claimed, was sent to the Groningers, in which the ancient law and the glory of ancestral liberty were compared with the shameful profession of a new servitude:

units.la: NATVRA rerum sanctissima Parens, Groningani non sui tantum amorem, sed & proximi humanis mentibus ingeneravit, & ita quidem, ut ex unius incommodo ac discrimine alterius sæpe periculum exsurgat. Quam naturæ legem confundi persæpe non exempla tantum veterum temporum, sed hæ tempestates Belgicæ recentibus aliis docuerunt. Sive errore humani consilij, quod suâ etiam varietate ex temperamentis corporum dissentit, sive instigatione hostium ac culpa. Equidem non credendum est illam pravitatem nostris ingenijs non subesse, à bono legitimoque fine abduci cum voluptate sepatiantur. Præsertim cum ea civilium bellorum, quibus cum luctamur, calamitas sit, ut vitiis gravis & aspera, ne victoribus quidem læta sit, quos ad lenitatem & legitimum prosperitatis humanæ usum erga victos miseratio impellit. Igitur satius fuisset jure potius ac pacto, quam armis egisse, parcendo illorum sanguini, quos legum & societatis communio conectebat. Quod cum vos imprimis concernat, Groningani, causam belli & armorum dissimulare non potestis. Neque enim hæc in socios atque amicos, in congeneres & legibus connexos sumpta per errorem reputabitis, aut ut ex unius damno alterius commodum increscat, sed odio tyranni & jurati hostis, tum amore libertatis, quæ honores, opes, omnemque prosperitatem, ac affluentiam rerum parit. Imprimis cum vestra libertas tanto sanctior atque eminentior vobis pra ceteris gentibus fuerit, ut in urbe civitateque vestra & per Omlandiam, non Principes, sed Præfectos Protectoresque agnoverit. Nunc vero pra ceteris nationibus, quas confines aut socias habetis, oppressa spectatur, erecto in urbe vestra regio & quidem validissimo castello quo externa peregrinaque colluvies, legibus vestris, corporibus atq; animis pro arbitrio & lubidine suâ imperitet. Hanc ut restitutam redditamq; nostris terris habeamus, arma sumpsimus, non mutuo exitio, aut ut in viscera nostra sanguinemque sæviremus, sed in Hispanos, qui sanctissimus etiamnum armorum nostrorum prætextus est. Apud nos verò imprimis, quibus inter omnia mortalium & fortunæ bona vitâ carior libertas habetur. Ut tanto nocentiores, haberi possint, qui arma, qui consilia cum tyranno miscent, subvertendis socijs, amicis atque contivibus, quorum omne studium in conservatione legum & libertatis & desiderio pacis concordiaque conquiescit. Quæ cum sine armorum subsidio haberi non possit, actu ac fraude hostium effectum est, ut ea in suos convertant, divisosque & communibus viribus destitutos singulos opprimant. Caterum nos ab oppressoribus legum, à violatoribus fœderum sacrorumque, à conjugum liberorumq; nostrorum pollutoribus alienos facit infelicis servitij fastidium, & ne libertas majoribus nostris pace belloque quæsita tyranno cedat. Quod certe levitate illorum alibi effectum est, qui fidem patriæ datam, venalem & enormis potentiæ servam ministramque fecerunt. Quibuscum cum vobis nihil commune mune sit, Groningani, aut saltem esse debeat, quos excelsa indoles & servitij pertæsa commendatos annalibus posterisque fecit, tamen hoc tempore vestrâ patientiâ & fœdissimæ servitutis ludibrio gloriam Frisici nominis attaminatis, quod multis abhinc sæculis, reliquarum gentium invidiâ, ut exterorum Principum imperia ita arma repressit. Quæ omnia ut ad animum revocetis, Groningani, hortamur, cogitetisq; eadem ingenia, easdem indoles, eosdem spiritus; eandem virtutem, eadem arma quæ vicinis vestris esse. Quo magis mirari ad miraculum usque libet, ita vos à virtute nobilissimorum fortissimorumque majorum & à vestrâ descivisse, ut tyrannorum dominationes ac imperia pro justis acceptisq; habeatis, quibuscum nulla vitæ jurisque communio est. Qui autores fuere, ut cum Omlandis intestina arma misceretis, disceptareti sque per vim de jure vestro, quod à peregrino, nec armato, sed à vobis ipsis, à proceribus vestris intra Curias vestras & comitia majorum more petendum fuisset. Cogitate plus damni datum illâ tempestate urbi, reipublicæque ac libertati vestræ fuisse, quam si totam Omlandiam perdidissetis. Reputate multos ex vestris ad paupertatem mendicitatemque propulsos, conjuges uxoresque vestras maritorum solatio & consuetudine viduatas, innocentes liberos & propaginem vestram æternitatem genti & imperio vestro daturam parentibus suis orbatam, optimos cives civiumque filios prædonum raptorumque contubernio ascriptos, multum sanguinis, ut sub Tyrannio essetis, profusum, multum æris cum jactura erarij & fortunarum vestrarum bello regio impensum, ne spe quidem vobis adhuc facta munitionum in Frisiâ Trans-Isulaniâque potiundi. Quin spectate Neozilandâ munitione ejectum cum ignominia Rennebergium, longèque abesse ut majorem Frisiam suæ potestatis faciat agerrimè ad defectorem violatoremque fœderis, in quod juraverat, rediturum. Econtra soli à socijs, à vicinis sejuncti agitis, sine commercio, sine subsidio tributi & pecuniæ, quam ex Hispania petendam invium mare, aut longinquitas loci intercipit, non sine rerum vestrarum detrimento & dispendio, quas aut hostilis vis, aut vestrorum militum insolentia depræatur. Qui etsi victores gentium se fore opinentur, quas ad Regem se reducturos extinctâ libertate gloriantur, tamen scitote urbem vestram medio Frisiam inter & Trans-Isulaniam loco positam, regiæ dominationis & simul vestræ servitutis perenne domicilium fore. Illos ipsos quoque Hispanos communi & vestrâ etiam ope manuque arcibus castellisque, quæ demoliti estis, exturbatos, magis magisque regni sui in securitatem emunituros, ne eadem arcium excidia, eadem præsidiorum exterminia patiantur, quæ ante pertulere. Ita illis perpetua durioris imperij tutela aut possessio, vobis perpetuæ servitutis urbe in vestra munimentum erit. Nam ita Italiam, ita Siciliam, ita Indias, loca natura & ingenio munita retinent ut erigere se nequeant, qui semel depressi sunt. Præter hoc urbem vestram, Groningani; aut omnium rerum penuriâ circumjacentibus hostibus vestris, aut internâ civium vestrorum seditione gravabitis. Quod si fiat, facile eveniet, ut vos ipsi qui spem vobis auctioris imperij facitis, fato & divinæ providentiæ ordinatione urbem cum dominatione amittatis. Utramque verò facile retinebitis, si cum amicis, cum vicinis vestris in gratiam redeatis, quorum intercessione adjudicabuntur aserenturque vobis, quæ fortunæ & magnis casibus obnoxia sunt. Hoc etiam expendite in Frisia & Omlandia non nisi per vos bellum esse, habituros pacem, quietem, prosperitatem, si æterna amicitia ac fide nobiscum jungamini. Nunc verò divinæ iræ satellites & flagella nostra auditis hinc, quibus ne belli quidem metus fœlicibus terris foret. Ea propter commonemus ac hortamur, ut an-
units.tr: Nature, the most holy parent of things, has implanted in human minds a love not only of oneself but also of one's neighbour, and so indeed that danger often arises for one man from another's misfortune and peril. That this law of nature is very often overturned, not only the examples of past times but also these recent Belgian storms have taught. Whether through the error of human counsel, which, by its very variety, differs according to the temperaments of bodies, or through the incitement and fault of enemies. Indeed, it must not be believed that this perversity is not present in our natures, that men allow themselves to be led away with pleasure from a good and lawful end. Especially since the calamity of civil wars, with which we are struggling, is so grievous and harsh in its vices that it is not happy even for the victors, whom compassion impels toward gentleness and the lawful use of human prosperity toward the conquered. Therefore it would have been better to act by right and by agreement rather than by arms, sparing the blood of those whom the common bond of laws and society joined together. Since this concerns you above all, Groningers, you cannot disguise the cause and the purpose of the war and of arms. For you will not judge that these have been undertaken through error against allies and friends, against kinsmen and men bound by the same laws, or so that one's gain may grow from another's loss, but from hatred of the tyrant and the sworn enemy, and also from love of liberty, which brings forth honours, wealth, and all prosperity and abundance of goods. Especially since your liberty has been so much holier and more eminent for you than for other peoples, that in your city and state, and throughout Omlandia, it has acknowledged not princes but prefects and protectors. Now, however, beyond the other nations which you have as neighbours or allies, it is seen to be oppressed, since in your city a royal fortress, and indeed a very strong castle, has been erected, by which a foreign and alien rabble may rule over your laws, your bodies, and your minds at its own will and pleasure. We have taken up arms so that we may have this liberty restored and returned to our lands, not for mutual destruction, nor to rage against our own vitals and blood, but against the Spaniards, which is still the most sacred pretext of our arms. Above all among us, for whom liberty is held dearer than life, among all the goods of mortals and of fortune. Those who mix arms and counsels with the tyrant, in subverting allies, friends, and fellow citizens, whose whole zeal rests on the preservation of laws and liberty and the desire for peace and harmony, may be thought all the more guilty. Since this cannot be had without the support of arms, it has come about, by the deed and deceit of the enemy, that they turn these arms against their own people and, dividing them and stripping them of common strength, crush them one by one. Yet the disgust of unhappy servitude, and the fear that liberty, won by our ancestors in peace and war, might yield to a tyrant, keep us apart from the oppressors of the laws, the violators of covenants and sacred things, and the defilers of our wives and children. This has certainly been brought about elsewhere by the fickleness of those who made the pledge given to their country a bargain, and made themselves the venal and servile instruments of an enormous power. You, Groningers, have nothing in common with them, or at least ought not to have; you whom a lofty character and weariness of servitude have commended to the annals and to posterity; yet at this time, by your patience and by the mockery of most shameful servitude, you have sullied the glory of the Frisian name, which for many centuries, despite the envy of other peoples, has repressed the rule of foreign princes as well as their arms. We exhort you to call all these things to mind, Groningers, and to consider that your minds, your natures, your spirits, your virtue and your arms are the same as those of your neighbours. Therefore we are moved to wonder all the more that you have so fallen away from the virtue of your most noble and brave ancestors, and from your own, that you regard the dominations and commands of tyrants as just and acceptable, with whom you have no community of life or law. Those who were the authors of this have brought it about that you mix internal arms with the Omlandians, and contend by force over your right, which should have been sought not from a foreigner, nor under arms, but from yourselves, from your nobles, within your own courts and assemblies, according to the custom of your elders. Consider that more harm was done in that storm to the city, to your commonwealth and your liberty, than if you had lost all of Omlandia. Reflect that many of yours have been driven to poverty and beggary, your wives deprived of the comfort and company of their husbands, innocent children, and your offspring, who were to give eternity to your nation and dominion, bereaved of their parents, your best citizens and the sons of citizens enrolled in the company of robbers and plunderers; much blood has been spilled so that you might be under a tyrant, much money has been spent from the treasury and your fortunes with the loss of the war's cost, and you have not yet been given even the hope of seizing the fortresses in Frisia and Trans-Lauwers. Look further at Nienortius's fortress, from which Rennenberg was expelled with disgrace, and it is far from the case that he will make the Greater Frisia subject to his power; he will soon return, as a deserter and violator of the covenant he swore to keep. On the contrary, you alone, cut off from your allies and neighbours, live without commerce, without the help of tribute and money, which the unsailable sea or the remoteness of the place cuts off from Spain, not without loss and expense of your goods, which are plundered either by hostile force or by the insolence of your own soldiers. Although they think they will be the conquerors of the nations, whom they boast they will bring back to the King with liberty extinguished, yet know that your city, placed midway between Frisia and Trans-Lauwers, will be a perpetual dwelling for royal domination and at the same time for your servitude. Those very Spaniards also, with your common help and labour, cast out from the citadels and castles which you have demolished, will fortify their kingdom ever more securely, lest they suffer the same destruction of fortresses and the same ruin of garrisons that they suffered before. Thus for them a perpetual guardianship or possession of harsher rule, and for you, in your city, the fortification of perpetual servitude will be the outcome. For thus they keep Italy, thus Sicily, thus the Indies, places fortified by nature and by skill, so that those who have once been cast down cannot raise themselves up. Besides this, Groningers, you will be burdened either by a want of all things, with your enemies surrounding you, or by the internal sedition of your own citizens. If this comes about, it will easily happen that you, who hold out to yourselves the hope of a larger empire, will by fate and by the ordering of divine providence lose the city together with its dominion. Yet you will easily keep both if you return to favour with your friends and neighbours, through whose intercession those things which are subject to fortune and great chances will be awarded and secured for you. Consider this as well: that in Frisia and Omlandia there is war only through yourselves, and you will have peace, rest, and prosperity if you join with us in eternal friendship and faith. But now you hear the satellites of divine wrath and our scourges from this quarter, for whom not even the fear of war would be in happy lands. Therefore we warn and exhort that you [shun] every evil from our country, from you and your city, from our borders and yours, which we have as neighbours, lest by divine disposition you suffer the misery that you have brought upon us. Indeed, this is the usual outcome of arms, and the turn of fortune, that for the wicked and for those

units.la: ferri à patriâ nostrâ, à vobis ac urbe vestrâ, à finibus nostris vestrisque quos contiguos habemus, omne malum cavetis, ne divinâ dispositione miseriam patiamini quam nobis intulistis. Equidem is armorum exitus, ea sortunæ vicissitudo esse solet, ut pravis ac ad bona sua obstinatis ac contumacibus ea rependat quæ merueré. Sed hæc ægræ urbis & levitatis vestræ ac inconstantiæ magna indicia sunt, ut modo harum, modo illarum partium, nec retinere libertatem nec imperia regia pasitis. Reputate equidem quanto cum gaudio, quantâ cum ovatione, post ejectum abductumque in captivitatem Roblesium urbem vestram impleveritis, quæ isto tempore alterum libertatis suæ natalem accepisse credebatur. Econtra quam peregrino imperio, quod servituti vestræ connexum est lædamini bodie, revocatis urbem in vestram Hispanis, qui omnem calamitatem vobis suo ingressu attulere. Quippe agri vastati, abacta pecora vestra, domus villæque incendia passæ, civibus inquilinisque manus injectæ, & ita quidem ut nihil malis vestris addi possit, nisi remedium. Sed cæcitatis vestræ, sed erroris divinæ cælestesque causæ sunt, quæ in abdito positæ bonæ mentis exsortes vos faciunt. Ita fit ut ex fragili arbitrio omnia agentes mala pro bonis, prava pro rectis intueamini. Quam mentium nubem ut dispellat Deus precabimur fideliter, ne vos in perpetuam caliginem demersi continuas tempestates, continua bella, aut saltem metum habeatis.
units.tr: You take care to keep the sword away from our country, from you and your city, and from our borders and yours, which lie next to each other, so that you do not suffer through divine arrangement the misery you have inflicted on us. Indeed, this is usually how the outcome of arms and the turn of fortune go: they repay those who are perverse, obstinate and stubborn in their own ways with what they have deserved. But these are great signs of your sick city's fickleness and inconstancy, that now on one side and now on the other you neither keep your liberty nor bear royal rule. Consider how great a joy, how great an ovation, you showed when Roblesius was driven out and carried off into captivity, and how your city was thought at that time to have received a second birthday of its freedom. On the other hand, consider how you are harmed today by the foreign rule that is bound up with your servitude, now that you have let the Spaniards back into your city, who brought every calamity upon you by their entry. For fields were laid waste, your herds driven off, houses and farms set on fire, citizens and tenants laid hands upon, and so thoroughly that nothing can be added to your troubles except a remedy. But the causes are your blindness, your error and divine and heavenly reasons, which, hidden away, make you lack a sound mind. So it comes about that, acting on a fragile judgment, you look on evils as goods and perverse things as right. We will faithfully pray that God disperses this cloud of minds, lest, plunged into perpetual darkness, you have continual storms, continual wars, or at least fear.

units.la: Invenio in actis post dimissum Dodonem Larium cohortis ductorem munitionis Aelsumanæ custodiam Utingeranis, ac post Rauerdijs Idardijsque demandatam, eosdemque Utingeranos, Rauerdios, ac Idardios supremæ Curiæ supplices factos, æquandæ solo munitionis mandatum sollicitasse. Curiam quoque Tiallengo Wickelio Jurisconsulto & Senatori, hac de re cum Præfecto provinciæ Ordinumque Delegatis potestatem accepisse, totumque negotium, novo metu indies ex vicino hoste auc-to, datâ operâ prolatum. Scipionem quoque Meckmannum cum Orichio Dojemo Amstelodamum pro legatis missos Aurantium Principem, ibi commorantem ordinandis tam pacis quam belli rebus in Frisiam evocasse, ipsumque Principem, etsi Frisiæ rectorem, variis curis sollicitudinibusque apud Batavos distractum, profectionis suæ consilium in tempus distulisse. Quo tempore Ordines inter generales Frisiosque de provinciarum Senatu rite constituendo, de jure Frisico asserendo, de supplendis copijs, de assignandâ Alençonio pensione, de militari disciplinâ corrigenda, de conscribendis tribus equitum millibus multa disceptabantur. Quibus postulatis cum gravari se Frisij quererentur, solenni comitio Leovardiæ indicto missis Delphos Leone Bejemo viro nobili, & Jacobo Jacobæo Consule Bolsuerdiano responderunt: Causam cunctationis & moræ, quod condicto die Ord. Generalium Legatorumque conventui interesse nequiverint, molem curarum occupationumque comitialium fuisse. Velle se quidem singulis ex provincijs Senatum constitui qui gerendis rebus præsit, cæterum sub cautione, ut numeri ratio habebatur, Frisijque ternos eo in Senatu habeant. Hoc quoque delegatis suis demandasse, ut eminentiæ, jurisque Frisici ratio habeatur, provinciæque prærogativa & dignitas, quam Carolo Philippoque per Frisiam rerum potiuntibus concessam possedissent, asseratur. Quod ad supplementa cohortium, intendendamque disciplinam militarem attinet ret, velle Frisios, ut ista fiant colliganturque quanto ocyus & ut mili- taris licentia severis legibus coërceatur. Propterea nolle, delectum Germanorum equitum, quorum insolentiam Geldri, Zutphanienses, Ultrajectini, Trans-Isulani, Drentini & Tubantes experti essent, institui; cæterum ut ex unitis provinciis tria equitum millia colligantur, tanto minus incommodum factura, quanto magis arctiusque natali solo obligarentur. Interim permittere ut Alençonio ex ærario provinciarum fœderatarum viginti aureorum millia quotannis præstentur, quam diu fœderatis in provinciis commoraturus sit, & quam diu illi de conditione aliâ prospectum fuerit. Extraordinarijs vero tributis, quæ petuntur, ante assensum præbere non posse, quam rationes ærarij omnium provinciarum initæ forent. Neque enim alia onera recipi per Frisiam posse, quæ menstruo 24. millium tributo gravata levamentum ad xii. M. accipere debeat, rapinis & vastationibus hostium suorumque militum exhausta. Hæc Leov. 15. Mart. perscripta ac Legatis communicata. Quibus difficultatibus etiam hoc accedebat, quod qui mos rerum mortalium, prosperis bellorum adversa innascerentur, forisque læta, domi ac in ipsis reip. visceribus exitiosa suborirentur. Præterquam enim, quod miles, sive disciplinæ neglectu, sive stipendiorum egentiâ in licentiam pronus conspiceretur, ita legionum tribuni cohortiumq; præfecti progressum quoque publicæ prosperitatis morabantur, magnâ stipendia facientium infrequentiâ, quos ad signa & recensionem pro more habendam publicæ autoritatis solemnitas vocabat. Reliquis malis, quod inter primos status & in rep. eminentissimos exorta, nullus accusator repertus, aut qui in melius corrigendis temporum vitijs consuleret, quæ paucos inter secretim alita, postmodum egressa publicum de primatu certamen aperuere. Quare adductâ magnum in discrimen rep. ad Gulielmum Aurantium provinciæ rectorem honestissima Legatio instituta, quo militaribus malis & languenti disciplinæ, tum magnorum æmulationibus discordijsque mederetur. Qui auditis Amstelodami Orichio Dojemo & Jacobo Jacobæus Legatis adscitisque in comitatum, ut nobilissimus vir Scipio Meckmannus notavit, uxore Loïsâ ac quatuor filiabus cum Gulielmo Nassovio filio naturali, seu ut alij, cum Hohenloo profectionem in Frisiam instituit, advectusque Harlingam, de quâ tanquam maritimâ urbe muniendâ cogitabat, magnâ procerum populique gratulatione exceptus est. Franckena in Ephemeride tradit, Novem-viros cmnes collegio & Senatus sede egressos Harlingamque salutando Principi provectos, omne honoris officijq; genus Provinciæ Gubernatori detulisse, Principemque Harlingæ adhuc agentem multa in secessionem partium eruptura salutaribus decretis composuisse. Igitur & Hohenloius, qui provincialium animos rerum ac fortunæ adversitate à se alienaverat, ad colloquium se Principi arbitro obtulit, speciosisque rationibus infoelicitati suæ & simul publicæ patrocinatus est.
units.tr: I find in the records that, after Dodo Larius, leader of a cohort, was dismissed, the guarding of the fortress of Aelsum was entrusted first to the people of Utingeradeel and afterwards to Rauerdi and Idardi; and that these same people of Utingeradeel, Rauerdi and Idardi, having made supplication to the Supreme Court, sought the order to level the fortress with the ground. The Court also gave Tiallingo Wickelius, jurist and senator, the power to deal with this matter together with the governor of the province and the deputies of the Estates, and the whole business was deliberately put off, while the new fear, increased daily by the nearby enemy, grew. Scipio Meckmannus, too, and Orichius Dojemus were sent as envoys from Amsterdam to summon the Prince of Orange, who was staying there, to Friesland to arrange both peace and war matters; and the Prince himself, although governor of Friesland, distracted by various cares and anxieties among the Batavians, postponed the plan of his journey to a later time. At that time the Estates-General and the Frisians disputed much over setting up a provincial senate properly, over asserting Frisian law, over supplying troops, over assigning a pension to Alençon, over reforming military discipline and over raising three thousand cavalry. When the Frisians complained that these demands weighed on them, they called a solemn assembly at Leeuwarden and sent Leo Beyema, a nobleman, and Jacobus Jacobaeus, consul of Bolsward, to Delft to reply: the cause of the delay and hindrance was that they had been unable to attend the meeting of the Estates-General and their envoys on the appointed day, because of the mass of cares and business of the assembly. They themselves wished a senate to be set up in each province to direct affairs, but on condition that the proportion of numbers be kept, and that the Frisians have three seats in that senate. They had also instructed their deputies to see that the eminence and the right of Friesland, and the privilege and dignity of the province, which it had possessed when Charles and Philip held sway over Friesland, be asserted. As to the supplementing of the cohorts and the tightening of military discipline, the Frisians wished this done and gathered as quickly as possible, and military licence to be restrained by strict laws. For this reason they did not want the levy of German cavalry to be instituted, whose insolence Gelderland, Zutphen, Utrecht, Overijssel, Drenthe and the Tubantes had experienced; rather, that three thousand cavalry be raised from the united provinces, which would be all the less burdensome the more closely and firmly they were bound to their native soil. Meanwhile they permitted that twenty thousand gold pieces be paid yearly to Alençon from the treasury of the United Provinces, for as long as he should remain in the United Provinces and until some other arrangement for him had been made. But they could not agree to the extraordinary taxes that were demanded before the accounts of the treasury of all the provinces had been drawn up. For no other burdens could be received through Friesland, which, weighed down by a monthly tax of twenty-four thousand, ought to receive relief to the extent of twelve thousand, exhausted by the plunder and devastation of the enemy and of their own soldiers. These things were written out at Leeuwarden on 15 March and communicated to the envoys. To these difficulties there was also added the fact that, as is the way of mortal affairs, adversities arise out of the prosperous fortunes of wars, and what is pleasing abroad comes up as harmful at home and in the very vitals of the commonwealth. For not only was the soldier seen to be prone to licence, whether from neglect of discipline or from lack of pay, but the tribunes of the legions and the prefects of the cohorts also delayed the progress of public prosperity, because of the great scarcity of men who served for pay and whom the solemnity of public authority summoned to the standards and to the customary muster. Besides these evils, there was the fact that among the first estates and the most eminent men in the commonwealth a quarrel had arisen, and no accuser was found, nor anyone who would take thought to correct the vices of the times; these, fostered in secret by a few, afterwards came out and opened a public contest over primacy. Therefore, with the commonwealth brought into great danger, a most honourable embassy was undertaken to William of Orange, governor of the province, so that he might remedy the military ills and the languishing discipline, and also the rivalries and discords of great men. He, having heard at Amsterdam Orichius Dojemus and Jacobus Jacobaeus as envoys, and having taken into his train, as the most noble man Scipio Meckmannus has noted, his wife Louise and four daughters, together with his natural son William Nassau, or, as others say, together with Hohenlo, began his journey into Friesland; and, carried to Harlingen, whose fortifying as a maritime town he was considering, he was received with great rejoicing by the nobles and the people. Franckena reports in his Ephemeris that all nine men (the Nine), leaving their college and seat of the senate, went out to Harlingen to greet the Prince, and offered every kind of honour and service to the governor of the province; and that the Prince, while still staying at Harlingen, settled with salutary decrees many things that were about to break out into the secession of parties. So too Hohenlo, who had alienated the minds of the provincials by his conduct of affairs and the adversity of fortune, offered himself for a conference with the Prince as arbiter, and with specious reasons defended both his own unhappiness and at the same time that of the public.

units.la: NEQVE enim, inquiebat, socordiæ meæ, FRISII, quid impu- tare potestis, quo minus dextrè pugnaverim, qui Senatum, qui Lega-tos ad vos misi, indicaviq; quantum periculi ac discriminis mihi exerci-tuiq; meo incumberet. Obtestatione quoq; honestissimâ usus sum, ut nisi
units.tr: For neither, he said, can you, Frisians, impute to my sloth that I did not fight skilfully, who sent a senate and envoys to you and made clear how great a danger and peril threatened me and my army. I also used a most honourable entreaty, that unless

units.la: nisi pecuniam, belli, ut nostis, nervum, nisi commeatum mitteretis, contineri militare corpus & turbidas legiones in officio non posse. Quorum omnium etsi fideliter vos monuerim, tamen discrimini meo & simul publico subventum non est. Igitur militari more & antiquis quoq; Imperatoribus usurpato mobilem exercitum, & jam seditioni furorique proximum dividere ac segregare coactus fui, ut locis disjun&ti obsequia inducrent, quae conjuncti sociatique suarum virium fiducia exuerant.
units.tr: unless you sent money, the sinew of war, as you know, unless you sent supplies, the military body and the restless legions could not be kept in order. Although I warned you of all these things faithfully, still no help was given to my peril and to the public at the same time. Therefore, by military custom and as commanders of old also practised, I was forced to divide and separate an army that was mobile and already close to mutiny and frenzy, so that, scattered apart, they might bring about obedience, which, united and banded together, they had cast off through confidence in their own strength.

units.la: Ad quae cum Frisij responderent, plusque in ipso fati infoelicitatem, quam neglectum boni ducis officium culparent, Aurantij arbitrio res permissa definitaque est. Qui frenando ambitus crimine, quod optima libertatis initia & comitiorum ordinem turbabat, legem edixit, ut ordinaria ad comitia conventusque annuos ex nobilitate & proprietariorum ordine patriae amantes rerumque periti vocarentur, eligendisque Deputatis aut Novem-viris Oostergoi, Westergoi, Sylvestres, Oppidani bis seni nuncuparentur, offerrerenturque Rectori provinciae, qui delectum haberet, delectosque in muneris possessionem mitteret. Hac tamen cautione interposita, ut propinquitatis consanguinitatisq; in quartum, affinitatis in tertium ratio haberetur, removendis conspirationibus, & ne sanguinis societatisque cognatione juncti potentiam acquirerent reip. & libertati gravem. Quae Principis constitutio a Deputatis Novem-viris approbata confirmataque usq; dum aliter solenni comitio statuererur, vim & efficaciam retinuit. Jam enim Aurantius postulata quaedam Delegatis Ordinum exhibuerat, quae amovendae rerum consusioni, stabiliendoq; bono in rep. Ordini perscripta Ipem emendandi status publici, pacisque inter discordes aemulosque conciliandae pollicebantur. Caeterum imperij cupido, optimis florentissimisq; rebus exitio orta Juridicum Ordinumq; Senatum adhuc committebat, postquam hic potiundae, ille retinendae dominationis desiderio captus Principis animum non sine acerbitate fatigaret. Unde utrinque multa odio partium perscripta, quae Philippici principatus & imperij prima aetate in consuetudinem perducta verso temporum statu innovanda libertati videbantur.
units.tr: When the Frisians replied to these things, and blamed the unhappiness of fate itself more than the neglect of a good commander's duty, the matter was left to the judgment of Orange and settled. He, checking the crime of electioneering, which was disturbing the excellent beginnings of liberty and the order of the assemblies, issued a law that for the ordinary assembly and annual meetings men from the nobility and the class of landowners who loved their country and were skilled in affairs should be summoned, and that for choosing deputies, or Nine Men, the twelve of Oostergo, Westergo, the Sylvestres and the townsmen should be named, and offered to the governor of the province, who would hold the selection and send those chosen into possession of their office. Yet this caution was added, that the reckoning of kinship and blood-relationship should extend to the fourth degree, and of marriage-relationship to the third, so that conspiracies might be removed, and lest men joined by ties of blood and alliance should gain a power burdensome to the commonwealth and to liberty. This constitution of the Prince, approved and confirmed by the deputies, the Nine Men, retained its force and effect until it should be otherwise settled at a solemn assembly. For Orange had already presented certain demands to the envoys of the Estates, which were drawn up to remove the confusion of affairs and to establish the good of the commonwealth for the Estates, and promised a reform of the public condition and the reconciling of parties at odds and rivals. But the desire for power, born to the ruin of the most excellent and flourishing affairs, still set the Juridical Court and the Senate of the Estates against each other, since the one, seized with a desire to gain dominion, and the other to keep it, wore down the mind of the Prince not without bitterness. Hence on both sides much was written out in hatred of the factions, which, having been made into custom in the first age of Philip's principate and rule, appeared to need renewing for liberty now that the state of the times had changed.

units.la: Quare Aurantius quo finem contentioni imponeret & ne resp. tenerrimis adhuc infantiae suae annis & foelicitate adhuc dubia, quae desertura regem credebatur, litem diremit, specieque edicti crescentem indies discordiam composuit.
units.tr: Therefore Aurantius, in order to put an end to the dispute, and so that the commonwealth, still in the tender early years of its infancy and with its prosperity still uncertain (which was believed to be about to desert the king), should not be torn apart, settled the growing discord by means of an edict.

units.la: LEGATIONE vestra, Frisii, mense praeterito sollicitatus sum ut in provinciam hanc venirem.
units.tr: BY your embassy, Frisians, I was summoned last month to come into this province.

units.la: LEGATIONE vestrâ, FRISII, mense praeterito sollicitatus sum ut in provinciam hanc venirem. Et quanquam excusari ab hac molestia potuissem, quod Ordinum Belgicae conventus praesentiae meae egeret, tamen amore vestri commodique publici in provinciam meo regimini & fidei commissam adveni, non sine spe an dicam fiducia consilia vestra in unum idemque conspiratura. Sed omnia aemulationum discordiarumque plena invenio, magno provinciae vestro damno, & cum jactura prosperitatis publicae, cujus cursum & incrementa fatalis secundis rebus dissensio subvertit. Ego vero ut pestilenti huic malo, remedium praescriberem, quaedam ordinandae reip. & sanandae animorum exacerbationi destinata conceperam, quae a vicario meo Bernardo Merodio, provinciali Curia & Deputatis Ordinum tamdiu servari retinerique volebam, donec pleniorem emendandae firmandaeque reip. occasionem nactus essem. Equidem ejus animi semper fui, ut me publica etiam provinciarum fata ac negotia gotia tractantem sustinentemque vestris commodis impenderem. Huic fini Præfecturam provinciæ vestræ non semel abnuendo tandem suscepi, svique ut post Rennebergij defectionem meæ fidei & imperio committeretur. Et quoniam cæteris quoque provinciis inserviendum mihi erat, petiistis, ut si ipse præesse rebus vestris non possem, Vicarium vobis darem mitteremque cum autoramento in provinciam, qui meo nomine res vestras & officium Præfecti expediret. Itaque Bernardum Merodium virum belli pacisque gloriâ, & multa majorum imagine clarum, prudentiaque per ætatem & rerum experientiam eximium ad vos misi, quo rectius vestra procederent, quæ privatæ dissensiones rectore atque arbitrio destitutæ distorserant. Cujus auctoritati ne quid decedat, de consilio tum Curiæ & Deputatorum, Nobilitatisque & Oppidanorum statutum est, ut eundem Merodium pro Vicario meo ex jure concessi à me diplomatis habeatis, neve quid impedimenti injiciatis potestati à me concessæ. Quin decerno petoque ut eundem tanquam Præsidem Justitiæ & Senatus juridici agnoscatis, Curiæque supremæ jus sartum tectum curetis, salvâ tamen præturarum oppidorumque jurisdictione, tam in criminalibus quam civilibus actionibus judicyisque, ne quid enorme ac recepto ordini adversum eveniat. Hoc etiam addo determinoque, ut Præsidis Rectorisque vicarij honor ac autoritas à Deputatis Ordinum præstetur, & ut habeat potestatem in commune de belli pacisque negotijs consultandi, deliberandi, decernendique quod è re provinciæ sit. Quare & fœdus Vtrajectinum, omniaque Ordines inter generales Frisiosque acta, ab illo approbari volo, & si quid imposterum sanciendum decernendumque erit, quod regis Dominia, Ecclesiastica bona, fiscales actiones, Canones, indictiones, reliquaque onera & erarij firmamenta in subsidium belli reperta concernet. Quæ ipsa quoque ut in erarium prompte statoque tempore inferantur Vicarius meus, & Deputati provinciæ effectum dabunt, & ne pecuniæ certis usibus decretæ in alios convertantur. Quod ut fiat, Tribunis erarij quæstoribusque; demandatur ut accepti expensique rationes actaque in indicem referant, eaque coram Delegatis Ordinum quovis tempore, aut ipsis Ordinibus solemni anniversarioque comitio exhibeant. Fiscalibus verò actionibus instituendis adversum eos, qui contra patriam, aut cum hostibus faciunt, potestatem faciendam procuratori fisci à Deputatis Ordinum censeo, ut coram supremo Senatu ijs judicium intentet, editorumque; & juris subsidio utatur. Quod ad aggeres, vias, aquæductus & emissaria attinet, ista omnia veteri ex jure & receptâ consuetudine Præfectus Deputatique administrabunt, aut si inter oppidanos agrariosque lis oriatur, eam Senatus Iuridicus sub formâ processus definiet. Religionis verò dissidia, meæ & Ordinum juxtaque Senatus Iuridici curæ erunt, sub hac interea tautione, ne quæ alia doctrina quam reformata publicè habeatur, doceaturque. Creandorum quoque Prætorum morem legitimum proximo comitio restituam, factâ interim provincialibus agrariisque potestate ut si, vacans prætura sit tres patriæ & libertati addictos nuncupent, eosque Præfecto provinciæ, aut per illius absentiam vicario eius offerant, deque consilio Curiæ, aut Deputatorum in prætutiæ possessionem dignitatemque mittant. Et quamvis tota gerendi belli militiaque ratio nobis commissa, aut Vicario nostro sit, tamen concordiæ pacisque causâ decerno, neque apparatum castrorum habeări, neque copias educi, neque oppida obsideri, neque præsidia locorum mutari, neque delectum institui, neque aliunde in Frisiam evocari debere, nisi Ordinum Deputatorumque assensus accesserit, pluriumque suffragijs firmetur. Quod ad exploratores mittendos, ordinandaque secreta consilia, strate-
units.tr: By your embassy, Frisians, I was summoned last month to come into this province. And although I could have been excused from this trouble, since the assembly of the Belgic Estates needed my presence, nevertheless, out of love for you and for the public good, I came into the province entrusted to my government and good faith, not without hope (or, should I say, confidence) that your counsels would combine into one and the same purpose. But I find everything full of rivalries and discords, to the great harm of your province and the loss of public prosperity, whose course and growth a disastrous quarrel has overturned after its favourable beginnings. Indeed, to prescribe a remedy for this pestilent evil, I had devised certain measures intended to set the commonwealth in order and to heal the inflamed minds of men. I wished these to be observed and kept by my deputy Bernard Merode, by the provincial Court and by the deputies of the Estates for as long as it took until I found a fuller opportunity of amending and firmly establishing the commonwealth. Indeed, I have always been of the mind to devote myself to your advantage, sustaining and handling even the public fortunes and affairs of the provinces. To this end I took up the prefecture of your province, after refusing it more than once, and I asked that, after the defection of Rennenberg, it be committed to my good faith and command. And since I had to serve the other provinces as well, you asked that, if I could not myself preside over your affairs, I should give you a deputy and send him into the province with full authority, to manage your affairs and the office of prefect in my name. Accordingly I sent to you Bernard Merode, a man renowned for his glory in war and peace and for the image of his ancestors, and outstanding in prudence through his age and experience of affairs, so that your business might go forward more rightly, since private quarrels, deprived of a ruler and arbiter, had distorted it. So that nothing may detract from his authority, it has been resolved, with the advice of the Court, the deputies, the nobility and the townsmen, that you are to recognise this same Merode as my deputy under the diploma granted to him by me, and that you are not to put any hindrance in the way of the power granted by me. Indeed I decree and ask that you acknowledge him as President of Justice and of the juridical Senate, and that you see to it that the rights of the supreme Court are kept whole and safe, saving however the jurisdiction of the magistracies and towns, in criminal as in civil actions and judgments, so that nothing unusual or contrary to the accepted order happens. I also add and determine this: that the honour and authority of the President and deputy-governor be rendered by the deputies of the Estates, and that he have power to consult, deliberate and decide in common on matters of war and peace, as is for the good of the province. Therefore I wish that the treaty of Utrecht, and all the acts of the Estates-General and the Frisians, be approved by him; and if anything is hereafter to be enacted or decreed concerning the royal domains, ecclesiastical goods, fiscal actions, the canons, the levies, and the other burdens and revenues of the treasury devised for the support of the war, my deputy and the deputies of the province shall see that these too are brought promptly into the treasury at the appointed time, and that the money decreed for fixed uses is not diverted to others. To ensure this, the treasurers and quaestors of the treasury are commanded to bring their accounts of receipts and expenditures and their proceedings into a record, and to present these before the deputies of the Estates at any time, or before the Estates themselves at the solemn annual assembly. As for instituting fiscal actions against those who act against the country or with the enemy, I advise that the fiscal prosecutor be given power by the deputies of the Estates to bring a charge against them before the supreme Senate, and to use the aid of the edicts and of the law. As for dykes, roads, aqueducts and drainage channels, the prefect and deputies shall administer all these according to the ancient law and accepted custom; or if a dispute arises between townsmen and landowners, the juridical Senate shall settle it by the form of legal process. But the disputes over religion shall be the care of myself, of the Estates and likewise of the juridical Senate, under this proviso meanwhile: that no doctrine other than the reformed be publicly held or taught. I shall also restore at the next assembly the lawful custom of creating praetors; meanwhile the provincials and landowners are given the power that, if a praetorship is vacant, they should nominate three men devoted to the country and to liberty, and offer them to the prefect of the province, or, in his absence, to his deputy, and send them, by the advice of the Court or of the deputies, into possession of the praetorship and its dignity. And although the whole conduct of war and of the militia is committed to us or to our deputy, nevertheless for the sake of concord and peace I decree that no camp be set up, no forces led out, no towns besieged, no garrisons of places changed, no levy instituted, and no troops called into Friesland from elsewhere, unless the assent of the Estates and of the deputies is given and confirmed by the votes of the greater number. As for sending scouts and arranging secret counsels and stratagems, I reserve these to myself or to my deputy to manage, from the necessity of a secret silence, and lest things entrusted in secret to many be divulged through carelessness or malice. Yet on this condition: that if the magnitude and exigency of affairs require it, they be communicated to fewer, whose loyalty and silence can be relied on. Moreover I grant my deputy Bernard Merode power to appoint and choose centurions and optiones, unless perhaps the deputies have in mind some inhabitants or others distinguished by military renown whom they commend, and these shall be preferred. To all these, and to each of them, officers as well as soldiers, I ask that their pay be counted out promptly; and that the form of military discipline promulgated throughout Friesland be confirmed by my deputy, and that the same, committed to the acts, punish severely the guilty and the offenders. This too will be all the more easily and conveniently achieved if the military pay is made good, lest from want of money the sweetness or necessity of plunder arise. And since further matters still need to be determined for the amendment and correction of the public state, and the shortness of time does not allow this to be done at the present moment, I shall enact written laws and decrees within a few days, to which the deputy governor, the Court and the deputies and the tribunes of the treasury shall submit. Meanwhile I decree this: that this edict be upheld without exception of sex or rank, and I command the officials, magistrates and Frisian inhabitants to direct their deeds and counsels according to its tenor. And that it may find public trust, I wish it to be published through the praetorships and towns by the provincial and supreme Court, by the deputies of the Estates and by the Nine-men, and that it be entered as quickly as possible in the records of the juridical Senate. Meanwhile I ask and admonish each and all, mindful of the oath and duty by which they are bound to the country and the province, to lay aside all harmful passions, and, devoted to peace and concord, to put off offences and hatreds, leaving not even the memory of those storms and acts, so that peace, safety and tranquillity may be held firm and eternal for this province. Given at Harlingen, 7 April 1581.

units.la: LXXXI.
units.tr: LXXXI.

units.la: gematagque attinet, ea mihi aut Vicario meo expedienda reservo ex artani silentij necessitate, & ne secreta pluribus commissa per imprudentiam aut malitiem evulgentur. Hac tamen conditione, ut si rerum magnitudo requirat exigatque, communicetur paucioribus, quorum fide & silentio committi possit. Vicario insuper meo Bernardo Merodio potestatem facio, centuriones, optionesque creandi eligendique, nisi forte Deputati inquilinos aliosque militari laude excellentes commendatos sibi habeant, qui praeferentur. Quibus omnibus quoque singulisque, tam officialibus quam militi prompte stipendia numerari peto, & ut formula disciplinae militaris per Frisiam promulgata a Vicario meo confirmetur, eademque actis commissa severe noxios delinquentesque puniat. Quod ipsum tanto quoque facilius commodiusque effectum daturum erit, si stipendiorum militarium solutio fiat, ne aeris egestate & penuria rapinarum dulcedo aut necessitas oriatur. Et quoniam plura adhuc determinanda ad emendationem correctionemque status publici forent, idque fieri hoc ipso tempore angustia non sinat, leges scriptas ac decreta paucos intra dies statuturus sum, quibus Vicarius Gubernator, Curia & Deputati Tribunique, ararioum pareant. Hoc interim decerno, ut huic Edicto sine exceptione sexus ordinisque stetur, mandoq; Officialibus, Magistratibus, Inquilinisque Friso, ut secundum eius tenorem facta sua consiliaque dirigant. Quod ipsum quoque, ut fidem publicam inveniat, per praeturas oppidaque a provinciali supremaque Curia, a Deputatis Ordinum Novem-virisque volo, & ut in acta juridici Senatus quanto ocyus referantur. Interim rogo moneoque ut omnes singulique sacramenti officiique sui memores, quo patriae provinciaeque obligantur, omnes noxios affectus deponant, pacique ac concordiae dediti offensas odiaque exuant, ne recordatione quidem istarum tempestatum actionumque relicta, quo huic provinciae pax, salus, atque tranquillitas aeterna stabilisq; habeatur. Datum Harlingae vii. April. cIↄ. Iↄ. LXXXI.

units.la: Quae etsi sedandis dissensionibus ac tollendae minuendaeve aemulationi reperta crederentur, tamen non defuere, qui veteres potentum discordias surdaque ad remedium vulnera refricarent. Quare Aurantius, Leovardiae adhuc agens, (quam urbem magna festivitatis gaudijque ostentatione xv. April. ingressus erat) postulata Deputatorum jam ante Harlingae perscripta Senatui juridico communicavit, quo omne controversum intermedia pace & arbitratu suo componeretur. Caeterum Senatus juridicus ordinariam legitimamque in Comitio creationem, optimum erga Religionem & Rempub. affectum criminationibus Novem-viralis Collegij obtendebat, paratumque se fore in omni actione consilioque publico optima suadentibus accedere. Neque enim cum regia tyrannide suum imperium, quod Deputati allegabant, aliquid commune habere, testabantur, seque voto juvaturos remp. ut regiae dominationis asperitas ab ea arceatur. Quod ad mutationem Curiae in deterius attinebat, respondebant, nihil quidem stabile ac aeternum in rebus mortalium esse, caeterum si cum annuis Deputatorum Novem-virorumque imperijs perpetuitas Senatoriae dignitatis conferatur, minus ab illa periculum fore. Id exemplis recentium annorum abunde doceri posse. Quare nihil sanctius meliusque concipi ad utilitatem reip. posse, quam si indivisa collegiorum potestas sit, publicaq; & communia consilia a Senatu juridico servandis in ordine rebus conferantur. Adeo inquiequiebant, impossibile esse, ut à juris dicundi officio reip. cura secerni queat, nisi cum detrimento rerum & confusionis extremae periculo. Quapropter Praetorum per Frisiam constitutionem adimi Curiae non posse, quae jus ad hoc quaesitum haberet, & quod praetorum potestas exequendis Curiae sententiis vicaria sit. Itaque petebant Princeps bono salubrique consilio instruere Deputatos Novem-virosq; vellet, quo creatio Praetorum & diplomatum concessio pro more & lege Senatui continuetur. Imprimis cum optimos quosq; & patriae fidos creari in Praetores Curia velit, cui nihil aliud propositum sit, quam divino honori & saluti publicae officia sua impendere. Econtra Deputati vim inferri tabulis mandatorum suorum affirmabant, curamque regundae reip. à proceribus populoque Frisico sibi commissam decreto Principis & interpositione novae legis infirmari. Quae quanquam veri speciem prae se ferrent, tamen hac moderatione Princeps usus est, ut tabulas mandataque Deputatorum firma sartaque esse declararet, usque dum populi comitium Principis & Praefecti consilio roboratum plenius de rep. & toto negotio disposuisset. Haec Leovard. xiv. April. perscripta.
units.tr: Although these measures were believed to have been devised to calm the dissensions and to remove or lessen rivalry, there were nevertheless some who stirred up again the old quarrels of the powerful and wounds that would not heal. Therefore Aurantius, still staying at Leeuwarden (which city he had entered on 15 April with a great display of festivity and joy), communicated to the juridical Senate the demands of the deputies, already drawn up earlier at Harlingen, so that every point in dispute might be settled by an intermediate peace and by his own arbitration. However, the juridical Senate, in answer to the accusations of the Nine-men's college, pleaded its ordinary and lawful creation in the assembly and its best disposition towards religion and the commonwealth, and declared that it was ready to comply in every action and public counsel with whatever the best advice recommended. For they affirmed that their power, which the deputies alleged, had nothing in common with royal tyranny, and that they would by their vow help the commonwealth so that the harshness of royal domination be kept away from it. As to the change of the Court for the worse, they replied that indeed nothing in human affairs is stable and eternal, but if the perpetuity of the senatorial dignity be compared with the yearly commands of the deputies and Nine-men, there would be less danger from the former. This, they said, could be sufficiently shown by the examples of recent years. Therefore nothing more sacred or better could be devised for the good of the commonwealth than that the power of the colleges be undivided, and that public and common counsels be entrusted to the juridical Senate for keeping order in affairs. So, they said, it was impossible that the care of the commonwealth could be separated from the office of administering justice without loss to affairs and the extreme danger of confusion. Therefore the appointment of praetors throughout Friesland could not be taken from the Court, which had a right to this by law, and the power of the praetors was subordinate to the Court in carrying out its sentences. Thus they asked that the Prince would deign to instruct the deputies and Nine-men with good and wholesome counsel, so that the creation of praetors and the granting of diplomas might continue for the Senate according to custom and law; especially since the Court wished the best and most faithful men to be made praetors, its only aim being to devote its duties to the honour of God and the safety of the public. On the other hand the deputies affirmed that violence was being done to the records of their mandates, and that the charge of governing the commonwealth, committed to them by the nobles and the Frisian people, was being weakened by the Prince's decree and the interposition of a new law. Although these claims bore an appearance of truth, the Prince nevertheless acted with this moderation: he declared that the records and mandates of the deputies were to stand firm and whole, until the assembly of the people, strengthened by the counsel of the Prince and the prefect, should more fully dispose of the commonwealth and the whole matter. Written at Leeuwarden, 14 April.

units.la: Reperio in actis horum temporum Petrum Everardum Durevoutium Rinsmageestanum jam ante Oeniae Witsmae Praetoris Dantumani praescripto consilioque instructum, colligendis per Frisiam vicinaque duobus militum signis mandatum à Rennebergio accepisse, eundemque agendis rebus pecuniam reliquaq; subsidia petentem, quo ministros verbi, praetores actuariosque in vincula ducere, aut multare damnis incommodisque posset, à Rennebergio post Steenvicanam obsidionem desertam aegritudine animi tabescente, ne nervum quidem foedissimae conjurationis impetrare potuisse.
units.tr: I find in the records of these times that Pieter Everaerd Durevoudt of Rinsmageest, already equipped beforehand with the instructions and advice of Oenia Witsma, praetor of Dantumadeel, received from Rennenberg a commission to raise two companies of soldiers throughout Friesland and the neighbouring lands. He sought money and other supplies for the business, so that he could throw the ministers of the Word, the praetors and the clerks into chains or fine them with losses and hardships. But after the siege of Steenwijk was abandoned, Rennenberg, wasting away in mental sickness, could not obtain for him even the sinews of this most foul conspiracy.

units.la: Douwoni quoque Sixmae, qui fiscalium bonorum capiendorum distrahendorum juxta Fisci advocatum potestatem nactus erat, Siboldum Aysmam suffectum mobilium immobiliumque bonorum actionumq; fiscalium, eorumque qui arma auxiliaque contra patriam sollicitaverant, indicem ac commentarios accepisse. Deputatorum quoque ac Novemvirali collegio Sibethum Sceltemam & Doconem Aysmam, ex Oostergois, Ielgerum Feitsmam ac Geroldum Intenium è Westergois, Auconem Edonium & Abelum Franckenam è Sylvestribus Douwonem, Sixmam & Ioannem Montsmam ascriptos plenam administrandae regundaeque provinciae potestatem mense Februario accepisse. Livium quoque Juckamam, Gisbertum Amsmam & Georgium Godefridi in Juridicum Senatum Ordinemque cooptatos judicandi auspicia fecisse.
units.tr: Douwo Sixma too, who had gained the power to seize and sell confiscated goods under the fiscal advocate, had received Sibold Aysma, appointed in his place, as informer and recorder of movable and immovable goods and fiscal actions, and of those who had incited others to arms and aid against the fatherland. In February, the deputies and the college of Nine also received full power to administer and regulate the province: Sibethus Sceltema and Doco Aysma from Oostergo, Jelger Feitsma and Gerold Intema from Westergo, Aucho Edonius and Abel Franckena from the Sylvestrine region, and Douwo, Sixma and John Montsma, who were enrolled among them. Livius Juckama, Gisbert Amsma and Georgius Godefridi, co-opted into the Judicial Senate and Order, also began to judge.

units.la: Quae quamvis in spem ordinandae firmandaeque reip. fierent, tamen eveniebat ut tota belli tempestas, velut circumagente malo fidere à Drentinis Tubantibusque in Frisiam se defecteret, insigni, ut mihi videtur, providentiae miraculo, ut tenerrima adhuc libertas domestica potentum aemulatione ipsis infantiae suae annis luxurians, haerentium in provinciae visceribus armorum hostiumq; vi cohiberetur. Ipse etiam Rennebergius oppugnando, etsi infeliciter, provinciam, quam odio regis defenderat, majore animi ex fortuna aegrotantis morbo corriperetur, discereteq; per eos adversis auspiciis res ut plurimum geri, qui foedera violavissent.
units.tr: Although these measures were taken in the hope of ordering and securing the commonwealth, it nevertheless came about that the whole storm of war, as though a ship's mast were swung round by the wind, withdrew from Drenthe and Tubantia into Friesland. This was, as it seems to me, a remarkable miracle of providence, so that a domestic liberty still very tender, flourishing in the years of its infancy through the rivalry of the powerful, was restrained by the force of arms and enemies lodged in the province's very heart. Rennenberg himself, though unsuccessfully, attacked the province he had defended out of hatred for the king; he was seized by a sickness of spirit from his ailing fortunes. Affairs were for the most part conducted, under adverse omens, by those who had violated their treaties.

units.la: Quo tempore mole belli provinciae gravi, novo quodam & majoribus cIↄ. Iↄ. bus nostris infrequente remedio impulsis ærarij rebus subventum, vul‑LXXXI. gatis publicatisque venalium rerum indictionibus, quas in superiora Bel‑ gicæ & fœderatæ reip. populum primo extrusas, Frisij quoque ac confortione publici fœderis acceperant. Quare v i. Eid. Mai (ut in Ephemeride Cl. Franckena notat) in comitio proclamatæ sequentibusq; diebus per præturas & oppida in usum perductæ locarijs publicanorum subfuere.
units.tr: At that time the province was burdened by the weight of war, and relief was given to the treasury by a new remedy, unusual and rare in our forefathers' times: public proclamations of auctions of goods. Our people had first seen these driven out of the Upper Netherlands and the united commonwealth, and the Frisians had also accepted them under the public alliance. Therefore they were proclaimed in the assembly on 10 May (the sixth day before the Ides of May, as Franckena notes in his Ephemeris), and on the following days they were brought into use through the praetorships and towns, and placed under the management of tax-farmers.

units.la: Quæ priscis olim gentibus vectigalium nomine ut firmamenta impe‑ rij usurpatæ, ita tum experiundo comprobarunt, recens inventum etsi libertati grave videretur, ut regundis domi rebus magnum præsidium ita munimentum adversum hostes attulisse. Unde status quoque æra‑ rij, quod à Saxonica usque dominatione canone censuque sustine‑ batur, penitius quoq; introspectus, urgente Bernardo Merodio, ut ex comitiali decreto Quæstores Tribunique ærarij rationes ad publicas constringerentur. Quod quanquam difficile istâ temporum ætate non ef‑set, quæ virtutem & innocentiam regio metu, aut quia malæ artes ignorabantur prodebat, tamen credebatur Merodius, revocato in Hollandiam Aurantio, hæc & similia efferendæ dominationi, aut in odium popularis licentiæ resuscitasse. Quibus & hoc accedebat, quod recente Aurantij præsentiâ & famâ suffultus modum imperij intenderet, &post exteros militiæ honoribus intrusos ipsa quoque procerum reip.suffragia suo arbitrio infirmaret. Criminantibus in secreto suo Ordinibus Aurantium solertis ne dicam an stupendæ prudentiæ Principem istum virum gubernandis Frisijs præfecisse, qui natalium modicus & pacis belliq; artium ignarus, nihil præter senilem ignaviam & impatiens militiæ corpus inutili Præfecturæ præferret. Qui in otio ac securitate rerum imbelles annos & superbam canitiem alens aulicos inter de bello dissere-ret, exiguumque quod haberet poreftatis in dominatum verteret priorum temporum Præfectis non usurpatum. Neque enim eum Egmondanis, Lignæis, Hyergijs ac Lalainijs accensendum, quos præter familiæ decus militaris gloria ad majora hæreditarijs imperia extulisset. Econtra hunc nominis obscuri dissitis terris evocatum Effætâ ac degeneri ætate ne vestigia quidem fortium clarorumque Ducum nosse, quæ sequeretur, neque satis capere, quibus moribus artibusque nova & tanto gratior libertas habenda sit. Quæ tum repetita & vulgaribus sermonibus familiaria homini ignavo & quidem in illo rerum discrimine reip. incurioso, contemptum peperere.
units.tr: Ancient peoples once used such levies as the foundations of their empires under the name of taxes. Experience then proved that this recent invention, though it seemed burdensome to liberty, brought as great a protection and fortification against enemies as it did for regulating affairs at home. Hence the state of the treasury, which had been sustained by levy and tax since the Saxon domination, was also examined more thoroughly, at the urging of Bernard Merode, so that by decree of the assembly the accounts of the quaestors and treasury tribunes were bound to public accounts. Although this would have been difficult in that age, which exposed virtue and innocence to royal fear, or because wicked arts were then unknown, Merode was believed, with Orange recalled to Holland, to have revived these and similar measures to extend domination or to stir hatred of popular licence. Added to this was that, supported by Orange's recent presence and fame, he was extending the mode of his rule, and, after foreigners had been thrust into military honours, he was even weakening the votes of the nobles of the commonwealth at his own pleasure. The Orders charged in their secret deliberations that Orange, shrewd (not to say of astonishing prudence), had set that prince over the government of Friesland: a man of modest birth, ignorant of the arts of war and peace, who offered nothing beyond senile sloth and a body unfit for military service in a useless governorship. Idle and secure, nourishing his unwarlike years and proud grey hair, he discussed war among courtiers, and turned the small power he had into domination, which earlier governors had not claimed. For he was not to be counted with Egmont, Ligne, Hierges and Lalaing, whom, besides the glory of their families and their military renown, hereditary commands had raised to greater things. On the contrary, this man, summoned from distant lands under an obscure name, in a worn-out and degenerate age, did not even know the footsteps of brave and famous leaders, nor sufficiently grasp by what manners and arts a new and so much more welcome liberty was to be kept. These things, repeated then and familiar in common talk, brought contempt upon a sluggish man, indifferent to the commonwealth in that crisis.

units.la: Jam enim Rennebergius per Omlandiam, circaque Lavicæ & amnis,qui majoribus Frisijs obtenditur, Reiderij ripas, copias contrahebat, distributisque per præsidia munitionum signis majoribus Frisijs imminebat. Quorum securitati Nienortius fœderatas quasdam cohortes per Omlandiam ac Translavicanos ducitabat, quo de hostium consilio, capti‑sq; cognosceret. Quem ut Rennebergici lambentibus Omlandiam æstuarijs ipsoque mari prohiberent, amni Reiderio, qui declivi prope mare alveo fertur, munitionem imponere constituerunt, quo belli fortunâ per continentem ancipite Oceani saltem prædonumq; per sinus maris errantium pericula anteverterent. Cæterum à Nienortio, ejus rei commonito, multis cæsis captisq; in fugam acti, cœnobio Adoardico amissis etiam signis se intulere.
units.tr: Now Rennenberg was gathering his forces through the Ommelanden, around the Lauwers and along the banks of the Reiderij, the river that lies before Greater Friesland. He distributed standards among the garrisons and threatened Greater Friesland. To secure it, Nienoord led some confederate cohorts through the Ommelanden and across the Lauwers, to learn the enemy's plans and take prisoners. So that Rennenberg's men, licking the estuaries of the Ommelanden and the sea itself, could not stop them, they resolved to place a fortification on the Reiderij, which flows in a steep channel near the sea, so that, with the fortunes of war uncertain on land, they might at least forestall the dangers of the ocean and of pirates wandering through the bays of the sea. But Nienoord, having been warned of this, cut down and captured many of them, put the rest to flight, and they withdrew, having lost their standards, to the monastery of Adoard.

units.la: Franckena tradit ingentis justique certaminis speciem illum confli-ctum habuisse, quadringentisq; ut notat, Geldris deletis, qui pro Phi-lippo militabant, reliquos urbem versus & Adoardiam abreptos majoris cladis periculum evasisse. Mox Nienortius, Winsumo, Marniorum vicus est, movens in Adoardios duxit, qui duarum Geldricarum cohortium praesidio defensi, Rennebergium de auxiliis commonuere, & ut quanto ocyus militem per vicina collectum admovendo praesentium discrimini decerneret. Qui etsi animi aeger, rejectâ in suos belli curâ, tamen contractas in unum copias Adoardiam ire Nienortiumque ut loco pellerent imperavit, qui modico vallo copijs suis praeducto, quo adventantes Rennebergicos Reiderij amnis ripâ arceret, pedestres quasdam copias emiserat. Caeterum istae, viso hostium adventu, mox terrore pavidos imbellesque subeunte retro in castra se recepere, quae ut Franckena tradit, ultro metus & formidinis plena suis ex retroactis, majore discrimine augebantur. Nienortius tamen velut pugnaturus ordines instruxit, plebemq; rusticam e majoribus Frisijs accitam militaribus cuneis immiscuit. In quam cum Rennebergici justo agmine ordinato impetum facerent, dubium casu an per exploratorem, tota rei fortuna inversa est, plebsque rustica superatis saltu fossis in fugam data, aut quae restiterat coesa animosi alias exercitus latera nudavit. Stuperus cohortis ductor deserto quem occupaverat loco ab hoste cum suis interceptus est. Igitur in Nienortium omnis tum hostium impetus furorque conversus, qui sensim recedens strenuisque militis & simul ductoris officium faciens, nullâ insigni clade affectum exercitum reduxit. E Frisijs centum & quinquaginta, ut commentarijs nostrorum traditum invenio, caesi e Nienortijs pauci desiderati. Id. x. Kal. Jun. factum Franckenae Ephemerides tradunt.
units.tr: Franckena relates that this encounter had the appearance of a great and just battle. As he notes, four hundred Gelderlanders who fought for Philip were destroyed, and the rest, seized, escaped the danger of greater disaster by fleeing towards the city and Adoard. Soon Nienoord, moving from Winsum (a village of the Marne) against Adoard, led his men there. The place was defended by the garrison of two Gelderland cohorts, who informed Rennenberg of the need for aid and urged him to end the present danger by bringing up, as quickly as possible, the soldiers gathered nearby. He, though sick in mind, had cast the care of the war upon his men, but nonetheless ordered the gathered forces to go to Adoard and drive Nienoord from the place. Nienoord had led his forces past a modest rampart, by which he could keep the approaching Rennenbergers off the bank of the Reiderij, and he had sent out some infantry. When those troops saw the enemy's approach, they were soon overcome by terror and cowardice and withdrew back into camp. As Franckena says, these men, already full of fear and dread from their earlier defeats, were made worse by the greater danger. Nienoord nonetheless drew up his lines as if about to fight, and mixed rustic commoners summoned from Greater Friesland into his military wedges. When the Rennenbergers charged in ordered column, the outcome, whether by chance or through a scout, was reversed. The rustic crowd, leaping over the ditches, was put to flight, and what was left of it was cut down, leaving the flanks of the otherwise brave army exposed. The commander of the cohort, Stuperus, deserted the post he had occupied and was cut off by the enemy with his men. Then all the enemy's assault and fury turned against Nienoord, who, withdrawing gradually and performing the duty of both a brave soldier and a leader, led his army back without any notable disaster. Of the Frisians, I find in the commentaries of our people, 150 were killed; few of Nienoord's men were missed. The Ephemerides of Franckena say this happened on 23 May.

units.la: Alij scriptores addunt, multos ex Nienortijs fugientes Adoardico emissario receptos fuisse victoresque Rennebergicos insecutos ipsum emissarium ter repetitâ oppugnatione deleto ad internecionem praesidio occupasse. Tres caedi superfuisse annotatum ab ijs, Sceltonemque Jargaeum centurionem, virum fortem & multis stipendijs rebusq; gestis clarum, isto in conflictu occubuisse. Franckena vii. Eid. Jun. id evenisse annotavit, deprehensumque mihi est fati vicissitudine actum in finibus Frisiorum & per Omlandiam belluin foelicibus prosperis adversa saepe manifesto humanarum rerum ludibrio miscuisse. Sive ut illas per tempestates arborum more tenerrima adhuc libertas firmaretur, sive ne securitatis opinioni locus foret & quidem apud eos, qui foelicitate projectae regiae servitutis elati fiduciam sui continuâ ex prosperitate captaturi credebantur.
units.tr: Other writers add that many of those fleeing from Nienoord were received by the emissary at Adoard, and that the Rennenbergers, pursuing the victors, attacked the emissary's post three times, took it, and destroyed the garrison to a man. They record that three survived the slaughter, and that Sceltonus Jargaeus, a centurion, brave and renowned for many campaigns and deeds, fell in that clash. Franckena notes that this happened on 7 June. I have found that the turn of fortune, in the bounds of the Frisians and across the Ommelanden, often mixed favourable events with adverse ones in the war, a clear mockery of human affairs. Whether this was done so that a tender liberty might be strengthened through such storms, as trees are made firm by the wind, or so that there would be no room for an opinion of security, especially among those who, elated by the good fortune of their cast-off royal servitude, were thought likely to draw confidence in themselves from continuous prosperity.

units.la: Mox hostium copiae Joanne Baptista Taxio duce, qui absentis & hecticâ ex febri aegrescentis Rennebergij partes sustinebat, Winsumum ductae, qui vicus Hunesi amnis flexu & modicâ munitione circumductus, omnium rerum & maxume annonâ commeatuq; destituebatur. Creditum fuit nostros, qui de successu Adoardicae expeditionis non dubitantes Winsumo excesserant, commeatum istius loci aere vendidisse, aesq; ex divendita distractaque annonâ contractum in stipendia seditiosae multitudinis & infidelis praesidij vertisse. Alij causam in Bernardi Merodij se-Yyy nilem cIↄ. Iↄ. nilem incuriam aut cunctabunda Ordinum Frisiæ consilia rejecere, quæ LXXXI. tardè capta etiam cum maximè festinandum foret, nascentem remp. grave crebrò in discrimen pertraxere. Ita Winsumum, nulla oppugnatione aut impetu hostili tentatum à Nienortio Rennebergicis deditum, certæ conditiones ea de re perscriptæ conventionem firmavere. Iis cautum fuit. Ut Niennortius cohortium præfecti milites, cum ægris & fœminis reliquoq; imbelli sexu munitione armati excederent, inque Frisiam aliaque loca quibus commodum foret deducerentur. Captivique apud Winsumanos Warfumanosque nullo lytro dato liberarentur, & quidem ipso conventionis die, exempto Cornelio Kempio, qui præfecti cohortis Matthiæ Keertzi curæ committeretur. Quæ Winsumi v I. Eid. Jun. acta Winsumanam munitionem Baptistæ Taxio Billianæ legionis pro-Præfecto permisere.
units.tr: Soon the enemy forces, led by Johann Baptist Taxis, who was holding the command for the absent Rennenberg (sickening with a hectic fever), advanced on Winsum. This village, enclosed by a bend of the river Hunze and a modest fortification, lacked everything, above all provisions and supplies. It was believed that our men, who had left Winsum not doubting the success of the Adorp expedition, had sold the supplies of that place for money, and had turned the proceeds into pay for the seditious mob and the faithless garrison. Others laid the blame on Bernhard Meroda's negligence or on the dawdling counsels of the Frisian States, which, taken too late when haste was most needed, often dragged the nascent commonwealth into grave danger. Thus Winsum, never attacked by siege or hostile assault, was surrendered by Nienoort to the Rennenbergers, and certain conditions drawn up on this matter confirmed the agreement. It was provided that Nienoort's soldiers of the cohorts, together with the sick, the women and the other unwarlike sex, should leave the fortification under arms and be conducted to Friesland or wherever else suited them. Captives held by the Winsumers and Warffumers were to be released without any ransom on the very day of the agreement, except Cornelius Kemp, who was to be committed to the care of Matthias Keertz, prefect of the cohort. These things were done at Winsum on the sixth day before the Ides of June, and they entrusted the Winsum fortification to Baptist Taxis, pro-prefect of Billy's legion.

units.la: Quare fœderatis præsidijs omni Omlandiâ & maritimâ imprimis orâ ejectis, Nienortius rebus suis diffisus, copias in Frisiam reduxit, quæ metu hostilium incursionum disparsum quaque versum militem recollegit, sociosq; ac Gulielmum Aurantium auxilia poposcit.
units.tr: Therefore, with the allied garrisons having driven out the whole of Omlandia and above all the seacoast, Nienoort, distrustful of his own position, led his troops back into Friesland. There, fearing hostile raids, he gathered the soldiers scattered everywhere, and he asked his allies and William of Orange for auxiliary forces.

units.la: Qui amissâ Omlandiâ magna rerum detrimenta & fati indignationem criminabantur, & quod dubijs rumoribus obnuntiaretur Carolum Gaurium Fresinium in arce Bredanâ captivum limitaneam Brabantiæ urbem & Hollandiæ conterminam corrupto præsidio prodidisse. Quæ quamquam de urbe dicerentur, ita arcis victæ expugnataque ab hostibus stabilem famam vulgavere, quæ Frisiorum quoque auribus acerba gentem bello implicitam majoribus curis exagitavit. Cui & hoc mali accedebat, quod exercitus ex Translavicanis in Frisiorum fines retractus importunius stipendia flagitaret, pridemque persoluta, ut Franckena notat, majore infamiâ repeteret. Ad quæ cum conniverent Frisij, quod provinciam suam licentioso & perfuso voluptatibus militè teneri scirent, ita murmurantibus legionibus I v. Kal. Iul. æs pensitatum, ne negato vitæ subsidio ferocius lasciverent, gravioribusque insuper exactionibus agrariorum fortunas attererent.
units.tr: They blamed the loss of Omlandia on the great damage to their affairs and on the misfortune of the times, and it was reported, in doubtful rumours, that Carolus Gaurius of Friesland, held captive in the fortress of Breda, had betrayed the frontier city of Brabant, which borders on Holland, by corrupting its garrison. Although these reports concerned the city, the news that the fortress had been taken and stormed by the enemy spread as established fact, and this bitter report, reaching the ears of the Frisians too, troubled a people already entangled in war with greater anxieties. To this was added the further evil that the army, withdrawn from the regions across the Lauwers into Frisian territory, demanded its pay more insistently, and sought again, as Franckena notes, with greater disgrace, wages paid long ago.
