Since the Frisians knew their province was held by a licentious soldiery sodden with pleasures, they overlooked this; but when the legions murmured, the money was paid on the 18th day before the Kalends of July, so that, denied the means of living, they would not run wilder in their wantonness, and would not, by even heavier exactions, wear down the fortunes of the farmers.

units.la: Quare Nienortio copias in Frisiam retrahente, magna per Ostergoam imprimis consternatio fuit, quod prima hostium, qui Nienortium insecuturi credebantur, irruptionibus exposita reliquarum Frisiæ partium minus discrimen expenderet. Unde Merodij delegatorumque Frisiæ de emuniendo Doccomio cogitatum, quod oppidum Roblesio Frisiam pro Philippo Gubernante à Valonibus non sine cæde incensum direptumque eadem hostilium furorum incommoda præformidabat. Caeterum fugâ rusticæ plebis aucto metu ab opere desitum, donec educto Rinsmageestum & mox Collumum exercitu allevatâ formidine intermissa ad officia fabrorum fossorumque multitudo rediret. Cl. Franckena tradit, tantam laborantium æmulationem in promovendâ accelerandaque oppidi munitione fuisse, ut à decimo Julij cæptam magnâ alacritate & industriâ ad Kal. Octob. confecerint. Curam quoque ordinandorum conficiendorumq; operum per Merodium Legatosque Ordinum Magistratui Doccumano commissam, qui publicum Oostergoæ munimentum curando privatæ quoque civium & suæ securitati nou ignobile studium impendebat.
units.tr: Therefore, when Nienoort was drawing his troops back into Friesland, great dismay arose throughout Oostergo, chiefly because the first places exposed to the enemy raids, which were expected to follow Nienoort, weighed the danger to the other parts of Friesland as lesser. Hence came the plan of Meroda and the deputies of Friesland to fortify Dokkum, because the town of Roblesio, which had been burned and plundered by the Walloons for Philip's governor, not without slaughter, feared the same disasters from the fury of the enemy. Otherwise, the fear, increased by the flight of the country people, brought the work to a halt, until, once the army had been led out to Rinsumageest and soon to Kollum, and the terror had been relieved, the crowd of craftsmen and diggers returned to their tasks. Franckena reports that the workers showed such rivalry in pushing forward and hastening the fortification of the town that, beginning it on the tenth of July, they finished it with great eagerness and diligence by the Kalends of October. The task of arranging and completing the works was also entrusted by Meroda and the deputies of the States to the magistrates of Dokkum, who, while caring for the public defence of Oostergo, devoted no small zeal to the private safety of the citizens as well as their own.

units.la: Mox auxilia à socijs, Aurantioque decreta, remissusque in Frisiam cum Anglorum legione Joannes Norritius, quasi fato quodam, ut liberandis nuper Steenvicanis vocatus, Frisiâ quoque pellendis Rennebergicis destinaretur. Igitur Lemmariam advectus, magnam melioris fortunæ spem per provinciam excitavit, quæ alternantibus prosperis adversisque sui in defensionem Anglicam Nienortijque legiones tum sustinebat. Plane ut belli sedem Frisiorum in finibus constituisse fati vicissitudo videretur, quæ ut aliis incommodis, ita exhaustam bello & aquarum diluvijs gentem militari maximè lascivià multabat. Quippe præter pecorum abactus vis atque rapina utraque in legione ingravescebat, ignorantibus Dongrijs suorum an hostium injurijs premerentur. Unde decretum à Norritio, ne per Anglos & legionis suæ militem pecora exportarentur quæ alio terrarum transvecta fertilissimos pascuis campos nudabant.
units.tr: Soon aid was decreed by the allies and by William, and John Norris was sent back into Friesland with the English legion, called as if by some fate to free Steenwijk, which had recently been freed, and destined now to drive the Rennenbergers out of Friesland too. Having arrived at Lemmer, he aroused a great hope of better fortune throughout the province, which at that time was sustaining the English and Nienoort's legions in turn, alternating good and bad fortune in their defence. It was as if a turn of fate had placed the seat of war in the borders of the Frisians; this people, already wasted by war and by floods of water, was afflicted by the soldiers' lust, above all for plunder. Indeed, besides the driving off of livestock, the violence and rapine grew worse in both legions, while the Dongeradeel men did not know whether they were oppressed by the injuries of their own people or of the enemy. Therefore Norris decreed that the English and the soldiers of his legion should not export livestock, which, carried elsewhere, were stripping of pasture the most fertile fields.

units.la: Franckena tradit villas quoque direptas passim & incensas, præterea; vim matronarum virginumque castitati illatam, omnia sacra & profana violentiæ militari subfuisse. Idem addit Norritium legionis Anglicæ, ut memoravi, tribunum, sumptuosum epulum Leovardiæ III. Kalend. Jul. instruxisse, ipsumque Merodium tum Legatos Ordinum & Curiæ Senatores diem illum geniali festivitate & profuturis reip. colloquijs extraxisse. Unde querelis rusticæ per Dongrios plebis auctis, cum hinc Anglorum legio, inde Nienortius in omnem insolentiam effunderentur, Merodius legatique Ordinum festino itinere Kal. Jul. Doccomium profecti, quo nascentibus legionum morbis mederentur, Dongriosq; extremam militaris immodestiæ patientiam professos ab illâ calamitate injuriâque militum sublevarent. Quod cum enervi disciplinâ, quæ castrensibus moribus vitijsque vincebatur, ægre fieret, animique feroces & pessimis assueti nec Merodij autoritate, nec legatorum provinciæ majestate deterrerentur, solâ pecuniæ ærisque pollicitatione, tanquam enormis luxuriæ fomento, evicti sunt. Quanquam Cl. Franckena tradat etiam sponsione stipendijs factâ necdum quievisse, auctamque villarum direptionem, militaremque ferociam soli castrorum otio imputatum. Ego crediderim aliam quoque militari licentiæ causam subfuisse, quod indictionibus per provinciam vulgatis, obligari quoque tenerique militem & exercitum publicanorum avaritia vellet hominesque parvo ære animam redimentes ijsdem tributorum oneribus obstringi. Quæ res si non initium saltem fomentum castrensibus malis incommodisque dedit. Quapropter à Merodio Gubernatore Ordinumque legatis decretum. Ne milites, lixæ, calones & quicquid castrorum commeatui annonæque serviret, istâ lege gravarentur & ut illi immunitatis exemptionisque privilegio gauderent, qui sacramento militiæ inligati corpora atque vitam publico discrimini objectarent. Unde ferox miles & prædandis agrariorum fortunis inhians remissiore licentiâ egit, deprehensis tamen qui etiam istâ indulgentiâ procerum abusi & mox inritati majorem licentiam spirarent.
units.tr: Franckena reports that villages were also plundered and burned here and there, and that violence was done to the chastity of matrons and virgins, and that all sacred and profane things were subject to military violence. He adds that Norris, the tribune of the English legion, as I have mentioned, laid on a sumptuous banquet at Leeuwarden on the third day before the Kalends of July, and that Meroda himself, with the deputies of the States and the senators of the Court, spent that day in cheerful festivity and in conversations useful to the commonwealth. Hence, as the complaints of the rural people in Dongeradeel increased, while the English legion on one side and Nienoort on the other poured out into every insolence, Meroda and the deputies of the States set out in haste for Dokkum on the Kalends of July, to remedy the diseases of the legions as they arose and to relieve the Dongeradeel men, who professed the utmost patience with military wantonness, from that calamity and injury done by soldiers. Since this was done with difficulty, owing to the slack discipline which was overcome by camp customs and vices, and since the fierce spirits, accustomed to the worst, were deterred neither by Meroda's authority nor by the dignity of the provincial deputies, they were won over only by the promise of money and bronze, as if these were fuel for an outrageous extravagance. Although Franckena also says that they had not yet quieted down even after a promise of pay had been made, and that the increase in the plundering of villages and the soldiers' ferocity were ascribed to the mere idleness of the camp, I should think that another cause of military licence also lay behind it. The levies published throughout the province wanted the soldier also to be bound and held by them, and the avarice of the tax-farmers wanted men who redeemed their lives for a small sum to be tied to the same burdens of taxes. If this did not give the beginning at least, it gave fuel and added to the evils and troubles of the camp. For this reason Meroda, the governor, and the deputies of the States decreed that the soldiers, the camp-followers, the sutlers and whoever served the camp's supplies and provisions should not be burdened by this law, and that they should enjoy the privilege of immunity and exemption, since they bound their bodies and lives to public danger by the oath of military service. Hence the fierce soldier, greedy for plundering the farmers' fortunes, acted with a looser licence, though some were caught who, abusing even this indulgence of the nobles, and soon emboldened, breathed a greater licence.

units.la: Quare Merodij Legatorumque jussu exercitus Dongriæ è finibus Rinsmagerestum ductus, quo hosti propior, qui circa Lavicam castra metabatur, periculi discriminisque metu corrigeretur. Mox octo dierum stipencIↄ. Iↄ. LXXXI. stipendia Nienortio numerata, conventumque ut accepto ære Dongriâ quanto ocyus excederet, Merodijque qui Doccomi tum erat, imperio obsecutus copias Collumo induceret. Quod quanquam raptis celeriter signis simularet, tamen exercitum, motis vix castris in Dongrios reduxit, militemque ultro mobilem & flagitiosum suo exemplo & parendi dedignatione corrupit.
units.tr: Therefore, by order of Meroda and the deputies, the army was led out of Dongeradeel to Rinsumageest, which was nearer the enemy, who was encamped near Leeuwarden, so that it might be corrected by fear of peril and danger. Soon eight days' pay was counted out to Nienoort, and, on receiving the money, they were ordered to leave Dongeradeel as quickly as possible; and obeying Meroda's command, he (who was then at Dokkum) led the troops into Kollum. Although he pretended this by quickly taking up the standards, nevertheless, the camp having scarcely been moved, he led the army back into Dongeradeel, and by his own example he corrupted the soldiers, who were already eager to move, and disgraceful in their contempt of obedience.

units.la: Cæterum positis Collumi Anglorum & Norritij castris, cum prope Groningam (quâ in civitate magna annonæ caritas tum erat) equitatus hostium faciendæ in Frisios irruptioni coïre diceretur, Dongriâ excessit, suumque exercitum Anglicis copijs pellendis Frisiâ hostibus conjunxit, qui transcenso amne Lavica Visfleto ac Virginum cœnobio sua jam præsidia induxerant. Quo cognito Norritius educta copiarum parte cum hoste congressus est, eumque Visfletum in ripâ Lavicæ situm & cœnobium Virginum deserere compulit. Multis hostium cæsis ac quadraginta captis Norritius Collumum reversus. Mox copijs auctus cedentemque trans Lavicam hostem Grypskerckam usque insecutus est, quo in pago, velut sparsas priduana clade & fuga copias recollecturus morabatur. Qui Norritio multitudine militum impar, & ob recentem cædis memoriam languens pavensque abjectis armis nullo ordine profugit, Norritioque insequenti ferienda more pecorum terga dedit.
units.tr: Moreover, when the camps of the English and Norris had been placed at Kollum, and it was said that the enemy cavalry were gathering near Groningen (a city where there was then a great scarcity of provisions) for a raid into Friesland, he left Dongeradeel and joined his army to the English forces to drive the enemy out of Friesland. The enemy had already crossed the river Lauwers and introduced their garrisons into Vispelt and the convent of the Virgins. When this was known, Norris, leading out part of his forces, engaged the enemy and forced them to abandon Vispelt, situated on the bank of the Lauwers, and the convent of the Virgins. Many of the enemy were killed and forty taken, and Norris returned to Kollum. Soon, strengthened with more troops, he pursued the enemy, who was retreating across the Lauwers, as far as Grijpskerk, where he stayed in that village, as if about to gather his scattered forces, broken by the defeat and flight of the previous day. Being unequal to Norris in the number of his soldiers, and languid and afraid from the recent memory of the slaughter, they threw down their arms, fled without any order, and, as Norris pursued, turned their backs to be struck down like cattle.

units.la: Cl. Franckena octingentos cæsos, signa septem, tria tormenta capta memorat, multosque & in ijs duos centuriones, tres vexilliferos in captivitatem abductos tradit. Meteranus septingentos hostium, alius scriptor mille & quingentos ibi perijsse notat, Norritioque victori sarcinas insuper impedimentaq; hostilium castrorum in prædam cessisse. Addit A. Franckena Norritij equites Groningam usque provectos, plurimos illuc fugientium cæcidisse, occupatâque Adoardiâ & Cœnobio Selverdico ipsam velut urbem Groningam rudibus castris clausisse. Reperio in actis publicis Norritium è prædicto cœnobio litteras ad Frisios dedisse, stipendiaque bimestria pro se & equitatu postulasse, ac ut ista Gulielmo Barckero Thesaurario suo placandis copijs & victoriæ præmium traderentur. Litteras è castris ad Groningam datas scribit. Angli victores Omlandiam Drentiæq; partem ita depopulati sunt, ut plurimæ familiæ majoris mali metu & amissis bonis agris atque possessionibus suis excesserint. Conflictum illum de quo dixi ad Grypskerckam v.11. Eid. Iul. habitum fuisse Franckena notat. Invenio in archivis provinciæ Ordines Belgicæ Kal. Iul. decretum perscripsisse. Ut de Ecclesiasticis per omnes provincias bonis statuendi singularum Ordinibus jus foret, addita cautelâ, ut in eorum dispensatione, usu ac alienatione honestatis quam maxime ratio haberetur. Adonem quoq; Harckamam Ordinum Frisiæ nomine Bolsuerdiam missum, quo de cœnobij S. Spiritus monialibus reliquorumque religiosorum moribus vitâque cognoscere t, probissimos quoq; civium ætate, aut prudentiâ venerabiles ad danda veritati testimonia in opprobrium dedecusque corruptissimi ordinis examinasse. Catharinam quoque Cyprianam è monialibus primam virginali cœnobio locoq; ejectam, quod Pontificia religione damnatâ & audiendis reformatorum concionibus frequens, mores quoq; pessimi & omni vitio ac turpitudine attaminati coetus aversaretur. Itaque tunc cœnobiobiorum Bolsuerdiensium vicinorumque luxus, & foedissimæ libidines vulgatæ, confessione etiam ipsarum quæ formæ decus ac venustatem nactæ præsulum cœnobitarumque amoribus ac desiderijs exponebantur. Addit Harckama virginem quandam Magdalenam formæ eximiam, in ipso ætatis flore circumventam ac mox compressam concepisse, uteroq; gestantem, & profiteri promiscuos virginum concubitus coram & in secreto loci vetitam locum illum tanquam sacrum execrandumq; proclamasse. Tres quoque Præsules Aengiummanum Præpositum & Ordinis Albatorum, istiusque cœnobij Bolsuerdiensis cottidianis compotationibus ætatem egisse, omnisque impuritatis ac temulentiæ liberrimâ professione ne vestigia quidem priscæ debitæque sanctitatis ostentasse.
units.tr: Franckena reports that eight hundred of the enemy were killed, seven standards and three cannon captured, and that many men, including two centurions and three standard-bearers, were led away into captivity. Meteranus notes that seven hundred of the enemy perished there, and another writer records fifteen hundred. Besides this, the baggage and supply wagons of the enemy camp fell as plunder to the victorious Norritius. A. Franckena adds that Norritius's horsemen advanced as far as Groningen and cut down most of those fleeing there, and that after seizing Adwerd and the monastery of Selwerd, he hemmed in the city of Groningen itself with a makeshift camp. I find in the public records that Norritius wrote letters to the Frisians from the said monastery, asking for two months' pay for himself and his cavalry, and that this money should be handed over to his treasurer Willem Barck to satisfy the troops, along with a reward for the victory. He writes that the letters were dated from the camp at Groningen. The English victors so ravaged Omlands and part of Drenthe that very many families, in fear of worse and having lost their goods, fields and holdings, left their homes. Franckena notes that the battle I mentioned took place at Grijpskerk on 11 July. In the archives of the province I find that the States of Belgium drew up a decree on 1 July, that each of the provinces' States should have the right to decide on the Church's goods, with the added caution that in their management, use and alienation the greatest regard be had for honesty. They also sent Addonis Harckama, on behalf of the States of Friesland, to Bolsward, to learn of the morals and manner of life of the nuns of the monastery of the Holy Spirit and of the other religious; and they examined the most upright citizens, venerable for their age or prudence, to give testimony of the truth to the disgrace and shame of that most corrupt order. Also Catharina Cyprian, the first of the nuns, was expelled from the virginal monastery and its place, because, having condemned the Papist religion and being a frequent hearer of the reformed sermons, she turned away from the company of the wicked, who were stained with every vice and filth. And so the luxury and most foul lusts of the monks and nuns of Bolsward and its neighbours became widely known, and by the confession of the women themselves, who had gained the beauty and charm of their looks, were exposed, along with their loves and desires for the prelates and monks. Harckama adds that a certain virgin, Magdalena, outstanding in beauty, was in the very flower of her age tricked and soon violated, and conceived, and, while pregnant, professed that the virgins had promiscuous intercourse both openly and in secret, and proclaimed that this forbidden place was to be execrated as if it were sacred. Three prelates too, Aengium Manus the provost and of the Order of the White Friars, and the monastery at Bolsward, passed their lives in daily drinking bouts, and by their most unrestrained profession of every impurity and drunkenness showed not even the traces of their former and due holiness.

units.la: Composita militari seditione Varckanæ cohortis miles qui commilitonum animos accendendo castrensi insolentiæ occasionem dederat, decreto Aurantij exauctorata provectaque Fletam, Leovardiæ suburbium est, flagitansque importunius stipendia Frisicis terris excedere jussa. Reliquæ copiæ, quarum rationibus conficiendis Ordines Merodiusque Gubernator occupabantur, per Omlandiam & Translavicanos sparsæ, pristinam obsequij fidem induerant, ne hostibus expositæ inter illa castrorum mala ac sacramenti ludibria solutæ & discriminum improvidæ, postquam pugnandum videretur, armorum neglectu turpi & flagitiosâ morte perirent. Jam enim Norritius Northormi castra, ad quæ præter Anglorum legionem & Nienortij copias Hollandicæ Geldricæque cohortes convenerant, metatus dicebatur, Frisiosque commeatum reliquaque bello necessaria poposcerat premendis ut præ se ferebat, Groningensibus, quos summâ rerum angustia teneri non inanium rumorum fide confirmabatur. Quorum urbi ac ruri suburbano majora ut damna daret Northormo castra Adoardiam movit, missoque ad urbem exploratore qui cuncta specularetur, sternendo amni Reiderio pontem destinavit. Igitur Adoardiæ agens Legatos Ordinum quo de singulis cognoscerent, per litteras in castra evocavit, monuitque Neozilum tanquam limitaneum & expositum hosti locum, quanto ocyus emunirent, commeatuque ac annonâ subjuvarent. Cæterum omnia, sicuti solent, deliberatu facilia, exitu tarda deprehendebantur, sive ingenio gentis, quæ fiducia suorum virtutis ferebatur, sive quod conficiendis rebus provinciæ ærarium non responderet. Cui sublevando omnes publicæ pecuniæ conquisitæ, delegatique Orichius Dojemus Frisiorum Syndicus & Abelus Franckena Novem-vir & Historiæ scriptor, qui ab Heronis Burmaniæ Thesaurarij viduâ Emckiâ Glinzia omne æs redimendis civitatum creditis collectum reposcerent. Cæterum vidua suorum consilijs usa, etsi primo abnueret, tamen cautione à delegatis acceptâ omnem ærarij pecuniam delegatis concessit, residuumque præturarum & agri Biltani, quod debebatur, per acta rationum exposuit. Ita debitum, quod exsolvendis nuper Valonibus contractum erat, civitatibusque persolvendum restabat, necessitati bellicæ impensum, quod è Frisiâ in Omlandiam velut reciprocante quodam æstu translatum, ne in Frisios, quasi syderum flexu se transferret formidine recentis mali exuentibus securitatem metuebatur. Unde aurigæ, equi, currus vehendis castrorum commeatibus impedimentisque Frisios petiti, ægrè affecto animi Norritio quod omnis belli fortuna & salubre consilium cunctatione & morâ Ordinum ac defectu rerum retardarentur. Quare Novem-viros litteris per nobilem quendam perlatis, commonuit, ut præter aurigas in usum castrorum fossores insuper è Frisiâ mitterent, ne necessarijs belli subsidijs destitutus castra movere, alioque locorum transferre exercitum in commodo reip. cogeretur. Ne, inquiebat, cum ignominiâ & contemptu hic hærendo operam perdam, qui alibi res gerendo majori gloriæ & progressui rerum me & exercitum impensurus sum. Quod scriptum eo magis Frisios urebat, quod nudari exercitu provinciæ fines non vellent, & quod Trans-Isulani Goræ Tubantum munitioni circumventæ tacitè auxilia missis quaquaversum litteris sollicitarent. Quæ Clantij viri nobilis & Translavicani litteris quoq; confirmata, Frisiorum in deliberando lentitudinem & impendia fossorum exploratorumque tarde transmissa criminabantur. Quamvis commentarijs traditum sit Renicum Burmaniam, sive castrorum legatum, sive censorem exercitus tum agentem stipendia cohortibus attulisse, quæ licentiæ pridem assuetæ, & patientiâ gentis indulgentius habitæ castrorum pacem & quietem continuis murmurationibus obturbabant.
units.tr: When the military mutiny of the Varck cohort was quelled, the soldier who by stirring up his fellow soldiers had given occasion for military insolence was discharged by decree of Orange and carried to Flet, a suburb of Leeuwarden, and, demanding his pay more insistently, was ordered to leave Frisian lands. The remaining troops, whose accounts the States and Governor Merode were busy settling, were scattered through Omlands and the lands beyond the Lauwers. They had resumed their former obedience, lest, exposed to the enemy, loosed amid those evils of the camp and the mockery of their oath, and heedless of dangers, they should perish a shameful and disgraceful death through neglect of arms once fighting seemed required. For already Norritius was said to have pitched camp at Northorn, to which, besides the English legion and the troops of Nienoord, Holland and Gelderland cohorts had gathered; and he had demanded from the Frisians provisions and other things necessary for war, as he gave out, to press the Groningers, who, as reports not without foundation confirmed, were held in the greatest straits. Northorn then moved his camp to Adorp, to inflict greater damage on the city and its suburban countryside; and, sending an explorer to the city to spy on everything, he planned to lay a bridge across the river Reider. Accordingly, Norritius, acting at Adorp, summoned the envoys of the States by letter to the camp, so that he might learn about each matter; and he warned that Nieuwe Zijl, as a border place exposed to the enemy, should be fortified as quickly as possible and aided with supplies and provisions. Otherwise, as usually happens, all matters, which seemed easy to decide, were found slow in their outcome, whether from the character of the people, who were said to trust in the valour of their own men, or because the province's treasury did not match the work to be done. To relieve this, all public money was collected, and Orichius Dojema, Syndic of the Frisians, and Abel Franckena, one of the Nine Men and writer of the history, were appointed to demand back from Heron Burmania's treasurer's widow, Emckia Glinzia, all the money collected for redeeming the cities' debts. However, the widow, relying on her advisers, although at first she refused, nevertheless, having received a bond from the delegates, handed over all the money of the treasury, and laid out in the accounts the remainder owed from the praetorships and the land of Bilt. Thus the debt that had been contracted for paying the recently hired Walloons, and still remained to be paid to the cities, was spent on the necessity of war; and what had been carried from Friesland into Omlands, as by a kind of reciprocating tide, was feared to move on into Friesland, as if by a turning of the stars, so that the people, freed from the fear of the recent evil, would lose their sense of security. Hence drivers, horses and carts were sought in Friesland for carrying the camp's supplies and baggage. Norritius was grievously affected in mind because every fortune of war and every wholesome plan was delayed by the hesitation and delay of the States and the lack of resources. Therefore, through a noble man who carried letters to the Nine Men, he warned them that, besides drivers, they should also send diggers from Friesland for the use of the camp, lest, deprived of the necessary supports of war, he be forced to move the camp and lead the army elsewhere to the convenience of the commonwealth. "Lest," he said, "by staying here I waste my effort with disgrace and contempt, when by doing things elsewhere I shall apply myself and my army to greater glory and progress." This letter stung the Frisians all the more, because they did not wish the province's borders to be stripped of their army, and because the Trans-Ijssel Gore, surrounded by the fortifications of the Tubantes, were quietly seeking help, sending letters in every direction. These complaints were confirmed by letters of Clant, a noble man and a man of the lands beyond the Lauwers, who accused the Frisians of slowness in deliberation and of sending the diggers and scouts late and at great expense. Although it is recorded in the commentaries that Renick Burmania, then acting as legate of the camp or as censor of the army, brought pay to the cohorts, which, accustomed to licence for some time and treated too indulgently out of the patience of the people, were disturbing the peace and quiet of the camp with constant murmurings.

units.la: Invenio in actis Ludovicum Halevinium rei monetariæ per Frisiam præfectum, à primarijs quibusdam civibus Henrico Jarichio & filio adulteratæ monetæ insimulatum, eundemque Halevinium injuriæ atrocitate & tuendæ existimationis desiderio impulsum, libellum supplicem Bernardo Merodio obtulisse. Merodium quoque & Delegatos Ordinum Novem-viros decrevisse, ut tam actores quam reus vinculis manciparentur, dum de crimine aut innocentiâ partium judicium cognovisset. Metuebant namque ne istiusmodi dicteria, etsi suspicionibus tantum initerentur, in plebem militesq; evulgata, turbida sponte populi & castrensia ingenia ad graviora anteactis flagitia impellerent. Tum è provinciâ, ut Franckena tradit, Carolus Roorda, Livius Bejemus & Godscalcus Hiddama pro legatis ad Senatum Belgicum missi, quo consessui provinciarum interessent, providerentque ne quid detrimenti & sociali jure illâ vicinorum æmulatione Frisijs incumberet.
units.tr: I find in the records that Lodewijk Halevinius, prefect of the coinage throughout Friesland, was accused by certain leading citizens, Hendrik Jarichius and his son, of adulterating the coin; and that the same Halevinius, driven by the atrocity of the injury and the desire to defend his reputation, offered a petition to Bernard Merode. Merode and the Nine Men, the delegates of the States, also decreed that both the accusers and the accused be put in chains until they had judged the matter of the crime or the innocence of the parties. For they feared that such slanders, even if they were only aired by suspicions, spread among the common people and soldiers, would of their own accord stir up the turbulent populace and the military mind to graver crimes than those already committed. Then from the province, as Franckena reports, Carel Roorda, Livius Bejema and Godschalk Hiddema were sent as envoys to the Belgian Senate, to take part in that assembly of the provinces and to see that nothing harmful and against the common law should fall upon the Frisians from that rivalry of neighbours.

units.la: Carolus Roorda scribit potissimam illius conventus partem majore acerbitate quam concordiâ votorum actam, deprehensis qui omnia ad se suasque provincias trahendo singularum magis incommoda quam publicam fœderis & communis ærarij prosperitatem respicerent. Itaque convectitium & simul nauticum æs, quod firmitati diuturnitatiq; rerum repertum credebatur, certissimo popularis imperij vitio, privatis provincijs, etiam contra pactorum conventionumque religionem, applicatum enormi certè licentiâ, quæ infirmando fœderi invalescens, non ut ante integro regis imperio, unius majestate coërcebatur. Quippe Geldri convectitiam portoriorumque pecuniam, quæ securati commerciorum aut exigendis telonijs apud Arnhemum & Neomagium à præsidiarijs navibus in Rheno & Vahali stantibus colligebatur, pro arbitrio distrahere dicebantur, volentibus ècontra Hollandis, ut æs istud in provincijs collectum adornandis instruendisque præsidiarijs navibus in Hollandiam mitteretur, quo provinciarum proventibus opibusq; adjuti, singularum commercia accepto maris imperio imminuerent. Quod cum FriFrisiorum Legatis probrosum detrimentosumq; videretur, quasi nuda colligendi æris nautici ministeria sibi reservarentur commoda & fructus. Hollandiæ cessura essent relationum jus imploravere, ne quid in præjudicium gentis suæ statueretur, & ne capiendi æris adornandarumque navium beneficium alijs ereptum publici juris æqualitatem, qua libertas & resp. starent, imminuerent. Quin satius judicabant pro tempore & dum aliter statutum foret, per Hollandiam colligi, quam colle &tum per Frisiam in Hollandiam remitti quæ citra hoc suarum navium ope socios defendi gloriaretur.
units.tr: Carel Roorda writes that the greater part of that gathering was conducted with greater bitterness than harmony of wishes, since it was found that each man, by drawing everything to himself and his own provinces, considered the inconveniences of his own province rather than the public prosperity of the covenant and the common treasury. Thus the money collected by convoy and at the same time for shipping, which was thought to be found for the firmness and durability of affairs, was, through the most certain vice of a popular government, assigned to private provinces, even against the sanctity of pacts and agreements, by a truly enormous licence, which, growing strong by weakening the covenant, was no longer restrained, as before, by the intact rule of a king, but by the majesty of one man. For indeed, the money from Gelderland's convoy duties and tolls, which was collected for the safeguarding of commerce or for exacting tolls at Arnhem and Nijmegen by the garrison ships lying on the Rhine and the Waal, was said to be disposed of at will; while, on the contrary, the Hollanders wished that this money collected in the provinces be sent to Holland, to equip and fit out garrison ships, so that, aided by the revenues of the provinces and their resources, having gained command of the sea, they might reduce the trade of each. Since this seemed shameful and harmful to the envoys of Friesland, as if the duties and profits of collecting shipping money were reserved for them alone, which would pass to Holland, they begged for the right of reports, so that nothing might be decided to the prejudice of their nation, and so that the benefit of raising the money and equipping the ships, taken from others, would not diminish the equality of public right on which freedom and the commonwealth depend. Indeed they judged it better, for the time being, and until it was otherwise decided, that the money be collected through Holland, than that it be collected through Friesland and sent back into Holland, since without this, by the strength of its own ships, it boasted of defending its allies.

units.la: Quo tempore prima socialis-diffidentiæ indicia ostendisse se mihi videntur, quæ ut in libertate ac plurium regimine solet, diversis ex causis aucta etsi dissimularentur, vim atq; memoriam apud posteros retinuere. Franckena notat i v. Eid. Iul. magnum agri palustris in Feenhusâ incendium exortum fuisse, ignoratumque an ardore cœli, qui tum intensissimus esse solet, an fortuito igne excitatum foret, prodigij saltem loco habitum secutam oræ istius calamitatem indicasse. Quippe provincialium animos enatus derepente pavor tum occupaverat, quod trans-rhenana auxilia hostibus destinari vulgatissimi rumores proderent, Francicumque Verdugium legionis tribunum liberandis Groninganis vastandæque Frisiæ magnum armorum apparatum decernere. Quamvis Aggæi Albadæ qui Coloniæ tum herebat, litteræ 17. Iul. in Frisiam perlatæ, de impotentia hostium & exhausto regis ærario palam testarentur, confirmantis spem securitatemque populi, quod nec supplementa cohortibus fore, nec delectus novos haberi circa Rhenum posse à Philippo assereret. Mox Neosylum, quod Norritius petierat, muniri à Frisijs cæptum, delegato Scipione Meckmans viro nobili, qui curando promovendoq; operi esset, quod tempestate, pluviâ, aut pondere nonnunquam fatiscens, justæ tamen munitionis formam vergente Septembri accepit. Quæ res Norritio castra ad Selverdiam tenenti commoda fuit, postquam famâ hostilium auxiliorum renascente Groningæ obsidionem, ad cujus orientale latus hostis recesserat, deserere coactus est. Franckena tradit Aggæum Albadam Frisiorum apud Agrippinenses legatum, alias à prioribus litteras de apparatu hostium ad Falckenburgum nuntiantes in Frisiam misisse, gentisque spem paucos ante dies conceptam alitamque magno metu & pavore commutasse. Unde in exercitu, qui Selverdiæ adhuc agebat murmura & mox tumultus cæpere, paucis primo mala in vetera pronis, qui bonos, sicuti pestilentiæ vitio, inquinando fertiles Frisiæ agros & amœnissimum Dongriæ tractum repetituros se comminabantur. Franckena notat Geldricas maxumè Hollandicasque copias, tum Nienortianum militem priorem in castris licentiam induisse, magisque prædæ & otio quam pugnæ & discrimini deditum omnem disciplinæ metum excussisse. Quâ occasione tumultuantium apud Selverdios castrorum hostium equites usi populabundi per Drentiæ fines in Stellinguersios irruerunt, direptisq; tribus pagis Haula, Donckerbroekio & Ofteruoldâ ad suos rediere. Quæ dum fiunt Georgij Lalainij Rennebergij valetudo cottidie igravescebat, ipseque inquies & conturbatæ mentis in malorum consiliorum autores acerbis sæpe diâterijs invehebatur. Cæterum Groningæ nomen ei maxu-mê me frequens, sive quod sumpti eâ in urbe imperij eum paeniteret, sive quod locum consulis Hildebrandij amicorumque caede ac sanguine temeratum vehementibus odijs execraretur. Certè tristissimam factorum imaginem animo ejus obversari ne illi quidem dissimulabant, qui aegri ministerio curaeque delecti juxta laetalis morbi periculum aperta quoque conscientiae vulnera introspiciebant. Neq; Corneliae sororis nomen dissimulabat. Itaque in illam invehi acerbè tum cubili ac colloquio prohibere, ne si forte admitteretur morti proximum vehementius commoveret, animumque infoelicem & laniatibus expositum nova inquietudine conturbaret: Quare amotâ sorore Corneliâ, quae sola è propinquis cum Montjoïo marito in aulâ erat, augeri malum, & imminere extrema praesentiens peculiares moribundis ceremonias sacraque conferri Pontificio ritu sibi jussit, quatriduumque post, qui dies in x. Kalend. Augusti incidebat, mortalitatem implevit. Creditum fuit, illum non remissiore erga Corneliam sororem odio decessisse, quod ne in extremis quidem solatio praesentis, & quod addo, unicae sororis refoveri mixtam angoribus infirmitatem permiserit. Tum facta visceratio cadaverq; aromate ac pretiosis odoribus condito, magnitudine juglandis cor defuncti se ostendisse autores rettulere. Unde facile judicatum, eum non veneno, quod propinatum vanis rumoribus ferebatur, sed aegritudine ac maerore animi confectum, qui deserti foederis poenitentiâ ac amissae florentis Praefecturae recordatione tum fallacium nuptiarum cum Mariâ Brimaeâ tristi eventu tactus vividae aetatis florem vigoremq; manifesto vitae taedio depavit. Postquam enim Maria Brimaea defuncto priore marito Lanceloto Barlamontio, Philippo Croïo principi Chimaeo nupta inritos infausti juvenis amores fecit, desperatione rerum correptus est, ac si fides tacitè, si ad Regem rediret, amanti data & mox elusa iratis sideribus & imminentibus fatorum adversitatibus praelusisset. Ipsa quoque Maria Brimaea illius levitate ac perjurio, quod occultè sollicitasse dicebatur, affectum concepti amoris vertit, verita ac indignata istius amantis nuptialibus sacris pactisque se credere qui publica violavisset. Quae etsi forte fingeret, ut ingeniosa indagandis malorum causis amantium infoelicitas est, ita & hoc acribus mordacibusque cogitationibus accedebat, quod Aurantij Principumque per Belgicam virorum amicitiâ ac societate prohiberetur, versique in odia provincialium favores inter infida peregrinorum servitia, inglorio contemptui manciparent. Ita omnem tolerati sub Albano exilij gloriam, actam sub litteris adolescentiam, adhaec formae ac virtutis decus, denique gestarum in bello clarissimarum rerum famam sola desertio foederis obscuraverat. Quippe Transisulaniae victor, Groningâ insuper partibus adjectâ tamdiu quoque laudabile apud Frisios laudabile imperium egerat, quamdiu spretâ Oyenbruggij allorumque aulicarum assentatione Aurantij procerumque consilijs usu fuisset, gratumq; libertatis & venerabile nomen regio servitio antepositisset. Caeterum per Corneliam sororem, alio pellectus à plerisque per Belgicam ac ab ipsis regijs neglectus humanis excessit, suffecto ei vixdum animam spiranti & necdum humato Francisco Verdugio. Decessit triginta & unum annos agens vigesimo secundo Iulij à templo Martiniano conditus cum Frisiae vicinisque locis præfuisset annis quatuor. Tradunt autores eum ab ambitione adeo acIↄ. Iↄ. lienum fuisse, ut etiam de deponendâ trium provinciarum honorabili Præfecturâ cogitaverit, nisi solius Pompei Ufkenij consilio (qui Hardenbergico prælio perijt magnâque apud eum gratiâ vigebat) à propo-sito revocatus fuisset. Excessus illius clam & per silentia habitus avertendis militum seditionibus, qui morte Ducis velut excusso rectoris imperio flagitaturi stipendia non inrito metu credebantur.
units.tr: At this time, it seems to me, the first signs of mutual distrust appeared. As is usual in a free state governed by many, these grew from various causes. Although they were concealed, they kept their force and were remembered by posterity. Franckena notes that on 12 July a great fire broke out in the marshland at Feenhusen. It was not known whether the heat of the sky, which is usually most intense at that season, or an accidental flame had kindled it. At least, people regarded it as a portent, and a disaster on that coast followed. For a sudden panic then seized the minds of the provincials, because the most widespread rumours reported that auxiliaries from beyond the Rhine were destined for the enemy, and that Francisco Verdugo, a tribune of the legion, was decreeing a great armament to relieve the Groningers and lay waste Friesland. Yet letters from Aggaeus Albada, who was then staying at Cologne, were delivered in Friesland on 17 July. They openly bore witness to the enemy's weakness and the exhausted royal treasury, and they confirmed the people's hope and sense of security, since he asserted that Philip could neither send reinforcements to the cohorts nor raise new levies near the Rhine. Soon the Frisians began to fortify Nieuwesluis, which Norritius had sought. They appointed Scipio Meckmans, a nobleman, to take charge of and advance the work. It sometimes gave way under storm, rain or its own weight, but as September drew on it took the form of a proper fortification. This suited Norritius, who was holding a camp at Selwerd. After the rumour of enemy auxiliaries revived, he was forced to abandon the siege of Groningen, from whose eastern side the enemy had withdrawn. Franckena relates that Aggaeus Albada, the Frisian envoy among the Agrippinenses, had sent letters to Falkenburg, reporting the enemy's preparations, and that the hope the people had conceived and nourished a few days earlier had changed into great fear and dread. Hence in the army, which was still at Selwerd, murmurs and then tumults began. A few men, already inclined to the old evils, threatened that they would go back to the good and fertile fields of Friesland and the most pleasant district of Dongeradeel, and would pollute them as if with a plague. Franckena notes that the troops from Gelderland and especially from Holland, and earlier the Nijmegen soldiers, had granted themselves licence in the camp. Given over more to plunder and idleness than to battle and danger, they had shaken off all fear of discipline. On this occasion, while the mutineers were at Selwerd, the enemy's horsemen took advantage, rode plundering through the territory of Drenthe into Stellingwerf, and, after sacking the three villages of Haule, Donkerbroek and Oosterwolde, returned to their own people. While these things were happening, the health of Georg de Lalaing, Count of Renneberg, grew worse every day. He himself, restless and troubled in mind, often railed bitterly against the authors of the evil counsels. His thoughts most often turned to Groningen, either because he regretted having taken up his command in that city, or because he cursed with fierce hatred the place defiled by the murder and blood of the consul Hildebrand and his friends. Certainly those who had been chosen to attend and care for him, and who looked even into the open wounds of his conscience beside the danger of his deadly illness, did not conceal that the most sorrowful picture of those deeds haunted his mind. Nor did he hide the name of his sister Cornelia. He forbade her, with harsh words, to be admitted to his bed or to speak with him, lest, if she were admitted, she might stir him more violently when he was close to death, and disturb his unhappy spirit, already torn apart, with fresh unrest. So his sister Cornelia, who alone of his relatives was at court with her husband Montigny, was removed. The illness grew worse, and sensing that the end was near, he ordered the special ceremonies and sacraments for the dying to be administered to him in the Papist rite. Four days later, which fell on 22 July, he completed his mortal life. It was believed that he died with no less hatred towards his sister Cornelia, since he did not allow her, even in his last hours, to bring the comfort of her presence to his weakness, a weakness mingled with anguish, and she was his only sister. Afterwards an autopsy was performed, and the body, embalmed with spices and precious perfumes, was shown to contain a heart the size of a walnut, as the authors reported. Hence it was easily judged that he had been worn out not by poison, which vain rumours said had been given to him, but by sickness and grief of mind. Stung by remorse for the broken covenant, by the memory of the lost flourishing governorship, and by the sad outcome of his deceitful marriage with Maria of Brimeu, he manifestly wasted the flower and vigour of his lively age through weariness of life. For after Maria of Brimeu, widow of Lancelot de Berlaymont, married Philip de Croÿ, Prince of Chimay, the young man's unhappy love came to nothing. He was seized by despair, as if the promise he had tacitly given to his lover, and which he had broken by returning to the King, had foreshadowed it under angry stars and the threatening adversities of fate. Maria herself, too, turned her affection away from him because of his fickleness and perjury, which he was said to have secretly solicited. She feared and scorned to trust herself to the nuptial rites and pacts of a man who had violated public faith. Perhaps she invented this, as the unhappiness of lovers is ingenious in searching for the causes of its misfortunes. Yet this too was added to his bitter and biting thoughts: the friendship and alliance of Orange and of the leading men of Brabant were forbidden him, and their favours, turned into hatred of the provincials, delivered him to inglorious contempt amid the faithless services of foreigners. Thus his desertion of the covenant alone had obscured all the glory of the exile he had endured under Alba, his youth spent in letters, the grace of his form and his virtue, and finally the fame of his most distinguished deeds in war. Indeed, as victor in Overijssel, and with Groningen added to his side, he had exercised a praiseworthy command among the Frisians for as long as, scorning the flattery of Oyenbrugge and the other courtiers, he followed the counsels of Orange and the chief men, and preferred the pleasing and venerable name of liberty to royal service. Drawn away by his sister Cornelia, and by many others in Brabant, and neglected even by the royalists themselves, he departed this life. Francisco Verdugo, who had hardly been drawing breath and was not yet buried, succeeded him. He died on 22 July, aged thirty-one, and was buried in the church of St Martin, having governed Friesland and the neighbouring places for four years. Authors relate that he was so free of ambition that he even considered laying down the honourable governorship of the three provinces, had he not been called back from that purpose by the counsel of Pompeius Ufkens alone, who perished at the battle of Hardenberg and enjoyed great favour with him. His death was passed over in secrecy and silence, to avert mutinies among the soldiers, who, as if the leader's rule had been shaken off with the Duke's death, were believed to demand their pay with no empty fear.

units.la: Quare illius morte per omne confinium & apud Agrippinenses (ubi magna pars nuperi Senatus regij & nobilitatis Frisicæ quæ Philippi sa-cramento innexa erat exilium sustinebat) vulgatâ ijdem profugi Alexandrum Farnesium Philippi proregem datis Coloniâ litteris sollicitarunt, ut successorem defuncto Rennebergio quanto ocyus daret Frisiæq; ac laboranti imprimis Omlandiæ succurreret.
units.tr: By his death the news spread through the whole border region and among the Agrippinenses, where a large part of the recent royal Senate and of the Frisian nobility, who had been bound by oath to Philip, were in exile. The same fugitives, hearing of it, petitioned Alexander Farnese, Philip's viceroy, by letters sent from Cologne, that he should give a successor to the late Renneberg as quickly as possible and come to the aid of Friesland, and especially of the afflicted Ommelanden.

units.la: LITTERÆ hæ erant:
units.tr: These were the letters:

units.la: EX epistolâ, quam nostræ subjunctam habes, ALEXANDER FARNESI, cognosces quis Groningæ & per Omlandiam rerum sta-tus sit. PHILIPPI regis nostri exercitus RENNEBERGIJ excessu fidei anceps est & ruinam imperio regis minari videtur, nisi FRANCISCUM VERDUGIUM virum strennuum & cuius virtuti multum dandum est, cum auxilijs stipendijsque isthuc miseris ocyssimè. Crastinus quidem dies ducendo in Frisiam auxiliario militi dictus est, sed requiritur ut arma in promptu sint, & ut VERDUGIO autoritatem potestatemque facias tam diu pacis bellique negotia administrandi, dum regiæ majestatis aut tuâ ordinatione Frisiæ Omlandiæque Gubernator datus fuerit. Quo nostrorum omnium vota & spes contendunt. Non dubitamus quin justissimo imperio provinciam recturus sit, foreque ut gratiâ quâ valet regis nostri subditos conciliaturus sibi sit, incussurusque terrorem hostibus & rebellibus PHILIP-PI, quem hoc ipsum, quod nos desideramus, præstando summe beneficio, quo majus mortalibus dari non potest, obligabis.
units.tr: From the letter which you have appended to ours, Alexander Farnese, you will learn what the state of affairs is at Groningen and throughout Omland. The army of our king Philip under Rennenberg is uncertain after Rennenberg's death and seems to threaten the ruin of the king's rule, unless you send Francisco Verdugo, a vigorous man to whose valour much must be given, with auxiliaries and pay to that place as quickly as possible. Tomorrow indeed has been fixed for leading the auxiliary soldiers into Friesland, but it is required that arms be ready and that you give Verdugo the authority and power to administer the affairs of peace and war until he is appointed governor of Friesland and Omland by the royal majesty's ordinance or by yours. To this the wishes and hopes of all of us tend. We do not doubt that he will govern the province with most just rule, and that by the favour he enjoys with our king he will win over the king's subjects and strike terror into the enemies and rebels of Philip. By granting this very thing that we desire, you will oblige us by the greatest kindness, than which none greater can be given to mortals.

units.la: Quæ epistola à Bucchone Ayta, Georgio Westendorpio, H. Dekama, Iacobo Vinckenburgio & Vito Commingha signata, maturandis rebus incitamentum addidit. Mox alteræ litteræ Georgij Westendorpij nuper Senatoris per Frisiam regij, ad Casparum Roblesium Billium Frisiæ jam antè Gubernatorem hunc in modum additæ.
units.tr: This letter, signed by Bucho Ayta, George Westendorp, H. Dekama, Jacob Vinckenburg and Vitus Commingha, added a spur to hasten matters. Soon afterwards another letter was added, in this manner, from George Westendorp, lately the king's senator throughout Friesland, to Casparus Robles Billius, formerly governor of Friesland.

units.la: HOC ipso litteræ à Magistratu Deputatisque Groningæ & Omlandiæ ad me perlatæ sunt, excessum Comitis RENNEBERGII, qui vigesimo secundo Iulij horâ Octavâ matutinâ ex hac vitâ à Deo evocatus est, nuntiantes. Cujus morte id incommodi datum est, quod regi rebellium copiæ in cœnobio Selverdico castra habentes auctæ sint, & quod in-tra urbem & turrim Martiniani fani tres legiones congregatæ seditiones moliantur, perque suburbanum rus & planos in agros effusæ villas provincialium diripiant. Neque minus à cive nostro periculum est, qui nudis auxiliorum pollicitationibus & cunctatione ALEXANDRI FARNESII frustratus coitiones facit in apertam haud dubiè vim eruptu ras. Adhæc quoniam metuendum est, ne Germanos hac in urbe præsidium habentes, AURANTIUS ad defectionem sol-licitet collocatis in proximo castris, ALEXANDRUM FARNESIUM
units.tr: By this same letter, letters from the magistrate and deputies of Groningen and Omland were brought to me, announcing the death of Count Rennenberg, who was called from this life by God at eight in the morning on 22 July. By his death this harm was caused: the rebels' forces encamped at the monastery of Selwerd have grown larger for the king, and in the city and in the tower of the church of St. Martin three legions have gathered and are plotting sedition, and pouring out into the suburban countryside and the flat fields they plunder the farmhouses of the provincials. No less dangerous is the position of our fellow citizen, who, cheated by the bare promises of aid and by the delay of Alexander Farnese, is making plans which will undoubtedly break out into open violence. Besides, since it is to be feared that Orange may incite the Germans holding the garrison in this city to defection, with camps placed nearby, I have warned and urged Alexander Farnese

units.la: monui ac hortatus sum, ut te Præfecturam in tuam quanto ocyus remitteret. Præsertim cum ita de te sentiam, teste Deo & meâ conscientiâ, ut nemo procerum Ducumque magis hoc tempore idoneus gerendis rebus videatur. Quapropter rogo ut occasione hac utaris, certus te materiem gloriæ & famæ tuæ illustrande habituum facturumque, imprimis gratiam Regi, quâ majorem nulli, qui hac ætate vivunt, præstituri erunt. Tuæ certè prudentiæ ista provinciæ egent, quam sine morâ aut deliberatione impendi regiis necessitatibus velim.
units.tr: to send you back to your command as quickly as possible. Especially since I think of you, God and my conscience being my witnesses, in such a way that none of the nobles and commanders seems more fitted at this time to conduct affairs. Therefore I ask you to use this opportunity, certain that you will have material for illustrating your glory and fame, and above all the king's favour, than which none of those living in this age will grant greater. Surely those provinces need your prudence, which I would wish to be devoted without delay or deliberation to the king's necessities.

units.la: Datum Coloniæ 27. Iul. 1581.
units.tr: Given at Cologne, 27 July 1581.

units.la: Simile adhortamentum Buchonem Aytam ad Roblesium, qui Namurci agebat perscripsisse reperio, quo Verdugio urbem ad Groningam Frisiosque præmisso, Roblesius trans-rhenanarum provinciarum imperio, quo exutus fœderatorum armorum vi erat, indulgentiâ Regis aut Alexandri Farnesij redonaretur. Addit Ayta Clareboo Melroïo, alijsque Philippi legatis Coloniæ effectum fuisse, ut Germanorum equites peditesque supplendis aut legendis copijs abundè habere rex posset, ita alienis econtra ab Alençonio Germanis, ut ne unus quidem insigni mutatione rerum sacramentum ei dicturus fit. Quin Gallorum, inquit, nomen adeo passim Germanis ingratum, ut nec ludibrij aut invisus vacuum fit. Quæ omnia stabiliendo Philippi per Frisiam Omlandiamque in quam exules perfugæque reditum sibi augurabantur, imperio enormi fœderatorum partium odio perscribebantur.
units.tr: I find that Bucho Ayta wrote a similar exhortation to Robles, who was then at Namur, so that, with Verdugo sent ahead to the city of Groningen and to the Frisians, Robles might be restored by the king's or Alexander Farnese's indulgence to the rule of the Trans-Rhenish provinces, of which he had been stripped by the force of the allied arms. Ayta adds that it had been arranged at Cologne by Clarebeeck, Melroy and the other envoys of Philip that the king would have German horsemen and foot soldiers in abundance to supply or levy his forces; on the contrary, the Germans were so estranged from Alençon that not even one would swear allegiance to him after this notable change of affairs. "Moreover," he says, "the name of the French is so everywhere hateful to the Germans that it is not free from mockery or hatred." All these things were written with bitter hatred of the allied party's enormous rule, while they hoped, by establishing it, for the return of Philip's rule through Friesland and Omland, into which the exiles and refugees were to return.

units.la: Quo tempore speciosò libertatis nomine neque improspero armorum successu, quæ Philippo II. Caroli filio ex malè usurpatâ dominatione, tot jam annis reponebantur, de eodem rege deserendo in consessu Ordinum generalium actum, quo ejurato ejus imperio, populoq, tam Belgico quam Trans-Rhenano in libertatem asserto, jus quoque belli tanto æquius, & ut fieri solet, fœliciusque procederet. Cui rei revocatus è Gallia Alençonius (frater unicus & regis sive totius regni auxilia, & per connubium Elisabethæ Anglorum societatem & potentiam ut putabatur secum tracturus) multum addidisse momenti credebatur, & quod mare securum ac patens commercijs opes & subsidia gerendis incontinente rebus promitteret. Sive regis Philippi imperium fastidientibus satis, quæ ultro mutandis mortalium rebus prona, post violentum & grave regnum his in terris exercitum passis enormia meliora tempora pollicebantur, sive auctâ gentium feroci virtute, quæ olim potentissimas quasque nationes Principesque lacessere ausæ sustinendis quoque Philippi armis, etsi per tot maria terrasque conquisitis, majorum exemplo præparabantur.
units.tr: At that time, under the specious name of liberty, and with no unfavourable success of arms, the things that had for so many years been kept in reserve against Philip II, son of Charles, on account of his badly usurped dominion, were debated in the assembly of the General States: whether to desert that king, and by renouncing his rule and asserting the people, both Belgic and Trans-Rhenish, to liberty, so that the right of war might also proceed more justly and, as usually happens, more happily. Alençon, recalled from France to this business (the king's only brother, who, through his marriage to Elizabeth, was thought to be bringing with him the aid of the whole kingdom and the alliance and power of the English), was believed to have added much weight, and because he promised that the sea would be safe and open for commerce, to supply resources and aid for carrying on affairs without delay. Whether it was because men had had quite enough of King Philip's rule, which of its own accord is prone to change in human affairs, and promised better times after the violent and heavy reign that the enormous army had imposed on these lands; or because of the increased fierce valour of the peoples, who once dared to challenge the most powerful nations and princes, and who were now preparing, following their ancestors' example, to withstand even Philip's arms, though gathered from so many seas and lands.

units.la: Quod factum, velut miraculo proximum & stupori gentium repertum, per omnem Europæ aliarumque orbis partium angulum famam populi Belgici fœderatique diffudit, quod maximum regum lacertos per Indiam Africamque ultra Gades longè Herculisque columnas movientem Belgicæ suæ circulo exutis sacramentis exclusissent.
units.tr: This deed, close to a miracle and a thing to astonish the nations, spread the fame of the Belgic and allied people through every corner of Europe and the other parts of the world: that they had excluded from their Belgic circle, stripped of their oaths of allegiance, the greatest king, who was moving his arms through India and Africa, far beyond Gades and the Pillars of Hercules.

units.la: EDICTI Sensus talis erat.
units.tr: THE EDICT. Its sense was as follows.

units.la: OMNIVM gentium, quas sol lustrat, opinione ac fide creditum est, populum non Principis causâ, sed Principem populi tutelae haberi. Quam cum negligit, aut ab officio à lege deficiens deteriore imperio commutat, non Principis, sed tyranni nomen meretur. Cui oblustari cum jure gentium possit, quas ad propulsandam vim atque injuriam, tum liberorum conjugumque defensionem sacer naturae instinctus armavit, ita majore tyrannicae immanitatis culpâ gravandus est, qui rejectis populi sui supplicationibus querimoniisque ad patientiam infelicis turbae efferatur. Quem nec lex, nec honestum, nec mos majorum, nec data in publico adivrataque sacris fides obligare modestiae ac officio possunt, apud ipsas praesertim gentes, quae Principes suos honestis semper conventionibus & saepe beneficijs obstrinxe-re. Ita PHILIPPUS à morte CAROLI patris rerum potitus, qui magnitudinem suam, qui victorias, qui triumphos populi sui armis atque fidei debuerat, nec paterno hortatu, quo reponi gratiam fidissimae genti volebat, morem gessit, nec acceptorum primis imperij ac principatus sui annis beneficiorum memoriam retinuit, usus eorum perverso consilio, qui à regimine BELGICARUM vicinarumq; provinciarum cautionum religione arcebantur. Qui Neapolitano ac Siculo regnis, qui Mediolanensium Principatui, qui dissitis Indijs imperare pro arbitrio sueti, ne hoc quidem PHILIPPO in Rege ferebant, ut absolutae dominationis regnum utrobivis exercens, ORDINUM BELGICAE liberiorisque populi praescripto regeret. Igitur primo specie religionis asserendae, sed revera ut Hispanae gentis invalescente imperio BELGAE servirent, jureque majorum exuerentur, Episcopi primarias in civitates suis cum Canonicis introducti, cum inquisitionis propagandae studio, tum ut ditium coenobiorum censu patrimonia Episcoporum locupletarentur, totumque quod libertatis titulo veniret, fedissimo servitio inumbraretur. Quod olim CAROLO à Caesare excogitatum cum abnuissent BELGAE magnâ potentissimi Caesaris prudentiâ omissum est. Igitur ut regnante PHILIPPO idem fieret, multae querimoniae libellique cum à civitatibus provinciisque tum à Legatis Belgicae authoritate Consilij Status oblati missiq; in Hispaniam regnante MARGARETA Ducissâ Parmensi, MONTINIUS & EGMONDANUS qui regij consilij severitatem mitigarent. Cujus etsi spem fecisset PHILIPPUS, tamen mutatâ in deterius mente litteras in BELGICAM misit, quae recipi Episcopos & patrimonia Episcopatibus applicari, Inquisitionem introduci, postremo decreta Concilij Tridentini valescere jubebant. Unde mentium primo stupor & consternatio orta, mox aversus à PHILIPPO rege populi amor atq; dilectio asperitatem decreti introspexit, quod non in corpora tantum sed animorum quoque secreta ac libertatem conscientiae DEO subjacentis distringeretur. Itaque indignatione tristis servitij & infelicis populi miseratione, ne tormentis laniatibusq; carnificum subesset, anno 1566. MARGARETAE Ducissae Parmensi nobilitas supplex facta, ablegatis simul in Hispaniam Marchione BERGENSI & MONTINIO, qui necessitatem remedy & medicinam turbatae affectaeque BELGICAE exponerent. Caeterum tantum abfuit, ut nobilitatis intercessio valuerit, quae efferato per Hispaniae Senatum rege Majestatis damnata (vulgare isti temporum aetati crimen) legatorum quoque in Hispaniâ carceres & contra omne gentium jus etiam barbaris sacrum ac inviolabilis supplicia mortesque
units.tr: It has been believed by the opinion and faith of all the nations the sun shines upon that the people are not held for the sake of the prince, but the prince for the protection of the people. When he neglects this, or departs from his duty under the law and exchanges it for a worse rule, he deserves the name not of prince but of tyrant. Just as the sacred instinct of nature has armed men with the right of nations to repel violence and injury and to defend their children and wives, so he is to be charged with the greater guilt of tyrannical savagery who, having spurned the entreaties and complaints of his people, is driven to harden himself against the sufferings of an unhappy multitude. Neither law, nor honour, nor the custom of our ancestors, nor the faith pledged publicly and confirmed by oaths can bind him to moderation and duty, especially among the very peoples who have always bound their princes by honourable agreements and often by benefits. So Philip, having taken control of affairs after the death of his father Charles, who had owed his greatness, his victories and his triumphs to the arms and loyalty of his people, followed neither his father's exhortation, by which Charles wished the favour of that most faithful nation to be restored, nor kept in memory the benefits received in the first years of his rule and principate. He acted on the perverse counsel of those who were kept away from the government of the Netherlands and the neighbouring provinces by the obligation of their pledges. Those who were accustomed to rule at will over the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily, over the principality of Milan, and over the distant Indies, could not even bear that Philip, as king, should rule over the Netherlands in accordance with the prescribed rights of the estates of Netherlands and of the freer people, exercising a kingdom of absolute dominion in both places. Therefore, first under the pretext of defending religion, but in truth so that, as Spanish power grew, the Belgians might become slaves and be stripped of the rights of their ancestors, bishops were introduced with their canons into the chief cities, partly with a zeal for spreading the Inquisition, and partly so that the bishops' estates might be enriched by the revenues of the wealthy monasteries, and everything that might come under the title of liberty might be overshadowed by the most foul servitude. When the Netherlanders had refused what Charles once contrived at the suggestion of the emperor, the plan was dropped through the great prudence of that most powerful emperor. Therefore, so that the same thing might happen under Philip, many complaints and petitions were presented, both by the cities and provinces and by the envoys of the Council of State of the Netherlands, and sent into Spain during the regency of Margaret, Duchess of Parma; among them Montigny and Egmont, who were to temper the severity of the royal council. Although Philip had given hope of this, yet, with his mind changed for the worse, he sent letters into the Netherlands ordering that the bishops be received, that the estates of the monasteries be assigned to the bishoprics, that the Inquisition be introduced, and finally that the decrees of the Council of Trent be enforced. Hence at first astonishment and dismay arose in men's minds, and soon the love and affection of the people turned away from King Philip, who perceived the harshness of the decree, since it was aimed not only at bodies but also at the inner recesses of minds and at the freedom of conscience, which is subject to God alone. Therefore, saddened by indignation at the wretched servitude and by pity for the unhappy people, lest they be subjected to torments and the mangling of executioners, the nobility in 1566 humbly petitioned Margaret, Duchess of Parma, and at the same time sent into Spain the Marquis of Berghes and Montigny, to set forth the necessity of a remedy for the troubled and afflicted Netherlands. Yet the intercession of the nobility was so far from prevailing that, the king having been goaded by the Spanish Senate, they were condemned for treason (a charge common in that age), and even the prisons of the envoys in Spain, and punishments and deaths, which by every law of nations are sacred and inviolable even among barbarians, were stirred up.

units.la: Edictum quo prodiuntur causa ob quas deferius fit Philippus. tesqᵘe concitaverit. Quo anno etsi muliebri MARGARETAE Gubernatricis prudentiâ ac solerti ingenio Belgica nonnihil tempestas consedissët fugatis, captis cæsisve partibus, tamen ad omne populi jus tollendum & ut hæ gentes, Indorum more, haberentur (quod ALANAE PHILIPPI Regis per Galliam Legati litteræ ad Gubernatricem prodiderant) missus cum exercitu & comitatu sanguinarij Senatus FERDINANDUS ALBANUS crudelis efferiqué ingenij vir, Belgicaeq, libertatis osor acerrimus, qui magna reverentiâ inermis & non contra luctantis populi exceptus Philippici imperij, qui venturus ipse adornatâ per Hispaniam Zelandiamq; classe credebatur, inauspicata funestaque initia titulo Gubernatoris Præfectiq; regij etsi sanguine non contingeret, infælici BELGICAE exhibuit. Quippe urbes ac castella mox præsidijs firmata, novæ arces validissimas per civitates extructæ, Belgicæ Principes specie officij & velut ad concilium convocati, vinculis ac custodiæ dati, & ne quid immanitatis deforet, ipso ALBANO judice aut Brabantiâ contra fas eductî, aut gladio percusi amantem libertatis sanguinem tanquam piaculares victimæ, effuderunt. Adhæc Nobilitatis clarorumque civium cruore fœdata pegmata, multi exterres patriâ exilia toleravere, profugorum domus militæ completæ, uxoribus atque liberis intentata stupra & ne vita subsidia forent, ditium patrimonia per fiscum distracta, qui centesimæ, vigesimæ decimæque exactione, adinstar lienis intumescens omne sacrum & profanum rapiebat. Scilicet quo impotens & inermis BELGICA virium suarum infirmitate Regi PHILIPPO sine exceptione pareret, crudelesque ministri inter spolia & sanguinem innocentissimæ multitudinis se explerent. Igitur Curiæ, judicia, collegia suffectis Hispanis ejectisq;, provincialibus contra jus fasque gentium rectoribus destituta, impedita decimis provinciarum commercia, invalidis civium procerumque querimonijs, quibus amovendam ad calamitatem tyrannı satellitumque vultus salutabantur. Quæ mala, velut æternæ Principis famæ & populi inopiæ destinata, perpetuitatem quoque suam habitura fuissent, nisi AURANTIJ Principis, tum profugæ proscriptæque nobilitatis impulsu, Hollandia Zelandiaque tantæ immanitatis odio ac fastidio ab ALBANI imperio defecivissent. Unde armorum vis illas in gentes conversa, factumque ut ista provinciæ aliarum armis, (quas aut horror aut veneratio regiæ potentiæ aut castella arcesque in metu ac obsequio continebant) impetitæ sint, non ALBANO tantum regnante, sed etiam REQUESENTIO, qui in speciem mitioribus, sed æque perniciosis artibus imperium exorsus Antverpiam, Aloslum; tentatis Bruxellis sede Principis, deinde Trajectum ad Mosam cæde ac direptione oppressit. Post quoque à morte REQUESENTII Concilio Status BELGICI, ita volente PHILIPPO, rerum potiunte & Hispanis hostium loco proclamatis, HYERONIMUS RODA sive ingenij superbiâ, sive regiæ autoritatis mandato, motus fultusque Ducem se ac patronum nefarijs Hispanorum actionibus declaravit repudiatoque Concilij STATUS sigillo regium adulteravit, non aliâ potentiæ usurpatione quam quæ Proregem deceret. Quare superiorum Provinciarum ORDINES cum AURANTIO Principe tum Hollandis Zelandisque pacem fœdusque ferire compulsi sunt, continuatis interim apud Regem provincialium officijs supplicationibusque quo Hispanos legum pacisque ruptores populatoresque opulentissimarum urbium suam in Hispaniam PHILIPPUS Rex revocaret. Quod quamvis facturum se Rex promitteret, insolentiamque suæ gentis & scelera detestari se simularet, boni Principis & paterno affectu obtentutentui dato, tamen (cognitum est, Regem in illo Hispanorum furore sibi pla-cuisse. Qui quoque ut majore dolo ac fallacia populum BELGICUM LXXXI. circumveniret, non multo post IOANNEM AUSTRIACUM tanquam regij sanguinis Principem in provincias misit, quo fœdus Gandavense & conventa ORDINUM approbando confirmandoque in Hispanos pacis publicæ ruptores animadverteret, jureque provincijs asserto libertatem redderet.
units.tr: The edict setting out the causes for which Philip has become a worse prince, and the horrors it has aroused. In that year, although by the prudence and skilful wit of Margaret, the governess, the storm in the Netherlands had somewhat subsided, the parties having been put to flight, captured or cut down, nevertheless, in order to abolish every right of the people and to have these nations treated as the Indians are (as the letters of King Philip's envoy through France had revealed to the governess), Ferdinand of Alba, a man cruel and fierce of temper, a most bitter hater of Netherlandish liberty, was sent with an army and the retinue of the bloodthirsty Senate. Though he was received with great reverence by an unarmed people who did not resist him, and though it was believed he would come himself with a fleet prepared through Spain and Zeeland, his inauspicious and deadly beginnings, under the title of governor and royal prefect, brought an unhappy time to the Netherlands, even if they were not yet touched by bloodshed. Indeed, cities and castles were soon fortified with garrisons, new and very strong citadels were built throughout the cities, and the princes of the Netherlands, summoned as though to a council under the pretext of duty, were given to chains and custody, and, lest any savagery be lacking, were either led out of Brabant against the law, with Alba as judge, or struck down with the sword, and they poured out their blood, which loved liberty, like sacrificial victims of expiation. Besides this, the scaffolds were defiled with the blood of nobles and distinguished citizens; many endured exile from their native land; the houses of fugitives were filled with soldiers; rapes were threatened against wives and daughters, and so that there might be no means of support for life, the estates of the wealthy were seized by the treasury. By the exaction of the hundredth, the twentieth and the tenth penny, swelling like a spleen, it snatched up everything sacred and profane. Clearly, so that the powerless and unarmed Netherlands, weakened in its strength, might obey King Philip without exception, and the cruel ministers might glut themselves on the spoils and the blood of an utterly innocent multitude. Therefore the courts, the tribunals and the colleges, with Spaniards installed and the provincial governors removed contrary to law and the rights of the nations, were left without order; commerce was hindered by the tithes of the provinces; the complaints of citizens and nobles were unheard, though they were greeted with faces that promised removal of their calamity by the tyrant and his henchmen. These evils, as if destined for the eternal disgrace of the prince and the poverty of the people, would have kept their perpetuity, had not Holland and Zeeland, at the instigation of Prince William of Orange and of the nobility, then in exile and proscribed, revolted from the rule of Alba in hatred and disgust at such monstrous cruelty. Hence the force of arms was turned against those nations, and it came about that these provinces were attacked by the arms of others, whom either terror or reverence for royal power, or fortresses and citadels, kept in fear and obedience; and this happened not only under Alba's rule, but also under Requesens, who began his government with milder, but equally pernicious, arts. He oppressed Antwerp and Aalst, and after attempts on Brussels, the seat of the prince, then Utrecht on the Maas, with slaughter and plunder. After the death of Requesens too, the Council of State of the Netherlands, since Philip willed it, took control of affairs, and the Spaniards were proclaimed enemies. Jeronimo de Roda, whether from the pride of his temper or by the king's command, was stirred up and supported, and declared himself the leader and patron of the wicked actions of the Spaniards; and having rejected the seal of the Council of State, he corrupted it with the royal seal, using no other usurpation of power than what would befit a viceroy. Wherefore the Estates of the Upper Provinces were compelled to conclude peace and a treaty with Prince William of Orange and with Holland and Zeeland, while in the meantime they continued to present their duties and supplications to the king, that King Philip would recall the Spaniards, breakers of laws and peace and plunderers of the most wealthy cities, back into Spain. Although the king promised that he would do so, and pretended to detest the insolence of his nation and its crimes, he gave a pretext of a good prince's paternal affection; yet it became known that the king was pleased with that Spanish fury. And so that he might ensnare the Netherlandish people with still greater guile and deceit, not long afterwards he sent John of Austria into the provinces, as a prince of royal blood, so that by approving and confirming the Treaty of Ghent and the agreements of the estates, he might punish the Spaniards as breakers of the public peace, and by asserting the rights of the provinces, restore their liberty.

units.la: Cæterum discordiam socias inter provincias serendo, conventionum fœderumque ruptor, quas perjurio temerabat, nihil aliud primâ imperij sui infantiâ molitus est, quam ut legionum Germanicarum fidem sollicitaret, quorum præsidio validissima per provincias castella attinebantur. Non alio certè fine, quam ut societate cum Germanis eorumque tribunis initâ castellisque in potestatem redactis gravius AURANTIO, Hollandiæ Zelandiæque bellum inferret, prælatâque pacis ostentatione, civilem discordiam & intestina arma concitaret. Quæ etsi occultè tegeret, tamen illius consilia fato quodam in apertum producta maturitatem non accepere, evenitque ut juratæ pacis loco crudis adhuc potentiæ suæ rebus bellum daret. Quæ omnia etsi deferendum ad Regem sufficiant, eligendumque alium Principem, qui mitiore imperio ac curâ desertas per vim inti annos à Rege provincias moderaretur, ita ab Austriaci morte non aliam regis mentem fuisse deprehensum est, quam ut Gandavensi Fœderi aliisque conventionibus illuderet, gravioribusque postulatis Belgicæ Proceres & omne pacis remedium turbaret. Igitur Regis actionibus diffisi Regum Principumque intercessiones sollicitavimus, quo cum Rege, si per arbitros fieri posset, ex æquo pacisceremur, missis insuper Coloniam legatis nostris, ut Cæsaris Electorumque Romani Imperij coitione pax perscriberetur. Cæterum id arcanum isti conventui subfuit, ut provinciam à provincia, socium à socio divelleret, quo provincialium vires ex concordiâ auctas discordia minueret. Inde publico mox edicto majestatis nos damnavit, proscriptiones instituit, assignato percussori pretio, qui Aurantium submoveret. Igitur omni spe pacis ruptâ destituti omni malorum remedio, desolatique naturæ legem instinctumque imitati, quo jura majorum asseramus, defendamusque, à vi & injuriâ conjuges, liberos, denique ipsam posteritatem nostram alio auxilio tutandis legibus nobisque reperto, Notum facimus nos ultima necessitate compulsos communi suffragio & consensu Regem Hispaniae jure dominationis, eminentiæ, jurisdictionis omnique imperij hæreditate privasse, non usuros Regio impositerum nomine tituloque, à cuius Sacramento Magistratus omnes populumque insuper absolvimus. Et quoniam cum Andium Duce singularum provinciarum mandatis fulti convenimus, Matthiæque Archiduci missionem petenti concessimus; ita volumus, ut Regis Hispaniae sigilla aboleantur, omittantur, tradanturque; Provinciarum Ordinibus, quisve suo, sive Andini, sive provincialis Senatus, sive Aurantii usuri erunt. Volumus quoque ne aurum argentumque, Regis nomine & insignibus signetur, & ut Præsides, Cancellarij, Senatores, Rationum magistri, reliquique Officiales sacramento quod Regi præstiterunt, soluti, nobis & quidem novâ sub formulâ dicant. Quæ omnia ut vim ac perpetuitatem obtineant demandamus Præsidi secreti Senatus Brabantiæ, Geldriæque, & Comitatus Zutphaniæ Cancellario Senatuique, Præsidi per Flandriam, per Hollandiam Senatuique; Rationum Magistris per Zelandiam, Præsidi Senatuique, per Frisiam, Prætori Mechliniensium, Præsidi Senatuque Vltraiectino aliisque;
units.tr: But sowing discord among the allied provinces, the breaker of the agreements and treaties which he defiled with perjury, he undertook nothing else in the first infancy of his rule than to solicit the loyalty of the German legions, by whose garrison the very strong castles throughout the provinces were held. Certainly to no other end than that, by forming an alliance with the Germans and their tribunes, and by bringing the castles under his power, he might wage war more harshly against William of Orange, Holland and Zeeland, and, under the pretence of peace, stir up civil discord and internal arms. Although he concealed this secretly, nevertheless by some fate his counsels were brought into the open and did not come to maturity, and it came about that, instead of the sworn peace, he waged war on affairs of his power which were still immature. All these things would be enough to be referred to the king, and to the choosing of another prince who might govern the provinces, deserted for years by the king through force, with a milder rule and care. But after the death of Austria it was discovered that the king's mind was no other than to mock the Treaty of Ghent and other agreements, and to disturb the Netherlandish nobles and every remedy of peace with harsher demands.
