CONSULES; Reverendissimi ac Doctissimi, Mysteriorum Divinorum Dispensatores, Animarum PASTORES Vigilanti- ssimi; Doctissimi ac Spectatissimi, DD. Doctores, Licentiati, ac Magistri; Amici, Consanguinei, & Affines denati Maκαρίτη; Cæteriq; Viri Doctiss. Honoratiss. ac Spectatissimi; Tuque Nobilissima, Doctissima, Lectissima, ac Ornatissima, Studiosorum Corona, Flos & decus Academiæ nostræ.
units.tr: Most noble, most distinguished, most wise and most respected CURATORS of this nourishing Academy; most grave DEPUTIES of the illustrious and mighty ORDERS OF FRIESLAND; MAGNIFICENT MR. RECTOR; most distinguished, most learned and most acute DOCTORS, PROFESSORS, honoured colleagues, NOBLE GENTLEMEN; most distinguished, most wise and most respected CONSULS; most reverend and most learned dispensers of the Divine Mysteries, most vigilant MINISTERS of souls; most learned and most respected Doctors, Licentiates and Masters; friends, kinsmen and relatives of the late, of blessed memory [μακαρίτη]; and the other most learned, most honoured and most respected men; and you, most noble, most learned, most select and most adorned crown of students, flower and glory of our Academy.

units.la: VANTIS calamitatum, miseriarum, ærumnarumque fluctibus gravissimis ac decumanis, genus humanum passim obnoxium sit: testatur continua ac jugis rerum humanarum tristis ac subitanea mutatio & catastrophe. Testatur in primis celeberrima ac famosissima hæc ACADEMIA PATRIAE, quæ proh dolor! non quotannis: verum singulis fermè semestribus aut trimestribus, gravissimo lethalique vulnere sauciatur ac lancinatur. Ut enim unda undam trudit: sic publicus luctus & squalor, publicum antecedentemque è vestigio subsequitur. Excessit, pronuper ex hac vita, camposq; Elysæos petijt, unde negant redire quenquam, Nobilissimus, Acutissimus nec non Theologorum hujus ævi facile Princeps JOHANNES MACCOVIUS S S. Theologiæ Doctor & Professor primarius, Collega conjunctissimus ac dilectissimus. Hoc gravissimo vulnere Academico non contenta, non
units.tr: Since the human race is everywhere exposed to the most grievous waves of calamities, miseries and troubles, the constant and unbroken sad and sudden change and overthrow of human affairs bears witness to it. It bears witness above all in this most famous and renowned Academy of our homeland, which, alas, is wounded and torn by a most grievous and deadly blow not yearly, but almost every six months or every three months. For as one wave drives on another, so public grief and squalor follow hard upon the heels of one another. There has lately departed from this life and gone to the Elysian Fields, from which they say no one returns, the most noble, most acute and, by far, the chief of the theologians of this age, JOHN MACCOVIUS, Doctor of Sacred Theology and first Professor, a most close and beloved colleague. Not content with this grievous academic wound, not

units.la: Laudatio Funebris
units.tr: Funeral Oration

units.la: satiata, dira ac implacabilis illa D E A M O R T A, iterum ex improviso, quasi per cuniculos aggreditur ac adoritur, ipsas Athenas Attico Frisiacas, ac incomparabilem summumque virum, Clarissimum Collegam Dominum P I E R I U M W I N S E M I U M, I. V. Doctorem, Eloquentiae Professorem, Patriae Historiographum, Academiae decus ac columen aeternum, praeter omnium bonorum ac doctorum virorum votum, praeter omnem expectationem in ipso florentis ac vigentis aetatis flore atque vigore (lucis praesentis) usura privavit. — — — — — — Nec non Fati Abstulit atra dies, & funere mersit acerbo.
units.tr: Not yet satisfied, the dire and implacable goddess D E A T H has again attacked unexpectedly, as if through tunnels, the very Athens of Friesland, the Attic Athens, and the incomparable and most eminent man, our most distinguished colleague, Mr. PIERIUS WINSEMIUS, Doctor of Law, Professor of Eloquence, Historiographer of the Fatherland, the eternal glory and pillar of the Academy. Contrary to the wish of all good and learned men, and beyond all expectation, she deprived him of the use of the present light in the very bloom and vigour of his flourishing age. — — — — — — And the black day of fate took him away and plunged him into a bitter death.

units.la: Ex hoc clarissimi ac celeberrimi viri discessu ex hac vita, quantum publica ac Academica res, detrimenti capiet, sentiet, testabuntur fortean seri nostri nepotes, omnesque illi quibus studia, bonaeque artes curaeque ac cordi imposterum erunt. Hujus igitur summi ac incomparabilis viri exequias, dum omnes ac singuli hodie pulla veste, longoque syrmate ex officio caritatis ac Christianae Συμπαθείας iverimus lessumque fecerimus. Unicum hoc tandem, Auditores Ornatissimi, restat, ut ex laudabili instituto huius Academiae pijs manibus denati Μακαρίτη parentemus: Quamvis quidem clarorum virorum fama, ex se aeterna, ex se quoque immortalis sit: Nihil tamen unquam sanctius habet habuitque reverentia superstitum, quam ut amissos cum pia veneratione ac memoria recordetur: dandum enim hoc illustrium virorum posteritati (Tacito teste) ut quomodo exequijs, a promiscua sepultura mortalium separentur. Ita in traditione supremorum accipiant, habeantque propriam memoriam ac laudem. Sic enim olim Atheniensium Oratores, eos qui bello Persico ad Plataeas mortem fortiter pro salute patriae oppetierant, funebri laudatione publice prosecuti sunt. Sic quoque Fabius Maximus Publium Scipionem, Sic Iulius Caesar Iuliam Cajj Marij uxorem, amitam suam, amplissimis ac magnificis verbis in supremo funere publice pro concione ornarunt ac laudarunt. Sic & Appij Decemviri defuncti funebrem laudationem sequutis temporibus, aequis auribus Plebs Romana audivit ac accepit.
units.tr: How much harm this death of our most distinguished and renowned man will bring to public and academic affairs, our late descendants will perhaps witness and testify, together with all those to whom learning and the good arts and their cares will be dear in future. Therefore, since all of us today have gone to this great and incomparable man's funeral in mourning dress and long cloaks, out of the duty of charity and Christian sympathy [Συμπαθείας], and have made lament, there remains for us, most adorned listeners, one thing only: that in keeping with the praiseworthy custom of this Academy we should pay honour to our departed colleague, the blessed one [Μακαρίτη], with pious tribute. Although the fame of famous men is in itself eternal and immortal, nothing has ever been held more sacred by the reverence of the survivors than to remember the departed with pious veneration and remembrance. For, as Tacitus testifies, it must be granted to posterity of illustrious men that by their funerals they are set apart from the common burial of mortals, so that in the handing down of their last rites they may receive and keep their own memory and praise. Thus of old the Athenian orators publicly honoured with a funeral oration those who had bravely met death at Plataea in the Persian war for the safety of the fatherland. Thus also Fabius Maximus adorned Publius Scipio, and Julius Caesar his aunt Julia, the wife of Gaius Marius, with the most ample and splendid words, publicly, before the assembly, at their last funerals and praised them. And the Roman people, in later times, listened to and received with fair ears the funeral praise of the deceased Decemvir Appius.

units.la: Qua quoque de causa indubie moti, proximi heredes ac amici denati nostri Collegae ac Μακαρίτη etiam atque etiam a me flagrantissime & instanter petierunt, ut hoc extremum Christianae pietatis officium in me reciperem. Accessit quoque praeterea Amplissimi S E N A T U S A C A D E M I C I decretum, quo, per Delegatum, hanc dicendi Provinciam impraesentiarum humeris meis imposuerunt, quod pietatis, quod humanitatis officium, tum S E N A T U I A C A D E M I C O Amplissimo, tum denati Μακαρίτη amicis, nullam excusationem plane pleneq; admittentibus, tum imprimis familiari amicitiae, quam cum demortuo, constanter, pie, religiose semper colui & habui, me debere existimavi. Verum enimvero cum probe novi, quid humeri valeant, quid ferre recusent, & quam curta domi nobis sit in dicendo supellex. Proinde omnes ac singulos (Auditores Ornatissimi) vos etiam atque etiam rogatos volo, ut praesentem hanc Oratiunculam non gravate accipere & excipere dignemini, in qua si fortean verborum pondus, elegantia, splendor, caeteraque oratoria ornamenta desiderentur, cogitate quaeso, non ab Rhetore, aut Rhetoris filio proficisci, verum ab eo, qui parum aut nihil a facundia possit. Ne igitur (Auditores Ornatissimi) diutius animos vestros, longa per exorsa, suspensos teneam, (novi enim optime quam odiosa ac taediosa sit Circensibus pompa) paucis & Laco-
units.tr: Moved undoubtedly by this same cause, the nearest heirs and friends of our departed colleague, the blessed one [Μακαρίτη], have most ardently and urgently asked me again and again to undertake this final office of Christian piety. Moreover, the most honourable decree of the A C A D E M I C S E N A T E was added, by which, through a delegate, they have now laid upon my shoulders this task of speaking; and I have judged that I owe this duty of piety and humanity both to the most honourable A C A D E M I C S E N A T E, which admits no excuse at all, and to the friends of the deceased blessed one [Μακαρίτη], and above all to the close friendship which I have constantly, devotedly and faithfully always cultivated and held with the departed. Yet, truly, since I know well what my shoulders can bear and what they refuse, and how meagre is the stock of speech I have at home. Therefore I want all and each of you, (most adorned listeners), to be asked again and again to deign to accept and receive this little oration without displeasure; if perhaps in it the weight of words, elegance, splendour and the other ornaments of oratory are lacking, please consider that it comes not from a rhetorician or a rhetorician's son, but from one who has little or no power of eloquence. So then, (most adorned listeners), that I may not hold your minds, kept in suspense by long preludes, any longer (for I know very well how tedious and wearisome the pageantry of the circus is), I shall speak in few words and Laconic-

units.la: in memoriam P. Winsemij.
units.tr: In memory of P. Winsemius.

units.la: Laconicè orationis penicillo adumbrabo, ac delineabo nostri Μακαρίτε nativitatem, educationem, studia, vitam, mores & mortem.
units.tr: In the brush-strokes of a few words, I shall sketch and outline the birth, upbringing, studies, life, character and death of our late lamented friend [ὁ Μακαρίτης].

units.la: Nativitatis locum quod concernit, natus est ὁ Μακαρίτης Leovardiæ Frisio- rum, Anno Æræ Christianæ Millesimo Quingentesimo Octuagesimo sexto, quæ totius provinciæ nostræ caput ac Metropolis est, claris ac stupendis ingenijs, clara ac superba, juxta illud Poëtæ.
units.tr: As to the place of his birth: the late man was born at Leeuwarden in Friesland, in the year of the Christian era 1586. It is the capital and metropolis of our whole province, bright and proud with its remarkable and distinguished minds, in keeping with the saying of the poet:

units.la: Doctorum genitrix LEOVARDIA clara Virorum.
units.tr: "Leeuwarden, bright mother of learned men."

units.la: Permagni ut plurimum refert an quis Vervecum in patria, crassoq; sub aëre,
units.tr: It matters very much, for the most part, whether a man is born in the land of sheep, under a thick sky,

units.la: Colchisne natus an enutritus Athenis sit.
units.tr: "whether he was born in Colchis or brought up in Athens."

units.la: Sic Plato (uti memoriæ proditum est) imprimis maximam fœlicitatis suæ partem urbi, in qua natus ac educatus erat, adscripsit: quotidie Dis immortalibus singulares gratias referens, quod Athenis non Thebis natus esset, non secus ac si tacitè Philosophorum Princeps innueret summa ac excelsa ingenia, & ad magna nata, non nisi in summis ac excelsis locis lucem aspicere. Quod nativitatis præsagium si verum unquam fuit, sane in nostro Μακαρίτη verissimum fuit.
units.tr: So Plato, as is recorded, above all ascribed the greatest part of his happiness to the city in which he had been born and brought up, daily giving thanks to the immortal gods that he had been born at Athens and not at Thebes. It is as if the prince of philosophers were quietly suggesting that lofty and exalted minds, born for great things, look upon the light only in lofty and exalted places. If this presage of birth was ever true, it was most true in the case of our late friend [ὁ Μακαρίτης].

units.la: Ad Parentes quod attinet: honestissimis ac præstantissimis est natus Parentibus; patrem habuit, Virum Clarissimum omnigenâ Literaturâ politiori & Philosophia, nec non arte Oratoriâ exercitatissimum, Liberalium artium Magistrum HAJONEM PIERII WINSEMIUM, Præfectum ludi literarij Leovardiensis vigilantissimum: Matrem habuit THOMULAM MENEMIAM, Matronam honestissimis civibus Leovardiensibus oriundam. Præterea fratrem MENELAUM WINSEMIUM, SS. Medicinæ Doctorem, πεῳξίως, Anatomices, & Botanices Professorem, donec patria Academia stetit, per viginti (& quod excurrit) annos longè celeberrimum. Scilicet (Poëta teste) FORTES creantur fortibus, & bonis: Est in juvencis, est in equis, patrum Virtus: nec imbellem feroces Progenerant aquilæ columbam.
units.tr: As to his parents: he was born to most honourable and excellent parents. He had as father that most distinguished man, thoroughly versed in every kind of polite literature and philosophy, and also in the art of oratory, a Master of the Liberal Arts, HAJO PIERII WINSEMIUS, a most vigilant Prefect of the Leeuwarden grammar school. He had as mother THOMULA MENEMIA, a matron descended from the most honourable citizens of Leeuwarden. Besides, he had a brother, MENELAUS WINSEMIUS, Doctor of Medicine, worthily [ἀξίως] Professor of Anatomy and Botany, who for twenty years and more, as long as the home academy stood, was by far the most celebrated of them all. Surely, as the poet bears witness: "Brave children are born of brave and good parents; the courage of the sires is in the young bullocks and in the horses; fierce eagles do not beget a dove that is unfit for war."

units.la: Hujus patris prædicti (ut revertar ad id unde digressus) ὁ Μακαρίτης noster & χειρογραφία, aut privatâ manuductione in studijs suis tantum profecit, ut postmodum accedente institutione Correctoris THEODORI LAVERMANNI, imprimis verò superveniente tandem institutione clarissimi viri JOHANNIS FUNGERI I. V. & Medicinæ Doctoris, Scholæ Leovardianæ Gymnasiarchæ quondam longè famosissimi ac felicissimi, ut brevi temporis spatio reliquos suos condiscipulos longis parasangis fœlicitate, dexteritate ingenij ac profectu studiorum antecesserit, ita ut anno ætatis suæ decimo-quarto, post varia singularis eruditionis specimina, in Latina ac Græca Poësi, nec non in Orationibus methodicè dispositis facundeque habitis, ex angustis studiorum carceribus emissus, & quasi à patre manumissus aut emancipatus, ad augusta, ingenua, ac liberalia Academica studia & exercitia publica fuerit admissus, ac receptus in album aut matriculam Academiæ, Anno millesimo sexcentesimo primo, decimo tertio Aprilis, Rectore ac Dictatore Academico magno illo (piæ memoriæ) JOHANNE ARCERIO THEODORETO, Græcæ linguæ Professore Celeberrimo,
units.tr: Under this father just described (to return to the point from which I digressed), our late friend [ὁ Μακαρίτης] made such progress in his studies, either by his own writing [χειρογραφία] or by private tuition, that afterwards, when the instruction of THEODORUS LAVERMANNUS, the corrector, was added, and above all when at length the instruction of the most distinguished JOHANNES FUNGERUS, Doctor of Both Laws and of Medicine, once by far the most famous and most fortunate headmaster of the Leeuwarden school, was added, he outstripped all his fellow pupils within a short span of time, by many long strides in good fortune, quickness of wit and progress in his studies. So it was that in his fourteenth year, after various remarkable specimens of learning in Latin and Greek poetry, and in orations methodically arranged and delivered with eloquence, he was released from the narrow prison-cells of his studies, as if manumitted or emancipated by his father, and was admitted to the noble, free and liberal academic studies and public exercises. He was received and enrolled in the register or matriculation roll of the Academy on the thirteenth of April, in the year 1601, when the Rector and Academic Dictator was that great man, of pious memory, JOHANNES ARCERIUS THEODORETUS, most celebrated Professor of the Greek language.

units.la: Laudatio Funebris
units.tr: Funeral Oration

units.la: Academiam hanc vix ac ne vix ingressus, mox Orationem publicam pro Rostris Academiæ habuit in solemni panegyri, ad admirationem ac stuporem Auditorum ac clarissimorum Dominorum Professorum, cum adhuc ejus esset staturæ ac proceritatis ut hypopodio statura sublevanda fuerit, ne forte alias sanna postica aut antica ab auditoribus exciperetur, aut explcderetur. Ingressus hanc Academiam mox invenit amicos ac Mecoenates magnos, imprimis in Græca Lingua JOHANNEM ARCERIUM THEODORETUM; in Logica clarissimum Dñum LOLLIUM AB ADAMA: in Physica magnum illum HENRICUM DE VENO I. V. & Medicinæ Doctorem, Liberaliumque Artium Magistrum, sub cujus præsidio plurimas quæstiones in publico congressu acute defendit, tantâ cum animi alacritate, tantâ promptitudine, tanto judicio, ut ipsus Præses in publica disputatione, Collegam ipsum nominare ac salutare, non dedignatus fuerit.
units.tr: Scarcely had he entered this Academy when he soon gave a public oration from the Rostra of the Academy at the solemn panegyric, to the admiration and astonishment of the audience and of the most distinguished Professors. He was then so small in stature and height that a footstool had to be used to raise him, lest some mocking hiss from behind or in front be directed at him from the audience, or he be hissed off. On entering this Academy he soon found friends and great patrons, above all in Greek JOHANNES ARCERIUS THEODORETUS; in Logic the most distinguished Mr. LOLLIUS AB ADAMA; in Physics the great HENRICUS DE VENO, I.V. and Doctor of Medicine, Master of the Liberal Arts. Under his presidency he defended very many questions acutely in public disputation, with such cheerfulness of spirit, such readiness and such judgement, that the Presiding officer himself did not disdain to name him and greet him as a colleague in a public disputation.

units.la: Horum fideli ne dicam paternâ institutione pro tempore usus, tandem ad studium Medicinæ animum applicuit: ut autem cum fructu fieret, nihil prius aut antiquius nostro Maxaeíty fuit, quam ut se in singularem favorem clarissimorum DD. Professorum, præsertim Clarissimi Domini AULAETIJ: nec non viri Celeberrimi RAPHAELIS CLING-BYL insinuaret, sub cujus quoq; præsidio publicè de igne elementari disputavit cum summa circumstantium admiratione: usq; adeo ut in publica disputatione Præses aut Moderator publice in hæc verba eruperit. Quis Spiritus hunc Juvenem ac Respondentem agit? videtur ad magna natus. Paulo post Athenas Frisicas é Maxaeíty deserens, ut uberiorem studiorum suorum fructum & messem consequi posset (tanquam ad uberiorem mercatum) se ex consilio patris, rectâ Lugdunum Batavorum contulit. In qua illustri ac celeberrima Academia itidem (uti Franequeræ secerat) in omnium Dominorum Professorum gratiam ac singularem favorem se insinuavit, præsertim in gratiam ac amicitiam clarissimorum Dominorum Professorum PAVIJ, VORSTIJ Medici, HUERNIJ, DANIELIS HEINSIJ, nec non MERULAE, quorum omnium institutione ac familiaritate quotidie uti frui nostro Maxaeíty in summis delitijs fuit, qui omnes & singuli ipsum singulari affectu, amore & favore prosequebantur, summasq; ingenij dotes admirabantur ac venerabantur. Ne tamen cochlearum instar, aut domi ad focum delitesceret, aut in una atq; altera Academia consenesceret aut oberraret, relictâ Leydâ censuit exteras regiones & Academias quoq; lustrandas esse, — — Et ire per omnes Terrasque tractusque maris. — — — Vt mores hominum multorum cernat & urbes.
units.tr: Under the faithful, I may even say paternal, instruction of these men he was for a time guided, and at length he applied his mind to the study of medicine. But so that this might bear fruit, nothing was more pressing or more important to our Maxaeíty than to insinuate himself into the special favour of the most distinguished Professors, especially the most distinguished Mr. AULAETIUS, and also the most celebrated man RAPHAEL CLINGBYL. Under the presidency of the latter he also disputed publicly on elemental fire, to the great admiration of those present, so much so that the Presiding officer or Moderator burst out publicly in these words during the disputation: What spirit drives this young man who is responding? He seems born for great things. Shortly afterwards he left Maxaeíty for Athens of Friesland, and on his father's advice went straight to Leiden, the Lugdunum Batavorum, so as to reap a richer harvest of his studies, as one goes to a richer market. In that illustrious and most celebrated Academy too, as he had done at Franeker, he insinuated himself into the favour and special goodwill of all the Professors, especially into the favour and friendship of the most distinguished Professors Paauw, Vorstius the physician, Heurnius, Daniel Heinsius, and also Merula. To use and enjoy their instruction and companionship every day was for our Maxaeíty a supreme delight. All of them, one and all, pursued him with singular affection, love and favour, and admired and revered his outstanding gifts of mind. Yet, lest like a snail he should hide at home by the hearth, or grow old and wander about in only one or two Academies, having left Leiden he judged that foreign regions and Academies too must be explored: "And to go through all lands and stretches of sea; to see the manners of many men and their cities."

units.la: Voluntariumq;, (amore literarum) exilium decennale in se é Maxaeíty suscepit, bisque se in Germaniam omnium nationum matrem, studiorumq; alumnam & altricem se recepit: ibidemque mutato studij Medici cursu, se ad divinarum ac humanarum rerum scientiam, justi atque injusti notitiam, artem æqui & boni, id est, ad Jurisprudentiam se contulit, sive hoc aut proprio Naturæ ductu ac instinctu factum sit, sive amicorum Mecoenatumque hortatu ac suasu, nec ne, non satis constat. In Germania ubi vixit Helmstadij, Erfordiæ, Jenæ alijsq; in locis, summam quoq; mox cum summis viris ac Juris-Consultis familiaritatem ac amicitiam inivit ac contraxit. Imprimis vero Jenæ cum magno
units.tr: He undertook, out of love of letters, a voluntary ten-year exile from Maxaeíty, and twice betook himself to Germany, the mother of all nations and the nurse and foster-mother of studies. There, changing the course of his medical studies, he turned to the knowledge of divine and human things, the knowledge of what is just and unjust, the art of the fair and good, that is, to jurisprudence. Whether this was done from his own natural bent and impulse, or at the urging and persuasion of friends and patrons, is not altogether clear. In Germany, where he lived at Helmstedt, Erfurt, Jena and other places, he soon also formed and entered into the closest familiarity and friendship with leading men and jurists. Especially at Jena, with great

units.la: in memoriam P. Winsemij.
units.tr: In memory of P. Winsemius.

units.la: gno illo Juris-Consultorum Coryphæo ac Dictatore conterraneo suo DOMINICO ARUMAEO Frisio, ex vicino pago Arum patricijs parentibus oriundo. Cum hoc Juris-Consulto, nec non cum Consiliario Ducis Brunsvicensis Doctissimo Domino FOPPIO AB ÆTSEMA conterraneo familiarissimè, quoque toto illo tempore quo in Germania hæsit ac vixit conversatus est. Postmodum relictâ Germaniâ contulit se ὁ Maxaeirns, ut alias quoque lustraret Academias longe celeberrimas, in Sueciam, nec non paulo post in Gallias, ut summis Galliæ Luminibus, Juris-Consultis, Politicis, & Historicis quoq; innotescere posset, quibus omnibus in locis, propter singulare ingenij acumen & naturæ donum, apud summos Juris-Consultos, Politicos, ac Historicos in summo honore ac æstimio fuit; qui omnes ac singuli, singulari amore & favore, qua publicè, quâ privatim Maxaeirns prosequebantur. In Gallijs dum agit, ut studiorum suorum fructum consequeretur, debitosque virtuti ac eruditioni honores ac dignitates reportaret, visum ipsi fuit, ad Lauream Doctoralem adspirare, eamq; Anno Millesimo, sexcentesimo, undecimo, vigesima prima Mensis Aprilis in Academia Cadomensi, post publicam Disputationem de Testamentis habitam, consecutus est præsentibus multis Proceribus, Clarissimis Dominis Professoribus, Doctoribus, Licentiatis & Magistris, postquam cum summo omnium applausu publicè disputavit, qua disputatione perac-ta, stupendum hoc ingenium omnes in admirationem sui rapuit. Relictâ Gallia postquam per continuum decennium proprijs sumptibus ætatem in diversis celeberrimis Academijs egisset, visum ipsi fuit, tandem rectâ in patriam ad amicos ac Mecoenates tendere, quos non paucos sibi addictissimos ac faventissimos habuit, invenit, & fecit, usque adeo ut quasi mutua æmulatio ac concertatio pia ac religiosa inter illos fuerit, dubiumque ac ambiguum sæpe foret, plusne noster Maxaeirns diligeret ac æstimaret Mecoenates: an verò vice versâ illi nostrum Maxaeirns Domum reversum, ne segne otium magnifico nomine velaret, Doctorisque Titulum ac Gradum ad inanem pompam ac ostentationem haberet, coram Suprema Frisiæ Curia (post immatriculationem) Praxin Forensem exercere cœpit; Verum nec illa res fœliciter ipsi ex animi voto ac sententia cessit, mox enim in ipso ingressu ac praxeos limine defecit, ac descivit, Foroq; valedixit, repudium misit, divortiumque à Foro fecit, jussitque (more solenni Romano) forenses res suas sibi habere. Moxq; ad theoreticum, tranquillum, modestum, ac placidum vitæ genus se contulit, rus in Tusculanum suum nimirum privatus, ut altum dormiret, nec non ut tanto liberius philosophari ac meditari posset remotis arbitris.
units.tr: With that great coryphaeus and dictator of jurists, his fellow countryman DOMINICUS ARUMAEUS of Friesland, who came of patrician parents from the nearby village of Arum. He was on very intimate terms with this jurist, and with the councillor of the Duke of Brunswick, the most learned Lord FOPPIUS AB ÆTSEMA, also a fellow countryman, throughout the whole time he stayed and lived in Germany. Afterwards, having left Germany, Maxaeirns went on to visit other very famous universities, in Sweden, and a little later in France, so that he might become known to the outstanding lights of France, among its jurists, politicians and historians. In all these places, on account of his singular keenness of mind and natural gift, he was held in the highest honour and esteem by the leading jurists, politicians and historians, all of whom, both individually and collectively, pursued Maxaeirns with a singular love and favour, both in public and in private. While he was in France, wishing to reap the fruit of his studies and to win the honours and dignities owed to virtue and learning, he decided to aspire to the doctoral laurel. In the year 1611, on the twenty-first day of April, at the Academy of Caen, after a public disputation on wills, he obtained it, in the presence of many nobles, the most distinguished Professors, Doctors, Licentiates and Masters. When he had disputed publicly with the great applause of all, and that disputation was finished, this astonishing talent captivated everyone with admiration. After he had left France and spent a continuous decade at his own expense in various famous academies, he decided at last to make straight for his homeland, to his friends and patrons, of whom he had, found and made not a few most devoted and well-disposed, so that there was, as it were, a mutual rivalry and pious and religious contest among them. It was often doubtful and uncertain whether our Maxaeirns loved and esteemed his patrons more, or whether, conversely, they esteemed our Maxaeirns more. Having returned home, so that he might not veil idle leisure under a grand name, and so that he might not hold the title and degree of doctor for empty display and ostentation, he began to practise law before the Supreme Court of Friesland (after his enrolment). Yet this venture did not turn out happily for him, according to his heart's desire and judgement, for at the very threshold of his practice he soon faltered and withdrew, bade farewell to the Forum, sent it a bill of divorce, and divorced himself from the Forum, and (in the solemn Roman manner) bade his legal affairs be kept by himself. Soon he turned to a theoretical, quiet, modest and peaceful way of life, retiring to his country estate, his Tusculan villa, as a private man, so that he might sleep soundly and, with observers removed, be able to philosophise and meditate all the more freely.

units.la: Scilicet, secessum scribentes & otia quærunt.
units.tr: Of course, those who write seek retreat and leisure.

units.la: Sylva placet Musis, urbs est inimica Poëtis.
units.tr: The forest pleases the Muses; the city is hostile to poets.

units.la: Vel quia cum Poëta Lyrico, beatum illum existimavit. — — Qui procul negotijs Ut prisca gens mortalium, Paterna rura bobus exercent suis Solutus omni fœnore Forumque vitat, & superba civium Potentiorum limina. — — —
units.tr: Either because, with the lyric poet, he judged that man blessed: — — He who, far from business, like the people of old, works his ancestral fields with his own oxen, free from all interest, and shuns the Forum and the proud thresholds of the more powerful citizens. — — —

units.la: Laudatio Funebris
units.tr: Funeral Oration

units.la: Dum totus in theoretico ac solitario hoc ruris tris vitae genere est, seque privatis Musis oblectat, ecce derepente ex improviso ad gravissimum ac praeclarissimum Historiographi munus ab Illustribus ac Praepotentibus Frisiae ORDINIBUS vocatur, non secus ac si patriae Proceres Clarissimo Μακαρίτη doctum hoc & solitarium otium inviderent, exi stimantes scilicet tam nobile ac portentosum ingenium ruri non debere in privatis speculationibus consenescere aut torpescere, verum illa meditari, aggredi, aeternaeque memoriae posterorum consecrare, quae ab ipso Regisugio inter Potentissimum REGEM HISPANIAE, nec non inter PROCERES hujus provinciae domi & foris gesta sunt, post violatas Leges fundamentales UNITARUM PROVINCIARUM, post violatum Jus Gentium, post violata Foedera, post violata Pacta publica, post violata pedibusque conculcata, (tyrannide Hispanica) Privilegia Majorum: Et quod caput rei est, post introductam tyrannicam Conscientiarum mortalium Inquisitionem, Orthodoxaeque Religionis Reformatae suppressionem & extirpationem. Hanc Historici Patriae Spartam ac Provinciam sibi ab Illustribus ac Praepotentibus ORDINIBUS hujus Provinciae concreditam, fideique suae commissam, quanta cum laude immortalique fama Μακαρίτης noster ad aeternam memoriam decusque Patriae exornarit, testabitur ipsa HISTORIA, quae jam sub prelo est, brevique lucem aspectura est, instantibus proximis comitiis Patriae. Ex eo enim tempore, quo primam Historiae suae partem publici fecit juris mox quasi agminatim per literarum commercium viri totius Europae celeberrimi ac famosissimi (profundam eruditionem Μακαρίτη admirantes) primas ipsi detulerunt, atq; ad coelum usque laudibus encomiisque extulerunt, uti videre est ex literis incomparabilis ac immortalis Heroïs JOSEPHI SCALIGERI, HUGONIS GROTIJ, PAULI LUBBERTI Legati Illustrissimi Regis Suecia, DANIELIS HEINSIJ, PONTANI, CATZIJ, GRASVINKELIJ, ZEVECOTIJ: nec non quoque liquet ex commendatione AMMIANI STRADAE Iesuitae Romani, qui non semel atque iterum verum multoties in Historia sua nostri Μακαρίτη honorificam mentionem facit, summèque commendat. Verum Historici Patriae munus cum per viginti quatuor aut quod excurrit annos, Μακαρίτης fideliter bona fide obivisset. Visum deinde Illustribus ac Praepotentibus Frisiae ORDINIBUS, nec non Nobilissimis ac Amplissimis Almae hujus Academiae CURATORIBUS, Μακαρίτη nostro propter summam spem quam de illo conceperant, injungere ac demandare quod; ordinariam Historiarum & Eloquentiae Romanae Professionem, quam Anno Millesimo sexcentesimo trigesimo sexto, die vii. Decembris, post publicam inaugurationem, Rectore clarissimo Collega GEORGIO PASORE, (piae memoriae) aggressus est, in qua professione quantus Μακαρίτης fuerit, vos Frisij, vos Belgae, Germani, Sueci, Sarmatae, Ungari, Dani, Norvegi, Galli & Angli, qui quotidie ad ipsius lectiones, publicas agminatim tanquam ad uberem mercatum confluxistis: testes omni exceptione majores esse potestis. In hac Academica dignitate ab Illustribus ac Praepotentibus Frisiae ORDINIBUS constitutus, Amplissimos quoque Academiae honores ac dignitates Anno cIↄ. Iↄc. xxxix. sustinuit, Rectoraeque honos ipsi concordibus SENATUS Academici suffragijs demandatus est, in qua summa dignitate ac Praefectura Academica positus, se muneri isti parem ostendit, juxta illud tritum Graecorum proverbium ἀρχὴ ἀνδρὶ δείκνυσιν [?], id est, Magistratus virum ostendit, cum alias, Tacito teste, Plurimi bo-
units.tr: While he lives wholly in this theoretical and solitary kind of country life, and delights himself with his private Muses, suddenly and unexpectedly he is summoned to the most weighty and distinguished office of Historiographer by the Illustrious and Most Powerful Estates of Friesland. It was as if the leaders of the fatherland begrudged our late Makaritês [μακαρίτης] this learned and solitary leisure, judging that so noble and remarkable a talent ought not to grow old and grow dull over private speculations in the countryside, but should take up and undertake those matters and consecrate them to the eternal memory of posterity: the things done by the Most Powerful King of Spain himself, and by the leaders of this province at home and abroad, after the fundamental laws of the United Provinces were violated, after the law of nations was violated, after covenants and public pacts were violated, and after the privileges of our ancestors were violated and trampled underfoot by Spanish tyranny. And, what is the heart of the matter, after the tyrannical Inquisition over men's consciences was introduced, and the Reformed orthodox religion was suppressed and rooted out. How greatly our late Makaritês adorned this History, which was entrusted to him and committed to his faith by the Illustrious and Most Powerful Estates of this province, to the eternal memory and honour of the fatherland, with what praise and immortal fame, the History itself will bear witness; it is already at the press and will soon see the light, with the coming assembly of the fatherland close at hand. For from the time when he first made public the first part of his History, men of renown and fame throughout Europe (admiring our late Makaritês's profound learning) quickly, as it were in a crowd and by correspondence, awarded him first place and raised him to the heavens with praise and eulogy. This is evident from the letters of the incomparable and immortal hero Joseph Scaliger, Hugo Grotius, Paul Lubbert, Ambassador of the Most Illustrious King of Sweden, Daniel Heinsius, Pontanus, Cats, Graswinckel, and Zevecotius; and it is also clear from the commendation of Ammianus Strada, Jesuit of Rome, who more than once, indeed many times, makes honourable mention of our late Makaritês in his History and commends him highly. But when the Historian of the fatherland had faithfully and in good faith discharged this office for some twenty-four years or a little more, it then seemed good to the Illustrious and Most Powerful Estates of Friesland, and to the most noble and distinguished Curators of this nourishing Academy, to assign and entrust to our late Makaritês, on account of the great hope they had conceived of him, the ordinary Professorship of History and Roman Eloquence, which he undertook on the 7th of December in the year 1636, after his public inauguration, under the most distinguished Rector and colleague Georgius Pasor, of blessed memory. In this professorship, how great a man Makaritês was, you Frisians, you Belgians, Germans, Swedes, Sarmatians, Hungarians, Danes, Norwegians, French and English, who flocked daily to his public lectures in crowds as to a rich market, can be witnesses above all exception. Appointed to this academic dignity by the Illustrious and Most Powerful Estates of Friesland, he also held the highest honours and offices of the Academy in the year 1639, and the honour of the Rectorship was conferred upon him by the united votes of the academic Senate. Placed in this highest dignity and academic headship, he showed himself equal to that duty, according to the well-known Greek proverb, "office shows the man" [ἀρχὴ ἀνδρὶ δείκνυσιν], that is, the magistracy reveals the man; whereas on other occasions, as Tacitus testifies, most men [the sentence breaks off here].

units.la: in memoriam P. Winsemij.
units.tr: In memoriam P. Winsemij.

units.la: boni sint ante imperium, pauci in imperio. Legesque Academicas quas sartas tectasque se conservaturum juraverat, pie, religiose & masculè defendit, & quidem eâ tempestate, quâ boni mores in hac Academia proh dolor! non colebantur, sed exulabant. In Academica hac dignitate positus ὁ Μακαρίτης cum per octennium firmâ solidâque valetudine ut plurimum praeditus fuisset, post varia edita eruditionis suae monumenta, post HISTORIAM ad umbilicum deductam, post SYRIUN editum, post AMORES editos, post varias editas ORATIONES FUNEBRES. Tandem pridie calendarum Novembris anni praesentis clɔ. Iɔc. xliv. qui dies erat Mercurij, mane Lethargo exquisito, ac legitimo corripitur ac infestatur, usque adeo ut mox neminem Amicorum aut Collegarum dignoscere aut alloqueretur, verum toto decubitus tempore omni loquelâ, & quantum extrinsecus dijudicare licuit, etiam omni rationis usu & sensu destitutus fuerit. Hoc gravi ac tristi spectaculo attoniti ac contristati Amici ac proximi Haeredes, evestigio atque confestim curaverunt vocari Clarissimum Dominum PHOCYLIDEM 'HOLVERDA, nec non Doctissimum VIBRANDUM REVIUM SS. Medicinae Doctores, qui post varias deliberationes ac consultationes, ultrò citròque habitas, judicabant ex re aegri esse, tertium Medicum vocari, ne quid temerè in tam periculoso symptomate aut morbo acuto statueretur. Evocatur igitur Harlinga, Dr. JOHANNES ANSTA, Medicus ejusdem Reipublicae Ordinarius, ac Practicus summus, ἰατρὸς πολλῶν ἀλόξιῳ ἄλλων. Hic ubi nocte concubia aut intempestà appulisset, communicato consilio, cum praedictis Medicis, suasit φλεβοτομίαν aut venae sectionem instituendam ac tentandam esse, quae etiam mox subsecuta est. Verum enimvero cum ne sic quidem, foeliciter hoc negotium succederet ex voto & opinione Medicorum, proinde de aliis quoque medijs aut remedijs inter Medicos deliberatum ac disceptatum fuit, quae tamen pro illo temporis momento dilata fuerunt, donec aut melior & commodior ἰυχαρίστια, occurreret, aut se offerret. Verum enimvero cum post tentata omnia remedia, quae in hoc casu, ex Medicorum opinione ac sententia, aut schola & adhiberi soleant & applicari, incassum cederent, decessit interim Μακαρίτης Vir Clarissimus ex hac vita, quarto Nonarum Novembris, circa mediam septimam vespertinam, Anno aetatis quinquagesimo octavo. O tristis, funesta, infausta nox! nigro signanda lapillo, quae omnium Doctissimorum virorum nostri aevi facile Principem nobis ademit ac sustulit! Sustulit Academiae nostrae Ocellum; sustulit Patriae Lumen ac Decus aeternum; sustulit consummatissimae eruditionis ac πολυ-Historias virum incomparabilem; de quo ipsa Fama mentiri veretur. Verum enimvero frustra lesso ac immodicis lachrymis denatum Μακαρίτην prosequimur, qui optimo jure illud Poëtae usurpare, sibique vindicare potuit.
units.tr: "Let them be good before they hold power, few in power," and he kept the academic laws, which he had sworn to preserve whole and intact, with piety, religious devotion and manly firmness; and that at a time when good morals in this Academy, alas, were not cultivated but were exiled. Placed in this academic dignity, the late man (ὁ Μακαρίτης), who for eight years had enjoyed generally firm and solid health, after various published monuments of his learning, after his HISTORY brought down to the navel, after his published SYRIUS, after his published AMORES, after various published FUNERAL ORATIONS, was finally seized and afflicted, on the day before the Kalends of November of this present year 1644, which was a Wednesday, in the morning, by a severe and genuine lethargy, to such a degree that soon he could recognise or address none of his friends or colleagues, but for the whole time he lay ill he was deprived of all speech and, as far as could be judged from outside, of all use of reason and of sense. Astonished and saddened by this grave and sorrowful sight, his friends and close heirs at once and without delay had summoned the most distinguished Mr Phocylides Holverda and the most learned Vibrandus Revius, Doctors of Medicine, who, after various deliberations and consultations held back and forth, judged that it was expedient for the patient that a third physician be called, so that nothing be rashly decided in so dangerous a symptom or acute disease. Therefore Dr Johannes Ansta, ordinary physician of the same Republic and a highly skilled practitioner, "a physician of many, others being useless" (ἰατρὸς πολλῶν ἀλόξιῳ ἄλλων), was summoned from Harlingen. When he arrived at night or at an unseasonable hour, after the plan had been shared with the aforesaid physicians, he advised that phlebotomy, or bloodletting, be undertaken and tried, which was soon carried out. But indeed, when even so the matter did not succeed happily, according to the wish and opinion of the physicians, then other means or remedies were also discussed and debated among the physicians; these, however, were put off for the present moment, until either a better and more suitable remedy (εὐχαριστία) should present itself or be offered. But indeed, when after all the remedies had been tried which in this case, by the opinion and judgement of the physicians, and by the schools, are commonly applied and used, had come to nothing, meanwhile the late most distinguished man departed this life on the fourth day before the Nones of November, about half past seven in the evening, in the fifty-eighth year of his age. O sad, deadly, unlucky night! to be marked with a black stone, which has easily taken from us the prince of all the most learned men of our age! It has taken from us the little eye of our Academy; it has taken the eternal light and glory of our Fatherland; it has taken from us a man of most complete learning and many-sided histories, incomparable, about whom Fame herself would fear to lie. But indeed it is in vain that we follow the dead man (Μακαρίτης) with mourning and immoderate tears, who could rightly claim for himself and make his own that saying of the poet.

units.la: Ille jam omnium calamitatum ac dolorum expers, in gremio Abrahæ con-quiescit. Nos hic quotidie morimur, singulæque horæ aliquid de vita no-stra demunt, ludibrium fumus fortunæ, fragilitatis exemplar, lachrymarum domus, curarum omnium carcer. Igitur quod restat, salve terque quaterque, mî beatissime W I N S E M I, qui supra orbes cœlestes evectus, curas mortalium despicis, qui jam in suprema cœlesti Curia maximus Professor; qui non purpurâ, verum niveo indutus es virtutis ac æternitatis Amiculo ac Stolâ, qui pro R E P U B L I C A, pro E C C L E S I A, pro A C A D E M I A nostra ad genua divinæ M A J E S T A T I S ac potentiæ humiliter te submittis ac incurvas. Iterum salve atque vale, beatissima W I N S E M I A N I M A. Nos ubi decretoria aut fatalis illa hora affulserit, rursus tuo grato ac venerabili adspectu fruemur in æternum, cum omnibus fidelibus, freti πληροφορία, ac meritis unici Salvatoris ac Mediatoris nostri I E S U, cui cum P A T R E & S P I R I T U S S A N C T O, D E O T R I N O & U N O, sit laus & gloria in secula. A M E N.
units.tr: Now free of all calamities and sorrows, he rests in the bosom of Abraham. We here die every day, and each passing hour takes something from our life: we are the plaything of fortune's smoke, a model of frailty, a house of tears, a prison of all cares. Therefore what remains is this: farewell, thrice and four times, my most blessed W I N S E M I, who, raised above the heavenly spheres, look down upon the cares of mortals, who now are the greatest Professor in the supreme heavenly Council; who are clothed not in purple but in the white garment and robe of virtue and eternity, who for the R E P U B L I C, for the C H U R C H, for our A C A D E M Y, humbly submit and bow your knees before the divine M A J E S T Y and power. Again, farewell and good-bye, most blessed W I N S E M I A N S O U L. When that decisive or fated hour shall shine upon us, we shall again enjoy your pleasing and venerable sight forever, with all the faithful, relying on full assurance [πληροφορία] and on the merits of our one Saviour and Mediator J E S U S, to whom, with the F A T H E R and the H O L Y S P I R I T, the triune and one God, be praise and glory for ever and ever. A M E N.

units.tr: Margaret, sister of Philip, is appointed governor of Belgium, 30. Commends the institution of the new bishopric, 47. Writes to the king about the league of Belgian nobles, 61, and to the Frisians about the same, 62. Promises a mitigation of the edicts, 64. Sends envoys about this to Spain, ibid. Her threatening letters to Arenberg, concerning the king's will that a change in religion must be guarded against, are put aside in the assembly of the estates and cause disturbance, 73. Accuses the Belgians in letters to Philip, 76. Writes to the Senate of Leeuwarden that the names of fugitive citizens be entered on the list, 93, and by threats of confiscation and capital punishment deters those planning flight, ibid. Leaves Belgium, 98.

Frisiam defendit contra Lalainium, 498. vita dissoluta. 507. Groningam obsidet & temerè omittit, 508. 509. turpiter fugit, 512.
units.tr: Philip of Hohenlohe has command of the war at Groningen (481); he prepares himself to ward off the enemy (490); against the order of the States he goes into battle with Schenck (491), fights bravely and is defeated (493). He defends Friesland against Lalaing (498); his life is dissolute (507). He besieges Groningen and rashly gives it up (508, 509); he flees shamefully (512).
